Initially created: 2025-12-17T20:38:41.707+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Basic Annals 1: Emperor Wǔ, Part 1
Gāozǔ Wǔ Huángdì, personal name Yǎn,
courtesy name Shúdá,
nickname Liàn'ér,
was a native of Zhōngdū Lǐ, Nánlánlíng,
and a descendant of Hán Xiàngguó Hé.
Hé begat Cuódìng Hóu Yán.
Yán begat Shìzhōng Biāo.
Biāo begat Gōngfǔ Yuàn Zhāng.
Zhāng begat Hào.
Hào begat Yǎng.
Yǎng begat Tàizǐ Tàifù Wàngzhī.
Wàngzhī begat Guānglù Dàfū Yù.
Yù begat Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng Shào.
Shào begat Guānglù Xūn Hóng.
Hóng begat Jìyīn Tàishǒu Chǎn.
Chǎn begat Wújun Tàishǒu Bīng.
Bīng begat Zhōngshān Xiàng Bāo.
Bāo begat Bóshì Zhōu.
Zhōu begat Shéqiū Zhǎng Jiǎo.
Jiǎo begat Zhōu Cóngshì Kuí.
Kuí begat Xiàolián Xiū.
Xiū begat Guǎnglíngjùn Chéng Bào.
Bào begat Tàizhōng Dàfū Yì.
Yì begat Huái'yīn Lìng Zhěng.
Zhěng begat Jìyīn Tàishǒu .
begat Zhōu Zhìzhōng Fùzǐ.
Fùzǐ begat Nántái Zhìshū Dàocì.
Dàocì begat the Imperial Father, personal name Shùnzhī,
who was a clan younger brother of Qí Gāodì.
He participated in assisting the establishment of the dynasty,
and was enfeoffed as Línxiāngxiàn Hóu.
He successively held the offices of Shìzhōng,
Wèiwèi,
Tàizǐ Zhānshì,
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Dānyáng Yǐn,
and was posthumously granted the title of Zhèn'běi Jiāngjūn.
Gāozǔ was born in the year Jiǎchén, the 8th year of Dàmíng of Sòng Xiàowǔ, at the Sānqiáo residence in Tóngxià Lǐ, Mòlíng Xiàn.
From birth, he displayed extraordinary signs:
his two hips had fused bones,
the top of his head was prominently raised,
and there was a character on his right hand that read
"Wǔ".
When the Emperor grew up,
he was extensively learned and widely informed,
fond of strategy,
and possessed both civil and military talents.
His contemporaries and peers all highly praised him.
The room where he lived was always filled with a cloud-like aura,
and anyone who passed by it
would immediately feel a sense of solemnity.
He started his career as Bālíng Wáng Nánzhōngláng Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn,
and was promoted to Wèijiāngjūn Wáng Jiǎn Dōnggé Jìjiǔ.
Wáng Jiǎn, upon their first meeting, was deeply impressed by his extraordinary qualities,
and said to Lújiāng Hé Xiàn:
"This Xiāo Láng will become Shìzhōng within thirty years;
beyond this, his nobility will be beyond words."
Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng opened the Xī'dǐ and
invited literary talents.
Gāozǔ, along with Shěn Yuē, Xiè Tiǎo, Wáng Róng, Xiāo Chēn, Fàn Yún, Rèn Fǎng, Lù Chuí, and others, associated there,
and were known as the "Eight Friends".
Wáng Róng was brilliant and discerning beyond others,
and especially respected Gāozǔ.
He often said to his close associates:
"The one who will govern the world
will definitely be this person."
He was successively promoted to Suí Wáng Zhèn'xī Zīyì Cānjūn,
and soon after resigned due to the mourning period for his Imperial Father.
In the early period of Lóngchāng,
Míngdì assisted in governance
and appointed Gāozǔ as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
stationed in Shòuchūn.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shùzǐ, Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
and was assigned to duty in the inner palace.
He participated in the meritorious service of strategizing with Xiāo Chén and others,
and was enfeoffed as Jiànyángxiàn Nán,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ,
Wèi dispatched generals Liú Chǎng and Wáng Sù leading a multitude to invade Sīzhōu.
Gāozǔ was appointed Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, Jūnzhu,
and was assigned to Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Wáng Guǎng for reinforcement.
When they were about a hundred *li* from Yìyáng,
the troops, seeing the might of the Wèi army,
hesitated and dared not advance.
Gāozǔ requested to be the vanguard,
and Wáng Guǎng immediately assigned elite soldiers from his command to Gāozǔ.
That very night, he advanced,
a few *li* from the Wèi army,
and went directly up Xiánshǒushān.
The Wèi army, unable to ascertain their numbers,
dared not press forward.
At dawn,
the city saw the reinforcements arrive,
and consequently dispatched troops to attack the Wèi palisade.
Gāozǔ led his command to engage from the outside.
The Wèi army was attacked from both sides,
so they abandoned their heavy siege and retreated.
After the campaign,
Gāozǔ was appointed Yòujūn Jìn'ān Wáng Sīmǎ, Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
He returned to become Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and held the post of Yǔlín Jiān.
After a short while,
he was sent out to garrison Shítou.
In the fourth year,
the Wèi Emperor personally led a large army to invade Yōngzhōu.
Míngdì ordered Gāozǔ to go to their aid.
In the tenth month,
he reached Xiāngyáng.
An imperial edict also dispatched Zuǒmín Shàngshū Cuī Huìjǐng to overall command all armies.
Gāozǔ and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Cáo Hǔ and others were all subject to his command.
In the third month of the following year,
Cuī Huìjǐng and Gāozǔ advanced to Dèngchéng.
The Wèi lord, leading over ten thousand cavalry, suddenly arrived.
Cuī Huìjǐng turned pale
and wished to retreat.
Gāozǔ resolutely stopped him,
but he did not comply
and hastily extricated himself.
The Wèi cavalry pursued them,
resulting in a great defeat.
Gāozǔ alone led his troops to resist the attack,
killing hundreds of people.
The Wèi cavalry gradually retreated,
and he was then able to form a defensive line to cover the rear,
reaching the boats by evening.
Cuī Huìjǐng's army suffered almost complete casualties,
only Gāozǔ returned with his entire force intact.
Soon after, Gāozǔ was made acting Yōngzhōufǔ Shì.
In the seventh month,
he was formally granted the titles of Chíjié, Dūdū Yōng Liáng Nánběi Qín Sìzhōu Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu Zhī Suíjùn Zhū Jūnsì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In that same month,
Míngdì passed away,
and Dōnghūn ascended the throne.
Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng, Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì, Shàngshū Yòupúyè Jiāng Shí, Yòujiāngjūn Xiāo Tánzhī, Shìzhōng Jiāng Sì, and Wèiwèi Liú Xuān took turns on duty in the inner palace,
issuing edicts on different days.
Gāozǔ, upon hearing this,
said to his maternal uncle Zhāng Hóngcè:
"With governance coming from many gates,
the path to chaos has begun.
The *Shī* says:
'With three dukes in one state,
whom shall I follow?'
How much more so now with six!
Can this be allowed?
If rifts appear,
they will eventually exterminate each other.
To avoid disaster now,
this is the only place.
Diligently practice benevolence and righteousness,
and one can sit and become a Xībó.
However, my younger brothers are in the capital,
and I fear they may suffer from worldly calamities;
I must plan this with Yìzhōu."
At that time, Gāozǔ's eldest brother, Yī, had returned from a posting in Yìzhōu,
and was still managing affairs in Yǐngzhōu.
Hóngcè was then sent to Yǐng,
where he presented his plan to Yī, saying:
"In the past, Jìn Huì, a mediocre ruler,
saw the various princes contend for power,
which led to nine internal rebellions
and three foreign invasions.
Now, six powerful officials are contending for power;
each wields the royal authority,
controls the ruler, dictates edicts,
and desires to monopolize power.
Grudges quickly escalate into animosity,
and naturally they will destroy each other.
Moreover, the heir apparent, while in the Eastern Palace, had no good reputation;
he was familiar with his attendants,
a cruel and malevolent person.
Once he takes control of all affairs,
and acts as he pleases,
how could he possibly sit idly, merely assenting to others' words,
and delegate governance to court officials?
Mutual suspicion will accumulate,
leading inevitably to great massacres.
Shǐ'ān wishes to emulate Zhào Lún;
his intentions are already manifest.
For a lame man to ascend to heaven—
truly there is no such principle.
Furthermore, his nature is very suspicious and narrow-minded;
he will only bring about chaos.
The only ones who could possibly hold power
are Jiāng and Liú.
Shí is timid and indecisive,
Xuān is weak and untalented;
the 'overturning of the tripod and spilling of the food' [i.e., impending failure]
can be awaited on tiptoe.
Xiāo Tǎnzhī is suspicious and jealous,
constantly speaking to harm others.
Xú Xiàosì's talent is not that of a pillar of state;
he lets others lead him by the nose.
If a rift opens and conflict arises,
the state will surely crumble from within and without.
Now that we have the fortune to guard an outer province,
let us plan for our own safety.
A wise man seizes opportunity;
he does not wait a full day.
Before suspicion and defensiveness arise,
it is advisable to summon your brothers to gather in due time.
Afterwards, if mutual suspicion
arises, there will be no way to extricate oneself.
Yǐngzhōu controls the key areas of Jīng and Xiāng,
and flows westward into Hàn and Miǎn;
the soldiers and horses of Yōngzhōu,
numbering tens of thousands in an instant,
stand here like tigers,
observing the empire.
If the world is well-governed, we will devote our loyalty to the imperial court;
if the times are chaotic, we will eliminate the tyrants for the state.
Thus, we can advance or retreat with the times.
This is indeed a foolproof strategy.
If you do not plan early,
regret will be too late."
Yī's countenance changed upon hearing this,
and he did not agree in his heart.
When Hóngcè returned,
Gāozǔ then requested to welcome his brothers Wěi and Dàn,
who arrived in Xiāngyáng that year.
Thereupon, he secretly manufactured weapons
and felled many bamboos and trees,
sinking them in Tánxī,
secretly preparing for naval equipment.
At that time, his residence often exhibited five-colored swirling light,
resembling a coiling dragon,
with purple qi rising above it,
shaped like a parasol.
All who saw it found it extraordinary.
In the winter of the second year of Yǒngyuán,

news arrived of Yī's assassination. Gāozǔ secretly summoned his chief clerk Wáng Mào, middle-ranking officer Lǚ Sēngzhēn, assistant prefect Liǔ Qìngyuǎn, and records officer Jí Shìzhān, among others, to strategize.
Once decided,
on the *yǐsì* day of the eleventh month, he summoned his subordinates to gather in the main hall,
and said:
"In the past, King Wǔ convened at Mèngjīn,
and all said, 'Zhòu can be attacked.'
Now, the depraved ruler's wickedness is complete,
his tyranny and cruelty extreme;
he has executed court officials,
leaving few survivors.
The people are in misery,
and Heaven commands his destruction.
You all share the same hatred for evil;
let us together initiate this righteous undertaking.
Titles of dukes, marquises, generals, and ministers
truly lie in this day.
Each of you, exert your merits to the utmost,
and I will not break my word."
On that day, the battle standard was erected.
Thereupon, he gathered over ten thousand armored soldiers,
over a thousand horses,
and three thousand boats,
using the bamboo and wood from Tánxī to equip the ships.
Initially,
Dōnghūn had appointed Liú Shānyáng as the Grand Administrator of Bāxī,
providing him with three thousand elite troops,
and sent him to pass through Jīngzhōu to carry out the mission of assisting Xiāo Yǐngzhòu in attacking Xiāngyáng.
Gāozǔ knew of their plan,
and so dispatched staff officers Wáng Tiānhǔ and Páng Qìngguó to Jiānglíng,
where they delivered letters to all the provincial offices.
When Shānyáng ascended westward,
Gāozǔ said to his generals:
"Jīngzhōu originally feared the people of Xiāngyáng.
Furthermore, with the saying 'when the lips are gone, the teeth feel cold,'
they are naturally in a critical situation,
so how can they not secretly agree with us?
If I were to command the armies of Jīng and Yōng,
and sweep clean the eastern region,
even if Hán Xìn and Bái Qǐ were reborn,
they would be unable to formulate a strategy.
How much more so with such an incompetent and deluded ruler,
who only commands a mob of compliant executioners?
I can make Shānyáng surrender as soon as he reaches Jīngzhōu.
All of you, let's see how it turns out."
When Shānyáng reached Bālíng,
Gāozǔ again ordered Tiānhǔ to carry a letter to Yǐngzhòu and his brothers.
After he left,
Gāozǔ said to Zhāng Hóngcè:
"The way of using troops,
attacking the heart is superior,
attacking the city is secondary;
mental warfare is superior,
armed warfare is secondary.
This is the case today.
Recently, I sent Tiānhǔ to the provincial offices,
and everyone received a letter.
Now, this dispatch is extremely urgent,
and there are only two sealed letters for the acting officials and their brothers,
saying, 'Tiānhǔ will explain verbally';
but when Tiānhǔ is questioned, he has nothing to say verbally.
The acting officials cannot communicate with each other,
and it is impossible for them to speak carelessly.
Tiānhǔ is a trusted confidant of the acting officials.
When they hear this, they will surely believe that the acting officials and Tiānhǔ are concealing the matter together,
which will cause everyone to become suspicious.
Shānyáng, misled by the multitude of voices,
will certainly suspect disloyalty,
and they will inevitably leak our plans.
This is to stabilize a province by sending two empty envelopes."
Shānyáng reached Jiāng'ān,
and upon hearing this,
indeed became suspicious and did not advance.
Yǐngzhòu was greatly alarmed,
and so he beheaded Tiānhǔ,
and sent his head to Shānyáng.
Shānyáng believed him,
and with several tens of men, galloped in.
Yǐngzhòu, who had hidden armed men, beheaded him,
and sent his head to Gāozǔ.
He then reported on the proposal for the Nánkāng Wáng's title,
and further said:
"This month is not auspicious,
we must wait until February of next year;
to hastily advance troops now,
I fear, is not a strategy for the ancestral temple."
Gāozǔ replied:
"Now we have a hundred thousand armored soldiers,
and our provisions are depleting.
Moreover, we rely on righteous hearts,
a temporary surge of bravery,
and with things happening one after another,
we still fear doubt and slackening;
if we delay troops for ten tens of days,
remorse will surely arise.
If even children form factions,
then great affairs cannot be accomplished.
Now the planet Venus appears in the west,
and we act righteously.
With the opportune time and human planning,
what disadvantage can there be?
The arrangements are already made,
how can we stop in the middle?
In ancient times, King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
going against the Grand Commander of the Year.
Did he still need to wait for the year and month?"
Cáo Jǐngzōng, Grand Administrator of Jìnglíng, sent Dù Sīchōng to persuade Gāozǔ to welcome the Nánkāng Wáng and make Xiāngyáng the capital,
to await the formal bestowal of the title,
and then advance the army.
Gāozǔ did not agree.
Wáng Mào also privately said to Zhāng Hóngcè:
"I serve Your Excellency,
and am bound by righteousness to advance or retreat with you;
however, by placing the Nánkāng Wáng in other people's hands now,
they will then hold the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords,
and Your Excellency will go forward to be commanded by others.
How can this be a plan for weathering the cold?"
Hóngcè reported it,
and Gāozǔ said:
"If the great enterprise ahead does not succeed,
then naturally both orchids and mugwort will be burned together;
but if the achievements are established,
and our prestige awe-inspiring throughout the four seas,
commanding all under heaven,
who would dare not obey!
How can I be an ordinary person accepting others' commands?
When we reach Shíchéng,
I will personally clarify this to Wáng Mào and Cáo Jǐngzōng."
They established Xīnyě Commandery in Miànnán
to gather the newly surrendered.
In the second month of the third year,
the Nánkāng Wáng was appointed Grand Chancellor,
and Gāozǔ was made General Who Conquers the East,
granted a set of drums and pipes.
On the day Wùshēn,
Gāozǔ departed Xiāngyáng.
He left his younger brother Wěi to guard Xiāngyáng city,
overseeing all provincial affairs, and his younger brother Dàn to guard the camp city.
The Registrar of the Prefecture, Zhuāngqiū Hēi, guarded Fánchéng.
The Director of Merits, Jí Shìxún, concurrently served as Chief Clerk.
The Commander of Báimǎ Outpost, Huáng Sìzǔ, concurrently served as Registrar.
The Magistrate of Ruò, Dù Yǒng, concurrently served as Aide-de-Camp.
The Sub-Prefectural Clerk, Guō Yǎn, was in charge of transport.
A proclamation was issued to the capital: "Indeed, the Dao is not always smooth,
and times do not perpetuate eternal transformation.
Peril and peace succeed each other,
and darkness and light are not constant.
All things endure hardship before flourishing,
relying on many difficulties to reveal sagacity.
Thus,
when Chāngyì deviated from virtue,
Emperor Xiàoxuān rose;
when Hǎixī plunged governance into chaos,
Emperor Jiǎnwén ascended the throne.
Both opened new lines of succession and established foundations,
continuing the precious mandate.
This truth is verified by past classics,
and these events are clearly
recorded in past strategies.
The solitary tyrant has disturbed the natural order,
destroying the virtue of a ruler.
His treachery, depravity, and indulgence
have intensified with each passing year.
He inflicted cruelty in the year of his coming of age,
and planted danger in his childhood
days.
His suspicion and viciousness
manifested at every turn;
his tyranny, brutality, and foolishness
erupted with every incident.
Since the late emperor's illness progressed,
his joyful countenance was seen prematurely.
While the imperial coffin was in mourning,
he showed no
sorrow.
His merrymaking and banqueting
exceeded the ordinary,
and his strange and awe-inspiring attire
became excessively ostentatious.
As for selecting concubines,
there was no distinction between sisters.
When inviting attendants for his personal service,
aunts and nieces were indistinguishable.
The imperial harem gained a reputation for promiscuity,
and noblewomen were forced to wear soldiers' armor.
He even exposed his body,
wearing his underclothes inside out,
and would behead people in their midst
for
amusement.
He indulged in unbridled licentiousness,
driving people from the suburbs.
The old and weak drifted,
men and women suffered dire straits.
Bodies littered the roads,
and coffins filled the thoroughfares.
Mothers could not embrace their children,
and children had no time to mourn.
Robbery and plunder continued day and night,
one after another.
They hid by day and roamed by night,
without rest.
He indulged in debauchery and drunkenness,
singing and reveling in taverns.
He favored foolish
youths,
and was misled by evil enchantresses.
Méi Chóng'ér and Rú Fǎzhēn, mere servants and low-ranking individuals,
monopolized power,
executed loyal and virtuous officials,
and slaughtered ministers and grand administrators.
Liú Zhènjūn, a respected
maternal uncle,
was utterly loyal to the state.
Jiāng Púyè, a prominent maternal relative,
served the emperor with utmost sincerity.
Xiāo Lǐngjūn, a distant relative,
was committed to supporting the pillar of the state.
Xú Sīkōng,
Shěn Púshè was among the ranks of high-ranking officials and nobles,
a man looked up to by all.
Some had the lingering devotion of Wèiyáng,
some were genuinely and reverently recognized for their great accomplishments,
some had shown sincere loyalty in times of hardship,
and some had labored diligently for the royal house;
they all
received the legacy and trust,
jointly participated in accepting the dying instructions,
managing the funeral rites and serving the incumbent ruler,
and exhausting their efforts.
It was fitting that their fortune should overflow in their time,
and their prosperity extend to their descendants;
yet in one morning they were crushed to powder,
not even a child
was spared.
The resentment of men and spirits boiled up,
and passersby sighed with indignation.
Xiāo Lìngjūn’s loyalty was like the support of a main pillar,
his sincerity piercing the visible and the invisible.
In previous years, when the bandits' roaming spirits
endangered Nánzhèng,
he drew his blade at Fēiquán,
and single-handedly secured the isolated city.
When the rebels defied the mandate in the central river regions
and oppressed the capital,
he offered strategies within the forbidden palace,
giving directions to the various commanders,
vanquishing the great villains,
and purifying our royal
domain.
Cuī Huìjǐng’s exceptional military edge was swift and terrifying.
Where his troops met battle at the Xiàngwěi gate,
martial courage lost its soul,
and righteous men lost their nerve.
Those who submitted their names and surrendered their allegiance
rushed from house to house,
carrying provisions
and following his shadow;
the foolish and the wise eagerly flocked to him.
Furthermore, he swore allegiance in the Jiāng fields,
fighting recklessly without regard for his own safety,
encouraging the righteous soldiers,
and swiftly overwhelming the strong enemy,
slaughtering the great evildoers,
to solidify the imperial foundation.
His achievements surpassed those of Huán and Wén,
his merits towered above Yī and Lǚ;
yet he was modest, cautious, and self-examining,
his sincerity was evident in his actions and thoughts.
When his task was accomplished, he withdrew,
seeking no glory or fullness.
Generous rewards were unheard of,
but dreadful disaster
quickly overtook him.
If he was aware of this in the afterlife,
who would not feel injustice and pain!
Meanwhile, the crowd of rebels acted wantonly,
harboring viperous venom.
They then dispatched Liú Shānyáng to incite and rally the fugitives,
luring and coercing the exiles,
plotting secretly,
and planning surprise attacks.
Xiāo Yòujūn and Xiàhóu Zhēnglǔ showed loyalty and determination early on,
their righteousness visible in their countenance.
Their brilliant strategies were widely implemented,
and the evildoers were instantly beheaded and hung up.
Heaven’s
Dào brings misfortune upon the licentious;
their crimes cannot be forgiven even by execution.
As for their acts of violating propriety and transgressing instruction,
damaging culture and oppressing the people—
even shooting at Heaven and bombarding the roads
would be relatively better than this.
Cutting open wombs and chopping off legs
cannot compare to their cruelty.
If all the bamboo of Nan
could be exhausted,
it would not be enough to record their faults;
if all the rabbits in the mountains and marshes
could be captured, they could not write down all their crimes.
Since the beginning of chaos,
as recorded in histories and annals,
no dim-witted ruler
or tyrannical empress
has been as extremely wicked as this one.
Now that men and spirits lack a sovereign,
the altars of state are in peril,
the area within the seas is boiling,
and the common people are in turmoil.
The populace trembles in fear,
as if their heads were about to collapse.
The common folk long for relief,
having no place
to set their feet.
My headquarters bore the favor of the previous court,
sharing in joy and sorrow equally.
Upwards, I harbor the grave responsibility of the entrustment;
downwards, I consider the pain of being abandoned in the plains.
How can I lie upon brushwood and draw fire near,
sitting
and watching the downfall!
The Supreme One is physically descended from Gāozōng,
and was uniquely blessed by his affectionate favor.
His brightness rivals the sun and moon,
his purity illuminates the sacred spirits.
Auspicious signs were heralded by the mystic tortoise;
verifications corresponded to the ritual disk.
He was established as the commander of the Shǎn
fiefdom,
and his civilizing influence spread to the Western Xià region.
He is the one whom the songs and praises uphold,
and whom all readily support.
Right Commander Xiāo Yǐngzhòu and General of the Campaign Against the Barbarians Xiàhóu Xiáng united their hearts in support and assistance,
immediately installing him in the former
Chǔ capital.
The Three Spirits shine brightly once more,
the Nine Regions are renewed.
The era of peace and prosperity
begins anew here;
the flourishing state celebrated in the Kāng Zāi song
is present on this day.
However, though the Emperor's virtue is manifest,
the realm
is not yet settled.
The prime evildoer has not been deposed,
and the Imperial City remains blocked.
Reverently following the Emperor's plan,
we lead the way forward.
Immediately, we dispatch the General of the Van, the Administrator of Jìnglíng Cáo Jǐngzōng, and others—
twenty army commanders—
with fifty thousand long spears.
Swift horses gather in herds,
like eagles they vie to be first,
like dragons they gallop abreast.
They cross the river at Héngjiāng on foot
and head directly towards Zhūquè.
Chief Clerk, General of the Van
and Administrator of Xiāngyáng Wáng Mào, and others—thirty army commanders—
with seventy thousand war vessels.
They ride the current like flashing lightning,
forcing their way through strategic bottlenecks,
and heading obliquely towards Báichéng.
Advisor to the Central
Gentleman and Army Commander Xiāo Wěi, and others—thirty-nine army commanders—
with giant ships and swift oars,
smashing through waves and choking the water.
Eighty thousand banners and drums
converge like fire upon Shítóu.
Advisor to the Central
Gentleman and Army Commander Xiāo Dàn, and others—forty-two army commanders—
with soldiers brave as bears and tigers,
one hundred thousand shields and armor.
They sail along the current in light boats,
and seize Xīntíng in a surprise attack.
The Governor of Yìzhōu Liú Jìlián, the Governor of Liángzhōu Liǔ Dàn, the Governor of Sīzhōu Wáng Sēngjǐng, the Administrator of Wèixīng Péi Shīrén, the Administrator of Shàngyōng Wéi Ruì,
and the Administrator of Xīnchéng Cuī Sēngjì
have all solemnly received the bright edict
to carry out Heaven’s punishment together.
The fierce warriors of Shǔ and Hàn
are coming downriver;
the strong and brave troops of Huái and Rǔ
are rushing
towards the wave.
My headquarters commands all the fierce warriors,
one million brave and gallant soldiers.
They repair their armor and Yàn bows,
station their troops and Jì horses.
Gongs clash, shaking the ground;
drums sound, overwhelming the sky.
Frosty spear points reflect the sun;
vermilion banners stretch like silk.
Boats line up for a thousand *lǐ*,
advancing continuously in succession.
Right Commander Xiāo has superior talent in strategy,
combining both civil and military abilities.
His brilliant strategy is profound and far-reaching;
he manages the affairs and rectifies the world.
He commands the troops of Jīngnán,
supervising the armies from the four directions,
coordinating the central command,
and guarding the imperial carriage.
Wherever his banners and flags point,
his awe-inspiring power is boundless.
Like dragons soaring and tigers striding,
they all gather at
Jiànyè.
We will depose the ignorant and deceitful,
treat the depraved of Hǎicūn equally,
purify the sacred region,
and sweep clean and settle the capital area.
This is analogous to collapsing Mount Tài upon an ant hill,
or bursting a hanging river to pour upon
flying cinders.
How could they not be annihilated!
The axes of war are now directed
only at Méi Chóng'ér and Rǔ Fǎzhēn.
All you gentlemen are scions of noble families, proper examples of the time,
whose merits are recorded in the royal government.
All of you have bowed before the wicked faction,
subject to baleful terror.
If you can achieve merit through change,
turning calamity into blessing,
and swear by the Hé (河) and Yuè (岳),
you shall forever wear the azure and purple.
If you remain stubbornly deluded and unenlightened,
resisting the Royal Army (Wáng Shī),
once the great multitude arrives,
punishment will be administered without pardon.
This is what is meant by, "The fire rages across the highlands,
and the orchid and the zhī (芝) are destroyed together."
Strive to seek great fortune,
and do not bequeath later regrets.
The statutes regarding reward and punishment,
are
as clear as white water.
Gāozǔ (高祖) arrived at Jìnglíng (竟陵),
and ordered Chief Clerk Wáng Mào (王茂) and Administrator Cáo Jǐngzōng (曹景宗) to serve as the vanguard,
with Staff Officer Zhāng Fǎ'ān (張法安) defending Jìnglíng City.
Mào and the others reached Hànkǒu (漢口),
crossed the river with light troops,
pressing toward Yǐngchéng (郢城).
Its Governor Zhāng Chōng (張沖) set up a formation and occupied Shíqiáopǔ (石橋浦).
The Righteous Army (Yì Shī) fought them but met with defeat,
and Army Commander Zhū Sēngqǐ (朱僧起) died there.
The various generals discussed combining forces to besiege Yǐng (郢),
and dividing troops to attack Xīyáng (西陽) and Wǔchāng (武昌).
Gāozǔ said:
"Hànkǒu is not even one *lǐ* (里) wide,
and arrows can easily cross.
Fáng Sēngjì (房僧寄) is holding it securely with heavy forces,
forming a pincer with the people of Yǐngchéng.
If we advance with all our troops,
the rebels will surely cut off our army's rear.
Should this be blocked even for one morning,
then regret will be too late.
Now I intend to dispatch the armies of Wáng and Cáo across the river,
to meet up with the Jīngzhōu (荊州) forces,
and put pressure on the rebel defenses.
I will personally besiege Lǔshān (魯山) from the rear,
to ensure the passage of the Miǎn (沔) and Hàn (漢) rivers.
Grain stored between Yúnchéng (鄖城) and Jìnglíng
will be floated down in a flotilla;
troops from Jiānglíng (江陵) and Xiāngzhōng (湘中)
will arrive continuously, flags following flags.
Once provisions are sufficient,
and the number of soldiers and followers gradually increases,
besieging and holding the two cities
will result in their fall without attack.
The affairs of the world
will simply be ours for the taking, even lying down."
All the generals said,
"Excellent."
Thereupon, he ordered Wáng Mào and Cáo Jǐngzōng to lead their troops across the shore,
and advance to station at Jiǔlǐ (九里).
On that day,
Zhāng Chōng led out his troops to meet them in battle.
Mào and the others intercepted and attacked,
routing them utterly,
so they all abandoned their armor and fled.
Jīngzhōu dispatched Champion General Dèng Yuánqǐ (鄧元起), Army Commander Wáng Shìxīng (王世興), Tián Ān (田安), and several thousand others,
to meet the army at Xiàshǒu (夏首).
Gāozǔ built a wall at Hànkǒu City to guard Lǔshān,
and ordered the naval commanders Zhāng Huìshào (張惠紹), Zhū Sīyuǎn (朱思遠), and others to patrol and block the middle of the river,
cutting off communication between Yǐng and Lǔ (魯) cities.
In the third month,
he commanded Yuánqǐ to advance and occupy Nántáng Xīdǔ (南堂西陼),
Tián Ān to camp north of the city,
and Wáng Shìxīng to camp at the former city of Qǔshuǐ (曲水).
At this time, Zhāng Chōng died,
and his followers subsequently nominated Army Commander Xuē Yuánsì (薛元嗣) and Chōng’s Chief Clerk Chéng Mào (程茂) as their leaders.
On the *yǐsì* (乙巳) day,
the Prince of Nánkāng (南康王) ascended the imperial throne at Jiānglíng,
changing the 3rd year of Yǒngyuán (永元) to the 1st year of Zhōngxīng (中興),
and remotely demoting Dōnghūn (東昏) to the Prince of Fúlíng (涪陵王).
Gāozǔ was appointed Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè),
and additionally granted the titles of General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Dà Jiāngjūn) and Area Commander-in-Chief of All Campaigning Armies (Dūdu Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì),
and granted the Ax of Authority (Jiǎ Huángyuè).
The Western Court (Xītái) also dispatched Champion General Xiāo Yǐngdá (蕭穎達) to lead troops and join the army.
On this day,
Yuánsì's Army Commander Shěn Nándāng (沈難當) led several thousand swift boats,
floating downstream chaotically to attack.
Zhāng Huìshào and others defeated them,
capturing them all.
In the fourth month,
Gāozǔ left the Miǎn River area,
ordering Wáng Mào, Xiāo Yǐngdá, and others to advance their forces and pressure Yǐngchéng.
Yuánsì's troops were quite exhausted from fighting,
and consequently dared not come out.
The generals wanted to enforce stricter measures against him,
but Gāozǔ did not permit it.
In the fifth month,
Dōnghūn dispatched General Who Pacifies the North Wú Zǐyáng (吳子陽) and Army Commander Guāng Zǐjīn (光子衿), commanding thirteen armies, to reinforce Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
advancing to occupy Bākǒu (巴口).
In the sixth month,
the Western Court dispatched Court Architect Xí Chǎnwén (席闡文) to console the troops,
bringing deliberations from Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (蕭穎冑) and others,
which he presented to Gāozǔ, saying:
"Now you have halted troops on both banks,
failing to combine forces to besiege Yǐng,
or securing Xīyáng and Wǔchāng,
or taking Jiāngzhōu (江州).
This opportunity is already lost;
it is better to seek aid from Wèi (魏),
and form an alliance with the north.
This would still be the best strategy."
Gāozǔ said to Chǎnwén:
"The road at Hànkǒu connects Jīng and Yōng (雍),
controlling Qín (秦) and Liáng (梁).
The transport of provisions and supplies
depends entirely upon this juncture,
which is why forces must be pressed upon Hànkǒu,
linking several provinces.
If we now combine forces to besiege the city,
and also divide troops to advance forward,
Lǔshān will certainly obstruct the Miǎn River route,
which is called 'seizing the throat.'
If supply transport is cut off,
the army will naturally disperse.
How can we speak of holding out indefinitely?
Recently, Dèng Yuánqǐ wished to take three thousand soldiers to pacify Xúnyáng (尋陽).
If the enemy joyfully understood the moment,
one Lì Shēng (酈生) would be sufficient;
but if they resist the Royal Army,
three thousand men will definitely not be enough to take it.
Advancing or retreating lacks reliable basis,
so I do not see how this is feasible.
Xīyáng and Wǔchāng
can be taken easily enough,
but once taken, they must be garrisoned.
Guarding the two cities requires no fewer than ten thousand men,
and the provisions must match that number,
which is something we currently cannot produce.
Should a rebel force move upstream,
ten thousand men attacking one city,
the two cities would be unable to support each other.
If we divide our army to provide reinforcement,
then both the head and the tail would be weakened;
if we do not send aid,
the isolated city is certain to fall.
Once one city is lost,
the various cities will crumble consecutively,
and the great enterprise of the world will consequently be gone.
If Yǐngzhōu is successfully captured,
we will sweep along the current,
and Xīyáng and Wǔchāng
will naturally submit.
Why should we hastily divide our forces and scatter our troops,
thus bringing about our own worries!
Moreover, the actions of a great man
should determine the stillness of Heaven's steps;
how much more so when commanding the armies of several provinces to execute a band of ruffians?
It is like pouring a suspended river upon a fire;
how could it fail to be extinguished?
How can we face north and beg for aid,
thereby demonstrating our own weakness!
They may not necessarily be trustworthy,
and we would merely create an ugly reputation for ourselves.
This is a bottom-tier plan;
how can it be called the best strategy?
You must report back to the Garrison Army Commander (Zhèn Jūn) for me: The future offensive and capture
should simply be entrusted to me.
Victory is right before my eyes,
there is no fear of failure.
We rely on the Garrison Army Commander to maintain stability."
Wú Zǐyáng and others advanced their forces to Wǔkǒu (武口).
Gāozǔ then ordered Army Commanders Liáng Tiānhuì (梁天惠) and Cài Dàoyòu (蔡道祐) to occupy Yúhú City (漁湖城),
and Táng Xiūqī (唐脩期) and Liú Dàomàn (劉道曼) to camp at Báiyáng Fort (白陽壘),
holding positions on both banks to await them.
Zǐyáng further advanced to occupy Jiāhú (加湖),
thirty *lǐ* from Yǐng.
Relying on the mountains and bordered by water,
they built forts and stockades to secure their position.
Fáng Sēngjì, the commandant of Lǔshān City, died,
and his followers again nominated Assistant Defender Sūn Lèzǔ (孫樂祖) to replace him.
In the seventh month,
Gāozǔ ordered Wáng Mào to lead Army Commanders Cáo Zhòngzōng (曹仲宗), Kāng Xuàn (康絢), Wǔ Huìchāo (武會超), and others in a covert maneuver to attack Jiāhú,
intending to put pressure on Zǐyáng.
The water level was too low for ships to pass,
but that night, the water suddenly rose greatly.
All the armies moved forward simultaneously, riding the current,
beating drums and shouting as they attacked.
The rebels were immediately and utterly defeated.
Zǐyáng and the others fled,
and all their remaining troops drowned in the river.
Wáng Mào captured the remainder and returned.
Consequently, the two cities of Yǐng and Lǔ looked at each other and lost their fighting spirit.
Before this,
Dōnghūn dispatched the General of the Champion Army, Chén Bózhī, to garrison Jiāngzhōu,
to act as reinforcement for Zǐyáng and others.
Gāozǔ then said to his generals:
"In military campaigns, it is not always necessary to rely on brute force;
what is heeded is (our) formidable reputation.
Now, after the defeat at Jiāhú,
who would not submit?
Chén Hǔyá is Bózhī’s son,
and he fled back in distress.
The sentiments of the people there
should logically be ones of anxiety and fear.
I believe Jiǔjiāng can be pacified simply by sending a proclamation."
Accordingly, he ordered a search among the captured prisoners
and found Sū Lóngzhī, Bózhī’s banner commander.
He awarded him richly
and sent him to deliver a message.
Sūn Lèzǔ, the commandant of Lǔshān City, Chéng Mào, the commandant of Yǐngchéng City, and Xuē Yuánsì subsequently requested surrender.
Originally,
when Yǐngchéng City was besieged,
there were over one hundred thousand people inside, including military commanders, officials, men, women, and common folk.
Seventeen or eighteen tenths (70-80%) died from epidemics and massive swelling.
When the city was opened,
Gāozǔ extended compassion and solace to all.
For the deceased, he ordered that coffins be provided.
Before this,
Hú Wénchāo of Rǔnán raised a righteous army at Shèyáng,
seeking to attack Yìyáng and Ānlù commanderies to demonstrate his effectiveness.
Gāozǔ also dispatched Army Commander Táng Xiūqī to attack Suí Jùn,
and they conquered both.
Wáng Sēngjǐng, the Inspector of Sīzhōu, sent his son Zhēnsūn as a hostage.
The Sī region was completely pacified.
Chén Bózhī sent Sū Lóngzhī back with a reply,
requesting that the army delay its advance.
Gāozǔ said:
"In uttering this, Bózhī
harbors indecision.
While he hesitates,
we must quickly press upon him.
With no scheme left to execute,
he will be forced to surrender."
He then ordered Dèng Yuánqǐ to lead the troops
and advance downstream immediately that day.
In the eighth month,
the Son of Heaven dispatched the Palace Attendant, Sū Huí, to comfort the troops.
Gāozǔ boarded a boat,
ordering his generals to advance sequentially.
He left Wéi Ruì, the Administrator of Shàngyōng, to guard Yǐngchéng City
and manage the affairs of the province.
When Dèng Yuánqǐ was about to reach Xúnyáng,
Chén Bózhī was still suspicious and fearful,
so he withdrew his troops and retreated to secure Húkǒu,
leaving his son Hǔyá to guard Pénchéng.
When Gāozǔ arrived,
Bózhī bound his armor and requested pardon for his offense.
In the ninth month,
the Son of Heaven issued an edict confirming that Gāozǔ had pacified the Eastern Xià,
and granted him full discretion in handling affairs.
In this month,
he left the Lesser Treasurer and Chief Clerk, Zhèng Shàoshū, to guard Jiāngzhōu City.
The vanguard reached Wúhú.
Shēn Zhòu, the Inspector of Nányùzhōu, abandoned Gūshú and fled.
At this time, the main army advanced and occupied it,
and subsequently dispatched Cáo Jǐngzōng and Xiāo Yǐngdá to lead the cavalry and infantry to camp at Jiāngníng.
Dōnghūn dispatched the General Who Conquers the Barbarians, Lǐ Jūshì, to lead infantry to meet the attack,
but Jǐngzōng attacked and drove them away.
Thereupon, Wáng Mào, Dèng Yuánqǐ, and Lǚ Sēngzhēn advanced to occupy Chìbí Luó.
Cáo Jǐngzōng and Chén Bózhī served as mobile forces.
On that day,
Jiāng Dàolín, the commandant of Xīntíng City, led troops out to battle.
The allied forces captured him on the battlefield.
The main army encamped at Xīnlín.
Gāozǔ ordered Wáng Mào to advance and occupy Yuèchéng,
Cáo Jǐngzōng to occupy Zàojiá Qiáo,
Dèng Yuánqǐ to occupy Dàoshì Dūn,
and Chén Bózhī to occupy Lí Mén.
Dàolín’s remaining troops retreated and camped south of the Great Bridge (Háng),
but the righteous army pressed them.
They dispersed and fled again,
retreating to secure Zhūjué,
relying on the Huái River to fortify themselves.
At that time, Lǐ Jūshì still held Xīntíng Fort
and requested Dōnghūn to burn the houses and villages on the south bank to clear a battlefield.
West of the Great Bridge and north of Xīntíng,
everything was utterly destroyed.
In the tenth month,
Zhū Sēngyǒng, the commandant of Dōnghūn’s Shítou troops, led two thousand naval soldiers in surrender.
Dōnghūn again dispatched the General Who Conquers the Barbarians, Wáng Zhēnguó, leading Army Commander Hú Hǔyá and others, to set up formation on the main road south of the Great Bridge.
They were entirely equipped with elite soldiers and sharp weapons,
still numbering over one hundred thousand men.
The eunuch Wáng Chāngzǐ held the White Tiger Banner and supervised all the armies.
They also opened the Great Bridge with their backs to the water,
cutting off any route for retreat.
Wáng Mào, Cáo Jǐngzōng, and others attacked them from flanking positions.
The officers and soldiers all fought desperately;
there was no one who could not fight a hundred men.
Their battle cries shook Heaven and Earth.
Zhēnguó’s troops
instantly collapsed like earth.
Those who jumped into the Huái River and died
accumulated so many bodies that they reached the level of the Great Bridge.
Those who arrived later crossed over using the bodies.
Thereupon, all the troops at Zhūjué, upon seeing this, scattered and disintegrated.
The righteous army pursued them to Xuānyáng Mén.
Lǐ Jūshì surrendered Xīntíng Fort, and Xú Yuányú surrendered the Eastern Palace City.
All the troops stationed at Shítou and Báixià scattered during the night.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Gāozǔ took up station at Shítou,
ordering the allied armies to surround the six gates.
Dōnghūn completely burned down everything within the gates,
driving and forcing the barracks, offices, and officials all into the city.
He had twenty thousand troops remaining.
Huán Hé, the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, tricked Dōnghūn into leaving the city to fight,
and then brought his troops to surrender.
Gāozǔ ordered all armies to construct a long siege wall.
Earlier,
when the righteous army approached,
Dōnghūn had dispatched Army Commander Zuǒ Sēngqìng to garrison Jīngkǒu,
Cháng Sēngjǐng to garrison Guǎnglíng,
and Lǐ Shūxiàn to camp at Guābù.
When Shēn Zhòu fled back from Gūshú,
Dōnghūn also sent him to camp at Pòdūn to serve as a northeastern reinforcement.
By this time,
Gāozǔ sent envoys to enlighten and persuade them,
and they all led their troops in surrender.
Gāozǔ then dispatched his younger brother Xiù, General Who Assists the State, to garrison Jīngkǒu;
his younger brother Huī, General Who Assists the State, to camp at Pòdūn;
and his cousin Jǐng, General Who Pacifies the North, to garrison Guǎnglíng.
Cài Yín, the Administrator of Wú Jùn, abandoned the commandery and rushed to join the righteous army.
On the morning of the day Bǐngyín in the twelfth month,
Zhāng Jì (acting Grand Commandant of the Guards) and Wáng Zhēnguó (Inspector of Běixúzhōu) decapitated Dōnghūn,
and sent his head to the righteous army.
Gāozǔ ordered Lǚ Sēngzhēn to marshal troops to seal the treasuries, armories, and archives.
He arrested the consort Pān Fēi and forty-one members of the wicked faction, starting with Wáng Xuānzhī, and handed them over to the officials,
who executed them.
Empress Xuāndé issued an order to depose the Prince of Fúlíng as the Marquess of Dōnghūn,
following the precedent of the Han Marquess of Hǎihūn.

Gāozǔ was granted the titles of Director of the Secretariat, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Yáng and Nánxú provinces, Grand Marshal, Recording Secretary of the Masters of Writing, General-in-Chief of Cavalry, and Inspector of Yángzhōu.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiàn'ān Commandery,
receiving ten thousand taxable households,
and granted forty men bearing ceremonial swords.
The Yellow Ax, Palace Attendant, and Commander of Expeditions titles remained as before.
This was following the precedent of the Jin Prince Zūn of Wǔlíng, who acted under imperial mandate.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
Gāozǔ entered and encamped at the Reviewing Hall.
He issued an order, saying:
"The Imperial House has suffered misfortune,
encountering this darkened wickedness.
Calamity has spread to living things,
and cruelty has afflicted both men and spirits.
The danger to the altars of the soil and grain
was like a dangling thread.
I belong to the Imperial Clan,
and benefited unduly from previous favors.
I was entrusted with responsibilities in the frontier regions,
pushing the wheels of government across ten thousand *lǐ*.
Looking upon the imperial residence,
the pain was present before my eyes.
Therefore, I acted out of loyalty to honor the sovereign,
steeling my resolve to disregard my own life.
Although the precious calendar has been re-established,
and the luminous mandate has been succeeded,
that solitary, wicked villain
was still inciting chaos in the capital.
I threw back my sleeve and grasped the spear,
successfully alleviating great hardship.
The cruel government spread unchecked
for a long time,
and those united in wickedness supported one another.
It is certainly not confined to a single faction.
Submissively upholding the imperial decree,
my duty lies in leading this sole punitive campaign.
I desire to spread the imperial benevolence
across the whole land.
All those who bear guilt
shall be allowed to begin anew.
A great amnesty shall be granted to all under Heaven;
except Wáng Xuānzhī and the other forty-one persons, who shall not be included in this amnesty."
He further issued an order, saying:
“Now, the establishment of a ruler is for the purpose of governance and oversight,
not for burdening the people to sustain one’s own life;
one should view the populace as if they were injured,
how could one recklessly rely on high status to indulge in cruelty?
The deposed ruler abandoned the constant principles
and severed himself from the ancestral temples.
The extremes of cruelty and perversity he reached
are unprecedented in written records.
Taxes and levies were not unified,
and severe and oppressive measures flourished.
Silk embroidery and earthworks,
beans, grain, dogs, and horses—
levies were issued on the households of the poor (lǘ zuǒ),
to fill the needs of construction and repair.
People wandered, exposed to heat and cold,
followed by epidemics and plagues;
they died and their bodies piled up in the ditches,
yet they received no rescue or relief.
Rotting flesh and withered bones
were consumed by crows and vultures.
Furthermore, natural disasters and human-caused fires
repeatedly burned down the imperial palaces (gōng yè);
government offices, terraces, and temples—
not a single beam or rafter was left.
The sorrow exceeded that of Shǔ Lí,
and the pain was greater than that of Mài Xiù.
This led the countless populace to become alienated,
and the borders and frontiers were invaded and weakened.
What transgression did these people commit
to suffer such misery?
Now, order and chaos alternate their operation,
and the Great Way is publicly enforced.
The people longing for good governance
have found relief (lái sū) on this very day.
Though I am crudely meager in virtue,
I have been entrusted with this great favor.
Although the time distance is far from the Central Revival (zhōng xīng),
the difficulties are comparable to the initial, nascent stages (cǎo mèi).
I intend to illuminate the Imperial Glory (huáng xiū)
and begin anew with the populace.
All chaotic decrees, erroneous taxation, excessive punishments, and unwarranted labor service
that can be thoroughly investigated externally according to former sources
shall all be abolished and cleared away.
Regarding items lost from public custodianship
and all things damaged or depleted,
strict regulations shall be established,
and all shall follow the original precedents.”
He further said:
“In the latter years of Yǒngyuán,
the cosmic order (qián wéi) was dislocated.
Government functions were indeed manifold (duō mén),
differing from the time of Wèi Wén;
power shifted downwards,
the situation resembling the era of Cáo Gōng.
This caused eunuchs (yān yǐn) to be referred to as ‘Aunts and Uncles’ (wēng ǎo),
and Gāo'ān (Gāo'ān) dared to speak of ‘emulating Yáo’ (fǎ Yáo).
They sold judgments and traded official positions,
monopolized mountains and guarded marshes.
The mechanism of opening and closing policies
was presented and established by petty villains (xiǎo chǒu).
The straight path and true justice
were suppressed and obstructed for years.
Those harboring grievances and holding righteous principles
knew not to whom they could appeal.
Corrupt officials took advantage of this,
making written revisions at their own discretion.
How can this merely compare to Jiǎ Shēng shedding tears
or Xǔ Bó weeping for the times!
Now, the principle of governance is renewed,
and governance and punishment are properly aligned.
Correcting these pervasive abuses
is incumbent upon this very day.
It is permitted to thoroughly examine the various bureaus of the Secretariat (Shàngshū zhòng cáo)
concerning all litigations from the time of Dōnghūn whose judgments were unfair or whose supervising officials delayed implementation,
and thoroughly investigate and distinguish them,
and discuss and report on them according to the facts.”
He further issued an order,
stating that those in the Army of Righteousness (yì shī) who died facing the enemy or died of illness,
should all be given funerals and burials,
and their bereaved orphans should be cared for and relieved.
He further ordered, saying:
“At the victory of Zhūjué,
the families of the rebels who died delivering themselves to death
are specially permitted to inter and bury them;
if there are no relatives,
or if the relatives are poor and suffering,
the magistrate (cháng) and commandant (wèi) of the two counties shall immediately bury them.
Within the city of Jiànkāng,
those who failed to recognize the Mandate of Heaven
and brought about their own ruin
shall also be treated according to this regulation.”
In the first month of the second year

the Son of Heaven dispatched concurrent Palace Attendant (Jiān Shìzhōng) Xí Chǎnwén (Xí Chǎnwén) and concurrent Palace Deputy (Jiān Huángmén Shìláng) Yuè Fǎcái (Yuè Fǎcái) to console the capital region (jīng yì).
Posthumous titles were conferred upon Gāozǔ's grandfather: Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Master of the Left Glorious Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū);
and upon his deceased father: Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
Gāozǔ issued an order, saying:
“Now, when those above transform those below,
the grass bends and follows the wind.
The purity or decadence of the age
is brought about by this.
Since Yǒngyuán lost virtue,
the records have not fully chronicled
the extremes of cruelty and perversity;
how can they all be recounted?
Subsequently, dazzling mansions (xuán shì) were constructed externally,
and towering palaces (qīng gōng) accumulated internally.
Strange crafts and exotic clothing
exhausted all things unseen before.
The high were arrogant and the low were violent,
and debauchery and extravagance competed for attention.
The mandates of the state and the power of the court
entirely shifted to close attendants (jìn xí).
They traded offices and sold titles,
and bribery circulated openly.
They built magnificent residences (jiǎ dì) along the main avenues (kāng qú),
with soaring terraces (jiàn tái) and vast rooms.
Their long sleeves rose and fell,
equaling the gifts given when making peace with the Rong (hé róng);
a hundred varieties of delicacies
matched the provisions of the great families (fá bīng zhī jiā).
The foolish people, influenced by this,
gradually formed a custom.
Arrogance and seductive display competed,
and ostentation and beauty sought to surpass one another.
It reached the point where families of the market and alleyways
wore sable and fox furs;
and the sons of merchants and artisans
were clothed in silk embroidery (tí xiù).
The time of sunset
would not see them return until midnight;
and the time of the dim morning light
they treated as the bright dawn.
The Sagely Brightness (shèng míng) initiates this operation,
diligently beginning anew.
Although it is called succession (zàn róng),
it is nearly equivalent to a complete creation and reform (chuàng gé).
Furthermore, following this indulgence and waste,
military expeditions ensued,
and great bridges (jù qiáo) and deer terraces (lù tái)
were completely depleted, one after another.
I, the lonely one (gū), am humbly burdened with this great favor,
and my duty lies in clearing away confusion.
I contemplate how to uphold the great simplicity (dà bó) principle of the Imperial Court (huáng cháo) above,
and how to implement the principle of the deer-skin garment (lù qiú zhī yì) for my humble self below;
to unbind and reorder things,
to transform carving into simplicity (pǔ).
Apart from that which is necessary for presenting sacrificial offerings (zì shèng),
repairing ceremonial robes (fú miǎn),
practicing the rites and music,
and preparing military defenses (jiǎ bīng zhī bèi),
all other diverse expenditures
shall be entirely prohibited.
The offices and departments within the imperial administration
shall be reduced and abolished as deemed appropriate.
The number of imperial concubines (bèi yù qiè) in the Inner Palace (yètíng)
shall be greatly curtailed, and the music of Zhèng and Wèi (Zhèng Wèi zhī yīn) shall be cut off.
Among these measures, those which can set an example for the ministers (qīng shì)
and serve as a standard for the common people (méng shù),
such as frugal eating and plain clothing,
I request to begin with myself.
Moreover, if all talents walk the same path,
and the nine officers (jiǔ guān) all attend to their duties,
and if everyone can strive to retreat and eat modestly,
and compete in maintaining self-restraint,
then transforming customs and changing habits
may be achieved within a single year.
In the past, when Máo Jiè was at court,
the scholar-officials dared not wear luxurious clothes or eat extravagantly.
Wèi Wǔ sighed and said: ‘My law is not as effective as Minister Máo (Máo Shàngshū)’s.’
Although I am deficient in virtue compared to the former sages
and bear a heavy responsibility like those who came before,
I truly hope that the many scholars can grasp this sentiment.
Externally, detailed regulations (tiáo gé) can be drafted.”
On the day Wù Xū,
Empress Xuāndé assumed court governance
and moved into the Inner Palace (Nèi Diàn).
The Emperor was appointed Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ),
and his authority to issue independent decrees (chéng zhì) was revoked,
but all officials paid homage to him as before.
An edict promoted Gāozǔ to Supervisor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì),
granted him the privilege of wearing a sword and shoes upon entering the palace hall (jiàn lǚ shàng diàn),
not having to hurry (bù qū) when entering court,
and having his name omitted when announced for audience (zàn bài bù míng).
He was further granted the feathered canopy (yǔ bǎo) and drums and pipes (gǔ chuī) for his front and rear divisions.
He was allowed to establish Left and Right Chief Clerks (Chángshǐ), Commandants (Sīmǎ), Attendant Secretaries (Cóngshì Zhōngláng), and four each of Clerks (yuàn) and Subordinates (shǔ),
all to recruit staff as before,
with all other aspects remaining unchanged.
The edict stated: “Now, the sun and moon are affixed to the heavens,
by which loftiness and brightness manifest virtue;
the mountains and peaks are grounded upon the earth,
by which gentleness and breadth achieve success.
Therefore, all things are born and find their beginning,
and the River
is stirred but does not overflow.
The two fundamental cosmic patterns (*Èr Xiàng*) are constant and observed,
and those who replace them are men.
Therefore, the Seven Assistants (*Qī Fǔ*) and the Four Uncles (*Sì Shū*),
achieved non-action (perfect governance) under *Xuān* and *Hào*;
*Wéi*, *Péng*, *Qí*, and *Jìn*,
stabilized the decline and chaos during the *Yīn* and *Zhōu* periods.
The Grand Marshal (*Dà Sīmǎ*) *Yōu* is released from Heaven,
embodying this complete sageliness,
his civil achievements encompass the Nine Merits (*Jiǔ Gōng*),
his martial spirit contains the Seven Virtues (*Qī Dé*).
Reverently considering his beginning,
his glorious plans were established early,
his sincerity was manifest in hardship
and distress,
his achievements participated in the imperial planning,
he was granted taxes and opened new territories,
thereby setting a standard for his merits.
When *Jiànwǔ* ascended the calendar (began the reign),
the border fissures were frequently opened.
The Duke (*Gōng*) abandoned his books and stopped lecturing,
managing affairs across the four directions.
*Sī* and *Yù* prefectures were perilously close,
*Fán* and *Hàn* were endangered,
he crushed the strong invaders on the banks of the *Miǎn* River,
and felled the Hu cavalry at *Dèngruì*.
When *Yǒngyuán* began his reign,
trouble arose from a group of villains,
they monopolized power and practiced
cruelty,
their poison covered all living beings,
all under Heaven were trembling,
life hung on a moment's shadow.
Misfortune reached its end point,
divine strategy emerged,
first establishing the great plan,
renewing the destiny of the dynasty (*Dǐng Zuò*).
He threw
up his sleeves to serve the ruler,
moving along the currents swift as lightning,
*Lǔchéng* was swiftly taken,
*Xiàruì* was unveiled like mist parting,
the bandits at *Jiāhú*,
were exterminated in one beat of the drum,
the connected banners at *Gūshú*,
were like ice
melting.
Taking the newly built ramparts was like picking up mustard seeds,
striking down the *Zhū Jué* was like sweeping away dust.
Thunder and lightning shocked the outside (world),
the Palace gates collapsed internally,
the remaining vile remnants and tiny pests,
like ants and locust larvae, were completely wiped out.
He rescued those already drowned,
and unbound those hung upside down,
joy filled the roads, and clapped hands filled the villages,
from near to far.
The capital region (*Jī Diàn*) is peaceful and harmonious,
the outlying regions are solemn and tranquil,
this cruel net was dissolved,
replaced by lenient
governance.
Accumulated evils and extreme darkness,
were suddenly swept clear in one morning,
his renowned instruction spread far,
there is no thought that is not reached.
Even if *Yī Yǐn* maintained this singular virtue,
and *Jī Dàn* brought glory to the Four
Seas,
compared to this, they are insignificant.
In the past, *Lǚ Wàng* assisted the sagely ruler,
yet he only received the mandate of the four tracks;
Duke *Wén Hóu* established merit for the peaceful Queen (*Píng Hòu*),
yet he merely received the bestowal of the two bows,
how much more so for this profound virtue and foundational merit,
surpassing all antiquity.
The common people (*Qián Shǒu*) were anxious and fearful,
depending on him for their lives,
saving what had already occurred,
rescuing what was about to be destroyed.
To display standards at the villages and markers at the graves,
none can compare;
but the Grand Carriage (*Dà Lù*) and the Main
Gate (*Qú Mén*),
have been delayed and not yet bestowed.
Looking back upon the previous precedents,
we should not forget (this duty) even for the time of a meal.
It is proper to respectfully elevate this great ceremony,
in order to fulfill the expectations of the masses.
Therefore, he is promoted to the position of Chancellor (*Xiàng Guó*),
in charge of all official duties (*Bǎi Kuí*),
and Governor (*Cì Shǐ*) of *Yángzhōu*;
enfeoffed with ten commanderies as the Duke of *Liáng* (*Liáng Gōng*),
granted the rituals of the Nine Bestowals (*Jiǔ Xī*),
additionally granted the seals, tassels, and the *Yuǎnyóu* Cap,
his rank is above all the Princes (*Zhū Wáng*),
and additionally granted the green-and-purple
cord (*Lǜ Lèi Shòu*) of the Chancellor.
His title of General of Agile Cavalry (*Piào Jì Dà Jiàng Jūn*) remains as before.
The hundred officials of *Liáng* shall be established as before.
The Edict says: The Two Modes (Heaven and Earth) (*Èr Yí*) are quiet,
yet they operate alternately through cold and heat,
the Three Powers (*Sān Cái*) are utilized together,
relying on the establishment of man as their treasure,
thus allowing them to manifest forms and categorized things,
serving on behalf of Heaven's work.
Truly, this Chief Minister (*Yuán Fǔ*),
answers the timely emergence and outstanding quality,
shaping and completing the merits of Heaven and Earth,
and secretly aligning with the virtue of the Divine Radiance (*Shén Míng*).
He eliminated chaos and restored the correct order,
saving the era and bringing peace to the people,
his great achievements shine
in the realm of governance,
his immense merit shakes all regions beyond the frontiers,
even if *Yī Zhì* protected and governed the Royal House,
or if Duke *Jī* possessed such grand instruction,
compared to this, they are insignificant.
We shall now bestow
upon the Duke this formal record (edict).
Reverently listen to Our command: Heaven was unkind,
disaster befell the Imperial House,
*Shì Zǔ* died early despite his brilliance and clarity,
*Shì Zōng* was unable to perpetuate his benevolent virtue,
*Gāo Zōng* succeeded the lineage,
but his imperial residence was not
everlasting.
Although he worked diligently day and night,
great peace was not attained.
The succeeding ruler was darkened and violent,
records of him are unseen.
Court authority and the handle of the state,
were entrusted to groups of eunuchs/favorites (*Qún Huàn*).
They murdered loyal
and worthy officials,
executing and crippling high ministers (*Tái Fǔ*),
grievances were held and pain was borne,
none of the living kind were spared.
The numerous deeds were not just one instance,
all monopolizing the nation's destiny.
Frowning or smiling caused disaster,
a glance of displeasure resulted in catastrophe.
Strict laws
and poisonous taxes,
brought suffering to every household,
all under Heaven suffered in anguish,
with no place to safely settle themselves.
Wronged victims committed suicide,
their bodies were seen hanging from trees along the roads,
neither near nor far,
crying to Heaven without anyone to tell.
The Duke
seized the opportunity between darkness and clarity,
following the desire of the common people (*Zhào Mín*),
supporting and leading the various nobles (*Qún Hòu*),
assisting in accomplishing the restoration (*Zhōng Xīng*),
the danger to the imperial ancestors (*Zōng Shè*) has been secured,
the hopes of Heaven and man have been truly fulfilled,
this is truly the Duke
restoring our broken bonds,
and greatly creating (a new foundation) for the Royal House.
In the final years of *Yǒngmíng*,
the border fissures greatly opened,
the governors of *Jīng* and *Hé*,
incited the foreign barbarians (*Róng Huāng*),
the *Jiāng* and *Huái* regions were disturbed and pressed,
the situation was like treading on a tiger.
The Duke accepted the orders of the current court,
leading light forces to rush and attack,
restraining them with long-term planning,
and controlling them within the center of the ring.
He pushed through danger and braved peril,
using severity and leniency alternately,
creating a tranquil frontier region,
which was restored as a dependent state (*Fān Fú*).
This, too,
is the Duke's merit.
In the past, during *Lóngchāng*,
the grand foundation had already waned,
*Gāo Zōng* worried deeply about the state (*Shè Jì*),
and intended to carry out expediency.
The Duke established the strategy within the tent,
promoting the great moral principles,
deposing
the Emperor and establishing the King,
his planning was deeply evident.
This, too, is the Duke's merit.
When *Jiànwǔ* expanded the enterprise,
although his plans were far-reaching,
the *Róng Dí* (barbarians) invaded internally,
riding roughshod over the mountain passes,
the *Sī* prefecture region...
The peril was imminent,
the day of collapse was fixed.
Gōng (公) commanded his troops to attack externally,
rolled up the armor and campaigned widely,
engaging closely and making peace (or fighting closely and yielding),
swift as lighting, sweeping like wind,
destroying fortifications and crushing the vanguard,
drinking [from] rivers and dyeing the plains [with blood],
capturing prisoners at Xiàngwèi (象魏),
presenting the severed heads on Hǎizhǔ (海渚),
burning huts and destroying tents,
wailing and proclaiming return.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
Fán (樊) and Hàn (漢) were in dire straits,
urgent military dispatches continually arrived.
Gōng
swiftly assembled his forces (or departed at dawn),
receiving orders to go on campaign,
but military strategy and command—
matters did not originate from him,
and good strategies and excellent plans
were suppressed and not permitted.
In the battle of Dèngchéng (鄧城),
the Hú (胡) cavalry suddenly
arrived.
The Yuánshuài (元帥) secretly approached,
but did not inform [Gōng],
abandoning armor and sacrificing the army,
feeding them into the tiger's mouth.
Gōng (公) gathered the scattered soldiers in the south,
repelled the Diāoqí (雕騎) (elite cavalry) in the north,
saving the entire population and proceeding steadily,
following the roads and slowly returning,
rescuing our border from peril,
and allowing [the people] to regain peace and security.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
Hánnán (漢南) was utterly weak,
a mere foot away from fierce bandits,
provisions were largely lacking,
and equipment
and armor were exhausted.
Gōng (公) began establishing defenses there,
relying on resources he could not depend upon,
organizing soldiers and training troops,
conducting military drills (sōushòu) in an orderly manner,
causing our imperiled city
to be transformed into a strong garrison.
This was yet another of Gōng’s
achievements.
When the reign title Yǒngyuán (永元)
was proclaimed, the Zānwū (瞻烏) (symbolic of disorder) had already arrived.
Although deposing the incompetent emperor had historical precedent,
the actions of Yī (伊) and Huò (霍) were still called difficult.
Gōng (公) first established the great plan,
thereupon installing the enlightened and sagely ruler,
his righteousness
surpassed Yìlún (邑綸),
his merit was higher than those who substituted [rulers] in previous generations,
transforming chaos into order through enlightenment,
making darkness become brightness.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
Although the influence of Wénwáng (文王)
covered the Jiāng (江) and the Hàn (漢),
the capital city (Jīngyì)
was in turmoil,
submerged in a great current (of chaos),
and the regions of Gōuwú (句吳) and Yúyuè (於越)
felt no different from nests hanging on curtains (precariousness).
Gōng (公) cast off his sleeves (i.e., took action) across ten thousand *lǐ*,
focusing solely on rescuing those drowning,
wherever his righteous fame reached,
there was no thought that was not approved.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
Lǔchéng (魯城) and Xiàruì (夏汭)
obstructed and occupied the middle course of the river,
utilizing mountains to establish ramparts,
winding around the streams to fortify themselves.
Gōng (公) resisted this flocking assembly (of bandits),
traversing these dangerous terrains,
stationing troops and resting in armor.
Winter departed and summer arrived (a long duration),
our campaign lasted long,
the soldiers forgot their desire to return,
guided by a far-reaching strategy,
resisted by a long-term plan.
The spending did not waste a single arrow,
the fighting did not exhaust the military,
they trampled upon the solid defenses of Huá (華),
and those defenses, visible to each other, were all captured.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
These various villains,
aiding each other in their wickedness,
relying on the Jiāng (江) and their perilous terrain,
swarming like ants at Jiāhú (加湖).
By water
and land they coiled and occupied [the area],
planning to assist Xiàshǒu (夏首).
Once Gōng’s (公) war boats arrived,
they immediately scattered and disintegrated.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
The treacherous rebels shook the Emperor (Huáng),
once again harboring the idea of raising the axe (i.e., revolt),
accumulating troops
at Jiǔpài (九派),
intending to emulate those who helped the emperor (Qínwáng).
Gōng (公) pointed his majestic authority directly [at them],
his force surpassing wind and lightning.
His banners barely arrived,
and the entire prefecture submitted respectfully.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
Gūshú (姑孰) was a vital strategic point,
close to the capital region (Jīngjī).
Fierce bandits gathered intensely,
blocking and sealing the thoroughfare.
Gōng (公) dispatched a detached force to open the route,
arrays of ships following one after another.
Shaken by the might of his troops,
upon seeing the banners, they were immediately
terrified,
burning their boats and abandoning their defenses,
rolling up their armor and fleeing during the night.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
The various petty men were reckless and rampant,
intending to seize a certain opportunity,
charging like pigs along the banks of the Huái (淮),
their armed cavalry numerous as clouds.
Gōng (公) thereupon ordered the brave and heroic men,
taking advantage of the opportunity to unleash their sharp force.
Their spirit excelled that of Bǎnquán (版泉),
their momentum surpassed that of Huánshuǐ (洹水).
They pursued the fleeing and chased the defeated,
suddenly seizing the thoroughfare (tōngjīn).
Xiǒng'ěr (熊耳), compared for its steepness,
is not worthy to be
likened to it,
if the Suīshuǐ (睢水) had stopped flowing,
how could it compare to this achievement?
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
Lángyé (琅邪) and Shíshǒu (石首)
were strategic and ruggedly fortified,
Xīnlěi (新壘) and Dōngyōng (東墉)
were comparable to walls of metal and moats of boiling water (impregnable).
They relied on the dangerous terrain for defense,
having both troops and provisions.
When Gōng’s (公) actions stirred like wind and shocked like lightning,
none failed to tremble and collapse.
The collapse of the city into a mere moat
was indeed found here.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achievements.
The lone despot (dúfū) was dull and cruel,
relying on the city walls without fear,
beating drums and chiming bells,
acting as if he had resources to spare.
He was intimate with wicked courtiers,
envying those who held high office (guānmiǎn),
and the malicious cunning [courtiers] took advantage of this,
planning to carry out executions
and enslavement.
Gōng (公) secretly employed extraordinary schemes,
and his grand strategy was secretly made known.
Those who were loyal and brave
were able to exert their efficacy.
The incident of the white banner (báiqí) in the Xuānshì (宣室)
cannot be compared to this.
This was yet another of Gōng’s (公) achieve
ments.
Gōng (公) possessed the merit of rescuing the common people,
further enhanced by his brilliant virtue.
When he first cultivated his ambition,
he studied the Dao in the Rúmén (儒門) (Confucian school),
he washed his tassel (i.e., prepared for official service) and came to serve,
his pure reputation illuminating the age.
The times
and fate were difficult,
the ancestral temples and altars (Zōngshè) were in peril.
Kūngāng (崐崗) was already ablaze,
jade and stone were consumed together.
He commanded and led fierce troops (Píxiū),
his actions rising and falling like thunder and lightning.
His righteousness was equal to Náncháo (南巢),
his merit matched Mùyě (牧野).
As
for the vast and silent achievement of Yǔ (禹),
who succeeded Wēiguǎn (微管)?
He rescued those who were about to become fish,
he drove away those with unbound hair.
He untangled this net of chaos,
sorted out this tangled silk,
restored ritual and order to the sleeping mats,
and returned joy
to the realm.
The historical events of Yǒngpíng (永平),
those who hear of them sigh;
the old regulations of the Sīlì (司隸),
those who see them shed tears.
He petitioned for the lives of our people,
returning them to the Dǒují (斗極) (the Pole Star, symbolizing stability).
Lamentably, those holding office...
Officials
shoulder the heavy burden of Heaven’s favor;
the miserable black-headed people
again receive the kindness of treading the earth.
His virtue surpasses Sōng [and] Dài,
his merit rivals the Creator;
how transcendent and remote he is,
exceeding what can
be spoken of.
I have also heard that: rewarding merits and appointing the virtuous,
establishing lords to serve as shields,
are all used to strengthen the Four Pillars (the state),
and perpetually elevate myriad generations.
Thus, the transforming influence flowed from the *Èr Nán*,
and the Jǐu Bó
were summoned,
the Kingly Way became pure and harmonious,
and punishments were set aside and not needed.
Overturning the government did not occur,
through this long permanence,
until destruction had arrived,
and Jìn [and] Zhèng had nothing to rely on.
Only you, honored Sir, govern Heaven
and Earth,
bringing peace and relief to the Central Domain (China);
your way surpasses Yī [and] Jì,
yet your rewards are meager compared to Huán [and] Wén.
How can this be a means to make Qí [and] Lǔ your model,
and long govern the universe?
Reflecting respectfully on past accomplishments,
I am greatly fearful.
Now, I grant the promotion to Minister of State (*Xiàngguó*),
change the Prefect of Yángzhōu to Governor (*Mù*),
and take ten commanderies: Liángjùn in Yùzhōu, Lìyáng, Yìxīng in Nán Xúzhōu, and Huáinán, Xuānchéng, Wú, Wúxīng, Kuàijī, Xīn'ān, [and] Dōngyáng
in Yángzhōu.
I invest you, Sir, as Liáng Gōng.
I bestow upon you this white earth,
wrapped in white thatch,
thereby establishing your
state,
and setting up the ancestral altars.
In the past, Dàn [and] Shì
entered the capital to protect and assist;
extending to Bì [and] Máo,
they also served as high ministers,
holding concurrent responsibilities both internal and external,
which ritual indeed deemed appropriate.
Now,
I command the Envoy with Credentials and concurrent Grand Commandant Wáng Liàng to present the seals and ribbons of the Minister of State [and] Governor of Yángzhōu,
and the seal and ribbons of the Liáng Gōng;
I command the Envoy with Credentials and concurrent Minister of Works Wáng Zhì to present the thatch and earth to the Liáng Gōng,
the gold tiger tally from number one to number five (left halves),
and the bamboo tally from number one to number ten (left halves).
The position of Minister of State ranks above all princes,
holding command over all offices;
the established duties
should be changed accordingly.
Let him, as Minister of State, oversee all governmental affairs,
relinquish the title of Director of the Secretariat (*Lù Shàngshū*),

and surrender the seals and ribbons of acting credentials, Attendant at the Palace (with the sable cicada ornament), Seal of the Director of the Palace Writers, and Commander-in-Chief of Internal and External
Military Affairs (*Dà Sīmǎ*),
and the seal and tablet of Jiàn'ān Gōng.
The title Grand General of Cavalry (*Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn*) remains as before.
Furthermore, I confer the Nine Bestowals (*Jǐu Xī*) upon you, Sir.
Listen respectfully to the following decree: Because you, Sir, cultivate
both ritual and law,
administering punishment and virtue equally,
judging cases with pity and compassion,
leaving nothing untouched by sincerity,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, one Grand Carriage and one War Carriage,
and two teams (eight horses) of black stallions.
You, Sir, have toiled in farming
and harvesting,
mindful that the people are Heaven,
greatly elevating essential tasks,
valuing only grain as treasure,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, the robes of the *Gǔnmiǎn*,
complete with red slippers.
Where your forging influence has reached,
customs have been changed
into refinement,
reforming traditions and molding the people,
bringing peace to the state and country,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, the full set of suspended bells and chimes,
and the Dance of Six Rows (*Liù Yì zhī Wǔ*).
Your civil virtue spreads widely,
your righteous fame extends afar;
people with bunned
hair and knotted heads (barbarians)
sing barbarian songs asking for officials,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, a vermilion door for your residence.
You, Sir, elevate the pure and suppress the corrupt;
official standards are orderly;
many talented men arise,
like the *Yù Pǔ* stanza in circulation,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, a ramp (*Nà Bì*) for ascending.
You, Sir, govern subordinates with a solemn demeanor,
using yourself as a standard for others,
restraining unforeseen events,
warding off enemies from afar,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, three hundred
Tiger Guard soldiers.
Your authority, Sir, is like the summer sun,
determined to eliminate evil and treachery;
those who defy orders and destroy their clans
are punished without pardon,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, one axe (*Fū*) and one battle-axe (*Yuè*).
You, Sir, step upon
Sōng and Míng (mountains and seas),
dominating the world;
comparing you to the sun and moon,
your brilliant light inevitably arrives,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, one red bow
and one hundred red arrows;
ten black bows,
and one thousand black arrows.
You,
Sir, always speak of filial piety,
your utmost sincerity reaches the spirits,
reverent and strict in sacrificial ceremonies,
offering sacrifices with exceeding reverence,
I therefore bestow upon you, Sir, one jug of black millet fragrant wine (*Jù Chàng*),
complete with a jade libation spoon.
Within the State of Liáng, the Chancellor
and all subordinate officials
shall entirely follow the old regulations.
Respect this!
May you respectfully follow the previous measures,
reverently observe these great rites,
respond to and proclaim Heaven's favor,
thereby receiving abundant blessings,
and thus glorify the auspicious mandate of Our Tàizǔ!
Gāozǔ firmly declined.
The officials of the administration urged him to accept, saying:
“We respectfully received the auspicious decree,
and clearly await the tablet of appointment.
Your Excellency's hesitation regarding these grand rites
is indeed an expression of humble respect,
but it fails to reach the ultimate attainment of greatness.
Why is this?
The successor monarch abandoned normalcy
and severed himself from the ancestral altars.
The national mandate required a sovereign of the people,
while the old ruler became an enemy.
When the ridgepole snapped and the rafters collapsed,
the crushing ruin came upon them automatically.
Ministers suffered the pain of being sliced and chopped,
and the black-headed people feared the execution of entire neighborhoods.
Your Excellency has performed deeds that illuminate the heavens,
saving the people from the critical danger of fire and water.
You have circled the sun and moon anew,
and reconnected the stars Shēn and Chén.
You returned the tortoiseshells and jades from the mud,
saving the people from pits and cliffs,
causing ordinary women and young children
to be ashamed to speak of Yī [and] Lǚ,
and village schools and neighborhood academies
to be embarrassed to discuss the Wǔ Bà.
Yet your rank is lower than that of Ā Héng,
and your territory is narrower than Qūfù;
the way of festive reward
has yet to be fully realized.
Now, the Great Treasure (the throne) is a public instrument;
it is not to be demanded nor rejected.
It is utterly impartial and utterly fair.
When faced with benevolence, who should yield?
