Your Excellency should reverently accept the will of Heaven and man,
and rightfully receive these great rites.
Do not allow the song of ‘I wish he had given it to me’
to become the same as the universal resentment,
causing a man who saves the multitude
to turn into one who merely seeks personal virtue.”
The Duke did not consent.
On the *xīnyǒu* day of the second month,
the subordinate officials of the government again requested, saying:
“Recently, by imperial command, we presented a memorial,
boldly expressing our utmost sincerity.
We have received a return order,
but it has not yet been genuinely accepted.
The officials are eagerly awaiting,
and are deeply perplexed.
We have heard that accepting gold from the government,
which great men do with magnanimous purpose,
or gracefully withdrawing to the corner of the sea,
which commoners do as a minor virtue,
is why Zhōu Gōng was not suspicious when Lǚ Shícéng [Lǚ Shí] rode in his carriage,
and Tài Gōng was not hesitant to accept a jade *huáng* as a gift.
Moreover, a worldly sage follows the path,
and his former virtue remains with the people.
In times of chaos and wilderness,
he sighs deeply like Wēi Guǎn.
In addition, during the campaign of Zhūfāng,
he relied on the Jīng and Hé rivers.
When the army returned triumphantly,
he greatly contributed to the royal house.
Although there were those who repeatedly spun cocoons to save Sòng,
and endured multiple calluses to preserve Chǔ,
looking at the past from the present,
what do these amount to?
Yet, feeling as if stealing a bell,
his功 *gōng* is doubted and unrewarded.
Heaven and Earth,
cannot endure such cruelty.
This is why a swift jade horse ran,
signifying the departure of Wēi Zǐ;
and a golden plate emerged from the earth,
announcing the injustice of Lóng Fēng.
Míng Gōng leaned on his saddle and stopped weeping,
arousing the will of the three armies.
Dwelling alone, he wiped away tears,
inspiring the hearts of righteous warriors.
Thus, he was able to make Hǎiruò and Dēngzhī [Dēng Qí] appear,
exhausting their efforts to bestow blessings.
Shān Róng and Gū Zhú,
bound their horses and followed him like shadows.
He took responsibility for their faults and consoled the people,
bringing order to chaos with one effort.
This was not boasting of heavenly achievements,
but truly diligent effort.
Moreover, Míng Gōng was originally a scholar,
who found joy in the doctrines of the sages.
His elegant conduct and plain theories
calmed both the refined and the common.
He did not study Sūn and Wú,
yet he encountered this divine martial prowess.
He drove away all the doomed populace,
and saved the customs that were destined to be enfeoffed.
If the tortoise shell and jade are not destroyed,
whose achievement is it?
If he alone is a gentleman,
what place will Yī and Zhōu have? ”
Thereupon, he finally accepted the mandate of Xiàngguó Liáng Gōng.
On this day,
sixty-two types of extravagant and bizarre clothing of Dōnghūn were burned in the capital street.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Bǎozhì plotted rebellion
and was granted death.
An edict posthumously conferred upon Liáng Gōng’s former wife the title of Liáng Fēi.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
Chén Wénxīng, the troop commander of Nánwǔzhōu, while digging a well within Huánchéng,
found two carved jade *qílín*, two carved golden jade *bì*, and two crystal rings.
Furthermore, Yáng Zhān, the magistrate of Jiànkāng, reported that phoenixes were seen under the paulownia trees in Lǐ, a village in his county.
Xuāndé Huánghòu praised the auspicious signs,
and they were presented to the Xiàngguófǔ.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
an edict stated:
“The state of Liáng has just been established,
and affairs need to be managed.
All important positions may be selected as before,
entirely in accordance with the system of the imperial court. ”
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial, saying: “Your subject has heard that if officials are selected by their words,
scholars will embellish their words;
if people are selected by their conduct,
people will exhaust their efforts in conduct.
It is said that talent is born into the world,
and success or failure depends on the times.
But the current
fashionable trends prevail,
and reckless competition has become customary.
Mediators boast and show off,
profiting from even the smallest gains.
This leads to the gates of officialdom
being crowded.
It is not merely that they brave the sun and rain,
not
avoiding heat or cold,
but they also gather their shoes and lean on their staffs,
sure to arrive in wind and rain.
This is truly because selection from villages and communities
does not follow ancient precedents.
They judge based on outward appearance and superficial qualities,
leaving them to manage trivial matters.
Furthermore, even those with great achievements like Shānhé and Liángbì,
lack the favor of imperial summons;
while Jīn, Zhāng, Xǔ, and Shǐ [referring to powerful families],
forget the decline of their old enterprises.
Alas,
how lamentable!
Moreover, genealogical records are erroneous,
and fraud is rampant.
People do not care
about the refinement or vulgarity of individuals.
Thus, those who falsely assume the lineage of good families
immediately become prominent clans;
those who carelessly tidy up their appearance
immediately become elegant scholars.
Those who have deep
faults against customs
are suddenly promoted and favored;
those whose grave trees have grown tall
are only then bestowed with honor.
Therefore, officials of previous dynasties,
all established selection rosters.
Those who were listed
had their own order of selection.
The rise and fall of family lineages,
and the good or bad of conduct and ability,
were either determined in advance,
or derived from public opinion.
Thus, guests could be easily distinguished,
and there was no need to sweep the gate for visitors.
[二四]In recent times, the system has declined
and fallen,
and the nine streams of thought have gone astray.
There are those who bravely retreat and forget advancement,
holding integrity and embracing truth.
However, the selection department sometimes considers them difficult to promote
because they have not yet made court appearances.
Or there are those who conceal their goodness
and hide their reputation,
burying themselves in humble dwellings.
They are also denied opportunities
because their names are not well-known.
One must present a name card and submit a petition,
and only then can one be an official.
This forces the modest
and encourages fierce competition.
Your subject humbly believes that from now on, the selection office should carefully review,
and establish rosters as before,
so that official positions match qualifications,
and names and realities do not diverge.
Then, people will know their limits,
and unsolicited requests will naturally cease.
Moreover, I have heard that an intermediate regulation stipulates
that prominent families may enter officialdom at twenty,
while lesser families must be probationary officials after passing the age of thirty.
To your subject’s humble understanding,
this is still not acceptable.
Why?
The establishment of offices and division of duties
should prioritize talent.
If the Eight Worthies, at a young age,
are suppressed even in humble positions;
while the Four Villains, at a young age,
are deemed worthy within prominent clans.
This would mean that families with hereditary
stipends
have no intention of doing good;
while commoners
freely indulge in evil.
How can this be to promote virtuous conduct
and inspire future generations?
This is a truly great evil,
which
should be abolished.
Otherwise,
it will cause the people of Zhōu to weep by the roadside,
and the officials of Jìn to sigh over fishing and hunting.
Furthermore, vulgarity and competition are prevalent,
and few people have a mind to withdraw.
If there is a limit
on age to enter court,
they will surely increase their age to seek office.
Thus, outwardly and truly ignorant children
will already claim to be over thirty in their registers.
This defiles the doctrines of the sages,
and is most egregious.
Your subject oversees both internal and external affairs,
and bears this responsibility with worry.
Regarding the successes and failures of court administration,
it is my duty not to conceal them.
I humbly beg Your Majesty to show your sagely and virtuous disposition,
and grant your
attention.
Then, proper human relations will naturally be harmonious,
and laws and regulations will be just. ”
An edict commanded that Gāozǔ’s memorial be put into effect.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
an edict said: “Sōng Gāo is a great mountain,
matching Heaven, thus its fame flows forth;
the grand opening of Nányáng,
thus its霸 *bà* virtue shines forth.
Loyalty and sincerity were observed by the Emperor;
the vassal lord received a high noble title,
revered.
Diligently serving the royal house,
Jī Gōng 姬公 extended the lands of the feudatories.
The former kings' excellent ordinances
were promulgated in all regions and records,
granting long-lasting prosperity to the populace;
none failed to follow these.
The Imperial Chancellor, Liáng Gōng 梁公,
embodies this supreme wisdom,
possessing a sagely and expansive depth.
His civilizing influence permeates internally,
his martial achievements flourish externally.
By promoting and establishing feudal lords,
his prestige and benevolence reach even distant
customs.
By training troops and teaching warfare,
his thunderous might reverberates across ten thousand li.
When the Way was lost and the times were dark,
slander and wickedness flourished greatly.
How could it merely be that the ancestral altars were in peril, and the divine regalia had no master?
Indeed!
As for the annihilation of the populace,
the extermination of the gentry,
the remaining survivors clinging to life,
facing death each morning,
all living beings trembling with fear,
with no place to turn their feet —
thus the mountains and rivers were over
turned,
and vegetation covered the ground.
Compared to the time when benevolence covered the flourishing reeds,
and trustworthiness reached even pigs and fish,
how immensely distant are these two eras!
The Duke commanded his forces to gather
and march,
pursuing the sun's shadow in a long campaign.
However, the capital was in dire straits,
Fán 樊 and Dèng 鄧 were far away,
water and land routes were in sight of each other.
From Gūshú 姑孰
to Xiàshǒu 夏首,
the strong troops of Yánchéng 嚴城
relied on the rivers for defense.
The Duke proceeded along the Hàn 漢 River and floated down the Jiāng 江,
moving like lightning and sweeping like wind.
Boats capsized in the water,
and strategic strongholds collapsed like clouds.
Relying on this righteous courage,
no strong
enemy formation stood before him.
He saved the endangered capital,
cleansed our imperial domain,
extinguished the spreading prairie fire,
and spared those facing execution from house to house.
The vast multitude,
whose fate was not in Heaven,
and the boundless six
directions
all received his beneficence.
He rectified customs and restored the fundamental,
so the people did not lose their livelihoods.
Benevolence and trustworthiness proceeded together,
ritual and music flourished in unison.
Yī Ī and Zhōu 周 are not enough to compare with him,
while Huán 桓 and Wén 文
would be greatly ashamed of their virtue.
However, his enfeoffment as a feudal lord,
with his territory extending only to Qín 秦 and Chǔ 楚,
is not sufficient to adequately reward his brilliant achievements
and truly acknowledge his great merit.
This is truly because the Duke's humility is fundamental,
manifesting itself in every action,
so his auspicious commendations have not yet been fully presented,
and we await them with increasing anticipation day by day.
It is appropriate to elevate this ritual rank
to truly fulfill the expectations of all, far and near.
Let Liáng Gōng 梁公 be advanced to the rank of King.

With the ten commanderies of Nánqiáo 南譙 and Lújiāng 廬江 from Yùzhōu 豫州, Xúnyáng 尋陽 from Jiāngzhōu 江州, Wǔchāng 武昌 and Xīyáng 西陽 from Yǐngzhōu 郢州, Nánlángyé 南琅邪, Nándōnghǎi 南東海, and Jìnlíng 晉陵 from Nánxúzhōu 南徐州, and Línhǎi 臨海 and Yǒngjiā 永嘉 from Yángzhōu
, these ten commanderies
are added to the State of Liáng 梁,
making twenty commanderies in total.
His positions as Imperial Chancellor, Grand Administrator of Yángzhōu 揚州, and General-in-Chief of Cavalry remain as before.
The Duke firmly declined.
An imperial edict ordered the cessation of further memorials.
The Imperial Chancellor's Chief Clerk of the Left, Wáng Yíng 王瑩, and others, led the hundred officials in earnestly imploring him.
On the *xīnmǎo* 辛卯 day of the third month,
Dài Chē 戴車, the warden of Huáyángluó 華陽邏 in Yánlíng Xiàn 延陵縣, submitted a dispatch stating:
"On the *yǐyǒu* 乙酉 day of the twelfth month,
sweet dew descended upon Máoshān 茅山,
spreading for several li.
On the *jǐyǒu* 己酉 day of the first month,
the warden Pān Dàogài 潘道蓋 found a hairy turtle in a rock cave on the mountain.
On the *xīnyǒu* 辛酉 day of the second month,
the warden Xú Língfú 徐靈符 again saw a white musk deer to the east of the mountain.
At dawn on the *bǐngyín* 丙寅 day,
clouds and mists gathered from all four directions on the mountain.
Soon there appeared a black and yellow color,
shaped like a dragon,
over ten *zhàng* 長 in length,
alternately hidden and revealed,
until after a long time it ascended to heaven from the northwest."
On the *dīngmǎo* 丁卯 day,
Mǎ Yuánhé 馬元和, the Cìshǐ 刺史 of Yǒngzhōu 兗州, reported:
"In the Dōngpíng Jùn 東平郡, Shòuzhāng Xiàn 壽張縣, under my jurisdiction, a *zōuyú* 騶虞 was seen."
On the *guǐsì* 癸巳 day,
he accepted the title of King of Liáng 梁.
The command stated:
"I, the lonely one, with my limited ability,
am entrusted with the national helm.
Although I diligently strive day and night,
my mind is set on promoting good governance,
yet cultivating virtue and bringing peace to the people
is still far off.
The sagely court, remembering old precedents,
has bestowed this great appointment upon me.
The grand ceremony of enfeoffing a duke,
is on par with the achievements of past exemplars;
the auspicious bounty is profoundly bestowed,
the rituals are clearly exalted.
To merely cling to my humble resolve
would ultimately impede understanding.
The multitude of dukes and all officials
have repeatedly urged and encouraged this,
compelling this thick-faced one
to accept this propitious fortune.
I gaze upon Kūn 昆 and Péng 彭 with longings,
and admire Huán 桓 and Wén 文 with sighs.
I wish to promote the path of governance,
but know not how to cross the ford.
As the state domain is newly established,
and the feudal realm is renewed,
I wish to extend auspicious blessings
to the subordinate states.
Within the state, all those below capital punishment,
prior to dawn on the fifteenth day of this month,
shall all be pardoned.
Widows, widowers, orphans, and the solitary who cannot support themselves
shall be granted five *hú* 斛 of grain.
Those under the jurisdiction of the governorates and prefectures
shall also receive the same remission."
On the *bǐngwǔ* 丙午 day,
he was granted a king's crown with twelve tassels,
was to erect the Son of Heaven's banners,
have outrider escorts when going out and clear the way when entering,
ride in a golden-wheeled chariot,
drawn by six horses,
equipped with five seasonal auxiliary chariots,
with *máotóu* 旄頭 and *yúnhǎn* 雲罕 standards,
perform an eight-row dance,
and set up *zhōngjù* 鍾虡 and *gōngxuàn* 宮縣 musical instruments.
The titles and appointments of the King's consort, princes, and princesses
shall all follow the old precedents.
On the *bǐngchén* 丙辰 day,
the Qí 齊 Emperor abdicated in favor of the King of Liáng 梁.
The edict stated: "Verily, the Five Virtues succeed each other,
and the Three Reigns rise in turn.
Governing affairs requires the worthy,
and promoting talent reveals the sagely.
Thus, the imperial legacy perpetually flourishes,
and the kingly Way shines anew.
Replacing darkness with light
has been the tradition for a long time.
The virtue of Qí 齊 declined and weakened,
with repeated dangers and destructions.
Lóngchāng 隆昌's brutality and tyranny
truly defied Heaven and Earth;
Yǒngyuán 永元's incompetence and violence
disordered both men
and spirits.
The Three Luminaries dimmed again,
and the Seven Ancestral Temples hung precariously.
The imperial enterprise was almost shifted,
and all conscious beings knew of annihilation.
The fortune of our Gāo 高 and Míng 明 ancestors
was faintly on the verge of collapse.
Constantly contemplating the difficulties,
I carry the weight of being in an ice-bound valley.
The Imperial Chancellor, King of Liáng 梁,
was born with sagely wisdom from Heaven,
and possesses divine and spiritual martial prowess.
His virtue reaches the obscure deities,
and his achievements are equal to the Creator.
He stopped the rampant flow of the ancestral altars and land,
and rescued the populace from
utter misery.
He supported the tottering edifice,
and saved those drowning in the rushing river.
The nine regions were re-stitched,
and the four pillars were re-tied.
Lost rituals were restored,
and collapsed music was revived."
Civil officials fill the gentry ranks,
border posts cease their alarms.
Throughout the seas and the world, the wind rushes forth,
all territories submit and receive the Calendar.
The eight directions present auspicious signs,
the Five Spirits bring forth blessings.
How can it be limited only to the wondrous fortune of
scales and feathers,
or the auspicious colors of clouds and stars?
Merits flourish beyond a hundred kings,
the Way is manifest for ten thousand generations;
thus, the brilliance matches the High Heaven,
and the splendor illuminates the sun and moon.
The rivers and mountains manifest the tokens of revolution,
the charts and prophecies record the destiny of the dynastic end.
The sentiment of joyful promotion [of the new ruler],
is universally accumulated, seen and unseen;
the sincerity of songs and praise,
is evident in both the central states (Huá) and the peripheral tribes (Yì).
Formerly, when the Water
Governance (Shuǐ Zhèng) had weakened,
the Wood Virtue (Mù Dé) ascended to power.
The calendar of Heaven’s destiny
truly had a destination,
grasping the mirror and the jade pivot (governance),
fittingly gathered by the wise and brilliant.
Although I am common and obscured,
ignorant of the Great Way,
having long observed the rise and fall
for many days,
how dare I forget the profound righteousness of past generations,
and the ultimate wish of men and spirits?
Now
I shall respectfully abdicate to Liáng,
and settle at Gū Shú,
following the precedents of Táng Yú and Jìn Sòng.
On the *xīn yǒu* day of the fourth month,
Empress Xuān Dé (Xuān Dé Huáng Hòu) issued an order, saying:
"The Western Edict has arrived.
The Emperor, taking earlier generations as models,
respectfully abdicates the Divine Utensil (Throne) to Liáng.
Tomorrow, we shall personally send an envoy from the veranda,
to respectfully present the seals and ribbons.
This widowed person shall then retire to a separate palace."
On the *rén xū* day,
the Proclamation said: "I address you, King of Liáng (Liáng Wáng): Regarding the records of remote antiquity,
when the people first began to exist,
the rulers of Huáng Xióng and Dà Tíng,
the successors of Hè Xū and Zūn Lú—
these were all before the Dragon Chart
and Bird Traces,
during a vague, dark, and remote age,
and thus cannot be fully known in detail.
Reaching the eras of Nóng, Xuān, Yán, and Hào,
and the sovereigns Fàng Xūn and Chóng Huá,
none
failed to rule the ten thousand surnames with the Great Way,
or govern the eight corners of the world with public instruments.
Dwelling in that position was like holding a rotten rope;
departing from it was like casting off a heavy burden.
Once riding to Fén Yáng,
they immediately had the profound
intention [of abdication];
briefly traveling to Jī Lǐng,
they instantly moved the heart of the one who would yield the kingship.
Therefore, we know that wearing the yellow canopy,
and utilizing the jade seal,
are not means by which to display nobility or claim supreme status;
riding the grand carriage,
and raising the flags
and banners,
are merely intended to ensure that those seeking refuge have a place [to turn].
For this reason, they forgot themselves and nurtured the common people,
devoting themselves to governance and ruling the four seas.
But when the essence within was exhausted,
and they were worn out by the toil of scoops and sleds outside (governing),
they embraced the returning destiny,
and only granted it to the capable.
How much more so when the reeds and pipes change their patterns,
the awe-inspiring charts reveal auspicious signs,
the asterism Shè Tí shines brightly at night,
and the fluorescent light erupts during the day!
The four hundred years
announced their end,
which is why the Great Hàn respectfully yielded;
the Yellow Virtue having already declined,
is why the Wèi Clan (Wèi Shì) joyfully ceded [the throne].
Extending this to Jìn and Sòng,
they also amplified this standard.
Our Grand Progenitor (Tàizǔ) grasped the River Chart
and received the Calendar,
responding to the token and commencing the Mandate.
Two generations saw renewed splendor,
and three sagely rulers followed the track.
The successor sovereign lost his virtue,
ignorantly abandoning the standards and regulations,
destroying and disrupting the Heavenly Order (Tiān Gāng),
severing the Earth’s Tie (Dì Niǔ).
The vast
nine regions
were cut up into enmity,
and throughout the whole world, people looked at each other,
their lives hanging by the shadow of the sundial.
Chopping off a person crossing the water, and dissecting a pregnant woman,
were already minor incidents compared to his acts;
seeking out a chicken or demanding a staff [acts of extreme tyranny],
are hardly worth comparing.
For this reason, valleys were filled and rivers dried up,
mountains flew and ghosts wailed.
The seven ancestral temples were already endangered,
and men and spirits were without a sovereign.
But you, O King (Wáng), embody this highest wisdom,
with sagely brilliance inherent in your person,
receiving spirit from the Five Planets (Wǔ Wěi),
your brightness equal to the sun and moon.
When the permanent relationships are in order,
you wear the ceremonial cap and bring harmony and prosperity;
when the times
are exceedingly difficult,
you advance the spear point and rescue those plunged into mire and charcoal.
Your achievements surpass the Creator,
your virtue saves the common people.
Your favor soaks everything,
your benevolence covers everything,
reaching upward to the azure heaven (Cāng Hào),
and downward to
the rivers and springs.
Your civilizing influence rises equally with the wings of the Great Róc,
and your military accomplishments move in parallel with the sun’s chariot.
Therefore, the minds of both the hidden and the manifest [world] are settled,
and songs of praise belong to you.
How could it merely be that the drum sounds spread across the land,
or that the purple clouds gather in the sky?
Even phenomena like seeing daytime competition for light,
arrows flying unjustly at night,
the earth sinking, comets piercing [the sky],
and the sun and stars vanishing—
the sign of abolishing the old is surely manifest,
and the token of changing
the surname (dynasty) is truly gathered.
Therefore, when the righteous army first trod the ground,
fragrant dew condensed sweetly.
Once the benevolent wind spread,
white patterns formed spontaneously.
The envoys from the northern palace gates and fragrant streets,
and the people from the region of wind carriages and fire
frontiers,
all prostrate themselves,
wishing to become your subjects and servants.
The bells and stones completely changed [their tune];
this event is symbolized by the abdication of Yú (Qiān Yú).
Dragons and fish appeared together;
this righteousness was manifest in serving Xià (Shì Xià).
If a person
leads the people and governs the multitudes,
acting as their shepherd,
fundamentally, he identifies himself with all things,
and must depend on the sentiments of the populace.
The precious Mandate has no permanent master;
Emperors and Kings do not belong to a single lineage.
Now, looking up,
I reverently comply with the Heavenly patterns (Qián Xiàng),
and looking down, I rely on the wishes of men.
I respectfully abdicate the Divine Utensil,
bestowing the Imperial Throne upon your person.
The great destiny has announced its exhaustion,
the Heavenly emoluments forever terminate.
Alas!
O King (Wáng), truly hold fast to the
Mean (Zhōng),
model yourself upon former precedents,
to fulfill the expectations of the Vast Heaven (Hào Tiān).
Sacrifice reverently to the Supreme Deity (Shàng Dì) and govern the immense populace,
communicate with the Civil Ancestors (Wén Zǔ) and receive the great undertaking,
thereby transmitting boundless fortune.
Is this
not glorious!
Furthermore, the Imperial Letter says: "Now, life is the great virtue of Heaven and Earth,
and humanity is the general term for all that contains life.
All share a common origin,
and the reason for differentiation is unknown.
Yet, having received spirit and transformation,
the dispositions of the worthy
and the foolish are not uniform;
relying on the nature of the Five Constants (Wǔ Cháng),
the distinction between the strong and the gentle may sometimes be divergent.
When the various princes are not unified,
conflicts and offenses frequently arise.
Therefore, a sovereign is established and a chief leader is set up,
to manage and
shepherd them.
This is not intended for the high and arrogant to be above others,
or to regard the world as their private property.
Moreover, the Three Beginnings (Sān Zhèng) are changed successively,
and the Five Phases (Wǔ Yùn) shift mutually.
Green text and red characters [signs of prophecy],
gather from the River Chart and manifest...
Luò.
In antiquity, Xūn, Huá,
deeply understood this principle,
sought out the brilliant and wise,
and entrusted them with the teeming populace.
The transfer from Yú to serve Xià,
was fundamentally based on the will of the hundred surnames;
the transformation of Yīn into
Zhōu,
was truly the reception of the mandate from Cānghào.
From the time of Hàn and Wèi,
none failed to follow this;
down to Jìn and Sòng,
they also adhered to this norm.
This is why Our Gāohuáng was able to align with Wénzǔ
to govern the return of destiny,
and reverence the Highest Heaven and respectfully hold the precious calendar.
Reaching the late age,
disasters and chaos repeatedly arrived,
the royal governance was thrown into confusion,
and wickedness and deceit intensely accumulated.
The millions of common
people,
had the knife and chopping board as their fate,
the pressure of imminent disaster,
was as perilous as a thread,
crouching under heaven and treading on earth,
they had nowhere to hide.
The group of villains incited disturbance,
intent on indulging in slaughter and massacre,
intending
to first annihilate the gentry,
and next shift the tortoise and tripod (symbols of state power).
Héng, Bǎo, Zhōu, Shào,
were all grouped with base men.
Nests on curtains and eggs stacked up,
compared to this, are not urgent.
If not for an heroic sage with foresight,
taking benevolence as their duty,
then the owls would have sharpened their beaks,
and destruction would have already struck.
Only the King holds high the standard of Heaven,
and widely and generously models himself on Earth,
fusing and casting the six directions,
shaping and cultivating all existence.
Banners and chariots sped forth,
shaking the spiritual military might to expand the territory;
clouds and thunder
were beginning to spread,
gathering the righteous troops to serve the King diligently.
Raising banners and pennants on distant roads,
executing evildoers at Wèiquè.
His Virtue surpasses the past beginnings,
and his accomplishments have no equal.
He broadly assisted in times of
difficulty and peril,
and continually brightened the Royal Way.
He pacified and cherished the myriad surnames,
and managed the four quarters.
He raised the upright and dismissed the crooked,
clear as if drawn on a diagram.
Waiting for dawn (diligence) he is similar to the Yīn Empress,
while working until sunset he surpasses
Zhōu Wén.
The transforming influence of his customs is solemn and respectful,
and the rites and music are comprehensively flourishing.
Furthermore, he pardons faults and remits crimes,
his divine military might does not kill unnecessarily,
his abundant Virtue shines upon the cosmos,
and his utmost righteousness moves ghosts and spirits.
As for entering that great dwelling,
and receiving this returning destiny,
the fierce winds do not cause confusion,
and rejoicing and recommendation are found therein.
He governed the five flaws amid pre-existing chaos,
and restored weight to the nine tripods already made light.
Wherever the sound of
teaching reached,
and wherever carts and books arrived,
people changed their ways and turned their heads (in submission),
singing praises of his Virtue and benevolence.
The miasma over the nine mountains has been extinguished,
and the four rivers flow peacefully.
Auspicious winds have started to rise,
and excessive rains have ceased.
Black tortoises roam among fragrant herbs,
and plain-patterned beasts are tame in the imperial parks.
They leap across the nine rivers in the clear sky,
and the six kinds of elephants trumpet on the high hills.
Spiritual omens crowd together,
and mysterious tallies are brightly manifest.
As for the comet sweeping the Purple Palace,
the water responding in the first month of summer,
flying swans filling the fields,
and the long comet spanning the sky,
the response indicating the taking of the new is already manifest,
and the omen of reforming the old will certainly be clear.
Furthermore,
his celestial appearance is remarkably outstanding,
his bearing resembles the mien of Yáo;
the tokens of his rule,
truly are not uniform.
The Shū says:
“Heaven observes his virtue,
and thereby concentrates the great mandate.”
The Shī says:
“Wénwáng
is above,
Oh, bright in Heaven.”
Therefore, the two cosmic forces look upon him,
and the realms of light and darkness sincerely agree.
How could this merely be about residing over these myriad states,
and compiling these songs and praises?
Therefore, I embrace the jade ornament, bow my head,
and entrust my heart to the saintly wisdom.
In the past, when the water element declared its satiety,
Our Tàizǔ already received the mandate to replace the end;
in the present day, the Heavenly emolument is said to have departed,
and it
is also by the Wood Element that it is transmitted to Liáng.
Searching far back through previous records,
and contemplating modern times,
the hundreds of officials, far and near,
none go against My will.
I now dispatch the emissary holding the tally, concurrently Grand Protector,
Attendant at the Court, Director of the Central Secretariat, concurrently President of the Board of Personnel, the founding Marquis of Rǔnán County, Liàng,
and concurrently Grand Commandant, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Director of the Central Secretariat, the founding Marquis of Xīnwú County, Zhì,
to present the Emperor's seal and ribbons.
The ceremony for receiving the termination (of the mandate),
shall entirely follow the precedents of Táng and Yú.
May the King ascend to this position of sovereign,
rule over the myriad directions,
formally transmit the grand merit,
in response to the Highest
Heaven's gracious mandate!
Gāozǔ submitted a memorial expressing refusal and concession,
but the memorial was not accepted.
Thereupon,
Qí officials including the Prince of Yùzhāng Yuánlín and eight hundred and nineteen others,
and the Liáng court attendants including Minister Yún and one hundred and seventeen others,
all submitted memorials urging him to assume the throne,
but Gāozǔ humbly refused to accept.
On that day,
the Grand Astrologer Jiǎng Dàoxiù presented sixty-four articles of astrological signs and prophetic tallies,
all matters being clearly manifest;
the ministers repeatedly submitted memorials urgently requesting,
and only then did he comply.
Basic Annals II: Wǔdì (Middle)
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監), summer, the fourth month, day Bǐngyín (丙寅),
Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended to the position of Emperor at the Southern Suburb.
He established the altar, piled wood (for sacrifice), and performed the burnt offering,
announcing the sacrifice to Heaven, saying:
"I, the Emperor's servant Yǎn (衍),
dare to use the dark bull (for sacrifice),
to clearly announce to the August Heaven and Supreme Ruler: Since the fortune of the Qí (齊) clan's mandate has now ended,
when obstruction ceases, prosperity follows.
Respectfully following the response of Heaven,
the mandate was given to me, Yǎn.
Truly, the appointment to rule this realm
is only conferred upon the capable;
the mandate of Heaven does not reside permanently,
and emperors and kings are not confined to a single lineage.
Táng (唐) resigned and Yǔ (虞) received,
Hàn (漢) was replaced and Wèi (魏) arose,
extending to Jìn (晉) and Sòng (宋);
these established patterns are ancient.
All relied on the virtue of the ruler to govern the four seas,
and offered great achievements to the myriad common people.
Therefore, they were able to greatly shelter the masses,
and brilliantly dwell within the whole territory.
When the Qí dynasty reached its decline,
the reigning lord was ignorant and cruel.
Sly and treacherous gangs of villains
were exalted and promoted.
They unleashed their treachery, perversity, tyranny, and chaos,
spreading cruelty throughout our state,
causing all under Heaven to tremble with fear,
about to fall into a deep ravine.
Within the Nine Domains and the Eight Desolations,
the lords of the regional commanders and mountain supervisors,
stumbled and knocked their heads (in despair),
but had no means to rescue or restore order.
Lying on brushwood, they awaited the burning,
crying to Heaven without response.
I, Yǎn, tossed up my sleeves and set out at dawn,
advancing the sharp edge (of the army) for ten thousand *lǐ* (里),
overcoming the feeling of wanting to resign (from office),
in order to urgently rescue the masses.
Grasping bile (to remind me of bitterness) and swearing before the multitude,
we overcame the strong vanguard and destroyed the fortified positions,
establishing a ruler,
and managing to eliminate the ignorant chaos.
Consequently, following the arrival of the time,
I governed the state,
saving the people and bringing peace to the age;
I truly achieved this labor.
Moreover, the sun's shadow and celestial latitude presented auspicious signs,
the rivers and mountains offered blessings,
(the territory extended) morning and evening to the borders and pastures,
(the mandate embraced) the regions near the capital day and night.
The signs marking the end of the previous dynasty were manifest,
and the time for changing the mandate had arrived.
Foreign customs and the hundred barbarians,
using repeated interpretation, offered allegiance.
Men and spirits, near and far,
there was none who did not gather in harmony.
Thereupon, the various Dukes, Ministers, and officials
all rendered their sincerity,
unanimously believing that the August Heaven had sent down its mandate,
which could not be humbly refused.
The Emperor of Qí cast off the world,
and conferred upon me the divine vessel (the throne).
I, Yǎn, considering myself lacking in virtue,
declined, but could not succeed in refusing.
Looking up, I was constrained by the favor of the Supreme Heaven,
and looking down, I considered the hearts of the millions of people.
The Imperial Seat must not long remain vacant,
and the people and spirits must not lack a lord.
Therefore, relying on this joyous promotion (by the people),
I accept this splendid fortune.
Though I am limited and meager,
I preside over the myriad regions.
Reflecting on my former aspirations,
I shall perpetually speak of reverence and vigilance.
I respectfully selected an auspicious day,
and reverently performed this great ceremony,
ascending the altar to accept the abdication,
and announcing the sacrifice to the Supreme Lord,
so that I may successfully spread glorious blessings,
in order to extend this grand achievement,
to pass down the pattern to my descendants,
thereby eternally securing our state of Liáng (梁).
May the Bright Spirits accept this sacrifice."
When the ceremony was complete,
He prepared the imperial carriage, proceeded immediately to Jiànkāng Gōng (建康宮),
and presided over the front hall of Tàijí (太極).
He issued an edict saying:
"The Five Elements succeed one another,
which is how enlightened Kings receive the mandate;
the four seas happily promote (the new ruler),
which is how Yīn (殷) and Zhōu (周) changed the institutions.
Although abdication and succession differ,
and the circumstances of meeting (the mandate) occurred at different times,
yet the obscure and the bright alternated in their application,
and the lineage (of rule) is far-reaching.
There was none who did not encourage the people and cultivate virtue,
extending brilliance to the common folk.
I, relying on my limited intelligence,
am neither first nor last in receiving the mandate,
but the achievement of bringing peace and stability
happens to belong to this era's fortune.
Availing myself of this opportune moment,
and relying on the hearts of all things (the people),
I shall consequently reinforce the loosened rope (rule),
and bring great creation to the central lands.
Perpetually speaking of the footsteps of my predecessors,
my righteousness is equally ashamed of my lack of virtue.
Since the Qí clan showed evidence of their dynasty's end,
and the calculation of the heavenly mandate had changed,
they respectfully followed the previous record
and gathered the great mandate upon my person.
Considering my meager virtue,
I declined, but could not reject the command.
Reverently fearing the Supreme Spirit,
I thus accept this splendid enterprise.
Performing the ceremony of burnt sacrifice,
I shouldered the fortune granted to the capable.
Following the path of the hundred kings,
I rule over the four seas,
as if crossing a great river,
not knowing how to reach the other shore.
As the grand foundation is first established,
and all things begin anew,
I wish to cause joyous favor
to extend universally across the land under Heaven.
A great amnesty is granted to all under Heaven.
The second year of Zhōngxīng (中興) of Qí is changed to the first year of Tiānjiān.
The common people are granted two ranks of nobility;
civil and military officials are promoted two grades;
those who are old, widowed, orphaned, or solitary and cannot support themselves,
shall each receive five *hú* (斛) of grain.
Outstanding tax obligations, head tax, and old debts shall not be collected again.
Those who violated local public opinion and pure discourse,
or committed corruption, depravity, licentiousness, or robbery,
shall all be cleansed,
have their former records wiped clean,
and be allowed to start anew."
The Qí Emperor was enfeoffed as the Prince of Bālíng (巴陵王),
fully enjoying the revenue of one commandery.
He was allowed to use the Son of Heaven's banners and flags,
and ride in the auxiliary carriage of the Five Seasons.
He was allowed to follow the Qí calendar.
The suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
and the institutions concerning rites and music,
all followed the Qí statutes.
Empress Xuāndé (宣德) of Qí was made the concubine of the Qí Emperor Wén (文帝);
Empress Wáng (王氏) of Qí was made the consort of the Prince of Bālíng.
An edict stated:
"The rise and fall of ruling fortunes
are the old statutes of the preceding dynasty.
The princely and noble titles of the Qí era
are all to be reduced and reviewed.
Those who displayed merit during the period of difficulty
will receive a later, separate command.
Only the Prince of Rǔyīn (汝陰王) of Sòng is not included in this removal order."
Another edict stated:
"As the great fortune newly arises,
and auspicious joy commences,
the remaining dependents of bandits and robbers who were confiscated and held in the government bureaus
shall all be exempted and released.
All households that were banished and displaced
are permitted to return to their native places."
His late Imperial Father was posthumously honored as Emperor Wén (文皇帝),
with the temple name Tàizǔ (太祖);
his late Imperial Mother was posthumously honored as Empress Xiàn (獻皇后).
His late Consort, Xī Shì (郗氏), was posthumously granted the title Empress Dé (德皇后).
His elder brother, Grand Tutor Yì (懿), was posthumously enfeoffed as the Prince of Chángshā Commandery (長沙郡王),
with the posthumous title Xuānwǔ (宣武);
his brother Fū (敷), Advisor on Military Affairs of the Rear Army during Qí, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yǒngyáng Commandery (永陽郡王),
with the posthumous title Zhāo (昭);
his younger brother Chàng (暢), Grand Minister of Ceremonies during Qí, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Héngyáng Commandery (衡陽郡王),
with the posthumous title Xuān (宣);
his younger brother Róng (融), Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Yellow Gate during Qí, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Guìyáng Commandery (桂陽郡王),
with the posthumous title Jiǎn (簡).
On this day,
an edict enfeoffed fifteen civil and military meritorious officials, including Xiàhóu Xiáng (夏侯詳), newly appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry, as Dukes and Marquises,
with differing amounts of tax households (fiefs).
His younger brother Hóng (宏), Commander of the Central Guard, was made Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州),
and enfeoffed as the Prince of Línchuān Commandery (臨川郡王);
Xiù (秀), Governor of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州), was made the Prince of Ānchéng Commandery (安成郡王);
Wěi (偉), Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州), was made the Prince of Jiàn’ān Commandery (建安郡王);
Huī (恢), General of the Left Guard, was made the Prince of Póyáng Commandery (鄱陽郡王);
Dàn (憺), Governor of Jīngzhōu (荊州), was made the Prince of Shǐxīng Commandery (始興郡王).
On the day Dīngmǎo (丁卯),
Wáng Mào (王茂), General Commander of the Army, was promoted to General Who Guards the Army.
Wáng Liàng (王亮), Director of the Imperial Secretariat, was made Prefect of the Masters of Writing and General of the Central Army,
Wáng Yíng (王瑩), Chief Clerk of the Chancellor, was made Director of the Imperial Secretariat and General Who Calms the Army,
Shěn Yuē (沈約), Minister of the Civil Service, was made Vice Prefect of the Masters of Writing,
and Fàn Yún (范雲), concurrently Palace Attendant, was made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Minister of the Civil Service.
An edict stated:
“Since the time of the Sòng (宋) clan,
they widely indulged in excess and luxury,
the wealth of the abandoned palaces
amounting to several thousands.
Calculating among the five capitals (wǔ dū),
distress and poverty filled all lands;
many were afflicted by unjust suffering,
and restraints and coercion were manifold.
For playing stringed instruments and ordering pipes,
women from respectable families (liáng jiā) were not exempted;
in the weaving bureaus and embroidery rooms,
those secluded in hardship were still put to service.
Nothing harms the state and damages harmony
more severely than this.
All those in the inner palace and the Music Bureau (Yuè Fǔ),
and those in the Western Detention Halls (Xī Jiě Bào Shì),
and others falling under these categories,
shall all be released and sent away.
If they are old and infirm and cannot support themselves,
the officials shall provide them with rations.”
On the day Wùchén,
Gāo Yún (高雲), King of Gāogōulí (高句驪) and General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn), was promoted to General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Dàjiāngjūn).
Yú Dà (餘大), King of Bǎijì (百濟) and General-in-Chief Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn), was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn).
Liáng Mí Dǐ (梁彌氐), King of Dàngchāng (宕昌) and General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn), was promoted to General Who Guards the West (Zhènxī Jiāngjūn).
Wǔ (武), King of Wō (倭) and General-in-Chief Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn), was promoted to General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn).
Tǔgǔhùn Xiūliúdài (吐谷渾休留代), King of Hénán (河南) and General Who Guards the West (Zhènxī Jiāngjūn), was promoted to General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn).
The Prince of Bālíng (Bālíng Wáng) died at Gūshú (姑孰);
he was posthumously titled Emperor Hé of Qí (Qí Hé Dì).
His funeral rites were entirely conducted according to past precedents.
On the day Jǐsì,
Zhāng Guī (張瓌), Grand Master of the Palace (Guānglù Dàfū), was appointed Right Grand Master of the Palace (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
On the day Gēngwǔ,
Chén Bózhī (陳伯之), General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ), was promoted to General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn).
An edict stated:
“Observing customs and inspecting practices
is the grand rule of enlightened rulers;
hunting on mountains and touring the territories
is the glorious path of sagacious kings.
Thus, when Zhònghuá (重華) was supreme,
the Five Relationships (wǔ pǐn) were swiftly cultivated;
when Wénmìng (文命) laid the foundation,
he spent four years walking the land.
Therefore, they were able to discern the obscure and minute,
and used butchers and fishermen as eyes and ears,
thereby leading the imperial enterprise to glory,
and extending pure influence far and wide.
I, being slight and inadequate,
ignorant of governing methods,
relying on the mandate of the previous dynasty having ended,
and receiving the heavy responsibility of the celestial decree,
look to previous antiquity for guidance,
trembling as if driving a rotting carriage.
I contemplate how to invigorate the people and nourish virtue,
abandon capital punishment and overcome cruelty,
loosen the nets and set them anew,
and establish them in benevolence and longevity;
but my wisdom is ashamed of illuminating afar,
and my knowledge is insufficient for all matters.
Furthermore, due to the difficulty of the year,
I have not yet found leisure to plan an inspection tour.
When I speak, I am watchful until evening,
and I do not forget my concern even when asleep.
Therefore, officials from the inner court (nèishì) should be dispatched separately,
to inspect all regions thoroughly,
observe administration and listen to popular songs,
and seek out the worthy and promote the neglected.
If there are those whose fields are uncultivated,
whose legal cases are without order,
who forget public duty and pursue private interests,
and whose work is centered on extortion and oppression,
report all such matters as they occur.
If there are those who possess talent but remain obscure in the state (mí bāng),
who hide their genius awaiting the right price,
who store up sound and conceal truth,
and who do not seek fame or advancement,
report them all by name immediately,
allowing none to remain hidden or overlooked.
Let the places reached by the light carriages (yóu xuān)
be as if I had personally examined them.”
Another edict stated:
“The substitution of gold for penal servitude
has been known since antiquity;
the payment of silk for exemption
was implemented in the middle ages.
The people were pleased and the laws were practiced;
nothing is superior to this.
Reflecting upon these latter ages (shú shì),
the tendency toward deceit and shallowness has become prevalent;
committing errors and falling into crime,
the paths are not singular.
The documents detailing execution methods
pile up daily for review;
the instruments of tattooing and cutting (qián zhī xíng)
accumulate yearly in prisons.
The dead cannot be brought back to life,
and the mutilated cannot restore themselves.
If we hope for greater prosperity from this,
how can it be achieved?
I contemplate governance with nightly vigilance,
thinking to uphold political methods,
weighing the methods of former kings,
and selecting their excellent statutes.
Whatever can serve as a constitutional model for the state,
nothing shall be left unadopted.
I seek to alleviate the shame (of harsh laws) throughout the world (sì hǎi),
and make manifest my sincere nature to all beings.
As customs have been false for a long time,
the legal restrictions have become increasingly numerous.
The (leniency of) Emperor Wén of Hàn (Hàn Wén) has been distant
for four hundred years.
Although I simplify affairs and purify my mind,
never forgetting my daily duties,
and have abandoned harsh penalties,
the matter has not yet been fully implemented.
It is permissible to follow the old statutes of Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢),
where those guilty may redeem their punishment.
Let the relevant authorities draft detailed regulations
and present them to me in due course.”
On the day Xīnwèi,
Cài Dàogōng (蔡道恭), General of the Central Command (Zhōng Lǐngjūn), was appointed Governor of Sīzhōu (Sīzhōu Cìshǐ).
Xiāo Bǎoyì (蕭寶義), recently created Duke of Xiè Mù County (Xiè Mù Xiàn Gōng), was made Prince of Bālíng (Bālíng Wáng),
to continue the sacrifices of Qí (齊).
The counties of Nán Lánlíng (南蘭陵) and Wǔjìn (武進) were reinstated,
according to the regulations of the previous dynasty.
Xiè Fěi (謝朏) was summoned to serve as Left Grand Master of the Palace (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) and Grandee Equipped with the Authority of the Three Excellencies (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī);
Hé Yìn (何胤) was summoned as Right Grand Master of the Palace (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
Nán Dōnghǎi (南東海) was renamed Lánlíng Commandery (Lánlíng Jùn).
The administration reorganized the jurisdiction (tǔ duàn) of the various temporary commanderies and counties in Nán Xúzhōu (南徐州).
On the day Guǐyǒu,
an edict stated:
“The practices of the market (shāng sú) have just shifted,
but lingering customs are still rampant.
The lower ranks are unable to reach the top,
and this has been the case for a long time.
As I ascend to the center (throne) and take control of the reins (yù suǒ),
my apprehension increases greatly.
Two boxes shall be placed next to the Censure Post (bàng mù) and the Stone of Complaints (fèi shí) at the Court of the Imperial Carriages (Gōngchē Fǔ).
If those who enjoy official emoluments (ròu shí) remain silent,
and private individuals (shān ā) wish to offer contrary opinions,
they should deposit them in the Censure Post box.
If someone follows my example in the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) regions,
whose accomplishments are worthy of recognition,
whose rhinoceros hides and buffalo armor are uselessly worn out,
and whose ‘dragons and snakes’ (talents) are still constrained;
or if secondary officials possess high and excellent talent,
but are suppressed and unable to advance,
harboring the arts of Fù (傅) and Lǚ (呂),
and bearing the lament of Qū (屈) and Jiǎ (賈);
or if their arguments are clearly sound,
but they suffer hardship and remain wrapped up (in obscurity);
or if great administrations infringe upon the small,
and powerful families bully the humble,
so that the four classes of people (sì mín) are exhausted,
and the grievances do not reach the nine heavens (jiǔ chóng);
if they wish to express themselves,
they may all cast their submissions into the Stone of Complaints box.”
On the day Jiǎxū,
an edict banned the presentation of congratulatory gifts by people near and far.
Another edict stated:
“In the Court of Ritual (Lǐ Wéi) and the Archives (Wén Gé),
old regulations should be followed.
Once the noble and the humble have their positions,
there must be differences in rank and order.
Bowing, rising, kneeling, and prostrating
must be done to clarify the royal measure (wáng dù);
this solemn grandeur,
requires universal observance.
Recently, due to numerous troubles,
the principles of governance have relaxed and fallen into disuse.
Official positions are not attained through accumulated effort,
but honors arrive by chance.
Officers of the Six Armies (liù jūn) occupy Fourth Rank positions;
wearers of blue and purple robes (high officials) perform the tasks of clerks (bái bù).
Shaking out their robes in the ranks of the court,
they salute ministers and chancellors with a casual bow (cháng yī);
they stride quickly through the main palace gate,
and drive alongside the assisting ministers (chéng láng).
Thus, caps and shoes are reversed (order is inverted),
and jade tablets (guī) and earthenware vessels (zèng) cannot be distinguished.
Reflecting silently causes me distress;
I wish to reverse these current ills.
Furthermore, officials who disregard the laws and slacken in their duty,
frequently incur arrears and neglect,
but punishing them with ordinary statutes
will ultimately not reform them.
The birch and cudgel (jiǎ chǔ) display their severity;
for the period, punishment included cutting off the toes.
If whipping and beating are regulated,
they may perhaps be employed.
Let the relevant authorities discuss this thoroughly and impartially,
and strive to clarify the rationale.”
Guǐwèi (day),
an edict
commanded: "Officials of the Prime Minister's Establishment (Xiāngguó Fǔ),
based on their qualifications and service, may be transferred to the central government (Tái).
If their term limits are already fulfilled,
the remainder of those transferred,
and those from the General of Agile Cavalry Establishment (Piàojì Fǔ),
shall all be granted their maximum salary/rank."
In the intercalary month, on Dīngyǒu (day),
Liáng Mǐyōng, the acting King of Dàngchāng, was made General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn) and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Héliáng (河涼) two prefectures (zhōu),
and formally enfeoffed as the King of Dàngchāng.
Rén'yín (day),
Xiàhóu Xiáng, General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn), was made Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
The edict stated:
"The completion of tasks and the spread of good customs,
rigorously maintaining order both internally and externally,
truly depend on establishing offices and dividing responsibilities,
so that officials can mutually restrain and correct each other.
However, recently, being strictly bound by conventional rules,
mistakes have been allowed before reporting them,
resulting in much tolerance for violations and idleness,
and no one willing to hold others accountable.
The net of the law daily slackens,
gradually becoming customary.
Now, officials of the highest ranks may present memorials based on rumors or hearsay (fēngwén zòushì),
following the old system of Yuánxī. "
In the fifth month, on the night of Yǐhài (day),
thieves entered the South and North Yè (gates/wings),
burned the Shénhǔ Mén and the Zǒngzhāng Guān,
and murdered Zhāng Hóngcè, Minister of the Imperial Guard (Wèiwèi Qīng).
Wùzǐ (day),
Chén Bózhī, Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, raised troops and rebelled.
Wáng Mào, General Who Leads the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn), was made General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu,
leading forces to suppress him.
In the sixth month, on Gēngxū (day),
Yáng Shàoxiān, the acting Inspector of Běi Qínzhōu, was made Inspector of Běi Qínzhōu and King of Wǔdū.
In this month,
Chén Bózhī fled to Wèi,
and Jiāngzhōu was pacified.
Liú Jìlián, the former Inspector of Yìzhōu, occupied Chéngdū and rebelled.
In the eighth month, on Wùxū (day),
the Three Offices (Sānguān) of Jiànkāng were established.
Yǐsì (day),
Xiàng Shūpén, General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Xī Liángzhōu, had his title advanced to General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn),
and was enfeoffed as the King of Dèngzhì.
Dīngwèi (day),
an edict commanded Wáng Yíng, Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Jiān), and seven others to participate in settling and finalizing the laws and statutes.
In this month,
an edict commanded the Cáo Láng officials of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) to present memorials as they did formerly.
The kingdoms of Línyì and Gānlì each sent envoys to present local products.
In winter, the eleventh month, on Jǐwèi (day),
the Minor Temple (Xiǎomiào) was established.
Jiǎzǐ (day),
the Imperial Son Tǒng was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
The twelfth month, on Bǐngshēn (day),
Zhāng Jì, Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ), was made General Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
Xīnhài (day),
Zhāng Jì, General Protector of the Army, was dismissed.
This year there was a great drought.
Rice cost five thousand (cash) per *dǒu*.
Many people starved to death.
The second year [503 CE], spring, the first month, the new moon, on Jiǎyín (day),
an edict stated:
"The 'Three Inquiries and Five Hearings' [methods of judicial interrogation],
are recorded in the sacred canons.
Compassionately concluding legal cases,
is a profound meaning emphasized in former injunctions.
These are the means by which the application of punishments is made clear and cautious,
and deep warnings are issued against suspected injustice.
The achievement of success and the realization of good governance,
none fails to stem from this.
When We were in the regional administration,
We always personally oversaw the inquiries and records,
seeking principle and discovering the facts,
exhausting all efforts in both major and minor cases.
In recent times, the net [of the law] has been slackened,
and this administration is again deficient.
Prisons are congested and suppressed,
and appeals have nowhere to turn.
We are charged with the current mandate,
reigning over countless people.
Although We reside purely in the Xuānshì Palace,
and diligently attend to hearings and judgments;
the distant regions of the Nine Provinces (Jiǔmù)
cannot be personally overseen.
We deeply fear that those harboring grievances and undergoing torture
are not limited to just one region.
Therefore, a repeated command shall be issued to all prefectures (zhōu),
that they must oversee inquiries once a month,
broadly seek out and select the good,
and strive for absolute factual accuracy."
Yǐmǎo (day),
Shěn Yuē, Prefect of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Púyè), was made Left Prefect of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè);
Fàn Yún, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), was made Right Prefect of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè);
Huī, Prince of Póyáng, former General (Qián Jiāngjūn), was made Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu;
Wáng Liàng, Director of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Lìng), was made Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū);
Liǔ Qìngyuǎn, General of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn), was made Central Leader of the Army (Zhōng Lǐngjūn).
Bǐngchén (day),
Wáng Liàng, Director of the Masters of Writing and newly appointed Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, was dismissed.
Summer, the fourth month, on Guǐmǎo (day),
Cài Fǎdù, Shàngshū Shāndìng Láng, presented the Twenty Chapters of the Liáng Code, the Thirty Chapters of Statutes, and the Forty Chapters of Regulations.
The fifth month, on Dīngsì (day),
Fàn Yún, Right Prefect of the Masters of Writing, died.
Yǐchǒu (day),
Dèng Yuánqǐ, Inspector of Yìzhōu, captured Chéngdū,
and granted a limited amnesty to Yìzhōu.
Rénshēn (day),
it was decreed that all commanderies and counties must cease presenting tribute to the Two Palaces (Èrgōng).
Only the various prefectures (zhōu) and Kuàijī [Prefecture],
whose duties include the governance of large territories,
were permitted to present local products suitable to their region.
If they were not native products,
they were also forbidden from contributing them.
The sixth month, on Dīnghài (day),
an edict noted that due to flooding in the three counties of Dōngyáng, Xìn'ān, and Fēng'ān,
the assets and livelihoods of the residents were washed away and damaged.
Envoys were dispatched to travel extensively,
to assess the situation and remit taxes and levies.
This summer had many epidemics.
Xiè Fěi, newly appointed Left Grand Master of Glorious Happiness, was made Minister over the Masses (Sītú) and Director of the Masters of Writing.
Jiǎwǔ (day),
Wáng Yíng, Central Secretariat Director, was made Right Prefect of the Masters of Writing.
Autumn, the seventh month,
the kingdoms of Fúnán, Qiūcí, and Central Tiānzhú each sent envoys to present local products.
Winter, the tenth month,
Wèi bandits raided Sīzhōu.
The eleventh month, on Yǐmǎo (day),
there was thunder, lightning, and heavy rain,
and it was dark.
That night there was thunder again.
Yǐhài (day),
Shěn Yuē, Left Prefect of the Masters of Writing, left office due to mourning his mother.
[Third year, 504 CE], spring, the first month, on Wùshēn (day),
Hóng, Prince of Línchuān, General of the Rear (Hòu Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Yángzhōu, had his title advanced to General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn).
Guǐchǒu (day),
Wáng Yíng, Right Prefect of the Masters of Writing, was made Left Prefect of the Masters of Writing;
Liǔ Dàn, Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì), was made Right Prefect of the Masters of Writing;
Shěn Yuē, former Left Prefect of the Masters of Writing, was made General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn).
The second month,
Wèi captured Liángzhōu.
The third month,
frost fell and killed the vegetation.
The fifth month, on Dīngsì (day),
Kéuchénrú Shéyē Bámó, King of Fúnán, was made General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn).
The sixth month, on Bǐngzǐ (day),
an edict stated:
"In the past, when sagacious kings ruled the world,
they annually determined their route [for inspection],
and personally carried out tours and inspections.
Popular customs, government policies, and punishments,
nothing was left unexamined.
In later generations, customs have withered,
and this regulation has long been neglected.
Although We wish to extend Our reach afar and disregard hardship,
and fully oversee the obscure and remote regions,
carrying out ancient practices in the present day
is not easily followed.
Therefore, We hesitate when the day grows late,
feeling the desire to inspect the people again.
Among the totality of the Nine Provinces (Jiǔzhōu),
the common people, both near and far,
some are in remote and distant valleys,
some are poor, emaciated, old, or sick.
Harboring grievances and holding to their principles,
they have no way to plead their case.
This is why the common woman of Dōnghǎi
brought disaster upon the state,
and the lonely soul of Xītǔ
ascended a tower to plead his case.
Thinking of this,
We sigh deeply in the middle of the night.
Officials shall be dispatched in groups to tour the prefectures and regions.
If there are those with deep grievances or who have suffered great harm,
who are oppressed and have nowhere to turn,
they are permitted to approach the envoys
and present their cases based on the facts.
Thus, the sentiment of pity and compassion
may brightly cover the Four Directions,
ensuring that distant pleas are heard widely,
and the matter is equivalent to Our personal inspection."
Guǐwèi (day),
a general amnesty was granted to the realm.
Autumn, the seventh month, on Dīngwèi (day),
Xiàhóu Xiáng, Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū), was made General of Chariots and Cavalry and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Yáng Gōngzé, Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, was made Central Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn).
Jiǎzǐ (day),
the Imperial Son Zōng was established as the Prince of Yùzhāng Commandery.
The eighth month,
Wèi captured Sīzhōu.
An edict ordered Sīzhōu to be re-established at Nán Yìyáng.
The ninth month, on Rénzǐ (day),
Fúlián Chóu, heir apparent of the King of Hénán, was made General Who Guards the West (Zhènxī Jiāngjūn), Inspector of Xīqínhé two prefectures, and King of Hénán.
The kingdom of Northern Tiānzhú sent envoys to present local products.
In the eleventh month of winter, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
an edict stated:
"The establishment of teachings adapts to the times;
purity and corruption necessitate different governance.
Punishments change with the eras,
varying in severity.
In the past, the customs of Shāng (商) had not yet shifted,
and the people had been scattered for a long time.
Trapped in nets and fallen into legal penalties,
they were sought out day and night.
If all were to be subjected to the proper law,
then those in red garments (convicts) would block the roads.
If all were granted broad pardons,
then it would be difficult to govern the state.
Therefore, those guilty were allowed to redeem themselves,
to preserve the lives of the common people (*yuán yuán*).
Now, those near and far know the prohibitions,
and the prisons are gradually emptying.
Proceeding thus,
it is hoped that punishments can be abolished.
The system of monetary redemption,
should now be removed.
The regulation for redeeming crimes can be abolished."
That year there were many epidemics.
In the first month of spring of the fourth year, on the *guǐmǎo* day, the first day of the month,
an edict stated:
"Currently, among the regular selections of the nine streams (official classes),
those under thirty years of age,
who have not mastered one classic,
shall not be granted their first official robes (*jiě hè*).
However, if there are talents comparable to Gān (甘) and Yán (顏),
they shall not be limited by age."
One Doctor of the Five Classics (*wǔ jīng bó shì*) was appointed for each classic.
Jiàn'ān Wáng Wěi (建安王偉), General Who Guards the North (*zhèn běi jiāng jūn*) and Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州), was appointed Governor of Nánxúzhōu (南徐州).
Póyáng Wáng Huī (鄱陽王恢), Governor of Nánxúzhōu, was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Liǔ Qìngyuǎn (柳慶遠), Central Army Commander (*zhōng lǐng jūn*), was appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day,
the performance art of phoenixes holding books was abolished.
On the *wùshēn* day,
an edict stated:
"When performing suburban sacrifices to offer to the Emperor (of Heaven),
the utmost reverence must be present.
One must offer sincerity and exert oneself to the utmost,
yet still fear deviation.
However, in past generations, court women were often allowed to watch this ceremony,
with vast curtained palaces set up,
and decorated carriages glittering on the roads.
This is not how one reverently worships the azure heavens
and demonstrates sincerity to the supreme spirits.
The presence of numerous attendant carriages
was criticized by previous generations;
this practice should be stopped from now on."
On the *xīnhài* day,
the imperial carriage personally performed sacrifices at the southern suburbs,
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
In the second month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
Wèi Wèi Qīng Yáng Gōngzé (衞尉卿楊公則) was dispatched to lead the palace guards to block Luòkǒu (洛口).
On the *rénchén* day,
Lǐ Kǎi (李凱), Governor of Jiāozhōu (交州), rebelled by seizing the prefecture.
His Chief Clerk (*zhǎng shǐ*), Lǐ Cè (李畟), suppressed him.
A partial amnesty was granted to Jiāozhōu.
On the *wùxū* day,
Cáo Jǐngzōng (曹景宗), formerly Governor of Yǐngzhōu, was appointed Central Protector General (*zhōng hù jūn*).
That month,
the Jiànxīng Yuàn (建興苑) was established in Jiànxīng Lǐ (建興里) of Mòlíng (秣陵).
In the fourth month of summer, on the *dīngsì* day,
Liáng Míbó (梁彌博), the acting King of Dàngchāng (宕昌), was appointed General Who Pacifies the West (*ān xī jiāng jūn*), Governor of Héliáng (河涼) two prefectures, and King of Dàngchāng.
That month,
from the *jiǎyín* day to the *rénxū* day,
sweet dew continuously fell in Huálínyuán (華林園).
In the fifth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
auspicious grain grew in Shuòyīn Lǐ (朔陰里) of Jiànkāng (建康) county,
with twelve ears on one stalk.
In the sixth month, on the *gēngxū* day,
a temple for Kǒngzǐ (孔子) was established.
On the *rénxū* day,
Jupiter was seen during the day.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
Zhāng Guī (張瓌), Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (*yòu guāng lù dà fū*), died.
In the eighth month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
the star Canopus was seen.
In the tenth month of winter, on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
a northern expedition was launched.

Línchuān Wáng Hóng (臨川王宏), General of the Central Army (*zhōng jūn jiāng jūn*) and Governor of Yángzhōu (揚州), was appointed Commander-in-Chief of all northern expeditionary forces (*dūdū běi tǎo zhū jūn shì*).
Liǔ Tàn (柳惔), Right Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (*shàng shū yòu pú shè*), was his deputy.
That year,
due to the expenses of raising the army,
princes (*wáng gōng*) and officials below them each offered state taxes and grain from their fields,
to assist with military funds.
In the eleventh month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
Zhāng Jì (張稷), Minister of Public Works (*dū guān shàng shū*), was appointed General of the Palace Guard (*lǐng jūn jiāng jūn*).
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
the sky was clear,
and there were three flashes of lightning in the southwest,
heard like thunder.
In the twelfth month,
Xiè Fěi (謝朏), Grand Commandant (*sītú*) and Director of the Department of State Affairs (*shàng shū lìng*), left his post
due to mourning for his birth mother.
That year saw a great harvest,
with rice priced at thirty *hú* per *shí*.
In the first month of spring of the fifth year, on the *dīngmǎo* day, the first day of the month,
an edict stated:
"In the past, during the Zhōu (周) and Hàn (漢) dynasties,
talented individuals were sought from all regions of the country.
In recent times, with corruption and decline,
the obscure and hidden are rarely reached.
When people are isolated and places are remote,
their voices are unheard and their situations unseen.
The integrity of scholars has declined universally,
and thus there is no encouragement.
How could it be that mountains and rivers, though possessing spiritual power,
are inherently partial?
It is truly due to knowing or not knowing, employing or not employing [talent].
I, with my meager virtue,
rule these myriad people.
Yet the fully enlightened and widely illuminated [talents]
are confined within their homes.
My flying ears and long eyes [i.e., intelligence-gathering network]
do not reach the four directions.
I constantly feel shame in my heart,
never forgetting it day or night.
Therefore, in all commanderies and states, if there are old families within the region who hold no court positions,
officials should be selected to seek them out,
so that each commandery has at least one such person."
On the *yǐhài* day,
Xiè Fěi, formerly Grand Commandant, was appointed Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (*zhōng shū jiān*), Grand Commandant, and General of the Guards (*wèi jiāng jūn*).
Shěn Yuē (沈約), General Who Guards the Army (*zhèn jūn jiāng jūn*), was appointed Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness.
Yùzhāng Wáng Zōng (豫章王綜) was appointed Governor of Nánxúzhōu.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Wáng Yíng (王瑩), Left Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Protector General (*hù jūn jiāng jūn*),
with his former post as Assistant Director remaining.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
Imperial Prince Gāng (綱) was enfeoffed as King of Jìn'ān Commandery (*Jìn'ān Jùn Wáng*).
On the *dīnghài* day,
Venus was seen during the day.
In the second month, on the *gēngxū* day,
Zhāng Chōng (張充), Grand Minister of Ceremonies (*tài cháng*), was appointed Minister of Personnel (*lì bù shàng shū*).
On the first day of the third month, *bǐngyín*,
there was a solar eclipse.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
Yì (翼), a cousin of Wèi Xuānwǔ Dì (魏宣武帝), led his younger brothers to surrender.
Liú Sīxiào (劉思效), General Who Assists the State (*fǔ guó jiāng jūn*), defeated Yuán Xì (元繫), Wèi's Governor of Qīngzhōu (青州), at Jiāoshuǐ (膠水).
On the *dīnghài* day,
Chén Bózhī (陳伯之) led his troops from Shòuyáng (壽陽) to surrender.
In the fourth month of summer, on the *bǐngshēn* day,
two bronze swords were unearthed at Rénshān (仁山) in Gāochāng (高昌) of Lúlíng (廬陵).
One eight-eyed tortoise was found in Shǐfēng (始豐) county.
On the *jiǎyín* day,
an edict stated:
"I, from dawn, residing in my fasting chamber,
am solely concerned with punishments,
the 'three punishments' and 'five hearings' constantly occupying my thoughts whether waking or sleeping.
Therefore, I placed the 'lung-stone' (a petition box) in the capital streets,
and increased officials in the imperial prison.
I diligently and personally review,
considering even the smallest matters with sincerity.
Yet, my discerning caution has not been fully effective,
and prisons are still congested.
I reflect with shame,
as if I had fallen into a pit.
Therefore, to all places of imprisonment,
I shall dispatch judicial officials and close attendants,
to take turns recording prisoners.
If there are any cases of injustice or prolonged detention,
they shall be reported in a timely manner."
In the fifth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
Zhāng Huìshào (張惠紹), Left Guard Commander of the Crown Prince (*tài zǐ zuǒ wèi shuài*), captured Wèi's Sùyù (宿預) city.
On the *yǐhài* day,
the vanguard of Línchuān Wáng Hóng captured Liángchéng (梁城).
On the *xīnsì* day,
Wéi Ruì (韋叡), Governor of Yùzhōu (豫州), captured Héféi (合肥) city.
On the *dīnghài* day,
Péi Suì (裴邃), Grand Administrator of Lújiāng (廬江), captured Yángshíchéng (羊石城).
On the *gēngyín* day,
he also captured Huòqiū (霍丘) city.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Venus was seen during the day.
In the sixth month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
Huán Hé (桓和), Governor of Qīng (青) and Jì (冀) prefectures, and his vanguard captured Qúshān (朐山) city.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
the state of Dèngzhì (鄧至) sent envoys to offer local products.
In the eighth month, on the *wùxū* day,
the star Canopus was seen.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
the Crown Prince's palace was constructed.
In the eleventh month of winter, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
there was an earthquake in the capital.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
because the military campaign had dragged on,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
The Wèi (魏) invaders attacked Zhōnglí (鍾離).
Cáo Jǐngzōng, Right General of the Guards (*yòu wèi jiāng jūn*), was dispatched to lead troops to reinforce them.
In the twelfth month, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
Xiè Fěi, Grand Commandant, died.
an imperial edict stated:
"A treasure measuring but an inch
may be hidden in the sand and mud;
rejecting words because of the person [speaking them]
is something the *jūnzǐ* (gentleman) guards against.
When We attend court and retire late,
We contemplate expounding upon the methods of governance.
Although the myriad officials and *qīngshì* (ministers)
must submit whatever they harbor in their minds,
voices amassed in distant frontiers
have not yet reached the Wèiquè (imperial palace gates).
They may be constrained by poverty and low standing,
or separated by mountains and rivers,
stomping their feet and craning their necks,
having no means to present their views.
How can this be the way to ensure that nothing sinks or is missed,
and that both the distant and the near are benefited?
If the scholar-officials and common people of the four directions
have anything they wish to present regarding judicial or political affairs,
beneficial to the state and advantageous to the populace,
but are prevented or isolated by obscurity or distance,
and cannot communicate themselves,
they may individually detail and express their concerns to the *cìshǐ* (inspectors) and *èrqiānshí* (governors).
If there is anything worthy of presentation and adoption,
whether large or small, it must be reported."
On the day Jǐmǎo,
an imperial edict stated:
"He who possesses All Under Heaven
does so based on righteousness, not for his own sake.
Famine, epidemics,
warfare, floods, or fires—
if any one of these occurs,
the blame rests with the sovereign head.
Now, the prayer officials request prayers
citing successive evils.
We shall bear them in Our own person,
so that calamities forever fail to reach the myriad people,
allowing the common populace to gradually attain peace and rest.
No prayers for Our personal blessing are permitted,
lest they increase Our faults.
This is specially distributed far and near,
that all may comply and respect it."
In the second month, on the day Jiǎchén,
the Lǎorén Xīng (Canopus) was visible.
In the third month, on the day Gēngshēn (the new moon),
frost fell, killing the vegetation.
In this month,
three elephants entered the Jīngshī (Capital).
Summer, the fourth month, on the day Rénchén,
the offices of the Zǔoyòu Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of the Left and Right Swift Cavalry) and the Zǔoyòu Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of the Left and Right Mobile Attack) were established.
On the day Guǐsì,
Cáo Jǐngzōng, Wéi Ruì, and others defeated the Wèi army at Shàoyáng Zhōu,
achieving tens of thousands of casualties and captures.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
Cáo Jǐngzōng, General of the Right Guard, was appointed *Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn* (General Regulating the Army) and Inspector of Xúzhōu.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wáng Mào, Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, was appointed *Shàngshū Yòu Púyè* (Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs).
Ānchéng Wáng Xiù, Prefect of the Central Secretariat, was appointed Píngnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Quells the South) and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
Héngzhōu was established by dividing Xiāngzhōu and Guǎngzhōu.
On the day Dīngsì,

Línchuān Wáng Hóng, General of the Central Army and Inspector of Yángzhōu, was appointed Piàoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry) and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (Establishment of a Mansion with the Honors of the Three Grandees).
Jiàn'ān Wáng Wěi, Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Stabilizes the Army), was appointed Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Shěn Yuē, Grand Master of the Right of the Glorious Palace, was appointed *Shàngshū Zǔo Púyè* (Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs).
Wáng Yíng, Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed General of the Central Army.
In the fifth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
Chángshā Wáng Shēnyè, newly appointed General of the Left Swift Cavalry, was made *Zhōng Hùjūn* (Central Protector of the Army).
On the day Guǐhài,
Yuán Áng, Palace Attendant, was appointed *Lìbù Shàngshū* (Minister of Personnel).
On the day Jǐsì,
the offices of *Zhōngwèi* (Central Guard) and *Zhōngquán* (Central Authority) Generals were established.
*Xiāoqí* (Swift Cavalry) was renamed *Yúnqí* (Cloud Cavalry),
and *Yóují* (Mobile Attack) was renamed *Yóuqí* (Mobile Cavalry).
On the day Xīnwèi,
Jiàn'ān Wáng Wěi, General of the Right and Inspector of Yángzhōu, was promoted in title to *Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn*.
In the sixth month, on the day Gēngxū,
Xiàhóu Xiáng, General of Chariots and Cavalry and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, was appointed Grand Master of the Right of the Glorious Palace.
Liǔ Tán, newly appointed Grand Master of the Glorious Palace with Gold and Purple, was appointed Ānnán Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the South) and Inspector of Xiāngzhōu.
Xīnwú Xiàn captured one turtle with four eyes.
Autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Tàibái (Venus) was visible during the day.
On the day Bǐngyín,
Guìzhōu was established by dividing Guǎngzhōu.
On the day Dīnghài,
Wáng Mào, newly appointed Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed *Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn*.
In the eighth month, on the day Wùzǐ,
a general amnesty was granted across the realm.
On the day Wùxū,
a great wind broke trees.
There was a great flood in the Jīngshī,
caused by the ingress of tides,
adding seven *chǐ* (feet) to the Imperial Way.
In the ninth month,
auspicious grain with nine ears on a single stalk
grew in Jiānglíng Xiàn.
On the day Yǐhài,
the Yuèwǔ Táng (Hall for Reviewing Military Skills) was renamed Déyáng Táng (Hall of Moral Radiance),
and the Tīngsòng Táng (Hall for Hearing Litigation) was renamed Yíxián Táng (Hall of Exemplary Worthies).
On the day Bǐngxū,
Lǚ Sēngzhēn, General of the Left Guard, was appointed Píngběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Quells the North) and Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu.
Xiāo Chāng, Administrator of Yùzhāng, was appointed Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Winter, the tenth month, on the day Rén'yín,
Xú Miǎn, Minister of the Five Armies, was appointed Minister of Personnel.
In the intercalary month, on the day Yǐchǒu,
Línchuān Wáng Hóng, Piàoqí Jiāngjūn and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*, was appointed *Sītú* (Minister of Instruction) and Acting Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Shěn Yuē, Assistant Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed *Shàngshū Lìng* (Director of the Department of State Affairs) and Acting Junior Tutor of the Crown Prince.
Yuán Áng, Minister of Personnel, was appointed Assistant Director of the Right.
