On the day Jǐchǒu,
Hé Jìngróng, Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè (Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs), was made Zhōng Quán Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Authority).
Xiāo Yuānzǎo, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (General Protecting the Army), was made Ān Yòu Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Right) and Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè.
Xiè Jǔ, Shàngshū Yòupúshè (Vice Director of the Right in the Department of State Affairs), was made Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Palace of Brilliance of the Right).
On the day Gēngyín,
Lúlíng Wáng Xù, Ān Nán Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the South), was made Zhōng Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Guard) and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the third month, on the day Wùxū,
the son of Zhāomíng Tàizǐ, Qǐ, was established as Wǔchāng Jùnwáng (Prince of Wǔchāng Commandery),
and Yìn was established as Yìyáng Jùnwáng (Prince of Yìyáng Commandery).
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Dīngmǎo,
Hédōng Wáng Yù, Prefect of the two commanderies of Nán Lángyá and Péngchéng, was made Cìshǐ of Nán Xúzhōu.
In the fifth month, on the day Bǐngshēn,
Wǔlíng Wáng Jǐ, formerly Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, was reinstated as Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
In the sixth month,
frost fell in the territory of Qúshān in Qīngzhōu.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Wèi sent an envoy to offer tribute.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Yìyáng Wáng Yìn died.
In this month,
snow fell in Qīngzhōu,
damaging the crops.
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎshēn,
the Star of the Old Man appeared.
On the day Xīnmǎo,
the Imperial Carriage proceeded to the Āyù Wáng Sì (King Aśoka Temple),
and a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
In the ninth month,
Nán Yǎnzhōu suffered a great famine.
In this month,
approximately two thousand *qǐng* of spontaneously grown rice and barnyard grass appeared within the borders of Běi Xúzhōu.
In the intercalary month, on the day Jiǎzǐ,
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì, Ān Xī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West) and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, was promoted to the title Zhèn Xī Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the West).
Wǔlíng Wáng Jǐ, Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu, was made Ān Xī Jiāngjūn and Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
the capital suffered an earthquake.
This year,
there was famine.
In the fourth year, spring, the first month, on the day Gēngchén,
Xuānchéng Wáng Dàqì, Zhōng Jūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Army), was made Zhōng Jūn Dàjiāngjūn (General-in-Chief of the Central Army) and Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu.
In the second month, on the day Jǐhài,
the Imperial Carriage personally plowed the Ceremonial Field.
In the third month, on the day Wùyín,
the state of Hénán sent an envoy to present local products.
On the day Guǐwèi,
the state of Ruìruì sent an envoy to present local products.
In the fifth month, on the day Jiǎxū,
Wèi sent an envoy to offer tribute.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jǐwèi,
Yuèyáng Wáng Chá, Prefect of the two commanderies of Nán Lángyá and Péngchéng, was made Cìshǐ of Dōng Yángzhōu.
On the day Guǐhài,
an edict declared a general amnesty throughout the realm
because Lǐ Yìnzhī, a convict from Dōngyě, had received a *shèlì* (relic) of the true form of the Tathāgata (Rúlái).
In the eighth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
an edict stated:
"Since the twelve provinces of Nán Yǎnzhōu, Běi Xúzhōu, Xī Xúzhōu, Dōng Xúzhōu, Qīngzhōu, Jìzhōu, Nánběi Qīngzhōu, Wǔzhōu, Rénzhōu, Tóngzhōu, and Suīzhōu
have experienced famine,
outstanding rents and old debts are partially pardoned,
and the Three Levies (*Sāndiào*) for this year shall not be collected."
In winter, the twelfth month, on the day Dīnghài,
Huáng Kǎn, concurrently Guózǐ Zhùjiào (Assistant Instructor of the Directorate of Education), presented his fifty-scroll commentary (*yìshū*) on the *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites).
In the fifth year, spring, the first month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
Lúlíng Wáng Xù, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, was made Pīaoqí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Xiāo Yuānzǎo, Ān Yòu Jiāngjūn and Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè, was made Zhōng Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Guard) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Hé Jìngróng, Zhōng Quán Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn (Governor of Dānyáng), was made Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs) retaining his original title.
Zhāng Zuǎn, Lìbù Shàngshū, was made Shàngshū Púshè (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs).
Liú Rǔ, Dūguān Shàngshū (Minister of the Ministry of Revenue), was made Lìbù Shàngshū.
On the day Dīngsì,
Hè Chēn, Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor Vice Director) and official participating in ceremonial affairs, memorialized:
"Currently, when traveling to and returning from the two suburbs, north and south, and the Ceremonial Field (*Jìtián*), the Imperial Carriage (*yǔ niǎn*) should be used,
and the Imperial Chariot (*lù*) should no longer be ridden.
For the two suburbs, I request the use of the plain palanquin (*sù niǎn*).
For traveling to and returning from the Ceremonial Field, the ordinary palanquin (*cháng niǎn*) should be ridden.
In both cases, the Shìzhōng (Attendant at the Court) should accompany the ride,
dispensing with the Grand General (*Dàjiāngjūn*) and the Grand Coachman (*Tàipú*)."
An edict referred this to the Department of State Affairs for extensive discussion and implementation.
The name of the plain palanquin (*sù niǎn*) was changed to the Great Harmony Palanquin (*Dàtóng Niǎn*).
When offering sacrifices at the ancestral temples, the Jade Palanquin (*Yù Niǎn*) was ridden.
On the day Xīnwèi,
the Imperial Carriage personally performed sacrifice in the Southern Suburb.
An edict decreed that those known for filial piety, fraternal duty, diligence in agriculture, and those called good people by the districts (*zhōuliú*) and villages (*xiāngdǎng*),
should each be bestowed one rank of nobility,
and their respective administrations were ordered to report these names promptly.
Third month, Jǐwèi [day],
an imperial edict said:
「My four faculties of hearing (sìcōng) are already deficient,
and the five senses (wǔshì) are often obscured.
What is drawn (in policy) and recorded externally
may result in errors.
Regarding all governmental affairs that are inconvenient for the people,
the Zhōus, Jùns, and Xiàns must report them immediately,
and must not conceal them through deception.
If complaints and litigation arise,
the responsibility lies with the official in charge of that area.
From now on,
let this be established as a permanent standard. 」
Autumn, seventh month, Jǐmǎo [day],
Pīnjì Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, the Prince of Lúlíng, Xù, was appointed Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng, Yì, was appointed Hùjūn Jiāngjūn and Ānyòu Jiāngjūn.
Eighth month, Yǐyǒu [day],
the Kingdom of Fúnán sent an envoy to present a live rhinoceros and local products (fāngwù).
Ninth month, Gēngshēn [day],
Dūguān Shàngshū Dào Gài was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
Winter, eleventh month, Yǐhài [day],
Wèi sent an envoy to request friendly relations (pìn).
Twelfth month, Guǐwèi [day],
Xiè Jǔ, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wú Jùn, was appointed Zhōngshū Jiān.
The newly appointed Zhōngshū Lìng, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, was appointed Zhōnglǐngjūn.
Sixth year, spring, first month, Gēngxū (the first day of the month),
a limited pardon was issued in the four Zhōus of Sī, Yù, Xú, and Yǎn.
Second month, Jǐhài [day],
the Emperor personally plowed the sacrificial field (Jìtián).
Bǐngwǔ [day],
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, the Prince of Shàolíng, Lún, was appointed Píngxī Jiāngjūn and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, the Prince of Yùzhāng, Huān, was appointed Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Qín Jùn presented one white deer.
Summer, fourth month, Guǐwèi [day],
an imperial edict said:
「Those commissioned by destiny who arose as kings,
succeeding the worthy and transmitting their great accomplishments,
their reputation is imperishable.
However, generations pass and shift,
while the two guests (Èrbīn) have been granted positions,
the duty of the three honored guests (Sānkè) remains.
As time and affairs grow distant,
the old burial mounds are overgrown with weeds and brambles.
Looking back at antiquity brings forth sentiment,
and recalling them deeply saddens me.
Regarding the imperial mausoleums of the three Dynasties—Jìn, Sòng, and Qí—
those who hold the relevant positions must diligently increase their protection,
and must not allow common people arbitrarily to encroach upon or damage them.
If there are too few guards (zuòbīng),
ensure that they are supplemented until sufficient.
For those (mausoleums) that previously lacked custodianship and surveillance,
provisions should be allocated as deemed appropriate. 」
Fifth month, Wùyín [day],
Yuán Luō, formerly Cìshǐ of Qīng and Jì Zhōus, was appointed Yòuguānglù Dàfū.
Jǐmǎo [day],
the Prince of Hénán sent an envoy to present horses and local products (fāngwù).
Sixth month, Dīngwèi [day],
Píngyáng Xiàn presented one white deer.
Autumn, seventh month, Dīnghài [day],
Wèi sent an envoy to request friendly relations (pìn).
Eighth month, Wùwǔ [day],
a general amnesty was granted to the realm.
Xīnwèi [day],
an imperial edict said:
「Governing the state has its standard methods;
one must always consult the court officials.
This is why the Secretariat (Shàngshū) establishes Lìng, Pú, Chéng, and Láng positions,
to attend court every morning
to deliberate on current affairs,
first consulting and planning together,
and only then reporting to the throne.
Recently, this has not been the case.
Whenever there is a doubtful matter,
officials stand leaning (waiting) and seek an immediate decision.
The ancients said,
'If the ruler is not Yáo or Shùn,
how can whatever he speaks be automatically correct?'
Therefore, even the sagely Fàngxūn (Emperor Yáo),
still consulted the Four Peaks (Sìyuè);
and the wise Chónghuá (Emperor Shùn),
also relied upon many scholars.
How can I, who possess meager virtue,
be capable of making unilateral decisions?
Henceforth, if there is a doubtful matter within the Secretariat (Shàngshū),
they must first consult and deliberate in the court hall,
and only then report it.
Do not follow the recent habit.
As for military secrets and urgent matters,
which require prior consultation and examination,
they shall continue to follow the former statutes. 」
The Kingdom of Pánpán sent an envoy to present local products (fāngwù).
Ninth month,
Ānzhōu was moved to establish Dìngyuǎn Jùn.
(It) received the Governorship (Dūdu) of Běixú Zhōu.
Dìngyuǎn Jùn was transferred and placed under Ānzhōu.
Shǐpíng Tàishǒu Cuī Shuò submitted a memorial presenting one stalk of auspicious grain (jiāhé) with twelve ears.
Wùxū [day],
Tèjìn, Zuǒguānglù Dàfū, and Sīkōng Yuán Áng died.
Winter, eleventh month, Jǐmǎo [day],
a limited pardon was issued in the Capital City (Jīngyì).
Twelfth month, Rénzǐ [day],
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ, the Prince of Yùzhāng, Huān, died.
Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, the Prince of Xiāngdōng, Yì, was appointed Zhènnán Jiāngjūn and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Guìzhōu was established in Shǐ'ān Jùn of Xiāngzhōu.
(It) received the Governorship (Dū) of Xiāngzhōu.
Twenty-four Jùns, including Nánguìlín, were abolished (shěng).
All were transferred to belong to Guìzhōu.
Seventh year, spring, first month, Xīnsì [day],
the Emperor personally performed the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb (Nánjiāo).
A general amnesty was granted to the realm.
Those who had become refugees or lost their ancestral homes (sāngzǐ)
were each to return to their fields and residences,
and their taxes were remitted for five years.
Xīnchǒu [day],
the Emperor personally performed the sacrifice at the Míngtáng.
Second month, Yǐsì [day],
Liáng Mǐtài, acting Prince of Dàngchāng, was appointed Píngxī Jiāngjūn,
Cìshǐ of Hé and Liáng Zhōus, and Prince of Dàngchāng.
Xīnhài [day],
the Emperor personally plowed the sacrificial field (Jìtián).
Yǐmǎo [day],
there was an earthquake in the capital (Jīngshī).
Dīngsì [day],
Zhōnglǐngjūn, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, was appointed Zhènběi Jiāngjūn and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Third month, Yǐhài [day],
the Prince of Dàngchāng sent an envoy to present horses and local products (fāngwù).
Gāolì, Bǎijì, and Huáguó each sent envoys to present local products (fāngwù).
Summer, fourth month, Wùshēn [day],
Wèi sent an envoy to request friendly relations (pìn).
Fifth month, Guǐsì [day],
Shìzhōng, the Prince of Nánkāng, Huìlǐ, concurrently took the post of Lǐngjūn.
Autumn, ninth month, Wùyín [day],
the Kingdom of Ruìruì sent an envoy to present local products (fāngwù).
Winter, tenth month, Bǐngwǔ [day],
Shìzhōng Liú Rǔ was appointed Lìbù Shàngshū.
Eleventh month, Bǐngzǐ [day],
an edict commanded the cessation of labor drafts (yìshǐ) of female adults (nǚdīng) in their respective locations.
Dīngchǒu [day],
an imperial edict said:
「The great fortune of the people
is the misfortune of the state.
Repeated application of benevolence and favor
only increases treachery and theft.
I also know that this is a flaw.
Yet, if I do not grant a generous pardon,
it would not be the heart of a benevolent person.
Regarding all shortages, losses, arrears, and debts,
arising before the dawn of the ninth day of the eleventh month of the seventh year (of Tiānjiān),
which exist among the common people, regardless of amount,
and have been reported to the Secretariat (Shàngshū) or Superintending Office (Dūsuǒ) but have not yet been collected,
all are hereby pardoned and canceled. 」
Another imperial edict said:
「Utilizing the principles of Heaven
and sharing the advantages of the land,
are the established guidelines of the former sages.
All abandoned fields, mulberry grounds, and ruined residences that have been confiscated (mòrù),
aside from those newly established for public use,
shall all be divided and allocated to the poor people.
Each shall receive a share of the land commensurate with their capability.
I have heard recently that
powerful and wealthy households
have frequently occupied public land,
leasing it out at high prices,
and then giving it to the poor people (as subleases).
This harms the times and damages governance,
and the corruption (dù) is excessive.
Henceforth, public land shall absolutely not be leased to powerful households;
those already leased are exceptionally permitted not to be recovered.
However, if wealthy households provide poor people with seed grain and work together to farm,
this is not included in the prohibited categories. 」
Jǐchǒu [day],
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū Zāng Dùn was appointed Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the twelfth month, on the day Rén'yín,
an edict stated:
"The ancients said,
that if a single thing lacks its proper place,
it is like throwing it into a ditch;
this is not an entirely accurate statement.
I have felt chilled at heart and disheartened,
for a long time now.
Whenever I eat, I cast down my chopsticks;
when I am about to sleep, I remove my pillow.
Sitting alone, I harbor worry,
indignant until dawn.
This is not for the sake of one person,
but for the sake of the myriad common people.
Many Provincial Governors (Zhōu Mù) are not talented individuals,
while the local Administrators (Shǒu Zǎi) are tigers equipped with wings.
It is for this reason that Yáng Fù worried and lamented,
and that Jiǎ Yì shed tears.
Furthermore, the demands imposed upon the common people are myriad;
sometimes they must supply tents,
sometimes they must supply provisions (to the treasury),
sometimes they must provide for dispatched envoys,
or sometimes they must host guests.
None of these officials cover the costs themselves,
but rather take their provisions from the people.
Moreover, many roving armies are dispatched,
nominally for stopping crime and defense,
yet treason and banditry do not cease,
and violent extortion and plundering are frequent.
Sometimes they demand supplies and installations,
or sometimes they demand labor (foot-service).
Furthermore, they commit robberies and act wantonly,
forcing and coercing one another.
The lives of good people are extinguished,
and the wealth of rich households is exhausted.
These acts cause resentment and cruelty,
and are not limited to one incident.
Although I have frequently prohibited these practices,
they still have not ceased.
Outer departments should clearly listen and investigate,
and submit reports according to the circumstances.
Furthermore, concerning public and private relay stations (zhuàn), agricultural garrisons (tún), official residences (dǐ), and foundries (yě),
and extending even to Buddhist monks and nuns (sēng ní),
they should only guard and oversee the lands within their designated boundaries according to the limits;
(they should only guard and oversee the lands within their designated boundaries according to the limits;)
yet they extensively impose seals and restrictions,
transgressing boundaries to divide and block off water and land for fishing, hunting, and the gathering of firewood and grass.
Consequently, the common people have nowhere to turn their hands.
Henceforth, anyone who transgresses boundaries and imposes prohibitions,
the person imposing the prohibition,
shall all be dealt with according to military law.
If it is established land belonging to the state,
one must merely not establish private garrisons rashly,
competing with the state’s operations to obtain private profit.
As for the common people gathering firewood and fuel to supply their cooking fires,
they must absolutely not be prohibited;
and regarding fishing and hunting,
they shall also not be reprimanded or interrogated.
If these orders are not followed,
the offenders shall all be officially penalized with the death penalty."
Wèi sent envoys to seek relations.
On the day Bǐng Chén,
the Shìlín Guǎn (Scholars’ Forest Hall) was established west of the palace city,
where scholars were invited to gather.
That year,
Lǐ Bēn, a native of Jiāozhōu, attacked the Inspector (Cìshǐ) Xiāo Zī.
Zī offered a bribe,
and was able to return to Yuèzhōu.
In the eighth year, spring, the first month,
Liú Jìnggōng, a citizen of Ānchéng Commandery, rebelled by employing heterodox doctrines (Zuǒ Dào).
The Grand Administrator (Nèishǐ) Xiāo Yuè abandoned the commandery and fled eastward.
Jìnggōng occupied the commandery,
advanced to attack Lúlíng,
and took Yùzhāng.
His demonic faction subsequently grew to tens of thousands,
pressing forward toward Xīngàn and Cháisāng.
In the second month, on the day Wù Xū,
Yì (Prince of Xiāngdōng), Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, dispatched Zǐ Yǐng, the Central Military Clerk (Zhōng Bīng Cáo), to suppress him.
In the third month, on the day Wù Chén,
he was completely routed,
Jìnggōng was captured and sent to the capital,
and executed in the marketplace of Jiànkāng.
That month,
the Sòngpíng Tún (Garrison) was established at Xīncài and Gāotáng in Jiāngzhōu,
reclaiming and cultivating barbarian fields.
The Inspectors of Yuèzhōu (Chén Hóu), Luózhōu (Níng Jù), Ānzhōu (Lǐ Zhì), and Àizhōu (Ruǎn Hàn) were dispatched,
to jointly attack Lǐ Bēn in Jiāozhōu.
In the ninth year, spring, the intercalary month, on the day Bǐng Shēn,
there was an earthquake,
and hair grew (from the ground/objects).
In the second month, on the day Jiǎ Xū,
thirty households of the people of Jiāngzhōu were ordered to supply one household of slaves and maids,
and distributed to Sīzhōu.
In the third month,
Xiè Jǔ, Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì), was appointed Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púshè).
Summer, the fourth month,
The King of Lín Yì destroyed Dézhōu,
and attacked Lǐ Bēn.
Bēn’s general Fàn Xiū again defeated the King of Lín Yì at Jiǔdé,
and the King of Lín Yì fled in defeat.
Winter, the eleventh month, on the day Xīn Chǒu,

Jǐ (Prince of Wǔlíng), General Pacifying the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Cìshǐ), was promoted in title to General Punishing the West (Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn) and given the privilege of establishing a staff and ranking with the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
In the twelfth month, on the day Rén Xū,
Zāng Dùn, General Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn), died;
Yù (Prince of Hédōng), General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn), was appointed General Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the tenth year, spring, the first month,
Lǐ Bēn usurped the title and rank in Jiāozhǐ,
and appointed various officials.
In the third month, on the day Jiǎ Wǔ,
the Imperial carriage proceeded to Lánlíng,
to visit the Jiànlíng Mausoleum.
On the day Xīn Chǒu,
they arrived at the Xiūlíng Mausoleum.
On the day Rén Yín,
an edict stated:
"Since I left my hometown (Sāngzǐ),
more than fifty years have passed.
When I turn my gaze eastward,
there is no day I do not think of it.
Now, the four directions have opened their borders,
the lands beyond the sea are orderly,
lawsuits have somewhat diminished,
and state affairs are slightly calmer.
I have finally been able to display reverence at the imperial mausoleums,
but this only increases my sorrowful emotion.
The elderly and young of my former hometown,
have arrived from far away in continuous succession,
their feelings earnest and sincere,
as if returning to their father.
It is proper that I comfort their hearts.
They shall all be granted one rank of office,
and gifts shall be bestowed upon them.
The counties and townships that the carriage passed through,
shall be exempted from this year's rent and taxes.
The people who owed obligations to the supervisors,
are hereby exempted (from those obligations) for two years.
Furthermore, all accompanying civil and military officials, army commanders, and personal attendants, both inner and outer, shall be bestowed money and rice in varying amounts."
Consequently, the *Poem on Returning to the Former Hometown* (*Huán Jiù Xiāng Shī*) was composed.
On the day Guǐ Mǎo,
an edict instructed the officials responsible for the imperial mausoleums (Yuánlíng),
who had served diligently and laboriously,
that they should all be granted one rank of office,
and have gifts bestowed upon them.
On the day Dīng Wèi,
Zhèngyì (Prince of Línchuān), General of Majestic Benevolence (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu (Nán Xúzhōu Cìshǐ), was promoted in title to General Pacifying the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn).
On the day Jǐ Yǒu,
the Imperial presence visited the Běigù Lóu (North Solid Tower) at Jīngkǒu City,
and its name was changed to Běigù.
On the day Gēng Xū,
the Imperial presence visited the Huíbīn Tíng (Returning Guest Pavilion),
where a banquet was held for the elderly of the Imperial hometown and the thousands of people, young and old, from the nearby counties who had waited to greet the carriage.
Each person was bestowed two thousand cash.
Summer, the fourth month, on the day Yǐ Mǎo,
the Imperial carriage returned from Lánlíng.
An edict ordered that provisions and relief be provided in varying amounts to the particularly poor among the widowed, the solitary, the orphaned, and the childless (and others in need).
In the fifth month, on the day Dīng Yǒu,
Hé Jìngróng, Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), was dismissed.
Autumn, the ninth month, on the day Jǐ Chǒu,
an edict stated:
"This year, both near and far,
the rain has been appropriate and timely.
The harvest is approaching,
and it is hoped that there will certainly be ten thousand baskets of grain.
It is proper that the common people should, because of this, live in peace and happiness.
Henceforth, all crimes throughout the realm, regardless of severity,
whether already discovered or not yet discovered,
and those who were pursued but not yet captured,
shall all be pardoned and forgiven.
Those who have misappropriated or wasted state property,
regardless of the amount,
are also all absolved and cleared.
Regarding fields that were neglected, or where nothing grew due to flood or drought, which were not officially documented at the time,
and for which taxes should be collected retrospectively,
as well as those who cultivated land but did not meet the state's standards,
collection shall be suspended for all of these.
All cases of officials of the inspection bureaus (Táizhōu) whose documents listed delays in payments,
their offenses shall all be forgiven.
Those who, driven by hunger, sought food,
and left their native villages and lands,
are all permitted to return to their occupations,
and their labor levies shall be exempted for five years."
Winter, the twelfth month,
there was heavy snow,
three feet deep on level ground.
In the spring, the third month, on the day Gēngchén, of the eleventh year [of Dàtóng],
an edict stated:
"When the August Kings (Huángwáng) were in the past,
their benevolent influence (zé fēng) had not yet faded far,
thus they dwelt tranquilly in Xuánhù [mythological location]
and remained silently attentive in the court hall (yán láng).
Since the Great Way (Dàdào) has fallen,
and the decadent tide (jiāo bō) has swept past,
strife and competition daily increase,
and falseness of sentiment (qíng wěi) continuously arises.
I have ruled as sovereign (jūn lín), standing before the screen (fù yǐ),
for nearly half a century.
Before the night watch has finished,
I personally toil over governance;
when the white sun sinks in the west,
I have no time even for a simple meal.
Though retired, I still wear coarse cloth,
and my sustenance consists of humble fare like weeds and beans (lí huò).
I would rather not consider possessing ten thousand chariots to be noble,
or controlling the four seas to be wealthy;
I only desire that the myriad people (yì zhào) be healthy and peaceful,
and the lower populace be tranquil and well-ordered (ān yì).
Although I consider my actions three times before executing them,
a hundred deliberations still result in many errors.

Regarding all distant and near installations, internal and external regulations (tiáo liú), the garrisons (tún), courier stations (chuán), residences (dǐ), and administrative offices (zhì) established in the four directions,
the market taxes (shì dài) and ferry crossings (héng dù),
the customs duties (jīn shuì) and fields,
the new and old governors (shǒu zǎi),
and the mobile armies and defense patrols (shù luó):
if there is anything inconvenient for the people,
the Shàngshū (Grand Secretariat) and the various provinces (zhōu jùn) should immediately itemize and report it quickly.
They shall be removed or curtailed according to the report,
so as to relieve the people's suffering."
In summer, the fourth month,
Wèi sent envoys to offer congratulations.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Jǐwèi,
an edict stated:
"Since the time of Yáo and Shùn,
the redemption of punishment (shú xíng) was instituted.
In middle age (zhōng nián), following ancient precedent,
those who had committed crimes were permitted to redeem themselves with property (rù zī).
Lower officials used this opportunity,
not without deceit and cunning (jiān huá),
which is why I once again issued an order prohibiting and stopping it.
A river's flow is hard to obstruct,
and the human heart is perilous.
This measure contradicted the meaning of compassion in the inner canon (nèi diǎn) [Buddhism]
and harmed the virtue of cherishing life taught by the outer doctrines.
The *Shū* (Book of Documents) says: 'Rather than killing an innocent person (bù gū),
it is better to err by neglecting law (bù jīng).'
Criminals may once again be permitted [to redeem themselves],
and all are allowed to enter redemption."
In the spring, the first month, on the day Dīngwèi, of the first year of Zhōngdàtóng,
the stone *qílín* (kylin) at the entrance tunnel of Jiànlíng in Qǔ'ē Xiàn (County) moved.
There was a large serpent fighting inside the tunnel,
one of which was wounded and fled.
On the day Guǐchǒu,
Yáng Tán (Yáng Tán), the Cìshǐ of Jiāozhōu, conquered Jiāozhǐ Jiāníng Chéng (Jiāníng City).
Lǐ Bēn (Lǐ Bēn) fled into Qūliáo Dòng (Cave).
Jiāozhōu was pacified.
In the third month, on the day Yǐsì,
a general amnesty was issued to the empire: Regarding all those who oversaw custody, misappropriated or stole, or dispersed government property,
and those involving military provisions, equipment, and armor,
and all those crimes not usually pardoned by amnesty,
dating back to before the first month of the eleventh year [of Dàtóng],
all shall receive grace.
For crimes committed after the first month of the eleventh year,
all shall be pardoned from increased penalties.
Those who fled, rebelled, or wandered away due to circumstances,
or who lost their hometowns and lands after the famine,
are permitted to resume their livelihoods.
Their taxes (juān kè) are remitted for five years,
and their corvée duties (yáo yì) are suspended.
Those whose persons were seized [as bondservants],
shall each return to their native commanderies,
and if their former property still exists,
it shall all be returned to them.
On the day Gēngxū,
the Imperial Carriage (fǎ jià) proceeded out for a great assembly at Tóngtài Sì (Temple),
staying at the temple to lecture on the *Jīnzì Sānhuì Jīng* (Gold Character Sānhuì Sūtra).
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐngxū,
the lecture concluded at Tóngtài Sì,
and a dharma assembly (fǎ huì) was held.
A grand amnesty was issued,
and the era name was changed.
Those who were filial and fraternal (xiào tì) and those who exerted themselves in farming (lì tián) and who succeeded their fathers were granted one rank of nobility.
Rewards were bestowed upon the civilian and military officials of the palace guard, varying according to rank.
That night,
Tóngtài Sì suffered a disaster (fire).
In the sixth month, on the day Xīnsì,
a sound spanned the heavens,
like wind and rain striking each other.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Xīnyǒu,
Wǔchāng Wáng Guǐ (Wǔchāng Wáng Guǐ) was appointed Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ.
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
an edict stated:
"Birds and beasts know their mothers but not their fathers.
Wayward youths surpass birds and beasts [in immorality],
as they disregard both parents entirely.
Many violate the royal statutes,
thereby affecting the elders.
It is greatly pitiful and distressing (shāng mǐn) when elderly people are seized and imprisoned.
From now on, when someone commits a crime,
their parents and grandparents shall not be held accountable (wù zuò).
Only crimes of great rebellion (dà nì) are excluded from this current grace."
On the day Bǐngyín,
an edict stated:
"Four in the morning and three in the evening,
and all the monkeys were delighted.
Though the name and reality (míng shí) were not diminished,
happiness and anger were still employed [by them].
Recently, I have heard that outsiders mostly use coins counted in groups of nine (jiǔ mò qián).
When the count is short (mò jiǎn), goods become expensive;
when the count is sufficient (mò zú), goods become cheap.
It is not that the goods themselves are noble or base,
but that the hearts are confused (diāndǎo).
In distant regions,
this practice daily grows worse.
How can it be that the state has differing policies,
even to the extent that families have distinct customs?
This merely confuses the royal system (wáng zhì)
and brings no benefit to the people's wealth.
Henceforth, only coins of sufficient count (zú mò qián) shall be generally used.
After this order is promulgated,
allowing a period of one hundred days,
if there are still violations,
men shall be punished by forced transport labor (zhé yùn),
and women by penal servitude (zhì zuò),
both for a duration of three years."
In the eighth month, on the day Dīngchǒu,
Wǔchāng Wáng Guǐ (Wǔchāng Wáng Guǐ), the Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu, died.
Línchuān Wáng Zhèngyì (Línchuān Wáng Zhèngyì), General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu, was immediately granted his original title of Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún (Shàolíng Wáng Lún), Intendant of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn), was made General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Nánxúzhōu.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
the state of Kèpán Guó sent envoys to present local products.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
Rǔyīn Wáng Liú Zhé (Rǔyīn Wáng Liú Zhé) died.
On the day Yǐhài,
Yuèyáng Wáng Chá (Yuèyáng Wáng Chá), the former Cìshǐ of Dōngyángzhōu, was appointed Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
In the first month, on the day Rén'yín, of the first year of Tàiqīng,

Lúlíng Wáng Xù (Lúlíng Wáng Xù), Grand General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Minister over the Masses with the Privileges of the Three Grandees (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, died.
Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì (Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì), General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu, was made General Who Guards the West (Zhènxi Jiāngjūn) and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the Imperial Carriage personally performed the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb.
An edict stated:
"Heaven’s movements encompass all,
the breadth of its covering and nurturing;
the transformation of the way of the Qían (Heaven/Creative) principle,
fulfills the virtue of initiating all things.
I bathed and fasted in the fasting palace (zhāi gōng),
reverently respecting the Supreme Di (Shàngdì),
solemnly serving the pile and the burning offerings (yǒu liáo),
and raising the flame to the Great Unity (Tàiyī).
The great rite was successfully executed,
filling me with a sense of gratitude and celebration.
I intend to share
this fortune and favor with the myriad people.
A grand amnesty shall be granted to the empire.
The particularly impoverished shall be exempted from paying the rent and tax (zū diào) for the current year.
Those banished by public opinion (qīng yì jìn gù) shall all be pardoned and released.
Regarding those who were sought out for running away and rebelling (bū pàn),
those who cunningly listed themselves to hide their age,
and those who secretly concealed households (nì kǒu),
a period of grace of one hundred days is opened.
They are each ordered to surrender themselves,
and their past crimes will not be questioned.
Those who wandered and moved to other areas
are permitted to resume their settled livelihoods,
and their taxes are remitted for five years.
The filial, fraternal, and those diligent in farming shall be granted one rank of nobility.
Officials who performed well in their bureaus (jū jú) and managed affairs will be rewarded and commended for two years.
This shall be publicized to near and far,
to extensively gather exceptional talent.
Whether they possess flourishing virtue in the province and village (zhōu lǘ),
or their actions are models for the local community (xiāng yì),
or they act independently and stand firm,
not seeking fame or prominence (wén dá),
all shall be instructed to report them upwards,
to be recruited when appropriate."
On the day Jiǎzǐ,
the Imperial Carriage personally performed the sacrifice at the Míngtáng (Luminous Hall).
In the second month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
a white rainbow pierced the sun.
On the day Gēngchén,

Hóu Jǐng (Hóu Jǐng), the Sītú (Minister of Works) of Wèi, requested that the thirteen provinces of Yù, Guǎng, Yǐng, Luò, Yáng, Xīyáng, Dōngjīng, Běijīng, Xiāng, Dōngyù, Nányǎn, Xīyǎn, and Qí be incorporated into the realm.
On the day Rénwǔ,
Jǐng (Hóu Jǐng) was appointed Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as Hénán Wáng,
and given the status of Grand Deputy (Dàxíngtái) to act with full authority,
following the precedent of Dèng Yǔ (Dèng Yǔ).
On the day Dīnghài,
the Imperial Carriage personally tilled the ceremonial field (jí tián).
In the Third month, day *gēngzǐ*,
Gāozǔ visited the Tóngtài Temple,
established the Wúzhē Great Assembly,
dedicated himself (to the temple),
and the dukes and ministers, etc., offered 100 million coins to redeem him.
Day *jiǎchén*,
sent the Administrator of Sìzhōu, Yáng Yārén; the Administrator of Yănzhōu, Huán Hé; and the Administrator of Rénzhōu, Zhàn Hǎizhēn, among others, to support Běi Yùzhōu.
Summer, Fourth month, day *dīnghài*,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace,
a general amnesty was granted to the realm,
the reign title was changed,
those who were filial, fraternal, and diligent in agriculture, and who were the successors of their fathers, were granted one rank of nobility,
and all civil and military officials serving at court and in the palace guard were additionally rewarded.
Fifth month, day *dīngyŏu*,
the imperial carriage visited the Déyáng Hall,
feasted the officials,
and established silk and bamboo music.
Sixth month, day *wùchén*,
appointed the former Administrator of Yōngzhōu, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, as General Who Conquers the North (Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn),
and overall supervisor of military affairs for the campaigns north of the Hàn River.
Autumn, Seventh month, day *gēngshēn*,
Yáng Yārén entered Xuánhù City.
Day *jiǎzǐ*,
an imperial edict stated:
“The division and establishment of the two Yùzhōu provinces
has a long history.
Now that Rŭ and Yĭng have been subdued and settled,
following the precedents of previous dynasties,
Xuánhù should be made Yùzhōu,
Shòuchūn should be made Nányù (South Yùzhōu),
Héféi should be changed to Hézhōu,
Běi Guănglíng should be made Huáizhōu,
Xiàngchéng should be made Yīnzhōu,
and Hézhōu should be made Nánhézhōu (South Hézhōu).”
Eighth month, day *yĭchŏu*,
the imperial armies marched north,
appointing the Administrator of Nányùzhōu, Xiāo Yuānmíng, as Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū).
An imperial edict stated:
“Now that Rŭnán has been newly recovered
and Sōng and Yĭng are again peaceful,
looking upon the remaining populace
causes Me anxiety and sleeplessness.
It is fitting to extend broad grace and benevolence,
allowing them a fresh start.
Regarding the common people within the prefectures along the frontier who have newly submitted,
any who previously bore guilt, fled, or were fugitives,
or who escaped and defected to the north,
all are fully pardoned;
past offenses shall not be investigated.
Furthermore, no one is permitted to harbor private grudges and seek vengeance against them.
If there are any violators,
they shall be strictly interrogated and judged.”
Day *wùzǐ*,
appointed the Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn), Hóu Jĭng, to oversee the affairs of the Mobile Secretariat (Xíngtái Shàngshū Shì).
Ninth month, day *guĭmăo*,
the Imperial Hunting Park was completed.
Day *gēngxū*,
the imperial carriage visited the park.
Winter, Eleventh month,
Wèi sent Grand General Mùróng Shàozōng and others to Hánshān.
Day *bĭngwŭ*,
a great battle occurred;
Yuānmíng was defeated,
and he, along with the Administrator of Běi Yănzhōu, Hú Guìsūn, and others, were captured by Wèi.
Shàozōng advanced and besieged Tóngzhōu.
Twelfth month, day *wùchén*,
sent the Palace Attendant of the Crown Prince, Yuán Zhēn, back north to the Wèi ruler.
Day *xīnsì*,
appointed the former General Who Conquers the North, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, as General Who Pacifies the North (Ān Běi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nányùzhōu.
Second year, Spring, First month, day *wùxū*,
an edict ordered officials currently in office to recommend those they knew to be capable.
Day *jĭhài*,
Wèi captured Guōyáng.
Day *xīnchŏu*,
appointed the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè), Xiè Jŭ, as Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng);
and Wáng Kè, acting Director of the Bureau of Personnel, as Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
Day *jiǎchén*,
the Administrator of Yùzhōu, Yáng Yārén, and the Administrator of Yīnzhōu, Yáng Sīdá,
both abandoned their cities and fled.
Wèi advanced and occupied them.
Day *yĭmăo*,
appointed Grand General Hóu Jĭng as Governor of Nányùzhōu (Nányùzhōu Mù);
and the General Who Pacifies the North and Administrator of Nányùzhōu, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, as Administrator of Hézhōu.
Third month, day *jiǎchén*,
the General Who Soothes the East (Fŭ Dōng Jiāngjūn) and King of Gāolì, Gāo Yán, died.
His son was appointed General Who Pacifies the East (Níng Dōng Jiāngjūn), King of Gāolì, and Duke of Lèlàng.
Day *jĭwèi*,

appointed the General Who Guards the East (Zhèn Dōng Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nánxúzhōu, the Prince of Shàolíng, Lún, as General Who Pacifies the South (Píng Nán Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Xiāngzhōu, and granted the ceremony rank equivalent to the Three Dukes (Tóng Sānsī zhī Yí);

and the General of the Central Guard (Zhōng Wèi Jiāngjūn) and Open Office with the Same Honors as the Three Dukes (Kāifŭ Yítóng Sānsī), Xiāo Yuānzǎo, as General Who Conquers the East (Zhēng Dōng Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nánxúzhōu.
On this day,
the Qū Liáo Caves tribes beheaded Lĭ Bēn,
and sent his head to the capital (Jīngshī).
Summer, Fourth month, day *bĭngzĭ*,
an edict ordered officials at court and in the prefectures and commanderies to each recommend honest people capable of governing the populace;
these were all to be respectfully escorted to the capital (Jīngshī).
Day *wùyín*,
appointed the General Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn), the Prince of Hédōng, Yù, as Administrator of Xiāngzhōu.
Fifth month, day *xīnchŏu*,

appointed the newly designated Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), the Prince of Shàolíng, Lún, as General Who Stabilizes the Front (Ān Qián Jiāngjūn) and Open Office with the Same Honors as the Three Dukes;
and the former Administrator of Xiāngzhōu, Zhāng Zăn, as General Controller of the Army (Lĭngjūn Jiāngjūn).
Day *xīnhài*,
limited amnesty was granted to Jiāo, Ài, and Dé three prefectures.
Day *guĭchŏu*,
an imperial edict stated:
“The successful governance of the state relies on many talented people,
and settling the realm depends on securing the right individuals.
I am ignorant in conducting affairs
and especially lacking in methods of governance.
Isolated in my high position,
I feel as if I am overlooking a deep abyss.
All of you who serve at court
must think of assistance and remedy,
presenting your proposals for acceptance or rejection,
to mutually guide and enlighten Me.
Officials below Me, including regional administrators,
must extensively seek out talented individuals,
searching among butchers and fishermen,
and throughout the mountain caves,
reporting them to the throne in a timely manner.”
This month,
two moons were seen at night.
Autumn, Eighth month, day *yĭwèi*,
appointed the General of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn), Zhū Yì, as General Controller of the Central Army (Zhōng Lĭngjūn).
Day *wùxū*,
Hóu Jĭng raised troops and rebelled,
arbitrarily attacking the garrisons of Mătóu, Mùzhà, and Jīngshān, among others.
Day *jiǎchén*,
appointed the General Who Stabilizes the Front and Open Office with the Same Honors as the Three Dukes, the Prince of Shàolíng, Lún, as commander-in-chief of all forces to suppress Jĭng.
Limited amnesty was granted to Nányùzhōu.
Ninth month, day *bĭngyín*,
added the title of General Who Guards the Right (Zhèn Yòu Jiāngjūn) to the Grand Master of the Left Glorious Happiness (Zuŏ Guānglù Dàfū), Yuán Luó.
Winter, Tenth month,
Hóu Jĭng attacked Qiáozhōu,
and captured the Administrator, Xiāo Tài.
Day *dīngwèi*,
Jĭng advanced and attacked Lìyáng,
and the Grand Administrator, Zhuāng Tiě, surrendered to him.
Day *wùshēn*,
appointed the newly designated Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū), the Prince of Línhè, Zhèngdé, as General Who Pacifies the North (Píng Běi Jiāngjūn),
commander-in-chief of all capital forces,
stationed in Dānyáng Commandery.
Day *jĭyŏu*,
Jĭng crossed the river from Héngjiāng at Căishí.
Day *xīnhài*,
Jĭng's army arrived at the capital,
and the Prince of Línhè, Zhèngdé, led his troops and defected to the rebels.
Eleventh month, day *xīnyŏu*,
the rebels attacked and captured Dōngfŭ City,
killing the Marquis of Nánpŭ, Xiāo Tuī, and the Central Army Staff Officer, Yáng Tūn.
Day *gēngchén*,
the Prince of Shàolíng, Lún, led the Administrator of Wŭzhōu, Xiāo Nòngzhāng, and the former Administrator of Qiáozhōu, Zhào Bóchāo, among others, to enter and reinforce the capital,
stopping at Àijìng Temple on Zhōngshān Mountain.
Day *yĭyŏu*,
Lún advanced his army to Hútóu,
fought the rebels,
and was defeated.
Day *bĭngxū*,
the General Who Pacifies the North, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, sent his heir Sī, and the General of Martial Trust, Péi Zhīgăo, among others, leading troops to reinforce the capital,
camping at Zhānggōngzhōu.
Twelfth month, day *wùshēn*,
the sky split open in the northwest quadrant,
with a light resembling fire.
The Director of the Department of State Affairs, Xiè Jŭ, died.
Day *bĭngchén*,

the Administrator of Sìzhōu, Liŭ Zhònglĭ; the former Administrator of Héngzhōu, Wéi Càn; the Administrator of Gāozhōu, Lĭ Qiānshì; and the former Administrator of Sìzhōu, Yáng Yārén, among others, all led their armies to reinforce the capital,
nominating Zhònglĭ as Grand Commander.
Third year, Spring, First month, day *dīngsì*, the first day of the month,
Liŭ Zhònglĭ led his troops to occupy positions along the south bank.
On this same day,
the rebels crossed the river at Qīngtáng,
attacked and destroyed Wéi Càn's camp,
and Càn died resisting the battle.
Day *gēngshēn*,
the Prince of Shàolíng, Lún, and the Administrator of Dōngyángzhōu, the Duke of Línchéng, Dàlián, among others, led troops to assemble on the south bank.
Day *yĭchŏu*,
the General Controller of the Central Army, Zhū Yì, died.
Day *bĭngyín*,
appointed the Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng), Fù Qí, as General Controller of the Central Army.
Day *wùchén*,
the Administrator of Gāozhōu, Lĭ Qiānshì, and the Grand Administrator of Tiānmén, Fán Wénjiăo, advanced their armies east of Qīngxī,
where they were defeated by the rebels,
and Jiāo Jiăo died there.
Day *rénwŭ*,
Yínghuò (Mars) stood guard over Xīn (the Heart constellation).
Day *yĭyŏu*,
Tàibái (Venus) was visible during the day.
Second month, day *dīngwèi*,
the Administrator of Nányănzhōu, the Prince of Nánkāng, Huìlĭ, and the former Administrator of Qīng and Jì Prefectures, the Marquis of Xiāngtán, Xiāo Tuì, led troops from Jiāngzhōu,
stopping at the Lántíng Park.
Day *gēngxū*,
the General Who Pacifies the North and Administrator of Hézhōu, the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn, was granted the Open Office with the Same Honors as the Three Dukes while retaining his original titles.
In the third month, on the day Wùwǔ,
the former Cìshǐ of Sīzhōu, Yáng Yārén (and others), advanced their army north of Dōngfǔ,
and fought with the rebels,
suffering a great defeat.
On the day Jǐwèi,
the Crown Prince's Consort, Wáng Shì, passed away (hōng).
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the rebels attacked and captured the Palace City,
letting their soldiers loose to plunder heavily.
On the day Jǐsì,
the rebels forged an imperial decree and sent Shíchéng Gōng Dà Kuǎn to dismiss the external reinforcing armies.
On the day Gēngwǔ,

Hóu Jǐng appointed himself Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (Grand Commander of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital), Dà Chéngxiàng (Grand Chancellor), and Lù Shàngshū (Director of the Affairs of the Secretariat).
On the day Xīnwèi,
the reinforcing armies scattered and retreated.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
Yínghuò (Mars) guarded the constellation Xīn (Heart).
On the day Rénwǔ,
Fù Qí, newly appointed as Zhōng Lǐngjūn, died.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Jǐchǒu,
the capital experienced an earthquake.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
there was another earthquake.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Gāozǔ, because what he requested was not provided,
became vexed with worry and fell ill.
In this month,
Míng Shǎoxiá, Cìshǐ of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu; Zhàn Hǎizhēn, Cìshǐ of Dōng Xúzhōu; and Wáng Fèngbó, Cìshǐ of Běi Qīngzhōu, each submitted their respective provinces to Wèi.
In the fifth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
Gāozǔ passed away (bēng) in the Jìngjū Diàn (Pure Dwelling Hall),
at the age of eighty-six.
On the day Xīnsì,
the coffin (zǐgōng) of the Dà Xíng Huángdì (Great Emperor on the Move) was moved to the front hall of the Tàijí Palace.
In winter, the eleventh month,
he was posthumously honored as Wǔ Huángdì,
and his temple title was Gāozǔ.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
he was buried at Xiūlíng.
Gāozǔ possessed pure filial piety from birth.
When he was six years old,
Xiàn Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Xiàn) passed away;
he took no water or gruel for three days,
and his weeping and sorrow
exceeded that of an adult.
Relatives, both inner and outer,
all accorded him reverence and distinction.
When mourning for Wén Huángdì occurred,
he was then an Advisor (Zīyì) to Qí Suí Wáng,
and the Prince’s establishment was stationed in Jīngzhèn.
Having barely received the news,
he immediately resigned his post and rushed like a shooting star,
neither sleeping nor eating,
doubling his journey speed to reach the road.
Raging through storms and startling waves,
he never stopped, even briefly.
Gāozǔ was originally robust in appearance,
but by the time he returned to the capital,
he was emaciated, only skin and bones.
His relatives, acquaintances, scholars, and friends
no longer recognized him.
Facing the residence to observe the taboo mourning,
he lost consciousness for a long time.
Every time he cried, he would vomit several pints of blood.
During the mourning period, he no longer tasted rice;
he subsisted only on barley,
limited to two yì (cups) per day.
When bowing and sweeping the imperial tombs (shānlíng),
the tears he shed
caused the pines and grasses to change color.
When he ascended the imperial throne,
he immediately built the Dà Àijìng Sì (Great Love and Reverence Temple) on Zhōngshān,
constructed the Zhìdù Sì (Wisdom Crossing Temple) by the Qīngxī stream,
and also established the Zhìjìng Diàn (Utmost Reverence Hall) and similar structures within the Palace complex.
He also established the Seven Ancestral Shrines (Qī Miàotáng),
visiting them twice a month
to set out pure offerings (jìngzhuàn).
Every time he went to pay respects,
his tears and snot flowed profusely,
moving all those around him with sorrow.
Furthermore, he was cultivated, thoughtful, revered, and enlightened,
capable of fully understanding any task.
He was devoted to learning from a young age,
thoroughly comprehending Confucianism and Daoism (Rúxuán).
Although burdened by a myriad of state affairs,
he still never let go of his scrolls.
Burning candles to use the reflected light,
he often continued until the fifth watch (late night).
He authored the *Zhìzhǐ Xiàojīng Yì* (Imperial Commentary on the Meaning of the Classic of Filial Piety),
the *Zhōuyì Jiǎngshū* (Commentary and Sub-Commentary on the Classic of Changes),
and commentaries on the sixty-four hexagrams, the Two Appendices (Èr Xì), the *Wényán*, and the *Xùguà*.
He wrote the *Yuèshè Yì* (Meaning of Music and Ritual),
*Máoshī Dáwèn* (Answers to Questions on the Mao Version of the Classic of Poetry),
*Chūnqiū Dáwèn* (Answers to Questions on the Spring and Autumn Annals),
*Shàngshū Dàyì* (Great Meaning of the Classic of Documents),
*Zhōngyōng Jiǎngshū* (Commentary and Sub-Commentary on the Doctrine of the Mean),
*Kǒngzǐ Zhèngyán* (Correct Words of Kǒngzǐ),
and *Lǎozǐ Jiǎngshū* (Commentary and Sub-Commentary on Lǎozǐ),
totaling over two hundred volumes.
These corrected the errors of previous Confucian scholars
and clarified the principles of the ancient sages.
Kings, marquises, and court officials all presented memorials questioning certain points,
and Gāozǔ explained them all.
He restored and adorned the National Academy (Guóxué),
increased the number of students,
established five colleges (Wǔguǎn),
and appointed Erudites of the Five Classics (Wǔjīng Bóshì).
Early in the Tiānjiān era,
Hé Tóngzhī, Hè Yáng, Yán Zhízhī, Míng Shānbīn, and others reviewed and reiterated the imperial commentaries,
and together compiled the Five Rituals (Jí, Xiōng, Jūn, Bīn, Jiā),
totaling over one thousand volumes.
Gāozǔ then issued an imperial decree resolving all doubts.
Thus, graciousness and sincerity prevailed,
and every household knew the rules of propriety.
During the Dàtóng era,
the Shìlín Guǎn (Scholarly Forest College) was established west of the Palace.
Zhū Yì (Lǐngjūn), Hè Chēn (Tàifǔ Qīng), Kǒngzǐ Qū (Shèrén), and others lectured on the subjects in turn.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) and Xuānchéng Wáng also initiated lectures in the Xuānyóu Táng (Hall of Spreading Excellence) in the Eastern Palace and at the Yángzhōu administration office.
Consequently, prefectures and states from all four directions
rushed to study and follow this trend,
gathering in the capital like clouds.
Moreover, he devoutly believed in the orthodox Dharma [Buddhism]
and was especially skilled in the Buddhist Canon.
He composed commentaries on the essence of the Nièpán (Nirvana), Dà Pǐn (Great Perfection of Wisdom), Jìng Míng (Vimalakirti), and Sānhuì (Three Wisdoms) sūtras,
again totaling several hundred volumes.
In his leisure time after listening to reports and governing,
he would lecture at the Chóngyún Diàn (Layered Clouds Hall) and Tóngtài Sì (Universal Peace Temple).
Famous monks, great scholars, and listeners from the four assemblies
regularly numbered over ten thousand.
He also compiled the *Tōngshǐ* (Comprehensive History),
personally writing the eulogies and prefaces,
totaling six hundred volumes.
His natural intellect was profound and sharp;
he completed essays the moment he put brush to paper.
A thousand *fù* (rhapsodies) and a hundred poems
were finished instantly in a straight draft.
All were beautifully balanced in substance and refinement (wén zhì bīnbīn),
surpassing both the present and the past.
His imperial edicts, inscriptions, eulogies (zàn, lěi),
admonitions, odes, memorials (jiān zòu),
from his beginning in the field
until he ascended the imperial throne (Bǎolì),
were all gathered into a collection of writings,
totaling another one hundred and twenty volumes.
He mastered all Six Arts,
reaching the highest level (yì pǐn).
Regarding Yīnyáng, astronomical phenomena (wěi hòu),
divination by tortoise shell and stalks (bǔ shì), and making judgments,
he was considered excellent in all.
He also compiled the *Jīncè* (Golden Plans) in thirty volumes.
In Cursive and Clerical script (Cǎolì) and writing letters (chǐ dú),
as well as mounted archery and horsemanship,
nothing was not exceptionally marvelous.
He was diligent in state affairs,
working tirelessly without rest.
Every winter month,
as soon as the fourth watch ended (around 3 AM),
he would immediately order the lighting of candles to review matters.
Holding his brush in the bitter cold,
his hands became chapped and cracked.
When investigating corruption and exposing hidden crimes,
he thoroughly understood the circumstances.
He often wept out of pity and compassion
before he would issue a ruling.
He ate only one meal a day;
his food contained no fresh or rich ingredients,
consisting only of bean soup and coarse grain.
If state affairs were numerous and pressing,
and the sun happened to pass midday,
he would merely rinse his mouth and continue.
He wore plain cloth robes,
used a black curtain made of floss silk,
wore the same hat for three years,
and used the same blanket for two years.
He was constantly self-restrained in frugality;
everything was of this nature.
After the age of fifty, he abstained from sexual relations.
In the Inner Palace, the officials and concubines below the rank of Guìfēi,
and throughout the six palaces, aside from the official robes (huī yú sān dí),
all wore garments that did not drag on the ground,
and no silk brocade was allowed nearby.
He did not drink wine,
nor listen to music.
Unless it was for sacrifices in the ancestral temple, grand assemblies and feasts, or various Buddhist rites,
he never had music performed.
His character was upright and proper.
Even when residing in a small hall or a private room,
he always adjusted his robes and cap;
when sitting down, he would press his clothes flat.
In the height of summer, during the hot months,
he never lifted his robes or exposed his body.
If he had not properly arranged his appearance,
he would not meet people.
Even when viewing internal attendants and minor officials,
it was as if he were meeting a great guest.
Looking through the ancient emperors and rulers,
few, if any, have possessed such combined attributes of reverence, frugality, solemnity, respect,
artistic skill, and extensive learning.
says: When the Qí (Nán Qí) dynasty came to an end,
the ruler was dark and tyrannical;
Heaven abandoned him and the spirits were enraged,
causing the masses to rebel and relatives to depart.
Gāo Zǔ was heroic, mighty, wise, and philosophical;
he righteously arose in Fán and Dèng,
raising his banner and establishing his title.
He wetted his feet to save those burning (i.e., acted urgently to save the state).
He commanded the armies of the *cāng sì* (fierce rhinoceros),
he deployed the battle formations of the Dragon and the Leopard.
Galloping like clouds and startling like thunder,
he cut down the violent and eliminated the vicious.
The myriad states joyfully supported him,
and the Three Spirits (Heaven, Earth, Man) changed their mandate.
Thereupon, he controlled the Phoenix Calendar (imperial reign),
and grasped the Dragon Chart (imperial plan).
He opened the four gates widely to promote the path of inviting the worthy,
he accepted the *Shí Luàn* (ten capable ministers) and introduced the honest and upright.
He promoted literature and scholarship,
he restored the suburban sacrifices (*jiāo sì*),
he managed the Five Rites,
and he fixed the Six Pitches.
With the opinions of the four quarters fully reached,
the myriad affairs of state were thus governed.
Governance was settled and achievements were established,
the distant regions were peaceful and the nearby regions were quiet.
Furthermore, auspicious signs from Heaven and propitious omens from Earth
never ceased throughout the years and seasons.
The territories where taxes and levies extended,
the lands where written characters and cart ruts universally reached,
stretched south beyond ten thousand *lǐ*,
and expanded west by five thousand.
The rare wealth and heavy treasures therein,
and the thousand men and hundred clans (from conquered peoples),
none failed to fill the royal treasury,
or bow their heads at the palace court.
For thirty or forty years,
this was truly magnificent.
Since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
there had never been anything like it.
But when he reached his old age,
he entrusted affairs to a group of favored sycophants.
Consequently, the clique of Zhū Yì (Zhū Yì zhī tú),
exercised authority and dispensed favors,
gathering associates and establishing factions.
Government policy was achieved through bribery,
and holding high office,
was determined by their grasp.
Because of this, the court structure was chaotic,
and rewards and punishments lacked principle.
"The way of the petty man prevailed,"
this is what that statement describes.
Jiǎ Yì once said,
"One may weep bitterly over this."
Consequently, the overwhelming Jié bandits
took advantage of the lapse and launched a surprise attack.
The vulture feathers (arrows) scattered upon the royal residence (Wáng Wū),
and the golden seal was humiliated along with the imperial carriage.
The common people were plunged into misery,
and millet grew in the palace grounds.
Alas!
How terribly cruel is the Way of Heaven!
Although the span of the mandate (lì shù) was depleted,
it was certainly also caused by human actions.
Annals Four: Emperor Jiǎn Wén.
Tàizōng, Emperor Jiǎn Wén, whose personal name was Gāng,
courtesy name Shìzǎn,
childhood name Liùtōng,
was the third son of Gāo Zǔ,
and the full younger brother of Crown Prince Zhāomíng.
In the 10th month, *Dīng Wèi* day, of Tiānjiān 2nd year (503 CE),
he was born in the Xiǎnyáng Palace.
In the 5th year,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn'ān,
with an assigned income household of eight thousand.
In the 8th year,
he was appointed General Yúnhuī,
concurrently managing the military affairs of the Shítóu Garrison,
and having an authorized quota for establishing assistant officials.
In the 9th year,

he was promoted to Minister with Credentials (*Shǐ Chí Jié*), Generalissimo (*Dūdū*) of military affairs of the five provinces of Nán Yǎn, Běi Yǎn, Qīng, Xú, and Jì, General Xuānyì, and Governor (*Cìshǐ*) of Nán Yǎn Province.
In the 12th year,
he was summoned to the capital and appointed General Xuānhuì and Prefect (*Yǐn*) of Dānyáng.
In the 13th year,

he was sent out as Minister with Credentials, Generalissimo of military affairs of the seven provinces of Jīng, Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín, Yì, and Níng, Commandant (*Xiàowèi*) of the Southern Man Tribes, and Governor of Jīng Province,
retaining his general title.
In the 14th year,
he was transferred to Generalissimo of military affairs of Jiāng Province, General Yúnhuī, and Governor of Jiāng Province,
retaining his credentials.
In the 17th year,
he was recalled and appointed General of the Gentlemen-of-the-Household of the West (*Xī Zhōng Láng Jiàng*), concurrently managing the military affairs of the Shítóu Garrison,
shortly thereafter he was again appointed General Xuānhuì and Prefect of Dānyáng,
and granted the additional post of Attendant-in-Ordinary (*Shì Zhōng*).
In Pǔtōng 1st year (520 CE),
he was sent out as Minister with Credentials, Generalissimo of military affairs of the seven provinces of Yì, Níng, Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín, and Shā, and Governor of Yì Province;
before he was inaugurated,
the assignment was changed to General Yúnhuī and Governor of Nán Xú Province.
In the 4th year,

he was transferred to Minister with Credentials, Generalissimo of military affairs of the four provinces of Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín, the commandery of Jìnglín in Yǐng Province, and the commandery of Suí in Sī Province, General Píngxī, Commandant Níngmán (Pacifying the Man Tribes), and Governor of Yōng Province.
In the 5th year,
his title was advanced to General Ānběi (Pacifying the North).
In the 7th year,
he was temporarily advanced to Generalissimo of military affairs of the three provinces of Jīng, Yì, and Nán Liáng.
In this year,
he was in mourning for the loss of his birth mother, Consort Mù Guì Pín,
and submitted a memorial requesting to relinquish his duties.
An imperial edict ordered him to return and manage his original post.
In Zhōngdàtōng 1st year (529 CE),
an edict ordered that he be granted one set of drums and pipes, as previously bestowed.
In the 2nd year,
he was recalled and appointed Generalissimo of military affairs of the two provinces of Nán Yáng and Xú, General Piàojì (General of Cavalry), and Governor of Yáng Province.
In the 4th month, *Yǐ Sì* day, of the 3rd year (531 CE),
Crown Prince Zhāomíng died.
In the 5th month, *Bǐng Shēn* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Without perfect fairness, one cannot preside over the realm;
without expansive love, one cannot oversee the four seas.
This is why Yáo and Shùn yielded,
only giving it to the virtuous;
and why King Wén bypassed Bó Yì Kǎo and established King Wǔ.
This resonates above and below,
and shines brightly across the four directions.
Now, Dàizōng (the throne) is unsettled,
the path of Heaven (the dynasty) is difficult,
the pure customs are still stifled,
and the common people are not yet settled.
Unless one is supremely enlightened and supremely wise,
truly martial and truly cultured,
how can one bear the weight of the Divine Utensil (the state),
and succeed to the venerability of the Dragon Chart?
The Prince of Jìn'ān, Xiāo Gāng,
is naturally endowed with literary talent and righteousness,
his filial piety and respect are spontaneous,
his authority and kindness are publicly known,
his virtuous conduct is inwardly astute,
all the nobles attribute excellence to him,
and the whole land places their trust in him.
He may be established as the Crown Prince."
In the 7th month, *Yǐ Hài* day,
he was officially invested with the office while standing before the covered way,
but due to the renovation of the Eastern Palace,
he temporarily resided in the Eastern Residence (*Dōng Fǔ*).
In the 9th month of the 4th year,
he moved back to the Eastern Palace.
In the 5th month, *Bǐng Chén* day, of Tàiqīng 3rd year (549 CE),
Gāo Zǔ died.
On the *Xīn Sì* day,
he ascended the throne as Emperor.
An imperial edict stated:
"I, because of my lack of fortune,
suffered early distress and misfortune.
The Great Departed Emperor suddenly abandoned the myriad states.
Clutching and yearning, I weep bitterly,
with no place to put myself.
Unworthily, with meager virtue,
I have been placed above the people.
Lonely and distressed by the mourning,
I know not where to rely.
Now I must rely on the protective princes and ministers,
so that the altars of the state (*shè jì*) may be secured.
Reverently following the late Emperor's will,
and the lasting favor of his final command,
it ought to be extended to the hundreds of millions.
Let there be a great amnesty throughout the realm."
On the *Rén Wǔ* day,
an imperial edict stated:
"Nurturing creatures requires broadness,
and governing the people requires kindness.
The Way is manifest through rising kings,
and fundamentally is not based on enslavement.
Some, upon opening the border to serve the state,
were immediately captured and taken captive;
others, dwelling in the borderlands,
were wrongfully plundered and kidnapped.
If two countries compete,
what crime have the common people committed?
I, being meager and ignorant,
have newly succeeded to this grand enterprise.
Having assumed governance over the whole land,
and having spread transformation across the universe,
how can I desire to make only them not citizens?
All northerners currently residing in the provinces as slaves or bondservants,
including their wives and children,
are hereby released and pardoned."
On the *Guǐ Wèi* day,
his consort, Lady Wáng (Wáng Shì), was posthumously honored as Empress Jiǎn.
In the 6th month, *Bǐng Xū* day,
Xiāo Huìlǐ, the heir-prince of Nánkāng, was made Minister of Works (*Sī Kōng*).
On the *Dīng Hài* day,
Xiāo Dàqì, the Prince of Xuānchéng, was established as the Crown Prince.
On the *Rén Chén* day,
Xiāo Dàxīn, the Duke of Dāngyáng, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xúnyáng Commandery,
Xiāo Dàkuǎn, the Duke of Shíchéng, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiāngxià Commandery,
Xiāo Dàlín, the Duke of Níngguó, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánhǎi Commandery,
Xiāo Dàlián, the Duke of Línchéng, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nán Commandery,
Xiāo Dàchūn, the Duke of Xīfēng, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Ānlù Commandery,
Xiāo Dàchéng, the Duke of Xīngàn, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Shānyáng Commandery,
Xiāo Dàfēng, the Duke of Línxiāng, was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yídū Commandery.
day, Yuán Jǐngzhòng,
the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, plotted to side with Hóu Jǐng. Chén Bàxiān,
the Regional Commander of Xījiāng, raised troops and attacked him. Jǐngzhòng
committed suicide. Bàxiān
welcomed Xiāo Bó, the Inspector of Dìngzhōu, and installed him as Inspector (of Guǎngzhōu). On the *wùchén*
day, Wú Zhōu
was established based on Wú Jùn. Ānlù Wáng
Dàchūn was made the Inspector (of Wú Zhōu). On the *gēngwǔ*
day, Sīkōng Nánkāng
Sìwáng Huìlǐ was additionally made Shàngshū Lìng. Nánhǎi Wáng
Dàlín was made the Inspector of Yángzhōu. Xīnxīng Wáng
Dàzhuāng was made the Inspector of Nánxúzhōu. In
this month, Jiǔjiāng
suffered a great famine. Four
or five out of every ten people resorted to cannibalism. The eighth month, on the *guǐmǎo*
day, Xiāo Yuānzǎo,
the General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East, Administrator-in-Chief with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes, and Inspector of Nánxúzhōu, died. In Winter, the tenth month, on the *dīngwèi*
day, there
was an earthquake. The twelfth
month, the state of Bǎijì Guó
sent envoys to present local products. Dàbǎo
First Year, Spring, the first month, on the *xīnhài* first day of the month, due
to the national mourning, court assemblies were suspended. An edict
stated: "The realm
(under Heaven) is the most
impartial sacred vessel. In antiquity, the Sān
(Three) and Wǔ (Five) Sovereigns were forced
to preside over it. Therefore, the achievements
of emperors and kings are but
supplementary tasks for a Sage; the glory
of high position and official carriages is merely
an incidental possession. Emperor
Wén, the Grand Ancestor, possessed a great and illuminating capacity, establishing
the foundation laid by Xībó. Emperor
Wǔ, the High Ancestor, had a *Dào* that harmonized with the Two Forms (Heaven and Earth), and a wisdom
that encompassed all things. When the Qí
dynasty declined and sickness spread, moral
bonds were destroyed and lost. Kinsmen
suffered the calamity of separation and death in the garden, and the sovereign
harbored insatiable desires. It was then
that the moment arrived for the joyful mandate, based
on the hearts of the hundreds of millions, to take
hold of the reins and horns (leadership), and wipe
away this shameful enmity. The task
was not for personal gain; the righteousness
truly derived from the people. Therefore, having achieved
merit, he did not claim it, living
in a humble palace with meager food. The work
of great compassion universally permeated, and edicts
like those of Fényáng were frequently issued. For
four *jì* (twelve-year cycles),
his virtue cannot be fully recounted. I,
due to my limited understanding, am gravely
afflicted by sorrow and loneliness. All living
things have perished, and I
have no desire to preserve myself. I force
myself to look towards the future, hoping
to carry on the great legacy. My anxiety,
like hanging a banner or walking on thin ice,
is insufficient to describe. My pain
is deep and slow to heal; my mourning
is intensely felt. I ought
now to maintain silence and introspection, resting
my heart outside worldly affairs. However, since
the Kingly Way is not yet straight and the path
of Heaven is still difficult, I must rely
upon the chief ministers
to manage and extend the manifold government duties. To begin
anew and establish a new reign title
is based on former regulations. Therefore, let
there be a general amnesty throughout the realm, and the fourth year
of Tàiqīng shall be changed to the first year of Dàbǎo." On the *dīngsì*
day, yellow
sand rained down from the sky. On the *jǐwèi*
day, the Grand
White (Venus) traversed the sky. It
ceased on the *xīnyǒu* day. The Xī Wèi
raided Ānlù, captured
Liǔ Zhònglǐ, the Inspector of Sīzhōu, and completely
seized the territory of Hàndōng. On the *bǐngyín*
day, the moon
was visible in daylight. On the *guǐyǒu*
day, Zǔ Hào,
the former Magistrate of Jiāngdū, started an uprising, attacked
Guǎnglíng, and beheaded
Dǒng Shàoxiān, the rebel Inspector of Nányǎnzhōu. Hóu Jǐng
personally led his naval and land forces to attack Hào. The second month, on the *guǐwèi*
day, Jǐng
attacked and captured Guǎnglíng, and Hào
and his followers were all killed. On the *bǐngxū*
day, Ānlù Wáng
Dàchūn was made the Inspector of Dōngyángzhōu. Wú
Zhōu was abolished,
reverting to its former status as a commandery (*Jùn*). An edict
stated: "Recently,
the eastern frontier was disturbed, and Jiāngyáng
was wild and unrestrained. The chief
ministers devised their plans, and brave
warriors fought valiantly. Wú
and Kuài were entirely pacified; Jǐ
and Yǎn were cleared and quieted. Within
the capital and the capital region, there
is no need for military attire. All high
officials of the court, and the attendants
within the palace,
may cease vigilance and stand down." On the *yǐsì*
day, Wáng Kè,
the Director of the Department of State Affairs, was made the Assistant Director of the Left. In
this month, Shàolíng Wáng Guānl
traveled from Xúnyáng to Xiàkǒu. Nánpíng Wáng
Kè, the Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, yielded his post to Guānl. On the *bǐngwǔ*
day, Hóu Jǐng
compelled Emperor Tàizōng to visit Xīzhōu. Summer, the fifth month, on the *gēngwǔ*
day, Póyáng Sìwáng
Fàn, the General Who Conquers the North and Administrator-in-Chief with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes, died. From
spring until summer, there
was a great famine. People
ate each other,
especially severely in the capital. The sixth month, on the *xīnsì*
day, Nánjùn Wáng
Dàlián was appointed Acting Administrator of Yángzhōu. On the *gēngzǐ*
day, Yáng Yārén,
the former Inspector of Sīzhōu, fled from the Department of State Affairs to Xīzhōu. Autumn, the seventh month, on the *wùchén*
day, the rebel Administrator Rèn
Yuē attacked Jiāngzhōu. Xúnyáng Wáng
Dàxīn, the Inspector, surrendered the province to Yuē. In
this month, Nánjùn Wáng
Dàlián was made the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu. The eighth month, on the *jiǎwǔ*
day, Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì
sent the Commander of the Guards, Wáng Sēngbiàn, leading troops to pressure Yǐngzhōu. On the *yǐhài*
day, Hóu Jǐng
promoted himself to Minister of State (*Xiàngguó*), and was
invested with twenty commanderies as Hàn Wáng. Shàolíng Wáng Guānl
abandoned Yǐngzhōu and fled. Winter, the tenth month, on the *yǐwèi*
day, Hóu Jǐng
again compelled Emperor Tàizōng to attend an informal banquet at Xīzhōu. He promoted
himself to Grand General of the Universe and Overall Commander of Military Affairs of the Six Directions. He established the imperial
sons Dàjūn as the Prince of Xīyáng Commandery, Dàwēi
as the Prince of Wǔníng Commandery, Dàqiú
as the Prince of Jiàn’ān Commandery, Dàxīn
as the Prince of Yì’ān Commandery, Dàzhì
as the Prince of Suíjiàn Commandery, and Dàyuán
as the Prince of Lèliáng Commandery. On the *rěnyín*
day, Jǐng
killed Nánkāng Sìwáng Huìlǐ. The eleventh
month, Rèn Yuē
advanced and occupied Xīyáng. He dispatched
troops to raid Qíchāng, captured
Héngyáng Wáng Xiàn and sent him to the capital,
where he was executed. Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì
sent Xú Wénshèng, the former Inspector of Níngzhōu, to command the armies and resist Yuē. Zhāng Biāo,
the former Middle General of Nánjùn Wáng, launched an uprising at Ruòxié Shān in Kuàijī, and attacked
and captured various counties in Zhèdōng. Second Year, Spring, the second month,
Shàolíng Wáng Guānl
fled to Dǒng Chéng in Ānlù. He
was attacked by Xī Wèi, his
army was defeated, and he
died. The third
month, Hóu Jǐng
personally led his forces west to raid. On the *dīngwèi*
day, he departed
the capital. From Shítou
to Xīnlín,
the ships’ bows and sterns touched each other. The fourth
month, he arrived
at Xīyáng. On the *yǐhài*
day, Jǐng
divided his forces and sent the false generals Sòng Zǐxiān and Rèn Yuē to assault Yǐngzhōu. On the *bǐngzǐ*
day, they captured
the Inspector Xiāo Fāngzhū. Intercalary month, on the *jiǎzǐ*
day, Jǐng
advanced and attacked Bālíng. Wáng Sēngbiàn,
the Commander of the Guards sent by Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì, engaged in continuous battles but could not defeat him. The fifth month, on the *guǐwèi*
day, Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì
sent the Mobile General Hú Sēngyòu and Lù Fǎhé, the Inspector of Xìnzhōu, to reinforce Bālíng. Jǐng
sent Rèn Yuē leading troops to resist the relief force. The sixth month, on the *jiǎchén*
day, Sēngyòu
and his forces defeated Rèn Yuē,
and captured him. On the *yǐsì*
day, Jǐng
lifted the siege and fled overnight. Wáng Sēngbiàn
commanded the armies to pursue Jǐng. On the *gēngshēn*
day, they attacked
Lǔ Shān Chéng,
capturing it. They
captured Zhāng Huàrén, the Wèi Minister of Works, and
Mén Hóngqìng, the Administrator-in-Chief. On the *xīnyǒu*
day, they advanced
and besieged Yǐngzhōu,
conquering it, and captured
the rebel commander Sòng Zǐxiān and others. Hóu Tián,
a former general of Póyáng Wáng, raised troops and attacked
the false Administrator-in-Chief Yú Qìng at Yùzhāng. Qìng
was defeated and fled. Autumn, the seventh month, on the *dīnghài*
day, Hóu Jǐng
returned to the capital. On the *xīnchǒu*
day, Wáng Sēngbiàn’s
army reached Pén Chéng. Fàn Xīróng,
the rebel acting administrator of Jiāngzhōu, abandoned the city and fled.
In the eighth month, on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
Wáng Sēngzhèn and Zhèng Chǒng of Jìnxī raised troops and attacked the commandery seat.
The pseudo-Inspector of Jìnzhōu, Xiàhóu Wēishēng, and the Companion, Rèn Yán, fled.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Hóu Jǐng sent the Minister of the Guards, Péng Jùn, and the Duke of Xiāng, Wáng Sēngguì, leading troops into the palace.
They deposed Tàizōng, making him the Prince of Jìn'ān,
and imprisoned him in Yǒngfú Province.
They murdered Crown Prince Dàqì, the Prince of Xúnyáng Dàxīn, the Prince of Xīyáng Dàjūn, the Prince of Wǔníng Dàwēi, the Prince of Jiànpíng Dàqiú,
the Prince of Yì'ān Dàxīn, and twenty sons of the Prince of Xúnyáng.
They forged an imperial edict for Tàizōng,
ceding the throne to the Heir Prince of Yùzhāng, Dòng.
A general amnesty was issued, and the reign year was changed.
They sent envoys to murder the Prince of Nánhǎi, Dàlín, in Wújùn;
the Prince of Nánjùn, Dàlián, in Gūshú;
the Prince of Ānlù, Dàchūn, in Kuàijī;
and the Prince of Xīnxīng, Dàzhuāng, in Jīngkǒu.
In winter, tenth month, on the *rén yín* day,
the Emperor said to the Palace Attendant Yīn Bùhài:
"Last night I dreamt I swallowed earth.
Try to interpret it for me."
Bùhài replied:
"In the past, Chóng'ěr was offered a clod of earth,
and eventually returned to the state of Jìn.
May Your Majesty's dream
be a sign matching this event."
When Wáng Wěi and others presented wine to the Emperor, they said:
"The Chancellor, seeing that Your Majesty has been worried and indignant for a long time,
has sent your servants to offer a toast for long life."
The Emperor laughed and said:
"A toast for long life—
can it not fulfill this purpose?"
Thereupon, they brought wine, food, and a bent-neck *pípá* (lute),
and drank with the Emperor.
The Emperor knew he could not escape,
so he drank deeply until fully intoxicated,
saying:
"I never expected that pleasure could reach such a point!"
Once he was drunk and asleep,
Wáng Wěi and Péng Jùn brought forward a sack of earth,
and Wáng Xiūzuǎn sat upon it.
Thereupon, Tàizōng died in Yǒngfú Province,
at the age of forty-nine.
The rebels gave him the false posthumous title of Emperor Mínghuáng,
and the temple name Gāozōng.
The following year,
in the third month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
Wáng Sēngbiàn led the former officials in carrying the coffin into the court hall.
Shìzǔ posthumously honored him as Emperor Jiǎnwén,
with the temple name Tàizōng.
In the fourth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
he was buried at Zhuānglíng.
Earlier,
when Tàizōng was imprisoned,
he inscribed a preface on the wall, saying:
"There is a true scholar of Liáng, Xiāo Shìzuǎn of Lánlíng,
who established himself by practicing the Way,
consistent from beginning to end.
Though the wind and rain darken the day,
the crowing of the cock does not cease.
I would not deceive a dark chamber,
how much less the Three Luminaries (Sun, Moon, Stars)?
That fate has come to this,
what is to be done!"
He also composed two pieces of *liánzhū* (linked pearls),
the writing being extremely sorrowful.
Tàizōng was sharp and wise in youth,
his perception surpassing others.
At six *suì*, he was already composing literature.
Gāozǔ was astonished at his precocity,
and did not believe it.
He then tested him personally before the court,
and the composition was exquisitely beautiful.
Gāozǔ sighed and said:
"This child
is the Dōng'ē of our house."
Once grown,
his disposition was broad and magnanimous;
he never revealed anger or joy.
He had square cheeks and a full jaw,
his beard and sideburns were like a painting.
When he glanced, his gaze illuminated others.
When reading, he read ten lines at once.
The Nine Schools and Hundred Masters—
what passed his eyes was certainly remembered.
For essays, verses, and *fù* (rhapsodies),
he took up the brush and finished immediately.
He widely studied the Confucian classics
and was skilled at discussing profound principles (*xuánlǐ*).
From the age of eleven,
he was able to personally handle administrative affairs.
He was tested in managing various feudal regions
and was praised wherever he went.
During the mourning period for Noble Consort Mù,
he grieved so severely that he was skin and bones,
wailing day and night without ceasing.
The mat he sat upon
rotted completely from being soaked (by tears).
In Xiāngyáng, he submitted memorials for a northern campaign,
sending the Chief Clerk Liǔ Jīn, the Cavalier Commander Dǒng Dāngmén, General Zhuàngwǔ Dù Huáibǎo, General Zhènyuǎn Cáo Yìzōng, and other troops to advance and suppress the enemy.
They conquered and pacified the commanderies of Nányáng and Xīnyě, etc.
Lǐ Zhì, the Wèi Inspector of Southern Jīngzhōu, surrendered with the city of Ānchāng.
The territory expanded by over a thousand *lǐ*.
When he served as overseer and administrator,
he showed great leniency and generosity.
