In documents and administrative registers,
he could not be deceived even in the slightest detail.
He introduced and received literary scholars,
rewarding and meeting them without fatigue.
They discussed various texts and books,
followed by literary compositions.
The commentaries on the Five Classics composed by Gāozǔ
were once respectfully narrated by him in Xuánpǔ;
listeners filled the court and the countryside.
He was generally fond of writing poems;
his preface stated:
"At seven *suì*, I acquired a poetry addiction,
and have not tired of it since growing up."
However, he was criticized for being light and glamorous (*qīngyàn*).
At the time, it was called
"Palace Style" (*gōngtǐ*).
His works include the Biography of Crown Prince Zhāomíng (five scrolls),
Biographies of the Various Princes (thirty scrolls),
Great Meaning of the Rites (twenty scrolls),
Meaning of the Lǎozǐ (twenty scrolls),
Meaning of the Zhuāngzǐ (twenty scrolls),
Record of the Meaning of Chángchūn (one hundred scrolls),
and Joined Jade Discs of the Dharma Treasure (three hundred scrolls).
All circulated in the world.
The official historian states: Tàizōng was bright and wise in his youth,
his fine reputation established early.
His genius was boundless,
surpassing all of the past and present.
However, his literature was occasionally hampered by superficial glamour (*qīnghuá*),
which the noble man does not approve of.
When he cultivated virtue in the Eastern Court (as Crown Prince),
his reputation spread throughout the barbarians and the Huá (Chinese).
When he succeeded to the lineage,
he truly possessed the excellence of a ruler.
Yet, corresponding to Wén and Jǐng (Emperors Wén of Hàn and Jǐng of Hàn),
his era coincided with the *Zhūn* and *Bō* hexagrams (representing difficulty and ruin).
He was controlled by rebellious subjects
and could not exhibit what he contained (his abilities).
In the end, he suffered the cruelty of Huái and Mǐn (Emperors Huái and Mǐn of Jìn).
Alas!
Basic Annals 5: Emperor Yuán
Shìzǔ, Emperor Xiàoyuán. His taboo name was Yì,
courtesy name Shìchéng,
and childhood name Qīfú.
He was the seventh son of Gāozǔ.
He was born in the eighth month of Tiānjiān 7 (508 CE), on the *dīngsì* day.
In year 13 (514 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xiāngdōng Commandery,
with a fief of two thousand households.
Initially, he served as General Níngyuǎn and Administrator of Kuàijī.
He entered the court as Attendant-in-Ordinary (*shìzhōng*), General Xuānwēi, and Governor of Dānyáng.
In Pǔtōng 7 (526 CE),

he was sent out to serve as Bearer of the Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the six provinces of Jīng, Xiāng, Yǐng, Yì, Níng, and Nánliáng, General of the Western Gentlemen, and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
In Zhōngdàtōng 4 (532 CE),
he was promoted to the title of General Píngxī (Pacifying the West).
In Dàtóng 1 (535 CE),
he was promoted to the title of General Ānxī (Pacifying the West).
In year 3 (537 CE),
he was promoted to the title of General Zhènxī (Garrisoning the West).
In year 5 (539 CE),
he returned to court as General Ānyòu (Pacifying the Right) and General Hùjūn (Protector of the Army),
in charge of military affairs at Shítou Garrison.
In year 6 (540 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Bearer of the Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Jiāngzhōu, General Zhènnán (Garrisoning the South), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In Tàiqīng 1 (547 CE),

he was transferred to serve as Bearer of the Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the nine provinces of Jīng, Yōng, Xiāng, Sī, Yǐng, Níng, Liáng, Southern Qín, and Northern Qín, General Zhènxī (Garrisoning the West), and Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
In the third month of year 3 (549 CE),
Hóu Jǐng attacked and captured the capital.
In the fourth month,
Palace Attendant Xiāo Sháo arrived at Jiānglíng to announce a secret imperial edict,

appointing Shìzǔ as Attendant-in-Ordinary, Acting Bearer of the Yellow Axe, Grand Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs domestic and foreign, and Minister of Education (*sītú*) with the authority to issue mandates.
All other posts remained as before.
In this month,
Shìzǔ mobilized troops from Xiāngzhōu,
but the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, Prince of Hédōng Yù, refused to send them.
In the sixth month, on the *bǐngwǔ* day,
he sent his Heir Apparent Fāngděng to lead forces to punish Yù.
Fāngděng was defeated and killed in battle.
In the seventh month,
he again sent General Zhènbīng Bào Quán to replace (Fāngděng) in attacking Yù.
In the ninth month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
the Inspector of Yōngzhōu, Prince of Yuèyáng Chá, raised troops and rebelled,
coming to attack Jiānglíng.
Shìzǔ entrenched himself behind the city walls and defended.
On the *yǐchǒu* day (later in the month),
Chá’s general Dù Zè, along with his brothers and Yáng Hùn, each led their forces to surrender.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
Chá fled.
Bào Quán attacked Xiāngzhōu but failed to capture it.
He then sent General of the Left Guards, Wáng Sēngbiàn, to take command.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (Great Treasure),
Emperor Shìzǔ (世祖) still referred to it as the fourth year of Tàiqīng (Great Clarity).
On the *xīnhài* day of the first month,
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯), General of the Left Guard, obtained thirty oranges attached to a single stem,
which he presented.
On the *jiǎxū* day of the second month,
Zhōu Hóngzhí (周弘直), Internal Historian of Héngyáng (衡陽), reported in a memorial that a phoenix had been seen within the commandery boundaries.
In the summer, on the *xīnwèi* day of the fifth month,
Wáng Sēngbiàn conquered Xiāngzhōu (湘州),
beheaded Yù (譽), the Prince of Hédōng (河東),
and Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
In the sixth month,
Dàkuǎn (大款), Prince of Jiāngxià (江夏), Dàchéng (大成), Prince of Shānyáng (山陽), and Dàfēng (大封), Prince of Yídū (宜都), came through secret paths from Xìn'ān (信安) to defect to us.
On the *xīnyǒu* day of the ninth month,

Kè (恪), the Prince of Nánpíng (南平) and former Inspector of Yǐngzhōu (郢州), was made General of the Central Guard, Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), and Head of the General Administration (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
Fāngzhū (方諸), the Heir Apparent and General of the Middle Garrison, was made Inspector of Yǐngzhōu.
Wáng Sēngbiàn, General of the Left Guard, was made General Overseer (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
Dàkuǎn was restyled as the Prince of Línchuān (臨川) Commandery,
Dàchéng as the Prince of Guìyáng (桂陽) Commandery,
and Dàfēng as the Prince of Rǔnán (汝南) Commandery.
In this month,
Rèn Yuē (任約) advanced to raid Xīyáng (西陽) and Wǔchāng (武昌).

Xu Wénshèng (徐文盛), General of the Left Guard, Yīn Zǐchūn (陰子春), General of the Right Guard, Xiāo Huìzhèng (蕭慧正), Commandant of the Heir Apparent's Right Guard, and Xí Wénxiàn (席文獻), Inspector of Suìzhōu (嶲州), were dispatched down to Wǔchāng to resist Yuē.
Kè (恪), the Prince of Nánpíng, General of the Central Guard, Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Head of the General Administration, was appointed Inspector of Jīngzhōu (荊州),
stationed at Wǔlíng (武陵).
On the *jiǎzǐ* day of the eleventh month,

Kè (恪), the Prince of Nánpíng, Dàkuǎn (大款), Prince of Línchuān and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Dàchéng (大成), Prince of Guìyáng, Yuánzhèng (圓正), Marquis of Jiāng'ān (江安) and Mounted Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), Zhāng Wǎn (張綰), Palace Attendant and General of the Left Guard, Tán (曇), Left Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works (Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ), and one thousand others from the palace administration, inspectorates, and states presented a memorial, saying: We humbly consider that when Mount Sōng (嵩岳) is steep,
clouds emerge from the mountains and rivers;
when a great state has protectors,
Shēn (申) and Fǔ (甫) are indeed its supports.
Is this not because the Emperor established this ultimate position,
using rank as his treasure,
and the teachings of the Sages distinguished
regions,
being cautious with names and instruments?
Thus we know that when the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) assisted the Emperor,
Chónghuá (重華) displayed the tally of the yellow jade;
when the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) surveyed the land,
Bóyǔ (伯禹) received the gift of the dark jade tablet (xuānguī).
We humbly consider that Your Highness the Illustrious
Duke and Great Prince,
was born at the command of fate, answering the cosmic order,
endowed with saintly wisdom upon birth.
Loyalty is your excellent virtue,
and filial piety is truly a natural law.
Your grounding is comparable to Yì (應) and Hán (韓),
and the trust placed in you is as deep as Dàn (旦) and Shì (奭).
The Five Relationships
are thereby instructed,
and the Seven Regulators are thereby aligned.
Your aspiration resides in protecting the state and society,
and your achievement delivered us from adversity and danger.
When the barbarians invaded internally,
you slept on your weapons, weeping blood.
While the whales and monsters were not yet swept away,
you threw on your robes to serve the Throne diligently.
You were able
to make the wandering souls request an alliance by kneeling,
and the ugly hordes offered up their jade tokens while terrified.
When close vassals rebelled externally,
their offense was equal to that of Wú (吳) and Chǔ (楚).
You manifested your authority through righteous campaigns,
and the battle was concluded without bloodshed.
The waves of the Xiāng (湘) River subsided on their own,
without needing to construct the fortifications of Dù Tāo (杜弢).
Xiànshān (峴山) was separated and estranged,
without having to attack the city of Liú Biǎo (劉表).
When Jiǔjiāng (九江) became obstructed,
and the two streams parted,
you only needed to command the war vessels,
and Qián (灊) and Huò (霍) were settled.
Tracing the stream to pursue and subdue the enemy,
the road for spying and trespassing was cut off.
When the Hu (胡) soldiers invaded our borders,
their iron cavalry gathered like a mist.
But with your divine strategy operating singularly,
they were all immediately displayed on poles,
turning to
broken wings,
and consequently they resumed offering tribute.
Liáng (梁) and Hàn (漢) formed an agreement,
brandishing their sharp and advantageous troops.
Bā (巴) and Hàn (漢) both submitted,
expending the ranks of the brave and fierce.
Southward, the Five Ridges are connected;
northward, you exert your strength in the plains.
The Eastern Yi (夷) do not complain,
and the Western Róng (戎) are immediately in order.
It can be said that in the upper reaches for a thousand *lǐ*,
there are a million soldiers holding halberds,
the most noble man in the world,
and one whom the four seas acclaim.
Now the sea clouds fly up,
Mount Kūnlún (崑山) arises in flames.
Wèi Wén (魏文) lamented the year of voluntary abdication;
Hán Xuān (韓宣) sighed over the day the rites were completed.
Beneath the Yángtái (陽臺),
only caps and carriages
are seen flocking together;
beside the Mèngshuǐ (夢水),
carriages still create tracks, hub to hub.
Two ears of wheat (móumài) appeared,
emerging from the state of Nánpíng;
sweet dew (gānlù) moistened the branches,
descending upon the territory of Dāngyáng (當陽).
Wild silkworms spun naturally,
how is this inferior to Ōusī (歐絲)?
Rice grew in fallow fields,
how is this different from raining grain?
Is this not because all things are prosperous,
which is called luminous civilization and great brightness?
How can your honorable title
not be displayed in the canons,
and your bright trial not be arrayed in the carriages and robes?
In the past, when Jìn (晉) and Zhèng (鄭) entered Zhōu,
they were still made Qing nobles;
when Xiāo (蕭) and Cáo (曹) assisted Hàn,
they were temporarily ranked as Prime Ministers (Xiàngguó).
It is fitting to exalt this grand ceremony
and clearly respond to the hopes of the multitude.
We, Kè (恪) and the others, have thoroughly
examined the existing laws
and broadly inquired of the sincere historians.
We respectfully bow twice and present this:
Advance him to the rank of Prime Minister,
to oversee all government affairs,
with one bamboo tally (zhúshǐ fú),
and separate standards for ceremonies.
Let him wield the golden axe to chop down the rebellious
and violent,
and ride in the jade carriage to settle the state and society.
His splendor covers the sun and moon in every direction,
and his integrity matches Heaven and Earth.
To assist the endangered and support the governance,
how glorious is that!
We, Kè and the others, lacking understanding of the great principle,
have blindly presented this petition for Your attention.”
Emperor Shìzǔ commanded a reply, saying:
“We have frequently encountered the ‘Nine of Yang’ (yángjiǔ) cycle,
and this time is within the ‘Hundred Six’ (bǎiliù) cycle.
The whales and monsters have not yet been eliminated,
and we suffer heartache day and night.
Zhōu (周) referred to the Heavenly Office,
and Qín (秦) called it the Prime Minister.
East reaches the sea,
west reaches the Yellow River,
south descends to Zhūyuān (朱鳶),
and north penetrates the Dark Pass (Xuánsè).
Leading these minor officials,
we promote this great virtue.
How can we follow in the footsteps of Qūfǔ (曲阜),
emulate the conduct of Huán (桓) and Wén (文),
and ultimately establish the great unification,
reverently performing the five bows?
Although righteousness belongs to conforming with the times,
and events are not recorded falsely,
traditions speak of yielding,
and the symbols demonstrate modesty (míng qiān).
Looking upon previous precedents,
We feel choked with shame again.”
On the *rénchén* day of the twelfth month,
Xiāo Bó (蕭勃), Inspector of Dìngzhōu (定州), was made General Who Pacifies the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
Yǐn Yuè (尹悅), General Protector of the Army, Wáng Xún (王珣), Inspector of Bāzhōu (巴州), and Dù Yòu'ān (杜幼安), Inspector of Dìngzhōu, were dispatched with troops down to Wǔchāng,
to assist Xú Wénshèng.
In the second year of Dàbǎo,
Emperor Shìzǔ still referred to it as the fifth year of Tàiqīng.
On the *jǐhài* day of the second month,
Wèi (魏) sent an envoy to pay respects.
In the third month,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) mobilized all his troops westward,
and joined Rèn Yuē's army.
On the *bǐngwǔ* day of the fourth month,
Jǐng dispatched his generals Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) and Rèn Yuē to attack Yǐngzhōu,
and captured the Inspector Xiāo Fāngzhū (蕭方諸).
On the *wùshēn* day,

it was fitting
to unify control,
and jointly elevate our headquarters,
truly making us the leader of the alliance.
I, though unworthy,
erroneously oversee the allied commanders.
Reflecting on the nation's long-term distress,
I have no time for peace or rest.
Managing the central command and the strong rear guard,
we respectfully execute Heaven's punishment,
carrying pikes and enduring peril,
prepared to sacrifice ourselves for this.
A thousand herds of celestial horses,
a million long pikes,
driving forth warriors like Bēn and Huò,
relying on the strength of wisdom and courage.
Dà Chǔ
crosses Jīngshān,
Qiǎnyuán crosses Pénglǐ,
our ships float on the water,
holding their southern flank,
our supply wagons deliver provisions,
striking their northern flank.
Chinese and the various tribes
carried provisions
and followed like shadows.
Like thunder shaking and wind frightening,
we marched straight toward Jiànyè.
When we press down on our swords and roar,
the River water flows backward;
when we draw out our pikes and wave them,
the bright sun retreats.
We are
driving forward swiftly,
entering by a hundred routes simultaneously,
leveling mountains and filling valleys,
filling the plains and covering the fields.
The comrades who shoulder cart shafts and pull oxen,
and the heroes who lift heavy posts and shatter stones,
their cavalry chases the sun and pursues
the wind,
their archery makes apes weep and geese fall.
It is like lifting Kūnlún Mountain to crush an egg,
or tilting the Bóhǎi Sea to drown a firefly.
It is like four horses drawing a feather,
or a charging bull hitting thin Lǔ
silk.
With such a host fighting,
who can withstand them!
Even if wasps and scorpions are poisonous,
a cornered beast will fight.
If they claim the mountains are high,
then our fortifications surround the four suburbs;
if they claim the land is
distant,
three thousand *lǐ* will not stop us.
They are like an angry frog,
or comparable to a small mouse.
We hardly need to expend ten thousand *jūn*,
nor trouble ourselves with a hundred *yì*.
Furthermore, the sun has reached the auspicious path,
the troops rise from the Jiàng
gōng.
The Three Gates are already opened,
and the Five Generals have all been dispatched,
raising orderly banners,
sweeping away the enemy's lofty spirits.
Thus, executing secret strategies at the crucial moment,
which the rebels cannot comprehend,
carrying out punishment righteously,
what villainy will not submit?

Now we dispatch the Envoy holding the Imperial Insignia, Grand Commander-in-Chief, General Who Conquers the East, Administrator of the Secretariat, Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Minister of the Secretariat, Founding Marquis of Chángníng County,
Wáng Sēngbiàn, leading a host of a hundred thousand,
to sweep straight toward Jīnlíng.
Beating drums deafens the heavens,
clashing cymbals shakes the earth.
Red banners raised in the evening
are like the rising clouds of Chìchéng;
warships moving at
night
are like the rushing currents of the dark sea.
Calculating those who share his evil,
they do not amount to a single company.
Noble men are marginalized,
while petty men form cliques.
Why should we worry about their complete destruction?
It will happen not in the morning, but in the
evening.
We will smash the throat of the Cháng Dí,
and bind the neck of Zhìzhī.
Now the Minister of Justice clearly announces the penalty,
that those justly executed by the axe
are only Hóu Jǐng and his immediate group.
What crime have the common people committed?
Not a single one
will be prosecuted.
Gentlemen, you who have for generations established loyalty and devotion,
personally bear favored aristocratic ranks,
whose conduct is exemplary among noble families,
and whose merits are recorded in the Princely Establishment—
having to bow your heads to these cunning villains,
and having no chance to demonstrate your worth—
how can you not quickly submit...?
and above, ashamed before August Heaven!
Having lost loyalty and righteousness
, it is hard for them to stand alone.
If you sincerely yearn for the Southern influence,
then look favorably West,
seize this opportunity to establish merit,
and turn disaster into fortune.
Anyone who can capture Hóu Jǐng and send his head will be enfeoffed as a Founding Duke (Kāiguó Gōng) over ten thousand households
, and given fifty thousand bolts of silk and cloth
Anyone who can mobilize the righteous masses
to respond to the governmental armies
, completely preserve their cities and
towns
, and refuse to be used by the bandit,
will be rewarded with ranks ranging from Regional Governor (Fāngbó)
at the highest, down to receiving a tally (Pōufú) at the lowest,
and will have territories granted
so they may wear the blue and purple robes of high office.
Formerly, when Yóu Yú entered Qín
, he was treated like a high minister and assistant. When Jì Mìdī
surrendered to Hàn
, he was even allowed to wear the golden sable
If you certainly possess the talent,
why worry about lacking a position?
If you cling to delusion and do not turn back
, resisting the Imperial Army,
the moment the great army arrives
, punishment will be applied without pardon.
When Mèngzhū is consumed by fire
, fragrant herbs and weeds are destroyed together. When the Xuānfáng River
bursts its banks
, jade and stone sink together.
The rules for reliable rewards
are as clear as the bright sun;
the system of dismissal and promotion
is as fair as clear water.
This proclamation is spread far and near
, so that all may hear and know
. In the third month
, Wáng Sēngbiàn and others pacified Hóu Jǐng
, and transmitted his head to Jiānglíng.
On the day Wùzǐ
, the pacification of the bandit was reported to the Míngtáng and the Tàishè.
On the day Jǐchǒu
, Wáng Sēngbiàn and others again respectfully presented a memorial, saying: All the armies gathered completely in Jiànkāng on the Wùzǐ day of this month.
Bandit Jǐng, like a hidden bird or an exhausted beast
, was frequently attacked and frequently frustrated.
His treachery was spent and his cunning exhausted
, so he fortified himself with deep trenches.
We
your servants divided and commanded our warriors
to advance simultaneously from a hundred directions
, with shock cavalry and short weapons
, rhinoceros armor and iron shields
, forming thousands of battalions
, and holding millions of halberds
. We stopped Zhòu
in seven steps and surrounded Xiàng
in three
cordons. There was a resounding great rout
, and the host of villains were scattered everywhere.
The young and old in the capital
all shouted "Long Live!"
The wine and food of Cháng’ān
fetch a high price due to this celebration.
The clouds lifted over the Nine Districts
, and the Six
Directions became clear and bright.
How much more so the common people
—who does not leap for joy!
We humbly reflect that Your Majesty has tasted pain and swallowed sorrow
, enduring wrath and bearing cruelty.
Since the Purple Court and Crimson Towers
, barbarian dust has risen in the four
directions. In Ruán Yuán and Hǎo Zhì
, the horses of Jì
gathered like clouds. [Your Majesty] managed the troops while weeping blood
, and swore the masses while tasting gall
Wú and Chǔ, united as one
, plotted rebellion just like the Seven States.
The rumors spread by Guǎn and Cài
led to chaos caused by the Three Supervisors (Sān Jiàn)
The righteous masses of Xīliáng
were blocked by powerful Qín and could not reach us.
The remaining people of Bìngzhōu
, crossing Fēihú Pass, were destroyed.
Jackals and wolves blocked the road
, and they were not limited to just one person.
If the great whale (Jīngní) had not been captured
, how could [this chaos have lasted] for five years
? Heroism and might have been manifested
, and all grievances have been cleared
. Eternally remembering the frost and dew (mourning the late emperor)
, how can words express [our grief]!
We, your servants
, promptly followed old precedents
by respectfully restoring the altars and temples
, and sending envoys holding tallies
to separately inform the tombs and mausoleums.
Since the successor ascended far away (died)
, his funeral carriage (Lóng Chūn) had not yet been interred.
The Empress (Chénghuá) concealed her brilliance
, and the Imperial Coffin (Zǐ Gōng) could not be located.
We immediately made preparations according to the circumstances
, ensuring the rites were complete despite the prevailing chaos.
The Four Seas share the sorrow
, and the Six Armies weep with bared shoulders.
Your Majesty's sacred devotion to filial piety and fraternal duty
logically means you must be deeply moved.
Recently
, all officials and regional governors (Yuè Mù)
have prayed and looked up to the Imperial Scrutiny.
They believe that the merit of receiving the jade tablet (Xī Guī)
has already returned to the possessor of the Way,
and the ceremony of accepting the jade disk (Dāng Bì)
truly belongs to the Sagely and Brilliant one (Your Majesty).
Yet, Your gracious edicts
express modesty and reserve
, and you remain obscurely aloof.
The Flying Dragon (Fēi Lóng) could ascend
, but the line of Qián remains at the fourth position.
Though voices shout at the Imperial Gate (Dì Hūn)
, the Heavenly Gate (Chāng Hé) has not yet opened.
Songs of praise are sent forth again
, and therefore
we crane our necks
. Thus, the people of Yuè were so insistent
that they smoked the Cinnabar Cave to seek their lord.
The people of Zhōu happily supported [their ruler]
, crossing Mount Qí to serve their sovereign
. If the King of Hàn (Hàn Wáng) had not immediately ascended the throne
, there would have been no way to honor his meritorious
ministers
. When Emperor Guāngwǔ (Guāngwǔ) stopped the claims of King Xiāo (Xiāo Wáng)
, how could he have continued the ancestral temple line
? When the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) wandered to Xiāngchéng
, he still inquired about the methods of governing the people.
When Fàng Xūn (Emperor Yáo) entered Gūyè
, he still ensured
that the ceremonial vessels had their rightful place.
This opportunistic arrival
is surely not what a sage desires,
nor what an Emperor should readily accept
, but it is done because there is no other choice.
We humbly read Your Imperial Document (Xǐ Shū)
and pondered the Imperial Directive (Zhì Zhǐ)
. [You] contemplate
matters outside the mundane world
, and have not yet accepted our compassionate request.
Your Majesty’s appearance, possessing the sun-horn and dragon countenance
, was manifested on the day you inspected Qí.
The auspicious sign of rosy clouds and pure aura
was established at the beginning of your response to the world.
Broadly observing, Your greatness is beyond naming
; speaking profoundly, Your insights are brilliantly illuminating.
Loyalty is a virtuous quality
, and filial piety truly moves Heaven.
Furthermore, Your heroic might and great strategy
, grand designs and martial calculations,
mean that when you give directions, the Dānpǔ requires no battle;
when you merely glance around, Bǎnquán disperses itself.
The mooring ropes of the earth, though snapped, have been re-tied.
The pillar of Heaven, though tilted, has been re-erected.
You have dredged the river crossings
at Mèngmén
, so that the hundred rivers flow again;
you mend the vault of the sky with five stones
, so that the ten thousand things are reborn.
Even if Your Majesty were to brush off your robes and wander to Guǎngchéng
, or climb Mount Qǔ and leave the Eastern
lands
, how could your assembled ministers petition you
, and to whom would the common people turn for benevolence?
Moreover, the suburban sacrifice matching Heaven (Jiāosì Pèi Tiān)
is neglected due to the absence of ritual vessels (Léi Fěi).
In the Purification Palace and Pure Temple (Zhāigōng Qīng Miào)
, the gourd and bamboo instruments are not displayed.
We look up and gaze at
Your Imperial Carriage (Luán Yú)
not just morning but evening.
When we look at the Imperial Procession (Fǎ Jià)
, we are parched and hungry.
How can you long delay the consensus of the masses
and neglect the proper standard!
The former suburban ritual sites have been restored.
Hán and Luò
are already pacified.
Although the palaces and residences in Gāonú and Lìyáng
are ruined
, the auspicious aura along the muddy River (Zhuó Hé) and the clear Wèi River (Qīng Wèi)
still remains.
Gāomén stands grandly
, Gānquán is open on all four sides
, and the earth gnomon measures the shadows
Receiving Dew.
This covers the Chìxiàn of the Nine Provinces,
and is the pivot and mechanism of the Six Directions.
The Erudites (Bóshì) held the diagrams and documents and gradually returned,
and the Grand Courtier (Tàicháng) established the rituals and they were arrayed.
How can one not raise the pure imperial carriage and proceed to the famous capital,
having prepared the jade bells (yù luán) to move through the main palace chamber!
Formerly, when the Eastern Zhōu had moved,
Hào Jīng was subsequently never recovered;
once Cháng'ān was in turmoil,
Jiá and Luò were taken as permanent residences.
Xià Hòu used the ten thousand states to hold court with the feudal lords,
and King Wén used the six provinces to rectify the world.
His traces were based on a hundred *lǐ*,
his sword and staff measured three *chǐ*.
Using
the remaining land of Chǔ,
he resisted the Nine Róng (Barbarians);
with the army of a single division,
he cut down and extinguished the Three Rebellions.
Smoothly and greatly settled,
the imperial carriage returned east.
He unyoked the five oxen in Jìzhōu,
and fed
the six horses in Qiáojùn.
If we seek distantly among antiquity,
can it be achieved?
Responding to and glorifying the Heavenly Mandate,
what virtues should be relinquished?
Since principles exist therein,
I dare to re-state my petition.
The Chancellor (Xiāngguó) replied:
“I have examined the memorial,
and prepared one or two responses.
All the Dukes, Ministers, and Officers,
and the countless common people,
all agree that August Heaven regards and mandates this,
and the destined loyalty belongs
to gather the precious throne upon Me, the Sole Man.
Wénshū's office of Commander of the Capital Guard (Jīnwú),
is a matter equivalent to previous desires;
Mèngdé's position of General Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī),
moreover, matches earlier statements.
Currently, the long whale of Huáihǎi,
although he is said to have surrendered his head;
the short fox of Xiāngyáng
has not yet completely changed his face.
When the Great Peace (Tàipíng) is like a jade candle,
then you may discuss this.”
On the *Xīnmǎo* day,
General Who Spreads Fierceness (Xuānměng Jiāngjūn) Zhū Mǎichén secretly executed Dòng, the Heir King of Yùzhāng,
along with his two younger brothers, Qiáo and Jiū.
This was the will of Shìzǔ.
In the fourth month, on the *Yǐsì* day,
Xiāo Jǐ, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, newly appointed Acting Grand Axe Bearer (Jiǎ Huángyuè), Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), and Prince of Wǔlíng, usurped the throne in Shǔ,
and changed the reign title to Tiānzhèng Yuánnián (First Year of Tiānzhèng).
Shìzǔ sent the Acting Minister of Works (Jiān Sīkōng) Xiāo Tài and the Minister of Rites (Cíbù Shàngshū) Yuè Zǐyún to pay homage and visit the imperial mausoleum,
and repair the altars of the land and grain (shè miào).
On the *Dīngsì* day,
Shìzǔ issued an order saying:
“Military appearance does not enter the capital,
and capital appearance does not enter the army.
Although Zǐchǎn presented victory,
he executed the matter in military attire,
and Yàfū refused to bow,
defining his duty as commanding troops.
Now, the fierce villains have been exterminated,
and the rebellious followers annihilated and routed.
The Nine Possessions (Jiǔ Yǒu) are secured,
and the Four Seas are peaceful and secure.
The majestic rituals of the Hàn officials
are now ready to display the grand ceremonies.
Wèi has many gentlemen;
this is entrusted to them as a model to behold.
You should immediately relax the security,
and announce this promptly.”
In this month,
Zhāng Biāo, the Administrator of Dōngyáng, was made General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn).
In the fifth month, on the *Gēngwǔ* day,
Kè, the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Prince of Nánpíng, along with imperial clansmen, kings, marquises, and the Grand Chief Controller (Dà Dūdū) Wáng Sēngbiàn,
once again bowed and presented a memorial advocating for the exalted title,
but Shìzǔ still firmly yielded and refused to accept it.
On the *Gēngchén* day,

Kè, the General Who Attacks the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn), Inspector of Xiāngzhōu, Minister of Works, and Heir Prince of Nánpíng, was made General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Yángzhōu,
the rest remaining as before.
On the *Jiǎshēn* day,

Wáng Sēngbiàn, the Prefect of the Palace Writers (Shàngshū Lìng), General Who Attacks the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn), Administrator with the Status of the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, was made Minister over the Masses (Sītú) and General Who Guards the Guards (Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn).
On the *Yǐyǒu* day,

the rebel Left Director of the Secretariat (Zuǒ Púyè) Wáng Wěi, Minister (Shàngshū) Lǚ Jìlüè, Minor Courtier (Shǎo Qīng) Zhōu Shízhēn, and Palace Attendant (Shèrén) Yán Dǎn were beheaded in the city market of Jiānglíng.
On this day,
Shìzǔ issued an order saying:
“The gentleman pardons faults,
recorded in the Zhōu Classics;
the sage loosens the net,
heard in the ordinances of Tāng.
Since the Xiǎnyǔn grew greatly rampant,
and the long serpent repeatedly consumed,
the Chìxiàn (Red Districts) were in imminent danger,
and the black-haired people (Qiánlí) fell into mud and charcoal.
I could not sleep throughout the night,
my resolve fixed on wiping away the shame.
The chief evil (Yuán'è) due for execution,
primarily belonged to Hóu Jǐng;
Wáng Wěi was his heart and backbone,
and Zhōu Shízhēn turned his back on grace and righteousness.
Now they have all been boiled in tripods and cauldrons,
and publicly displayed in the market and court.
However, since the distress and suffering from the bandit disturbances
have accumulated for years,
the former nobility in robes and caps,
were forced to steal life (survive illegally),
while fierce warriors and heroic merit-men
obscured their brilliance and barely escaped.
All those who were accomplices in evil,
certainly were not of a single clan.
I now specially proclaim the royal benevolence,
and erase the record of punishment.
From before dawn on the twentieth day of the fifth month of Tàiqīng 6th year,
let all be renewed.”
In this month,
Wèi sent Grand Tutor (Tàishī) Pān Yuè, Xīn Shù, and others to invade Qínjùn.
Wáng Sēngbiàn sent Dù Zè to lead troops to resist them.
Chén Bàxiān was made General-in-Chief Who Attacks the North (Zhēngběi Dà Jiāngjūn), Administrator with the Status of the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Inspector of Nán Xúzhōu.
In this month,
Wèi sent envoys to congratulate [the court] on suppressing Hóu Jǐng.
In the eighth month,
Xiāo Jǐ led the vast armies of Bā and Shǔ, linking boats to move eastward downstream.
[Shìzǔ] sent Army Protector (Hù Jūn) Lù Fǎhé to garrison Bāxiá to resist him.
Xú Líng, concurrently Gentleman-Consultant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì) and envoy to Wèi, presented a memorial at Yè saying: I have heard that Fēng Táng possessed a sage,
who eventually succeeded the house of Dì Kù;
dwelling in Dài with only virtuous men,
he eventually succeeded the heritage of Gāo Huáng.
Non-action (Wúwéi) was praised regarding the leather sandals,
and perfect governance was manifest
by merely letting robes hang down,
yet setting right chaos and restoring correctness
were not separate from antiquity.
As for the Metal Element performing again,
its source came from Dōngguǎn;
the Fiery Destiny remains prosperous,
its branch splitting off from Nándùn.
How
can one conceal the illustrious surname of Xuānyuán,
or fail to possess the talented son of Zhuānxù?
None fail to, in times of great difficulty,
simultaneously succeed the Divine Ancestor.
I humbly reflect that Your Majesty,
arising from Zhèn
equals Xūn and Huá,
and your clear yielding is the same as Dàn and Shì.
Grasping the Diagram and holding the Axe,
you are prepared to rule Heaven.
The jade clasp and pearl beam
first signify the Supreme Sovereign (Yuán Hòu).
The command of the Spirits of Heaven and Earth
is not
only the auspicious sign of Tàishì;
the diagrams and documents return to this place,
how can it be limited to the good omen at the gate of Yáo?
Regarding Great Filial Piety being the heart of the sage,
and the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhōngyōng) being the virtue of the gentleman,
naturally,
these serve as instruction for the people,
bequeathing custom to numerous scholars.
Day after day,
you investigate and review all affairs;
truly civil and truly martial,
encompassing all arts.
Likening this to the Three Great Ones,
and receiving guests at the Four
Gates,
enduring all trials,
all diverse achievements are glorious—
these cannot be adequately praised.
Since the reckless (wú wàng) rose in violence,
the imperial heritage has gradually diminished.
The large boar (Fēng Xī) and the long snake (Xiū Shé)
wreaked havoc upon the Central States (Zhōngguó).
Where the spiritual heart dwells,
the successor (Xià Wǔ) must arise.
Gazing at the Purple Zenith
and wailing aloud,
looking toward Dānlíng and falling in grief.
The family grievance was about to be avenged;
Heaven granted the banner of the yellow bird.
The national blight ought to be executed;
the spirits presented the mandate of the black fox.
Duke Téng embracing the standard (or tree),
his heroic spirit was imposing.
Zhāng Xiù engaging in battle,
his divine demeanor was increasingly courageous.
Loyalty and sincerity crown the sun and moon,
filial piety and righteousness move ice and frost.
Like thunder (tíng), like mighty crash (léi),
like the *Pí* (a mythical ferocious beast), like
The tigers
in the vanguard gave their lives,
and the chief villains were thus annihilated.
Since their gallbladders are hung up in the Western Prefectures,
they are now having their navels burned in the Eastern Market.
The three tombs of Chīyóu—
how can they be called severe execution?
Wáng Mǎng's
thousand slices
cannot be said to be clear penalties.
The Qīngqiāng and the Chìdí
were equally given to the jackals and wolves;
those in Hú clothing and Yí speech
were all made into jīngguān (mounds of bodies).
The capital region is orderly and prosperous,
once more seeing peace established; the ancestral
temple is
solemn,
now receiving abundant blessings.
Since the age of mists and primordial chaos,
and the sovereigns Lílián and Lìlù,
the hexagrams arose from the Dragon Chart,
and writing followed the bird tracks.
The Cloud
Master and the Fire Emperor
were not without the ways of battle and formation;
Yáo took oaths and Tāng campaigned,
all employing the means of shields and spears.
When the star aligned with Dōngjǐng,
Xiáo and Tóng were then broken;
when thunder shook Nányáng,
Xún
and Yì were initially pacified.
There has never been anyone who assisted the already fallen Three Powers,
or saved the scattered multitudes of the Four Seas,
so glorious and shining,
so reverently executing Heaven's punishment,
as the mighty one of today.
Thereupon,
auspicious clouds resembling a canopy
shone at dawn upon Yáoxiāng;
sweet dew like pearls
adorned Jǐng Qǐn in the morning.
The auspicious fungi, responding to virtue,
all emerged from the bronze pool;
the míngjiá plant tracks the hours,
negating the need for the silver
arrow (clepsydra).
Furthermore, reaching eastward to Xuántú,
and crossing westward beyond Báiláng;
Gāoliǔ produces wind,
Fúsāng enjoys the magnificent sun—
none fail to register their names as dependent states,
presenting hostages to the Hónglú.
The distant regions come as
guests,
near and far sharing the blessings.
His civil brilliance and martial reverence,
his assistance and support, are like that;
Heaven is made peaceful and Earth complete—
his achievements are like this.
It is high time that custodians of history were sought out widely,
that Heaven Officials were
consulted,
that Fánchāng was considered,
and Gāoyì planned.
The imperial lineage establishes its hegemony,
there is no need to trouble the Marquis of Yángwǔ;
the imperial road is clear of danger,
why dwell in the residence in Cháng'ān?
It is entirely proper to raise the bells and banners to offer sacrifices to the Emperor (God),
and to face the Phoenix Screen to receive the Mandate of Heaven.
The Mandate of Heaven rests upon your person,
to whom would you yield it?
On the twentieth day of last month,
Liǔ
Huī, who also holds the post of Sǎnqí Chángshì, and others arrived at Yè.
We humbly received the sacred decree, which expresses great modesty,
doing great deeds but not taking the throne.
Some say that Jīngyáng has not yet been recovered,
or that Hángǔ is free of obstructions,
and that by returning the imperial carriage to Jīnlíng,
Your Majesty will then receive Heaven’s blessing.
I foolishly believe that Dàtíng and Shǎohào
did not have fixed residences;
Hànzǔ and Yīnzōng
all had no permanent capitals.
When performing the Feng sacrifice on Mount Dài,
they still established the Míngtáng;
when touring Zhānglíng,
they sometimes
traveled through the Sīlì region.
Why must one look west to where the tiger squats
to establish the royal palace;
or gaze south toward Niútóu
to be called the Heaven's Gate?
Furthermore, I have heard this: Since the black jade scepter has been bestowed,
the dark green
jade is not yet offered,
which means the firewood has been delayed past the due time,
not that the bundled grass was not presented in tribute.
The Yúnhé lutes
have long been neglected at Gānquán;
the Gūzhú pipes
are unheard at Fāngzé.
How
can one not be fearful?
I humbly beg Your Majesty to comply with the desires of the people,
and save the destiny of the myriad states.
How can you hesitate and firmly decline,
only then seeking the farmer of Shíhù;
or loftily decline to rule,
merely
citing the recluse of Jīshān!
We do not know the non-virtue inherent in the highest virtue,
we only see the lack of benevolence in the Sage.
The entire realm is anxious,
what hope do the common people have?
In the past, Sū Jì and Zhāng
Yí,
leaving their home and defying custom,
were still able to recruit the three regions to serve Zhào,
and urge the six states to honor Qín.
How much more we, your servants, who clearly carry the imperial credentials,
and personally received the court mandate!
Jade scepters were
specially conveyed,
announcing the mission in Héyáng,
we wore mink tail hats with dignity,
seeking alliance by the Zhāng River.
The increase of sacrifices (or degradation of lodging)
depended upon the prevailing power;
gazing towards our homeland,
we truly share equally in joy and sorrow.
But we are of humble origin and lack fortune;
our destiny is out of sync with the times.
We are shamefully serving as mere envoys,
sharing the distant banishment of Sānwēi.
Gaining a moment in the Inner Palace,
the treatment is entirely lacking the favor shown to Gěng Yǎn;
sealing
memorials from the border town,
we privately match the weeping of Liú Kūn.
Unable to suppress these humble feelings,
we respectfully submit this memorial for Your hearing.
In the ninth month, on the day Jiǎxū,
Kè, Prince of Nánpíng, who held the titles of Sīkōng, General Who Guards the East, and Governor of Yángzhōu, passed away.
In the winter, tenth month, on the day Yǐwèi,
Xiāo Xún, the former Governor of Liángzhōu, arrived at Jiānglíng from Wèi.
Xún was appointed General Who Pacifies the North and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
On the day Wùshēn,
Wáng Lín, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu, was seized inside the palace.
Lín’s deputy general, Yīn Yàn, was jailed and died.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
his son, Fānglüè, was appointed Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
On the day Gēngxū,
Lín’s Chief Clerk Lù Nà and his general Pān Wūlěi, among others, raised troops in revolt,
attacking and capturing Xiāngzhōu.
In this month,
the kings, dukes, ministers, and gentlemen governing and garrisoning the four directions again urged Shìzǔ to assume the revered title (Emperor),
but he still modestly declined and had not agreed.
When the memorial was submitted three times,
he finally acquiesced.
In the winter of the 1st year of Chéngshèng, 11th Month, day Bǐngzǐ,
Shìzǔ ascended the throne as emperor at Jiānglíng.
An imperial edict stated:
"Now, establishing a ruler
is for supervising and tending the common people (qiánshǒu).
The heart of Dì Yáo
surely did not value the yellow canopy (Huángwū, the imperial standard),
but truly found it impossible to avoid taking charge.
Our august ancestor, Tàizǔ Wénhuángdì, accumulated virtue in Qí and Liáng,
his transforming influence spread through the Jiāng and Hàn regions,
his Way shone brightly in the land,
and all looked up to him.
Our deceased august father, Gāozǔ Wǔhuángdì, was as bright as the sun and moon,
his merit reached the ends of the earth,
responding to Heaven and following the people,
truly wise and a sage.
Tàizōng Jiǎnwén Huángdì's status equaled Qǐ and Sòng,
and his standard matched Wén and Jǐng.
When the Jié bandits encroached,
the difficulties of the time were extremely urgent.
We greatly rescued [the realm] from devastation,
and succeeded in restoring the ancestral temples and the state (zōngshè).
The various dukes, ministers, scholars, and all officials
unanimously believed that the Imperial Spirit favored the mandate,
that the opportunity for sovereignty had arrived,
that the Mandate of Heaven could not be long delayed,
and that the Imperial Throne could not be long vacant.
Following the precedents of previous records,
modeling the excellent standards,
fearing the majesty of Heaven,
calculating the elevation of the Imperial Calendar (bǎolì),
they thereby brought the divine instrument [of rule] upon Us alone.
In the past, Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu
had no auspicious designations for years,
but Hàn, Wèi, Jìn, and Sòng
have continued this tradition for a long time.
Although We claim to have put down rebellion,
We are not founding a new dynasty;
We wish to connect upward to the ancestral lineage (zōngtiāo)
and bestow favor downward upon the myriad people.
The 6th year of Tàiqīng is hereby changed to the 1st year of Chéngshèng.
Outstanding taxes and old debts
are all permitted to be extensively forgiven (hóngdài);
filial sons and righteous grandsons
shall all be granted titles of nobility.
Long-term exiles and the banished
shall receive special clemency and pardon;
those under lifetime political prohibition and those deprived of official position
shall all be broadly absolved."
On that day, Shìzǔ did not ascend the main hall;
the dukes and ministers merely lined up in attendance.
Day Dīngchǒu,
Xiāo Xún, General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn) and Kaifu Yítóng Sānsī, was appointed General of Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
All other appointments remained as before.
Day Jǐmǎo,
the King's Heir Fāngjǔ was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
and his name was changed to Yuánliáng.
Imperial Son Fāngzhì was established as Prince of Jìn'ān Commandery (Jìn'ān Jùnwáng),
and Fānglüè was established as Prince of Shǐ'ān Commandery (Shǐ'ān Jùnwáng).
His birth mother, Ruǎn Xiūróng, was posthumously honored as Empress Dowager Wénxuān (Wénxuān Tàihòu).
In this month,
Lù Nà sent his generals Pān Wūlěi and others to attack and defeat Dīng Dàoguì, the Governor of Héngzhōu, at Lùkǒu.
Dàoguì fled to Línglíng.
12th Month, day Rénzǐ,
Lù Nà divided his troops and attacked Bālíng.
Xiāo Xún, the Governor of Xiāngzhōu, attacked and defeated them.
In this month,
Lǐ Hóngyǎ, the Governor of Yíngzhōu, led his forces from Línglíng and exited Kōnglíngtān,
intending to descend and attack Nà.
Nà sent his general Wú Zàng and others to attack and defeat Hóngyǎ.
Hóngyǎ retreated and defended Kōnglíngchéng.
Second Year, Spring, 1st Month, day Yǐchǒu,
an edict ordered Wáng Sēngbiàn to lead the massed forces to campaign against Lù Nà.
Day Wùyín,
Wáng Bāo, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), was appointed Assistant Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè),
and Liú Jué was made Minister of Personnel.
Xī Wèi sent its great general Yùchí Jiǒng to attack Yìzhōu.
3rd Month, day Gēngwǔ,
an edict stated:
"Food is the people's heaven,
and agriculture is the root of governance.
Handed down over a thousand years,
transmitted to hundreds of kings,
none failed to respectfully grant the people their seasons [for farming],
or to personally plow the imperial field.
For this reason, cropping is treasured,
and the Songs of Zhōu praised their musical composition.
If grains failed to mature,
the scribes of Lǔ recorded it in their historical documents.
The people of Qín had regulations encouraging agricultural effort,
and the Hàn dynasty opened up the benefits of military farming (túntián).
Recently, times have been difficult,
multiple calamities have repeatedly arrived,
and as shields and spears were not sheathed,
We were unable to attend to this matter.
Orders to expand fields
were not heard in the commanderies and states;
the duties of the Minister of Agriculture (Zàishī)
were deficient in the official system.
Now the primary evil has been eliminated,
and the land within the seas is unified.
It is right to greatly shelter the common people (qiánshǒu),
in order to rescue those suffering from the turmoil.
If one farmstead neglects its duties,
our hearts are troubled daily;
if one man abandons his profession,
no salt flats will be left uncultivated.
May the state be prosperous and punishments light,
and may families be well-supplied and the people satisfied.
Those persons who exert effort in farming
shall be granted tax exemptions wherever they are.
Let this be promulgated externally
to convey Our intent."
Day Xīnwèi,
Lǐ Hóngyǎ surrendered Kōnglíngchéng to the bandits.
The bandits seized him and returned.
Originally,
Dīng Dàoguì fled to Línglíng and sought refuge with Hóngyǎ.
Hóngyǎ ordered the remnants of the forces to be collected,
and they surrendered together with him.
Since Hóngyǎ had surrendered to the bandits,
the bandits then executed Dàoguì.
Day Bǐngzǐ,
the bandit general Wú Zàng and others led troops to occupy Chēlún.
Day Gēngyín,
two dragons were seen in the western river of Xiāngzhōu.
Summer, 4th Month, day Bǐngshēn,
Sēngbiàn's army encamped near Chēlún.
5th Month, day Jiǎzǐ,
the combined forces attacked the bandits
and thoroughly routed them.
Day Yǐchǒu,
Sēngbiàn's army arrived at Chángshā.
Day Jiǎxū,
Yùchí Jiǒng advanced and pressured Bāxī.
Yáng Qiányùn, the Governor of Tóngzhōu, surrendered the city
and received Jiǒng.
Day Jǐchǒu,
Xiāo Jì's army arrived at Xīlíng.
6th Month, day Yǐmǎo,
Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
In this month,
Yùchí Jiǒng besieged Yìzhōu.
Autumn, 7th Month, day Xīnwèi,
the people of Bā, Fú Shēng and Xú Zichū, killed Gōngsūn Huǎng, the commandant of the bandit city,
and brought the city to surrender.
Jì's forces suffered a massive defeat
and he died encountering troops.
Day Yǐwèi,
Wáng Sēngbiàn returned his army to Jiānglíng,
and an edict ordered the various armies to return to their respective garrisons.
8th Month, day Wùxū,
Yùchí Jiǒng captured Yìzhōu.
Day Gēngzǐ,
an edict stated:
"Now, when [Tāng] first resided in Bó,
he did not abandon the capital of the former king.
When the Mandate was received by Zhōu,
the eulogies for the old state were not changed.
Recently, military flags have ceased to wave,
and the border passes are free of alarms.
When departing Lǔ, one sighs,
feeling deeply moved at midnight;
when passing Pèi, one sheds tears,
truly disturbing rest in the evening.
Furthermore, because Xiāo and Xiāng were in revolt,
and Yōng and Shǔ held up troops,
We appointed generals and granted them military codes,
setting a date for the conquest and pacification.
Now the Eight Regions are settled and clear,
and the four suburbs are without ramparts.
It is fitting to follow the precedent of the azure canopy
and return to the land of Báishuǐ.
The supplies from Jiāng and Xiāng [regions]
have flat-bottomed boats lined up stern to stern;
the ships and vessels from the Bā Gorges
have a million elite soldiers.
They shall first proceed to Jiànyè,
which shall truly act as the capital;
thereafter, the Six Armies shall swiftly set out,
the Nine Banners shall raise their pennants,
We shall pay homage at the imperial tombs,
and restore the ancestral temples and the state (zōngshè).
Let the responsible officials diligently follow the old precedents
and promulgate this promptly."
9th Month, day Gēngwǔ,
Sītú Wáng Sēngbiàn returned to his garrison.
Day Bǐngzǐ,
Lù Fǎhé, General of the Guards (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn), was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Day Yǐyǒu,
Fāngzhì, Prince of Jìn'ān, was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
In this month,
Wèi sent Guō Yuánjiàn to train naval forces at Héféi,
and further dispatched great generals Xíng Gǎoyuǎn, Bù Dàhánsà, and Dōngfāng Lǎo to lead their forces to join him.
Wáng Sēngbiàn
arrived at Gūshú, and immediately remained there to garrison the area.
He dispatched the Inspector of Yùzhōu, Hóu Zhèn,
to occupy the rampart at Dōngguān, and summoned the Administrator of Wúxīng, Péi Zhīhéng,
to lead troops to follow up. On the day Wùxū,
Wáng Bāo, the Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs, was appointed Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs;
Zhāng Wǎn, the Administrator of Xiāngdōng, was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs.
In the twelfth month,
Dōngfāng Guāng, a native resident of Sùyù, occupied the city and surrendered. All the prefectures and commanderies of Wèi west of the river rose up in arms in response to him.
In the spring of the third year, the first month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Hóu Zhèn, the Inspector of Nányùzhōu, was given the additional titles of General Who Attacks the North and Founder of a Staff with the Honors of the Three Dukes.
Chén Bàxiān led troops to attack Guǎnglíng City.
Yán Chāodá, the Inspector of Qínzhōu, besieged Jīngzhōu from Qín Jùn;
Hóu Zhèn and Zhāng Biāo went out to Shíliáng
to serve as their support. On the day Xīnchǒu,
Chén Bàxiān dispatched Dù Sēngmíng, the Administrator of Jìnlíng, to lead troops to assist Dōngfāng Guāng.
In the third month, on the day Jiǎchén,
Wáng Sēngbiàn, the Minister of Education (Sītú), was appointed Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry.
On the day Dīngwèi,
Wèi dispatched its general Wáng Qiú to lead seven hundred troops to attack Sùyù.
Dù Sēngmíng intercepted and attacked them,
and utterly defeated them. On the day Wùshēn,
Lù Fǎhé, the General of the Guards and Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, was appointed Minister of Education (Sītú).
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
Chén Bàxiān, the General-in-Chief Who Attacks the North and Founder of a Staff with the Honors of the Three Dukes, was appointed Minister of Works (Sīkōng).
In the sixth month, on the day Rénwǔ,
Wèi again dispatched the general Bù Dàhànsà to lead troops to relieve Jīngzhōu.
On the day Guǐwèi,
a black vapor, resembling a dragon,
appeared inside the palace hall.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Jiǎchén,
Zōng Lǐn, the President of the Board of Justice, was appointed President of the Board of Civil Office.
In the ninth month, on the day Xīnmǎo,
Shìzǔ, at the Lóngguāng Hall, expounded upon the meaning of the *Lǎozi*;
Wáng Bāo, the Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, served as the reader of the text.
On the day Yǐsì,
Wèi dispatched its Pillar of the State, Wànniǔ Yú Jǐn, to lead a large army to invade.
In winter, the tenth month, on the day Bǐngyín,
the Wèi army arrived at Xiāngyáng,
and Xiāo Chá led his forces to join them.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
the lectures were halted,
strict military discipline was imposed internally and externally,
and the imperial carriage traveled outside the capital's barricade.
On this day,
a great wind uprooted trees.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
the armies of Wáng Sēngbiàn and others were summoned.
In the eleventh month,
Hú Sēngyòu, the General Commandant of the Army, was appointed Overall Supervisor of Military Affairs for the troops east and north of the city;
Zhāng Wǎn, the Vice Director of the Right, served as his deputy.
Wáng Bāo, the Vice Director of the Left, was appointed Overall Supervisor of Military Affairs for the troops west and south of the city;
Yuán Jǐngliàng of the Palace Attendant Bureau served as his deputy.
The princes, dukes, ministers, and gentlemen each took up defensive positions.
On the day Bǐngxū,
Shìzǔ personally toured all parts of the capital's barricade.
The Crown Prince toured the city towers,
ordering the residents to assist in transporting water and stones.
At all vital defensive points,
troop deployments were increased.
On the day Dīnghài,
the Wèi army reached the foot of the barricade.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
Wáng Lín, the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu, was summoned to enter and provide relief.
On the day Dīngyǒu,
there was a great wind,
and a fire broke out inside the city.
Hú Sēngyòu was appointed Founder of a Staff with the Honors of the Three Dukes;
Péi Jī, the Inspector of Kuízhōu, was appointed General Commandant of the Army.
On the day Gēngzǐ,
Xú Shìpǔ, the Inspector of Xìnzhōu, and Rèn Yuē, the Commander (Sīmǎ) for the Prince of Jìn'ān, arrived with their armies at Mǎtóu Àn.
On the day Wùshēn,
Hú Sēngyòu, Zhū Mǎichén, and others led their troops out to battle.
Mǎichén was defeated.
On the day Jǐyǒu,
Wáng Bāo, the Vice Director of the Left, was demoted to General of the Guards.
On the day Xīnhài,
the Wèi army launched a major assault.
Shìzǔ went out through the Pípá Gate,
personally overseeing and supervising the battle.
Hú Sēngyòu was struck by a stray arrow and died.
The Six Armies were utterly defeated.
Traitors cut down the Western Gate barrier to admit the Wèi army,
and the city fell to Western Wèi.
Shìzǔ was captured.
He was taken to Xiāo Chá’s camp,
and then relocated back inside the city.
In the twelfth month, on the day Bǐngchén,
Xú Shìpǔ and Rèn Yuē retreated and garrisoned Bālíng.
On the day Xīnwèi,
Western Wèi killed Shìzǔ.
He thus passed away,
being forty-seven years old at the time.
The Crown Prince Yuánliáng and the Prince of Shǐ'ān, Fānglüè, were both killed.
Tens of thousands of common people, men and women,
were then selected, divided into slaves,
and driven into Cháng'ān;
those who were young and weak were all killed.
In the fourth month of the following year,
he was posthumously honored as Emperor Xiàoyuán,
with the temple name Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ was intelligent, astute, outstanding, and brilliant;
his natural talent was superb and bright.
When he was five years old,
Gāozǔ asked:
"What book are you reading?"
He replied:
"I can recite the *Qǔlǐ*."
Gāozǔ said:
"Recite some of it for me."
He immediately recited the first chapter,
and none of those around him failed to express astonishment and admiration.
When he was first born, he suffered from an eye ailment.
Gāozǔ personally took pains to treat it,
but he ended up blind in one eye.
(Gāozǔ) felt even deeper pity and affection for him.
Once grown, he was fond of learning,
comprehensively mastering many books.
He could form a composition as soon as he put brush to paper;
his pronouncements became established arguments.
His talent, eloquence, sharpness, and speed
were unparalleled in his generation.
Gāozǔ once asked him:
"When Sūn Cè was previously in Jiāngdōng,
how old was he then?"
He replied:
"Seventeen."
Gāozǔ said:
"That is exactly your age."
Hè Gé served as Consultant (Fǔ Zīyì) in his administration.
He ordered Hè Gé to lecture on the *Sānlǐ* (Three Rites).
Shìzǔ by nature disliked sensuous pleasures,
and possessed considerable renown.
He maintained friendships of equals (cloth-garment exchanges) with Péi Zǐyě, Liú Xiǎn, Xiāo Zǐyún, Zhāng Zuǎn, and other talented figures of the time.
His compositions and literary writings
circulated widely in the world.
When he was in Xúnyáng,
he dreamed that a person said:
"The world is about to fall into chaos,
but the Prince will surely stabilize it."
Furthermore, he had a black mole on his back.
A shamaness saw it and said:
"This is an omen of great nobility,
which should not be spoken of."
Initially,
when Hè Gé traveled west,
he was extremely unhappy about it.
He stopped to bid farewell to Jiāng Gé, the Palace Assistant Imperial Censor,
and informed him of his feelings.
Jiāng Gé said:
"I once dreamed that His Majesty reviewed all his sons.
When he reached the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
he personally removed his hat and conferred it upon him.
This man is certain to possess the imperial seal later on.
You should go!"
Hè Gé followed this advice.
When the disaster of the Tàiqīng era occurred,
he alone was able to overcome and restore order.
Therefore, people near and far gladly supported him,
and he successfully received the sacred mandate.
The works he compiled include *Xiàodé Zhuàn* (Biographies of Filial Virtue), thirty scrolls;
*Zhōngchén Zhuàn* (Biographies of Loyal Ministers), thirty scrolls;
*Dānyáng Yǐn Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Governor of Dānyáng), ten scrolls;
Annotation of the *Hàn Shū* (Book of Hàn), one hundred and fifteen scrolls;
*Zhōu Yì Jiǎngshū* (Commentary on the Zhou Changes), ten scrolls;
*Nèidiǎn Bóyào* (Extensive Essentials of Buddhist Texts), one hundred scrolls;
*Liánshān*, thirty scrolls;
*Dònglín*, three scrolls;
*Yù Tāo*, ten scrolls;
*Bǔ Quēzǐ*, ten scrolls;
*Lǎozi Jiǎngshū* (Commentary on the *Lǎozi*), four scrolls;
*Quándé Zhì*, *Huáijiù Zhì*, *Jīngnán Zhì*, *Jiāngzhōu Jì*, *Gòngzhí Tú*, and *Gǔjīn Tóng Xìngmíng Lù* (Record of Identical Names, Ancient and Modern), one scroll;
*Shì Jīng* (Classic of Divination), twelve scrolls;
*Shì Zàn*, three scrolls;
and a Collected Works (*Wénjí*), fifty scrolls.
In the disaster of the decline of the Liáng dynasty,
massive bandits relied on fortresses.
Shìzǔ was then positioned as the Chief Commander (Cháng Liánshuài),
holding the resources of the whole of Chǔ.
He should have personally led the multitude of nobles,
resting on spears and pioneering the way.
He falsely displayed reliance on external aid,
actions distinct from serving the sovereign diligently (Qínwáng).
Regarding the movement of troops,
it was never far.
Only later did he exterminate the great villains,
thereby pacifying the ancestral altars (Zōngshè).
Grasping the Mandate and facing south,
he gloriously initiated the restoration (Zhōngxīng).
This was also due to Shìzǔ’s heroic talent and brilliant strategies,
allowing him to inherit this precious destiny.
However, his disposition was suspicious and jealous,
treating distant and close associates alike (with suspicion).
He had no skill in managing subordinates,
treading on ice without fear.
Therefore, the merit of the Fèng Què (Palace Gate) anticipating the dawn,
lacked the beauty of the fire lighting itself from within.
Given Shìzǔ’s divine wisdom and unique insight,
and his focus on the way of governance,
why did he not restrain evil doctrines,
move his carriage to Jīnlíng,
and neighbor a powerful enemy on the left?
How could he possibly succeed?
Thus, Heaven did not repent the misfortune,
and destroyed this existence.
Alas!
Basic Annals Six: Jìng Dì
Emperor Jìng’s taboo name was Xiāo Fāngzhì,
his courtesy name was Huìxiàng,
and his childhood name was Făzhēn.
He was the ninth son of Shìzǔ.
In the third year of Tàiqīng [549 CE],
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīngliáng.
In the first year of Chéngshèng [552 CE],
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jìn'ān,
with a fiefdom of two thousand households.
In the second year [553 CE],
he was sent out as General Pacifying the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu.
In the eleventh month of the third year [554 CE],
Jiānglíng fell.
Wáng Sēngbiàn, Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Governor of Yángzhōu, and Chén Bàxiān, Minister of Works (Sīkōng) and Governor of Nán Xúzhōu, reached an agreement
to appoint the Emperor (i.e., Prince Fāngzhì) as Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi) and regent (Chéngzhì),
and escort him back to the capital (Jīngshī).
On the *Guǐchǒu* day of the second month of the fourth year [555 CE],
he arrived from Xúnyáng,
and entered to reside in the court hall (Cháotáng).

Wáng Sēngbiàn, the Grand Commandant, was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān), Recorder of the Masters of Writing (Lù Shàngshū), General of the Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn), and Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì).
Chén Bàxiān, the Minister of Works, was granted thirty guards carrying ceremonial swords (Bājiàn).
Hóu Tián, Governor of Yùzhōu, was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
Xiāo Xún, Dignitary with the Same Privileges as the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī) and Governor of Xiāngzhōu, was appointed Grand Commandant.
Xiāo Bó, Dignitary with the Same Privileges as the Three Ducal Ministers and Governor of Guǎngzhōu, was appointed Minister of Education (Sītú).
Zhāng Biāo, General Guarding the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn), was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
In the third month,
Qí sent Gāo Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, to escort Xiāo Yuānmíng, Marquis of Zhēnyáng, to assume the succession of Liáng.
When they reached Dōngguān,
Pèi Zhīhénɡ, Prefect of Wúxīng, was dispatched to fight them.
(The Liáng forces) suffered a defeat,
and Zhīhénɡ died.
Grand Commandant Wáng Sēngbiàn led his troops out to garrison Gūshú.
In the fourth month,
Minister of Education Lù Fǎhé defected with Yǐngzhōu to Qí.
Hóu Tián, Governor of Jiāngzhōu, was dispatched to suppress him.
On the *Xīnchǒu* day of the seventh month,
Wáng Sēngbiàn accepted Xiāo Yuānmíng, Marquis of Zhēnyáng.
He crossed the river from Cǎishí.
On the *Jiǎchén* day,
(Yuānmíng) entered the capital,
and the Emperor (Fāngzhì) was made Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
On the *Jiǎchén* day of the ninth month,
Minister of Works Chén Bàxiān launched his righteous campaign (Jǔyì),
attacked and killed Wáng Sēngbiàn,
and deposed Xiāo Yuānmíng.
On the *Bǐngwǔ* day,
the Emperor (Fāngzhì) ascended the throne.
In the winter, on the *Jǐsì* day of the tenth month of the first year of Shàotài [555 CE],
an imperial edict stated:
“The royal house failed,
engulfed by disaster and calamity.
The Western Capital (Xīdū) was lost,
and the court fell into ruin.
The coffin of the former emperor (Xiāndì)
was scattered and displaced.
The royal foundations collapsed,
and the whole land lacked a sovereign.
I, though young and inexperienced,
faced these ongoing difficulties.
We wept tears of blood and rested on spears,
determined to avenge the rebels.
The great shame has not yet been washed away;
morning and night, I am choked with indignation.
The numerous dukes, ministers, and magistrates
urged me with the great principle of righteousness (Dàyì),
forcing me, the unskilled, to ascend (the throne),
and inherit this great enterprise.
Considering my original intention,
I never expected to reach this position.
I hope to rely on the spirit of my ancestors,
and be aided by generals and ministers,
to successfully eradicate the chief villains
and offer redress at the imperial tombs (Língqǐn).
Now that the fallen Mandate has been renewed,
and the ancestral temple (Zōngbēng) is receiving sacrifices again,
the celebration flows to the myriad people,
not just to me alone.
Therefore, the fourth year of Chéngshèng shall be changed to the first year of Shàotài.
There shall be a general amnesty across the empire,
and all civil and military officials, internal and external, shall be promoted one rank.”
Xiāo Yuānmíng, Marquis of Zhēnyáng, was appointed Minister of Education,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiàn'ān Commandery,
with a revenue of three thousand households.
On the *Rénzǐ* day,

Chén Bàxiān, the Minister of Works, was appointed Prefect of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Lìng), Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside the Capital, General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yángzhōu and Nán Xúzhōu.
He retained his title as Minister of Works.
Dù Kān, Governor of Zhènzhōu, raised troops
and attacked Chén Qiàn, General Establishing Martiality (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), at Chángchéng.
Wéi Zài, Prefect of Yìxīng, occupied his commandery and responded to (Dù Kān).
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
Xiāo Xún, the Grand Commandant, was promoted to Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo).
Yuānmíng, the newly appointed Minister of Education and Duke of Jiàn'ān, was promoted to Grand Mentor (Tàifù).
Xiāo Bó, the Minister of Education, was appointed Grand Commandant.

Wáng Lín, General Guarding the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn), was appointed General of Chariots and Cavalry and Granted the Privileges of Establishing a Staff and the Same Privileges as the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
On the *Wùwǔ* day,
Xià Guìfēi, his birth mother, was honored as Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu).
His consort, Lady Wáng, was established as Empress (Huánghòu).
Zhāng Biāo, General Guarding the East and Governor of Yángzhōu, was promoted to General-in-Chief Pacifying the East (Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn).
Xú Sìhuī, General Guarding the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Qiáo and Qín prefectures, was promoted to General-in-Chief Pacifying the North (Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn).
Rèn Yuē, General Pacifying the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Nán Yùzhōu, was promoted to General-in-Chief Pacifying the South (Zhēngnán Dàjiāngjūn).
On the *Xīnwèi* day,
an edict ordered Minister of Works Chén Bàxiān to campaign east to suppress Wéi Zài.
On the *Bǐngzǐ* day,
Rèn Yuē and Xú Sìhuī raised troops and rebelled.
Taking advantage of the capital being unprepared,
they stealthily occupied Shítóu.
On the *Dīngchǒu* day,
Wéi Zài surrendered,
and Yìxīng was pacified.
Zhōu Wényù, Prefect of Jìnlíng, was dispatched to lead troops to reinforce Chángchéng.
On the *Gēngchén* day of the eleventh month,
Zhái Zǐchóng, Governor of Ānzhōu (of Qí), Liú Shìróng, Governor of Chǔzhōu, and Liǔ Dámó, Governor of Huáizhōu, led their forces to join Rèn Yuē,
and entered Shítóu.
On the *Gēngyín* day,
Minister of Works Chén Bàxiān returned to the capital.
On the *Gēngxū* day of the twelfth month,
Xú Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē again led their men to Cǎishí,
to welcome Qí reinforcements.
On the *Bǐngchén* day,
Hóu Āndū, General Fierce and Ardent (Měngliè Jiāngjūn), was dispatched with a naval force to intercept them at Jiāngníng.
The rebel forces suffered a great rout,
and Sìhuī and Yuē fled to the west of the river (Jiāngxī).
On the *Gēngshēn* day,
Zhái Zǐchóng and others requested surrender,
and they were all released back to the north.
In the spring, on the *Wùyín* day of the first month of the first year of Tàipíng [556 CE],
there was a general amnesty across the empire.
Those who had allied and conspired with Rèn Yuē and Xú Sìhuī
were entirely pardoned.
Posthumous titles were conferred upon the various sons of Emperor Jiǎnwén.
The son of the late Marquis of Yǒng'ān, Xiāo Què, was subsequently granted the hereditary title of Prince of Shàolíng,
to manage the succession of Prince Xié.
On the *Guǐwèi* day,
Dù Kān, General Guarding the East and Governor of Zhènzhōu, surrendered.
An edict ordered him to commit suicide (Cìsǐ).
A partial amnesty was granted to Wúxīng Commandery.
On the *Jǐhài* day,
Xiāo Xún, Grand Guardian and Marquis of Yífēng, inherited the title of Prince of Póyáng.
Zhāng Biāo, Governor of Dōng Yángzhōu, besieged Wáng Huáizhèn, Prefect of Línhǎi, at Shànyán.
On the *Gēngxū* day of the second month,
Zhōu Wényù and Chén Qiàn were dispatched to attack Kuàijī
and suppress Biāo.
On the *Guǐchǒu* day,
Biāo's Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) Xiè Qí, Marshal (Sīmǎ) Shěn Tài, Army Commander Wú Băozhēn, and others offered the city in surrender.
Biāo was defeated and fled.

Xiāo Dàkuǎn, Prince of Línchuān and General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn), was granted the Privileges of Establishing a Staff and the Same Privileges as the Three Ducal Ministers with his current title.
Xiāo Dàchéng, Prince of Guìyáng and Central Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn), was made Protector of the Army General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
On the *Bǐngchén* day,
the people of Ruòyé Village executed Zhāng Biāo
and sent his head to the capital.
A partial amnesty was granted to Dōng Yángzhōu.
On the *Jǐwèi* day,
Zhènzhōu was abolished,
and restored to Wúxīng Commandery.
On the *Guǐhài* day,
the rebels Xú Sìhuī and Rèn Yuē attacked the Cǎishí garrison,
captured the garrison commander Zhāng Huáijūn, Governor of Míngzhōu,
and fled to Qí.
On the *Jiǎzǐ* day,
because the eastern territories had suffered severely from the pillaging of Dù Kān and Zhāng Biāo,
a grand envoy (Dàshǐ) was dispatched to tour and inspect the area.
In the third month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Dōngyángzhōu was abolished,
and Huìjī Jùn was restored.
On the day Rénwǔ,
it was proclaimed that ancient and modern coins could be used together throughout the realm.
On the day Wùxū,
Qí sent Major General Xiāo Guǐ out of Shàkǒu,
heading toward Liángshān.
Sīkōng Chén Bàxiān’s military commander Huáng Zhōu counterattacked,
and routed him completely.
Guǐ retreated and secured Wúhú.
Zhōu Wényù and Hóu Āndū were dispatched with the combined armies
to occupy Liángshān and resist him.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Dīngsì,
Sīkōng Chén Bàxiān petitioned to proceed to Liángshān to inspect and comfort the generals.
On the day Rénshēn,
Hóu Āndū led light troops to raid the Qí Mobile Chancellery (Xíngtái) Sīmǎ Gōng at Lìyáng,
thoroughly defeating him,
and capturing tens of thousands.
In the fifth month, on the day Guǐwèi,
Grand Tutor (Tàifù) Jiàn'ān Gōng Yuānmíng passed away.
On the day Gēngyín,
the Qí forces, both naval and infantry, entered Dānyáng Xiàn.
On the day Bǐngshēn,
they reached the old seat of Mòlíng.
An imperial order instructed Zhōu Wényù to return and encamp at Fāngqiū,
Xú Dù to encamp at Mǎmù,
and Dù Léng to encamp at Dàhéng.
On the day Guǐmǎo,
the Qí army advanced and occupied Értáng.
The imperial carriage moved out to encamp at the old hedge gate of Zhào Jiàn,
and strict security was enforced both inside and outside the palace.
In the sixth month, on the day Jiǎchén,
the Qí forces secretly reached the Dragon’s Tail (Lóngwěi) of Jiǎngshān,
angled toward the north of Mòfǔshān,
and arrived northwest of Xuánwǔ Hú.
On the day Yǐmǎo,
Sīkōng Chén Bàxiān was invested with the authority to command all armies.
He engaged the Qí forces in battle,
utterly defeating them.
He executed Dù Fāngqìng, the Qí Inspector of Běiyǎnzhōu, along with Xú Sìhuī and his younger brother Sìzōng.
He captured alive Xú Sìyàn, Xiāo Guǐ, Dōngfāng Lǎo, Wáng Jìngbǎo, Lǐ Xīguāng, Péi Yīngqǐ, Liú Guīyì, and others,
and all of them were executed.
On the day Wùwǔ,
a general amnesty was declared throughout the realm.
Soldiers who perished on the battlefield
were all ordered to be collected and given sacrifices.
Those without family members
were immediately given proper burial.
On the day Xīnyǒu,
the state of alert was lifted.
In autumn, the seventh month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) and Sīkōng Chén Bàxiān was promoted to Minister of Education (Sītú),
and additionally appointed Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
His other titles remained as before.
On the day Dīnghài,
Hóu Tián, who held the title of Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, was appointed Sīkōng.
In the eighth month, on the day Jǐyǒu,
Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) Pōyáng Wáng Xún passed away.
In the ninth month, on the day Rén'yín,
the era name was changed and a great amnesty was declared.
Those who showed filial piety, fraternal duty, and diligence in farming were granted one rank of nobility.
People of exceptional talent and unusual conduct were to be reported by their localities.
Those displaced due to famine and distress were compelled to return to their native lands.

The newly appointed Sītú Chén Bàxiān was promoted to Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), Director of the Affairs of the Secretariat (Lù Shàngshū Shì), General-in-Chief Guarding the State (Zhènwèi Dà Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Mù).
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Yìxīng Commandery (Yìxīng Jùn Gōng).
General of the Central Authority (Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn) Wáng Chōng was granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī based on his current rank.
Wáng Tōng, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), was appointed Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè).
On the day Dīngsì,
Xú Dù, Inspector of Yǐngzhōu, was appointed General Leader of the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
In winter, the eleventh month, on the day Yǐmǎo,
the Yúnlóng Gate and the Shénhǔ Gate were constructed.
In the twelfth month, on the day Rénshēn,
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and General Guarding the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn) Xiāo Bó was promoted to Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) and General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
The newly appointed General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn) Ōuyáng Wěi was made General Pacifying the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Héngzhōu.
On the day Rénwǔ,
General Pacifying the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) Liú Fǎyú was promoted to the title Ānnán Jiāngjūn.
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
Liú Ruì, former Prefect of Shòuchāng, was made Prince of Rǔyīn (Rǔyīn Wáng),
and Xiāo Dǎn, former Judicial Officer (Fǎcáo) under the General Guarding the West and acting Staff Officer, was made Prince of Bālíng (Bālíng Wáng),
to maintain the sacrifices for the preceding Sòng and Qí dynasties.
In the second year, spring, the first month, on the day Rén'yín,
an imperial edict stated:
"The Master (Fūzǐ), endowed with sacred spirit and embodying wisdom,
wove together benevolence and rectified righteousness.
He truly illuminated the Uncrowned King (Sù Wáng),
and continually expounded profound merits.
Those who look up to him find him ever higher;
those who receive his teachings find him tireless.
He established loyalty and filial piety,
and his virtue covered the common people.
He formulated rites and composed music,
his Way surpassed all sovereigns.
Although Mount Tài has crumbled and fallen,
not one elder has been abandoned;
and the lingering ripples of the Sì Shuǐ
still remain after a thousand years.
Since the imperial plan was obstructed and stalled,
the sacrifices have not been maintained.
At the gates of the temple honoring the Sage,
the descendants have been extinguished.
In the chamber revering the divine spirit,
the sacrificial vessels (fǔguǐ) are empty and desolate.
When reflecting upon his reputation and brilliance,
deep admiration and sorrow are truly combined.
Furthermore, search for and identify descendants of the Lǔ state clan
to serve as successors who maintain the sacrifices to the Sage.
Simultaneously, repair the temple hall
and provide for the sacrificial ceremonies.
The four seasonal offerings
shall all follow the old customs."
On this day,
another edict ordered:
"Let all prefectures (zhōu) establish Central Appraisers (Zhōngzhèng)
to interview and nominate candidates as before.
Officials shall not be arbitrarily appointed based on single petitions.
All nominations must be countersigned by the Zhōngzhèng
before positions are assigned according to rank.
They must rigorously adhere to the ranking system,
ensuring accuracy and trustworthiness.
Although Jīngzhōu, Yōngzhōu, Qīngzhōu, and Yǎnzhōu are temporarily cut off,
many gentry reside along the Huái and the sea (Huáihǎi),
and thus the functions of the officials overseeing them should still not be abandoned.
Huìjī, although its status as a zhōu was abolished,
remains a major commandery.
As the population of gentry is numerous and widespread,
a separate residential district (yìjū) may be established there.
Regarding commanderies and counties that have been newly divided,
or those newly titled Zhōu Mù,
they are all affiliated with their original districts
and do not require concurrent establishment [of separate appraisal offices].
When selecting the Zhōngzhèng,
one must always seek out senior men of virtue who are comprehensive and knowledgeable,
and they shall hold the position concurrently with another office."
Wáng Lín, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Jiāngjūn) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, was appointed Sīkōng and Grand General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dà Jiāngjūn).
The five commanderies of Xúnyáng, Tàiyuán, Qíchāng, Gāotáng, and Xīncài were divided
to establish Xījiāng Zhōu,
with Xúnyáng serving as the prefectural seat and garrison.
Another edict stated:
"Members of the Imperial Clan who hold office and established states or inherited families,
but are currently still referred to as heir apparent (shìzǐ),
are all permitted to succeed to their original noble ranks."
Wáng Tōng, Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè), was appointed Vice Director of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè).
On the day Dīngsì,
Chángshā Wáng Sháo, General Guarding the West (Zhènxī Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Yìzhōu, was promoted to General Campaigning in the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn).
In the second month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
General Leader of the Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn) Xú Dù entered Dōngguān.
Grand Guardian (Tàibǎo) and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu Xiāo Bó raised troops in rebellion.
He sent the false commanders Ōuyáng Wěi, Fù Tài, and Bó’s cousin Zī to serve as the vanguard,
and Yú Xiàoqǐng, Inspector of Nánjiāng Zhōu, joined them with troops.

An edict ordered General Pacifying the West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn) Zhōu Wényù, General Pacifying the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn) Hóu Āndū, and others to lead the combined armies in a punitive expedition to the south.
On the day Wùzǐ,
Xú Dù arrived at Héféi
and burned three thousand Qí ships.
On the day Guǐsì,
Zhōu Wényù’s army, positioned at Bāshān, captured Ōuyáng Wěi alive.
In the third month, on the day Gēngzǐ,
Dīng Fǎhóng, Zhōu Wényù’s vanguard commander, captured Fù Tài alive at Zhíkǒu.
The armies of Xiāo Zī and Yú Xiàoqǐng retreated and fled.
