On the day Jiǎchén,
the newly appointed Sīkōng Wáng Lín was made Inspector of Xiāngzhōu and Yǐngzhōu.
On the day Jiǎyín,
Chén Fǎwǔ, Inspector of Dézhōu, and Tán Shìyuǎn, former Inspector of Héngzhōu, attacked and killed Xiāo Bó at Shǐxīng.
In summer, the fourth month, on the day Guǐyǒu,
a partial amnesty was granted to Jiāngzhōu, Guǎngzhōu, and Héngzhōu;
also, all those within the metropolitan area (dū nèi) who had been constrained or coerced by the rebels
were all pardoned.
On the day Jǐmǎo,
four-pillar coins (Sìzhù Qián) were minted,
with one coin equivalent to twenty [standard coins].
Qí sent an envoy to request peace.
On the day Rénchén,
the four-pillar coin was changed to be equivalent to ten [standard coins].
On the day Bǐngshēn,
the use of thin coins (xì qián) was again prohibited.
Lán Yǎn, Xiāo Bó’s former chief commander and former Director of the Imperial Chambers (Zhí Gé), launched a surprise attack and killed Tán Shìyuǎn.
Yǎn, in turn, was killed by the fugitive Xiàhóu Míngchè.
Lǐ Bǎozàng, Xiāo Bó’s former Registrar (Jìshì), supported Huái’ān Hóu Xiāo Rèn in occupying Guǎngzhōu and raising rebellion.
On the day Wùxū,
Hóu Āndū advanced his army.
Yú Xiàoqǐng abandoned his forces and fled.
Xiāo Zī requested surrender,
and Yùzhāng was pacified.
In the fifth month, on the day Yǐsì,
General Pacifying the West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn) Zhōu Wényù was promoted to the title General Guarding the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn),
and Hóu Āndū was promoted to the title General Guarding the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn).
Both were granted the title Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī based on their current ranks.
On the day Bǐngwǔ,
General Guarding the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn) Xú Dù was appointed Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
On the day Wùchén,
Yú Xiàoqǐng sent an envoy to the Chancellor’s (Chéngxiàng) residence to beg for surrender.
In autumn, the eighth month, on the day Jiǎwǔ,
Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) Chén Bàxiān was granted the Yellow Axe (Huáng Yuè),
put in charge of the Grand Tutor (Tàifù) office,
permitted to wear his sword and shoes when ascending the hall,
exempted from hurried steps during court attendance,
exempted from naming during the announcement of audience,
and provided with feathered canopies and court music (gǔchuī).
In the ninth month, on the day Xīnchǒu
, Grand Councilor Chóng was made Prime Minister (Xiàng Guó),
controlling all governmental affairs.
He was enfeoffed with ten commanderies as the Duke of Chén (Chén Gōng),
granted the ceremonies of the Nine Distinctions (Jiǔ Xī),
given an imperial seal and sash, and a Yuǎnyóu Crown (Yuǎnyóu Guān),
his rank being above that of the princes and dukes.
The Prime Minister (Xiàng Guó) was granted a green silk sash.
A complete official bureaucracy was established for the State of Chén.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day Wùchén,
the Duke of Chén (Chén Gōng)'s peerage was advanced to Prince (Wáng),
and he was granted an additional ten commanderies,
making a total of twenty commanderies including the previous grant.
The Prince of Chén (Chén Wáng) was ordered to wear a crown (miǎn) with twelve strings of beads (liú),
to erect the Emperor's banners and standards,
to have imperial clearance procedures upon exiting and entering,
to ride the Golden-Axle Carriage,
drawn by six horses,
and to be accompanied by the five seasonal auxiliary carriages.
The Māotóu and Yúnhǎn standards were established.
Music included the Eight-Row Dance (Bā Yì),
and bells were arranged using the gōngxuán display.
The regulations governing the titles and appointments of the Prince's consort, sons, and daughters
entirely followed the former standards.
On the day Xīnwèi,
an imperial edict stated: "The Five Phases (Wǔ Yùn) change their cycle,
and the Three Beginnings (Sān Zhèng) alternate;
the shepherding of the common people
belongs to the sage and worthy,
who is thus able to order Heaven and Earth,
encompass the universe,
greatly shelter the black-haired people,
and propagate great glory.
Replacing darkness with light
has been the continuous practice throughout the ages;
a hundred kings have followed these steps,
all adhering to this principle.
The virtue of Liáng has withered and declined,
and calamity and distress have repeatedly arisen: from the beginning of the Tàiqīng
era,
we were plagued by the 'Long Serpent';
during the Chéngshèng year,
we again suffered from the 'Great Boar';
and arriving now at Tiānchéng,
the sacred instruments have been seized again.
The Three Luminaries frequently change,
the Seven Ancestral Temples (Qī Miào) lack sacrifices,
all sentient
life is extinguished,
and the Mandate of the Cauldron has fallen.
The inheritance of Our Emperor
is tiny, like a hanging tassel.
Quietly contemplating the Tún and Bō hexagrams,
we bear anxiety day and night.
The Prime Minister, the Prince of Chén (Chén Wáng),
possesses talents bestowed by Heaven,
a divine spirit descended from the sacred mountains.
His virtue aligns with Heaven and Earth;
his brilliance equals the sun and moon.
He rescued the State from overwhelming ruin,
lifting the millions
from mud and charcoal.
In the east, he punished the rebels;
in the north, he eliminated the Xūn Chǒu savages.
His majesty extends over the four seas,
and his benevolence permeates all nations.
He restored broken music,
and re-established forgotten rites.
The halls of Confucian scholarship have been repaired,
while border posts
remain empty.
Although great merit rests with Shùn,
and splendid achievements belong to Yǔ,
his greatness is sublime and immeasurable,
beyond description.
The offering of the white ring
is not limited only to the time of the Sovereign Yú;
the presentation of the white
pheasant as tribute
is not restricted only to the glorious era of Zhōu.
Therefore, treasures are offered from river and land,
auspicious signs appear in mist and clouds:
Jade Dew and Sweet Springs,
condense and flow forth morning and evening;
fine grain and auspicious grasses
propagate in the suburbs and fields.
His Way shines through distant ages,
and his merit reaches the August Heaven.
Bright is the High Heaven,
its brilliance matching the sun and moon.
Changing the old order is manifested in celestial phenomena,
and the succession of virtue is clearly displayed in prophecies and charts.
When injustice in prisons and lawsuits
has been removed,
the songs of the people turn towards him.
Heaven's calendar and destiny
truly rest in his place.
Although We are mediocre and small,
ignorant of antiquity,
We have long examined the rise and fall of states,
and this day has been long in coming.
How dare We forget the enduring precedents of successive dynasties,
and the utmost desire of humanity and the spirits!
We now immediately relinquish the throne and retire to a separate palace,
respectfully ceding the rule to Chén.
All procedures shall follow the precedents set by Táng and Yú, and Sòng and Qí."
The Prince of Chén (Chén Wáng) ascended the throne.
The Emperor was honored with the title Prince of Jiāngyīn (Jiāngyīn Wáng).
He died in an outlying residence
at the age of sixteen.
He was posthumously granted the title Emperor Jìng (Jìng Huángdì).
The Official Historian comments: When Liáng approached collapse and disintegration,
disaster and chaos repeatedly arrived.
At this time,
the Heavenly Mandate was already gone.
Emperor Jìng (Jìng Huáng) readily yielded,
which was akin to releasing a burden.
(魏徵), said:
"Gāozǔ (高祖) was indeed exceptionally endowed by Heaven,
intelligent and knowledgeable about antiquity.
His Way was second only to inherent knowledge,
his learning made him extensively erudite,
truly cultured and truly martial,
possessing many skills and many talents.
Starting from his status as a scholar,
he had an unrestrained bearing.
When the darkened tyrant indulged in tyranny,
and the heavenly relations (family) suffered disaster,
he gathered righteous armies,
intending to avenge his family’s grievance.
He declared that Zhòu (紂) could be conquered,
meeting (the opportunity) without prior arrangement.
He was like a dragon leaping over Fán (樊) and Hàn (漢),
and lightning striking Xiāng (湘) and Yǐng (郢).
He cut down those lacking virtue as easily as shaking off dry leaves,
and seized the lone tyrant as easily as picking up something discarded.
His heroic talents and grand strategies
are indeed beyond adequate praise.
Since he raised the banner of the white flag (submission),
he aligned with the favor of August Heaven.
He spread virtue and bestowed kindness,
making those nearby happy and bringing in those from afar.
He opened the broad Kingly Way,
and reformed the decadent customs of Shāng (商).
He greatly promoted culture and education,
elaborately adorned ceremonial conduct,
propagated the subtle teachings (Daoism),
and publicized Confucian scholarship.
He wore benevolence and righteousness as armor,
resolving conflicts at the ceremonial table (diplomacy),
his fame shook the universe,
and his beneficence flowed to distant descendants.
Weapons were sheathed
for several decades in total.
How numerous and capable they were!
How flourishing and grand!
Since the era of Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉),
there has been no such flourishing period.
However, he could not stop focusing on the superficial and strengthen the fundamentals;
transforming the ornate into the simple;
admiring fame and indulging in extraordinary deeds,
highly valuing superficial splendor.
He alternately praised and disparaged Kǒng (孔) and Mò (墨) (Confucianism and Mohism),
and lingered excessively upon Shì (釋) and Lǎo (老) (Buddhism and Daoism).
Sometimes he would go the whole night without sleep,
sometimes he would go the whole day without eating.
This was not to broaden the Way to benefit creatures,
but merely to embellish cleverness in order to astound the foolish.
Moreover, his heart had not yet abandoned glory,
though he falsely placed himself among the ranks of common servants;
he spoke loftily of casting off the world,
but ultimately clung to the dignity of the Yellow Canopy (the throne).
The great desires of man
lie in food, drink, and sexual relations.
As for carriages, crowns, palaces, and halls,
these are not matters of immediate personal necessity.
Gāozǔ (高祖) suppressed his appetites and desires,
but was strongly attached to carriages and crowns.
He achieved what was difficult, yet was held back by what was easy.
It can be said that his spirit did not fully comprehend,
and his wisdom was not entirely unimpeded.
When his vitality gradually dried up,
and his phoenix-like virtue had waned,
he was misled by what he heard and accepted,
and power fell into the hands of the treacherous and cunning.
The Heir Apparent and the assembled officials
were unable to speak their minds fully.
His dangerous and volatile heart
grew worse in his later years.
He acted merely upon seeing profit,
rejected counsel and disregarded divination,
opened the gate and welcomed thieves (traitors),
abandoned friends and approached enemies.
Trouble arose within the palace walls,
and disaster was brought about by the Róng Jié (戎羯) tribes.
He died by unnatural means,
and calamity afflicted the common people.
Officials and gentry perished under the blades and arrows,
the old and young were crushed beneath the horses' hooves of the invaders.
Looking at the millet growing lushly [in the ruins],
the pain is deeper than that at the temples of Zhōu (周);
speaking always of the wheat growing tall,
the sorrow is greater than at the ruins of Yīn (殷).
Since ancient times, when security turned to danger,
and success was followed by defeat,
the speed of this collapse
is unprecedented in written records.
The *Yì* (易) says: ‘Heaven assists those who are sincere,
men assist those who are compliant (obey the Way).’
That Gāozǔ (高祖) encountered such distress and ruin,
and did not die a natural death,
was because his actions led to danger,
not proceeding from sincerity and compliance,
thus losing the aid of Heaven and men.
How could he have avoided this?
"Tàizōng (太宗) was exceptionally intelligent and wise,
his spiritual radiance was outstanding,
he was widely read and highly accomplished,
rich and versatile in literary expression.
However, his writings were ornate but of little practical use,
flowery but lacking substance;
his style exhausted excessive beauty,
and his meaning was rarely clearly articulated.
His sounds of sorrowful reflection
thus altered the customs.
To rectify all states based on this
is different from the recitation of Zhōu (周) or the solemnity of Hàn (漢).
I was born at an unlucky time,
encountering many troubles.
Rebellious tyrants plotted and incited,
great scoundrels surged up to the heavens.
Starting with the imprisonment at Yǒulǐ (牖里),
it ultimately resembled the disaster at Wàngyí (望夷).
Oh, distant Azure Heaven,
can you be questioned?
"In the past, when the nation’s fate first fell into difficulty,
and troops amassed at the Wèiquē (魏闕) gate,
the regional lords relinquished their positions,
throwing up their sleeves to aid the Emperor.
Yuándì (元帝), as a member of the bedrock imperial clan,
accepted the responsibility of governing a separate territory,
faced with difficulties affecting both ruler and family,
occupying the highest position among the regional governors.
Yet he was unable to grasp his sword and taste bile (pledge resolution),
rest on his weapon and weep blood,
personally lead the troops,
or dedicate his life as a vanguard;
instead, he held back his army and hesitated,
harboring discontent and ambition inwardly,
sitting back to observe the changes of the time,
considering it a fortune for himself.
He did not hasten to punish Mǎng (莽) or Zhuó (卓) (usurpers),
but first executed his own brothers.
Moreover, he was deeply suspicious, jealous, and cruel,
often acting without propriety.
He employed clever arguments to mask his wrongs,
and unrestrained his rage and perversity to harm others.
His fierce generals, his claws and teeth,
and his most trusted advisors,
some were glanced at and immediately imprisoned,
others met with mincing and brine (execution) for a single word.
The upright men of the court
looked at each other in fear.
He considered himself as secure as Mount Tàishān (泰山),
and that all his actions were without oversight.
Frightened by perverse theories,
he sought comfort in Jīngchǔ (荊楚).
Although the main villain was subdued,
the nation was not yet at peace,
and when the western neighbor sent reproaches,
disaster and ruin quickly followed.
High Heaven looked down in judgment,
merely borrowing the hand of another here.
The Way of Heaven and human affairs—
how can they be misled?
He devoted himself earnestly to literature and art,
selecting the frivolous and excessive while rejecting loyalty and sincerity.
In military renown and resolute firmness,
he placed kinsmen before enemies.
Although he recited the Six Classics from memory,
and his mind grasped the Hundred Schools,
possessing the learning of Zhòngní (仲尼),
and the talent of Gōngdàn (公旦),
this merely served to increase his arrogance and pride,
and compounded his misfortune.
How did it aid the overthrow of Jīnlíng (金陵)?
How did it save Jiānglíng (江陵) from destruction?
"Jìngdì (敬帝) encountered disaster in his family (the country),
succeeding to this troubled fate.
Expeditions and punitive actions originated from others,
and government and punishment were not decided by himself.
Since there was no aid from Yī (伊) or Huò (霍) (wise ministers),
how could he avoid making the supreme concession (abdication)? ”

Biography Series One: Empress Zhāng (張), wife of Tàizǔ (太祖); Empress Xī (郗), wife of Gāozǔ (高祖); Empress Wáng (王), wife of Tàizōng (太宗); Noble Consort Dīng (丁), wife of Gāozǔ (高祖); Lady Rǔan Xiūróng (阮脩容), wife of Gāozǔ (高祖); Consort Xú (徐), wife of Shìzǔ (世祖).
The *Yì* says:
“After Heaven and Earth existed, then the myriad things existed.
After the myriad things existed, then men and women existed.
After men and women existed, then husbands and wives existed.”
The principle of husband and wife is indeed lofty!
In the *Zhōu Lǐ*,
the ruler establishes the Empress, six palaces,
three *Fūrén*, nine *Pín*, twenty-seven *Shìfù*, and eighty-one *Yùqī*,
to oversee the internal governance of All Under Heaven.
Therefore, the principle of marriage states:
“The Son of Heaven and the Empress
are like the sun and the moon,
the *Yīn* and the *Yáng*,
things that rely upon each other to complete their function.”
At the beginning of the *Hàn* dynasty, they followed the titles of *Qín*:
The Emperor’s mother was called *Huáng Tàihòu*;
The Empress was called *Huánghòu*;
and ranks such as *Měirén*, *Liángrén*, *Bāzǐ*, and *Qīzǐ* were added.
Reaching the reign of *Xiàowǔ*, he established the rank of *Jiéyú* and others, totaling fourteen grades.
Descending to the *Wèi* and *Jìn* dynasties,
the titles for empresses and empress dowagers
all followed the *Hàn* precedents;
but from the rank of *Fūrén* downward,
there were increases and decreases throughout the generations.
*Gāo Zǔ* quelled disorder and restored correctness,
he deeply recognized the dangers of extravagance and excess,
wore coarse clothing, ate simple food,
and focused foremost on frugality.
His consort of virtue died early,
leaving the *Chángqiū* position empty.
The number of concubines and palace women
was not modified or added to.
*Tài Zōng* and *Shì Zǔ* came from collateral princely lines,
and their consorts likewise died prematurely,
nor did they establish the inner palace.
The current compilation of records
merely serves to fill in the gaps.
Empress *Xiàn* of *Tài Zǔ*, née *Zhāng*, personal name *Shàngróu*,
was a native of *Fànyáng Fāngchéng*.
Her grandfather, *Cìhuì*,
was the Administrator of *Púyáng* during the *Sòng*.
The Empress’s mother, née *Xiāo*,
was the paternal cousin of Emperor *Wén Dì*.
The Empress,
during the *Yuánjiā* era of the *Sòng*, was a consort to Emperor *Wén Dì*.
She gave birth to *Chángshā Xuānwǔ Wáng Yì* and *Yǒngyáng Zhāowáng Fū*,
and subsequently gave birth to *Gāo Zǔ*.
Initially,
the Empress was once indoors
when she suddenly saw calamus growing flowers in the courtyard,
shining with brilliant colors
unlike anything found in the world.
The Empress looked in astonishment
and said to her attendants:
“Do you see it?”
They replied:
“We do not see it.”
The Empress said:
“I have heard that those who see it will attain wealth and nobility.”
She immediately took and swallowed it.
That month she gave birth to *Gāo Zǔ*.
On the night she was about to give birth,
the Empress saw figures wearing robes and caps lined up in attendance in the courtyard.
Next, she gave birth to *Héngyáng Xuānwáng Chàng* and *Yìxīng Zhāo Cháng Gōngzhǔ Lìngyì*.
In the seventh year of *Sòng Tàishǐ* [471 CE],
she died in the residential quarter of *Tóngxià Lǐ* in *Mòlíng* County,
and was buried on the hill in *Dōngchéng Lǐ*, *Wǔjìn* County.
In the fifth month, *Jiǎchén* day, of the first year of *Tiānjiān* [502 CE],
she was posthumously granted the honored title of Empress (*Huánghòu*),
with the posthumous name *Xiàn*.
Her father was *Mùzhī*,
courtesy name *Sījìng*,
the sixth-generation descendant of *Jìn Sīkōng Huá*.
Her great-grandfather, *Yú*, was implicated in *Huá*'s execution
and was banished to *Xīnggǔ*.
Before arriving, he was recalled.
Upon crossing the river,
he served as an Attendant to the Chancellor
and a Retainer to the Crown Prince.
*Mùzhī* was upright and refined in his youth,
and possessed keen judgment.
During the *Sòng Yuánjiā* era,
he served as *Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng*.
He was friends with *Lìbù Shàngshū Jiāng Zhàn* and *Tàizǐ Zuǒshuài Yuán Shú*.
*Shú* recommended him to *Shǐxīng Wáng Jùn*,
and *Jùn* greatly welcomed and accepted him.
*Mùzhī* perceived the seeds of impending disaster
and sought to avoid the misfortune,
so he spoke to *Zhàn*, requesting an outside posting.
*Zhàn* intended to employ him in an eastern county,
but he resolutely begged for a distant commandery.
After some time,
he was appointed *Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn* and Administrator of *Jiāozhǐ*.
His administration achieved unusual success.
When the Regional Inspector died,
the region of *Jiāo* fell into great chaos.
*Mùzhī* used a combination of might and kindness to stabilize and soothe the people,
and the territory became peaceful.
Emperor *Wén Dì* of *Sòng* heard of this and praised him,
intending to make him the Regional Inspector of *Jiāozhōu*,
but he died of illness.
His son, *Hóngjí*,
courtesy name *Zhēnyì*,
served as *Zhènxī Cānjūn* at the beginning of the *Qí* dynasty,
and died in office.
When *Gāo Zǔ* ascended the throne,
he posthumously presented *Mùzhī* with the title *Guānglù Dàfū*,
and added the Golden Seal.
Furthermore, an edict stated:
“My late maternal uncle, the *Qí Zhènxī Cānjūn*,
possessed an inherent refinement and elegant virtue,
and long shared the ranks of the famous.
His allotted years were not long,
and his brilliance was hidden by an early demise.
Having endured hardship in Our youth,
Our feeling for him is intensely deep.
Although we were able to establish our residence,
we were unable to present him with carriages (due to his early death).
Thinking of him long gone,
Our heart aches at every sight.
He shall be posthumously presented with the title *Tíngwèi Qīng*.”
*Hóngjí* had no son.
His paternal cousin *Hóngcè* allowed his third son, *Zuǎn*, to become the heir.
He has a separate biography.
Empress *Dé* of *Gāo Zǔ*, née *Xī*, personal name *Huī*,
was a native of *Gāopíng Jīnxiāng*.
Her grandfather, *Shào*,
was the Libationer of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐ Jìjiǔ*),
and concurrently served as the Tutor to the Prince of *Dōnghǎi*.
Her father, *Yè*,
was a Retainer to the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Shèrén*),
and died young.
Initially,
when the Empress's mother, Princess *Xúnyáng*, was pregnant,
she dreamed she would give birth to a noble child.
When the Empress was born,
a red light shone inside the room,
making all objects clearly visible.
The family members were all astonished by this.
A sorceress said that this girl’s radiance was extraordinary
and might cause harm,
so they performed an exorcism ritual by the riverbank.
The Empress was bright and intelligent as a child,
excelled at clerk script (*Lìshū*),
and read histories and biographies.
As for needlework and domestic tasks,
there was nothing she did not practice proficiently.
Emperor *Hòu Fèi Dì* of *Sòng* intended to take her as his Empress;
At the beginning of the *Qí* dynasty,
*Ānlù Wáng Miǎn* also wished to marry her. Lady *Xī* declined both, citing female ailments,
and the arrangements ceased.
At the end of the *Jiànyuán* era,
*Gāo Zǔ* first married her.
She gave birth to Princess *Yǒngxīng Yùyáo*,
Princess *Yǒngshì Yùwǎn*,
and Princess *Yǒngkāng Yùhuán*.
In the fifth year of *Jiànwǔ* [498 CE],
when *Gāo Zǔ* was made Regional Inspector of *Yōngzhōu*,
he first proceeded to the post,
and only later summoned the Empress to join him.
Not long after arriving in the province,
in the eighth month of the first year of *Yǒngyuán* [499 CE], she died in the official residence in *Xiāngyáng*,
at the age of thirty-two.
That year she was brought back and buried on the hill in *Dōngchéng Lǐ*, *Wǔjìn* County, *Nán Dōnghǎi*, *Nán Xúzhōu*.
In the second year of *Zhōngxīng* [502 CE],
the *Qí* court advanced *Gāo Zǔ*’s position to Chancellor (*Xiàngguó*),
enfeoffed him with ten commanderies,
as *Liáng Gōng*.
An imperial edict posthumously conferred the title of *Liáng Gōng Fēi* upon the Empress.
When *Gāo Zǔ* ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Empress (*Huánghòu*).
The relevant officials deliberated on her posthumous name.
Minister *Yuē*, who was *Lìbù Shàngshū* and concurrent *Yòu Púshè*, offered the following deliberation:
“Establishing a title and leaving a name
is a principle that illuminates the everlasting.
The former Empress responded to the auspicious lunar virtue,
matching the spiritual potency of the Earth.
Her gentle example fostered the *Yīn* transformation,
and her ceremonial demeanor extended far.
She was the worthy match established by Heaven,
the meaning of her union predating the marriage itself.
Yet her divine virtue was concealed too soon,
preventing her from witnessing the ascent to the mandate.
It is proper to follow her glorious conduct as a model
to illuminate this grand ceremony.
Reverently examining the law of posthumous naming:
The loyal, harmonious, and purely complete is called *Dé*.
The noble who loves ritual is called *Dé*.
It is fitting to honor her as Empress *Dé*.”
The imperial edict followed this recommendation.
Her tomb was named *Xiūlíng*.
The Empress’s father, *Yè*,
was posthumously presented by imperial edict with the title *Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū*.
*Yè* married Princess *Xúnyáng*, daughter of Emperor *Wén Dì* of *Sòng*.
At the beginning of the *Qí* dynasty, she was demoted and enfeoffed as *Sōngzī Xiànjūn*.
*Yè*'s son, *Fàn*,
was the Secretary and Staff Officer to the Prince of *Línchuān* in the Central Army (*Zhōngjūn Línchuān Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn*).
was a person from Línyí, Lángxié.
Her grandfather, Jiǎn,
was the Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and Duke Wénxiàn of Nánchāng.
The Empress was gentle, intelligent, and virtuous in her youth.
Her uncle, Jiǎn, saw her and said:
“She is the female model of our family.”
In the eleventh year of Tiānjiān (512 CE),
she was appointed Consort of the Prince of Jìn'ān.
She gave birth to Crown Prince Āi, Dàqì,
the Prince of Nánjùn, Dàlián,
and Princess Chángshān, Miàosì.
In the tenth month of the third year of Zhōngdàtōng (531 CE),
she was appointed Crown Prince Consort.
In the third month of the third year of Tàiqīng (549 CE),
she passed away in the Yǒngfú Palace Chamber,
at the age of forty-five.
That year,
Tài-zōng ascended the throne,
and posthumously elevated her to Empress,
with the posthumous title Jiǎn.
In the ninth month of the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
she was interred at Zhuānglíng.
Earlier, an imperial edict stated:
“The interment of Empress Jiǎn has been scheduled.
In the past, Bālíng of the Western Capital,
used the mountain as the tomb;
Shòulíng of the Eastern Hàn,
was merely a flowing stream.
We happen to be facing difficult times,
with famine and exhausted populace.
We intend to personally lead Our subjects
to forever demonstrate thrift and simplicity.
The construction currently underway at Zhuānglíng
must prioritize frugality and moderation.”
Furthermore, he commanded Xiāo Zǐfàn, the Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal), to compose the lamentation inscription.
Her father, Qiān,
courtesy name Sījì,
was originally named Xuánchéng.
Because his name shared a character with the taboo name of Emperor Gāo of Qí,
he thus changed it.
As a son of a nobleman, he began his career as a Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Gentleman),
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (Attendant at the Crown Prince’s Gate).
He inherited the title of Duke of Nánchāng County,
and was sent out as the Grand Administrator of Yìxīng.
Returning, he served as a Consultative Advisor to the Pylot Cavalry General (Piàojì Zīyì),
and was successively promoted to Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gates),
and Right Chief Clerk of the Sītú (Minister of the Masses).
His character was stable and simple,
and he did not associate closely with the powerful figures of the time.
He once casually said to his sons:
“Our family status
is known as a common lineage (Sùzú).
We can naturally advance steadily with the flow,
and there is no need for us to seek position through improper means.”
At the end of Yǒngyuán (c. 500 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
but he did not accept the post.
When Gāo-zǔ established his governing headquarters (Bàfǔ),
he was appointed as Consultative Counselor to the Dàsīmǎ (Grand Marshal).
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
concurrently holding the post of Yuèqí Xiàowèi (Commander of the Swift Cavalry).
When Gāo-zǔ received the abdication,
an edict stated:
“The generations-long sacrifices of Tíngjiān
were not abolished in Zōngzhōu.
Yuè Yì being granted territory
was clearly displayed in the mighty Hàn.
The late Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and Duke of Nánchāng of Qí
embraced distinction and practiced the Way.
During the founding of Qí from obscurity,
his bright plans and assisting counsel
matched the examples of the past.
Although Zǐfáng (Zhāng Liáng) became a magnificent Imperial Mentor,
and Wénruò (Xún Yuè) achieved eminence comparable to a King’s Assistant,
they were no greater than he.
We have received the mandate of the calendar and the imperial charts (Lì Shòu Tú).
In renewing this precious destiny,
the abundant presentation of jade and silk
follows fixed regulations for promotion and demotion.
Reflecting upon the previous dynasty,
We respectfully consider his glorious achievements.
Not only should his great accomplishments be recognized,
but righteousness requires honoring and establishing his line.
Qiān shall be demoted in title from Duke of Nánchāng County to Marquis,
with a stipend of one thousand households.”
Qiān inherited the noble rank,
and was promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū (Minister of the Treasury).
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (505 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng,
and soon after transferred to Wújùn.
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he returned to the capital as Tàifǔ Qīng (Minister of the Privy Treasury),
concurrently holding the title of Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Rear Army),
and was promoted to Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
In the eleventh year (512 CE),
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Secretariat),
and granted the additional title of Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary).
At that time, Gāo-zǔ was constructing the Dà'àijìng Temple on Zhōngshān.
Qiān’s old villa was near the temple,
possessing more than eighty *qǐng* of fertile land,
which was originally the land granted by Prime Minister Wáng Dǎo of the Jìn dynasty.
Gāo-zǔ sent a Chief Scribe to announce his intention and ask Qiān to sell the land,
intending to donate it to the temple.
Qiān replied to the intention, saying:
“This land is not for sale;
if it is an imperial order to seize it,
then I dare not speak against it.”
His response was also casual and slighting.
Gāo-zǔ was angered,
and consequently instructed the market office to appraise the land’s value,
and forcibly returned the payment to him.
Because of this insubordination to the imperial will,
he was sent out as Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
While in the commandery, he stayed in bed sick and did not attend to affairs.
He was recalled,
and reinstated as Dùzhī Shàngshū (Minister of the Treasury),
granted the additional title of Jǐshì Zhōng (Attendant at the Palace Gate),
and concurrently held the post of Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Commander of the Archery Division).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
In the tenth month of the third year of Pǔtōng (522 CE), he died,
at the age of forty-nine.
An edict granted him posthumously the titles of Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal),
with the posthumous title Ān.
His son, Guī, inherited the rank,
and has a separate biography.
Dīng Guìpín (Honored Consort Dīng) of Gāo-zǔ, whose personal name was Lìngguāng,
was a native of Qiáoguó,
whose family had resided in Xiāngyáng for generations.
The Guìpín was born in Fánchéng.
There was an unusual occurrence of divine light,
and purple vapor filled the room.
Therefore,
the character
“guāng”
was used as her personal name.
The physiognomist said:
“This girl will become exceedingly noble.”
When Gāo-zǔ governed the province,
the Dīng family managed to inform him through an intermediary.
The Guìpín was then fourteen years old,
and Gāo-zǔ took her into his household.
Initially,
the Guìpín had been born with a red mole on her left arm;
medical treatments could not remove it.
However, at this time, it suddenly disappeared without effort.
Serving Empress Dé (Dégōng), she was cautious, reverent, and respectful.
Once, while beside the table holding the scriptures used for offerings,
she faintly saw a divine being,
and she privately considered this extraordinary.
When Gāo-zǔ raised his righteous army,
and Crown Prince Zhāomíng was just being born and raised,
the Guìpín and the Crown Prince remained in the provincial capital.
When the capital was pacified,
they returned to the Imperial Capital.
In the fifth month of the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
the relevant department petitioned for her to be designated a Guìrén (Honored Lady),
but she was not yet formally installed;
in the eighth month of that year,
she was again designated Guìpín (Honored Consort),
her rank being above the Sān Fūrén (Three Ladies),
residing in the Xiǎnyáng Palace.
When the Crown Prince was established,
the relevant department submitted a memorial stating: According to the rites,
the mother is ennobled because of her son’s nobility.
It is unacceptable for the birth mother of the Imperial Heir
to receive no deference.
In the sixth month of the first year of Tàiyù of Sòng (472 CE),
it was debated whether the hundred officials should honor Chén Tàifēi,
the Emperor’s birth mother, with the deference due to a superior official.
This implies that when Emperor Míng of Sòng was alive,
the hundred officials had not yet shown deference.
We humbly believe
that the principle,
“the mother is ennobled because of her son’s nobility,”
The Crown Prince acts as the assistant to the Imperial
Pinnacle.
Everyone throughout the land pays him the deference due to a superior official.
Since full rites are paid to the Imperial Heir,
it is unacceptable for his birth mother to receive no deference.
However, as consorts and concubines of the Emperor,
they are conceptually separated from the external world.
Based on principle and precedent,
there is no standard way for deference to be paid (by external officials).
Now, the Crown Prince possesses sagacity and wisdom,
and the rites due to the Heir have been fully prepared since early times.
The principle of the son’s nobility ennobling the mother
is also covered by old statutes.
All princely consorts and imperial princesses who regularly maintain
communications,
as well as the consorts of the Six Palaces and the Three Ladies (Sān Fūrén)—although ranked equally with the Guìpín—
should all honor the Guìpín with the same rites used to honor the Crown Prince.
During the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
the ministers of the principalities of Shǐ
xīng and Wǔlíng began to honor the birth mothers, Consort Pān Shūfēi and Lady Lù Shūyuán, with the deference due to a superior official.
Although the Guìpín is not considered the Lady of the Palace (Xiǎojūn) by the palace officials,
the principle is not different,
and should be applied as it was in Sòng
During the Tàiyù era, the court officials debated that all officials should pay respect to the mother who gave birth to Jìng Dì,
the principle of the matter being exactly the same.
They proposed that palace eunuchs rendering respect
should follow the same rites as officials:
proceeding to the Shénhǔmén (Gate of Divine Tigers) to present memorials
and offer salutations;
and celebrating on annual festivals
should also be the same way.
Women had no duties outside the inner chambers.
Congratulations, inquiries, and memorials
should merely be reported by the relevant officials.
In the way of the married
woman,
morally she has no independent authority;
if she does not rely upwardly on her husband,
then she must rely downwardly on her son.
The way to honor one’s parents
should fully achieve the honor deserved,
and there has never been a case where the actions of the son
were performed yet the source of the honor was insufficient.
Therefore, in the *Chūnqiū* (Spring and Autumn Annals), whenever the King appointed someone as *Fūrén*,
her ritual rank was equal to that of the son.
Although the feudal states differed regarding the Crown Prince,
the principle of according
supreme honor was not different.
Precedent from previous dynasties
is widely available in historical records.
The *Guìpín*, having borne the primary heir
and secured the great enterprise,
should enjoy rites equal to those of the Crown Prince;
this truly is an old statute.
Reviewing
how the *Guìpín* rank was first established in former dynasties:
her position ranked below the Empress,
but her noble rank had no precedent (in terms of matching officials);
for the official next in line below her,
the position was regarded as equal to that of the Xiàngguó (Chancellor),
and the noble rank comparable to that of a Prince (Zhūhóu Wáng).
The rites accorded to this *Guìpín*
were already higher than the general court ranks;
how much more so when she is the mother model of the Spring Palace (Crown Prince's residence),
a position whose significance far exceeds ordinary reckoning.
Moreover, the Crown Princess serves as the consort,
following grand regulations;
for the wife (Crown Princess) to surpass the mother-in-law (*Guìpín*),
greatly violates the proper order.
It was thus proposed
that the system and regulations for the *Guìpín*
should be identical to those of the Crown Prince.
Consequently, the *Guìpín* was fully accorded the system, regulations, and rites
identical to those of the Crown Prince,
and when speaking (of her decree), the term *Lìng* was used.
The *Guìpín*'s nature was benevolent and forgiving.
While residing in the palace,
her interactions and governance of those below her
won all their affection.
She disliked extravagant adornments,
and her utensils and clothing contained nothing rare or beautiful.
She never used her position for private visits with relatives.
When Gāozǔ promoted Buddhism,
the *Guìpín* embraced it and practiced it,
completely eliminating rich meats
and continuously eating vegetarian meals.
On the day she received the precepts,
sweet dew (*Gānlù*) descended in front of the palace hall,
covering an area fifteen *chǐ* square.
She grasped the core teachings
of all the scriptures established by Gāozǔ.
She was particularly proficient in the *Jìng Míng Jīng* (Vimalakīrti Nirdeśa Sūtra).
All the offerings and grants she received
were used to fund Buddhist rites.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng, on the *gēngchén* day of the eleventh month, she died,
and was interred temporarily at the Línyún Diàn in the Eastern Palace,
aged forty-two.
An imperial edict commanded Zhāng Zuǎn, Assistant Administrator of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù Láng*), to compose the Eulogy (*Āicè Wén*), which read: The path to the grave having been opened,
the cinnamon jar (of wine) stands empty and still;
the dragon canopy has been spread,
the elephant robes are about to be lifted up.
The Emperor grieves that the Jade Terrace is forever closed,
mourning that the Lofty City is no longer trod upon.
He has ceased the rustic songs of entertainment
and abolished the complete fasting from the ritual canon.
The customs of the *Cǎifán* ode persist,
her influence extended throughout the Southern State.
Therefore, he commanded the official historians
to spread the virtues of the consort.
The text reads: The essence of Xuān Wěi,
the brilliance of the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers;
returning to the sovereign’s sleeve,
giving birth to this radiating brightness.
Born from the very beginning,
she was raised during this age;
the pivoting lightning encircled the suburb,
divine light
illuminated the house.
When she reached the age of marriage,
she possessed brilliance and early grace;
her reputation reached Qǐyáng,
her fame spread throughout the Central Valley.
The Dragon Virtue was in the field,
and thus offered this sacrifice respectfully;
the transformation of the feminine principle ended the previous era,
and the royal
influence thus began.
In every movement, she sought counsel on ritual forms;
when speaking, she consulted historical precedents;
she brought order to her household,
modeling behavior for the national regulations.
Receiving this compassionate mandate,
she settled her heart upon it;
wearing the embroidered *Dí* skirt and adorned *héng* pendants,
her jades chimed with refined tones.
At midday, she contemplated caution,
at the full moon, she remembered admonitions;
how could she not be reverent,
as Heaven is high and oversees all.
The profound harmony could not be maintained,
the ritual robes were prematurely incomplete;
who
can complete all things?
Her fragrant legacy is glorious.
The pure soul was chaste and bright,
illuminating the Purple Palace clearly;
extending kindness to subordinates without hurting them,
seeking the virtuous without obscuring them.
She practiced frugality as a principle,
and served the ancestors with reverence;
precious metals and jades
were not played with,
baskets and hampers were not discarded.
Auspices flowed from her virtuous transformation,
good fortune marked her kin and the worthy;
she emulated Zhēnchāng and Yìqǐ,
educating Lǔ and influencing Yān.
Just when discussing wifely instruction,
clarifying and displaying proper conduct in the inner chambers,
the dark
pool was early sealed,
and the Xiāng and Yuán Rivers flowed to the tomb.
Displayed clothing lost its brilliance,
the red curtain stopped its activity;
longing binds the Crown Prince’s palace,
grief runs deep among the vassal princes.
Alas!
The sacred tortoise shell yielded favorable divination,
allowing the coffin to follow the ancestral route;
the assembled officials lined up,
following the grandeur step by step.
The sun is dim and hides the spring,
the wind is mournful and weaves sorrow;
leaving the Lofty
Chambers reluctantly,
adorning the new palace (tomb) while pausing for a long time.
Alas!
Raising the starry banner of the vermilion flag,
brandishing the embroidered skirt of the ceremonial carriage;
placing the spirit money causing profound sadness,
floating the desolate pipes causing frozen grief.
Leaving prepared items in the burial chamber,
closing
the heavy gates upon the earth mound;
the pepper-scented warmth remains as before,
but the orchid hall is dark and sunless.
Alas!
The exalted righteousness of the side chambers,
the female historiographers (*tóngguǎn*) are pleased;
her Way transformed the customs of Yú,
her merit matched the traces of Táng.
Such a gentle person,
with splendid virtue and red slippers;
imparting this to Heaven and Earth,
lasting without
end.
Alas!
The relevant officials proposed the posthumous title Mù.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
she was posthumously honored as Mù Tàihòu.
The Tàihòu's father, Zhòngqiān,
at the beginning of Tiānjiān,
held the official post of Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (*Cìshǐ*).
Gāozǔ's Rǔan Xiūróng, personal name Lìngyíng,
was originally named Shí,
and was a native of Yúyáo, Kuàijī.
Yáo Guāng, Prince of Shǐ'ān during Qí, took her in.
When Yáo Guāng was defeated,
she entered the palace of Dōnghūn.
When Jiànkāng city was pacified,
Gāozǔ accepted her as a *Cǎinǚ*.
In the eighth month of the seventh year of Tiānjiān,
she gave birth to Shìzǔ.
Soon after, she was appointed *Xiūróng*,
and always followed Shìzǔ when he governed his feudal state.
In the sixth month of the sixth year of Dàtóng (大同),
she passed away (hōng) in her inner chambers in Jiāngzhōu (江州),
at the age of sixty-seven.
In the eleventh month of that year,
she was returned and interred on Tōngwàng Shān (通望山) in Jiāngníng Xiàn (江寧縣).
Her posthumous title (shì) was Xuān (宣).
When Shìzǔ (世祖) ascended the throne,
the relevant authorities proposed posthumously honoring her as Wénxuān Tàihòu (文宣太后).
In the second year of Chéngshèng (承聖),
the Empress Dowager's (Tàihòu) father, Qí (齊), formerly Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請), Língbǎo Sànqí Chángshì (靈寶散騎常侍), and Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn (左衞將軍), was posthumously granted these titles.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wǔkāng Xiàn (武康縣侯),
with an estate of five hundred households;
his mother, Madame Chén (Chén Shì),
was titled the Marchioness of Wǔkāng (Wǔkāng Hóu Fūrén).
The Imperial Consort Xú (Xú Fēi) of Shìzǔ (世祖), personal name Zhāopèi (昭佩),
was a person from Tán (郯) in Dōnghǎi (東海).
Her grandfather was Xiàosì (孝嗣),
Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Duke Wénzhōng (Wénzhōng Gōng) of Zhījiāng (枝江).
Her father was Gǔn (緄),
Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of Xìnwǔ (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn).
In the twelfth month of the sixteenth year of Tiānjiān (天監),
she was appointed Princess Consort (Fēi) of the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng).
She gave birth to the Heir Apparent Fāngděng (方等) and Princess Hánzhēn (含貞) of Yìchāng (益昌).
In the fifth month of the third year of Tàiqīng (太清),
she was condemned and died,
and was buried at Wǎguān Sì (瓦官寺) in Jiānglíng (江陵).
The Official Historian comments: The conduct of the Empresses and Consorts supports the imperial ways,
spreading transformation throughout the world,
likely derived from the principles found in the *Gě Tán* (葛覃) and *Guān Jū* (關雎) odes.
As for Noble Consort Mù (Mù Guìpín),
her brilliance and splendor were manifest early,
she gave birth to the primary worthy successor,
and her virtue excelled throughout the six palaces.
Truly beautiful!
That the Imperial Consort Xú (Xú Fēi) of Shìzǔ (世祖) was without proper conduct
and thus brought about her own destruction,
is fitting.
Biography 2 (Lièzhuàn Dì Èr): Crown Prince Zhāomíng (昭明 Tàizǐ), Crown Prince Āi (哀 Tàizǐ), Crown Prince Mǐnhuái (愍懷 Tàizǐ)
Crown Prince Zhāomíng (Zhāomíng Tàizǐ), personal name Tǒng (統), courtesy name Déshī (德施),
was the eldest son of Gāozǔ (高祖).
His mother was Noble Consort Dīng (Dīng Guìpín).
Initially,
Gāozǔ had no sons.
When the righteous army rose,
the Crown Prince was born in Xiāngyáng (襄陽) in the ninth month of the first year of Zhōngxīng (中興) of Qí (齊).
When Gāozǔ had accepted the abdication,
the relevant authorities petitioned to establish the Heir Apparent,
but Gāozǔ, believing that the realm was only newly settled
and that the hundred regulations were mostly incomplete,
did not grant permission.
The assembled ministers insisted,
and in the eleventh month of the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
At that time, the Crown Prince was young,
and according to the old customs, he resided within the inner court.
He was appointed to the officials of the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng),
and both civil and military officials were assigned duty tours in the Yǒngfú Shěng (永福省).
The Crown Prince was intelligent and astute from birth;
at the age of three, he studied the *Classic of Filial Piety* (Xiàojīng) and the *Analects* (Lúnyǔ);
by the age of five, he had read all Five Classics (Wǔjīng)
and could recite them entirely from memory.
In the *gēngxū* day of the sixth month of the fifth year,
he first moved out to reside in the Eastern Palace.
The Crown Prince was inherently benevolent and filial.
Since moving out of the palace,
he felt sorrowful longing and was unhappy.
Gāozǔ knew this,
and commanded him to offer respects once every five days,
often keeping him to stay overnight in the Yǒngfú Shěng,
and sometimes he would not return to the palace until after three or five days.
In the ninth month of the eighth year,
he lectured on the *Classic of Filial Piety* in the Shòu'ān Diàn (壽安殿),
fully grasping the profound meanings.
After the lecture was finished,
he personally presided over the *shìdiàn* (sacrifice to Confucius) at the National University (Guóxué).
On the first day of the first month of the fourteenth year,
Gāozǔ presided over the court,
and performed the capping ceremony (guān) for the Crown Prince in the Tàijí Diàn (太極殿).
According to the old system,
the Crown Prince wore the Yuǎnyóu Guān (遠遊冠),
adorned with a golden cicada and kingfisher feathers as tassels;
but on this occasion,
an edict commanded the addition of the Golden Bóshān (Jīnbóshān) ornament.
The Crown Prince had handsome features
and fine manners.
When reading, he could take in several lines at once,
and remembered everything he saw.
Whenever he traveled, feasted, or performed the Zǔ Dào (road god) ceremony,
he composed poems of ten or more rhymes.
Sometimes he was commanded to compose *fu* (rhapsodies) using difficult rhymes,
and he would instantly gather his thoughts and complete them,
without needing any corrections or revisions.
Gāozǔ greatly promoted Buddhism
and personally gave lectures;
the Crown Prince also highly revered and believed in the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
reading all the various scriptures.
Therefore, he established a separate Huìyì Diàn (慧義殿) within the palace,
dedicated solely to holding Dharma assemblies.
He invited famous monks,
and their discussions were continuous.
The Crown Prince established his own interpretations of the concepts of the Two Truths (Èrdì) and the Dharma Body (Fǎshēn),
both containing original insights.
In the fourth month of the first year of Pǔtōng (普通),
sweet dew descended upon the Huìyì Diàn (慧義殿).
Everyone believed this was due to the inspiration of his utmost virtue.
In the eleventh month of the third year,
Dàn (憺), the Prince of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Wáng), passed away (hōng).
According to previous precedent,
since the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng) was exempt from mourning rites for collateral relatives,
written correspondence was carried out according to the usual protocol.
The Crown Prince felt uncertain about this,
and commanded his attendant (pú) Liú Xiàochuò (劉孝綽) to deliberate on the matter.
Xiàochuò deliberated, saying:
"Consulting the *Records of Eastern Palace Rituals* (Dōng Gōng Yíjì) compiled by Zhāng Jìng (張鏡),
it states: 'For those who express mourning during the three days after death,
no music shall be played for more than a month;
drumming and wind instruments shall cease performance,
and the limit of mourning attire is the same.'
Considering the principle of 'exemption for collateral relations,'
the meaning lies in the removal of mourning attire.
Although the attire may be omitted,
how can the emotion not contain grief?
The cessation of military music and songs [nàogē]
is indeed due to this.
Since there is grief,
it is appropriate to use the expression of joint mourning (jiān mù).
After the completion of the *zú kū* ceremony,
music should resume as normal.
The statement that the expression of grief ceases
corresponds to this precedent.
I suggest that the expression of joint mourning should still be used
until *zú kū*."

The Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Púyè), Xú Miǎn (徐勉), the Left Commandant (Zuǒ Shuài), Zhōu Shě (周捨), and the Household Administrator (Jiā Lìng), Lù Xiāng (陸襄), all agreed with Xiàochuò's proposal.
The Crown Prince issued an order, saying:
"Zhāng Jìng's *Records of Rituals* state: 'Following the rites for a common scholar,
mourning is expressed until the end of the required month of mourning attire.'
It also says: 'Generally, those who express mourning during the three days after death,
shall not play music for more than a month.'
The deliberation by Attendant Liú (Liú Pú)
says: 'The principle of 'exemption for collateral relations'
lies in the removal of mourning attire.
Although the attire may be omitted,
how can the emotion not contain grief?
After the *zú kū* ceremony,
music resumes as normal.
The statement that the expression of grief ceases
corresponds to this precedent.'
Reflecting on the argument regarding emotional grief,
it does not cease immediately after *zú kū*.
If the argument is based on emotion,
this is the first difficulty.
To adopt Zhāng Jìng's instruction regarding playing music
but abandon Zhāng Jìng's instruction regarding expressing grief—
from the words of a single source, Zhāng Jìng,
the choices made (acceptance and rejection) are different.
This is the second difficulty.
Household Administrator Lù (Lù Jiālìng) only mentioned 'it has been practiced for many years'
which I fear is not a factual verification.
Although this has been adopted for many years,
I have always felt uneasy about the intention.
Recently, I often brought this up outside for inquiry,
and my original intent
was that there should still be words of mourning and commemoration.
How could Zhāng not know that playing music is a major matter
and expressing grief is a minor matter?
The reason he adopted the minor (grief) and ignored the major (music)
must have had a basis.
Regarding events like the New Year's Day *Liù Yì* (six-row dance),
these matters constitute the laws of the state.
Although one's feelings may be unsettled,
the rites cannot be abolished.
The military music of drums and pipes,
compared to this, is also similar.
However, compared to written correspondence,
the matter becomes minor,
and can be governed by personal feeling.
Ritual music originates externally,
written correspondence originates internally.
Music pertains to others,
writing pertains to oneself.
The proposal by Attendant Liú
immediately fails to settle my feelings.
Let the scholars deliberate further on the inner meaning."
The Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng), Míng Shānbīn (明山賓), and the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi), Zhū Yì (朱异), deliberated,
stating:
"The relief from expressing mourning
should be at the end of the mourning month."
Thereupon, he ordered the officials in charge of records to comply and implement this,
making it a permanent standard.
In the eleventh month of the seventh year,
Imperial Consort Guìpín became ill.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) returned to Yǒngfú Residence
to attend to her sickness morning and night,
not loosening his belt.
When she passed away,
he walked, following the procession back to the palace.
When reaching the temporary interment site,
no water or liquid passed his lips.
Every time he wept, he was overcome by grief and fainted.
Gāozǔ sent the Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Gù Xié to issue an edict, saying:
“Harming oneself without destroying one's nature
is the rule established by the Sages.
According to the Rites,
failing to survive mourning rituals is comparable to being unfilial.
While I am still here,
how can you destroy yourself like this!
You must immediately force yourself to take food and drink.”
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) obeyed the imperial command,
and then consumed several *gě* (measures).
From that time until the burial,
he consumed one *shēng* of barley gruel daily.
Gāozǔ again issued an edict, saying:
“I hear that what you are consuming is excessively little,
and you are becoming increasingly emaciated and ill.
I currently have no other sickness,
but precisely because you are like this,
my chest is also blocked up and becoming sick.
Therefore, you should force yourself to take gruel and congee,
so as not to make my heart anxious.”
Although he repeatedly received imperial commands urging and compelling him,
he stopped at only one *yì* (measure) daily,
and did not taste the flavor of vegetables or fruit.
His body was naturally robust;
his waist was ten spans (*wéi*) around.
By this point, he had shrunk and lost more than half his size.
Every time he entered court,
none of the officials or common people who saw him failed to weep.
Since the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) came of age,
Gāozǔ had made him oversee all affairs of state.
Those from the hundred offices, internal and external, who presented memorials crowded before him.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) was lucid regarding general affairs;
even the minutest detail he understood thoroughly.
Whenever a memorial presented contained errors, mistakes, clever deceit, or falsehoods,
he would immediately investigate and analyze it,
showing whether it was acceptable or not,
and then calmly order corrections.
He never impeached or punished a single person.
In settling legal cases and judgments,
he granted complete pardon in many instances.
The whole world called him benevolent.
His nature was broad, peaceable, and tolerant of the masses.
Joy or anger did not show in his countenance.
He attracted and received learned and talented gentlemen,
rewarding and cherishing them without tiring.
He personally discussed classical texts and documents,
sometimes consulting with scholars regarding antiquity and the present;
when free, he would follow this up with literary composition and writing,
making this his consistent habit.
At that time, the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng) contained nearly thirty thousand volumes of books,
and famous talents were all gathered there.
The flourishing state of literature
had not been seen since the Jìn and Sòng Dynasties.
His nature loved mountains and rivers.
In Xuánpǔ, he dug and built,
establishing additional pavilions and lodges,
and wandered there with court officials known for their simplicity.
He once floated a boat on the rear pond.
The Marquis of Pānyú, Guǐ (Pānyú Hóu Guǐ), highly praised the spot, saying,
“This place is suitable for performing female music (nǚyuè).”
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) did not reply.
He recited a line from Zuǒ Sī’s Poem on Summoning the Recluse (Zhāo Yǐn Shī), saying:
“Why must there be strings and bamboo (music)?
The mountains and waters have a clear sound.”
The Marquis was ashamed and stopped.
For more than twenty years since leaving the palace,
he had not kept instruments or musicians.
When he was young,
he was commanded to receive a troupe of female performers from the Bureau of Court Music (Tàiyuè),
but they were entirely against his preferences.
During the Pǔtōng era,
when the great army campaigned in the north,
grain in the capital became expensive.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) therefore ordered plain clothing and reduced his meals,
changing his regular feast to simple fare.
Whenever there was continuous rain or heavy snow,
he would send his trusted attendants,
to go around the villages and alleys,
to observe impoverished families.
If there were any wandering destitute along the roads,
he secretly increased the relief and gifts given to them.
He also provided cotton and silk from his personal wardrobe,
making many jackets and trousers.
In the winter months, he distributed these to the poor and freezing.
If someone died and there was nothing available for burial,
he provided coffins and caskets.
Whenever he heard that the common people near and far were suffering hardship from taxes and forced labor,
he would immediately change his expression.
He constantly felt that because the census figures were not accurate,
it was crucial to avoid disturbing them with labor.
Wúxīng Commandery (Wúxīng Jùn) had repeatedly suffered crop failure due to floods.
Someone submitted a memorial proposing to dredge a major canal to drain into the Zhè Jiāng river.
In the spring of the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
an imperial edict was issued dispatching the former Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāozhōu, Wáng Biàn, granting him temporary authority,
to mobilize male laborers from the three commanderies: Wú Commandery (Wú Jùn), Wúxīng, and Yìxīng, for the work.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ) submitted a memorial, saying:
“I humbly hear that you intend to mobilize the male laborers of the three eastern commanderies under Wáng Biàn and others,
to open irrigation channels and canals,
to divert and drain Lake Zhèn Zé,
so that the entire territory of Wúxīng
will no longer suffer flood damage.
This is truly the ultimate benevolence in showing compassion and concern,
and a far-reaching objective of strategic planning.
A temporary hardship for permanent ease
will surely yield future benefits.
However, before the trouble manifests, it is hard to observe,
and I humbly hold a foolish opinion.
I have heard that Wúxīng has suffered repeated crop failures for several years,
and the populace has largely scattered and migrated.
The ten cities of Wú Commandery (Wú Jùn)
also did not have a complete harvest.
Only Yìxīng had a harvest last autumn,
but they are not the people accustomed to corvée labor.
Currently, grain and crops in the eastern territory are still expensive,
and robberies frequently occur.
The officials in charge
do not report everything.
Now, troops sent on campaigns have not yet returned,
and strong adult males are sparse.
This, although a small undertaking,
I fear will be difficult to assemble.
Once officials call at the gate,
it quickly becomes harmful to the people.
Moreover, the locations where the laborers are mobilized
are not uniform in distance.
By the time they can be assembled together,
it will already interfere with silk farming and agriculture.
Last year was called a year of plenty,
but the public and private sectors still lack sufficient food.
If they again lose their livelihood this year,
I worry the resulting calamity will be even deeper.
Furthermore, bandits often watch for opportunities regarding the local populace's strength or weakness.
If good people are mobilized for the labor,
then plundering and robbery will greatly increase.
Wúxīng has not yet received its benefit,
but the interior regions will already suffer the resulting troubles.
I wonder if it would be possible to temporarily suspend this project
and wait until resources are plentiful and the population stable?
The Sacred Heart shows compassion for the common people,
and the divine strategy has long been established.
My views are shallow and mediocre,
and I do not understand the proper conduct of affairs,
but having this foolish thought,
I wish to submit it to Your Majesty.”
Gāozǔ issued a gracious edict to clarify the matter to him.
The Crown Prince (Tàizǐ)'s filial piety and reverence were heaven-sent.
Every time he attended court,
he would wait for the city gate to open before the fifth watch.
Although he rested in the inner hall of the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng),
one time he sat down and one time he rose up,
facing the southwest tower (where Gāozǔ often resided).
If he was summoned the night before and was due to enter the palace,
he would sit upright until dawn.
In the third month of the third year,
he fell ill.
Fearing he would burden Gāozǔ with worry,
when asked about his health,
he always forced himself to write a reply by hand.
When his condition worsened slightly,
his attendants wished to report it to the throne,
but he still refused,
saying,
“How can I let the Supreme One (Zhìzūn) know I am this unwell?”
and thereupon sobbed.
On the *Yǐsì* day of the fourth month, he passed away,
at the age of thirty-one.
Gāozǔ went to the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng),
and cried over him, expressing his deepest grief.
An edict commanded that he be encoffined in imperial robes and crown (*gǔnmiǎn*).
His posthumous title was Zhāomíng.
On the *Gēngyín* day of the fifth month,
he was interred at Ānníng Líng.
An edict commanded the Left Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ), Wáng Yún, to compose the funerary inscription (*āicè*).
The text read: The carriage decorated with clamshells suddenly stops,
the dragon steeds pace slowly;
the feather banners drive before,
the cloud streamers escort to the north.
The Emperor grieves that the successor to the bright light has dimmed,
grieves that the fragrant virtue of the heir has perished;
he stands by the military tent and sorrowfully mourns,
he overlooks the armored viewing platform and increases his sadness.
Following the customary rites,
we hereby extol his vast accomplishments;
an edict is issued to record his virtue on the banners and plumes,
and forever transmit his fine reputation in the sequence of dances.
truly he was Shàoyáng;
He was already called the Supreme Heir,
and also called the Prime Virtuous One.
His conduct mirrored Heaven, comparable in loftiness,
paired with the sun, illuminating brightly;
He maintained the sacrifices, extending blessings,
He guarded the regalia
and
passed down fragrance.
Wise and sagacious, he met the age,
morning and evening, he was present;
Externally, he broadly displayed solemnity and reverence,
internally, he contained peace and joy.
His knowledge penetrated deep secrets,
his capacity encompassed Yínghǎi;
Establishing virtue, he was not limited to one function,
his ultimate
merit was not self-controlled.
Generosity resided in his heart,
warmth and reverence formed his nature,
He followed the times in filiality and fraternity,
guiding (the nation) through strict reverence.
Everyone possessed his inherited virtue,
his kindness and harmony made him comparable to the sages.
The Three Virtues were successively proclaimed,
the myriad states celebrated together.
The stellar coordinates of Xuānwěi concealed their brilliance,
Yīn Xī loosened its structure;
Wailing sorrow was held internally,
profound grief contained lamentation.
The child wept ceaselessly,
vegetables and gruel did not overflow;
The *tán* sacrifice was observed over the months,
the cries of sorrow
were not yet finished.
Truly, he supervised governance,
and also succeeded in the suburban sacrifices;
When inquiring about health, he was solemn and grave,
when attending to meals, he was sincere and earnest.
Jīnhuá Yùzǎo,
dark steeds arrayed the chariot wheels;
He elevated the family and supported the state,
presiding over
sacrifices and bringing peace to the people.
He gloriously carried out his prescribed duties,
the myriad affairs were managed;
He was compassionate and cautious regarding common lawsuits,
diligently attending to the concerns of passes and markets.
Sincerity resided in his hidden empathy,
his demeanor showed neither anger nor extreme joy.
Earnestly and diligently, he provided widespread charity,
closely weaving together principles of grace.
Since the beginning, respecting his studies,
separating lines and punctuating sentences of the classics;
Offering wine vessels and honoring his teachers,
humbly waiting upon his tutors.
He preferred relying on guidance and practice,
not needing laborious review or instruction.
Breadth and conciseness were his domain,
timely diligence
was his effort.
He analyzed and investigated the subtle void,
his thoughts explored the intricate depths of omens.
His spirit raced through the túwěi,
his mind studied the yáohuà.
Pondering the canons and rites,
roaming freely among the volumes of texts;
He feasted heavily on the rich classics,
savoring
and chewing the core substance.
He encompassed the trends and outlines of thought,
embracing all arts and writings;
Comprehensively mastering the yellow and white silk texts,
exhausting the scope of the Qiū Fén classics.
Rolls filled the piles,
distinguishing between the Rú and Mò schools;
Gazing at the river (diagrams), he elucidated teachings,
looking toward Lǔ, he spread renown.
Chanting poems of inner nature and spirit,
how could this be merely a minor skill?
Composing words that were graceful and restrained,
following emotion, they were beautiful and delicate.
Not a single character needed correction,
the brush never stopped on the paper;
Mighty thoughts flowed like a spring,
pure stanzas accumulated like clouds.
He comprehensively reviewed the talents of the age,
netting and gathering the outstanding heroes;
Their learning was thorough and abundant,
their rhetoric tended toward richness and profusion.
Some excelled in the fields of discussion,
some were praised as gardens of literature;
The Sì Yǒu admired his virtue,
the Qī Zǐ
were ashamed of their own talent.
He invited the virtuous to his Wàng Yuàn,
cherishing guests at the Huá Chí;
Sharing his chariot and sailing in the same boat,
linking carriages and joining seats.
Spreading out writings and projecting literary brilliance,
flying cups and overflowing wine.
His grace surpassed the ceremony of setting out sweet wine,
his rewards
exceeded the gift of jade disks.
His fine customs spread far,
his grand achievements were renewed daily;
The vessel of benevolence was not weighted down,
virtue, though light, was easy to follow.
His beneficence flowed to the common people,
blessings descended from the Hundred Spirits;
The four quarters longed for righteousness,
all under Heaven returned to benevolence.
Cloud signs announced the portent,
evil influences lifted their appearances;
Stars dimmed their radiance,
mountains crumbled into rotten earth.
The spiritual presence became a guest above,
the virtuous voice departed forever;
The assembled officials lost their protective shade,
how can we seek guidance
and rely on him in peace?
Alas! How sorrowful!
The Imperial heart mourns with compassion,
deeply distressed and wailing in pain;
The successor cried out long,
the siblings increased their grief.
Admiration bound us in close association,
grief moved the masses of people;
The sorrow is like the destruction of the state,
the fear is like
the collapse of the main beam.
Alas! How sorrowful!
Early summer governed the opening,
wheat harvest marked the season;
The ceremonial guard stands vigilant in vain,
the refined essence is utterly gone.
The study curtain is hung empty,
the discussion mats have ceased to be laid out;
The empty offerings are piled high,
the lone lamp
flickers dimly.
Alas! How sorrowful!
We selected the hour and requested the day,
divinations by yarrow and tortoise shell agreed.
The secluded tomb passage was opened early,
the Dark Palace was presented complete.
The military ranks were uniformly arrayed,
civilian and military decorations shone brighter.
Formerly, when he traveled to Zhāng Fǔ,
the accompanying
retainers were silent;
Now returning to the outer suburbs,
the footmen and drivers stare in alarm.
Alas! How sorrowful!
Turning his back on the Jiàng Què, he departs afar,
slowly turning past the Qīng Mén;
Pointing toward the imperial carriage road, yet unable to advance,
gazing at the national capital but not setting foot there.
Crossing the vast slopes that rise high,
ascending
the plains, distant and profound;
The noble horses stumble and whinny sorrowfully,
the funeral chant is mournful, causing tears to flow.
Alas! How sorrowful!
Mournful sounds mingle with the flutes and pipes,
changing the sorrowful countenance of Heaven and sun;
Although the summer trees are deeply shaded,
they revert to the desolate chill of winter woods.
Having just intended to return, yet doubting again,
as if
seeking something that is suddenly lost;
We say that Heaven and Earth are without feeling,
yet he suddenly hides his form forever.
Alas! How sorrowful!
He proceeds to the shadowy silence of the Dark Palace,
resting the spirit in quiet seclusion;
His glorious reputation is passed down through great ceremonies,
his virtuous achievements are seen in his fine posthumous name.
His loyalty and integrity hang in the sun and moon,
his vast
name is broadcast between Heaven and Earth;
These are the recorded words of this humble minister,
truly written with the brush and without shame.
Alas! How sorrowful!
benevolence and virtue were well-known. When he
died, the court
and the populace were dismayed and astonished. Men and women of the capital
rushed to the palace gates,
their wailing and crying
filling the roads. The common people
of the four directions,
and the residents of the frontier regions,
all wept bitterly upon hearing the news of his death. His collected writings comprised twenty volumes;
he also compiled ancient and modern standard
pronouncements and literary speeches,
which he titled *Zhèng Xù* (正序) in ten volumes; the best of the five-character poems
were compiled as *Wénzhāng Yīnghuá* (文章英華) in twenty volumes;
and a selection of literature
(*Wénxuǎn*) in thirty volumes.
Crown Prince Āi
Dàqì (哀太子大器), courtesy name Rénzōng (仁宗), was Tàizōng's
legitimate eldest son. He was born
on the *dīngyǒu* day in the fifth month of the fourth year of Pǔtōng (普通). In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (中大通),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince
of Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery,
with a stipend of two thousand households. Soon after, he became Shìzhōng
(Attendant Counselor) and General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn),
and was granted a military band (gǔchuī). In the fourth year of Dàtóng (大同),
he was appointed as the Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe),
Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs in Yángzhōu (揚州) and Xúzhōu (徐州), Grand General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Dà Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yángzhōu,
retaining his position as Shìzhōng. In the tenth month of the second year of Tàiqīng (太清),
Hóu Jǐng
invaded the capital. The Crown Prince was ordered
to serve as the Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū) within the Palace. In the fifth month of the third year,
Tàizōng
ascended the throne. On the *dīnghài* day of the sixth month,
he was established
as the Imperial Crown Prince. In the eighth month of the second year of Dàbǎo (大寶),
the bandit Jǐng deposed
Tàizōng,
and planned to harm the Crown Prince.
At that time, Jǐng’s faction claimed they had his order to summon the Crown Prince. The Crown Prince
was lecturing on the *Lǎozǐ* (老子).
He was about to step down from his couch
when the executioners rushed in. The Crown Prince’s
expression did not change.
Calmly, he said:
“I have known this event was coming for a long time;
I merely regret that it is so late.” The executioners wanted
to use a sash to strangle him.
The Crown Prince said:
“This cannot kill me.”
He then pointed to a rope tied below the canopy pole,
ordered them to take it and strangle him until he died.
He was twenty-eight years old at the time. The Crown Prince’s
nature was broad and temperate,
and his mental fortitude was upright and majestic.
While in the hands of the bandits,
he never compromised his resolve. Previously,
when Hóu Jǐng
marched westward,
he brought the Crown Prince along.
When Jǐng returned defeated,
his troops were no longer well-disciplined. The Crown Prince’s
boat lagged behind
and did not catch up with the bandit forces.
His attendants and trusted associates all advised him to use this chance to flee north. The Crown Prince said:
“The state and the family are ruined and defeated;
I have no intention
of scheming for my survival.
Since my lord is suffering humiliation,
how can I bear to abandon him?
If I were to escape and hide now,
it would be rebelling against my father,
not simply avoiding the bandit.” He then wept
and sobbed deeply,
ordering them to immediately proceed forward. Because the bandits recognized the Crown Prince’s talent and bearing,
they always feared him,
worrying he would become a future menace.
Therefore, they inflicted disaster upon him first. In the fourth month of the first year of Chéngshèng (承聖),
he was posthumously honored with the title Crown Prince Āi (哀太子). Crown Prince Mǐnhuái
Fāngjǔ (愍懷太子方矩), courtesy name Déguī (德規),
was the fourth son of Shìzǔ (世祖). Initially,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nán'ān (南安) County,
and accompanied Shìzǔ while he was stationed in Jīng (荊). Early in Tàiqīng (太清),
he was appointed as the Commissioner with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe),

Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs in the seven provinces of Xiāngzhōu (湘州), Yǐngzhōu (郢州), Guìzhōu (桂州), Níngzhōu (寧州), Chéngzhōu (成州), Hézhōu (合州), and Luózhōu (羅州), General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiāngzhōu. Soon after, he was summoned
to serve as Shìzhōng (Attendant Counselor) and General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn),
and was granted a military band. Shìzǔ,
acting by imperial prerogative,
appointed him as the Prince Crown Prince (Wáng Tàizǐ),
and changed his name to Yuánliáng (元良). On the *bǐngzǐ* day in the eleventh month of the first year of Chéngshèng,
he was established
as the Imperial Crown Prince. When the army of Xī Wèi
captured Jīngchéng,
the Crown Prince and Shìzǔ were both killed by the Wèi people. The Crown Prince was intelligent
and somewhat inherited
the manner of Shìzǔ,
but he was fierce, violent, and suspicious. Emperor Jìng (Jìng Dì),
acting by imperial prerogative,
posthumously honored him with the title Crown Prince Mǐnhuái. Yáo Chá (姚察),
Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén (陳), said: Mèng Kē (孟軻, Mencius) stated:
“Those who rise at cock-crow
and diligently strive to do good
are followers of Shùn (舜).” If a commoner, wearing coarse clothes and a leather belt,
lives among the fields,
and practices this (goodness)
throughout the day,
the resulting benefit is vast. How much more so for one who occupies
the supremely enlightened position,
residing in the dignity of the rightful body,
who is able to contemplate without negligence,
and sincerely practices filiality?
How far removed
is his virtue from that of the great Shùn! Biographies, Part Three:
Wáng Mào (王茂), Cáo Jǐngzōng (曹景宗), Liǔ Qìngyuǎn (柳慶遠). Wáng Mào,
courtesy name Xiūyuǎn (休遠),
was a man from Qí (祁) in Tàiyuán (太原). His grandfather,
Shēn (深),
was the Sīmǎ of the General of the Northern Gentlemen (Běi Zhōngláng Sīmǎ). His father,
Tiānshēng (天生),
was a commander at the end of the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
At Shítou (石頭), he defeated the Minister of Instruction (Sītú), Yuán Càn (袁粲).
For his merit, he reached the position of Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies of Bāxī (巴西) and Zǐtóng (梓潼),
and was enfeoffed as the Baron (Nán) of Shànghuáng County. When Mào
was several years old,
his grandfather Shēn recognized his extraordinary talent
and often told relatives and acquaintances:
“This is the thousand-mile colt of our family;
the one who will establish our house
must be this child.” When he grew up,
he loved to read military texts,
grasping their broad outlines and main principles. His character
was reserved and discreet;
he did not socialize carelessly.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
fair-skinned, and handsome in appearance. When Emperor Wǔ of Qí (Qí Wǔ Dì)
was still a commoner,
he saw him and sighed, saying:
“Wáng Mào is young,
yet so imposing and magnificent.
He is surely a vessel fit to be a Duke or Minister.”
At the end of the Shēngmíng
he began his career as an Attendant for Summons (Fèng Cháoqǐng).
He successively held the posts of Acting Staff Officer of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Xíng Cānjūn),
Cavalry Officer under the Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and Staff Officer of the Central Army under the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn). When the Wèi
general Lǐ Wūnú (李烏奴) invaded Hànzhōng (漢中),
Mào received an imperial order to campaign against him in the west.
When the Wèi army retreated,
he returned and served as Sīmǎ of the General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Sīmǎ),
concurrently holding the position of Magistrate (Lìng) of Línxiāng. He then entered the capital to serve as Commandant of the Rapid Cavalry (Yuèqí Xiàowèi).
When the Wèi
invaded Yǎnzhōu (兗州),
Mào was serving as the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) for the General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn), reinforcing the northern border.
He later returned to the capital to serve as Sīmǎ under the Prince of Jiāngxià, General of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn). He was then promoted
to General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Interior Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Jiāngxià. Early in the Jiànwǔ
era,
Wèi besieged Sīzhōu (司州).
Mào led the Yǐngzhōu (郢州) army to relieve the siege. Gāozǔ
personally led the troops to ascend Mount Xiánshǒu (賢首山) first.
The Wèi generals Wáng Sù (王肅) and Liú Chǎng (劉昶) came to fight.
Mào followed Gāozǔ to resist them,
and they heavily defeated Sù and the others. When the Wèi
army retreated,
Mào returned to Yǐng,
and was subsequently promoted to Chief Clerk of the General Who Supports the State (Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
When Gāozǔ’s army of righteousness arose,
Mào privately spoke to Zhāng Hóngcè,
urging Gāozǔ to welcome back Emperor Hé (Hé Dì).
Gāozǔ considered this incorrect,
and the details are recorded in the annals of Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ Jì).
When Gāozǔ launched (his forces) from Yōng Bù,
he always sent Mào to be the vanguard.
When the army reached Yǐng Chéng,
Mào advanced and pacified Jiā Hú,
defeating Guāng Zǐjīn, Wú Zǐyáng, and others,
slaughtering tens of thousands (of enemies),
and returned to present the victory report at Hàn Chuān.
After Yǐng and Lǔ were pacified,
he followed Gāozǔ eastward,
again acting as the military vanguard.
When the army reached Mòlíng,
Dōng Hūn (Hòu Fèi Dì) sent the great general Wáng Zhēnguó,
massing troops at Zhūquè Mén (Gate),
whose numbers were declared to be 200,000,
crossing the ferry to request battle.
Mào joined with Cáo Jǐngzōng and others to attack them,
and utterly defeated them.
He unleashed his troops to pursue the fleeing enemy;
the piled corpses were level with the ferry railings,
