and those who rushed into the Huái (River) and died,
were countless.
He drove straight up to Xuānyáng Mén (Gate).
When Jiànkāng city was pacified,
Mào was appointed Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Imperial Guard).
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General Governing the Army).
When the bandits burned Shénhǔ Mén (Gate),
Mào led his subordinates to Dōngyè Mén (Eastern Side Gate) to respond and engage,
and was shot at by the bandits.
Mào spurred his horse and charged forward,
whereupon the bandits fled in reverse.
Mào felt he had failed to suppress the treacherous bandits,
and submitted a memorial requesting release from office.
An imperial decree of praise refused permission.
He was given the additional title of Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Army),
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Wàngcài Xiàn (Wàngcài County),
with a stipend of 2,300 households.
That year,
the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Chén Bózhī, raised troops and rebelled.

Mào was sent out as the Commissioner with Staff (Shǐchíjié), Cavalier Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), Area Commander of all military affairs of Jiāngzhōu (Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Attacks the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ),
granted a full set of drums and pipes (Gǔchuī Yībù),
to campaign south against Bózhī.
Bózhī fled to Wèi.
At that time, Jiǔjiāng had newly suffered from military banditry,
and the people wished to return to their occupations.
Mào focused on agriculture and reduced labor services;
the common people were settled because of this.
In the fourth year,
Wèi invaded Hànzhōng.
Mào received an imperial decree to march west and suppress them,
whereupon Wèi withdrew its army.
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Right (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè);
his position as Cavalier Attendant remained as before.
He firmly declined the appointment and did not take office.
He was instead appointed Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Guard),
concurrently serving as Mentor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Chēqí Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry),
with the Tàizǐ Zhānshì position remaining as before.
In the eighth year,
retaining his original title, he was granted the authority to establish a government (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) and appointed Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn),
with the Shìzhōng position remaining as before.
At that time, the world was peaceful,
and Gāozǔ was relying heavily on refined literary officials.
Mào felt quite discontented.
After getting drunk while attending imperial banquets,
he often displayed this through his words and demeanor;
Gāozǔ always pardoned him and did not punish him for it.
In the eleventh year,
he was advanced to the position of Sīkōng (Minister of Works),
with the Shìzhōng and Yǐn titles remaining as before.
Mào declined the position of Capital Governor (Jīng Yǐn),
and was instead appointed Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Authority).
Mào was by nature tolerant and generous.
Although his tenure in office brought no remarkable fame,
he brought stability to the officials and the populace.
His daily bearing was proper and upright;
even when alone in a room, he maintained his formal attire and cap strictly,
and even servants and concubines never saw him in a relaxed manner.
His appearance was splendid and magnificent,
his beard and eyebrows were like a painting.
Whenever he attended court assemblies,
he was always gazed upon by the crowd.
The following year,

he was sent out as the Commissioner with Staff (Shǐchíjié), Cavalier Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàoqí Jiāngjūn), granted the prestige of establishing a government similar to the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī zhī Yí), Area Commander of all military affairs of Jiāngzhōu (Dūdū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
He held office for three years,
and died in the commandery [Jiāngzhōu],
at the age of sixty.
Gāozǔ deeply mourned and regretted his loss,
bestowing 300,000 cash [as funeral gifts],
and 300 bolts of cloth.
The imperial decree stated:
“To distinguish virtue and record merit
is the admirable rule of wise kings;
to honor the deceased and commemorate the past
is the clear instruction of ancient codes.

The late Commissioner with Staff (Shǐchíjié), Cavalier Regular Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), General of Agile Cavalry (Piàoqí Jiāngjūn), Minister of State Granted Authority to Establish a Government (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Inspector of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ), Mào,
had broad understanding and immense breadth of mind,
and his character was composed and upright.
From the very beginning of the founding,
he devoted his utmost sincerity and exerted his strength,
closely sharing happiness and sorrow,
through difficulty and ease.
We were relying on his plans and strategies
to eternally advance the state’s trust;
but he suddenly perished and died.
We mourn him deeply in Our heart.
It is proper to increase the ritual observances [for him],
to thereby display his great achievements.
He is posthumously granted Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant),
an increase of twenty attendants bearing swords,
and a full set of drums and pipes.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōngliè (Loyal and Illustrious/Ardent).”
In the beginning,
because Mào was a foundational meritorious minister,
Gāozǔ bestowed upon him the music of bells and chimes (Zhōngqìng zhī Yuè).
While Mào was in Jiāngzhōu,
he dreamt that the bells and chimes hanging on their stand,
suddenly fell without cause.
He found this ominous in his heart.
When he awoke,
he ordered the music to be played.
When the instruments were arranged,
the bells and chimes were hanging on the stand,
and indeed, all the ropes suspending them snapped without cause,
and they fell to the ground.
Mào said to the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ), Jiāng Quán:
“This music,
was given by the Son of Heaven to favor and reward his minister.
Since the enjoyment has reached its end,
how can I not worry?”
Soon after, he fell ill,
and died within a few days.
His son, Zhēnxiù, succeeded him.
Because he behaved improperly during the mourning period,
he was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and banished to Yuèzhōu.
Later, there was an imperial decree allowing him to remain in Guǎngzhōu.
He then secretly allied with Dù Jǐng, the Military Advisor in the household of Rénwēi,
planning to attack the capital of the commandery.
The Inspector, Xiāo Áng, suppressed them.
Jǐng
was a surrendered man from Wèi;
he was executed along with Zhēnxiù.
Cáo Jǐngzōng, courtesy name Zǐzhèn,
was a native of Xīnyě.
His father, Xīnzhī,
served as a general for Sòng,
reaching the rank of General Who Campaigns Against the Captives (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ).
Jǐngzōng was skilled at mounted archery from youth,
and fond of hunting.
He often chased roe deer and stags in the marshes with several dozen youths.
Whenever many riders pursued a deer,
and the deer and horses were mixed together,
Jǐngzōng would shoot it amidst the crowd.
Everyone else feared hitting a horse's leg,
but the deer would invariably drop dead upon being struck by his arrow.
He enjoyed this immensely.
Before reaching manhood (before age 20),
Xīnzhī sent him out of Xīnyě to the commandery.
With a single horse and only a few attendants,
he suddenly encountered several hundred Mán bandits surrounding him on the road.
Jǐngzōng carried over a hundred arrows.
He then galloped his horse, shooting in all directions.
Each arrow killed one Mán bandit,
and the Mán then scattered and fled.
Because of this, his courage and bravery became famous.
He was quite fond of historical texts,
and whenever he read the biographies of Ráng Jū or Yuè Yì,
he would put down the scroll and sigh, saying:
“A true man should be like this!”
He was invited to serve in Xī Cáo but did not accept the post.
During the Yuánhuī era of Sòng,
he followed his father out to the capital.
He served as Attendant for Imperial Audience (Fèng Cháoqǐng) and Supernumerary Official (Yuánwài),
and was promoted to Secretariat Director of the Left Division of Population (Shàngshū Zuǒ Mín Láng).
Soon after, he left office due to his father's death,
and returned to his hometown.
When the mourning period ended,
the Inspector Xiāo Chìfǔ appointed him Military Advisor of the Central Army for the General Who Stabilizes the Army (Guànjūn Zhōng Bīng Cānjūn),
concurrently serving as the Grand Administrator of Tiānshuǐ (Tiānshuǐ Tàishǒu).
At the beginning of Jiàn-yuán,
the Mán bandits rose en masse.
Jǐng-Zōng campaigned against them in the east and west,
capturing and defeating many.
Qí's Pān-yáng Wáng Qiāng was Governor of Yōng-zhōu,
and he again appointed Jǐng-Zōng as Cóng-lǔ Zhōng-bīng Cān-jūn,
holding the concurrent title of Fēng-yì Tài-shǒu,
supervising all military affairs south of Xiàn-shān.
He was appointed Tún-qí Xiào-wèi.
When he was young, he was very friendly with Zhāng Dào-mén from his home province.
Dào-mén
was the youngest son of Qí's Chē-qí Jiāng-jūn Jìng-ér,
and served as Wǔ-líng Tài-shǒu.
When Jìng-ér was executed,
Dào-mén was put to death in his commandery.
His relatives and former subordinates dared not collect his body.
Jǐng-Zōng sent men and boats from Xiāng-yáng to Wǔ-líng,
collected his remains,
brought them back, and buried them.
The local people honored him for this righteous act.
In the second year of Jiàn-wǔ,
Wèi Zhǔ Tuòbá Hóng attacked Zhě-yáng.
Jǐng-Zōng served as a subordinate general.
Whenever he charged into strongholds and broke through formations,
he always achieved captures and kills.
For his merits, he was appointed Yóu-jī Jiāng-jūn.
In the fourth year,
Tài-wèi Chén Xiǎn-dá led a large army north to besiege Mǎ-quān.
Jǐng-Zōng followed him,
setting an ambush with two thousand armored soldiers,
and defeated forty thousand Wèi reinforcements under Tuòbá Yīng.
When Mǎ-quān was captured,
Xiǎn-dá discussed merits,
but placed Jǐng-Zōng at the rear.
Jǐng-Zōng withdrew without a word of complaint.
When the Wèi Zhǔ arrived with a large army,
Xiǎn-dá fled by night.
Jǐng-Zōng guided him through mountain paths,
thus allowing Xiǎn-dá and his son to escape safely.
In the fifth year,
Gāo-Zǔ became Yōng-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
Jǐng-Zōng deeply attached himself to him,
repeatedly inviting Gāo-Zǔ to his residence.
At that time, the world was in turmoil,
and Gāo-Zǔ also paid him close attention.
At the beginning of Yǒng-yuán,
he was memorialized as Guàn-jūn Jiāng-jūn and Jìng-líng Tài-shǒu.
When the righteous army rose,
Jǐng-Zōng gathered his forces,
and sent his trusted man Dù Sī-chōng to advise Gāo-Zǔ to first welcome Nán-kāng Wáng in Xiāng-yáng to ascend the throne,
and then dispatch the army,
as a plan for absolute safety.
Gāo-Zǔ did not follow this advice;
the details are in the Gāo-Zǔ Jì.
When Gāo-Zǔ arrived at Jìng-líng,
he assigned Jǐng-Zōng and Guàn-jūn Jiāng-jūn Wáng Mào to cross the river,
and besiege Yǐng-chéng.
From the second month until the seventh month,
the city finally surrendered.
He again led his troops as the vanguard to Nán-zhōu,
commanding cavalry and infantry to take Jiàn-kāng.
On the way to Jiāng-níng,
Dōng-hūn's general Lǐ Jū-shì was garrisoned with a large force at Xīn-tíng.
On that day, he selected a thousand elite cavalry to encamp in Jiāng-níng.
Jǐng-Zōng had just arrived,
and his camp was not yet established;
furthermore, the army had been campaigning for a long time,
and their weapons and armor were worn out.
Jū-shì looked at them and underestimated them,
then beat drums and shouted, pressing forward against Jǐng-Zōng.
Jǐng-Zōng donned his armor and galloped into battle.
As soon as the short weapons met,
Jū-shì abandoned his armor and fled.
Jǐng-Zōng captured them all,
then advanced with drums,
straight to Zào-jiá-qiáo where he built a camp.
Jǐng-Zōng also coordinated with Wáng Mào and Lǚ Sēng-zhēn,
and defeated Wáng Zhēn-guó at Dà-háng.
Mào charged into their central stronghold,
which fell immediately,
and Jǐng-Zōng unleashed his troops to exploit the victory.
Jǐng-Zōng's soldiers were all unruly and lawless.
Along the imperial road,
there was no household that was not wealthy,
and they plundered property,
and abducted women and children.
Jǐng-Zōng could not restrain them.
When Gāo-Zǔ entered and encamped at Xīn-chéng,
he strictly reissued orders,
and then the situation gradually subsided.
He again joined the various armies in a prolonged siege of the six gates.
When the city was pacified,
he was appointed Sàn-qí Cháng-shì and Yòu-wèi Jiāng-jūn,
and enfeoffed as Xiāng-xī Xiàn-hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand six hundred households.
He was then promoted to Chí-jié, Dū-dū Yǐng Sī Èr-zhōu Zhū-jūn-shì, Zuǒ Jiāng-jūn, and Yǐng-zhōu Cì-shǐ.
In the first year of Tiān-jiān,
he was advanced to Píng-xī Jiāng-jūn,
and his title was changed to Jìng-líng Xiàn-hóu.
While Jǐng-Zōng was in the province,
he engaged in commercial activities and accumulated wealth.
He built a residence south of the city,
east of the long dike,
and north of Xià-kǒu.
He opened streets and erected gates,
stretching several li east and west.
His subordinates were cruel and rampant,
and the people were quite weary of them.
In the tenth month of the second year,
Wèi bandits raided Sī-zhōu,
besieging Cì-shǐ Cài Dào-gōng.
At that time, the Wèi attacks were fierce,
and people in the city had to carry boards to draw water.
Jǐng-Zōng stayed behind his gates,
merely displaying his troops and hunting.
When Sī-zhōu city fell,
he was impeached by Yù-shǐ Zhōng-chéng Rèn Fǎng.
Gāo-Zǔ, considering him a meritorious minister, did not pursue the matter,
and recalled him as Hù-jūn.
Upon his arrival,
he was again appointed Sàn-qí Cháng-shì and Yòu-wèi Jiāng-jūn.
Wèi
Tuòbá Yīng attacked Zhōnglí,
and besieged Chāng Yìzhī, the Administrator of Xúzhōu.
Gāozǔ commanded Jǐngzōng to supervise the armies and reinforce Yìzhī.
Wéi Ruì, the Administrator of Yùzhōu, was also involved,
but was under Jǐngzōng’s command.
Gāozǔ commanded Jǐngzōng to camp at Dàorén Zhōu,
and wait until the various armies were fully assembled before advancing together.
Jǐngzōng firmly petitioned,
asking to first occupy the tail of Shàoyáng Zhōu,
but Gāozǔ did not permit it.
Jǐngzōng wished to claim the merit entirely for himself,
so he disobeyed the edict and advanced.
He encountered a sudden strong gale,
resulting in many drownings and losses,
and he returned to guard his previous camp.
When Gāozǔ heard of this,
he said:
"This is exactly how we will defeat the bandits.
Jǐngzōng’s failure to advance,
must be the will of Heaven!
If he had gone alone with an isolated army,
the fortress would not have been established in time,
and he certainly would have been utterly exposed.
Now that he must wait for the armies to advance together,
we shall achieve a great victory."
When Wéi Ruì arrived,
he and Jǐngzōng advanced and encamped at Shàoyáng Zhōu,
setting up ramparts about a hundred paces away from the Wèi fortress.
Wèi fought consecutive battles but could not repel them,
resulting in twenty to thirty percent killed or wounded.
From then on, the Wèi army dared not approach closely.
Jǐngzōng and the others’ equipment and armor were excellent and new,
and their military bearing was extremely magnificent.
The Wèi troops, looking upon them, lost heart.
The great Wèi general Yáng Dàyǎn established a fortress on the northern bank opposite the bridge,
in order to maintain transport of supplies.
Whenever herdsmen crossed the river to cut fodder and straw,
they were all seized by Dàyǎn.
Jǐngzōng then recruited over a thousand brave soldiers,
crossed directly a few *lǐ* south of Dàyǎn’s fortress and constructed a rampart,
personally leading the construction.
Dàyǎn led his troops to attack,
but Jǐngzōng fought and defeated him,
thereby allowing the rampart to be completed.
He ordered the subordinate general Zhào Cǎo to guard it,
and it was therefore named Zhào Cǎo Chéng (Zhao Cao’s Fortress).
After this, grazing and foraging were carried out freely there.
Dàyǎn occasionally sent out raiding parties,
but they were repeatedly captured by Zhào Cǎo instead.
Before this,
Gāozǔ had commanded Jǐngzōng and the others to equip high ships,
making them as tall as the Wèi bridges,
planning for a fire attack.
He ordered Jǐngzōng and Ruì to each attack one bridge;
Ruì would attack the southern one,
Jǐngzōng would attack the northern one.
In the third month of the sixth year,
the spring waters rose,
and the Huái River suddenly surged up six or seven *chǐ*.
Ruì dispatched the generals under his command, Féng Dàogēn, Lǐ Wénzhāo, Péi Suì, Wéi Jì, and others, to board the ships and land,
attacking and utterly destroying the Wèi troops on the islet.
Jǐngzōng then ordered all the armies to beat their drums, shout loudly, and rush to scale the various fortresses,
their shouts shaking heaven and earth.
Dàyǎn burned his camp on the west bank,
and Yīng abandoned his fortress on the east bank and fled.
The various ramparts crumbled one after another,
they all abandoned their equipment and armor,
scrambling to jump into the water and drown.
The flow of the Huái River was blocked by them.
Jǐngzōng ordered the Army Commander Mǎ Guǎng to pursue Dàyǎn up to the Huì River,
for over forty *lǐ*,
where the fallen corpses lay piled upon one another.
Yìzhī emerged and chased Yīng to Luòkǒu,
and Yīng entered Liáng Chéng with only a single horse.
Along the Huái River for over a hundred *lǐ*,
the corpses lay strewn about.
More than fifty thousand people were captured alive,
their military provisions and equipment were collected,
piled up like mountains.
Cattle, horses, donkeys, and mules
were beyond counting.
Jǐngzōng then selected from what the army had obtained over ten thousand captives,
and one thousand horses.
He sent them to report the victory,
but Gāozǔ commanded that they be returned to the army.
Jǐngzōng entered the capital with his triumphant army.
His stipend was increased by four hundred households,
making his total previous and current stipend two thousand households,
and his noble rank was promoted to Duke.
An edict appointed him Shìzhōng and Lǐng Jūn Jiāngjūn,
and granted him a military band.
Jǐngzōng’s personality was self-confident and competitive.
Whenever he wrote a document,
if there was a character he did not understand,
he would not ask anyone,
but would invent it according to his own idea.
Even when facing the highest ministers (Gōngqīng), he offered no deference;
only Wéi Ruì,
being older and a leading figure from his home region,
did he specifically respect and honor.
When dining together at imperial banquets,
he would also bow and show modesty.
Gāozǔ praised him for this.
Jǐngzōng enjoyed women,
having several hundred singing girls and concubines,
dressed in the finest silks and embroideries.
His nature was restless and lively,
and he could not remain quiet or reserved.
When traveling out, he always wanted to lift the curtains of his carriage.
His attendants frequently remonstrated, saying that his rank and prestige were too high and serious,
and everyone was watching him,
so it was improper to do so.
Jǐngzōng said to his close associates:
"When I was back in my hometown,
I rode swift horses like dragons,
with dozens of young companions on horseback,
drawing our bowstrings to make a thunderclap sound,
and the arrows whistled like starving owls.
We chased roe deer across the flat marshes,
shooting them in the ribs,
when thirsty we drank their blood,
and when hungry we ate their meat,
sweet as nectar.
We felt the wind rising behind our ears,
and fire blazing from our noses.
This joy made a man forget death,
unaware that old age was approaching.
Now I have come to Yángzhōu to be a noble,
unable to move freely.
If I travel and open the carriage curtain,
my attendants immediately say it cannot be done.
Shut up inside the carriage,
I am like a bride on her third day.
Experiencing this gloom,
makes a man spiritless."
He was fond of wine and enjoyment.
In the twelfth month (Làyuè), he stayed in his residence
and had men act out the *yě hú* ritual to drive away pestilence,
and they went everywhere begging for wine and food from people’s homes.
Originally, this was intended as a game,
but many of his subordinates were unruly and frivolous.
Consequently, they molested people’s women
and stole people's property.
Gāozǔ learned of this,
and Jǐngzōng stopped the practice.
Gāozǔ often held banquets for his meritorious ministers,
and they talked about old times.
After Jǐngzōng became drunk, he would forget himself and speak absurdly,
sometimes mistakenly referring to himself as "your subordinate official."
Gāozǔ deliberately indulged him for entertainment.
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng, Zhōng Wèi Jiāngjūn, and Administrator of Jiāngzhōu.
He died on the road while proceeding to his post,
at the age of fifty-two.
An edict granted funeral expenses of two hundred thousand cash,
and three hundred rolls of cloth.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn, Administrator of Yōngzhōu, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His posthumous name was Zhuàng.
His son, Jiǎo, succeeded him.
Liǔ Qìngyuǎn, courtesy name Wénhé,
was a native of Xiè in Hédōng.
His paternal uncle Yuánjǐng
was the Sòng Tàiwèi.
Qìngyuǎn began his career as Registrar of Yǐngzhōu,
and early in the Qí dynasty served as Director of the Department of State Affairs, Staff Officer in the Central Army under the Grand Marshal, Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Administrator of Wèixīng.
The commandery suffered severe flooding,
sweeping away residents.
Officials requested to move the people and offer sacrifices to the city walls.
Qìngyuǎn said:
"Heaven sends down rain and water;
how could the city walls know about it?
I have heard that rivers and streams do not rise for more than three days.
What is there to worry about?"
He only ordered earthworks to be built.
Soon after, the water receded,
and the common people respected him for it.
He entered the capital to serve as Commandant of Chángshuǐ,
and later went out to serve as Píng Běi Lùshì Cānjūn and Magistrate of Xiāngyáng.
When Gāozǔ governed Yōngzhōu,
he asked the Jīngzhào native Dù Yùn to recommend someone for the core provincial administration.
Yùn nominated Qìngyuǎn.
Gāozǔ said:
"I already know Wénhé,
I was asking for someone I didn't know yet."
Nevertheless, he then invited him to serve as Biéjià Cóngshì Shǐ.
When the Qí dynasty was facing many troubles,
Qìngyuǎn said to his close associates:
"Now the empire is about to fall into chaos,
a hero is surely going to rise.
He who protects the people and establishes hegemony,
must be our Lord (Gāozǔ)!"
Therefore, he offered full sincerity and collaboration.
When the righteous army arose,
Qìngyuǎn always stayed in the tent, serving as the chief strategist.
Zhōngxīng,
he was selected by the Western Terrace to be a Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate).
He was promoted to Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Champion Army) and Zhēngdōng Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the General Who Conquers the East).
Following the army eastward,
he personally led the troops.
When Gāozǔ inspected the camps and fortifications,
he saw that Qìngyuǎn's temporary quarters were orderly and strict.
He often sighed, saying:
"If every person were like this,
what worry would I have?"
After Jiànkāng city was pacified,
he entered the court as a Shìzhōng (Attendant in Ordinary),
holding the post of Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard),
and simultaneously held the posts of Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Huáilíng and Qíchāng commanderies.
Once, a fire broke out at night within the city walls,
causing panic and alarm within the Forbidden Precincts.
Gāozǔ, who was then residing in the palace,
gathered all the keys,
and asked,
"Where is Attendant Liǔ (*Liǔ Shìzhōng*)?"
When Qìngyuǎn arrived,
all keys were handed over to him.
This shows the extent to which he was trusted.
When the Duke's Administration (Bàfǔ) was established,
he was appointed Tàiwèi Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Aide to the Grand Commandant).
When Gāozǔ received the abdication (of the throne),
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard),
given the additional title Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians),
and enfeoffed as the Marquis of Chóng'ān,
with a thousand taxable households.
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother,
but was ordered to return to duty in his former capacity,
yet he firmly declined the appointment.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (503 CE),
he was promoted to Zhōng Lǐngjūn (General of the Central Army Command),
and his title was changed to Marquis of Yúndù.
In the fourth year (505 CE),

he was sent out to serve as Shǐ Chíjíe (Emissary with Credentials), Grand Governor of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, and Běi Qín Four Provinces, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Barbarians), Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel Who Pacifies the Man Barbarians), and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yōng Province.
Gāozǔ held a farewell feast for him at Xīntíng,
and said:
"You are returning to your home province, adorned in embroidered robes (glory),
and I shall have no worries looking westward."
In the seventh year (508 CE),
he was recalled to be Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (General Protector of the Army),
holding the concurrent post of Tàizǐ Shùzǐ (Aide to the Crown Prince).
Before taking up this post,
he was immediately promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant Who Passes Through) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard),
holding the concurrent post of Yòuxiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Valiant Cavalry).
When he arrived at the capital (Jīngdū),
it happened that the city of Sùyù, held by Wèi, requested surrender.
He received an imperial decree to provide support.
Consequently, he was granted the temporary authority (jiǎjié) to guard Huáiyīn.
The Wèi army retreated.
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he returned to the capital (Jīngshī),
and was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (Palace Attendant), Tàizǐ Zhānshì (Controller of the Household of the Crown Prince), and Grand Judge (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Yōng Province.
In the tenth year (511 CE),
he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Attendant in Ordinary) and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General Commanding the Army),
granted the privilege of the walking staff,
and a full military band.
In the twelfth year (513 CE),
he was promoted to Ānběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel Who Pacifies the Man Barbarians), and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yōng Province.
Qìngyuǎn, serving again in his home province,
greatly emphasized integrity and purity,
and was cherished by both the gentry and the common people.
In the spring of the following year,
he passed away,
aged fifty-seven.
The imperial edict stated:
"To remember the past and honor the end
is the excellent rule of former kings;
To greatly increase honors
is the standard for successive generations.

Liǔ Qìngyuǎn, Emissary with Credentials, Grand Governor of Military Affairs of Yōng, Liáng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín Four Provinces, and the Commanderies of Jìnglíng in Yǐng Province and Suí in Sī Province, Ānběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), Níngmán Xiàowèi (Colonel Who Pacifies the Man Barbarians), Inspector of Yōng Province, and Founding Marquis of Yúndù County,
possessed profound ability and broad insight,
and his thoughts and demeanor were refined and elegant.
In the earliest days of uncertainty,
he participated in planning state affairs;
long since the establishment of peace,
he has endured hardships in the Imperial Guards.
Having twice governed the western border regions,
he was expanding the path of good governance,
when his sudden death occurred,
causing deep grief in Our heart.
It is fitting to posthumously bestow honor upon him,
to display his magnificent achievements.

He is posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng (Attendant in Ordinary), Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Army), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishment of a Government Bureau with the Ceremonial Privileges of the Three Dukes).
The military band and the marquisate title shall remain as before.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōnghuì (Loyal and Benevolent).
A funeral grant of two hundred thousand coins
and two hundred rolls of cloth is awarded."
When the coffin returned to the capital (Jīngshī),
Gāozǔ personally went out and wept over it.
His son, Jīn, inherited the title.
Previously,
Qìngyuǎn's cousin, Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Guard) Shìlóng, once said to Qìngyuǎn:
"I once dreamed that the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) bestowed a mattress upon me,
and subsequently I became second only to the Three Dukes (Táisī);
just now I dreamed that my mattress was given to you.
You will surely bring glory to our ducal clan."
By this time,
Qìngyuǎn had also followed in Shìlóng's footsteps.
Yáo Chá, Minister (Shàngshū) of Personnel (Lìbù) of Chén, commented: Although Wáng Mào, Cáo Jǐngzōng, and Liǔ Qìngyuǎn were hereditary military families,
they had not yet displayed extraordinary integrity.
When Liáng arose,
they took advantage of the final brilliance of the sun and moon (the twilight of the previous dynasty),
to achieve their ambitions.
Their achievements matched those of Fāng and Shào,
and their merits were inscribed on bells and tripods—
how magnificent!
In the past, Emperor Guāngwǔ of Hàn fully cherished his meritorious officials;
their official ranks did not exceed Cháoqǐng or Tèjìn (Adviser or Specially Advanced officials).
Kòu, Dèng, Gěng, and Jiǎ all did not fully utilize their abilities and strength.
Mào and the others repeatedly held provincial governorships (Fāngyuè),
and their positions culminated in that of Supreme General,
the relationship between ruler and minister
surpassed that of previous generations.
Collected Biographies Four: Xiāo Yǐngdá, Xiàhóu Xiáng, Cài Dàogōng, Yáng Gōngzé, Dèng Yuánqǐ
Xiāo Yǐngdá,
was a native of Lánlíng, Lánlíng Commandery,
and the fifth son of Chìfǔ, Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of Remonstrance) of Qí.
When young, he was fond of courage and energetic.
He began his career as Guànjūn (Champion).
His elder brother, Yǐngzhòu,
served as Acting Governor of Jīng Province at the end of the Qí Jiànwǔ period,
and Yǐngdá also served as Wàibīng Cānjūn (Military Adjutant in Charge of Outer Forces) under the Western Central Commandant,
both being at the Western Headquarters.
During the troubled times at the close of Qí,
they were rather uneasy about their own safety.
At that time, Dōnghūn dispatched Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State) Liú Shānyáng to serve as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Bāxī.
On his way, he passed through Jīng Province.
He had secretly instructed Yǐngzhòu to attack Yōng Province.
At that time, Gāozǔ was already prepared.
Yǐngzhòu then sent Wáng Tiānhǔ, one of his close associates, with a letter to sow suspicion in him (Shānyáng).
When Shānyáng arrived,
he indeed dared not enter the city.
Yǐngzhòu, finding himself without options,

sent Zhū Jǐngsī of Qiántáng at night to summon Xí Chǎnwén, Military Adjutant of the City Bureau under the Western Central Commandant, and Liǔ Chén, Consultant Adjutant, to close the retreat and settle on a plan.
Chǎnwén said:
"Xiāo, the Inspector of Yōng Province (*Xiāo Yōngzhōu*), has been accumulating troops and horses
for a long time, not just since yesterday.
Jiānglíng has always feared the people of Xiāngyáng,
and our forces are not equal to theirs.
If we attempt to seize it, we will certainly be unable to control it;
(Even if) we controlled it,
we would eventually not be tolerated by the Imperial Court.
If we now kill Shānyáng,
and launch an undertaking alongside the Inspector of Yōng Province,
installing a Son of Heaven to command the various feudal lords,
then our hegemony will be established.
Shānyáng remains suspicious and has not advanced;
this shows he does not trust us.
If we now execute and send Wáng Tiānhǔ's head,
his suspicion can be dispelled.
Once he arrives, we can plot against him,
and nothing will fail."
Chén also urged this course of action.
Yǐngdá said:
"Excellent."
When dawn broke,
Yǐngzhòu said to Tiānhǔ:
"You are acquainted with General Liú (*Liú Fǔguó*),
but now I must regrettably borrow your head."
He then executed Tiānhǔ and showed the head to Shānyáng.
Shānyáng was overjoyed,
and lightly led a few hundred infantry and cavalry to the provincial seat.
Chǎnwén mustered troops and waited at the gate.
When Shānyáng's carriage crossed the threshold, the gate was closed.
He was immediately seized and executed,
and his head was sent to Gāozǔ.
They also sent word informing Gāozǔ of the plan to support the Prince of Nánkāng.
Gāozǔ granted permission.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,

Yǐngzhòu was appointed Jiǎjié (Temporary Credentials), Shìzhōng (Attendant in Ordinary), Shàngshū Lìng (President of the Department of State Affairs), holding the concurrent post of Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel), Grand Governor of Military Affairs of Traveling and Remaining Forces, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Army), and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Jīng Province,
remaining to guard the Western Court.
Yǐngdá was appointed Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Champion Army).
When Yáng Gōngzé and others led their armies to follow Gāozǔ,
Gāozǔ besieged Yǐng City.
Yǐngdá rendezvoused his forces at Hànkǒu,
and along with Wáng Mào and Cáo Jǐngzōng, attacked Yǐng City,
and captured it.
He followed Gāozǔ to pacify Jiāng Province.
Gāozǔ advanced from Jiāng Province,
ordering him and Cáo Jǐngzōng to first lead cavalry and infantry to march rapidly toward Jiāngníng,
where they defeated Dōnghūn's general Lǐ Jūshì,
and subsequently took Dōngchéng.
Initially,
when the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) arose,
Xiāo Huìxùn's (蕭惠訓) son, Guī (璝), the Governor of Bā Dōng (巴東 Tàishǒu), and Lǔ Xiūliè (魯休烈), the Governor of Bā Xī (巴西 Tàishǒu), refused to follow.
They raised troops and invaded Jīngzhōu (荊州),
defeating the General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), Rèn Yàngzhī (任漾之), at Xiákǒu (硤口),
and routing the Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) Liú Xiàoqìng (劉孝慶) at Shàngmíng (上明).
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (穎冑) dispatched troops to resist them;
but Gāozǔ (高祖) had already pacified Jiāng (江) and Yǐng (郢),
and was planning the capture of Jiànkāng (建康).
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, considering his position as a high-ranking general,
was unable to curb or control Guī (璝) and his confederates.
He was anxious, ashamed, and unhappy,
fell ill for several days, and died.
Those in the prefecture concealed his death,
and employed someone whose handwriting resembled his to fake imperial decrees (jiàomìng).
When Guī (璝) and the others heard that Jiànkāng (建康) was about to be pacified,
their forces panicked and scattered.
Only then was the mourning announced.
Emperor Hé (和帝) posthumously granted Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (穎冑) the title of Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
At the beginning of the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) campaign,
Yǐngdá's (穎達) younger brother, Xiāo Yǐngfú (穎孚), fled the capital (Jīngshī).
Xiū Jǐngzhì (脩景智), a native of Lúlíng (廬陵), secretly led him south to return home.
When they reached Lúlíng,
Jǐngzhì (景智) and his kinsman Líng Yòu (靈祐) raised troops for him,
gathering several hundred men.
They garrisoned at Yàoshānhú (藥山湖) in Xīchāng (西昌).
When Xiāo Yǐngdá (穎達) heard of this,

He provisionally granted Yǐngfú (穎孚) the staff of authority (jié), the supervision of military affairs for the five commanderies of Lúlíng (廬陵), Yùzhāng (豫章), Línchuān (臨川), Nánkāng (南康), and Ānchéng (安成), the title of General Who Subdues the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn), and Prefect of Lúlíng (Lúlíng Nèishǐ).
Yǐngfú (穎孚) led Líng Yòu (靈祐) and others to advance and occupy Xīchāng.
Emperor Dōng Hūn (東昏) dispatched the Governor of Ānxī (Ānxī Tàishǒu), Liú Xīzǔ (劉希祖), who entered the lake from Nánjiāng (南江) to resist them.
Yǐngfú (穎孚) could not maintain his position.
Taking his troops, he fled again via Jiàn'ān (建安) to Chángshā (長沙).
Xīzǔ (希祖) pursued him.
Yǐngfú (穎孚) climbed along mountains and jumped across ridges,
barely managing to escape.
While on the road, he ran out of provisions.
Later, he died from overeating after finally getting food.
When the city of Jiànkāng (建康) was pacified,
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed Xiāo Yǐngdá (穎達) as General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
When the Emperor (Shàng) received the abdication (shàn),
an imperial edict stated:
“To consider merit and esteem virtue
is common practice across successive dynasties.
To honor those long gone and cherish the individual
is to further emphasize commitment to the task.
The late Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Chancellor (Chéngxiàng), and President of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng) of Qí (齊), Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (穎冑),
had a majestic and far-reaching character,
with profound and ample capacity.
His pure conduct and great achievements
garnered universal respect.
He established the righteous cause at its beginning,
laying the foundation for the royal enterprise.
Through hardship and ease,
he embodied his dedication.
As We now receive Heaven’s mandate and transform the world,
brilliantly dwelling over the realm,
looking toward Mount Dài (岱) and observing the Yellow River (Hé),
We weep and mourn eternally.
He is hereby granted the title of Founding Duke of Bādōng Commandery (Bādōng Jùn Kāiguó Gōng),
with a stipend of three thousand households.
His original official rank remains unchanged.”
Xiāo Yǐngfú (穎孚) was posthumously granted the title General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
Xiāo Yǐngdá (穎達) was promoted to Cavalry Attendant in Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì),
but was dismissed shortly thereafter due to official matters.
When great deliberations were held concerning merits and rewards,
Yǐngdá (穎達) was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Wúchāng County (Wúchāng Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of one thousand five hundred households.
Soon after, he became Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
His title was changed to Marquis of Zuò Táng (Zuò Táng Hóu),
but the county and stipend remained the same as before.
He was promoted to General Who Subdues the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Commander of the Crown Prince's Left Guard (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài).
The Imperial Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), Rèn Fǎng (任昉), memorialized, saying:
“Your servant has heard that one should observe what a man takes when he is poor,
and what he refrains from doing when he is destitute.
If even a commoner,
living in poverty, maintains resolute conduct,
he can still inspire the greedy and warn the common customs,
and make generous these frivolous
men;
how much more so for a house of high rank (fábīng zhī jiā),
to contend for the profits of chickens and pigs?
Or for a scholar in embroidered robes,
to assume the mantle of a merchant.
We have heard rumors that the General Who Subdues the Barbarians, your servant Xiāo Yǐngdá (蕭穎達), requested the tax revenue derived from fish
for his army supplies.
We immediately summoned Péng Nándāng (彭難當), the overseer (dū) of Yǐngdá’s (穎達) household, to the court for questioning and clarification.
He stated: ‘Regarding the standard tax on live fish,
it was originally requested by Dèng Sēngyǎn (鄧僧琰).
The period of his privilege expired
on the fourteenth day of the fifth month this year.
My master, Yǐngdá (穎達),
at that time, believing the tax was not newly established,
still petitioned to succeed Sēngyǎn (僧琰) in collecting the revenue.
Permission was immediately granted for him to take up the tax collection,
and based on historical precedent,
the annual revenue was calculated to be 500,000 cash.’
If the detailed statement is accurate,
then it corresponds precisely with the rumors,
and Yǐngdá (穎達) is indeed the principal involved.

Your servant respectfully observes: The General Who Subdues the Barbarians, Commander of the Crown Prince's Left Guard, and Founding Marquis of Zuò Táng County (Zuò Táng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu), your servant Xiāo Yǐngdá (穎達),
holds the position of a great minister,
and is knowledgeable in upholding the law.
Yet private petitions
are frequently presented by him,
while matters of ultimate public interest are neglected.
A heart set on the market should
be different from the demands of a fishmonger (Bào Sì).
The resources gained from fish and turtles
ought not to require calculation of subtle ownership.
He has proceeded to reiterate this text
twice,
and pursued that eleventh point.
If his conduct is like this,
then the standard rules (zhǔn shéng) must be applied.
Your Majesty, valuing and cherishing meritorious officials,
often bends the law for them;
but your servant, holding office and upholding the statutes,
dares not fail to straighten
the rope (apply justice strictly).
We, your servants, have discussed this and
request that Xiāo Yǐngdá (穎達) be dismissed from his current official posts due to this matter,
and retire to his residence as a Marquis.”
There was an imperial edict pardoning him.
He was transferred to Cavalry Attendant in Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì) and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he returned to the post of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
He was posted out as General Who Commands Trust and Awe (Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Nèishǐ),
with an added salary rank of Zhōng Èrqiān Shí.
His governance was formidable and fierce,
and the people of the commandery feared him.
He was promoted to Bearer of the Staff of Authority (Shǐ Chí Jié), Supervisor of Military Affairs for Jiāngzhōu (江州), and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His generalship title remained as before.
After a short time,
he was recalled to serve as Cavalry Attendant in Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì) and General of the Right Galloping Cavalry (Yòu Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
Since he was now in a comfortable position,
he especially indulged in music and women (shēng sè),
drank excessively,
and thereby greatly damaged his health.
In the ninth year (510 CE),
he was promoted to General Who Commands Trust and Awe (Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn) and General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
He died that year,
at the age of thirty-four.
The Emperor (Chē Jià) personally attended the mourning,
and provided secret implements from the Eastern Park (Dōngyuán Mìqì),
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
two hundred thousand cash,
and two hundred bolts of cloth.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn),
and a full military band (gǔchuī).
His posthumous name was Kāng (康).
His son, Mǐn (敏), succeeded him.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu's (穎冑) son, Mǐ (靡),
inherited the title of Duke of Bādōng (Bādōng Gōng).
His highest position reached Secretary of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
but he died young.
Xiàhóu Xiáng (夏侯詳), courtesy name Shū Yè (叔業),
was a native of Qiáo (譙) in Qiáojùn (譙郡).
At the age of sixteen,
he suffered the death of his father,
and his mourning was filled with grief and physical deterioration.
He lived in a hut by the tomb for three years.
Once, a three-legged sparrow
flew to perch on the door of his hut,
and everyone regarded it as extraordinary.
When the mourning period was complete,
In the beginning of the Sòng Tàishǐ reign era,
Yǎn raised Yùzhōu in rebellion.
Sòng Míngdì dispatched the General Guarding the State, Liú Miǎn, to suppress him.
The attack and defense lasted for months,
the populace was terrified and afraid,
and were about to request aid from Wèi.
Xiáng advised Yǎn, saying:
"Today’s action,
fundamentally aims to demonstrate loyalty and integrity.
If the state has a sovereign to serve,
one should immediately submit oneself to the Imperial Court.
How can you humble yourself, face north, and submit to a foreign region?
Moreover, the troops of the Wèi clan now
are close to the Huái River.
We cannot ascertain the intentions of their single army regarding advance or retreat;
I fear they harbor ulterior motives.
If we now send an envoy to submit,
they will surely comfort and accept us generously,
which would be more than merely pardoning our crimes.
If you believe otherwise,
I request to serve as the envoy."
Yǎn agreed to this.
Xiáng met with Miǎn and said:
"Your Excellency has established a strict siege and steep fortifications;
arrows and blades are like frost.
The foolish people inside the city
are truly like cornered beasts.
Officers and commoners alike fear execution,
and all wish to defect to Wèi.
The reason I climbed over the wall and submitted to Virtue
is to boldly reveal what is in my heart.
I wish Your Excellency would extend boundless grace
and bestow sweeping favor.
If you lift the siege and withdraw,
they will all lead each other out and arrive."
Miǎn consented.
Xiáng said:
"If it is truly so,
and it shall be as you have said,
then I, Xiáng, request to return and report the command."
Miǎn sent him to the base of the city wall.
Xiáng called out to the people inside the city,
telling them Miǎn's words.
That very day, Yǎn and his followers all came out,
and the entire prefecture was preserved.
Miǎn became the Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ),
and Xiáng was appointed Commandant (Zhǔbù).
After a short time,
he became the Magistrate of Xīnjí County (Lìng).
His governance showed outstanding achievements.
Regional Inspector Duàn Fórōng circulated a notice throughout the territory,
making him a model for the subordinate counties.
He was transferred to be the Administrator/Recorder (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Shǐ),
and subsequently promoted to Chief Clerk (Biéjià).
He successively served eight generals,
and was praised by the provincial authorities.
Qí Míngdì, when he was the Regional Inspector,
greatly appreciated and valued him.
When he began administering the government,
he summoned Xiáng to the capital,
intending to employ him extensively.
He often brought Xiáng and his fellow townsman Péi Shūyè in to talk day and night,
but Xiáng often summarized briefly and offered no response.
The Emperor asked Shūyè about this.
Shūyè informed Xiáng.
Xiáng said:
"Do not initiate fortune,
nor be the forerunner of disaster."
Because of this, he incurred slight displeasure.
He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk to the General Who Punishes the Captives (Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ) and Governor of Yìyáng Commandery (Tàishǒu).
After a short time,
the garrison at Jiàn'ān Shù was besieged by Wèi.
Accordingly, Xiáng was made Commander of the Jiàn'ān Garrison,
holding the concurrent post of Governor of the two commanderies, Biānchéng and Xīncài,
and simultaneously commanding the troops from the three commanderies of Guāngchéng, Yìyáng, and Rǔyīn to go to its relief.
When Xiáng arrived at Jiàn'ān,
the Wèi army withdrew.
Previously,
Wèi had also established the Jīngtíng Garrison on the Huái River,
which constantly raided and pillaged.
Repeated attacks failed to stop them.
Xiáng led crack troops to attack it,
and the bandit forces were utterly routed;
they all abandoned the city and fled.
At the end of the Jiànwǔ reign era,
he was summoned to serve as General of Light Cavalry (Yóují Jiāngjūn).
He was then sent out to serve as Adjutant to the Southern Central General (Nán Zhōngláng Sīmǎ) and Governor of Nán Xīncài Commandery.
When the Prince of Nánkāng of Qí was in Jīngzhōu,
Xiáng was promoted to Adjutant to the Western Central General (Xī Zhōngláng Sīmǎ) and Governor of Xīnxīng Commandery.
He proceeded directly to Jiāngyáng.
At that time, Prince Yáoguāng of Shǐ'ān raised troops in the capital.
The Chief Clerk of the Prince of Nánkāng, Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, had not yet arrived.
The Staff Officer of the Central Army (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn), Liú Shānyáng, was already in the province.
Shānyáng's deputy, Pān Shào, planned to stage a rebellion.
Xiáng pretended to summon Shào for consultation,
and immediately executed him at the city gate.
The provincial administration was thus stabilized.
He was promoted to Regional Inspector of Sīzhōu,
but he declined the post.
When Emperor Gāozǔ raised his righteous army,
Xiáng and Yǐngzhòu together initiated the great mobilization.
When the Western Administration (Xītái) was established,
Xiáng was appointed Commandant of the Central Guard (Zhōng Lǐngjūn),
and granted the additional titles of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Governor of Nánjùn Commandery.
For all major military and state affairs,
Yǐngzhòu mostly relied on Xiáng for decisions.
When Gāozǔ besieged Yǐngchéng but had not yet taken it,
Yǐngzhòu sent the Palace Commandant (Wèiwèi), Xí Chǎnwén, to Gāozǔ’s army.
Xiáng presented a proposal, saying:
"A desperate stronghold is easy to defend,
and conquering it by assault is difficult.
Remaining arrayed before a strong city
is frowned upon by military strategists.
It is truly advisable to greatly extend strategic planning,
and seek and accept diverse opinions.
From military commanders down to common soldiers,
all should be ordered to present their views,
and fully express their thoughts.
Choose what is good and follow it,
select the capable and employ them.
Do not reject advice because of the person offering it,
nor let the majority impose upon the minority.
Furthermore, you must assess the strength of our forces,
estimate the enemy's firewood and provisions,
observe their morale,
and weigh their overall situation.
If the enemy has many troops but little food,
then it is proper to calculate the days and maintain the siege.
If they have plenty of food but few strong fighters,
then it is proper to gather all forces and attack them.
If both provisions and strength are sufficient,
and they cannot be subdued by either attack or siege,
it is expedient to distribute gold and valuables,
and launch counter-intelligence operations,
so that their wise men are not trusted,
and their fools harbor suspicion.
This is how Emperor Wèi Wǔ secured his great accomplishment.
If these three methods are not feasible,
one should consider flexibility and change,
observe the mood of the populace,
and calculate our own provisions.
If virtue is felt,
and ten thousand miles align with the standard;
if benevolence is embraced,
and people near and far return to righteousness;
if gold and silk have long been accumulated,
and food supplies are abundant—
then one can establish a siege but relax the blockade,
drawing it out over months and years.
This is how Wáng Jiǎn conquered Chǔ.
If surrounding them does not ultimately result in surrender,
attacking them cannot subdue them,
using covert pathways is impractical,
and gold and grain are not accumulated by the populace,
if the world is not yet united under one house,
and public sentiment is difficult to predict,
then one should definitely think of a new changing strategy.
The key to a changing strategy
truly relies on heroic decision-making.
The deepest essentials of this
are difficult to convey on paper.
I have already presented my thoughts to Palace Commandant Xí;
I especially hope they will be adopted."
Gāozǔ praised and accepted the advice.
Shortly thereafter,
Yǐngzhòu died.
At that time, Gāozǔ’s younger brother, Prince Dàn of Shǐxīng, was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng.
Xiáng then sent an envoy to welcome Dàn,
to participate jointly in military and state affairs.
Emperor Hé added Xiáng to the Imperial Guards,
allowing him to enter and exit the palace buildings,
but he firmly declined the acceptance.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè).
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), General Who Guards the Army (Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn), and Regional Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
Xiáng again firmly yielded this post to Dàn.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry).
Upon discussion of his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Níngdū Xiàn,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
Xiáng repeatedly declined the offers,
doing so with great sincerity.
He was then instead appointed Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of the Right of Splendid Happiness),
with the position of Shìzhōng remaining as before.
He was granted twenty close attendants,
and his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Fēngchéng Xiàn,
with the same number of households as before.
In the second year,
he presented a memorial requesting retirement.
An imperial edict relieved him of the Shìzhōng position,
and promoted him to Tèjìn (Special Advanced Rank).
In the third year,
he was transferred to be an Envoy with Credentials, Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant), Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiāng Zhōu.
Xiáng was skilled in official administration.
He served in the province for four years,
and was praised by the common people.
To the south of the provincial capital, overlooking the water, there was a steep peak.
The elders traditionally passed down the saying,
that
“whenever a Governor (Cìshǐ) ascends this mountain, he is immediately replaced.”
Because of this, successive administrations dared not visit it.
Xiáng built pavilions and terraces on that spot,
hosting his subordinates,
to show his lack of superstitious apprehension.
In the sixth year,
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant) and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of the Right of Splendid Happiness).
He was granted twenty close attendants.
Before he arrived,
he was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè (Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs),
Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple),
with the Shìzhōng title remaining as before.
He died of illness on the road.
He was seventy-four years old at the time.
The Emperor wore plain mourning clothes and expressed grief for him.
He was posthumously granted Yòu Guānglù (Grand Master of the Right of Splendid Happiness).
Before this,
Jí Shìzhān, the Cānjūn (Staff Officer) of the Jīng Fǔ City Bureau, employed ten thousand men to dredge the fire prevention pool of the military armory.
A gold belt hook was found,
with raised carvings that were extremely intricate and ingenious.
The seal script read:
“Grant you a gold hook,
to be both Duke and Marquis.”
Shìzhān
was the son-in-law of Xiáng’s elder brother.
The daughter secretly gave it to Xiáng,
and Xiáng happily wore it.
Within a year, he attained high rank.
Cài Dàogōng, courtesy name Huáijiǎn,
was a native of Guānjùn, Nányáng.
His father, Nà,
was Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yì Zhōu during the Sòng dynasty.
In his youth, Dàogōng was generous, magnanimous, and possessed great capacity.
When Emperor Wén of Qí was in Yōng Zhōu,
he summoned him to fill the post of Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk),
and later appointed him Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (Supernumerary Cavalry Regular Attendant).
Later, he repeatedly achieved military merits,
and was promoted to Yuèqí Xiàowèi (Colonel of Agile Cavalry) and Hòujūn Jiāngjūn (General of the Rear Army).
Toward the end of the Jiànwǔ era,
he was sent out to be Fǔguó Sīmǎ (Military Advisor of the State-Aiding General) and Prefect (Lìng) of Rǔnán.
When the Prince of Nánkāng of Qí was in Jīng Zhōu,
he recommended Dàogōng to be Xīzhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Central Army of the Western Gentleman-of-the-Household),
and added the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (State-Aiding General).
When the Righteous Army arose,
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, viewing Dàogōng as a veteran general
who had long demonstrated authority and strategy,
trusted him completely and appointed him
to be Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Subdues the Army) and Xīzhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn (Staff Officer of Consultative Affairs of the Western Gentleman-of-the-Household).
He was subsequently transferred to Sīmǎ (Military Advisor).
In the first year of Zhōngxīng,
when Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard).
When Lǔ Xiūliè, the Administrator of Bāxī, and others gathered troops from Bā and Shǔ and attacked Shàngmíng,
Dàogōng was given credentials and appointed Supervisor of the various armies dispatched to suppress the west.
Upon reaching Tǔtái,
he engaged the rebels in battle.
Dàogōng secretly deployed surprise troops behind them,
and utterly defeated them in a single battle.
Xiūliè and his forces surrendered at the army gate.
Based on his merit, he was promoted to Zhōnglǐngjūn (Commander of the Central Army),
but he firmly declined the acceptance.
He was sent out to be Envoy with Credentials, Yòu Jiāngjūn (General of the Right), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sī Zhōu.
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
upon discussion of his merits, he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Hànshòu Xiàn,
with a stipend of seven hundred households,
and his title was advanced to Píngběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North).
In the third year,
the Wèi surrounded Sī Zhōu.
At that time, the troops within the city numbered fewer than five thousand,
and the food supplies could only last half a year.
The Wèi army attacked,
without stopping day or night.
Dàogōng resisted and defended based on the situation,
and all their advances were crushed immediately.
The Wèi then built large carts loaded with earth,
advancing simultaneously from four sides,
intending to fill the moat.
Dàogōng, however, always lined up covered assault ships and fighting vessels inside to wait for them,
so the Wèi troops could not advance.
They also secretly constructed covered tunnels to drain the water,
but Dàogōng countered by loading earth to block them.
They held out against each other for more than a hundred days,
and the number of heads taken and captives seized was countless.
The Wèi extensively built siege ladders and battering rams,
and the siege intensified daily.
Dàogōng built earthen mountains inside the city,
more than twenty *zhàng* thick;
He also made many great pikes,
twenty-five feet long,
equipped with long blades,
and ordered brave men to stab the Wèi troops who tried to scale the walls.
The Wèi army greatly feared this,
and was about to withdraw.
It happened that Dàogōng’s illness worsened severely.
He summoned his elder brother’s son, Sēngxié, his cousin, Líng'ēn, and the various generals and commanders, and told them:
“I have received profound grace from the state,
but I have failed to destroy the bandits and rebels.
Now my suffering is getting much worse,
and I cannot sustain myself for long.
You must hold fast to your loyalty even unto death,
do not let me die with regrets.”
He then ordered them to bring his credentials (jié) and said to Sēngxié:
“When I received the order to go beyond the borders,
I relied solely on this;
Since I cannot bring it back to court in service,
I intend to take it with me when I depart.
It must accompany my coffin.”
Everyone wept.
He died in the fifth month of that year.
When the Wèi learned of Dàogōng’s death,
their attacks became fiercer.
Previously,
the imperial court had dispatched Cáo Jǐngzōng, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐng Zhōu, leading troops to reinforce the city.
Jǐngzōng reached Zuòxiàn,
but halted his troops and did not advance.
By the eighth month,
the grain inside the city was exhausted,
and the city fell.
An imperial edict stated:
“Dàogōng, Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Sī Zhōu, Píngběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sī Zhōu, and Founding Earl of Hànshòu Xiàn,
possessed cautious temperament and capable talent,
with outstanding ability and ambition.
When the foundation of the imperial enterprise was laid,
he exerted his strength in Shǎnxī.
Receiving appointment on the frontier,
his achievements were manifest wherever he served.
When bandits and rebels were aggressive,
he dedicated his sincerity to defense and resistance.
His ingenious strategies were implemented repeatedly,
and reports of victory arrived daily.
Unfortunately, he became ill,
and soon died.
The defense he maintained through his remaining stratagems
allowed the resistance to continue into the next period of time.
If he had not sacrificed himself for the state and forgotten himself,
with both loyalty and decisiveness reaching their utmost,
how could the defense have persisted after his death,
only yielding when utterly exhausted?
Thinking of this causes deep sorrow and lamentation,
exceeding normal sentiment.
To posthumously increase his honors
is appropriate under the circumstances.
He is hereby posthumously granted Zhènxi Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the West),
with the titles Envoy with Credentials, Supervisor, Governor (Cìshǐ), and Earl remaining as before.
Furthermore, efforts should be made to purchase his coffin and funeral supplies,
providing resources as deemed appropriate.”
In the eighth year,
Wèi agreed to return Dàogōng’s remains.
His family exchanged female musicians for them,
and he was buried in Xiāngyáng.
His son, Dàn, succeeded him,
and died while serving as Administrator of Hédōng.
His grandson, Gù, died young,
and the peerage was abolished.
Yáng Gōngzé, courtesy name Jūnyì,
was a native of Xī Xiàn, Tiānshuǐ.
His father, Zhònghuái,
served as a general under Yīn Yǎn, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yù Zhōu, at the beginning of the Tàishǐ era (Sòng dynasty).
When Yǎn rebelled,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (State-Aiding General) Liú Miǎn campaigned against Yǎn.
Zhònghuái fought bravely,
and died at Héngtáng.
Gōngzé was with his father in the army.
Though he had not yet reached adulthood,
he risked the battlefield, embraced the corpse, and wept loudly,
losing consciousness for a long time.
Miǎn ordered Zhònghuái’s head to be returned.
After Gōngzé completed the funeral preparations,
he carried the coffin on his back, walking back to his home village.
Because of this, he became well known.
He served successively as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (Supernumerary Cavalry Attendant-in-Waiting).
Fàn Bónián, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Liáng Zhōu, commissioned him as Administrator of Sòngxī and concurrently Commandant of Báimǎ Garrison.
The Dī bandit Lǐ Wūnú started a rebellion,
attacking Báimǎ.
Gōngzé held fast to the defense for a considerable time.
Arrows were exhausted and provisions were depleted,
and he fell captive to the bandit.
He raised his voice and cursed the rebels.
Wūnú admired his spirit,
and treated him with greater generosity,
requesting that he work together with him.
Gōngzé falsely agreed but plotted against him.
The plot was exposed,
and he escaped back alone on horseback.
The Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu, Wáng Xuánmiǎo, reported the matter in a memorial,
and Qí Gāodì issued an edict highly praising him.
He was appointed Jìnshòu Tàishǒu.
While in office, he maintained integrity and self-restraint.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
he served as Zhènběi Chángliú Cānjūn.
He was promoted to Fúfēng Tàishǒu.
He left office due to mourning for his mother.
The Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu, Chén Xiǎndá, recalled him to serve as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn,
and he concurrently resumed the post of Tàishǒu.
Soon after,
the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, Bādōng Wáng Zǐxiǎng, stirred up rebellion.
Gōngzé led his troops forward to suppress him.
When the matter was settled,
he was promoted to Wǔníng Tàishǒu.
He served in the commandery for seven years;
his private wealth amounted to nothing measurable in baskets or piculs,
and the common people found his rule agreeable.
He entered the capital to serve as Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Nánkāng Wáng became the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
he again served as Xī Zhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiāo Yǐngzhòu joined the righteous endeavor,
and appointed Gōngzé as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and concurrent Xī Zhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn,
with the post of Zhōngbīng remaining as before.
He led his forces eastward.
At that time, the Xíngshì of Xiāngzhōu, Zhāng Bǎojī, mobilized troops and held his position,
not yet knowing whom to support.
When Gōngzé's army reached Bālíng,
he turned his army back to launch a campaign southward.
When the army reached Báishā,
Bǎojī became fearful,
and took off his armor, awaiting him.
When Gōngzé arrived,
he pacified and accepted him.
The Xiāng region was thus stabilized.
When Hé Dì ascended the throne,
he was granted the credentials of Chíjìe, Dūdū Xiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Gāozǔ led the masses of troops to Miǎnkǒu.
Sūn Lèzǔ, the Chéngzhǔ of Lǔshān,
and Zhāng Chōng, the Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu, each held their respective cities and had not yet surrendered.
Gōngzé led the forces from the Xiāng administration to join the gathering at Xiàkǒu.
At that time, all the armies of Jīngzhōu received their orders from Gōngzé,
and even Xiāo Yǐngdá, though of noble imperial lineage, was subordinate to him.
He was repeatedly promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
retaining his Chíjìe and Cìshǐ positions as before.
When Yǐngchéng was pacified,
Gāozǔ ordered all the armies to advance downstream immediately that same day.
Gōngzé received the order to serve as the vanguard,
going directly to seize Cháisāng.
Once Jiāngzhōu was settled,
they marched eastward continuously,
heading straight for the Jīngyì (Capital).
Gōngzé's commands and orders were strict and clear;
he did not violate (loot) even the smallest item,
and wherever they went, everyone relied upon him.
When the main army reached Xīnlín,
Gōngzé moved his camp from Yuèchéng to the North Tower of the Lǐngjūn Fǔ fortress,
which faced the Nányèmén.
He once ascended the tower to observe the battle.
Those inside the city saw his pennant and carriage canopy from afar,
and fired a *shénfēng nǔ* (divine-tipped crossbow) bolt at him.
The arrow pierced his folding chair (*húchuáng*).
His attendants all turned pale.
Gōngzé said:
"It almost hit my leg."
He continued to talk and laugh as if nothing had happened.
Dōnghūn secretly selected brave warriors by night to attack Gōngzé's palisade.
The army camp was alarmed and disturbed,
but Gōngzé remained firmly lying down and did not rise.
He calmly ordered them to counterattack,
and Dōnghūn's forces consequently retreated.
Most of the troops led by Gōngzé were people from Xiāngxī,
who were timid and weak by nature.
The defenders inside the city held them in contempt,
believing they would be easy to deal with,
and whenever they sallied forth to sweep the area,
they always attacked Gōngzé's camp first.
Gōngzé encouraged his soldiers,
and they achieved many victories and captures.
When the city was finally pacified,
some of those exiting the city were stripped and robbed.
Gōngzé personally led his subordinates,
forming a battle array at the Dōngyèmén,
to guard and escort officials, nobles, gentry, and commoners.
Therefore, most of those who exited passed through Gōngzé's camp.
He was promoted to the title of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
retaining his Chíjìe and Cìshǐ positions as before,
and returned to garrison the Nánfān region.
Initially,
when Gōngzé advanced eastward,
most of the commanderies in the Xiāng region had not yet submitted.
When Gōngzé returned to the prefecture,
only then did all the various settlements and garrisons disperse (submit).
In Tiānjiān Yuánnián (the first year of the Tiānjiān era),
he was promoted to the title of Píngnán Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as the Níngdū Xiànhóu,
with an estate of 1,500 households.
Xiāngzhōu had suffered from banditry and chaos for several years,
and many people had scattered and fled.
Gōngzé used light punishments and low taxes.
After a short time,
the population was replenished.
Although his governance lacked stern authority,
he maintained his personal integrity and caution,
and was well-liked by the officials and common people.
It was the custom in Xiāng region for ordinary families to seek provincial posts through bribery.
When Gōngzé arrived,
he completely stopped this practice.
Those he recruited were all prominent families from the prefectures and commanderies,
and Gāozǔ transmitted this policy to all the prefectures as a standard practice.
In the fourth year (of Tiānjiān),
he was summoned to serve as Zhōng Hùjūn.
When his replacement arrived,
he departed immediately, traveling on two small boats.
He accepted none of the farewell gifts.
He was subsequently promoted to Wèiwèi Qīng,
and additionally granted the position of Sǎnqí Chángshì.
At that time, the court began to discuss a northern expedition.
Because Gōngzé’s imposing reputation was already well-known,
upon reaching the capital,
an edict granted him temporary Chíjìe status and ordered him to first garrison Luòkǒu.
Gōngzé contracted a disease after receiving the command.
He said to his close relatives:
"In the past, Lián Pō and Mǎ Yuán were passed over because of old age,
yet they exerted themselves to request employment.
Now the state does not consider me decrepit and cowardly,
but trusts me to be the vanguard.
Compared to the ancients,
this is indeed a great honor.
Although I am suffering from illness right before setting out,
how can I reluctantly decline this duty?
To be buried wrapped in a horse hide,
that is my aspiration."
He then forced himself to rise and board the boat.
When he reached Luòkǒu,
several thousand households of officials and commoners from Shòuchūn surrendered.
The Cìshǐ of Wèi Yùzhōu, Xuē Gōngdù, dispatched his Chief Clerk Shí Róng and others as a vanguard to engage in battle.
Gōngzé immediately beheaded Shí Róng,
and pursued the routed enemy to Shòuchūn.
He only turned back when he was dozens of *lǐ* away from the city.
He died of his illness while with the army,
aged sixty-one.
Gāozǔ grieved deeply over his death,
and held a mourning ceremony that same day.
He was posthumously granted Chējì Jiāngjūn,
and provided with one set of drums and pipes (for ceremonial use).
His posthumous title was Liè.
Gōngzé was a genuinely honest and benevolent person.
At home, he was profoundly harmonious;
he treated his brother’s sons better than his own,
entrusting all his family wealth to them.
He was fond of learning by nature,
and even when residing with the army,
his hands never stopped handling books.
The scholar-officials praised him for this.
His son Piāo succeeded him.
Due to a crime, the peerage was abolished.
Because Gāozǔ considered Gōngzé an meritorious official,
he issued a special edict allowing his eldest concubine-born son, Tiǎo, to succeed.
Tiǎo firmly declined,
and only accepted after several years had passed.
Dèng Yuánqǐ, courtesy name Zhòngjū,
was a native of Dāngyáng in Nánjùn.
In youth, he possessed courage and capability,
and his physical strength surpassed that of ordinary men.
He was chivalrous by nature,
and enjoyed giving relief and aid.
Many young men in his village and hometown attached themselves to him.
He began his career when the prefecture appointed him Zhōu Pì Yìcáo Cóngshì Shǐ.
He was transferred to Fèng Cháoqǐng.
The Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu, Xiāo Miǎn, appointed him Huáilǐ Lìng.
He was promoted to Hóngnóng Tàishǒu and Píngxī Jūnshì.
At that time, Mǎ Róng of Xīyáng led a band to plunder along the river,
causing commercial travel to cease.
Cìshǐ Xiāo Yáoxīn ordered Yuánqǐ to lead troops to suppress and pacify them.
He was promoted to Wǔníng Tàishǒu.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
the Wèi army pressed upon Yìyáng,
and Yuánqǐ led troops from the commandery to reinforce it.
The barbarian leader Tián Kǒngmíng attached himself to Wèi,
styling himself the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu.
He plundered the Sān Guān
and planned to attack Xiàkǒu.
Yuánqǐ led elite soldiers to attack him.
Within ten days to a month,
he frequently captured six citadels,
slaying or capturing tens of thousands.
The remaining rebels all dispersed and fled.
He then garrisoned the Sān Guān.
Zhāng Chōng, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu, supervised military affairs north of the Héběi.
Yuánqǐ repeatedly wrote letters to Zhāng Chōng
requesting to recall his army.
Zhāng Chōng replied, saying:
“Since Your Excellency is there,
and I am here,
this forms the strategic configuration of inner and outer defense,
what is called a ‘metal city and boiling moat.’
Should you abandon this post suddenly,
then thorns and brambles will grow there.”
Thereupon, he memorialized that Yuánqǐ be appointed Píngnán Zhōngbīng Cānjūnshì.
From then on, he was victorious in every battle,
his valor surpassing his contemporaries.
More than ten thousand soldiers, ready to die, were happy to serve under his command.
When the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) arose,
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu sent a letter inviting him.
Zhāng Chōng had always treated Yuánqǐ generously,
and the masses all feared Zhāng Chōng.
When the letter arrived,
many of Yuánqǐ’s subordinate troops urged him to return to Yǐng.
Yuánqǐ spoke loudly to the assembly, saying:
“The imperial court is tyrannical,
executing chief ministers.
Base men are being employed,
and the way of the high officials is exhausted.
Jīng and Yōng Provinces have jointly launched this great undertaking;
why worry that we shall not succeed?
Furthermore, my aged mother is in the West (Xī);
how can I betray my origins?
If the endeavor fails,
I would rather be executed by the ignorant court
and fortunately avoid the crime of unfilial conduct.”
On that very day, he prepared his equipment and set out.
When he reached Jiānglíng,
he was made Xī Zhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and given the additional title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
He led his troops and joined Gāozǔ at Xiàkǒu.
Gāozǔ ordered Wáng Mào, Cáo Jǐngzōng, and Yuánqǐ, among others, to besiege the city,
constructing defensive walls extending nine *lǐ*.
Zhāng Chōng fought repeatedly,
but was always soundly defeated,
so he withdrew behind the city walls and held fast.
When Emperor Hé Dì ascended the throne,
Yuánqǐ was granted the titles of Jiǎ Jié, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu.
He was later promoted to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and moved his headquarters to Nántáng Xīzhǔ.
In the seventh month of the first year of Zhōngxīng,
Yǐng Citadel (Yǐng Chéng) surrendered.
He was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yìzhōu with his existing title,
and remained the vanguard force,
first securing Xúnyáng.
When the main army advanced to the Capital (Jīng Yì),
Yuánqǐ built a fortress at Jiànyáng Mén,
joining Wáng Mào and Cáo Jǐngzōng in forming a long siege line.
He personally faced the sharp points of the enemy's arrows.
After Jiànkāng Chéng was pacified,
he was promoted to the title of Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis (Hóu) of Dāngyáng County,
with a taxable population of one thousand two hundred households.
He was further promoted to the title of Zuǒ Jiāngjūn,
with his governorship (Cìshǐ) remaining as before.
He then formally commenced his duties.
Initially,
when the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) first arose,
Liú Jìlián, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yìzhōu, maintained neutrality;
but upon hearing that Yuánqǐ was about to arrive,
he consequently raised troops to resist and defend.
This account is found in the Biography of Jìlián.
When Yuánqǐ arrived at Bāxī,
the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Bāxī, Zhū Shìlüè, opened the gates and received him.
Previously, many Shǔ people had fled.
Now, they came out and submitted to Yuánqǐ,
all claiming to have risen in righteousness to answer the court.
The army, new and old recruits, numbered over thirty thousand.
Yuánqǐ had been on the march for a long time,
and army provisions were exhausted.
Someone advised him, saying:
“The administration in the land of Shǔ is lax,
and many people feign illness.
If you examine the household registers of Bāxī Commandery
and subsequently punish them,
the gain will surely be substantial.”
Yuánqǐ agreed with this.
Lǐ Yīng, the Magistrate (Lìng) of Fú, remonstrated, saying:
“My Lord, you have a strong enemy ahead
and no reinforcements following.
The mountain people have only just submitted
and are observing our virtue.
If we correct them with harshness and severity,
the people will certainly be unable to bear it.
Once the people’s hearts are alienated,
it will be too late for regret.
Why must feigning illness be used to supply the army?
I, Yīng, request permission to go out and devise a plan;
there is no need to worry about insufficient provisions.”
Yuánqǐ said:
“Excellent.
I shall entrust the entire matter to you, Sir.”
Lǐ Yīng withdrew,
and led the wealthy citizens to present grain for military use.
Soon, thirty thousand *hú* were obtained.
Yuánqǐ first dispatched generals Wáng Yuánzōng and others,
who defeated Jìlián’s general Lǐ Fèngbó at Xīnbā,
and Qí Wǎnshèng at Chìshuǐ.
The forces advanced and encamped at Xīpíng.
Jìlián then withdrew behind the city walls and defended himself.
Qí Wǎnshèng subsequently defeated Yuánqǐ’s general Lǔ Fāngdá at Húshí,
and more than a thousand soldiers died.
The entire army was struck with fear.
Yuánqǐ then personally led his troops and slowly advanced to Jiǎng Qiáo,
twenty *lǐ* from Chéngdū,
leaving his baggage train at Pí.
Jìlián again dispatched Lǐ Fèngbó and Qí Wǎnshèng with two thousand men
to use side roads and launch a surprise attack on Pí.
They captured it,
and all the military supplies were lost.
Yuánqǐ sent Lǔ Fāngdá's troops to rescue it,
but they were defeated and returned,
and thus failed to regain control.
Yuánqǐ abandoned Pí
and proceeded directly to besiege the provincial capital,
fencing off three sides and digging a trench.
Yuánqǐ went out to inspect the siege fence.
Jìlián sent elite warriors to ambush him.
When they were about to reach his command banner,
Yuánqǐ dismounted from his sedan, held his shield, and shouted at them.
The crowd scattered and dared not advance.
At that time, military conflict in the Yì region had lasted for a long time.
The people abandoned farming.
Both inside and outside the city suffered from famine;
many people resorted to cannibalism.
Roads were cut off,
and Jìlián's resources were exhausted.
Coincidentally, the following year,
Gāozǔ sent an envoy to pardon Jìlián's crimes,
allowing him to surrender.
Jìlián immediately opened the city gates that day and received Yuánqǐ.
Yuánqǐ escorted Jìlián to the Capital (Jīngshī).
With the city opened,
Pí then surrendered.
He executed Lǐ Fèngbó and Qí Wǎnshèng.
Gāozǔ, discussing the merits of pacifying Shǔ,
restored Yuánqǐ’s title of Píngxī Jiāngjūn,
and increased his enfeoffment by eight hundred households,
totaling two thousand households including the previous grant.
Yuánqǐ appointed his townsman Yǔ Qiánlóu as Lùshì Cānjūn,
and also acquired Jiǎng Guāngjì, a former retainer of Xiāo Yáoxīn, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jīngzhōu.
He treated them both generously
and entrusted them with provincial affairs.
Yǔ Qiánlóu was very upright and honest,
and Jiǎng Guāngjì was rich in strategies.
Both urged him to implement good governance.
When Yuánqǐ conquered Jìlián,
he kept none of the city’s wealth or treasures for himself.
He diligently cared for the affairs of the people,
and spoke no word of wealth or beauty.
By nature, he was originally able to drink wine,
up to one *hú* without confusion,
but at this time, he completely stopped.
The people of Shǔ universally praised him.
Yuánqǐ’s maternal cousin, Liáng Jīnsūn, was frivolous and unstable by nature.
His ambition and conduct differed from Yǔ Qiánlóu’s,
so he spoke to Yuánqǐ, saying:
“People in the city say there are three governors (Cìshǐ).
How can Your Excellency tolerate this?”
Because of this, Yuánqǐ alienated Yǔ Qiánlóu and Jiǎng Guāngjì,
and his administrative effectiveness subsequently declined.
He was in the prefecture for two years.
Because his mother was elderly, he requested to return home to care for her.
The imperial edict permitted this.
He was summoned to serve as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was replaced by Xīchāng Hóu Xiāo Yuānzǎo.
At this time,
Liángzhōu Chángshǐ Xiàhóu Dàoqiān rebelled at Nánzhèng.
He invited the Wèi people (Northern Wèi) in.
The commandant of Báimǎ Garrison, Yǐn Tiānbǎo, immediately sent a messenger to report to Shǔ.
Wèi generals Wáng Jǐngyìn and Kǒng Líng raided Dōng and Xī Jìnshòu.
They both sent pleas for urgent help.
The multitude urged Yuánqǐ to rush to their rescue.
Yuánqǐ said:
"The Imperial Court is ten thousand *lǐ* away,
and the army cannot arrive suddenly.
If bandits and invaders spread their harm,
it will be necessary to suppress and eliminate them.
The responsibility for overall command and supervision,
if not mine, then whose?
Why hurry so quickly to the rescue?"
