Qián Lóu and others earnestly remonstrated with him,
but he did not heed any of them.
Gāozǔ also granted Yuánqǐ the credentials (jié) to command all punitive expedition forces (Dūdu Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì),
to save Hanzhōng.
By the time he arrived,
Wèi had already attacked and captured the two Jìnshòu areas.
When Yuānzǎo was about to arrive,
Yuánqǐ busied himself greatly with preparing his return.
Stored grain, provisions, and equipment—
he left virtually nothing behind.
When Yuānzǎo entered the city,
he greatly resented and was disappointed by this.
He consequently memorialized that Yuánqǐ had lingered and neglected military affairs.
Yuánqǐ was arrested and handed over to the prefectural prison.
He hanged himself in the prison,
at the age of forty-eight.
The relevant authorities subsequently impeached him and requested the stripping of his title and territory.
An imperial edict reduced his fiefdom by half.
He was then re-enfeoffed as Sōngzī Xiànhóu,
with a thousand households.
Previously,
when Yuánqǐ was in Jīngzhōu,
the Inspector (Cìshǐ), Prince of Suí, appointed Yuánqǐ as Cóngshì Biéjià.
Yǔ Bì strongly maintained that this was unacceptable.
Yuánqǐ resented him for this.
When the main army had reached the capital (Jīngshī),
Bì was inside the city,
and was extremely afraid.
When the city was pacified,
Yuánqǐ first sent someone to welcome Bì,
telling people:
"If Administrator Yǔ (Yǔ Biéjià) were killed by the rebellious soldiers,
I would have no means of clearing my name."
He then gave him generous gifts.
When he was young, he also once visited his farmstead in Xīzǔ.
A *shāmen* (Buddhist monk) approached him, begging.
Yuánqǐ asked the farmer:
"How much rice do you have?"
He replied:
"Twenty *hú*."
Yuánqǐ gave it all away to the monk.
People at the time praised him for having great magnanimity.
When Yuánqǐ was first appointed to Yìzhōu,
he passed through Jiānglíng to welcome his mother.
His mother, serving the Dao (a reference to religious practice or moral rectitude),
was staying in a lodging house,
and refused to come out.
Yuánqǐ bowed and requested her to travel with him.
His mother said:
"A child of a poor and humble family who suddenly achieves wealth and status,
how can he maintain it for long?
I would rather die than enter into disaster and ruin with you."
When Yuánqǐ arrived at Bādōng,
and heard that Shǔ was in chaos,
he ordered Jiǎng Guāngjì to perform a divination.
The result was the hexagram *Jiǎn* (Obstruction).
He sighed deeply, saying:
"Am I perhaps Dèng Ài, reaching this point?"
Later events indeed matched the divination.
His son, Kēng, succeeded him.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, commented: At the end of Yǒngyuán,
Jīngzhōu had not yet had a crisis,
but Xiāo Yǐngzhòu mobilized all the troops of Chǔ,
and was the first to answer the righteous uprising.
Was this perhaps inspired by Heaven,
or planned by man?
If not,
how could the ensuing swift adhesion have been so resolute?
Yǐngdá, nephew and uncle, brought fortune down to later generations.
Xiàhóu, Yáng, and Dèng all enjoyed great reputations.
How splendid!
Xiáng was cautious and sincere;
Yáng and Cài were incorruptible and upright.
Gentlemen may learn from them.
Biographies V: Zhāng Hóngcè (Yǔ Yù), Zhèng Shàoshū, Lǚ Sēngzhēn
Zhāng Hóngcè, courtesy name Zhēnjiǎn,
was a native of Fányáng Fāngchéng.
He was the younger paternal cousin of Empress Wénxiàn.
In youth, he was famous for his filial piety.
His mother once fell ill.
For five days she ate nothing.
Hóngcè also refused to eat.
His mother forced herself to eat congee for him.
Only then did he eat what his mother had left over.
During the mourning period for his mother,
he did not eat salt or vegetables for three years,
almost destroying his health.
The brothers were loving toward one another,
and could not bear to be separated even briefly.
Although they each had their own households,
they always slept and rose together.
People of the time compared them to the Jiāng Hóng brothers.
He began his career as Chángshì of Qí’s Principality of Shàolíng Wáng.
He was promoted to Fèng Cháoqǐng, and then Xī Zhōngláng Jiāngxià Wáng Xíng Cānjūn.
Hóngcè and Gāozǔ were similar in age.
From youth, they were close and intimate.
He followed Gāozǔ wherever he traveled or resided.
Whenever Gāozǔ entered a room,
Hóngcè always sensed a cloudy, smoky aura,
and his body would immediately become reverent.
Hóngcè thus held Gāozǔ in special respect.
At the end of Jiànwǔ,
Hóngcè lodged with Gāozǔ.
After they were well into their cups,
they moved their mats beneath the stars.
They spoke about current affairs.
Hóngcè then asked Gāozǔ:
"What do the astrological portents indicate?
Will the state certainly remain safe?"
Gāozǔ said:
"Is that something that can be spoken of?"
Hóngcè responded:
"Please tell me the omens."
Gāozǔ said:
"North of the Hàn River, the earthly *qì* is failing.
East of the Zhè River, there is an omen of urgent military action.
At the beginning of this winter,
Wèi will certainly move.
If they move, the territory north of the Hàn will be lost.
The Emperor is now suffering a prolonged illness,
and there are many dissenting opinions.
Should someone watch for a crisis,
Jībù will seize the opportunity to act.
But this, too, will achieve nothing;
he will merely clear the way for others.
Next year, there will be chaos in the capital and surrounding areas.
The dead will be more numerous than tangled hemp.
The mandate of Qí,
will perish from this point on.
A hero must rise up in Liáng, Chǔ, and Hàn regions."
Hóngcè said:
"Where is this hero now?
Is he already wealthy and noble,
or is he among the common people?"
Gāozǔ laughed and said:
"Guāngwǔ once said,
'How do you know it is not me?'"
Hóngcè stood up and said:
"What has been said tonight
is the will of Heaven.
I request that we establish the division between sovereign and subject."
Gāozǔ said:
"Are you, my maternal uncle (jiù), seeking to emulate Dèng Chén?"
That winter,
the Wèi army raided Xīnyě.
Gāozǔ led troops as reinforcement,
and also received a secret command,
subsequently replacing Cáo Hǔ as Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
Hóngcè rejoiced upon hearing this,
and said to Gāozǔ:
"What was spoken in the night
must truly be verified now."
Gāozǔ laughed and said:
"Do not speak too much."
Hóngcè followed Gāozǔ westward,
and participated in military strategy sessions.
He personally engaged in hard labor,
and did not shirk hardship.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
Míngdì (明帝) died.
The dying edict appointed Gāozǔ (高祖) as the Governor (Cìshǐ 刺史) of Yōngzhōu (雍州).
Gāozǔ then memorialized that Hóngcè (弘策) be made Record-keeping Adjutant (Lùshì Cānjūn 錄事參軍),
concurrently holding the post of Magistrate (Lìng 令) of Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Gāozǔ saw that chaos was imminent throughout the realm,
and harbored the desire to rectify and save the world.
He secretly made preparations and accumulated resources.
The scope of his planning,
extended only to Hóngcè.
At that time, the Prince Xuānwǔ (宣武王) of Chángshā (長沙) returned after being relieved of his command in Yìzhōu (益州),
and was subsequently made Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ 長史) of the General of the Western Central Department (Xī Zhōngláng 西中郎),
managing the affairs of Yǐngzhōu (郢州).
Gāozǔ sent Hóngcè to Yǐng,
to lay out his strategy before Prince Xuānwǔ.
The details are recorded in the annals of Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ Jì 高祖紀).
Hóngcè then persuaded the Prince, saying:
“In the past, when the Zhōu (周) House declined,
the feudal lords fought vigorously.
Qí Huán (齊桓) was merely an ordinary person,
yet he was able to rectify the realm and unite the lords (Yī Kuāng Jiǔ Hé 一匡九合).
The people praise him even now.
Now the virtue of Qí (齊) is diminished,
and the world is heading toward chaos.
The fate of the common people,
must eventually find a master.
Given that Yǐngzhōu occupies the strategic center of the river,
and the territory of Yōng (雍) has abundant war horses,
you and your brother are heroes and martial,
without equal today.
If you hold these two provinces like tigers,
dividing the empire into three parts,
and rally the righteous armies,
to petition for the lives of the populace,
dethroning the obscured ruler and establishing the enlightened one,
it will be as easy as turning over your palm.
If you do this,
then the accomplishments of Huán (桓) and Wén (文) can be achieved,
and glory unequaled for generations can be established.
Do not be deceived by mere rascals (shùzǐ 豎子),
and become a joke after your death.
Yōngzhōu has been thoroughly considered.
I hope you will plan this well.”
The Prince was somewhat displeased but had no means to refuse.
When the Righteous Army (Yìshī 義師) was about to rise,
Gāozǔ summoned Hóngcè and Lǚ Sēngzhēn (呂僧珍) into his residence at night to finalize the plan.
At dawn, the troops were dispatched.
Hóngcè was appointed General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn 輔國將軍) and Commander of the Army (Jūnzhǔ 軍主),
leading ten thousand men and supervising the military affairs of the rear division.
When the Western Administration (Xītái 西臺) was established,
he was made Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi 步兵校尉).
He was promoted to Consultant Adjutant (Zīyì Cānjūn 諮議參軍) to the General of Cavalry and Chariots (Chējì 車騎).
When the city of Yǐng was pacified,
generals like Xiāo Yǐngdá (蕭穎達) and Yáng Gōngzé (楊公則) all wanted to halt the army at Xiàkǒu (夏口).
Gāozǔ believed it was appropriate to seize the momentum and drive straight forward,
heading directly for the capital (Jīngyì 京邑).
He discussed this strategy with Hóngcè,
and Hóngcè agreed completely with Gāozǔ.
He also consulted with General Who Pacifies the Distant (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn 寧遠將軍) Yǔ Yù (庾域).
Yù also concurred.
So, Gāozǔ ordered all the armies to immediately set out on the road,
traveling along the river to Jiànkāng (建康).
For every rugged shoreline (jī 磯), inlet (pǔ 浦), or village (cūnluò 村落),
where the army marched, rested for the night, or established camps,
Hóngcè had preemptively mapped and analyzed them;
they were all mentally indexed.
When the Righteous Army reached Xīnlín (新林),
Wáng Mào (王茂) and Cáo Jǐngzōng (曹景宗) were engaged in battle at Dàháng (大航).
Gāozǔ sent Hóngcè, bearing the credentials (jié 節), to reward and encourage them.
The troops were all highly motivated.
On that very day,
they subsequently defeated the Zhūquè (朱雀) army.
Gāozǔ entered and encamped at Shítóuchéng (石頭城).
Hóngcè garrisoned the gates and served as a guard,
receiving and guiding local gentry and officials.
Many were fully spared.
When the city was pacified,
Gāozǔ sent Hóngcè and Lǚ Sēngzhēn ahead to enter and clear the palace,
and to seal and inspect the treasury.
At that time, rare treasures in the city were piled up.
Hóngcè repeatedly cautioned and restrained his division,
such that not a single thing was violated.
He was promoted to Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng 衞尉卿),
and granted the title Gentleman of the Palace (Jǐshì Zhōng 給事中).
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
he was given the concurrent post of Palace Attendant Consultant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍),
ennobled as the Marquis (Hóu 侯) of Táoyáng County (洮陽縣),
with a stipend of two thousand two hundred households.
Hóngcè served the ruler with utmost loyalty,
doing everything he knew how to do.
His friends and old acquaintances,
were recommended and promoted according to their talent.
All the gentry (jìnshēn 搢紳) flocked to him.
At that time, the remnants of Dōng Hūn (東昏)'s faction, having just received the amnesty,
were mostly unsettled.
Several hundred men used bundled reeds as torches and strapped weapons to themselves.
They managed to enter the Northern and Southern Flanking Gates (Nánběi Yè 南北掖) and cause a disturbance,
burning the Shénhǔ (神虎) Gate and the Zǒngzhāng (總章) Tower.
Lǚ Sēngzhēn, Aide to the General of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn Sīmǎ 前軍司馬), who was on duty inside the palace,
used the palace guards to resist and defeat them.
Some of the bandits split off and entered the office of the Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Fǔ 衞尉府).
Hóngcè was then fighting the fire,
when the bandits secretly attacked him from behind and killed him.
He was forty-seven years old at the time.
Gāozǔ grieved deeply and regretted his loss.
He was granted a prime residential plot,
one set of clothes,
one hundred thousand coins,
one hundred bolts of cloth,
and two hundred *jīn* (斤) of wax.
The imperial edict stated:
“The deceased Minister of the Guards, my cousin-maternal uncle (cóngjiù 從舅),
due to the suddenness of the incident which he overlooked,
lost his life to wicked rascals.
His disposition was pure and upright,
his talent and knowledge were vast and helpful.
From the time he served in the frontier provinces (fān 藩) until he ascended to court,
he remained constant through difficulty and ease, obstruction and smoothness.
Moreover, since the maternal clan (wàishì 外氏) has been declining,
the rites and sacrifices have often ceased.
I felt moved by the sentiments of Wèiyáng (渭陽),
and my affection was entirely placed in him.
We were counting on his loyal service,
to assist and promote this unworthy person.
Now his repayment of service is unfulfilled,
and remembering him increases my perpetual sorrow.
He is posthumously appointed Palace Attendant Consultant (Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍) and General of Cavalry and Chariots (Chējì Jiāngjūn 車騎將軍).
He is granted one set of drums and pipes (gǔchuī 鼓吹).
His posthumous title (Shì 謚) shall be Mǐn (愍).”
Hóngcè was broad-minded, generous, and easygoing by nature,
and devoted to old friends.
When he achieved high rank and status,
he did not become arrogant due to his noble power.
He treated his old friends and guests,
with the same courtesy as when he was a commoner (bùyī 布yī).
His salary and stipends were all distributed among relatives and friends.
When he met his death,
there was no one who did not mourn and regret it.
His son, Miǎn (緬), succeeded him.
A separate biography for him exists.
Yǔ Yù (庾域), courtesy name Sīdà (司大),
was a native of Xīnyě (新野).
When the Prince Xuānwǔ of Chángshā was in Liángzhōu (梁州),
he appointed Yǔ Yù as Record-keeping Adjutant,
concurrently holding the post of Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu 太守) of Huáyáng (華陽).
At that time, the Wèi (魏) army attacked and besieged Nánzhèng (南鄭).
The province had several dozen empty granaries.
Yù sealed them, wrote labels, and showed them to the officers and soldiers, saying:
“The grain inside these is all full,
enough to last for two years.
Just strive hard and hold fast.”
The morale of the troops was thus stabilized.
When the enemy retreated,
due to his merit, he was appointed Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín Jiān 羽林監),
and promoted to Secretariat Adjutant (Jìshì Cānjūn 記室參軍) to the General of the Southern Central Department (Nán Zhōngláng 南中郎).
At the end of the Yǒngyuán (永元) era,
Gāozǔ raised his army,
and sent a letter inviting Yù.
When the Western Administration was established,
he was appointed General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn 寧朔將軍),
and oversaw personnel selection (xíngxuǎn 行選).
He followed Gāozǔ eastward.
When the army reached Yángkǒu (楊口),
Hédì (和帝) sent Zōng Jué (宗夬), Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞), bearing the imperial mandate to comfort the troops.
Yù then implicitly suggested to Jué, saying:
“The yellow ceremonial axe (huáng yuè 黃鉞) has not yet been granted,
which is unsuitable for commanding all the marquises and nobles.”
When Jué returned to the Western Administration,
the yellow ceremonial axe was immediately conferred upon Gāozǔ.
Since Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (蕭穎冑) was the Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs inside and outside the capital (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì 都督中外諸軍事),
some argued that Gāozǔ should send a memorandum (jiān 牋) to him.
Yù strongly argued against this, and it was not allowed.
So, it stopped there.
When the city of Yǐng was pacified,
the counsel of Yù and Zhāng Hóngcè (張弘策) was in agreement with Gāozǔ's intention,
and he immediately commanded all the armies to advance downstream.
Whenever he offered plans,
they were mostly adopted.
When the Marshal's Administration (Bàfǔ 霸府) was first established,
he was appointed Consultant Adjutant.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he was ennobled as the Viscount (Zǐ 子) of Guǎngmù County (廣牧縣),
and made Aide to the General of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Sīmǎ 後軍司馬).
He was sent out as General Who Pacifies the North, and Grand Administrator of the two commanderies of Bāxī (巴西) and Zǐtóng (梓潼).
Xiàhóu Dàoqiān (夏侯道遷), Chief Clerk of Liángzhōu, rebelled with the entire province and defected to Wèi.
The Wèi cavalry was about to attack Bāxī.
Yù held firmly for over a hundred days.
The provisions in the city were exhausted.
The officers and soldiers all gnawed on grass and ate dirt.
More than half died,
but none lost loyalty.
When the Wèi army retreated,
an imperial edict increased his stipend by two hundred households,
and advanced his noble rank to Earl (Bó 伯).
In the sixth year,
he died in the commandery.
Zhèng Shàoshū, courtesy name Zhòngmíng,
was a man of Kāifēng in Xíngyáng
, whose family had lived for generations in Shòuyáng.
His grandfather, Kūn
, was the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Gāopíng under the Sòng.
Shàoshū was orphaned and poor in his youth.
When he was a little over twenty,
he served as the Magistrate (Lìng) of Ānfēng.
While administering the county, he gained a reputation for competence.
The local province summoned him to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
and he was subsequently transferred to be the Assistant Officer in Charge of Governance (Zhìzhōng Cóngshìshǐ).
At that time, the Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ), Xiāo Dàn, was executed because his brother, Chén, had been executed.
When the court dispatched troops to arrest him arrived,
all those around him were startled and fled.
When Shàoshū heard of the trouble,
he alone rushed to his side.
When Dàn died,
he attended and escorted the coffin.
Everyone praised him for this.
When he arrived at the capital (Jīngshī),
the Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Xú Xiàosì, saw him and was impressed,
saying:
"He is of the same caliber as Zǔ Tì."
When Gāozǔ administered Sīzhōu,
he ordered Shàoshū to be Adjutant in Charge of Military Affairs (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn)
and concurrently Prefect of Chángliú (Zhǎnglú).
Because of this, Shàoshū strongly attached himself to Gāozǔ.
When Gāozǔ resigned his post in the province and returned to the capital,
he dismissed his retainers and guests.
Shàoshū alone firmly requested permission to stay.
Gāozǔ said to him:
"Your talent is certainly useful in its own right,
but I cannot benefit you now.
You should seek another path."
Shàoshū replied:
"My dedication (to you) is set;
by righteousness, I cannot have a second allegiance."
Gāozǔ firmly refused his request,
so he returned to Shòuyáng.
The Provincial Governor, Xiāo Yáochāng, strenuously tried to recruit Shàoshū,
but he ultimately refused the appointment.
Yáochāng became angry
and planned to imprison him,
but intervention saved him from punishment.
When Gāozǔ became the Provincial Governor of Yōngzhōu,
Shàoshū took a shortcut west to rejoin him.
He was appointed Chief Clerk of the Pacification of the Man (Níngmán Zhǎngshǐ) and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Fúfēng.
Since Dōnghūn had already murdered the court officials,
he grew rather suspicious of Gāozǔ.
Shàoshū’s elder brother, Zhí, was a Palace Attendant (Zhíhòu) under Dōnghūn.
Dōnghūn dispatched him to Yōngzhōu,
ostensibly to visit Shàoshū,
but in reality, he secretly intended for him to act as an assassin.
Shàoshū knew this
and secretly informed Gāozǔ.
When Zhí arrived,
Gāozǔ hosted a banquet for him at Shàoshū’s residence,
and joked to Zhí, saying:
"The court sent you here to assassinate me.
This relaxed gathering today
is an excellent opportunity for you to do so."
Both host and guest laughed heartily.
He ordered Zhí to climb the city walls and ramparts
and thoroughly inspect the government offices.
The soldiers, equipment, ships, and warhorses
were all numerous and well-provisioned.
Zhí retired and said to Shàoshū:
"The military strength of Yōngzhōu
is not easily countered."
Shàoshū said:
"When you return,
report everything fully to the Son of Heaven.
If you try to take Yōngzhōu,
I, Shàoshū, request to fight against you with these troops."
He escorted his brother to Nánxiàn,
where they embraced, wept bitterly, and parted.
When the righteous army arose,
he was appointed General Who Routs the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn),
later changed to General of Swift Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
He accompanied Gāozǔ eastward down to Jiāngzhōu,
where Shàoshū was left behind to supervise the affairs of the province,
overseeing the transport of provisions for Jiāngzhōu and Xiāngzhōu.
There was no shortage or lack in the supplies.
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he entered the capital to serve as Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
Shàoshū was loyal in serving his sovereign.
Everything he heard or learned from outside
was reported without the slightest concealment.
Whenever he spoke to Gāozǔ about matters,
if they succeeded,
he would say,
"Your servant is too foolish to have reached this conclusion;
these are all strategies of the sagely ruler."
If they failed,
he would say,
"Your servant's consideration was shallow and brief.
I thought the matter should be handled thus,
and I have probably misled the court by this.
Your servant's crime is grave."
Gāozǔ trusted and relied on him greatly.
He resigned his post due to mourning for his mother.
Shàoshū possessed profound sincerity (filial piety).
Gāozǔ often had people moderate his crying.
Soon after,
he was recalled to serve as General Who Routs the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) and Military Commander of the Right (Yòujūn Sīmǎ).
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yíngdào County (Yíngdào Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
Shortly thereafter, he was again appointed Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng),
with the added title of General Who Routs the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn).
Because the households in Yíngdào County were poor and depleted,
he was re-enfeoffed as the Marquis of Dōngxīng County (Dōngxīng Xiàn Hóu),
with the same stipend of households as before.
Originally,
Shàoshū lost his father when he was young.
He was famous for his filial piety in serving his mother and grandmother
and was respectful and careful in supporting his elder brother.
When he held a prominent position,
all the salary, stipends, and gifts received from the four directions
were handed over to his brother's family.
In the third year [of Tiānjiān],
when the Wèi army besieged Héféi,
Shàoshū, holding his existing title, supervised the various armies stationed at Dōngguān.
When the matter was settled,
he was again appointed Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
Soon after, Yìyáng was captured by Wèi,
and Sīzhōu moved its headquarters south of the pass (Guānnán).
In the fourth year,
Shàoshū was appointed as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), General Who Conquers the Captives (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn), and Provincial Governor of Sīzhōu (Sīzhōu Cìshǐ).
Shàoshū established new city walls and moats,
repaired weapons,
expanded farmland, accumulated grain,
and welcomed refugees.
The common people found peace under his rule.
His nature was somewhat arrogant and impatient,
and he relied on his power and influence.
Nevertheless, he was able to sincerely interact with others
and made many recommendations,
for which the gentry also respected him.
In the sixth year,
he was summoned to court as General of the Left (Zuǒ Jiāngjūn),
given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
and concurrently served as the Grand Impartial Judge (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Sīzhōu and Yùzhōu.
Shàoshū became gravely ill upon reaching home.
The appointment was administered to him in his residence,
and he was carried back to his official quarters.
Imperial envoys bearing medicine
visited several times a day.
In the seventh year,
he died in his official residence,
at the age of forty-five.
Gāozǔ intended to personally attend his wake,
but the lane of Shàoshū’s residence was narrow and humble,
unable to accommodate the imperial carriage,
so he stopped.
An edict stated:
"To pursue the past and remember merit
is what previous kings held dear;
to focus on sincerity toward former servants
is a rule shared across different ages.
The Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì), General of the Right Guards (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn),
Founding Marquis of Dōngxīng County (Dōngxīng Xiàn Kāiguó Hóu), Shàoshū,
established himself as pure and upright,
served his superior with loyalty and reverence.
In difficult times, both in the provinces and at court,
his sincerity and achievements were outstanding.
Starting from the beginning of our righteous cause,
he truly established magnificent feats.
When serving as governor in the border regions,
his achievements were manifest in the places he oversaw.
We were just about to rely on him
to assist Us as Our closest confidant;
his sudden death
fills Our heart with grief.
It is appropriate to bestow special honors
and enhance this benevolent mandate.
He is posthumously appointed Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and General Protecting the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
granted one set of drums and pipes (gǔchuī),
burial accessories from the Eastern Garden (dōngyuán mìqì),
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
and whatever else is required for the funeral rites
shall be supplied upon request.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōng (Loyal)."
After Shàoshū died,
Gāozǔ once wept and said to his court officials:
"Zhèng Shàoshū established a loyal and virtuous character.
When things went well, he praised his sovereign;
when they went wrong, he blamed himself.
Today, there is almost no one comparable to him."
The extent to which he was valued and cherished was thus.
His son, Zhēn, inherited his title.
Lǚ Sēngzhēn, courtesy name Yuán Yú,
was a man from Fàn in Dōng Píng.
His family resided in Guǎng Líng for generations.
He started from humble origins.
When he was a young boy,
he studied under a teacher.
A physiognomist observed the students
and pointed at Sēngzhēn, saying to the professor:
“This one has a rare voice
and the physiognomy of a marquis.”
When he was over twenty,
he attached himself to Liú Bǐng, the Administrator of Dān Yáng under Sòng.
After Bǐng was executed,
he served Tàizǔ (Emperor Wén Huáng) as a clerical assistant in the palace secretariat (mén xià shū zuǒ).
He was seven feet five inches tall
and had a very imposing appearance.
Among his peers, he rarely engaged in overly familiar banter,
and his colleagues all respected him.
When Tàizǔ was the Inspector of Yù Zhōu,
he made Sēngzhēn a record keeper (diǎn qiān),
also holding the post of Magistrate of Méng.
He performed his duties commendably.
When Tàizǔ was promoted to General of the Palace Guard (lǐng jūn),
Sēngzhēn was appointed Chief Clerk (zhǔ bù).
When the demon rebel Táng Yǔ attacked Dōng Yáng,
Tàizǔ led the troops on an eastern campaign,
and instructed Sēngzhēn to manage the administrative affairs of the campaigning army.
Sēngzhēn’s residence was east of Jiàn Yáng Gate.
From the day he received the command to depart,
he passed through Jiàn Yáng Gate daily,
but did not visit his private residence.
Tàizǔ esteemed him even more because of this.
When Tàizǔ became the Administrator of Dān Yáng,
he again appointed Sēngzhēn as the Commander of the Commandery Posts (jùn dū yóu).
When Zǐ Lóng, the Prince of Suí under Qí, was sent out as the Inspector of Jīng Zhōu,
Emperor Wǔ of Qí appointed Sēngzhēn as Zǐ Lóng’s personal guard commander (fáng gé),
and he accompanied Zǐ Lóng to the garrison.
In the ninth year of Yǒng Míng (491 CE),
when Wáng Huàn, the Inspector of Yōng Zhōu, rebelled,
an imperial decree ordered Sēngzhēn to join Cáo Hǔ, the General Pacifying the North (píng běi jiāng jūn), on his western campaign,
serving as a record keeper (diǎn qiān),
and concurrently holding the post of Magistrate of Xīn Chéng.
When the Wèi army invaded north of the Miǎn River,
Chén Xiǎndá, the Minister of Works (sī kōng), marched out to suppress them.
Upon seeing Sēngzhēn, he considered him extraordinary,
and therefore, dismissing the attendants, he called him forward
and said:
“You possess the physiognomy of nobility.
In the future, your achievements will not be inferior to mine.
Strive hard for this.”
In the second year of Jiàn Wǔ (495 CE),
Wèi launched a major invasion southward,
advancing simultaneously along five routes.
Gāozǔ led the army to reinforce Yì Yáng,
and Sēngzhēn was with him in the army.
The Prince Xuān Wǔ of Cháng Shā was then the Inspector of Liáng Zhōu,
and Wèi forces had besieged him for months.
Espionage networks were completely cut off,
and the road between Yì Yáng and Yōng Zhōu was severed.
Gāozǔ wished to send an envoy to Xiāng Yáng
to inquire about the situation in Liáng Zhōu.
Everyone was apprehensive
and dared not go.
Sēngzhēn firmly requested to serve as the envoy
and immediately set off in a single boat.
Upon reaching Xiāng Yáng,
he oversaw the dispatch of reinforcement troops,
and furthermore, obtained a letter from Prince Xuān Wǔ and returned.
Gāozǔ praised him greatly.
After the matter was settled,
he was appointed Supervisor of the Feathered Forest (yǔ lín jiān).
When Dōng Hūn ascended the throne,
Xú Xiàosì, the Minister of Works, managed the government.
He wanted Sēngzhēn to work with him,
but Sēngzhēn anticipated that the situation would not remain peaceful for long
and ultimately did not go.
At that time, Gāozǔ had already taken charge of Yōng Zhōu.
Sēngzhēn persistently requested to return west
and was appointed Magistrate of Qí.
Upon arrival,
Gāozǔ appointed him Adjutant to the Army Chief of Staff (zhōng bīng cān jūn)
and entrusted him with vital military matters.
Sēngzhēn secretly trained loyal combatants,
and many people attached themselves to him.
Gāozǔ often recruited brave warriors,
and both soldiers and commoners responded and followed,
with over ten thousand people gathering.
Consequently, Gāozǔ ordered Sēngzhēn to inspect the empty land west of the city,
planning to construct several thousand rooms
for barracks.
He heavily felled timber and bamboo,
sinking it in Tán Stream,
and stacked hay for roofs as high as hills,
but none of it was used immediately.
Sēngzhēn alone understood the underlying purpose
and also privately prepared several hundred shields.
When the righteous army rose,
Gāozǔ summoned Sēngzhēn and Zhāng Hóngcè at night to decide on the plan.
The next morning, they gathered the masses and mobilized the army.
All the timber and bamboo from Tán Stream were retrieved,
and constructed into lofty warships (lóu jiàn).
They were roofed with the hay,
and everything was prepared rapidly.
When the armies were about to depart,
the generals indeed competed for shields.
Sēngzhēn then brought out those he had prepared beforehand,
issuing two shields to each boat,
and the competition then ceased.
Gāozǔ appointed Sēngzhēn General Assisting the State (fǔ guó jiāng jūn) and Commandant of Infantry (bù bīng xiào wèi).
He had access to the inner chamber
to transmit Gāozǔ’s instructions.
When the army reached Yǐng Chéng,
Sēngzhēn led his subordinates to encamp at Yǎn Yuè Bulwark,
and shortly thereafter advanced to occupy Qí Chéng.
After Yǐng Zhōu was pacified,
Gāozǔ promoted Sēngzhēn to Grand General of the Vanguard (qián fēng dà jiāng jūn).
When the main army reached Jiāng Níng,
Gāozǔ ordered Sēngzhēn and Wáng Mào to lead elite troops and be the first to ascend Chì Bí Watchtower.
On that day,
Lǐ Jūshì, a general under Dōng Hūn, attacked with his forces.
Sēngzhēn and others intercepted the attack
and decisively defeated them.
Then, he and Mào advanced to construct a bulwark at Bái Bǎn Bridge.
Once the bulwark was established,
Mào moved his encampment to Yuè Chéng,
while Sēngzhēn still guarded Bái Bǎn.
Lǐ Jūshì secretly spied and learned that the forces were few.
He led ten thousand elite soldiers
and came straight to attack the bulwark.
Sēngzhēn said to his officers and men:
“Our current strength is no match for them,
so we must not engage in battle.
Also, do not shoot arrows from afar.
Wait until they reach the trenches and palisades,
then we must exert all our strength to crush them.”
Soon after, they all crossed the trenches and pulled out the palisades.
Sēngzhēn divided his men to go up the bulwark,
and arrows and stones were launched simultaneously.
He personally led three hundred cavalry and infantry to emerge behind the enemy.
Those defending the corners also scaled the bulwark and descended,
striking simultaneously from inside and outside.
Jūshì was immediately routed and scattered,
and the quantity of armor and weapons captured was countless.
Sēngzhēn further advanced and occupied Yuè Chéng.
Wáng Zhēnguó, the Grand General of Dōng Hūn, arranged his chariots in formation to create a camp,
arrayed with their backs to the Huái River.
Wáng Mào and the other armies attacked them,
and Sēngzhēn deployed fire chariots to burn their camp.
It disintegrated instantly that day.
When Jiàn Kāng city was pacified,
Gāozǔ ordered Sēngzhēn to lead his subordinates to be the first to enter and secure the palace,
and along with Zhāng Hóngcè, they sealed and inspected the government treasuries and armories.
On the same day, he was given the concurrent post of Administrator of Nán Péng Chéng with his original office,
and was promoted to Gentleman-Consultant, Prefect of the Yellow Gate (gěi shì huáng mén shì láng),
and concurrently Commandant of the Tiger-Banners (hǔ bēn zhōng láng jiāng).
When Gāozǔ received the abdication (of the Qí dynasty),
Sēngzhēn was appointed General of the Champions (guàn jūn jiāng jūn), Front Army Chief Clerk (qián jūn sī mǎ),
and enfeoffed as Marquis of Píng Gù County,
with an estate of one thousand two hundred households.
Shortly after, he was promoted to Gentleman-Consultant (gěi shì zhōng) and General of the Right Guard (yòu wèi jiāng jūn).
After a while,
he was transferred to General of the Left Guard (zuǒ wèi jiāng jūn),
and granted the additional title of Cavalry Regular Attendant (sǎn qí cháng shì).
He entered the palace to oversee the Secretarial Bureau (mì shū shěng)
and was generally responsible for the palace guard.
In the winter of the fourth year of Tiān Jiān (505 CE),
a major northern expedition was launched.
From then on, there were many military affairs.
Sēngzhēn was on duty at the Central Secretariat (zhōng shū shěng) during the day,
and returned to the Secretarial Bureau at night.
In the summer of the fifth year (506 CE),
Sēngzhēn was again ordered to lead the elite and brave soldiers of the Feathered Forest Guard out to Liáng Chéng.
In the winter of that year, the army returned,
and he concurrently held the post of Chief Administrator to the Crown Prince (tài zǐ zhōng shù zǐ) with his original office.
Sēngzhēn had been away from home for a long time,
and submitted a memorial requesting to visit his ancestors' tombs.
Gāozǔ, wishing to honor him,
appointed him to his home province,
and thus granted him the title of Administrator with Imperial Authority, General Who Pacifies the North, and Governor of Southern Yānzhōu.
While Sēngzhēn was in office,
he treated his subordinates fairly
and showed no favoritism to relatives.
His paternal cousin’s son had previously made a living by selling onions.
When Sēngzhēn arrived,
he abandoned his trade, hoping to secure a provincial official position.
Sēngzhēn said:
"I owe a great debt of gratitude to the state,
and have no way to repay it.
You all have your ordinary lot;
how can you recklessly seek undue advancement?
You should just quickly return to your onion stall."
Sēngzhēn's old house was north of the market.
In front of it was the Dūyóu's office.
His fellow villagers all urged him to move the office to enlarge his residence.
Sēngzhēn angrily said:
"The Dūyóu's office is a government building.
Since its establishment,
it has been in this location.
How can it be moved to enlarge my private residence!"
His elder sister, who had married into the Yú clan,
lived west of the market
in a small house facing the road,
mingled with the rows of shops.
Sēngzhēn would often lead his retinue and imperial guard to her house,
not feeling ashamed of it.
After a hundred days in the province,
he was recalled to serve as General of the Palace Guard,
and soon after was promoted to Palace Attendant,
granted an imperial band,
and continued to supervise the Imperial Secretariat as before.
Sēngzhēn had performed great services,
and held positions of crucial importance.
His favor and intimacy with the emperor were profound,
unequaled by any other.
He was naturally extremely respectful and cautious.
When on duty in the forbidden palace,
he dared not remove his robes even in the height of summer.
Whenever he attended the imperial presence,
he held his breath and bowed,
never touching his chopsticks even for fruit.
Once, after getting drunk,
he took an orange and ate it.
Gāozǔ laughed and said to him:
"This is indeed great progress!"
Beyond his official salary,
he was also given one hundred thousand coins monthly;
other grants and gifts were continuous at the time.
In the tenth year,
he fell ill.
The imperial carriage personally visited,
and imperial envoys delivered medicine
several times a day.
Sēngzhēn said to his relatives and old friends:
"When I was in Méngxiàn long ago,
I suffered from a fever that caused jaundice.
At the time, I certainly thought I wouldn't recover.
But the emperor saw me and said,
'You have the appearance of wealth and nobility,
you will surely not die,
and will soon recover on your own.'
Soon after, I indeed recovered.
Now I am already wealthy and noble, and yet the jaundice has returned.
The suffering is exactly the same as before,
so I will certainly not recover again."
It turned out exactly as he said.
He died in the residence of the General of the Palace Guard,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Gāozǔ personally attended the funeral on that very day,
and issued an imperial edict which read:
"Cherishing the old and honoring the end of life is a venerable practice of previous kings;
conferring posthumous honors and promotions is a common rule throughout generations.
Sāngì Chángshì, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, Pínggùxiàn Kāiguó Hóu Sēngzhēn,
possessed profound thought and broad understanding,
and a sagacious and resourceful mind.
He exhausted his loyalty and fulfilled his duties,
sparing no effort in what he knew to be right.
He shared the joys and sorrows with Us,
his feelings encompassing both our struggles and prosperity.
In the early days of establishing Our great enterprise,
he made splendid achievements.
When he served in the imperial guard,
he displayed utmost sincerity morning and night.
He was about to participate in the important affairs of the court and the state,
and to greatly advance the imperial trust;
but suddenly met with death.
We are deeply grieved and saddened in Our heart.
It is proper to confer generous honors
to magnify this imperial decree.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of General of Agile Cavalry, Minister over the Masses, and his former titles of
Palace Attendant, imperial band, and Marquis remain unchanged.
He shall be provided with secret treasures from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
and all necessary funeral provisions shall be supplied as appropriate.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōngjìng Hóu."
Gāozǔ lamented him deeply,
and shed tears when speaking of him.
His eldest son Jùn had died young;
Jùn's son Dàn succeeded him.
Chén Lìbù Shàngshū Yáo Chá said:
Zhāng Hóngcè was honest, generous, and prudent;
Lǚ Sēngzhēn was diligent and tireless;
Zhèng Shàoshú was loyal and sincere.
In the establishment of the imperial enterprise,
these three men all played significant roles.
Sēngzhēn's solemn respect in the forbidden palace,
and Shàoshú's discreet counsel and astute advice,
demonstrated their understanding of the principles of being a minister.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 6: Liǔ Dàn (younger brother Chén), Xí Chǎnwén, Wéi Ruì (clan brother Ài).
Liǔ Dàn, courtesy name Wéntōng,
was a native of Jiě in Hédōng.
His father, Shìlóng,
was the Grand Commandant of Qí.
When Dàn was seventeen,
Emperor Wǔ of Qí, then Commander of the Central Army,
appointed him as his staff officer,
then promoted him to Chief Clerk.
At the beginning of Qí,
he entered as a Secretary of the Board of Civil Office and Three Dukes,
and was successively promoted to Palace Middle Attendant to the Crown Prince,
and a friend of Zǐxiǎng, the Prince of Bādōng.
When Zǐxiǎng became Governor of Jīngzhōu,
Dàn accompanied him to the garrison.
Zǐxiǎng associated closely with petty men,
and Dàn knew that disaster was imminent,
so he feigned illness and returned to the capital.
When the rebellion broke out,
Dàn escaped due to his earlier return.
He successively served as Secretary to the Grand Secretariat,
and Chief Clerk to the Commander of the Central Army.
He was sent out as Administrator of Xīn'ān.
While governing the commandery,
he was dismissed and returned home
due to lack of administrative achievements.
After a long time,
he became Consulting Staff Officer to the General of the Right.
At the end of Jiànwǔ,
he was appointed Commandant of the Western Rong, and Governor of Liángzhōu and Nánqínzhōu.
When Gāozǔ raised his army,
Dàn raised Hànzhōng in response to the righteous cause.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
he was appointed Palace Attendant,
and concurrently General of the Vanguard.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was recalled as Commander of the Imperial Guard.
Before taking office,
he was further promoted to Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant.
For his merits, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Qǔjiāng County,
with an estate of a thousand households.
Gāozǔ once composed a poem during a banquet and presented it to Dàn, saying:
"You are indeed the crown of all lords,
and I truly remember your meritorious deeds."
He also once attended the imperial presence,
and Gāozǔ said:
"Xú Yuányú disobeyed orders in Língnán,
but the Book of Zhōu states that crimes do not extend to descendants.
I have already pardoned all his sons,
what do you think?"
Dàn replied:
"Punishments do not extend to heirs,
and rewards extend to future generations.
This is now seen again in Your Sacred Dynasty."
At the time, people considered his words wise.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Master of Ceremonies of the Right.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān,
a large northern expedition was launched.
Prince Hóng of Línchuān was appointed commander-in-chief of all forces,
and Dàn was made his deputy.
Upon the army's return,
he resumed his position as Grand Master of Ceremonies.
Due to prolonged illness,
he was transferred to Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon,
given the additional title of Palace Attendant,
and granted twenty personal guards.
Before taking office,
he was sent out as Administrator with Imperial Authority, General Who Pacifies the South, and Governor of Xiāngzhōu.
In the tenth month of the sixth year,
he died in the province,
at the age of forty-six.
Gāozǔ wore plain clothes and mourned for him.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant, General Who Soothes the Army,
and provided with an imperial band.
His posthumous title was Mù.
Dàn authored the Rénzhèng Chuán (Biographies of Benevolent Governance) and various poems and rhapsodies,
which possessed considerable literary merit.
His son Zhào succeeded him.
Tán’s fourth younger brother, Chéng,
also had a fine reputation.
He successively held the posts of Shìzhōng and Zhènxī Zhǎngshǐ.
In the twelfth year of Tiānjiān (513 CE),
he died.
He was posthumously granted the titles Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Yùzhōu Cìshǐ.
Chén, courtesy name Wénruò,
was Tán’s fifth younger brother.
When he was several years old,
his father Shìlóng and mother, née Yán, were confined by illness.
Chén did not untie his sash for a full year.
When observing mourning,
he became known for his extreme emaciation.
He started his official career as Sītú Xíng Cānjūn,
and was repeatedly promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
Xī Zhōngláng Zhǔbù,
and Gōngcáo Shǐ.
Qí Dōnghūn (Márquess of Dōnghūn) sent the Administrator of Bāxī, Liú Shānyáng, via Jīngzhōu to attack Gāozǔ.
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu, the Zhǎngshǐ of Xī Zhōngláng, had not settled on a plan,
so he summoned Chén and his trusted associate Xí Chǎnwén, among others, to enter and discuss it at night.
Chén said:
"The court is frantic and perverse,
and their evil deeds multiply daily.
Recently, I heard that the elders in the capital (Jīngshī),
all stand on doubled feet, stacking their breath (living in extreme fear).
Now, fortunately, we are far away,
and can temporarily enjoy peace and security.
The matter concerning Yōngzhōu
is merely a means by which they are destroying each other.
Have you alone not seen Xiāo Lìngjūn?
He used a few thousand elite troops
to defeat the hundred thousand men of the Cuī clan,
yet he was ultimately entrapped by a group of villains,
and disaster and cruelty followed one another.
That which happened before should not be forgotten;
it is a guide for subsequent events.
If their malevolent intentions have already succeeded there,
how can we know that the Lord (Shǐjūn) will not be pursued closely afterward?
Furthermore, Yōngzhōu has sharp soldiers and ample grain,
and Lord Xiāo (Xiāo Yǎn) possesses heroic qualities unmatched in the age.
He certainly cannot be equaled by Shānyáng.
If Shānyáng is defeated,
Jīngzhōu will again be subject to the blame for military failure.
There is no good choice in advancing or retreating.
Please consider this deeply."
Chǎnwén also strongly advised joining Gāozǔ.
Yǐngzhòu subsequently lured and executed Shānyáng,
and appointed Chén as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
Chén became Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
and was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Nánpíng.
Soon after, he was moved to Shìzhōng and Guànjūn Jiāngjūn,
retaining his post as Tàishǒu.
He was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū,
but did not assume the office.
When Yǐngzhōu was pacified,
Yǐngzhòu debated moving the capital to Xiàkǒu.
Chén repeatedly and firmly remonstrated,
believing that Bāxiá had not yet submitted,
and it was improper to lightly abandon the foundation
and disturb the will of the people.
Yǐngzhòu did not heed him.
Soon after, the Bādōng troops arrived at Xiákǒu,
and the discussion of moving the capital then ceased.
Commentators considered him to have recognized the critical moment.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Chén as Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
concurrently serving as Xiāojì Jiāngjūn.
Discussing his merit in establishing the righteous cause,
he was enfeoffed as the Earl of Zhōulíng,
with an estate of seven hundred households.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (503 CE),
he was sent out as Ānxī Zhǎngshǐ, Guànjūn Jiāngjūn, and Administrator of Nánjùn.
In the sixth year (507 CE),
he was summoned to be Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì and Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài.
Before he departed,
he was promoted to Chíjié, Dū Xiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Xiāngzhōu.
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he was removed from office for arbitrarily dismissing military service men.
Soon after, he entered (the capital) to become Mìshūjiān,
was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì,
and transferred to Cíbù Shàngshū.
Before he took the oath of office, he fell ill.
An imperial decree changed his appointment to Jìshìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū,
but as his illness was grave, he did not take the oath.
In the tenth year (511 CE),
he died at home,
aged forty-one.
He was posthumously granted Zhōngshū Lìng,
and given the posthumous title Mù.
His son, Fàn, succeeded him.
Xí Chǎnwén
was a native of Línjīng, Āndìng Commandery.
He was poor and orphaned in youth,
but dabbled in books and history.
Early in the Qí Dynasty,
he served as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn for Xiāo Chìfǔ, the Cìshǐ of Yōngzhōu.
Because of this, he maintained a close relationship with Chìfǔ’s son, Yǐngzhòu.
He subsequently held the post of Xī Zhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
concurrently overseeing the Chéngjú (City Bureau).
When Gāozǔ was about to raise the righteous army,
Chǎnwén strongly encouraged him.
Yǐngzhòu agreed
and subsequently sent Tián Zǔgōng to privately inform Gāozǔ,
and also presented a silver-mounted sword.
Gāozǔ replied with a golden Rúyì scepter.
When Emperor Hé assumed the honored title,
Chǎnwén served as Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and soon moved to Wèiwèi Qīng.
When Yǐngzhòu suddenly died,
the provincial administration was thrown into turmoil.
Chǎnwén, observing that Emperor Hé was young and weak,
and that the responsibilities in the central region were heavy,
and that Shǐxīngwáng Dàn was then stationed and governing the Yōng region,
therefore joined the officials of the Western Court to welcome the Prince to take overall charge of the provincial affairs.
Thus, reliance on him brought peace and stability.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
Chǎnwén was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū and Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
He was enfeoffed as the Earl of Shānyáng,
with an estate of seven hundred households.
He was sent out to serve as the Administrator of Dōngyáng,
and his title was changed to the Earl of Xiāngxī,
with the number of households remaining the same.
After governing for two years,
he became famous for his purity and integrity,
and died in office.
An imperial decree granted funeral expenses of thirty thousand coins
and fifty bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title was Wēi.
Wéi Ruì, courtesy name Huáiwén,
was a native of Dùlíng, Jīngzhào Commandery.
Since Xián, the Chancellor of Hàn,
his family had been a prominent clan in Sānfǔ for generations.
His grandfather, Xuán,
avoided officials and lived hidden in the Southern Mountains of Cháng’ān.
When Sòng Wǔdì entered the pass,
Xuán was summoned to serve as Tàiwèi Yuàn,
but he did not go.
His paternal uncle, Zǔzhēng,
was Guānglù Xūn at the end of the Sòng Dynasty.
His father, Zǔguī,
was Níngyuǎn Zhǎngshǐ.
Ruì was known for his filial piety toward his stepmother.
Ruì’s elder brothers, Zuǎn and Chǎn,
were both famous early in life.
Zuǎn and Ruì were both fond of learning;
Chǎn possessed pure integrity.
Zǔzhēng served as Jùnshǒu repeatedly.
He always took Ruì with him to his posts
and treated him like a son.
At that time, Ruì’s wife’s elder brother, Wáng Chéng, and his maternal cousin, Dù Yùn,
both enjoyed great local fame.
Zǔzhēng said to Ruì:
"What do you think of yourself compared to Chéng and Yùn?"
Ruì was humble and dared not answer.
Zǔzhēng said:
"Your literary talent might be slightly less,
but your learning and knowledge certainly surpass theirs.
However, in serving the state
and achieving great accomplishments,
neither of them can reach you."
His maternal cousin, Dù Yǒuwén, was Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
He requested Ruì to travel with him.
The territory of Liáng was rich and fertile.
Those who went there often failed due to bribery.
Although Ruì was young at the time,
he alone was known for his integrity.
Yuán Yǐ was the Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
saw Wéi Ruì and considered him extraordinary,
and appointed him Chief Clerk (*Zhǔbù*).
When Yǐ arrived at the province,
he raised troops with Dèng Wǎn.
Wéi Ruì requested to be sent out to Yìchéng Commandery,
thus escaping the disaster Yǐ faced.
Later, he served as Left Attendant (*Zuǒ Chángshì*) to the Prince of Jìnpíng.
He was promoted to Acting Staff Officer (*Xíng Cānjūn*) for the Minister of Works (*Sīkōng*), the Prince of Guìyáng.
He followed the Qí Minister of Works, Liǔ Shìlóng, in defending Yǐngchéng (Yǐng City),
resisting Shěn Yōuzhī, the Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
When Yōuzhī was defeated,
he was promoted to Mid-Army Staff Officer (*Zhōngbīng Cānjūn*) for the General of the Vanguard (*Qiánjūn*).
After a long time,
he became Magistrate of Guǎngdé.

He accumulated promotions to Administrator of Qíxīng, Assistant to the Inspector of his home province (*Biejia*), Colonel of Chángshuǐ (*Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi*), and General of the Right Army (*Yòujūn Jiāngjūn*).
At the end of Qí, many troubles arose,
and he did not wish to be far from his hometown.
He requested to be Administrator of Shàngyōng,
with the additional title General Who Establishes Might (*Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn*).
Soon after, the Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*) Chén Xiǎndá and the General Protecting the Army (*Hùjūn Jiāngjūn*) Cuī Huìjǐng repeatedly pressed the capital.
The people were panicked and agitated,
with nothing yet settled.
The people of the western territories consulted Wéi Ruì about the matter.
Wéi Ruì said:
“Although Chén Xiǎndá is an old general,
he is not a talent ordained by fate.
Cuī Huìjǐng is rather experienced,
but he is timid and not martial.
Their families being exterminated
is fitting.
The true lord of the realm,
will likely rise from our province!”
He then sent his two sons
to ally himself with Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng).
When the summons of the righteous army arrived,
Wéi Ruì led the people of the commandery to cut bamboo to make rafts,
traveling twice the normal speed to hasten to the meeting.
He had two thousand troops,
and two hundred horses.
Gāozǔ was extremely pleased upon seeing Wéi Ruì,
and slapped the table, saying:
“On another day, I saw your face,
today I see your heart.
My enterprise is complete.”
When the righteous army captured Yǐng and Lǔ,
and pacified Jiāhú,
Wéi Ruì presented many strategies,
all of which were accepted and used.
When the main army departed Yǐng,
they debated who should remain to guard the area.
Gāozǔ found it difficult to select the right person;
After a long time,
he looked at Wéi Ruì and said:
“If I abandon a magnificent steed (*Qíjì*) and do not ride it,
why should I frantically search for another?”
That same day, he was appointed General Who Subdues the Army (*Guànjūn Jiāngjūn*) and Administrator of Jiāngxià,
concurrently managing the affairs of the Yǐng administration.
Originally,
when Yǐngchéng was under siege and defended,
the population of men and women was nearly one hundred thousand.
The barracks were closed for a year,
and seven or eight tenths of them died from sickness and plague.
Corpses were piled up beneath the beds,
while the living slept above them,
every house being filled to capacity.
Wéi Ruì investigated, organized, and provided relief,
making arrangements for all.
Consequently, the dead received burial,
and the living returned to their livelihoods.
The common people relied on him.
When the Liáng Dynasty was founded,
he was summoned to serve as Grand Judge (*Dàlǐ*).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Palace Commandant (*Tíngwèi*),
enfeoffed as Viscount of Dūliáng (*Dūliáng Zǐ*),
with a stipend of three hundred households.
In the second year of *Tiānjiān* (503 CE),
his title was changed to Viscount of Yǒngchāng,
the number of households remaining as before.
When the Eastern Palace was established,
he was promoted to Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài*).
He was then sent out as General Assisting the State (*Fǔguó Jiāngjūn*), Inspector of Yùzhōu, and concurrently Administrator of Lìyáng.
In the third year [of *Tiānjiān*],
Wèi sent troops to invade.
He led the provincial troops and attacked, driving them away.
In the fourth year,
the royal army launched a northern expedition.
Wéi Ruì was ordered to supervise all the armies.
Wéi Ruì sent his Chief Clerk (*Zhǎngshǐ*) Wáng Chāozōng and the Administrator of Liáng Commandery, Féng Dàogēn, to attack Wèi’s Xiǎoxiàn City,
but they were unable to capture it.
Wéi Ruì toured the surrounding palisades.
Suddenly, several hundred Wèi troops emerged from the city and formed ranks outside the gate.
Wéi Ruì wished to attack them.
All the generals said:
“We originally came lightly,
and are not yet prepared for battle.
If we slowly retreat to put on armor,
then we may advance.”
Wéi Ruì said:
“Not so.
The more than two thousand Wèi troops inside the city,
by closing the gates and defending stoutly,
are sufficient to protect themselves.
To send men outside without reason,
means they must be their fiercest and bravest.
If we can defeat them,
the city will take itself.”
The masses were still hesitant.
Wéi Ruì pointed to his staff of authority (*jié*) and said:
“The court granted me this
not as decoration.
Wéi Ruì’s command
cannot be violated.”
Thereupon, he advanced the troops.
All the soldiers fought desperately.
The Wèi army indeed suffered a crushing defeat and fled.
Taking advantage of this, they quickly attacked,
and the city was captured overnight.
They then advanced to attack Héféi.
Before this,
Hú Lüè, the Marshal (*Sīmǎ*) of the Right Army, and others had arrived at Héféi,
but had long been unable to take it.
Wéi Ruì surveyed the mountains and rivers,
and said:
“I have heard that ‘the Fén River can inundate Píngyáng,
and the Jiàng River can inundate Ānyì’—
this situation is exactly that.”
He then dammed the Féi River.
He personally directed the effort.
After a short while,
the dam was complete and the water flowed,
and ships and boats arrived in succession.
Wèi had initially built small cities to the east and west, flanking Héféi.
Wéi Ruì first attacked these two cities.
Soon after, the Wèi relief general Yáng Língyìn led an army of fifty thousand and arrived suddenly.
The troops feared they would be outnumbered,
and requested a petition for reinforcements.
Wéi Ruì laughed and said:
“The bandits have already reached the city walls.
If we only now start seeking troops,
it is like forging weapons when facing danger—
how can it reach the horse’s belly?
Furthermore, if I request relief forces,
they will also mobilize troops.
It is just like Wú reinforcing Bāqiū,
and Shǔ increasing Bái Dì.
‘Victory for an army lies in unity, not in numbers,’
is an ancient maxim.”
Consequently, he engaged them in battle,
and defeated them.
The soldiers were somewhat reassured.
Initially,
the Fěishuǐ Yàn (Feishui Dam) was constructed.
Jūnzhǔ Wáng Huáijìng (Wang Huaijing) was ordered to build a city on the bank and guard it.
The Wèi attacked and captured Huáijìng Chéng (Huaijing City),
more than a thousand men were all lost.
The Wèi forces, capitalizing on their victory, arrived below the dike of Wèi Ruì,
and their momentum was extremely strong.
Jūnjiān Pān Língyòu (Pan Lingyou) advised Wèi Ruì to retreat back to Cháohú,
and the other generals also requested to flee and secure Sānchā.
Wèi Ruì said angrily:
"How can such a thing happen!
A general maintains order until death;
we only advance, we do not retreat."
He then ordered umbrellas, fans, flags, and banners to be taken
and erected below the dike,
showing his resolve not to move.
Wèi Ruì was inherently frail;
he never rode a horse in battle,
but carried himself in a wooden litter,
supervising and encouraging all the armies.
The Wèi soldiers came to dig through the dike.
Wèi Ruì personally fought for control of it.
The Wèi army withdrew slightly,
and he then built fortifications upon the dike to secure himself.
Wèi Ruì constructed fighting ships
that were as tall as Héféi Chéng (Hefei City),
and positioned them to overlook the enemy on all four sides.
The Wèi people were out of ideas,
and wept together in sorrow.
Once Wèi Ruì's siege equipment was completed,
and the dam waters were full,
the Wèi relief forces were rendered useless.
The Wèi defending general Dù Yuánlún (Du Yuanlun) climbed the wall to supervise the battle,
was hit by a crossbow bolt and died,
and the city subsequently collapsed.
More than ten thousand heads were captured,
cattle and horses numbered in the tens of thousands,
and silk filled ten rooms;
all were distributed as military rewards.
Wèi Ruì spent every day receiving guests and travelers,
and calculating military documents at night;
he would rise at the third watch, light his lamp, and work until dawn.
He looked after his troops
as if he constantly feared he was failing them.
Therefore, men who offered themselves for service flocked to him.
Wherever he stopped, the lodging houses were well-maintained;
the buildings, fences, and walls
all strictly adhered to standards.
Once Héféi was pacified,
Gāozǔ ordered the armies to advance and camp at Dōnglíng.
Dōnglíng was twenty *lǐ* from Wèi Pìchéng (Wei Picheng).
Just as they were about to engage in battle,
an imperial edict ordered the army to return.
As they were close to the enemy,
fearing they would be pursued,
Wèi Ruì sent all the baggage train ahead,
while he personally rode in a small litter guarding the rear.
The Wèi forces respected Wèi Ruì's prestige and reputation,
and looking upon him, dared not approach,
so the entire army returned safely.
At this time, Yùzhōu was moved to Héféi.
In the fifth year,
Yuán Yīng, Prince Zhōngshān of Wèi, invaded Běi Xúzhōu,
and besieged Cìshǐ Chāng Yìzhī (Chang Yizhi) at Zhōnglí.
His host was said to number a million,
and they had constructed over forty continuous fortifications.
Gāozǔ sent Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn Cáo Jǐngzōng (Cao Jingzong),
Dūdū (Area Commander) of twenty myriad troops, to resist them.
They camped at Shàoyáng Zhōu,
built ramparts, and held their positions.
Gāozǔ ordered Wèi Ruì to lead the Yùzhōu forces to join them there.
Wèi Ruì traveled directly from Héféi, passing through the vast marsh of Yīnlíng.
When he encountered ravines and valleys,
he would immediately build pontoon bridges to cross.
The troops feared the strength of the Wèi army
and many advised Wèi Ruì to proceed slowly.
Wèi Ruì said:
"Zhōnglí is currently trapped, living by digging holes
and fetching water by leaning on their doors (under duress).
Even if chariots race and soldiers rush,
I still fear being late,
how much less can we afford to go slowly!
The Wèi people have already fallen into our trap (stomach);
you should not worry."
In ten days, they arrived at Shàoyáng.
Initially,
Gāozǔ had instructed Cáo Jǐngzōng, saying:
"Wèi Ruì
is your relative and superior;
you must treat him with respect."
When Cáo Jǐngzōng saw Wèi Ruì,
his courtesies were extremely meticulous.
Gāozǔ heard of this,
and said:
"If the two generals are harmonious,
the campaign will surely succeed."
Wèi Ruì, twenty *lǐ* in front of Cáo Jǐngzōng’s camp,
dug a long trench overnight,
erected chevaux de frise,
and cut off the islet to form a city.
By dawn, the camp was established.
Yuán Yīng was greatly alarmed,
striking the ground with his staff, saying:
"What kind of spirit is this!"
The next morning,
Yuán Yīng personally led his troops to battle.
Wèi Ruì rode in a plain wooden litter,
holding a white horn *rúyì* (scepter) to command the army.
There were several clashes that day,
and Yuán Yīng greatly feared his strength.
The Wèi army returned again that night to attack the city,
and flying arrows fell like rain.
Wèi Ruì’s son, Wèi Àn, requested to descend from the wall to avoid the arrows,
but Wèi Ruì refused permission.
When the troops became alarmed,
Wèi Ruì shouted loudly at them from the top of the wall,
and they settled down.
The Wèi forces had previously built two bridges connecting the two banks of Shàoyáng Zhōu,
erecting fences hundreds of paces long,
to cross the Huái River and open a thoroughfare.
Wèi Ruì equipped large battleships,
and ordered Liángjùn Tàishǒu Féng Dàogēn (Feng Daogen), Lújiāng Tàishǒu Péi Suì (Pei Sui), Qínjùn Tàishǒu Lǐ Wénzhāo (Li Wenzhao), and others to lead the naval forces.
As the Huái River water suddenly swelled,
Wèi Ruì immediately dispatched them.
The fighting ships launched fiercely,
all moving to overlook the enemy ramparts.
They loaded small boats with reeds,
doused them with grease,
and used them to burn the bridge.
The wind raged and the fire grew fierce,
smoke and dust darkened the sky.
The dare-to-die soldiers
tore out the fences and hacked at the bridge.
The water also flowed rapidly,
and in an instant,
the bridges and fences were completely destroyed.
Meanwhile, Féng Dàogēn and the others all fought personally hand-to-hand.
The soldiers fought bravely,
their shouts shaking heaven and earth.
Every man was equal to a hundred opponents,
and the Wèi forces suffered a massive defeat.
Yuán Yīng, seeing the bridge cut off,
escaped and fled.
More than 100,000 Wèi soldiers rushed into the water and died,
and the number beheaded was similar.
The remainder discarded their armor and bowed their heads to the ground,
begging to be made prisoners or slaves;
they still numbered several hundred thousand.
The military supplies, cattle, and horses captured
were too numerous to count.
Wèi Ruì sent a message to Chāng Yìzhī.
Chāng Yìzhī was both sad and joyful,
and had no time to speak a response,
but only shouted:
"Given a second life!
Given a second life!"
Gāozǔ sent Zhōngshū Láng Zhōu Shě (Zhou She) to offer condolences on the banks of the Huái.
Wèi Ruì piled the captured goods outside the army gate.
Zhōu Shě viewed them
and said to Wèi Ruì:
"The volume of your captures here is equal to Xióng'ěr Shān (Mount Xiong'er) again."
For his merit, he was granted an additional seven hundred households in his fief,
promoted in rank to Hóu (Marquis),
and summoned to serve as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (Attendant-in-ordinary, Gentleman-in-Waiting) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Right Guard).
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard).
Soon after, he became Ānxī Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West) and Nánjùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nanjun),
with a salary rank of Middle Two Thousand *Dàn*.
Coincidentally, when Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Mǎ Xiānpín (Ma Xianpin) returned from his northern campaign,
he was pursued by the Wèi forces.
The Sānguān passes were agitated,
and an imperial edict ordered Wèi Ruì to command the armies and reinforce the area.
When Wèi Ruì arrived at Ānlù,
he added over twenty feet to the city walls,
newly dug large trenches,
and erected tall towers.
The crowd somewhat criticized him for showing weakness.
Wèi Ruì said:
"Not so;
a general must sometimes appear fearful;
one cannot rely entirely on courage."
At this time, Yuán Yīng was again pursuing Mǎ Xiānpín,
intending to avenge the shame of Shàoyáng.
Hearing of Wèi Ruì's arrival,
he retreated,
and the Emperor also issued an edict to disband the army.
The following year,
he was transferred to Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Commands Military Trust) and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiangzhou).
In the ninth year,
he was summoned to serve as Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (Attendant-in-Ordinary, Gentleman-in-Waiting, Supernumerary) and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was successively transferred to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn and Tàizǐ Zhānshì (Supervisor of the Crown Prince's Household),
and shortly after was granted the additional title Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
In the thirteenth year,
he was transferred to Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Wise Valor) and Dānyáng Yǐn (Administrator of Danyang).
He was dismissed due to an official matter.
After a short while,
he was reinstated as Zhōnghù Jūn (Protector of the Army).
In the fourteenth year,
he was sent out to serve as General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn), Commandant Who Soothes the Barbarians (Níngmán Xiàowèi), and Administrator of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Earlier,
when Ruì raised troops in his hometown,
the retainer Yīn Jùnguāng wept and tried to stop Ruì.
When Ruì returned to serve in the prefecture,
Jùnguāng waited for Ruì on the road.
Ruì smiled and said to him:
"If I had followed your words,
I would be begging for food by the roadside now."
He presented Jùnguāng with ten oxen for plowing.
Regarding his old friends and acquaintances,
Ruì spared nothing,
and he frequently granted temporary county magistracies (jiǎbǎn xiànlìng)
to scholar-officials aged seventy or older.
His local community held him in high regard.
In the fifteenth year,
he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but the gracious imperial edict did not permit it.
In the seventeenth year,
he was summoned to serve as Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and General of the Guard (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was granted a set of drums and pipes (gǔchuī),
and entered to serve duty in the Palace Secretariat (Diànshěng).
While in court,
he was respectful and mild (xúnyú) and never looked upon others defiantly.
Emperor Gāozǔ treated him with great respect.
He was naturally benevolent and loving.
He cared for his deceased elder brother's sons better than his own sons.
All the salary and rewards he received throughout his career
he distributed to his relatives and old friends.
His family had no accumulated wealth.
Later, when he served as General of the Guard (Hùjūn),
and had nothing to do at home,
he admired the conduct of Wàn Shí and Lù Jiǎ,
and therefore painted their portraits on the wall for his own appreciation.
Although he was old at the time,
on leisure days he still instructed his various sons in study.
His third son, Léng,
was especially knowledgeable in the Classics and Histories (jīngshǐ).
The generation praised him for his extensive learning.
Ruì would often sit and have Léng explain books,
but the points he raised (Ruì's)
Léng still could not fully grasp.
Emperor Gāozǔ was intensely devoted to Buddhism (Shì Shì),
and the whole empire followed the trend and was transformed.
Ruì considered his own faith and acceptance to be inherently shallow,
and occupying the position of a great minister,
he did not wish to conform easily to popular trends.
His conduct remained largely the same as it had always been.
In the summer of the first year of Pǔtōng (Pǔtōng Yuánnián),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn),
but due to illness, he was not invested.
In the eighth month,
he died at home,
at the age of seventy-nine.
His dying instructions were for a simple burial,
using only contemporary clothing for the shroud.
Emperor Gāozǔ mourned the death deeply on that very day.
He bestowed 100,000 cash,
200 bolts of cloth,
precious burial artifacts from the Eastern Garden (Dōngyuán mìqì),
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothes.
The expenses for the funeral were supplied by the government,
and a Palace Writer (Zhōngshū Shèrén) was dispatched to supervise.

He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), General of the Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn), and Founder of a Government Office with the Privileges of the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
His posthumous name was Yán.
Earlier,
during the campaign at Shàoyáng,
Chāng Yìzhī greatly admired Ruì
and invited Cáo Jǐngzōng to meet with Ruì.
They then set aside 200,000 cash for them to gamble with.
Jǐngzōng rolled a 'pheasant' (zhì).
Ruì slowly rolled a 'deer' (lú).
He quickly took one die and reversed it,
saying,
"A strange incident,"
and thus created a tie (sè).
At that time, Jǐngzōng and the other commanders competed fiercely to be the first to report victory,
but Ruì alone held back.
His refusal to value winning
was generally like this,
and the generation especially respected him for this.
His sons were Fàng, Zhèng, Léng, and Àn.
Fàng has a separate biography.
Zhèng, courtesy name Jìngzhí,
began his career as Acting Staff Officer (Xíng Cānjūn) for the Prince of Nánkāng (Nánkāng Wáng),
gradually moving up to Palace Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
and was sent out to serve as Administrator of Xiāngyáng (Xiāngyáng Tàishǒu).
Earlier,
Zhèng was close friends with Wáng Sēngrú (Wáng Sēngrú), the Prince of Dōnghǎi.
When Sēngrú became Director of the Personnel Bureau of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng),
participating in the major selections of officials,
all his guests, friends, and old acquaintances showed him special consideration,
but Zhèng alone remained detached.
After Sēngrú was disgraced and dismissed,
Zhèng remained dedicated to their ordinary relationship,
even more so than in previous days.
Commentators praised this behavior.
He eventually served up to the rank of Attendant at the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
Léng, courtesy name Wēizhí,
was quiet and simple in nature.
He devoted himself to books and history.
He was widely knowledgeable and had a strong memory.
The scholars of the time
all came to him to clarify doubts.
He began his career as Acting Staff Officer (Xíng Cānjūn) in the establishment of the Prince of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Wáng),
gradually moving up to Palace Investigator (Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ),
Servant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Pú),
and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Guānglù Qīng).
He authored the three-volume *Hànshū Xù Xùn* (Extended Commentary on the Book of Han).
Àn, courtesy name Wùzhí,
was strong and upright in nature.
In his youth he studied the Classics and Histories (jīngshǐ),
and possessed literary talent.
He began his career as Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
gradually moving up to Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Qīng),
Administrator of Nányùzhōu (Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ),
and Minister of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng).
When Hóu Jǐng crossed the Yangtze River,
Àn was stationed at Liùmén.
He was soon changed to be Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs West of the City (Dūdū Chéngxī Miàn Zhū Jūnshì).
At that time, Jǐng built two mounds of earth, one east and one west, outside the city.
Those inside the city also built mounds to counter them.
Tàizōng personally carried earth,
and Crown Prince Āi and those below him personally took up baskets and spades.
Àn guarded the western earthen mound
and fought bitterly day and night.
For his merit, he was granted General of Swift Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn),
and given the insignia of Authority (Chíjié).
He died inside the city.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
Ài was a cousin of Ruì.
Ài, courtesy name Xiàoyǒu,
was reserved, quiet, and possessed great capacity.
His great-grandfather was Guǎng,
General of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Běipíng (Běipíng Tàishǒu) during the Jìn dynasty.
His great-grandfather was Guǐ.
At the beginning of the Tàiyuán era of Emperor Xiàowǔ,
he moved south to Xiāngyáng,
where he served as Chief of Protocol (Biejà) for the local prefecture
and Palace Attendant Consultant (Sànqí Shìláng).
His grandfather was Gōngxún,
Administrator of Yìyáng (Yìyáng Tàishǒu) during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Yìzhèng,
died young.
Ài was orphaned at a young age
and was known for his filial piety toward his mother.
He was pure and strict in character
and did not socialize indiscriminately.
He was devoted and fond of learning.
Whenever he sat alone in an empty room,
immersing his mind in ancient texts (fén sù),
dust and dirt would accumulate on his mat,
as quiet as if no one were there.
At the age of twelve,
he once traveled to the capital (Jīngshī).
He happened upon the Son of Heaven traveling out to the Southern Park (Nányuàn).
The villages and neighborhoods were noisy,
and old and young rushed to watch.
Ài alone sat upright reading a book,
never letting the scroll leave his hand.
All his clan members who saw him
were impressed.
When he grew up,
he was widely learned and possessed literary talent,
especially mastering the meanings of the *Zhōuyì* (Book of Changes) and the *Chūnqiū Zuǒshì Yì* (Commentary of Zǔo on the Spring and Autumn Annals).
When Yuán Yǐ was Administrator of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ),
he recruited him to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
When he experienced mourning for his mother,
he built a hut beside the grave
and carried earth to raise the tomb mound.
When Emperor Gāozǔ governed Yōngzhōu,
hearing of this,
he personally went to visit and condole.
When the mourning period ended,
he promoted him to Staff Officer of Military Affairs (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn).
When the righteous army arose,
Ài was appointed General of Martial Might (Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Marshal (Sīmǎ) for the Champion Prince of Nánpíng (Guànjūn Nánpíng Wáng),
simultaneously holding the post of Magistrate of Xiāngyáng (Xiāngyáng Lìng).
At that time, the capital (Jīngyì) was unsettled,
and Yōngzhōu was vulnerable.
The Administrator of Wèixīng (Wèixīng Tàishǒu), Yán Sēngdū, and others seized their commandery and rebelled.
The prefecture was alarmed and disturbed,
and the common people wavered in their loyalty.
Ài was calm, astute, and resourceful,
and had long been trusted and obeyed by the prefecture.
He therefore comforted and managed the people with sincerity,
clearly explaining the difference between rebellion and loyalty.
He also led recruitment efforts among the local populace,
gathering over a thousand men.
He fought Sēngdū and the others south of Shǐpíng Commandery (Shǐpíng Jùn),
routing them decisively.
The common people were then pacified.
When Xiāo Yǐngzhòu died,
Emperor Hé levied troops in Xiāngyáng.
[Shěn] Āi followed the Prince of Shǐxīng, Dàn, and proceeded there.
Before this,
the Administrator of Bādōng, Xiāo Guī, and the Administrator of Bāxī, Lǔ Xiūliè, raised troops and pressed upon Jīngzhōu.
When Dàn arrived,
he ordered [Shěn] Āi to write a letter persuading them.
Xiāo Guī immediately requested surrender that day.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng,
he followed Emperor Hé down east.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication (of the Qí throne),
[Āi] was promoted to the title General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn),
and remained General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
Soon thereafter, he was appointed Administrator of Níngshǔ.
He ascended west with the Inspector of Yìzhōu, Dèng Yuánqǐ, to attack Liú Jìlián.
When he traveled to Gōng'ān,
he became sick and died on the road.
He was posthumously granted the title Minister of the Palace Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
His son, Gānxiàng,
rose to the offices of General of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn),
Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi Chángshǐ),
and Administrator of the two commanderies Rǔyīn and Zhōnglí.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, said: "In the past, Dòu Róng returned Hányòu to Hàn,
and ultimately became a distinguished clan;
Liǔ Dàn raised Nánzhèng and followed [the cause] immediately,
and his family reputation did not fall.
What opportune timing!
Shěn [Āi]'s planning and strategies
also led to achievements.
How wise!
Wéi Ruì rose up in Shàngyōng to join the righteous cause.
His territory was humble compared to Dàn's.
Yet, in the campaigns of Héféi and Shàoyáng,
his achievements were immense.
He declined ownership [of the credit] and did not claim them for himself.
What a noble man (jūnzǐ)!
Biography Seven: Fàn Yún, Shěn Yuē.
Fàn Yún, courtesy name Yànlóng,
was a man of Wǔyīn, Nánxiāng.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Wāng, the General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn) of Jìn.
When he was eight years old,
he met Yīn Yǎn, the Inspector of Yùzhōu under Sòng, on the road.
Yǎn was struck by him
and invited him to a seat.
Yún's demeanor and responses
suggested he was oblivious to those around him.
Yǎn ordered him to compose a poem.
He grasped the brush and finished immediately.
Those seated sighed in admiration.
He once studied under his relative Yuán Zhào.
He worked tirelessly day and night.
Zhào patted his back and said,
"Your spirit is bright and clear, and you are diligent in your studies.
You possess the talent for becoming a minister."
In his youth, he was quick-witted
and had insight.
He was skilled in composing literature
and adept at writing letters.
Whenever he put brush to paper, he completed the work immediately,
never needing to draft it beforehand.
People often suspected he had pre-composed the material.
His father, Kàng,
served as Staff Officer (Cānjūn) in the Yǐng Prefecture.
Yún followed his father and lived there.
At that time, Shěn Yuē of Wúxīng and Yǔ Gǎozhī of Xīnyě were in the same prefecture as Kàng,
and upon seeing Yún, they befriended him.
He began his career as Clerk in the Western Bureau (Xīcáo Shūzuǒ) of Yǐngzhōu,
and was later transferred to Provisional Staff Officer of the Judicial Bureau (Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn).
Soon thereafter, Shěn Yōuzhī raised troops and besieged the city of Yǐng.
Kàng was then the Registrar (Zhǎnglìu) of the prefecture;
he entered the city and held it firmly,
leaving his family outside.
Yún was captured by the soldiers.
