Shěn Yōuzhī summoned him for a talk.
His manner and voice were very stern.
Yún's appearance did not change;
he calmly presented his case.
Shěn Yōuzhī then laughed and said,
"You are truly a promising young man.
You may leave and reside in a dwelling."
The next morning,
he was summoned again and ordered to send a letter into the city.
Some people inside the city wanted to execute him.
Yún said:
"My old mother and young brother
have their lives dependent on the Shěn clan.
If I disobey his order,
disaster will certainly befall my relatives.
To suffer execution today
would be as sweet to my heart as water caltrop."
The Chief Clerk, Liǔ Shìlóng, had always been friendly with Yún,
and thus spared him.
In the beginning of the Jiànyuán era (of Qí),
Xiāo Ziliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng, became the Administrator of Kuàijī.
Yún first followed the Prince,
but the Prince did not yet know him well.
It happened that they toured Qínwàng.
The Prince sent someone to examine the carved stone inscription.
At the time, no one could recognize it.
Yún alone recited it.
The Prince was delighted,
and from then on, [Yún]'s favor surpassed all others in the prefectural administration.
When the Prince became the Governor of Dānyáng,
he summoned Yún to be his Chief Clerk,
greatly trusting and employing him.
At that time, [Yún] was introduced to Qí Gāodì.
It happened that someone presented a white crow.
The Emperor asked, "What sort of auspicious omen is this?"
Yún's rank was low,
and he answered last, saying:
"Your subject has heard that when a king reveres the ancestral temples,
then the white crow arrives."
At that time, the visit to the temple had just been concluded.
The Emperor said,
"Your words are correct.
The principle of sympathetic response
truly extends to this degree!"
He was transferred and appointed Military Advisor for Judicial Affairs (Xíngyù Cānjūnshì) to the Prince of Nánjùn, General Who Conquers the North (Zhēngběi),
concurrently retaining his position as Chief Clerk.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Diànzhōng Láng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
When Zǐliáng became Minister of Education (Sītú),
[Yún] was again appointed Military Advisor in Charge of Records (Jìshì Cānjūnshì).
Soon after, he was granted Gentleman-Consultant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng) and concurrently held the position of Grand Impartial Judge (Dà Zhōngzhèng) for his home province.
He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Línglíng.
While in office, he kept himself clean,
reduced burdensome regulations,
and eliminated frivolous expenditures.
The hundred families were content with this.
Emperor Míng recalled him to the capital.
When he arrived,
he was appointed Gentleman-in-Attendance (Sànqí Shìláng).
He was again sent out to be Administrator of Shǐxīng.
The commandery had many powerful, cunning, great clans.
If a Two Thousand Picul Official was not good,
they would conspire together to murder him,
or else drive him away.
The border areas bordered the Barbarians,
and especially abounded in bandits and thieves.
Previous Administrators all had to protect themselves with weapons.
When Yún entered the territory,
he soothed them with kindness and virtue.
He abolished the patrol posts.
Merchants could sleep openly.
The people in the commandery called him divine and brilliant.

He was subsequently promoted to Bearer of the Ax (Jiǎjié), General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn), General and Colonel Who Pacifies the Yuè (Píngyuè Zhōngláng Jiāng), and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Initially,
Yún was close with Jiāng Shí, the Assistant Minister of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè).
Shí’s maternal cousin, Xú Yì, was the Prefect of Qǔjiāng.
Shí strongly entrusted Yì to Yún.
There was a man named Tán Yǎn,
a powerful clan member in the county.
Yì flogged him.
Yǎn considered this a great humiliation
and went to the capital to accuse Yún.
Yún was recalled, imprisoned, and held responsible.
He was exempted due to a general amnesty.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
he was reinstated as Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì).
Previously,
Yún had met Gāozǔ at the residence of Xiāo Zǐliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng of Qí.
They had also often been neighbors in the district.
Gāozǔ highly valued him.
When the righteous army reached the capital,
Yún was inside the city at the time.
Once Dōnghūn was executed,
the Palace Attendant, Zhāng Jì, ordered Yún to carry a message out of the city.
Gāozǔ then detained him,
and he immediately participated in strategy planning.
He was subsequently appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Shìláng),
and collaborated wholeheartedly with Shěn Yuē in assisting [Gāozǔ].
Soon after, he was promoted to Military Advisor (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ), and concurrently held the position of Secretariat Director (Lùshì).
When the Liáng state was established,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
At that time, Gāozǔ had taken the remaining imperial concubines of the dethroned Emperor Dōnghūn of Qí,
which somewhat interfered with governing affairs.
Yún had previously remonstrated about this,
but Gāozǔ had not accepted the advice.
Later, Yún entered the inner chamber together with Wáng Mào.
Yún again remonstrated, saying:
"In the past, Hàn Zǔ lived east of the mountains,
coveting wealth and fond of women.
But when he entered the Pass and settled Qín,
he took none of the treasures and silks,
and did not take any women to wife.
Fàn Zēng believed this was because his ambition had become great.
Now, the Duke has just settled the world.
People everywhere look forward to hearing about your reputation.
How can you adopt the ways of the misguided and chaotic ruler
and be burdened by female charms?"
Wáng Mào then rose, bowed, and said,
"Fàn Yún's words are right.
The Duke must take the world into consideration,
and should not keep or cherish these women."
Gāozǔ remained silent.
Yún then wrote an instruction ordering that the Yú women be bestowed upon Wáng Mào.
Gāozǔ admired his intention and permitted it.
The next day,
he gifted Yún and Mào one million cash each.
Gāozǔ received the abdication (of the former emperor),
offering sacrifices (chái liǎo) at the Nánjiāo,
Yún, as the Shìzhōng (Attendant at the Palace), accompanied him in the carriage.
When the ceremony was complete,
Gāozǔ ascended his imperial carriage,
and said to Yún:
"My current position,
is what is called trembling as if driving six horses with a rotten rope.”
Yún replied:
"I also wish Your Majesty would exercise greater caution day by day."
Gāozǔ praised him for this.
On that same day,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Attendant in Ordinary) and Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel);
based on his merit in supporting the establishment of the dynasty (Zuǒmìng Gōng), he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xiāochéng County,
with a stipend of a thousand households.
Yún was promoted due to the Emperor's former favor,
leaping into the position of supporting the founding of the dynasty.
He diligently assisted and advised (the Emperor) with full sincerity,
leaving nothing undone that he knew needed doing.
Gāozǔ also entrusted him completely,
and many of his memorials were approved.
Once, while attending a banquet,
Gāozǔ said to the Prince of Línchuān, Hóng, and the Prince of Póyáng, Huī:
"When I was young, Fàn Shàngshū and I were close friends.
We shared the reverence of all within the four seas.
Now that I am the ruler of All Under Heaven,
this formality has changed.
You should call Fàn 'Elder Brother' on my behalf."
The two princes descended from their seats and bowed,
and returned to the Shàngshū Xiàshěng (Ministerial Secretariat) in the same carriage as Yún.
People at the time considered this a great honor for him.
In that same year,
the Eastern Palace was established.
Yún concurrently held the post of Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Crown Prince) with his main office.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàngshū Yòu Púyè (Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs),
still concurrently managing the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel).
After a period,
he was implicated for violating an imperial edict in appointing personnel,
and dismissed from the Ministry of Personnel,
though he remained Púyè.
Yún was fundamentally deeply affectionate (or loyal).
He served his widowed elder brother's wife with utmost courtesy,
and concerning household matters, he would always consult her before acting.
He admired integrity and cherished the unconventional,
being solely dedicated to helping people in urgent need.
When he was young, he was close friends with Wáng Gē, the Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General of the Palace Guard).
Gē died in his official residence,
being poor and without a private dwelling.
Yún therefore brought the coffin back to his own home,
and personally managed the embalming and interment arrangements.
His respect and courtesy toward Jìnglínɡ Wáng Zǐliáng were exceptionally great.
Whenever Yún offered criticism or advice,
he never tailored his words to please him.
Zǐliáng once memorialized Qí Wǔdì (Emperor Wǔ of Qí) regarding Yún’s performance as a Commandant (Jùn).
The Emperor said:
"He is an ordinary man.
I heard that he betrayed (or mocked) others.
I will not exhaust the law [against him],
but he should be pardoned by sending him far away."
Zǐliáng said:
"That is not so.
Yún constantly advised and remonstrated with me,
and the remonstrance documents are all preserved.
I request permission to fetch them and present them to you."
When they arrived,
there were over a hundred pages,
and the language was entirely pointed and frank.
The Emperor sighed,
and consequently said to Zǐliáng:
"I did not expect Yún capable of such things.
I should keep him here to assist you;
why should he be sent out to govern a province?"
Qí Wénhuì Tàizǐ (Crown Prince Wénhuì of Qí) once went out to the Eastern Fields to observe the harvest.
He looked back and said to his assembled retainers:
"Reaping this is truly a marvelous sight."
Everyone assented obediently.
Yún alone said:
"The tasks of the three seasons [of farming]
are truly long and arduous work.
I sincerely wish that Your Highness might understand the difficulties of sowing and reaping,
and not pursue the pleasure and ease of a single morning."
After leaving,
the Shìzhōng Xiāo Miǎn, who had not known him previously,
approached his carriage, grasped Yún's hand, and said:
"I did not expect to hear such righteous advice again today."
When he held the post related to selecting officials,
his responsibilities were substantial and weighty.
Memorials and documents filled his desk,
and guests crowded his gate.
Yún responded to them fluently,
without obstruction or delay.
Concerning official paperwork,
his critical insight was like that of a spirit.
People at the time universally admired his intelligence and capability.
He was inclined to be fervent and sharp,
and lacked gravitas.
Whenever he judged something right or wrong,
it immediately showed in his bearing.
Scholars sometimes slighted him because of this.
Initially,
when Yún served as a Commandant, he was known for his integrity and honesty.
But when he occupied high and important positions,
he accepted quite a few gifts and tributes;
however, his family accumulated no wealth,
as he immediately distributed it among relatives and friends.
In the second year [of Tiānjiān],
he passed away,
being fifty-three years old at the time.
Gāozǔ wept for him,
and that same day, he drove his imperial carriage to attend the funeral rites.
An edict stated:
"To mourn those long gone and to be roused to grief
is the firm sentiment of common human nature;
how much more so for one whose reputation was present among us,
and who held a profound trust from the court!
The late Sànqí Chángshì, Shàngshū Yòu Púyè, and Marquis of Xiāochéng, Yún,
had a character that was firm and upright,
and his thoughts embraced far-reaching principles.
From the time he first established his ambitions,
his pure conduct was renowned.
Once he cast off his civilian headwear and entered service,
his pure achievements became consistently prominent.
Harmonizing affairs while rising in the court,
he was deemed trustworthy by all observers.
His careful assistance and support
were ethically reassuring to Our heart.
Although his diligence did not involve carrying the imperial reins [i.e., serving as the chief minister],
he was an old friend with whom We shared discussions.
Just as he was setting out on a long journey [i.e., career],
to forever assist the various state affairs;
his sudden death
brings grief and sadness to Our heart.
It is proper to add titles to his rank,
to fulfill the grand statutes.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Shìzhōng, Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Guards), Púyè, and Marquis status remains as before.
Furthermore, he is granted one set of drums and pipes (Gǔchuī)."
The official in charge of rites requested the posthumous name Xuān,
but an imperial order granted the posthumous name Wén.
His collected works comprised thirty volumes.
His son, Xiàocái, succeeded him,
and rose to the post of Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (Attendant in the Crown Prince’s Palace).
Shěn Yuē, courtesy name Xiūwén,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His grandfather, Línzǐ,
was the Sòng Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the North).
His father, Pú,
was the Grand Administrator of Huáinán.
Pú was executed near the end of the Yuánjiā period.
Yuē hid in his youth,
until he met with an amnesty and was spared.
Thereafter, he lived as a destitute orphan in exile.
He was devoted to study
day and night without tiring.
His mother, fearing he would fall ill from overwork,
often made him reduce the oil and put out the lamp fire.
But what he read during the day,
he would recite every night.
Consequently, he gained a broad mastery of all texts
and was skilled at composition.
He began his career as Fèngcháoqǐng (Gentleman Usher).
Cài Xīngzōng of Jìyáng heard of his talent and admired him.
When Xīngzōng became the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu,
he recruited Yuē as the Ānxī Wàibīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer for External Military Affairs to the General Who Pacifies the West),
concurrently serving as Jìshì (Recorder).
Xīngzōng once told his sons:
"Shěn Jìshì is a model teacher for human relations;
you should serve him well."
When Xīngzōng later served in Jīngzhōu,
Yuē again served as Zhēngxī Jìshì Cānjūn (Staff Officer and Recorder to the General Who Subdues the West),
and concurrently held the post of Magistrate (Lìng) of Juéxī.
After Xīngzōng died,
Yuē first served as Fǎcáo Cānjūn (Staff Officer for Judicial Affairs) to the Prince of Jìn'ān, General Who Pacifies the West,
then transferred to Wàibīng (External Military Affairs),
concurrently holding the post of Recorder for both.
Upon entering the central government, he became Shàngshū Dùzhī Láng (Director of Finance in the Department of State Affairs).
Early in the Qí dynasty, he served as Secretary to the General Who Conquers the North (Zhēnglǔ Jìshì),
concurrently holding the post of Magistrate of Xiāngyáng (Xiāngyáng Lìng).
The Prince he served
was Crown Prince Wénhuì (Qí Wénhuì Tàizǐ) of Qí.
When the Crown Prince moved into the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
he became Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
managing secretarial affairs,
on duty at the Yǒngshòu Chamber (Yǒngshòu Shěng),
and collating the maps and books of the Four Sections.
At that time, the Eastern Palace was filled with scholars.
Shěn Yuē was treated with particular intimacy and favor.
Whenever he went in for his audience (while on duty),
he would only leave when the shadow was slanted.
At that time, when kings and marquises arrived at the palace,
some were unable to be admitted.
Shěn Yuē frequently spoke about this.
The Crown Prince said:
“I have always been lazy to rise,
which you know well.
When I have your discussion,
only then do I forget sleep.
If you want me to rise early,
you should enter early.”
He was transferred to Palace Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Jiālìng).
Later, he concurrently held the post of Drafting Clerk (Zhùzuò Láng) with his original office.
He was transferred to Central Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Láng),
Regional Impartial (Zhōngzhèng) of his home county,
Right Chief Clerk (Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ) to the Minister of the Multitudes,
and Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng).
At that time, the Prince of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Wáng) also recruited scholars.

Shěn Yuē, along with Xiāo Chēn (Xiāo Chēn) of Lánlíng, Wáng Róng (Wáng Róng) of Lángyé, Xiè Tiǎo (Xiè Tiǎo) of Chénjùn, Fàn Yún (Fàn Yún) of Nánxiāng, Rèn Fǎng (Rèn Fǎng) of Yuè'ān, and others, all associated there,
and the age hailed them as having acquired the best men.
Shortly thereafter, he concurrently held the post of Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng).
Soon after, he became Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng),
and was transferred to Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) to the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì).
In the first year of Lóngchāng (Lóngchāng yuánnián),
he was appointed Director of the Bureau of Civil Office (Lìbù Láng),
and was sent out to serve as General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
When Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) ascended the throne,
his title was advanced to General Who Aids the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
He was recalled to serve as Minister of the Five Bureaus (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and transferred to Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
When Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) died,
governance returned to the Chief Minister (Zhǒngzǎi).
The Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Xú Xiàosì (Xú Xiàosì), ordered Shěn Yuē to draft and finalize the dying injunctions.
He was transferred to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was given the additional title of Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (Yǒngyuán èrnián),
citing his mother's old age, he submitted a memorial requesting to be relieved of his duties.
He was reassigned as General of the Vanguards (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) and Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) to the Minister of the Multitudes (Sītú),
and General Who Conquers the North (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Nán Qīnghé (Nán Qīnghé Tàishǒu).
When Gāozǔ was in the Western Residence (Xī Dǐ),
he had associated with Shěn Yuē for a long time.
When Jiànkāng city was pacified,
he appointed him Cavalry Commandant (Piàojì Sīmǎ),
with his General title remaining as before.
At that time, Gāozǔ’s meritorious achievements were complete,
and Heaven and men truly inclined towards him.
Shěn Yuē once broached the subject,
but Gāozǔ remained silent and did not answer.
On another day, he advanced and spoke again:
“The present differs from antiquity;
one cannot expect all things to adhere to the pure ways.
Scholars and officials who cling to the dragon and attach themselves to the phoenix
all hope to achieve some measure of merit,
so as to protect their good fortune and emolument.
Now, even children and herd-boys
all know that the Qí mandate has ended,
and everyone says that the Illustrious Duke (Míng Gōng) is the man.
The signs of Heaven and human affairs
indicate the portents of a changed destiny.
Since Yǒngyuán,
this has been especially clear and manifest.
The prophecy says, ‘The movement conforming to Water
becomes the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ),’
and this, too, is clearly recorded.
The heart of Heaven cannot be violated,
and the will of the people cannot be lost.
If this is truly where the Heavenly mandate rests,
even if you wish to show modesty,
you cannot stop yourself.”
Gāozǔ said:
“I am still considering this.”
He replied:
“When you first took up arms at Fán and Miǎn,
that was the time you should have considered it.
Now the imperial achievement is complete,
what more is there left to consider?
In the past, when King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) attacked Zhòu (Zhòu),
as soon as he entered,
the people immediately called him ‘Our Lord.’
King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) did not violate the people’s wishes,
and also had nothing to consider.
Since you arrived at the capital (Jīngyì),
the natural order has already shifted.
Compared to King Wǔ of Zhōu (Zhōu Wǔ),
the speed is different.
If you do not quickly settle the great enterprise,
delaying the hopes of Heaven and man,
should just one person take a divergent view,
it would damage your prestige and virtue.
Moreover, men are not made of metal or stone,
and current affairs are difficult to secure.
How can you leave the enfeoffment of Jiàn'ān (Jiàn'ān)
to be inherited by your sons and grandsons?
If the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) returns to the capital,
and the Dukes and Ministers assume their posts,
then the division between ruler and minister will be fixed,
and there will be no more divergent hearts.
With the ruler enlightened above
and the ministers loyal below,
would there still be anyone willing to join you again as a rebel?”
Gāozǔ agreed with him.
When Shěn Yuē went out,
Gāozǔ summoned Fàn Yún (Fàn Yún) and informed him.
Yún’s reply was generally the same as Shěn Yuē’s intent.
Gāozǔ said:
“That wise men should agree in secret like this!
You should bring Xiūwén (Xiūwén) to come again early tomorrow.”
Fàn Yún went out and told Shěn Yuē.
Shěn Yuē said:
“You must wait for me.”
Fàn Yún promised,
but Shěn Yuē went in earlier than planned.
Gāozǔ ordered him to draft the required documents.
Shěn Yuē then produced the imperial edict and all the appointments from his sleeve.
Gāozǔ initially made no changes whatsoever.
Shortly thereafter, Fàn Yún arrived from outside,
but upon reaching the palace gate, he could not enter.
He paced back and forth outside the Shòuguāng Gate (Shòuguāng Gé),
only saying
“Duō duō!”
When Shěn Yuē came out,
Fàn Yún asked:
“How was I placed?”
Shěn Yuē raised his hand toward the left (Zuǒ, referring to the Left Executive rank).
Fàn Yún smiled and said:
“This does not disappoint my hopes.”
A moment later,
Gāozǔ summoned Fàn Yún and said:
“In the past, when I associated with Shěn Xiūwén (Shěn Xiūwén) in a group,
I did not sense that he was extraordinary;
but today, his talent and wisdom flow freely—
he can be called brilliant and perceptive.”
Fàn Yún replied:
“Your Grace knows Shěn Yuē today,
which is no different from Shěn Yuē knowing Your Grace today.”
Gāozǔ said:
“It has been three years since I raised the army.
The meritorious officials and various generals
certainly exerted themselves;
however, those who established the imperial enterprise
are actually the two of you.”
When the Liáng (Liáng) administration was established,
he served as Grand Master of Remonstrance (Sànqí Chángshì) and Minister of the Bureau of Civil Office (Lìbù Shàngshū),
concurrently holding the post of Right Executive (Yòu Púyè).
When Gāozǔ accepted the abdication,
he became Executive of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè),
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiànchāng County (Jiànchāng Xiànhóu),
with one thousand households,
and his Grand Master title remained as before.
He also appointed Shěn Yuē’s mother, Xiè (Xiè), as Grand Lady of the State of Jiànchāng (Jiànchāng Guó Tàifūrén).
On the day of the conferment ceremony,
Right Executive Fàn Yún (Fàn Yún) and more than twenty others all came to pay their respects,
and the court and the public considered this a great honor.
Soon after, he was transferred to Left Executive of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè),
his Grand Master title remaining as before.
Not long after, he concurrently served as Commander of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn),
and was given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the second year of Tiānjiān (Tiānjiān èrnián),
he suffered the mourning of his mother.
The Imperial Carriage personally visited to express condolences.
Since Shěn Yuē was advanced in years
and should not undergo the destructive rites of mourning,
the Emperor sent a Court Attendant (Zhōngshū Shèrén) to prohibit visitors and limit his wailing.
He was recalled to office as General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn),
and given subordinate staff.
When mourning was concluded,
he was transferred to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Grand Master of Radiance of the Right (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū),
concurrently leading Palace Grandee to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì),
Grand Impartial (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Yángzhōu,
and attending to eight matters of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Bā Tiáo Shì).
He was transferred to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
His Palace Attendant, Palace Grandee, and Impartial titles remained as before.
He repeatedly submitted memorials petitioning to decline the appointment.

He was reassigned as Left Executive of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), concurrently leading Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), and General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn),
and given subordinate staff,
his Palace Attendant title remaining as before.
Soon after, he was transferred to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng),
concurrently leading Junior Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shàofù).
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to Grand Master of Radiance of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū).
His Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Junior Tutor (Shàofù) titles remained as before,
and he was granted one set of drums and horns (Gǔchuī).
Initially,
Xuě Yuē, having long held the position of Duānkuǐ,
had aspirations for the post of Táisī.
Commentators all considered this appropriate,
but the Emperor ultimately did not appoint him.
Thereupon, he requested to be sent out (to a provincial post),
but this was also not granted.
He was always on good terms with Xú Miǎn,
and thus presented his feelings in a letter to Mǐan, saying:
“I was lonely and suffering in my youth,
with no close relatives nearby.
In the past, I was on the verge of collapsing,
separated, troubled, and distressed,
struggling day and night.
I plodded through humble official service;
the tasks were not for my own gain,
but in hopes of obtaining a small salary,
relying on this to return East.
More than ten years passed
before I was finally humbled to serve as the Magistrate of Xiāngyáng County.
The calculations involving public and private concerns
were not fully clear to me;
using my person to aid matters,
I had no choice but to undertake human affairs.
At the end of the Yǒngmíng era,
I was sent out to govern Dōngyáng,
my intention being to halt and be content;
but when the Jiànwǔ era inaugurated its rule,
human society became intertwined,
and once I departed, there was no returning,
making it difficult to proceed.
When the reign of the darkened and suspicious ruler began,
the imperial administration was fragmented.
I therefore planned retirement,
hoping it might succeed.
I entrusted you to express my sentiments to Xú Lìng;
I imagine you have not forgotten that memory.
Now that the Sagely Way has swiftly arisen,
I wrongly encountered this excellent opportunity.
My former ambition and long-held intention
again resulted in contradiction and disappointment.
This year begins anew,
and the conventional age for retirement has arrived.
My request to retire
was overruled by imperial favor.
I sincerely cannot broadly proclaim excellent administration
or glorify and clarify court principles,
yet I am still required to examine documents and records
and deliberate on the commonalities and differences of current proposals.
However, since the beginning of the year,
my illness has worsened and my worries are urgent.
This must be because the vital spirit is limited,
and the exertion has been excessive,
leading overall to this decline and exhaustion,
which is attributed to my later years.
I force myself to move and rest,
striving diligently to attend to matters.
Viewed externally and observed casually,
I still seem like a whole person,
but my body and energy
do not coordinate with each other.
I constantly need to greatly restrain myself;
only then can I reluctantly carry out my duties.
If I loosen my robes and lie down,
my limbs seem to lose connection.
I suffer from heat above and cold below,
worsening month by month and day by day.
If I seek warmth, I become agitated;
if I add cold, it invariably brings relief.
Later periods of improvement are inferior to earlier periods,
and later periods of severity are certainly worse than earlier periods.
Over a hundred days or a few weeks,
my leather belt must constantly be moved a hole;
if I grasp my arm with my hand,
it is calculated to shrink by half a *fēn* each month.
Based on this calculation,
how can I possibly last long?
If this continues without stopping,
day after day,
I will leave the Sagely Lord the regret of being unable to recall (this situation in time).
I dare to submit this report,
begging for the rank of retired elder.
If Heaven grants me more years
and I regain normal health,
to the extent my ability and strength allow,
I will only consider how to serve in office.”
Xú Miǎn spoke on his behalf to Gāozǔ,
requesting the ceremonial honors of the Sān Sī (Three Dukes).
He was not permitted,
only the drums and wind instruments were added.
Xuě Yuē was by nature not a drinker,
and had few desires.
Although he was greatly honored at the time,
his residence was simple and plain.
He built his house in Dōngtián,
gazing upon the suburbs and hills.
He once composed the *Jiāojū Fù* (Rhapsody on Suburban Dwelling).
Its text says: Only the ultimate person considers things other than the self,
and thus forgets both the world and the self.
As for those below middle intelligence,
all take nature as their field of action.
Beasts run freely because of their dens,
birds soar only after securing a nest.
Chén was poor in the alley yet his work was great,
Yīng lived in cramped quarters yet his virtue prospered.
Qiáo resided in benevolence in Dōnglǐ,
Fèng concealed his traces in Xītáng.
Alas, my own narrow ambition
lacks the great methods for ordering the world.
I desire to rely on the forest and fold my wings,
I wish to entrust myself to the water and conceal my scales.
Truly, I have no desire for magnificent mansions,
nor any
wish for grand thoroughfares.
I expose myself to the vastness of the eastern suburbs,
entering the wild expanse of weeds and thistles.
I build vertically and construct horizontally,
and clear away obstructions by wind and rain.
When the Western Hàn Dynasty marked its conclusion,
my ancestors' dispersal and migration began.
They left Lìjiàn in Hǎihūn,
and first established their livelihood along the riverbanks.
It was like the Hé and Jǐ rivers, returning to prominence,
surpassing the ten generations of Bān Shēng.
Some resigned their salaries and returned to farming,
some dusted their hats and came to serve.
When it reached the Lóng'ān era of the Jìn Dynasty,
hardship and distress accumulated in the course of Heaven.
The world was contested and drifted like waves,
the people lost their stability and looked around fearfully like wolves.
Disorder spread like tangled hemp across the towns and villages,
and the exposed dead lay like wild grass on the thoroughfares.
The great earth was vast but offered no refuge,
and High Heaven was distant—to
whom could one appeal?
Alas, when the Imperial Ancestor was young,
he encountered a time of extreme hardship.
He left the dangerous state in distress and shock,
sought a place of safety, and moved there.
He first built his dwelling in the Zhū
region,
and closed off the quiet courtyard to rest peacefully.
He met the glorious rise of the Dragon Visage,
and relied on the wind to stretch his wings.
He pointed his carriage south toward the Imperial Capital,
driving along the long road to exert his strength.
He moved the decorated doors and came to open them,
raising high beams and installing posts.
He bordered the long, level side roads,
facing the clear, straight flow of the Huái River.
Fragrant dust settled and time passed far away,
the ways of the world
suddenly became uneven.
Four generations have continued until this day,
completing one hundred years upon my humble person.
Alas, this humble dwelling is hard to maintain,
like a falling bamboo sheath carried by the wind.
Sometimes clearing the thatch and
trimming the thorns,
sometimes having gone west, returning east.
Sometimes accommodating myself in Bái Shè,
and also entrusting my family to Bó Tōng.
Tracing my upright conduct throughout life,
I truly intended to depart alone.
I think of secluded people with deep concern,
gazing toward the eastern marsh with prolonged longing.
Originally forgetting my emotions regarding external pursuits,
I am merely constrained by Heaven and Earth.
I often lament being controlled by the thread (of fate/office),
and Lù composed his words about the net of the world.
Affairs rush forth yet do not suit me,
my resolve is distressed but remains untainted.
The path is nearly
exhausted yet grows steeper,
my sentiment deepens as twilight approaches.
I hold a small heart, pure as an orchid;
why is this wish so immense?
I chant "Let me return" but hesitate,
gazing fondly at the cliffs and
clapping my hands.
I met a ruler of the time who lost virtue;
how furiously chaotic was the dark malevolence!
It was what the Battle of Mù did not display,
it was truly what Shēng'é did not record.
The clamoring common people
were about to hang themselves as bait for beasts.
Looking up at the vast sky, there was no place to return;
though not in a pen, they were treated like meat.
I first lamented the silk thread (of fate) but did not witness (peace),
finally relaxing the official sash, I encountered it afterwards.
Seeking
to bestow love upon High Heaven,
truly nothing is more important than the people.
The hidden token was granted in the constellations of Jǐng and Yì;
this was truly bestowed by the spiritual mandate.
At the first moment of descent and oversight,
it coincided with accumulated evil.
The fruition is called ripe.
Preferring to manage the lower platform (the land),
dispelling the heavy atmosphere from the upper heavens.
Personally having no leisure for breakfast,
always seeking clothing from the night pillow.
Having already encompassed
Guī and Xià,
and furthermore driven along Xuān and Xù.
Virtue covers everywhere, no matter how distant,
light illuminates everywhere, no matter how subtle.
Spreading profound grace throughout the Great Wilderness,
sowing the wind of benevolence among distant
customs.
Opening up eternal ages and extending contemplation,
believing that the kingly plan is like jade.
Happening upon the glorious age of receiving the Mandate,
meeting the auspicious time when the Sage arises.
Declining the court attendant role in the early days,
accepting the honor of assisting at this time.
Lacking the fierce ambition of casting stones,
possessing no eloquent words like flying arrows.
Arranging the orientation (of the sun/birds) and naming the city,
aligning with rivers and mountains to establish the foundation.
Assisting the stored brilliance in the three excellences,
overseeing the royal duties among the hundred offices.
Fearing the simplicity of loss for a humble
man,
worrying about the difficulty of maintaining favor and emolument.
As for the noble officials of former generations,
rarely did they bend their minds toward humble caves and mounds.
Like flowers clustered in Chǔ and Zhào,
they always surpassed one another in
arrogance and extravagance.
Constructing foremost mansions near the bronze gate,
placing high gates alongside the Běiquè.
Opening heavy inner doors in splendid residences,
how could these be obscured by weeds and brambles?
Arrogantly hoping to pass on succession in barren
soil,
how can one settle the body in impoverished land?
Pondering the words of the ancient sages,
this is certainly what my heart delights in.
I do not covet power in the city market,
nor would I seek fame in the butcher shops.
Chanting about the subtle and examining the dwelling,
fortunate that it can shelter against wind and frost.
Therefore, next to the poor wilderness,
arriving at the desolate outskirts;
Weaving reeds frosted by winter,
patching up cold thatch.
Constructing where roosting and chirping gather,
building where paths and tracks intersect.
Because they touched the eaves,
trees were felled,
because they obstructed the foundation, nests were removed.
Draining the stagnant pools and ponds,
filling the sunken pits of bricked wells.
Planting fragrant trifoliate oranges by the northern ditch,
growing tall willows by the southern bank.
Moving the simple jar window to the orchid room,
joining the walls shoulder-to-shoulder with the painted fence.
Weaving dormant brushwood to form the gate,
utilizing the outer shutter as the door.
Having taken shade from the courtyard trees,
also relying on the
fence of fragrant thoroughwort.
Opening upper chambers to oversee the distance,
building high balconies to view the surroundings.
Digging small pools where the roof drip line falls,
surrounding the hall with ridges and paths below.
Its aquatic plants are
water clover, duckweed, water caltrops, and hornwort,
algae, rush, and wild rice shoots;
rock moss and sea hair,
yellow fringed water-lily, and green cattail.
Red lotus blossoms move with the light ripples,
green leaves cover the clear lake.
Eating the fine fruits and
repelling old age,
shaking the feathered garments in the Qīngdū.
Its terrestrial herbs are purple turtle-like plant and green burr,
heavenly milfoil and mountain leek;
goose teeth and elk tongue,
ox lip and pig head.
Spreading luxuriantly
on the sunny side of the Southern Pond,
profusely flourishing behind the Northern Tower.
Some curtain the islet and overshadow the ground,
some twine around the windows and peer through the openings.
As for garden residences of unique design,
and fields and orchards in different sections.
Lǐ Héng had a thousand tangerine trees,
Shí Chóng had ten thousand mixed fruit trees.
Both were extensions of extravagant emotions,
not the pleasure of a frugal mind.
Wishing them to be dense and lush,
spitting green and gathering crimson;
Covering the windows and reflecting the doors,
catching the eaves drip and filling the corners.
Opening crimson buds to illuminate all directions,
spreading emerald leaves over the nine paths.
Drawing forth red flowers from purple stems,
bearing white
pistils on green calyxes.
The forest birds alight and hover up and down,
their lingering songs rising and falling;
The Chǔ sparrows have many names,
warbling notes mix with the sounds.
Some have patterned tails and brocaded wings,
some have green
breasts and crimson foreheads.
Fond of hiding among the leaves and concealing among the branches,
sometimes singing charmingly as they come and go.
The aquatic fowl are large swans and small geese,
sky dogs and marsh fowl;
autumn kingfishers and cold plovers,
long petrels and short [bird].
Dragging the uneven, tender algae,
playing with their light bodies in the splashing water;
Their wings strike the current raising foam,
their feathers beat the waves forming pearls.
The fish include red
carp and green bream,
slender dace and giant catfish.
Jade scales and vermillion tails,
long skulls and slanting [mouths].
The small ones play by the banks forming patterns,
the large ones spout water stirring up white spray.
They do not excite envy in the
rivers and seas,
but find peace forgotten in my residence.
The bamboo is uniquely flourishing in the southeast,
the nine prefectures boast its rarity.
It was not transplanted from the Qí River,
nor were its roots divided from the Yuèchí.
Autumn cicadas hum among the leaves,
cold sparrows chatter on the branches.
The wind comes beneath the Southern Balcony,
snow rests on the eaves of the Northern Hall.
Investigating the deep tracks of past paths,
observing the sincerity and falseness of those who knew first.
Always punishing the empty and seeking the existent,
everyone points to difficulty while calling it easy.
Not restraining oneself but seeking sufficiency,
acquiring treasures that lead to troubles.
This is what the scholars of the past were deluded by,
and what I
now avoid.
Reflecting on the origin established by the Nónghuáng,
examining the beginning of sowing.
He initiated the change from raw meat to grain food,
this is what sustains human life.
Tracing the old records of the well-field system,
examining the paths and boundaries in former writings.
Yán was content with a bamboo basket of food,
Zhèng had high granaries but remained empty.
Four hundred *qǐng* are insufficient,
fifty *mǔ* are more than enough.
Comforting my secluded
heart with confined thoughts,
fortunately drawing sustenance from my courtyard hut.
Plowing the eastern fallow with the old spade,
irrigating the northern fields with the new ditch.
Not needing to move the cooking fire early in the morning,
not harboring hunger while eating
morning vegetables.
Rejecting external things equally and sending them away,
the only thing that burdens me is within myself.
Why bother with the accumulation of thousands of things,
I do not envy the great market of Wènyáng.
Facing the southeast corner and letting my gaze gallop,
turning my eyes toward the stacked mounds.
Although these mountains are mere hillocks,
they were the place of feasting for Wénjìng.
Driving the four stallions that rise and fall,
echoing the clear trills of numerous reed pipes.
Arranging square and circular objects in splendid array,
offering delicacies from both sea and land.
Why is a single power worthy of admiration?
Squandering a thousand gold pieces as if they were thread.
Trying to touch my
chest and speak (from the heart),
how can such customs be encouraged?
This is the profound meaning known to the enlightened,
not what common minds perceive.
For a moment shifting my thoughts and changing my gaze,
recognizing the emerging mounds at the
home ferry crossing.
Belted by long shoals at the laurel islet,
where the shovels were first raised by powerful Qín.
The road wound through Wú and reached Yuè,
the path covered the sea and connected to Mǐn.
Holding the three birds in prolonged
memory,
alas, the old hometown is truly precious.
Truly, I arrived late in the year,
having not missed my chance in early spring.
Why does the Eastern River flow so smoothly,
yet tears flow uniquely for us?
I wrongly participated among the worthy of former generations,
and frequently wandered to this place.
Attending by the painted yak-tail banners, we aligned our reins;
escorting the dragon boat, we followed the waterside.
Sometimes we arranged seats and composed poetry,
sometimes we distributed
cups and spoke at the banquet.
When the gauze curtain suddenly became dark and silent one morning,
Xīlíng (西陵) suddenly became lush and verdant.
Gazing at Shāng (商), I let out a long sigh,
always finding joyous harmony in this spectacle.
At first, bells and stones
resounded brightly and loudly;
finally, fish and dragons danced wildly (in the water).
Some ascended and descended in order,
others floated cups without count.
The noble included Bǐng (丙), Wèi (魏), Xiāo (蕭), and Cáo (曹);
the intimate included Liáng Wǔ (梁武) and Zhōu
Dàn (旦).
None failed to perish amid the frost and fog,
and dissipate along with the wind and clouds.
I gaze at the tomb fields of Sūn Hòu (孫后),
searching for the heroic achievements left by the conquerors.
Truly he followed the later
kings of Hàn (漢),
and indeed initiated [the reign of] the wise ruler of Wú (吳).
He pointed to Héngyuè (衡岳) to serve as his bastion,
encompassing the Jiāng (江) and Hàn (漢) to form his domain.
Vainly were words engraved on the stone sarcophagus,
and subsequently disaster was invited upon the golden threads (of the shroud).
Suddenly
it is overgrown and neglected,
identical to the vast mounds of Yuánlíng (原陵).
How could they know the ants and the foxes and rabbits,
not to mention the woodcutters and the stable boys?
I look towards the eastern peaks
and cast my gaze,
my heart mournful and uneasy.
This was formerly the old garden of the Crown Prince,
and truly the remaining foundation of Bówàng (博望).
The long woods are marked by cassia trees,
the rows of grasses are crowned by fragrant
língzhī (芝).
Wind towers pile up their wings,
moon pavilions have double brackets.
A thousand brackets are quickly deployed,
a hundred interlocking supports hold each other up.
Black shafts drive the carriages (in the woods),
orchid oars propel the water games.
More than three years have passed
since those events,
and suddenly two cycles (24 years) have elapsed since then.
All are leveled and cleansed,
not that ancient and modern are different times.
I turn my eyes back towards the northeast region,
to see the high manor on this ridge.
Although it is formed by coalescence and leaves no trace,
truly its inherited teachings can be maintained.
First, one sips the clouds and exhales the mist;
finally, one traverses the void and casts a reverse shadow.
Riding the continuous stream of the female rainbow,
floating on the boundless expanse of the Heavenly River.
Pointing to Xiánchí (咸池) for a brief rest,
gazing towards Yáotái (瑤臺) and soaring high,
not that I boast
with empty words,
but I hope that divine methods can be sought.
Only the hidden lushness of Zhōngyán (鍾巖)
stands out as steep and lofty for the imperial capital,
truly the place where ranks of gods are venerated,
enveloping wind and clouds and exhaling
moisture.
As for its appearance,
it is majestic and towering,
with tall branches brushing the sun;
it is rugged and lofty,
with fallen stones piled up like stars.
The peaks are high and prominent,
sometimes concave, sometimes flat;
resting on
hard rocks,
with strange and varying shapes.
Solitary peaks jut out horizontally,
caves pass through diagonally;
a thousand *zhàng* (丈) and ten thousand *rèn* (仞),
three tiers and nine sections.
It stretches around the prefectures and cities,
and spans across the suburbs and countryside;
Plain smoke girdles it in the evening,
white mist coils around it in the morning.
Observed closely, one cliff shows various colors;
viewed from afar, a hundred ridges are all green.
I observe the tombs of the two dynasties,
and see the remnants of destruction
of those brought low by tyrannical subordinates,
and those who straightened their robes before empty vessels;
of Mù (穆), who respectfully regulated himself in the court hall,
and Jiǎn (簡), who
simplified his emotions in the mystical marketplace;
of Liè (烈), who brought disaster by excessive drinking,
and Ān (安), who forgot worry and received misfortune.
How magnificent was the patriarch Zōngzǔ (宗祖),
whose might traversed heaven and surpassed earth.
Only Shèngwén (聖文)
continued his martial deeds,
and perhaps great peace could be achieved.
I, whose generation has been ruled by virtue,
look up at the remaining territory and wipe away tears.
The divine shrines are not one,
the spiritual halls are separated by distance.
Mats are spread for
the reddish colt (divine guest),
cassia wine flows in the hall.
The Purple Emperor descends from the Heavenly Palace,
the two consorts are invited from the Xīangzhǔ (湘渚).
Floating orchid smoke rises over the cassia beams,
Wūyáng (巫陽) is summoned from Nánchǔ (南楚).
Wielding
jade drumsticks,
holding pepper grain offerings.
Dazed, facing the wind, I chant loudly,
breaking off fragrant reeds and standing long.
I respectfully consider that the ethereal path is distant,
and divine traces are far-reaching.
Thoughts are greatly startled,
life is like accumulated foam.
I turn the marvelous wheel towards the One Vehicle,
and open the mysterious door towards the Three Paths.
If one desires to cease the mind and discard burdens,
one must violate human conventions before becoming enlightened.
Sometimes rafters are joined at
the base of the cliff,
sometimes windows are opened at the tips of trees.
The rooms are darkened by ivy,
the eaves are covered by pines and cypresses.
Since I have attained principle by shedding both (worldly things and self),
I naturally forget about hunger and thirst.
Sometimes I cling to branches
and wander alone far away,
sometimes I traverse the clouds and soar high.
Because I repair the thatch and establish a name (for the hermitage),
I still observe the void and establish a designation.
If I can forget the self on this day,
why should I anticipate rewards in the future?
Heaven grants me great virtue,
I bear this boundless favor.
I receive the good praise for an old man,
and distribute the ceremonial feast in the Supreme School.
I lack the excellent quality of desiring to follow a *jì* (驥, swift horse),
and am deficient in the admirable reputation of Rúguī (如
I received favor in the past from the former ruler,
and am again not employed by the present Emperor.
I look up to the great rule of respecting the aged,
and ask for my humble self [to retire] in the setting sun.
I am burdened by management duties
but am granted leave,
yet I still serve in the Eastern Palace (Spring Hall).
At times I speak of returning to my humble dwelling,
and casually wander during leisure days.
I settle my aspirations in the Pure Land,
I return my heart to the *dàochǎng* (道場, place of cultivation).
Beasts rest by the steps without being startled,
fish fill the pond and are not netted.
I turn from the confused path of my former track,
and value the later thought of the fleeting time.
Late trees open their flowers,
the first blossoms shed their petals.
Sometimes different woods separate the crimson and azure,
suddenly they mingle the red and purple due to the wind.
Purple lotuses bloom at night,
red lotuses unfold at dawn.
A light breeze stirs slightly,
its fragrance assaults me.
Wind
rustles among the garden trees,
the moon covers the contiguous pond bamboos.
Vines lengthen their branches on the eaves' cassia,
yellow flowers bloom on the courtyard chrysanthemums.
Ice hangs in the hollows and borders the mounds,
snow surrounds the pine
and covers the plains.
Ducks gather in flight but do not disperse,
geese soar high and are about to descend.
These are all seasonal sights to be cherished,
although they come from outside, they are not false (or borrowed).
They are truly what my nature
is attached to and detains,
and what I intend to keep and cannot abandon.
I grieve that my emotions are worn and old,
afflicted by multiplying worries and misfortunes.
Sadness comes from different carts but meets at the same destination,
joy comes from different directions but is simultaneously lost.
Sometimes I again entrust my feelings to fish and birds,
Beside him, the Wú wá were lacking,
and in front of him, there was no Zhào sè zither.
He used this (lifestyle) to end his life,
thereby passing the days.
He regretted only that the grace of Heaven and Earth was left unpaid,
and the office dedicated to recording affairs
could not be recounted (or accomplished fully).
He only held importance in the place of high gates,
but was not recorded by the brushes of worthy historians.
He sighed deeply—what could he say?
Truly, his feeling of shame was not slight.
Soon thereafter, he was promoted to Tèjìn,
while his titles of Guānglù, Shìzhōng, and Shàofù remained as before.
In the twelfth year,
he died in office,
aged seventy-three at the time.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him his former office,
bestowed 50,000 cash,
and 100 bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title was Yǐn.
Yuē had double pupils in his left eye,
a purple mark on his waist,
and his intelligence surpassed others.
He loved classical texts and books,
accumulating up to 20,000 scrolls,
unmatched in the capital.
When young, he was orphaned and poor.
He begged among his relatives (zōngdǎng),
receiving several hundred hú of rice.
He was insulted by a relative,
who spilled the rice and left.
When he became noble,
he held no grudge against the relative,
and employed him as a messenger in the commandery (jùnbù).
Once, while attending a feast,
there was a singing mistress (jìshī) who had been a palace attendant of Qí Wénhuì.
The Emperor asked if she recognized the guests present.
She replied:
"I only recognize Shěn Jiālìng."
Yuē prostrated himself and wept,
the Emperor was also saddened by this,
and consequently stopped the drinking.
Yuē served successively under three dynasties.
He was comprehensive and familiar with the old regulations.
He was knowledgeable about nature and widely informed,
serving as a model for his generation.
Xiè Xuánhuī was skilled at composing poetry,
Rèn Yànshēng was adept at literary writing.
Yuē possessed both talents,
but he could not surpass them.
He prided himself on his great talent,
but was dim concerning glory and profit.
However, taking advantage of the times and relying on influence,
he somewhat stained (or compromised) his reputation for pure discussion (qīngtán).
When he held the high position (duānkuí),
he gradually upheld the principle of contentment (zhǐzú).
Every time he was promoted,
he earnestly requested retirement,
yet ultimately could not leave.
Commentators compared him to Shān Tāo.
He held power for more than ten years,
but never once recommended or promoted anyone.
Regarding the success or failure of governance,
he merely offered perfunctory agreement (wéiwéi).
Initially,
Gāozǔ held a grievance against Zhāng Jì.
When Jì died,
[Gāozǔ] spoke of the matter with Yuē.
Yuē said:
"The Minister of Personnel, Chief Executive of the Left (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè), was sent out to serve as the Inspector (Cìshǐ) of a border province.
Past matters
are not worth discussing again."
The Emperor thought that since they were related by marriage (hūnjiā), Yuē was defending him,
and in great anger said:
"For you to speak like this,
is that the mark of a loyal minister?"
Thereupon, he was carried back to the inner palace chamber.
Yuē was frightened,
and did not realize that Gāozǔ had risen,
still sitting as before.
When he returned,
before reaching his bed,
he stumbled heavily below the door threshold for no apparent reason.
Subsequently falling ill,
he dreamed that Emperor Hé of Qí cut off his tongue with a sword.
He summoned a shaman (wū) to examine him.
The shaman's words confirmed the dream.
He then summoned a Dàoshì priest to submit a "crimson memorial" (chìzhāng) to Heaven,
declaring that the matter of the abdication (chándài)
did not originate with him.
Gāozǔ sent Xú Zhuàng, a physician from the Imperial Medical Department (Shàngshěng Yī), to examine Yuē's illness,
who returned and fully reported the situation.
Before this,
Yuē had once attended a feast.
It happened that Yùzhōu presented chestnuts,
one and a half cùn (inch) in diameter.
The Emperor marveled at them,
and asked:
"How many historical anecdotes concerning chestnuts are there?"
He and Yuē each listed what they remembered,
but the Emperor listed three fewer items than Yuē.
Yuē went out and said to others:
"That gentleman (the Emperor) was protecting his reputation (hùqián).
If I hadn't deferred, he would have been mortified."
The Emperor considered these words disrespectful (bú xùn),
and wished to punish him.
Xú Miǎn firmly remonstrated, and only then did the Emperor stop.
When he heard about the matter of the crimson memorial (chìzhāng),
he became extremely angry.
The imperial envoys sent to rebuke Yuē were numerous,
and Yuē died of fear.
The relevant officials proposed the posthumous title Wén,
but the Emperor said:
"Harboring feelings that are not fully expressed is called Yǐn."
Therefore, it was changed to Yǐn.
His written works include the Jìn Shū (Book of Jìn) in 110 volumes,
the Sòng Shū (Book of Sòng) in 100 volumes,
the Qí Jì (Annals of Qí) in 20 volumes,
the Gāozǔ Jì (Annals of Gāozǔ) in 14 volumes,
the Ěr Yán (Recent Sayings) in 10 volumes,
the Shì Lì (Examples of Posthumous Titles) in 10 volumes,
the Sòng Wénzhāng Zhì (Treatise on Literature in Sòng) in 30 volumes,
and a literary collection (wénjí) of 100 volumes: all circulated throughout the world.
Furthermore, he compiled the Sī Shēng Pǔ (Manual of the Four Tones),
believing that poets of the past,
for thousands of years, had not been awakened (to this realization),
and that he alone had grasped the essence (xiōngjīn),
exhausting its subtle principles.
He called it a work that "entered the spirit" (rùshén zhī zuò),
but Gāozǔ was fundamentally displeased with it.
The Emperor asked Zhōu Shě:
"What are the Four Tones?"
Shě replied:
"'The Son of Heaven is wise and brilliant' (Tiānzǐ Shèngzhé)
are examples."
Nevertheless, the Emperor ultimately did not follow or use it.
His son, Xuán,
had already served as Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng) by the time of Yuē,
Grand Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
Attendant Officer of the Minister of Works (Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
and Chief Clerk of the Right for the Minister of Works (Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ).
After completing mourning for Yuē,
he served as Palace Assistant to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Pú).
He again left office due to mourning for his mother,
surviving only on vegetables and abstaining from grain (bìgǔ).
When the mourning period ended,
he still abstained from polished and coarse grains (jīngliáng).
He served as Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng) and Chief Clerk of the Central Pacification Army (Zhōng Fǔjūn Chángshǐ).
He was sent out to serve as General Who Beckons Afar (Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Nánkāng (Nánkāng Nèishǐ).
While in the commandery, he was praised for his pure administration.
He died in office,
with the posthumous title Gōng Hóu.
His son, Shí, succeeded him.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, said: In the past, when the Virtue of Wood (Mù Dé, referring to the Sòng Dynasty) was about to decline,
the incompetent successor indulged in cruelty and oppression.
The fearful common people (qiánlí),
their lives hung in the balance, like the passing shadows on a sundial or water in a clepsydra.
Gāozǔ righteously rescued the collapsing state,
aiming to pacify the Chinese realm (qūxià).
Planning and deliberation in the military tent (wéiwò),
truly relied upon [figures like] Liáng and Píng (i.e., Zhāng Liáng and Chén Píng).
As for Fàn Yún and Shěn Yuē,
they participated in the founding and establishment [of the new dynasty],
assisting in the completion of the imperial enterprise.
Furthermore, Yún was quick-witted, perceptive, and knowledgeable,
his practical assistance benefiting the era.
Yuē had great talent and broad knowledge,
his fame second only to Qiān and Dǒng (i.e., Sīmǎ Qiān and Dǒng Zhòngshū).
Both belonged to the era of rising fortune,
truly they were heroic figures of their generation.
Collected Biographies 8: Jiāng Yān, Rèn Fǎng
Jiāng Yān, courtesy name Wéntōng,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng Commandery.
When young, he was orphaned, poor, and fond of learning.
He was quiet, reserved, and had few social contacts.
He began his career as an Attendant Officer (Cóngshì) in Nánxú Prefecture,
and was later transferred to the position of Fèng Cháoqǐng.
Jǐngsù, the Prince of Jiànpíng during the Sòng Dynasty, was fond of talented men.
Yān followed Jǐngsù to Nányǎn Prefecture.
Guō Yànwén, the Magistrate of Guǎnglíng, incurred a crime,
and the charges implicated Yān.
He was detained in the prefectural prison.
While in prison, Yān submitted a memorial, stating:
"In the past,
a humble minister (Jiànchén) beat his heart, and falling frost struck the land of Yān;
an ordinary woman appealed to Heaven,
and a violent wind swept over the terrace of Qí.
This humble official (Xiàguān) has never
failed
to put down the scroll and weep when reading their accounts.
Why?
Because scholars possess established views,
and women possess unwavering conduct.
When sincerity is met with suspicion,
and loyalty leads to execution,
I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), heard that benevolence
cannot be relied upon,
and goodness cannot be depended on.
I initially thought these were mere words,
but now I know the truth.
I humbly pray that Your
Majesty (Dàwáng) will briefly dismiss those around you
and grant me a measure of pity and consideration.
I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), was originally a person of thatched dwellings and humble doors,
a scholar (shì) of plain clothes and leather belts.
In retirement, I did not embellish poetry and books to startle the ignorant;
when advancing, I did not purchase fame among the world.
Recently,
I was wrongly permitted to ascend and descend the Chéngmíng Gate-Tower
and enter and exit the Jīnhuá Palace Hall.
When was it that I did not constrain my shadow in solemn reverence
and keep my body humbly within the restricted palace quarters?
I secretly admired Your
Majesty's (Dàwáng) righteousness,
serving as a guest beneath your gate.
I was counted among the insignificant practitioners of minor skills,
participating in the lowest ranks of petty talents.
Your Majesty (Dàwáng) favored me with grace and glory,
and looked upon me with kind regard.
I truly felt I received the gift of gold bestowed upon Jīng Qīng,
and secretly felt the devotion of a man of integrity (guóshì) like Yù Ràng.
I always desired to tie up my official sash and fall upon my sword
to repay even a ten-thousandth part,
splitting my heart and wearing down my heels
in order to repay
the One Whom Heaven Bestows.
I did not anticipate that I, a small person (xiǎorén), being stubborn and vulgar,
would incur slander and fault,
causing my tracks to fall short of the illustrious standard (Zhāoxiàn),
and my body to be confined to a dark prison (yōuyǔ).
Walking among shadows, my heart grieves;
my nose aches and my bones hurt.
I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), heard that
losing one's reputation is humiliation,
and losing one's body (injury/death) is second to that.
Therefore, whenever this thought arises,
I suddenly feel as if something has been lost.
Moreover, having passed through months,
now nearing the end of autumn (Jìqiū),
the light of the sky is heavy and overcast,
and the surroundings
are without color.
I am not made of wood or stone,
yet I am confined with jailers.
This is why Shào Qīng (Sīmǎ Qiān) looked up to heaven and beat his chest,
weeping until his tears ran out and were followed by blood.
I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān),
although lacking local renown,
have nevertheless heard of the conduct of the virtuous gentleman (jūnzǐ).
The highest among them hide themselves among markets,
or lie beneath rocky cliffs;
next, they tie their official seals
in the courtyard of Jīnmǎ,
or offer lofty counsel atop Yúntái;
next, they capture the ruler of Nányuè,
or bind the neck of the Chányú: all are recorded in the red documents,
and depicted together in the green histories.
How could
they fight over the minutiae of an inch or a foot,
or compete for the profits of a knife or an awl!
However, I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), have heard that accumulated slander can dissolve metal,
and accumulated calumny can grind down bones.
In antiquity, Zhí Shēng was suspected of stealing gold;
more recently, Bó Yú received a reputation for unrighteousness.
Those two talented men,
still met such fates;
how much more so for me, the subordinate official (Xiàguān)?
How can I escape?
Formerly, the disgrace of a supreme general (shàngjiàng) saw
the Marquis of Jiàng (Jiàng Hóu)
imprisoned;
the shame of a famous minister (míngchén) saw
Shǐ Qiān (Sīmǎ Qiān) confined to the lower chambers (prison).
Compared to them, what further words can I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), offer?
The wisdom of Lǔ Lián (Lǔ Zhònglián)
caused him to refuse emoluments and not look back;
the worthiness of Jiē Yú
led him to wander singing and forget to return home.
Zǐ Líng (Yán Zǐlíng) closed himself off in Dōngyuè,
and Zhòng Wèi (Jiǎng Wěi) shut his gate in Xī Qín.
This, too, is understandable.
If the matter concerning me, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), were not baseless,
and the guilt were truly mine,
I should clamp my mouth shut and swallow my tongue,
and fall upon a dagger to perish.
How could I face the men of exceptional integrity from Qí and Lǔ,
or the tragic singing gentlemen of Yān and Zhào?
Currently, the Holy Reign (Shènglì) is revered and enlightened;
the world is content in its occupations;
auspicious clouds float over Luò (Luòyáng),
and glorious light fills the Hé (Yellow River).
Westward extending to Líntáo and Dí Dào,
and north to Fēihú and Yáng
Yuán,
all are immersed in benevolence and bathed in righteousness,
shining brightly and drinking sweet wine.
Yet I, the subordinate official (Xiàguān), harbor sorrow within the prison gate (huánmén),
holding resentment at the jail door.
For such a trivial creature,
this is truly regrettable.
I look up
and pray that Your Majesty (Dàwáng) will briefly grant clarity,
then the soul of Wú Qiū
will not be shamed when sinking his head (in submission);
and the spirit of Hú Tíng
will harbor no regrets when his bones turn to ash.
Unable to bear the intensity of my feelings,
I respectfully rely on this official (zhíshì) to present this.
If this heart is understood,
I will not perish even in death. Jǐng Sù
read the letter and released him (from prison) that same day.
Soon after, he was nominated as an outstanding talent (xiùcái) from Nán Xúzhōu,
excelled in the policy examination,
and was transferred to the post of Left Attendant (Zuǒ Chángshì) for the Kingdom of Bālíng.
When Jǐng Sù became Governor of Jīngzhōu,
Yān followed him to that post.
When the Young Emperor (Shàodì) ascended the throne,
he displayed many faults in virtue.
Jǐng Sù monopolized the upper reaches of the Yangtze,
and everyone urged him to seize this opportunity to launch an affair.
Yān repeatedly offered calm remonstrance, saying:
"Spreading rumors brought disaster,
which is why the Two Shū (Èr Shū) perished together;
staking everything and holding grievances,
led to the collective downfall of the Seven States (Qī Guó).
If Your Highness (Diànxià) does not seek the security of the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
but instead trusts the schemes of those around you,
then we shall once again see deer and elk dwelling amid the frost and dew upon the Terrace of Gū Sū."
Jǐng Sù did not heed his advice.
When Jǐng Sù garrisoned Jīngkǒu,
Yān again served as the Military Advisor (Cānjūnshì) to the General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn),
concurrently holding the position of Assistant Prefect (Jùnchéng) of Nán Dōnghǎi Commandery.
Jǐng Sù consulted with his confidantes day and night,
and Yān, knowing that the plot was about to be launched,
presented him with fifteen poems as a veiled critique.
It happened that Lù Chéng, the Administrator of Nán Dōnghǎi, was mourning his parent's death (dīng jiān),
Yān believed himself, as the Commandery Assistant (jùn chéng), should manage the commandery affairs,
but Jǐngsù employed the Commandant (Sīmǎ), Liǔ Shìlóng.
Yān firmly requested the position,
Jǐngsù became greatly angered,
and spoke to the selection office,
demoting him to be the Magistrate (lìng) of Wúxīng in Jiàn'ān.
Yān remained in the county for three years.
In the beginning of Shēngmíng,
Qí Dì assisted in governance,
heard of his talent,
and summoned him to be the Director (Láng) of the Carriage Bureau (Jià Bù) under the Secretariat (Shàngshū) and Staff Officer (Cānjūnshì) to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì).
Soon after, Shěn Yōuzhī, the Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Jīngzhōu, rebelled.
Gāo Dì said to Yān:
“The world is in such great turmoil.
What is your opinion, Sir?”
Yān replied, saying:
“In the past, Xiàng Yǔ was strong while Liú Bāng was weak;
Yuán Shào had many followers while Cáo Cāo had few.
Yǔ issued commands to the feudal lords,
but ultimately suffered the humiliation of a single sword.
Shào spanned four provinces,
but finally became a captive fleeing north.
This is what is meant by ‘Authority lies in virtue (dé), not in the ritual tripod (dǐng).’
Why does Your Grace have doubts?”
The Emperor said:
“Many have expressed this sentiment,
but try to offer an analysis.”
Yān said:
“Your Grace is valiant, martial, and possesses extraordinary strategies—
this is the first victory;
You are magnanimous, benevolent, and forgiving—
this is the second victory;
the worthy and capable devote their full strength—
this is the third victory;
the people's hopes converge upon you—
this is the fourth victory;
You uphold the Son of Heaven and attack the rebels—
this is the fifth victory.
As for the other side, his ambition is sharp but his capacity is small—
this is the first defeat;
he possesses might but lacks kindness—
this is the second defeat;
his officers and soldiers are demoralized—
this is the third defeat;
the gentry feel no loyalty toward him—
this is the fourth defeat;
he hangs his army thousands of *lǐ* away,
without allies of like malice to assist him—
this is the fifth defeat.
Therefore, although he commands a hundred thousand jackals and wolves,
he will ultimately be captured by us.”
The Emperor smiled and said:
“Your discussion is excessive, Sir.”
At this time, all military letters, memorials, and declarations,
were drafted entirely by Yān.
When he was established as the Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
he was appointed as Staff Officer for Records (Jìshì Cānjūnshì).
In the beginning of Jiànyuán,
he was again made the Secretary (Jìshì) to the Prince of Yùzhāng, the General of Agile Cavalry,
concurrently holding the post of Magistrate of Dōngwǔ,
participating in managing imperial edicts and pronouncements,
and concurrently presiding over the National History.
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Assistant Secretary (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
In the beginning of Yǒngmíng,
he was promoted to General of Gallant Cavalry (Xiāojì Jiāngjūn),
and maintained custody of the National History.
He was sent out to serve as General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Inner Clerk (Nèishǐ) of Lúlíng.
He held this post for three years,
and returned as General of Gallant Cavalry,
concurrently Assistant Director of the Left (Zuǒ Chéng) under the Secretariat.
Soon after, he again used his original post to concurrently lead the Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì).
In the beginning of the reign of Shào Dì (the Young Emperor),
he concurrently held the position of Palace Affairs Monitor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng) using his original post.
At that time, Míng Dì was serving as Chancellor (Xiàng),
and thereupon said to Yān:
“When you were previously in the Secretariat,
you did not act improperly unless it was official business;
in office, you were able to strike a balance between leniency and severity.
Now, serving as the Southern Controller (Nán Sī),
you are capable of striking awe and maintaining discipline among all officials.”
Yān replied, saying:
“The matter today
can be described as proceeding appropriately for the office,
but I fear that my talent is inferior and my will is weak,
and that I will be unable to live up to Your clear instructions.”

Thereupon, he impeached Xiè Fěi, the Director of the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng), Wáng Huì, the Chief Clerk of the Left (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) under the Minister of the Multitudes (Sītú), and Yǔ Hóngyuǎn, the Chief Clerk to the Protector-General (Hùjūn Zhǎngshǐ),
all for long-term illness preventing them from participating in the public affairs regarding the imperial tomb;
he also memorialized against Liú Quān, the former Inspector of Yìzhōu, and Yīn Zhìbó, the former Inspector of Liángzhōu,
both of whom had amassed millions in illicit goods (zāng huò),
and immediately had them arrested and handed over to the Commandant of Justice (Tíngwèi) for punishment.
Shěn Zhāolüè, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Línghǎi, Yǔ Tánlóng, the Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
and the officials holding salaries of two thousand *dàn* (èr qiān shí) in various commanderies, as well as the chief officials of the major counties,
were mostly impeached and investigated,
creating internal and external discipline.
Míng Dì said to Yān:
“Since the era of Sòng,
there has not been a stern and brilliant Palace Affairs Monitor again.
Today, Sir, you may be described as unique in recent times.”
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
Yān became the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Línghǎi, the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Jūqí).
Soon after, he was appointed Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng),
and granted Attendant in the Palace (Jǐshì Zhōng).
He was promoted to Chief Clerk to the General Who Protects the Army (Guànjūn Zhǎngshǐ),
and granted General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
He was sent out to be the Administrator of Xuānchéng,
retaining the General title as before.
He remained in the commandery for four years,
and returned as Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng), concurrently leading the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
Soon after, he became Director of the Palace Library (Bìshū Jiān).
During the Yǒngyuán period,
Cuī Huìjǐng raised an army and besieged the capital city.
All high officials (yī guān) submitted their name cards (míng cì),
but Yān claimed illness and did not go.
When the incident was settled,
people admired his foresight.
At the end of Dōng Hūn,
Yān, as Director of the Palace Library, concurrently held the post of Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
He firmly declined but could not be excused,
and thus personally carried out the duties.
He said to others:
“This is not my proper responsibility,
as passersby know.
They are merely taking advantage of my empty reputation.
Furthermore, the time decreed by Heaven and the affairs of men
will soon undergo reversal.
Confucius said: ‘One who handles civil affairs (wén shì) must also possess military readiness (wǔ bèi).’
I shall plan according to the situation,
what cause is there for worry?”
Shortly thereafter,
he also served as Deputy to Wáng Yíng, the General Protector (Lǐng Jūn).
When the righteous army (yì shī) reached Xīnlín,
Yān fled to them in plain clothes.
Gāo Zǔ appointed him General Who Protects the Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn),
retaining his post as Director of the Palace Library,
and soon concurrently Chief Clerk of the Left under the Minister of the Multitudes.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng,
he was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
In the second year,
he was transferred to Chief Clerk of the Right (Yòu Zhǎngshǐ) under the Chancellor,
retaining the title of General Who Protects the Army as before.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he became Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn),
and was enfeoffed as the Founding Count (Kāiguó Bó) of Línjǔ County,
receiving an income of four hundred households.
Yān then said to his sons and younger brothers:
“I originally pursued a simple official career,
and did not seek wealth and high status.
That I have now humbly attained these things,
has led me even to this point.
What I have always spoken of regarding knowing when to stop and be content (zhǐ zú zhī shì),
is now sufficiently accomplished.
A person’s life is merely about pursuing pleasure.
When must one wait for wealth and nobility?
Since my merit and fame are already established,
I simply wish to retire myself to the wilderness.”
In that same year,
due to illness, he was promoted to Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple (Jīn Zǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
and his enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Lǐlíng (Lǐlíng Hóu).
In the fourth year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-two.
Gāo Zǔ wore plain clothes and held mourning rites for him.
He was granted thirty thousand coins,
and fifty bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title (shì) was Xiàn Bó.
Yān was famous for his literary compositions in his youth,
but his talent and intellect slightly diminished in his later years.
People at the time all said his talent was exhausted.
In total, he authored more than one hundred essays and books,
and compiled them himself into Anterior and Posterior Collections (qiánhòu jí),
as well as the Ten Treatises (Shí Zhì) of the History of Qí (Qí Shǐ),
all of which circulated throughout the world.
His son Wěi succeeded to the title,
serving successively as Assistant to the Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng) and Magistrate of Chángchéng.
Having committed a crime, he was stripped of his rank.
In the fourth year of Pǔtōng,
Gāo Zǔ remembered Yān’s achievements,
and restored Wěi's enfeoffment as Count of Wúchāng (Wúchāng Bó),
with the same number of households as before.
was a man from Lè'ān Bóchāng.
He was a descendant of the Hàn Grandee Secretary Ōu.
His father, Yáo,
was a Zhōngsàn Dàfū of Qí.
Yáo's wife, Péi-shì,
once slept during the day.
She dreamt there was a canopy of colorful banners with bells hanging from its four corners,
falling from the sky.
One of the bells fell into Péi's bosom.
Her heart pounded.
Shortly thereafter, she became pregnant
and gave birth to Fǎng.
He was seven *chǐ* and five *cùn* tall.
As a child, he loved studying,
and became famous early.
Liú Bǐng, the Dānyáng Yǐn of Sòng, appointed him as Chief Clerk.
At the time, Fǎng was sixteen,
and offended Bǐng's son with his temperament.
After a long while,
he served as Fèng Cháoqǐng,
was recommended as a Xiùcái from Yǎnzhōu,
and was appointed Tài Cháng Bóshì.
He was promoted to Aide to the Generalissimo Who Conquers the North.
In the beginning of the Yǒngmíng era,
Wáng Jiǎn, General of the Guards, served concurrently as Governor of Dānyáng,
and again engaged Fǎng as Chief Clerk.
Jiǎn greatly admired and valued Fǎng,
believing him to be peerless in his time.
Fǎng was promoted to Aide to the Minister of Works concerning Penal Affairs,
then entered court service as Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng,
and transferred to Records Officer for the Prince of Jìnglíng, the Minister of Works.
He resigned due to mourning for his father.
His nature was extremely filial;
he observed the mourning rites perfectly.
When the mourning period ended,
he subsequently suffered mourning for his mother.
He often lived in a hut beside the tomb,
and in the spots where he wept,
the grass would not grow.
When mourning was completed,
he was appointed Commandant of Infantry for the Heir Apparent, managing the documents of the Eastern Palace.
Previously,
after Qí Míngdì had deposed the Prince of Yùlín,

he initially held the titles of Attendant Official, Director of the Central Secretariat, General-in-Chief of Cavalry, establishing a subordinate government equal in status to the Three Dukes, Inspector of Yángzhōu, and Director of the Affairs of the Masters of Writing.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Xuānchéng Commandery,
and granted an additional five thousand troops.
He ordered Fǎng to draft the formal memorial.
The text said:
"Your subject was originally a man of mediocre talent,
whose intellect and strength are shallow and weak.
Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gāo, showed sincere love as if I were his nephew,
and bestowed kindness as if I were a relative;
Revered Progenitor, Emperor Wǔ, treated me as an equal commoner,
placing deep trust in me as a brother.
When Emperor Wǔ was gravely ill,
I truly received his verbal imperial decree.
Although the wisdom to see oneself clearly
is often obscured by mediocrity and shortsightedness,
this ignorant man reached a point
where he chanced to know his own limitations.
I truly could not bear to persist in maintaining my position during the time of the hanging robes,
or to disobey while beside the jade armrest,
and thus bore the burden of the trust and commission,
announcing the last commands.
Although the successor ruler abandoned the norm,
and offended the virtue that should be proclaimed,
that the royal house met misfortune
is the responsibility of your subject.
Why?
In terms of closeness, I was like Dōngmóu,
and in terms of responsibility, I was like Bólù.
I merely harbored the ambition of Zǐmèng to stabilize the state,
but failed to avert the censure aimed at the officials who contested Chāngyì.
The judgment of the four seas—
how can I escape this blame?
The earth on the imperial tomb is not yet dry,
and the instructions and oaths still ring in my ears.
That the affairs of the family and state
have come to this point—
if it is not the fault of your subject,
upon whom does the blame rest?
How shall I solemnly pay my respects at the lofty shrine
and devoutly serve the Wǔ Mausoleum?
