My heart is grieved that I failed the plan,
weeping tears of blood as I await the morning.
How can I be allowed to seek honor amid the family's disgrace,
and enjoy peace and comfort while the state is in peril?
The primary merit of the Grand General of Cavalry,
the towering example for the Divine Land—
the Secretariat is called the regulator of affairs,
and the Central Secretariat truly manages the sovereign's words.
Moreover, merely bestowing empty honors
and entrusting the defense against insult—
your subject knows this is unsatisfactory,
and who among the people would deem it appropriate?
However, my life is lighter than a swan's feather,
but my responsibility is heavier than mountains.
Whether living or dead, the outcome will be the same;
calumny and praise are unified throughout.
Resigning one office will not reduce the burden on myself,
and adding one post already defiles the principles of the court.
I ought immediately to align myself with the concerns of the state,
and not merely make a show of refusal.
As for merits equal to Yīkuāng,
rewards equal to a thousand households,
being gloriously settled in the inner domain,
and suddenly possessing the entire state—
I regard perishing and falling as my goal,
and dare not accept the command.
I also wish that Your Majesty would graciously retain and consider my request,
and immediately deign to hear and grant it.
If the sincere earnestness of Jùpíng must be upheld,
and the loyal sincerity of Yǒngchāng is allowed to be expressed,
then I shall know that the Way of Sovereign and Subject
still possesses great latitude.
If it is said that this is easy to manifest,
I dare to maintain that it is hard to renounce."
The Emperor disliked the frankness of the language
and was greatly displeased.
Consequently, throughout the Jiànwǔ era, Fǎng's
position never surpassed that of a Colonel.
Fǎng was skilled in literary composition,
especially proficient at drafting documents.
His talent and creativity were inexhaustible.
The memorials and petitions of the contemporary princes and dukes
were all requested from him.
Fǎng would draft the text instantly,
without needing revisions or deletions.
Shěn Yuē, the master poet of his generation,
highly praised and admired him.
When Emperor Míng died,
Fǎng was promoted to Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán era,
he became Chief Clerk of the Right for the Minister of Works.
When Gāozǔ conquered the capital,
and his administrative headquarters were first established,
he appointed Fǎng as Records Officer to the General of Cavalry.
Originally, Gāozǔ had met Fǎng at the Western Residence of the Prince of Jìnglíng.
Leisurely, he said to Fǎng:
"When I attain the rank of the Three Ducal Offices,
I shall make you my Records Officer."
Fǎng jokingly replied to Gāozǔ:
"If I reach the rank of the Three Ducal Offices,
I shall make you my Cavalryman."
This was because Gāozǔ was good at riding.
When this time arrived,
he engaged Fǎng, fulfilling his old promise.
Fǎng presented a memorial, saying:
"I humbly learn that on a propitious day this month,
Your Excellency solemnly received the charge and mandate.
Your virtue is manifest and Your achievements lofty,
gloriously matching the hopes of the four seas.
All living beings
have a place to find protection;
how much more so for Fǎng, who has received instruction from Your Lordship,
for nearly twenty years.
Your coughs and spittle became kindnesses,
Your glances became adornments.
This humble person cherishes Your favor,
and looks back knowing where he should die.
Previously, during a clean gathering,
there were related remarks,
the intention to lift and guide me
was expressed in pleasant jest.
How could I know that I was so fortunate
that this word would remain unchanged?
Although my feelings erred regarding Your foresight,
my track fell into the lure of pride.
The bath and cleansing water are prepared, but there is no need for condolence;
the great mansion is built, and we share joy.
Your Excellency’s Way surpasses Heaven and Earth,
and Your achievements transcend deep antiquity.
Though You will cause Yī and Zhōu to hold the reins,
and Huán and Wén to assist the chariot axle,
Your divine merit is boundless,
and how can the transformation of the world be described?
The administration of the headquarters is newly established,
and talented worthies raise their heads.
Only this fish eye
rudely intrudes among the precious jade.
Looking at myself and observing my limits,
I truly know I am a disgrace and a speck of dust.
Such an encounter happens but once in a thousand years;
this second creation is difficult to repay.
Even if I should die in service,
I still know it would not be sufficient repayment."
When the Liáng administrative structure was established,
many of the documents and proclamations concerning the abdication
were prepared by Fǎng.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Fǎng was appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gates,
promoted to Director of the Bureau of Personnel,
and soon managed the works of the court while holding his original post.
he was sent out to serve as the Administrator of Yìxīng.
While holding the post, he was clean and incorruptible;
his children and concubines ate only wheat.
His friend Dào Gài of Péngchéng,
and Gài’s younger brother, Qià,
often journeyed to the mountains and marshes with Fǎng.
When he was replaced and boarded the vessel,
he possessed only five *hú* of rice.
When he arrived, he was without suitable clothes,
so the General Who Guards the Army, Shěn Yuē, sent him robes and shirts to welcome him.
He was reappointed as Attendant Gentleman of the Ministry of Personnel,
participating in the management of major selections,
but he did not prove worthy of the post.
Soon after, he was transferred to Imperial Censor-in-Chief,
Director of the Imperial Library,
and concurrently held the title of General of the Vanguard.
Since the Yǒngyuán era of Qí,
the Four Divisions in the Imperial Archive
were chaotic with numerous scrolls and chapters.
Fǎng personally collated and proofread them by hand,
and consequently, the catalog was established.
In the spring of the sixth year,
he was sent out as General Who Pacifies the North and Administrator of Xīn'ān.
While in the commandery, he disregarded formality.
Carelessly dragging his staff,
he walked alone through the towns and suburbs.
Citizens who presented lawsuits or petitions
had them decided right there on the road.
His governance was clear and simple,
and the officials and common people found it convenient.
After overseeing affairs for a full year,
he died in his official residence,
at the age of forty-nine.
The entire territory grieved and lamented,
and the common people together erected a memorial hall south of the city.
When Gāozǔ heard the news,
he observed mourning rituals that very day,
weeping uncontrollably for him.
He was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
and given the posthumous name Jìngzǐ.
Fǎng was fond of forming friendships
and promoting scholarly friends.
Those who received his praise
were mostly promoted,
hence all gentry and noble travelers
vied to establish good relations with him,
and the guests at his table
numbered several dozen.
People of the time admired him
and called him Rèn Jūn,
implying that he was like the Three Gentlemen of the Hàn Dynasty.
Yīn Yún of Chénjùn wrote a letter to the Administrator of Jiàn'ān, Dào Gài, saying:
“The wise man has passed away,
the standard of virtue is forever gone.
Where shall the great oracle shell be placed?
Who shall be entrusted with the lodestar?”
This is how highly he was praised by his scholarly friends.
Fǎng did not manage his estate,
to the extent that he did not even possess a proper house.
People sometimes mocked him for frequently borrowing,
but he immediately distributed it to his relatives and friends.
Fǎng often sighed and said:
“Those who understand me judge me by Shūzé,
and those who do not understand me also judge me by Shūzé.”
Fǎng had read every book and document.
Although his family was poor,
he accumulated over ten thousand scrolls of books,
mostly rare editions.
After Fǎng died,
Gāozǔ ordered the scholar Hè Zòng, together with Shěn Yuē, to examine his book catalog,
and those that the court library lacked
were taken from Fǎng’s home.
Fǎng’s written works numbered several hundred thousand characters,
and were widely circulated in the world.
Initially,
when Fǎng established himself among the scholar-gentry,
he greatly helped and promoted others.
If someone treated him kindly, he amplified their reputation.
When he died,
all his sons were young,
but few people provided for or helped them.
Liú Xiàobiāo of Píngyuán wrote a discourse about this, saying: A guest asked the host:
“Is Zhū Gōngshū’s Treatise on Breaking Off Friendships
correct,
or is it wrong?”
The host said:
“Why do you ask this, sir?”
The guest replied:
“When grass insects chirp, the locusts leap.
When the sculpted tiger roars, the clear wind rises.
Thus, when vapors intertwine, they sense each other,
fog surges and clouds steam;
when calls echo, they summon each other,
stars stream and lightning flashes.
Therefore, when Wáng Yáng ascended, Gòng Gōng was happy,
and when Hǎn Shēng passed away, Guózǐ was sorrowful.
Furthermore, hearts are like the *qín* and *sè* zithers,
their words fragrant like orchid and iris;
principles adhere like glue and lacquer,
their ambitions are harmoniously
sweet like the *xūn* and *chí* instruments.
The sages and worthies used this to engrave on gold tablets and carve on basins and dishes,
to write on jade slips and carve on bells and tripods.
Should the master craftsman abandon the wondrous skill of ‘Achieving Wind,’
or Bó Yá
cease the elegant melody of ‘Flowing Waves,’
Fàn Shì and Zhāng Shào were affectionate at Xiàquán,
Yǐn Jí and Bān Gù were joyful throughout the long night.
Constantly flowing and crisscrossing,
scattering like smoke and falling like rain,
all these phenomena are unknown
to clever calculation,
and cannot be measured by mental planning.
Yet Zhū Yìzhōu disregarded,
transgressed moral teachings,
struck out fairness and sincerity,
and severed friendships,
viewing the common people like hawks and falcons,
comparing humanity
to jackals and tigers.
I have doubts about this,
and request that you clarify this confusion.”
The host listened attentively and said:
“What you speak of, sir, is plucking the strings for beautiful music,
yet you fail to understand how dryness and moisture alter the sound;
casting nets in low marshes,
yet failing to see the swans and wild geese flying high.
The sages
held the golden mirror,
expounding upon moral character and deeds.
Like dragons soaring or inchworms contracting,
they follow the rise and fall of the Way.
Sun and moon linked like jade discs,
extolling the earnest achievement;
clouds flying and lightning flashing,
manifesting the subtle meaning
of the Dì Huá.
Just like the variation of the Five Tones,
completing the wondrous melodies of the Nine Achievements.
This Mr. Zhū obtained the dark pearl from the Red River,
planning with spiritual wisdom in his words.
As for
weaving benevolence and righteousness,
polishing virtue and the Way,
rejoicing in their happiness,
and grieving over their decline—
bonding beneath the spiritual terrace,
leaving traces above the rivers and lakes;
though the wind and rain are severe,
their sounds do not cease,
and though frost and snow fall, their colors do not change.
This is the pure friendship of the worthy and eminent,
rarely encountered even across ten thousand ages.
Reaching this declining age, where people are deceitful,
cunning and deceitfulness rise like a whirlwind.
The deep ravines cannot surpass their danger,
and ghosts and spirits cannot exhaust their variations.
They compete for things as light as feathers,
and rush toward the tip of an awl or knife blade.
Thus, pure friendships ended,
and beneficial friendships
arose.
The world is turbulent and noisy,
startled like birds and frightened by thunder.
However, beneficial friendships share a common source,
but their streams diverge.
Comparing their summaries,
there are five methods:
“If one’s favor rivals Dǒng Xián or Shí Xiǎn,
and their power suppresses Liáng Jì or Dòu Xiàn.
They command all craftsmen,
refining and forging ten thousand things.
A spit or a cough raises clouds and rain,
a breath brings down frost and dew.
The Nine
Regions raise dust for them,
the Four Seas are overwhelmed by their dazzling power.
None fail to see their shadow and rush like stars,
relying on their reputation, they flock like ducks to a stream.
As soon as the court announcer proclaims dawn,
the canopies of high officials form shade,
the tall gates open in the morning,
carriages line up like flowing water.
All wish to sacrifice themselves completely,
tearing open their guts and drawing out their hearts,
making vows like Yāo Lí, who burned his wife and children,
swearing loyalty like Jīng Qīng, who suffered the extermination of seven clans.
This is called Power
connection,
this is the first category.
“Wealth rivaling Táo [Zhū] and Bái [Guǐ],
assets exceeding those of Chéng and Luó;
their mountains monopolize Tónglíng,
their homes harbor gold mines.
When they leave the flat lands, their carriages are linked;
when they reside in the village gates, bells chime.
Then
there are the guests from poor alleys,
scholars who live behind rope-hinged doors,
hoping for the last glimmer of the night torch,
seeking the smallest favor of the flourishing house.
They file in like fish, leaping,
gathering thick as scales.
They share the
rice and millet meant for geese and ducks,
and drink the remaining drops from the jade goblets.
They cherish this favor and encounter,
offering sincere gratitude,
grasping the green pine to show their steadfast hearts,
pointing to the white water to symbolize their trust.
This is called Bribery Connection (Huì Jiāo),
this
is the second category.
“Lù Dàfū enjoyed banquets in Xīdū;
Guō Yǒudào was the paradigm of humanity in Dōngguó.
Dukes and ministers valued their great reputations,
officials and gentry envied their ascent to immortality.
Furthermore, they pout their jaws and wrinkle their
noses,
with mucus and saliva flying.
They race like a yellow horse in vehement discussion,
unleashing the eloquence of a green rooster.
When they speak warmly, cold valleys become mild;
when they discuss with solemn severity, spring thickets drop their leaves.
The rise and fall (of fortunes) depend on their glance and gesture,
honor and disgrace are fixed by their single word.
Consequently, young noble heirs,
and sons of wealthy families in silk and fine clothes,
whose accomplishments are not yet recognized by the wise,
whose fame has not yet reached the Cloud
Pavilion,
climb onto their scale-wings,
begging for their superfluous opinions,
attaching themselves to the forelock of the *qíjì* steed,
soaring past the homing swan at Jiéshí.
This is called Discourse Connection (Tán Jiāo),
this is the third category.
“The sun offers ease, the shade brings sorrow—
this is the great condition of the living;
sorrow brings convergence, joy brings departure—
this is the nature of all things.
Thus, fish, when their spring dries up, spit bubbles to moisten each other,
and birds, when about to die, mournfully
cry.
Those sharing the same suffering pity one another,
composing the sad melodies of the riverbank;
fear placed in the breast
gives rise to the great ceremony of the *Gǔ Fēng* (Odes).
In this way, friendship stronger than metal arises from distress,
and throat-slitting friendship begins
under thatched coverings.
Therefore, Wǔ Yuán was cleansed and aided by Zǎi Pǐ;
Zhāng Wáng sheltered and protected Chén Xiàng.
This is called Desperate Connection (Qióng Jiāo),
this is the fourth category.
“In customs that rush headlong,
among people who are shallow and fickle,
none fail to grasp the scale and balance,
or hold the fine floss.
The scale is used to measure their weight,
and the floss is used to test their breath (life/influence).
If the scale cannot be lifted (they are worthless),
or the floss cannot be moved (they have no breath of influence),
even if Yán and Rǎn are like dragon quills and phoenix chicks,
or Zēng and Shǐ are fragrant as orchids and white as snow,
or Shū and Xiàng are like gold, jade, abysses, and seas,
or Qīng and Yún possess ceremonial robes as vast as the River
of Heaven (the Milky Way),
they are regarded as drifting dust,
treated like clay clods.
No one is willing to spend half a bean on them,
and rarely does a single hair fall for them.
If the scale weighs even a trifle,
and the floss barely
drifts,
even if they possess the wickedness of Gòng Gōng,
the concealment of righteousness of Huān Dōu,
the arrogance of Nán Jīng,
or are the great villains of Dōng Líng,
everyone will crawl and fawn,
breaking branches and licking hemorrhoids.
Gold balm and kingfisher feathers are used to curry their favor,
while flattery and obsequiousness lead them to sincerity.
Therefore, where the covered carriages travel,
it is certainly not the house of Yí or Huì;
where gifts and presents enter,
it truly goes to the house of Zhāng
or Huò.
They plan before acting,
making few mistakes, even by a hair's breadth.
This is called Measurement Connection (Liàng Jiāo),
this is the fifth category.
“All these five connections,
their principle is the same as trading and selling.
Therefore, Huán Tán compared them to the marketplace,
and Lín Huí likened them to sweet wine.
Now, cold and heat alternate,
and prosperity
and decline follow one another.
Some flourish early and wither later,
some begin wealthy and end poor,
some initially survive and finally perish,
some were meager in the past and are magnificent today.
The cycle rotates and inverts,
swift as
waves and ripples.
In this, the desire for gain never changes,
but the way of transformation cannot remain constant.
Viewing it thus,
the reasons why Zhāng and Chén ended disastrously,
and why Xiāo and Zhū
fell out at the end,
can be decisively known.
Yet Zhái Gōng still meticulously inscribed his gate to warn off guests—
how late was his realization?
“However, from these five connections,
three harms arise: destroying virtue and annihilating righteousness,
making men like beasts—
this is the first harm;
hard to solidify, easy to sever,
gathering feuds and lawsuits—
this is the
second harm;
reputation trapped in gluttony and greed,
shamed by the pure and principled—
this is the third harm.
The ancients knew that the three harms caused obstruction,
and feared that the five connections would quickly lead to blame.
Therefore, Wáng Dān chastised his son
with the *jiǎchǔ* rod,
and Zhū Mù spoke openly to show his severance.
How profound!
“In recent times there was Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān,
a talent within the seas,
who early grasped the silver and yellow seals (held high office),
and quickly attracted public fame.
His strong writings and beautiful prose
rivaled Cáo and Wáng;
his exceptional
talent and distinction
matched Xǔ and Guō.
He resembled Tián Wén in loving guests,
and was the same as Zhèng Zhuāng in appreciating worthies.
Seeing a single virtue, he would stare and grip his wrist;
encountering a single talent, he would raise
his eyebrows and clap his hands.
The yellow (disapproval) came from his lips,
and red and purple (high official rank) were determined by his monthly appraisals.
Consequently, officials and nobles converged like spokes,
clothes gathered like clouds,
carriages collided at the axles,
and the seated guests
were full.
Treading his threshold
was like ascending the hall of Quèlǐ;
entering his inner chambers
was said to be climbing the slope of Lóngmén.
As for his glances, they doubled their value;
his grooming made
them roar loudly.
Those wearing ribbons at Yúntái rubbed shoulders,
and those rushing about the Dānchí (vermilion steps) crowded their footsteps.
All established favor and familiarity,
forming deep bonds,
hoping for the pure legacy of Huì and Zhuāng,
and aspiring
to the noble deeds of Yáng and Zuǒ.
When he closed his eyes in Dōng Yuè,
and his remains returned to Luòpǔ,
the coarse mourning curtain was still hanging,
but few gentlemen came to sprinkle wine at his gate;
the grave had no old grass yet,
but the fields were devoid of turning wheels
of guests.
His pitiful several orphans,
not planning for the morrow,
were scattered south of the great sea,
entrusting their lives to lands of miasma and pestilence.
Among the heroes who previously grasped his arm,
those of golden-orchid (friendship)
Friendship,
never possessing the benevolence of Yángshé (Yángshé) who wept upon descending,
preferring instead to admire the virtue of Hòu Chéng (Hòu Chéng) who divided his home.
Alas!
The path of the world is dangerous and precipitous,
having come to this!
Tàiháng (Tàiháng) and Mèngmén (Mèngmén),
how can they even be called rugged and precipitous?
Therefore, resolute and upright gentlemen,
angered by such a state of affairs,
tear their robes to wrap their feet,
abandoning it to flee far away.
Standing alone atop high mountains,
happy to be
amongst elk and deer,
brightly separating themselves from the hazy filth,
truly ashamed of it,
truly fearful of it. 」
Yú Fǎng (Yǔ Fǎng) compiled 247 volumes of miscellaneous biographies,
252 volumes of geographical records,
and 33 volumes of essays.
Yú Fǎng’s (Yǔ Fǎng’s) fourth son Dōnglǐ (Dōnglǐ),
largely inherited his father’s style,
and his official post reached Shàngshū Wàibīng Láng (Shàngshū Wàibīng Láng).
Yáo Chá (Yáo Chá), Minister (Shàngshū) of Personnel (Lìbù) of the Chén (Chén) dynasty, said: Observing that the two Hàn (Hàn) dynasties sought the worthy
by leading with classical scholarship;
in recent generations, the selection of men
is mostly achieved through literature and history.
The works of these two men,
possessing magnificent rhetoric,
truly match their time.
Zhōu Yān (Zhōu Yān) was capable and reserved,
Yú Fǎng (Yǔ Fǎng) maintained his moral character,
both concluded their lives with high reputation and status;
this is proper.
Had Jiāng (Jiāng) not been perceptive,
or Rèn (Rèn) lacked old favor,
then attaining high rank and conspicuous honors
would not have been possible for them either.
Collected Biographies Number Nine: Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) (His nephew Lǎn [Lǎn]).
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi), courtesy name Jìngchōng (Jìngchōng),
was a native of Yángxià (Yángxià) in Chén Jùn (Chén Jùn).
His grandfather, Xiè Hóngwēi (Xiè Hóngwēi),
was Tàicháng Qīng (Tàicháng Qīng) of Sòng (Sòng);
his father, Xiè Zhuāng (Xiè Zhuāng),
was Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū).
Both were famous in previous generations.
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) was intelligent in his youth;
Xiè Zhuāng (Xiè Zhuāng) valued him highly
and always kept him at his side.
At the age of ten,
he was able to write compositions.
Xiè Zhuāng (Xiè Zhuāng) visited Tǔ Shān (Tǔ Shān) and composed a poem,
instructing Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) to title the piece;
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) immediately grabbed the brush and completed it.
Wáng Jǐngwén (Wáng Jǐngwén) of Lángxié (Lángxié) said to Xiè Zhuāng (Xiè Zhuāng):
"Your talented son can truly be called a Divine Prodigy (Shéntóng),
and will furthermore achieve singular eminence later."
Xiè Zhuāng (Xiè Zhuāng) laughed,
and consequently patted Xiè Fěi’s (Xiè Fěi’s) back, saying:
"He is truly the 'thousand pieces of gold' of my family."
Emperor Xiàowǔ (Xiàowǔ Dì) traveled to Gūshú (Gūshú),
commanding Xiè Zhuāng (Xiè Zhuāng) to bring Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) with the imperial carriage.
An edict ordered him to compose a Eulogy for the Cave Well (Dòngjǐng Zàn),
which he presented from his seat.
The Emperor said:
"Although small,
he is a marvelous child."
He began his official career as Acting Staff Officer of the Judicial Section under the General Pacifying the Army (Fǔjūn Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn),
was promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
but resigned his post due to mourning his father.
When the mourning period concluded,
he resumed the post of Shèrén (Shèrén),
successively served as Director of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
and Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) under General-in-Chief (Wèijiāngjūn) Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn).
Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn) was naturally aloof and severe,
rarely receiving visitors.
People of the time compared him to Lǐ Yīng (Lǐ Yīng).
After Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) withdrew from his audience,
Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn) said:
"Xiè Ān (Xiè Lìng) is not dead."
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
He was sent out to serve as Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Línchuān (Línchuān);
he was impeached for bribery.
Since the case passed through Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn),
Yuán Càn (Yuán Càn) suppressed it.
When Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì) of Qí (Qí) became General of Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) assisting in governance,
he selected Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) as his Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ).

He commanded Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi), along with Chǔ Xuàn (Chǔ Xuàn) of Hénán (Hénán), Jiāng Xiào (Jiāng Xiào) of Jìyáng (Jìyáng), and Liú Yǔ (Liú Yǔ) of Péngchéng (Péngchéng), to attend upon the Sòng (Sòng) Emperor.
At the time, they were referred to as the Four Friends of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ Sì Yǒu).
Subsequently, he was appointed Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and managed the imperial edicts and documents for the two departments, Zhōngshū (Zhōngshū) and Sǎnqí (Sǎnqí).
When Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì) advanced to Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi),
he again appointed Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ),
concurrently holding the title of Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nán Dōnghǎi (Nán Dōnghǎi).
Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì) was then planning the transfer of the throne,
and sought ministers to assist in establishing the new mandate.
Because Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) possessed great renown,
he deeply admired and relied upon him.
Discussing the historical events of Wèi (Wèi) and Jìn (Jìn),
he then said:
"The signs for the Jìn (Jìn) revolution had long been evident.
Shí Bāo (Shí Bāo) failed to advise Jìn Wén (Jìn Wén) early,
and only wept bitterly upon his death.
Compared to Féng Yì (Féng Yì),
he did not recognize the opportune moment."
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) replied:
"In the past, there was a minister of Wèi (Wèi) who urged Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) of Wèi (Wèi) to take the imperial throne.
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) of Wèi (Wèi) said: 'If anyone were to make use of me,
I would rather be like King Wén (Wén Wáng) of Zhōu (Zhōu)!'
Jìn Wén (Jìn Wén) served the Wèi (Wèi) clan for generations
and was certain to die facing north [as a subject];
even if Wèi (Wèi) had followed the examples of Táng (Táng) and Yú (Yú) earlier,
he still ought to have refused three times to elevate his status."
The Emperor was displeased.
He subsequently appointed Wáng Jiǎn (Wáng Jiǎn) as Chief Clerk of the Left (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ),
while appointing Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) as Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng),
concurrently leading the Palace Library (Mìshū Jiān).
When Qí (Qí) accepted the imperial abdication,
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) was on duty that day.
All the officials attended the ceremony.
The Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng) was required to hand over the imperial seal,
but Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) pretended ignorance,
saying:
"What public matter is this?"
The conveyor of the edict said:
"The seal is to be handed over to the Prince of Qí (Qí Wáng)."
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) said:
"Qí (Qí) should naturally have its own Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng)."
He then pulled up a pillow and lay down.
The conveyor of the edict was frightened,
and instructed him to claim illness,
hoping to find a substitute.
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) said:
"I am not ill;
why should I claim it?"
Thereupon he put on his court robes,
walked out of the East Side Gate (Dōng Yèmén),
found his carriage,
and returned directly to his residence.
That day, Wáng Jiǎn (Wáng Jiǎn) was consequently appointed Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng) to hand over the seal.
Afterwards, Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ Dì) spoke to Emperor Gāo (Gāo Dì),
requesting that Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) be executed.
The Emperor said:
"If we kill him, he will merely achieve his desired fame;
we should simply tolerate him, excluding him from further consideration."
Consequently, he was dismissed and remained at home.
In the first year of Yǒngmíng (Yǒngmíng),
he was reappointed Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì (Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì).
He was successively promoted to Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng),
concurrently serving as Erudite of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Bóshì).
In the fifth year,
he went out to serve as General of the Vanquishing Army (Guànjūn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yìxīng (Yìxīng),
his emolument being augmented to that of Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí (Zhōng Èr Qiān Shí).
While in the commandery, he did not concern himself with miscellaneous affairs,
entrusting everything to his subordinates,
saying:
"I cannot function as an officer handling specific duties;
I can only function as the Administrator (Tàishǒu)."
After governing for three years,
he was summoned to serve as Minister of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū) and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
In the first year of Lóngchāng (Lóngchāng),
he was again appointed Shìzhōng (Shìzhōng),
concurrently serving as Tutor (Shī) to the Prince of Xīn'ān (Xīn'ān Wáng).
Before being inaugurated,
he strenuously requested an outside appointment.
Consequently, he became General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wúxīng (Wúxīng).
Upon receiving the summons, he immediately took up his post.
At that time, Emperor Míng (Míng Dì) was planning to succeed to the throne,
and all the veteran court ministers were invited to participate in the planning and strategy.
Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) internally sought contentment,
and was truly attempting to avoid political involvement.
His younger brother, Xiè Lǎn (Xiè Lǎn),
was serving as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) at that time.
When Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) arrived at the commandery,
he sent several *hú* (hú) of wine to Xiè Lǎn (Xiè Lǎn),
and included a letter saying:
"You must drink this heartily,
and do not involve yourself in political affairs."
While serving in the commandery, Xiè Fěi (Xiè Fěi) never governed diligently,
but constantly focused on accumulation and hoarding.
The populace somewhat criticized him for this,
but he did not mind.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
an imperial edict summoned him to be Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
but he immediately submitted a memorial resisting the summons.
He sent his sons back to the capital (Jīngshī),
remaining alone with his mother,
building a residence in the western suburbs of the commandery.
Míngdì (明帝) issued an edict saying:
"Those who transcend worldly honors,
their noble spirit keeping them distant;
walking the path of recluses,
their brilliance is rarely encountered.
Thus, the man who offered a long bow to the Chancellor of Chǔ (Chǔ Xiàng),
was praised in the Southern State (Nánguó);
and the man who loftily declined service under the Hàn (Hàn chén),
earned fame from esteemed historians.
Fěi (朏), newly appointed Shìzhōng (侍中) and Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
long possessed ceremonial dignity,
and early demonstrated purity and refinement.
He established achievements when serving at court,
and gained renown when governing outside.
He subsequently withdrew his footsteps from the broad avenues,
shook his robes among the woods and pools,
cherishing the lingering fragrance of Jī (箕) and Yǐng (潁),
willing to endure emaciation without distress.
Considering these matters and cherishing the man,
we hold him in respectful regard.
It is fitting to grant him exceptional courtesy,
in order to commend his simple integrity.
He shall be granted a bed, curtains, mattresses, and mats,
his stipend shall be that of a Minister,
and it shall be regularly delivered to his place of residence."
At that time, Hé Yìn (何胤) of Lújiāng (廬江), who was Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒), also submitted a memorial to return to Kuàijī (會稽).
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (永元),
an edict summoned Fěi (朏) to be Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監);
Yìn (胤) was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿).
Both refused to yield.
In the third year,
an edict again summoned Fěi (朏) to be Shìzhōng (侍中) and Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅);
Yìn (胤) was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍) and Tàizǐ Zhānshì (太子詹事).
At that time, Dōng Hūn (東昏) sent mandates to their residences,
forcing them to depart,
but it happened that the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) was already approaching,
thus both were unable to reach the capital.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) pacified the capital region,
he advanced to the position of Chancellor (Xiàngguó).
He memorialized, requesting Fěi (朏) and Yìn (胤), saying:
"When impoverished, one perfects oneself alone;
when successful, one benefits the world as well.
Although the principles of serving or retiring,
are not the same in their measure,
accepting or rejecting service depends on the timing,
and the wise and virtuous abide by this.
The former newly appointed Shìzhōng (侍中) and Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅), Fěi (朏),
and the former newly appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Tàizǐ Zhānshì (太子詹事), and Dūtíng Hóu (都亭侯), Yìn (胤),
are scions of noble families who uphold standards,
their excellent conduct ranks them above others,
their moral achievements and virtuous reputation
bring peace and benefit to both the cultured and the common.
Previously, when residing among the ranks of the court,
they fundamentally lacked ambition for office.
Their association with guests was select,
and high officials rarely participated.
Even before their official insignia were removed,
they had already shaken off the dust of the world.
Moreover, in literature and classical scholarship,
they mutually hold preeminence;
in pure principle and refined judgment,
they both excel.
Both possess profound insight and clear understanding,
having foreseen the beginning of disorder,
observing the mediocre nature [of the rulers] as it was from the start,
knowing that the inheritance could not be entrusted to them.
Shaking off their robes at Dōngshān (東山),
they definitively abandoned the tracks of the mundane world.
Although they resigned their seals during a time of prosperity,
in reality, they were escaping an age of darkness.
Their families deserved sumptuous meals,
yet they willingly ate acorns and wild plants;
their lineages inherited high office,
yet they were content with tattered garments.
Since the frivolous trends first spread,
it became customary in the South,
but pure currents and simple conduct
still retain some residual influence.
Who stimulated the greedy [to relinquish their desires]?
The merit belongs to those who possess the Way.
To bring peace to customs and stir up the people,
the court and the countryside must be unified in purpose.
Although they reside among the rivers and seas,
their merits are equivalent to those established at the palace gate (Wèiquè).
Now that the great fortune has just opened,
poverty is deemed shameful;
how much more so for those who have long contained the talents of sacrificial vessels,
and temporarily withdrew from the Chéngmíng [Palace]?
How can they be allowed to fulfill their aspirations on the seashore,
forever emulating Sōngzǐ (松子)?
I bear an exceptionally heavy responsibility,
participating in and assisting with all affairs of state.
I truly rely on a multitude of talents
to jointly form the foundational pillars.
I wish to draw from pure sources,
and take still water as a mirror.
I foolishly wish to ask them to condescend to hold the top official positions,
seeking their counsel morning and evening,
hoping thereby to assist and proclaim my limited ability,
and model the Royal Way (wáng dù).
I request that both be appointed to my administrative staff as Jūn Zī Jìjiǔ (軍諮祭酒),
and that Fěi (朏) be additionally granted Hòu Jiāngjūn (後將軍)."
Neither arrived.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he summoned Fěi (朏) to be Shìzhōng (侍中), Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (左光祿大夫),
and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (開府儀同三司);
Yìn (胤) was summoned to be Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍), Tèjìn (特進), and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū (右光祿大夫).
Again, both refused to yield.
Subsequently, he sent Wáng Guǒ (王果), the Lǐngjūn Sīmǎ (領軍司馬), to proclaim the imperial intent and earnestly persuade them.
In the sixth month of the following year,
Fěi (朏) departed in a light boat,
traveling to the palace to personally present his case.
When he arrived,
an edict appointed him Shìzhōng (侍中), Sītú (司徒), and Shàngshū Lìng (尚書令).
Fěi (朏) declined to perform the formal prostration and audience, citing a foot ailment.
Instead, wearing a cornered turban and carried in a sedan chair,
he proceeded to Yúnlóng Mén (雲龍門) to express his gratitude.
An edict granted him an audience at Huálín Yuán (華林園),
where he rode a small carriage to his seat.
The next morning,
the Emperor's carriage proceeded to Fěi's (朏) residence,
where they feasted and conversed merrily.
Fěi (朏) firmly stated his original aspiration,
but it was not granted.
He then requested permission to return east himself to fetch his mother,
and this was granted.
Just before his departure,
the imperial carriage again paid a visit,
and poems were composed to bid him farewell.
Imperial envoys sending him off and welcoming him back
were visible to each other along the road.
When he arrived back at the capital (Jīngshī),
an order commanded carpenters to construct his administrative residence (fǔ) at his former dwelling.
Gāozǔ (高祖) presided from the imperial hall,
and sent an Usher (yè zhě) to confer the official seal upon him in the residence.
An edict ordered the suspension of all routine official business and the semi-monthly court audiences for him.
During the Grand Assembly of the third year,
an edict allowed Fěi (朏) to ride a small sedan chair up the steps to the palace hall.
In that same year,
he encountered the mourning period for his mother.
Soon after, there was an edict restoring him to his position in an acting capacity, as before.
Five years later,
his appointment was changed to Zhōngshū Jiān (中書監), Sītú (司徒), and Wèi Jiāngjūn (衞將軍),
but he firmly declined them all.
An Usher was sent to earnestly confer the posts upon him,
whereupon he finally performed the obeisance and accepted.
That winter he died in his residence,
at the age of sixty-six.
The Emperor's carriage went out to preside over the lamentations,
and an edict granted imperial funerary objects (Dōngyuán Mìqì),
one set of court robes (cháo fú),
one suit of clothes,
100 bolts of cloth,
and 100 catties of wax.
He was posthumously given Shìzhōng (侍中) and Sītú (司徒).
His posthumous name was Jìngxiào (靖孝).
The books and writings authored by Fěi (朏)
are all circulated throughout the world.
His son, Xuān (諼),
rose to the office of Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ (司徒右長史),
but was dismissed from office for killing an ox,
and died at home.
His second son, Zuǎn (篹),
had considerable literary talent,
and served up to the post of Jìn'ān Tàishǒu (晉安太守),
and died in office.
Lǎn (覽), courtesy name Jǐngdí (景滌),
was the son of Fěi's (朏) younger brother, Qiú (𦵩).
Lǎn (覽) was selected to marry the Qí (齊) Princess of Qiántáng (錢唐公主).
He was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (駙馬都尉), Bìshū Láng (祕書郎), and Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) was Dà Sīmǎ (大司馬),
Lǎn (覽) was summoned to be appointed Dōnggé Jìjiǔ (東閤祭酒),
and then transferred to the post of Xiàngguó Hùcáo (相國戶曹).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he became Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
managing the affairs of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù),
and shortly thereafter he assumed the proper post.
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) was handsome and elegant in demeanor,
skilled in rhetoric.
Gāozǔ (高祖) deeply valued him.
He once attended a sitting,
and was ordered to compose and exchange poems with Grandee Remonstrant Wáng Jiǎn (王暕).
His writing was very skillful.
Gāozǔ (高祖) praised it,
and then made him compose again,
which again matched the emperor's intent.
Then a poem was bestowed, saying:
"Shuāng Wén (雙文) is indeed a junior,
while the two youths are truly renowned families;
Is it merely that their pillars are strong,
nay, they are truly the nation's glory."
He left his post due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Middle Palace Secretary.
He also managed the affairs of the Secretariat Bureau Director,
and soon was appointed Secretariat Bureau Director,
then promoted to Grandee Remonstrant.
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) was quite fond of wine,
and during a banquet, he and Regular Cavalry Grandee Remonstrant Xiāo Chēn (蕭琛) exchanged insults,
which was reported by the authorities.
Gāozǔ (高祖) considered Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) to be young and not entirely at fault,
so he was sent out as Chief Clerk of the Central Headquarters.
After a while,
he was ordered to manage the Eastern Palace's records,
and promoted to General Mingwēi (明威) and Administrator of Xīn'ān (新安).
In the summer of the ninth year,
the mountain bandit Wú Chéngbó (吳承伯) captured Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery.
The remaining bandits scattered into Xīn'ān (新安),
and rebellious officials such as Bāo (鮑) joined them,
attacking and seizing Yī (黟) and Shè (歙) counties.
They advanced their troops to attack Xiè Lǎn (謝覽).
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) sent the Commandery Assistant Zhōu Xīngsì (周興嗣) to build a stockade at Jǐnshā (錦沙) to resist the attack.
They were defeated,
and consequently abandoned the commandery and fled to Kuàijī (會稽).
After the imperial army pacified the mountain bandits,
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) returned to the commandery.
He was demoted to Consultative Adjutant to the Minister of Works, Chief Clerk of Rénwēi (仁威), Acting Administrator of Nánxú (南徐) Prefecture,
and Minister of Five Military Bureaus.
Soon after, he was promoted to Minister of Personnel.
From Xiè Lǎn's (謝覽) grandfather to his grandson,
three generations served in the selection department,
which was considered an honor at the time.
In the spring of the twelfth year,
he was sent out as Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).
The Palace Secretary Huáng Mùzhī (黃睦之) resided in Wūchéng (烏程),
and his sons and younger brothers were domineering.
Former administrators all humbled themselves to serve them.
Before Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) arrived at the commandery,
Mùzhī's (睦之) sons and younger brothers came to greet him.
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) drove their boats away,
and beat the officials who had allowed their passage.
From then on, Mùzhī's (睦之) family kept their doors shut,
not daring to have any public or private contact.
The commandery was rife with robbers,
causing trouble for the eastern route.
As soon as Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) took office, it became peaceful,
and the whole region was quiet.
Originally,
Emperor Míng of Qí (齊明帝), Xiè Lǎn's (謝覽) father Xiè Yǔ (謝𦵩), and Xú Xiàosì (徐孝嗣) of Dōnghǎi (東海),
all served as Administrators of Wúxīng (吳興),
and were known as famous administrators.
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) wished to surpass them all!
Previously, Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) had accumulated much wealth in Xīn'ān (新安),
but now he was known for his integrity.
People at the time compared him to Wáng Huáizǔ (王懷祖).
He died in office,
at the age of thirty-seven.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title of Central Palace Secretary.
His son, Xiè Hǎn (謝罕),
died young.
Minister of Personnel Chén Yáochá (姚察) said: Xiè Fěi (謝朏) in the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
was he perhaps a loyal and righteous person?
During the Jiànwǔ (建武) era of Qí (齊),
he shook off his official robes and was content to retire.
During the troubled Yuǒngyuán (永元) period,
he steadfastly maintained his own virtue.
He was like the likes of Shū (疏) and Jiǎng (蔣).
When Gāozǔ (高祖) rose to power,
seeking out talented individuals from all sides,
he came to serve in a plain cap,
and was the first to ascend to the highest offices.
He reached the pinnacle of both official service and retirement.
Xiè Lǎn (謝覽) was ultimately able to govern well,
and gentlemen praised him.
Collation Notes
Biographies, Chapter 10: Wáng Liàng (王亮), Zhāng Jì (張稷), Wáng Yíng (王瑩)
Wáng Liàng (王亮), courtesy name Fèngshú (奉叔),
a native of Línyí (臨沂), Lángyá (琅邪),
was the sixth-generation descendant of Jìn (晉) Chancellor Wáng Dǎo (王導).
His grandfather, Wáng Yǎn (王偃),
was Grand Master of Guanglu of the Right and Grandee with Special Precedence in the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
His father, Wáng Yōu (王攸), was Attendant-in-ordinary to the Palace Gate.
Wáng Liàng (王亮), being from a distinguished family,
was chosen to marry a princess at the end of the Sòng (宋) dynasty.
He was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-law and Secretary of the Imperial Library,
then successively promoted to Scholar of Prince Guìyáng (桂陽),
Friend of Prince Nánjùn (南郡),
and Assistant Secretary of the Imperial Library.
Prince Zǐliáng (子良) of Jìnglíng (竟陵) of Qí (齊) opened the Western Residence,
inviting talented and outstanding individuals to form the Forest of Scholars Hall,
and had artists paint their portraits;
Wáng Liàng (王亮) was also among them.
He was promoted to Palace Secretary and General of the Grand Marshal's Retainers,
and then sent out as Administrator of Héngyáng (衡陽).
Because the southern lands were low and damp,
he declined the office.
He was then promoted to Attendant-in-ordinary to the Palace Gate.
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator of Jìnlíng (晉陵),
where he governed with integrity and achieved good administration.
At that time, Emperor Míng of Qí (齊明帝) was serving as Chancellor;
hearing of this, he praised him,
and brought him in as Chief Clerk of the Garrison Commander,
and he was greatly appreciated and accepted.
Upon the Emperor's accession,
he was successively promoted to Middle Palace Secretary to the Crown Prince,
Minister of Personnel,
where his selection and ranking of officials were renowned.
He was then promoted to Grandee Remonstrant.
At the end of the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
he served as Minister of Personnel.
At that time, the Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat, Jiāng Shí (江祏), managed court affairs,
and promoted many,
to whom scholars rallied.
Wáng Liàng (王亮), finding himself in the selection department,
often held dissenting opinions.
Initially, before Wáng Liàng (王亮) became Minister of Personnel,
because Jiāng Shí (江祏) was the emperor's maternal relative,
he was deeply friendly with Jiāng Shí (江祏).
Jiāng Shí (江祏) praised him,
which further endeared him to the emperor;
but by this time, his relationship with Jiāng Shí (江祏) had become strained,
though Jiāng Shí (江祏) still treated him as before.
When Jiāng Shí (江祏) was executed,
petty individuals ran rampant,
and all appointments
were made through imperial favorites.
Wáng Liàng (王亮) was unable to stop it.
Outwardly, he appeared thorough and judicious,
but inwardly, he lacked clear discernment.
His selections
were merely based on seniority and sequence.
People at the time did not consider him capable.
He was repeatedly given the titles of Palace Attendant and Regular Cavalry Grandee, and Commandant of the Right Guard of the Crown Prince,
then served as Right Assistant Director of the Imperial Secretariat and Central Protector-General.
Thereafter, when Dōnghūn (東昏) indulged in tyranny,
and cruel punishments were rampant,
Wáng Liàng (王亮) swayed and accommodated to save himself,
and thus escaped execution.
When the righteous army reached Xīnlín (新林),
all officials inside and outside the city went to greet them.
Those who could not leave
also sent their sincere regards through intermediaries,
but Wáng Liàng (王亮) alone did not send anyone.
When the city was pacified,
only Wáng Liàng (王亮) was pushed forward as the leader.
Wáng Liàng (王亮) came out to see Gāozǔ (高祖),
and Gāozǔ (高祖) said:
"If one falls and is not helped,
what use is such a chancellor?"
Yet, he did not punish him.
When the Duke's Headquarters was established,
he was made Chief Clerk to the Grand Marshal, General Fǔjūn (撫軍), and Administrator of the two commanderies of Lángyá (琅邪) and Qīnghé (清河).
When the Liáng (梁) dynasty was founded,
he was appointed Grandee Remonstrant and Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
He firmly declined the appointment,
so he became Grandee Remonstrant and Supervising Secretary,
concurrently holding the post of Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) accepted the abdication,
he was promoted to Grandee Remonstrant, Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and Central Army General,
and was invited to participate in the founding of the dynasty.
He was enfeoffed as Duke of Yùníng (豫寧) County,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he was transferred to Grand Master of Guanglu of the Left,
with Grandee Remonstrant and Central Army General remaining as before.
On New Year's Day, when all nations paid respects at court,
Wáng Liàng (王亮) claimed illness and did not ascend the hall.
He had a meal set in a separate chamber,
and laughed and chatted as usual.
A few days later,
an imperial edict ordered the high officials to inquire about his health.
Wáng Liàng (王亮) showed no signs of illness.
Censor-in-chief Yuè Ài (樂藹) impeached him for grave disrespect,
advocating for the death penalty in the marketplace.
An imperial edict stripped him of his titles and reduced him to a commoner.
In the fourth year, in the summer,
Gāozǔ held a banquet at the Huáguāng Diàn,
and said to his assembled ministers:
“I attend to governing until the afternoon,
and I desire to hear about successes and failures.
You gentlemen may be called talented men;
you should each fully present your proposals for implementation or rejection.”
Fàn Zhěn, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒchéng), rose and said:
“Sītú Xiè Fěi originally had an undeserved reputation,
yet Your Majesty promotes him like this;
whereas the former Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Wáng Liàng, possessed considerable administrative substance,
yet Your Majesty discards him like that.
This is what your foolish minister fails to understand.”
Gāozǔ’s expression changed, and he said:
“You may speak of other things.”
Fàn Zhěn was resolute and would not stop,
and Gāozǔ was displeased.
Rèn Fǎng, Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), consequently presented a memorial, saying: “Your minister hears that
when Xīfū criticized publicly, the Hàn dynasty applied proper laws;
when Bái Bāo submitted a memorial,
the Jìn dynasty thereby clarified punishments.
How much more so when one denigrates those above by flattering those below,
and slander and praise come straight from one’s mouth!
It is rumored that your minister Fàn Zhěn, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
upon returning from Jìn’ān,
told people, saying:
‘I did not visit other people,
only visited Wáng Liàng;
I did not present gifts to other people,
only presented gifts to Wáng
Liàng.’
I immediately had Fàn Zhěn arrested and brought to the court from the side of Wàn Xiū [a subordinate] to be interrogated and questioned,
and this matched the rumors.
Furthermore, on the tenth day of this month,
when Your Majesty personally saw off your minister Zhēn
Guó, the Inspector of Liángzhōu,
and the private banquet had concluded smoothly,
and all the ministers had already taken leave and retired,
Your Majesty decreed that your minister Āng, Attendant-in-ordinary (Shìzhōng), and ten others remain,
to be consulted about the way of governance.
Fàn Zhěn did not answer the questions posed,
but rather arbitrarily
stirred up controversy with his deliberations,
and proceeded to disparage and criticize Sītú Xiè Fěi,
while praising and elevating the commoner Wáng Liàng.
Your minister was present at that time, having been honored to remain,
standing shoulder-to-shoulder with others;
what my eyes and ears perceived
was somewhat
different from the rumors.
I humbly reflect that the King enjoyed a delightful outing,
personally ascending the imperial steps;
the meaning was profound in promoting capable men,
and the feeling was equal to the gathering dew.
When the drinking was over and the banquet concluded,
he stood straight by the screen,
recording matters
that happened before,
and recording words that followed,
expressing his concern for the morning court,
and deeply seeking to know the people’s suffering.
Yet Fàn Zhěn’s words were disrespectful,
he arbitrarily presented praise and criticism,
injuring the spirit of respectful solemnity,
and failing the expectation of
the proximity to the Emperor.
If there is no severe judgment,
the constitutional standards will collapse.
Fàn Zhěn is the main culprit.
Your minister respectfully submits this case: Your minister Fàn Zhěn, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
is a remnant of the gentry,
whose words and actions are contradictory and confused;
he boasts and jokes in the villages
and noisily disputes in public streets.
His distorted learning and flattering reputation
are unknown in later generations;
his trifling with words and wagging tongue
are only sufficient to cover up his faults.
Recently,
when the army of righteousness (referring to Gāozǔ's forces) was nearby,
Fàn Zhěn, suffering distress and difficulties,
did not even call upon his gate [in mourning],
but wore black sackcloth and hastily followed,
somewhat like those who foresaw the change,
and indeed served the Dragon Face (the Emperor).
But now, taking advantage of the remnants of factional strife,
he turns to being a spear and shield [for others].
A man who lacks [integrity]
commits this kind of treachery and crookedness.
Formerly,
when rewards for merit were presented at the victory banquet,
his achievement was minor but his reward was great;
he was sent out to govern a famous commandery,
and brought back to oversee administrative functions.
Baskets and boxes [of gifts] were not overlooked,
yet he falsely claimed his carriage axle was broken [due to poverty],
and that his skirt and gown were worn out,
inciting malicious suggestions about lack of provision,
which was permitted
to become an exception and a failure,
publicly humiliating the noble clans.
Having held a central constitutional position,
his impeachments have been silent and sparse.
He looks around and indulges himself,
lacking the deliberations of absolute fairness;
he hates the upright and reviles the honest,
engaging in private slanderous
talk.
He should be put in fetters,
to enforce strict compliance with the national law.
Your ministers have conferred,
and request that Fàn Zhěn be dismissed from his current official post based on the evident facts,
and that he be immediately ordered to be taken into custody outside and handed over to the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi) for legal
prosecution and punishment.
Regarding those who should be implicated and apprehended,
they are entrusted to the prison officials,
to be dealt with according to the law.
Fàn Zhěn’s rank requires a yellow document [for notification],
but your minister immediately presents a white document [for urgency].
The Emperor decreed, 'Heard and approved.'
The imperial sealed letter challenged Fàn Zhěn, saying
“Wáng Liàng was lacking in talent when young,
and was not recognized by his contemporaries.
He previously managed to sneak into the assembly of heroes,
but his interaction with them was slight.
In his later years, he fawned upon Jiāng Shí,
and served as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù).
Finally, he joined in allegiance with Méi Chóng’ér and Rú Fǎzhēn,
and consequently upheld misguided governance.
Every household suffered disaster,
their entire families were plunged into misery;
the four seas boiled over,
and the empire was swept away in devastation.
Whose fault was this?
He ate the emolument of a disordered ruler,
yet did not die in a period of orderly governance.
Wáng Liàng was firmly allied with the atrocious faction,
exerting influence and acting like a tyrant.
In silken robes and jade meals,
his rooms were full of female musicians.
When the situation became perilous and matters pressed upon them,
they devoured each other.
He erected a stone with a title inscribed,
and submitted a flimsy petition of apology.
We recognized his coming over with a white flag,
and spared him the fault of his past.
Wáng Liàng was treacherous and disloyal,
his corruption and bribery openly manifest—
what is there worthy of discussion,
that you arbitrarily speak of him?
Provide a full explanation of the situation.”
Of the ten points raised in the challenge,
Fàn Zhěn’s reply was merely rambling and evasive.
Wáng Liàng subsequently isolated himself, closing his doors and sweeping his dwelling,
and cut off contact with guests.
When he suffered the bereavement of his mother,
he fulfilled the mourning rites completely.
In the eighth year,
an edict summoned him to serve as Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat (Mìshū Jiān).
Soon after, he was appointed General in Attendance and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
A few days later, he was transferred to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
He died that year.
An edict posthumously granted him thirty thousand coins
and fifty bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title was Yángzǐ.
Zhāng Jì, courtesy name Gōngqiáo,
was a native of Wú Jùn.
His father, Yǒng,
was Right Grand Master of Glorious Happiness (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū) during the Sòng dynasty.
Zhāng Jì’s birth mother contracted a long-term illness.
When Zhāng Jì was only eleven,
he cared for her without removing his clothes at night,
and Yǒng considered this extraordinary.
When his mother died,
he became extremely emaciated, more so than others,
and could only rise with the aid of a cane.
He was naturally casual and straightforward,
brightly discerning and possessed of talent and strategy.
He, along with his cousins Chōng, Róng, and Juǎn, were all famous,
and people at the time referred to them, saying:
“Chōng, Róng, Juǎn, and Jì,
these are the Four Zhāngs.”
He began his career as an Assistant Gentleman of the Secretariat (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng)
but did not accept the appointment.
He frequently endured mourning for his parents,
living in a hut beside the grave for six years.
When the mourning period ended,
he served as Law Clerk and Acting Adjutant of the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn),
and was promoted to Adjutant of External Military Affairs (Wàibīng Cānjūn).
During the Yǒngmíng period of Qí,
he served as the Magistrate of Shàn County,
barely attending to official duties,
spending much time touring mountains and rivers.
When the bandit Táng Yǐn raised a rebellion,
Jì led the people of Lì County
and secured the county border.
He entered the court to become a Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (Attendant at the Crown Prince’s Gate),
Dà Sīmǎ Dōngcáo Yuàn (Secretary of the Eastern Division under the Grand Marshal),
Jiàn'ān Wáng Yǒu (Companion to the Prince of Jiàn'ān),
and Dà Sīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Aide-de-camp to the Grand Marshal).
Wǔlíng Wáng Wěi (Prince of Wǔlíng) was appointed Hùjūn (Protector of the Army),
and Jì was transferred to Hùjūn Sīmǎ (Registrar under the Protector of the Army).
Soon after, he became the Zhìzhōng (Chief Secretary) of his original province.
When Emperor Míng took charge of the province,
he remained as Biéjià (Assistant Administrator).
At that time, Wèi forces raided Shòuchūn.
Jì was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North) and Jūnzhǔ (Army Commander),
serving as the deputy to Shàngshū Púyè (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs) Shěn Wénjì, who was defending Yùzhōu.
The Wèi multitude claimed a million men,
and besieged the city for several days.
During the strategic planning and deployment,
Wénjì entrusted everything to Jì.
When the Wèi army withdrew,
he was promoted to Píngxī Sīmǎ (Registrar under the General Who Pacifies the West), Níngshuò Jiāngjūn, and Nánpíng Nèishǐ (Administrator of Nánpíng Commandery).
Wèi again raided Yōngzhōu.
An imperial edict appointed him, retaining his former title, Dūdū Jīng, Yōng Zhūjūn Shì (Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Jīng and Yōng Provinces).
At that time, the Governor of Yōngzhōu, Cáo Hǔ, crossed the river bank at Fánchéng,
and Jì was entrusted with managing the affairs of the province.
The Wèi army retreated.
Jì returned to Jīngzhōu
and was appointed Huángmén Shìláng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
and then again Sīmǎ (Registrar), and Tàishǒu (Administrator) of the two commanderies of Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng.
Since the name of the commandery violated a personal taboo,
Yǒngníng was changed to Chángníng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Sītú Sīmǎ (Registrar under the Minister of Works),
and granted the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State).
When the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Chén Xiǎndá, raised troops in rebellion,
Jì was appointed, retaining his general title, to defend Lìyáng and serve as Tàishǒu of Nánqiáo Commandery.
He was then promoted to Zhènnán Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk under the General Who Guards the South), Tàishǒu of Xúnyáng, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Xíng Jiāngzhōu Shì (Acting Governor of Jiāngzhōu).
Soon he was recalled (to the capital).

He was appointed Chíjíe (Bearer of Credentials), Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Běixúzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Běixú Province), and Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Běixú Province).
He went out and stationed himself at Báixià,
and was subsequently promoted to Dūdū Nányǎnzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Nányǎn Province), and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nányǎn Province).
Shortly after, he was advanced to Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in the five provinces of Běixú, Xú, Yǎn, Qīng, and Jì,
his general title remaining unchanged.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán period,
he was summoned to be Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant),
stationed to guard the palace city.
When the righteous army arrived,
Jiāng Yān, who concurrently held the title Wèiwèi (Palace Guard Commander), fled.
Jì concurrently held the title Wèiwèi,
assisting Wáng Yíng as Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs inside the city.
At that time, Dōnghūn (the Deposed Emperor) was tyrannical and cruel.
The righteous army had besieged the city for a long time,
and those inside the city wished for surrender but no one dared to make the first move.
Wáng Zhēnguó, the Governor of Běixú Province, approached Jì to plot the matter.
They then dispatched the Zhígé officer Zhāng Qí to assassinate Dōnghūn in Hándé Hall.
Jì summoned Shàngshū Yòupúyè (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs) Wáng Liàng and others to sit in a line below the west bell in front of the palace hall.
He addressed them, saying:
“In the past, when Jié possessed depraved virtue,
the Mandate (the tripod) shifted to Yīn;
when Shāng Zhòu was tyrannical and cruel,
the Mandate shifted to Zhōu.
Now the tyrant has cut himself off from Heaven,
and the four seas have already returned to the Sagely Lord.
This is truly the time for Wēizǐ to leave Yīn,
and the day for Xiàng Bó to return to Hàn.
Should you not strive to do so?”
Then he sent Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University) Fàn Yún, Shèrén (Gentleman-in-Attendance) Péi Chángmù, and others as envoys to Shítóuchéng (Stone City) to meet Gāozǔ (Emperor Gāo).
Gāozǔ appointed Jì as Shìzhōng and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard).
When Gāozǔ controlled all governmental affairs,
Jì was promoted to Dà Sīmǎ Zuǒ Sīmǎ (Left Registrar under the Grand Marshal).
When the court of Liáng was established,
he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant) and Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat).
When Gāozǔ received the abdication,
for his merit, he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jiāng'ān County (Jiāng'ān Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
He was also appointed Shìzhōng and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the National University),
concurrently holding the title Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn (General of the Valiant Cavalry).
He was promoted to Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (General Protector of the Army) and Yángzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng (Great Impartial Judge of Yáng Province),
but was dismissed due to an incident.
Soon after, he became Dùzhī Shàngshū (Director of the Ministry of Finance), Qián Jiāngjūn (General of the Vanguard), and Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ (Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard),
but was again dismissed due to official business.
Shortly, he was Cíbù Shàngshū (Director of the Ministry of Rites).
He was transferred to Sànqí Chángshì, Dūguān Shàngshū (Director of the Ministry of Census), and Yángzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng,
and retained his original rank while overseeing Lǐng Jūn Shì (Affairs of the Central Army Command).
Soon he was promoted to Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General Commanding the Central Army),
his titles of Impartial Judge and Marquis remaining as before.
At that time, Wèi forces raided Qīngzhōu.
An imperial edict granted him Jiǎjié (Temporary Credentials) and allowed him to manage the affairs of the province.
The Wèi army happened to withdraw,
and he was subsequently sent out to serve as Sànqí Chángshì, General, and Administrator of Wúxīng Commandery (Wúxīng Tàishǒu),
holding the salary rank of Zhōng Èrqiān Shí.
Upon taking office, he visited and comforted the elderly and established officials,
promoting their children and grandchildren,
and placing them in important positions.
His administration was praised for its leniency and forgiveness.
He was advanced in title to Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn (General of Cloud Cavalry),
and summoned to be Shàngshū Zuǒpúyè (Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs).
The Emperor’s carriage was about to proceed to Jì’s residence,
but due to the intense summer heat,
He stayed instead at the Vice Director’s office.
Traditionally, all provisions supplied for an imperial visit were reimbursed at the cost of the Imperial Kitchen meals.
However, the Emperor considered Jì to be poor and honest,
and personally issued an edict exempting him from payment.

He was sent out to serve as Shǐ Chíjíe (Envoy Bearing Credentials), Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Zhūjūn Shì (Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Qīng and Jì Provinces), Ānběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North), and Governor of Qīng and Jì Provinces.
When Wèi forces raided Qúshān,
an edict ordered Jì to temporarily halt at Liùlǐ,
and command all the armies.
Upon his return,
he was advanced in title to Zhènběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the North).
Originally, Yùzhōu bordered the frontier,
and the local people often engaged in trade with the Wèi people.
When Qúshān rebelled,
some (people of Yùzhōu) communicated with Wèi,
and they were already feeling uneasy;
moreover, Jì was lenient and lacked strict defenses,
and his subordinates often exploited and oppressed the people.
The provincial residents, led by Xú Dàojiǎo, among others, attacked the provincial capital by night,
and murdered Jì.
He was sixty-three years old at the time.
The responsible authorities proposed stripping him of his title and fiefdom.
Jì was upright and honest in nature,
and skillful in dealing with others.
Throughout his career, he accumulated no wealth.
His salary was all distributed among his relatives and old friends.
His household had no surplus assets.
When he first departed Wúxīng Commandery,
having been summoned as Vice Director (Púyè),
his route passed through Wú (Danyang/Jiankang area).
The local people who waited for Jì filled both the land and the waterways.
Jì traveled light, heading directly back to the capital (Jīngshī).
Few recognized him,
such was his simplicity and integrity.
Jì’s eldest daughter, Chǔ Yuàn,
married into the Kǒng family of Kuàijī.
She returned to her family lineage (due to having no sons).
When Jì was attacked,
his daughter shielded the weapon with her body,
dying before her father.
Jì’s son, Shèng,
has a separate biography.
Juǎn, courtesy name Lìngyuǎn,
was Jì’s older cousin.
In his youth, he was famous for his understanding of principle
and skilled in pure conversation (qīngyán).
He served up to the position of Dūguān Shàngshū (Director of the Ministry of Census).
He died at the beginning of the Tiānjiān era.
Wáng Yíng, courtesy name Fèngguāng,
was a native of Línyí in Lángyé.
His father, Mào,
was Guānglù Dàfū (Grand Master of Splendid Happiness) and the Marquis Xī of Nánxiāng (Nánxiāng Xī Hóu).
Yíng was selected to marry the Sòng Princess Línhuái,
appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi (Cavalry Commandant),
and subsequently Zhùzuò Zuǒláng (Assistant in the Bureau of History).
He was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén (Gentleman-in-Attendance to the Crown Prince),
Fǔjūn Gōngcáo (Merit Officer under the General Who Soothes the Army),
Sànqí Shìláng (Cavalry Attendant Gentleman),
and Sītú Zuǒxīshǔ (Subordinate Official of the Left/West under the Minister of Works).
When Emperor Gāo of Qí was Piàojí Jiāngjūn (General of Agile Cavalry),
he invited Yíng to be his Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Aide-de-camp).
After a while,
he was sent out to be the Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu),
replacing Xiè Chāozōng.
After Chāozōng left the commandery,
he became hostile toward Yíng.
Upon returning (to the capital),
he slandered Yíng to Mào.
Mào spoke of it to the imperial court,
accusing Yíng of failing in filial support.
Consequently, Yíng was dismissed and stripped of his position as Administrator.
After a long time,
he was appointed Qiánjūn Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Advisor for the General of the Vanguard),
Zhōngshū Shìláng (Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Central Secretariat),
and Dà Sīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Aide-de-camp to the Grand Marshal).
Before he could accept the appointment,
he entered mourning for his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he became Gěishì Huángménláng (Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Yellow Gate).
He was sent out to be Xuānchéng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xuānchéng),
and promoted to Piàojí Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk under the General of Agile Cavalry).
He returned to serve as Huángmén Shìláng, Sīmǎ, and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Secretary to the Crown Prince).
He was then promoted to Shìzhōng,
but resigned due to mourning for his father.
When the mourning period ended,
he again became Shìzhōng,
concurrently holding the title Shèshēng Xiàowèi (Colonel of the Archers).
He was also appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the Army) and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Dōngyáng).
While governing the commandery, he implemented beneficial policies,
and was promoted to Wúxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wúxīng).
As Emperor Míng was diligent and concerned about the affairs of the state,
and Yíng had served successfully in both commanderies,
having a reputation for competence in both,
he was greatly praised.
He returned to become Tàizǐ Zhānshì (Supervisor of the Crown Prince’s Household) and Zhōng Lǐngjūn (Commander of the Central Army).
At the beginning of Yǒngyuán (era),
government was controlled by petty officials,
Wáng Yǐng maintained his post but could not distinguish right from wrong.
As Yǐng’s cousin, Wáng Liàng, was already holding court office,
although he traditionally had a poor relationship with Yǐng,
at that time, he wished to invite Yǐng to serve alongside him.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè.
Before he formally accepted (the post),
it happened that the Hùjūn, Cuī Huìjǐng, brought the Prince of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Wáng) from Jīngkǒu to invade the capital.
Wáng Yǐng was granted the *jié* (credentials),
and led troops to resist Huìjǐng at Hútóu.
He was attacked by Huìjǐng during the night;
his troops scattered.
Wáng Yǐng jumped into the water,
boarded a small boat, and entered Lèyóu,
and thus managed to return to Táichéng.
When Huìjǐng was defeated,
he returned to residing at the Lǐngjūn Fǔ (office of the General Leading the Army).
When the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) arrived,
he was again granted the *jié*,
and served as Dūdū Gōngchéng Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of All Military Matters in the Palace City).
When Jiànkāng was pacified,
Emperor Gāozǔ became Xiàngguó (Chancellor),
and appointed Wáng Yǐng as Zuǒ Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Left),
with the added title of Guānchūn Jiāngjūn,
and was ordered to take the Imperial carriage (*fǎjià*) to welcome Emperor Hé Dì from Jiānglíng.
When the Emperor reached Nánzhōu,
he abdicated in a separate palace.
When Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Yǐng was promoted to Shìzhōng and Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as the Duke of Jiànchéng County (Jiànchéng Xiàn Gōng),
with a stipend of a thousand households.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
retaining his posts as Shìzhōng and Fǔjūn.
After a while,
he served as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and was again promoted to Sànqí Chángshì, Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
He held office for three years,
then was promoted to Shìzhōng and Guānglù Dàfū,
concurrently leading the Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn.
Shortly thereafter, he was promoted to Shàngshū Lìng and Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn,
retaining his post as Shìzhōng.
He was successively advanced in title to Zuǒ Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn,
and granted a set of drums and pipes (*gǔchuī*).
Wáng Yǐng was naturally pure and careful;
he was respectful and diligent in office.
Emperor Gāozǔ deeply valued him.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
retaining the posts of Dānyáng Yǐn and Shìzhōng.
When Wáng Yǐng was about to take office,
the seal maker cast his official seal.
It was cast six times, and the turtle (knob) was ruined six times.
When it was finally finished,
the neck (of the turtle) was hollow and incomplete.
It was patched up and used.
After holding the post for six days,
he died suddenly of illness.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of the Chén Dynasty, said: Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) stated,
“Yīn had three men of benevolence:
Wēizǐ departed from it;
Jīzǐ became its slave;
Bǐ Gān remonstrated and died.”
Wáng Liàng lived during a chaotic age,
and held visible power and position.
Regarding his choices of action,
how different was he from those three men of benevolence?
When he served the rising monarch,
and received lenient treatment,
he served as an aid to the new dynasty,
which must have caused him shame in his heart.
That he brought about his own ruin and failure
was not due to bad luck.
The *Yì* (Classic of Changes) states:
“To hold a position which is not yours to hold,
your person will surely be endangered.”
Liàng’s advances and retreats
lost sight of the basis (of his position).
A pity!
Zhāng Jì acted due to timely circumstance and change;
this was also his moment.
Wáng Yǐng’s official seal being ruined six times,
was this perhaps the displeasure of the spirits regarding overfullness?
Biography Eleven: Wáng Zhēnguó, Mǎ Xiānpǐn, Zhāng Qí
Wáng Zhēnguó, courtesy name Dézhòng,
was a native of Xiāng, Pèiguó Commandery.
His father, Wáng Guǎngzhī,
was a good general during the Qí Dynasty,
and his office reached Sànqí Chángshì and Chējì Jiāngjūn.
Zhēnguó began his career as Guānchūn Xíng Cānjūn,
and was successively promoted to Hǔbēn Zhōngláng Jiāng and Governor of Nánqiáo (Nánqiáo Tàishǒu).
His administration earned him a reputation for capability.
At that time, the commandery suffered from famine.
He then distributed grain and scattered his wealth
to save the poor and destitute.
Emperor Gāodì of Qí issued a personal decree, saying:
“You love the people and govern the state,
which greatly aligns with my wishes.”
At the beginning of Yǒngmíng (era),
he was promoted to Administrator of Guìyáng (Guìyáng Nèishǐ).
He campaigned against and arrested bandits,
and the region became thoroughly pacified.
When he retired from his post and returned to the capital,
his route passed through Jiāngzhōu.
The Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ), Liǔ Shìlóng, saw him off by the shore.
Seeing that Zhēnguó’s returning baggage was light and simple,
he sighed and said:
“This one truly deserves to be called a Worthy Governor (Liáng Èrqiānshí).”
Upon returning, he became Dàsīmǎ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
Emperor Wǔ Dì deeply recognized and appreciated him,
and often exclaimed with a sigh:
“Among the military descendants of the late generation,
those like Zhēnguó are few indeed.”
He was again sent out to serve as Administrator of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Nèishǐ).
He returned to the capital to become Yuèqí Xiàowèi,
Guānchūn Chángshǐ, and Governor of Zhōnglí (Zhōnglí Tàishǒu).
He was subsequently promoted to Governor (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies of Bādōng and Jiànpíng.
Returning, he became Yóují Jiāngjūn (General of Mobile Cavalry).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his father.
At the end of the Jiànwǔ (era),
when Wèi troops besieged Sīzhōu,
Emperor Míng Dì sent the Provincial Governor of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ), Péi Shūyè, to attack and capture Wōyáng,
in order to create a diversion.
Zhēnguó was reinstated as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn,
and led troops to assist.
When the large army of the Wèi general Yáng Dàyǎn suddenly arrived,
Shūyè became fearful,
abandoned his army, and fled.
Zhēnguó led his own troops as a rearguard,
and thus prevented a total rout.
In the first year of Yǒngtài (era),
when Wáng Jìngzé, the Governor of Huìjī (Huìjī Tàishǒu), rebelled,
Zhēnguó again led troops to resist him.
After Jìngzé was suppressed,
Zhēnguó was promoted to Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Provincial Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qīng and Jì Provinces,
retaining the rank of General.
When the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) rose up,
Dōnghūn summoned Zhēnguó and his troops back to the capital (Jīngshī).
They entered and encamped in Jiànkāng City.
When the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) arrived,
Dōnghūn ordered Zhēnguó to go out and garrison at Zhūquè Mén,
but he was defeated by Wáng Mào’s forces,
and consequently retreated back into the city.
He then secretly dispatched Xī Zuǎn to present a “bright mirror” (Míng Jìng) to Emperor Gāozǔ as an offering of loyalty.
Emperor Gāozǔ broke off a piece of gold (as a token) to reply to him.
At that time, everyone in the city wished to follow the righteous cause,
but no one dared to strike first.
The Shìzhōng and Wèiwèi (Guard Commander), Zhāng Jì, was Dūdū Zhòngjūn (Supervisor of All Forces).
Zhēnguó secretly allied with Zhāng Jì's confidant, Zhāng Qí, to urge Jì,
and Jì agreed.
On the morning of *bǐngyín* in the twelfth month,
Zhēnguó led Jì to the Wèiwèi Fǔ,
mustered troops, and entered through Yúnlóng Mén.
They immediately beheaded Dōnghūn in the inner palace hall,
and met Jì and Shàngshū Púyè Wáng Liàng, and others, below the Western Bell (Xī Zhōng).
They then ordered the Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretarial Court Gentleman), Péi Chángmù, and others, to present Dōnghūn’s head to Emperor Gāozǔ.
For this merit, he was granted the title Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn.
He declined the appointment and did not accept it.
He was also offered the post of Provincial Governor of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ),
but he firmly pleaded to remain in the capital (Jīngshī).
He was again bestowed gold and silk.
Zhēnguó firmly declined this, too.
An imperial decree replied:
“In the past, Tián Zǐtài firmly declined silk and grain.
Your profound sentiment for the state,
is truly commendable.”
Later, while attending an imperial banquet,
the Emperor asked:
“Is your Míng Jìng (Bright Mirror) still intact,
and where is the gold from the past?”
Zhēnguó replied:
“The gold is respectfully kept on my arm,
I dared not lose it.”
He was again appointed Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn,
with the added post of Jǐshì Zhōng.
He was promoted to Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn,
with the added post of Sànqí Chángshì.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān (era),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Shèyáng County (Shèyáng Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of a thousand households.
He was appointed Dūguān Shàngshū,
retaining his post as Chángshì.
In the fifth year,
Yuán Chéng (Prince Rènchéng of Wèi) invaded Zhōnglí.
Gāozǔ dispatched Zhēnguó,
and subsequently asked him for strategies to suppress the rebels.
Zhēnguó replied:
"Your servant is constantly concerned that the Wèi forces are too few,
and is not troubled by their multitude."
Gāozǔ admired his words,
and thereupon granted him the staff (jié),
and he joined the massed armies in the suppression campaign.
The Wèi army retreated,
and the forces returned to the capital.
