He was appointed external official as Envoy with Staff (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Liáng and Qín Provinces (Dūdū Liáng Qín Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nánqín and Liáng Provinces.
Coincidentally, Xiàhóu Dàoqiān, Chief Clerk of Liáng Province, surrendered the province to Wèi.
Zhēnguó traveled by foot through Wèixīng,
intending to launch a surprise attack against him,
but did not succeed,
so he remained there to garrison the area.
Since he had achieved no merit,
he repeatedly memorialized requesting to be relieved of duty,
but Gāozǔ did not permit it.
His enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Yíyáng County (Yíyáng Xiàn Hóu),
with the same number of households and territory as before.
He was recalled to serve as Supernumerary Palace Attendant (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì) and Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Yòu Wèishuài),
and was additionally given the post of General of the Rear (Hòujūn).
Shortly thereafter,
he again served as General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn).
In the ninth year,

he was appointed external official as Envoy with Staff (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Xiāng Province (Dūdū Xiāng Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of Trustworthy Valour (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Xiāng Province (Xiāng Zhōu Cìshǐ).
After administering the office for four years,
he was recalled to serve as General Protecting the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
and then promoted to Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì) and Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
In the fourteenth year,
he died.
An imperial edict granted him posthumously the title General of Chariots and Cavalry (Jūqí Jiāngjūn),
provided a set of drum and wind instruments (gǔchuī),
bestowed 100,000 cash for funeral expenses,
and 100 bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title was Wēi.
His son, Sēngdù, inherited his title.
Mǎ Xiānpǐn, courtesy name Língfù,
was a native of Méi in Fúfēng.
His father, Bólúan,
was Grand Marshal (Sīmǎ) to the General Championing the Army (Guànjūn) under Sòng.
Xiānpǐn was known in his youth for his decisiveness and courage.
When mourning his father,
he grieved and wasted away beyond the customary rites,
carrying earth to build the grave mound,
and personally planting pines and cypresses.
He began his career as Clerk (Zhǔbù) of Yǐng Province,
was promoted to Palace Attendant and Cavalier (Wǔqí Chángshì),
served as a minor general,
and followed Xiāo Miǎn, Prince Ānlù of Qí.
When Miǎn died,
he served Emperor Míng.
During the Yǒngyuán reign period,
when Xiāo Yáoguāng and Cuī Huìjǐng rebelled,
he accumulated battle merits,
and based on these achievements, reached the rank of General of the Vanguard (Qián Jiāngjūn).
He was appointed external official as General Who Soars Like a Dragon (Lóngxiáng Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nánrǔyīn and Qiáo Commanderies.
At the time, Shòuyáng had recently fallen,
and the Wèi general Wáng Sù invaded the border.
Xiānpǐn fought fiercely,
defeating larger forces with fewer men.
The Wèi people greatly feared him.
Again based on his merit, he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Yù Province (Yù Zhōu Cìshǐ).
When the Army of Righteousness (Yìshī) arose,
many regions responded.
Gāozǔ sent Yáo Zhòngbīn, a former friend of Xiānpǐn, to persuade him.
Xiānpǐn executed Zhòngbīn in the army camp as a public warning.
When the Army of Righteousness reached Xīnlín,
Xiānpǐn still held his forces west of the river,
daily raiding supply transports.
When the city of Jiànkāng fell,
Xiānpǐn cried out and wept for an entire night,
then disbanded his troops and surrendered.
Gāozǔ comforted him, saying:
"Shooting the hook and severing the sleeve—
the ancients did not bear grudges over this.
You should not feel estranged simply because you executed the messenger who was sent."
Xiānpǐn bowed and replied:
"A humble man is like a dog that has lost its master;
when a new master feeds it,
it immediately becomes useful again."
Gāozǔ laughed and praised him.
Shortly thereafter, Xiānpǐn’s mother died.
Gāozǔ, knowing his poverty,
provided very generous funeral supplies.
Xiānpǐn cried and wept,
saying to his younger brother Zhòngài:
"Having received the grace of the Great Creator,
I have not yet managed to repay it.
Now I am further burdened with extraordinary kindness;
I shall dedicate my whole heart and strength to serving him, together with you."
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (507 CE),
when the Royal Army launched a northern campaign,
Xiānpǐn, in every battle,
displayed courage surpassing the entire army.
Those who faced his assault
were invariably crushed and broken.
When discussing matters with the various generals,
he never once mentioned his own merits.
When people asked the reason,
Xiānpǐn said:
"For a true man to be recognized by his age,
he should advance without seeking fame,
and retreat without evading punishment.
This is my lifelong aspiration.
What merit is there to discuss!"
He was appointed General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Sòng'ān and Ānmán Commanderies,
and then promoted to Grand Administrator of Nányìyáng.
He repeatedly defeated the Mountain Man (Shānmán),
and the commandery borders became peaceful and quiet.
Based on his merits, he was enfeoffed as Earl of Qùkuàng County (Qùkuàng Xiàn Bó),
with four hundred households.
He was subsequently promoted to Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Sī Province (Dūdū Sī Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì) and Governor of Sī Province (Sī Zhōu Cìshǐ).
His rank of General Who Assists the State remained as before.
Shortly after, his title was advanced to General of Loyal Awe (Zhēn Wēi Jiāngjūn).
Bái Zàoshēng, a man from Yù Province of Wèi, killed its Governor, Sīmǎ Qìngzēng (Prince of Lángyé).
He declared himself General Who Pacifies the North (Píng Běi Jiāngjūn),
elevated his fellow villager Hú Xùn as Governor,
and subsequently surrendered Xuánhù.
Gāozǔ dispatched Xiānpǐn to go to their aid,
and also sent Generals of the Inner Enclosure (Zhí Hé Jiāngjūn) Wǔ Huìchāo and Mǎ Guǎng to lead troops as reinforcements.
Xiānpǐn advanced and encamped at Chǔwáng Chéng (King Chǔ’s City).
He sent his deputy general Qí Gǒu'ér with two thousand troops to assist in defending Xuánhù.
Yuán Yīng, Prince Zhōngshān of Wèi, led a force of 100,000 to attack Xuánhù.
Xiānpǐn sent Guǎng, Huìchāo, and others to guard the Three Passes (Sānguān).
In the twelfth month,
Yīng broke Xuánhù,
capturing Qí Gǒu'ér.
He then advanced to attack Mǎ Guǎng,
and again defeated Guǎng,
capturing him alive,
and sending him to Luòyáng.
Xiānpǐn was unable to rescue them.
Huìchāo and the others also successively retreated and scattered,
and the Wèi army consequently advanced and occupied the Three Passes.
Xiānpǐn was implicated and recalled,
serving as General of Cloud Cavalry (Yúnqí Jiāngjūn).
He was appointed external official as Grand Marshal (Sīmǎ) under the General of Benevolent Awe (Rén Wēi Jiāngjūn).
The head of the establishment, the Prince of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Wáng), changed his title to General of Cloud Command (Yúnhuī),
and Xiānpǐn again served as Grand Marshal,
additionally holding the title General Who Arouses Distant Peoples (Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
In the tenth year (511 CE),
the people of Qúshān killed Liú Zhé, the Grand Administrator of Lángyé,
and surrendered the city to Wèi.
An imperial edict granted Xiānpǐn the temporary staff (jié),
to lead a punitive expedition against them.
Lú Chǎng, Governor of Xú Province of Wèi, went to the aid [of Qúshān] with over 100,000 troops.
Xiānpǐn engaged him in battle,
repeatedly defeating him,
and Chǎng fled.
Xiānpǐn unleashed his troops to press the pursuit.
Only ten or twenty percent of the Wèi forces escaped,
and the captured weapons, provisions, oxen, horses, and equipment
were countless.
He returned to the capital with a victorious army,
was promoted to Commander of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zuǒ Wèishuài),
his rank was advanced to Marquis (Hóu),
and his households were increased by six hundred.
In the eleventh year (512 CE),

he was promoted to Envoy with Staff (Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yù, Běiyù, and Huò Three Provinces (Dū Yù Běiyù Huò Sān Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of Trustworthy Valour (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yù Province (Yù Zhōu Cìshǐ),
concurrently holding the position of Grand Administrator of Nánrǔyīn.
Originally,
Xiānpǐn’s childhood name was Xiānbì.
When he grew up,
finding the name
'Bì' (slave girl)
inappropriate,
he replaced the radical
'jade' (yù)
for the radical
'woman' (nǚ),
thereby forming the character
'Pǐn'
(it is said).
From the time he served as a general and governed provinces and commanderies,
he was able to share hardships and ease with his officers and troops.
He personally wore no more than plain cloth,
and his residence contained no curtains, canopies, or screens.
While traveling, his food and drink were the same as the lowest ranking servants and grooms.
When he was on the frontier,
he often went alone stealthily into enemy territory,
scouting out the critical locations of the fortifications, villages, and strategic points.
Therefore, he won many battles,
and the officers and troops were also willing to serve under him.
Gāozǔ greatly admired and relied upon him.
He spent four years in the province,
then died.
He was posthumously granted the title General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn).
His posthumous title was Gāng.
His son, Yánfū, inherited his title.
Zhāng Qí, courtesy name Zǐxiǎng,
was a man from Féngyì jùn.
His family had resided for generations in Héngsāng,
or some say he was a man of Héngsāng.
When young, he possessed courage and spirit.
Initially, he served Yuán Lìshēng, the Sīmǎ (Army Supervisor) of the Jīng Commandery Administration.
Lìshēng was an alcoholic,
and treated his subordinates severely and cruelly,
thus he did not greatly value (Qí).
When Lìshēng was dismissed from office and returned home,
Zhāng Jì of Wú jùn became the Sīmǎ of the Jīng Commandery Administration.
Qí followed him again.
Jì greatly valued and respected him,
considering him a trusted confidant.
Even minor household matters,
he entrusted entirely to him.
Qí served Jì wholeheartedly,
without shirking any task.
He followed Jì back to the capital (Jīngshī).
When Jì became Governor of Nányān Zhōu,
Qí was promoted to Bīng Cānjūn (Military Aide) of the administration,
and it was then that he first handled military affairs.
During the Yǒngyuán period,
when the righteous army (Yìshī) arose,
Dōnghūn summoned Jì back,
appointed him Dūdū Gōngchéng Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor General of all Military Affairs in the Palace City),
and he resided in the Department of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Shěng).
When the righteous troops (Yìbīng) arrived,
and the external siege became increasingly urgent,
Qí visited Wáng Zhēnguó daily,
secretly settling a plan with him.
Once the plan was settled,
he led Zhēnguó by night to Jì for a secret meeting,
and Qí personally held the candle to finalize the plot.
The next morning,
he, Jì, and Zhēnguó immediately executed Dōnghūn in the inner palace hall.
Qí personally wielded the blade.
The following year,
Gāozǔ received the abdication,
enfeoffed Qí as the Marquis of Ānchāng Prefecture (Ānchāng Xiàn Hóu),
with an income of five hundred households,
and retained him as General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Lìyáng (Lìyáng Tàishǒu).
Qí could not write by hand,
nor recognize characters by sight,
yet while governing the prefecture he maintained clean governance,
and administrative affairs were highly organized.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (503 CE),
he was recalled to serve as Colonel of the Tiger’s Might (Hǔbēn Zhōnglángjiāng).
Before taking up the post,
he was transferred to be Prefect of Tiānmén (Tiānmén Tàishǒu),
retaining the title of Níngshuò Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year (505 CE),
the Wèi general Wáng Zú attacked Bā and Shǔ.
Gāozǔ appointed Qí as General Assisting the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) to relieve Shǔ.
Before he arrived,
Zú retreated and fled.
Qí then advanced to garrison Nán'ān.
In the autumn of the seventh year (508 CE),
he ordered Qí to establish the two garrisons of Dàjiàn and Hánzhǒng,
and the army returned to Yì Zhōu.
That same year,
he was promoted to General of the Martial Encampment (Wǔlǚ Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Bāxī (Bāxī Tàishǒu),
and shortly thereafter was granted the title General Who Campaigns Afar (Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
In the tenth year (511 CE),
the local man Yáo Jǐnghé gathered the non-Han peoples (mányán),
plundered and blocked the river routes,
and attacked and destroyed Jīnjǐng.
Qí campaigned against Jǐnghé at Píngchāng,
and defeated him.
Previously,
Nánzhèng had been lost to Wèi,
so Nánliáng Zhōu was established to the west of Yì Zhōu.
The administrative center was newly established,
and everything depended on Yì Zhōu for supply.
Qí requested voluntary grain tax from the indigenous tribes (Yí Liáo),
obtaining 200,000 *hú* of rice.
He also established official relay stations (tái chuán),
promoted metal smelting and casting,
in order to meet the needs of Nánliáng.
In the eleventh year (512 CE),
he was promoted to receive the *jiǎjié* (temporary imperial accreditation) and supervised all armies outside the rivers of Yì Zhōu.
In the twelfth year (513 CE),
the Wèi general Fù Shǔyǎn attacked Nán'ān.
Qí led his forces to resist him.
Shǔyǎn retreated and fled.
In the fourteenth year (515 CE),
he was promoted to General of Martial Trust (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of the two prefectures, Bāxī and Zǐtóng.
That year,
Rèn Lìngzōng of Jiāméng, taking advantage of the common people's suffering under Wèi rule,
killed the Wèi Prefect of Jìnshòu,
and surrendered his city.
Pōyáng Wáng, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yì Zhōu, sent Qí, leading a force of 30,000,
to supervise Xí Zōngfàn, the Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) of Nánliáng Zhōu, and other forces to receive Lìngzōng.
In the fifteenth year (516 CE),
Yuán Fǎsēng, the Wèi Governor of Dōng Yì Zhōu, sent his son Jǐnglóng to resist Qí's army.
Huángfǔ Chén, the Prefect of Nán'ān, along with Zōngfàn, counterattacked,
severely defeating the Wèi army at Jiāméng,
capturing more than ten cities.
The Wèi generals Qiū Tú, Wáng Mù, and others all surrendered.
However, Wèi further reinforced the troops of Fù Shǔyǎn,
who came again to resist the fight.
Qí’s troops suffered a slight disadvantage,
and the army withdrew and returned.
Thus, Jiāméng fell back into Wèi hands.
Qí served in the Yì region for many years,
campaigning against the indigenous tribes (Mán Liáo),
finding no peaceful year for himself.
While stationed with the army,
he personally engaged in demanding and arduous tasks,
sharing the hardships with his officers and soldiers.
From planning barracks and camps to fortifications,
he ensured every detail was convenient and well-arranged.
He managed the distribution of clothing, food, and supplies,
ensuring everyone was free from distress and want.
Since he was supported by the sentiment of the people,
the Mán Liáo also dared not encroach upon the territory.
Therefore, his reputation for power spread throughout Yōng and Shǔ.
Bāxī Prefecture bordered half of Yì Zhōu,
and also occupied a vital position on the eastern route.
When governors passed through,
or when the military administration traveled long distances,
they often faced destitution.
Qí accumulated grain along the route,
and planted vegetables,
so travelers could all obtain provisions.
His ability to achieve things
was often demonstrated in this manner.
In the seventeenth year (518 CE),

he was promoted to Chíjìe (Imperial Accredited), Supervisor General of all Military Affairs in Nánliáng Zhōu, General of Brilliant Martiality (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Nánliáng Zhōu (Nánliáng Zhōu Cìshǐ).

he was promoted to General of Martial Trust (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), Sīmǎ to the Prince of Pōyáng Who Campaigns in the West (Zhēngxī Pōyáng Wáng Sīmǎ), and Prefect of the two prefectures, Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng.
He died before taking up the post,
at the age of sixty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì) and General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
He was bestowed 100,000 cash
and 100 bolts of cloth.
His posthumous name was Zhuàng.
Yáo Chá, the Minister (Shàngshū) of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) of Chén, said: Wáng Zhēnguó, Shēn Zhòu, Xú Yuányú, and Lǐ Jūshì,
were all generals at the end of Qí,
commanding strong armies.
Some submitted with faces bound seeking punishment,
others broke gates and offered victory;
among those who submitted later,
there was only Mǎ Xiānpǐn.
How constant are benevolence and righteousness?
If one follows them, he becomes a noble person (jūnzǐ)—
indeed!
When they took command of the border and pacified the populace,
not even Lǐ Mù could surpass them.
Zhāng Qí's administrative achievements
were also exceptional.
The records of Zhòu, Yuányú, and Jūshì after entering Liáng service are sparse,
therefore biographies were not written for them.
Collective Biographies Twelve: Zhāng Huìshào, Féng Dàogēn, Kāng Xuàn, Chāng Yìzhī.
Zhāng Huìshào, courtesy name Déjì,
was a man of Yìyáng.
When young, he possessed military talent.
During the reign of Qí Míngdì, he served as a Zhíhé (Palace Attendant),
later dispatched to serve as Garrision Commander (Shùzhǔ) of Héngsāng in Jìnglíng.
In the early Yǒngyuán period,
his mother died, and he returned to his hometown for the burial.
Hearing that the righteous army (Yìshī) had risen,
he rushed to join Gāozǔ.
He was provisionally appointed Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Central Military Aide),
and given the titles Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Jūnmǔ (Army Commander).
When the army reached Hànkǒu,
Gāozǔ ordered Huìshào and Jūnmǔ Zhū Sīyuǎn to patrol and blockade the middle of the river,
cutting off the grain supply lines to the two cities of Yǐng and Lǔ.
Shěn Nándāng, the Naval Commander (Shuǐ Jūnmǔ) of Yǐng city, led dozens of light ships to challenge them.
Huìshào defeated him,
beheaded Nándāng,
and captured all his military equipment.
When the righteous army (Yìshī) reached Xīnlín and Zhūquè,
Huìshào repeatedly achieved military merits.
After Jiànkāng city was pacified,
he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, Qiánjūn (Vanguard General),
Zhíhé, and Commander of the Left Minor Guard (Zuǒ Xìzhàng Zhǔ).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Shíyáng Prefecture (Shíyáng Xiàn Hóu),
with an income of five hundred households.
He was promoted to General of Gallant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn),
retaining the titles of Zhíhé and Commander of the Minor Guard (Xìzhàng Zhǔ).
At that time, several hundred remnants of Dōnghūn's faction
secretly entered the North and South Yèmén Gates,
burned the Shénhǔ Gate,
and killed Zhāng Hóngcè, the Commandant of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
Huìshào swiftly led his subordinates to the battle,
beheading dozens of enemy soldiers.
The rebels then scattered and fled.
Due to his merit, his income was increased by two hundred households,
and he was promoted to Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard (Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài).
four (505 CE),
a major expedition was launched against the north.
Huìshào, along with the General of the Central Army Chángshǐ Hú Xīnshēng and the General Quelling the North Zhāng Bàozǐ, attacked Xùyù,
capturing the city lord Mǎ Chénglóng,
and sending him to the capital.
He ordered his subordinate general Lán Huáigōng to establish a city south of the water to serve as a supportive flanking position.
Soon thereafter, the Wèi reinforcements arrived in great numbers,
defeating and trapping Huáigōng.
Huìshào could not hold the position.
That night he fled back to Huáiyīn,
and Wèi consequently regained Xùyù.
In the sixth year (507 CE),
the Wèi army attacked Zhōnglí.
An imperial edict commanded the General of the Left Guard Cáo Jǐngzōng to oversee the assembled forces as relief.
They advanced and occupied Shàoyáng.
Huìshào, along with Féng Dàogēn and Péi Suì, etc., attacked and severed the Wèi pontoon bridges.
Engaging in close-quarters combat,
the Wèi army was completely routed.
For his achievements, his stipend was increased by three hundred households,
and he returned to serve as the General of the Left Swift Cavalry.

Soon thereafter, he was sent out as Administrator with Credentials (Chíjǐe), Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Běiyǎnzhōu (Dūdū Běiyǎnzhōu zhū Jūnshì), General of the Central Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Běiyǎnzhōu (Běiyǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
The two Wèi cities of Xùyù and Huáiyáng internally submitted (defected).
Huìshào was credited with successfully pacifying and assimilating them.
He was promoted in title to General of Wise Martiality (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn),
and his feudal grant was further increased by two hundred households.
He returned to court as Minister of the Palace Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng),
and was promoted to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).

He was sent out as Administrator with Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Sīzhōu, General Trustworthy and Awe-Inspiring (Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn), Governor of Sīzhōu (Sīzhōu Cìshǐ), and concurrently Administrator of Ānlù (Ānlù Tàishǒu).
While in the province, he governed justly and harmoniously,
and the officials and common people loved him dearly.
He was summoned back to serve as General of the Left Guard,
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant in Ordinary (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
with one hundred armed guards,
who guarded the palace interior.
In the eighteenth year (519 CE),
he died,
aged sixty-three.
The imperial edict stated:
“Zhāng Huìshào’s will and strategy were broad and helpful,
his administrative ability was steadfast and effective.
He began with sincerity and diligence toward righteousness,
his achievements were recognized throughout his many appointments.
Having been placed in the Imperial Guard,
he applied himself wholeheartedly day and night.
That he suddenly met his demise
causes me deep sorrow.
It is fitting to posthumously grant him honors
to make manifest his meritorious achievements.
He is hereby posthumously presented with the title General Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
granted one set of drums and pipes (Gǔchuī),
one hundred rolls of cloth,
and two hundred catties of wax.
His posthumous name (Shì) shall be Zhōng.”
His son, Chéng, succeeded him.
Chéng first served as General of the Palace Gate Guard (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn).
He mourned his father,
was ordered to resume duty as Administrator of Jìnxī (Jìnxī Tàishǒu),
and followed the Governor of Yùzhōu, Péi Suì, on the northern expedition.
He accumulated several military achievements.
He and Zhàn Sēngzhì, Hú Shàoshì, and Yú Hóng were regarded as fierce generals of that time.
He successively held the positions of Minister of the Palace Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng) and Commander of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài).
He died while in office.
His posthumous name was Mǐn.
Féng Dàogēn, courtesy name Jùjī,
was a native of Guǎngpíng Zàn.
He lost his father young.
His family was poor,
and he hired himself out for labor to support his mother.
If he acquired sweet and fatty food during his travels,
he dared not eat it first;
he would quickly return to present it to his mother.
At the age of thirteen,
his filial piety was known throughout the local community.
The commandery summoned him to be Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
but he refused the appointment.
At the age of sixteen,
a fellow villager, Cài Dàobān, was the Garrison Commander of Húyáng.
Dàobān attacked the Mán (barbarian) city of Xīchéng,
but was instead surrounded by the Mán.
Dàogēn went to his rescue.
Fighting alone on horseback,
he inflicted heavy casualties.
Dàobān was thus spared,
and because of this, Dàogēn became famous.
At the end of the Qí Jiànwǔ era (493-494 CE),
the Wèi ruler Tuòbá Hóng invaded and seized Nányáng and four other commanderies.
Emperor Míng sent Grand Commandant Chén Xiǎndá to lead forces to retake them.
When the army entered Jūn Kǒu (mouth of the Jūn River),
Dàogēn and local gentry brought oxen and wine to meet the army,
and then spoke to Xiǎndá, saying:
“The Jūn River current is swift and rapid,
making advance difficult and retreat easy.
If Wèi guards the passes,
then both our vanguard and rearguard will be imperiled.
It is better to abandon all ships and vessels at Zànchéng,
proceed on foot along the straight paths,
setting up successive camps,
and advance while beating the drums.
If this is done,
we will defeat them immediately.”
Xiǎndá did not listen.
Dàogēn still followed the army with his private retainers.
When Xiǎndá was defeated,
the soldiers fled by night,
many not knowing the mountain paths.
Whenever Dàogēn reached a strategic bottleneck or danger point,
he would stop his horse and point the way for them.
The masses relied on this guidance to survive.
Soon after, he served as the Deputy Commander of the Jūn Kǒu Garrison.
During the Yǒngyuán era (499–501 CE),
he returned home due to his mother’s funeral.
Hearing that Emperor Gāozǔ (Liáng Wǔ Dì) had raised an army of righteousness,
he said to his close associates:
“Warfare overrides ritual obligations;
the ancients did not shy away from this.
To make one's name famous for posterity,
is that not filial piety?
The time must not be missed.
I must go.”
He led the young men of his community who were capable fighters
and all submitted to Emperor Gāozǔ.
At that time, Cài Dàofú was serving as a general in the army.
Gāozǔ appointed Dàogēn as his deputy,
and both were placed under the command of Wáng Mào.
When Mào attacked Miǎn,
assaulted Yǐngchéng,
and conquered Jiāhú,
Dàogēn constantly served as the vanguard, breaking enemy lines.
Subsequently, Dàofú died in the field.
Gāozǔ ordered Dàogēn to concurrently lead his troops.
When the main army reached Xīnlín,
he followed Wáng Mào in a great battle at Zhūquè Háng (Zhuque Bridge),
where he achieved especially great kills and captures.
When Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he appointed Dàogēn General of the Swift Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
He was enfeoffed as Baron of Zēngchéng County (Zēngchéng Xiàn Nán),
with a stipend of two hundred households.
He was concurrently appointed Commander of Wéndé (Wéndé Shuài),
and later promoted to General of Roving Cavalry (Yóují Jiāngjūn).
That same year,
the Governor of Jiāngzhōu, Chén Bózhī, rebelled.
Dàogēn followed Wáng Mào to suppress and pacify him.
In Tiānjiān two (503 CE),
he was appointed General Quelling the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nánliáng (Nánliáng Tàishǒu),
concurrently commanding the Fùlíng City Garrison.
When he first arrived at Fùlíng,
he repaired the city walls and moats,
and sent out scouts far afield.
Others thought an enemy general was approaching,
and many people ridiculed him.
Dàogēn said:
“Cautious defense and brave fighting—
this is what that means.”
Before the repair of the city was finished,
the Wèi generals Dǎng Fǎzōng and Fù Shǔyǎn led a force of twenty thousand men,
suddenly appearing beneath the city walls.
Dàogēn’s trenches and ramparts were not yet secure,
and the troops inside the city were few.
Everyone turned pale.
Dàogēn ordered the gates to be opened wide,
leisurely climbed the wall in his civilian clothes,
selected two hundred elite troops,
and went out to fight the Wèi army,
defeating them.
The Wèi observed his composure,
and since the fighting was also disadvantageous to them,
they consequently retreated.
At that time, Wèi had divided its troops at the Greater and Lesser Xiàn, Dōngsāng, and other locations,
holding successive fortified positions.
The Wèi general Gāo Zǔzhēn stationed three thousand cavalry among them.
Dàogēn led one hundred cavalry and attacked them sideways, defeating them,
and capturing their drums, horns, and military standards.
Since the supply lines were completely cut,
the various Wèi forces subsequently withdrew.
Dàogēn was promoted to General Assisting the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
conquered it.
Dàogēn advanced
with the various armies,
achieving merit wherever he went.
In the sixth year (507 CE),
Wèi attacked Zhōnglí.
Gāozǔ again ordered Wéi Ruì to rescue it.
Dàogēn led three thousand men as Wéi Ruì’s vanguard.
Upon arriving at Xúzhōu,
he proposed a strategy to occupy Shàoyáng Zhōu,
building ramparts and digging trenches,
thus pressuring the Wèi city.
Dàogēn was capable of surveying the terrain by horseback,
calculating the distance covered by the horses’ hooves to apportion the labor;
the city walls and moats were immediately completed.
When the Huáishǔi rose,
Dàogēn took warships
and attacked and severed the Wèi pontoon bridge, which stretched several hundred *zhàng*.
The Wèi army suffered a defeat.
His stipend was increased by three hundred households,
and his noble rank was advanced
to *bó* (Earl). Upon returning, he was transferred to Yúnqí Jiāngjūn, concurrently holding Zhíhé Jiāngjūn.
His enfeoffment was changed to Yùníng Xiàn,
the number of households remaining
as before. He was successively promoted to Zhōngquán Zhōng Sīmǎ, Yòu Yóujī Jiāngjūn, Wǔlǚ Jiāngjūn, and Prefect of Lìyáng (*Lìyáng Tàishǒu*).
In the eighth year (509 CE),

he was transferred to Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn, granted the *jiǎjié* (temporary imperial accreditation), made Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yùzhōu (*Dū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì*), *Yùzhōu Cìshǐ*, and concurrently Prefect of Rǔyīn (*Rǔyīn Tàishǒu*).
His administration was clean and simple,
and the territory was stable.
In the eleventh year (512 CE),
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ (Right Commander of the Crown Prince’s Guard).
In the thirteenth year (514 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Xuānhuì Sīmǎ, and Prefect of the two commanderies of Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng.
In the fourteenth year (515 CE),
he was recalled to serve as Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì, and Yòu Yóujī Jiāngjūn,
concurrently holding Zhūyī Zhíhé.
In the fifteenth year (516 CE),
he was made Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (Right Guard General).
Dàogēn was careful and sincere by nature,
slow of speech and quiet.
As a general, he was able to restrain and manage his subordinates and troops.
In the villages and fields through which
they passed, the officers and men dared not loot or plunder.
Whenever he undertook a campaign,
he would never speak of his achievements.
While the other generals clamored and competed,
Dàogēn would simply remain silent.
Sometimes his subordinates complained about his lack of ambition.
Dàogēn instructed them, saying:
"The enlightened ruler will judge the magnitude of the achievements
himself. Why should I do anything?"
Gāozǔ once pointed to Dàogēn and showed him to Shàngshū Lìng Shěn Yuē,
saying: "This man's mouth does not discuss merit."
Shěn Yuē replied:
"This is Your Majesty's Dàshù Jiāngjūn (General of the Great Tree)."
When administering commanderies and prefectures,
he governed harmoniously, clearly, and quietly,
and was cherished by his subordinates.
When in the imperial court,
though he was esteemed and prominent, he was frugal and restrained by nature.
The residence where he lived was without embellished walls or buildings.
He lacked fine utensils, clothing, or attendants.
When entering his room, it was desolate and quiet, like that of a poor and humble common scholar.
People at the time admired his purity and modesty,
and Gāozǔ also highly respected him.
He did not study when he was humble.
After becoming noble,
he roughly read books.
He considered himself to have little literary talent,
and often admired the gravitas of Zhōu Bó.
In the sixteenth year (517 CE),
he was again granted the *jiǎjié*, made Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yùzhōu (*Dūdū Yùzhōu Zhū Jūnshì*), Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and *Yùzhōu Cìshǐ*.
When he was about to depart,
Gāozǔ gathered court officials and held a farewell banquet for Dàogēn in the Wǔdé Diàn hall.
He summoned artisans to observe Dàogēn
and ordered them to paint his portrait.
Dàogēn deferentially offered his thanks, saying:
"What this subject can use to repay the state
is only one death;
however, the realm is at peace,
and I regret that I have no place where I can die (for the country)."
The region of Yùzhōu was delighted to have Dàogēn back,
and all the people rejoiced.
Gāozǔ often praised him, saying:
"Wherever Féng Dàogēn is situated,
he is able to prevent the court from having to worry about that province."
After residing in the province for a short time,
he contracted an illness,
and petitioned to be recalled to court.
He was summoned and appointed Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
After arriving, his illness worsened.
Imperial envoys repeatedly came to inquire about his health.
In the first month of the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
he died,
at the age of fifty-eight.
On that day, the imperial carriage was performing the spring sacrifice at the Two Temples.
After leaving the palace,
the relevant official reported the news.
Gāozǔ asked Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhū Zhāo:
"Auspicious and inauspicious events fall on the same day.
Should I proceed (with the sacrifice) now?"
Zhū Zhāo replied:
"Formerly, Liǔ Zhuāng was ill.
Wèi Xiàngōng was about to perform the sacrifice.
He petitioned the impersonator of the dead (*shī*) saying: 'I have a minister, Liǔ Zhuāng.
He is not merely the subject of this insignificant ruler,
he is a subject of the State (*Shèjì*).
Having heard of his death,
I request to go.'
He went without removing his sacrificial robes,
and then presented the burial garments to him.
Although Dàogēn might not yet be considered a subject of the State,
he also labored greatly for the Royal House.
It is proper ritual to attend to his passing."
Gāozǔ immediately proceeded to his residence
and wept deeply in mourning.
The imperial edict stated:
"Féng Dàogēn, Founding Earl of Yùníng Xiàn, newly appointed Sànqí Chángshì, and concurrently Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
served his superiors with loyalty;
he had achievements but did not boast;
he governed people with enduring affection;
and his defense of the borders was difficult to breach.
Jì Zūn, Féng Yì, Guō Jí, and Lǐ Mù
could not surpass him.
His sudden death
causes sorrow in Our heart.
He is to be posthumously appointed Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and granted one set of drums and pipes (*gǔchuī*).
An offering of one hundred thousand cash
and one hundred bolts of cloth is granted.
His posthumous title is Wēi."
His son Huái succeeded him.
Kāng Xuàn, courtesy name Chángmíng,
was a native of Lántián, Huàshān.
His ancestors originated from Kāngjū.
Initially,
when Hàn established the Protectorate General (*Dūhù*),
making all the Western Regions its vassals,
Kāngjū also sent a hostage prince (*shìzǐ*) to await summons west of the Yellow River (*Héxī*).
He consequently stayed and became a commoner.
His descendants then adopted Kāng as their surname.
During the Jìn dynasty, Lǒngyòu was in chaos,
and the Kāng clan relocated to Lántián.
Kāng Xuàn’s great-grandfather, Yīnwèi, was Fú Jiān’s Crown Prince Tutor (*Tàizǐ Zhānshì*).
He begot Mù.
Mù was Yáo Cháng’s Prefect of Hénán (*Hénán Yǐn*).
During the Yǒngchū era of the Sòng dynasty,
Mù led his kin and clan, numbering over three thousand households,
to settle south of Xiàn (Xiànnán) in Xiāngyáng.
The Sòng dynasty established Huàshān Jùn and Lántián Xiàn for them,
temporarily settling them in Xiāngyáng.
Mù was appointed *Cìshǐ* of the two provinces of Qín and Liáng.
Before he could accept the appointment,
he died.
Kāng Xuàn's paternal cousin Yuánlóng
and father Yuánfǔ
were both supported by the displaced people (*liúrén*).
They successively served as Prefect of Huàshān (*Huàshān Tàishǒu*).
When Kāng Xuàn was young, he was outstanding and had great ambition.
When Qí Wéndì was *Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ*,
the people he recruited were all selected from famous families.
Kāng Xuàn, specifically for his talent and strength, was summoned to be Xīcáo Shūzuǒ (Secretary of the Western Bureau).
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485 CE),
he was appointed Fèngcháoqǐng.
When Qí Wéndì was in the Eastern Palace (as Crown Prince),
based on their previous friendship, he recruited him to be Zhíhòu.
He left his post due to mourning his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn and *Huàshān Tàishǒu*.
He acted with sincerity and treated the people kindly;
the remaining scattered population submitted willingly.
He was transferred to Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn,
and again served as *Huàshān Tàishǒu*.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán,
the righteous army rose.
Xuàn led the entire commandery to respond to Gāozǔ,
personally commanding three thousand brave and daring men
and two hundred fifty private horses to join.
He was appointed Central Army Staff Officer to the King of Nánkāng, Xīzhōngláng,
and granted the title of Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
When the righteous army was besieging Zhāng Chōng at Yǐngchéng,
it dragged on for a long time.
Dōnghūn's general, Wú Zǐyáng, set up camp at Jiāhú,
and his military might was formidable.
Xuàn followed Wáng Mào in a forceful attack and conquered it.
From then on, he often led roving troops,
responding to emergencies,
and his captures and beheadings were numerous.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as the County Baron of Nán'ān,
with a stipend of three hundred households.
He was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Jìnglíng Tàishǒu.
When Wèi besieged Liángzhōu,
the Inspector Wáng Zhēnguó sent a plea for help.
Xuàn led the commandery troops to relieve it,
and the Wèi army retreated.
In the seventh year,
the three passes of Sīzhōu were threatened by Wèi.
An imperial edict provisionally granted Xuàn a jíe and the title of Wǔlǚ Jiāngjūn,
ordering him to lead his troops to reinforce them.
In the ninth year,
he was promoted to provisional jíe, General Administrator of all military affairs along the Huái River in Běiyǎnzhōu, Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Běiyǎnzhōu.
When the fugitives from Qúshān surrendered the city to Wèi,
Xuàn swiftly dispatched his Sīmǎ, Huò Fèngbó, to lead a detachment to hold the strategic passes.
When the Wèi army arrived,
they could not bypass Qúchéng.
The following year,
the Inspector of Qīngzhōu, Zhāng Jì, was killed by the local leader Xú Dàojiǎo.
Xuàn again dispatched his Sīmǎ, Máo Róngbó, to suppress him.
He was summoned to be the Sīmǎ to the Prince of Línchuān, the Piàoqí,
and granted the title of Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Zhūyī Zhíhé.
In the thirteenth year,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài,
with a hundred armored guards,
and along with the Língjūn, Xiāo Jǐng, was stationed directly within the palace.
Xuàn was eight *chǐ* tall,
with extraordinary looks.
Though he held a prominent office,
he still practiced martial arts.
Gāozǔ visited Déyángdiàn to watch horseplay,
and commanded Xuàn to perform equestrian archery.
He drew his bow and hit the target,
which delighted the onlookers.
On that day,
the emperor ordered a painter to draw Xuàn's portrait,
and sent a palace envoy to hold it and ask Xuàn:
"Do you recognize this painting?"
Such was the closeness he enjoyed.
At that time, Wáng Zú, a defector from Wèi, proposed a plan,
requesting to dam the Huái River to flood Shòuyáng.
Zú quoted a northern children's rhyme:
"Jīngshān forms the upper gate,
Fúshān forms the lower gate,
Tóngtuó serves as the rushing channel,
all combined to flood Jùyěz. "
Gāozǔ believed it to be true
and sent the hydraulic engineer Chén Chéngbó and the Artisan General Zǔ [⿰耳幾] to inspect the terrain.
They all stated that the sand and soil inside the Huái River were light and easily swept away,
not firm,
and thus the project could not be completed.
Gāozǔ did not accept this
and mobilized people from Xú and Yáng,
requiring five strong men for every twenty households to build it.
Xuàn was provisionally granted a jíe, made General Administrator of all military affairs along the Huái River,
and also put in charge of the dam construction.
The laborers and soldiers
numbered two hundred thousand.
They started building from Fúshān in the south of Zhōnglí
to Chánshí in the north,
building up the earth along the banks,
and joining the crest in the middle of the river.
In the fourteenth year,
as the dam was about to be completed,
the swift currents of the Huái River
repeatedly broke through and collapsed it.
The multitude was distressed by this.
Some said that there were many *jiāo* (water dragons) in the Jiāng and Huái rivers,
capable of riding the wind and rain to break cliffs and banks,
and that their nature was averse to iron.
Therefore, iron implements from the eastern and western foundries were brought,
large ones like cauldrons and kettles,
small ones like hoes and picks,
tens of millions of *jīn* in weight,
and sunk at the dam site.
Still, it could not be completed.
Then trees were cut to form well-frames,
filled with huge stones,
and earth was added on top.
Within a hundred *lǐ* along the Huái River,
all hills, mounds, wood, and stones,
whether large or small, were completely used up.
The shoulders of the bearers were all chafed through.
In summer, there was a severe plague,
and the dead lay piled upon each other.
Flies and insects buzzed day and night in unison.
Gāozǔ, sympathizing with the prolonged suffering of the laborers,
sent the Shàngshū Yòupúyè Yuán Áng and the Shìzhōng Xiè Jǔ with a provisional jíe to comfort them,
and also granted tax exemptions and remissions.
That winter was also extremely cold;
the Huái and Sì rivers were completely frozen.
Seventy or eighty percent of the soldiers died.
Gāozǔ again sent clothes and trousers as a gift.
In the eleventh month,
Wèi dispatched General Yáng Dàyǎn to loudly declare his intention to break the dam.
Xuàn ordered his armies to dismantle their camps and wait in the open.
He sent his son, Yuè, to challenge them,
and Yuè beheaded Xú Fāngxīng, the Sīmǎ of the Wèi King of Xiányáng's mansion.
The Wèi army retreated slightly.
In the twelfth month,
Wèi dispatched its Shàngshū Púyè Lǐ Tándìng to oversee the armies coming to battle.
Xuàn and Xúzhōu Cìshǐ Liú Sīzǔ, among others, resisted them.
Gāozǔ also sent Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn Chāng Yìzhī, Tàipú Qīng Yú Hóngwén,
and Zhíhé Cáo Shìzōng and Xú Yuánhé in succession to resist and defend.
In the fourth month of the fifteenth year,
the dam was finally completed.
It was nine *lǐ* long,
one hundred forty *zhàng* wide at the bottom,
forty-five *zhàng* wide at the top,
twenty *zhàng* high,
and nineteen *zhàng* five *chǐ* deep.
It was flanked by dikes,
and willow trees were planted.
The soldiers settled down safely,
lining its top.
The water was clear,
and looking down, one could clearly see the graves of the residents
all beneath it.
Someone said to Xuàn:
"The Four Great Rivers
are how Heaven regulates its energy;
they cannot be blocked for long.
If the *qiū* (pond) is dug to flow eastward,
then the flowing waves will be broad and slow,
and the dam will not be damaged."
Xuàn agreed with this,
and opened the *qiū* to flow eastward.
He also spread a counter-espionage message to Wèi, saying:
"The people of Liáng fear the opening of the *qiū*,
but do not fear open battle."
The Wèi people believed this
and indeed dug the mountain five *zhàng* deep
to open the *qiū* to flow northward.
The water split day and night,
but the *qiū* did not diminish.
In that month,
the Wèi army finally collapsed and returned.
The water reached several hundred square *lǐ* of land along the Huái River.
The Wèi garrison at Shòuyáng city gradually moved to Bāgōngshān,
and the residents south of this area scattered to the hills and ridges.
Initially,
when the dam started in Xúzhōu territory,
the Inspector Zhāng Bàozǐ declared throughout his jurisdiction
that he would certainly be in charge of the matter.
Later, Xuàn came as an official from another post to supervise the construction,
and Bàozǐ was greatly ashamed.
Soon after, an edict ordered Bàozǐ to follow Xuàn's directives,
and he would first consult him on every matter.
Because of this, Bàozǐ then slandered Xuàn, accusing him of communicating with Wèi.
Although Gāozǔ did not accept this,
he still summoned Xuàn after the project was completed.
Soon after, Xuàn was appointed bearer of a jíe, General Administrator of all military affairs in Sīzhōu, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Sīzhōu,
and concurrently Governor of Ānlù,
with an additional enfeoffment of two hundred households.
After Xuàn returned,
Bàozǐ did not maintain the dam.
By the eighth month of that autumn,
the Huái River violently swelled,
the dam completely broke and collapsed,
and the surging water flowed into the sea.
Zǔ [⿰耳幾] was imprisoned for this.
Xuàn was in the province for three years,
and greatly repaired the city walls and moats,
known for his strict governance.
In the eighteenth year,
he was summoned to be Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently Líng Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi,
and along with Hùjūn Wéi Ruì
and Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài Zhōu Shě, was stationed directly in the palace secretariat.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he was appointed Wèiwèi Qīng.
Before he could take office,
he passed away,
at the age of fifty-seven.
The imperial carriage personally visited and mourned on that very day.
He was posthumously granted the title of Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn,
and given a set of drums and pipes.
A funeral gift of one hundred thousand *qián*
and one hundred bolts of cloth was bestowed.
His posthumous name was Zhuàng.
Kāng Xuàn 康絢 was generous and rarely showed joy or fear.
In the imperial court,
he appeared as if he could not speak to people,
and was known as "Ever Sincere" (長厚).
In the provincial office,
every cold month he saw the provincial officials in thin clothes,
and always gave them padded robes,
such was his generosity.
His son, Yuè 悅, succeeded him.
Chāng Yìzhī 昌義之,
was a native of Wūjiāng 烏江, Lìyáng 歷陽.
From a young age, he possessed military talent.
During the Qí 齊 dynasty, he followed Cáo Hǔ 曹虎 in campaigns,
and accumulated many military merits.
When Hǔ 虎 became the Governor of Yōngzhōu 雍州,
he appointed Yìzhī 義之 as a guard (防閤),
and later sent him out as the Commander (戍主) of Féngyì 馮翊.
When Hǔ 虎 returned due to an imperial decree,
Yìzhī 義之 remained to serve Gāozǔ 高祖.
At that time, the world was in turmoil,
and Gāozǔ 高祖 also treated him generously.
When the righteous army rose,
he was appointed as General Who Assists the State (輔國將軍) and Army Commander (軍主),
and was made a Staff Officer (中兵參軍) to the Prince of Jiàn'ān 建安.
At that time, Jìnglíng Qiānkǒu 竟陵芊口 had a granary (邸閣).
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent him to attack it,
and he was victorious in every battle.
When the main army reached Xīnlín 新林,
he followed Wáng Mào 王茂 to Xīntíng 新亭,
and fought vigorously alongside Zhūquèháng 朱雀航,
capturing and killing many.
When Jiànkāng 建康 city was pacified,
he was made General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) and Commander of the Right Cavalcade (馬右夾轂主).
In the first year of Tiānjiān 天監 (502 CE),
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngfēng County 永豐縣侯,
with a fief of five hundred households.
He was appointed General of Elite Cavalry (驍騎將軍).
He was sent out as the Administrator of Xūyí 盱眙 (Xūyí Tàishǒu 盱眙太守).
In the second year (503 CE),
he was promoted to Acting Imperial Commissioner (假節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (督北徐州諸軍事), General Who Assists the State (輔國將軍), and Governor of Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (北徐州刺史),
stationed at Zhōnglí 鍾離.
When the Wèi 魏 invaders encroached upon the prefecture,
Yìzhī 義之 defeated them.
In the third year (504 CE),
he was advanced in rank to General Who Quells the Army (冠軍將軍),
and his fief was increased by two hundred households.
In the fourth year (505 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched.
The Prince of Línchuān 臨川, Governor of Yángzhōu 揚州, led the various armies to encamp at Luòkǒu 洛口.
Yìzhī 義之, with the provincial troops, received orders
to be the vanguard.
He attacked the Wèi 魏 garrison at Liángchéng 梁城,
and captured it.
In the fifth year (506 CE),
Gāozǔ 高祖, finding the military campaign protracted,
issued an imperial decree recalling the armies.
The various armies dispersed and retreated.
Yuán Yīng 元英, the Prince of Zhōngshān 中山 of Wèi 魏, seized the opportunity to pursue them,
attacking and capturing Mǎtóu 馬頭.
The grain stores within the city
were all moved north by Wèi 魏.
All the strategists said:
"The Wèi 魏 are transporting grain back north,
so they will not advance south again."
Gāozǔ 高祖 said:
"Not so.
They will surely advance their troops;
this is not the truth."
He then sent skilled artisans to repair and fortify Zhōnglí 鍾離 city,
[一一] and ordered Yìzhī 義之 to prepare for defense.
That winter,
Yīng 英 indeed led his Prince of Ānlè 安樂 Yuán Dàomíng 元道明, General Who Pacifies the East (平東將軍) Yáng Dàyǎn 楊大眼, and a host of several hundred thousand men,
to invade Zhōnglí 鍾離.
Zhōnglí 鍾離 city was blocked to the north by the Huái Huái River.
The Wèi 魏 people built a pontoon bridge on the west bank of Shàoyáng Zhōu 邵陽洲,
crossing the Huái Huái River to open a path.
Yīng 英 occupied the east bank,
and Dàyǎn 大眼 occupied the west bank,
to attack the city.
At that time, the city only had three thousand troops.
Yìzhī 義之 commanded them,
resisting the attacks from all directions.
The Wèi 魏 army then used carts loaded with earth to fill the moat,
making their soldiers carry earth to follow,
while heavily armored cavalry pressed them from behind.
If anyone did not turn back in time,
they were crushed by the earth.
Soon, the moat was full.
Yīng 英 and Dàyǎn 大眼 personally supervised the battle,
attacking relentlessly day and night,
taking turns in shifts.
They fell and rose again,
none retreating.
They also deployed flying towers (飛樓) and battering rams (衝車) to strike,
wherever they hit, the city walls would collapse.
[一二] Yìzhī 義之 then used mud to repair the breaches.
Although the battering rams penetrated, they could not destroy the wall.
Yìzhī 義之 was skilled in archery.
Wherever the attack was most critical and dangerous,
he would gallop there to rescue.
Every time he drew his bow,
no one failed to fall when the arrow was released.
In one day, they fought dozens of engagements,
with tens of thousands killed and wounded before and after.
The Wèi 魏 dead piled up as high as the city walls.
In the fourth month of the sixth year (507 CE),
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Cáo Jǐngzōng 曹景宗 and Wéi Ruì 韋叡 to lead an army of two hundred thousand to relieve them.
Upon their arrival,
they fought with the Wèi 魏,
and utterly defeated them.
Yīng 英, Dàyǎn 大眼, and others all escaped and fled.
Yìzhī 義之 then led light cavalry in pursuit as far as Luòkǒu 洛口 before returning.
The number of beheaded and captured alive
was incalculable.
For his merit, he was advanced in rank to General of the Army Adviser (軍師將軍),
his fief was increased by two hundred households,

and he was promoted to Imperial Commissioner (持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Qīngzhōu 靑州 and Jìzhōu 冀州 (督青冀二州諸軍事), General Who Conquers the Barbarians (征虜將軍), and Governor of Qīngzhōu 靑州 and Jìzhōu 冀zhōu (青冀二州刺史).
Before he was formally appointed,

he was changed to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu 南兗州, Yǎnzhōu 兗州, Xúzhōu 徐州, Qīngzhōu 靑州, and Jìzhōu 冀zhōu (督南兗兗徐青冀五州諸軍事), General Who Assists the State (輔國將軍), and Governor of Nányǎnzhōu 南兗州 (南兗州刺史).
He was impeached by the authorities for allowing contraband goods to leave the province
and was dismissed.
That same year,
he was appointed 朱衣直閤 (zhūyī zhíhé, an official of the inner enclosure wearing red robes),
and made General of the Left Elite Cavalry (左驍騎將軍),
with his position as Inner Enclosure guard remaining as before.
He was promoted to Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (太子右衞率),
also holding the position of Colonel of Yue Cavalry (越騎校尉),
and Acting Imperial Commissioner (假節).
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he was sent out as Imperial Commissioner (持節), Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xiāngzhōu 湘州 (督湘州諸軍事), General Who Conquers from Afar (征遠將軍), and Governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘zhōu (湘州刺史).
In the ninth year (510 CE),
he returned to court with his original rank,
and shortly after became the Grand Secretary (司馬) for the Prince of Línchuān 臨川, who was the Minister of Works (司空),
retaining his generalship as before.
In the tenth year (511 CE),
he was promoted to General of the Right Guard (右衞將軍).
In the thirteenth year (514 CE),
he was transferred to General of the Left Guard (左衞將軍).
That winter,
Gāozǔ 高祖 sent Kāng Xuàn 康絢, Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (太子右衛率), to lead the armies in building the Jīngshān Jing Mountain Weir 荊山堰.
The following year (515 CE),
Wèi 魏 sent General Lǐ Tándìng 李曇定 with a large army to approach Jīngshān 荊山,
and spread rumors that they intended to destroy the weir.
An imperial decree granted Yìzhī 義之 a commissioner's staff,
and he was ordered to lead Grand Minister of the Imperial Stud (太僕卿) Yú Hóngwén 魚弘文, General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) Cáo Shìzōng 曹世宗, Xú Yuánhé 徐元和, and others to reinforce Xuàn 絢.
Before the army arrived,
Xuàn 絢 and his forces had already defeated the Wèi 魏 army.
Wèi 魏 again sent the great general Lǐ Píng 李平 to attack Xiáshí 峽石,
besieging General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) Zhào Zǔyuè 趙祖悅.
Yìzhī 義之 again led Zhūyī Zhíhé 朱衣直閤 Wáng Shénniàn 王神念 and others to relieve them.
At that time, the Wèi 魏 forces were strong,
and Shénniàn 神念 could not capture the pontoon bridge at Xiáshí 峽石,
so the relief forces could not advance in time,
and Xiáshí 峽石 subsequently fell.
Yìzhī 義之 returned with his army,
and was impeached by the authorities.
Gāozǔ 高祖, considering him a meritorious minister,
did not pursue the matter.
In the fifteenth year (516 CE),
he was again appointed Imperial Commissioner with Staff (使持節), Area Commander-in-Chief of Xiāngzhōu 湘州 (都督湘州諸軍事), General Who Commands with Trust (信威將軍), and Governor of Xiāngzhōu 湘zhōu (湘州刺史).
That same year,

he was reappointed Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs along the Huái Huái River in Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (都督北徐州緣淮諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the North (平北將軍), and Governor of Běixúzhōu 北徐州 (北徐州刺史).
Yìzhī 義之 was by nature generous and magnanimous,
and as a general, he was able to soothe and control his subordinates,
earning their utmost loyalty.
When he served in a provincial capacity,
the officials and people found peace under him.
Shortly after, he was granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments (鼓吹一部),
and was re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Yíngdào County 營道縣侯,
with his number of households remaining as before.
In the third year of Pǔtōng 普通 (522 CE),
he was summoned to be General Protector of the Army (護軍將軍),
with the drum and wind instruments remaining as before.
In the tenth month of the fourth year (523 CE),
he passed away.
Gāozǔ 高祖 deeply mourned him,
and issued an edict saying:
"Chāng Yìzhī 昌義之, General Protector of the Army and Founding Marquis of Yíngdào County,
was resourceful and composed in strategy,
and his heart was generous and forbearing.
His sincerity was manifest at the beginning of the reign,
and his achievements were prominent in the border regions.
He was just about to be further used as a trusted aide,
entrusted with the imperial guard;
suddenly, he met his demise,
which saddens my heart.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (散騎常侍) and General of Chariots and Cavalry (車騎將軍),
along with a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
A 'Secret Vessel from the Eastern Garden' (東園祕器) is granted,
and one set of court robes.
A funeral gift of twenty thousand coins,
two hundred bolts of cloth,
and two hundred catties of wax.
His posthumous name shall be 'Liè' 烈."
His son, Bǎoyè 寶業, succeeded him,
and his highest official post was General of the Inner Enclosure (直閤將軍) and Governor of Qiáozhōu 譙州 (譙州刺史).
Chén Lìbù Shàngshū Yáo Chá said: Zhāng Huìshào, Féng Dàogēn, Kāng Xuàn, Chāng Yìzhī,
initially rose from the ranks of the followers of the Emperor,
their achievements were therefore minor.
However, when the bandits set fire to the gates,
Huìshào distinguished himself through fierce fighting;
when Héféi and Shàoyáng were under siege,
Dàogēn and Yìzhī made significant contributions;
when the campaign of Fúshān began,
Kāng Xuàn took charge of the matter: they each had their own merits,
and it was fitting that they were promoted and honored.
Before this, the Zhenxing star guarded the Tiānjiāng river, and the weir was built;
when it retreated from its station, the weir broke.
This was not merely a matter of human affairs,
but also involved the Way of Heaven.
Jiàokān Jì
Lièzhuàn dì shí sān Zōng Jué Liú Tǎn Yuè Ài
Zōng Jué, courtesy name Míngyáng,
was from Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His family had long resided in Jiānglíng.
His grandfather, Bǐng,
was offered the position of Prince's Grand Tutor during the Sòng dynasty but declined,
holding a high reputation.
His father, Fán,
was a Xīzhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn.
Jué was diligent in his studies when young,
and had a firm and capable character.
At twenty,
he was recommended as Xiùcái in Yǐngzhōu,
and successively served as Línchuān Wáng Chángshì and Piàojì Xíngcānjūn.
When Qí Sītú Jìnglǐng Wáng gathered scholars at the Western Mansion,
and all viewed the paintings and calligraphy,
Jué was also among them.
During the Yǒngmíng era,
a peace agreement was made with Wèi.
Jué was commanded to receive the Wèi envoys along with Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng Rèn Fǎng,
both being selections of the time.
When Emperor Wǔ's legitimate grandson, Nánjùn Wáng, resided in Xīzhōu,
he appointed Jué to manage his correspondence.
Jué was known for his literary skills
and also admired for his integrity and uprightness,
which is why he was appointed.
Shortly thereafter, Wénhuì Tàizǐ died,
and the King became the Imperial Grandson.
Jué continued to manage his correspondence.
When the Grandson ascended the throne,
he often acted improperly.
Jué gradually distanced himself,
obtaining the position of Línglìng,
and later promoted to Shàngshū Dūguānláng.
At the end of the Lóngchāng era,
the Young Emperor was executed,
and many of his former favorites suffered misfortune.
Only Jué and Fù Zhāo escaped due to their integrity and uprightness.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he appointed Jué as Yǐngzhōu Zhìzhōng.
He was well-regarded and competent in his duties.
Due to his father's old age, he resigned and returned to his hometown.
When Nánkāng Wáng became Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he appointed Jué as Biéjià.
When the Righteous Army rose,
he was promoted to Xīzhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn,
while retaining his position as Biéjià.
At that time, among the dignitaries in Xītǔ,
only Jué, Yuè Ài, and Liú Tǎn from the same commandery were trusted and recommended by the people of the province.
Therefore, Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Xiāo Yǐngzhòu greatly relied on them,
consulting them on every matter.
When Gāozǔ's army departed from Yōngzhōu,
Yǐngzhòu sent Jué from Yángkǒu
to personally report on military strategies
and to escort military supplies.
Gāozǔ treated him with great respect.
In the early days of Zhōngxīng,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
but resigned due to mourning for his father.
He was then appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Wèijūn Zhǎngshǐ.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Zhǎngshǐ and Dōnghǎi Tàishǒu,
retaining his general title.
In the second year,
he was summoned to be Tàizǐ Yòuwèishul.
In the winter of that year,
he was promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū,
participating in the major selections.
In the third year,
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
His son, Yàoqīng, inherited his position.
Jué's cousin, Yuè,
had a good reputation and conduct,
and was praised by the people of the province,
surpassing Jué.
He successively served as Shàngshū Kùbùláng,
Yǐngzhōu Zhìzhōng,
and Běizhōngláng Lùshì Cānjūnshì.
Liú Tǎn, courtesy name Déduó,
was from Ānzhòng, Nányáng,
a seventh-generation descendant of Jìn Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn Qiáo.
Tǎn was recognized by his cousin Qiú at a young age.
In the early Jiànchuán era of Qí,
he served as Nánjùn Wángguó Chángshì,
and was soon appointed Cánlíng Lìng,
then promoted to Nánzhōngláng Lùshì Cānjūn.
He was known for his capability and efficiency wherever he served.
When Nánkāng Wáng became Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
Tǎn served as Xīzhōngláng Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
concurrently holding the position of Zhǎnglìu.
When the Righteous Army rose,
he was promoted to Zīyì Cānjūn.
At that time, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn Yáng Gōngzé, who was Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
led his army to Xiàkǒu.
The Western Court deliberated on who should govern the provincial affairs.
Tǎn said to the assembly:
"The disposition of the people in the Xiāng region
is easily disturbed and difficult to trust.
If only military men are used,
the common people will fear encroachment and exploitation;
if literati are sent,
their authority and strategy will not be asserted.
If you truly wish to pacify the provincial capital
and ensure sufficient food for both the army and civilians,
there is no one superior to this old minister.
In the campaign against the Xiānliú,
I secretly offered myself."
So they followed his suggestion.
He was then appointed Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ and Chángshā Tàishǒu,
acting as Xiāngzhōu Shì.
Tǎn had previously served in Xiāngzhōu
and had many old favors.
Many people welcomed him along the road.
Upon arrival, he selected capable officials,
assigned them to the ten commanderies,
mobilized all able-bodied men,
transported over three hundred thousand hú of grain,
delivering it to the Righteous Army,
thus providing ample provisions.
At that time, Dōnghūn sent Ānchéng Tàishǒu Liú Xīzǔ to defeat Fàn Sēngjiǎn, the Tàishǒu selected by Xītái, at Píngdū.
Xīzǔ then sent a proclamation to the Xiāng region,
whereupon Shǐxīng Nèishǐ Wáng Sēngcàn responded.
The people of Shàolíng drove out their Nèishǐ Chǔ Jiàn,
and Zhōu Huī of Yǒngyáng raised an army to attack Shǐ'ān Commandery,
both siding with Sēngcàn.
Shào Tánnòng and Dèng Dàojiè of Guìyáng sought revenge for private feuds,
and consequently formed a party and joined them.
Sēngcàn proclaimed himself Píngxī Jiāngjūn and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ,
appointing Zhōu Shū of Yǒngyáng as his chief strategist,
and headquartered his army in Jiànníng.
From then on, all the commanderies in the Xiāng region
rose up like swarms;
only the four counties of Línxiāng, Xiāngyīn, Líuyáng, and Luó remained intact.
The people of the province all wanted to flee by boat,
but Tǎn gathered all the boats and burned them.
He dispatched general Yǐn Fǎlüè to resist Sēngcàn,
and they were in a stalemate.
The former Xiāngzhōu Zhènjūn Zhōng Xuánshào secretly plotted to join Sēngcàn,
recruiting hundreds of gentry and commoners,
all signing their names and setting a date
to rebel against the provincial capital.
Tǎn heard of their plot,
but pretended not to know.
He prolonged a lawsuit until night,
thus the city gates were not closed,
which made them suspicious.
Xuánshào had not yet acted.
The next morning, he went to Tǎn to ask why.
Tǎn detained him and conversed with him for a long time,
secretly sending his personal soldiers to search his house for documents.
Xuánshào was still sitting and had not yet left,
when the soldiers returned, reporting that they had found all the documents and their contents.
Xuánshào immediately confessed,
and was executed on the spot.
His documents were burned,
and no questions were asked of his other confederates.
The people were ashamed and yet submitted,
and the province was thus pacified.
Fǎlüè and Sēngcàn were in a stalemate for several months.
When the city of Jiànkāng was pacified,
Gōngzé returned to the province,
and the bandits began to disperse.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
for his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Lìpǔ Xiànzǐ,
with three hundred households.
He was promoted to Píngxī Sīmǎ and Xīnxīng Tàishǒu.
In the third year of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Xīzhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ,
and died
at the age of sixty-two.
His son, Quán, inherited his position.
Yuè Ǎi ěr Wèiyuǎn
was a native of Yùyáng in Nányáng.
He was a sixth-generation descendant of Jìn’s Shàngshū Ling, Guǎng.
His family had resided in Jiānglíng for generations.
His maternal uncle, the Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ Zōng Zhì,
once displayed various artifacts
to test his nephews.
Ǎi was still young at the time,
but the only things he chose were books.
Zōng Zhì thus considered him exceptional.
He then took one scroll each of historical narratives and biographies and gave them to Ǎi and the others,
telling them to read them completely
and relate what they remembered.
Ǎi read them briefly but recounted everything in full,
which pleased Zōng Zhì even more.
When Sòng’s Prince Jiànpíng, Jǐngsù, was the Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he appointed Ǎi as his Zhǔbù.
When Jǐngsù was assigned to Nánsúzhōu,
Ǎi again served as the Zhēngběi Xíngyù Cānjūn,
and was then transferred to be the Xiàng of Lóngyáng.
Due to mourning his father, he resigned his post.
The officials and common people went to the provincial government to petition for his return,
and he resumed his post after the burial was complete.
At that time, Qí’s Prince Yùzhāng, Yí, was the Wǔlíng Tàishǒu.
He was deeply impressed with Ǎi’s governance.
When Yí became the Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
he appointed Ǎi as the Piàojì Xíng Cānjūn and concurrently the Zhōu Zhǔbù,
participating in managing the affairs of the province.
Yí once asked Ǎi about the local customs and traditions,
the foundations and layout of the city walls,
and the dangerous and easy parts of the mountains and rivers.
Ǎi immediately answered every question,
as if consulting a map or record.
Yí held him in even higher regard.
The people in the province were jealous of him.
Some slandered Ǎi, saying the gate to his office was like a marketplace.
Yí sent someone to secretly observe him,
who found Ǎi closing his door and reading books.
When Yí returned to the capital,
he appointed Ǎi as the Tàiwèi Xíngyù Cānjūn,
managing documentation,
and subsequently promoted him to Zhījiāng Lìng.
He returned to serve as the Dàsīmǎ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn,
and was subsequently transferred to be Jìshì.
In the eighth year of Yǒngmíng,
Bādōng Wáng Zǐxiǎng, the Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ, raised troops and rebelled.
After he was defeated,
the government offices were burned down,
and the official documents
were all destroyed at once.
Emperor Wǔdì granted Ǎi an audience
and questioned him about the affairs of the West.
Ǎi’s response was detailed and astute,
and the Emperor was pleased.
He was appointed as the Jīngzhōu Zhìzhōng,
and was instructed to be responsible for restoring the provincial government offices.
When Ǎi returned to the province,
he repaired and renovated several hundred government quarters.
They were all completed after a short time,
and the corvée labor did not overburden the people.
The Jīng region believed that since Jìn’s Wáng Chén moved his garrison here,
such an achievement had never been seen.
In the ninth year,
Prince Yùzhāng, Yí, died.
Ǎi resigned his office to attend the funeral
and, leading the former officials of Jīng and Xiāng provinces,
erected a stele at the tomb site.
He was successively promoted to Chējì Píngxī Lùshì Cānjūn and Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He requested to join the western garrison and return home.
When the Prince Nánkāng served as Xīzhōngláng,
he appointed Ǎi as his Zīyì Cānjūn.
When the righteous army rose,
Xiāo Yǐngzhòu invited Ǎi, Zōng Kuài, and Liú Tǎn
and entrusted them with strategic planning.
When the Liáng court was established,
he was promoted to Zhèn Jūn Sīmǎ, Zhōngshū Shìláng, and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
At that time, the manufacturing of weapons and armor,
ships and military provisions,
and the court's ceremonial regulations
were all dependent on Ǎi.
Soon after, he was promoted to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
while retaining the position of Zuǒchéng.
When Emperor Hé went east,
he concurrently served as Wèiwèi Qīng on the road.
In the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Xiāojì Jiāngjūn and concurrently the Shǎofù Qīng.
Shortly thereafter, he was transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng
and concurrently served as the Dàzhōngzhèng of his home province.
Originally,
when Ǎi departed Jiānglíng,
he inexplicably found eight chariot wheel spokes on his boat,
resembling the quick-footed runners who clear the way for the Zhōngchéng.
It was indeed at this time that he was promoted to that office.
Ǎi was strong in his public duties,
and performed very ably while holding the censorial office.
When the Prince Xuānwǔ of Chángshā was about to be buried,
the carriage office suddenly lost an oiled net from its storeroom,
and wanted to investigate the person responsible.
Ǎi said:
“In the past, when Jìn’s armory caught fire,
Zhāng Huá believed that if ten thousand stones of oil were piled up, fire was inevitable.
Now, if there is ash in the storeroom,
it is not the fault of the officials.”
When they subsequently inspected it,
there was indeed a pile of ash.
People at the time praised his extensive knowledge and great tolerance.
In the second year,
he was dispatched out as Chíjìe, Dū Jìao Yuè Sānzhōu Zhū Jūn, Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng, and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ.
When the previous Cìshǐ, Xú Yuányú, was dismissed and returned home,
he encountered people from Shǐxīng rebelling on the road.
They chased away the Nèishǐ Cuī Mùshū,
and consequently looted Yuányú’s property.
Yuányú fled back to Guǎngzhōu,
borrowing troops from Ǎi,
ostensibly to suppress the rebels,
but actually plotting to attack Ǎi.
Ǎi realized this
and executed Yuányú.
Soon after, his title was advanced to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and he died in office.
Ǎi’s elder sister married the hermit Liú Qiú from the same commandery.
She was also intelligent, knowledgeable, and observant of ritual instructions.
When Ǎi was Cìshǐ,
he welcomed his sister to live in the official residence
and divided his salary and rank three ways.
The people in the West praised this.
His son, Fǎcái,
whose courtesy name was Yuánbèi,
had a good reputation along with his younger brother Fǎzàng from a young age.
In his youth, he traveled to the capital
and visited Shěn Yuè.
Yuè met him and praised him.
When Qí’s Emperor Hé was Xiàngguó,
Fǎcái was summoned to be a Fǔ Cānjūn.
Zhèn Jūn Xiāo Yǐngzhòu appointed him as Zhǔbù.
When the Liáng court was established,
he was appointed as Qǐbù Láng.
In the second year of Tiānjiān,
Ǎi was sent to govern the regions south of the Five Ridges.
Fǎcái remained appointed in the capital city,
and was promoted to Jīnbù Láng.
He resigned due to mourning his father.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén,
and was then sent out to be Biéjià of his home province.
He returned to the capital to serve as Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng,
and was again put in charge of Tōngshì.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
When the Prince Jìn’ān served in Jīngzhōu,
Fǎcái was again appointed as Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ.
He was again summoned to serve as Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and then sent out as Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Jiànkāng Lìng.
He did not accept his salary and emoluments.
By the time he left office,
the amount was nearly one hundred catties of gold,
which the county administration reported for transfer to the court treasury.
Gāozǔ commended his integrity and purity,
saying:
“Serving in office like this
can set an example for a hundred cities!”
He was immediately promoted to Tàizhōu Qīng.
Soon after, he was appointed Nánkāng Nèishǐ,
but he was ashamed to gain fame by declining salary,
so he declined the appointment and did not take office.
Shortly, he was transferred to Yúnqí Jiāngjūn and Shǎofù Qīng.
He was sent out to serve as Xìnwǔ Chángshǐ and Jiāngxià Tàishǒu.
After being replaced,
he submitted a memorial to return to his hometown via the shortest route.
Upon reaching home,
he partitioned his residence to form a temple,
dedicating his heart beyond material concerns.
The Crown Prince, regarding Fǎcái as a veteran minister,
repeatedly issued generous decrees
summoning him to travel east.
He died before he could depart,
at the age of sixty-three.
Chén’s Lìbù Shàngshū Yáo Chá said: Xiāo Yǐngzhòu raised the masses of the great province to gather in righteousness.
At that time,
people’s hearts could not yet comprehend it.
These three men
were the anchors of Chǔ.
In planning and establishment,
they were indeed instrumental.
In regional achievements,
Tǎn achieved the most;
in holding office and managing affairs,
Ǎi surpassed him.
That they all attained prestigious ranks
is fitting!
Memoir Fourteen: Liú Jìlián, Chén Bózhī.
Liú Jìlián, courtesy name Huìxù,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His father, Sīkǎo,
was prominent during the Sòng era as a distant relative of Sòng Gāozǔ,
and reached the position of Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Jì Lián had fame and reputation,
having served in prestigious offices early on.
When Qí Gāo Dì received the abdication,
he executed all close relatives of the Sòng imperial house.
(The purge) was about to reach Jì Lián and others,
but Tàizǎi Chǔ Yuān had always been good to him,
and insisted on pleading for him, so he was spared.
During the Jiànyuán era,
Jì Lián served as Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng.
At the beginning of the Yǒngmíng era,
he was sent out as the Internal Prefect (Nèishǐ) of Jiāngxià.
He was successively promoted to Píngnán Chángshā Nèishǐ,
Guànjūn Zhǎngshǐ, and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Guǎnglíng,
and concurrently managed the affairs of the headquarters and the province.
He returned to the capital to serve as Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
and was transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he was again sent out as Zhǎngshǐ to Píngxī Xiāo Yáoxīn, and Administrator of Nán Jùn.
At that time, all the sons of Míng Dì were young and weak.
For close internal relatives, he relied on Yáoxīn and his brothers;
for external relatives, he relied on the Empress's younger brother Liú Xuān, and the internal younger brother Jiāng Shí.
When Yáoxīn garrisoned Jiānglíng,
the expectations placed on him were very high.
However, after Yáoxīn arrived at the province,
he frequently recruited retainers and guests,
and greatly enriched himself.
Míng Dì greatly disliked this.
Jì Lián's nephew by clan, Wáng Huì of Lángxié, served as Yáoxīn's Cányì Cānjūn.
He had a beautiful appearance,
and was quite talented and articulate.
Yáoxīn treated him extremely well.
Wáng Huì was often neglectful (or arrogant).
During public meetings, he competed with Yáoxīn in insulting Jì Lián.
Jì Lián resented this,
and secretly submitted a memorial to Míng Dì,
stating that Yáoxīn displayed unusual behavior.
Míng Dì accepted the report,
and consequently made Yáoxīn the Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yōngzhōu.
Míng Dì secretly favored Jì Lián.
In the fourth year,
he made him Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Inspector of Yìzhōu,
ordering him to occupy the upstream region relative to Yáoxīn.
Jì Lián's father,
had served as (Inspector of) Yìzhōu during the Sòng dynasty.
He had been greedy, contemptible, and lacked administrative achievements,
yet the provincial people, due to a sense of loyalty (or propriety),
treated Jì Lián well.
When Jì Lián arrived at the post,
he visited and inquired after former elders,
comforted and welcomed both newcomers and old residents.
When he saw former officials who had served his father,
he would weep before them.
He appointed Gōng Qiè of Suìníng as the Headquarters Clerk (Fǔ Zhǔbù).
Qiè
was the grandson of Gōng Yǐng.
His family had generations of scholarly conduct,
which is why he was recruited.
When Dōng Hūn ascended the throne,
in the first year of Yǒngyuán (499 CE),
Jì Lián was summoned to serve as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
The roads were blocked, and he did not arrive.
Jì Lián heard that Dōng Hūn lacked virtue,
and that the capital was rife with turmoil.
He gradually became arrogant and conceited.
Originally known as a civil official,
he was naturally jealous and narrow-minded.
At this point, he became harsh, headstrong, cruel, and vicious,
and the local people began to harbor resentment and dissatisfaction.
In the ninth month of that year,
Jì Lián, using a gathering as an excuse,
mobilized five thousand able-bodied men,
claiming it was for military exercises.
He then dispatched Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Sòng Mǎi to lead them and attack Zhōngshuǐ.
Lǐ Tuō of Ráng knew about this in advance,
made preparations and defended the strategic pass.
Mǎi fought but was unsuccessful.
When he returned to the province,
many commanderies and counties had already rebelled.
In this month,
Zhào Xùbó of Xīnchéng killed the Magistrate (Lìng) of Wǔchéng,
and drove out the Administrator of Shǐpíng.
In the tenth month,
Yuè Bǎochēng and Lǐ Nándāng of Jìnyuán killed their Administrator.
Bǎochēng proclaimed himself Inspector of Nán Qínzhōu,
and Nándāng proclaimed himself Inspector of Yìzhōu.
In the twelfth month,
Jì Lián dispatched Cānjūn Cuī Màozǔ to lead two thousand men to attack them,
carrying three days' rations.
It happened to be a year of great cold.
The bandits gathered together,
felled trees to block the roads.
The soldiers could find neither water nor fire (provisions),
suffered a major defeat and returned.
Seventy or eighty percent of them died.
In the first month of the following year,
Bó Yǎng of Xīnchéng drove out Qiáo Xīyuān, the Administrator of Suìníng.
In the third month,
Yōng Dàoxī of Bāxī led over ten thousand bandits and approached Bāxī,
just a few *lǐ* away from the commandery seat.
Dàoxī proclaimed himself Zhènxī Jiāngjūn,
and adopted the title Jiànyì.
Lǔ Xiūliè, the Administrator of Bāxī, and Lǐ Yīng, the Magistrate of Fú, barricaded themselves within the city and defended it.
Jì Lián dispatched Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Lǐ Fèngbó to lead five thousand troops to rescue them.
When Fèngbó arrived,
he and the commandery troops defeated and captured Dàoxī,
and executed him in the market of Fú.
Fèngbó then advanced alone into the eastern district of Bāxī to suppress the remaining bandits.
Lǐ Yīng stopped him and said:
"The troops are weary and the general is arrogant.
Relying on victory to traverse dangerous terrain
is not a good strategy.
It would be better to delay slightly,
and think about subsequent plans."
Fèngbó did not accept this,
and led all his troops into the mountains.
He was greatly defeated and forced out,
and fled back to the province.
In the sixth month,
Chéng Yánqī of Jiāngyáng rebelled,
and killed the Administrator Hé Fǎzàng.
Lǔ Xiūliè, fearing he could not protect himself,
fled and sought refuge with the Chancellor (Xiāng) of Bādōng, Xiāo Huìxùn.
In the tenth month,
Zhào Xùbó of Bāxī rebelled again.
He commanded twenty thousand men,
and emerged from Guǎnghàn.
He rode in a Buddhist carriage,
wrapped a black stone in five colors of silk,
and deceived the common people, saying:
"Heaven has given me a jade seal,
and I shall rule Shǔ."
Many foolish people followed him.
Jì Lián advanced to suppress him,
and sent Zhǎngshǐ Zhào Yuècháng as the vanguard.
The troops were defeated,
so Jì Lián again dispatched Lǐ Fèngbó to attack them via the Fú road.
Fèngbó’s separated division met the main army at Chántíng and joined them at the city.
They advanced and attacked the bandit stockade,
and greatly defeated them.
At that time, Shí Wén'ān, courtesy name Shǒuxīu, a man from Kuàijī,
lived in seclusion in his hometown,
devotedly practicing ritual and yielding.
He had replaced Jì Lián as Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng,
was sent out as Internal Prefect of Jiāngxià,
and had again replaced Jì Lián in returning to serve as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He was friendly with Jì Lián.
His son, Zhòngyuān, courtesy name Qīnhuí,
heard that the righteous army (Yì Shī) had risen,
and led his local people to respond to Gāo Zǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng).
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed Biéjià of Yǐngzhōu,
and followed Gāo Zǔ to pacify the capital district (Jīngyì).
The next spring,
he dispatched the attendants Chén Jiànzūn (陳建孫) to send Jìlián's (季連) younger brother, the Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎) Zǐyuān (子淵), and Jìlián's (季連) two sons as envoys to Shǔ (蜀),
conveying the imperial decree to comfort and console them.
Jìlián (季連) received the order
and prepared for their return.
Gāozǔ (高祖) appointed Dèng Yuánqǐ (鄧元起), a general from Xītái (西臺), as the Governor of Yìzhōu (益州).
Yuánqǐ (元起)
was from Nánjùn (南郡).
When Jìlián (季連) was in Nánjùn (南郡),
he had always looked down on Yuánqǐ (元起).
A record-keeper named Zhū Dàochēn (朱道琛),
who had once served as a Dūlù (都錄) in Jìlián's (季連) administration,
