was a lawless ruffian.
Having committed a crime,
Jìlián (季連) wanted to kill him,
but he escaped by fleeing.
At this time, he spoke to Yuánqǐ (元起), saying:
"Yìzhōu (益州) has been in chaos for a long time;
the public and private treasuries must have suffered great losses.
Liú Yìzhōu (劉益州) left completely empty-handed when he departed,
how could he possibly arrange for messengers to be sent far away again?
Dàochēn (道琛) requests to go first to inspect
and welcome you along the way;
otherwise,
provisions for a thousand li
will not be easy to obtain."
Yuánqǐ (元起) agreed to this.
Once Dàochēn (道琛) arrived,
his words were disrespectful,
and he also visited various officials and gentry in the prefecture and province,
seizing any objects he saw.
If he didn't get what he wanted,
he would say:
"It will eventually belong to others,
why be so reluctant to part with it?"
At this, the military and the government were greatly alarmed,
believing that when Yuánqǐ (元起) arrived, he would surely execute Jìlián (季連)
and bring disaster upon his allies,
and they all spoke of this to Jìlián (季連).
Jìlián (季連) also believed this to be true;
moreover, he regretted his past disrespect towards Yuánqǐ (元起),
and became increasingly resentful.
The Sīmǎ (司馬) Zhū Shìlüè (朱士略) persuaded Jìlián (季連)
to ask for Bāxī Jùn (巴西郡),
leaving his three sons as hostages,
and Jìlián (季連) agreed.
Soon after,
Jìlián (季連) summoned his assistants,
falsely claiming an order from Qí Xuāndé Huánghòu (齊宣德皇后),
gathered troops, rebelled again,
and captured and killed Zhū Dàochēn (朱道琛).
He sent a letter to Zhū Shìlüè (朱士略),
and also summoned Lǐ Yīng (李膺).
Yīng (膺) and Shìlüè (士略) both refused the summons.
When the envoy returned,
Yuánqǐ (元起) gathered his troops in Bāxī (巴西) to await him,
and Jìlián (季連) executed Shìlüè's (士略) three sons.
In the sixth month of the first year of Tiānjiān (天監) (502 CE),
Yuánqǐ (元起) arrived in Bāxī (巴西).
Jìlián (季連) sent his general Lǐ Fèngbó (李奉伯) and others to resist.
The armies engaged,
with gains and losses on both sides.
After a long time,
Fèngbó (奉伯) was defeated and retreated to Chéngdū (成都).
Jìlián (季連) herded the residents,
closed the city gates, and held firm.
Yuánqǐ (元起) gradually advanced and besieged him.
That winter,
Jiāng Xīzhī (江希之) and others, who were Jìlián's (季連) Chéngjú Cānjūn (城局參軍), plotted to surrender the city,
but it did not succeed,
and Jìlián (季連) executed them.
Shǔzhōng (蜀中) had been in turmoil for two years,
food in the city ran out,
a shēng (升) of rice cost three thousand (coins),
and there was nowhere to buy it.
Those who starved to death lay piled upon each other.
Those without relatives or friends
were even killed and eaten.
Jìlián (季連) ate porridge for months,
in dire hunger and with no plan.
In the first month of the second year (503 CE),
Gāozǔ (高祖) sent the Zhǔshū (主書) Zhào Jǐngyuè (趙景悅) to proclaim an imperial decree for Jìlián (季連) to surrender,
and Jìlián (季連) bared his upper body to beg for punishment.
Yuánqǐ (元起) moved Jìlián (季連) outside the city,
and soon after visited him,
treating him with courtesy.
Jìlián (季連) thanked him, saying:
"If I had known this earlier,
how could there have been the events of the other day?"
Yuánqǐ (元起) executed Lǐ Fèngbó (李奉伯) and all the other rebel leaders,
and sent Jìlián (季lián) back to the capital.
When Jìlián (季連) was about to depart,
no one saw him off,
except Gōng Qiè (龔愜).
Initially,
when Yuánqǐ (元起) was en route,
fearing the campaign would not succeed
and that he would have nothing to reward with,
he promised all who joined him
official appointments.
Thus, those who received the official documents of Biéjià (別駕) and Zhìzhōng (治中)
numbered nearly two thousand men.
After Jìlián (季連) arrived,
he went to the palace gate to express his apologies,
and Gāozǔ (高祖) granted him an audience.
Jìlián (季連) entered through the Dōngyèmén (東掖門),
bowing his head to the ground every few steps
until he reached Gāozǔ (高祖).
Gāozǔ (高祖) smiled and said to him:
"You wanted to emulate Liú Bèi (劉備), but you didn't even reach the level of Gōngsūn Shù (公孫述).
Did you have no '臥龍 (Wòlóng, Crouching Dragon)' minister?"
Jìlián (季連) bowed his head again to apologize.
He was pardoned and reduced to a commoner.
In the first month of the fourth year (505 CE),
while leaving through the Jiànyángmén (建陽門),
he was killed by Lìn Dàogōng (藺道恭) from Shǔ (蜀).
When Jìlián (季連) was in Shǔ (蜀),
he had killed Dàogōng's (道恭) father,
and Dàogōng (道恭) had fled.
Now, he took his revenge.
Chén Bózhī (陳伯之) was
from Suīlíng (睢陵), Jìyīn (濟陰).
As a child, he possessed great physical strength.
At thirteen or fourteen,
he liked to wear an otter fur hat
and carry a dagger.
He would watch for ripe rice in the neighboring fields
and steal and cut it.
Once, he was seen by a field owner,
who reprimanded him, saying:
"Chǔzǐ (楚子), don't move!"
Bózhī (伯之) said to the field owner:
"Your rice is fortunately abundant,
what's the harm in one load?"
The field owner was about to seize him,
but Bózhī (伯之) advanced with his staff-knife,
intending to stab him,
saying:
"Chǔzǐ (楚子) will definitely show you!"
The field owners all ran away,
and Bózhī (伯之) leisurely carried the rice home.
When he grew older,
he frequently committed robberies in Zhōnglí (鍾離).
Once, he used his face to spy on someone's boat,
and the boatman chopped at him,
cutting off his left ear.
Later, he followed Wáng Guǎngzhī (王廣之), a Chējì Jiāngjūn (車騎將軍) from his hometown.
Guǎngzhī (廣之) admired his bravery,
and whenever he lay down at night,
he always brought Bózhī (伯之) with him on campaigns.
Qí Ānlù Wáng (齊安陸王) Zǐjìng (子敬) was in Nányánzhōu (南兗州),
and held a considerable armed force for self-defense.
Míngdì (明帝) dispatched Guǎngzhī (廣之) to suppress Zǐjìng (子敬).
When Guǎngzhī (廣之) reached Ōuyáng (歐陽),
he sent Bózhī (伯之) as a vanguard.
When the city gate opened,
he entered alone and decapitated Zǐjìng (子敬).
He also repeatedly achieved military successes,
and was successively promoted for his merits to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn (冠軍將軍) and Piàojì Sīmǎ (驃騎司馬),
and enfeoffed as the Earl of Yúfù Xiàn (魚復縣),
with a stipend of five hundred households.
Dōnghūn granted Chén Bózhī the credentials (Jié), appointed him Supervisor of the various advance armies (Dū Qiánqū Zhū Jūnshì), and Governor of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ).
His generalship remained as before.
Soon after, he was transferred to Jiāngzhōu.
He occupied Xúnyáng
to resist the righteous army (Yìjūn).
When Yǐngchéng
was pacified, Gāozǔ captured Bózhī’s banner master, Sū Lóngzhī.
He sent Lóngzhī to persuade Bózhī,
and immediately appointed him General Who Pacifies the East (Āndōng Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Although Bózhī
accepted the appointment, he still held doubts,
falsely stating:
“The main army does not yet need to advance immediately.”
Gāozǔ said to his generals:
“Bózhī’s
answer shows that his heart is not yet settled.
While he is still hesitant,
we should press him.”
The assembled armies then approached Xúnyáng.
Bózhī retreated to defend Nánhú,
and only then submitted.
He was promoted to the title General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn),
and advanced along with the forces.
Bózhī camped at Límén (the Fence Gate),
and soon advanced to Xīmíng Mén (the West Bright Gate).
Before Jiànkāng
city was pacified, whenever someone surrendered and came out,
Bózhī would summon them and whisper in their ear.
Gāozǔ feared that he might again harbor rebellious intentions,
and secretly told Bózhī:
“I heard that those in the city are extremely angry that you handed Jiāngzhōu
over and surrendered. They intend to send assassins to strike you.
You should take heed of this.”
Bózhī did not believe this yet.
At that time, Zhèng Bólún, a general under Dōnghūn, surrendered.
Gāozǔ sent Bólún to visit Bózhī,
and instructed him to say:
“Those in the city are extremely angry with you.
They plan to send a messenger to lure you back with noble titles and rewards.
If you surrender to them again,
they will surely chop off your hands and feet while you are alive.
If you do not surrender,
they plan to send assassins to kill you.
You must be deeply prepared.”
Bózhī was terrified,
and from then on, he harbored no divergent intentions.
He fought vigorously and achieved merit.
When the city was pacified,
he was promoted to the title General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn),
enfeoffed as the Duke of Fēngchéng County (Fēngchéng Xiàn Gōng),
with a tax household quota of two thousand,
and sent back to guard his post.
Bózhī was illiterate.
When he returned to Jiāngzhōu,
if he received official documents, memorials, or lawsuits,
he would only make a large “Nuo” (Affirmation/Yes) mark.
When business arose,
the Secretary (Diǎnqiān) would relay the verbal instructions,
and all decisions regarding granting or denying were determined by the responsible officials.
Bózhī had old friendships with Dèng Shàn of Yùzhāng and Dài Yǒngzhōng of Yǒngxīng.
Shàn had previously hidden Bózhī’s son Yīng, saving him from disaster,
and Bózhī especially appreciated this favor.
When he was in the province,
he appointed Shàn as Biéjià
(Vice Governor) and Yǒngzhōng as Secretary (Jìshì Cānjūn).
Chǔ Yuè
of Hénán, was a man of shallow conduct in the capital.
At the end of Qí, he served in the West Office (Xīcáo) of Yángzhōu.
When the chaos occurred, he resided in his neighborhood;
while many lightweight opportunists managed to achieve status,
only Yuè remained unsuccessful.
When Gāozǔ
ascended the throne, Yuè repeatedly visited the Minister Fàn Yún.
Yún
did not like Yuè and firmly refused him entry.
Yuè grew angrier,
and privately said to his acquaintances:
“Since the Jiànwǔ
era, those from the lowest, common ranks
have all transformed into noble persons.
What crime have I committed to be rejected?
Now the country is newly founded,
famine is unending,
and the chaos is yet undetermined.
Chén Bózhī commands powerful troops in Jiāngzhōu.
He is not a hereditary subject
and harbors self-doubt.
Moreover, the planet Mars (Yínghuò) guards the Southern Dipper (Nándǒu)—
surely this sign is manifesting for me!
If I make a move now,
and if the affair does not succeed,
I can enter Wèi.
Why should I lose status by serving in Hénán Jùn?”
Thereupon, he attached himself to Bózhī’s clerk, Wáng Sīmù,
and was greatly favored and trusted.
When Bózhī’s townsman Zhū Lóngfú became Assistant to the Governor (Zhǎngliú Cānjūn),
they both exploited Bózhī’s ignorance and stupidity
to act villainously and dangerously without restraint.
Matters of punishment and governance, success and obstruction,
were all monopolized by them.
Bózhī’s son Hǔyá,
was then General of the Inner Chamber (Zhígé Jiāngjūn).
Gāozǔ personally drafted Lóngfú’s
crimes, handing the document directly to Hǔyá.
Hǔyá sealed it and showed it to Bózhī.
Gāozǔ also sent a replacement for the Jiāngzhōu Biéjià, Dèng Shàn, but Bózhī
refused to accept either order.
He replied to Gāozǔ:
“Lóngfú is a fierce and brave young man.
Dèng Shàn’s services have been effective.
I request that the Biéjià
sent by the court be made the Zhìzhōng (Administrative Assistant).”
Shàn thereupon constantly urged Bózhī, saying:
“The imperial treasury and storehouses are exhausted,
they lack weaponry,
the three granaries have no rice,
and the eastern regions are afflicted by famine and migration.
This is a chance that happens once in ten thousand generations,
and the opportunity must not be missed.”
Yuè and Yǒngzhōng regularly supported this plan.
Bózhī said to Shàn:
“I shall submit a petition for you this time.
If I fail again,
I will immediately go downriver with you and rebel.”
Gāozǔ commanded that Shàn be placed in charge of one commandery within the region.
Bózhī then assembled his staff and provincial subordinates and said:
“By the decree of the Prince of Jiàn’ān (Jiàn’ān Wáng) of Qí,
I have mobilized 100,000 righteous volunteers north of the Jiāng (Yangtze River).
They have already reached Liùhé.
I am now ordered to use the resources of Jiāngzhōu to quickly transport provisions downstream.
I have received the great favor of Emperor Míngdì,
and I vow to repay it with my life.
I will now immediately prepare and make arrangements.”
He instructed Yuè to falsely write a letter from Xiāo Bǎoyín,
which he showed to his subordinates.
He erected an altar in front of the main hall,
sacrificed animals, and swore an oath.
Bózhī drank first,
and the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) and others below him then ritually drank the blood in sequence.
Yuè advised Bózhī:
“Now that we are undertaking a great matter,
we should draw upon popular support.
Chéng Yuánchōng is not wholeheartedly with us.
The Administrator of Línchuān (Línchuān Nèishǐ), Wáng Guān,
is the grandson of Sēngqián,
and his personal character is not bad.
He should immediately be summoned and made the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ),
replacing Yuánchōng.”
Bózhī agreed,
and appointed Yuè
as the Administrator of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng Tàishǒu), adding the title General Who Suppresses Rebellion (Tǎonì Jiāngjūn);
Yǒngzhōng was made General Who Assists Righteousness (Fǔyì Jiāngjūn);
Lóngfú was made Governor of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ)
and led five hundred men to guard Dàléi.
The commander of the Dàléi garrison was Shěn Huìxiū,
and his General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán) military assistant was Lǐ Yánbó.
He also sent his townsmen Sūn Lín
and Lǐ Jǐng to take orders from Lóngfú. Lín
was appointed Governor of Xúzhōu, and Jǐng was appointed Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
Zhèng Bólún, the Administrator of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Tàishǒu), raised the commandery troops to resist and defend.
As Chéng Yuánchōng
had already lost his post, he gathered several hundred men at his home,
and used Bózhī’s Secretaries Lǚ Xiàotōng and Dài Yuánzé as internal contacts.
Every morning, Bózhī habitually watched performances,
and he regularly went to sleep in the late afternoon.
His attendants and bodyguards were all resting.
Yuánchōng took advantage of this lapse in vigilance,
entered through the North Gate,
and went straight to the front of the main hall.
Bózhī, hearing the shouting,
personally led his men out to counterattack.
Yuánchōng’s strength was insufficient to fight,
so he fled and escaped to Lúshān.
Initially,
Yuánchōng (元沖) raised an army.
He sought Zhāng Xiàojì (張孝季) of Xúnyáng (尋陽),
and Xiàojì (孝季) followed him.
After their defeat,
Bózhī (伯之) pursued Xiàojì (孝季) but did not catch him.
He captured Xiàojì's (孝季) mother, Lady Láng (郎氏),
and killed her by pouring hot wax on her.
He sent a messenger back to the capital to report to Hǔyá (虎牙) and his brothers.
Hǔyá (虎牙) and others fled to Xūyí (盱眙).
The people of Xūyí (盱眙), Xú Ān (徐安), Zhuāng Xīngshào (莊興紹), and Zhāng Xiǎnmíng (張顯明), ambushed them.
They could not resist
and were instead killed.
Gāozǔ (高祖) dispatched Wáng Mào (王茂) to attack Bózhī (伯之).
When Bózhī (伯之) heard that Mào (茂) was coming,
he said to Chǔ Quán (褚𥱰) and others:
"Since Wáng Guān (王觀) has not accepted the command,
and Zhèng Bólún (鄭伯倫) is unwilling to follow,
we should be trapped empty-handed.
Now, we should first pacify Yùzhāng (豫章),
open up the southern route,
mobilize more manpower,
and transport more provisions and grain.
Then, we can sweep northwards
to strike at their hungry and weary troops.
There will be no worry of failure."
So, he left the local man Táng Gàirén (唐蓋人) to guard the city,
and they all headed towards Yùzhāng (豫章).
The Grand Administrator, Zhèng Bólún (鄭伯倫), held his ground firmly,
and Bózhī (伯之) attacked but could not take it.
When Wáng Mào's (王茂) vanguard arrived,
Bózhī (伯之) arranged his troops to face the enemy.
He was defeated and fled,
escaping along a secret path to north of the Jiāng (江),
entering Wèi (魏) with his son Hǔyá (虎牙) and Chǔ Quán (褚𥱰).

Wèi (魏) appointed Bózhī (伯之) as Envoy with Credentials (使持節), Palace Attendant (散騎常侍), Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Huáinán (都督淮南諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the South (平南將軍), Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (光祿大夫), and Marquis of Qǔjiāng County (曲江縣侯).
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (天監) [505 CE],
an imperial edict commanded the Grand Commandant (太尉), Prince Hóng (宏) of Línchuān (臨川), to lead a large army to attack the north.
Hóng (宏) ordered his secretary Qīu Chí (丘遲) to write a private letter to Bózhī (伯之), saying: "General Chén (陳), are you well?
Most fortunately.
Your bravery surpasses all three armies,
and your talent is unique in the world.
You abandoned the small ambition of the sparrow,
and yearned for the wild goose to soar
high.
In the past, you adapted to opportunities,
met an enlightened lord,
achieved great deeds,
founded a state and inherited a family.
With crimson wheels and ornate hubs,
commanding banners across ten thousand li,
how magnificent that was!
How
is it that in one morning you became a fugitive captive,
trembling at the sound of a whistling arrow,
kneeling before a nomad's yurt?
How ignoble is that!
Examining your decision to leave or stay,
there was no other
reason,
but simply that you could not examine yourself internally
and were influenced by external rumors,
becoming lost and reckless,
leading to this.
The Sacred Court pardons crimes and evaluates merits,
overlooking flaws and employing talents,
gathering
loyal hearts from all under heaven,
and reassuring the wavering in all things.
This is known to you, General,
and requires no lengthy discourse from me.
Zhū Wěi (朱鮪) shed the blood of his kin,
Zhāng Xiù (張繡) raised a
weapon against his beloved son,
yet the Han (漢) lord did not doubt them,
and the Wei (魏) ruler treated them as before.
Moreover, General, you have not committed the crimes of those men of old,
and your achievements are significant in this age.
To know to turn back from a迷途 (lost path)
is what the ancient sages approved;
to return from not far off
is highly praised by old canons.
Our Emperor bends the law to extend grace,
letting even a swallowed boat escape.
General, your pines
and cypresses are not cut down,
your relatives live in peace;
your high platform has not collapsed,
your beloved concubine is still there.
Your lingering thoughts,
how can they not be mentioned!
Now, meritorious officials and famous generals,
arranged in an orderly line
like wild geese.
Wearing yellow and purple sashes,
they advise on strategies in the command tent;
riding light chariots and carrying credentials,
they undertake responsibilities on the frontier.
They have all sworn oaths by killing a horse,
to be passed down to their descendants.
General, are you alone
to shamelessly beg for your life,
and gallop about in a foreign land?
Is this not lamentable!
For with the strength of Mùróng Chāo (慕容超),
his body was sent to the eastern market;
with the might of Yáo Hóng (姚泓),
he was bound and presented at the western capital.
Therefore, it is known that where frost and dew are equally distributed,
no different species can grow;
in the old lands of Jī (姬)
and Hàn (漢),
no mixed breeds should be taken.
The northern barbarians have usurped the Central Plains,
for many years.
Their evil has accumulated and their misfortune is full,
it is time for them to be utterly destroyed.
Moreover, the false usurpers are foolish and cunning,
slaughtering
each other.
Their tribes are scattered,
and their chieftains are suspicious and disloyal.
They are about to be led by the neck to the barbarian mansion,
and have their heads displayed in the Straw Street.
Yet you, General, are like a fish swimming in a boiling cauldron,
and nesting atop a flying banner,
is this not bewildering!
In the late spring, the third month,
the grass in Jiāngnán (江南) grows long,
varied flowers blossom on trees,
flocks of birds fly about.
Seeing the banners and drums of your old country,
remembering your past in those days,
stroking the lute
and ascending the parapet,
would you not feel sorrow and regret?
Thus, Lián Gōng (廉公)'s longing for the Zhao (趙) general,
and Wú Zǐ (吳子)'s weeping by the Xīhé (西河),
are human emotions.
General, are you alone without feelings!
I hope
you will soon make a good plan,
and seek much fortune for yourself."
Bózhī (伯之) then, with 8,000 troops, returned to Shòuyáng (壽陽).
Hǔyá (虎牙) was killed by the Wèi (魏) people.
When Bózhī (伯之) arrived,

he was appointed Envoy with Credentials (使持節), Area Commander-in-chief of all military affairs in Xīyù Prefecture (都督西豫州諸軍事), General Who Pacifies the North (平北將軍), Governor of Xīyù Prefecture (西豫州刺史),
Marquis of Yǒngxīn County (永新縣侯),
with a fief of one thousand households.
Before he took up the post,
he was again appointed Palace Attendant (通直散騎常侍), General of Agile Cavalry (驍騎將軍),
and then Grand Master of the Middle (太中大夫).
After a long time,
he died at home.
Some of his sons remained in Wèi (魏).
Chǔ Quán (褚𥱰) was in Wèi (魏),
and the Wèi (魏) people wanted to promote him.
At a Wèi (魏) imperial banquet,
Quán (𥱰) playfully composed a poem, saying:
"On my cap I wear a caged crown,
over my trousers I wear a crimson robe;
I do not know if this present is right,
I do not know if the past was not wrong."
The Wèi (魏) people were angered,
and exiled him to become the Grand Administrator of Shǐpíng (始平).
He hunted daily,
fell from his horse, and died.
The historian comments: "Liú Jìlián (劉季連) was a minor official of letters,
yet he could not preserve himself; this is indeed the result of accustomed chaos.
Chén Bózhī (陳伯之) was a small man who commanded the instruments of a gentleman,
and the bandits falsely accused and stripped him of them.
How could he last long?"
Collation Notes

Biographies, Chapter 15: Wáng Zhān (王瞻), Wáng Zhì (王志), Wáng Jùn (王峻), Wáng Jiǎn (王暕) (son Xùn (訓)), Wáng Tài (王泰), Wáng Fèn (王份) (grandsons Xī (錫), Qiān (僉)), Zhāng Chōng (張充), Liǔ Yùn (柳惲), Cài Zūn (蔡撙), Jiāng Qiàn (江蒨).
Wáng Zhān (王瞻), courtesy name Sīfàn (思範),
was from Línyí (臨沂), Lángyé (琅邪), a grand-nephew of Sòng (宋) Grand Preceptor Hóng (弘).
His grandfather, Liǔ (柳),
was Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (光祿大夫) and Marquis of Dōngtíng (東亭).
His father, Yóu (猷),
was Minister of Justice (廷尉卿).
When Zhān (瞻) was a few years old,
he once received instruction from a teacher.
At that time, an entertainer passed by his gate,
and all his classmates went out to watch,
but Zhān (瞻) alone did not look,
continuing to recite as before.
His paternal cousin, Minister of the Secretariat (尚書僕射) Sēngdá (僧達), heard of this and was impressed,
saying to Zhān's (瞻) father:
"Our clan will not decline;
its future rests with this child."
At the age of twelve,
he mourned his father,
and was known for his filial piety.
When the mourning period ended, he inherited the title of Marquis of Dōngtíng (東亭).
Zhān in his youth was frivolous and careless,
enjoyed leisure wandering,
and was considered a nuisance by the local community.
When he grew up,
he largely corrected his ways and possessed the integrity of a scholar.
He dabbled in books and records,
and was especially skilled at archery.
He began his career (*qǐjiā*) as a Zuòzuò Zuǒláng,
and was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén, Tàiwèi Zhǔbù, and Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
After a while,
he was sent out to serve as the Nèishǐ of Póyáng,
and when his term of office was complete,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén.
He then served as a Yǒu (attendant) to the Prince Nánhǎi of Qí,
shortly thereafter transferring to Cóngshì Zhōngláng for the Sītú, Prince Jìnglíng.
The Prince treated him with great respect as a guest.
When the Prince Nánhǎi became Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
Zhān served as his Zhǎngshǐ.
He was again sent out to fill the position of Biéjià Cóngshìshǐ of Xúzhōu,
and was promoted to Zhǎngshǐ of Piàojì Jiāngjūn, Wáng Yàn.
After Wáng Yàn was executed,
Zhān was sent out to serve as the Tàishǒu of Jìnlíng.
Zhān governed conscientiously and honestly,
but his wife and children did not escape hunger and cold.
At that time, Dàsīmǎ Wáng Jìngzé raised troops and rebelled.
Their route passed through Jìnlíng,
and many people in the commandery sided with Jìngzé.
After the rebel forces were defeated,
the imperial forces hunted down the rebel followers.
Zhān spoke to the court, saying:
"Ignorant people are easily swayed,
and the law should not be enforced exhaustively against them."
Emperor Míng agreed to this,
and tens of thousands of people were thereby saved.
He was summoned to court and appointed Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng,
Fǔjūn, Zhǎngshǐ of the Prince Jiàn'ān,
and Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
When Gāozǔ established his administrative headquarters (*Bàfǔ*),
Zhān was made Dàsīmǎ Xiàngguó Zīyì Cānjūn,
overseeing Lùshì.
When the government of Liáng was established,
he became Shìzhōng,
promoted to Zuǒmín Shàngshū,
and shortly thereafter transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
Zhān was naturally straightforward and honest.
While managing the personnel selection department,
his recommendations often followed his personal judgment.
He was quite fond of wine;
whenever he drank, it might last the whole day,
yet his mind became more lucid and capable,
and he did not neglect his bureaucratic duties.
Gāozǔ often praised Zhān for possessing three talents:
archery, *jué* (a board game), and wine.
Shortly thereafter, he was given the additional title of Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn,
but due to illness, he did not take the post.
He continued as Shìzhōng,
overseeing Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn.
Before formally taking that post,
he died,
at the age of forty-nine.
His posthumous title was Kāng Hóu.
His son, Zhǎngxuán,
was a Zuòzuò Zuǒláng,
but died young.
Wáng Zhì, courtesy name Cìdào,
was a man from Línyí, Lángyé.
His grandfather, Tánshǒu,
was Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Yùníng Wén Hóu during Sòng;
his father, Sēngqián,
was Sīkōng and Jiǎnmù Gōng during Qí: both had great reputations.
When Zhì was nine years old,
he observed mourning for his birth mother,
and his appearance, marred by grief and emaciation,
was remarkable to his relatives.
Upon reaching adulthood,
he was selected to marry Princess Āngù, daughter of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
and was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi and Mìshū Láng.
He was successively promoted to Tàiwèi Xíng Cānjūn,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and Wǔlíng Wáng Wénxué.
When Chǔ Yuān became Sītú,
he appointed Zhì as his Zhǔbù.
Chǔ Yuān said to Sēngqián:
"The favor of the court,
is essentially extraordinary;
the glory that can be bestowed
lies in humbly appointing your worthy son."
He was successively promoted to Gōngcáo Shǐ for Zhènběi, Prince Jìnglíng, and Yǒu (attendant) to the two princes of Ānlù and Nánjùn.
He entered the court to become Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed Nèishǐ of Xuānchéng.
He was pure, cautious, and benevolent.
Two commandery residents, Zhāng Ní and Wú Qìng, disputed a field,
and the case remained unresolved for a year.
When Zhì arrived in office,
the elders said to one another:
"Prefect Wáng Fǔjūn practices virtuous governance,
yet our community still has this dispute."
Ní and Qìng consequently held hands and asked for pardon,
and the land they had disputed was thereafter left fallow.
He was summoned and appointed Huángmén Shìláng,
and shortly thereafter promoted to Lìbù Shìláng.
He was sent out to serve as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Dōngyáng.
In the commandery prison, there were more than ten serious criminals.
On the day of the Winter Solstice, he released them all to return home.
After the festival, they all returned,
except for one who was late.
The prison officers reported this.
Zhì said:
"This is strictly the affair of the Tàishǒu.
Those in charge need not worry."
The next morning,
the man indeed came personally to the prison,
apologizing that his wife was pregnant.
The officials and people admired and submitted to him even more.
After holding office for three years,
in the second year of Yǒngmíng of Qí,
he entered the court to become Shìzhōng.
Before being formally invested,
he was transferred to Lìbù Shàngshū.
In personnel selection, he was praised for being harmonious and reasonable.
When Cuī Huìjǐng was defeated,
he was, following standard practice, given the additional title of Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Línrǔ Hóu.
He firmly declined the appointment and did not accept it.
Instead, he was appointed to oversee Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
When the righteous army arrived,
people within the city harmed Dōnghūn (Emperor Hūn),
and all the officials signed a document accompanying his head when it was sent away.
Zhì heard of this and sighed, saying:
"Although a cap may be worn out,
should it be placed underfoot?"
He then took a leaf from a tree in the courtyard, crushed it, and pretended to take medicine,
feigning unconsciousness,
and did not sign the document.
When Gāozǔ reviewed the memorial and saw that Zhì had not signed it,
he secretly admired him,
and did not reprimand him for it.
When the administrative headquarters (*Bàfǔ*) was opened,
Zhì was made Yòujūn Jiāngjūn and Zhǎngshǐ to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
When the government of Liáng was established,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngshū Lìng.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he retained his current office while overseeing Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn.
In that same year,
he was promoted to Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
His governance was pure and tranquil,
eliminating burdensome regulations.
There was a widow in the capital who had no son.
When her mother-in-law died,
she borrowed money to arrange the funeral and burial.
After the burial, she had no means to repay the debt.
Zhì pitied her righteousness,
and used his salary to pay it off for her.
As it was a year of famine,
every morning he prepared congee at the commandery gate,
to distribute to the populace.
The people praised him endlessly.
Three years later,
he became Sànqí Chángshì and Zhōngshū Lìng,
overseeing Yóují Jiāngjūn.
After Zhì served as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and occupied the office of the Capital Prefecture,
he developed an attitude of being content with his lot.
He often told his sons and nephews:
"Xiè Zhuāng, during the reign of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
only reached the position of Zhōngshū Lìng.
Looking at myself, how could I possibly surpass him?"
Consequently, he frequently declined duties citing illness,
and restricted contact with visitors.
He was promoted to Qián Jiāngjūn and Tàicháng Qīng.
In the sixth year,
he was sent out to serve as Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, Zhǎngshǐ of the Prince Shǐxīng of Ānxī, and Tàishǒu of Nánjùn.
The following year,
he was promoted to Jūnshī Jiāngjūn, Zhǎngshǐ of the Prince Póyáng of Píngxī, and Tàishǒu of Jiāngxià,
receiving the additional salary rank of Zhōng Èrqiān Shí for both positions.
In the ninth year,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
In the twelfth year,
he died,
at the age of fifty-four.
Zhì was skilled in the *cǎo* and *lì* scripts (cursive and clerical),
which were considered models of calligraphy at the time.
Xú Xīxiù, Yóují Jiāngjūn of Qí, who was also known for his excellent calligraphy,
often referred to Zhì as
the "Sage of Calligraphy" (Shū Shèng).
Shì’s family resided generation after generation in Jìankāng’s Jìnzhōng Lǐ, Mǎfān Xiàng.
Since his father Sēngqián,
the family ethos was largely one of leniency and forgiveness;
Shì was especially generous and kind.
In all the offices he held,
he never impeached anyone for faults or transgressions.
A guest of his once stole the axle-pin from Shì’s carriage and sold it.
Shì knew but did not question him,
treating him as before.
For guests who frequented his home,
he would specifically cover up their faults and praise their good qualities.
His brothers, sons, and nephews were all earnest, modest, and amiable.
People of the time called the various princes of Mǎfān “the elders.”
In the fourth year of Pǔtōng,
Shì was reburied.
Gāozǔ bestowed a generous funeral stipend and gifts upon him,
and posthumously named him Ān.
He had five sons:
Jī, Xiū, Yīn, Cāo, and Sù,
all of whom were renowned.
Wáng Jùn, courtesy name Màoyuǎn,
was a native of Lángxié Línyí.
His great-grandfather, Jìnghóng,
was highly reputed in the Sòng dynasty,
holding positions up to Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His grandfather, Zànzhī,
was Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
His father, Xiùzhī,
was Wúxīng Tàishǒu.
Jùn was handsome in appearance in his youth
and had refined manners.
He began his career as a Zhùzuò Zuǒláng,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngjūn Lúlíng Wáng Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
Shàolíng Wáng Wénxué,
and Tàifù Zhǔbù.
The prefect, Zǐliáng, Prince of Jìnglíng of Qí, greatly appreciated and valued him.
He was promoted to Sītú Zhǔbù,
but resigned due to his father’s mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ
and Jìan’ān Wáng Yǒu.
He was sent out as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Guìyáng Nèishǐ.
At that time, when the righteous army arose,
many commanderies in the upper reaches of the river were alarmed and disturbed.
Jùn closed the city gates and remained calm,
and the entire commandery was pacified,
for which the common people relied on him.
In the early Tiānjian era,
he was recalled and appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Gāozǔ was very pleased with his demeanor and conduct,
and he was appreciated and promoted alongside Xiè Lǎn of Chénjùn.
Soon after, he was promoted to Lìbù.
He was not considered competent in that office,
so he was transferred to Zhēnglǔ Ānchéng Wáng Chángshǐ.
He also served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ and Yóují Jiāngjūn.
He was sent out as Xuānchéng Tàishǒu.
His governance was pure and harmonious,
and the officials and people were at peace with him.
After serving for three years,
he was summoned and appointed Shìzhōng,
then promoted to Dùzhī Shàngshū.
He also concurrently held the original office of Qǐbù Shàngshū
and supervised the construction of the Tàijí Diàn.
After the project was completed,
he was sent out as Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, Píngxī Chángshǐ, and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
Soon after, he was appointed Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn, Zhènxī Chángshǐ, and Shǔjùn Tàishǒu.
Upon his return, he served as Zuǒmín Shàngshū
and concurrently Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū,
where he gained an excellent reputation for his selections.
Jùn was by nature meticulous and elegant,
without any desire for competition or advancement.
He once made an agreement with Xiè Lǎn
that once they reached the office of Shìzhōng,
they would no longer seek further promotion.
Lǎn, after serving as Lìbù Shàngshū, was sent out as Wúxīng Jùn Tàishǒu.
He was impartial and unafraid of powerful oppressors,
which was also due to his indifferent attitude towards worldly affairs.
After Jùn became Shìzhōng,
although he did not withdraw,
he remained detached and self-possessed,
not pursuing any further engagements.
After a long time,
he submitted a memorial due to illness requesting to resign his post.
He was promoted to Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
but did not accept the appointment.
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
he died
at the age of fifty-six,
and was posthumously named Huìzǐ.
His sons were Cóng
and Wán.
Cóng was a Guózǐ Shēng
and married the daughter of Shǐxīng Wáng, Fánchāng Xiànzhǔ.
He was not intelligent
and was ridiculed by the students,
which led to a divorce.
Jùn thanked the prince,
and the prince said:
“This was the emperor’s intention;
I truly did not wish for this to happen.”
Jùn replied:
“My great-grandfather was the maternal grandson of Xiè Rénzǔ;
we do not rely on Your Highness’s marriage connection for our family status.”
Wáng Jiǎn, courtesy name Sīhuì,
was a native of Lángxié Línyí.
His father, Jiǎn, was Qí Tàiwèi and Nánchāng Wénxiàn Gōng.
When Jiǎn was a few years old,
his spirit and bearing were sharp and outstanding,
possessing the demeanor of an adult.
At that time, Wénxiàn served as chancellor,
and guests filled his home.
Upon seeing Jiǎn, they remarked to each other:
“The Duke’s talent and reputation
are present here again.”
At twenty years of age,
he was selected to marry Princess Huáinán,
appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
and then Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
He did not accept the appointment
and was instead appointed Jìn’ān Wáng Wénxué,
then promoted to Lúlíng Wáng Yǒu and Mìshū Chéng.
Emperor Míng issued an edict seeking extraordinary talents.
Shǐ’ān Wáng Yáoguāng submitted a memorial recommending Jiǎn and Dōnghǎi Wáng Sēngrú,
saying:
“I have heard that seeking worthy individuals is momentarily arduous,
but allows for eternal ease in governing with folded hands,
akin to cultivating sparse soil
or guiding a river.
I humbly observe that Your Majesty’s virtue is veiled by your imperial attire,
and your trust is complete in your seals.
White colts roam in empty valleys,
and egrets gather in the court.
Yet I fear that hidden dragons and diviners,
and treasured vessels among butchers and porters,
are being sought beyond the passes,
or found on the banks of the river.
This is not about making a single choice,
but rather seeking flavor from diverse sources.
And so, when the five notes weary the ear,
the nine artisans are consulted.
Deliberations sleep in the imperial ancestral temple,
while ears listen to the common people.
My position and responsibilities are weighty,
and my duty extends to the state and family.
I truly wish to ensure that reputation and reality do not diverge,
and that the path of opportunism is cut off.
Even powerful families of the highest rank
should be judged by their pure discourse;
talented young men of lower rank
should not be limited by their position or appearance.
I secretly observe Mìshū Chéng Wáng Jiǎn of Lángxié,
aged twenty-one,
whose family has shone brilliantly for seven generations,
the foremost scholarly clan within the seas.
His spirit is pure and his essence vibrant,
truly embodying moderation and harmony.
His discussions are as clear as Shūbǎo’s rational discourse,
and his joy in moral teachings rivals Yànfǔ’s.
Therefore, he already shines among his predecessors
and leads the younger generation.
His dwelling is free from worldly dust,
and his family possesses imperial gifts of books.
His prose and poetry are fresh and pure,
his essays profound and distant.
Though his chamber is close, his person is expansive;
though things are distant, the Dao is near.
He cultivates his virtue in retirement,
leaving official positions vacant.
Yet in the imperial court,
tens of thousands look up to him.
How can he be merely like Xún Lìng, who can be imagined,
or Lǐ Gōng, who is not forgotten?
He is truly a secret treasure of the eastern order,
a magnificent vessel of the state.”
He was appointed Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
When *Gāozǔ* opened his supreme headquarters,
he was appointed as an aide in the Household Department,
and promoted to Chief Clerk of the Establishment.
In the first year of *Tiānjiān* (502 CE),
he was appointed as Central Attendant of the Crown Prince,
holding concurrently the title of General of Valiant Cavalry,
and later entered the court to serve as Court Attendant.
He was sent out to serve as General Who Pacifies the North and Chief Clerk of the Central Army.
He again served as Court Attendant,
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of the Archery Division,
and promoted to Minister of the Five Armaments,
with the added title of Palace Attendant.
He was sent out to serve as Administrator of *Jìnlíng*.
He was recalled to serve as Minister of Personnel,
and soon concurrently held the position of Libationer of the Imperial University.
*Wáng Jiǎn* was a famous noble son,
and gained high praise in his youth.
When he managed the selection office,
his official duties were well-ordered;
however, being of noble and distinguished lineage,
he kept a distance from many people,
and failed to show concern for the humble and impoverished.
The public generally considered him rather harsh.
He was promoted to Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and shortly thereafter was additionally given the title of Court Attendant.
He was again promoted to Left Vice Director,
but resigned his office due to mourning for his mother.
He was recalled from mourning to serve as General of the Cloud Banners and Administrator of *Wú* County.
Upon returning, he served as Court Attendant and Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently holding the position of Libationer of the Imperial University.
In the winter of the fourth year of *Pǔtōng* (523 CE),
he died suddenly from illness,
aged forty-seven.
An imperial edict granted him posthumously the titles of Court Attendant, Director of the Central Secretariat, and General of the Central Army,
and provided him with the secret funerary objects from the Eastern Garden,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
and 100 bolts of cloth.
His posthumous name was *Jìng*.
He had four sons:
*Xùn*, *Chéng*, *Zhì*, and *Xū*,
all of whom became prominent.
*Wáng Xùn*, courtesy name *Huáifàn*,
was intelligent, alert, perceptive, and possessed good judgment in his youth.
The invited scholar *Hé Yìn* saw him and regarded him as exceptional.
At the age of thirteen,
when *Wáng Jiǎn* died, he was so overwhelmed by grief,
that his family members barely recognized him.
At sixteen,
he was summoned for an audience at the *Wéndé* Palace,
and his responses were clear and thorough.
The Emperor gazed after him for a long time,
turning to *Zhū Yì*, he said:
“It can truly be said that within a minister’s family, there is a future minister.”
He was appointed as a student of the Imperial University,
achieved the highest grade in the policy examination,
and was appointed Secretary of the Palace Library,
then promoted to Palace Attendant of the Crown Prince and Vice Director of the Palace Library.
He was transferred to Literary Scholar for the Prince of *Xuānchéng*, Mentor, and Central Attendant of the Crown Prince,
in charge of records.
Soon he was promoted to Court Attendant.
After he was formally appointed and entered for an audience,
*Gāozǔ* leisurely asked *Hé Jìngróng*:
“At what age did *Chǔ Yànhuí* become a chief minister?”
*Hé Jìngróng* replied:
“Slightly over thirty.”
The Emperor said:
“The present *Wáng Xùn*
is no less capable than *Yànhuí*.”
*Wáng Xùn* had a handsome appearance and fine deportment,
and was skilled in court movements.
The beauty of his literary works
made him the leader of the rising generation.
While serving in the Eastern Palace, he received special favor and courtesy.
He died in office due to illness,
aged twenty-six at the time.
He was granted his original office posthumously.
His posthumous name was *Wēnzǐ*.
*Wáng Tài*, courtesy name *Zhòngtōng*,
was the son of *Wáng Zhì*'s elder brother, *Wáng Cí*.
*Wáng Cí*,
during the *Qí* dynasty, successively served as Court Attendant and Administrator of *Wú* County,
and his reputation surpassed that of *Wáng Zhì*.
*Wáng Tài* was quick-witted and astute in his youth.
When he was a few years old,
his paternal grandmother gathered all the grandsons and nephews,
and scattered jujubes and chestnuts on the bed.
All the children rushed to seize them,
but *Wáng Tài* alone did not take any.
When asked the reason,
he replied:
“If I do not take them,
I will naturally be given a grant.”
Because of this, his maternal and paternal relatives regarded him as extraordinary.
When he grew up,
he was broad-minded, harmonious, gentle, and refined.
People never saw him display signs of joy or anger.
He started his career as Secretary to the Imperial Library,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was reassigned as Secretary of the Palace Library,

then promoted to Acting Assistant in the Judicial Department of the General of the Vanguard, Libationer of the Eastern Gate of the Establishment, and Chief Clerk of the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
When *Gāozǔ*'s supreme headquarters was established,
*Wáng Tài* was made Merit Officer of the General of Cavalry.
In the first year of *Tiānjiān*,
he was promoted to Vice Director of the Palace Library.
At the end of the *Yǒngyuán* era of *Qí* (c. 501 CE),
the rear palace caught fire,
and the flames spread to the Palace Library,
where the maps and books were scattered and almost entirely destroyed.
*Wáng Tài*, as Vice Director,
submitted a memorial requesting to review, verify, and copy the texts.
*Gāozǔ* complied with his request.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Gentleman Attendant of the Central Secretariat.
He was sent out to serve as Aide-in-Waiting to the Governor of *Nán Xú* Prefecture,
and gained a reputation for competence in his post.
He was again recalled to serve as Gentleman Attendant of the Central Secretariat,
and ordered to manage the affairs of the Director of Personnel.
He was progressively promoted to Palace Attendant and Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates,
and Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
still managing the Personnel Department as before.
Soon thereafter, he officially held the position.
Since the relocation south of the Yangtze River,
the Director of Personnel had ceased to preside over major selections;
for clerks and lower ranks,
the common people seeking appointment crowded in great numbers.
Few of his predecessors were able to fully meet the duties required.
When *Wáng Tài* held the office, he allowed no private influence or lobbying,
appointing clerks immediately based on who arrived first,
and did not change his decisions due to requests or recommendations, whether from the noble or the humble.
The entire realm praised his fairness.
He was progressively promoted to Grand Judge,
and Chief Clerk of the Establishment.
He was sent out as General Who Manifests Awe and Administrator of *Xīn'ān*.
While in the commandery, his harmonious administration gained the people's hearts.
He was recalled to serve as General Who Pacifies Afar,
and Chief Clerk of the Security Department.
Soon he was promoted to Court Attendant.
Shortly after, he was made Chamberlain of the Crown Prince, concurrently holding the position of Commandant of Infantry,
and again served as Court Attendant.
Subsequently, he was promoted to Chief Clerk of the General of Benevolent Awe and Administrator of Southern *Lánlíng*,
managing the affairs of the establishment, prefecture, and state of the Prince of *Nánkāng*.
When the Prince changed positions,
he again served as Chief Clerk of the Northern General of the Gentlemen, managing the affairs of the establishment, prefecture, and state of the Prince of *Yùzhāng*,
retaining the position of Administrator as before.
He entered the court to serve as Minister of the Metropolitan Departments.
*Wáng Tài* was skilled at interacting with officials and scholars.
Many scholars held affection for *Wáng Tài*,
always hoping he would hold a position in the personnel selection office.
Shortly thereafter,
he was appointed Minister of Personnel.
The high officials and gentry looked upon him with hope.
Before he could carry out any selections,
he became ill,
and his post was changed to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of the Left Valiant Cavalry.
Before he formally accepted the appointment,
he died,
aged forty-five.
His posthumous name was *Yízǐ*.
Initially, *Wáng Tài* had no sons,
and adopted *Qí*, the son of his elder brother.
Later, he had a son named *Kuò*.
*Wáng Fèn*, courtesy name *Jìwén*,
was a man from *Lángyé*.
His grandfather, *Wáng Sēnglǎng*,
was Grand Commandant with Honorary Privileges and Duke *Yuán* during the *Sòng* dynasty.
His father, *Wáng Suì*,
was Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates.
*Wáng Fèn* was orphaned at fourteen,
and began his official career as Chief Clerk of the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
He was sent out as General Who Pacifies Afar and Internal Administrator of *Shǐ'ān*.
When *Yuán Càn* was executed,
none of his friends or old acquaintances dared to look upon him;
*Wáng Fèn*
Because of this, he gained a prominent reputation.
He was promoted to Central Attendant of the Crown Prince,
and Aide to the Grand Commandant.
He was sent out as Internal Administrator of *Jìn'ān*.
He was progressively promoted to Gentleman Attendant of the Central Secretariat,
and transferred to Minister of Agriculture.
*Wáng Fèn*'s elder brother, *Huàn*, was executed in *Yōng* Prefecture.
*Huàn*'s son, *Wáng Sù*, fled to *Wèi*.
*Wáng Fèn* voluntarily confined himself and requested punishment.
Emperor *Shìzǔ* of *Qí*, knowing his sincerity,
admonished him and sent him away.
As *Wáng Sù* repeatedly led *Wèi* forces to invade the borders,
Emperor *Shìzǔ* once, while *Wáng Fèn* was in attendance,
casually addressed *Wáng Fèn*, saying:
“Have you recently received news from the North?”
*Wáng Fèn*, straightening his demeanor, replied:
“Since *Wáng Sù* has already forgotten his ancestral graves,
how could he possibly remember that he has me, his servant?”
The Emperor also held him in high regard because of this display of loyalty.
Soon after, he was appointed General Who Pacifies the North and Internal Administrator of *Línglíng*.
He was recalled to serve as Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates.
Because his father had died holding this office,
he firmly declined the appointment.
He was promoted to Director of the Palace Library.
he was appointed *Sànqí Chángshì*, concurrently holding the position of Commandant of Infantry (*Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi*), and additionally serving as *Qǐbù Shàngshū*.
*Gāozǔ* once asked his officials at a banquet:
"Am I existence (*yǒu*) or non-existence (*wú*)?"
*Fèn* replied:
"Your Majesty, in responding to the myriad things, is existence;
in embodying the ultimate principle, is non-existence."
*Gāozǔ* praised the answer.
He went out to serve as the Administrator of *Xuānchéng* (*Xuānchéng Tàishǒu*),
and was transferred to Administrator of *Wú Jùn* (*Wú Jùn Tàishǒu*).

He was promoted to General Tranquilizing the North (*Níngshuò Jiāngjūn*), Chief Clerk to the Prince of *Yùzhāng* (*Yùzhāng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ*) in the Northern Central Palace Administration, and Administrator of *Lánlíng* (*Lánlíng Tàishǒu*),
acting concurrently as the Governor of *Nánxú* Commandery.
He was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Qīng*), Right Commander of the Heir Apparent's Guard (*Tàizǐ Yòulǜ*), and *Sànqí Chángshì*,
serving in the Eastern Palace.
He was appointed *Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū*.
He again served as General Wise and Martial (*Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn*) and Chief Clerk to the Prince of *Nánkāng* (*Nánkāng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ*),
with a salary rank of medium two thousand *dàn* (*Zhōng Èrqiānshí*).
He returned to the court to serve as *Sànqí Chángshì*, *Jīnzǐ Guānglù*, and Grand Centralizer (*Dà Zhōngzhèng*) of *Nánxú* Province,
and was granted twenty personal attendants.
He was promoted to Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè*),
and shortly thereafter was additionally granted the title of Attendant at Court (*Shìzhōng*).
At that time, the two suburban altars were being rebuilt,
and *Fèn*, retaining his original office, served concurrently as Minister of the Grand Architect (*Lǐng Dàjiàng Qīng*).
He was promoted to *Sànqí Chángshì* and Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (*Yòu Guānglù Dàfū*),
and the number of his personal attendants was increased to forty.
He was promoted to *Shìzhōng*, Special Advanced Officer (*Tèjìn*), and Left Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (*Zuǒ Guānglù*),
and again retained his original office to supervise the Governor of *Dānyáng* (*Dānyáng Yǐn*).
In the third month of the fifth year of *Pǔtōng*,
he died,
aged seventy-nine *suì*.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him his original office,
bestowed forty thousand cash,
four hundred bolts of cloth,
four hundred *jīn* (catties) of wax,
granted funerary instruments from the Eastern Park (*Dōngyuán Mìqì*),
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothes.
His posthumous title was *Húzǐ*.
His eldest son was *Lín*,
courtesy name *Xiàozhāng*.
He was nominated as Flourishing Talent (*Xiùcái*) from *Nánxú* Province.
Upon entering officialdom, he became the Legal Officer (*Fǎcáo*) to the Prince of *Jiàn'ān* who was General Pacifying the Caitiffs (*Zhēnglǔ*),
Libationer of the Eastern Office (*Dōng Gé Jìjiǔ*) under the Minister over the Masses (*Sītú*),
and Erudite for the Prince of *Nánpíng* (*Nánpíng Wáng Wénxué*).
He married Princess *Yìxīng* (*Yìxīng Gōngzhǔ*),
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Son-in-Law (*Fùmǎ Dūwèi*).
He was repeatedly promoted to Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shìláng*),
Chief Clerk to General of the Guards (*Wèijūn*) *Xiè Fěi*,
and Attendant at Court Extraordinarily Designated (*Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì*).
He went out to serve as General Manifesting Might (*Míngwēi Jiāngjūn*) and Administrator of *Dōngyáng* (*Dōngyáng Tàishǒu*),
and was recalled to be Left Chief Clerk to the Minister over the Masses (*Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ*).
*Xī*, courtesy name *Gōnggǔ*,
was the second son of *Lín*.
From childhood he was vigilant and perceptive.
When receiving instruction with his brothers,
when it was time for them to rest and disperse,
he alone always stayed and did not rise.
When he was seven or eight *suì*,
he still followed the Princess into the palace.
*Gāozǔ* praised his intelligence and quickness,
and often spoke of him to the court officials.
His mental energy was tireless,
causing damage to his right eye.
The Princess often limited his studies
and decorated his dwelling place.
Even among children's pastimes,
he had no interest in anything.
At twelve *suì*,
he became a student of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐshēng*).
At fourteen,
he was nominated as Pure and Splendid (*Qīngmào*),
and was appointed Palace Receptionist of the Imperial Library (*Mìshū Láng*).
He was equally famous as *Zhāng Bóxù* of *Fànyáng*,
and both became Gentlemen of the Household of the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Shèrén*).
When mourning the death of his father,
he observed the funeral rites perfectly.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Mounted Escort of the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ*).
At that time, *Zhāomíng* (the Heir Apparent) was still young
and had not yet begun interacting with his officials.
*Gāozǔ* issued an imperial order:
"Mounted Escort of the Heir Apparent *Wáng Xī* and Palace Receptionist of the Imperial Library *Zhāng Zuǎn*
are distinguished models of brilliance,
and eminent talents in the court.
You may treat them as your teachers and friends."
Because he was related by marriage to the imperial family, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of *Yǒng'ān* (*Yǒng'ān Hóu*).
He was appointed Mentor to the Prince of *Jìn'ān* (*Jìn'ān Wáng Yǒu*),
but citing illness, he did not take up the post.
An imperial order permitted him to receive the edict while remaining in the capital.
On the day the Prince came of age,
he acted for the Prince's staff to manage the ceremonies.
Early in the *Pǔtōng* reign,
the *Wèi* (Northern Wei) first established peace and alliance,
sending *Liú Shànmíng* to offer tribute and establish relations.
An imperial order directed Gentleman of the Household of the Palace Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shèrén*) *Zhū Yì* to receive him.
All those attending the banquet were northern converts.
*Shànmíng*, relying on his own talent and vigor,
said to *Yì* when the wine was flowing freely:
"How many people in the Southern State have rhetorical learning like yours, Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat?"
*Yì* replied:
"The reason *Yì* has the duty of receiving the guest at this banquet
is simply that this task falls under my official function.
The two states are communicating in peace,
to strengthen their friendly relationship.
If the purpose were to elevate those skilled in talent and rhetoric,
then I would certainly not have been permitted to be sent."
*Shànmíng* then said:
"*Wáng Xī* and *Zhāng Zuǎn*
are known in the North.
How might I be able to see them?"
*Yì* reported this fully to the Emperor.
An imperial order immediately commanded a banquet to be set up in the Southern Park (*Nányuàn*),
attended only by *Xī*, *Zhāng Zuǎn*, *Zhū Yì*, and *Shànmíng* (four people in total).
When *Shànmíng* arrived at the meeting,
he discussed widely the classics and histories,
and also used mockery and jesting.
*Xī* and *Zuǎn* responded to every point,
without hesitation or doubt.
They never once needed to question him about anything.
*Shànmíng* admired and respected them greatly.
On another day, he said to *Yì*:
"To see two wise men in one day
truly fulfills what I had hoped for.
If there were no noble men,
how could the state be governed?"
He was transferred to Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Láng*),
and promoted to Yellow Gate Attendant for Deliberative Matters (*Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng*) and Director of the Bureau of Civil Office in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Lìbù Lángzhōng*).
He was then twenty-four *suì*.
He said to his close friends:
"I, being a maternal relative of the imperial family,
was mistakenly recognized by the era,
and have received many unwarranted noble offices;
this was not my original intention.
Furthermore, recently I have been frail and ill,
and it is difficult to attend to manifold official duties.
How can I abandon what I love and pursue what I am incapable of doing?"
He then cited illness and refused the appointment.
He immediately dismissed his staff and assistants,
refused guests,
closed his door, and immersed himself in deep thought.
His chambers were utterly desolate.
In the first month of the sixth year of *Zhōngdàtōng*,
he died,
aged thirty-six *suì*.
He was posthumously granted *Shìzhōng*,
funerary instruments from the Eastern Park (*Dōngyuán Mìqì*),
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothes.
His posthumous title was *Zhēnzǐ*.
His sons were *Fàn* and *Shí*.
*Qiān*, courtesy name *Gōnghuì*,
was the fifth younger brother of *Xī*.
At the age of eight *suì*, he mourned his father's death,
his grief and self-neglect exceeding the rites.
When the mourning period ended,
he was summoned to fill the post of student of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐshēng*).
The Libationer (*Jìjiǔ*), *Yuán Áng*, called him profoundly rational.
He was ranked top in the examination,
and appointed concurrently Palace Receptionist of the Imperial Library (*Cháng Jiān Mìshū Lángzhōng*).
He successively held the posts of Director of the Palace Hall in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng*),
Gentleman of the Middle Household of the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén*),
where, along with *Lù Xiāng* of *Wú Jùn*, he jointly managed the records and documents of the Eastern Palace.
He went out to serve as Administrator of *Jiàn'ān* (*Jiàn'ān Tàishǒu*).
The mountain chieftains *Fāng Shàn* and *Xiè Xī* gathered followers and occupied strategic passes,
repeatedly causing trouble for the populace.
*Qiān* secretly laid out strategies,
led his troops, and subdued them.
There was an imperial edict praising him highly,
which was distributed and shown to the provinces and commanderies.
He was appointed General of Martial Might (*Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn*)
and Administrator of *Shǐxīng* (*Shǐxīng Nèishǐ*).
When mourning the death of his birth mother,
he firmly declined the appointment.
He was again appointed General Pacifying the Distance (*Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn*) and Administrator of *Nánkāng* (*Nánkāng Nèishǐ*).
Coinciding with the rebellion of *Xún Lú*,
*Qiān* was transferred again to Administrator of *Ānchéng* (*Ānchéng Nèishǐ*),
in order to pacify and stabilize the area.
Returning [to the capital], he was appointed Yellow Gate Attendant (*Huángmén Shìláng*).
Shortly after, he became Chief Clerk to the Prince of *Wǔlíng*, who was General Pacifying the West (*Ānxī Wǔlíng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ*), and Administrator of *Shǔ Jùn* (*Shǔ Jùn Tàishǒu*).
*Qiān* feared the rugged mountains,
and firmly resigned, citing illness.
Consequently, he was dismissed from office.
After a long time,
he was appointed General Manifesting Military Prowess (*Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn*) and Left Aide in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng*).
He was again appointed Yellow Gate Attendant (*Huángmén Shìláng*).
He was promoted to Palace Assistant to the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ*),
managing the records and documents of the Eastern Palace.
In the twelfth month of the second year of *Tàiqīng*,
he died,
aged forty-five *suì*.
He was posthumously granted *Shìzhōng*,
funerary instruments from the Eastern Park (*Dōngyuán Mìqì*),
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothes.
In the third year of *Chéngshèng*,
*Shìzǔ* issued a retroactive edict, saying:
"Being worthy but not boastful is called reverence (*gōng*).
His posthumous title shall be *Gōngzǐ*."
Zhāng Chōng, courtesy name Yánfú,
was a native of Wújùn.
His father, Xù,
was a Tèjìn and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū in the Qí dynasty,
and had a good reputation in previous generations.
When Chōng was young,
he did not uphold moral conduct,
and enjoyed idle roaming.
Xù once took leave to return to Wú.
As he first entered the western suburb (guō),
he chanced upon Chōng going out hunting,
an eagle on his left arm,
and a dog on a leash in his right hand.
When he met Xù's boat arriving,
he immediately released the leash and removed his falconer's glove,
bowing by the water's edge.
Xù said,
"Engaged in two activities at once,
is it not tiring?"
Chōng knelt and replied,
"I have heard that one stands firm at thirty (sānshí ér lì).
Now I am twenty-nine.
Please allow me until next year to respectfully change my ways."
Xù said,
"To be able to correct one's faults (guò ér néng gǎi),
Yán Shìzǐ (Yán Huí) had this quality."
By the next year,
he indeed cultivated himself and changed his conduct.
He had not studied for a full year,
yet had extensively read much,
especially excelling in Lǎo (Lǎozi) and Yì (Yìjīng),
and was skilled in pure conversation (qīngyán).
He and his paternal uncle Jì both enjoyed high renown.
He began his official career as an Xíng Cānjūn for the Fǔjūn,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén, Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng, and Wǔlíng Wáng Yǒu.
At that time, Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn held significant power in the court,
and Emperor Wǔ made all his decisions based on Wáng Jiǎn's advice.
Emperor Wǔ once wanted to appoint Chōng's father Xù as Shàngshū Púshè.
He consulted Jiǎn,
who replied,
"Zhāng Xù has had a clear reputation since he was young,
and is indeed an excellent choice;
however, people from the East (dōngshì) have rarely taken a firm stand (bǐ wú suǒ zhí),
and Xù's sons are mostly of loose conduct.
I believe this should be carefully considered."
The Emperor then stopped the plan.
Previously, Chōng's brothers were all rather wild (qīngxiá),
and Chōng himself did not pay attention to minor conduct (xìxíng) when he was young,
which is why Jiǎn spoke as he did.
Chōng heard this and was displeased,
so he wrote a letter to Jiǎn, saying: "Zhāng Chōng, a man from the state of Wú, respectfully sends this letter to His Excellency, Lord Wáng of Lángxié: Recently, the journey has been long,
and the continuous rain has kept things hidden.
The cool and hot seasons are not yet balanced;
I trust you are well
and taking care.
Fortunately, during my leisure from fishing
and free time from gathering herbs,
I occasionally amuse myself with scrolls,
leisurely exploring ancient histories.
Across myriad ages,
the paths of action and inaction are manifold;
in the hustle and bustle of a hundred years,
the ways of rising and falling are not uniform.
[一０] Thus, round for movement and square for stillness,
is the difference of instruments;
diamond hard and water soft,
is the distinction of natures.
One who is skilled
at managing nature
does not go against the essence of metal and water;
one who is skilled at making instruments
does not alter the function of round and square.
This is why Běihǎi (Kǒng Róng) held his hairpin high (guà zān dài zhī gāo),
and Hénán (Zhōng Yáo) received
the honor of imperial edicts.
[一一] Throughout my life, I have had few companions;
I have not allowed desires for profit to disturb my mind.
For thirty-six years,
I have managed to live in humble tranquility.
My resolute will
stands towering like a frosty
cliff;
my steadfast feelings
stretch like peaks across the coastline.
Hanging my cap in the celestial pavilion (piāo yīng tiān gé)
means I have renounced the splendor of the court;
adorning the Cloud Terrace with official cords (zhuì zǔ yún tái)
means I ultimately feel shame at the brilliance of high officials.
This is why
I have retired to the riverside (jiāng gāo)
and feigned madness by the hills (lǒng pàn),
truly because my disposition is lofty and reserved,
and my feelings are unyielding and detached.
I abide by my own unique sentiments,
not accepted by ordinary people;
my solitary brilliance on a spiritual
precipice
often faces twists and turns in this world.
Thus, Jūnshān (Shào Jiē), who went straight up,
was pressured in his time;
Shúyáng (Xu Shúyáng), who soared far,
was admired a thousand years later.
This is why I [Chōng] choose to live among
fish and birds,
spending my days beneath the pines.
Half an acre of land
is enough to pay taxes;
five acres of homestead
planted with mulberry and hemp.
I sing and chant by the rivers and lakes,
savoring verses
by the Mǐnchí,
indulging in the fisherman's pastime,
and resting in a chosen dwelling.
That is all.
What have I, Chōng, to regret?
As for towering cliffs that shade the sun,
and the vast sea that meets the sky;
precipitous rocks crumbling for fathoms,
dividing dangers and dropping for measures.
Cassia and orchids exquisitely bloom,
mingled in the mountain's depths;
pines and cypresses densely
shade,
intertwining along the winding streams.
Yuánqīng (Rì Yuánqīng) did not return from here,
and Bóxiū (Liú Bóxiū) also departed forever from this place.
If one were to cast a fishing rod by the islet,
and wash one's feet in the clear waters;
alone roaming
through mist and clouds,
reposing loftily among the wind and moon.
Distant zither and wine,
who comes from afar to the mountain peak;
brilliant literary conversations,
in vain, cease in one's mind.
Unconsciously, a thousand miles stretch,
the road blocked by rivers
and streams.
Whenever the west wind blows,
how can one not gaze back?
Taking advantage of this period of illness,
I briefly express my feelings;
holding these few words,
I lightly trespass upon your esteemed attention.
Your Excellency, your years are not yet advanced,
yet you excel in learning and serve in office;
you assist the common people with your Dao,
your achievements are as vast as the sea.
When in court, you harmonize with Chángqiàn's (Wèi Chángqiàn's) sincerity;
when debating, you uphold
Zhòngzǐ's (Bāo Zhòngzǐ's) integrity.
One can truly say you are a great virtue of the age,
a lone pine that stands out.
My own conduct is not yet fully understood,
and this journey is still obscure.
The talented men of Máolíng
look upon the noble retinues
with long-held aspirations;
the common folk of Bàshān
await the carriages and robes with sighs.
Could this not be regrettable?
If a swan were to pull a carriage,
and a crane were to soar empty,
then the riverbank would not refuse to wither,
and the mountain would be moistened by its influence.
Strange birds with exotic feathers
might be met by the cliffside;
tender mists and light smoke
suddenly gather at the forest's edge.
The Eastern Capital (Dōngdū) is not exceptional,
why should the Southern Mountains (Nánshān)
be considered precious?
I, Chōng, am one of the common people west of the Kūn (Kūn Wén),
one citizen on the periphery of Mount Dài (Dài Biǎo).
I raise silkworms for clothes,
and cultivate the land for food.
I cannot serve princes and kings,
nor seek confidants,
nor visit contemporaries,
nor display my persuasive
speeches.
Like tumbleweeds, I drift among butchers and markets,
and my joy is exceedingly great.
Your Excellency met with favor early on,
and later encountered great courtesy.
The attention from the highest positions
overflowed in your early days;
the words from your hometown
were mistakenly prolonged on occasion.
However, the whole world calls me, Chōng, mad.
What can I, Chōng, possibly tell all of you gentlemen about this?
Thus, I reveal what I have heard and seen,
Cleansing the heart and mind,
narrating my life,
discussing speaking and silence,
the means by which dreams are joined and souls interact,
those who bare their breasts and embrace affection—
this can only be done by you, venerable sir.
Passes and mountains are vastly separated;
having finished the letter, there is no means of conveyance.
If perchance I meet a woodcutter,
I will presumptuously entrust this matter to him.
Someone spoke critically of him to Emperor Wǔ (Wǔdì),
and Chōng (Chōng) was dismissed from office,
remaining in disfavor for a long time.
Later, he served as Adjutant in the Secretariat of the Minister of Works (Sītú Zīyì Cānjūn).
He, along with Wáng Sīyuǎn (Wáng Sīyuǎn) of Lángyá (Lángyá) and Lù Huìxiǎo (Lù Huìxiǎo) of the same commandery,
all served as retainers (bīnkè) to the Minister of Works (Sītú), the Prince of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Wáng).
He entered the court as Palace Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
and soon transferred to Palace Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
When Emperor Míng (Míngdì) acted as Chancellor,
he appointed Chōng (Chōng) as Chief Clerk to the General Who Guards the Army (Zhèn Jūn Zhǎngshǐ).
He went out to serve as Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu).
His governance was pure and tranquil,
and the people and officials benefited from it.
Soon after, due to mourning for his mother, he resigned his post.
When the period of mourning ended,
he was appointed Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
and promoted to Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng).
When the Righteous Army (Yì Shī) drew near,
Emperor Dōng Hūn (Dōng Hūn) summoned all officials into the palace grounds.
Court gentlemen feared disaster;
some went about indulging in drunken banquets.
Chōng (Chōng) alone remained in the Attendant at Court Bureau (Shìzhōng Shěng),
and did not leave his chamber.
Once Emperor Dōng Hūn (Dōng Hūn) was assassinated within the city,
all officials gathered beneath the Western Bell (Xī Zhōng).
Chōng (Chōng) was summoned but did not arrive.
When Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) established his administrative headquarters (bà fǔ),
he appointed Chōng (Chōng) as Adjutant in the Secretariat of the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ Zīyì Cānjūn).

He was promoted to Prefect of the Gentlemen of the Palace for the State of Liáng (Liáng Wángguó Lángzhōng Lìng), Minister of the Bureau of Sacrifices (Cíbù Shàngshū), and concurrently Commandant of Cavalry (Tún Qí Xiàowèi).
He transferred to General Who Penetrates the Army (Guàn Jūn Jiāngjūn) and Chief Clerk of the Left to the Minister of Works (Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ).
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān (Tiānjiān) era,
he was appointed Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
He was soon promoted to Minister of the Bureau of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and in this selection post, he was known for being fair and equitable (píng yǔn).
Soon after, he served as Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sàn Qí Cháng Shì) and General of Cloud Cavalry (Yún Qí Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu),
receiving the salary grade of Two Thousand Shi (Èr Qiān Shí).
He was recalled and appointed Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sàn Qí Cháng Shì) and Libationer of the Directorate of National Academy (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
Chōng (Chōng) excelled in philosophical principles.
He ascended the hall to lecture,
and the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) and all those below him attended.
At that time, many princes and marquises were studying there,
holding classics and bowing [to him].
Chōng (Chōng) stood in his court robes,
not daring to accept the honor.
He was transferred to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn),
the post of Libationer (Jìjiǔ) remaining as before.
He entered the court as Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè).
After a while,
he was appointed General of Cloud Triumphs (Yún Huī Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wú Commandery (Wú Jùn Tàishǒu).
Upon taking office, he showed compassion for the poor and elderly,
and none of his old acquaintances were unhappy.
He pleaded his case due to illness,
and was recalled as Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sàn Qí Cháng Shì),
and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
Before he could return to court,
in the thirteenth year [of the era],
he died in Wú (Wú),
aged sixty-six.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng) and General Protecting the Army (Hù Jūn Jiāngjūn).
His posthumous title was Mùzǐ (Mùzǐ).
His son, Zuì (Zuì), succeeded him.
Liǔ Yùn (Liǔ Yùn), courtesy name Wénchàng (Wénchàng),
was a man from Xiè (Xiè) in Hédōng (Hédōng).
In youth he possessed ambition and good conduct,
loved learning,
and excelled at letter writing.
He was a neighbor of Xiè Yǎo (Xiè Yǎo) of Chén Commandery (Chén Jùn),
and Yǎo (Yǎo) cherished him deeply.
Previously,
during the Sòng (Sòng) era, there were Jī Yuánróng (Jī Yuánróng) and Yáng Gài (Yáng Gài),
both skilled at playing the qín zither.
It was said they transmitted the method of Dài Āndào (Dài Āndào).
Yùn (Yùn) studied under them in his youth,
and especially grasped the profundity of their art.
The Prince of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Wáng) of Qí (Qí) heard of him and invited him,
appointing him Acting Adjutant in the Legal Section (Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn).
He was greatly admired and treated intimately.
The Prince once held a banquet in the rear garden.
A famous qín zither used by the Jin (Jìn) Chancellor Xiè Ān (Xiè Ān) was present.
He handed it to Yùn (Yùn),
and Yùn (Yùn) played an elegant tune.
Zǐliáng (Zǐliáng) said:
“Your skill surpasses the mind of Jī (Jī),
and your subtlety reaches the form of Yáng (Yáng).
Such excellent talent and beautiful handiwork
are truly present today.
Not only are you praised as marvelous by your contemporaries,
but you are surely able to follow the path of the ancient masters.”
He was repeatedly promoted to Mounted Escort to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
Due to mourning for his father, he resigned from office.
When mourning ended,
he was appointed Acting Chancellor of Póyáng (Póyáng Xiàng).
He allowed his subordinate officials to complete the three-year mourning rite,
and dedicated himself to cultural instruction,
for which the common people praised him.
He returned and was appointed Gentleman of the Palace Attendant to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojí Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
When Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) arrived at the capital city (Jīng Yì),
Yùn (Yùn) went to Shítou (Shítou) to pay his respects,
and was appointed General Who Penetrates the Army (Guàn Jūn Jiāngjūn) and Commander of the Expeditionary Forces in the East (Zhēng Dōng Fǔ Sīmǎ).
At that time, Emperor Dōng Hūn (Dōng Hūn) was not yet pacified,
and the soldiers were still fighting fiercely.
Yùn (Yùn) submitted a memorial discussing expediency,
requesting that when the city was settled,
the maps and census registers should first be collected,
and that the principle of Emperor Hàn Zǔ’s (Hàn Zǔ) broad-mindedness and love for the people should be followed.
Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) adopted his suggestion.
Coincidentally, Xiāo Yǐngzhòu (Xiāo Yǐngzhòu) died in Jiānglíng (Jiānglíng).
Yùn (Yùn) was sent west to welcome Emperor Hé (Hé Dì).
He was then appointed Palace Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
concurrently Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
and promoted to Commander of the Right to the Chancellor (Xiàngguó Yòu Sīmǎ).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (Tiānjiān),
he was appointed Perpetual Concurrently Attendant at Court (Zhǎng Jiān Shìzhōng),
and worked with Vice Director Shěn Yuē (Shěn Yuē) and others to establish the new legal code.
Yùn’s (Yùn) conduct was steadfast and pure.
As a noble son, he acquired an excellent reputation early.
In youth, he excelled at composing poetry.
His first poem said:
“In the pavilion, the tree leaves fall,
over the mountain ridges, autumn clouds drift.”
Wáng Yuáncháng (Wáng Yuáncháng) of Lángyá (Lángyá) saw it and exclaimed in admiration,
and subsequently wrote it on his study wall.
Thereafter, whenever he attended a private banquet,
he was invariably commanded by imperial edict to compose a poem.
He once respectfully matched Emperor Gāozǔ’s (Gāozǔ) poem composed upon ascending Jǐngyáng Tower (Jǐngyáng Lóu), which said:
“On Tàiyè (Tàiyè) Lake, blue waves arise,
tall poplars reach the autumn sky.
Jade pennants follow the Hàn (Hàn) far off,
the carved carriage chases the wind and roams.”
This was deeply praised by Emperor Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ).
At that time, everyone commonly praised and transmitted it.
Yùn (Yùn) was skilled at Go (yì).
The Emperor often commanded him to attend court,
and then ordered him to establish rankings [for players],
grading their superiority and inferiority.
In the second year,
he went out to serve as Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu).
In the sixth year,
he was recalled as Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sàn Qí Cháng Shì),
and promoted to Minister of the Bureau of the Left People (Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū).
In the eighth year,

he was appointed Bearer of Credentials (Chí Jié), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Guǎng (Guǎng), Jiāo (Jiāo), Guì (Guì), and Yuè (Yuè), General of Benevolent Martiality (Rén Wǔ Jiāngjūn), Gentleman of the Palace, Pacifier of the Yuè (Píng Yuè Zhōngláng Jiāng), and Inspector of Guǎngzhōu (Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ).
He was recalled as Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān),
and concurrently General of the Left Army (Zuǒ Jūn Jiāngjūn).
He again served as Administrator of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu) for six years.
His governance was pure and tranquil,
and the people and officials cherished him.
He contracted an illness in the commandery,
and personally requested to be relieved of his duties.
Over a thousand elders bowed and presented a memorial pleading [for him to stay],
but the request had not yet been acted upon.
In the sixteenth year of Tiānjiān (Tiānjiān),
he died,
aged fifty-three.
He was posthumously granted Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng) and General Protecting the Central Army (Zhōng Hù Jūn).
Since Yùn (Yùn) was skilled at the qín zither,
he often feared that contemporary music tended to abandon ancient methods.
Therefore, he wrote the Discussion of Pure Modes (Qīng Diào Lùn),
which contained detailed principles and categories.
His youngest son was Yǎn (Yǎn),
courtesy name Yàn Yóu (Yàn Yóu).
At age twelve, he was granted an audience.
The Emperor inquired what book he read.
He replied, the Book of Documents (Shàngshū).
The Emperor further asked:
“What beautiful sentences does it contain?”
He replied:
“Virtue consists of good governance,
and governance lies in nourishing the people.”
Everyone was impressed by this.
By imperial edict, he married Princess Chángchéng (Chángchéng Gōngzhǔ),
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Equipage (Fùmǎ Dūwèi),
Marquis of Dūtíng (Dūtíng Hóu),
Gentleman of the Palace for the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Mounted Escort (Xǐmǎ),
and Internal Administrator of Lúlíng (Lúlíng) and Póyáng (Póyáng).
In the first year of Dàbǎo (Dàbǎo),
he died.
Cài Zǔn (Cài Zǔn), courtesy name Jǐngjié (Jǐngjié),
was a man from Kǎochéng (Kǎochéng) in Jìyáng (Jìyáng).
His father, Xīngzōng (Xīngzōng),
was Grand Master of Splendid Happiness of the Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) and Minister with Honors Equal to the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sān Sī) during the Sòng (Sòng) dynasty,
and held a weighty reputation in the previous generation.
He and his elder brother Yín (寅) were both famous.
He was selected and appointed as a Guózǐshēng (國子生).
He achieved high marks (gāodì, 高第).
He served as Sītú Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn (司徒法曹行參軍).
Wáng Jiǎn (王儉), General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn) of Qí (齊), highly selected staff for his residence.
He appointed Zǔn (撙) as Zhǔbù (主簿).
He was repeatedly promoted to Jiàn'ān Wáng Wénxué (建安王文學),
Sītú Zhǔbù (司徒主簿), and Zuǒ Xīshǔ (左西屬).
When Emperor Míng (明帝) was Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn (鎮軍將軍),
he summoned (Zǔn) to be Cóngshì Zhōngláng (從事中郎).
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
Zhōngjūn Zhǎngshǐ (中軍長史),
and Jìshì Huángmén Shìláng (給事黃門侍郎).
He experienced the mourning period for his mother.
He built a hut beside the tomb.
The end of Qí (齊) was fraught with difficulty.
When the mourning period concluded,
he remained living at the gravesite.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子),
and Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ (太尉長史).
He did not take up either post.
