When the Liáng (梁) Dynasty was established (Táijiàn, 臺建),
he was made Shìzhōng (侍中).
He was promoted to Tàishǒu (太守) of Línhǎi (臨海).
Due to an official matter, he was demoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子).
He subsequently became Shìzhōng (侍中) again,
and Tàishǒu (太守) of Wúxīng (吳興).
In Tiānjiān (天監) ninth year,
Wú Chéngbó (吳承伯), a clerk from Xuānchéng (宣城) Commandery, gathered a mob using heterodox teachings and attacked Xuānchéng.
He killed the Tàishǒu (太守), Zhū Sēngyǒng (朱僧勇).
He then proceeded to slaughter the neighboring counties.
He crossed the mountains and raided Wúxīng (吳興).
Everywhere he passed was ravaged and destroyed.
His followers numbered twenty thousand.
They suddenly attacked the commandery city.
The eastern region was unaccustomed to military conflict.
The officials and people were frightened, troubled, and scattered,
and all urged Zǔn (撙) to avoid (the attackers).
Zǔn (撙) held firm and did not move.
He recruited brave men to secure the commandery.
Chéngbó (承伯) used all his elite forces to attack Zǔn (撙).
Zǔn ordered his men to go out and resist.
They fought at the gate.
(The enemy) was immediately crushed and routed.
Chéngbó (承伯) was killed on the battlefield.
The remaining rebels were all pacified.
He was given the title Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (信武將軍).
He was summoned to be Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書).
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
He subsequently became Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (信武將軍) and Tàishǒu (太守) of Jìnlíng (晉陵).
Upon returning (to the capital), he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍) and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (國子祭酒).
He was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū (吏部尚書).
While in charge of appointments,
his breadth and simplicity earned him fame.
He was also made Shìzhōng (侍中),
concurrently leading Mìshū Jiān (祕書監).
He was transferred to Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令),
retaining his position as Shìzhōng (侍中).
In Pǔtōng (普通) second year,
he went out to serve as Xuānyì Jiāngjūn (宣毅將軍) and Tàishǒu (太守) of Wú Jùn (吳郡).
In the fourth year,
he died,
aged fifty-seven.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng (侍中), Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (金紫光祿大夫), and Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn (宣惠將軍).
His posthumous name was Kāngzǐ (康子).
His son, Yànxī (彥熙),
successively held the offices of Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎),
and Nèishǐ (內史) of Xuānchéng (宣城).
Jiāng Qiàn (江蒨), courtesy name Yànbiāo (彥標),
was a native of Kǎochéng (考城) in Jìyáng (濟陽).
His great-grandfather, Zhàn (湛),
was Zuǒ Guānglù (左光祿) and Yítóng Sānsī (儀同三司) during the Sòng (宋) Dynasty.
His father, Jù (鉅),
was Tàicháng Qīng (太常卿) during the Qí (齊) Dynasty. Both held high reputations in previous generations.
Qiàn (蒨) was intelligent and sharp when young.
When reading, he could recite (the text) immediately after glancing through it.
He was selected as a Guózǐshēng (國子生).
He mastered the *Shàngshū* (尚書).
He achieved high marks.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng (祕書郎).
He was repeatedly promoted to Sītú Dōnggé Jìjiǔ (司徒東閤祭酒) and Lúlíng Wáng Zhǔbù (廬陵王主簿).
During the mourning period for his father, he became known for his filial piety.
He built a hut beside the tomb.
Emperor Míng (明帝) issued an imperial decree sending twenty fasting guards to guard the gravesite.
When the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬).
He was repeatedly promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ (司徒左西屬),
Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén (太子中舍人),
and Mìshū Chéng (祕書丞).
He went out to serve as Nèishǐ (內史) of Jiàn'ān (建安).
After governing for about a month,
the righteous army approached Jiāngzhōu (江州).
(The enemy) sent Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍) Liú Jiǎnzhī (劉諓之) to take the commandery.
Qiàn (蒨) led the officials and people to hold the commandery and resist him.
When Jiànkāng (建康) city was pacified,
Qiàn (蒨) was temporarily imprisoned.
Soon thereafter, he was pardoned.
He rose to become Hòujūn Línchuān Wáng Wàibīng Cānjūn (後軍臨川王外兵參軍).
He was repeatedly promoted to Línchuān Wáng Yǒu (臨川王友),
Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎),
Tàizǐ Jiālìng (太子家令),
Huángmén Shìláng (黃門侍郎),
concurrently overseeing Dà Zhōngzhèng (大中正) of Nányǎnzhōu (南兗州).
He was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (太子中庶子).
His position as Zhōngzhèng (中正) remained unchanged.
He was transferred to Zhōngquán Shǐxīng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ (中權始興王長史).
He went out to serve as Fúbō Jiāngjūn (伏波將軍) and Nèishǐ (內史) of Jìn'ān (晉安).
While governing, he was clean and restrained.
His efforts focused on leniency and kindness.
The officials and people benefited from this.
An imperial edict summoned him to be Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (寧朔將軍), Nánkāng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ (南康王長史), concurrently managing the affairs of the Residence, Prefecture, and State.
After a short time,
he was promoted to Tàiwèi Línchuān Wáng Zhǎngshǐ (太尉臨川王長史).
He was transferred to Shàngshū Lìbù Láng (尚書吏部郎),
and Yòu Jiāngjūn (右將軍).
Qiàn (蒨) was upright, refined, and possessed outstanding demeanor.
Pūyè (僕射) Xú Miǎn (徐勉) regarded himself highly due to his great authority.
Those in office, all seasoned scholars, respected him.
Only Qiàn (蒨) and Wáng Guī (王規) treated him with equal courtesy,
and did not yield to him.
Miǎn (勉) used Zhaí Jǐng (翟景), a retainer of Qiàn (蒨), to seek Qiàn's daughter in marriage for his seventh son, Yáo (繇).
Qiàn (蒨) did not reply.
When Jǐng (景) spoke of it again,
(Qiàn) punished Jǐng (景) with forty strokes of the cane.
Because of this, he clashed with Miǎn (勉).
He was appointed Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
He refused the post.
At that time, Miǎn (勉) also sought the daughters of Qiàn's (蒨) younger brother Qì (葺) and Wáng Tài (王泰) for his sons.
Both men refused him.
Qì (葺) was Lìbù Láng (吏部郎).
He was dismissed from office for the offense of caning a subordinate.
Tài (泰) used illness as an excuse to leave his residence.
He was then promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍).
All these actions were Miǎn’s (勉) intention.
Originally,
in Tiānjiān (天監) sixth year,
an edict stated that Shìzhōng (侍中) and Chángshì (常侍) both attended the imperial court.
The two departments of the Ménxià (門下) were divided and incorporated into the Jíshū (集書) office.
Although the rank of this office was equal to that of Shìzhōng (侍中),
it was not favored by the noble families.
Therefore, Miǎn (勉) deliberately pushed Tài (泰) into this position.
Soon after, Qiàn (蒨) was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ (司徒左長史).
Earlier,
when Wáng Tài (王泰) left the court,
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) said to Miǎn (勉):
"Jiāng Qiàn's (江蒨) experience
qualifies him to oversee the Appointment Department."
Miǎn (勉) replied:
"Qiàn (蒨) suffers from an eye ailment,
and he is not thoroughly familiar with men of talent."
Gāozǔ (高祖) then dropped the matter.
He was promoted to Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
In Dàtōng (大通) first year,
he died,
aged fifty-three.
An edict posthumously conferred upon him his original office.
His posthumous name was Sùzǐ (肅子).
Qiàn (蒨) loved learning,
and was especially knowledgeable about court rituals and precedents.
He compiled thirty volumes of *Jiāng Zuǒ Yí Diǎn* (江左遺典).
He died
before completing it.
His collected writings numbered fifteen volumes.
His son, Fú (紑),
is recorded in the Biography of Filial Conduct (*Xiàoxíng Zhuàn*, 孝行傳).
The Historiographer states: Since the Wáng (王) clan originated from the Jī (姬) surname,
up until the Qín (秦) and Hàn (漢) dynasties,
they continuously produced brilliant and wise men.
When Wáng Màohóng (王茂弘) of the Eastern Jìn (東晉) Dynasty managed the affairs of Jiāngzuǒ (江左),
people of the time compared him to Guǎn Zhòng (管仲).
Thereafter, high officials shone forth together.
Ministers succeeded one another.
Their names were recorded in the imperial registry.
Blessings flowed down to their descendants.
This was truly a flourishing clan.
Wáng Zhān (王瞻) and others inherited this foundation,
esteemed as the glory of the state.
Their sons possessed talent and conduct
and are worthy of praise.
Zhāng Chōng (張充) lacked integrity when young,
but later corrected his behavior.
When presiding over appointments,
he was truly known as honest and impartial.
Liǔ Yùn (柳惲) was renowned for his many skills.
Cài Zǔn (蔡撙) was famous for his upright refinement.
Jiāng Qiàn (江蒨) was conspicuous for his demeanor and style.
All of them were famous scholars of the Liáng (梁) court.
Collective Biographies Sixteen: The Five Princes of Tàizǔ.
Empress Zhāng
gave birth to Yǐ, Prince Xuānwǔ of Chángshā; Fū, Prince Zhāo of Yǒngyáng; Gāozǔ (the future Emperor); and Chàng, Prince Xuān of Héngyáng.
Consort Lǐ gave birth to Róng, Prince Jiǎn of Guìyáng.
Yǐ and Róng
were harmed by Dōnghūn during the Yǒngyuán reign period of Qí.
Fū and Chàng
died during the Jiànwǔ reign period. When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
they were all posthumously enfeoffed as Commandery Princes.
Consort Chén gave birth to Hóng, Prince Jìnghuì of Línchuān;
and Wěi, Prince Yuánxiāng of Nánpíng.
Consort Wú gave birth to Xiù, Prince Kāng of Ānchéng;
and Dàn, Prince Zhōngwǔ of Shǐxīng.
Consort Fèi gave birth to Huī, Prince Zhōngliè of Póyáng.
Hóng, Prince Jìnghuì of Línchuān, courtesy name Xuāndá,
was the sixth son of Tàizǔ.
He was eight *chǐ* tall,
had fine beard and eyebrows,
and his appearance and demeanor were impressive.
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng of Qí,
he served as Adjutant in the Judicial Office of Lúlíng Wáng (Prince of Lúlíng) of the Garrison Army,
and was later promoted to Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent.
At that time, Yǐ, Prince of Chángshā, was garrisoned at Liángzhōu,
and was besieged by Wèi.
The following year,
Hóng was given a thousand elite soldiers to go to his aid.
Before he arrived,
the Wèi army retreated.
He was transferred to Chief Clerk for the General of Agile Cavalry and Prince of Jìn'ān.
Soon after, he became Registrar for the General of the Northern Center and Prince of Guìyáng.
Chàng, Prince of Héngyáng,
had a good reputation
and was treated with respect by Xiāo Yáoguāng, Prince of Shǐ'ān.
When Yáoguāng launched his rebellion,
he forced Chàng to enter the Eastern Administration.
Chàng, fearing disaster,
went immediately to the Imperial Secretariat.
Gāozǔ, while in Yōngzhōu,
constantly feared that his younger brothers would meet disaster.
He said to Wěi, Prince of Nánpíng:
"The sixth brother (Hóng) understands the nature of things;
he must have already returned to the Imperial Secretariat."
When the report arrived,
it was indeed as Gāozǔ had predicted.
When Gāozǔ's righteous army descended,
Hóng went to Xīnlín to greet and welcome him,
and was appointed General Supporting the State.
After Jiànkāng was pacified,
he was promoted to General of the Western Center and Central Protector of the Army,
and commanded the garrison affairs of Shítóu.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as Prince of Línchuān Commandery,
with two thousand households in his stipend.
Soon after, he was made Bearer of Credentials, Palace Attendant Consultant, Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, General of the Rear, and Governor of Yángzhōu.
He was also granted a complete set of drum and wind instruments.
In the third year,
he was additionally granted the title of Attendant in Ordinary,
and promoted to the title of General of the Center Army.
In the fourth year,
Gāozǔ commanded a northern expedition.
Hóng was made Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs for the Northern Campaign in the eight provinces of Nán Yǎn, Běi Yǎn, Běi Xú, Qīng, Jì, Yù, Sī, and Huò.
As the emperor's immediate younger brother,
Hóng's forces were supplied with excellent new equipment and weapons.
His military display was extremely grand.
People in the north believed that such a sight had not been seen for a hundred years.
When the army reached Luòkǒu,
Hóng's vanguard captured Liángchéng
and executed the Wèi general Cháo Qīng.
As the campaign had lasted a long time,
an edict ordered the army to withdraw.
In the summer of the sixth year,
he was promoted to General of Agile Cavalry
and was granted the privilege of establishing an administration equal to the Three Councilors. His position as Attendant in Ordinary remained the same.
That same year,
he was promoted to Minister of Works,
and additionally served as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent.
In the summer of the eighth year,
he was made Bearer of Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, Minister of Education, and Governor of Yángzhōu.
His position as Attendant in Ordinary remained the same.
In the winter of that year,
due to an official matter, he was demoted to General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry.
His privileges of establishing an administration equal to the Three Councilors and his position as Attendant in Ordinary remained the same.
Before he was formally invested,
he was transferred to Bearer of Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu and Xúzhōu, and Governor of Yángzhōu.
His positions as Attendant in Ordinary and General remained the same.
In the twelfth year,
he was promoted to Minister of Education.
His positions as Bearer of Credentials, Attendant in Ordinary, Area Commander-in-Chief, Governor, and General all remained the same.
In the spring of the fifteenth year,
his birth mother, Consort Chén, fell ill.
Hóng and his full younger brother, Wěi, Prince of Nánpíng, attended to her illness.
They did not loosen their belts.
Whenever the envoys from the two palaces inquired after her health,
they wept openly before them.
When the Consort died,
Hóng did not take water or liquid food for five days.
Gāozǔ frequently visited to comfort and encourage him.
Hóng had been filial and careful since youth.
In the final years of Qí,
when he was hiding to avoid danger,
he was separated from Consort Chén.
He still regularly sent messengers to inquire after her well-being.
Someone said to Hóng:
"When fleeing disaster,
you must maintain secrecy; it is unwise to send messengers back and forth."
Hóng, holding back his tears, replied:
"I may be dispensable,
but this matter cannot be neglected even for a moment."
Soon after, he was recalled to serve as Director of the Central Secretariat.
His titles of General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, Bearer of Credentials, and Area Commander-in-Chief remained the same.
He firmly declined, but permission was not granted.
In the summer of the seventeenth year,
due to an official matter, he was demoted to Attendant in Ordinary, General of the Center Army, and acting Minister of Works.
In the winter of that year,
he was transferred to Attendant in Ordinary, Director of the Central Secretariat, and Minister of Works.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he was transferred to Bearer of Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, Grand Commandant, and Governor of Yángzhōu.
His position as Attendant in Ordinary remained the same.
In the second year,
when the Southern and Northern Altars were reconstructed,
he concurrently served in his current capacity as Minister of the Board of Works.
When the work was completed, he was relieved of the post.
In the third month of the seventh year,
suffering from illness, he repeatedly submitted memorials requesting relief.
An imperial edict permitted him to relinquish the Governorship of Yángzhōu,
but the rest of his titles remained the same.
In the fourth month,
he passed away,
aged fifty-four.
From the onset of his illness until his death,
the imperial carriage visited him seven times to check on his condition.
Upon his burial,
an imperial edict stated:
"Hóng, Prince of Línchuān, Attendant in Ordinary and Grand Commandant,
possessed a noble and eminent demeanor,
and his elegant tolerance was broad and far-reaching.
Starting from his tender years,
his conduct showed the sincerity of his character.
When he came to serve in office,
his excellent strategies were consistently effective.
Since the inception of the imperial enterprise,
his rank as the immediate younger brother
led him to long administer the capital region
and successively occupy high official positions.
When discussing policy in court,
no one ever offered a dissenting opinion.
My fraternal affection
combines the feelings of family and state.
I planned for him to greatly assist
and serve as a model for the various princes.
Heaven did not spare him,
and he suddenly passed away too soon.
My grief is profound and penetrating,
shaking my heart with sorrow.
It is proper to increase his esteemed rites and honors,
thereby highlighting his meritorious career.
He is posthumously granted Attendant in Ordinary, Grand General, Inspector of Yángzhōu, and Authorized to use the Yellow Battle-Axe.
His title of Prince remains the same.
He is also granted a complete set of feathered parasols, drums, and wind instruments,
and the number of honor guards with drawn swords is increased to sixty men.
He is to be provided with the *wēnmíng* secret funerary ware,
and dressed in the imperial ceremonial robe for his interment.
His posthumous title is Jìnghuì."
Hóng was naturally broad-minded, gentle, and profoundly sincere.
He served as Governor for over twenty years,
during which he never used administrative affairs to harass the commanderies or counties.
People at the time praised him as a venerable elder.
Hóng had seven sons: Zhèngrén,
Zhèngyì,
Zhèngdé,
Zhèngzé,
Zhènglì,
Zhèngbiǎo,
and Zhèngxìn.
The Heir Apparent, Zhèngrén,
served as the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng
and showed governing capability.
In the tenth year of Tiānjiān,
he died,
receiving the posthumous title of Āi Shìzǐ (Sorrowful Heir Apparent).
Since he had no son,
Gāozǔ issued an edict making Zhènglì, Marquis of Luópíng, the new Heir Apparent.
This was Hóng's intention.
After Hóng passed away,
Zhènglì submitted a memorial yielding the succession to Zhèngyì.
Gāozǔ commended this action and granted permission.
Zhènglì was consequently re-enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiàn'ān,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
When he died,
his son Bēn succeeded him.
Zhèngyì had previously been enfeoffed as Marquis of Pínglè;
Zhèngdé, as Marquis of Xīfēng;
Zhèngzé, as Marquis of Lèshān;
Zhènglì, as Marquis of Luópíng;
Zhèngbiǎo, as Marquis of Fēngshān;
and Zhèngxìn, as Marquis of Wǔhuà.
A separate biography exists for Zhèngdé.
was
the seventh son of Tàizǔ.
When
he was twelve years old, his birth mother, Grand Consort Wú, died.
Xiù's full younger brother, Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn, was nine years old at the time,
and both were renowned for their filial piety.
While observing mourning,
for many days they took neither gruel nor drink.
Tàizǔ personally took gruel and fed it to them.
Grieving their early orphanhood,
he ordered Concubine Chén to jointly act as mother to the two sons.
Chén herself also had no children,
possessing maternal virtue,
she regarded the two sons as if they were her own offspring.
After Xiù matured,
he possessed beautiful manners and bearing,
and his nature was principled and composed.
Even those attending him closely,
if not properly dressed and capped, he would not meet them.
Because of this, his relatives, friends, and household members all respected him.
During the Qí era,
upon reaching adulthood, he served as Zuòzhù Zuǒláng,
gradually rising to Hòujūn Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn,
and Tàizǐ Shèrén.
During the Yǒngyuán period,
Chángshā Xuānwǔ Wáng Yì entered the capital and pacified Cuī Huìjǐng,
becoming Shàngshū Lìng,
dwelling in the highest ministerial position.
His younger brother, Héngyáng Wáng Chàng, became Wèiwèi,
managing the keys and seals.
Dōnghūn (the dethroned Emperor) escaped and wandered day and night,
entering and exiting without restraint.
Many people strongly urged Yì to take advantage of the Emperor's absence,
close the gates, raise troops, and depose him.
Yì did not heed them.
The Emperor's attendants, already disliking Yì's high merit,
and also fearing deposition and enthronement,
all worked to sow discord against Yì.
Yì also felt endangered,
and from then on, all the princes and marquises prepared for trouble.
When the catastrophe occurred,
Línchuān Wáng Hóng and the younger brothers and nephews below him were all able to flee and hide.
While they were escaping,
none of them left the capital.
Few were discovered,
only Guìyáng Wáng Róng suffered disaster.
When Gāozǔ's army of righteousness arrived at Xīnlín,
Xiù and the various princes and marquises all extracted themselves and joined the army.
Gāozǔ appointed Xiù as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
At this time, Dōnghūn's younger brother, Jìnxī Wáng Bǎosōng, was Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nán Xúzhōu,
garrisoned at Jīngkǒu.
His Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ), Fàn Xiù, managed the affairs of the headquarters and the province,
and sent envoys to surrender.
He also requested troops from Gāozǔ,
who appointed Xiù as Guānjūn Zhǎngshǐ and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nán Dōnghǎi,
garrisoning Jīngkǒu.
After Jiànkāng was pacified,
he remained as Envoy Holding Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs of Nán Xú and Yǎn provinces, and Governor of Nán Xúzhōu,
with the title Fǔguó Jiāngjūn as before.
In Tiānjiān first year (502 CE),
he was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn,
and enfeoffed as Prince of Ānchéng Commandery (Ānchéng Jùnwáng),
with an estate of two thousand households.
Since Cuī Huìjǐng raised rebellion, Jīngkǒu
had repeatedly suffered warfare.
The households were scattered and displaced.
Xiù invited, comforted, and welcomed them,
and his benevolence and affection were widely known.
It then happened that the year brought famine,
and he used his private wealth to provide for the common people.
The number of lives he saved was very large.
In the second year,
he was summoned using his existing title to oversee the garrison affairs at Shítou,
and granted the additional post of Sǎnqí Chángshì.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Yòujiāngjūn.
In the fifth year,
he was granted the additional posts of Lǐngjūn and Zhōngshū Lìng,
and bestowed one section of drums and pipes (Gǔchuī).
In the sixth year,
he went out to serve as Envoy Holding Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs of Jiāngzhōu, Píngnán Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
When he was about to depart,
the official in charge requested sturdy boats to serve as the ritual vessels (Zhāifǎng).
Xiù said:
"How can I value property while failing to value my subordinates?"
He then instructed the personnel
to give the sturdier ones to the staff and aides,
and the inferior ones to carry the ritual supplies.
Soon afterward, they encountered a storm,
and the ritual boat was consequently wrecked.
When he arrived at the province,
he heard that the previous governor had appointed the great-grandson of the solicited scholar Táo Qián as a Village Head (Lǐsī).
Xiù sighed and said:
"The virtue of Táo Qián—
how can it not be extended to later generations!"
That very day, he appointed him to the Western Bureau (Xīcáo).
At that time, in the height of summer, the water rose high,
and ferries and bridges were cut off.
The external officials requested to hire passage as before,
and collect the corresponding fee.
Xiù instructed them, saying:
"The Governor lacks virtue,
causing the floods to become a disaster;
how can profit be made from this!
Just provide the boats."
In the seventh year,
he suffered the mourning of his kind mother, Grand Consort Chén.
An imperial edict ordered him to rise and attend to his duties.

Soon after, he was transferred to Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs of the nine provinces: Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Níng, Nán Běi Liáng, and Nán Běi Qín; Píngxī Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Jīngzhōu.
That same year,
he was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
He established schools,
and invited recluses.
He issued an instruction, saying:
"The birds of Chúnhuǒ
do not conceal their shadows in the Scarlet Mountains;
the treasure of Zhāohuá
briefly shines its radiance in Lántián.
Therefore, Jiāng and Hàn have the song of washing the cap-strings,
and the empty valley bears the ode 'Come, O Mindful Man!'
Promoting customs and clarifying the Way
must proceed from these.
The gentlemen-scholars (Chǔshì) Hédōng Hán Huáimíng, Nánpíng Hán Wàng, Nánjùn Yǔ Chéngxiān, and Hédōng Guō Má,
all cast off worldly affairs
and upheld their lofty conduct.
The two Háns are profoundly filial and fraternal,
while Yǔ and Guō show withered physical forms.
Some subsist on acorns and wild herbs,
concerned only that the day is too short,
others dwell with reed walls and artemisia mats,
finding joy therein.
Formerly, Bó Wǔ, steadfast and firm,
accepted office in Hèněi.
Shǐ Yún, isolated and self-disciplined,
submitted his will in Chénliú.
How can one merely speak of the sprouting grain,
when in reality, one is carving jade?
They should be summoned and appointed,
and envoys sent to explain the intent.
Since this request parallels Wèi Hóu's act of showing courtesy,
may we avoid the sigh of Pì Qiáng's threefold silence."
That year,
the people of Xuánhù city in Wèi revolted,
killed the Governor of Yùzhōu, Sīmǎ Yuè,
and invited Sīzhōu Governor Mǎ Xiānpǐn.
Xiānpǐn sent a request to Jīngzhōu asking for support.
Everyone said they should wait for the court's reply.
Xiù said:
"They are waiting for our support;
support must be swift.
Although awaiting the imperial decree is customary,
it is not suitable for an emergency."
He immediately dispatched troops to go there.
Earlier than this,
the Mán barbarians of Bālíng Mǎyíng were committing robbery and causing harm along the Jiāng River.
The Hòujūn Sīmǎ Gāo Jiāngchǎn attacked them with troops from Yǐngzhōu,
but failed,
and Jiāngchǎn died.
The Mán consequently grew stronger.
Xiù sent Defender Wén Chì to lead forces to suppress them.
He burned their forests,
and blocked their trails and paths.
The Mán lost their strategic defensive terrain.
Within a year, the river routes were clear,
and consequently, banditry within the province ceased.
When the Jǔ River suddenly swelled,
it damaged the people's fields significantly.
Xiù used twenty thousand *hú* of grain to relieve them.
He ordered Chief Clerk Xiāo Chēn to review the poor, elderly, and single-male officials in the headquarters and province.
In one day, over five hundred people were dismissed and dispersed.
The common people were greatly pleased.
In the eleventh year,
Zhēng was appointed Shìzhōng, General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn),
concurrently serving as Minister of the Imperial Clan Court (Zōngzhèng Qīng) and overseeing the affairs of Shítou Garrison (Shítou Shùshì).
In the thirteenth year,

he was again sent out to serve as Emissary with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Cavalry Regular Attendant (Sǎnqí Chángshì), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Three Provinces of Yǐng, Sī, and Huò (Dūdū Yǐng Sī Huò Sān Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yǐng Province (Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Dāngtú in Yǐng Province was a demanding region.
The common people were poor;
they were reduced to using women for labor service,
such was the extent of the hardship.
When Xiù arrived at the garrison,
he made stabilizing the people his priority.
The administrators sometimes requested the recruitment of more officials.
Xiù said:
"They do not understand the methods of saving the distressed;
this province is worn out and withered,
it must not be disturbed."
Thereupon, he diligently practiced self-restraint,
reduced unnecessary expenses,
and the common people settled peacefully,
and the region was tranquil.
Previously, Xiàkǒu had often been a battlefield;
exposed skeletons and piled bones lay beneath Huánghè Tower (Huánghè Lóu).
Xiù performed sacrifices and buried them.
One night,
he dreamed that hundreds of people bowed in thanks and departed.
Every winter month,
he always made padded jackets and trousers to bestow upon those suffering from the cold.
At that time, Tián Lǔshēng, a rebellious barbarian from Sī Province (Sīzhōu),
along with his brothers Lǔxián and Chāoxiù,
occupied Ménglóng and came to surrender.
Gāozǔ appointed Lǔshēng as Governor of Northern Sī Province (Běi Sīzhōu Cìshǐ),
Lǔxián as Governor of Northern Yù Province (Běi Yùzhōu Cìshǐ),
and Chāoxiù as Governor of Dìng Province (Dìngzhōu Cìshǐ),
to serve as a defensive screen for the northern border.
However, Lǔshēng and Chāoxiù slandered each other,
and considered leaving or switching allegiance.
Xiù soothed and reconciled them, embracing them (in good faith),
allowing each to fulfill his usefulness,
and the region relied on them at the time.
In the sixteenth year,

he was promoted to Emissary with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Four Provinces of Yōng, Liáng, Northern Qín, and Southern Qín, Jìnglíng Commandery (part of Yǐng Province), and Suí Commandery (part of Sī Province) (Dūdū Yōng Liáng Nán Běi Qín Sì Zhōu Yǐngzhōu zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu zhī Suíjùn Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Guards the North (Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn), Commandant Who Pacifies the Man (Níng Mán Xiàowèi), and Governor of Yōng Province (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ).
He proceeded to his garrison by the quickest route.
In the spring of the seventeenth year,
he traveled as far as Shífàn in Jìnglíng,
and died,
aged forty-four.
Gāozǔ heard of this
and mourned him deeply.
He dispatched his Imperial Son, the Prince of Nánkāng, Jì, to meet the coffin along the route.
Previously,
when Xiù traveled west,
the people of Yǐng Province escorted him out of the border.
Hearing of his illness,
the common people and merchants all prayed for his recovery.
After he died,
the people of the four provinces tore their clothes to make white caps,
and mourned and wept as they received and escorted the funeral procession.
The Mán people of Yōng Province went to welcome Xiù;
hearing of his death,
they performed sacrifices, wept, and departed.
When the mourning procession reached the Capital (Jīngshī),
Gāozǔ sent an envoy to bestow (posthumously) the titles Shìzhōng and Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
and gave him the posthumous name Kāng.
Xiù possessed a handsome appearance;
every time he attended court,
the hundreds of officials gazed upon him.
His nature was benevolent and forgiving;
joy and displeasure were not shown in his countenance.
A servant once threw a stone and killed a swan that Xiù kept.
The commander of the guards requested that the servant be punished.
Xiù said:
"How could I injure a man over a bird?"
While he was in the Capital (Jīngshī),
he attended to public affairs one morning.
When someone brought him food,
they accidentally spilled it.
He left and mounted his carriage,
did not eat the entire morning,
but did not rebuke the person either.
He was dedicated to scholarly arts and learning,
collecting classics and records.
He summoned the scholar Liú Xiàobiāo of Píngyuán
and commissioned him to compile the *Lèiyuàn*.
Although the book was not finished,
it was already circulating in the world.
Xiù was a brother to Gāozǔ from their commoner days.
After they became ruler and subject,
he was cautious and reverent,
more so than even those of lower or unrelated status.
Gāozǔ esteemed him even more highly because of this.
As a youth, he was partially orphaned;
he was particularly devoted to Prince Dàn of Shǐxīng.
When the Liáng dynasty arose,
Dàn served as Governor of Jīng Province (Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ) for a long time.
Starting from the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he habitually divided his official salary and shared it with Xiù.
Xiù accepted it willingly,
nor did he refuse when it was a large amount.
The harmony between the brothers
was praised by contemporary opinion.
His former subordinates, such as Xiàhóu Dǎn, memorialized requesting the erection of a tomb stele,
and an imperial edict granted permission.
High talents of the age who frequented the Prince's residence—
Wáng Sēngrú of Dōnghǎi, Lù Chuí of Wú Commandery, Liú Xiàochuò of Péngchéng, and Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng—
each composed an inscription for it.
This was unprecedented in antiquity.
His heir apparent, Jī, succeeded him.
Jī, whose courtesy name was Zhìtōng,
in the second year of Tiānjiān,
was appointed Heir Apparent of Ānchéng State.
In the sixth year,
he became General Who Pacifies Afar (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Kuàijī (Kuàijī Tàishǒu).
Upon returning, he served as Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng).
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he inherited the title Prince of Ānchéng Commandery (Ānchéng Jùn Wáng).
That same year, he became Groom of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
and was promoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
In the second year,
he was promoted to General of Awesome Brightness (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
In the third year,

he was promoted to Emissary with Credentials (Chíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Three Provinces of Xiāng, Héng, and Guì, General Who Pacifies Afar (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Xiāng Province (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the second year of Dàtōng,
he died in the province,
aged thirty.
Jī was handsome in appearance
and skilled in breath techniques (tǔnà).
Since his family possessed many books,
he was widely learned and had a strong memory;
however, he enjoyed frivolous games,
valued physical strength,
distanced himself from scholars,
and favored petty individuals.
While serving as governor, he focused entirely on extortion,
and showed no administrative achievements,
frequently being investigated and impeached.
When the funeral was being prepared,
the officials concerned requested a posthumous name.
Gāozǔ issued an edict saying:
"The Prince was indulgent in private affairs and negligent in governance.
He may be given the posthumous name Yáng."
The poems and rhapsodies he composed amounted to several thousand words,
which Shìzǔ collected and wrote a preface for.
His son, Cāo, succeeded him.
The Marquis of Nánpǔ, Tuī,
whose courtesy name was Zhìjìn,
was Jī’s second younger brother.
As a youth, he was pure and quick-witted,
enjoyed composing literature,
and was deeply appreciated by Tàizōng.
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng,
he was enfeoffed according to the precedent for imperial sons.
He subsequently served as General Who Pacifies Afar (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Huáinán (Huáinán Tàishǒu).
He was promoted to General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu),
Palace Attendant (Jǐshìzhōng),
Groom of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
and Director of the Palace Library (Mìshū Chéng).
He was sent out to serve as General Who Illustrates Military Might (Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wú Commandery (Wú Jùn Tàishǒu).
Wherever he served, the land inevitably became scorched earth and suffered great drought.
The people of Wú called
him "Mother of Drought"
During Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion,
he defended Dōngfǔ City.
The rebels set up siege towers
and attacked with all their might.
Tuī resisted everywhere,
frequently repelling and defeating them.
By evening,
Xǔ Yùhuá, the officer in charge of the northeast tower, opened the gate and welcomed the rebels inside.
The city was consequently taken,
and Tuī died, holding his official staff (jié).
Wěi, the Prince Yuánxiāng of Nánpíng, whose courtesy name was Wéndá,
was Tàizǔ’s eighth son.
As a child, he was pure, alert, and fond of learning.
During the Qí dynasty,
he began his career as an Acting Staff Officer in the Judicial Section of the General Who Guards the North in Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Zhèn Běi Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn).
His superior’s headquarters was promoted to that of the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì),
and he was transferred to External Military Affairs.
When Gāozǔ was in Yōng Province,
fearing that the realm would soon be in chaos,
he sought to summon Wěi and Prince Dàn of Shǐxīng to Xiāngyáng.
Soon after, he heard they had already entered the Miǎn River area.
Gāozǔ happily told his subordinates:
"I have nothing to worry about now."
When the righteous army arose,
the Prince of Nánkāng acted by imperial authority
and appointed him General Who Defeats the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn),
remaining behind to manage the affairs of the Yōng Provincial government.
After the righteous army departed,
the province's stores and manpower were completely depleted.
Péi Shīrén, Administrator of Wèixīng, and Yán Sēngdū, Administrator of Qíxīng, both held their commanderies and refused to accept orders,
raising troops intending to attack Yōng Province.
Wěi and Prince Dàn of Shǐxīng dispatched troops to Shǐpíng Commandery to await Shīrén and the others,
intercepted and heavily defeated them,
and the provincial border was consequently secured.
having already conquered *Yǐng* and *Lǔ*,
moved down upon *Xúnyáng*,
and besieged *Jiànyè*.
However, *Xiāo Huìxùn*'s son, *Guī*, the Administrator of *Bādōng*, and *Lǔ Xiūliè*, the Administrator of *Bāxī*, raised troops and pressed upon *Jīngzhōu*.
They garrisoned their forces at *Shàngmíng*,
and repeatedly defeated *Jīngzhōu*.
The Garrison Commander *Xiāo Yǐngzhòu* dispatched generals *Liú Xiàoqìng* and others to resist them,
but they were instead defeated by *Guī*.
*Yǐngzhòu*, consumed by grief and anger, died suddenly from illness.
The Western Court was terrified.
*Shàngshū Púyè* (Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs) *Xiàhóu Xiáng* proposed drafting troops from *Yōngzhōu*.
*Wěi* therefore assigned the generals and officials of the provincial administration,
to accompany the Prince of *Shǐxīng*, *Dàn*, to proceed there.
Once *Dàn* arrived,
*Guī* and his associates all surrendered.

Emperor *Hé* issued an edict appointing *Wěi* as *Shǐchíjié* (Bearer of Credentials), Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of *Yōng*, *Liáng*, *Nán Qín*, *Běi Qín* (the four provinces), *Jìnglíng* Commandery of *Yǐngzhōu*, and *Suí* Commandery of *Sīzhōu*; *Níngmán Xiàowèi* (Colonel Pacifying the Barbarians); and Governor of *Yōngzhōu* (*Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ*),
retaining his previous general title.
Shortly thereafter, he was additionally granted the title of *Shìzhōng* (Palace Attendant),
and his general title was advanced to *Zhènběi Jiāngjūn* (General Who Guards the North).
In the first year of *Tiānjiān* (502 CE),
he was additionally granted the title *Sànqí Chángshì* (Cavalry Regular Attendant),
and his military command was advanced to include *Jīng* and *Níng* provinces,
the remainder remaining as before.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of *Jiàn'ān* Commandery,
with an income fief of two thousand households,
and was provided with a set of drums and pipes (*gǔchuī*).
In the fourth year (505 CE),
he was transferred to be Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of *Nán Xúzhōu* and Governor of *Nán Xúzhōu*.
His titles *Shǐchíjié*, *Chángshì*, and General remained as before.
In the fifth year (506 CE),
upon arriving at the capital,
his position was changed to *Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn* (General Who Stabilizes the Army) and *Dānyáng Yǐn* (Prefect of *Dānyáng*),
retaining *Chángshì* as before.
In the sixth year (507 CE),
he was promoted to *Shǐchíjié*, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of *Yáng* and *Nán Xú* provinces, *Yòujūn Jiāngjūn* (General of the Right Army), and Governor of *Yángzhōu*.
Before he accepted the appointment,
his general title was advanced to *Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn* (General of Central Authority).
In the seventh year (508 CE),
citing illness, he memorialized to relinquish the provincial post.
His position was changed to *Shìzhōng* and *Zhōngfǔjūn* (Central General Who Stabilizes the Army),
and he supervised the affairs of the *Sītú* (Minister of Education).
In the ninth year (510 CE),
he was promoted to *Hùjūn* (Protector of the Army) and placed in charge of the military affairs of *Shítou* Garrison.
*Shìzhōng*, General, and the *gǔchuī* remained as before.
That same year,
he was sent out as *Shǐchíjié*, *Sànqí Chángshì*, Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs of *Jiāngzhōu*, *Zhènnán Jiāngjūn* (General Who Guards the South), and Governor of *Jiāngzhōu*.
The *gǔchuī* remained as before.
In the eleventh year (512 CE),
by his existing titles, he was additionally granted *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī* (Establishment of a Governorship with Honors Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers).
That same year,
he again pleaded to be relieved due to illness.
In the twelfth year (513 CE),
he was recalled to be *Fǔjūn Jiāngjūn*.
The titles *Yítóng* and *Chángshì* remained as before,
but due to illness, he did not accept the appointment.
In the thirteenth year (514 CE),
his position was changed to *Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū* (Grand Master of the Palace, Left).
He was additionally granted forty trusted attendants,
an annual stipend of ten thousand *hú* of rice,
five thousand bolts of linen and silk,
two million four hundred thousand cash for medicine,
and two hundred thousand cash monthly for kitchen supplies.
In addition, two hundred miscellaneous laborers from the Two Guards and Two Battalions,
double the previous amount,
and one hundred staff members for the *fánggé* and *báizhí* offices were appointed.
In *Wěi*'s later years, his illness grew severe,
and he no longer left the capital (as a regional lord).
Therefore, his emoluments and ranks were increased.
In the fifteenth year (516 CE),
his biological mother, Consort Dowager *Chén* (*Chén Tàifēi*), fell ill.
*Wěi* and the Prince of *Línchuān*, *Hóng*, attended her illness,
neither removing their belts.
When the Consort Dowager passed away,
their grief and devastation exceeded the proper rituals.
They did not let water or gruel pass their lips for several successive days.
*Gāozǔ* personally visited them repeatedly to console and restrain them.
Although *Wěi* obeyed the edicts,
his devastation and emaciation were almost unbearable for the mourning.
In the seventeenth year (518 CE),
because *Gāozǔ* considered the land of *Jiàn'ān* to be poor,
he changed *Wěi*'s enfeoffment to Prince of *Nánpíng* Commandery.
The households of the fief remained as before.
He was promoted to *Shìzhōng*, *Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū*, and *Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*.
In the fourth year of *Pǔtōng* (523 CE),
his fief was increased by one thousand households.
In the fifth year (524 CE),
his title was advanced to *Zhènwèi Dàjiāngjūn* (Grand General Who Guards the Garrisons).
In the first year of *Zhōngdàtōng* (529 CE),
by his existing office, he concurrently led the duties of *Tàizǐ Tàifù* (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince).
In the fourth year (532 CE),
he was promoted to *Zhōngshū Lìng* (Director of the Central Secretariat) and *Dàsīmǎ* (Grand Marshal).
In the fifth year (533 CE),
he passed away,
at the age of fifty-eight.
An imperial edict commanded that he be entombed in the ceremonial robe and crown (*gǔnmiǎn*),
and supplied with secret implements from the Eastern Park.
Another edict stated:
"Honoring virtue and recording merit
is the commendable standard of former kings.
Paying careful respect at the end and recalling the distant past
is the common rule of successive generations.
The late *Shìzhōng*, *Zhōngshū Lìng*, *Dàsīmǎ*, Prince of *Nánpíng*, *Wěi*,
possessed a vast and generous disposition,
and his discernment and understanding were broad and concise.
Since his youth,
his pure reputation has been reverent.
He assisted Us during the chaos (of the dynasty's founding),
his merit was high at *Fán* and *Miǎn*,
enduring great hardship and difficulty,
and fulfilling the responsibilities entrusted to him with diligence.
When he later assisted in governance and discussed the Way,
he magnified the duties of the highest officials.
His sudden passing,
causes Us intense grief in Our heart.
It is fitting to confer high honors upon him,
thus manifesting the great standard.
He is hereby granted the posthumous titles of *Shìzhōng* and *Tàizǎi* (Grand Tutor),
retaining his princely rank.
He shall be provided with one set of feather canopies and drums and pipes,
along with forty honor guards wielding swords.
His posthumous name shall be *Yuánxiāng*."
When *Wěi* was young, he loved learning,
was earnest, sincere, tolerant, and forgiving.
He pursued the worthy and respected scholars,
always acting as if he could never achieve enough.
Because of this, wandering scholars from all directions,
and those famous in their generation,
all came to him.
During the *Qí* era,
the *Qīngxī* Palace had been renamed *Fānglín Yuàn* (Fragrant Forest Park).
In the early *Tiānjiān* period,
it was bestowed upon *Wěi* as his residence.
*Wěi* further excavated and constructed grounds,
planting beautiful trees and rare fruits,
making it extremely ornate and magnificent.
Whenever he strolled within it with his guests,
he commanded the Aide *Xiāo Zifàn* to write a record of it.
Among the mansions of the imperial kinsmen in the *Liáng* era,
none could surpass it.
Moreover, his nature was benevolent,
and he especially pitied the poor and needy.
He often sent his trusted confidants and attendants
to visit people in the neighborhoods and villages.
If there were those who were poor and unable to handle auspicious or inauspicious events,
he would immediately send aid and relief.
When *Wáng Mǎnyǐng* of *Tàiyuán* died,
his family was poor and lacked means for the funeral preparations.
His friend *Jiāng Gé* went to mourn him.
*Mǎnyǐng*'s wife and children wept and appealed to *Gé*.
*Gé* said:
"The Prince of *Jiàn'ān* will surely know of this,
and he will certainly manage the arrangements for you."
Before he had finished speaking, an envoy from *Wěi* arrived,
providing for the funeral affairs,
and thus they were fully aided.
Whenever there was severe cold and accumulated snow,
he would dispatch people carrying firewood and rice,
immediately distributing them to those suffering from shortages.
In his later years, he greatly revered Buddhist principles,
and was particularly skilled in the study of the Dark Learning (*Xuánxué*).
He authored the *Èr Zhǐ Yì* (Meaning of the Two Purposes),
which created a new form of understanding.
He also composed treatises on *Xìngqíng* (Nature and Emotion) and *Jīshén* (Subtle Spirit).
Regarding his theories,
the monk *Chǒng*, along with *Zhōu Shě*, *Yīn Jūn*, and *Lù Chuí*, all famous for their expertise and understanding,
were unable to refute him.
*Wěi* had four sons: *Kè*,
*Gōng*,
*Qián*,
and *Zhī*.
The Heir Apparent *Kè* succeeded him.
*Gōng*'s courtesy name was *Jìngfàn*.
In the eighth year of *Tiānjiān* (509 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of *Héngshān* County.
Due to *Yuánxiāng*'s merit,
his fief was increased to one thousand households.
Previously,
when the Marquis of *Lèshān*, *Zhèngzé*, committed a crime,
an imperial command reprimanded the various princes,
but addressed *Yuánxiāng* alone, saying:
"Not only are your sons without fault,
they all adhere to the path of righteousness."
*Gōng* began his career as *Jǐshìzhōng* (Attendant in the Palace Secretariat).
He was promoted to *Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ* (Equerry to the Crown Prince).

He was sent out as the Supervisor of the Military Affairs of eleven commanderies including *Qí'ān*, *Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn* (General Who Pacifies Afar), and Administrator of the two commanderies of *Xīyáng* and *Wǔchāng*.
He was recalled to serve as *Mìshū Chéng* (Vice Director of the Palace Library),
and promoted to *Zhōngshū Láng* (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat).
He oversaw the Prefect of *Dānyáng*.
He temporarily managed the affairs of *Xú* and *Nán Xú* provinces.
He was transferred to be Governor of *Héngzhōu*.
He left office due to mourning his mother.
Shortly after, he was reactivated as *Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn* (General of the Cloud-Maneuvers) and Governor of *Xiāngzhōu*.
Gōng was skilled in handling official affairs,
and was praised wherever he went.
However, his nature favored extravagance,
and he extensively constructed residences,
emphasizing living quarters and walkways,
mimicking palace halls.
He especially enjoyed entertaining guests and friends,
feasting deeply all day long;
his seating area was full of guests,
and he never tired of conversation.
At that time, Shìzǔ
resided in his fiefdom, somewhat dedicated to reputation,
diligently focusing his mind on writing;
he never recklessly consumed a cup of wine.
Gōng often leisurely said to people:
"I, your subordinate, have observed the people of the world;
many do not enjoy happiness,
instead lying face up on their beds,
looking at the roof beams while writing books.
A thousand autumns and ten thousand years—
who will transmit this?
To exhaust the spirit and bitterly contemplate,
yet ultimately fail to achieve fame—
How can that compare to facing the clear breeze,
looking at the bright moon,
climbing mountains and floating on waters,
freely and heartily singing!"
Soon after, because the Mán (barbarians) of Yōngzhōu, led by Wén Dào, detained and attracted Wèi
bandits, an edict ordered Gōng to go and assist.
Consequently, he was appointed Chíjié, Rénwēi Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ,
proceeding directly to his post.
Tàizōng, having associated with Gōng since youth,
especially appreciated and favored him.
Thereupon, he issued a personal order saying:
"The scholarly class there is honest and straightforward,
possessing residual customs of Guānfǔ;
the black-haired people are defiant and obstinate,
knowing only to value their swords and lightly regard death.
The surrendered Hú only prize greed,
and the border Mán do not know reverence or deference.
Their intentions cannot be clearly discerned (white from black),
and laws have no use when applied.
I hope you will strengthen the border garrisons,
avoid frequent relocations,
keep espionage far-reaching,
ensure stores and granaries are accumulated,
use strength to control weakness,
and use calm to manage turbulence.
Having long received your affection and consideration,
I dare to express my innermost feelings."
When Gōng arrived at the prefecture,
his governance indeed achieved reputation and merit.
The hundred surnames presented a memorial,
requesting permission to erect a stele south of the city to praise his virtue;
an edict granted this.
Previously, Xiān Gāozǔ had designated Yōng as a border defense post,
transporting grain from several prefectures
to fill the reserve granaries.
Later, Gōng frequently took official rice
to supply his private residence.
This was reported by Lúlíng Wáng, the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
Because of this, he was dismissed from office and stripped of his title.
For several years thereafter, he was not employed.
During the chaos of Hóu Jǐng,
he died within the city
at the age of fifty-two.
An edict specially restored his original title.
Shìzǔ posthumously appointed him Shìzhōng and Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn.
His posthumous title was Xī.
His heir, Jìng,
courtesy name Ānrén,
had a fine reputation
and was called an outstanding young member of the imperial clan.
He had literary talent,
and was devoted and fond of learning.
Since he was internally wealthy,
he accumulated many classics and historical works.
Books were spread across his mat,
and he personally collated them by hand.
Hé Jìngróng wanted to give his daughter to him in marriage,
but Jìng was wary of the family being too powerful;
he refused and did not accept.
Public opinion at the time admired this.
He successively held the posts of Tàizǐ Shèrén and Dōnggōng Lǐngzhí.
He was promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng,
then Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
He was deeply cherished and appreciated by Tàizōng.
In the third year of Tàiqīng,
he died,
and was posthumously appointed Shìzhōng.
Huī, the Zhōngliè Wáng of Póyáng, courtesy name Hóngdá,
was the ninth son of Tàizǔ.
In his youth, he was intelligent and bright;
at the age of seven,
he could understand the meaning of the Xiàojīng and the Lúnyǔ,
leaving nothing unanalyzed or unexposed.
Once grown,
he possessed a fine appearance and demeanor,
and widely studied historical records.
During the Lóngchāng period of Qí,
when Míng Dì was Chancellor,
there were many troubles both internal and external.
Míng Dì asked Chángshā Xuānwǔ Wáng Yì for advice on which of his younger brothers could be entrusted with important matters.
Xuānwǔ recommended Huī.
Míng Dì appointed Huī as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn,
provided 100 armed guards to protect the Eastern Residence,
and also drew him in as Piàojì Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn.
When Míng Dì ascended the throne,
and the Eastern Palace was established,
Huī was made Tàizǐ Shèrén.
He was repeatedly promoted to Běi Zhōngláng Wàibīng Cānjūn,
and Qiánjūn Zhǔbù.
During the rebellion of Xuānwǔ,
he fled and stayed in the capital.
When Gāozǔ’s righteous army arrived,
Huī received him at Xīnlín,
and was appointed Fǔguó Jiāngjūn.
At that time, the Sānwú region was rife with unrest,
so Gāozǔ ordered him to move out and garrison Pògāng.
When Jiànkāng was pacified,
he returned and was appointed Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was made Shìzhōng, Qián Jiāngjūn, and concurrently in charge of the Shítóu garrison affairs.
He was enfeoffed as the Prince (Wáng) of Póyáng Commandery,
with a stipend of two thousand households.
In the second year,
he was sent out as Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of Nán Xúzhōu, Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Nán Xúzhōu.
In the fourth year,
he was reassigned as Dūdū of the military affairs of Yǐng and Sī Prefectures, Hòu Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Yǐngzhōu,
retaining his title of Chíjié.
Early in the righteous army campaign,
many people in Yǐngchéng died from disease and plague,
and there was no time to bury them.
When Huī arrived at his post,
he immediately ordered them to be buried and covered up.
He also dispatched four envoys to tour the prefectural regions,
and the territory achieved great order.
In the seventh year,
his title was advanced to Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn,
and he was further appointed Dūdū of Huòzhōu.
In the eighth year,
his title was again advanced to Píngxī Jiāngjūn.
In the tenth year,
he was recalled to serve as Shìzhōng, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, in charge of the Shítóu garrison affairs,
and concurrently Zōngzhèng Qīng.
In the eleventh year,

he was sent out as Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū of the military affairs of the Nine Prefectures: Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Yì, Níng, North and South Liáng, and North and South Qín, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
He was granted a set of drums and horns.
In the thirteenth year,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of the military affairs of the Seven Prefectures: Yì, Níng, North and South Qín, and Shā,
Zhènxī Jiāngjūn, and Cìshǐ of Yìzhōu.
His title of Shǐ Chíjié remained unchanged.
He proceeded directly to his post.
Chéngdū was five hundred *lǐ* from Xīnchéng.
When traveling by land,
private horses were all requisitioned.
The common people suffered from this,
a practice which successive administrations failed to change.
Huī then purchased one thousand horses
and distributed them to the households that had previously been requisitioned,
providing them with mounts for riding.
When needed, they were dispatched in sequence.
The common people depended on him for this relief.
In the seventeenth year,
he was recalled to serve as Shìzhōng, Ānqián Jiāngjūn, and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the eighteenth year,

he was sent out as Shǐ Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of the military affairs of the Eight Prefectures: Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, North and South Qín, Zhēngxī Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
In the fifth year of Pǔtōng,
his title was advanced to Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn.
In the ninth month of the seventh year,
he died at his post
at the age of fifty-one.
An imperial edict stated:

"The deceased Shǐ Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū of the military affairs of the Eight Prefectures: Jīng, Xiāng, Yōng, Liáng, Yì, Níng, North and South Qín, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, Prince Huī of Póyáng,
possessed an open and bright demeanor,
and his character and disposition were solid and true.
Since his tender years,
his fine reputation was fully proclaimed.
Extending to his participation in government,
his excellent plans were thoroughly implemented.
He was just about to enter the highest council to discuss the Way
and vastly assist the officials of the court.
Unexpectedly, he passed away.
We are therefore profoundly grieved in Our heart.
It is proper to bestow generous posthumous honors,
in accordance with court regulations.
He shall be posthumously appointed Shìzhōng and Sītú.
His princely title remains as before.
Furthermore, he is granted twenty men bearing ceremonial swords.
His posthumous title shall be Zhōngliè (Loyal and Illustrious)."
Liú Xiǎn, a Zhōngshū Shèrén, was dispatched to oversee the funeral arrangements.
Huī possessed filial piety.
When he first governed Shǔ,
his birth mother, Fèi Tàifēi, was still staying in the capital (dū).
Later, she became unwell in the capital.
Huī did not yet know of this.
One night, he suddenly dreamt of returning to attend to her illness.
After waking, he was worried and distraught,
and thereupon neglected sleep and food.
Soon after, a message arrived from the capital,
stating that the Tàifēi had already recovered.
Later, he also had an eye disease,
which long prevented him from seeing.
There was a Daoist monk, Huìlóng, who had crossed over from the north and possessed the art of treating eyes.
Huī invited him.
When he arrived,
Huī suddenly saw a divine monk (shèngsēng) in the air,
and as soon as Huìlóng inserted the needle,
his sight was immediately and clearly restored.
Everyone said this was due to his utmost sincerity (jīngchéng).
Huī was broad-minded and forgiving by nature.
He lightly regarded wealth and loved giving charity.
He governed four prefectures in total,
and scattered the stipends he received as soon as he got them.
While in Jīngzhōu,
he often casually asked his staff and guests, saying:
“Zhōngshān liked wine,
Zhào Wáng liked officials (lì).
Which of the two is superior?”
No one in the assembly had an answer.
He looked at Chief Clerk Xiāo Chēn and said:
“During the Hàn Dynasty, kings and marquises
were merely territorial governors (fānpíng).
Attending to affairs and interacting closely with the people
belonged naturally to their respective roles.
Zhōngshān listening to music
could be considered indulging his nature;
but Péng Zǔ replacing officials
was close to infringing on official duties.
The kings and marquises of today
do not merely guard their territories (fānguó);
they ought to assist the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) in governing the people.
Purity and integrity (qīngbái)—are these not superior?”
The guests in attendance were all convinced.
His heir was Fàn.
Fàn’s courtesy name was Shìyí.
He was gentle, mild, and possessed talent and insight.
He started his career as Crown Prince’s Equerry (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ) and Palace Writer (Mìshū Láng),
served successively as Palace Gate Attendant (Huángmén Láng),
and was promoted to Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
Every night, he personally patrolled for security.
Gāozǔ praised him for his diligence.
He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Cìshǐ).
He opened up the Jiàndào route
and succeeded in recovering Huàyáng.
His fiefdom was increased by one thousand households,
and he was granted military music (gǔchuī).
He was recalled to serve as General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn) and Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Although Fàn lacked scholarly knowledge,
he prided himself on his military strategy (chóu lüè).
He loved the unusual and appreciated antiquity,
and gathered literary talents.
He wrote inscriptions and memorials impromptu,
which sometimes showed surprising elegance.

He was again sent out to serve as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of the Five Prefectures of Yōng, Liáng, Dōng Yì, and Nán Běi Qín (Dūdū Yōng Liáng Dōng Yì Nán Běi Qín Wǔ Zhōu Zhū Jūnjì), General Guarding the North (Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn), and Administrator of Yōngzhōu (Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ).
Fàn, in his capacity as governor, managed the people
and earned great contemporary praise.
He pacified and consoled the officers and soldiers,
and completely won their devotion.
In the first year of Tàiqīng (547 CE),
a major northern expedition was launched.

Fàn was appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), General-in-Chief Campaigning in the North (Zhēng Běi Dà Jiāngjūn), and Supreme Commander of All Military Affairs for the Northern Expedition (Zǒngdū Běi Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnjì),
and advanced to attack Rángchéng.
Soon after, he was promoted to General Pacifying the North (Ān Běi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nán Yùzhōu (Nán Yùzhōu Cìshǐ).
Hóu Jǐng was defeated at Guōyáng
and retreated to defend Shòuyáng.
Fàn was then reassigned as Administrator of Hézhōu (Hézhōu Cìshǐ),
stationed at Héféi.
At that time, Jǐng had already harbored treacherous schemes,
and his disloyalty was about to be exposed.
Fàn repeatedly memorialized concerning this,
but Zhū Yì consistently suppressed the reports and did not present them.
When Jǐng besieged the capital (Jīngyì),
Fàn sent his heir, Sì, along with Péi Zhī Gāo and others, to enter and provide assistance.
He was promoted to Governor-General with Rank Equal to the Three Dukes (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
and advanced in title to General Campaigning in the North (Zhēng Běi Jiāngjūn).
When the capital could not be held,
Fàn abandoned Héféi,
exited through Dōngguān,
requested troops from Wèi,
and sent his two sons as hostages.
The Wèi people occupied Héféi
but ultimately did not send out troops to assist Fàn.
Fàn had no strategy for advancing or retreating,
so he sailed westward upstream,
camped at Cóng Yáng,
and sent a messenger to inform the Prince of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng Wáng).
The Prince of Xúnyáng asked him to return to Jiǔjiāng,
intending to raise troops together and proceed west.
Fàn received the letter and was greatly pleased.
He then led his army to Pénchéng,
designated Jìnxī as Jìnzhōu,
and sent his son Sì to be the Administrator (Cìshǐ).
The commanderies and counties of Jiāngzhōu
were frequently altered and changed.
The administrative orders issued by Xúnyáng
only covered one remaining commandery.
Contemporary opinion criticized him for this.
Since trade and travel were cut off,
and communications were completely severed,
Fàn’s several tens of thousands of troops
were all left without food.
Many people died of starvation.
Fàn became angry/distressed
and died from a tumor on his back (fā bèi hōng),
at the age of fifty-two.
The heir, Sì,
courtesy name Cháng Yìn.
His appearance was robust and great,
and his waist measurement was ten standard girths (shí wéi).
He was brave, decisive, and strategically bold by nature.
He was unconventional and did not care for minor conduct,
but he was capable of dedicating himself to supporting soldiers,
all of whom were willing to fight for him until death.
When Fàn died,
Sì still held Jìnxī.
Food ran out in the city,
and the troops were utterly exhausted.
Jǐng sent Rèn Yuē to attack.
Sì personally donned armor
and emerged from the ramparts to resist them.
At that time, the momentum of the rebels was great.
Everyone advised him to stop for the moment.
Sì grasped his sword and shouted at them, saying:
“In the current battle,
how can there be retreat?
This is the moment for Xiāo Sì to dedicate his life and die a loyal death.”
He was consequently struck by a stray arrow,
and died on the battlefield.
Dàn, the Prince Zhōngwǔ of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Zhōngwǔ Wáng), courtesy name Sēng Dá,
was the eleventh son of Tàizǔ.
When he was a few years old,
his birth mother, Wú Tàifēi, died.
Dàn’s grief moved those around him.
During the Qí Dynasty,
when he reached manhood (ruò guàn), he served as Acting Aide to the Legal Section of the General of the West (Xī Zhōng Láng Fǎ Cáo Xíng Cānjūn),
and was promoted to Aide to the External Military Section (Wài Bīng Cānjūn).
When the righteous army (yì shī) rose up,
the Prince of Nánkāng (Nánkāng Wáng) acted by imperial decree
and appointed Dàn as General of the Champion Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn) and Military Counselor Aide to the General of the West (Xī Zhōng Láng Zīyì Cānjūn).
He was promoted to Retainer within the Grand Counselor's Staff (Xiàngguó Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
and remained in defense with Wěi, the Prince of Nánpíng (Nánpíng Wáng).
Hé Dì ascended the throne,
appointing Dàn as Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
At that time, Xiāo Huìxùn’s son Guī, Administrator of Bādōng, along with Lǔ Xiūliè, Administrator of Bāxī, raised troops and threatened Jīngzhōu.
They garrisoned their forces at Shàngmíng.
When Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn Xiāo Yǐngzhòu died suddenly of a severe illness,
the Xī Cháo (Western Court) was terrified.
Shàngshū Púyè Xiàhóu Xiáng proposed levying troops from Yōngzhōu,
and Nánpíng Wáng Wěi dispatched Dàn to handle the situation.
Dàn used a letter to persuade Guī and the others,
and within ten days, they all requested surrender.
That winter,
Gāozǔ pacified Jiànyè.
In the spring of the following year,
Hé Dì was about to depart from Jiānglíng.
An imperial edict appointed Dàn as Shǐchíjié, Dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yì Níng Nán Běi Qín liù zhōu zhū jūnshì, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ,
though he had not yet formally accepted the post.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
he was promoted to Ānxī Jiāngjūn.
His posts as Dūdū and Cìshǐ remained unchanged.
He was invested as Shǐxīng Jùnwáng,
with an allotted fief of two thousand households.
Following the recent military campaigns,
public and private resources were depleted.
Dàn exerted himself diligently in governing,
extensively opening up military agricultural colonies (túntián),
reducing corvée labor,
offering condolences to the families of soldiers who had died,
and providing for those in extreme poverty.
The populace greatly benefited from this security.
Dàn, conscious that he was young yet held such a weighty responsibility,
wished to foster openness and guide the sentiments of the people.
He then addressed his assisting officials, saying:
“If administration is not good,
gentlemen and officials should collectively regret it.
If a suggestion is useful,
it may be used;
if it is not used,
how does that harm me?
My heart is open,
so you should not hold back.”
Consequently, the petty people realized his kindness,
and the gentlemen exerted their full efforts.
When the common people came with disputes and lawsuits,
they would stand waiting for his ruling or instruction,
and decisions were made in an instant.
The government offices had no backlog of business,
and the lower courts had no prolonged imprisonments.
The people were increasingly pleased.
In the third year,
an imperial edict added one set of drums and pipes (for ceremonial music).
In the sixth year,
the prefecture suffered a great flood.
The river overflowed and the dike was broken.
Dàn personally led his prefectural officers and subordinates,
braving the rain, assigning measurements, and supervising the construction and repair.
The rain was severe and the water level rose dangerously.
Everyone was afraid,
and some requested Dàn to withdraw.
Dàn said:
“Even Wáng Zūn desired to personally block the river dike;
why should I alone seek exemption?”
He then sacrificed a white horse to the Jiāngshén (River God).
Soon after, the water receded and the dike was secured.
Bǐngzhōu was on the south bank.
Several hundred households, seeing the water rising, ran in panic,
climbing onto roofs and clinging to trees.
Dàn offered a reward for people to save them,
offering ten thousand coins per person rescued.
Dozens of traveling merchants answered the call and went to the rescue,
and thus the prefectural citizens were spared.
He also sent representatives to all the commanderies.
Those who had died in the flood were provided with coffins,
and those who had lost their fields were given grain seed.
That year,
auspicious grain (jiāhé) grew within the prefecture's borders.
The officials and common people attributed the merit to him,
but Dàn modestly declined to accept it.
In the seventh year,
his loving mother, Címǔ Chén Tàifēi, passed away.
For six days, he took neither water nor gruel into his mouth.
He observed the mourning rites beyond what was prescribed by ritual.
Gāozǔ issued a gracious edict encouraging him,
and ordered him to temporarily manage the affairs of the prefecture.
That winter,
an imperial edict summoned him back to the court with his original title.
The people sang a song about him, saying:
“Shǐxīng Wáng,
father of the people,
(Pronounced tú-kě-fǎn) Rushing to help those in peril,
like extinguishing fire or water.
When will he return again to nourish us?”
In the eighth year,
he was made Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, and Put in charge of Shítóu Garrison Affairs (lǐng Shítóu shù shì).
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn and Zhōngshū Lìng,
and shortly managed the office of Wèiwèi Qīng.
Dàn was by nature diligent and humble.
He lowered his status to receive scholars and officials,
often sitting with his guests on couches placed side by side.
Contemporary opinion praised this conduct.
That autumn,
he was sent out as Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Dūdū Nán Běi Yǎn Xú Qīng Jì wǔ zhōu zhū jūnshì, Zhènběi Jiāngjūn, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the spring of the ninth year,
he was transferred to Dūdū Yì Níng Nán Liáng Nán Běi Qín Shā liù zhōu zhū jūnshì, Zhènxī Jiāngjūn, and Yìzhōu Cìshǐ.
He established schools,
encouraging people to attend classes and take up studies.
He sent his son Yìng to personally receive instruction in the classics there,
and consequently, many people were inspired to follow this example.
At that time, Wèi attacked Bānán
and besieged Nán'ān from the west.
Yuán Jìguī, the Administrator of Nán'ān, firmly defended the city walls.
Dàn dispatched troops to rescue him.
The Wèi forces retreated,
and a great amount of captured equipment was obtained.
In the fourteenth year,
he was transferred to Dūdū Jīng Xiāng Yōng Níng Nán Liáng Nán Běi Qín qī zhōu zhū jūnshì, Zhènyòu Jiāngjūn, and Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ.
His elder brother by the same mother, Ānchéng Wáng Xiù, who was traveling to Yōngzhōu,
died en route.
When Dàn heard the news of the death,
he threw himself onto the ground,
wept while sitting on a mat of straw,
and abstained from drinking and eating for several days.
He poured out his wealth to provide funeral gifts and provisions,
and all those in the convoy, high and low, received sufficient aid.
The entire realm praised his fraternal devotion.
In the eighteenth year,
he was summoned to court and appointed Shìzhōng, Zhōngfǔ Jiāngjūn, Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the eleventh month of Pǔtōng three (522 CE),
he passed away,
at the age of forty-five.
He was posthumously granted the titles Shìzhōng, Sītú, and Piàojì Jiāngjūn.
He was granted thirty guards bearing ceremonial swords,
and one set of feather canopy, drums, and pipes.
The document of investiture read:
“Alas, the late Shìzhōng, Sītú, Piàojì Jiāngjūn, Shǐxīng Wáng: Indeed, loyalty is a fine virtue,
and martial valor means stopping conflict.
The manner in which these virtues were utilized
is recorded in previous histories.
The Prince possessed the foundational merit of aiding the Mandate,
and the profound virtue of benefiting the people.
Over two cycles of twelve years (24 years),
he remained constant from beginning to end.
Therefore, following the path of the worthy men of the past,
and examining ancient precedents,
his great reputation and noble righteousness
truly reached their pinnacle.
We now dispatch Chéng Shuǎng, acting Grand Herald (Jiān Dà Hónglú),
to grant him the posthumous title Zhōngwǔ (Loyal and Martial).
If your spirit has awareness,
accept this glorious title.
Alas, mournful indeed!”
Before Dàn passed away,
he dreamed that his title was changed to Zhōngshān Wáng,
and the investiture document was bestowed upon him as on other days.
He felt quite ill-omened by this,
and died a few weeks later.
The heir apparent, Liàng, succeeded him.
The Court Historian remarks: Since ancient times, when kings established their dynasties,
they widely planted the seeds of kinship,
dividing provinces and states,
and enfeoffing their sons and younger brothers.
Thus, Dàqí Shǎobó
were honored in Lǔ and Wèi,
and the firm foundation of Pánshí Níngzhī (Impregnable Stone and Solid Fat)
was established in Liáng and Chǔ.
Gāozǔ followed these ancient standards,
using his honored kin as protecting screens.
As for Ānchéng, Nánpíng, Póyáng, and Shǐxīng,
all were distinguished by their reputation and achievements,
and they may be likened to Hàn zhī Jiān and Píng of the Hàn Dynasty.
Biography Seventeen: Heir Yè of Chángshā, Heir Bóyóu of Yǒngyáng, Heir Yuánjiǎn of Héngyáng, Heir Xiàng of Guìyáng.
Chángshā Sì Wáng Yè, courtesy name Jìngkuàng,
was the son of Gāozǔ's elder brother, Yì.
Yì, courtesy name Yuándá,
had a fine reputation when young.
He relinquished his commoner status to serve as Acting Staff Officer to Qí's Prince Ānnán of Shàolíng,
succeeding to the noble title of Marquis of Línxiāng County.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén), Crown Prince's Groom (Xǐmǎ), and Companion to the Prince of Jiàn'ān.
He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Jìnlíng,
and in less than a full year,
his judicial administration was harmonious,
and it was lauded as good governance.
He returned to the court to serve as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
In the final year of Yǒngmíng (period),

he was granted the Staff of Authority, made Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs in the four provinces of Liáng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín, and Shā, Commandant for the Western Barbarians (Xīróng Xiàowèi), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Liáng and Nán Qín provinces,
with the added title of General Who Guards the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn).
That year,
the Wèi people entered Hànzhōng,
and consequently besieged Nánzhèng.
Yì adapted to the situation and resisted the attack,
inflicting heavy casualties,
whereupon the siege was lifted and they fled.
Yì also dispatched the Dī chief Yáng Yuánxiù to attack six Wèi garrisons, including Lìchéng, Gāolán, Luògǔ, and Kēngchí,
and captured them.
The Wèi people were alarmed and fearful,
and the border regions subsequently became peaceful.
He was promoted to the title General Who Conquers the Captives (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn),
and his fiefdom was increased by three hundred households.
He was transferred to Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Yì and Níng provinces, and Governor of Yì Province.
He returned to the court to serve as Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard (Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài), Director of the Personnel Bureau (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng), and Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
In the second year of Yǒngyuán,
Péi Shūyè occupied Yù Province and rebelled.
Yì was granted the Staff of Authority, made General Who Conquers the Captives, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Yù Province, and Governor of Yù Province,
concurrently serving as Administrator of Lìyáng and Nánqiáo Commanderies,
to suppress Shūyè.
Shūyè became fearful
and surrendered to Wèi.
Soon thereafter, General Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī Jiāngjūn) Cuī Huìjǐng invaded the capital region,
taking Jiāngxià Wáng Bǎoxuán as his figurehead and besieging Táichéng.
The Qí house fell into great disorder,
and an imperial edict summoned Yì.
Yì was eating at the time;
he threw down his chopsticks and stood up.
He led three thousand elite soldiers to reinforce the city.
Huìjǐng sent his son, Jué, to resist him.
Yì attacked rapidly and heavily defeated him;
Jué fled alone on horseback.
Taking advantage of the victory, Yì advanced,
Huìjǐng's troops collapsed,
and he was pursued and decapitated.
Yì was appointed Attendant at the Palace (Shìzhōng) and Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòupúshè).
Before he formally took the post,
he was immediately promoted to Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Area Commander-in-Chief of all land and naval forces for expeditions,
with the Staff of Authority and the rank of General remaining as before.
His income fief was increased by two thousand five hundred households.
At that time, Dōnghūn (the Eastern Degenerate) indulged in cruelty;
Rú Fǎzhēn, Wáng Xuānzhī, and others held power.
Long-serving officials and veteran generals
were all executed.
Since Yì had established great merit
and alone occupied a high position at court,
he was deeply feared by Fǎzhēn and the others.
They consequently spoke to Dōnghūn, saying:
"Yì is planning to repeat the precedent of Lóngchāng;
Your Majesty's life is hanging by a thread."
Dōnghūn believed them,
and intended to inflict a cruel death upon Yì.
However, someone close to Yì learned of this,
and secretly prepared a boat on the riverbank,
urging him to flee west.
Yì said:
"Everyone must die eventually.
How could a Director of the Department of State Affairs flee as a rebel?"
Consequently, he met disaster.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng,
he was posthumously granted Attendant at the Palace, Supervisor of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān), and Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
When Empress Dowager Xuāndé supervised the court (acting as regent),
this was changed to the posthumous grant of Grand Tutor (Tàifù).
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was posthumously elevated to Chancellor (Chéngxiàng),
enfeoffed as Prince of Chángshā Commandery,
and given the posthumous title Xuānwǔ.
He was provided with the nine-streamer banner, the carriage decorated with luan birds, the covered carriage (wēnliáng chē),
the yellow canopy, the great left banner (zuǒdú),
feathered canopies and drums and fifes for the front and rear divisions,
two divisions of mourning songs,
and one hundred Bāan Jiàn Hǔbēn (Tiger Guards with Swords of Office).
The funeral rites followed entirely the precedent of the Prince Ānpíng of Jìn.
Yè was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and his wisdom and tolerance surpassed ordinary men.
While serving Qí, he was Literary Draftsman (Zhùzuò Láng) and Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince.
During the disaster involving Xuānwǔ,
he fled and hid along with his two younger brothers, Zǎo and Xiàng.
When Gāozǔ arrived,
Yè went to his army
and was made General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn).
In the second year of Zhōngxīng,
he was appointed General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Nán Lángyá and Qīnghé Commanderies.
In the second year of Tiānjiān,
he succeeded to the title Prince of Chángshā,
was summoned to court as General Who Guards the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn),
and was allowed to establish staff officers according to scale.
He was promoted to Supervisor of the Imperial Secretariat (Mìshū Jiān).
In the fourth year,
he was reassigned as Attendant at the Palace (Shìzhōng).
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and Commander of the Crown Prince's Right Guard.
He was promoted to General of the Left Gallant Cavalry (Zuǒ Xiāojì Jiāngjūn),
and shortly thereafter became Protector-in-Chief (Zhōng Hùjūn),
overseeing military affairs at Shítou Garrison.
In the seventh year,

he was sent out to be Commissioner with Staff of Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the five provinces of Nán Yǎn, Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, and Jì, General of Benevolent Awe (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Nán Yǎn Province.
In the eighth year,
he was summoned back as Protector of the Army (Hùjūn).
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
He was reassigned as General Who Pacifies the Rear (Ānhòu Jiāngjūn), stationed in Lángyá and Péngchéng Commanderies, and concurrently served as Administrator of Nán Lángyá.
In the tenth year,
he was summoned back as General Who Pacifies the Right (Ānyòu Jiāngjūn) and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
In the fourteenth year,
he again served as Protector of the Army,
overseeing Nán Lángyá and Péngchéng,
and stationed at Lángyá.
He was again summoned back as Director of the Central Secretariat,
and sent out to be General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Xiāng Province.
Yè was naturally sincere and loyal,
leaving kindness wherever he served.
He deeply believed in cause and effect (karma),
and sincerely upheld the Buddhist Dharma.
Gāozǔ often praised him admirably.
In the third year of Pǔtōng,
he was summoned back as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Protects the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
In the fourth year,
he was reassigned as Attendant at the Palace and Grand Master of Remonstrance with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
In the seventh year,
he died,
aged forty-eight.
His posthumous title was Yuán.
