A collection of his literary works circulated in the world.
His son, Xiàoyǎn, succeeded him.
Xiàoyǎn, courtesy name Xīzhuāng,
was intelligent and had literary talent.
He achieved the highest rank (Jiǎkē) in the examination (shècè),
and was appointed Gentleman of the Imperial Secretariat (Mìshū Láng) and Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince.
He accompanied the emperor on a visit to Huálínyuán Garden.
During the gathering, he presented *sòng* (eulogies) regarding the Xiàngfēng Wū (Wind-indicating Bird), Huáguāng Diàn Palace, and Jǐngyáng Shān Hill.
His writings were exquisite,
and Gāozǔ deeply appreciated and admired him.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he died,
aged twenty-three.
His posthumous title was Zhāng.
His son, Shèn, succeeded him.
Zǎo, courtesy name Jìngyì,
was the younger brother of Prince Yuán.
When young, he established a reputation for good conduct,
and his integrity was pure.
At the beginning of Qí's Yǒngyuán (period),
he relinquished his commoner status to become Assistant Literary Draftsman (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng).
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xīchāng County,
with an income fief of five hundred households.

He was sent out to be Commissioner with Staff of Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Yì and Níng provinces, General Who Guards the Army (Guānjūn Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yì Province.
At that time, the state was newly founded,
and the frontier was unsettled.
Jiāo Sēnghù, a commoner of the province, gathered tens of thousands of followers,
occupying Pí and Fán to revolt.
Zǎo was not yet twenty years old,
and gathered his aides to deliberate.
He intended to attack them himself.
Some argued that this was impossible,
whereupon Zǎo became greatly enraged
and had the man decapitated beside the steps.
He then rode in a flat, shoulder-borne carriage,
patrolling the rebel camps.
The rebels shot wildly with their bows;
arrows fell like rain.
His attendants raised shields to block the arrows,
but Zǎo ordered them removed.
Because of this, morale became greatly settled.
The rebels subsequently fled during the night.
Zǎo ordered his cavalry to pursue them,
decapitating several thousand heads,
and thus pacified the revolt.
He was promoted to the title General of Trustworthy Awe (Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn).
In the ninth year,
he was summoned to court as Central Secretariat Officer of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ).
In the tenth year,
he became General of the Left Gallant Cavalry and concurrently Administrator of Nán Lángyá.
He returned to the court as Attendant at the Palace.
Zǎo's nature was humble and retiring,
not seeking fame or advancement.
He was skilled at writing essays and poems,
especially fond of ancient styles.
Unless it was for public banquets,
he never wantonly engaged in writing.
Even if he had a small piece,
he would discard the original as soon as it was finished.
In the eleventh year,

he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of Yōng, Liáng, and Qín three prefectures, and Jìnglín and Suí two commanderies, General of Awe-Inspiring Might (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn), Superintendent of the Barbarians of Níng (Níngmán Xiàowèi), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yōng Prefecture.
In the twelfth year,

he was recalled to be Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the five prefectures of Nányǎn, Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, and Jì, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǎn Prefecture.
His military title remained as before.
He frequently served in several garrisons,
and the people and officials praised him.
He promoted good people and humbled himself before others,
always as if he was not good enough.
He was recalled to be Grand Mentor (Zhānshì) to the Crown Prince.
In the third year of Pǔtōng (普通),
he was promoted to General of the Palace Guard (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn),
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the sixth year,
he served as General of the Military Adviser (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn),
and with Hóu Zhèngdé (侯正德), the Marquis of Xīfēng (西豐), campaigned northwards to Wōyáng (渦陽).
He then withdrew the troops.
He was impeached by the appropriate officials (yǒusī),
dismissed from office and stripped of his rank and fief.
In the seventh year,
he was reinstated as Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng).
In the eighth year,
his rank and fief were restored.
Soon after, he was appointed General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn),
and concurrently commanded the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
In the first year of Dàtōng (大通),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Protector-General of the Army (Zhōnghùjūn).
At that time, Wōyáng (渦陽) had just surrendered.
So, Zǎo was appointed Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Expedition (Běitǎo Dūdū), and Grand General of the Pacification of the North (Zhēngběi Dàjiāngjūn),
garrisoned at Wōyáng (渦陽).
In the second year,
he was appointed General of the Central Command (Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn), [一０]Grand Master of Remonstrance with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
had his own staff appointed,
and was given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng (中大通),
he was promoted to Protector-General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn),
while his position as General of the Central Command (Zhōngquán) remained as before.
In the third year,
he was appointed General of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jiāngjūn), [一一]Grand Mentor (Zhānshì) to the Crown Prince,
and sent out to serve as Administrator (Yǐn) of Dānyáng (丹陽).
Gāozǔ (高祖) often sighed and said:
“If all my sons and nephews were like Jiāyè (迦葉),
what worries would I have?”
Jiāyè (迦葉)
was Zǎo's (藻) informal name.
He was recalled to serve as General of Pacifying the Left (Ānzuǒ Jiāngjūn) and Left Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒpúshè),
with the additional title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
Zǎo (藻) firmly declined,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
In the fifth year of Dàtóng (大同),

he was promoted to General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn), Open the Residence with the Three Dukes' Privileges (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī), and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng),
his title of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) remaining as before.
Zǎo's (藻) nature was tranquil and calm.
He lived alone in a room,
his bed had knee marks,
and the imperial clan and high officials
all took him as a model.
He always felt that his rank and emolument were excessive,
and constantly thought of retiring.
His gate and courtyard were quiet and solitary,
and visitors were rare.
Tàizōng (太宗) especially respected and loved him.
Since suffering family misfortune,
he wore coarse cloth and sat on rush mats,
did not eat fresh fowl,
and unless in a public court,
did not listen to music.
Gāozǔ (高祖) always praised him for this.
He was sent out to serve as Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nánxú (南徐) Prefecture.
When Hóu Jǐng's (侯景) rebellion broke out,
Zǎo (藻) sent his eldest son Yù (彧) to lead troops in support.
When the city gates were opened,
he was given the additional titles of Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand General (Dàjiāngjūn).
Jǐng (景) sent his Commissioner of Ceremonial (Yítóng) Xiāo Yōng (蕭邕) to replace him,
who occupied Jīngkǒu (京口).
Zǎo (藻) then fell ill with a qi disorder,
and did not treat himself.
Someone advised him to flee north of the river,
but Zǎo (藻) said:
“I am a pillar of the state,
my position and responsibility are particularly high.
Since I cannot eliminate the rebel,
I should die with the imperial court.
How can I abandon myself to another kind,
wishing to preserve the rest of my life?”
Thereupon, he did not eat for several days.
In the third year of Tàiqīng (太清),
he died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
Yǒngyáng (永陽) Successor Prince Bóyóu (伯游), courtesy name Shìrén (士仁),
was the son of Gāozǔ's (高祖) second elder brother Fū (敷).
Fū (敷), courtesy name Zhòngdá (仲達),

first served in Qí (齊) as Campaigning Army Administrative Officer (Xíngcānjūn) to the Rear Army Conqueror-General (Hòujūn Zhēnglǔ). [一二]He was transferred to Crown Prince's Household Administrator (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
then Palace Attendant (Xǐmǎ),
and promoted to Assistant Administrator (Chéng) of Dānyáng (丹陽) Commandery.
He was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant (Zhōngshèrén) to the Crown Prince,
and then appointed General of Establishing Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Suí Commandery.
He rallied and comforted those near and far,
and the common people were at peace because of him,
believing that no previous administration had equaled his.
He was promoted to General of Pacifying the North (Níngshuò Jiāngjūn),
and recalled to serve as Consultant (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Lúlíng (廬陵).
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ (建wǔ),
he died.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
ennobled as Prince of Yǒngyáng (永陽) Commandery,
and given the posthumous name Zhāo (昭).
Bóyóu (伯游) had a beautiful demeanor and spirit,
and was skilled at discussing profound theories.
In the fourth month of the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
an imperial edict stated:
“My nephew Bóyóu (伯游),
though his knowledge is not yet extensive,
his intentions are roughly acceptable.
The remote region of Zhèdōng (浙東)
requires administration and governance.

He is to be Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the five commanderies of Kuàijī (會稽), Dōngyáng (東陽), Xīn'ān (新安), Yǒngjiā (永嘉), and Línhǎi (臨海), General Assisting the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Kuàijī (會稽).”
In the second year,
he inherited the title of Prince of Yǒngyáng (永陽) Commandery.
In the fifth year,
he died,
at the age of twenty-three.
His posthumous name was Gōng (恭).
Héngyáng (衡陽) Successor Prince Yuánjiǎn (元簡), courtesy name Xīyuǎn (熙遠),
was the son of Gāozǔ's (高祖) fourth younger brother Chàng (暢).
Chàng (暢) served in Qí (齊) up to Grand Minister of Sacrifices (Tàicháng),
was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jiānglíng (江陵) County,
and then died.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),

he was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), and Open the Residence with the Three Dukes' Privileges (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Héngyáng (衡陽) Commandery.
His posthumous name was Xuān (宣).
Yuánjiǎn (元簡) inherited the title in the third year.
He was appointed Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
and promoted to Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Kuàijī (會稽).
In the thirteenth year,
he was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng),

and sent out to serve as Envoy with Credentials (Chíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the three prefectures of Guǎng (廣), Jiāo (交), and Yuè (越), Central Commander of Pacifying the Yue (Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎng (廣) Prefecture.
He returned to serve as Central Palace Attendant (Zhōngshùzǐ) to the Crown Prince,

and was promoted to Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of the three prefectures of Yǐng (郢), Sī (司), and Huò (霍), General of Trusty Martiality (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yǐng (郢) Prefecture.
In the first month of the eighteenth year,
he died in the prefecture.
His posthumous name was Xiào (孝).
His son Jùn (俊) succeeded.
Guìyáng (桂陽) Successor Prince Xiàng (象), courtesy name Shìyì (世翼),
was the ninth son of Prince Xuānwǔ (宣武) of Chángshā (長沙).
Initially,
his uncle Róng (融) served in Qí (齊) up to Palace Attendant (Xǐmǎ) to the Crown Prince.
During the Yuányuán (永元) period,
during the misfortune of Xuānwǔ (宣武),
Róng (融) was killed.
When Gāozǔ (高zǔ) pacified Jīngyì (京邑),
he was posthumously granted the title of Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he was given the additional titles of Regular Mounted Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand General of the Pacifying Army (Fǔjūn Dàjiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed as Prince of Guìyáng (桂陽) Commandery.
His posthumous name was Jiǎn (簡).
He had no sons,
so an imperial edict designated Xiàng (象) as his successor,
to inherit his rank and title.
Xiāo Xiàng's countenance and bearing were composed and elegant,
and he was skilled in social interactions.
He was known for his filial piety towards his birth mother.
He began his career as Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Not long after arriving at his post,
Princess Jiǎn Wángfēi passed away,
and he resigned his office.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was again appointed Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Xiāo Xiàng had grown up in the deep palace,
and this was his first direct involvement in common administration.
His conduct was without fault,
and the imperial court praised him.
He was dispatched as Chíjié, Dū Sīhuò Yǐng Sān Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn, and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Soon after, he was transferred to Xiānghéng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, and Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
Xiāngzhōu had previously suffered greatly from tiger attacks,
but during Xiāo Xiàng's tenure,
these ceased,
and the elders all attributed it to the influence of his virtuous governance.
He was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng.
Soon after, in his original capacity, he temporarily oversaw the military affairs of Shítóu Shù,
then was transferred to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng, concurrently leading the army (jiān lǐngjūn),
and again, in his original capacity, concurrently served as Zōngzhèng Qīng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Shìzhōng and Tàizǐ Zhānshì.
Before he could take up the post,
he was reassigned as Chíjié, Dū Jiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ.
He was relieved of duty due to illness.
Soon after, he was appointed Tàicháng Qīng,
given the additional title of Shìzhōng,
and then promoted to Mìshū Jiān, concurrently Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he died,
and was posthumously granted the title Dūn.
His son, Xiāo Zào, inherited.
The imperial historian says: The successive princes of Chángshā,
all inherited their territories,
and brilliantly governed their feudal states.
Guìyáng Wáng Xiāo Xiàng was known for his filial piety,
and when he governed Xiāngzhōu,
ferocious tigers ceased their violence,
which was indeed due to his benevolent virtue.
How could the excellent governance of old surpass this?

Biographies, Chapter 18: Xiāo Jǐng (Younger brothers: Xiāo Chāng, Xiāo Áng, Xiāo Yù)
Xiāo Jǐng, courtesy name Zǐzhāo,
was a cousin of Gāozǔ.
His father, Xiāo Chóngzhī, courtesy name Màojìng,
was the son of Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū Xiāo Dàocì.
Xiāo Dàocì had three sons: The eldest, Xiāo Shàngzhī,
courtesy name Màoxiān;
the second, Tàizǔ Wén Huángdì;
the third, Xiāo Chóngzhī.
Initially,
the Zuǒ Guānglù resided in his hometown,
exclusively practicing propriety and humility,
and was highly esteemed by the multitude.
His career included serving as a Cānjūn for Sòng Tàiwèi, Jiāngxià Wáng,
and he ended as Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
At the end of Qí,
he was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
Xiāo Shàngzhī was honest and possessed virtuous character,
serving as Zhōngbīng Cānjūn for Sītú, Jiàn'ān Wáng.
The entire administration referred to him as an elder.
Lángyá Wáng Sēngqián particularly esteemed him,
and often sought his counsel on many matters.
He was promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
and died in office.
In the early Tiānjiān era (502 CE),
he was posthumously granted the title Wénxuān Hóu.
Xiāo Shàngzhī's son, Xiāo Língjūn,
served as Guǎngdé Lìng in Qí.
When Gāozǔ's righteous army arrived,
he temporarily managed the affairs of Kuàijī Jùn,
and died shortly thereafter.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Dōngchāng Xiàn Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
His son, Xiāo Jiǎn, inherited.
Xiāo Chóngzhī distinguished himself through his competence and ability,
and his governance leaned towards severity.
He rose to the rank of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn and Dōngyáng Tàishǒu.
In the Yǒngmíng era (483-493 CE),
when Táng Yǐn of Qiántáng rebelled,
his separate forces breached Dōngyáng,
and Xiāo Chóngzhī was killed.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he was posthumously granted the title Zhōngjiǎn Hóu.
Xiāo Jǐng, at eight years old, followed his father to the prefecture.
He was known for his extreme grief during mourning.
As he grew up, he was fond of learning,
and possessed eloquence and decisive judgment.
In the Jiànwǔ era (494-498 CE) of Qí,
he was appointed Zuǒ Chángshì for Jìn'ān Wángguó,
then promoted to Yǒngníng Lìng,
and his administration was considered the best among all cities.
Fàn Shù, the Tàishǒu of Yǒngjiā, who had previously governed the prefecture,
was renowned for his integrity and fairness.
He greatly admired Xiāo Jǐng's governance,
and thus posted a notice at the prefecture gate saying:
"For any unresolved or difficult matters in other counties,
you may consult the Yǒngníng Lìng for a decision."
Soon after,
he left office due to illness.
One thousand people from Yǒngjiā, including Hú Zhòngxuān, went to the imperial court,
to petition for Xiāo Jǐng to be appointed to the prefecture,
but it was not granted.
He returned to serve as Piàojì Xíng Cānjūn.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (500 CE),
due to the meritorious service of Chángshā Xuānwǔ Wáng Xiāo Yì,
he was appointed Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
That winter,
Xuānwǔ Wáng was killed,
and Xiāo Jǐng also fled for safety.
When Gāozǔ's righteous army arrived,
Xiāo Jǐng was appointed Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Acting Military Affairs of Nányǎnzhōu.
At that time, the empire was not yet settled.
The "Cángchǔ" (barbarian/southern people) north of the Yangtze River each occupied fortified settlements.
Xiāo Jǐng demonstrated his authority and trustworthiness,
and the chieftains came forward, binding themselves, to plead guilty.
Within ten days, the entire region was pacified.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng (502 CE),
he was promoted to Dū Nányǎnzhōu Zhū Jūnfù, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, and Jiān Nányǎnzhōu.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was enfeoffed as Wúpíng Xiàn Hóu,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
He continued to serve as Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū Nánběi Yǎnqīng Jì Sì Zhōu Zhū Jūnfù,
Guānjūn Jiāngjūn, and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
An imperial edict granted Xiāo Jǐng's mother, Lady Máo, the title Guótàifūrén,
with ceremonies equivalent to a Wángguó Tàifēi,
and she was granted a golden seal and purple ribbon.
When Xiāo Jǐng governed the prefecture,
he was pure, diligent, and authoritative.
He had a clear understanding of official duties,
so paperwork was never delayed.
Subordinates dared not deceive him,
and officials and common people feared and respected him as a god.
It happened to be a year of famine,
so he calculated provisions per person and provided relief,
distributing porridge along the roads.
The deceased were provided with coffins and burial equipment,
and the people greatly relied on him.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (505 CE),
the imperial army launched a northern expedition.
Xiāo Jǐng led his troops out of Huáiyáng,
and advanced to slaughter Sùyù.
He entered mourning for his mother,
but an imperial edict ordered him to temporarily resume his duties.
In the fifth year (506 CE),
the army returned,
and he was appointed Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ,
then promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wèiwèi Qīng.
In the seventh year (508 CE),
he was promoted to Zuǒ Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn,
concurrently Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
The Lǐngjūn was in charge of all critical military affairs,
and oversaw the officials in the bureau.
Previously, many were arrogant and extravagant,
but Xiāo Jǐng's strictness in office
made the official departments solemn.
The Zhìjú Jiān were all favored intimates,
and many were quite resentful of his orders.
For this reason, he could not remain in the central government for long.
Soon after, he was dispatched as Shǐ Chíjié, Dū Yōngliáng Nánběi Qín Yǐngzhōu Zhī Jìnglíng Sīzhōu Zhī Suí Jùn Zhū Jūnfù, Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, Níngmán Xiàowèi, and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the third month of the eighth year (509 CE),
Yuán Zhì, the Wèi Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, led an army of seventy thousand to invade Chán'gōu,
pressing the various Mán tribes.
All the Mán crossed the Hànshuǐ to surrender.
Debaters suggested that since the Mán had repeatedly been a border problem,
this was an opportunity to eliminate them.
Xiāo Jǐng said:
"Those who are in dire straits and come to us
should not be executed; it would be inauspicious.
Furthermore, when the Wèi people invade,
they always face resistance.
If we execute all the Mán,
then the Wèi army will have no obstacles,
which is not a wise strategy."
So, he opened Fánchéng to accept their surrender.
He then ordered his Sīmǎ Zhū Sīyuǎn, Níngmán Chángshǐ Cáo Yìzōng, and Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Mèng Huìjùn to attack Yuán Zhì at Chán'gōu,
where they utterly defeated him,
capturing Yuán Zhì's Chángshǐ Dù Jǐng alive.
Over ten thousand heads were cut off,
and the floating corpses covered the Hànshuǐ.
Xiāo Jǐng sent Zhōngbīng Cānjūn Cuī Huì to lead soldiers to collect and bury them.
initially arrived at the prefecture (zhōu).
He abolished the elaborate paraphernalia and ritual attire used for welcoming and escorting,
ensuring that officials and the populace were not burdened or disturbed.
He repaired and constructed city walls and fortifications,
reinforced vigilance regarding border defenses,
managed legal disputes,
and encouraged agriculture and sericulture.
The commanderies and counties all changed their standards and exerted themselves.
Within the prefecture, conditions were clean and solemn (qīngsù).
For over a thousand *lǐ* along the Hànshǔi (river), both by land and water,
robbery and raiding ceased entirely.
In the eleventh year,
he was summoned to serve as Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn (Right Guard General) and concurrently Administrator of the Garrison Affairs of Shítóu (Shítou Shù Jūngshì).
In the twelfth year,

he was again made Shǐ Chíjié (Bearer of the Credentials), Dū Zhū Jūngshì (Area Commander) of five prefectures: Nányǎn, Běiyǎn, Běixú, Qīng, and Jì, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Trust and Awe), and Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture).
In the thirteenth year,
he was summoned to serve as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn (General Governing the Armies),

Xiāo Jǐng was naturally a man of elegant vigor (fēnglì)
and skilled in rhetoric and speech (cílìng).
When he was at court,
he was looked up to and admired by the multitude.
Although he was a cousin (cóngdì) related to Gāozǔ,
the courtesy and trust accorded him were extremely grand.
All important military and state affairs
were discussed and settled with his involvement.
In the fifteenth year,
he was given the additional title Shìzhōng (Attendant at Court).
In the seventeenth year,
Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yáng Prefecture), Wáng Hóng, Prince of Línchuān, was dismissed due to legal infractions.
An imperial edict stated:
"Yáng Prefecture requires organization and management,
and the right person should be obtained.
Shìzhōng and Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, Xiāo Jǐng, Marquis of Wúpíng, has the talent suitable for this task.
He shall be appointed Ānyòu Jiāngjūn (General Who Guards the Right) and Overseer of Yáng Prefecture (Jiān Yángzhōu),
and staff assistants (zuǒshǐ) shall be appointed concurrently.
His title Shìzhōng shall remain as before,

Xiāo Jǐng, taking office in Yáng Prefecture despite his close kinship,
pleaded urgently and sincerely to decline the post,
even to the point of weeping,
but Gāozǔ did not permit it.
While in the prefecture, he was particularly renowned for his insightful decisions (míngduàn),
and his official documents and decrees (fújiào) were severe and precise.
An old woman from the countryside once filed a complaint and received his official warrant (fú).
Upon returning to the county seat,
the county clerk did not immediately process it.
The old woman said:
"The warrant from Overseer Xiāo Jǐng

He was thus respected and feared by the people.
In the eighteenth year,

The following year,

he was dispatched externally as Shǐ Chíjié, Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant), Dū Zhū Jūngshì (Area Commander) of three prefectures: Yǐng, Sī, and Huò, Ānxī Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the West), and Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yǐng Prefecture).
As he was about to depart,
Gāozǔ personally visited Jiànxīng Yuàn (park) to hold a farewell banquet,

After returning to the palace,
an edict ordered the provision of a full ensemble of military music (gǔchuī yībù).
While in this prefecture, he again gained a reputation for competence.
The commanderies of Qí'ān and Jìnglíng bordered the territory of the Wèi (Northern Wèi),
and were prone to banditry.
Xiāo Jǐng sent official letters giving notice;
the Wèi immediately burned their earthworks and garrisons and protected their own borders,
no longer engaging in invasion or encroachment.
In Pǔtōng fourth year (523 CE),

An edict posthumously granted him the titles Shìzhōng, Zhōng Fǔjūn (Central General Who Consoles the Armies), and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Staff Equal to the Three Dukes).
His posthumous title was Zhōng (Loyal).
His son, Mài, succeeded him.
Chāng, courtesy name Zǐjiàn,

At the end of the Yùzhāng (period) of Qí,
he served as Zuǒ Chángshì (Left Regular Attendant) to the Prince of Jìn'ān.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),

In the fifth year,
he was given the additional title Níngshuò Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North).
In the sixth year,

he was promoted to Chíjié, Dū Zhū Jūngshì (Area Commander) of four prefectures: Guǎng, Jiāo, Yuè, and Guì, Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General Who Assists the State), Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiàng (Gentleman of the Household Who Pacifies the Yuè), and Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Guǎng Prefecture).
In the seventh year,
his military title was advanced to Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Attacks Afar).
In the ninth year,
Hēng Prefecture was established by dividing Xiāng Prefecture.

Chāng was made Chíjié, Dū Zhū Jūngshì (Area Commander) of Suījiàn (in Guǎng Prefecture) and Shǐ'ān (in Xiāng Prefecture), Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn (General of Trust and Valour), and Hēngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Hēng Prefecture).

In the thirteenth year,
he was reappointed Sànqí Shìláng (Cavalry Gentleman),

In that year,
he was dispatched externally as Ānyòu Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General Who Guards the Right).

Xiāo Chāng was also a man of clarity and intelligence,
but he was naturally fond of alcohol,
and committed many errors when drunk.
When serving in commanderies and prefectures,
whenever he was drunk, he would walk straight into people's homes,
or sometimes go alone into the wilderness.
Regarding punishments and executions (xínglù),
he was often erratic and without measure.
If he killed someone while drunk,
he might search for that person when sober,
and yet felt no remorse.
Due to being impeached by the relevant authorities,
he returned and remained in the capital.
He became anxious and unhappy,
and consequently indulged in drink and suffered from panic.
While at the Eastern Study (Dōngzhāi) in Shítóu,
he drew a knife and stabbed himself.
His attendants saved him,
and he did not die.
In the seventeenth year,
he died.
He was thirty-nine years old at the time.
His son was Bóyán.
Áng, courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was Xiāo Jǐng’s third younger brother.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was repeatedly promoted to Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works, Right).
He was dispatched externally as Qīngchē Jiāngjūn (General of Light Chariots) and Overseer of Nányǎn Prefecture (Jiān Nányǎnzhōu).
Previously,
his elder brother Jǐng had served in Nányǎn twice,

When Áng came to replace him,
people at the time compared him to Fēng Shì (Lord Fēng).
He was summoned to serve as Tàishǒu (Administrator) of the two commanderies of Lángyé and Péngchéng,

He was again dispatched externally, with the title Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, to serve as Guǎngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Guǎng Prefecture).
In Pǔtōng second year,
he served as Sànqí Chángshì and Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to Sànqí Shìláng, Zhōng Lǐngjūn (General Governing the Central Armies), and Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant Secretary to the Crown Prince).
He was dispatched externally as Wúxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wúxīng).
In Dàtōng second year,
he was summoned to serve as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Benevolent Awe) and Wèiwèi Qīng (Minister of the Guards).
Shortly thereafter, he became Shìzhōng,
concurrently serving as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In Zhōng Dàtōng first year,
he became Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the second year,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Xiāngyīn County (Xiāngyīn Xiànhóu),
with a thousand households in his demesne.
He was dispatched externally as Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiāng Prefecture).
In Dàtóng first year,
he died.
He was fifty-three years old at the time.
His posthumous title was Gōng (Reverent).
Yù, courtesy name Zǐzhēn.
He was the fourth younger brother of Xiāo Jǐng.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed as Mìshū Láng (Secretary).
He was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
Xǐmǎ (Groom),
Zhōngshū Shèrén (Attendant Secretary),
and Zhōngshū Shìláng (Secretariat Gentleman).
He constantly requested an opportunity to test himself,
but Gāozǔ offered him the commanderies of Huáinán, Yǒngjiā, and Xiāngyáng.
He did not accept any of them.
He aspired to serve in a frontier prefecture,
but Gāozǔ, considering him flighty, unreliable, and lacking prestige,
suppressed his request and did not permit it.
He was promoted to Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng (Palace Attendant).
He submitted a memorial, saying:
“The petition presented at the beginning of summer,
has yet to be acknowledged and examined.
Recalling it fills me with shame and fear,
truly causing anxiety in my heart.
I have heard that during hot rains and intense cold,
even commoners complain;
as for glory and decline, favor and disgrace,
who can remain indifferent?
I rely on past causes,
and have attained the importance of being a member of the imperial family.
Since my karma (consequences/rewards) is mixed,
I sometimes encounter periods of adversity and failure.
In the past, at the end of the Qí Dynasty,
at the start of the righteous army's campaign,
I was still young and weak,
but had a rough understanding and awareness.
Blocked off east and west,
I had no means to join the returning forces.
Although I could not bear the spear and don the armor,
I truly suppressed my tears and felt immense indignation.
Hiding in the eastern territory,
I endured every kind of hardship and danger.
For three full years,
I frequently moved to several different locations.
Although hunger and cold afflicted my body,
I did not consider freezing and starvation a hardship.
Every time I encountered alarm or doubt,
I was terrified and beside myself.
Since I missed the opportunity to sacrifice my life according to morality,
I only bore the worry of losing my head in vain.
I hoped for a period of peace and prosperity,
trusting to share in the general joy;
how could I expect that after more than twenty years,
my achievements and reputation would be unrecorded?
If I finish this life
only to fill a ditch or ravine,
my sincere devotion and fundamental wishes
will suddenly cease forever.
Looking down and pitying myself,
how can I not feel distressed and sigh!
Indeed, to self-promote and boast,
is truly contemptible;
to praise oneself and brag,
is really shameful.
However, measuring oneself and assessing one’s limitations,
the self-knower is discerning.
To display one's strength and seek office,
how dare one speak empty words?
Therefore, I constantly wished for a trial,
and repeatedly made appeals.
Indeed, responding to the Heavenly Signs above
is truly not easy to presume upon;
brocade is not lightly cut,
it is indeed difficult to fashion.
Past karmic obstacles
are the reason why I have deviated from expectations and estimations.
Since the Sacred Observer has deemed me foolish and inadequate,
and unfit for trial use,
how can I be permitted to remain long in prominent and forbidden offices,
merely polluting the central bureaucracy?
If my undeserved tenure accumulates further,
I fear I will invite public criticism.
I request to resign my current post,
and beg to withdraw to my private dwelling.
I humbly pray that the Heavenly Light
will specially grant this permission.
Although I have undeservedly enjoyed honors in both palaces,
I have had no opportunity to offer service in return.
As I am about to leave the palace offices,
I am filled with deep attachment and trepidation.”
Gāozǔ replied with an imperial decree written in his own hand, saying:
“Yù's memorial is as stated.
In antiquity, when employing men,
they must first be clearly tested.
All must wait until service and merit are established,
only then can one claim the moral high ground of self-withdrawal.
In the past, Hán Guāngwǔ's elder brother's sons, Zhāng and Xīng, the two men,
were both famous members of the imperial clan,
and when they wished to practice official duties,
Zhāng was appointed no higher than Prefect of Píngyīn,
and Xīng was Magistrate of Gōushì.
Only when their administration showed competence
were they then transferred to become commandery governors.
Their promotion was not merely because their administrative achievements were praised,
but also because they were Guāngwǔ's nephews.
Yù's talent and standing,
how can they be compared to them!
Last year, I placed him in command of Huáinán Commandery,
but he was unwilling to go;
next I appointed him Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Summons the Distant), Chief Clerk to the Commander of the North, and Administrator of Xiāngyáng,
and again he declined, citing the distance to the frontier;
I changed the appointment to Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
and he again said that an inland posting was not his wish;
I further asked him about Jìn’ān and Línchuān,
to choose whichever he preferred,
and still he would not go.
To lay aside the scholar's cloth cap and oversee a commandery,
this post is not to be considered insignificant.
With several instances of declining the post,
what is your intention?
Moreover, all of Yù's elder brothers have successively held posts as commandery governors,
following one another in high office,
never missing a year.
His full brother, Jǐng,
is currently holding a regional military post.
How can I favor Jǐng and slight Yù?
It is simply the order of the court and public opinion
that determines the rank as it stands.
Regarding his entire family,
I feel somewhat without shame.
Leaving aside the fact that things should not be this way now;
when Yù and his brothers were commoners,
they lived their youth and grew up
by what standard did they establish themselves?
How can they act arbitrarily and contradict the Way,
turning their backs on Heaven and Earth?
Who says the imperial court lacks statutes and regulations?
It is just that I have not yet wished to subject you to legal proceedings.
Since you have memorialized requesting resignation,
it may be granted as petitioned.”
Consequently, he was dismissed from office.
Following this, he shut his door and ceased attending court,
and no longer communicated with the state regarding celebrations or condolences.
In the fifth year of Pǔtōng (524 CE),
he was implicated for privately minting coins inside his residence,
and was impeached by the relevant authorities.
He was handed over to the Tíngwèi (Chief Justice).
He was spared the death penalty,
and exiled to Línhǎi Commandery.
When he reached Shàngyú,
an imperial edict ordered his return,
and moreover commanded him to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts.
When Yù arrived,
he was humble and observed every propriety.
He changed his mindset and embraced the Way,
maintaining the precepts with great precision and purity.
Gāozǔ greatly praised him,
and appointed him Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Administrator of Jìnlíng.
Upon arriving at his post, he strove for a good reputation,
eliminated oppressive regulations,
clarified the laws and statutes,
was severe toward corrupt officials,
and generously cared for the common people.
Within ten days,
the commandery was greatly reformed.
Soon thereafter, he died suddenly from an acute illness.
The common people, whether walking or sitting, wailed,
and the markets and streets were in an uproar because of it.
More than four hundred people set up sacrifices and memorials in the commandery courtyard.
In the countryside, there was a woman of the Xià clan,
over a hundred years old,
who, leaning on her great-grandson, came out to the commandery seat,
grieving and unable to control herself.
Such was the extent of the moving influence of his benevolent administration.
The common people, leading one another, erected a temple and built a stele for him,
to commemorate his virtue.
They also went to the capital to request posthumous honors and a title.
An imperial edict posthumously appointed him Cǐshǐ (Governor) of Xiāngzhōu.
His posthumous title was Gōng.
The imperial historian comments: When Gāozǔ illuminated and possessed the realm,
the mandate of fortune flowed outward.
The extended relatives and kin,
were all entrusted with appointments and treated well.
The talent, eloquence, knowledge, and decisiveness of Xiāo Jǐng,
which benefited governance and assisted the era,
made him truly a respected member of the Liáng imperial house.
Biographies, Chapter Nineteen: Zhōu Shě, Xú Miǎn
Zhōu Shě, courtesy name Shēngyì,
was a native of Ānchéng, Rǔnán.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Yǐ, who served as Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Left, Minister of Ceremonies) during the Jìn Dynasty.
His father, Yóng,
was Zhōngshū Shìláng (Secretariat Gentleman) during the Qí Dynasty,
and was famous in his time.
Shě was exceptionally intelligent in his youth,
and Yóng regarded him as extraordinary.
As he was about to die, he told him:
“You need not worry about failing to achieve wealth and honor;
you should only strive to maintain them through morality and virtue.”
When he grew up,
he was widely learned and knowledgeable,
especially skilled in metaphysical principles.
He was good at reciting texts,
reciting and explaining them from memory;
his voice and delivery were clear and eloquent.
He started his career as an Erudite of the Imperial University (*Tàixué Bóshì*) of Qí.
He was transferred to be Acting Adjutant (*Xíng Cānjūn*) to the General of the Rear Army (*Hòujūn*).
During the Jiànwǔ era,
Wú Bāo, a man from Wèi, came south.
He possessed Confucian learning.
The Assistant Director of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Púyè*), Jiāng Shí, invited Bāo to debate.
Shě attended the session.
He repeatedly refuted Bāo,
his logic and rhetoric being powerful and outstanding.
From this, he became famous for his verbal eloquence (*Kǒu Biàn*).
When Wáng Liàng was the Governor of Dānyáng (*Dānyáng Yǐn*),
he heard of him and was pleased,
appointing him Chief Secretary (*Zhǔbù*).
Many government affairs were entrusted to him.
He was transferred to Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Tàicháng Chéng*).
When the Liáng regime (*Liáng Tái*) was established,
he served as Vice Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (*Fèngcháng Chéng*).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he widely sought officials of unusual ability.
Fàn Yún, the Director of the Personnel Bureau (*Lìbù Shàngshū*), was already well-acquainted with Yóng.
He valued Shě's talent and capacity,
and spoke of him to Gāozǔ.
He was summoned and appointed Attendant Gentleman of the Bureau of Sacrifices (*Shàngshū Cíbù Láng*).
As the state was newly founded at that time,
many changes and additions to the rites and ceremonies
mostly originated from Shě.
Soon after, he served as Adjutant Secretary (*Jìshì Cānjūn*) to the General of the Rear Army (*Hòujūn*) and Prefect of Mòlíng (*Mòlíng Lìng*).
He entered the court as Palace Attendant for Communications (*Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén*).
He was repeatedly promoted to Attendant to the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ*),
Gentleman-in-Attendance (*Sànqí Chángshì*),
Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shìláng*),
and Minister of the Court of the Imperial Entertainments (*Hónglú Qīng*).
At that time, Wáng Liàng was disgraced and returned home.
None of his former friends visited him.
Shě alone maintained the old friendship.
When he died,
Shě personally managed the funeral and burial arrangements.
People at the time praised this deed.
He was promoted to Attendant Gentleman of the Personnel Bureau (*Shàngshū Lìbù Láng*),
Commander of the Right Guard of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Yòuwèishuài*),
and General of the Right Guard (*Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn*).
Although his official post changed frequently,
he always remained within the Palace Secretariat,
rarely getting time off.
National histories, imperial edicts, and pronouncements,
ceremonial forms and statutes,
and military strategies and deliberations,
were all under his concurrent responsibility.
He attended the Emperor day and night,
participating in classified matters.
For more than twenty years, he was never far from the Emperor’s side.
Shě was naturally quick-witted and eloquent;
when engaging in broad discussions or banter with others,
he could talk incessantly all day,
yet ultimately, not a single word leaked state secrets.
Everyone especially admired and respected him for this.
His nature was frugal and plain.
His clothes and utensils,
his living quarters and bedding,
were like those of the poorest commoners.
Whenever he entered an official residence,
even if it had broad mansions and splendid halls,
with deep and layered inner chambers,
Shě residing there meant dust and dirt accumulated.
He used reeds as screens,
and if they broke, he would not attend to them.
While serving as General of the Right Guard (*Yòuwèi*),
he left office to mourn his mother.
He was recalled to duty as General Who Displays Awe (*Míngwēi Jiāngjūn*) and General of the Right Valiant Cavalry (*Yòu Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn*).
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Gentleman of the Palace (*Shìzhōng*),
and concurrently held the position of Commander of the Infantry (*Bùbīng Xiàowèi*).
Before he formally accepted the post,
he was transferred to Extraordinary Gentleman-in-Attendance (*Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì*) and Commander of the Left Guard of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài*).
A little later,
he was given the concurrent title of Gentleman-in-Attendance (*Sànqí Chángshì*) and Great Arbiter (*Dà Zhōngzhèng*) of his home province.
He was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Zhānshì*).
In the fifth year of Pǔtōng (Pǔtōng Wǔ Nián),
the southern ferry station captured a letter from Bái Wō, the Governor of Wǔlíng (*Wǔlíng Tàishǒu*).
The letter promised to give Shě one million *miànqián*.
The ferry officials reported this matter.
Although the letter originated externally,
he was still impeached by the relevant authorities.
Shě was dismissed from office due to this charge.
He was transferred to General of the Right Valiant Cavalry (*Yòu Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn*),
and managed the affairs of the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Zhānshì*).
He died in that same year,
aged fifty-six.
The Emperor personally came and wept,
his sorrow moving those around him.
An imperial edict stated:
“Shě, the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Zhānshì*) and Great Arbiter of Yùzhōu (*Yùzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng*),
has suddenly met his demise,
causing sorrow in Our heart.
His learning and reflection were firm and brilliant,
his disposition and conduct were open and keen.
He labored tirelessly in handling confidential matters
for many years.
His talents had not been fully realized,
making this loss deeply lamentable.
It is proper to confer high honors posthumously
to distinguish this good man.
He is posthumously granted Gentleman of the Palace (*Shìzhōng*) and General Protecting the Army (*Hùjūn Jiāngjūn*),
one set of drums and pipes (*gǔ chuī*),
and provided with ritual burial vessels from the Eastern Park storehouse (*Dōng Yuán Mì Qì*).
He is also granted one set of court robes,
one complete suit of clothes,
and funds shall be provided for his funeral according to necessity.
His posthumous title (*shì*) shall be Jiǎnzǐ.”
The following year,
another imperial edict stated:
“The late Gentleman of the Palace (*Shìzhōng*) and General Protecting the Army (*Hùjūn Jiāngjūn*), Jiǎnzǐ Shě,
had principles that encompassed both Mysterious Learning (*Xuán*) and Confucianism (*Rú*),
and extensively mastered literature and history.
He served his parents filially,
and served the sovereign with total loyalty.
He successively managed classified matters,
maintaining integrity and purity in his life.
His meals lacked complex flavors;
his person owned no excess clothing.
On the day of his death,
he had no inner household wealth,
and externally, he owned no fields or grand residence.
His two sons are alone and poor,
surpassing the distinguished examples of antiquity.
In the past,
concerning the impeachment by the Southern Authority regarding Bái Wō,
We feared external opinion might suggest We acted partially,
which led to his dismissal.
We now regret that good qualities were not acknowledged, even in this single instance.
In addition, suitable extraordinary honors shall be conferred
to distinguish this good man.”
He had two sons: Hóng Yì,
and Hóng Xìn.
Xú Miǎn, whose courtesy name (*zì*) was Xiūrén,
was a native of Tán in Dōnghǎi Commandery.
His grandfather, Cháng Zōng,
was Acting Adjutant (*Xíng Cānjūn*) in the Headquarters (*Bà Fǔ*) of Sòng Gāozǔ.
His father, Róng,
was the Chancellor of Nánchāng (*Nánchāng Xiàng*).
In his youth, Miǎn was orphaned and poor,
and early on strove for integrity and purity.
At the age of six,
during a period of continuous rain,
his family prayed for the weather to clear.
He casually wrote a composition
that was praised by the respected elders.
When he grew older,
he was devoted to learning.
He started his career as a student of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐ Shēng*).
Wáng Jiǎn, the Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*) and Duke Wénxiàn (*Wénxiàn Gōng*), was serving as Libationer (*Jìjiǔ*) at the time.
He often praised Miǎn as having the capacity of a Chief Minister (*Zǎifǔ*).
He passed the strategy examination with high honors,
and was appointed Attendant Gentleman (*Shìláng*) in the Kingdom of Xīyáng.
Soon after, he was transferred to Erudite of the Imperial University (*Tàixué Bóshì*),
Adjutant to the General Who Guards the Army (*Zhènjūn Cānjūn*),
and Attendant Gentleman of the Palace (*Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng*).
He was dismissed due to an official matter.
Later, he was appointed Attendant Gentleman of the Central Military Bureau (*Zhōngbīng Láng*) and Chief Clerk to the Commander of the Guards (*Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ*).
Prince Yuáncháng of Lángxié (*Lángxié Wáng Yuáncháng*) had a very great reputation for talent.
He often wished to meet Miǎn,
frequently relying on others to summon him.
Miǎn said to people:
“Young Lord Wáng’s fame is high, but his outlook is limited.
It is difficult to rashly go and meet him.”
Soon after, Yuáncháng met with disaster.
People at the time were all impressed by his astute foresight.
He initially associated with the Prince Xuānwǔ of Chángshā,
and Gāozǔ deeply valued and admired him.
When the righteous army reached the capital city,
Miǎn requested an audience at Xīnlín,
and Gāozǔ showed him great favor and courtesy,
entrusting him with managing documents and records.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Miǎn was appointed Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shìláng*).

He was transferred to General Who Establishes Awe (*Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn*), Consultant Adjutant (*Zīyì Cānjūn*) to the General of the Rear Army (*Hòujūn*), Arbiter (*Zhōngzhèng*) of his home district, and Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng*).
Since taking charge of pivotal laws and regulations,
he frequently impeached and recommended officials.
Contemporary opinion held that he was competent for his office.
, he was appointed Gentlemen-in-Attendance at the Yellow Gate (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng) and Secretary of the Bureau of Civil Office (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng)
. He participated in managing the Great Selections
. He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng)
. At that time, the royal army was campaigning in the north (Běifá)
, and couriers and post stations were overloaded
. Miǎn participated in managing military correspondence
, toiling day and night
, often spending several ten-day periods
before returning home once
. Whenever he returned
, the pack of dogs would bark in surprise
. Miǎn sighed, saying
: "I worry for the state and forget my family
, reaching this point
. If I die later
, this incident will also be recorded in my biography
." In the sixth year
, he was appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary (Gěishì Zhōng) and Secretary of the Five Bureaus of Military Affairs (Wǔbīng Shàngshū)
. He was promoted to Secretary of the Bureau of Civil Office (Lìbù Shàngshū)
. When Miǎn served as the selecting official
, ethical relationships (yílún) were correctly ordered
. He was already skilled in writing documents (chǐdú)
and also excelled at verbal expression
. Although official documents piled up
and guests filled his seat
, he responded fluently
, his hand never ceasing to write
. Furthermore, he covered and synthesized the Hundred Schools
, and everyone avoided naming taboos (bìhuì)
around him. He often gathered with his disciples at night
. A guest, Yú Gǎo
, sought the post of Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Zhānshì Wǔguān)
. Miǎn immediately refused, replying
: "Tonight, we should only discuss poetry and nature (fēngyuè)
." Thus, the people of the time all admired his impartiality
. He was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì)
, concurrently commanding the General of Agile Cavalry (Yóují Jiāngjūn)
. Before he formally assumed the post
, this was changed to commanding the Commandant of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Yòuwèi Shuài)
. He was promoted to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn)
, concurrently commanding the Palace Secretary to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ)
, attending the Eastern Palace
. As Crown Prince Zhāomíng Tàizǐ was still young
, he was ordered to oversee palace affairs
. The Crown Prince treated him with great respect
, consulting him on every matter
. He once lectured on the *Classic of Filial Piety* (*Xiàojīng*) inside the hall
. The Prince Jìnghuì of Línchuān (Línchuān Jìnghuì Wáng) and the Director of the Department of State Affairs Shěn Yuē (Shàngshū Lìng Shěn Yuē) served as the two tutors (fù)
. Miǎn and the Libationer of the Directorate of Education Zhāng Chōng (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Zhāng Chōng) served as the script holders (zhíjīng)
. Wáng Yíng, Zhāng Jì, Liǔ Chéng, and Wáng Jiǎn served as attending lecturers (shìjiǎng)
. The selection at that time prioritized the most intimate and worthy individuals
, perfectly capturing the current renown
. Miǎn submitted pleas declining the post several times
. He also wrote a letter to Shěn Yuē
, asking to switch his role to attending lecturer (shìjiǎng)
. The imperial edict refused
, and only then did he accept the position
. He was transferred to Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhānshì)
, concurrently commanding General of the Cavalry of the Clouds (Yúnqí Jiāngjūn)
. Soon after, he was granted the rank of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì)
. He was promoted to Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púshè)
, while his post as Zhānshì remained as before
. He was again changed to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng)
. He frequently petitioned to be relieved of his palace duties
, but the gracious imperial edict refused
. At that time, among the common people, funerary rites
were largely non-compliant with ritual (lǐ)
. Ending life in the morning and interring the body by evening
, they competed in speed
. Miǎn submitted a memorial, saying
: "The *Lǐ Jì* (Record of Rites), in the 'Wèn Sāng' (Inquiry Regarding Mourning), states
: 'The reason the great encoffining (liǎn) occurs after three days
is to await the return to life;
if life is not restored after three days
, then life will not be restored
, this system has not been followed
. For the ceremony of escorting the deceased
, the temporary coffin placement (bìn) should take a full year
. Yet, even among wealthy and influential families
, it sometimes lasts only half a day
. Regarding clothes, shrouds, coffins, and outer casings (guó)
, speed is considered honor
. Relatives and servants
only think of resting and returning
. Therefore, as soon as the testing of breath (shǔ kuàng) is completed
, the ash-nails are already prepared
. They forget the lingering steps of the fox and the rat
and shame the circling flight of the swallow and sparrow
. For injuring sentiment and destroying principle
, there is nothing greater than this
. Moreover, when a person’s child attends to the deceased
, his will is distressed and his heart is broken
. The necessary preparations for the funeral
are all handed over to others
. The depth of their affection or resentment
is difficult to verify in reality
. If the observation of life is perhaps mistaken
, resulting in violation and error regarding survival or death
, even if it happens one in ten thousand times
, the bitterness and cruelty are immense
. How can this compare to delaying the morning when the encoffining is announced
and extending the hope for resurrection
? I request that from now on, officials and commoners
should all follow the ancient practice
of the great encoffining on the third day
. If anyone fails to comply
, they should be disciplined
." An imperial edict approved his memorial
. Soon after, he was appointed General Xuānhuì (Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn)
, and given supporting staff (zuǒshǐ)
. His posts as Shìzhōng and Púshè remained as before
. He was again appointed Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púshè) and General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn)
. Due to his long-standing favor
, Miǎn had leaped to high office
. He served the Emperor with complete dedication
. If he knew something should be done, he did it
. Starting from minor selections
until this present office
, he always participated in managing the scales of office (héngshí, i.e., selection of officials)
, and greatly won the hearts of the scholarly class
. Affairs within the palace forbidden area (jǐn shěng)
were never leaked
. Whenever he submitted a memorial
, he would immediately burn the rough draft
. He was broadly conversant with the Classics and Histories (jīng shǐ)
, and was knowledgeable about past records
. Court rituals and state statutes
, marriage, capping, auspicious, and inauspicious events
, Miǎn was involved in the planning and discussion of all
. In the sixth year of Pǔtōng
, he submitted a memorial on revising the Five Rites (Wǔ Lǐ), which said
: Your servant has heard
that "The Way of Heaven is established
by Yīn and Yáng;
the Way of Man is established
by Benevolence (Rén) and Righteousness (Yì)"
: "Guide them by virtue (dé)
, and regulate them by ritual (lǐ)
." Ritual
is that which settles the ruler and governs the people
, promotes customs and instructs morals
, administers the state
, and benefits later generations
. Táng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties (Sāndài)
all necessarily followed it
. During the Zhōu dynasty
, the rules and statutes (xiàn zhāng)
. Based on the reformation of the Xià by the Yīn
were especially complete
, the additions and deletions (sǔn yì) are evident
. Although there are three hundred major rituals (jīng lǐ)
, three thousand minute rituals (qǔ lǐ)
; three hundred major texts
, and three thousand solemn ceremonies (wēiyí)
, their main categories
total five
. These are the rites managed by the Zōngbó (Minister of Rites)
: Auspicious Rites (Jí) are the highest
, Guest Rites (Bīn) are next
, Military Rites (Jūn) are next
, and Festival Rites (Jiā) are the lowest
. Therefore, if sacrifices are not conducted according to ritual
, they are neither orderly nor solemn
. If mourning is not conducted according to ritual
, then those who turn away from the dead and forget the living will be numerous
. If guest receptions are not conducted according to ritual
, then audience rituals will lose their propriety
. If military campaigns are not conducted according to ritual
, then disorder will be brought upon military discipline
. If capping (guān) and marriage (hūn) are not conducted according to ritual
, then men and women will lose the proper timing
. For governing the state and cultivating oneself
, this is critical
. When the royal house of Zhōu suffered great decay
and the kingly way was already weakened
, the officials who maintained these texts
daily lost their proper sequence
. Ritual, music, and military expeditions (zhēngfá)
originated from the feudal lords (zhūhóu)
. The Lesser Odes (Xiǎoyǎ) were completely abandoned
, and the ancient statutes (jiù zhāng)
. Thus, when Hán Xuān traveled to Lǔ
were incomplete
, he learned of the virtue of the Duke of Zhōu (Zhōu Gōng)
. When Shū Hóu was in Jìn
, he distinguished the ceremony of comforting guests in the suburbs (jiāo láo)
. During the Warring States period (Zhànguó), when vertical and horizontal alliances prevailed
, government and education were further extinguished
. The tyrannical Qín destroyed scholarship
, sweeping everything away
. Although the Hàn Dynasty (Hàn Shì) flourished
, time was too short for comprehensive efforts
. Yet, they still ordered Shúsūn
in the outer fields, only then realizing the preciousness of imperial majesty
. In the later period
numerous and complex,
successively there were rises and falls,
sometimes due to sharp ambition in military merit,
sometimes favoring the doctrines of Huáng-Lǎo.
The regulations of rites and righteousness
therefore ceased.
When Cáo Bāo of Dōngjīng
composed and narrated in the Nán
gōng,
collecting scattered outlines,
resulting in over a hundred chapters.
Although they were written on short slips,
they ultimately lacked unified memorials.
Afterwards, wars followed one another,
unorthodox teachings arose mutually.
Chapters
and sentences were lost,
and sacrificial utensils ceased use.
The demeanor of square collars and measured steps,
its practice vanished amidst flags and drums;
the documents of Lántái and Shíshì,
were fully utilized (or consumed) for tents and canopies.
Reaching the
early Jìn period,
new Rites were established.
Xún Yǐ formulated them first,
and Zhì Yú edited them later.
Thereafter, the Zhōngyuán fell into chaos,
rarely leaving anything remaining;
Jiāngzuǒ started crudely,
merely following old customs.
The trend toward reform
there was simply no time for.
Humbly reflecting, Your Majesty (Bìxià), wise and brilliant, initiated the Mandate,
changing the world before Heaven decreed it.
You suppressed chaos solely through military force,
and governed the world through culture.
The composition of music depended on the achievement of success,
and the formulation of rites was broadened after
the establishment of governance.
You brilliantly inaugurated the two schools,
where imperial relatives ranked equally with noble visitors;
You opened these five halls,
promoting those from the common populace with high rank.
From the time of receiving the Mandate,
until completion was announced,
the form and features of your great
virtue are complete,
and all capable affairs under Heaven are finished.
Bright and profound,
there is no virtue left unpraised.
As for the auspicious signs of profound talismans and spiritual bounty,
and the rare gifts from crossing the ocean and climbing the mountains
they are surely recorded daily by the Left Historian,
preserved in the relevant offices,
and can now be briefly mentioned.
Therefore, you commanded the assembled talents,
to search for the methods of Gānquán;
You summoned these
great scholars,
to expound the ceremonies of Qǔtái.
The Confucians from Zīshàng and Yānzhōng,
followed closely, one after the other;
the distinguished men carrying satchels and bearing writing implements
worked day and night.
We trust that transformation has rendered the Sān
yōng harmonious,
and the people follow the Wǔdiǎn,
and the teaching of the Zhìzōng
has flourished vigorously.
I humbly recall that the established Five Rites
began in the third year of Yǒngmíng of the Qí dynasty,
when Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi Fú Màróng memorialized requesting the creation of the Rites and Music for the current dynasty.
At that time, ten new and old scholars were appointed
to participate in the deliberation,
solely dedicated to revising the Five Rites.
They consulted with Wèi Jiāngjūn, Dānyáng Yǐn Wáng Jiǎn.
The scholars were also divided and housed in the commandery,
working for years,
but still unable to complete the work.
When Wénxiàn died,
the remaining documents were scattered and lost.
Later, the matter was entrusted to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ Hé Yìn.
Nine years passed,
yet it was still not finished.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
Hé Yìn returned to Dōngshān,
and Emperor Míngdì of Qí ordered Shàngshū Lìng Xú Xiàosì to take charge.
The details of the old project
were kept in the southern residence.
During the Yǒngyuán period,
Xú Xiàosì
met with misfortune there,
and much was again scattered and lost.
At that time, what remained was gathered up,

They jointly managed the
affair.
At that time, the Bureau for the Revision of Rites was housed outside the central gate of the Guózǐ Xué.
During the reign of Dōnghūn,
there were frequent military fires,
and what was scattered and lost
exceeded more than half again.
In the first
year of Tiānjiān,
Hé Tóngzhī memorialized seeking deliberation on whether the Bureau should be retained or abolished,
and an imperial edict commanded officials outside to deliberate.
At that time, the Shàngshū office deliberated,
believing that since the realm was newly reformed,
and all affairs were just beginning,
it was proper to wait for peaceful prosperity,
and then
discuss compilation and editing.
They wished to temporarily abolish the Bureau of Rites,
and merge its duties back into the Ceremonial Section (Yí Cáo) of the Shàngshū.
The imperial decree stated:
"Rites were destroyed and Music deficient,
thus states differed and houses varied.
It is truly proper to revise and
establish them promptly,
to serve as a perpetual standard.
However, recent revisions and compilations
selected people based on personal favor,
not advancing them based on scholarship;
those in charge of the knowledge
unified the work based on rank,
not based on historical investigation.
That is
why it has not been completed over the years,
having the name but lacking the substance.
Since this is paramount for governing the state,
the external officials may deliberate on suitable personnel.
Once the people are settled,
compilation and organization shall immediately begin."
Thereupon, Shàngshū Púyè
Shěn Yuē and others consulted and deliberated,

and that each scholar nominate two additional scholars

If there were doubts among them,
following the precedent of the Shíqú of the Former Hàn and the Báihǔ of the Later Hàn,
they were to be reported according to the source,
requesting an imperial decision to settle the matter.
accordingly, the senior scholar, Yòujūn Jìshì Cānjūn Míng Shānbīn, was put in charge of the Auspicious

After Hé Tóngzhī’s death,

Therefore, Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn, Dānyáng Yǐn Shěn Yuē, Tàicháng
Qīng Zhāng Chōng, and I, your servant (Chén), were further instructed to participate in these duties.
I, your servant, also received a separate edict,

Finally, Zhōngshū Shìláng Zhōu Shě and Yǔ Yúlíng

If there were doubtful meanings,

consult generally with the senior scholars of the Five Rites and the participating officials,
each stating their agreement or disagreement,

Since the doubtful matters were numerous,
and years have accumulated,
the imperial decisions rendered
were considerable in number.
All of them encompass the classics and injunctions,
striking like a jade chime
or a bronze bell (perfectly harmonious wisdom),
their meaning penetrates the subtle and obscure,
and their principle achieves divine resonance,
matters which previous Confucians failed to elucidate,
and which later scholars had not yet heard.
All matters determined by memorial
are recorded at the beginning of the chapters,
listing the full sacred
decrees,
serving as unchangeable rules.
These great regulations and flourishing standards
surpass all hundred former kings;
these splendid accomplishments and brilliant fame
will extend for a thousand years.
How could Xiàoxuān be compared to them?
How could Xiàozhāng
are sufficient to mention.
The duties of the Five Rites (Wǔ Lǐ),

volumes,

they were copied and finalized,

I humbly observe that the compilation and rectification of ritual systems
has rarely been achieved throughout the ages,
but with the ascent of the Illustrious Dynasty (Huáng Míng),
this achievement has been successfully completed.
The Zhōu Dynasty had three thousand [rules],
that being the full count used;
the current eight thousand [articles]
reflect additions made according to circumstances.
As essence and ornamentation change,
thus the number is multiplied,
just like the lines of the Bāguà (Eight Trigrams),
which are doubled,
forming the sixty-four [hexagrams] through combination and arrangement.
In the past, the
two Kings Wén and Wǔ
used this to manage the laws of the Zhōu Shì [court],
and rule the world.
Gōng Dàn (the Duke of Zhōu) revised them,
thereby achieving the great peace signified by the auspicious omens of the dragon and phoenix.
Since then,
they have been fully completed only
in these present days.
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) said:
"If there be any who succeed Zhōu,
though it be a hundred ages, we can know them."
Could this be what is meant by equaling that accomplishment and matching its beauty!
Your servant, relying on his ordinary understanding,
was mistakenly placed in charge of
this responsibility.
Detained and lingering for many years,
I sincerely accepted this charge.
Moreover, at the beginning of the compilation and completion [of the Rites],
I did not have time to present them in a memorial,
truly because my talent was slight and the task was vast,
and my mental power was inadequate.
I constantly feel ashamed and fearful,
never
forgetting this whether waking or sleeping.
Since this spring, when the imperial carriage was about to personally inspect the Six Armies,
the Military Rites (Jūnlǐ) were sought out,
and upon reviewing their articles and chapters,
nothing was found to be incomplete or inadequate.
It is indeed what is meant by "how splendid is the pattern!"
radiant
and overflowing,
truly worthy of being hung up alongside the sun and moon,
and promulgated throughout the world.
My foolish heart rejoiced and clapped its hands,
and I felt an increasing urge to present this statement;
moreover, the officials who held concurrent positions before and after [me]
have all
passed away,
and although your servant is fortunate to still be alive,
old age is imminent.
Fearing that the great canon of the Imperial Dynasty
might lack a formal transmission through a memorial,
unable to bear this sentiment,
I took the liberty of fully detailing the beginning and end of the compilation,
together with the names of the responsible
personnel, the number of fascicles, volumes, and articles completed,
and respectfully presented this memorial for announcement.
An imperial edict stated:
"The essential Rites (Jīnglǐ) are greatly complete,
and the governing statutes are correspondingly vast.
We now command the relevant authorities
to adopt these precedents and implement them."
Another imperial edict stated:
"The memorial by Miǎn is thus.
The traditional systems have been truly clarified through reform and change,
and the legal codes are fully comprehensive.
The achievement is accomplished and the foundational work is established,
resting herein.
This can illuminate the eight quarters,
and be applied for a hundred generations,
ensuring that for ten thousand generations hereafter,
they will know that this culture (wén) rests here.
Let the officials in charge adhere to this and follow it,
without any loss or oversight."
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhōngshū Lìng (Prefect of the Palace Writers),
and granted twenty trusted attendants.
Miǎn pleaded his illness,
requesting relief from his inner court duties.
The edict did not permit it,
but instead ordered him to remain in the palace annex (Xià Shěng),
attend court once every three days,
and send a chief clerk (Zhǔshū) to discuss and decide matters when necessary.
His leg ailment worsened,
and he was absent from court for a long time.
He firmly petitioned again for release from duty.
The edict then granted him leave,
requiring him to return to the palace annex once his illness was cured.
Although Miǎn held a high position,
he did not manage property or commerce,
his family had no savings,
and his salary was distributed to support relatives who were impoverished.
His disciples and old friends sometimes gently raised the matter.
Miǎn then replied:
"Others leave their descendants wealth,
I leave them integrity (qīngbái).
If my descendants are talented,
they will naturally acquire carriages and luxury;
if they are untalented,
[the wealth] will ultimately belong to others."
He once wrote a letter admonishing his son, Sōng, saying: Our family has been incorruptible for generations,
and therefore we have always maintained a life of poverty and simplicity.
As for the matter of property,
it is something we have never discussed,
and not simply something we fail to engage in.
This humble person happened
to meet with fortune,
thus reaching the present day,
where I hold an honorable office and substantial salary,
which can be considered complete provision.
Whenever I consider that I have falsely obtained such things,
it is certainly not achieved through my own talent,
but rather thanks to the high standards and good fortune
of my ancestors;
thus have I reached this point.
The ancients said,
"To bequeath integrity to one's descendants,
is it not generous?"
They also said:
"To leave a son a basket full of gold,
is not as good as
one classic text (jīng)."
Carefully considering these words,
I believe they are certainly not empty phrases.
Although I am not clever,
I truly possess this original ambition,
hoping to be able to follow and uphold this principle,
daring not to let it fall away.
This is why, since gaining prominence
and rank,
nearly thirty years ago,
disciples and old friends
have repeatedly offered favorable opportunities,
sometimes advising me to establish farms and gardens,
sometimes urging me to set up shops and inns,
or wanting to use fleets of ships for transport,
or suggesting I engage in commerce and hoarding wealth.
All such numerous matters
I have refused and not accepted.
This is not to say that I would pull up mallow or abandon weaving [i.e., reject all labor],
but rather that I desire to lessen the distractions of the world.
That I casually established a small garden among the eastern fields in my middle years
was not for the purpose of sowing and cultivating [crops],
seeking profits,
but simply desiring to dig a pond and plant trees,
so as to briefly indulge my sentiments in appreciation.
Moreover,
as the suburban area is spacious and quiet,
it could eventually serve as a residence.
If I am fortunate enough to retire from office (literally, hang up the carriage),
I truly wish to spend my time singing and weeping there.
Huìrì, Shízhù, and others,
since they need to arrange marriages,
also require residences...
Stop.
My residence at Qīngmíng mén,
there is no room for co-existence.
The reason for this
also has its grounds.
Previously, the western side was given to Xuānwǔ Sì,
and having lost the west wing,
it is no longer
spacious.
I also thought of this as merely an inn,
why should it need to be grand?
I often regret that people of the time call it my residence.
From ancient times to the present,
the rich and powerful have followed in succession,
with high gates
and grand mansions,
connected courtyards and deep chambers.
When they are dead,
whose rooms are they truly?
But I cannot help but build a small mound-like hill,
gathering stones and moving fruit trees,
mixing them with flowers,
to
enjoy leisure and rest,
and to entrust my spirit.
I built it casually,
not aiming for grandeur,
but where the merits are,
I preferred it to be small.
Therefore, the interior is cramped,
without additional
rooms.
Recently, I have been building two residences for my sons and grandsons on the east side,
relying on the funds for the return journey of the ten who went south.
The required expenses for these
are still considerable.
Since the funds did not arrive as expected,
and it was
unacceptable to stop midway,
the garden in the suburbs
could not be maintained.
It was sold to Wéi Àn,
from which I obtained a hundred catties of gold,
to complete the two residences,
which consumed half of it.
How did the garden's
value
reach such an amount?
Because I started it years ago,
and it had largely taken shape.
The peach and plum trees were lush,
the paulownia and bamboo provided shade,
the paths and lanes were interconnected,
and the canals and ditches were
linked.
With elegant buildings and lofty pavilions,
it had considerable beauty for gazing afar;
solitary peaks and dense thickets,
not without an intricate charm.
The waterways were rich in water oats and hornwort,
and the ponds were especially abundant in water caltrops and
lotuses.
Although it was said to be outside human habitation,
it was close to the city walls.
Wéi Shēng desired it,
and it indeed possessed elegant charm.
Recounting this matter
is not due to a stingy heart,
but rather where the flow of writing
led.
I recall Xiè Língyùn's poem "Mountain Dwelling" which says:
"In the midst of heaven and earth,
it now belongs to a rustic fellow."
This garden of mine has been mine for twenty years,
now it belongs to heaven
and earth.
What difference is there between things and me,
when compared?
What I have left here,
I now divide for you,
to build a small farmhouse.
Since relatives and dependents are many,
it is reasonable that this is needed.
Moreover, the teachings of Buddhism
consider wealth as external life;
Confucian classics also state,
"What gathers people is wealth."
How could your common feelings
forget this?
I hear
that the land you bought in Gūshú
is very saline and barren,
how can you be at peace there?
The reason for this is
not due to competition among things.
Although the matter is different from "sleeping on a mound,"
it can somewhat
resemble it.
Confucius said:
"Managing a household well
can be transferred to official duties."
Since you have already begun it,
you should ensure its completion.
To fail in both advancing and retreating
would only bring more ridicule.
If
there is any harvest,
you can distribute it among the family, inside and out, young and old.
It should be appropriately allocated,
which is not for me to know.
Also, the daughters should receive their share.
Since you are the
eldest,
this responsibility falls to you.
Being the eldest for anyone
is indeed not easy.
You must ensure harmony within and without,
so that no one has cause for complaint,
prioritizing others before yourself.
Only then can you be esteemed.
The Old Master said:
"Put yourself last, and you will be first."
If you can do this,
you will attract even greater benefits.
You should strive hard,
see worthy people and emulate them,
and not neglect your days by idleness.
Not
only are you wasting days,
you are wasting yourself.
How great are the good or bad of one's reputation
and person!
Should you not be careful?
What I am now instructing
briefly states this intention:
that since I became
a household head,
I have not pursued assets.
Now that a villa has been established,
it deviates from my old ways.
To recount its beginning and end
leaves no shame in my heart.
Moreover, my years are decaying and old,
my mental and physical strength are gradually
exhausted.
I can barely manage to fulfill my official duties,
and almost fail to perform them.
Any remaining leisure
is barely enough for me to rest.
Perhaps in the winter sun,
or the summer shade,
during good seasons and beautiful scenery,
in the gaps between official documents,
leaning on my staff and wearing sandals,
strolling freely in my humble dwelling,
watching fish by the pond,
listening to birds in the woods,
with a cup of浊jiǔ,
playing a tune on the qín,
seeking a few moments of
temporary joy.
I hope to live out my days in this manner,
and should not again be burdened by trivial family affairs.
Since your contacts are established,
and this letter is issued,
all necessary provisions
will be supplied as
specified elsewhere.
From now on,
I will no longer speak of land matters,
nor should you speak of them to me again.
Even if there were a flood like Yáo's or a drought like Tāng's,
how would I know what to do;
if
your granaries are full and your chests overflowing,
that is your good fortune.
Such matters
do not require me to be informed.
The *Book of Rites* says:
"Filial piety means
skillfully continuing the aspirations of others,
and skillfully
carrying on their undertakings."
Now I hope that you will fully carry out this aspiration of mine,
then I will have no regrets.
Urging his second son, Fěi, upon his death,
deeply grieved,
not wishing to long neglect the affairs of the state,
he then composed "An Explanation to a Guest."
Its words are: In the second month, Dīngchǒu day, of spring in the fifth year of Pǔtōng,
the news of the death of my second son, Fěi, the Internal Historian of Jìn'ān, arrived,
and the whole family was grief-stricken,
our spirits as if fallen.
Two
The palaces both sent down imperial messengers
to express condolences and encouragement.
His close friends and guests
all came to offer their sympathies and inquire after him.
He would invariably weep bitterly and lose his voice,
unable to restrain his grief.
It was the so-called natural bond between father and son;
he did not know where the tears came from.
Thereupon, his disciples, worried that by indulging the intensity of his emotion,
it might lead to his collapse,
straightened their robes and stepped forward, saying:
“I have heard that the passing of the ancient and the coming of the modern
is the regular constant of the rational cycle;
the flourishing of spring and the falling of autumn
is the fixed schedule of cosmic phenomena.
Man dwells within this,
like staying in an inn.
Being born is a sojourn, and dying is a return—
this is established in common discourse.
Therefore, gentlemen of profound insight
calmly
dismiss such thoughts.
The principle of Guīwú from Dōngmén [Dōngmén Guīwú]
was praised by former sages;
the excessive grief of Xīhé [Xīhé] over losing his sight
was mocked by his friends.
Your Excellency has received favorable treatment from the court,
holding the position of Chief Minister
on the right.
Your worries are profound, and your responsibilities are heavy;
you share equally in the good fortune and sorrow of the state.
It is appropriate that you should put aside your grief for those below,
stop mourning, and resume eating,
to preserve your service to the nation above,
and demonstrate the prosperity of your family below.
How can you indulge this profitless
grief,
behaving like children,
damaging your spirit and harming your judgment,
or perhaps neglecting your vital duties?
We, your disciples, have privately discussed this,
and unanimously agree that Your Lordship should not allow it.”
I [Xú Miǎn] wiped away my tears and replied:
“The ultimate meaning of Pénzǔ and Shāngzi [Péngshāng zhī dáyì],
and the refined words of Yánzǐ and Wúqǐ [Yán Wú zhī yǎyán],
I have also often heard of;
