however, the reason I have been unable to quell my feelings,
please allow me to explain
the reasoning.
When planting trees in the courtyard,
we admire the lushness of their branches and leaves;
when building a mountain pile by the measure,
we regret the failure of the final basket of earth.
Therefore, when something flowers but bears no fruit,
the Master Ní [Nífù] sighed
for it;
the breaking off at diverging paths
was why Yángzǐ lingered with sorrow.
When a matter is worthy of deep emotion,
sages and worthies do not suppress it.
My current sorrow
is also because Fěi [Fěi] had just passed the age of thirty;
his filial
piety and brotherly respect were exceptional,
from his youth onward;
the beauty of his literary compositions
was derived naturally;
he was tirelessly fond of learning,
and his dwelling was free of vulgarity and confusion.
He produced many writings,
filling bundles and cabinets.
Regarding gain and loss, he was indifferent,
never showing
expressions of joy or anger.
When he ascended to the Eastern Court [dōngcháo],
he was counted among the prominent officials;
those he associated with
were all talents and elites of the time.
They composed poems and chanted
songs,
forgetting fatigue all day long.
He often calmly advised me that since I had encountered a favorable time,
and my position was lofty and my responsibilities vital,
I should recommend worthy men and humble myself before scholars,
putting the needs of others first and myself last,
only then could I
repay the kindness of the enlightened sovereign [míngzhǔ]
and maintain great fortune.
The reason I have, in the space of two cycles [24 years],
held this undeserved high rank,
and fortunately committed no major faults,
is entirely due to the help of this son.
Since he left
the Mǐn region [Mǐn Qū],
his governance has been pure and peaceful.
I hoped for his prompt return
to provide some comfort in my declining years.
To think that today,
he has vanished into the long journey.
Furthermore, he closed his coffin a thousand *lǐ* away,
and the date of
his remains being returned is unknown.
Even those without natural feelings
—how could they not feel pain at this event!
When Yífǔ [Yífǔ] lost the child he was holding,
he still wept bitterly when meeting guests;
Ānrén [Ānrén] had not yet reached seventy
years,
but still diligently produced poems and *fù*.
How much more so when one’s fame is established and career is successful,
only to be abandoned midway—
how can I simply stop [my grief]?
Seeking the reason for this feeling,
it may be described
as the meaning of the plant and the fruit [Miáoshí zhī yì].
Since all you gentlemen have provided wise counsel [géyán],
and enlightened me with the great principle,
I shall cease mourning today
and order my carriage to resume my official duties.”
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng [Zhōngdàtōng],
he again pleaded illness,
and was transferred and appointed as Tèjìn,
Yòuguānglù Dàfū, Shìzhōng, and Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn.
He was granted auxiliary staff [zuǒshǐ],
the rest of his titles remaining as before.
Forty personal attendants were added.
The two palaces inquired after him,
and the carriages of officials formed continuous tracks [gūnyà gēzhé].
His clothing, food, and medicine
were all provided by the Imperial Treasury [tiānfǔ].
When there was an imperial decree that the emperor intended to personally visit him,
he excused himself by stating that his bowing and kneeling would be deficient,
and frequently memorialized requesting the visit be canceled.
The emperor granted the decree,
and thereupon halted the imperial carriage [yújià].
In the first year of Dàtóng [Dàtóng],
he died,
aged seventy.
Gāozǔ heard of it and shed tears,
and immediately drove his carriage to the funeral.
He then issued a decree posthumously awarding him the titles Tèjìn, Yòuguānglù Dàfū, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī,
with all other positions remaining as before.
He was provided with secret utensils from the Eastern Park [Dōngyuán Mìqì],
one set of court robes,
and one suit of clothes.
He was posthumously granted 200,000 cash [qián]
and 100 bolts of cloth [bù].
The Crown Prince [Huáng Tàizǐ] also mourned in the court hall [cháotáng].
His posthumous title was Jiǎnsù Gōng.
Miǎn [Miǎn] was skilled at composing literature [shǔwén]
and worked diligently on writings.
Although preoccupied with state affairs [jīwù],
he never ceased writing.
He once found the *Jūzhù* [Qǐjūzhù] records cumbersome and disorganized,
so he added deletions and compilations, creating the *Liúbié Qǐjūzhù* in 600 scrolls;
the *Zuǒchéng Tánshì* in five scrolls;
while in the election office [xuǎncáo],
he compiled the *Xuǎnpǐn* in five scrolls;
during the Qí [Qí] period,
he compiled the *Tàimiào Zhùwén* in two scrolls;
believing that the doctrines of Confucius [Kǒng] and Śākyamuni [Shì] (Buddhism) led to the same destination despite different paths,
he compiled the *Huìlín* in fifty scrolls.
In total, his complete works included the former and latter collections [jì] in forty-five scrolls,
and he also compiled the *Fùrén Jí* in ten scrolls,
all of which circulated in the world.
In the third year of Dàtóng,

his former auxiliary staff, including the Left Administrator of the Department of State Affairs [Shàngshū Zuǒchéng], Liú Lǎn [Liú Lǎn], went to the palace gate [què] and presented the biography of Miǎn’s conduct [xíngzhuàng],
requesting that a stone be carved to record his virtues.
An imperial decree was immediately issued, permitting the erection of a stele at his tomb.
Fěi [Fěi], courtesy name Jìngyè [Jìngyè],
was intelligent and sensitive in his youth,
and skilled at literary composition.
He started his career as a Recorder and Aide [Zhùzuò Zuǒláng],
then transferred to Aide to the Crown Prince [Tàizǐ Shèrén],
where he was responsible for secretarial duties [shūjì].
He was successively promoted to Grand Master of the Stud [Xǐmǎ] and Inner Aide [Zhōng Shèrén],
still managing secretarial matters.
He served in the palace quarters [gōngfāng] for several years.
Due to a foot illness, he left to become Advisor to the Prince of Xiāngdōng [Xiāngdōng Wáng Yǒu],
and was later promoted to Administrator of Jìn'ān [Jìn'ān Nèishǐ].
Chén [Chén] Minister of Personnel [Lìbù Shàngshū], Yáo Chá [Yáo Chá], said: Xú Miǎn [Xú Miǎn] was determined from a young age, forgetting to eat,
exerting himself to cultivate his character,
being cautious in speech and conduct,
and selective in choosing friends.
Furthermore, his destiny coincided with the rise of the ruling house [xīngwáng],
basking in the light of the sun and moon.
Thus, he was able to illuminate classical scholarship to hold high official ranks [qīngzǐ],
and emerge from the common lanes to achieve the position of Minister [qīngxiàng].
When he held heavy responsibilities,
he served his sovereign with utmost sincerity,
his actions modeled on ancient beginnings,
his principles guided by the former kings,
maintaining balance and upright standards,
so that there were no dissenting opinions among the populace.
He was a great minister of Liáng [Liáng Zōngchén],
truly magnificent.
Biographies, Chapter 20: Fàn Xiù [Fàn Xiù], Fù Zhāo [Fù Zhāo] (younger brother Yìng [Yìng]), Xiāo Chēn [Xiāo Chēn], Lù Gǎo [Lù Gǎo]
was a man from Kǎochéng,
Jìyáng. His great-great-grandfather, Xuān,
was a Gentleman Recluse of the Jìn [dynasty].
His father, Xī,
was the Chief Commandant of Yǎnzhōu
during the Sòng [dynasty]. Xiù
was orphaned young.
He was known for his filial piety in serving his mother,
and he and Shěn Yuē of Wúxīng were both treated with respect by Cài Xīngzōng.
During the Tàishǐ period,
he started his career as a Gentleman of the Imperial Service.
When Xīngzōng was General Who Guards the West,
he appointed Xiù as Chief Clerk.
He was successively promoted to Prefect of Línhǎi and Chángchéng counties, Pìyáo Cavalry Consultative Assistant,
Gentleman of the Secretariat for Drafting
in the Chancellery, Cavalier Major,
and Secretariat Consultative Assistant to Xiāo Ziliáng,
Prince of Jìnglíng and Grand Minister of the Masses of Qí.
He was subsequently promoted to Household Manager of the Heir Apparent.
When Crown Prince Wénhuì was in the Eastern Palace,
Shěn Yuē and his associates were drawn in due to their literary talent,
and Xiù was also among them.
Although Xiù's literary output did not equal Yuē's,
his reputation and conduct were highly regarded by his contemporaries.
He studied widely and was broadly learned,
being particularly knowledgeable about the auspicious and inauspicious historical precedents (rituals) dating from the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards.
Yuē often praised him, saying:
"Lord Fàn's
knowledge of historical events is vast; Hú Guǎng could not surpass him."
Fàn Yún of Nánxiāng told people:
"Gentlemen, regarding propriety of movement and deportment,
you must ask Fàn Chángtóu (Long-head)."
This was because Xiù possessed extensive knowledge of previous dynasties' ancient precedents.
He was promoted to Erudite of the National University.
During the Yǒngmíng period,
when envoys from Wèi arrived,
an imperial edict mandated the careful selection of court officials possessing rhetorical skill
to meet the envoys at the border.
Xiù was appointed concurrently as the Chief Commandant of Huáiyīn to receive them.
Upon return, he was promoted to Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs.
He resigned due to mourning for his mother,
but was soon reinstated to supervise the duties.
He was sent out as General Who Pacifies the North, Chief Commandant of the Southern Man, and Administrator of Nán Yìyáng Commandery.
Before taking up the post,
he was promoted to Consultative Assistant to the General of the Right,
retaining the commandery post as before.
He was appointed Cavalier Major of the General Who Soothes the Army.
He was sent out as General Who Establishes Might and Internal Administrator of Ānchéng.
He returned to court as Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gates,
then was promoted to Imperial Censor, concurrent General of the Van, and Grand Director of the Centralized Selection for the two provinces of South Yǎn and North Yǎn.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán period,
he was sent out as General Who Assists the State, Chief Commandant to the Prince of Jìn'ān, General of the Champions,
and acted as the administrator of Nán Xúzhōu.
When the righteous army pacified the capital,
he received authorization to be summoned as Gentleman of the Bureau of Official Selection in the Department of State Affairs,
participating in the major selections.
When the Liáng court was established,
he became Minister of Finance.
In the fifth year of Tiānjiān (506 CE),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant, Grand Master of Guanglu,
served the Crown Prince,
and was granted an escort.
In the sixth year (507 CE),
he concurrently held the post of Commander of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent.
In the seventh year (508 CE),
he was transferred to Regular Palace Attendant, General of the Right Guard,
retaining his position as Grand Director of the Centralized Selection as before.
That year, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but an edict forbade it.
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he was sent out as Administrator of Jìnlíng Commandery,
holding the rank of Two Thousand Piculs (Middle Grade).
In the ninth year (510 CE),
he returned to court as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
concurrently holding the position of General of the Right Swift Cavalry.
That same year, he was promoted to Grand Master of Guanglu with Gold and Purple Seal,
and was granted twenty confidential retainers.
In the thirteenth year (514 CE),
he died in office,
aged seventy-five.
He was granted 50,000 cash
and 100 bolts of cloth as funeral gifts.
Xiù was seven feet eight inches tall.
He was respectful and solemn in character,
and his every action followed propriety.
After the funeral of his parent,
he ate vegetables and wore coarse cloth for the rest of his life.
In every office he held,
he was noted for his integrity and honesty.
When he was Prefect of Chángchéng,
he had a writing box made of catalpa wood which he used for several decades;
though it eventually became valuable, he never replaced it.
In Jìnlíng,
he only had one pair of ivory-handled brushes made,
yet he still considered it an extravagance.
His compiled writings, *Lǐ Lùn* (Discussions on Ritual), *Zá Yí* (Miscellaneous Protocols), and *Zì Xùn* (Explanations of Characters) circulated in the world.
His two sons were Bāo
and Wěi.
Fù Zhāo,
courtesy name Màoyuǎn,
was a man from Língzhōu, Běidì,
and a seventh-generation descendant of Fù Xián, Commandant of Retainers of Jìn.
His grandfather was Hézhī,
and his father, Dàn,
was skilled in the Three Rites
and was well-known during the Sòng era.
Dàn served Liú Dàn, Prince of Jìnglíng of Sòng.
When Dàn rebelled,
Dàn was executed due to his association.
Zhāo was orphaned at six years old;
his grief and emaciation were like that of an adult,
and all his clan members regarded him highly.
At eleven,
he followed his maternal grandfather and sold almanacs at the Zhūquè Háng (Vermilion Sparrow Bridge).
He was a retainer of Yuán Yǐ,
Inspector of Yōngzhōu.
Yǐ once visited Zhāo's residence,
and Zhāo continued reading composedly,
his expression unchanged.
Yǐ sighed and said:
"This child’s spirit and demeanor are extraordinary;
he will certainly become a fine vessel."
Liú Xiūrén, Prince of Jiàn'ān and Grand Minister of the Masses, heard this and was pleased,
intending to invite Zhāo to serve.
However, since the Sòng clan was afflicted by many troubles,
Zhāo did not go.
Someone recommended Zhāo to Yú Yuàn, Minister of Justice,
so Yuàn dispatched a carriage to welcome Zhāo.
At that time, Yuàn's clansman Tōngzhī was present,
along with other famous contemporaries. Tōngzhī presented Zhāo with a poem, saying:
"The brilliant talents dominate east of the mountains,
the gifted scholars inspire Luòyáng.
Who can inherit their pure essence?
It is you who encounters the lingering fragrance."
Wáng Yánxiù of Tàiyuán recommended Zhāo to Yuán Càn, Governor of Dānyáng.
Càn treated him with great respect
and appointed him as the Commandery Chief Clerk,
making his sons study under Zhāo.
When Emperor Míng died,
Càn composed the elegiac edict
and invited Zhāo to finalize the text he had drafted.
Whenever he passed by Zhāo's door,
he would sigh and say:
"Passing by his door,
it is silent as if uninhabited;
lift the curtain,
and the person is there.
Is this not a virtuous scholar?"
Soon after, he became a Scholar of the Zǒngmíng Academy and Gentleman of the Imperial Service.
During the Yǒngmíng period of Qí,
he was successively promoted to Supernumerary Gentleman, Consultative Assistant to Prince Ziliáng
of Jìnglíng and Grand Minister of the Masses, and Gentleman of the Bureau of Ritual in the Department of State Affairs.
Previously, Liú Xiū, the Imperial Censor, had recommended Zhāo to Emperor Wǔ.
At the start of Yǒngmíng,
Zhāo was made Attendant Reader to the Prince of Nánjùn.
When the Prince succeeded to the imperial throne,
his former subordinates competed for power and favor.
Only Zhāo and Zōng Guài of Nányáng
protected themselves and upheld righteousness,
participating in nothing, and thus avoided misfortune.
When Emperor Míng ascended the throne,
he appointed Zhāo as Gentleman of the Central Secretariat for Transmissions.
At that time, those holding this office
generally had power that shook the world.
Zhāo alone remained honest and quiet,
involving himself in nothing.
His vessels and attire were generally crude,
and he was content with coarse food.
He usually stuck a candle onto a wooden plank bed.
Emperor Míng heard of this
and bestowed upon him lacquered boxes, candle stands, etc.,
issuing an instruction:
"You possess the demeanor of the ancients,
thus I grant you the implements of the ancients."
He was subsequently promoted to Secretariat Consultative Assistant to the Prince of Línhǎi, General of Chariots and Cavalry,
Commandant of Chángshuǐ,
Household Manager of the Heir Apparent,
and Consultative Assistant to the Prince of Jìn'ān, General of Pìyáo Cavalry.
Soon after, he was appointed Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs and Grand Director of the Centralized Selection for his home province.
When Jiànkāng chéng was pacified,
he appointed him as Adjutant (Lùshì Cānjūn) to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
When the Liáng Dynasty was established,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
concurrently holding the position of Director of the Imperial Archives (Zhùzuò Láng).
Soon after,
he concurrently served as Vice President of the Censorate (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
His positions as Huángmén (Palace Attendant), Zhùzuò (Director of Imperial Archives), and Zhōngzhèng (Administrator of Justice) all remained as before.
In Tiānjiān third year,
he concurrently served as Minister of the Five Armies (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
participating in selection affairs.
In the fourth year,
he took the substantive position.
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Minister of State Revenue (Zuǒmín Shàngshū).
Before he took up the post,
he was sent out as General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Ānchéng (Píngnán Ānchéng Wáng), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xúnyáng Commandery.
In the seventh year,
he entered the capital to serve as General Who Arouses Distance (Zhènyuǎn
Jiāngjūn) and Chief Clerk of the Central Authority (Zhōngquán Zhǎngshǐ).
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì),
concurrently holding the post of Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
and again concurrently holding the Grand Administrator of Justice (Dà Zhōngzhèng) for his native province.
In the tenth year,
he again became Minister of State Revenue (Zuǒmín Shàngshū).
In the eleventh year,
he was sent out as General Who Inspires Military Prowess (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Nèishǐ).
Ānchéng had suffered from military disturbances since the Sòng Dynasty.
The commandery office was considered ill-omened.
When Zhāo governed the commandery,
people within the commandery dreamed at night of a great host of soldiers, horses, and armor,
and heard someone say,
"They must avoid the good person."
The troops dispersed, flying away into the void.
The dreamer woke up in alarm.
Presently, fierce winds and torrential rain
suddenly arrived.
Several rooms completely collapsed,
which was exactly the area the dreamer had seen the troops and horses trampling.
Thereafter, the commandery office became peaceful,
and everyone believed this was due to Zhāo's integrity and uprightness.
There were no fish in the commandery's streams.
Sometimes, during the summer months, someone would present Zhāo with fish.
Zhāo neither accepted them
nor wished to refuse them outright;
so he fed them to animals outside his gate.
In the twelfth year,
he entered the capital to serve as Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān),
concurrently holding the position of General of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Jiāngjūn).
In the fourteenth year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng).
In the seventeenth year,
he was sent out as General of Sagacious Prowess (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Línhǎi (Línhǎi Tàishǒu).
In the commandery, there was a Honey Cliff (Mì Yán).
Previous Administrators had all personally sealed it off
and monopolized the profit.
Zhāo, citing the park of King Wén of Zhōu,
shared it with the common people.
Applying a large principle to a small matter,
he ordered that it not be sealed.
The County Magistrate often presented him with chestnuts,
placing silk beneath the container.
Zhāo laughed and returned it.
In Pǔtōng second year,
he entered the capital to serve as Palace Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Master of Remonstrance (Guānglù Dàfū),
concurrently holding the Grand Administrator of Justice (Dà Zhōngzhèng) for his native province.
Soon after, he also concurrently held the Directorship of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Master of Remonstrance with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
The post of Zhōngzhèng remained as before.
In all the offices Zhāo administered,
he always governed with purity and tranquility,
and did not favor strictness or solemnity.
When residing at court,
he made no requests or petitions.
He did not keep private protégés
and did not engage in private gain.
He sat upright all day,
finding joy in scholarly writings,
and though old, his vigor did not decline.
His learning was extensive, reaching into the past and present.
He was especially skilled in understanding historical figures.
Regarding the lineage and achievements of officials and eunuchs
since the Wèi and Jìn Dynasties,
and their intermarriage inside and outside the court,
when he spoke of them,
he never made any omissions or mistakes.
His nature was especially careful and discreet.
His son's wife once obtained beef sent by her family and presented it.
Zhāo summoned his son and said:
"If we eat it, we violate the law;
if we report it, it is improper.
Take it and bury it."
His conduct and self-cultivation,
never betraying conscience even in private,
were all of this nature.
The later generation in the capital
honored his learning
and respected his integrity,
everyone feeling they could not measure up to him.
In Dàtōng second year, ninth month,
he died,
aged seventy-five.
An imperial edict granted 30,000 cash
and fifty rolls of cloth for his funeral.
Mourning was declared that very day,
and he was given the posthumous title Zhēnzǐ.
His eldest son, Xū,
was a Secretary of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Láng)
and Magistrate of Lín'ān.
His second son was Gōng.
Yìng, courtesy name Huīyuǎn,
was Zhāo's younger brother.
He was orphaned at the age of three.
The brothers were harmonious and affectionate,
cultivated their conduct, and refined their practice.
If it was not proper ritual, they would not perform it.
When Zhāo first governed Línhǎi,
Lù Chuí hosted a farewell feast for him.
Both host and guest were greatly joyous,
and as dusk fell, Zhāo did not return.
Yìng, considering Zhāo’s advanced age,
thought it improper for him to prolong the revelry late into the night.
He personally went to meet and escort him back,
returning together in the same carriage.
Both brothers already had gray hair,
and people of the time admired and respected this act.
When Zhāo died,
Yìng mourned him as if he were his father.
Although he was over seventy years old,
his sorrow and grief exceeded the prescribed rites.
Even after the mourning period was over,
whenever he spoke of Zhāo, he was overcome with emotion.
Yìng broadly studied histories and biographies
and possessed literary talent,
but he did not assert himself through poetry and prose.
When young, he was friendly with Liú Huì and Xiāo Chēn.
When Huì served as Chancellor (Xiāng) of Nánkāng,
Yìng served as Administrator Assistant (Fǔ Chéng) at the time.
Many of the official documents and edicts were drafted by him.
Chǔ Yànhuí heard of this and was pleased,
and condescended to associate with him and his son Bēn.
Before Yìng reached the age of twenty,
Yànhuí wanted him to enter official service.
Yìng, knowing Zhāo had not yet taken office (lifted his simple robes),
firmly declined,
waiting until Zhāo held office before accepting a position.
In Yǒngyuán first year,
he participated in the military affairs of the Prince of Jiāngxià, General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngxià Wáng),
and was sent out as Magistrate of Wǔkāng.
When Gāozǔ's army reached Jiànkāng,
Yuán Áng, the Administrator of Wúxīng, believing his family lineage to be loyal and righteous,
strongly maintained his fidelity and integrity.
He consulted Yìng, saying:
"What is your opinion regarding the current situation?"
Yìng replied:
"At the end of Yuánjiā era,
there was an unprecedented disaster.
The late Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) sacrificed himself to demonstrate his integrity,
and the Minister of Education (Sītú) held a position of heavy responsibility entrusted to him.
Naturally, he could not simply preserve himself,
and thus, regardless of danger or safety,
he died for reputation and righteousness.
Now the current ruler is perverse and tyrannical,
associating closely with base individuals.
The worthy and related parties are being executed,
and the way of the gentleman is diminishing.
External calamities repeatedly arise,
yet there is no change or improvement.
Now Jīng and Yōng Provinces have raised forces in accord,
seizing the upper reaches of the river.
Turning their backs on darkness and moving toward light,
the situation guarantees success.
The common people desire good governance,
showing the clear intent of Heaven and man.
Since it is both clear and wise,
the path of loyalty and filial piety allows no deviation.
I urge you, respected Administrator, to consider this carefully,
lest you regret it later."
Soon after, he was dismissed due to an official matter.
Early in the Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed Adjutant (Cānjūn) to the Prince of Póyáng, General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Póyáng Wáng);
Adjutant (Lùshì Cānjūn) of the Central Authority for the Prince of Jiàn'ān;
Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of the Leader of the Army (Lǐngjūn);
and Magistrate of Wūchéng.
The stipends and emoluments he received
were all transferred to his elder brother.
He again served as Adjutant (Lùshì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Línchuān,
Overseer of Documents for the Southern Secretariat (Nántái Zhìshū),
Adjutant (Lùshì) for the Prince of Ānchéng,
Commandant of the Heir Apparent’s Supporting Army (Tàizǐ Yìjūn Xiàowèi).
He was repeatedly promoted to Grand Master of the Household (Zhōngsàn Dàfū) and Minister of the Court of the Imperial Insignia (Guānglù Qīng),
and then Grand Master of the Household (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
In Dàtóng fifth year,
he died,
aged eighty-three.
His son was Hóng.
Xiāo Chēn, courtesy name Yànyú,
was a native of Lánlíng.
His grandfather, Sēngzhēn,
was the Minister of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng) during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Huìxùn,
was a Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū).
Chēn, when several years old,
his paternal uncle, Huìkāi, patted his back and said:
"He will surely make our clan prosperous."
Chēn, while young, was bright and perceptive,
possessing strategic and rhetorical talent.
He started his career as Erudite of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì) during the Qí dynasty.
At that time, Wáng Jiǎn was dominant at court.
Chēn was young,
and not yet recognized by Jiǎn.
Relying on his talent and spirit,
he sought an audience with Jiǎn.
At that time, Jiǎn was holding a banquet at the Yuèyóu Garden (Yuèyóu Yuàn).
Chēn therefore put on tiger-skin boots,
carried a peach branch staff,
and went directly to where Jiǎn was seated.
Jiǎn spoke with him,
and was greatly pleased.
When Jiǎn became the Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn),
he appointed him Principal Registrar (Zhǔbù),
and he was nominated as an Elite Talent (Xiùcái) of Nán Xúzhōu.
He was successively promoted to Record Keeper (Jìshì) for the Minister of Works (Sītú).
In the ninth year of Yǒngmíng (491 CE),
when Wèi first established friendly relations,
Chēn was twice entrusted with a mission to Sānggān.
Upon return, he became a Gentleman-Consultant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng).
At that time, Wèi dispatched Lǐ Dàogù as an envoy to come,
and the Qí Emperor held a feast for him.
Chēn, at the imperial banquet, raised a cup of wine to Dàogù, urging him to drink.
Dàogù refused to accept,
saying:
"In a public court, there are no private formalities,
and I cannot accept this solicitation."
Chēn slowly replied:
"The Odes (Shī) say, 'Let it rain on our public fields,
and then reach our private ones.' "
All those seated were impressed,
and Dàogù then accepted Chēn's wine.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Right (Yòu Zhǎngshǐ) for the Minister of Works (Sītú).
He went out to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Jìnxī (Jìnxī Wáng), managing the affairs of Nán Xúzhōu.
Returning, he additionally served as Minister of the Privy Treasury (Shǎofǔ Qīng) and Vice Director of the Left (Zuǒchéng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
When Dōnghūn first succeeded to the throne,
there was debate at the time because the rite of Mìao Jiàn (visiting the ancestral temple) was lacking.
Chēn argued that based on the Odes of Zhōu (Zhōu Sòng), specifically the sections "Liè Wén" and "Mǐn Yǔ," these were rites for visiting the temple upon accession.
Consequently, his suggestion was followed.
When Emperor Gāozǔ stabilized the capital,
he brought him in as Consultant (Zīyì) to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì),
and concurrently Registrar (Lùshì).
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
When the Liáng regime was established,
he became Vice Minister of the Censorate (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
he was promoted to Tutor (Shùzǐ),
and went out to serve as Governor of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Tàishǒu).
He was recalled to serve as Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
Soon after, he was promoted to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì).
In the third year (504 CE),
he was appointed Palace Administrator to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhōng Shùzǐ) and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
In the ninth year (510 CE),
he went out to serve as General Who Pacifies Afar (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the General Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī), and Governor of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Tàishǒu).
When Chēn was first in Xuānchéng,
a northern monk crossed south,
carrying only a gourd,
which contained the Preface and Biography sections of the *Hàn Shū*.
The monk said:
"The elders of Sānfǔ (the three capital commanderies) passed it down,
believing it to be the true original text by Bān Gù."
Chēn firmly requested and obtained it.
That book contained many parts different from the current version,
and the paper and ink were ancient.
Many of the characters followed the style of *lóng jǔ* (dragon script),
being neither clerical (lì) nor seal script (zhuàn).
Chēn greatly treasured it.
When he undertook this journey,
he presented the book to the Prince of Póyáng, Fàn (Póyáng Wáng Fàn).
Fàn then presented it to the Eastern Palace (the Heir Apparent).
Chēn was subsequently promoted to Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Zhǎngshǐ) and Governor of Nánjùn (Nánjùn Tàishǒu).
He resigned his office due to mourning for his mother,
and subsequently experienced the difficulty of mourning for his father.
He was recalled to serve as General of Martial Trust (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Chief Clerk to the Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Zhǎngshǐ).
Soon after, he became General of Loyal Resolve (Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn) and Chief Clerk to the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ).
He went out to serve as General of Trust and Might (Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
He was promoted to Governor of Wúxīng (Wúxīng Tàishǒu).
In the commandery, there was a temple to Xiàng Yǔ.
The local people called him the "Vexed King" (Fèn Wáng).
He was extremely efficacious.
Consequently, in the commandery's administrative hall, a bed and curtains were set up as the divine seat.
Both officials and common people offered prayers and petitions.
All previous Governors (who held the salary of two thousand *dàn*) bowed and sacrificed in the hall,
and avoided residing in that room.
When Chēn arrived,
he moved the spirit back to the temple,
occupying the hall without hesitation.
He also prohibited the killing of cattle for sacrificial offerings,
using dried meat instead of fresh meat.
Chēn frequently governed large commanderies,
but did not manage assets (or acquire property).
If there was a deficiency, he would take (what was needed),
and did not regard it as shameful.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
he was recalled to serve as Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng).
He was promoted to Minister of the Left Populace (Zuǒmín Shàngshū),
concurrently holding the position of Grand Arbiter (Dà Zhōngzhèng) for Nán Xúzhōu,
and Commandant of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèishuài) to the Heir Apparent.
He was transferred to Minister of Revenue (Dùzhī Shàngshū),
General of the Left Valiant Cavalry (Zuǒ Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn),
General of the Leading Army (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn),
then transferred to Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān) and General of the Rear Army (Hòujūn Jiāngjūn).
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
When Emperor Gāozǔ was at the Western Residence,
he had long been intimate with Chēn.
Whenever there was a court banquet,
he received him with old affection,
calling him "Venerable Elder of the Clan" (Zōng Lǎo).
Chēn, too, presented his gratitude for past kindness,
saying:
"I was early ranked among the central figures,
and long shared the same neighborhood.
Although I was confused (and missed) the start of the rising dynasty,
I still bear the great grace."
The Emperor replied:
"Although we spoke of meeting long ago,
you were certainly not of the same will;
Do not speak of the beginning of the rising dynasty,
just speak of the differences of the wild slave."
Chēn often said:
"When I was young and strong, I had three enjoyments:
music, books, and wine.
Since growing older,
two of those are completely abandoned.
Only books and reading have not waned."
Chēn was naturally unconstrained and easygoing.
He often personally managed the cooking.
When the work was done and leftovers consumed,
he would invariably become pleasantly drunk.
In the second year of Dàtōng (528 CE),
he was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū),
and additionally given the rank of Special Advanced (Tèjìn).
He was granted thirty personal retainers.
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtōng (529 CE),
he became General of the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu).
Holding a salary rank equivalent to two thousand *dàn*,
he resigned himself due to illness.
He was reassigned as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Special Advanced (Tèjìn), and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
He died,
at the age of fifty-two.
He left instructions to his sons
to share the same grave mound as his wife but be buried in separate chambers,
to sacrifice with vegetables,
and for the burial day to use only ten carriages,
maintaining simplicity in all matters.
The Emperor personally attended the mourning, weeping deeply.
An imperial edict conferred him the titles of his original office,
added the title General of the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn),
provided funerary items (Mìqì) from the Eastern Park,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothing,
a burial grant of two hundred thousand coins,
and one hundred bolts of cloth.
His posthumous name was Píngzǐ.
Lù Gǎo, courtesy name Míngxiá,
was a native of Wú in Wú Commandery (Wú Jùn).
His grandfather, Huī,
was General Assisting the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Yìzhōu (Yìzhōu Cìshǐ) during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Ruì,
was Administrator of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng).
Gǎo was fond of learning from a young age,
skilled in calligraphy and painting.
His maternal uncle, Zhāng Róng, had a high reputation.
Gǎo’s demeanor and conduct
were quite similar to Róng’s.
People at the time praised them, saying:
“Under the sun, there are none comparable,
except the uncle and the nephew.”
He started his career as an Acting Staff Officer of the Middle Army Judicial Section of Qí,
then Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince,
and Registrar under Wáng Jiǎn, the Commander of the Guards.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Palace Affairs Section of the Secretariat,
but on the day he was appointed,
all the Chief Secretaries and Gentlemen of the Eight Seats went up to the central secretariat to exchange courtesies,
and Gǎo arrived late,
missing the scheduled time.
Consequently, he was dismissed from office.
After a long period,
he was appointed Staff Officer of the Outer Military for the Minister of Education, the Prince of Jìnglíng.
He was promoted to Chief Recorder for the General Who Attacks the Enemy, the Prince of Yídū,
then Consultant and Staff Officer for the General of Agile Cavalry, the Prince of Jìn’ān,
and subsequently Director of Retainers for the Minister of Education.
When the Liáng regime was established,
he was appointed Recorder and Staff Officer for the General of Agile Cavalry,
and was promoted to Western Bureau Director for the Chancellor.
In the first year of Tiānjiān [502 CE],
he was appointed Chief Clerk to the General Who Comforts the Army,
but left office due to mourning for his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed General Who Establishes Might and Consultant and Staff Officer for the Prince of Línchuān, the General of the Central Army.
Soon after, he was promoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Yellow Gates,
and Chief Clerk to the Prince of Ānchéng, the General of the Right Army.
In the fifth year [506 CE],
he was promoted to Palace Assistant Imperial Censor.
Gǎo was naturally resolute and forthright,
and showed no concern for favors or influence.
Yú Jiān, the Magistrate of Shānyīn, was in office
and embezzled several million [coins].
Gǎo submitted a memorial to have him arrested and investigated.
Huáng Mùzhī, a Secretariat Drafter, asked Gǎo to intercede in Jiān’s case,
but Gǎo did not respond.
When Gāozǔ heard of this,
he asked Gǎo about it.
Gǎo replied:
“It is true.”
Gāozǔ said:
“Do you know Mùzhī?”
Gǎo replied:
“I do not know the person.”
At that time, Mùzhī was standing near the Emperor’s seat.
The Emperor pointed him out to Gǎo and said:
“This is the person.”
Gǎo said to Mùzhī:
“You are a petty man!
How dare you recommend a criminal to the Southern Bureau?”
Mùzhī turned pale.
Zhāng Jì, the General Who Leads the Army,
was Gǎo’s maternal cousin.
Gǎo once impeached Jì concerning a public matter.
Jì, while attending a banquet, complained to Gāozǔ, saying:
“Lù Gǎo is my close relative,
yet he shows no mercy in impeaching me over minor issues.”
Gāozǔ said:
“Gǎo is merely carrying out his duty;
how can you hold that against him?”
When Gǎo was in the Censorship Bureau,
he was renowned for not fearing the powerful and arrogant.
In the sixth year [507 CE],
he was promoted to Director of the Imperial Library.
A short while later, he became Chief Gentleman of the Crown Prince’s Household and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In the eighth year [509 CE],
he was sent out as the Administrator of Yìxīng.
While in the commandery, he was benevolent and lenient,
and was praised by the common people.
Upon returning, he served as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Línchuān, the Minister of Works, and concurrently Director of the Great Central Secretariat of Yángzhōu.
In the fourteenth year [515 CE],
he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
and shortly thereafter, to Cavalier Regular Attendant,
retaining his post as Director of the Central Secretariat as before.
In the fifteenth year [516 CE],
he was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Left to the Minister of Education.
In the sixteenth year [517 CE],
he entered the government as Minister of Personnel for the Left,
and was then promoted to Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In the second year of Pǔtōng [521 CE],
he was sent out as General Who Manifests Awe and Administrator of Línchuān.
In the fifth year [524 CE],
he returned to serve as Gold and Purple Grand Master of the Palace,
and concurrently retained the post of Director of the Great Central Secretariat of Yángzhōu.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng [529 CE],
he was given the special title of Attendant-in-Chief,
retaining the post of Director of the Central Secretariat as before.
In the fourth year [532 CE],
he died,
at the age of seventy-four.
His posthumous title was Zhǐzǐ.
Gǎo was naturally devout in Buddhism,
keeping the precepts very strictly.
He wrote thirty scrolls of the Biographies of Śramaṇas (Buddhist Monks).
His younger brother, Xū,
was broadly learned and possessed profound reasoning.
In the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he successively served as Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Central Secretariat,
Assistant Director of the Left in the Secretariat,
and Prefect of the Crown Prince’s Household.
He died [in this post].
He had not completed compiling the History of Jìn.
He also authored fifteen scrolls of the History of Lù,
and one scroll of the Records of Lìquán of the Lù Clan,
both of which circulated widely.
His son, Zhào,
was earnest in his studies from a young age
and possessed literary talent.
He rose in office to Chief Gentleman of the Crown Prince’s Household and Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
The Historian comments: Fàn Xiù and Fù Zhāo
were both earnest in their conduct, clean, and prudent,
finishing well what they started.
They were disciples of Shí Jiàn and Shí Qìng.
Xiāo Chēn and Lù Gǎo were both renowned for their talent and learning.
Chēn was bright, insightful, and articulate,
and moreover thoroughly conversant with court institutions.
When Gāozǔ was still a commoner,
he had a long-standing friendship with Chēn,
and when he ascended the throne,
he entrusted and treated him with great respect.
This was admirable.
Gǎo was naturally resolute and forthright,
with nothing to fear or avoid.
When he held office in the Censorate,
he enforced the law without sparing the powerful or favored.
He may be called true to the color of integrity.
The Poem says:
“That gentleman,
is the rectifier of the state.”
Gǎo exemplified this.
Biography Twenty-one: Lù Chuí, Dào Qià, Míng Shānbīn, Yīn Jūn, Lù Xiāng
Lù Chuí, courtesy name Zuǒgōng,
was a native of Wú County in Wú Commandery.
He was a sixth-generation descendant of Wán, the Grand Commandant of Jìn.
His grandfather, Zǐzhēn,
was the Administrator of Dōngyáng for Sòng.
His father, Huìxiǎo,
was the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices for Qí.
Chuí was diligent in study from a young age
and skilled in literary composition.
He built two thatched rooms inside his residence,
cut off contact with visitors,
and read day and night,
doing this for several years.
Every book he read once
he could recite by heart.
He once borrowed the Hàn Shū from someone
and lost four scrolls of the Wǔ Xíng Zhì (Treatise on the Five Elements).
He secretly rewrote them from memory and returned them,
with virtually nothing missing or incorrect.
As a child, he was considered extraordinary by his maternal grandfather, Zhāng Dài.
Dài often said to his sons:
“This child is the Yáng Yuán of your family.”
At age seventeen,
he was recommended as a Cultivated Talent by his commandery.
Zǐliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng and Prefectural Governor, opened the Western Residence to invite outstanding talents,
and Chuí was among them.
He was appointed Staff Officer of the Discussion Section, and Acting Staff Officer of the Judicial Section for the Prince of Lúlíng.
In the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he served as Staff Officer of the Outer Military for the Prince of Ānchéng, the General of the Right Army,
and then transferred to Registrar.
Lù Chúi and Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān were good friends.
He composed the Rhapsody on Feeling Understood (Gǎn Zhī Jǐ Fù) and presented it to Fǎng.
Fǎng used a poem of the same title to reply, saying:
“Truly, your great lineage is profound and enduring,
Its origins rooted in the domain of the feudal lords in Lù Xiāng.
I recall the refined manner and the simple Daoist virtue,
Inheriting the ceremonial robes and embroidered skirts.
The gentleman (Yī Rén) returns, carried through the generations,
Equaling the three mighty steeds in brilliant splendor.
Passing through Lóng Jīn for a brief rest,
Gazing at Fèng Tiáo before soaring high.
Although that white jade is pure,
This deep orchid is truly fragrant.
My thoughts seek analogies in nature,
Not measurable by pints or pecks.
Matched to the towering Eastern Peak (Dōng Yuè),
Compared to the sharp severity of autumn frost.
Never wasting a single meal,
But often throwing three coins into the Wèi River.
He dares not sigh while hiding his face in his sleeve,
Nor can the ditches and ravines clothe him.
He is both possessed of abundant cultivation and reserve,
And yet simple and unpretentious.
When content, he shares the desire to withdraw and keep his talents hidden,
When disagreeing with convention, he seems to rely on temperament.
Like Hè Yán (Píngshū) but without adornment,
Like Yáng Xióng (Zǐyún) but not unrefined.
Crowning all virtues and leaving a legacy of conduct,
Synthesizing all doctrines, giving fame to his learning.
Surpassing Gāo and Dài at the Imperial Secretariat (Hòutái),
Different from Zōu and Yán in Dǒng Zhòngshū’s academy.
Collecting the three versions of the *Book of Odes* in Héjiān,
Visiting the nine masters of the Rites in the bends of the Huái River.
His methods include orally transmitted texts,
His skills encompass the resonant sounds of music.
Sometimes sitting asleep with hair tied to the beam,
Cutting thorny wood and grasping an awl.
His writing is smooth, yet his meaning is profound,
His reasoning excels, yet his language is rich.
Alas, my life fades swiftly,
I am near the year's end, and my spirits are low.
I gauge the passing shadows beneath the hall,
Listening to the sounding bells in Luòchéng.
Only Master Lù (Lù Zǐ), who disregards age differences,
Is destined for a spontaneous meeting, sitting upon thorns.
I have obtained the worth of Tián and Sū's friendship,
You have gained a reputation across the sea.
Truly, I am downcast and without property,
Yet I will ultimately live long opposite a short life.
Hunger is revealed by a slow gait,
Avoiding debt is evident in swift running.
You compared me to Shū Zé,
And also likened me to Yào Qīng.
Hearts illuminating each other, emotions intertwined,
Rumors cannot confuse us.
All things are sought in darkness,
Yet they are found suspended a thousand *lǐ* away.
Words and images can be discarded,
The snares and fish traps fall silent.
We do not live in joined houses,
But when traveling, we share a carriage.
In winter, the day is too short,
In summer, there is no time left over.
Feasting and dining are not our lure,
How can strings and flutes amuse us?
I have not yet set down my carriage,
And you have already turned your chariot around.
Looking at each other during the midday meal,
We feel moved and melancholic.
Our territories are already different,
Our partings and meetings are unpredictable.
When alive, we are unlike the residents of Shānyáng,
When dead, we will not lie beside Yāo Lí.
It is like glue poured into lacquer,
How could Lí Lóu recognize it?"
He was highly valued by scholars and friends in this manner.
He was transferred to be the Eastern Bureau Aide (Dōng Cáo Yuàn) for the General of Cavalry, the Prince of Línchuān (Piàojì Línchuān Wáng).
At that time, the systems of rites and music,
Were largely being newly established and reformed.
Emperor Gāo (Gāozǔ) greatly admired Chúi’s talent,
and therefore commanded him to compose the Inscription for the New Clepsydra (Xīn Lòukè Míng).
His composition was extremely fine.
He was transferred to be Palace Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén),
Managing the Eastern Palace’s (Crown Prince’s) documents.
He was also ordered by imperial decree to write the Record Inscription on the Stone Watchtower (Shí Quē Míng Jì),
And he presented it.
The imperial decree stated:
“The Stone Watchtower Inscription (Shí Quē Míng) composed by Lù Chúi, Palace Aide to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén),
Has elegant language and lofty meaning,
Sufficient to be considered a fine work.
In the past, Yú Qiū distinguished objects,
And Hándān presented a *fù*,
And were rewarded with gold and silk—
This is well spoken of in earlier histories.
He may be granted thirty rolls of silk.”
He was transferred to be Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shùzǐ) and Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì).
Due to mourning for his mother, he left office.
When the mourning period ended,
He became Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
And Vice Administrator (Biéjià Cóngshì Shǐ) of Yángzhōu.
He requested resignation due to illness.
He was transferred to Minister of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglú Qīng),
And entered the capital to serve as Director of the Personnel Department (Lìbù Láng),
Participating in selection matters.

He left the capital to serve as Chief Clerk to the General of the Flying Cloud, Prince of Jìn'ān (Yúnhuī Jìn'ān Wáng Zhǎngshǐ), Administrator of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng Tàishǒu), and Acting Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
He was dismissed due to official matters,
And demoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
Marshal to the Minister over the Masses (Sītú Sīmǎ),
Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi Qīng).
He again became Attendant-in-Ordinary (Zhōngshùzǐ),
Given the additional title of Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Zhōng),
And Senior Arbiter of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
He was reappointed Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì),
With the posts of Attendant-in-Ordinary (Zhōngshùzǐ) and Arbiter (Zhōngzhèng) remaining as before.
He served as Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng),
The post of Arbiter (Zhōngzhèng) remaining as before.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng [526 CE],
He died,
At the age of fifty-seven.
His collected works, in twenty volumes,
Circulated throughout the world.
His fourth son, Lù Yì,
Was precociously intelligent;
At ten years old, he had mastered the Classics.
He served as Gentleman-Service-Carriage (Fèngchē Láng) while still a child,
And died.
Dào Qià, courtesy name Mào,
Was a native of Wǔyuán in Péngchéng.
He was the great-grandson of Dào Yànzhī, General of Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) during the Sòng dynasty.
His grandfather, Dào Zhòngdù,
Was Gentleman-Service-Official (Cóngshì Zhōngláng) to the General of Cavalry, the Prince of Jiāngxià (Piàojì Jiāngxià Wáng).
His father, Dào Tǎn,
Was Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng) during the Qí dynasty.
When Qià was eighteen,
He became Acting Western Bureau Official (Yíng Xī Cáo Xíngshì) for Nán Xúzhōu.
Qià was famous early in life;
He was pure, alert, talented, learned, and proper in his conduct.
Xiè Tiǎo's literary compositions were renowned during that era.
Upon meeting Qià, he greatly appreciated and favored him,
Inviting him daily for conversation and discussion.
He often said to Qià:
“You are not just a famous gentleman,
But also possess both civil and military talents.”
Later, when Tiǎo was in the Personnel Department (Lìbù),
Qià left his post.
Tiǎo wished to recommend him,
But Qià saw that the world was heading toward chaos,
And resolutely declined.
He was appointed Left Attendant of the Princely State of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Wángguó Zuǒ Chángshì),
But did not take the post.
Consequently, he built a house beneath a cliff,
Living in seclusion for several years.
Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān possessed the ability to judge men.
He was on good terms with Qià’s elder brothers, Dào Zhǎo and Dào Gài.
He once visited Qià at his rural residence,
And upon seeing him, sighed and said:
“This young man is unequaled under Heaven.”
He then paid him the ritual respect due to a close relative.
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
Zhǎo and Gài were both promoted and appointed.
Qià, especially, was recognized and valued.
His cousin, Dào Hàng, also shared renown with them.
Emperor Gāo (Gāozǔ) asked Qiū Chí (Expectant Appointee):
“How does Dào Qià compare to Hàng and Gài?”
Chí replied:
“His integrity and purity surpass Hàng,
His writings are no less than Gài’s;
Furthermore, concerning philosophical discussion,
He is probably hard to equal.”
He was immediately summoned to be Gentleman of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
The Emperor held court at Huáguāng Palace (Huáguāng Diàn),
And ordered Qià, Hàng, Xiāo Chēn, and Rèn Fǎng to attend the feast,
And compose a twenty-couplet poem.
Qià’s verses were judged the most skillful,
And he was bestowed twenty rolls of silk.
Emperor Gāo (Gāozǔ) said to Fǎng:
“The Dào family members may truly be called talented men.”
Fǎng replied:
“Your servant often secretly considers that,
The Sòng dynasty obtained their military strength,
And the Liáng dynasty obtains their literary refinement.”
In the second year,
he was transferred to become Registrar (Zhǔbù) to the Minister of Works (Sītú).
He served directly in the Imperial Secretariat (Dài Zhào Shěng),
receiving an imperial edict to copy the works of the Jiǎ Department.
In the fifth year,
he was transferred to become Palace Affairs Clerk (Diànzhōng Láng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
*Qià*’s (Qià) brothers and cousins
successively held this position,
and people at the time honored this.
In the seventh year,
he was transferred to be Central Attendant (Zhōng Shèrén) to the Crown Prince,
and together with the Palace Steward (Shùzǐ), Lù Chuí (Lù Chuí), he jointly managed the records of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
Soon after, he became Attendant Reader (Shìdú).
The Attendant Reader Office (Shìdú Shěng) subsequently established two Academicians (Xuèshì),
and *Qià* (Qià) was again chosen to fill one of these posts.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to be Erudite (Bóshì) of the Imperial University (Guózǐ),
receiving an imperial edict to compose the Stele for the Grand Academy (Tài Xué Bēi).
In the twelfth year,
he was sent out to serve as Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Línchuān (Línchuān),
and was praised for his performance while in the commandery.
In the fourteenth year,
he returned to the capital to become Household Administrator (Jiālìng) to the Crown Prince,
transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng),
concurrently holding the post of Erudite (Bóshì) of the Imperial University (Guózǐ).
In the sixteenth year,
he was transferred to Central Principal Secretary (Zhōng Shùzǐ) to the Crown Prince.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (Pǔtōng),
he held the post of Erudite (Bóshì) using his current official capacity.
After a short time,
he returned to the capital to become Director (Láng) of the Bureau of Personnel (Lìbù) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
He did not permit any requests or lobbying.
Soon after, he was transferred to Supernumerary Palace Attendant (Yuánwài Sǎnqí Chángshì),
and again held the post of Erudite (Bóshì).
He left office due to mourning for his mother.
In the fifth year,
he again became Central Principal Secretary (Zhōng Shùzǐ) to the Crown Prince,
concurrently commanding the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
Before he was formally invested,
he was subsequently transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng),
concurrently commanding Assistant Director of the Left (Zuǒ Chéng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
In applying the standards and rules, he did not spare the powerful or imperial relatives,
and bribery could not pass through the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Shěng).
At that time, when the Emperor intended personally to lead the troops,
the military and state protocols
mostly originated from *Qià* (Qià).
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Palace Assistant Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
His impeachment and correction were carried out without regard or hesitation,
and he was renowned for being strong and upright;
the atmosphere at the time was rigorously purified.
He was demoted due to a public matter,
but still remained in his post.
According to old regulations,
the Palace Assistant Censor (Zhōngchéng) was not permitted to enter the inferior residence of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Xiàshě).
*Qià*’s (Qià) elder brother, *Gài* (Gài), was Minister (Shàngshū) of the Bureau of Public Works (Zuǒ Mín).
*Qià* (Qià) argued that close relatives should not be obstructed,
and referred the matter to the Secretariat for detailed decision.
Assistant Director of the Left (Zuǒ Chéng) Xiāo Zǐyún (Xiāo Zǐyún) argued that he should be allowed to enter *Gài*’s (Gài) office,
also considering that the brothers were generally devoted,
and should not be separated.
In the seventh year,
he was sent out to be General of Majestic Rectitude (Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of the Cloud-Charging Cavalry (Yúnhuī), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng).
In the first year of Dàtōng (Dàtōng),
he died in the commandery,
aged fifty-one.
He was posthumously granted Attendant-in-Ordinary (Shìzhōng).
His posthumous title was Lǐzǐ (Lǐzǐ).
Crown Prince Zhāomíng (Zhāomíng Tàizǐ) issued an order to the Prince of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Wáng), Gāng (Gāng), saying:
“Lord Míng of Běi Yǎn (Míng Běi Yǎn) and Chief Clerk Dào (Dào Zhǎngshǐ) have successively and continuously passed away.
My sorrow is profound and my grief is aching,
and I cannot stop myself.
Last year, Grand Minister Lù (Lù Tàicháng) died;
this year, these two worthies have also departed forever.
Mr. Lù (Lù Shēng) possessed loyalty and practiced rectitude,
pure as ice and clear as jade.
His writings encompassed the Four Beginnings,
and his learning covered the Nine Schools.
His sentiments were lofty and his spirit outstanding,
truly ascending straight up.
Lord Míng (Míng Gōng) studied the Classics, investigated antiquity,
was pure, sincere, and profoundly trustworthy.
In establishing himself and practicing the Way,
he was consistent from beginning to end.
If he were to meet Confucius (Fūzǐ),
he would surely ascend the Hall of Kǒng (Kǒng Táng).
Master Dào (Dào Zǐ) had a broad and refreshing demeanor,
his writings and principles were worth viewing,
and when holding office and conducting affairs,
he was steadfastly impartial.
They were all distinguished talents within the realm,
and hidden treasures of the Eastern School (Dōng Xù).
What more needs to be said
about this cause for lamentation and pity?
However, having associated and interacted with them,
and having spent years with them,
the loyal advice offered privately
cannot be fully enumerated.
That I have happily avoided error and regret
is truly due to the efforts of these few gentlemen.
Our conversations feel like yesterday,
their voices still resonate in my ears.
Their continuous passing,
turning them all into things of the past,
every time I think of it,
how can words describe it?
For the treasures of the world,
it is natural to feel pain and sorrow.
Recently, Zhāng Xīn'ān (Zhāng Xīn'ān) also passed away.
His literary style and writing were grand and refined,
also worthy of lamentation and pity.
Since following his younger brother to the governmental court,
he has been traveling East and West for a long time;
this loss is particularly heartbreaking.
Recently, there has been a great falling off of talent,
which is particularly lamentable and sorrowful.
Since I have received this current communication,
I mention it again.”
*Qià*’s (Qià) collected writings circulate in the world.
His sons were Bóhuái (Bóhuái) and Zhòngjǔ (Zhòngjǔ).
Míng Shānbīn (Míng Shānbīn), courtesy name Xiàoruò (Xiàoruò),
was a native of Gè (Gè) in Píngyuán (Píngyuán).
His father, Sēngshào (Sēngshào),
lived as a recluse and did not take office.
During the late Sòng (Sòng) dynasty, he was summoned by the Erudite (Bóshì) of the Imperial University (Guózǐ),
but did not accept the post.
Shānbīn (Shānbīn) at age seven could discuss philosophical concepts.
At thirteen, he was widely knowledgeable in the Classics and Commentaries.
While observing mourning, he fulfilled all the rites.
When the mourning period concluded,
the commandery appointed him to be Aide (Cóngshì Shǐ).
He started his official career by being summoned to Court (Fèng Cháoqǐng).
His elder brother, Zhòngzhāng (Zhòngzhāng), suffered from a chronic illness,
and the family resources were frequently depleted.
Shānbīn (Shānbīn) thus sought official salary.
Xiāo Yáoguāng (Xiāo Yáoguāng), Prince of Shǐ'ān (Shǐ'ān Wáng) of Qí (Qí), recruited him to be Acting Aide (Xíng Cānjūn) to the General Who Controls the Army (Fǔ Jūn).
Later, he became Prefect (Lìng) of Guǎngyáng (Guǎngyáng).
After a short while, he left the office.
When the righteous army arrived,
Gāozǔ (Gāozǔ) recruited him to be Aide (Cānjūn) in the Land Affairs Bureau (Tián Cáo) of the Chancellor’s establishment.
When the Liáng (Liáng) state was established,
he became Director (Láng) of the Bureau of Carriages and Horses (Jiàbù) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū).
He was transferred to Archivist Censor (Zhìshū Shì Yùshǐ),
and Aide (Cānjūn) and Secretary (Jìshì) to the General of the Right (Yòujūn),
tasked with managing the auspicious rites.
At that time, the Erudites of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng Bóshì) were first established,
and Shānbīn (Shānbīn) was the first to be selected for this position.
He was transferred to Consultant Aide (Zīyì Cānjūn) to the Central Leader of the North (Běi Zhōng Láng),
and attended the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) in reading.
He was successively transferred to Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng),
Erudite (Bóshì) of the Imperial University (Guózǐ),
Prefect (Lìng) of the Crown Prince’s Palace (Tàizǐ Shuàigēng),
Central Principal Secretary (Zhōng Shùzǐ),
while his post as Erudite (Bóshì) remained unchanged.
In the fifteenth year of Tiānjiān (Tiānjiān),

he was sent out as Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié), Supervisor of Military Affairs Along the Huái River (Dū Yuán Huái Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Subdues the Distant (Zhēng Yuǎn Jiāngjūn), and Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Běi Yǎnzhōu (Běi Yǎnzhōu).
In the second year of Pǔtōng (Pǔtōng),
he was recalled to serve as Commander of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Shuài) to the Crown Prince,
was granted Attendant-in-Ordinary (Gěishìzhōng),
and was transferred to Palace Assistant Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
Due to a public matter, he was demoted to Cavalier Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng) and Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng).
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to Palace Attendant (Sǎnqí Chángshì),
concurrently commanding Grand Impartial Judge (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Qīngzhōu (Qīngzhōu) and Jìzhōu (Jìzhōu).
The Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) newly established the post of Academician (Xuèshì),
and Shānbīn (Shānbīn) was again appointed to it.
Soon after, he concurrently held the post of Libationer (Jìjiǔ) of the Imperial University (Guózǐ) using his existing official capacity.
Previously,
when Shānbīn (Shānbīn) was in the province,
Pínglù County (Pínglù Xiàn), which was under his jurisdiction, suffered a poor harvest.
He petitioned to release grain from the stores to relieve the people.
Later, a Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ) inspected the provincial administration,
and finding the records missing,
he held Shānbīn (Shānbīn) responsible for the loss and deficiency.
The responsible authorities sought repayment,
and confiscated his residence for the government.
Shānbīn (Shānbīn) remained silent and did not defend himself,
but instead bought land and built a new residence.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng (Zhāomíng Tàizǐ), hearing that the construction of the house had not been completed,
issued an order saying:
“Although Libationer Míng (Míng Jìjiǔ) went out to govern a great dependency,
carrying banners and riding in chariots,
wearing gold and trailing purple,
his affairs frequently come to nothing.
Hearing that the construction has not been finished,
I now send a small contribution.”
He also gifted a poem, which said:
“Píng Zhòng (Píng Zhòng) was renowned as exceptional in antiquity,
Yí Wú (Yí Wú) was praised for his virtuous actions.
The law highlights those who are truly worthy;
Eastern Qín (Dōng Qín) certainly has many scholars.
Build your house not by the roadside,
but locate your dwelling in the Hamlet of Benevolence (Rén Lǐ).
Gēng Sāng (Gēng Sāng) had his lineage to follow,
Yuán Shēng (Yuán Shēng) is easily paralleled today.
The men of the Three Paths (Sān Jìng) will surely arrive,
and the scholars of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng) will be summoned.”
Shān Bīn 山賓 was of a sincere and honest nature.
His family often lacked resources,
so he sold the ox he rode.
After selling it and receiving the money,
he then said to the buyer:
"This ox once suffered from hoof-rot,
and although it has been cured for a long time,
I fear it might relapse later.
I cannot but tell you this."
The buyer immediately pursued him to reclaim the money.
Ruǎn Xiàoxù 阮孝緒, a recluse, heard of this
and sighed, saying:
"These words are enough to make people return to simplicity and sincerity,
and to stir up the generous and stop the vulgar!"
Five years later,
he was again appointed Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士,
while Chángshì 常侍 and Zhōngzhèng 中正 remained as before.
That year, he was granted the Jiǎjié 假節 with his original official post,
and provisionally oversaw the affairs of Běiyǎnzhōu 北兗州.
In Dàtōng 元年 (527 CE),
he died,
at the age of eighty-five.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Shìzhōng 侍中 and Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn 信威將軍.
His posthumous title was Zhìzǐ 質子.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ 昭明太子 held a mourning ceremony for him,
bestowing a funeral gift of one hundred thousand coins,
and one hundred bolts of cloth,
and also sent his Shèrén 舍人, Wáng Yǒng 王顒, to supervise the funeral arrangements.
He also sent a letter to the former Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ 司徒左長史, Yīn Yún 殷芸, which read:
"News from Běiyǎnzhōu indicates that
the esteemed Chángshì 常侍 has finally passed away.
Hearing this, I am deeply saddened.
This worthy scholar's learning was comprehensive and profound,
his aspirations and conduct adhered to ancient principles,
and he was warm, kind, simple, and harmonious,
cultured, elegant, and profoundly steadfast.
Since he began teaching the classics,
two cycles (twenty-four years) have passed.
His refusal to flatter superiors,
and his loyal remonstrances delivered face-to-face,
were not for outward show,
but came from his heart,
and indeed accumulated over time.
He took on the heavy responsibility of a provincial governor,
and was about to return home as expected,
but alas, he departed forever,
becoming a memory of days gone by.
Recalling our conversations,
they all turn into sources of sorrow.
Alas, what can be done now!
Having served together in the past,
it is only natural to feel profound grief."
Shān Bīn 山賓 repeatedly held positions in educational institutions,
and was very beneficial in his teaching and guidance.
However, his nature was rather open and free,
and in his interactions with students,
he was often familiar and close,
so everyone loved him.
His published works included the Jílǐ Yízhù 吉禮儀注 in two hundred twenty-four volumes,
Lǐyí 禮儀 in twenty volumes,
and Xiàojīng Sānglǐ Fúyì 孝經喪禮服義 in fifteen volumes.
His son, Zhèn 震,
whose courtesy name was Xīngdào 興道,
also carried on his father's profession.
He successively held posts as Tàixué Bóshì 太學博士,
Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人,
Shàngshū Cíbù Láng 尚書祠部郎,
and Yúyáo Lìng 餘姚令.
Yīn Jūn 殷鈞, whose courtesy name was Jìhé 季和,
was from Chénjùn Chángpíng 陳郡長平.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Jìn Tàicháng Róng 晉太常融.
His father, Ruì 叡,
was talented and eloquent,
well-known during the Qí 齊 dynasty,
and successively held the post of Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng 司徒從事中郎.
Ruì's 叡 wife was the daughter of Wáng Huàn 王奐.
Wáng Huàn 王奐, serving as Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ 雍州刺史 and Zhèn běi Jiāngjūn 鎮北將軍,
then petitioned the court
to appoint Ruì 叡 as Zhèn běi Zhǎngshǐ 鎮北長史 and Hénán Tàishǒu 河南太守.
When Wáng Huàn 王奐 was executed,
Ruì 叡 was also killed.
Jūn 鈞 was nine years old at the time
and was known for his filial piety.
As he grew up,
he was calm and quiet, with few companions,
and loved learning and reflective thinking.
He excelled at Lìshū 隸書 (clerical script),
serving as a model for the time.
Fàn Yún 范雲 from Nánxiāng 南鄉
and Rèn Fǎng 任昉 from Yuè'ān 樂安 both praised him.
Gāozǔ 高祖 and Ruì 叡 had been old acquaintances since youth,
and Gāozǔ 高祖 gave his daughter in marriage to Jūn 鈞,
who was Yǒngxīng Gōngzhǔ 永興公主.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān 天監 (502 CE),
he was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi 駙馬都尉,
starting his career as Mìshū Láng 祕書郎,
then Tàizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人,
Sītú Zhǔbù 司徒主簿,
and Mìshū Chéng 祕書丞.
While in office, Jūn 鈞
requested to revise and collate the four divisions of books in the Mìgé 祕閣,
and create a new catalogue.
He also received an imperial edict to inspect the calligraphic works and ancient artifacts in the Xīshěng 西省,
and classify them into different categories.
He was promoted to Piàojì Cóngshì Zhōngláng 驃騎從事中郎,
Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎,
Tàizǐ Jiālìng 太子家令,
managing the records of the Eastern Palace.
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng 給事黃門侍郎,
Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
Shàngshū Lìbù Láng 尚書吏部郎,
Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ 司徒左長史,
and Shìzhōng 侍中.
When scholars were established in the Eastern Palace,
Jūn 鈞 was again appointed to that position.
He was dismissed due to official business.
He was again made Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
concurrently holding the posts of Guózǐ Bóshì 國子博士 and Zuǒxiāoqí Jiāngjūn 左驍騎將軍,
with his role as Bóshì 博士 remaining unchanged.
He was sent out as Míngwēi Jiāngjūn 明威將軍 and Línchuān Nèishǐ 臨川內史.
Jūn's body was frail and frequently ill.
He stayed behind closed doors to govern,
yet the common people were transformed by his virtue,
and all bandits fled beyond the borders.
Once, he captured a bandit leader,
but did not subject him to torture or interrogation,
only gently rebuking him.
The bandit leader knocked his head to the ground, begging to reform,
and Jūn immediately ordered him released.
Afterward, he became a good person.
The commandery previously suffered much from mountain malaria,
which would invariably recur with the summer heat.
But ever since Jūn took office,
there was no more malaria in the commandery.
When his mother died, he left his post,
mourning beyond the rites.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ worried about him,
and personally wrote a letter of admonition and instruction, saying:
"I know that among your many virtues,
your excessive grief is a fault.
Moreover, what you consume is barely more than a single grain,
which greatly distresses me.
You are a solitary person,
and the continuity of your family rests upon you.
To destroy oneself and extinguish one's nature
is not permitted by the sagely teachings.
You should slightly moderate your self-denial,
and humbly adhere to the established rites.
For gruel, porridge, fruits, and vegetables,
make a little more effort.
Since your worries are profound,
I will instruct Míu Dàozhēn to fully explain the specifics in person."
Jūn replied:
"I have received your imperial handwritten decree,
and Míu Dàozhēn has conveyed your instructions.
As I prostrate myself and read, I am choked with emotion;
my heart and liver are as if spilled on the ground.
I am a humble person without much emotion,
and my actions often fall short of the rites.
However, I was born with a weak constitution,
and as the years passed,
sins and transgressions accumulated,
further compounded by chronic illness.
Recently, I have been frail,
keeping vigil day and night,
my eyes blurring with confusion,
my heart lost in sorrow and joy.
I only seek to relieve this dangerous suffering,
unable to restrain myself with distant principles.
The nourishment of ginger and cinnamon
is indeed mentioned in ancient texts.
Not avoiding meat and fine grains,
I am also blessed by your present kindness.
Who am I,
to receive such concern and pity?
I will respectfully follow the sagely words,
and contemplate how to recover.
If I should fail to extend my life,
it will truly be due to fate."
After the mourning period concluded,
he was promoted to Wǔbīng Shàngshū.
Still suffering from chronic illness,
he was unable to accept the appointment,
so he was instead given the title Sànqí Chángshì,
and concurrently served as Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
attending the Eastern Palace.
Soon after, he was reappointed as Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Zhāomíng Tàizǐ passed away,
his officials were dismissed.
He was then appointed Yòuyóujī,
and made Guózǐ Jìjiǔ,
with his Chángshì title remaining.
In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (532 CE),
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
His posthumous title was Zhēnzǐ.
He had two sons: Gòu
and Wò.
Lù Xiāng, courtesy name Shīqīng,
was a native of Wú Commandery.
His father, Xián,
served as Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng for Qí Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
Yáoguāng rebelled, occupying the Eastern Palace.
Someone advised Xián to leave him.
Xián said:
"I am his official;
how can I escape death?"
When the imperial army attacked and captured the city,
Xián was seized.
As he was about to be executed,
his second son, Jiàng, asked to die in his place,
but was not permitted.
He then shielded his father with his body,
and both were killed by the executioner.
Xiāng was deeply pained by the tragic deaths of his father and brother,
and his mourning exceeded the rites.
Even after the mourning period ended, he still seemed to be grieving.
In the third year of Tiānjiān (504 CE),
Dūguān Shàngshū Fàn Xiù submitted a memorial recommending Xiāng.
He was appointed Xuèzuò Zuǒláng,
and then appointed Yǒngníng Lìng.
After his term of office,
he was successively promoted to Sīkōng Línchuān Wáng Fǎcáo,
Wàibīng,
and Qīngchē Lúlín Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ heard of Xiāng's conduct and studies,
and memorialized Gāozǔ to invite him for companionship.
He was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and then promoted to Zhōngshèrén,
concurrently overseeing the records.
He was sent out to serve as Yángzhōu Zhìzhōng.
As Xiāng's father had died in this office,
he firmly declined the post.
Gāozǔ did not permit it,
but allowed him to exchange residences with the Fǔsīmǎ.
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ respected elders,
and Xiāng's mother was nearly eighty.
Along with Xiāo Chēn, Fù Zhāo, and Lù Gǎo, he would regularly send greetings and inquiries each month,
additionally bestowing rare delicacies and clothing.
Xiāng's mother once suddenly suffered heart pain.
The medical prescription required three sheng of millet gruel.
It was winter at the time,
and evening was approaching.
They searched everywhere but found none.
Suddenly, an old man came to the gate selling gruel,
the quantity exactly matching the prescription.
Just as they were about to pay,
he vanished without a trace. People at the time believed this was due to Xiāng's filial piety.
He was successively promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì,
Tàizǐ Jiālìng,
and again oversaw the records.
When his mother died, he left his post.
Xiāng was already fifty years old,
and his grief and debilitation exceeded the rites.
The Prince worried about him,
sending envoys daily to admonish and instruct him.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
and again oversaw the records.
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng (531 CE),
Zhāomíng Tàizǐ passed away,
and his officials were dismissed.
His consort, Cài Shì, moved to reside in Jīnhuá Gōng,
and Xiāng was made Zhōngsàn Dàfū, concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi, Jīnhuá Gōng Jiālìng, and was put in charge of Jīnhuá Gōng affairs.
In the seventh year,
he was sent out to be the Interior Historian of Póyáng.
Prior to this,
a local man named Xiānyú Chēn practiced Dàofǎ by consuming substances,
and once entered the mountains to gather herbs.
He picked up a five-colored banner and a ceremonial staff,
and also found a stone seal in the ground,
which secretly puzzled him.
Chēn had previously separated his living quarters from his wife.
Looking towards where Chēn resided,
there was often an unusual aura,
which made her increasingly believe he was divine.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he then gathered his followers,
killed Wáng Jūn, the Magistrate of Guǎngjìn,
proclaimed the first year of Shàngyuàn,
and appointed officials.
His partisans continued to delude each other,
accumulating a crowd of over ten thousand people.
When they were about to attack the commandery,
Xiāng had already led the local people and officials to repair the city walls and moats,
preparing defenses.
When the bandits arrived,
he repeatedly fought and defeated them,
capturing Chēn alive.
The remaining crowd fled and dispersed.
At that time, the governors and magistrates of neighboring commanderies like Yùzhāng and Ānchéng
investigated the partisans,
and took the opportunity to demand bribes.
None of them found the truth,
and some good people suffered misfortune and their whole families were separated.
Only in Xiāng's commandery were the innocent and guilty distinguished without excess.
The people composed a song saying:
"After Xiānyú was pacified, good and evil were divided,
the people did not die unjustly,
thanks to Lord Lù."
There were also two families, Péng and Lǐ,
who had previously had a quarrel,
and then falsely accused each other.
Xiāng brought them into his inner chamber,
and did not reprimand them,
but only used gentle words to explain and mediate.
The two men were grateful,
and deeply blamed and regretted themselves.
He then prepared wine and food for them,
allowing them to enjoy themselves to the fullest.
After the wine,
they rode home together in the same carriage,
and became close friends.
The people again sang:
"Lord Lù's administration,
no one bears resentment,
when the fight is over,
enemies share a carriage."
He governed for six years,
and the commandery was greatly pacified.
Four hundred and twenty people, including the commoner Lǐ Xiàn, went to the palace gate and submitted a memorial,
describing Xiāng's virtuous influence,
and requesting to erect a stele in the commandery.
An imperial edict permitted it.
They also petitioned to keep Xiāng,
but Xiāng steadfastly requested to return.
He was summoned to be the Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
then promoted to Secretarial Court Director,
concurrently serving as the Grand Moderator of Yángzhōu.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Minister of the State Treasury,
retaining his concurrent post as Grand Moderator.
In the second year,
Hóu Jǐng raised troops and besieged the imperial palace.
Xiāng was in charge of the Ministry of the Imperial Attendants.
In the third month of the third year,
the city fell.
Xiāng fled back to Wú.
The bandits soon invaded the eastern border,
overwhelming Wújùn.
Jǐng's general Sòng Zǐxiān advanced to attack Qiántáng.
At that time, Lù Àn of Hǎiyán raised an army of righteousness,
with several thousand followers.
He launched a night attack on the commandery,
killed the false Grand Administrator Sū Dān Yú,
and nominated Xiāng to act as the commandery administrator.
At that time, Xiāo Níng, Marquis of Wénchéng and Grand Administrator of Huáinán, fled from the bandits into Wú.
Xiāng sent for Níng to be the leader of the alliance,
and dispatched Àn and his elder brother's son Yìnggōng to lead the troops to resist Zǐxiān.
Zǐxiān, hearing that an army had risen,
then retreated.
He fought with Àn and others at Sōngjiāng.
Àn was defeated and fled.
The Wúxià army, hearing of this,
also dispersed.
Xiāng hid in a tomb,
and died of grief and indignation overnight,
at the age of seventy.
Xiāng suffered a family misfortune in his youth,
and for the rest of his life ate vegetables and wore coarse cloth,
did not listen to music,
and did not speak of killing for about fifty years.
When Hóu Jǐng was pacified,
Emperor Shìzǔ posthumously appointed him Grand Attendant and General of Yúnhuī.
For his meritorious service in raising the righteous army,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as Marquis of Yúgān County,
with five hundred households.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel for Chén, said: Lù Chuí was extensively learned in literature and principles,
Dào Qià was steadfast and vigorous, dedicating himself to public service,
Míng Shānbīn was refined, sincere, and pragmatic,
Yīn Jūn was quiet, simple, peaceful, and harmonious,
Lù Xiāng was pure, profound, and filial.
Although their appointments and treatment differed,
they were all ranked among the famous ministers.
Collated Notes
Biographies Twenty-two: Péi Suì (his elder brother's sons Zhīgāo, Zhīpíng, Zhīhéng), Xiàhóu Dǎn (his younger brother Kuí, Yú Hóng appended), Wéi Fàng.
Péi Suì, courtesy name Yuānmíng,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
