He was a descendant of Chuò, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu in the Wèi dynasty.
His grandfather, Shòusūn, lived temporarily in Shòuyáng and served as the Army Commander for Emperor Wǔ of Sòng.
His father, Zhòngmù, was a Galloping Cavalry General.
Suì could compose essays at the age of ten
and was skilled in the Zuǒ Shì Chūnqiū.
In the early Jiànwǔ era of Qí,
Inspector Xiāo Yáochāng appointed him as his Household Registrar.
There was an Eight Dukes Mountain Temple in Shòuyáng;
Yáochāng had a stele erected for it
and commissioned Suì to write the inscription,
which was highly praised.
He was recommended as an outstanding talent,
achieved a high rank in the policy examination,
and served as an Imperial Attendant.
When Emperor Dōnghūn ascended the throne,
Xiāo Yáoguāng, Prince of Shǐ'ān, was appointed General of the Pacified Army and Inspector of Yángzhōu.
He appointed Suì as a Staff Officer.
Later, when Yáoguāng was defeated,
Suì returned to Shòuyáng.
At that time, Inspector Péi Shúyè surrendered Shòuyáng to Wèi,
and the powerful families of Yùzhōu were all driven out and plundered.
Suì then followed the crowd north.
The Wèi sovereign, Emperor Xuānwǔ, highly esteemed him,
and appointed him as a Subordinate of the Minister of Works,
Director of the Central Secretariat,
and Grand Administrator of Wèijùn.
Wèi dispatched Wáng Sù to govern Shòuyáng.
Suì firmly requested to accompany Sù,
secretly planning to return south.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he escaped and returned to court,
and was appointed Military Advisor to the Rear Army.
Suì requested to prove himself on the border,
and was appointed General of the Stabilizing State and Grand Administrator of Lújiāng.
At that time, Wèi general Lǚ Pó led five thousand troops to suddenly attack the commandery.
Suì led his subordinates to resist and defeat them,
and was promoted to General of the Right Army.
In the fifth year,
he campaigned in Shàoyángzhōu.
The Wèi people built a long bridge to cross the Huái River.
Suì built fortifications to press against the bridge,
winning every battle.
Thereupon, he secretly built submerged assault ships.
Just then, there was heavy rain,
and the Huái River suddenly overflowed.
Suì rode the ships directly to the side of the bridge.
The Wèi troops were shocked and dispersed.
Suì took advantage of the victory to pursue,
and greatly defeated them.
He then captured Yángshí City,
beheading its lord Yuán Kāng.
He also captured Huòqiū City,
beheading its lord Níng Yǒngrén.
He pacified Xiǎoxiàn
and attacked Héféi.
For his achievements, he was enfeoffed as Viscount of Yílíng County,
with three hundred households.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Champion General and Grand Administrator of Guǎnglíng.
Péi Suì, together with his fellow villagers, entered the Temple of Wèiwǔ (Cáo Cāo).
Consequently, they discussed the achievements of emperors and kings.
His wife’s nephew, Wáng Zhuǎnzhī, secretly reported to Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng),
saying,
"Péi Suì speaks excessively boastful words,
and shows signs of disloyalty."
Because of this, he was demoted and made Administrator of Shǐ'ān (Shǐ'ān Tàishǒu).
Suì aspired to achieve merit on the frontiers,
and did not wish for a leisurely, distant post.
He therefore sent a letter to Lǚ Sēngzhēn, saying:
"In the past, Ruǎn Xián and Yán Yán lamented the 'Two Shǐs' (Èr Shǐ)
(posts starting with the character Shǐ).
My talent does not reach that of the ancients,
yet now I hold the 'Three Shǐs' (Sān Shǐ).
This is not my desire.
What am I to do about it?"
Before he could reach the commandery,
it happened that Wèi (Northern Wèi) attacked Sùyù.
An imperial edict ordered Suì to repel them.
When he marched to Zhídú,
the Wèi forces retreated.
He was promoted to Consultant and Adjutant to the Right Army (Yòujūn Zīyì Cānjūn) and Commandant (Sīmǎ) in the Yùzhāng Wáng Cloud-Maneuvering Headquarters (Yùzhāng Wáng Yúnhuī Fǔ Sīmǎ).
Leading his subordinates, he helped guard Shítóu.
He was then sent out to be Administrator of Jìnglíng (Jìnglíng Tàishǒu).
He opened up and established military agricultural colonies (túntián);
both the government and private citizens benefited.
He was promoted to General of Mobile Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn), Zhūyī Zhíhé (an official attending the emperor, wearing red robes),
serving duty in the palace hall.

Soon thereafter, he was promoted to receive temporary authority (Jiǎjié), General Who Manifests Awe (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn), Colonel of the Western Barbarians (Xīróng Xiàowèi), and Inspector of the two provinces of Běiliáng and Qín (Běiliáng Qín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ).
He again initiated the creation of several thousand qǐng of military agricultural colonies.
The granaries were full,
reducing and relaxing frontier transportation burdens,
and the people and officials enjoyed peace.
They subsequently came together and offered him more than a thousand bolts of silk.
Suì calmly said:
"You should not do this;
yet, I cannot refuse you."
He accepted only two bolts of silk.
Returning to the capital, he became Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Zhōng), General of Cloud Cavalry (Yúnqí Jiāngjūn), and Zhūyī Zhíhé General (Zhūyī Zhíhé Jiāngjūn).
He was promoted to Minister of Works (Dàjiàng Qīng).
In the second year of Pǔtōng (521 CE),
Wén Sēngmíng, the Inspector of Yìzhōu, rebelled with his province and defected to Wèi (Northern Wèi).
The Wèi army came to support him.
Suì was appointed Jiǎjié, General Who Is Trustworthy and Martial (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn),
and placed in command of the various armies to suppress the rebellion.
Suì penetrated deep into Wèi territory,
taking the route past the border cities,
catching them by surprise.
Fēng Shòu, the Wèi-appointed Inspector of Yìzhōu, occupied Tángōng Xiàn.
Suì attacked and defeated him,
and then surrounded his city.
Shòu bound himself and asked to surrender.
Yìzhōu was pacified.
He was appointed Bearer of Credential (Chíjié), Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in Běixúzhōu (Dū Běixúzhōu Zhūjūn Shì), Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Běixúzhōu (Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ).
Before he took office,
he was again promoted to Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in the three provinces of Yùzhōu, Běiyù, and Huò (Dū Yùzhōu Běiyù Huò Sānzhōu Zhūjūn Shì), and Inspector of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ),
garrisoned at Héféi.
In the fourth year (Pǔtōng 4, 523 CE),
he was advanced to the title General Who Proclaims Valor (Xuānyì Jiāngjūn).
That same year,
when the Grand Army was about to campaign north,
Suì was appointed Commander-in-Chief of the Campaigning and Punitive Armies (Dū Zhēngtǎo Zhūjūn Shì).
He led three thousand cavalry
to launch a preliminary attack on Shòuyáng.
In the ninth month, on the Rénxū day,
he arrived at Shòuyáng at night.
He attacked its outer wall (fú),
broke through the gate, and entered.
In one day, they fought nine engagements.
Because the rear army, led by Cài Xiùchéng, lost its way and failed to arrive,
Suì withdrew due to lack of reinforcement.
Thereupon, Suì reorganized his forces again
and gathered his soldiers.
He ordered his generals to distinguish themselves by the color of their clothing.
Suì himself led the Yellow Robe Cavalry (Huángpáo Qí).
He first attacked Díqiū, Pìchéng, Líjiāng, and other cities,
capturing them all.
He slaughtered the garrisons (shù) at Ānchéng, Mǎtóu, Shālíng, and others.
That winter,
he began repairing the Quèpí (irrigation works).
The following year,
he again defeated the Wèi forces in Xīncài Commandery,
seizing territory as far as Zhèngchéng.
People throughout the Rǔ and Yǐng regions responded to him.
The Wèi generals defending Shòuyáng, Zhǎngsūn Zhì and Yuán Chēn, Prince of Héjiān, led fifty thousand troops.
They emerged from the city to challenge him.
Suì ordered his generals to form four battle arrays (zhēn) to await them.
He commanded Zhíhé General Lǐ Zǔlián to feign retreat to lure Zhì,
and Zhì and the others pursued him with their entire force.
The four arrays charged simultaneously,
and the Wèi forces were greatly defeated.
More than ten thousand heads were taken.
Zhì and the others fled,
closed their gates to secure themselves,
and dared not venture out again.
In the fifth month of that year,
he died in the camp.
He was posthumously granted the titles Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn).
He was provided with a set of court music instruments (gǔchuī).
His noble rank was advanced to Marquis (Hóu),
and his stipend increased by seven hundred households.
His posthumous name was Liè.
Suì seldom spoke or smiled;
he was deep-thinking and strategic.
His governance was lenient and enlightened,
and he was able to win the hearts of the educated class.
His personal conduct was upright and he possessed dignity and weight,
causing generals and officials to fear him;
few dared to violate the law.
When he died,
everyone between the Huái River and Féi River shed tears,
believing that if Suì had not died,
Luòyáng would not have been difficult to capture.
His son, Zhīlǐ,
courtesy name Zǐyì,
passed the examination as a National University Student (Guózǐ Shēng),
and was appointed Left Regular Attendant of the Shàolíng Royal State (Shàolíng Wángguó Zuǒchángshì) and Acting Adjutant of Trustworthy Might (Xìnwēi Xíng Cānjūn).
When the Prince (Shàolíng Wáng) served in Nányǎn,
Zhīlǐ was appointed Adjutant of the Commander's Staff (Chángliú Cānjūn).
Before he departed for the post,
he remained stationed in the imperial guard
and was appointed Zhíhé General (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn).
He observed mourning for his father.
After the mourning period concluded, he inherited the enfeoffment.
He then requested to follow the army to campaign against Shòuyáng.
He was appointed General of Cloud Maneuvers (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn).
He was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
He also separately attacked the Wèi city of Guǎnglíng.
Having pacified it,
he was appointed Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn and Inspector of Xīyùzhōu (Xīyùzhōu Cìshǐ).
He was granted the title General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn).
He was appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Huángmén Shìláng).
He was promoted to Commandant (Sīmǎ) under the Prince of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Wáng) in the Central Army (Zhōngjūn).

Soon after, he became Commander-in-Chief of Military Affairs in the three provinces of Běixú, Rén, and Suī (Dū Běixú Rén Suī Sānzhōu Zhūjūn Shì), Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Inspector of Běixúzhōu (Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ).
He was recalled to serve as Commander of the Crown Prince's Left Guard (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài),
concurrently holding the position of Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi Qīng).
He was transferred to Minister of the Lesser Treasury (Shǎofǔ Qīng).
He died.
His posthumous name was Zhuàng.
His son, Zhèng,
during the Chéngshèng era,
held office up to Palace Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
When Jiānglíng fell,
he followed the standard procedure and entered Western Wèi (Xī Wèi).
Zhīgāo, courtesy name Rúshān,
was the son of Suì’s elder brother, Máo, who was a Grand Master of the Central Household (Zhōngsǎn Dàfū).
He started his career as a Provincial Subordinate (Zhōu Cóngshì), Magistrate of Xīndū (Xīndū Lìng), and received the Imperial Summons (Fèngcháoqǐng).
He was promoted to Adjutant (Cānjūn).
He read extensively,
and possessed spirited courage from a young age.
He constantly followed his uncle Suì on campaigns,
achieving merit wherever he went.
He was greatly valued and respected by Suì,
and all military affairs were entrusted to him.
During the campaign at Shòuyáng,
Suì died in the military camp.
Zhīgāo assisted Xiàhóu Kuí,
pacified Shòuyáng,
and was consequently appointed Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Yùzhāng Zhǎngshǐ) and Administrator of Liáng Commandery (Liángjùn Tàishǒu).
He was enfeoffed as Baron of Dūchéng County (Dūchéng Xiàn Nán),
with a stipend of two hundred and fifty households.
At that time, Rǔyīn of Wèi defected and joined (Liáng).
Zhīgāo was ordered to receive and handle the situation.
He was then appointed Jiǎjié, General of Rushing Valor (Biāoyǒng Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Yǐngzhōu (Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ).
The soldiers and people rebelled at night,
climbing over the wall to enter.
Zhīgāo led his household servants and subordinates in a vigorous counterattack,
and the bandits scattered and fled.
He returned to the capital to mourn his father.
Rising from mourning, he was appointed General Who Shines Afar (Guāngyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
He joined the campaign to suppress the bandits in Yīnlíng,
and pacified them.
He was appointed Inspector of Qiáozhōu (Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ).
He later returned to become General of the Left Army (Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn).
He was sent out to be Administrator of Nánqiáo (Nánqiáo Tàishǒu) and Overseer of Běixúzhōu (Jiān Běixúzhōu).
He was promoted to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì).
Soon after, he was appointed General of Heroic Trust (Xióngxìn Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Xīyùzhōu (Xīyùzhōu Cìshǐ).
All other positions remained as before.
Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
Zhī Gāo led his troops to reinforce the defense.

The Governor (Cìshǐ) of Nányùzhōu, Fàn, the Heir Prince of Póyáng, commanded Zhī Gāo to serve as the General Supervisor of All Military Affairs of the Reinforcing Armies East of the Yangzi River (Jiāng Yòu).
He set up camp at Zhānggōngzhōu.
When Liǔ Zhònglǐ arrived at Héngjiāng,
Zhī Gāo dispatched more than two hundred ships and boats to escort Zhònglǐ.
He and Wéi Càn and others gathered at Qīngtáng and established a camp,
occupying Jiànxīng Yuàn.
When the city fell,
Zhī Gāo returned to Héféi.
He traveled west with Prince Fàn of Póyáng.
Gradually, they reached Xīncài.
Their troops numbered ten thousand,
but they had not yet submitted to any authority.
Emperor Yuán sent Xiāo Huìzhèng to summon him,
appointing him as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
Upon arriving at Jiānglíng,
he was provisionally appointed as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Tèjìn) and Grand Master of Glorious Happiness with Gold and Purple Seal (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
He died
at the age of seventy-three.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Paramount Chief (Yítóng Sānsī),
along with a set of drums and horns (gǔchuī).
His posthumous name was Gōng.
His son, Jī,
rose through the ranks to be Right Commander of the Crown Prince’s Guards (Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jùnzhōu.
When the Western Wèi attacked and captured Jiānglíng,
Jī fought bravely and died there.
Zhī Píng, courtesy name Rúyuán,
was the fifth younger brother of Zhī Gāo.
While young, he also followed Suì in campaigns,
and for his military achievements, he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Dūtíng.
He successively held the positions of Palace Attendant to the Prince of Wǔlíng, and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies of Fúfēng and Hóngnóng.
He did not take up those posts.
He was appointed Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of Qiáozhōu and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yángpíng.
He resisted Hóu Jǐng.
After the city fell,
he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì), General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn), and Supervisor of the Crown Prince’s Household (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
Zhī Héng, courtesy name Rúyuè,
was the thirteenth younger brother of Zhī Gāo.
When young, he enjoyed hosting guests
and travel, valuing spirit and chivalry,
and did not concern himself with property or livelihood.
Zhī Gāo, considering him undisciplined and profligate,
deliberately gave him narrow bedding and meager food to motivate him.
Zhī Héng sighed and said:
"If a great man achieves wealth
and honor, he must make a hundred-sheet quilt."
Consequently, with several hundred servants
and retainers, he extensively developed farms and estates at Sháopí,
thereby becoming rich and prosperous.
When Tàizōng was in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
hearing of this, he sought him out and summoned him,
appointing him Attendant to the Prince of Hédōng and Commander of the Palace Retainers (Zhí Diàn Zhǔshuài).
He was promoted to General of the Inner Guard (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn).
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
he was sent out as General of Rectified Awe (Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn),
following Prince Fàn of Póyáng to attack Jǐng.
When Jǐng crossed the Yangzi River (Jiāng),
he then entered the capital for reinforcement with Sī, Fàn’s eldest son.
He linked his camps and crossed the Huái River,
occupying the Eastern City (Dōngchéng).
When the capital fell,
he retreated back to Héféi.
He and Fàn traveled upstream to Pénchéng.
Jǐng sent Rèn Yuē to press north toward Jìnxī.
Fàn ordered Zhī Héng to go down and reinforce them.
Before he could arrive,
Fàn died.
Zhī Héng then returned.
At that time, Dàxīn, Prince of Xúnyáng, was in Jiāngzhōu.
Fàn’s deputy, Méi Sīlì, secretly urged Dàxīn to attack Pénchéng.
Zhī Héng beheaded Sīlì and resisted Dàxīn.
Dàxīn surrendered the province to Jǐng.
Zhī Héng led his troops and, along with his elder brother Zhī Gāo, submitted to Emperor Yuán.
He was provisionally appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and Minister
of Justice (Tíngwèi Qīng). He was sent out to serve as Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Hédōng.
He subsequently followed Wáng Sēngbiàn to resist Hóu Jǐng at Bālíng.
When Jǐng retreated,
he was promoted to Bearer of Credential (Chíjié), General Pacifying the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dōngxúzhōu,
(and) Central Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn),
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yùníng,
with a stipend of three thousand households.
He again followed Sēngbiàn to pursue Jǐng,
pacifying Yǐngzhōu, Lǔzhōu, Jiāngzhōu, Jìnzhōu, and other provinces,
serving as the vanguard and breaking the enemy lines.
He then reached Shítóu,
defeated Jǐng.
Jǐng fled eastward.
Sēngbiàn ordered Zhī Héng and Dù Zè to enter and guard Táichéng.
When Lù Nà occupied Xiāngzhōu and rebelled,
he again followed Wáng Sēngbiàn to campaign in the south.
He killed Nà’s general Lǐ Xiánmíng in battle,
and subsequently suppressed the rebellion.
He also defeated the Prince of Wǔlíng at Xiákǒu.
Upon returning, he was appointed Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wúxīng.
He then made a hundred-sheet quilt,
thus fulfilling his initial aspiration.
Later, when Jiānglíng fell,
Qí sent Gāo Huàn, Prince of Shàngdǎng, assisting the Marquis of Zhēnyáng, to attack Dōngguān.
Fāngzhì, Prince of Jìn'ān, provisionally issued a decree,
appointing Zhī Héng as Bearer of Credential (Shǐ Chíjié), General Guarding the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu,
commanding all the armed forces,
and granting him a set of drums and horns (gǔchuī).
He was sent out to defend Qíchéng.
Zhī Héng’s camps and ramparts were not yet complete,
when the Qí army arrived in massive force.
His soldiers were depleted and his arrows exhausted,
and he consequently died in battle,
at the age of forty-one.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and Minister of Works (Sīkōng Gōng).
His posthumous name was Zhōngzhuàng.
His son, Fèngbǎo, inherited the title.
Xiàhóu Dǎn, courtesy name Shìlóng,
was the eldest son of Xiáng, the General of Cavalry and Chariots (Jūqí Jiāngjūn).
In the early period of Qí,
he entered official service as Suppliant (Fèng Cháoqǐng).
At the end of the Yǒngyuán era,
Xiáng served as Military Advisor (Sīmǎ) to the Prince of Nánkāng under the General of the Western Barbarians (Xī Zhōngláng).
He followed the administration and was stationed in Jīngzhōu.
Dǎn remained in the capital (Jīngshī),
serving as the Chief Commander (Zhǔshuài) overseeing political affairs for Dōnghūn.
When Cuī Huìjǐng raised a rebellion,
Dǎn, due to his achievements in defense and resistance,
was appointed General of the Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
When Gāozǔ raised an army,
Xiáng and his Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) Xiāo Yǐngzhòu cooperated in the righteous uprising.
They secretly sent a messenger to the capital to welcome Dǎn.
Dǎn thus carried the command of Empress Xuāndé,
instructing Zuǎn, Prince of Nánkāng, to assume the great succession,
granting him ten commanderies and enfeoffing him as Prince of Xuānchéng,
promoting his rank to Chancellor (Xiàngguó),
establishing official staff,
and selecting all civil and military officials.
When Jiànkāng city was pacified,
Dǎn was appointed Director (Láng) of the Personnel Bureau of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìbù).
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and presented the Imperial Seal to Gāozǔ.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
he was sent out to serve as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xuānchéng.
Soon after, he was recalled to serve as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
concurrently holding the post of General of the Right Valiant Cavalry (Yòu Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
In the sixth year (507 CE),
he was sent out as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Shǐxīng, General Pacifying the West (Píngxī), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nánjùn.
He resigned due to mourning for his father.
He observed the mourning rites completely,
building a hut beside the grave.
He ceded all inherited property to his younger brothers.
In the eighth year (509 CE),
he was reactivated as Bearer of Credential (Chíjié), Supervisor of All Military Affairs of Sīzhōu, General of Trustworthy Valor (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sīzhōu,
concurrently holding the post of Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Ānlù.
When the mourning period was complete,
he inherited the title of Duke of Fēngchéng County.
While in the province, he administered with great authority and benevolence,
and was respected and obeyed by the border populace.
In the twelfth year (513 CE),
he returned to court with his original rank,
and was appointed Minister of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū).
He was promoted to Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretary (Jǐshì Zhōng), General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn), concurrently holding the position of Grand Moderator
of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng). In the fifteenth year (516 CE),
he was sent out as General of Trustworthy Valor (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the General Pacifying the West (Ānxī), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Jiāngxià.
In the seventeenth year (518 CE),
he was recalled to serve as Grand Master of Remonstrance (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì) and Right Commander
of the Crown Prince’s Guards (Tàizǐ Yòuwèilǜ). He was promoted to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn),
concurrently holding the position of General of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was sent out as General of Illustrious Awe (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wúxīng.
While in the commandery, he again implemented benevolent policies;
the officials and common people drew his portrait
and erected a stele to praise his merits.
In the third year of Pǔtōng (522 CE),
he was recalled to serve as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
concurrently holding General of the Right Valiant Cavalry (Yòu Xiāoqí Jiāngjūn).
He was transferred to Minister of the Imperial Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng),
his status as Chángshì remaining unchanged.
He was dismissed due to an official matter,
but not long after,
by gracious imperial decree, he was reinstated.
In the fifth year (524 CE),
he was promoted to Central Protector of the Army (Zhōng Hùjūn).
In the sixth year,
a large-scale northern expedition was launched.
First, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu, Péi Suì, was dispatched, leading the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Qiáozhōu, Zhàn Sēngzhì, and the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Lìyáng, Míng Shàoshì,
the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nánqiáo, Yú Hóng, and the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Jìnxī, Zhāng Chéng,
all of whom were fierce generals of the time,
to campaign against Shòuyáng City from the southern route.
They had not yet overcome it when Suì died.
Thereupon, Dǎn was given the title Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié),
and rushed by courier post to replace Suì.
He resisted the Wei generals, Yuán Chēn, the Prince of Héjiān, and Yuán Yù, the Prince of Línhuái, among others,
and repeatedly fought and achieved victory.
Soon after, there was a secret imperial edict
to withdraw the army to Héféi,
to rest the troops and horses,
and to advance again when the embankment was completed.
In the summer of the seventh year,
the Huái River embankment waters rose high,
and Shòuyáng City was about to be submerged.
Gāozǔ again dispatched the Northern Route Army, Yuán Shù, leading Péng Bǎosūn, Chén Qìngzhī, and others, to advance slowly.
Dǎn led Zhàn Sēngzhì, Yú Hóng, Zhāng Chéng, and others to clear the Qīngliú Stream
in preparation for entering the Huái and Féi Rivers.
The Wei army built a fort alongside the Féi River
and came out behind Dǎn's army.
Dǎn and Sēngzhì returned and attacked them,
defeating them.
They advanced to attack Líjiāng,
where General Zhēnwēi, Wéi Fàng, met them from the northern route.
Once the two armies merged,
every place they went surrendered.
In total, fifty-two cities surrendered,
capturing seventy-five thousand men and women,
and two hundred thousand *shí* of rice.
An imperial edict reinstated Yùzhōu at Shòuyáng, following the previous dynasty's precedent,
and the Héféi Garrison was changed to Nányùzhōu.

Dǎn was made Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the military affairs of Yùzhōu, the Huái River border regions, Nányùzhōu, Huòzhōu, Yìzhōu, and Dìngzhōu, General of Cloud Cavalry (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn), and Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu and Nányùzhōu.
Shòuchūn had long suffered from warfare and famine,
and many of the common people had fled and dispersed.
Dǎn lightened punishments and reduced taxes,
focused on farming, and curtailed forced labor.
After a short while, the households were replenished.
In Dàtōng second year (528),
he was promoted to the title General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn).
In the third year,
he died at his provincial garrison.
When Gāozǔ heard this,
he wore plain clothes and mourned on that very day,
and posthumously granted him the title General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn).
His posthumous name was Xiāng.
Five hundred people from the province, including Xiàhóu Jiǎn, petitioned requesting to erect a stele and establish a shrine for Dǎn.
An imperial edict permitted it.
Dǎn was a man of fine appearance and bearing,
generous and possessing great capacity,
well-read in literature and history,
eloquent and capable of handling diplomatic missions alone.
When his kinsman, Xiàhóu Yì, was appointed Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Héngyáng,
and came to take his leave,
Dǎn was attending the Emperor's seat.
Gāozǔ said to Dǎn:
“Is Xiàhóu Yì closely related to you or distantly?”
Dǎn replied:
“He is my cousin (paternal uncle's son).”
Gāozǔ knew that Yì was already distantly related to Dǎn,
and said:
“You rustic man,
you are fond of not distinguishing between clan kin (zú) and cousins (cóng).”
Dǎn replied:
“Your servant has heard that those related by mourning attire become easily distant,
therefore I cannot bear to speak of clan kin (zú).”
At the time, this was considered an able response.
Dǎn served successively in six commanderies and three provinces.
He did not accumulate property;
what he received in stipends and awards
he immediately distributed among relatives and friends.
His nature was frugal and simple;
his housing and clothing
were merely sufficient,
and he did not pursue luxury or extravagance.
In his later years, he became quite fond of music.
He had over ten singing girls (jìqiè),
but none of them wore ornate clothes or possessed great beauty.
Whenever he had guests,
he always had them perform separated by a screen,
thus, the screen was referred to at the time as "Xiàhóu's courtesan clothing."
Dǎn had two sons: Yì
and Sǔn.
Yì inherited the title Duke of Fēngchéng.
He successively held the posts of Palace Attendant (Shèrén) to the Crown Prince
and Groom (Xǐmǎ) to the Crown Prince.
During the Tàiqīng reign,
when Hóu Jǐng launched an invasion,
Yì and his younger brother Sǔn led their own troops into the city,
and both died within the siege.
Kuí, courtesy name Jìlóng,
was Dǎn's younger brother.
He started his career as Acting Military Counselor (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Residence of the Prince of Nánkāng of Qí.
At the beginning of Zhōngxīng,
he was promoted to Aide to the Minister of the Masses (Sītú Shǔ).
In Tiānjiān first year (502),
he became Groom (Xǐmǎ) to the Crown Prince,
Palace Attendant (Zhōngshèrén),
and Secretariat Director (Zhōngshū Láng).
He mourned his father's death.
When the mourning period was over,
he was appointed Minister of Works (Dàjiàng Qīng),
overseeing the construction of the Tàijí Hall.
In Pǔtōng first year (520),
he became Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Shàolíng, assisting in military matters (Xìnwēi),
and managed the affairs of the princely residence and the state.
In that same year,
he was sent out as Provisional Envoy (Jiǎjié) and General Who Attacks from Afar (Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn),
to campaign against the north as opportunities arose.
Upon return, he was appointed Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
In the second year (521),
he served as deputy to Péi Suì in attacking Yìzhōu,
and pacified it.
In the third year (522),
he replaced his elder brother Dǎn as Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wúxīng.
Soon after, he was transferred to Provisional Envoy (Jiǎjié), General Who Attacks from Afar (Zhēngyuǎn Jiāngjūn), and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xīyáng and Wǔchāng Commanderies.
In the seventh year (526),
he was summoned to be Minister of the Guards (Wèiwèi).
Before taking up the post,
he was reassigned as Envoy with Credentials (Chíjié), Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of military affairs of Sīzhōu, General of Martial Trust (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Sīzhōu,
and concurrently Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Ānlù.
In the eighth year (527),
Kuí was ordered to lead General of Mighty Martiality (Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn) Péi Zhīlǐ and General of the Inner Apartments (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn) Rèn Sīzǔ out along the Yìyáng route,
to attack the three passes: Píngjìng, Mùlíng, and Yīnshān.
He conquered them.
At this time, the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Qiáozhōu, Zhàn Sēngzhì, besieged the Wei Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Dōngyùzhōu, Yuán Qìnghé, at Guǎnglíng,
and entered the outer wall of the city.
The Wei general Yuán Xiǎnbó led troops to aid them.
Sēngzhì intercepted and defeated them.
Kuí traveled from Wǔyáng to meet Sēngzhì,
cutting off the retreat route of the Wei army.
Qìnghé built a stockade inside the city to secure himself.
When Kuí arrived,
Qìnghé immediately requested to surrender.
Kuí deferred the surrender to Sēngzhì.
Sēngzhì said:
“Qìnghé intends to surrender to Your Excellency,
and does not wish to surrender to Sēngzhì.
If I go now, I will certainly violate his intention.
Moreover, the troops Sēngzhì commands are a chaotic collection of recruited men,
and cannot be managed strictly by law.
Your Excellency has always maintained strict military discipline,
and there will certainly be no violation of orders.
For receiving the surrender and accepting their allegiance,
it is highly appropriate that you do so.”
Thereupon, Kuí ascended the city walls, tore down the Wei banners,
and established the banners and drums of the government forces.
None of the populace dared to move rashly.
Qìnghé gathered his troops and came out,
and the army committed no private plunder.
In total, they captured over forty thousand men and women,
six hundred thousand *hú* of grain,
and other goods in commensurate measure.
Xiǎnbó heard this and fled by night.
The combined armies pursued him,
capturing alive over twenty thousand people,
while the number killed or captured could not be fully counted.
An imperial edict appointed Sēngzhì to oversee Dōngyùzhōu,
and garrison Guǎnglíng.
Kuí led his army to garrison Ānyáng.
Kuí also dispatched a subsidiary general to massacre Chǔchéng City,
capturing all its inhabitants.
From this point, the northern route of Yìyáng was completely cut off from Wei.
In Dàtōng second year (528),
the Wei Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu, Yuán Yuàndá, requested to surrender.
Gāozǔ ordered the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Yǐngzhōu, Yuán Shù, to go and receive Yuàndá.
Kuí also joined them from Chǔchéng,
and subsequently remained there to garrison the area.
An imperial edict changed the Wei Yǐngzhōu to Běisīzhōu,
and made Kuí its Prefect (Cìshǐ),
concurrently serving as Area Commander (Dūdū) of Sīzhōu.
In the third year (529),
he was promoted to Envoy with Credentials (Shǐchíjié),
received the advanced title General of Benevolent Might (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn),
and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Bǎochéng County (Bǎochéng Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of fifteen hundred households.
In Zhōngdàtōng second year (530),
he was summoned to be General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn).
He resigned his post due to mourning the death of his birth mother.
At that time, Liú Míng, the Inspector of Nányànzhōu of Wèi, defected with Qiáochéng.
An imperial edict was issued, sending the General Who Guards the North, Yuán Shù, to lead troops to meet him.
Hóu Kuí was promoted to General of the Cloud Banners,
and was ordered to march north based on circumstances.
He was soon granted the Staff of Authority, made Supervisor of Military Affairs of Nányùzhōu, and Inspector of Nányùzhōu.
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Staff of Authority, Supervisor of Military Affairs of the Seven Provinces of Yù, Huái, Chén, Yǐng, Jiàn, Huò, and Yì, and Inspector of Yùzhōu.
Yùzhōu had suffered from years of banditry and warfare,
and the people had largely lost their livelihoods.
Kuí therefore led his troops to construct a weir at Cānglíng,
irrigating over a thousand qǐng of fields,
yielding over a million shí of grain annually,
which was used to fill the storehouses,
and also to aid the poor.
The region depended on this.
Kuí's elder brother, Hóu Dǎn, had previously held this post,
and now Kuí occupied it again.
The brothers both showed benevolence to the people of the region,
and the common folk sang of them, saying:
"Our prefecture,
has repeatedly had the Xiàhóu;
First the elder brother, then the younger,
their governance is excellent."
He served in the province for seven years,
achieving great fame and accomplishments,
and many from near and far attached themselves to him.
He had ten thousand private troops,
and two thousand horses,
all well-trained, highly skilled, and formidable,
constituting a great power at the time.
His nature was extravagant and luxurious;
his inner chambers, entertainers, and concubines, who wore silk gauze adorned with gold and kingfisher feathers, also numbered in the hundreds.
He cherished and supported talented individuals,
and did not elevate himself due to his wealth or power.
Scholars, military men, and guests constantly filled his seats.
People at the time praised him for this as well.
In the fourth year of Dàtóng,
he died in the province,
aged fifty-six.
An imperial edict ordered mourning,
and bestowed 200,000 cash
and 200 bolts of cloth.
He was posthumously granted Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Pacifies the North.
His posthumous name was Huán.
His son, Hóu Zhuàn, inherited the title,
and his highest office reached Minister of the Imperial Stud.
Zhuàn’s younger brother, Hóu Pān,
was rough, treacherous, and immoral in his youth.
He often stayed in the local area,
commanding his father's private troops,
and assisted the province's defense.
Inspector Xiāo Yuānmíng appointed him Chief Clerk of his administration.
When Yuānmíng was killed in battle at Péngchéng,
Pān became Hóu Jǐng’s Chief Clerk.
Jǐng soon raised an army and rebelled.
Pān served as the vanguard crossing the Yangtze River,
and stationed his troops at Shìlín Guǎn west of the capital city.
He looted and plundered residences and the wealthy households of residents,
seizing all their daughters, sons, valuables, and goods.
Yuānmíng had four concubines in the province,
Zhāng, Yú, Wáng, and Ruǎn,
all possessing exceptional beauty.
When Yuānmíng died in Wèi,
his concubines were all returned to the capital residence.
When Pān arrived,
he broke into the residence and took them in.
Yú Hóng was
a native of Xiāngyáng.
He was eight feet tall,
fair-skinned, handsome, and well-formed.
He served in campaigns numerous times,
always leading the military vanguard,
and successively held the posts of Administrator of Nánqiáo, Xūyí, and Jìnglíng.
He often told people:
"When I govern a commandery,
it is what is called the 'Four Exhaustions': the fish and turtles in the water are exhausted,
the roe deer and ordinary deer in the mountains are exhausted,
the rice and grain in the fields are exhausted,
and the common people in the villages are exhausted.
A man living in this world
is like light dust resting on weak grass,
or a white colt glimpsed through a crack.
How long does the happiness and wealth of a human life last?"
Thereupon, he indulged in reckless enjoyment.
His serving maids and concubines numbered over a hundred,
overloaded with gold and kingfisher adornments.
His attire, playthings, carriages, and horses
were the most exquisite of the age.
He was promoted to Army Supervisor for the Prince of Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West, and Administrator of the two commanderies of Xīnxīng and Yǒngníng,
and died in office.
Wéi Fàng, courtesy name Yuánzhí,
was the son of Wéi Ruì, the General of Chariots and Cavalry.
Initially, he served as Principal Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the North, the Prince of Jìn'ān of Qí.
When Emperor Gāozǔ took command of Yōngzhōu,
he summoned Fàng to serve as Principal Clerk again.
Fàng was seven feet seven inches tall,
with a waist measurement of eight wéi,
and a very imposing appearance.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
he became Administrator of Xūyí.
Upon returning, he was appointed Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he became Internal Military Advisor to the Prince of Jìn'ān, General of Light Chariots.
He was transferred to Consultative Attendant to the Prince of Shǐxīng, General Who Guards the Right,
but left office due to mourning his father.
When the mourning period ended,
he inherited the title Marquis of Yǒngchāng County.
He was posted out as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánpíng, General of Light Chariots, and Administrator of Xiāngyáng.
He was then transferred to Staff of Authority, General of Manifest Might, and Administrator of Jìnglíng.
In the commandery, he governed harmoniously and justly,
and was praised by the officials and the people.
In the sixth year,
a major northern expedition was launched.
Fàng was made General of Loyal Might,
and ordered to meet up with Hú Lóngyá and Cáo Zhòngzōng's advancing forces.
In the seventh year,
when Xiàhóu Dǎn failed to conquer Líjiāng,
Emperor Gāozǔ again ordered Fàng to lead troops from the northern route to converge at Shòuchūn city.
Soon after, he was transferred to Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánkāng, General of the Cloud Banners, and Administrator of Xúnyáng.
Fàng served as a princely aide numerous times,
and consistently achieved fame and accomplishments.
In the eighth year of Pǔtōng,
Emperor Gāozǔ sent Cáo Zhòngzōng, who was also Acting Commander of the Palace Guard, and others to attack Wōyáng.
Fàng was again made General of Manifest Might,
and led troops to meet them.
The great Wèi General Fèi Mù arrived suddenly with his forces.
Fàng’s military camp was not yet established,
and he had only over two hundred men under his banner.
Fàng’s cousin Xún was brave, fierce, and possessed great strength,
and was the reliance of the entire army.
Fàng ordered Xún to charge and strike alone on horseback,
and he repeatedly broke the Wèi forces.
Xún’s horse was also wounded and could not advance,
and Fàng’s helmet was struck by three stray arrows.
Everyone turned pale with fear
and requested Fàng to make a breakout retreat.
Fàng sternly shouted at them, saying:
"Today, there is only death!"
He then removed his helmet and dismounted,
sitting on a camp stool to issue orders.
Consequently, all the soldiers fought to the death,
each man matching a hundred.
The Wèi forces subsequently retreated,
and Fàng pursued them north to Wōyáng.
Wèi again dispatched Yuán Zhāo, the Prince of Chángshān, and the great generals Lǐ Jiǎng, Qǐfó Bǎo, Fèi Mù, and others, totaling fifty thousand troops, to reinforce the area.
Fàng led the generals under his command, Chén Dù and Zhào Bó'chāo, to attack them from both sides,
and thoroughly routed them.
Wáng Wěi, the commander of Wōyáng city, surrendered the city.
Fàng then ascended the city wall
and counted out four thousand two hundred captured soldiers,
whose weaponry filled the place.
He also sent thirty surrendered men
to separately inform Lǐ Jiǎng and Fèi Mù.
The Wèi men abandoned all their camps and strongholds,
fleeing in utter collapse.
The combined forces took advantage of this
and slaughtered and captured nearly all of them.
They captured Mù's younger brother Chāo,
and sent both him and Wáng Wěi to the capital.
Upon returning, he became Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent,
and was transferred to Palace Attendant and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.

He was posted out as Staff of Authority, Supervisor of Military Affairs of the Two Provinces of Liáng and Nánqín, General of Trustworthy Martiality, and Inspector of the Two Provinces of Liáng and Nánqín.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he was transferred to Supervisor of Military Affairs of Běixúzhōu and Inspector of Běixúzhōu.
His fief was increased by four hundred households,
and his titles of Staff of Authority and General remained the same.
He died after serving at the garrison for three years,
aged fifty-nine.
His posthumous name was Yíhóu.
Fàng was generous, sincere, and trustworthy by nature.
He held wealth lightly and enjoyed charity,
and was particularly harmonious with his younger brothers.
Whenever they were about to part for a distant journey or when they first returned from a campaign,
they always slept and rose in the same chamber.
He was known at the time as
the "Three Jiāngs."
Previously,
Fàng and Zhāng Shuài of Wújùn both had concubines who were pregnant,
and they agreed to arrange a marriage by indication.
Later, they each bore a son and a daughter.
Before they grew up, Shuài died,
leaving his heirs orphaned and weak.
Fàng always provided for and comforted them.
When he became Inspector of Běixúzhōu,
there were powerful families who requested marriage alliances.
Fàng said:
"I cannot break my promise to an old friend."
He then had his son Qí marry Shuài's daughter,
and also married his daughter to Shuài's son.
At the time, Fàng was praised for his deep loyalty to old friendships.
His eldest son Càn inherited the title,
and has a separate biography.
literary talent was noted early,
and his planning was profound and deep;
Xiàhóu Dǎn was fond of learning and eloquent;
Kuí was extravagant, generous, and loved scholars;
Wéi Fàng was broad-minded, generous, and earnest in conduct;
all met a good ruler and encountered their time,
displaying their talents and usefulness.
When they governed provinces and administered commanderies,
defeated enemies, and stabilized the frontiers,
they all established achievements,
truly fulfilling the duties of both civil and military officials.
They were surely famous ministers of the Liáng dynasty.
Collected Biographies, Number Twenty-Three: The Three Princes of Gāozǔ Gāozǔ had eight sons: Consort Dīng Guìpín gave birth to Crown Prince Zhāomíng Tǒng,
Emperor Tàizōng Jiǎnwén,
and the Prince of Lúlíng Wēi, Xù;
Ruǎn Xiūróng gave birth to Emperor Shìzǔ Xiàoyuán;
Wú Shūyuán gave birth to the Prince of Yùzhāng, Zōng;
Dǒng Shūyí gave birth to the Prince of Nánkāng Jiǎn, Jì;
Dīng Chōnghuá gave birth to the Prince of Shàolíng Xié, Lún;
Gě Xiūróng gave birth to the Prince of Wǔlíng, Jì.
Zōng and Jì have separate biographies.
Jì, the Prince of Nánkāng Jiǎn, courtesy name Shìjǐn,
was the fourth son of Gāozǔ.
In Tiānjiān eight year (509),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánkāng Commandery,
with two thousand taxable households.
He was sent out as General of Light Chariots,
simultaneously overseeing the military affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
In the tenth year (511),
he was promoted to Commissioner with Special Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs in Nánxú Prefecture, and Governor of Nánxú Prefecture,
and advanced to the title of General Rénwēi.
Jì was then seven years old.
The official in charge accepted bribes,
erasing and altering official documents.
The Chief Clerk, Wáng Sēngrú, did not notice it.
When Jì saw it, he immediately questioned the man,
and the man immediately confessed.
Everyone praised his sharp intelligence.
In the sixteenth year (517),
he was recalled to serve as General Xuānyì, overseeing the military affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
In the seventeenth year (518),
he was sent out as Commissioner with Special Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in five prefectures (Nán Yǎn, Běi Yǎn, Xú, Qīng, and Jì), and Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture.
He gained renown while in the prefecture.
Soon, an imperial edict summoned him back.
Jiā Lè and 370 others from the civil office went to the palace gates to submit a memorial,
listing fifteen exceptional accomplishments by Jì,
requesting that he be allowed to remain in his provincial post.
A gracious edict granted the request,
and he was promoted to the title of Commandant of the Northern Gentlemen-of-the-Household.
In Pǔtōng four year (523),
he was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant and General Yúnhuī,
overseeing the military affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
In the fifth year (524),
he was sent out as Commissioner with Special Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Jiāng Prefecture, and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture.
Upon the death of Dǒng Shūyí,
his mourning observance exceeded the prescribed rites.
Gāozǔ personally issued an edict to encourage him,
instructing him to temporarily assume the duties of the prefecture.
He firmly requested to resign his position.
Consequently, he was recalled and appointed General Ānyòu, overseeing the military affairs of Shítóu Garrison,
and soon thereafter was granted the position of Protector of the Army.
He was weak and emaciated and unable to attend to business.
In Dàtōng three year (529),
due to the grief that brought on illness, he died in office,
at the age of twenty-five.
He was posthumously granted Palace Attendant, General of the Central Army, and Opener of the Palace, Rites Equal to the Three Dukes,
and provided with a set of drums and pipes.
His posthumous title was Jiǎn.
Jì had few interests in playthings,
and little desire for pleasures.
He kept no servants or concubines in his residence,
personally practicing austerity and frugality.
All the rents and emoluments he received,
he entirely deposited in the Imperial Treasury.
After his death,
the treasury of the State of Nánkāng held tens of millions in unlisted currency.
His son, Huìlǐ, succeeded him;
courtesy name Chángcái.
He was intelligent and quick-witted from a young age,
and fond of literature and history.
He was orphaned at the age of eleven,
and was particularly beloved by Gāozǔ.
His clothes and ritual ranks were no different from those of a principal prince.
At the age of fifteen,
he was appointed General of Light Chariots and Governor of Xiāng Prefecture,
and also oversaw the military affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant,
simultaneously holding the post of General Commandant.
Soon after, he was appointed General Xuānhuì and Administrator of Dānyáng,
and provided with assisting officials.

He was sent out as Commissioner with Special Authority, Area Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in seven prefectures (Nán Yǎn, Běi Yǎn, Běi Xú, Qīng, Jì, Dōng Xú, and Qiáo), General Pacifying the North, and Governor of Nányǎn Prefecture.
In Tàiqīng first year (547),
he commanded various armies in a northern campaign.
When he reached Péngchéng,
he was defeated by the Wèi forces,
and retreated back to his original commandery.
In the second year (548),
Hóu Jǐng besieged the capital city.
Huìlǐ prepared his forces to enter and provide aid.
Coincidentally, Zhèng Biǎo, the Marquis of Fēngshān and Governor of Běixú Prefecture, was about to join his elder brother, Zhèng Dé.
Outwardly, he claimed he was rushing to provide assistance,
but in reality, he planned to raid Guǎnglíng.
Huìlǐ attacked and defeated him,
only then clearing the route forward.
When Táichéng fell,
Hóu Jǐng sent Dǒng Shàoxiān, the former Administrator of Línjiāng, with an autograph edict from Gāozǔ to summon Huìlǐ.
All his subordinates advised him to refuse the summons,
but Huìlǐ said:
“Your intentions, gentlemen,
are different from mine.
The Son of Heaven is advanced in years
and is controlled by the bandit enemy.
Now there is an autograph edict summoning me to the capital.
How can a minister or a son
dare disobey it?
Furthermore, remaining far away near the Jiāng [River],
it is difficult to accomplish great deeds.
It is better to personally proceed to the capital
and plan action from close proximity.
My decision is fixed.”
Thereupon, he packed up and departed quickly,
handing the city over to Shàoxiān.
When he reached the capital,
Jǐng appointed him Palace Attendant, Minister of Works, and concurrent Director of the Central Secretariat.
Although he was in the hands of the bandit,
he constantly thought of aiding in the restoration.
He secretly exchanged confidences with Quàn, the Marquis of Xīxiāng, and others,
gathering brave men.
At that time, Zǔ Hào of Fànyáng killed Shàoxiān,
occupying the city of Guǎnglíng and raising a righteous army.
He planned for Huìlǐ to act as an inside supporter.
When Hào was defeated,
the testimony implicated Huìlǐ.
Jǐng issued a forged imperial edict dismissing Huìlǐ from his offices,
but still allowed him to serve as Director of the Department of State Affairs in civilian dress.
That winter,
Jǐng traveled to Jìnxī.
The capital was weak and vulnerable.
Huìlǐ again plotted with Liǔ Jìnglǐ.
Jìnglǐ said:
“To undertake a great matter, one must have resources.
We now lack even a single soldier.
How can we act?”
Huìlǐ said:
“At Húshú, I have more than three thousand old troops.
We contacted them recently,
and fixed a date for them to gather quickly.
Once I fix the date,
they will arrive immediately at the capital.
I estimate the bandit guards are no more than a thousand men.
If our main force attacks from outside,
and we respond from inside,
directly seizing Wáng Wěi,
the plan is certain to succeed.
Even if Jǐng returns later,
he will be powerless.”
Jìnglǐ said,
“Excellent,”
and thereupon supported the plan.
At that time, the common people were weary of the bandit [Hóu Jǐng],
and all wished to dedicate their lives.
From Dānyáng to Jīngkǒu,
everyone was of the same mind.
Later, the affair did not come to fruition,
and he was killed along with his younger brother, Tōnglǐ, the Marquis of Qíyáng.
Tōnglǐ, courtesy name Zhòngxuān,
held the post of Groom of the Heir Apparent,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Qíyáng.
Tōnglǐ’s younger brother, Lǐ, courtesy name Jìyīng,
was Huìlǐ’s sixth younger brother.
The Prince of Jiǎn died when Lǐ was ten months old.
When he reached three years old and was able to speak,
he saw the palace women being dismissed,
weeping as they said goodbye.
Lǐ asked the reason.
Someone replied:
“These are the palace women of the Prince of Jiǎn,
who are leaving now that the mourning period is over.”
Lǐ immediately cried out loudly,
his sorrow overwhelming him.
When the palace women saw this,
none were unmoved with grief.
Three of them decided to stay for his sake.
After the mourning observance was completed,
he was presented to Gāozǔ,
and again he wept bitterly, unable to control his sorrow.
Gāozǔ wept because of him,
and said to his attendants:
“When this child grows up, he is certain to become a remarkable man.”
In Dàtóng eight year (542),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Ānlè County,
with five hundred taxable households.
Lǐ Xìng
admired the establishment of meritorious fame.
Every time he read books and saw loyal ministers and valiant warriors,
he never failed to lay aside his scroll and sigh, saying:
"Throughout my life,
I must not be unworthy of the ancients."
He was widely read and knowledgeable,
and possessed literary talent.
He once offered sacrifices at Kǒng Wénjǔ's tomb,
and also erected a stele for him,
composing a very beautiful inscription.
During the Tàiqīng reign,
Hóu Jǐng launched an internal invasion.
Lǐ Xìng gathered several hundred retainers
and lightly equipped, hastened to Nányān Zhōu,
following his elder brother Huìlǐ to provide aid.
He personally faced arrows and stones,
leading the soldiers.
When the city fell,
he again followed Huìlǐ back to Guǎnglíng,
then entered Qí as a hostage
to beg for troops.
After two days of travel,
it happened that Hóu Jǐng had sent Dǒng Shàoxiān to occupy Guǎnglíng,
who then pursued Huìlǐ,
and thus Lǐ Xìng was captured by him.
Shàoxiān guarded him very strictly,
preventing him from seeing his brothers.
So he falsely requested to return to the capital first
to bid farewell to his mother.
He told his elder sister, the princess Āngù Gōngzhǔ:
"Since matters have come to this,
how can the whole family suffer death?
If elder brother arrives,
I wish you would speak to him for me.
Encourage him to make good plans to exert himself,
and not to think of this as a burden.
The family and state are in dire peril;
though I die, there is no regret.
I also wish to achieve something in the future,
but I do not know what Heaven's will is."
Upon reaching the capital,
considering that Yuán Zhēn, a surrendered man from Wèi, was upright and loyal
and could be entrusted with his family,
he presented him with a jade-handled fan.
Zhēn found this strange
and refused to accept it.
Lǐ Xìng said:
"You will remember this later,
please do not decline."
At that time, Zǔ Hào raised an army.
Lǐ Xìng fled to Chánglú,
and gathered over a thousand soldiers.
Among his retinue, there were those who sided with the bandits,
and they seized an opportunity to abduct Huìlǐ.
His troops then dispersed in panic,
and he was killed by Hóu Jǐng
at the age of twenty-one.
Yuán Zhēn then understood his previous words
and went to collect and bury him.
Lúlíng Wēi Wáng Xù, courtesy name Shìxīn,
was the fifth son of Gāozǔ.
In the eighth year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as King of Lúlíng Commandery,
with an income of two thousand households.
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Light Chariot General and Administrator of Nánpéngchéng and Lángyá.
In the thirteenth year,
he was transferred to be Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the sixteenth year,
he became Overseer of All Military Affairs of Jiāngzhōu, General of Agile Cavalry, and Regional Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he was summoned to be General Who Manifests Valour,
and concurrently supervised military affairs at Shítóu Garrison.
Xù was brave and decisive in his youth,
with extraordinary physical strength.
He was skilled in horse archery and hunting,
hitting the target with every shot.
Gāozǔ often sighed, saying:
"He is my Rènchéng!"
He once competed in horse archery before Gāozǔ with Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé, Hú Guìtōng, Zhào Bózhāo, and others.
Xù excelled among all of them,
and Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
In the third year,

he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Yǒng, Liáng, Qín, and Shā, West Central Inspector-General, and Regional Inspector of Yǒngzhōu.
In the seventh year,
he was given the additional title of General Who Manifests Valour.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,

he was again appointed Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Yǒng, Liáng, Qín, and Shā, General Who Pacifies the North, Commandant for Pacifying the Man, and Regional Inspector of Yǒngzhōu,
and granted a set of drums and pipes.
Xù accumulated many horses and weapons,
and maintained brave and powerful men.
His gold and silk filled his inner chambers,
and his granaries were fully stocked.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the North.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he was appointed Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of Jiāngzhōu, General Who Pacifies the South, and Regional Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the third year,
he was summoned to be Protector-General, and concurrently supervised military affairs at Shítóu Garrison.
In the fifth year,
he was appointed Cavalry General and Minister without Portfolio.

He then departed to be Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Nine Prefectures of Jīng, Yǐng, Sī, Yǒng, Nánqín, Běiqín, Liáng, Bā, and Huá, and Regional Inspector of Jīngzhōu.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtóng,
he died in the prefecture
at the age of forty-four.
He was posthumously granted the titles of Minister of Works, Palace Attendant, and Grand Cavalry General,
a set of drums and pipes,
and given the posthumous name Wēi.
His eldest son was Ānsì.
Shàolíng Xié Wáng Lún, courtesy name Shìdiào,
was the sixth son of Gāozǔ.
He was intelligent in his youth,
widely learned and skilled in composition,
especially proficient in writing letters.
In the thirteenth year of Tiānjiān,
he was enfeoffed as King of Shàolíng Commandery,
with an income of two thousand households.
He went out to serve as General Who Pacifies the Distant, and Administrator of the two commanderies of Lángyá and Péngchéng,
then promoted to Light Chariot General and Administrator of Kuàijī.
In the eighteenth year,
he was summoned to be General Who Manifests Awe.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he concurrently supervised military affairs at Shítóu Garrison,
and soon after became Regional Inspector of Jiāngzhōu.
In the fifth year,
as West Central Inspector-General, he provisionally governed Nányān Zhōu.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he was restored to his title,
and soon after, given the additional title of General Who Manifests Awe,
and assigned assistant officials.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he became Governor of Dānyáng.
In the fourth year,
he became Palace Attendant, General Who Manifests Favor, and Regional Inspector of Yángzhōu.
Because he exploited the common people,
the Vice Director of the Privy Treasury, Hé Zhìtōng, reported the matter.
Lún learned of this
and ordered his guest, Dài Zǐgāo, to stab him to death in the capital's lane.
Zhìtōng's son complained at the imperial court.
Gāozǔ ordered Lún's residence to be surrounded
and Zǐgāo to be arrested.
Lún hid him,
and he was never produced.
For this, Lún was dismissed and reduced to commoner status.
After a short while,
he was restored to his title.
In the first year of Dàtóng,
he became Palace Attendant and General of Agile Cavalry.
In the seventh year,

he went out to serve as Bearer of the Imperial Seal, Overseer of All Military Affairs of the Four Prefectures of Yǐng, Dìng, Huò, and Sī, General Who Pacifies the West, and Regional Inspector of Yǐngzhōu,
In the first year of Zhōngdàtóng,
he went out to serve as General Who Guards the East and Regional Inspector of Nánsúzhōu.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Central Guard) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Bureau-Founding Commissioner with Rights and Privileges Equal to the Three Ducal Ministers).
When Hóu Jǐng instigated a rebellion,
he was additionally appointed Zhēngtǎo Dàdūdū (Grand Commander of the Punitive Expedition)
and led his troops to suppress Jǐng.
As he was about to depart,
Gāozǔ cautioned him, saying:
“Hóu Jǐng is a mere upstart,
quite skilled in military formations.
He cannot be annihilated in a single battle;
you must plan to subdue him over months and years.”
Lún reached Zhōnglí,
but Jǐng had already crossed Cǎishí.
Lún then traveled day and night,
sending his mobile forces to respond.
〔一三〕As they crossed the Yangtze River, a strong wind arose in mid-stream,
and one or two tenths of the men and horses drowned.
He then led Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the Distant) Xīfēng Gōng Dàchūn, Xīngàn Gōng Dàchéng, and others,
〔一四〕with thirty thousand infantry and cavalry,
departing from Jīngkǒu.
General Bó chāo said:
“If we follow the main road through Huángchéng,
we will certainly encounter the rebels.
It would be better to take a direct route straight to Zhōngshān,
catching them by surprise.”
Lún agreed.
When the combined forces arrived suddenly,
the rebel band was greatly alarmed
and divided into three columns to attack Lún.
Lún fought them
and utterly defeated them,
beheading over a thousand.
The next day,
the rebels attacked again.
The stalemate lasted until late evening,
when the rebels gradually retreated.
Nán'ān Hóu Jùn (Marquis Jùn of Nán'ān) chased them with dozens of cavalry.
The rebels turned to resist Jùn,
and Jùn’s troops fell into disarray.
The rebels then pressed the main army,
which subsequently disintegrated.
Lún reached Zhōngshān
with barely a thousand men.
The rebels surrounded them,
and they were defeated again,
so he fled back to Jīngkǒu.
In the spring of the third year,
Lún again entered to provide aid with Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Dōngyáng Prefecture) Dàlián and others,
arriving at Piàojìzhōu.
He was promoted to Sīkōng (Minister of Works).
When Táichéng fell,
he fled to Yǔxué.
In the first year of Dàbǎo,
Lún arrived at Yǐngzhōu.
The Cìshǐ (Governor) Nánpíng Wáng Kè (Prince Kè of Nánpíng) yielded the prefecture to Lún,
but Lún refused it.
Kè then proposed Lún be appointed Jiǎ Huángyuè (Acting Imperial Axe) and Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of All Military Affairs, Internal and External).
Lún then established his officials
and renamed the administrative hall Zhèngyáng Diàn (Hall of the Correct Yang).
There were frequent omens of disaster,
which Lún greatly disliked.
At that time, Yuándì had long besieged Hédōng Wáng Yù (Prince Yù of Hédōng) in Chángshā,
cutting off internal and external communications.
Lún, hearing of his plight,
wanted to go rescue him,
but due to insufficient military provisions,
he stopped.
He then wrote to Shìzǔ, saying: "I humbly reflect that the sagely virtue of the former dynasty
governed the world with filial piety.
The nine degrees of kin were harmonious and affectionate,
and the four corners of the realm held no grievances.
This was truly the nation's governance,
and indeed also the family's tradition.
Only I and you
have jointly upheld the divine instruction;
we should adhere to this teaching
and together maintain it unchanged.
Moreover, this path is beautiful
and values harmony above all.
How much more so when the timing and geographical advantage
are less important than human concord.
How can
limbs and supports
slaughter each other?
Recently, I heard that Yù was self-willed and ignored instruction,
and as a junior, trespassed against a senior.
Within Xiāng and Xiá,
this eventually led to conflict.
As for Fāng and others, they
met with mutinous soldiers
and perished in battle,
dying in Wú.
Their fate in this regard was not unjust.
Hearing this news, I cried out in sorrow and pain,
only increasing my heartbreak and indignation.
My thoughts are tinged with mourning;
how can I express them?
My residence in the prefecture is remotely separated;
though I know the situation,
I do not understand the reasons.
When I reached this border region,
I made thorough inquiries.
Everyone said that Yù's responses and treatment were often inconsistent,
and his military provisions
were obstructed.
His younger brother's teachings also did not correct him,
thus an army was raised to attack.
Yù did not understand the greater principles;
he acted on his own will.
Though he was in dire straits,
how could he know our secret thoughts?
He was unable to politely
contend,
and instead brought an army.
Strife arose within the family,
turning close relatives into enemies.
To reach this point in one day,
how can one not sigh?
Since there are letters and inquiries,
spreading like clouds and rain,
there are rumors
in between,
making it impossible to fully investigate the details.
Currently, the nation is in peril and shame,
with deep wounds and profound pain.
Humans are not birds or beasts;
they know their ruler and father.
At present, the great enemy is still strong,
and the heavenly vengeance has not been avenged.
We, your
brothers,
are three outside.
If we do not assist in this crisis,
what use are we as ministers and sons?
We should only lay bare our hearts and taste gall,
weep blood and sleep on spears,
swear to the vast sky,
and rely on the spirits of the ancestral
sacrifices,
planning day and night,
together contemplating restoration.
As for other minor grievances,
perhaps they should be treated with leniency.
Truly, if a son's resentment is momentary,
what will be done about the nation's unavenged grievance?
It is proper to weigh the heavy and the light,
to prioritize the great over the small,
to discard unbeneficial emotions,
and to cut off lower-level mourning.
Broad-mindedness should guide us,
and sagacious understanding should strive for this.
Now that Zhōngshān has been lost,
and a nephew is again executed,
is this not like trying to stop boiling water by pouring in hot water,
or curing cold by swallowing ice?
If Yù's unrighteousness is such that
near and far equally resent him,
and his younger brother again follows his bad example,
then it is not his
sole fault.
Hopefully, you will be lenient with the general opinion
and endure until affairs are settled.
If external invaders are not yet eliminated,
and family disasters continue to arise,
then comparing the present with the past,
none have failed to perish.
The principle of warfare
lies in achieving victory;
as for battles between kin,
the more one wins, the more cruel it becomes.
Victory is not merit,
and defeat brings loss.
It exhausts soldiers and harms
righteousness,
resulting in many losses.
The reason Hóu Jǐng's army has not yet ventured beyond the river
is precisely because the frontier defenses are solid
and the imperial kinsmen are strong and numerous.
If we slaughter each other,
this is
to wage war on behalf of Jǐng.
Jǐng would then not need to expend military strength,
but would achieve success sitting idle.
When the ugly rebels hear of this,
what could please them more?
Furthermore, Zhuāng Tiě, a petty upstart, caused rebellion,
and has long held Guānníng and Huái'ān,
the two marquises,
as his pretext.
Dāngyáng is preoccupied with matters and constrained,
greatly neglecting its defensive border.
Upon hearing of punitive expeditions,
it again causes troops to be divided.
This is to slice
extending to Xiāng and Yōng
were all battlegrounds,
completely exhausting our troops.
Hóu Jǐng finally took advantage of the weakness and exploited the rift,
crossing the Jiāng [river] and rampaging wildly.
How could this not indicate danger and create anxiety,
making it difficult
to reinforce both ends?
This is truly chilling,
and the matter is already critical.
If you, my younger brother (dì), suffer from being trapped at Dòngtíng,
and warfare does not cease,
Yōngzhōu will feel threatened and pressed.
How can it remain secure?
It will certainly
invite the Wèi army to advance,
seeking physical aid.
The situation with Hóu Jǐng is like an internal abscess;
externally, Xī Qín is like a large tumor.
Merely maintaining Guānzhōng
is already exhausting.
Moreover, their greed is difficult
to fathom,
and they are bound to invade and swallow us up.
If you, my younger brother, are not secure,
the family and the state will be lost.
It is not that I possess profound insight
or can establish this policy solely myself.
Rather, I have collected rumors and folk songs,
broadly consulting
public opinion,
and all consider this suspicious,
and all desire a solution to break up the current situation.
Since our state was established fifty or so years ago,
our favor has matched the dark vault of heaven,
and our virtue has filled the realm of Chìxiàn.
Although there have been rebellions and difficulties,
peace and prosperity have not yet been destroyed.
Throughout the whole world,
loyal officials are filled with indignation
and passion.
As every household suffers calamity,
loyalty and righteousness are aroused;
there is no one who does not bear armor and carry a spear,
whose hair does not stand up to pierce their cap and whose eyes are not split in fury.
All wish to plunge a blade into Hóu Jǐng’s belly;
what is needed is simply a military commander to lead
the call.
Now, men are ready to die happily;
those who rush forward are like a stream.
Your glorious strategy, younger brother, resonates far and wide,
dominating this generation as a hegemon.
You possess both virtue and skill,
equipped with both scholarly and martial abilities.
To save those drowning and rescue those in distress,
the court and the common people look to you.
To restore order and unite the realm,
if not you, my younger brother, then who?
How can you ignore public expectation
and thus incur widespread criticism!
The distress between us
is just as I have explained.
This
principle is perfectly clear,
requiring no elaborate writing to set forth;
verifying it with facts,
why must detailed examples be cited?
The reason I traveled through rugged and perilous roads,
coming out of Dōngchuān,
was precisely because I expected the various feudal lords upstream
would certainly join forces and approach quickly.
I hoped that with my remaining life,
I could participate among the ranks.
When I arrived at Jiǔjiāng,
Ānběi-xiōng consequently sailed upstream again.
This was entirely because provisions had been completely cut off,
forcing us to eat meager rations.
Hindered by starvation,
there was no way to advance.
Hóu Jǐng is currently prolonging his temporary reprieve
and delaying the execution of punishment,
doubling our cries of anger and resentment,
leaving us with no place to rest.
Considering the grain and millet of Xiāo
and Xiāng,
they ought to pile up high.
If you, my younger brother, hold back your strictly controlled army,
focusing only on internal conflicts,
then regarding transportation,
I fear there will be no time to dispatch it.
Immediately, the wishes of myriad hearts
depend
solely on the people's Mandate of Heaven.
If you consequently treat this as equal to Xīhé,
the current situation will be imperiled.
I earnestly hope that you, my esteemed younger brother, will clearly understand this path,
lift the siege of Mìchuān,
and preserve the plans for the state.
Ensure that
transportation of provisions and supplies
fully supports the armies,
so that we can cooperate in one unified action,
and peace will be restored immediately.
The Imperial Ancestral Temples will be secure again,
and the realm will be cleansed and recovered.
Judging your merit, younger brother,
will it not be a great
fortune?
My talent is weak and my soldiers few;
how can I accomplish this task?
I place my hope in you, my esteemed younger brother,
that I may express my feelings.
If I hear success in the morning and die in the evening,
I would have no regrets in perishing.
I merely set forth what I have heard and seen.
Please
do not be offended.
Writing this, I cry out in confusion;
many points lack sequence.
Shìzǔ replied to the letter,
stating that Hédōng was guilty
and the siege could not be lifted.
Lún read the letter, weeping, and said:
"Affairs of the world,
how have they come to this!"
Those around him heard this,
and none failed to cover their faces and weep.
Thereupon, he greatly repaired his weapons and armor,
preparing to attack Hóu Jǐng.
Yuándì heard of his strength
and then sent Wáng Sēngbiàn to lead a naval force of ten thousand men to press Lún.
Lún's generals, Liú Lóngwǔ and others, surrendered to Sēngbiàn.
Lún's army collapsed,
and he subsequently fled to Wǔchāng in a light boat with his son Zhì and more than ten others.
At that time, Lún's Chief Clerk, Wéi Zhì, and Marshal, Jiāng Lǜ, were previously stationed outside.
Hearing of Lún's defeat,
they rushed to meet him.
Thereupon, they gathered the scattered troops again
and garrisoned Qíchāng Jùn,
intending to bring in the Wèi army to jointly attack Nányáng.
Hóu Jǐng's general, Rèn Yuē, heard of this
and sent two hundred armored cavalry to assault Lún.
Lún was unprepared,
and again fled to Dìngzhōu after defeat.
Tián Lóngzǔ, the Governor of Dìngzhōu, welcomed Lún.
However, Lún knew Lóngzǔ had been appointed by the Jīng commandery
and feared being captured by him,
so he returned to Qíchāng.
Traveling to Rǔnán,
the Lord of Rǔnán City appointed by Xī Wèi was Lǐ Sù.
His eldest son was Jiān,
courtesy name Chángbái.
In the first year of Dàtóng (535 CE),
he was typically enfeoffed as the Marquis of Rǔnán,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
He was also skilled in running script,
but his character was rather mediocre and shortsighted.
When Hóu Jǐng besieged the city,
Jiān was stationed at Tàiyángmén.
He spent the whole day drinking,
paying no attention to military administration.
If officers or soldiers achieved merit,
he never acknowledged or rewarded them.
When plague struck,
he offered no care or relief.
All the soldiers were consequently resentful.
In the third month of the third year of Tàiqīng (550 CE),
Jiān's clerks Dǒng Xūnhuá and Bái Tánlǎng used ropes to pull the bandits up onto the ramparts.
The city was thus breached,
and Jiān was killed.
His younger brother was Què,
courtesy name Zhòngzhèng.
When young, he was brave and fierce,
and possessed literary talent.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Zhèngjiē,
with a stipend of five hundred households.
Later, his title was transferred to Yǒng'ān.
He often practiced horsemanship and archery in his residence
and studied military strategy.
People at the time all considered him eccentric.
When his attendants offered remonstrance,
Què said:
"Wait until I defeat the bandits for the state,
then you will understand."
He was appointed Secretary of the Palace Library (Mìshūchéng)
and Gentleman of the Eastern Palace (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén).
In the battle of Zhōngshān,
Què fought bitterly;
wherever he charged, the enemy lines broke,
and the mass of captives feared him.
Whenever Què faced the enemy in battle,
his spirit and resolve were abundant and composed.
Wearing armor and seated on his saddle,
from morning until evening,
he galloped back and forth,
not deeming it exhausting.
All the generals respected his strength and courage.
When Hóu Jǐng sued for peace,
Què was outside (the city).
Fearing he would cause future trouble,
a memorial was submitted requesting Què be summoned into the city.
The imperial edict then summoned Què and made him Nánzhōng Lángjiàng and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu,
increasing his feudal allotment by two thousand households.
Què knew this alliance was full of duplicity
and that the city would inevitably be overrun.
He therefore intended to flee south.
When Xié Wáng heard this,
he compelled Què to enter the city.
Què still refused.
Xié Wáng wept and said to him:
"Are you intending to rebel?"
At that time, the court envoy Zhōu Shízhēn was present.
Què said to Shízhēn:
"Although Hóu Jǐng says he wishes to leave,
he does not lift the prolonged siege.
Judging by his behavior,
his intentions are manifest.
Now summoning me inside,
I do not see the advantage."
Shízhēn said:
"The imperial decree is thus.
How can you decline?"
Què remained resolute in his stance.
Xié Wáng was greatly enraged
and said to Zhào Bó Chāo:
"O, Qiáozhōu!
You execute him for me,
and carry his head to the Palace."
Bó Chāo brandished his blade, looking menacingly at Què, and said:
"I recognize you,
but how can the knife recognize you?"
Què thereupon wept and went out,
and subsequently entered the city.
When Jǐng broke the alliance and again besieged the city,
and the city fell,
Què pushed open the gate and went in,
reporting to Gāozǔ, saying:
"The city has already fallen."
Gāozǔ said:
"Is it still possible to fight one last battle?"
He replied:
"It is not possible.
Your servant just personally engaged in the fighting,
but the momentum could not be stopped.
I lowered myself down from the city wall by rope
and barely managed to reach this place."
Gāozǔ sighed and said:
"I gained it myself,
I lost it myself.
What regret can I possibly have?"
He then ordered Què to write a document of conciliation.
When Què came out and met Jǐng,
Jǐng admired his muscular strength
and ordered him to remain nearby.
Later, while accompanying Jǐng on an outing,
they saw a flying kite in the sky.
The crowd of followers competed to shoot it but missed.
Què shot at it,
and it fell the moment the bowstring sounded.
The bandit followers were furious and jealous,
and all urged that he be removed.
Prior to this, Xié Wáng had secretly sent a man to guide Què.
Què said to the envoy:
"Hóu Jǐng is frivolous and unstable;
he can be handled by the strength of one man.
Què does not fear death;
I only wish to slay him with my own hands.
I just haven't found the right opportunity yet.
When you return, report this to our family's Prince,
and ask him not to worry about it."
Before the task was accomplished, he was killed by the bandits.
The Historian says: Since the Zhōu and Hàn Dynasties widely established feudal defense screens,
solidifying the foundation and deepening the roots,
Gāozǔ’s system of enfeoffment
was intended to follow the ancient regulations.
Nánkāng and Lúlíng, both noble due to their kinship with the imperial house,
held positions as heavy as a cornerstone.
Their merits were first known for filial piety,
and subsequently renowned for bravery.
Lún was intelligent, perceptive, and talented in learning,
but his character was dangerous and impetuous.
He was repeatedly dismissed due to offenses.
Yet, during the chaos of Tàiqīng,
his loyalty and filial piety alone remained intact.
This is truly praiseworthy.
Biographies Twenty-Four: Péi Zǐyě, Gù Xié, Xú Chī, Bào Quán.
Péi Zǐyě, courtesy name Jīyuán,
was a native of Wénxǐ, Hédōng.
He was the eighth generation descendant of Kāng, Chief of Staff to the Crown Prince during the Jìn Dynasty.
His elder brother was Lí,
and his younger brothers were Kǎi and Chuò.
All had great reputations,
and were what are called
"The Four Péis."
His great-grandfather was Sōngzhī,
Grand Master of the Middle (Tàizhōng Dàfū) during the Sòng Dynasty.
His grandfather was Yīn,
Administrator of External Military Affairs for the Nánzhōng Director.
His father was Zhāomíng,
Attendant Counselor (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì).
Zǐyě was orphaned young.
He was raised by his grandmother.
When he was nine years old
and his grandmother died,
he mourned so deeply that he wept blood.
His family found this remarkable.
In his youth he loved learning
and was skilled in composition.
He began his career as Left Attendant-in-Waiting (Zuǒ Chángshì) for the Qi Principality of Wǔlíng,
and then Administrator (Cānjūn) for the Prince of Jiāngxià, the Right General (Yòujūn).
He resigned his post to mourn his father.
He observed the mourning rites completely.
Every time he went to the grave site,
the grass where he wept withered.
A white rabbit stayed tamely by his side.
Early in the Tiānjiān era,
the Secretariat Director (Shàngshū Púshè) Fàn Yún admired his conduct
and intended to submit a memorial recommending him.
However, Yún died,
and the recommendation was not realized.
Rèn Fǎng of Lè'ān had a great reputation
and was admired by younger scholars.
Of those who associated with him,
Fǎng would surely recommend and advance them.
Zǐyě was Fǎng's cousin,
but he alone did not visit;
Fǎng regretted this.
After a long time,
he was appointed Administrator (Cānjūn) for the Prince of Ānchéng and Right General (Yòujūn).
Soon thereafter, he was promoted to acting Chief Justice (Tíngwèi Zhèng).
At that time, the three judicial officials jointly signed the legal documents.
Zǐyě happened to be absent,
and his colleagues simply signed his name.
When a proposal was rejected,
Zǐyě was consequently implicated and dismissed from office.
Someone advised him to speak to the relevant authorities
so that he could avoid the penalty.
Zǐyě smiled and replied:
