"Although I am ashamed to follow the ways of Liǔ Jì,
how can I submit to the judgment by making a plea?"
From this point, he remained dismissed for a long time,
yet he never harbored any feelings of resentment.
In the second year,
Xiāo Jǐng, the Marquis of Wú Píng, was the Administrator of Nányǎnzhōu.
He was appointed Record Keeper (Lùshì) of the Guān Jūn establishment.
When the establishment was moved, his position ended.
At that time, Fàn Zhěn of the Secretariat had not yet met Zǐyě,
but hearing of his conduct and accomplishments, he admired him.
When Fàn Zhěn was about to be transferred to the post of Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University),
he submitted a memorial declining it, saying:
“I humbly observe that Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng, formerly a Lùshì Cānjūn (Record Keeper and Adjutant) in the Guān Jūn establishment,
is forty years old,
with the courtesy name Jīyuán.
In his youth, he maintained the conduct of a perfect man;
in adulthood, he exhibited the demeanor of a national scholar.
He followed the rites during mourning;
his wasting away brought him near death.
Even after the period of official mourning was over,
he would not partake of vegetables or water.
Although he dwells in a low position,
his status is humble and his name obscure,
yet his nature is not anxious,
and his disposition is not urgent.
Therefore, discerning people sigh in admiration,
and the local populace praises and submits to him.
Moreover, his family passed down their traditional studies;
for generations, they have practiced Confucianism and history.
He immerses himself in the classics and records,
resting and relaxing in literature and arts.
He authored the Sòng Lüè (Outline of Sòng) in twenty volumes,
organizing it from beginning to end,
compiling the history of a whole era.
His choice of words and presentation of facts
are worthy of observation.
Furthermore, his grasp of chapters and verses is comprehensive,
and his explanations of ancient meanings are transmissible.
If he were placed in the schools,
to promote and encourage the younger generation,
then perhaps the debate of Yī Kuí could be traced,
and the doubts concerning Sān Shǐ would be free from error.
I humbly consider that the Imperial House is pure and glorious,
with many scholars filling the court.
The selection of officials surpasses that of the Yǒu Guī,
and the selection of raw talents (Yù Pǔ) exceeds that of the Jī Shì.
If even a small good deed should be recorded,
regardless of importance,
and if a single worthy person is sought,
it is not limited by rank.
I have historically observed the sovereigns of antiquity and the present who respected the worthy and loved the good,
but none have reached the level of diligence shown by Your Sacred Dynasty.
Daring to follow this principle,
I presumptuously present my dull views.
I beg that the post I unworthily hold
be transferred to Zǐyě.
If this is done,
then the worthy and the unworthy
will each hold their proper place.
If one questions public opinion,
who would say it is not justified?
Although I have never shared a drink with Zǐyě,
inquiries in the villages confirm
that this estimation is certainly not false.
Overwhelmed by my sincere, minor observations,
I rashly present this for consideration.
I humbly pray that Your Majesty will take pity on this simple sincerity,
examine the truth behind this humble petition,
and grant forgiveness
for the transgression of having presumed to speak.”
The relevant authorities deemed his qualifications not yet sufficient,
and did not approve the transfer.
Soon after, he was appointed Shàngshū Bǐbù Láng (Secretary of the Bureau of Statistics),
and Rén Wēi Jìshì Cānjūn (Record Keeper and Adjutant for the General Rén Wēi).
He was sent out to be the Magistrate of Zhūjì.
While in the county, he did not use whipping or punishment.
When people had disputes,
he demonstrated the principles of reason to them.
The hundred families praised and were pleased,
and throughout the whole jurisdiction there were no lawsuits.
Earlier,
Zǐyě’s great-grandfather, Péi Sōngzhī,
received an imperial edict during the Yuánjiā era of the Sòng to continue compiling Hè Chéngtiān’s Sòng Shǐ (History of Sòng).
He died before completing it.
Zǐyě always wished to continue and complete this ancestral work.
By the end of the Yǒngmíng era of the Qí,
after the Sòng Shū compiled by Shěn Yuē had been circulated,
Zǐyě instead revised and compiled his own work into the Sòng Lüè in twenty volumes.
His commentary on the events was mostly excellent.
Shěn Yuē saw it and sighed, saying:
“I did not reach that level.”
Xiāo Chēn of Lánlíng, Fù Zhāo of Běidì, and Zhōu Shě of Rǔnán all highly esteemed it.
Up to this point,
Xú Miǎn, the Minister of Personnel, spoke of him to Gāozǔ,
who appointed him Zuòzhù Láng (Court Gentleman for Editorial Review),
in charge of the official national history and the Imperial Diary.
Shortly after,
he concurrently held the post of Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (Secretarial Court Gentleman for Transmission of Edicts),
and soon after was appointed Tōngzhí Zhèngyuán Láng,
retaining his posts as Zuòzhù and Shèrén.
He was further commanded to oversee the drafting of imperial edicts and pronouncements in the Secretariat.
At this time, beyond the northwestern frontier there were the Bái Tí and the Huá Guó,
who sent envoys via the Mín Shān route to present tribute.
These two states had never submitted in previous dynasties,
and no one knew their origin.
Zǐyě said:
“The Marquis of Yǐngyīn of the Hàn dynasty beheaded one Hú general named Bái Tí.
Fú Qián’s commentary says: ‘
Bái Tí is the name of the Hú.’
Furthermore, when the Marquis of Dìngyuǎn of the Hàn dynasty attacked the captives,
eight Huá tribes followed him.
Are these perhaps their descendants?”
People at the time admired his extensive knowledge.
An edict then instructed him to compile the Fāngguó Shǐ Tú (Illustrations of Envoys from Foreign States),
extensively describing the flourishing nature of attracting foreigners,
from those tribes nearest to the central government up to those beyond the sea,
totaling twenty states.
Zǐyě, along with Liú Xiǎn of Pèiguó, Liú Zhīlín of Nányáng, Yīn Yún of Chénjùn, Ruǎn Xiàoxù of Chénliú, Gù Xié of Wújùn, and Wéi Léng of Jīngzhào,
were all widely versed in many books.
They admired each other deeply,
and Liú Xiǎn especially held him in high regard.
At that time, Xiāo Mài, the Marquis of Wú Píng, and Zhāng Zuǎn of Fànyáng,
whenever they discussed ancient texts,
always referred to Zǐyě for the final authoritative decision.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng,
the Imperial Army launched a northern campaign.
An edict ordered Zǐyě to draft a proclamation to Wèi.
Upon receiving the command, he completed it instantly.
Because Gāozǔ considered the matter of great magnitude,

he summoned the Director of the Department of State Affairs Xú Miǎn, the Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent Zhōu Shě, the Minister of Dependencies Liú Zhīlín, and the Vice Minister of the Secretariat Zhū Yì,
to gather at the Shòuguāng Diàn (Shòuguāng Palace Hall) to read it.
All present expressed admiration.
Gāozǔ looked at Zǐyě and said:
“Although his physique is weak,
his writing is extremely strong.”
Soon after, he was again commanded to draft a letter to Yuán Yì, the Chancellor of Wèi.
He received the instruction that night.
Zǐyě thought he could wait until dawn before submitting it,
and thus did not write it immediately.
When the fifth drum sounded,
an edict urgently commanded him to open his chamber and submit it quickly.
Zǐyě slowly rose, took up his brush,
and completed it just as the sky began to lighten.
Once submitted,
Gāozǔ greatly praised it.
From this point onward, all major documents and official communications
were entrusted to him for drafting.
Zǐyě’s writing was elegant yet swift,
not favoring ornate and extravagant language.
His compositions often imitated antiquity.
Being different from the contemporary literary style,
some people at the time criticized it,
but eventually, everyone universally came to respect it.
Someone asked him why his writing was so fast.
Zǐyě replied:
“Others compose with their hands,
but I compose only with my mind.
Although there is a difference in visible output,
the amount of revision required is the same.”
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Secretariat),
with his other duties remaining as before.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he was transferred to Hónglú Qīng (Minister of Dependencies),
and soon concurrently took charge of the Commander of Infantry.
Zǐyě served within the Inner Court for over ten years,
maintaining silence and self-restraint,
never making any requests or solicitations.
His maternal relatives and cousins were impoverished,
and he distributed all his salary to them.
He owned no house,
borrowing two *mǔ* of government land
to build a few thatched huts.
His wife and children suffered from hunger and cold.
He focused solely on teaching and instruction.
His sons and nephews respected and feared him
as if serving a strict lord.
In his later years, he deeply believed in Buddhism,
upholding its precepts.
For the rest of his life, he ate grains and vegetables.
In the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
he died in office,
aged sixty-two.
this, Zǐyě had predetermined the date of his death,
which would not be later than the year Gēngxū.
That year, he reported illness and retired,
saying to his colleague Liú Zhīhēng:
"I am about to depart."
His dying instructions emphasized frugality
and moderation in all things.
Gāozǔ lamented and regretted his loss,
shedding tears for him.
The imperial edict read:

"Péi Zǐyě, the Grand Herald (Hónglú Qīng), concurrently Commandant of the Infantry (Lǐng Bùbīng Xiàowèi), managing the affairs of the Gentleman of the Palace Library (Zhī Zhùzuò Láng), and concurrent Attendant Secretary in the Central Secretariat (Jiān Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén),
possessed sufficient talent in literature and history,
maintained integrity and purity,
diligently serving as Attendant Secretary
for many years.
His sudden passing
evokes deep sorrow in Our heart.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
We grant 50,000 cash for funeral expenses,
and 50 bolts of cloth.
Let mourning commence immediately.
His posthumous title shall be Zhēnzǐ."
In his youth, Zǐyě
compiled the *Commentary on Mourning Rites* (*Jìzhù Sāngfú*) and the *Continuation of the Péi Clan Genealogy* (*Xù Péishì Jiāzhuàn*), two volumes each.
He also compiled and synthesized events from the Later Hàn (Hòuhàn) into over forty volumes,
and was commanded to compile the *Biographies of Monks* (*Zhòng Sēngzhuàn*) in twenty volumes,
(*Bǎiguān Jiǔpǐn*) in two volumes,
an expansion on the *Rules for Posthumous Titles* (*Fùyì Shìfǎ*) in one volume,
*Maps of Envoys from Neighboring States* (*Fāngguó Shǐtú*) in one volume,
and a Collected Works (*Wénjí*) in twenty volumes,
which all circulated in the world.
He also intended to compile the *Spring and Autumn Annals of Qí and Liáng* (*Qí Liáng Chūnqiū*),
which he had begun to draft,
but he died before completing it.
His son, Jiǎn,
served as Aide-in-Ordinary (Tōngzhí Láng).
Gù Xié, courtesy name Zhènglǐ,
was a man of Wú county in Wújùn (Wú Commandery).
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Hè (Hé), the Minister of Works (Sīkōng) of the Jìn Dynasty.
Xié was orphaned young,
and was raised by his mother among her maternal relatives.
His mother's cousin's ancestor, Zhāng Yǒng, the Right Minister of Ceremonies (Yòu Guānglù) of the Sòng Dynasty, once took his grandsons and nephews, both paternal and maternal, to tour Mount Hǔqiū.
When Xié was a few years old,
Yǒng patted him and said:
"What game do you want to play, child?"
Xié replied:
"I merely wish to pillow myself on stones and rinse my mouth in the stream."
Yǒng sighed and remarked:
"The Gù clan will flourish through this child."
When he grew up,
he loved studying,
and was noted for his energy and keenness.
Many members of his maternal Zhāng clan were wise, prominent, and discerning;
his cousin Shuài particularly esteemed him.
He began his career as Clerk in the Advisory Section (Yìcáo Cóngshìshǐ) of Yángzhōu,
concurrently serving as Erudite of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì).
He was recommended as a Cultivated Talent (Xiùcái).
Shěn Yuē, the Prefect of the Masters of Writing (Shàngshū Lìng), reviewed his policy paper and sighed, saying:
"Since the establishment of Jiāngzuǒ (East of the Yangtze),
there has been no work like this."
He was promoted to Left Attendant (Zuǒ Chángshì) of the Kingdom of Ānchéng,
concurrently serving as Court Judge (Tíngwèi Zhèng).
The Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), Prince of Línchuān, heard of his reputation,
summoned him to manage the archives (Zhǎng Shūjì),
and he subsequently attended Xīfēng Hóu Zhèngdé while he studied.
When Zhèngdé was appointed Governor of Bāxī and Zǐtóng Commanderies,
Xié was appointed Magistrate of Āndū county within his jurisdiction.
Before reaching the county,
he suffered the mourning period for his mother.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Vice Administrator of Xīyáng Commandery (Xīyáng Jùnchéng).
Returning, he was appointed Provisional Staff Officer to the Commandant-in-Chief of the North (Běi Zhōngláng Xíng Cānjūn),
and again concurrently served as Court Judge (Tíngwèi Zhèng).
After some time,
he was sent out to serve as Vice Administrator of Lúlíng Commandery (Lúlíng Jùnchéng),
but before taking up the post,
Xīfēng Hóu Zhèngdé happened to be appointed Governor of Wújùn (Wú Commandery).
Xié was appointed Staff Officer to the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Cānjūn),
overseeing the five officials of the commandery.
He was promoted to Staff Officer (Cānjūnshì) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng), General of Light Chariots (Qīngchē),
concurrently serving as Recorder (Jìshì).
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng,
Zhèngdé received an edict to campaign in the north.
He engaged Xié as Registrar Staff Officer (Lùshì Cānjūn) in his establishment,
managing the archives.
When the army returned,
there happened to be an imperial edict recommending scholars for promotion.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng submitted a memorial recommending Xié, saying:
"Your servant has heard that those who offer jade
come from Rùnshān;
those who discuss pearls
come from the barren shore.
Therefore, even the words of grass-cutters
are chosen and valued in the court (Lángmiào).
Gù Xié of Wújùn, Staff Officer and concurrent Recorder in Your servant’s establishment,
is praised for his conduct in the villages,
his learning encompasses both civil and military arts,
he adheres devoutly to virtue and simplicity,
his noble disposition is profound and far-reaching.
He is content in poverty and maintains tranquility,
dedicated to public duty and upright,
close to the palace gate but reserved about his own merit,
and does not seek personal gain.
Though he is nearing sixty,
his home contains neither wife nor child.
If Your servant were to speak to officials
to advance him from his constrained position,
Xié would certainly insist on his integrity and retirement,
his resolve being hard to sway.
He can truly be called a hidden treasure of the Southeast.
I humbly note that Your Majesty seeks attire before dawn,
and thirsts for the virtuous.
You have consequently issued a clear edict,
asking everyone to recommend those they know.
Although Your servant’s judgment is not that of Xǔ or Guō,
and I lack the ability to judge men completely,
if I stubbornly remain silent,
I fear incurring the blame of concealing worthy talent.
Previously, Kǒng Yú praised the talent of Hán Jì,
and Yǔ Liàng recommended the virtue of Zhái Tāng.
Although Your servant cannot compare to these two ministers,
Xié truly holds no shame when compared to those two scholars."
He was immediately summoned and appointed Aide-in-Ordinary, Cavalier Attendant (Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng),
concurrently serving as Attendant Secretary in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén).
He was successively promoted to Commandant of the Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
Provisional Grand Herald (Shǒu Hónglú Qīng),
and Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì).
His titles of Grand Herald and Attendant Secretary remained unchanged.
In the eighth year of Dàtóng,
he died,
aged seventy-three.
Gāozǔ mourned and regretted his loss,
issuing a handwritten edict:
"Gù Xié, Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì), Grand Herald (Hónglú Qīng), and concurrent Attendant Secretary in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén),
maintained his integrity and purity,
his conduct undiminished even in old age.
Having long served in the court and palace,
he was praised by those inside and outside the government.
His sudden demise
fills Our heart with deep sorrow
that cannot be easily set aside.
He has no close relatives nearby,
which makes his loss even more pitiable.
Once the main burial rites are complete,
his coffin shall immediately be escorted back to his hometown.
His grave mound and outer coffin shall also be constructed.
All necessary resources shall be provided
to ensure everything is thoroughly taken care of.
He is hereby posthumously granted the title of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
Let mourning commence immediately.
His posthumous title shall be Wēnzǐ."
In his youth, Xié was pure, straightforward, and possessed high integrity.
When he first served as Court Judge (Tíngwèi Zhèng),
his winter clothing was thin.
Cài Fǎdù, the Court Administrator (Sì Qīng), said to others:
"I wish I could take off the jacket I am wearing and give it to Lord Gù,
but I fear Lord Gù would find it hard to accept provisions."
Ultimately, he dared not give it to him.
When he became Attendant Secretary (Shèrén),
his colleagues all enriched their homes.
Xié served in the secretariat for sixteen years,
yet his utensils, clothing, and diet
never changed from the ordinary.
A disciple, newly come to serve Xié,
knowing his integrity,
dared not offer a generous gift,
sending only two thousand cash.
Xié grew angry,
giving him twenty strokes of the cane.
After this, subsequent servants ceased giving gifts.
From the time he encountered the grief of mourning (for his mother),
he wore coarse cloth and ate vegetarian food for the rest of his life.
When he was young, he was planning to marry the daughter of his maternal uncle.
Before the marriage took place, Xié’s mother died.
After the mourning period, he did not marry again.
When he reached over sixty years of age,
this woman still had not married anyone else.
Xié, acting out of righteousness, welcomed her (as his wife).
Although they were finally united late in life,
he ultimately had no heir.
Xié studied widely among numerous books,
and was especially renowned for his meticulous knowledge of characters, as well as birds, beasts, grasses, and trees.
He compiled *Yìxìng Yuàn* in five volumes,
and *Suǒyǔ* in ten volumes,
which both circulated in the world.
Xú Chī, courtesy name Shìxiù,
was a man of Tán county in Dōnghǎi.
His grandfather, Píngdào,
was the Administrator of Hǎilíng (Hǎilíng Tàishǒu) under the Sòng Dynasty.
His father, Chāozhī,
served up to the position of Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì) at the beginning of the Tiānjiān era.
Xú Chī was fond of study from a young age;
when he grew up,
he extensively read the Classics and Histories.
In composition, he favored novelty and change,
not being constrained by old styles.
He began his career as a Tàixué Bóshì (Erudite of the Imperial University);
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Sīmǎ (Cavalry Administrator of the Left Guard).
When Jìn'ān Wáng Gāng (Prince of Jin'an, Xiāo Gāng) went out to garrison Shítou,
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) said to Zhōu Shě:
“Seek one person for me,
who excels in both literature and conduct,
I want him to associate with Jìn'ān (Wáng).”
Shě said:
“My younger cousin, Xú Chī,
is physically humble and small,
as if he could not bear the weight of clothes,
but he is worthy of this selection.”
Gāozǔ replied:
“If he truly possesses the talent of Zhòngxuān (Wáng Cān),
then his appearance shall not be scrutinized.”
He appointed Chī as Shìdú (Attendant Reader).
Later, when the Prince went out to govern Jiāngzhōu,
Chī was retained and appointed Yúnhuī Fǔ Jìshì Cānjūn (Secretary and Staff Officer of the Cloud-Banner Commandery);
he was then transferred to Píngxī Fǔ Zhōng Jìshì (Secretary in the Headquarters of the General Who Pacifies the West).
When the Prince moved his garrison to Jīngkǒu,
he again followed the commandery, transferring to Ānběi Zhōng Lùshì Cānjūn (Central Registrar and Staff Officer of the General Who Pacifies the North),
concurrently serving as the Magistrate of Tán;
he left office due to mourning his mother.
When the Prince became Dānyáng Yǐn (Governor of Danyang),
he reinstated Chī as Líng Lìng (Magistrate of Líng).
In Pǔtōng fourth year (523 CE),
the Prince went out to govern Xiāngyáng;
Chī firmly requested to follow the commandery westward,
and was promoted to Jìn'ān Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn (Counsellor and Staff Officer of the Prince of Jin'an).
At the beginning of Dàtōng (527 CE),
the Prince led the army in a northern campaign;
Chī was appointed concurrent Níngmán Fǔ Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Commandery for Pacifying the Barbarians),
participating in and assisting military affairs.
His instructional orders and military documents
mostly originated from Chī himself.
When the Prince entered the capital to become Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince),
Chī was transferred to Jiālìng (Chief Steward),
concurrently overseeing secretarial duties,
and shortly thereafter was additionally appointed Lǐngzhí (Director of the Attendants).
Since Chī’s literary style was distinct,
all those in the Crown Prince's court (Chūnfāng) imitated it;
the appellation “Gōngtǐ” (Palace Style)
arose from this.
Gāozǔ heard of this and was angry.
He summoned Chī and rebuked him.
When they met,
Chī’s responses were clear and quick,
and his rhetoric and meaning were commendable.
Gāozǔ’s anger was appeased.
He then questioned Chī about the great principles of the Five Classics,
followed by questions on the histories of successive dynasties and the miscellaneous theories of the various schools,
and finally discussed Buddhism (Shìjiào).
Chī discussed and debated extensively and freely;
his replies were instantaneous, like an echo.
Gāozǔ greatly praised and admired him,
and Chī was subsequently treated with greater intimacy;
his favor and treatment increased daily.
Zhū Yì, the Lǐngjūn (Commander of the Palace Guard), was displeased.
He said to his confidants:
“Old Xú (Xú Sǒu) goes in and out of the two palaces,
and is gradually encroaching upon my position.
We must deal with him soon.”
He then took advantage of an opportunity and reported to Gāozǔ, saying:
“Chī is old,
and he loves springs and rocks (nature).
He desires a commandery,
so he can rest and recuperate.”
Gāozǔ believed that Chī desired this,
so he summoned Chī and said:
“Xīn'ān has wonderful scenery;
Rèn Fǎng and others have previously governed it.
You shall govern this commandery for me in a leisurely manner (Wòzhì).”
In Zhōngdàtōng third year (531 CE),
he was consequently sent out to be Xīn'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xin'an).
Upon arriving at the commandery,
his governance was pure and tranquil.
He instructed the people in rites and righteousness,
and encouraged farming and sericulture.
Within a year,
the local customs were transformed.
When his term expired,
he returned to serve as Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
and was granted the title Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Military Prowess).
At this time, Línchéng Gōng (Duke of Lincheng) married Lady Wáng,
who was the niece of Tàizōng’s (Xiāo Gāng’s) consort.
Since the Jìn and Sòng Dynasties,
on the third day after the initial marriage,
when the wife greeted her husband’s parents (jiùgū),
all the guests would line up to watch.
They cited the principle in the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chūnqiū), which states:
“On the day Dīngchǒu,
Lady Jiāng arrived.
On the day Wùyín,
the Duke sent the Grandee and the principal wife to present gifts upon sight.”
Wùyín
is the day immediately following Dīngchǒu.
Therefore, the officials of ritual, based on this,
all said that it should follow the old tradition.
Tàizōng asked Chī about this.
Chī said:
“The Yílǐ (Book of Etiquette and Rites) says, ‘At dawn, the usher presents the wife to the husband’s parents.’
The Zájì (Miscellaneous Records of Rites) also says, ‘When the wife greets her husband’s parents,
brothers and sisters all stand below the hall.’
The purpose is that the wife is from an external clan,
and it is not yet known if she is adept at propriety,
so she is kept waiting for three mornings (Sānzhāo),
to observe her Seven Virtues (Qīdé).
The father-in-law invites outside guests,
and the mother-in-law leads the inside guests;
the ceremony below the hall
is to complete the grand rite.
In recent generations, the wife and her husband’s parents
often have existing relations,
and thus do not gaze upon one another.
This lady is the niece of the Consort,
which is different from other marriages.
The ritual of presentation upon sight
I suggest ought to be omitted.”
Tàizōng followed his suggestion.
Chī was appointed Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài (Commander of the Crown Prince’s Left Guard).
In Tàiqīng third year (549 CE),
Hóu Jǐng attacked and captured Táichéng (the Imperial City).
At that time, Tàizōng was residing in Yǒngfú Shěng (Yongfu Palace).
The multitude of rebels rushed in;
they raised their weapons and ascended the hall.
The attendants and guards fled and scattered,
with none remaining.
Chī alone stood firm and unmoving as an attendant.
Slowly, he addressed Jǐng:
“Lord Hóu (Hóu Gōng) should present himself with proper rites;
how can you act like this?”
The brutal display of force was immediately checked.
Hóu Jǐng then bowed,
and thereafter always respected Chī.
When Tàizōng succeeded to the throne,
Chī was promoted and granted the title Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard),
but he firmly declined the appointment.
Later, Tàizōng was confined;
Chī was unable to attend the court.
He succumbed to a respiratory illness and died,
at the age of seventy-eight.
His eldest son, Líng (Xú Líng),
was the most famous.
Bào Quán, courtesy name Rùnyuè,
was a man from Dōnghǎi.
His father, Jī (Bào Jī),
was Zīyì Cānjūn (Counsellor and Staff Officer) to the Xiāngdōng Wáng (Prince of Xiangdong).
Quán extensively studied historical narratives,
and also possessed literary talent.
While young, he served Yuán Dì (Emperor Yuán);
he was promoted and appointed early.
When Emperor Yuán assumed official authority (chéngzhì),
Quán was repeatedly promoted until he reached the position of Xìnzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Xinzhou).
In Tàiqīng third year (549 CE),
Emperor Yuán ordered Quán to campaign against Hédōng Wáng Yù (Prince of Hedong) in Xiāngzhōu.
Quán arrived at Chángshā,
and constructed interconnected fortifications to press him.
Yù led his troops to attack Quán;
Quán occupied the stockade and defended firmly,
and Yù could not overcome him.
Quán took advantage of their exhaustion and sallied out to strike them.
Yù suffered a major defeat,
and all his troops were captured.
Quán then besieged the city,
but was unable to take it for a long time.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Yuán) then enumerated Quán’s faults,
and sent Píngnán Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngbiàn (General Who Pacifies the South) to replace Quán as Dūdū (Area Commander).
When Sēngbiàn arrived,
Quán was astonished.
He looked around at his subordinates and said:
“If only I had Wáng Jìnglíng (Prince of Jingling) to help me plan,
the rebels would be nothing to pacify.”
Once Sēngbiàn entered the camp,
he sat down with his back toward Quán,
and said:
“Bào Láng (Young Bao) is guilty.
The Imperial Edict instructs me to chain you,
do not rely on our old acquaintance.”
He then produced the order and showed it to Quán,
and chained him beneath the bed.
Quán said:
“I have delayed the royal army;
it is my lot to accept the punishment.
I only fear that later generations will miss the confusion (incompetence) of Bào Quán.”
He then submitted a memorial acknowledging the crime of undue delay.
Shìzǔ soon restored him to his post,
ordering him and Sēngbiàn to lead the naval forces eastward to pressure Shàolíng Wáng (Prince of Shaoling) at Yǐngzhōu.
When Yǐngzhōu was pacified,
Yuándì appointed his eldest son, Fāngzhū, as Cìshǐ (Governor),
and Quán as Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk),
managing the affairs of the prefecture and province.
Hóu Jǐng secretly dispatched the generals Sòng Zixiān and Rèn Yuē to lead elite cavalry and attack them.
Fāngzhū and Quán paid no attention to military administration,
only indulging themselves in gambling and wine.
When the enemy cavalry arrived,
the common people rushed to report it.
Fāngzhū and Quán were playing *shuānglù* (a dice game)
and did not believe it,
saying:
"Xú Wénshèng's great army is in the east;
how could the bandits possibly get here?"
Subsequently, the number of reporters multiplied,
and only then did they order the closing of the gates.
The bandits set fire and burned them down.
No one resisted,
and the enemy cavalry entered.
The city then fell.
They captured Fāngzhū and Quán and sent them to Hóu Jǐng's location.
Later, Hóu Jǐng attacked Wáng Sēngbiàn at Bālíng,
but did not succeed.
He returned defeated,
and subsequently killed Quán at Jiāngxià,
sinking his corpse in the Huánghú Jī (Yellow Crane Reef).
Initially,
when Quán was Nántǎo Dūdū (Area Commander for the Southern Campaign),
his friend dreamed that Quán had incurred the displeasure of Shìzǔ.
He woke up and told Quán this.
Less than ten days later,
Quán was indeed captured and imprisoned.
A short time later,
the friend again dreamed that Quán was wearing vermillion robes and walking upon the water.
He again told Quán:
"Sir, do not worry;
you will soon be released."
He then described the dream.
Quán secretly recorded it.
Soon after, he was reinstated,
all just as in the dream.
Quán was especially proficient in ceremonial rites (*Yílǐ*).
He compiled the *Xīnyí* (New Rites) in forty volumes,
which circulated in the world.
Chén Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Ministry of Personnel for Chén) Yáo Chá said: Ruǎn Xiàoxù often said,
Zhongní (Confucius) discussed the Four Disciplines;
they begin with virtuous conduct (Déxíng),
and conclude with literary study (Wénxué).
Those who possess conduct often value simplicity and honesty,
while those with literary talent rarely adhere to rules and standards.
Thus, Wèi and Shí left no writings that could be transmitted,
while Qū and Jiǎ had no reputation for established virtue.
If one were to follow the model of Yóu and Xià,
and draw inspiration from Huí and Qiān,
possessing both literary talent and conduct,
this is seen in Péi Jǐyuán.
Biographies, Chapter 25: Yuán Áng (son Jūnzhèng)
Yuán Áng, courtesy name Qiānlǐ,
was a native of Yángxià, Chén Jùn (Chén Commandery).
His grandfather, Xún,
was Sòng Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the North) and Wú Jùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wu Commandery).
His father, Yǐ,
was Guànjūn Jiāngjūn (General Who Leads the Army) and Yōngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yong Province).
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ reign,
he raised troops to support Jìn'ān Wáng Zixūn.
The affair failed, and he was executed.
Áng was five years old at the time.
His nurse carried him and hid in Lúshān (Mount Lu).
He was released when an amnesty was granted,
but was still exiled to Jìn'ān.
He was permitted to return during the Yuánhuī period,
at which time he was fifteen.
Previously,
when Yǐ was defeated,
his head was sent to the capital
and stored in the Imperial Armory.
It was only now that it was returned.
Áng wailed loudly and vomited blood,
fainting and then reviving.
His cousin (paternal uncle's son), Tuàn, often comforted and advised him to control his grief.
Áng then prepared mourning attire
and built a mourning hut near the tomb.
Later, he and Tuàn together visited their cousin's uncle, Sītú (Minister of Education) Càn.
Càn said to Tuàn:
"That he was orphaned young and yet reached this level [of sincerity],
shows that his innate talent and capacity reside naturally within him."
In the beginning of the Qí Dynasty,
he started his career as Guànjūn (General Who Leads the Army), Ānchéng Wáng Xíng Cānjūn (Acting Staff Officer to the Prince of Ancheng).
He was promoted to Zhēnglǔ Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk to the General Who Conquers the North),
Tàizǐ Shèrén (Attendant to the Crown Prince),
and Wáng Jiǎn Zhènjūn Fǔ Gōngcáo Shǐ (Merit Officer in Wáng Jiǎn's General Who Guards the Army headquarters).
At that time, Jiǎn was Jīngyǐn (Prefect of the Capital).
He often invited Áng to his back hall for a private audience.
Pointing to the North Hall, he said to Áng:
"You will surely reside here [in a high position]."
He was repeatedly promoted to Mìshū Chéng (Palace Secretary),
and Huángmén Shìláng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate).
Áng's original name was Qiānlǐ.
During the Yǒngmíng reign of Qí,
Wǔdì said to him:
"The towering (*ángáng*) colt covers a thousand *lǐ* (*qiānlǐ*).
You possess this quality.
I will now change your personal name to Áng,
and use Qiānlǐ as your courtesy name."
He was assigned externally as Ānnán (General Pacifying the South), Pōyáng Wáng Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Prince of Poyang), and Xúnyáng Gōng Xiāng (Chancellor to the Duke of Xunyang).
Returning, he served as Tàisūn Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant to the Imperial Grandson) and Wèijūn Wǔlíng Wáng Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Prince of Wuling, General Protecting the Army).
He retired due to a maternal mourning period (*Dīng Nèiyōu*),
grieving and weakening his health beyond the prescribed rites.
Before the mourning period was complete, his cousin Tuàn died.
Áng was orphaned young
and had been raised by Tuàn.
Thus, he prepared mourning clothes for a full year (*jīfú*).
Someone was surprised and questioned him about it.
Áng sent a letter to explain, saying:
"I have heard that rites are determined by affection,
and mourning clothes are extended according to sentiment.
Thus, for *xiǎogōng* (minor mourning) in another state,
the severity of mourning is increased by one degree.
For those sharing a hearth, there is *sī* (the lightest mourning cloth),
which is clearly stated in the classics.
This orphan son was unfortunate from an early age,
losing his father's protection when young.
The filial duty of support was not rendered,
and the instructions imparted in the courtyard were not received.
I was a small, ignorant youth,
unable to distinguish between vermillion and purple (high and low status).
My cousin raised and instructed me,
showing me the path of righteousness.
He always exaggerated my worth in conversation
and praised my reputation falsely,
allowing me to achieve success among others;
this truly had its source in him.
Moreover, he expanded my residence
and provided me with luxurious and spacious living quarters.
We shared wealth in common,
allowing me to take as much as I needed.
For more than thirty years since then,
his extreme affection
was no different than that for himself.
My sisters and orphaned nephews
were all supported by him.
The depth of his heartfelt concern
was even stronger at the end.
This kindness and this love
cannot be repaid even unto the grave.
Since the feeling was like that of a full brother,
yet the mourning duty is only for a cousin (*zhūcóng*),
speaking of my heart and the facts,
I truly cannot bear to rest easily.
In the past, Mǎ Léng lived together with his younger brother Yì.
When Yì died,
Léng performed inner mourning for three years.
My failure to put off my mourning clothes
is also caused by my sentiment and thus I institute this observance.
Although my understanding is not equal to the ancients,
my heart sincerely holds feelings of gratitude and longing.
I always wished that after a thousand autumns (death),
I could share a full year of mourning with him.
I did not anticipate that my family would decline
and misfortune would gather suddenly,
leaving me, a remnant surviving among the weeds and dirt,
to again suffer this current hardship.
Whenever I contemplate this, I am plunged into extreme grief,
ever more severe and profound.
Now, while I still have breath remaining,
I wish to fulfill my long-held desire,
hoping to express my grief and unending sorrow,
and slightly extend these boundless feelings.
Although the rites lack explicit scriptural basis for this,
this situation has historical precedents.
I follow my distress and arrive at this decision,
and I must carry it out.
You asked about the proper course of the rites;
I respectfully use this letter to inform you.
Facing the paper, I weep and choke up;
my words are disorganized."
When the mourning period was complete,
he was appointed Yòujūn Shàolíng Wáng Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Prince of Shaoling, General of the Right).
Soon after, he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor).
At that time, the younger brother of Shàngshū Lìng (President of the Department of State Affairs) Wáng Yàn, named Xǔ, was Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
He accepted many bribes and goods.
Áng impeached him according to the facts,
not fearing powerful and influential figures.
He was consequently known at the time as upright and honest.
He was assigned externally as Yùzhāng Nèishǐ (Administrator of Yuzhang).
He left his post due to mourning for his birth mother (*Dīng Suǒshēng Mǔ Yōu*).
When returning with the coffin during the mourning period,
the river route was subjected to violent storms and massive waves.
Áng then tied his clothes to the coffin,
swearing to sink and drown together with it.
When the wind stopped,
the other boats had all sunk.
Only the boat Áng was aboard survived.
Everyone said this was achieved by his sincere spirit.
After the burial was completed,
he was recalled to serve as Jiànwǔ Jiāngjūn (General Who Establishes Might) and Wúxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wuxing).
At the end of the Yǒngyuán period,
the Righteous Army arrived at the capital.
Provincial governors (zhōumù) and commandery administrators (jùnshǒu) all surrendered upon seeing the approach,
but Án​g (昂) alone defended the border and refused to receive orders.
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) personally wrote a letter of instruction, saying:
“Indeed, misfortune and fortune have no fixed gateway,
but rise and fall have their measure.
If Heaven has cast someone aside,
who can save them?
Opportunity comes but once;
it is advisable to plan for it early.
I have recently heard rumors
that you intend to occupy one corner and remain hesitant,
but as I do not fully know your true, refined intentions,
I shall briefly express my views.
That solitary man's (Xiāo Bǎo Juàn's 蕭寶卷) madness and perversity
are unheard of throughout history.
His extreme violence and tyranny
have grown worse over the months and years.
Heaven has not yet destroyed Qí (齊),
and a sagely and enlightened one has initiated the mandate.
The millions of people have someone to rely on,
and the populace is reviving.
I bore the responsibility of leading the charge,
sweeping clean the capital region (Jīngyì),
and am currently restoring order and returning to righteousness,
punishing the guilty and comforting the people.
Since my forces arrived,
there have been no hostile battle arrays facing us.
Now, the Imperial might is present in all four directions,
the protracted siege has closed,
forces far and near are all gathered,
and men and gods cooperate in the effort.
We have elite troops numbering tens of thousands
and thousands of groups of armored cavalry.
Using these forces to attack and fight,
where would we go and not conquer?
Moreover, Jiànyè (建業) is an isolated city,
and its people harbor thoughts of leaving and resisting.
Those bound and brought before the army headquarters
succeed one another day and night.
The date of its collapse and destruction
is clearly not far off.
Furthermore, Mars (Yínghuò 熒惑) has emerged at the Duānmén (端門) gate,
and Venus (Tàibái 太白) has entered the Dī Shì (氐室) lunar mansion.
Heavenly signs are manifested above,
and human affairs correspond below;
this congruence, achieved without planning,
is truly occurring at this very moment.
Furthermore, Fàn Xiù (范岫) and Shēn Zhòu (申冑)
have long offered sincere submissions;
each leads his subordinates
and acts as a supporting force.
Shěn Fǎ Yǔ (沈法瑀), Sūn Xī (孫肸), and Zhū Duān (朱端)
have already pacified the Wú Huì (吳會) region in advance.
Yet you wish to use your insignificant commandery
to resist a massive and imposing army.
Since the root is already toppling,
how can the branches and leaves attach themselves?
Even children and herders
all say this is mistaken.
To demand such a clear judgment
is something you truly have not attained.
Now, exhausting your efforts for a debauched ruler
is not sufficient to be called loyalty,
and causing your household to be exterminated
is not what is called filiality.
If both loyalty and filiality are lost,
upon what will you rely?
How is this comparable to promptly changing your plans
and thereby inviting great fortune upon yourself?
If you advance, you will avoid disaster and preserve your life;
if you retire (remain in office), you will long maintain your stipend and position.
The propriety of leaving or joining
I hope you will carefully consider and choose.
If you stubbornly cling to delusion and continue thus,
sharing the evil and refusing to repent,
the moment the great army arrives,
punishment will extend to the three kindreds.
Although this may leave you with later regret,
how could it possibly be rectified?
Wishing to lay bare what is in my heart,
I therefore send this message now.”
Án​g replied, saying:
“The official arrived,
and I received your instruction with honor.
I understand that relying on public opinion,
you say that I, your servant, have actions supporting the royal cause,
and I am further rebuked
for alone failing to offer submission.
Reflecting upon your severe decree,
I feel as if standing upon a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.
The interior territory of Sān Wú (三吳)
is not a place for military deployment.
Moreover, with one commandery in a remote corner,
how could it be of use?
I recently received an imperial decree,
stating that this border was highly distressed,
and I was dispatched to pacify and console it.
Since I heard your banners and pennants arrived,
all others have knelt submissively before the army headquarters.
I am the only servant who dares to be late,
precisely because I inwardly measure myself as ordinary and humble,
having no ability in civil or martial matters;
I am simply a humble man from the Eastern Region.
Although I wish to offer my devotion,
it would not increase the bravery of the great army,
nor would my foolish silence,
diminish the might of the assembled forces.
Fortunately, relying on the great tolerance and magnanimity of the General (Jiāngjūn),
I may proceed with courtesy and ease.
I humbly reflect that even a small bestowal of one meal
inspires one to sacrifice oneself;
how much more so, when eating a man's stipend,
to instantly forget him?
Not only would public opinion forbid it,
but I also fear that Your Excellency (Míng Gōng 明公) would disdain it.
This is why I hesitated
and have not yet hastened to present my submission.
Consequently, due to my insignificant status,
a weighty command has been issued.
It shakes and burns in my heart,
making me forget where I stand.
Truly considering the principles and reflecting clearly,
I still fear your majestic arrival.”
When Jiànkāng city was pacified,
Án​g presented himself bound at the palace gates.
Emperor Gāozǔ pardoned him and did not hold him accountable.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (天監),
he was appointed Aide to the Prince of Línchuān (Línchuān Wáng 臨川王) for the Rear Army.
Án​g respectfully submitted a memorial of thanks, saying:
“Grace has descended at a moment of utter despair,
and joy has gathered on the day my heart was cold with fear.
A flame returning from ashes is not an adequate analogy;
a withered plant sprouting new growth does not compare.
Tucking up my robe and gathering my feet,
my confusion and distress are beyond bearing.
I, your servant, have perused the Sān Fén (三墳)
and fully examined the Liù Diǎn (六典),
reviewed the statutes concerning reward and punishment,
and investigated the laws of life and death.
None fail to strictly enforce the Five Punishments (Wǔ Pì) in the court of an enlightened ruler,
nor to rigorously uphold the Three Chapters (Sān Zhāng) in the age of the sages.
Thus, when the assembly at Túshān (塗山) first took place,
it resulted in the execution of Fángfēng (防風).
When the city of Fēng Yì (酆邑) was first established,
there was the campaign against the Marquis of Chóng (Chóng Hóu 崇侯).
Never has the constitution been lenient toward one deserving of execution,
nor has punishment been deferred for a family worthy of death,
yet I, your servant, have passed through ten thousand deaths and gained a single life.
Extending grace even to the guilty—
this is truly magnificent concerning your servant.
Tearing open my heart and dripping blood,
I dare to beg permission to speak of it.
I, your servant, am a humble man from the Eastern Region;
what merit is there in my learning or conduct?
Since I differ from the calling goose and the straight tree,
I never expected to tie the official sash or brush my cap.
I merely borrowed the court’s grace
and exchanged farming for officialdom.
In past years, I unworthily held office,
maintaining rank in the eastern corner.
I looked up as your majestic army marched,
driving forward like the wind and sweeping across like lightning.
At that time,
those offering the symbols of rule arrived daily,
and those bearing jade and silk (tribute) were visible everywhere.
I alone, your foolish servant,
suddenly became confused about the great principle of righteousness,
sacrificing myself for something as light as a swan's feather,
forgetting the importance of uniting in virtue.
However, the Sān Wú region is treacherous and frivolous,
and the Five Lakes (Wǔ Hú) connect to all directions.
It often gives rise to revolts like that of Tián Dān (田儋),
and I always feared disaster like that of Yīn Tōng (殷通).
I futilely admired Jūn Yú (君魚) for protecting his border,
and consequently missed the opportunity to submit like Shī Juān (師涓).
Those who arrive late are executed;
I accept this punishment.
Who would say
that enforcing clear justice to satisfy the multitude is inappropriate?
Fortunately, the simplification of the law is magnanimous,
and I received forgiveness like the loosening of the net.
I ought still to be demoted to gathering firewood,
but instead, I was immediately released from shackling and tattooing.
You gathered my bones and breathed life back into my soul,
returning me to the registry of the common people.
You washed away my faults and cleansed my filth,
allowing me to enter Chǔ (楚) and travel to Chén (陳).
Heaven’s wave has already cleansed me,
and the soothing clouds have immediately bathed me.
The ancients had a saying: ‘It is not difficult to die;
it is difficult to manage one's death.’
What your servant has received
is unrecorded in history.
The place where your servant ought to have died
I do not yet know where it lies.”
Gāozǔ replied:
“I give the *Shègōu*,
you, Minister (Qīng), must not treat yourself as an outsider.”
Soon after, he was appointed Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
That year, he was promoted to Shìzhōng.
The following year,
he went out to serve as the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Xúnyáng,
acting as the Governor (*xíng* jiāng zhōu shì) of Jiāngzhōu.
In the sixth year (of the reign period),
he was summoned to become the Minister (Shàngshū) of the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
He repeatedly submitted memorials declining the post.
He was transferred to become the Minister (Shàngshū) of Zuǒmín,
and concurrently served as Yòu Púyè.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Guózǐ Jìjiǔ;
his concurrent position as Púyè remained unchanged,
and he oversaw the Grand Director (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Yùzhōu.
In the eighth year,
he went out to serve as General of Majestic Benevolence (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wú Jùn.
In the eleventh year,
he returned to the capital to serve as the Minister (Shàngshū) of the Five Ministries of War (Wǔbīng),
and again concurrently served as Yòu Púyè.
Before formally accepting the post,
there was an imperial edict granting him the substantive (i.e., full) title.
Soon after, holding his original office, he was appointed to oversee the Minister (Shàngshū) of the Ministry of Public Works (Qǐbù),
and was granted the title of Shìzhōng.
In the fourteenth year,
Mǎ Xiānpǐn defeated the Wèi army at Qú Shān,
and an edict temporarily authorized Áng to carry the credentials,
and go to comfort the troops.
In the fifteenth year,
he was promoted to Zuǒ Púyè,
and soon became Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng) and General of Manifest Favor (Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn).
In Pǔtōng three years (3rd year of Pǔtōng era),
he became Central Drafting Supervisor (Zhōngshū Jiān) and Governor (Yǐn) of Dānyáng.
That year, he was advanced to the title General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn),
and again became Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng).
Based on this title, he was granted the honor of establishing a government office and enjoying privileges equal to the Three High Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
and was provided with musicians for drum and wind instruments (*gǔchuī*).
Before formally accepting the post,
he again oversaw the Guózǐ Jìjiǔ.
In Dàtōng first year (1st year of Dàtōng era),
he was additionally granted the title of Central Drafting Supervisor (Zhōngshū Jiān),
and was granted thirty personal retainers (qīnxìn).
Soon after, he memorialized to resign the post of Jìjiǔ,
was advanced to the title Grand General Stabilizing the Army (Zhōng Fǔjūn Dà Jiāngjūn),
and was promoted to Minister of Works (Sīkōng), Shìzhōng, and Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng).
His retainers and musicians remained as before.
In the fifth year,
he was additionally granted Tèjìn and Grand Master of the Left Glorious Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū),
and his personal retainers were increased to eighty people.
In Dàtóng six years (6th year of Dàtóng era),
he died,
at the age of eighty.
An imperial edict stated:
“Shìzhōng, Tèjìn, Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū, and Sīkōng Áng,
has suddenly passed away,
causing sorrow and grief in Our heart.
The Duke’s temperament was solid and pure,
his resolve was sincere, loyal, and upright,
he regulated affairs in the court,
and his excellent counsel was always respected.
Bestowing posthumous honors to display virtue,
is truly a fine regulation.
He shall be posthumously granted his original offices,
one set of musicians (gǔchuī),
provided with special funeral implements from the Eastern Garden (Dōngyuán Mìqì),
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
twenty thousand coins,
one hundred bolts of silk and cloth,
two hundred catties of wax,
and mourning rituals shall commence this very day.”
Originally,
Áng, in his final memorial before death,
refused posthumous grants and titles,
commanding his sons not to submit a biography (*xíngzhuàng*) to the throne or to erect a tomb inscription (*zhìmíng*).
Anything that was generally required (for the funeral),
was all to be stopped and reduced.
He further said:
“I began my official career having left my humble status,
I did not expect wealth or high status,
but my official sequence did not deviate from proper ranks,
and my clothing and food roughly knew honor and disgrace (i.e., were appropriate for my status).
Closing the coffin with this realization,
I have no shame before my hometown.
Previously, I disgraced Wúxīng (referring to his governorship there),
it was a time between darkness and light (i.e., political transition),
I was ignorant of former knowledge,
and unrecognized by the sacred dynasty (Shèngcháo).
Not knowing the Mandate of Heaven,
I willingly brought upon myself public execution (or disgrace),
but fortunately, I received exceptional grace,
and thus my entire household was saved.
I considered myself guilty and marginalized,
with all hopes of honor cut off;
to preserve my life,
I considered the greatest fortune.
I never expected to receive so much favor and spiritual grace,
to reach this point.
I always wished to exhaust my sincerity in repaying this debt,
to express my true feelings.
Therefore, whenever the court raised an army for a northern expedition,
I always requested permission to go,
swearing my profound devotion—
this was truly not false speech.
Since I am useless and weak, with nothing to offer,
I was never permitted to go.
Although I wished to expend my life,
the means for that attempt were not followed.
Today, as I close my eyes,
my regret is complete in the grave.
If my soul possesses consciousness,
I look forward to repaying the kindness by weaving grass.
The sacred dynasty (Shèngcháo) follows ancient customs,
knowing my reputation and rank,
there might be posthumous grace;
although this is a standard institutional practice of the state,
for me, it should not be applied.
Should there be any posthumous grant of office,
my sons must carefully avoid accepting it.”
His sons repeatedly submitted memorials presenting this request,
but the imperial edict did not permit it.
He was granted the posthumous title Mùzhèng Gōng (Reverent and Upright Duke).
His son, Jūnzhèng,
had an elegant appearance,
and was skillful in managing his life and affairs,
and as the son of a high official, he gained fame and reputation among his contemporaries.
After a short time,
he concurrently served as Clerk (Láng) in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
He resigned his office due to mourning for his mother.
When the mourning period was complete,
he served as Mentor (Yǒu) to Shàolíng Wáng, Chief Clerk (Chángshǐ) to the Northern Central Commandant (Běi Zhōngláng), and Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Dōngyáng.
Soon after, he was summoned back to the capital,
but three hundred local citizens and scholars, including Xú Tiānyòu, went to the palace gates requesting that he be allowed to stay for one more year.
The imperial edict did not permit this,
and he was immediately appointed Commander (Nèishǐ) of Yùzhāng,
and soon transferred to become Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wú Jùn.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
he led several hundred men to follow Shàolíng Wáng to provide aid.
When the capital city fell,
he returned to his commandery.
Jūnzhèng had a good reputation for administering affairs while in office,
but he accumulated wealth and property,
and his clothes and decorations were luxurious.
The rebel sent Yú Zǐyuè to attack him.
Dài Sēngyì, the Commandant (Shùzhǔ) of Xīnchéng, urged him to resist and defend,
but Wú Lù Yìnggōng and others feared that if the rebels won,
they would seize their assets.
They then said:
“The rebel army is extremely sharp;
their advance cannot be countered.
If we resist them now,
we fear the hearts of the people will not follow us.”
Jūnzhèng was naturally timid and cowardly,
so he sent rice, oxen, and wine,
and went out of the city to welcome Zǐyuè.
Once Zǐyuè arrived,
he plundered his wealth, goods, sons, and daughters,
and because of this event, Jūnzhèng fell ill and died.
The historian comments: Heaven is high and Earth is low—
this establishes the position of ruler and minister.
The pine and the bamboo share the same steadfast character;
they do not change their resolve in the winter cold.
Yuán Qiānlǐ’s fate coincided with collapse and disintegration,
his body met with a disastrous era.
Although the sole ruler (Sòng) had lost virtue,
the minister's resolve did not waver.
When he submitted a strongly worded memorial to Gāozǔ,
he did not lose his loyalty and integrity.
This also preserved the spirit of Yí and Shū (Bó Yí and Shū Qí).
Ultimately, he became a pillar of the Liáng court—
how beautiful that is!
Biographies, Chapter 26: Chén Qìngzhī, Lán Qīn
Chén Qìngzhī, courtesy name Zǐyún,
was a man from Guóshān, Yìxīng.
In his youth, he followed Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ naturally loved (reading/chess),
and often continued without stopping from night until dawn.
His peers were all tired and asleep,
only Qìngzhī did not sleep.
Hearing a call, he would immediately arrive,
and was highly favored and appreciated.
He followed Gāozǔ in moving east to pacify Jiànyè,
and gradually became a Secretary (Zhǔshū).
He distributed wealth and gathered scholars,
constantly thinking of ways to serve.
He was appointed Grand Master of the Court (Fèng Cháoqǐng).
During Pǔtōng,
Yuán Fǎsēng (the Inspector of Xúzhōu for Wèi) at Péngchéng requested to defect internally.
Qìngzhī was made General of Martial Awe (Wǔwēi Jiāngjūn),
and with Hú Lóngyá and Chéng Jǐngjùn, he led various armies to meet and receive him.
Upon returning, he was appointed General Who Proclaims Fierceness (Xuānměng Jiāngjūn) and Chief Commander of Wéndé.
He then led two thousand troops
to escort Zōng, the Prince of Yùzhāng, into Xúzhōu to take up his post.
Wèi sent Yuán Yánmíng, the Prince of Ānfēng, and Yuán Yù, the Prince of Línhuái, leading twenty thousand troops to resist,
and they camped at Zhìdí.
Yánmíng first dispatched his auxiliary general Qiū Dàqiān to build a fortress at Xúnliáng,
observing the troops near the border.
Qìngzhī advanced and assaulted the fortress;
it immediately collapsed after a single drum roll.
Later, the Prince of Yùzhāng abandoned the army and fled to Wèi.
The troops all scattered and dispersed.
None of the generals could stop them,
so Qìngzhī cut open the gates and retreated by night,
allowing the soldiers to be saved.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng (526 CE),
General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn) Yuán Shù went out to campaign at Shòuchūn.
Qìngzhī was appointed Acting Governor (jiǎjié) and Overall Supervisor of Military Affairs (zǒng zhī jūnshì).
Lǐ Xiàn, the Inspector of Yùzhōu for Wèi, sent his son Chángjūn to build two separate cities to resist.
Qìngzhī attacked them,
and Xiàn’s strength failed, whereupon he surrendered.
Qìngzhī entered and occupied his city.
He was transferred to be an Attendant in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng Zhíhé),
and was granted the title Marquis of Guānzhōng (Guānzhōng Hóu).
In the first year of Dàtōng (527 CE),
he served under Commander Cáo Zhòngzōng in the campaign against Wōyáng.
Wèi sent General Who Conquers the South (Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn) Yuán Zhāo, Prince of Chángshān, and others, leading one hundred fifty thousand cavalry and infantry to reinforce the area.
The vanguard reached Tuójiàn,
forty *lǐ* away from Wōyáng.
Qìngzhī wanted to meet them in battle.
Wéi Fàng argued that the enemy’s vanguard must be lightly equipped and elite.
If we fight and win,
it will not be considered a great achievement.
But if we are unsuccessful,
it will damage the morale of our army.
The military classic speaks of waiting, well-rested, for the weary enemy;
it is better not to attack.
Qìngzhī said:
“The Wèi troops have traveled far
and are all exhausted.
Since they are still far from us,
they surely won't suspect us.
Before they can concentrate their forces,
we must break their morale
by taking them by surprise;
there is no reason why we should fail to defeat them.
Furthermore, I heard that the camp occupied by the barbarians
is surrounded by abundant woods,
so they certainly will not venture out at night.
If you, gentlemen, have doubts,
Qìngzhī requests permission to capture them alone.”
Thereupon, he led two hundred cavalry from his command and swiftly attacked,
smashing their vanguard.
The Wèi troops were greatly terrified.
Qìngzhī then returned and advanced with the other generals, setting up continuous camps.
They occupied the city of Wōyáng
and entered into a standoff with the Wèi army.
From spring until winter,
they fought dozens or hundreds of battles.
The troops grew weary and morale declined.
The Wèi reinforcements again wanted to build a fortress behind their army.
Zhòngzōng and the others, fearing attack from both front and rear,
planned to withdraw the army.
Qìngzhī stood holding his staff of authority (jié) at the camp gate and said:
“We came here together
and have passed through a full year.
The consumption of provisions and weaponry
has been extremely high.
Now all the armies lack the will to fight
and are planning to retreat.
Is this how one seeks to establish merit and fame?
It is merely gathering together to plunder and commit violence!
I have heard that placing troops in a position of certain death
allows them to seek life.
We must wait until the barbarians have fully concentrated
and then fight them.
If you truly wish to return the troops,
Qìngzhī has a separate, secret imperial decree.
Whoever violates orders today
will immediately be dealt with according to the clear edict.”
Zhòngzōng admired his plan
and followed it.
The Wèi troops, supporting each other in formation, built thirteen fortresses.
Qìngzhī, with gags in their mouths, went out at night,
and captured four of their fortified camps.
Wáng Wěi, the commander of Wōyáng city, begged for surrender.
The remaining nine cities
still had abundant troops and weapons.
He displayed the captives and severed heads,
then attacked them with drums beating and shouts.
They consequently collapsed in a great rout,
and almost all were killed or captured.
The Wō River was choked with bodies,
and more than thirty thousand men and women surrendered from the city.
An imperial edict established Xī Xúzhōu in the region of Wōyáng.
The combined armies, following up on their victory, advanced to Chéngfù.
Gāozǔ praised this
and bestowed upon Qìngzhī a handwritten edict which said:
“You are fundamentally not of military lineage,
nor from a powerful clan,
yet you yearned for success and seized the opportunity,
leading you to this point.
You must deeply contemplate extraordinary strategies
and skillfully achieve a good conclusion.
To open red gates to welcome guests,
and to spread your fame upon bamboo and silk—
is this not the mark of a great man?”
In the beginning of Dàtōng (527 CE),
Yuán Hào, the Prince of Běihǎi for Wèi, having fled because of the great chaos in his court,
came to surrender,
and requested to be established as the ruler of Wèi.
Gāozǔ accepted him,
appointed Qìngzhī Acting Governor (jiǎjié) and General of Rushing Courage (Biāoyǒng Jiāngjūn),
and sent Yuán Hào back north.
At Huànshuǐ, Hào assumed the title of Wèi Emperor

and granted Qìngzhī the titles of Commissioner with Staff (Shǐ Chíjíe), General Who Guards the North (Zhènběi Jiāngjūn), Protector of the Army (Hùjūn), and Grand Commander of the Vanguard (Qiánjūn Dà Dūdū).
Starting from Zhìxiàn,
he advanced and captured Xíngchéng,
and subsequently reached Suīyáng.
Wèi General Qiū Dàqiān had seventy thousand troops
and divided them into nine fortresses to resist.
Qìngzhī attacked them,
and from dawn until the Hour of Shēn (3-5 PM),
he captured three of the camps.
Dàqiān then surrendered.
At that time, Wèi General Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn) Yuán Huīyè, Prince of Jìyīn, led twenty thousand Yǔlín troops and minor officials to rescue Liáng and Sòng.
They advanced and camped at Kǎochéng.
The city was surrounded by water on all four sides,
and the defenses were stern and secure.
Qìngzhī ordered the construction of a rampart upon the water,
attacked and captured the city,
took Huīyè alive,
and seized seven thousand eight hundred carriages loaded with grain.
He then rushed toward Dàliáng;
upon seeing his banners, the populace pledged allegiance.
Hào promoted Qìngzhī to General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn), Inspector of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ), and Duke of Wǔdū (Wǔdū Gōng).
He then led the troops westward.
led the imperial guard, the Yǔlín (Feathered Forest), and the masses of imperial clansmen and their sons, totaling seventy thousand men.
They occupied Xíngyáng to resist Hào.
Since their troops were elite and powerful,
and the city was also dangerous and secure (well-fortified),
Qìngzhī's attack could not take it.
The Wèi General Yuán Tiānmù's main army was also about to arrive.
He first dispatched his General of Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn) Ěrzhū Tǔmò'ér leading five thousand Hu cavalry.
The Cavalry Commander Lǔ Ān led nine thousand infantry and cavalry from Xiàzhōu,
to reinforce Yáng Yù.
He further sent the Right Vice Director Ěrzhū Shìlóng,
and the Inspector of Xījīngzhōu Wáng Pí, with ten thousand cavalry,
to occupy Hǔláo.
Tiānmù and Tǔmò'ér successively arrived, one after the other.
Their flags and drums were visible to each other.
At that time, Xíngyáng had not yet been taken.
All the officers and men were frightened.
Qìngzhī then unsaddled and fed his horses (i.e., prepared for battle),
and announced to the troops, saying:
"Since I arrived here,
the number of cities we have slaughtered and territories we have seized
is truly not small.
You gentlemen have killed the fathers and elder brothers of others,
and abducted the daughters and sons of others,
which is also countless.
The forces of Tiānmù
are all our bitter enemies.
We only number seven thousand,
while the barbarians number more than three hundred thousand.
Regarding the matter today,
righteousness means we should not seek survival.
I believe that since the barbarian cavalry cannot be matched on the open plain,
and before they have all arrived,
we must flatten their city walls and fortresses.
Gentlemen, do not harbor doubts,
thereby bringing slaughter upon yourselves."
With a single drum beat, he ordered them all to climb the city walls.
The brave warriors Sòng Jǐngxiū of Dōngyáng and Yú Tiānmǐn of Yìxīng climbed over the parapets and entered.
They subsequently overcame the city.
Shortly afterward, the Wèi forces converged outside the city.
Qìngzhī led three thousand cavalry to fight them, facing away from the city.
He thoroughly defeated them.
Lǔ Ān begged for surrender on the battlefield.
Yuán Tiānmù and Ěrzhū Tǔmò'ér escaped with only their single horses.
They collected the stores and supplies of Xíngyáng;
the cattle, horses, grain, and silk cloth were beyond counting.
They advanced to Hǔláo.
Ěrzhū Shìlóng abandoned the city and fled.
The Wèi sovereign Yuán Zǐyōu was terrified,
and fled to Bìngzhōu.
His King of Línhuái Yuán Yù and King of Ānfēng Yuán Yánmíng led the multitude of officials,
sealed the government offices and treasuries,
prepared the imperial carriage,
and respectfully welcomed Hào into the Luòyáng Palace.
He took control of the main hall,
changed the reign title, and granted a general amnesty.
Hào appointed Qìngzhī as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chējì Dàjiāngjūn), and Left Grand Master of Radiant Favor (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū),
and increased his stipends by ten thousand households.
The Wèi Grand General, King of Shàngdǎng, Yuán Tiānmù, Wáng Lǎoshēng, and Lǐ Shūrén again led forty thousand troops.
They attacked and captured Dàliáng.
They separately dispatched Lǎoshēng and Fèi Mù with twenty thousand troops,
to occupy Hǔláo.
Diāo Xuān and Diāo Shuāng entered Liáng and Sòng (territories).
Qìngzhī attacked and raided in every direction,
and they all submitted.
Tiānmù, with more than ten cavalrymen, crossed the Yellow River northwards.
Emperor Gāozǔ again bestowed an imperial edict (by his own hand), praising him.
All the troops under Qìngzhī's command wore white robes.
Wherever they went, the enemy scattered.
Before this, a nursery rhyme in Luòyáng went:
"Famous strategists and great generals, do not secure yourselves!
A thousand troops and ten thousand horses must avoid the white robes."
From setting out at Zhìxiàn to reaching Luòyáng, it took fourteen *xún* (140 days).
He pacified thirty-two cities,
fought forty-seven battles,
and met no resistance wherever he went.
Initially,
Yuán Zǐyōu had only fled with a single horseman,
but the palace guards and imperial concubines were unchanged from their usual state.
Once Hào had achieved his ambition,
he became dissolute in wine and women.
He therefore feasted and reveled day and night,
and no longer attended to affairs of state.
He conspired wickedly with the Kings of Ānfēng and Línhuái,
intending to betray the favor shown by the (Liáng) Court,
and sever the tribute relationship.
It was only because the current situation was unstable
and they still required Qìngzhī's military assistance
that they appeared amicable externally while differing internally.
Their words were often resentful and harsh.
Qìngzhī knew this in his heart,
and secretly made his own plans.
He then advised Hào, saying:
"We have traveled far to reach this place.
There are still many who have not submitted.
If people learn of our true strength,
they will join forces again.
Being safe, one must not forget danger,
so we must prepare strategies in advance.
It is proper to petition the Son of Heaven (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng),
to request more elite troops.
Furthermore, order all the surrounding prefectures
that any southerners captured here
must all be organized and sent to us."
Hào wanted to follow this advice.
Yuán Yánmíng advised Hào, saying:
"Chén Qìngzhī's troops do not exceed several thousand,
yet they are already difficult to control.
If we now increase his forces,
would he still be willing to serve us?
Once the reins of power are gone,
every action will be dictated by others.
The ancestral shrines of Wèi
will perish here."
Hào thereby became suspicious,
and gradually grew distant and mistrustful.
Fearing that Qìngzhī would send a secret memorial (to Emperor Wǔ),
Hào memorialized Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ), saying:
"Héběi and Hénán have been settled simultaneously.
Only Ěrzhū Róng still dares to be arrogant and unruly.
Your servant and Qìngzhī are perfectly capable of capturing and eliminating him.
The prefectures and commanderies have newly submitted,
and they currently require appeasement and comfort.
It is inappropriate to send more troops
and disturb the populace."
Gāozǔ then ordered all the armies to halt at the border.
The southerners remaining in Luòyáng did not exceed ten thousand.
The Qiāng and Yí (local barbarians) outnumbered them tenfold.
The Deputy Commander Mǎ Fúniàn spoke to Qìngzhī, saying:
"Merit that is too great to be rewarded,
and fame that shakes the ruler endangers the person.
Since both these conditions exist,
how can the General not be worried?
Since antiquity,
those who depose the incompetent and establish the worthy,
or support the endangered and settle difficulties,
rarely achieve a good end.
Now the General’s might shakes the Central Plain,
his fame moves the regions north of the Yellow River.
If you were to slay Hào and occupy Luò (Luòyáng),
it would be a unique opportunity in a thousand years."
Qìngzhī did not follow the advice.
Hào had previously appointed Qìngzhī as the Inspector of Xúzhōu.
He therefore strongly requested to be assigned to that post.
Hào secretly feared him,
and consequently did not send him.
He then said:
"The Emperor has entirely entrusted you with the territory of Luòyáng.
Upon hearing that you wish to abandon this court duty
and go to Péngchéng (Xúzhōu seat),
he believes that you are hastily grasping for wealth and honor,
and not planning for the state.
His handwritten edicts are frequent and urgent,
and I fear I will incur the blame of a servant."
Qìngzhī dared not speak of it again.

The Wèi General Tiānzhù Ěrzhū Róng, Right Vice Director Ěrzhū Shìlóng, Grand Commander Yuán Tiānmù, General of Cavalry Ěrzhū Tǔmò'ér, Róng’s Chief Clerk Gāo Huān, the Xiānbēi, and the Rùiruì (Rouran),
amassed troops, estimated at one million,
and, bringing the Wèi sovereign Yuán Zǐyōu, came to attack Hào.
Hào occupied Luòyáng for sixty-five days.
All the cities he had captured
rebelled simultaneously.
Qìngzhī crossed the Yellow River and defended Běizhōngláng Chéng (Northern Zhonglang City).
In three days, he fought eleven battles,
inflicting massive casualties.
Róng was about to retreat.
At that time, there was a man named Liú Língzhù,
skilled in astronomy.
He then told Róng:
"Within ten days,
Hénán will be completely settled."
Róng then tied logs into rafts,
and crossed from Xiáshí.
He fought Hào at Héquiáo (River Bridge).
Hào suffered a massive defeat.
He fled to Línyǐng,
encountered bandits, and was captured.
Luòyáng fell.
Qìngzhī, with several thousand cavalry and infantry,
formed a defensive square and turned eastward to retreat.
Róng personally came to pursue him.
He happened upon the Sōnggāo Mountain floodwaters overflowing,
and his soldiers perished and scattered.
Qìngzhī then shaved his beard and hair to become a *shāmén* (monk).
He traveled covertly to Yùzhōu.
The people of Yùzhōu, including Chéng Dàoyōng, secretly escorted him out via Rǔyīn.
Upon reaching the capital (Jiànkāng),
he was subsequently appointed General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn) for his merit,
enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngxīng County,
with a tax base of one thousand five hundred households.
He was sent out as a Chief Bearer of the Imperial Ensign and Grand Supervisor of all military affairs along the Huái River, Fènwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Běiyǎnzhōu.
At that time, there was a demonic rebel Buddhist monk Sēngqiáng who proclaimed himself emperor.
The local magnate Cài Bólóng raised an army in support of him.
Sēngqiáng had considerable knowledge of magical arts,
and they incited and deluded each other.
Their forces reached thirty thousand.
They attacked and captured Běixúzhōu.
Jìyīn Tàishǒu Yáng Qǐwén abandoned the city and fled.
Zhōnglí Tàishǒu Shān Xībǎo was killed.
Qìngzhī was sent to suppress them.
The imperial carriage proceeded to Báixià to see him off.
Gāozǔ said to Qìngzhī:
"The soldiers of Jiāng and Huái are strong;
their vanguard is difficult to withstand.
You should use strategy to control them,
and not engage in a decisive battle."
Qìngzhī accepted the order and departed.
Less than a full day had passed,
when he beheaded Bólóng and Sēngqiáng,
and sent their heads as a report.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he was appointed Grand Supervisor of the military affairs of the four prefectures of Nán Sī, Běi Sī, Xī Yù, and Yù, and Governor of Nán Sī and Běi Sī prefectures.
All other titles remained as before.
When Qìngzhī arrived at his post,
he then besieged Xuánhù.
He defeated Wèi Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ Lóu Qǐ and Yángzhōu Cìshǐ Shì Yúnbǎo at Zhēnshuǐ.
He also defeated Xíngtái Sūn Téng, Dàdūdū Hóu Jìn, Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yáo Xióng, and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Sīmǎ Gōng at Chǔchéng.
He disbanded the garrison troops at Yìyáng,
ceased water and land transport,
and the various prefectures along the rivers and lakes were all able to rest.
He opened six thousand qǐng of farmland.
Two years later,
the granaries were full.
Gāozǔ always praised and rewarded him.
He also memorialized to abolish Nánsīzhōu,
restore Ānlù Jùn,
and establish Shàngmíng Jùn.
In the second year of Dàtóng,
Wèi dispatched general Hóu Jǐng leading seventy thousand men to invade Chǔzhōu.
Cìshǐ Huán Hé was captured.
Jǐng then advanced his army to the Huái River,
and sent a letter to Qìngzhī asking him to surrender.
An imperial edict ordered Xiāngtán Hóu Tuì, Yòuwèi Xiàhóu Kuí, and others to go to their aid.
When the army reached Líjiāng,
Qìngzhī had already defeated Jǐng.
At that time, there was a severe cold and snow.
Jǐng abandoned his baggage and fled.
Qìngzhī collected it and returned.
He was promoted to the title of Rénwēi Jiāngjūn.
In that year,
Yùzhōu suffered from famine.
Qìngzhī opened the granaries to provide relief,
saving many lives.
Eight hundred people, including Lǐ Shēng from the prefecture, presented a memorial requesting a stele to be erected to praise his virtue.
An imperial edict granted it.
In the tenth month of the fifth year,
he died,
at the age of fifty-six.
He was posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
with a set of drum and wind instruments.
His posthumous title was Wǔ.
An imperial edict ordered Yìxīng Jùn to dispatch five hundred able-bodied men to attend the funeral.
Qìngzhī was reverent and cautious by nature.
He did not wear fine silks,
did not enjoy music,
was not skilled in archery,
and was not good with horses,
but he was good at comforting his soldiers
and could obtain their utmost loyalty.
His eldest son, Zhāo, inherited his titles.
His fifth son, Xīn,
had the courtesy name Jūnzhāng.
At seven, he could ride and shoot.
At twelve, he followed his father to Luòyáng,
but fell ill on the way
and returned to the capital.
He went to Hónglú Qīng Zhū Yì,
who inquired about the situation in the north.
Xīn gathered earth and drew on the ground,
pointing and explaining clearly.
Zhū Yì was very impressed by him.
In the fourth year of Dàtóng,
he became Shàolíng Wáng Chángshì, Wéndé Zhǔshuài, and Yòuwèi Zhàngzhǔ.
An imperial edict ordered him to assist in the defense of Yìyáng.
Wèi Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Yáo Xióng was
a fierce general in the north,
and his nephew Bǎolè
was particularly brave and daring.
When Qìngzhī besieged Xuánhù,
Xióng came to his aid.
Bǎolè asked for a single horse to challenge him to battle.
Xīn spurred his horse directly towards Bǎolè.
Yáo Xióng immediately dispersed and fled.
He then captured Zhēnchéng.
In the sixth year,
he was appointed Wēiyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Master of Xiǎoxiànchéng,
but was dismissed for an official matter.
In the tenth year,
the demonic rebel Wáng Qínzōng rose up in Bāshān Jùn.
Xīn was made Xuānměng Jiāngjūn
and given a temporary imperial seal to suppress him.
After Qínzōng was pacified,
he was appointed Yīnlíng Shùzhǔ and Běiqiáo Tàishǒu,
but did not take up the post due to illness.
He was then appointed Piàojì Wàibīng,
and soon became Línchuān Tàishǒu.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
Hóu Jǐng besieged Lìyáng.
An imperial edict summoned Xīn back.
Xīn reported:
"Cǎishí urgently needs a strong garrison.
Wáng Zhì's naval forces are weak and light;
I fear they will not suffice."
Thereupon, Xīn was appointed Yúnqí Jiāngjūn,
replacing Zhì.
Before he could reach Zhǔ,
Jǐng had already crossed the river.
He was then ordered to lead his subordinates to patrol outside the city,
and was not allowed to enter and guard it.
He wanted to flee to Jīngkǒu,
but was captured by Jǐng.
Jǐng saw Xīn's earnestness,
and so he kept him and drank heavily with him,
saying:
"I have obtained you here;
no one else can do anything."
He ordered Xīn to gather his troops
and intended to use him.
Xīn vowed not to comply.
Jǐng had his Yítóng Fàn Táobàng strictly guard him.
Xīn then persuaded Táobàng to lead his subordinates to surrender,
and to attack and kill Wáng Wěi and Sòng Zǐxiān as proof.
Táobàng agreed,
and they made an alliance.
A letter was shot into the city,
and Xīn was sent to rappel down at night and enter.
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased,
and issued an edict to immediately accept the surrender.
Tàizōng hesitated for several days and did not make a decision.
The external matter was exposed.
Xīn did not know this,
and still descended according to the appointed time.
Jǐng intercepted and captured him,
then forced Xīn to shoot another letter into the city,
saying
"Táobàng will lightly lead a few dozen men in first."
Jǐng wanted to follow him with armored troops.
Xīn, however, refused to write the letter,
determined to die.
He was then killed by Jǐng
at the age of thirty-three.
Lán Qīn, courtesy name Xiūmíng,
was a person from Zhōngchāng Wèi.
during the Tiānjiān period,
reached the official position of Yúnní Jiāngjūn due to military achievements,
and Governor of Jìzhōu.
Qīn was resolute and decisive in his youth,
and his swiftness surpassed others.
He followed his father in the northern campaigns
and was appointed Zhíhé of the Eastern Palace.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he attacked Wèi Xiāochéng
and captured it.
He then defeated Péngchéng Biéjiāng Jiāo Zhòng,
advanced to attack Nǐshān Chéng,
and defeated their Dàdūdū Liú Shǔ's forces of two hundred thousand.
He advanced to attack Lóngchéng
and captured over a thousand horses.
He also defeated their Dàjiàng Chái Jí, as well as Xiāngchéng Tàishǒu Gāo Xuān, Biéjiāng Fàn Sīniàn, Zhèng Chéngzōng, and others.
