He then attacked Juégù, Zhāng Lóng, and Zǐchéng.
Before they were captured,
Wèi Péngchéng Shǒujiàng Yáng Mù dispatched his son Yáng Xiàoyōng to lead light troops to reinforce.
Qīn intercepted and repelled him.
He also defeated Qiáozhōu Cìshǐ Liú Hǎiyóu,
then returned and captured Juégù,
taking its households.
Yáng Mù again dispatched Dūdū Fàn Sīniàn and Biéjiāng Cáo Lóngyá with tens of thousands of troops to reinforce.
Qīn engaged them in battle
and beheaded Cáo Lóngyá on the battlefield,
sending his head to the capital.
Moreover, Lán Qīn was granted the jǐe (credentials),
and was appointed Grand Commander (Dūdū) of the forces of the three commanderies in Héngzhōu,
to suppress the rebellious Mán tribes in Guìyáng, Yángshān, and Shǐxīng.
Upon arrival, he immediately pacified and defeated them.
He was enfeoffed as the County Baron (Xiàn Nán) of Ānhuái,
with an estate of five hundred households.
He also defeated Wǎnshídé, the Mán chieftain of Tiānqī.
At that time, Yuán Qìnghé, the Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Héngzhōu, was besieged by Yán Róng of Guìyáng.
An envoy was dispatched to request urgent aid.
Qīn went to respond and reinforce them.
He defeated Róng at Luóxī.
Consequently, all the settlements (dòng) in Chánglè were simultaneously pacified.
He was then secretly commanded to head toward Wèixīng,
passing through Nánzhèng.
It happened that the Wèi general Tuòbá Shèng was raiding Xiāngyáng,
so he was immediately commanded to proceed to reinforce it.

He was appointed Bearer of the Jǐe (Chíjǐe), Grand Commander of all military affairs in the four provinces of Nánliáng, Nán Qín, Běi Qín, and Shā (Dū Nánliáng Nán Běi Qín Shā Sìzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of Brilliant Strength (Guāngliè Jiāngjūn), Colonel Who Pacifies the West (Píngxī Xiàowèi), and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Liáng and Nán Qín provinces.
His enfeoffment was increased by five hundred households,
and his noble rank was advanced to Marquis (Hóu).
He defeated Tōngshēng,
capturing Yuán Zǐlǐ (the Acting Secretariat Director), and the major generals Xuē Jùn and Zhāng Púsà.
Yuán Luó, the Wèi Inspector of Liángzhōu, subsequently surrendered.
Liáng and Hàn were thus settled.
His title was advanced to General of Wise Martiality (Zhìwǔ Jiāngjūn),
and his enfeoffment was increased by two thousand households.
Soon after, he was reassigned as Bearer of the Jǐe, Grand Commander of all military affairs in Héng and Guì provinces, and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Héngzhōu.
Before he could take up his post,
Wèi sent the Grand Commanders Dǒng Shào and Zhāng Xiàn to attack and besiege Nánzhèng.
Dù Huáiyáo, the Inspector of Liángzhōu, requested aid.
Qīn led his troops to reinforce him.
He utterly defeated Shào and Xiàn at Gāoqiáo Chéng (High Bridge Fortress),
beheading over three thousand men.
Shào and Xiàn retreated swiftly.
Qīn pursued them into Xiégǔ,
slaughtering and capturing nearly all of them.
Yǔwén Hēitài, the Chancellor (Xiàng) of Western Wèi, sent two thousand horses,
requesting to establish good neighborly relations.
An imperial edict appointed him Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
and advanced his title to General of Benevolent Awe (Rénwēi Jiāngjūn).
His enfeoffment was increased by five hundred households,
and he was finally ordered to proceed to his post.
Passing through Guǎngzhōu,
he took the opportunity to defeat Chén Wénchè and his brothers, the Lǐ chieftains,
and captured them all.
When he arrived at Héngzhōu,
his title was advanced to General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn),
and his enfeoffment was changed to County Duke (Xiàn Gōng) of Qǔjiāng.
His estate was increased by five hundred households.
While governing the province, he implemented beneficial policies.
The officials and common people went to the palace gates requesting permission to erect a monument to praise his virtue.
The emperor granted permission by edict.
He was summoned to serve as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was reassigned as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán Jiāngjūn), and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu.
Once he arrived at his assigned post,
the former Inspector, the Marquis of Nán'ān, secretly sent a cook to place poison in his food.
Qīn was poisoned and died,
at the age of forty-two.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the titles Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng) and General of the Central Guard (Zhōng Wèi Jiāngjūn),
along with a set of drums and pipes (gǔchuī).
His son, Xiàlǐ,
when Hóu Jǐng reached Lìyáng,
led his troops to intercept and attack Jǐng.
His army was defeated and he died.
The Imperial Historian (Shǐ Chén) remarks: Chén Qìngzhī and Lán Qīn both possessed military strategy.
In winning battles and taking objectives,
they were perhaps secondary only to Pō, Mù, Wèi, and Huò.
Qìngzhī was alert and perceptive,
serving Gāozǔ early on.
Since he was included in the old favors,
and moreover was cautious and solemn,
his cicada hat, ribbon seal, and pendants (symbols of high office),
constituted the glory of an entire generation.
Biography Twenty-seven: Wáng Sēngrú, Zhāng Shuài, Liú Xiàochuò, Wáng Yún
Wáng Sēngrú, courtesy name Sēngrú,
was a native of Tán in Dōnghǎi.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Wèi Sù, General of the Guard (Wèi Jiāngjūn).
His great-grandfather, Yǎ,
was Grand Master of Remonstrance, Left (Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū) and Commissioner Bearing the Insignia (Yítóu Sānsī) during the Jìn dynasty.
His grandfather, Zhǔn,
was Left Chief Clerk (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) to the Minister over the Masses (Sītú) during the Sòng dynasty.
When Sēngrú was five years old,
he read the *Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng)*.
He asked his teacher what the book contained and described.
The teacher replied:
"It discusses the two matters of loyalty (zhōng) and filial piety (xiào)."
Sēngrú said:
"If that is the case,
I constantly desire to read it."
At six, he was able to compose prose.
When he grew up, he loved learning.
His family was poor,
and he often earned money by copying books to support his mother.
Once he had finished copying,
he had also mastered the recitation and meaning.
He served the Qí dynasty,
starting his career as Left Attendant-in-Ordinary of a Princely State (Wángguó Zuǒ Chángshì) and Academician of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì).
Wáng Yàn, the Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Púyè), greatly appreciated and admired him.
When Yàn became the Administrator of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn),
he summoned Sēngrú to fill the post of Meritorious Official of the Commandery (Jùn Gōngcáo).
He made Sēngrú compile the *New Records of the Eastern Palace*.
He was promoted to Acting Staff Officer (Xíng Cānjūn) to the Prince of Yùzhāng, the Grand Marshal (Dà Sīmǎ).
He concurrently served as Academician of the Imperial University.
Xiāo Zǐliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng and Minister over the Masses (Sītú), opened his Western Residence (Xī Dǐ) to recruit men of letters,
and Sēngrú also frequented it.
Crown Prince Wénhuì heard of his reputation,
summoned him into the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
and stationed him at Chóngmíng Diàn.
He intended to nominate him for a position among the palace staff,
but Wénhuì died,
and the plan was not realized.
At that time, Wáng Déyuán, the son of Wáng Yàn, went out to govern Jìn'ān Commandery.
He appointed Sēngrú as Assistant Administrator of the Commandery (Jùn Chéng),
and Sēngrú was then appointed Magistrate (Lìng) of Hòuguān.
Early in the Jiànwǔ era,
there was an imperial edict recommending scholars.
Xiāo Yáoguāng, Prince of Shǐ'ān and Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yángzhōu, memorialized recommending Wáng Jiǎn, the Secretarial Aide (Mìshū Chéng), and Sēngrú, saying:
"Wáng Sēngrú of Dōnghǎi, former Magistrate of Hòuguān,
is thirty-five years old.
His principles still lean toward simplicity and restraint,
and his thinking leads to keen understanding.
Since he used his writing brush (bǐ gēng) to earn a living,
he also attained scholarship by copying books for hire.
As for illuminating fireflies and reflecting snow (metaphors for studiousness),
binding rush scrolls and stitching willow tablets,
ancient sayings and past deeds,
the refinement and vulgarity of people,
the surviving ceremonies of Gānquán,
and the historical precedents of Nángōng,
he can draw diagrams on the ground,
and relate them with a slap of his hand;
he does not merely possess the debating skill (like the small rat in the story) to answer every question,
nor does he make the error of dropping bamboo slips from the historical records (zhúshū).
If one consults him, he replies tirelessly,
capable of resolving doubts."
He was appointed Director (Láng) of the Ceremonial Bureau (Yícáo) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
and promoted to Palace Censor Supervising Documents (Zhìshū Shì Yùshǐ).
He was sent out to serve as Magistrate (Lìng) of Qiántáng.
Previously,
Sēngrú and Rèn Fǎng of Luò'ān had met at the Western Residence of the Prince of Jìnglíng.
They had formed a friendship based on their shared literary interests.
When Sēngrú was about to go to the county post,
Fǎng presented him with a poem.
The main points were:
"I am the only one who truly knows you,
and you are the only one who truly knows me.
Observing your actions and viewing your words,
the ending is as important as the beginning.
I respect you and esteem you,
like the orchid or the angelica.
Form responds and shadow follows,
you were going forward, and now you pause.
Among the hundred good actions,
establishing oneself as a person is foremost.
You possess this quality;
who can blame you, and who can praise you?
Since your good reputation is established,
why rush toward old age?
Who will hold the whip?
I shall drive the carriage for you.
The compendium of Liú [Xiàng] and the arts of Bān [Gù],
the histories of Yú [Xǐ] and the records of Xún [Xuē],
we once cherished these ideals,
and mutually encouraged each other joyfully.
Do not grow weary of hanging the curtain (to study in seclusion),
when ascending high there are those related to you.
I admire your morning lamp,
and cherish my remaining night candle."
This shows how much he was admired and esteemed by his fellow scholars and friends.
In the early years of Tiānjiān,
he was appointed Adjutant in the Rear Army Secretariat for the Prince of Línchuān (Línchuān Wáng),
and served as an Expectant Appointee in the Wéndé Palace Library (Wéndé Shěng).
Soon after, he was sent out to serve as the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nánhǎi Commandery.
The commandery regularly received people from Gāoliáng and seabourne vessels arriving several times each year.
Foreign merchants exchanged goods for currency.
In the past, the prefecture and commanderies would acquire them at half price in the market,
then buy and immediately resell them,
profiting several times over.
This had been the norm throughout successive administrations.
Sēngrú then sighed, saying:
"In the past, a man served as the Chief Secretary (Zhǎngshǐ) in Shǔ (Sichuan)
and acquired no local Shǔ goods throughout his life.
What I wish to pass down to my descendants
is not this 'Yuè (Guangdong) wealth.'"
He took nothing at all.
After supervising affairs for one full month,
an imperial edict summoned him back.
Six hundred people from the commandery, both clerical and lay, went to the palace gates requesting that he be allowed to stay,
but permission was denied.
Upon his arrival (at the capital),
he was appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng) and concurrently Supervisor of the Imperial Archives (Lǐng Zhùzuò).
He again served in the Wéndé Shěng,
compiling the registers of the Imperial Clan (Zhōng Biǎo Bù) and the Diary of Activity and Repose (Qǐjū Zhù).
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng),
retaining his post as Supervisor of the Imperial Archives.
Soon after, he was appointed General of the Light Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn),
concurrently serving as Palace Assistant Imperial Censor (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
Sēngrú was poor in his youth.
His mother sold fine silk and cloth to sustain their livelihood.
She once brought Sēngrú with her to the market,
where they encountered the equipage (Lǔ Bù) of a Zhōngchéng on the road,
and were forced into a ditch.
When it came to the day of his own appointment,
his attendants cleared the road,
and he was overcome with sorrowful emotion.
Soon after, due to official matters, he was demoted to General of the Cloud Cavalry (Yúnqí Jiāngjūn),
retaining his concurrent post as before.
A short time later, he was restored to the substantive rank.
At this time, Gāozǔ composed a poem titled "Chūnjǐng Míng Zhì Shī" (Poem on Spring Scenery and Manifesting Aspiration) consisting of five hundred characters.
He commanded all officials at court, from Shěn Yuè downwards, to compose matching verses.
Gāozǔ judged Sēngrú's poem to be the finest.
He was promoted to Minister of the Lesser Treasury (Shǎofǔ Qīng),
and sent out to supervise Wújùn Commandery.
Upon returning, he was appointed Director of the Personnel Bureau (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng).
He participated in the Grand Selection (Dà Xuǎn, civil service screening),
and requests for audience (favors) were unsuccessful.
He was sent out to serve as Chief Secretary (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Nánkāng (Nánkāng Wáng), commander of the Rénwēi military forces,
managing the affairs of the Prince’s establishment, the prefecture, and the feudal state.
Tāng Dàomǐn, the prince's document steward (Diǎn Qiān), was favored by the Prince
and exercised authority within the establishment.
Sēngrú consistently restrained and suppressed him.
Dàomǐn subsequently slandered and impeached Sēngrú,
resulting in his arrest and appearance before the Southern Tribunal (Nán Sī).
He respectfully presented a memorial departing from his post, saying:
"This humble official was unable to avoid being suspected of drowning at the corner of a mountain,
nor of adjusting my cap beneath a plum tree (avoiding suspicion).
Since I have already incurred fault and disgrace,
I now face the disciplinary ropes (legal measures).
Taking off my official tally and retrieving my hairpins (resigning my post),
I shall return for the time being to the garments I first wore.
I humbly recall that Dǒng Shēng (Dǒng Zhòngshū), a great vessel,
only served a proud prince;
and Master Jiǎ (Jiǎ Yì), a supreme talent,
was sent to govern a humble territory.
This humble official has been fortunate in his life,
mistakenly aspiring to your noble presence.
Using my borrowed wings in Xīyōng (west region),
I secretly walked the steps of Dōnggé (the eastern chamber, i.e., official post).
I am often ashamed of my fine official robes,
disturbing the long robes of others.
Elevated couches face each other,
and I was positioned directly to the right of the seat of honor.
The long staircase was like a painting,
and I alone stood at the head of the officials.
I received your unrestrained words
and was granted your benevolent and gentle expression.
Your grace and courtesy far exceeded Shēn (Shēn Péng) and Bái (Bái Wǔ),
and my honor and standing were often placed alongside Yìng (Yìng Yáng) and Xú (Xú Gàn).
Great virtue is hard to encounter,
but petty men are easily swayed.
I had intended that tearing out my guts and giving up my head
would not be enough to repay a single word of yours;
and revealing my honesty and stripping bare my sincerity
how could that repay your frequent regards?
Who would have thought that as the net was only just being lifted,
the insignificant bird would fall first;
that as the Gate of Heaven (Chānghé) had just begun to blow,
the tiny grass would already be cast down.
Once departing the Nine Orchards (Jiǔ Wǎn),
I now leave the Five-Colored Clouds (Wǔ Yún).
Even if the net of heaven has holes,
and the sage's grace could be relied upon,
where else can I entrust my body and mind,
or where can I show my face?
I am about to cross pools and traverse the chaotic sea,
joining the fish and turtles as companions;
I will push through thorns and feel the trees,
associating with vipers and snakes as my peers.
How can I ever again look up and hear your golden voice,
or observe your jade countenance?
As I look back at your lofty carriage,
my sorrow descends like hail;
Hesitating on the step below the mat,
my tears flow like ropes."
Sēngrú was stripped of his office because of this charge,
and for a long time was not reassigned.
His friend Hé Jiǒng of Lújiāng was still serving as the Chief Clerk (Jìshì) in the princely establishment.
He then sent a letter to Hé Jiǒng
to convey his feelings.
It reads: "Since our recent separation,
we have been divided by warmth and cold (time/seasons).
Thoughts of you have brought me weariness,
and I have been unable to forget or put them aside.
In the past, when Elder Lǐ (Lǐ Yì) entered Qín,
and Master Liáng (Liáng Hóng) went to Yuè,
they still felt melancholy
regret,
and sometimes sang lamentations.
How much more so on the day of separation,
when I was about to leave the harsh net (of justice),
having no defense that could elicit pity,
and having committed a crime whose consequences were unpredictable.
Indeed, marking the ground and carving the wood
were hated by men of old.
Once the bundle of thorns (prison) accumulates,
how can one be heard?
Therefore, we clasped hands affectionately,
and valued our farewell.
My brotherly love was the same as Zōu Jì's,
and tears moistened my eyelashes.
Yet I still firmly raised
my hand and turned my back,
ashamed to imitate women.
The white bells initiate the season,
and the golden gale heralds the order (Autumn).
I trust your daily life is well,
and your movements and stillness are appropriate.
Zǐyún’s (Yáng Xióng) documents
and Yuányú’s (Wáng Cān) correspondence
are trustworthy and reliable,
which is deeply gratifying.
They also brighten the eyes
and can dispel headaches.
Very good, very good.
I lack the talent of the men of old but suffer their ailments.
Vertigo frequently strikes,
and my wasting-thirst (diabetes) continually worsens.
I surrender to destiny and accept my span of life,
hence I no longer call physicians or drink medicine.
I only regret
that one day I incurred great disgrace,
stepping into the clear law (court proceedings).
I left being pure and undefiled, not having disgraced myself,
but I harbor deep frustration with no one to tell.
The merits accumulated in my prime years
have perished with this (disgrace).
I merely stole high
prestige and great renown,
and wrongfully occupied official positions and human titles.
My wisdom and talent have nothing to repay,
and my strength and vigor have not compensated them.
Therefore, sorrow leads me to pound my chest,
and when tears are exhausted, they are replaced
by blood.
Considering my inadequacy,
neither refinement nor substance reached its mark.
I was primarily constrained by clothing and food,
and pressed by hunger and cold.
Relying on recluses and changing to farming,
my aspiration did not exceed obtaining provisions for a Zhōng (ancient measure) or a Yǔ.
For a long time, I served
as an official holding a foot-long tablet and earning a measure of grain,
engaging in the service of black robes and dark ribbons.
I did not possess extraordinary talent or unique scholarship,
nor heroic strategy or profound planning;
I could not utter a word that could correct customs and arouse the people,
or move an argument that could stabilize the state and revitalize the nation.
Returning the entire jade disk to Zhào,
or using flying arrows to save Yān;
resting and breathing easy in Wèi (Fán Wèi),
or sleeping peacefully in Yǐng (Gān Wò Ān Yǐng);
breaking the brains of the Rìzhú (tribe),
or extracting the marrow of the Yuèzhī (tribe);
commanding
a hundred thousand men to march unimpeded,
or leading five thousand into deep territory;
being able to hold the jade tablet (signifying rank) and partition territory,
having achievements engraved on the Jǐng Bell,
wearing embroidered silk robes,
and having crimson paint covering the wheels—
these are the aspirations
of a great man,
and are not what people like us can achieve.
I possess merely the minor talent of composition and rhetoric,
the insignificant skill of seal-carving (Chóng Zhuàn),
breathing life into yellow and azure scrolls (literature),
and fluttering beside the honored wine-vessels and cutting boards (feasting/court life)."
Trivial matters likened to
needle and thread, intricate details compared to rice and salt—
how could these lead to prominence and glory,
how could one reach high positions?
Furthermore, my nature is lax
and clumsy at advancement,
never having frequented
Xǔ and Shǐ,
nor roamed with Liáng and Dòu,
bowing my head and shrugging my shoulders,
anticipating and obeying every command.
This is why through three generations [of officials], I was never encountered,
not keeping pace with the times.
After ten years, I had not moved [up].
Was this not due to my
limited ability?
But when the old was discarded and the new inaugurated,
and the clear light dawned,
bearing music and containing maps,
and all praises and songs had a master,
I was still confined as a minor official in Cénshí,
separated by a thousand *lǐ* in Quántíng,
unable to serve as an attendant [Zhōngjuān] with a memorial tablet,
or participate in the assembly of the high officials,
holding a spear among the rear guards,
or be counted among the strategies of dragons and leopards.
When I resigned my post and returned,
favor was equally bestowed upon this former humble servant.
I ascended the polished
stone [stairs],
and mounted the jade steps.
Upon a single meeting, he lowered his countenance [to speak to me];
upon a second sight, he engaged in conversation;
it was not thanks to the kindness of the attendants,
nor was it necessary to trouble the assistance of the assembled nobles.
Moreover, we had not previously met,
sharing the same mat and studying together,
nor had we been early acquaintances sharing food from a hamper and wine from a cup.
Yet suddenly, I attended beneath the military tent,
gazed up at the civil steps,
served beneath the pillar like Dān and Yì,
and sat at the table filling the places of Yán and Zhū.
Entering, I ranked among the highest officials (the Nine Thorns),
leaving, I was entrusted with the governance of a thousand *lǐ*;
I held a crucial and powerful office,
participating in a prominent position concerning human affairs.
Although in antiquity, titles were bestowed without order [of rank],
and scholars were selected regardless of reputation,
there has never
been one who treads on shadows and chases the wind,
surging forward as rapidly as this.
However, the foundation was thin and the walls high;
the path was long but my strength faltered.
Falling and collapsing was inevitable,
stumbling and crawling could be expected.
Ultimately, excessive fortune begat disaster;
people pointed fingers and ghosts glared.
It was as if the vessel meant to contain
generosity
was testing the limits of an over-full goblet.
Therefore, I could not quickly follow the obscure path [of retreat],
and consequently incurred suspicion by following the wrong track.
Thus, the officials were apprehensive and severe,
wishing to strike the target.
I am like a beast
suspended,
or a bird escaped from the snare,
soon to fill the cooking pot
and become bait for hawks and falcons.
Although the charges were different from flaying the skin,
and the indictment did not pierce the bone,
yet based on the point of this tongue,
and realized through the tip of this
brush,
at best, I might be thrown into the northern regions;
at worst, I might be condemned to the Left Workshop,
becoming crimson and vermilion,
serving there chopping wood for the mortar.
Fortunately, the sagely ruler retained the virtue of great clemency,
extending the
mercy of loving life,
untying the net and praying for the captured beasts,
dismounting his carriage to weep over the condemned.
He pitied this disgrace and shame,
felt compassion for my trembling fear,
added flesh to rotting bones,
spread leaves upon a withered stump,
stopped the firewood and quenched the flames.
Thus, I escaped dissolution and decay.
This is what is meant by returning the soul to the Northern Dipper,
and recalling the spirit from Tàishān.
I was merely stripped of my rank and returned to common citizenry,
wearing a simple cloth wrap in my home neighborhood.
This, after fifty years [of life],
is the
gift of the ruler.
Wood and stone are influenced by Yin and Yang;
dogs and horses recognize kindness and neglect.
Being round-headed and square-footed [human beings],
who does not wear Heaven on their head?
Yet, secretly, I have my own sorrow:
For whether a scholar is worthy or
unworthy,
when in court, he is envied;
whether a woman is beautiful or ugly,
upon entering the palace, she is subject to jealousy.
My family is poor,
having no gifts to offer colleagues and peers.
I detest those who are hypocritical,
and feel shame for those who flatter.
How can I follow others?
How can I seek worldly gain?
Externally, I lack influential friends who run errands [for favors],
internally, I am short of powerful relatives nearby.
Therefore, the rumor-mongers
used every opportunity to stir up trouble.
And
when I was cast aside one morning,
to satisfy the hearts of those who held grudges—
alas, how sorrowful!
Indeed, being noble first and then humble,
rich in the past and poor now—
this is why Jìlún uttered this lamentable sound,
and why Yōngmén harmonized his mournful tune.
Furthermore, pressed by the lethal
*qì* of severe autumn,
all things are filled with sadness.
Throughout the long night, I toss and turn,
a hundred worries arriving together.
Moreover, the frost dims the color of the grass,
and the wind shakes the shadows of the trees.
Cold insects chirp in the evening,
blending high and low notes
in shared sorrow;
autumn leaves are wounded by the late season,
mingling yellow and purple as they all fall.
Spiders weave their webs across the curtains,
and fireflies flit about.
Naturally, there are no wheel tracks or sound of horses,
how could one hear the crowing of roosters or the barking of dogs?
I lower my gaze to serve my wife and children,
and raise my hand to turn away visitors.
Now I dwell alongside birds and beasts,
destined forever to be submerged in weeds and brambles.
Sighing long breaths,
suddenly I do not feel that life is
important.
I have always lacked even a small plot of land,
but I have the burden of several mouths to feed.
How can I say that I am a gourd that is not eaten?
I must perpetually work as a servant,
barely subsisting,
until suddenly I die in a ditch
or canal,
filling the stomachs of moles and ants.
Alas!
How can I ever again meet with two or three scholarly friends,
embracing the joy of sitting knee-to-knee,
shuffling feet and rubbing shoulders,
composing clear writings like brocade and silk gauze,
and discussing the profound
philosophy of the Way and Virtue.
I can only hope for Wú Féng to meet Xià Fù,
or Fàn Shì to encounter Kǒng Sōng,
pitying me for staying in servitude,
or having compassion for me reduced to begging.
If you do not consider me defiled
and burdened,
and occasionally keep a short note from me,
then even if I die first like a dog or horse,
I shall still feel like Sōng and Qiáo [immortals].
Farewell, Hé Shēng,
may you hold high your fragrant virtue.
I write this letter instead of meeting you face-to-face,
my tears fall together with the brush strokes.
After a long time,
he rose to become the staff officer (*cānjūn*) for the Prince of Ānchéng, Ānxī;
repeatedly promoted to Central Secretary (*zhōng jìshì*) for the Prince of Shǐxīng, Zhènyòu;
and Consultant (*zīyì cānjūn*) for the Prince of Nánkāng, Běizhōngláng.
He entered the Western Department (*Xīshěng*) for duty,
and oversaw the compilation of genealogies.
In the third year of Pǔtōng,
he died,
at the age of fifty-eight.
Sēngrú loved literature and records,
amassing over ten thousand scrolls of books,
most of which were rare editions,
comparable to the family collections of Shěn Yuē and Rèn Fǎng.
When young, he was dedicated and energetic,
reading every book there was.
His writing was elegant and unrestrained,
often utilizing new anecdotes
that people had never seen before;
the world valued its richness.
Sēngrú compiled the Genealogy of Eighteen Zhōu, seven hundred and ten scrolls;
A Collection of One Hundred Family Genealogies, fifteen scrolls;
A Transcript of the Southeast Genealogy Collection, ten scrolls;
Collected Writings, thirty scrolls;
Impeachments from the Two Bureaus, five scrolls, which were not included in the main collection;
and the New Records of the Eastern Palace.
These all circulated throughout the world.
Zhāng Shuài, courtesy name Shìjiǎn,
was a native of Wú County, Wú Jùn.
His grandfather, Yǒng,
was Grand Master of the Right Glorious Happiness (Yòu Guānglù Dàfū) during Sòng.
His father, Guī,
was famous and noble during the Qí era,
and returned to his home village in retirement.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān [era],
he was appointed Grand Master of the Right Glorious Happiness (Yòu Guānglù),
and given the additional title Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Zhōng).
Shuài was twelve years old
when he could write prose and verse,
often limiting himself to composing one poem per day,
gradually progressing to writing fù and sòng.
By the age of sixteen,
he had composed about two thousand pieces.
When Xiāo Yáoguāng, the Prince of Shǐ'ān of Qí, served as Governor of Yángzhōu,
he summoned Shuài to be Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
but he did not accept.
He began his career as Assistant Editor (Zhùzuò Zuǒ Láng).
In the third year of Jiànwǔ,
he was nominated as an Outstanding Talent (Xiùcái),
and appointed Palace Aide to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
He and Lù Chuí, who was from the same commandery, were close friends in youth,
and they often rode together to visit General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn) Shěn Yuē.
It happened that Rèn Fǎng was also there.
Yuē then said to Fǎng:
“These two young men are brilliant talents,
both are ‘Southern Gold’ (nánjīn).
You should establish a friendship with them.”
Thereupon, he became good friends with Fǎng.
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Palace within the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng).
He was sent out to serve as Administrator (Gōngcáoshǐ) for the Prince of Nánkāng under the General of the Western Central Army (Xī Zhōngláng),
but did not accept due to illness.
After a long time,
he was appointed Equerry to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
When Gāozǔ established his Prime Ministerial headquarters (bàfǔ),
he was brought in as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) to the Chancellor of State (Xiàngguó).
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān [era],
the Prince of Línchuān and those below him were all assigned Mentors (Yǒu) and Tutors (Xué).
Shuài was made Mentor (Yǒu) to the Prince of Póyáng.
He was promoted to Aide (Yuàn) under Minister of the Masses (Sītú) Xiè Fěi,
and served as Expectant Appointee (Dàizhào) in the Wéndé Palace Office.
He was commanded by imperial edict to copy books from the Yǐ division,
and also commissioned to compile over twenty sections concerning women's affairs,
organizing them into a hundred scrolls.
He had skilled scribes—Wáng Shēn of Lángyá,
Fàn Huáiyuē of Wú Jùn, Chǔ Xún, and others—copy them out,
to be provided to the inner palace (hòugōng).
Shuài also composed a Rhapsody on the Expectant Appointees (Dàizhào fù) and presented it.
He was highly praised and admired.
The Emperor replied with an autograph edict, saying:
“I have examined your Rhapsody, and it is exceptionally excellent.
Xiāngrú (Sīmǎ Xiāngrú) was skillful but slow,
Méi Gāo was fast but not skillful;
you can be said to possess the qualities of both men within the Jīnmǎ [Gate].”
He also attended a banquet and composed poetry.
Gāozǔ specially bestowed a poem upon Shuài, saying:
“The Southeast possesses a talented man,
thus he is capable of government service.
Though I am ashamed compared to antiquity,
in acquiring men of talent, I am now prosperous.”
Shuài composed several responding poems in obedience to the decree.
That same year,
he was promoted to Vice Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng),
and granted an audience in the Yùhéng Hall.
Gāozǔ said:
“The Vice Director of the Imperial Library is the purest office in the realm,
and no noble house from the Southeast has yet held it.
Now that I appoint you to it,
it is sufficient honor for you, my lord.”
His favor and treatment were like this.
In the third month of the fourth year,
the Purification Rite (Xìyǐn) was held at the Huáguāng Hall.
On that day,
the state of Hénán presented a dancing horse.
An edict commanded Shuài to compose a Rhapsody on it,
saying: Your servant has heard
“For the use of Heaven, there is none like the dragon;
for the use of Earth, there is none like the horse.”
Therefore, the rites praise the líyuán,
and the odes sing of the liúluò.
The excellence of the lingering customs of previous rulers
is what the world
hears;
the wonders of displaying auspicious signs and brilliant forms
emerge from time to time.
Extending to our great Liáng dynasty,
whose glory covers the entire land (qūxià),
its vast movements originate from the center,
its complete illumination has no boundaries.
In the places where the sun sets,
floating treasures are offered as tribute;
in the regions touched by its virtue (fēng),
they traverse dangers to present rarities.
They possess swift steeds known as língfú and wūháo,
and the names táotú and huànlóng.
And now Hénán has again presented a red 'dragon colt' (chìlóngjū),
possessing a wondrous appearance and unmatched legs,
capable of kneeling in obeisance and skilled in dancing.
The Son of Heaven regarded it as extraordinary,
and commanded your servant to compose a Rhapsody,
which states: Indeed, the Liáng dynasty has received the Mandate for four years,
the primordial omens have all arrived,
affairs concerning the harmony of music have been fully established,
the teachings of the schools (jiāoxiáng) are certainly set forth,
the use of the simple cart (tányú) has been discontinued,
and the riding of the jade chariot (yùlù)
is now in progress.
Upon examining the imperial writings, all is clear;
upon opening the imperial charts, the view is grand.
Auspiciousness precedes only those who follow the Way,
if not for a Sage, who could aid the spirits?
We see the auspicious river dragon of
Táng,
and gaze upon the propitious heavenly horses of Hàn.
Since the omens match and the virtues correspond,
and they share the same lineage and are connected by the same thread.
Seeking the nation's beauty in this present time,
it surpasses the sovereigns of the past.
Dispensing great light to illuminate the obscure,
raising the voice of righteousness to ward off distant [evils].
Indeed, it is bestowed without exhaustion,
truly having no concern for morning or evening.
All follow the currents of influence and request officials,
all turn toward
the custom (fēng) and perform their duties.
They present marvelous tributes from remote areas,
delivering dragon steeds (lóngméi) from distant lands.
Indeed, like the red markings of antiquity,
here now is the crimson wing.
It has displayed its virtue in
the Element of Fire (Yányùn),
and also symbolized auspiciousness for the honored color [red].
It relies on the bright moon in its birth,
and inherits outstanding qualities from the constellation Hé Fáng.
It is of the unparalleled lineage of Běi Táng,
and heir to the noble stock of Xī Yuān.
Endowed with marvelous legs, surpassing its peers,
it has a unique form and is exceptionally flourishing.
It is skilled in circling (huán xuán) during the Summer Solstice dance (Jìxià),
and knows how to step and tread to the metallic music.
It surpasses the six breeds of Zhōu stables,
and exceeds the eight
classes of Hàn.
Since it naturally possesses this essence,
how could its appearance change whether fat or thin?
How could it merely submit to the halter and live in safety,
or be used for advancing the carriage and speeding forth?
As for the difference of the
chǐxuánzáo [markings],
the distinctions of the fùchán fútù [bones],
the forms of the ten shapes and five observations,
and the features of the three hairs and eight muscles—
how can your servant describe them?
They have certainly been detailed in
previous compositions.
We merely observe its divine vigor,
and see its noble uniqueness,
dashing across the wilds and suddenly surpassing the chariot wheel,
equaling the finest qí horses and ranking with the best carriages.
It minimizes Dàipán and deems Xiǎohuà crude,
it surpasses
Dìngdān and holds the Heavenly Steed (Tiānjì) inferior.
Truly, none can equal its smooth face (lòumiàn);
who would choose a split nose (juébí)?
It can trace paths that Zhāng and Hài have not traveled,
and leap past places that Yǔ and Yì
have not reached.
It is impossible to count its accomplishments on the fingers,
and where is the time to manage the reins?
If it traveled everywhere and forgot to return,
that would not be the purpose of Our Sovereign.
It now adorns the writings of
antiquity,
far exceeding ornate prose and stored thought.
Furthermore, since there is much leisure in affairs of state,
and the green spring (qīngchūn) has not yet passed.
The season is the Shangsì festival,
and beautiful scenery is present here.
We follow the old customs of the Hào banquet,
and display the former ceremonies of the Luò feast.
to split its currents,
channeling swift water to circle the pool.
Gathering the nation’s worthies among the people’s elite,
lining up abundant trees around the imperial branches.
Numerous tall caps connected sleeves,
jangling sounding
jades as they followed shoulder to shoulder.
Clearing the imperial carriage path in the Shànglín park,
solemnizing the golden seats of the splendid terrace.
Watching the colors emerge from the green buds,
anticipating the fragrance wafting from the purple wrappings.
Hearing the sounding stones and large bells
completely raised,
listening to the music of Sháo and Xià all being played.
Following the conclusion of the Six Performances,
and after the Nine Changes were completed.
Matching the ceremonial birds of the Táng lineage,
resembling the dancing beasts in the Yú
court.
Recalling the nine generations of the Xià Hòu lineage,
thinking of the purple-red horse of Chén Wáng.
Thereupon, the palace attendants were commanded,
to bring forth fine steeds,
pass through the defensive ranks,
and enter the Gōuchén formation.
Announcing that the steed led by the right has already
arrived,
it would rather hold a simple rod and then advance.
It first tilted its head in time with the music,
then stamped its feet when the drums sounded.
Raising its dragon head,
turning its deer body,
glancing sideways at the two mirrors,
contracting its double mane.
Having reached the arena, it bowed gracefully,
sometimes rushing towards the melody, sometimes slowly trotting.
Its rapid agitation coincided with the quickened tempo,
its swift complexity exceeded the startling drumstick.
Qí steeds walked and Jì steeds moved,
tigers started and dragons soared;
sparrows leaped and swallows gathered,
swans stretched and flew.
Its beauty was graceful like the Qī Pán dance,
surpassing the rises and falls of the Jiǔ Jiàn.
Why borrow mannerisms from wide sleeves,
how could it need instruments from the hairy horse?
It gracefully arched its spine to receive the eulogy,
lowered its chest to conform to the standard tune.
Dewy foam sprayed red,
moist sweat streamed vermillion.
Then it retreated back to the Jílíng hall,
having been tamed and nourished during the abundance of summer.
The magnificent heart,
filled with the spirit of wind and thunder,
longed to stretch its legs in the Southern Wilderness.
If those numerous omens and auspicious signs
could reach the great mound to display the completion of achievement,
the assembled nobles and high officials,
truly hoped for this final brilliance,
but the Son of Heaven considered profound dignity as the standard,
and had not
yet inquired about it.
Why is that?
Advancement and yielding are different matters;
is this not the Emperor's grand display of culture?
Now that the Four Guards protect the external borders,
and the Five Sacred Mountains are internal commanderies,
it is fitting to extend the regulation of the Shàn Sacrifice below,
and increase the instruction regarding the Fēng Sacrifice above.
Turning away from Qīngdū as the sun travels,
pointing towards the cloud-filled suburb as the sky revolves.
Soon cutting off the dust and stopping the ruts,
resembling flying birds and mules.
Controlling the Three Powers
to drive forward,
following the Five Methods of Driving to swiftly spread forth.
Shading the auspicious cloud on the splendid canopy,
flanking the gentle breeze beside the attached carriages.
Not driving recklessly with the jade shaft,
not allowing the reins to slacken in the golden
chariot.
Decorating the unique path on the Central Peak,
establishing the old site of Fènggāo.
The instructions are abundantly manifested to both men and spirits,
broadly applying nurturing governance to the black-haired people and the virtuous.
Hanging down bright glory for endless generations,
gathering numerous blessings for these myriad people,
When I, your humble subject, am still young and vigorous,
I harbor the great wish to follow the army.
I shall certainly display my talents starting from this point,
and be bestowed along with Páo Huī.
I mourn the surviving writings of Cháng Qīng,
and pity the lasting regret of Zhōu Nán.
At that time, [Zhāng] Shuài, along with Dào Qià
and Zhōu Xīngsì, received an imperial decree to compose a *fu*.
Gāozǔ considered Shuài and Xīngsì to be the most skilled.
That same year,
he left office due to mourning his father.
His father had several dozen serving courtesans,
and one skilled singer possessed beauty.
A local man, the Secretary of Ceremonies Gù Wánzhī,
sought to marry her. The singer was unwilling
and consequently left home to become a nun.
She once held a vegetarian assembly at [Zhāng] Shuài's residence.
Wánzhī then wrote a letter claiming she had an illicit affair with [Zhāng] Shuài.
The Southern Office reported the matter to the throne.
Gāozǔ cherished his talent
and shelved the report,
but nevertheless, it generated public discussion.
After the mourning period concluded,
he did not hold office for a long time.
In the seventh year,
he was summoned by imperial decree
and appointed as Secretary to the Center Military Governor and Prince of Jiàn'ān,
included in the official roster for consultations,
without daily restrictions.
Shortly thereafter, there was an imperial decree appointing him directly to Shòuguāng Shěng,
where he was tasked with managing the copying of documents in the Bǐng and Dīng Sections.
In the eighth year,
when the Prince of Jìn'ān
was garrisoned at Shítóu, [Zhāng] Shuài was made Secretary to the General of Cloud-like Cavalry.
When the Prince moved to Nányǎn Zhōu,
[Zhāng] Shuài was transferred to be Counselor to the General Who Spreads Awe,
while concurrently serving as Secretary.
When the Prince returned to the capital,
[Zhāng] Shuài was appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
In the thirteenth year,
when the Prince became Governor of Jīngzhōu,
[Zhāng] Shuài was again made Counselor to the General Who Spreads Favor,
and concurrently Magistrate of Jiānglíng.
When the administrative seat moved to Jiāngzhōu,
he served as Counselor concurrently leading the Secretariat,
and was sent out to oversee the commanderies of Yùzhāng and Línchuān.
[Zhāng] Shuài served in the administration for ten years,
and the kindness and courtesy shown to him were extremely warm.
Upon returning, he was appointed Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince,
and was successively promoted to General Who Beckons Afar, Right Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education, and Supervisor of Yángzhōu.
Although [Zhāng] Shuài had held various official positions,
he never devoted his mind to administrative records.
When he served as Supervisor and presented reports,
Gāozǔ examined the documents and questioned him,
but he had no replies,
only respectfully responding,
"The matter is contained within the document."
Gāozǔ was displeased.
Soon after, he was transferred to be Household Manager to the Crown Prince,
sharing the responsibility of managing the Eastern Palace records with the Palace Steward Lù Chuí
and the Palace Assistant Liú Xiào Chuò, and then promoted to Gentleman of the Yellow Gates.
He was sent out to serve as Governor of Xīn'ān.
When his term was complete, he returned to the capital,
but before he arrived,
he entered mourning for his birth mother.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
while still in mourning,
he died,
aged fifty-three.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng sent an envoy to bestow gifts and burial expenses,
and issued an order to the Prince of Jìn'ān, Gāng, saying:
"Recently, Zhāng Xīn'ān has also passed away.
His talent and literary style were expansive and refined,
and he is indeed worthy of sorrow and regret.
Having followed your administrative court,
traveling East and West for many days,
you must feel particularly pained.
Lately, talented figures have been scattered,
which is especially tearful and regrettable.
Since this messenger is here now,
I mention this matter again."
[Zhāng] Shuài loved wine,
was lenient and forgiving in all matters,
and was particularly unconcerned with household affairs.
While serving in Xīn'ān,
he dispatched household servants to transport three thousand *shí* of rice back to his Wú residence.
When they arrived,
more than half had been consumed.
[Zhāng] Shuài asked the reason,
and the reply was:
"It was consumed by sparrows and rats."
[Zhāng] Shuài smiled and said:
"What magnificent sparrows and rats!"
In the end, he did not investigate further.
When he was young, he enjoyed composing literature,
and for the poems and *fu* recorded in the Qī Lüè
and the Yìwén Zhì
whose texts are now lost, he composed replacements for all of them.
He authored *Wénhéng* in fifteen scrolls,
and a literary collection in thirty scrolls,
which circulated in the world.
His son was Zhǎng Gōngsì.
Liú Xiào Chuò, courtesy name Xiào Chuò,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His original name was Rǎn.
His grandfather was Miǎn,
Duke Zhōngzhāo, Minister of Works of Sòng.
His father was Huì,
Gentleman-in-Attendance in the Administration of the Commander-in-Chief of Qí.
Xiāo Zhuó was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth;
at seven, he was able to compose essays.
His maternal uncle, Wáng Róng (Secretary in the Chancellery of Qí), deeply appreciated and marvelled at him,
often travelling with him in the same carriage when visiting relatives and friends,
calling him a "Divine Child" (Shéntóng).
Wáng Róng often said:
"If I were not the foremost writer in the world,
the distinction would certainly belong to Āshì."
Āshì
was Xiāo Zhuó's childhood name (xiǎozì).
[His father] Xiāo Huì,
held the charge of imperial edicts during the Qí era.
Though Xiāo Zhuó had not yet reached the age of study (zhi xué),
Huì often had him draft them in his stead.
His father's contemporaries, Shěn Yuè, Rèn Făng, Fàn Yún, and others, heard of his reputation,
and all ordered their carriages to visit him first.
Rèn Făng especially admired and favored him.
Fàn Yún was over ten years older than Huì;
his son, Xiāo Cái, and Xiāo Zhuó were both fourteen or fifteen years old.
When Fàn Yún met Xiāo Zhuó,
he immediately treated him as an elder or younger brother (bó jì) [i.e., as an equal or senior],
and ordered Xiāo Cái to bow to him.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān reign,
he began his career as an Assistant Gentleman of the Secretariat (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng).
He composed the "Poem on Returning for Ablutions" (Guī Mù Shī) and presented it to Rèn Făng.
Făng replied in verse, saying:
"That handsome youth from Luòyáng,
has cast upon me a work contemplating autumn.
How can it comfort this aged, sighing man?
It only deepens the trust of this old man.
The straight historian includes praise and censure;
the official in charge focuses on denouncing evil.
A nine-fold bend often suffers from wonderful sores;
I cannot repay you, but perhaps this is good medicine.
May you elevate your sharp talent,
exerting yourself in spring plowing for the autumn harvest."
This shows the high regard in which he was held by famous literati.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
Soon thereafter, while retaining his original post, he was concurrently appointed Chief of the Waterways Bureau (Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng).
He submitted a memorial expressing his thanks;
the emperor replied with an edict written in his own hand, saying:
"Fine brocade cannot be immediately tailored;
paperwork and administration should also be gradually learned."
After a short time, he took up the substantive post.
Emperor Gāozǔ was fond of literature and calligraphy (chóng zhuàn),
and often, during imperial banquets,
he commanded Shěn Yuè, Rèn Făng, and others to express their ambitions and compose poems.
Xiāo Zhuó was also invited.
Once, while attending a banquet,
he composed seven poems at the gathering.
Gāozǔ read his works,
praising and admiring every single piece.
Due to this, the court and the populace changed their view of him.
Soon, there was an imperial edict appointing him to oversee the affairs of the three provinces: Qīng, Běixú, and Nánxú.
He was sent out to serve as Recorder (Jìshì) to the Prince of Ānchéng (Píngnán),
accompanying the Prince's administration to its post.
Soon, he was appointed Cavalier Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
He was promoted to Chief of the Treasury Bureau (Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng),
and then returned to serve again as Cavalier Attendant to the Crown Prince,
overseeing the records and documents of the Eastern Palace.
He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Shàngyú (Shàngyú Lìng).
Upon returning, he was appointed Secretariat Aide (Mìshū Chéng).
Gāozǔ said to the Palace Attendant Zhōu Shě:
"The foremost official post ought to employ the foremost man."
Therefore, Xiāo Zhuó was placed in this office.
He was dismissed due to an administrative matter.
Soon after, he was reappointed Secretariat Aide.
He was sent out to serve as Advisor (Zīyì) to the Prince of Ānchéng (Zhènnán).
Upon returning to the capital, he was dismissed due to an incident.
He was reinstated as Recorder to the General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jìshì).
He was successively promoted to Advisor and Consultant to the General Who Pacifies the West and Commander of the Swift Cavalry (Ānxī Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn).
By imperial edict, he was temporarily put in charge of the affairs of the Right Chief Clerk to the Minister of Education (Sītú Yòu Chángshǐ).
He was promoted to Minister of the Grand Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng) and Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Pú),
and again oversaw the records and documents of the Eastern Palace.
At that time, Crown Prince Zhāomíng appreciated talent and loved literature.
Xiāo Zhuó, along with Yīn Yún of Chénjùn, Lù Chuí of Wújùn, Wáng Yún of Lángyé, and Dào Qià of Péngchéng,
were all treated with guest rituals.
The Crown Prince built the Hall of Joyful Sages (Lèxián Táng),
and commanded the painter to depict Xiāo Zhuó first.
The Crown Prince's literary works were numerous and rich.
All the talented writers wished to compile and record them,
but the Crown Prince exclusively tasked Xiāo Zhuó with collecting them and writing the preface.
He was promoted to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì),
concurrently serving as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi Qīng).
After a short while, he took up the substantive post.
Initially,
Xiāo Zhuó and Dào Qià were good friends,
and both frequented the Eastern Palace.
Xiāo Zhuó considered his talent superior to Qià's,
and often during banquets and gatherings,
he ridiculed and scorned Qià's writings.
Qià bore a grudge because of this.
When Xiāo Zhuó served as Minister of the Court of Judicial Review,
he brought his concubine into the government office,
while his mother remained at their private residence.
Qià was soon appointed Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
He dispatched a clerk (lìshǐ) to investigate the matter,
and subsequently impeached and reported him to the throne,
stating:
"He brings his young sister (mèi) into the magnificent palace office,
and abandons his aged mother in the lesser residence."
Gāozǔ, seeking to conceal the severity of the offense,
changed
the character for 'sister' (mèi)
to
'beautiful woman' (shū).
He was dismissed from office due to this transgression.
All of Xiāo Zhuó's younger brothers,
who were serving in various princely administrations, were then in Jīng and Yōng prefectures.
He then wrote a letter to them discussing ten instances where Dào Qià had treated him unfairly,
the language of which wholly disparaged the Dào family.
He also copied a separate version and sealed it to present to the Eastern Palace.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng ordered it to be burned,
without opening it to look.
At that time, Shìzǔ departed to become Jīngzhōu,
and upon reaching the garrison, wrote a letter to Xiàochuò, saying:
“You reside in seclusion with much leisure,
and are somewhat able to devote yourself to the classics and records,
reciting and expressing your emotions and nature.
Compared to the rare few among the ancients,
you do not restrain yourself through modesty, yet you are able to keep your skill from becoming restless (kè yǎng 伎癢);
and furthermore, Yú Qīng and Sī Qiān created works because of this.
I imagine the urge to compose and compile
must be considerable.
In Luòdì, paper is expensive;
in the capital (Jīngshī), reputations soar.
These two places are experiencing this simultaneously—
how prosperous!
Recently, when I was free from official duties on the road,
I managed slightly to pen some words.
Although I have no works recording my journey,
I have several pieces expressing nostalgia for the past.
Since arriving here,
various matters have kept me occupied with trivial tasks.
I fear the criticism from juniors (xiǎo shēng zhī dǐ)
will bring shame upon Lújiāng;
the evil intercepted on the road (zhē dào zhī jiān)
gives rise to the worry that schemes will be plotted against the Administrator (cóngshì).
I am currently raising the curtains (qīng wéi 褰帷) to discipline myself
and ceaselessly seeking out suffering (qiú mò 求瘼).
How can I possibly have leisure
for the efforts of brush and ink?
However, concerning the affection in my heart (xīn hū ài yǐ),
it has never ceased.
I miss your delightful voice (huì yīn 惠音),
but the refreshing wind (qīng fēng 清風) is not heard.
It is like dreaming of warm jade (wēn yù 溫玉)
or thirsting for bright pearls (míng zhū 明珠).
Although I am ashamed to compare myself to Biàn [Hé] and Suí [Hóu],
I am still fond of such things (hào shì 好事).
If you have newly composed anything,
I hope you can show it to me.
Do not treat it lightly,
thereby disappointing my request.
Having no way to fully appreciate (shǎng xī 賞悉) it,
I send this to convey my feelings.
Several travel routes are calculated;
I await the return of your fragrant letter (fāng zhá 芳札).”
Xiàochuò replied:
“I have respectfully learned that since you took leave of the Imperial City (Huáng Yì),
you have arrived at Jīngtái.
Before you have even labored at inspection and recommendation (cì jǔ 刺舉),
you are already displaying your high talent (gāo lí 高麗).
Although I recently had the privilege of viewing a short sample of exquisite writing (chǐ jǐn 尺錦),
I have not seen the complete jade (quán yù 全玉).
In the past, the literary compositions of Línzī [Wáng]
were entirely given to Yáng Xiū.
I have not exhausted my treasure chest (bǎo sì 寶笥),
but I am ashamed when I look back upon the former sages (xiān zhé 先哲).
According to the old customs of Zhǔgōng,
many court robes have been worn out (cháo yī duō gù 朝衣多故).
The recommendation of two worthies by Lǐ Gù,
and the memorializing concerning five commanderies by Xú Qiú—
Your way of inspiring awe and benevolence (wēi huái zhī dào 威懷之道)
encompasses both.
You surely intend to let your achievements flow like metal and stone (jīn shí liú gōng 金石流功),
and disdain using brush and ink to leave traces (hàn mò chuí jì 翰墨垂迹).
Although this deviates from the principle of ‘knowing two things’ (zhī èr 知二),
it happens to accord with the Saintly Heart (shèng xīn 聖心).
Since I retired to the common village (sù lǐ 素里),
sweeping away the dust from my humble gate (qióng hàn 窮閈),
I am comparable to Yáng Lún who did not leave home,
and likened to Zhāng Zhì who kept his door closed.
In the past, when Zhào Qīng was distressed by poverty,
he freely expressed opinions on success and failure;
when Hàn officials harbored frustrated ambitions,
they extensively discussed rise and decline.
These circumstances occurred at the same time,
but I am unfit to be compared to them.
I secretly feel, why should the patterned leopard (wén bào 文豹) be guilty,
and be judged criminal because of its markings?
If we discuss this matter,
how easy is it (yòu hé róng yì 又何容易)?
Therefore, I have concealed my brush and restrained my ink (tāo hàn shǔn mò 韜翰吮墨)
through many cold and hot seasons.
I lack Zǐ Yòu’s ‘Song of Nánshān,’
and also lack Jìng Tōng’s ‘Fù on the Wèishǔi.’
I have nothing with which to offer myself and invite laughter (xiàn xiào 獻笑),
or slightly repay your encouragement and guidance (bāo yòu 褒誘).
Furthermore, my talent is insufficient to describe objects (tǐ wù 體物),
and I do not intend to compose works like Xuán Gēn.
The circumstances are different from previous promises,
so how could I cause fear to Zhū Hài?
Looking back at myself and reflecting on my conduct,
I heave continuous sighs.
But looking toward the expansive Han River (Hàn Guǎng 漢廣) mentioned in your words,
it is as distant as the edge of heaven.
My humble heart,
divides the night soaring nine times [to reach you].
Your Highness condescends to visit my humble dwelling (bái wū 白屋),
inquiring about me and seeking me out.
Eating mulberries, I cherish your voice (shí shèn huái yīn 食椹懷音)—
how much more so when it is a person like you!”
Xiāo Zhuó was dismissed from office,
Gāo Zǔ frequently sent the Minister of the Secretariat, Xú Miǎn, to convey the imperial decree and console and comfort him.
Whenever there was a court banquet, he was always invited to participate.
And when Gāo Zǔ composed the poem for the Ritual Plowing Field,
he again ordered Miǎn to show it to Xiāo Zhuó first.
At that time, there were several tens of people who had received the edict to compose,
but Gāo Zǔ considered Xiāo Zhuó especially skilled.
On that very day, an imperial edict was issued,
appointing him as Western Gentleman of the Household and Consultant to the Prince of Xiāngdōng.
His Memorial expressing gratitude stated:
"I, your servant, was unable to hold the pearl to avoid danger,
or bend the branch to protect my feet.
Because of this blunt fortune
of mine, I frequently clashed with others.
Moreover, I met friends who concealed their resentment,
and thus I occupied a position targeted by slander.
They fabricated right and wrong,
resulting in false accusations.
The sun and moon shine brightly,
clarifying injustice and justice.
Whenever the case files
were reviewed by the Emperor, he immediately recognized the injustice suffered by Jiǎng Jì;
the intense scrutiny revealed the truth clearly,
not depending on the eloquence of Chén Zhèng.
Thus, I slipped through the dense net
and escaped those severe restraints,
allowed to return among the ranks of the people,
residing neighbor to neighbor with the citizens of Táng.
Bringing the dead back to life and putting flesh on the bones—
how could that equal this beneficence?
I, your servant, truly lack wisdom,
but who does not respect Heaven?
Far removed in the fields and furrows,
having utterly despaired of the lofty palace gates,
yet you condescended to receive and guide me,
graciously issuing imperial instructions.
For me, a trivial being,
this is sufficient to cause overwhelming honor.
Moreover, like stiff branches and fallen leaves,
I suddenly received the cloud and dew of imperial favor;
where positions are established in the imperial court,
I am again ranked among the flourishing officials.
But being decaying wood and rotten dust,
I merely result in protracted encouragement;
catching shadows and tying up the wind,
ultimately there will be no effective repayment."
He also sent a Memorial expressing gratitude to the Eastern Palace (the Crown Prince), saying:
"I, your servant, have heard that
the Former Sage said, 'If the masses hate it,
you must investigate it;
if the masses love it,
you must investigate it.'
Is it not the case that if one is isolated, they are subjected to accumulated slander,
and if one forms cliques, then accumulated praise is trusted?
To understand the difference between likes and dislikes,
one must rely on bright discernment.
Therefore, Yàn Yīng twice served as the Chief Minister of Ā,
being criticized first and praised afterwards.
The later praise stemmed from flattery,
while the earlier criticism was due to his straightforward conduct.
Thus, if one dog bites,
fine wine may exchange its sweetness for sourness;
if one hand shakes it,
the good tree changes between life and death.
Moreover, Zōu Yáng had a saying:
scholars, whether wise or foolish,
are met with jealousy upon entering court.
Such examples include Zāng Wén maligning Zhǎn Jì,
Jìn Shàng banishing Líng Jūn,
the Marquis of Jiàng rejecting Jiǎ Shēng,
and Píng Jīn framing Zhǔ Fù.
Since this time onwards,
their examples have truly been numerous.
Slanderous writing and brief words,
I have no time to fully enumerate them,
but what I observe through my limited perspective
is always born of intense resentment.
Your Highness instructs in the Way and studies books,
condescending to share a love of learning.
The injustice and justice of past events
are fully understood in your divine inspection.
Formerly, when I was standing in attendance,
I personally received your guiding words.
Comparing the swirling wind and the striped mat
to slander and wickedness,
Your Highness’s sincere instruction
deeply lamented the situation.
I, your servant, relying on my foolishness and treading the path of uprightness,
was unable to stop the beginning or prevent the slightest sign of trouble.
It was not long after
that I met with blame and suffered calamity.
Although finding fault through meticulous scrutiny,
those at court still sympathized;
but with strict laws and severe statutes,
the malicious were allowed to succeed in their schemes.
They disregarded betraying friends,
determined to seek favor with the ruler.
If it were not for the Emperor displaying his surpassing brilliance,
revealing the cruelty of the penal laws of Língyáng,
their manipulation of documents and false slanders
would not have been believed by the imperial sagacity.
In chains and fetters,
fortunately, I was able to be cleansed of ignorant obscurity.
You issued the decree removing my disgrace,
and furthermore promulgated the instruction allowing me to attend court assemblies.
I, the humble person, did not yet understand the proper way,
so I tied up my horse and suspended my carriage,
completely ceasing court attendance.
I was just wishing to hide my shadow and conceal my voice,
and relocate to the forests and valleys.
I did not realize that the imperial notice never ceases,
and that even trivial matters are certainly revealed.
You did not consider my resistance a flaw,
and again ordered me to enroll at the imperial court.
You bestowed a benevolent and harmonious countenance,
and offered simple and sincere words.
To display this for a thousand years,
the favor I received is already vast;
moreover, this grace is equal to a special summons,
and this honor is like the start of an official career.
Looking back at antiquity and reflecting on myself,
I increasingly feel profound unworthiness.
However, my loyalty, like cinnabar and stone, is unchanged,
eternally following the proper path,
unlike those skilled in speech
who fabricate malicious slander.
Furthermore, I am like the winter plant that has
already withered its branches and leaves.
I only receive prolonged virtuous favor,
yet have no repayment for the spring sunshine [of imperial grace]."
Later, he served as Director of the Crown Prince’s Household.
Due to mourning his mother, he left office.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Consultant and Aide to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West.
He was promoted to Palace Aide to the Imperial Secretary,
then Director of the Bureau of Personnel in the Department of State Affairs.
Because he accepted one bundle of silk from someone,
and was sued by the person who gave the gift,
he was demoted to Chief Clerk to the Prince of Línhè, Commandant of Trust and Awe.
After a while,
he was promoted to Director of the Imperial Library.
In the fifth year of Dàtóng
(539 CE), he died in office,
aged fifty-nine.
Xiāo Zhuó had a great reputation in his youth,
but he relied on his temper and presumed upon his talent,
often insulting and slighting others.
If anything was not to his liking,
he would criticize and denigrate it in the strongest terms.
Zāng Dùn, the Commander of the Guards, Shěn Sēnggǎo, the Minister of the Imperial Treasury, and others
were all respected by their contemporaries,
but Xiāo Zhuó especially slighted them.
Whenever he was at court gatherings or meetings,
he would speak with none of the dukes and ministers;
instead, he would call upon stable hands and servants to ask them about matters of the road.
Because of this, he frequently offended others.
Xiāo Zhuó’s literary style was revered by later generations,
and the world valued his writing.
Whenever he composed a piece,
it was completed in the morning and widespread by evening.
Those fond of literature all recited, copied, and transmitted it,
and its fame flowed to distant regions.
His collected works contained several hundred thousand words
and circulated throughout the world.
Xiāo Zhuó’s brothers, cousins, children, and nephews
totaled seventy people at that time,
all capable of writing literary compositions.
This had not been seen in recent antiquity.
His three younger sisters married Wáng Shūyīng of Lángyá, Zhāng Shěng of Wújùn, and Xú Fěi of Dōnghǎi.
All had talent and learning;
Fěi’s wife’s writing was especially clear and outstanding.
Fěi
was the son of Xú Miǎn, the Minister of the Secretariat.
He served as Prefect of Jìn’ān Commandery
and died.
When his coffin returned to the capital,
his wife composed a funeral address,
the diction of which was extremely sad and mournful.
Miǎn had originally intended to write a mourning composition,
but when he saw this composition,
he thereupon abandoned the attempt.
Xiāo Zhuó’s son was Liàng,
whose courtesy name was Qiúxìn.
In his youth, he loved learning
and possessed literary talent.
He especially had a wide understanding of the history of the Jìn Dynasty.
Contemporaries called him
"Pí Líng Jìn Shū."
He successively held office as Aide to the Director of the Imperial Archives,
Attendant of the Crown Prince’s Household,
Clerk to a Princely Establishment,
Clerk in Charge of Merits,
and Registrar and Aide to the Prince of Xuānchéng.
Wáng Jūn, courtesy name Yuánlǐ,
also known as DéRóu,
was a native of Línyí, Lángyá.
His grandfather, Sēngqián,
was Duke Jiǎnmù, Minister of Works (Sīkōng) of Qí.
His father, Jí,
was a Grand Master of the Center.
Wáng Yún
was sharp and observant as a child,
and at sixteen,
he composed the
fù
When he grew up,
he was quiet, devoted to study,
and was as famous as his paternal cousin, Tāi.
Xiè Lǎn
of Chénjùn,
and Lǎn's younger brother Jǔ,
also enjoyed high reputations.
At that time, people made a saying about them:
"The Xiè family has Lǎn and Jǔ;
The Wáng family has Yǎng and Jù."
Jù was Tāi,
and Yǎng was Yún;
they were both their courtesy names.
He began his career as an aide to the Prince of Línchuān, who was in charge of the Central Army,
then was promoted to the Crown Prince's Retainer,
and was appointed as the Palace Attendant in the Department of the Palace Affairs.
Since the Wáng clan crossed the river,
none of its members had served in the Bureau of Attendants.
Some advised him to hesitate and decline the position,
but Yún said:
“Lù Píngyuán
was the preeminent talent of the southeast,
and Wáng Wéndù was unmatched in Jiāngdōng.
Since I can compare my path to these predecessors,
what is there to regret?”
Thus, he happily accepted the post.
Shěn Yuē,
the Minister of Personnel,
who was the literary authority of the age,
would sigh and chant every time he saw Yún's writings,
believing that he himself could not match him.
He once said to Yún:
“In the past, Cài Bójiē,
upon seeing Wáng Zhōngxuān,
praised him, saying:
‘You are the grandson of Lord Wáng;
all the books in my family
should be given to you.’
Though I am not quick-witted,
I beg to attach myself to this statement.
Since Xiè Tiǎo
and other virtuous men have fallen away,
my lifelong literary aspirations
were almost entirely extinguished.
I did not expect that in my weary later years,
I would meet you again.”
Shěn Yuē
built a tall pavilion in his suburban residence.
Yún composed "Ten Songs on Grass and Trees"
and inscribed them on the wall,
writing only the words
without adding titles to the pieces.
Yuē told people:
“These poems point to objects and present their forms;
they do not need titles.”
Yuē composed the Rhapsody on the Suburban Residence,
pondering the composition for a long time,
but still had not completed it.
He then invited Yún to look at his draft.
When Yún read to the line
“The female rainbow (ní, pronunciation wǔ jī fǎn) is continuously curling,”
Yuē clapped his hands and exclaimed happily,
“I was worried that people would pronounce this as ní (pronunciation wǔ jī fǎn)!”
Next, when they reached
“Falling rocks pile up like stars,”
and
“Ice hangs in the deep pit and is girdled by the rising bank,”
Yún praised them,
beating time with his hand.
Yuē said:
“Those who understand music are few;
true appreciation is almost extinct.
The reason I invited you
is precisely because of these few lines.”
Yún also once composed a poem and presented it to Yuē.
Yuē immediately replied in a letter, saying:
“Upon reading the poem you presented,
I find it truly beautiful and exemplary.
The harmonious sound permeates the paper;
the light and shadow fill the characters.
Even Kúi and Yá,
if they were to respond,
would feel more than ashamed;
how could the flying peacocks
not feel greatly embarrassed?
My old, clumsy eyes
constantly await new wonders,
and now they have all brilliantly arrived;
the beginning has already exhausted itself.
The magnificent brilliance is revealed,
like the fragrance of orchids and the resonance of jade.
The meaning of perfect harmony
cannot be compared to flutes and reeds.
The reach of your thought and strength
has attained this level.
I sigh in admiration, chant, and ponder,
wandering in thought and forgetting everything.
In my youth and prime,
I quite loved this literature;
even in the midst of chewing and tasting,
how can I tire in my later years?
Not being able to match later talents
is certainly not limited to one person,
but the exclusive beauty and superior ability
truly belong to you, my son.
I await a leisurely day
to renew our pure meeting.”
Wáng Yún
was skilled in composing texts that pressed difficult rhymes.
Whenever there were public gatherings
and joint compositions,
his prose was inevitably refined and beautiful.
Shěn Yuē
often casually spoke to Gāozǔ, saying:
“Among the famous writers of recent times,
only Wáng Yún is truly unmatched.”
He was successively promoted to the Crown Prince's Marshal,
and Middle Retainer,
and was put in charge of the clerical records for the Eastern Palace.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng
cherished men of letters,
and often socialized with Yún, Liú Xiàochuò, Lù Chuí, Dào Qià, and Yīn Yún
in the Xuánpǔ park.
The Crown Prince
alone grasped Yún's sleeve
and patted Xiàochuò's shoulder, saying:
“This is what is called: ‘Grasping the sleeve of Fúqiū
with the left hand,
and patting the shoulder of Hóngyá
with the right.’”
Such was the esteem in which he was held.
Yún
and Yīn Yún
were also treated with respect
due to their dignified elegance.
He was transferred out
to serve as the Attendant Secretary of Dānyáng,
and Consultative Counselor to the Commander of the Northern Central Army,
then promoted to Central Secretary.
He was commanded by imperial decree
to compose the stele inscription
for the Venerable Master Bǎozhì
of Kāishàn Temple.
The prose was exceptionally beautiful and elegant.
He was again commanded by imperial decree
to compile thirty volumes of memorials and presentations
from the Central Secretariat,
along with the fù
and sòng
he had submitted,
all into one collection.
Soon after,
he concurrently served as Chief Clerk
to the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
General of Níngyuǎn,
and managed the affairs of the headquarters,
the state, and the commandery.
He was appointed Household Manager
to the Crown Prince,
and was again put in charge of the clerical records.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
he resigned his post
due to mourning his mother.
Yún
was naturally filial;
he wasted away and suffered excessive grief beyond the prescribed rites.
After the mourning period ended,
he was ill and incapacitated for a long time.
In the sixth year (525 CE),
he was appointed Bureau Director in the Ministry of Personnel,
Yún's appearance was small and unattractive;
his height did not reach six *chǐ*.
His nature was broad and generous;
he did not use his artistic skills to elevate himself above others,
but from a young age he excelled in talent and reputation,
and was highly regarded by the people of his time, along with Liú Xiàochuò.
His self-preface says:
"When I was young, I loved books,
and as I aged, this became even more profound.
Even if I happened to see a book and glanced at it,
I immediately made notes and recorded it.
Later, when I reviewed it again,
the joy and inspiration were even deeper.
Habit became second nature,
and I did not feel fatigue from the pen.
From the age of thirteen or fourteen,
from the *yǐhài* year (495 CE), the second year of Qí Jiànwǔ, until the sixth year of Liáng Dàtóng (540 CE),
forty-six years have passed.
In my youth, I read the Wǔ Jīng
all seventy or eighty times.
I loved the Zuǒshì Chūnqiū,
and reciting it constantly became a verbal habit.
I broadly abridged, deleted, and selected passages,
performing three comprehensive readings and five complete transcriptions.
The other classics, including the Zhōuguān, Yílǐ, Guóyǔ, Ěryǎ, Shānhǎijīng, and Běncǎo, I transcribed twice.
The works of the masters and histories, and various collections I transcribed once.
I never hired someone to lend a hand;
I personally transcribed them all,
amounting to more than a hundred scrolls, large and small.
This is not worthy of transmission to literary enthusiasts;
it is merely intended to guard against forgetting."
He also wrote a letter to his sons discussing the family collections, saying:
"Historical biographies state that the Cuī clan of Ānpíng and the Yìng clan of Rǔnán
have both possessed literary talent for generations.
This is why Fàn Wèizōng said of the Cuī clan, 'For generations they have excelled at the carving of dragons [fine literary composition].'
However, this was only for two or three generations, father and son;
it was not the case that over seven generations,
famous virtue shone brightly,
titles and ranks followed one another,
and everyone had their own collection,
as is the case with my family generationally.
Shěn Shàofù Yuē told people: 'I have loved the words of the Hundred Schools since youth,
and I have served as the historian for four dynasties.
Since the beginning of time,
there has never been such a flourishing case
of titles and ranks linked continuously, and literary talent succeeding itself,
as with the prosperity of the Wáng clan.'
You all should look up to the foundations of the hall [the achievements of your ancestors]
and think of striving hard."
Yún compiled his own writings,
using one official post as one collection.
The collections corresponding to his posts as Xǐmǎ, Zhōngshū, Zhōng Shùzǐ, Lìbù, Zuǒ Zuǒ, Línghǎi, and Tàifǔ were each ten scrolls,
and the Shàngshū collection was thirty scrolls,
totaling one hundred scrolls,
which circulated throughout the world.
The Historian Yáo Chá, Minister of the Personnel Bureau of Chén, commented: Given Wáng Sēngrú's immense learning
and Liú Xiàochuò's literary brilliance,
the sovereign was certainly not unfavorable to them,
nor was their talent left unused.
To attain the 'blue and purple' [high official rank]
and achieve the utmost nobility—
how difficult could that have been?
However, Xiàochuò did not restrain his speech and conduct,
thus tripping up his own career and reputation.
He merely suffered depression in his later years;
it was not that he failed to meet with opportunity.
Biography Twenty-Eight: Zhāng Miǎn (Younger brothers: Suì and Wǎn)
Zhāng Miǎn, courtesy name Yuáncháng,
was the son of General of Cavalry Hóngcè.
When he was several years old,
his maternal grandfather, Liú Zhòngdé of Zhōngshān, found him extraordinary,
and once said:
"This child is an unusual vessel;
he will be a treasure to the Zhāng clan."
Toward the end of Qí Yǒngyuán,
when the Righteous Army arose,
Hóngcè followed Gāozǔ in launching the campaign.
He left Miǎn in Xiāngyáng.
Miǎn was then only ten years old.
Whenever he heard of a victory or defeat by the army,
worry or joy showed in his expression.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
Hóngcè, serving as Wèiwèi Qīng,
was murdered by rebels.
Miǎn grieved excessively over his father’s cruel death,
and his mourning rites exceeded the prescribed rules.
Gāozǔ sent an official to admonish him.
When the mourning period ended,
he inherited the title of Marquis of Táoyáng County,
and was summoned to serve as a Guózǐ Shēng.
He started his career as Mìshū Láng,
and was then sent out to be the Administrator of Huáinán.
He was eighteen years old at the time.
Gāozǔ doubted that he was too young and unfamiliar with administrative affairs,
so he sent a chief clerk to seal and retrieve the official court documents of the commandery.
Seeing that Miǎn's judgments were consistent and satisfactory,
the Emperor praised him highly.
He returned and was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén and Yúnhuī Wàibīng Cānjūn.
Miǎn was diligent in his studies from youth,
setting his own curriculum for reading,
and never letting a scroll leave his hand.
He was particularly knowledgeable about the Hòu Hàn and the various schools of the Jìn era.
If a guest held a scroll and questioned Miǎn,
he would answer immediately according to the question,
with virtually nothing missed or forgotten.
When the post of Diànzhōng Láng was vacant,
Gāozǔ said to Xú Miǎn:
"This office traditionally employs men of literary talent,
and moreover, it ranks among the foremost of court officials.
It is appropriate to choose the person carefully."
Miǎn recommended Miǎn for the selection.
After a while,
he was sent out as the Administrator of Wǔlíng.
He returned and was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and then Zhōng Shèrén.
Miǎn’s mother, Lady Liú,
because her father had died and the family was poor,
and the funeral rites had been incomplete,
never lived in the main quarters for the rest of her life,
and did not follow her son into the official residences.
The salary and emoluments Miǎn received while serving in the commandery, he dared not spend.
Even his wife and children did not change their clothing often.
When he returned to the capital,
he used it all to support his mother and relieve his relatives.
Although he had accumulated this wealth over several years,
it was used up in a single morning.
Miǎn’s private chambers were always quiet and simple, like those of a poor person.
He was successively promoted to Advisory Counselor to the Northern Central Commandant and Chief Clerk of Níngyuǎn.
He was then sent out as Administrator of Yùzhāng.
