Miǎn governed by relying on kindness and benevolence,
and did not employ subtle entrapments or deception.
The officials and common people were transformed by his virtue
and dared not deceive him.
The old people all said,
"We have not seen this for several decades."
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he was summoned to be Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ,
but declined the appointment due to illness.
His post was changed to Tàizǐ Zhōng Shùzǐ,
concurrently holding the title of Chief of the Feathered Forest Guard.
Soon after, he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
He was temporarily demoted because he arrested a person who had fought with a foreign envoy,
being reduced to Huángmén Láng,
while concurrently holding his previous post.
Soon, he was restored to his true position.
While Miǎn served in the judicial office,
he investigated and punished without fear or favor,
and was known as strong and upright.
Gāozǔ therefore sent an artist to paint his likeness in the governmental ministries
to encourage officials.
In the third year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
he was promoted to Shìzhōng,
but before he could take up the post,
he died,
aged forty-two.
An imperial edict conferred upon him the posthumous title of Shìzhōng,
and added the title of Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn.
His rank as Marquis remained as before.
He was granted fifty thousand coins
and fifty bolts of cloth for the funeral.
Gāozǔ personally expressed his sorrow.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng also went to mourn,
and wrote to Miǎn’s younger brother, Zǎn, saying:
"Your esteemed elder brother’s scholarship was thorough and comprehensive,
and he handled affairs with insight and agility.
Even comparing him to Yǐ Xiàng studying the ancient archives
or Qiè Hú devoted to the *Shi* and *Shu* classics,
looking from the present back at antiquity,
none could surpass him.
Since he entered the court,
nearly two *jǐ* (24 years) have passed.
In duty, we were colleagues,
and in sentiment, we were truly close friends.
At literary banquets and academic lectures,
whether gathering in the morning or feasting in the evening,
when did we not share in this excellent enjoyment
and participate in these conversations?
How could he depart forever,
suddenly passing away and never returning?
Moreover, he was only just reaching the age of full strength,
and was still able to fully exert his talent and ability.
The falling of the flower and the shattering of the ear [premature death]
makes the sorrow even deeper.
Thinking of your natural familial harmony,
to suddenly lose one another
is beyond words.
As I speak of this, my throat tightens,
and I take up my brush without coherence."
Miǎn loved books by nature,
accumulating over ten thousand scrolls.
He copied the differences and similarities between the histories of Hòu Hàn and Jìn written by various scholars,
resulting in the Hòu Hàn Jì in forty scrolls
and the Jìn Chāo in thirty scrolls.
He also copied the Jiāng Zuǒ Jí,
but did not finish it.
His Wén Jí comprises five scrolls.
His son was Fù Sì.
(whose) courtesy name was Bóxù,
was Miǎn’s third younger brother.
He was adopted to be the heir of his paternal uncle Hóngjí.
Hóngjí
was Gāo Zǔ’s maternal uncle,
and was posthumously granted the title Tíngwèi Qīng at the beginning of the Liáng dynasty.
When Zhàn
was eleven years old, he married Gāo Zǔ’s fourth daughter, Princess Fùyáng.
He was appointed Fùmǎ Dūwèi,
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Lìtíng,
and summoned to serve as a Guózǐ Shēng.
He began his official career as Mìshū Láng,
at which time he was seventeen years old.
His height was seven *chǐ* and four *cùn*,
his eyebrows and eyes were prominent and clear,
and his spirit and demeanor were bright and vigorous.
Gāo Zǔ
regarded him as extraordinary, and once said:
"Zhāng Zhuàngwǔ said, 'Eight generations later, there will be one who reaches my standard.'
Is this perhaps that person?"
Zhàn
loved learning. His elder brother Miǎn had over ten thousand scrolls of books.
He continuously read them day and night,
hardly ever letting go of the texts.
There were four positions of Mìshū Láng.
Since the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
this post was considered the starting selection for noble families beginning their careers,
and they would wait their turn to fill the vacancy.
When holding the office,
they generally moved to a new post after several tens or hundreds of days.
Zhàn
firmly requested not to be moved, wishing to observe all the maps and documents within the palace library.
He once held the catalog of the Four Divisions of Literature and said:
"If I finish reading these,
then I can speak of having an excellent start to my career."
After several years of this,
he was finally promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén,
then transferred to Xǐmǎ and Zhōng Shèrén,
all the while managing records.
Zhàn shared equal fame with Wáng Xī of Lángxié.
At the beginning of Pǔtōng (era),
Wèi sent Liú Shànmíng of Péngchéng to the capital to request peace,
and he sought to meet Zhàn.
Zhàn
was twenty-three years old at the time, and Shànmíng met him and sighed in admiration.
He was successively promoted to Tàiwèi Zīyì Cānjūn,
Shàngshū Lìbù Láng,
and shortly thereafter served as Cháng Jiān Shìzhōng.
People at the time considered this an early achievement.
Péi Zǐyě
of Hédōng said: "That Director Zhāng Lìbù is holding the position of the tongue and throat (critical communication post)
is already regrettable for being late."
Zǐyě's
character was broad and open-minded, and he claimed
that "once I passed thirty,
I no longer visited people."
Although he had not met Zhàn initially,
he nonetheless highly esteemed him,
and consequently, they became friends who overlooked the difference in age.
In the first year of Dàtōng (era),
he went out (from the capital) to serve as the Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Duke of Huáróng, Níngyuǎn (General),
and concurrently managed the affairs of the two commanderies and states of Lángxié and Péngchéng.
In the second year,
he was transferred to Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Duke of Huáróng, Běi Zhōngláng (General), and Administrator of Nánlánlíng,
awarded the title Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently managed the affairs of the prefecture and state.
In the third year,
he entered the capital to serve as Dùzhī Shàngshū,
but resigned due to mourning for his mother.
When the period of mourning was completed,
he went out to serve as the Administrator of Wúxīng.
When Zhàn
governed the commandery, he reduced burdensome laws,
striving for clarity and tranquility.
The people and officials benefited from this.
In the second year of Dàtóng (era),
he was recalled to serve as Shàngshū Lìbù.
When Zhàn
held the selection post, if someone from a humble or poor family
possessed even minor ability, they were promoted.
He did not bend his will to the powerful or influential,
and scholars unanimously praised him.
In the fifth year,
Gāo Zǔ personally issued an edict saying:
"Zhàn's maternal clan is distinguished,
a leader in the court.
Following Sīkōng (Zhāng) after Sīkōng,
his reputation crowns Fànyáng.
He may be Shàngshū Púyè."
Previously,
Zhàn did not agree in outlook with Hé Jìngróng, who was concurrently in charge of affairs.
Jìngróng held the reins of power,
and guests flocked to him.
If someone who had visited Jìngróng subsequently came to see Zhàn,
Zhàn would immediately refuse to receive them,
saying:
"I cannot deal with Hé Jìngróng's leftovers."
When he was promoted (to Shàngshū Púyè),
he submitted a memorial which stated:
"Since leaving to govern the commanderies as a limb of the state,
and upon returning to oversee the measuring standards of government,
I have been able to raise my head and extend my brow
to discuss and list right and wrong.
However, the lingering annoyance in my heart
has recently obscured my ears and eyes,
and how could I possibly have anticipated
the depth or clarity of matters?
Furthermore, to feign humility and embellish one's appearance
is truly not something I am skilled at.
I dislike vulgar people
and serving alongside them."
These words were aimed at Jìngróng.
While Zhàn
was in office, he proposed that during the southern suburban sacrifice, the emperor should ride in a plain carriage,
which was appropriate to both ancient and modern ideals.
He also proposed that officials possessing seals and cords who wore court attire
should all wear their official cords.
Both proposals were implemented at the time.
In the ninth year,
he was transferred to Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn and Dānyáng Yǐn.
Before he took office,
this was changed to Emissary with Credentials, Supervisor of Military Affairs of Xiāng, Guì, and Dōngníng three provinces, and Governor of Xiāng Zhōu.
While traveling to report on his duties,
he composed the *Fù* on the Southern Expedition (*Nánzhēng Fù*).
The text says: The year star was in Jūzī,
the month was Zhōnglǚ.
I paid respects to the Emperor in Chéngmíng Palace,
about to report on my duties in the Southern Chǔ region.
Suddenly, I looked back from mid-stream,
longing for my old home and standing
gazing;
the road stretched infinitely long and endless,
my feelings were overwhelmed, and there was no one to share them with.
So I halted my steps and sighed, saying: When a person resides in the universe,
how is it different from the battling
snails on a horn,
or gnats flying around?
Yet (we experience) fullness and emptiness, dependence and concealment,
looking up and down, floating and sinking.
We pride ourselves on glory and splendor in a fleeting moment (literally, a foot-long shadow),
and encompass ten thousand thoughts in a single inch of time.
Those who forget schemes in a pure
day,
that is the clear admonition of the sagely enlightened.
Observing the subtlety of things in true contemplation,
what is there worth troubling the mind with?
Considering the minor trajectory of my own self,
I belong to the flourishing era of an ascendant ruler.
I received
the excellent favor of the three generations,
and bore the great kindness shown to my whole family.
I ascended the three halls of Shíqú,
overseeing the collation of texts in the Six Arts.
I shook my long tassel in Chénghuá,
looking upon the Crown Prince’s
supreme wisdom.
While residing there, we held cups and shared mats;
when going out, we shared the same boat to cross together.
Those glorious mansions and imperial gardens
were constantly bustling at night and restful by day.
I recall the virtuous words still in my
ears,
as if the fresh dust has not yet departed.
Two *jì* (twenty-four years) have passed up until now,
I grieve that the brilliant one (the Prince) has forever departed.
Considering my limited ability throughout my life,
I truly wished to rest and retreat.
I am ashamed to sink thousands of miles away,
bidding farewell, mournfully, like Hán Āi, to the distant reaches.
(Serving) is like using a straw cloak in place of something better,
or like the crookedness or straightness of wheels and shafts.
I am ashamed of Zhōu Rèn's clear principles (about officials' duties),
and truly have nothing
praiseworthy in exerting my strength.
I met with the auspicious fortune of washing my cap tassels (taking office),
and encountered a wise era like drawing water from the well.
Cherishing the imperial favor yet having failed to repay it,
I look back toward the palace gates with hesitation.
I oversaw the central government
as the deputy,
leading the multitude of officials and being called master.
It was like a short rope in a deep well,
or a high wall without a foundation.
Alas, my offenses are minor (but enough to warrant removal),
how could I have maintained this position?
I received the Imperial mandate for this appointment,
and now I drive the post horses toward Héngyí.
Following the nightly stops, I proceed on my journey,
preparing my morning gear and departing forever.
My passage sways southward,
while my heart lingers
westward in sorrow.
Thereupon, I cross the Ox constellation (Niú),
and gaze laterally at the Pheasant Granary (Zhìkù);
looking ahead at the hidden mountain ranges,
and behind at the spreading clouds.
I recall how the Jìn clan initiated conflict,
overturning the tripod of the central plain...
Suì.
nourished the three rivers (Sānchuān) among lush grass,
moistening the two capitals (Liǎng Jīng) with morning dew.
Therefore, the Yellow Banner and Purple Canopy,
their destiny lay in the Eastern Quarter (Zhèn Fāng);
the omen of Jīnlíng,
truly accorded with its auspicious nature.
When
those who surrendered (guī mìng) bore the jade disks,
they then presented the seal to Wǔwáng;
initiating the illustrious lord of the restoration,
proclaiming ten generations and renewed glory.
Observe how internally he garnered popular support,
externally driving back invaders and establishing the
governance;
founding Jiāngnán from scratch,
building up the foundation and base.
How could he merely have been able to spread his virtue,
keep the sacrifices of the Jìn dynasty going,
or be praised in poems like Yúnhàn,
or lauded in Sīgān?
Rather,
the rightful calendar (zhèng shuò) was passed down sequentially,
for four generations until now;
having passed through many years,
over two hundred years.
partitioning territories between Huá and Róng,
saving the common people within the realm;
preventing (them) from disheveled hair
and wearing clothes fastened on the left (zuǒ rèn),
truly, illustrious virtue bestowed this.
Next, we approach the stacked peaks overlooking the river,
seeking the former burial chamber of Shúbǎo;
containing the lingering richness of pearls and jades,
displaying the remaining
beauty of silks.
When thinking of the profound principles of such a person,
how could joy or anger move him?
Although the soul is buried for a hundred generations,
it still illuminates clearly in the Nine Springs (jiǔ quán).
Passing by the Buddhist temple of Fǎwáng,
observing the jumping forward or backward depending on the situation;
following the will of the Four Seas,
thus taking advantage of chaos to punish tyranny.
When the Azure Essence (Cāng Jīng) was coming to an end,
great branches were pruned and fell away;
already having witnessed the scorpion
asserting its punishment,
and then employing beasts for mockery.
Watching for high beacons with forced smiles,
awaiting the long star with laughter of revelry.
How frightened and apprehensive were the common people,
thinking of borrowing life but having no
recourse.
Truly, when human desires are met, Heaven follows;
thus, all things witnessed the Sage arising.
Our August Emperor (Huángdì) received the Mandate and accepted the Charts,
intelligent, brilliant, divine, and martial,
capitalizing on the rift and setting things in motion,
sweeping across Sānchǔ.
The military victory lay in harmony,
benevolence and righteousness were surely secured;
the form was like accumulated water
breaking a dam,
the response was like a sudden gust of wind.
Thereupon, he slew the wild boar of Sānglín,
captured the great wind of Qīngqiū;
putting away shields and spears to illuminate virtue,
spreading it across the realm and achieving success.
Banishing
licentious music from Zhèng and Wèi,
barring seductive beauty from the decadent palaces;
matching Xuānhuáng in his great achievements,
how could Shāng and Zhōu compare in majesty?
Transformation led to Supreme Peace,
lasting four epochs until now;
the Six Yí kowtowed,
the Eight Mán followed the same tracks.
instruction was harmonious in the Imperial Academy,
grievances were redressed in the Grand Court (Dà Lǐ);
manifesting the illumination of the Three Lights,
descending the auspicious blessings of the Five Spirits.
Truly, his extraordinary
achievements surpassed a hundred kings,
certainly beyond the power of words to praise.
We trace the swift sandbar of Jīnniú,
observing the majestic splendor of Língshān,
truly a ruined mound in Jiāngnán,
its form rising level with the clouds and sky.
marking the white ridge against the green cliffs,
adorning
red patterns on the emerald peaks;
huge rocks leaped amid startling rapids,
striking against rushing cliffs with terrifying waves.
carving out thousand-fathom steep shores,
and the great ravine where ten thousand streams flow;
concealing the sun and moon
until they seem to wane,
rolling up wind and mist and twisting around.
Cliffs reflect in the river, brightly illuminated,
water rises, glimmering and shining;
accumulating hoarfrost and hail coming and going,
urging the waves and billows forward
and back.
Below, foam flows, increasing the peril,
above, the mountain peaks seem about to topple;
Hearing that knowing fate is a matter of apprehension,
therefore, running counter to the trend provides no refuge.
Asking about the strange appearance of the accumulated bones,
saying that
the furious buffalo came rushing.
When the fisherman casts his bait,
sinking and hiding, locked away in the great deep.
Examining the dark road concerning Zhōngwǔ,
driving a high carriage with four horses.
Not speaking of spirits
to summon the strange,
keeping the feelings present without discussing them.
Displaying the ancient calendar of Gūshú,
visiting the remains of Xuānwǔ;
possessing the heroic spirit of Zhòngmóu,
retiring his robe in the morning to serve as an assistant.
having served successive illustrious lords of the ancestors,
still carrying a burden for the great ruler;
his power tipped the River and overturned Mt. Dài,
his prestige turned back Heaven and shook the universe.
Although his profound sincerity was brilliant and honest,
it was not yet displayed by Yī
and Jì;
Much less those who have merit but lack ambition,
how could they remain in the latter generations?
Fearing to become a laughingstock to Wén and Jǐng,
worrying that the imitation of the worthy would lead to overturned cauldrons (failure);
although sprouts
burst forth and flourished generationally,
in the end, the lineage was wiped out and the clan destroyed.
Those who accumulate meager measures of reserves,
still seek them out and wait for blessings;
much less the great treasure of divine illumination,
which secretly interferes with the Heavenly Emolument.
Setting up guards at the barred and locked gates,
dispatching official documents to the border commandants;
occupying Huányuán in Yī and Luò,
guarding Héngjīn on the Hé and Wèi Rivers.
Not acting pretentious to attract guests,
nor lacking the act of giving up the official seal
while waiting for honor.
Truly, respecting the royal statutes,
containing humble deference and holding one's breath.
Thinking of Hángǔ Pass as a vital artery,
resembling the elite troops stored in the armory.
Gathering folksongs from the
past,
hearing about the nursing tiger in Níngchéng.
Now, affairs are simple and easy,
merely criticizing and examining hidden treachery;
despising Wén Zhòng for abandoning his post,
scorning Rěn Mén for living off taxes.
Thereupon, we look closely at Zhěcén,
gazing distantly at Què'àn,
the islets are vast and boundless,
wind and clouds disperse quietly.
Following a new clearing after seasonal rain,
viewing the vast and flowing Hundred Rivers;
the water is deep and clear by dark evening,
the mountains are uneven, making dawn distinguishable.
Suddenly looking down upon my hometown,
the river and sky stretch boundlessly;
going against the upstream current, hindered on the right,
following the long thicket
and penetrating on the left.
Alone, facing the wind to express my feelings,
plucking flowers from the fragrant islet—who would appreciate this?
Stopping at Tóngshān and mooring the boat,
visiting the sacred dwelling of Shúwén;
discovering the old name
still existing,
all choked with weeds and accumulated thorns.
Thinking of the gentleman's good reputation,
truly known throughout ancient times;
saving the failed endeavors of Bā and Hàn,
thus matching his name with Zōu and Lǔ.
Distinguishing
mountain spirits to stop lawsuits,
facing the sacrificial stars to enlighten the ruler.
Every time I handle affairs, I remember that person,
those with superficial learning cannot see this.
Praising the filial daughter of Méigēn,
still riding fat horses
among concubines;
Alas, the severe punishments imposed by the Wú people,
worrying that harsh nets would be inflicted.
One submerged a melon to manifest righteousness,
pointing to the vast blue waves as a promise;
this one floated a shoe to clarify
restraint,
hastening toward the blazing fire—what hesitation is there?
Truly, principle inspires feeling and stirs grief,
genuinely distressed by my sorrow;
Vainly I sigh deeply with distant thoughts,
ashamed of the wonderful words of Hándān.
Gazing toward
Nánlíng to rest my eyes,
I admire the commitment maintained at the *yámén*.
When the Jìn armies swept over the land,
how could the barrier not offer protection?
Taking the old and weak into a desolate city,
yet striving earnestly for
one basketful.
Although it was the small virtue of drawing water with a jar,
it is truly recognized by the *jūnzǐ*.
(One line missing) This is called the rite of serving others.
Entering the long bank of Léichí,
I recall the fragrant legacy of Gōng and Dài.
Approaching Yúguān, I stop eating,
treading upon cold cattails where bamboo shoots emerge.
Furthermore, some, while living, possessed excellent virtue,
and upon death became bright spirits.
Some sacrificed their families to serve their lord,
while others held hands
to pay respects to their parents;
Or some upheld integrity and died for righteousness,
moving the market people to sorrow.
Thus, families call them purely filial,
and the state titles them capable ministers.
Their pure glory is heralded in the highest ranks,
standing together with those of different ages as
neighbors.
Setting out from the dawn islet against the wind,
struggling with the difficulty of navigating Shénwú.
The banks shine, but the boat does not advance,
the water boils and the sand rises, causing sudden alarm.
The sky darkens, casting shadow,
and the drizzling rain gathers;
Pitying the exhaustion of the traveler,
I frequently draw aside the curtain and stand waiting.
Following the branch of the river,
gazing toward the thoroughfare of Pénghuì,
The journey is not yet halfway
to Jiàng,
and a full cycle of ten days has already passed.
At this point, a thousand streams converge,
and ten thousand peaks divide their forms;
Inverted reflections hang high,
overflowing the sky with grandeur.
The clear river washes clean,
the level lake is smooth and vast;
Light flips and color shifts,
appearing and disappearing, rippling gently.
Mín Shān and Bō Zhǒng,
are distant and desolate;
Qīngpén and Chì'àn
control the runoff and draw the tide.
Gazing at the gathering homebound clouds,
raising the pure wind, gently
fluttering;
The flying current borders the dark green thicket,
a brilliant long rainbow arches in the azure sky.
As for the dense thickets along the riverbank,
and the deep pools, the palaces of the waters,
Where swimming creatures go and return,
and where loudly crying things
gather together.
Flocks fly over the sand swells,
covering the grassy islet;
Strange shells and unusual scales,
patterned markings and brightly colored feathers.
Hearing the lonely crane’s solitary call,
listening to the solitary swan yearning for its companion;
A traveler’s journey is filled with thoughts,
lonely and mournful, causing deep sadness.
Admiring the crucial importance of the midstream location,
relying on the *xíkǎn* (repeated peril) to maintain its stronghold.
Having secured it and established natural barriers,
they also dwell
there and cultivate virtue.
To the south, it connects to Zhūyá and Yèláng,
to the west, it reaches Yùjīn and Huámò.
None fail to clear out internal treachery,
or suppress external cruelty and vice,
Serving as a defensive screen for the capital,
its service
is equal to the virtue of Qí.
Gazing at Kuāng Lǐng with hesitation,
imagining the robes of mist on the cloud-high cliffs;
The lingering sound of Héng'é's soaring music,
the pure melody evoked by the Prince.
If the luminous pearl can be offered,
how can
glory and splendor be difficult to discard?

Like

Making the river spirit ascend in a watery carriage,

When the people resent and the spirits are angry,

Thereupon, dismounting the carriage and entering the department,

Visiting and inquiring about the elders,

How ancient and flourishing it is!

Then I toured the provincial offices and courtyards,

Ceding Qiánzhōng to establish a governorship,

Touring the high mountains piled up in heights (rèn),

those eight kings who were not of the Liú family,

In Chángshā, he promulgated decrees,

knowing that the Way of Heaven (tiāndào) blesses the humble,

Seeking the former residence of the Grand Tutor (Tàifù, Jiǎ Yí),

the town has not changed the old well,

Cherishing the political arts of Yī (Yī Yǐn) and Guǎn (Guǎn Zhòng),

finally

Grieving that King Huái (Huái Wáng of Chǔ) was not distinguished,

Establishing fixed sacrifices outside the northern wall (běiguō),

hoping to offer fresh fragrance,

Jǐng (King Wǔ of Chángshā, Liú Jǐng) established

until the middle decline of the Fiery Dynasty (Yánzhèng, Han),
this tributary state (fān) was truly relied upon.
Looking at the abundance of the four mounds (fù),

examining
the face and belt of the mountains and rivers,

Below, it is vast and brightly elevated,

Lowering the light that shines in four directions from Ruòhuá (mythical flower),
raising the Jiànmù tree a thousand fathoms (xún).
Hoping that the clamor and dust can be screened out,
I ascend the steep crag and stay overnight awake.
Abandoning the common attachments
within the world,
yearning for the spirit kin who roam as immortals.
It is the time of cool wind and late season,
all plants achieve fruition in the West,
the splendid pond is distant and remote,
the flying pavilion is desolate and bright.
Admiring the fiery virtue (Yándé) of the southern region,
I love the autumn brilliance of the orchids and *huì* (fragrant plants).
I pick famed mandarins beneath the winding pavilion,
and gather fragrant chrysanthemums upon the high wall.
Trees line the corridor and stand side by side,
bamboos cover the ridge and grow thickly.
I watch the roosting
birds returning in the evening,
and see off the traveling geese departing in the morning.
Grieving that I have left my home village and am a distant sojourner,
I occupy myself by observing nature to soothe my emotions.
As for where the relay carriages speed to,
it is truly where the powerful (like a soaring eagle)

Some resign their posts to establish their prestige,
suddenly displaying their robes and receiving extra rewards.
Following the benevolent laws of the Sagely Ruler,
I bear the profound virtue of Heaven and Earth.
The moistening influence spreads over the nine *lǐ*,
its beneficence starting with my own family and extending to serve as a model for the state.
Although the minor paths are lacking in things worth observing,
how can one fear that the path of danger is easily overcome?
Looking longingly at the great avenue, I wish to gallop forth,

I hear that relying on a troublesome
stone is not a secure position,

I am ashamed to be the remaining disciple of Shòulíng,

When Zuǎn arrived at the prefecture,
he stopped the sending out of ten prefectural comfort missions,
released aged and sick officials and laborers,
and concerning the former persons assigned to guard duties at passes, markets, garrisons, and patrols,
all were canceled and merged.
In the prefectural boundaries of Línglíng, Héngyáng, and other commanderies,
there were the Mòyáo Mán people,
who made their homes by relying on treacherous mountains.
They had never submitted throughout previous administrations,
but because of this, they turned towards civilization.
In Yìyáng County, a man farmed two *qǐng* of land,
where all the stalks, though in different fields, bore the same heads of grain.
Zuǎn was in office for four years.
Exiled people returned voluntarily,
and the census population increased by over a hundred thousand,
bringing great peace to the prefectural territory.
In the second year of Tàiqīng
he was summoned to be the Lǐngjūn.
Soon after, he was reassigned the titles Shǐ Chíjié, Dūdū of military affairs of Yōng, Liáng, Běiqín, Dōngyì, Jìnglíng in Yǐngzhōu, and Suíjùn in Sīzhōu, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, and Níngmán Xiàowèi.
Zuǎn first heard that Prince Lún of Shàolíng was supposed to replace him in Xiāngzhōu.
Later, it was definitively decided that Prince Yù of Hédōng would be used instead.
Zuǎn had always held the young prince in low regard,
and the arrangements for his reception and official provisions were extremely meager.
Yù deeply resented this.
When he arrived at the prefecture,
he immediately claimed illness and refused to see Zuǎn.
He then inspected and restricted all general affairs of the prefecture and government,
holding them up and refusing to release them.
Just then, news arrived that Hóu Jǐng was attacking the capital.
Yù prepared his gear, intending to go down and offer assistance.
At that time, the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu, Prince of Xiāngdōng, was marching to aid,
and his army was stationed at Wǔchéng in Yǐngzhōu.
Zuǎn quickly sent a message reporting:
“Hédōng has already rigged his masts and put to water;
he intends to launch a surprise attack on Jīngzhōu.”
The Prince believed him,
and immediately recalled his army to garrison,
and thus, Jīngzhōu and Xiāngzhōu formed a rift of enmity.
Soon after, (Zuǎn) abandoned his unit
and went alone by boat to Jiānglíng.
The Prince immediately sent an envoy to rebuke Yù
and demand Zuǎn’s subordinates back.
Once Zuǎn arrived,
he was then sent to Xiāngyáng.
The former Cìshǐ, Prince Chá of Yuèyáng, delayed his departure from the post and had not yet left the garrison,
so Zuǎn was merely housed at the Báimǎ Sì (White Horse Temple) west of the city.
Just then, upon hearing that the rebels had captured the capital,
Chá consequently refused to hand over command.
The prefectural assistant defender Dù Àn deceived Zuǎn, saying:
“Observing His Highness Prince of Yuèyáng, he will certainly not tolerate you, my lord.
You, my lord, have always won the hearts of the people.
If you flee into the Western Mountains,
and gather a righteous host,
people from near and far will certainly flock to you.
Moreover, your subordinates will arrive sequentially under your leadership.
With this righteous undertaking,
there is nowhere you will not be victorious.”
Zuǎn believed him,
and swore an oath with him.
He then fled into the mountains by night.
Àn, in contrast, informed Chá,
who then sent Àn to lead a force to pursue Zuǎn.
When Zuǎn’s followers saw Àn’s troops, they were greatly rejoiced,
believing they had come as arranged.
When they arrived,
they immediately seized Zuǎn and his followers,
and sent them all away as captives.
He was then imprisoned and bound.
Soon after, Zuǎn was forced to shave his head and become a Daoist monk.
That same year,
Chá raised troops to attack Jiānglíng,
always taking Zuǎn along with the army following behind.
When the army retreated after suffering a defeat,
and reached the south of Jiǎnshuǐ,
those guarding Zuǎn feared that the pursuing troops were approaching,
so they killed him,
abandoned his body, and left.
He was fifty-one years old at the time.
Emperor Yuán, acting under imperial authority,
posthumously granted Zuǎn the titles Shìzhōng, Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn, and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
His posthumous title was Jiǎnxiàn Gōng.
Zuǎn possessed sharp discernment.
From the moment he met Emperor Yuán,
he offered his sincerity and devoted himself entirely.
When Emperor Yuán ascended the throne,
he fondly remembered him
and once composed a poem.
Its preface said:
“Jiǎnxiàn, as a person,
did not serve princes or marquises.
Proud of his talent and trusting his spirit,
when he met Us, he conversed from morning until nightfall,
unable to stop himself.
Bearing the virtue of this man in mind,
how can I ever forget him?”
Zuǎn authored the *Hóngbǎo* in one hundred scrolls
and a collected works (*wénjí*) in twenty scrolls.
His second son was Xī,
courtesy name Zǐyán.
He was known early on
and was selected to marry Tàizōng’s ninth daughter, Princess Hǎiyán.
At the beginning of Chéngshèng,
his official position reached Huángmén Shìláng.
Wǎn, courtesy name Xiàoqīng,
was Zuǎn’s fourth younger brother.
He first served as a Guózǐ Shēng,
and attained a high grade in the imperial examination.
He began his career as Chángjiān Mìshū Láng,
and was promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén,
Xǐmǎ,
and Zhōngshèrén,
in all of which positions he was responsible for record-keeping.
He was repeatedly promoted to Zhōngshū Láng
and Guózǐ Bóshì.
He went out to serve as Běizhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ and Tàishǒu of Lánlíng.
Upon returning, he was appointed Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì.
At that time, Xiāo Yuānzǎo, Marquis of Xīchāng and Yǐn of Dānyáng, had not taken up his post due to long illness.
An imperial decree ordered Wǎn to provisionally manage the affairs of the Yǐn.
He was promoted to Zhǎngshǐ to the Prince of Xuānchéng, who held the rank of Zhōngjūn,
and soon after, he was transferred to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Gāozǔ sent his younger brother, Zhōngshū Shèrén Xuàn, to convey the imperial decree, saying:
“The most urgent task for the state
is entirely about upholding the law and maintaining rectitude.
The use of personnel is fundamentally not restricted by promotion or demotion.
During the Jìn and Sòng eras,
Zhōu Mǐn and Cài Kuò both held this post while being Shìzhōng.
My Lord, do not suspect this is a demotion.”
At that time, the residence of the Prince of Xuānchéng commanded great prestige,
which is why this decree was issued.
On the New Year’s Day of the fourth year of Dàtóng,
according to the old system, the seating positions of the Pūshè and the Zhōngchéng were opposite each other, corresponding East and West.
At that time, Wǎn’s elder brother, Zuǎn, was Pūshè.
When the hundreds of officials lined up for duty,
the brothers led their retinues,
separating to rush up the two staircases.
This had never happened in previous generations,
and people at the time considered it an honor.
A little over a year later,
he went out to serve as Yùzhāng Nèishǐ.
While Wǎn was in the commandery,
he lectured on the imperial annotations to the meaning of the *Lǐjì Zhèngyán Yì* (Commentary on the Rectified Words of the Book of Rites).
There were usually several hundred scholars and gentlemen from the Four Great Clans listening.
In the eighth year,
Liú Jìnggōng, a man from Ānchéng, espoused a heterodox Dao,
and subsequently gathered followers to attack the commandery.
The Nèishǐ Xiāo Tuō abandoned the city and fled.
The rebels shifted their attacks to Nánkāng and Lúlíng,
slaughtering and destroying counties and towns.
They had tens of thousands of followers
and advanced to attack Xīngàn County in Yùzhāng.
Nánzhōng had long been unused to military conflict,
and the officials and populace were terrified, disturbed, and scattered in flight.
Some advised Wǎn that he should avoid the rebel vanguard,
but Wǎn did not comply.
Instead, he repaired the city walls and moats,
set up battle defenses,
and recruited brave volunteers,
obtaining over ten thousand men.
The Cìshǐ, Prince of Xiāngdōng, sent the Sīmǎ Wáng Sēngbiàn to lead troops to suppress the rebels.
He accepted Wǎn’s command and direction.
Within a period of ten days to a month,
the rebel faction was entirely pacified.
In the tenth year,
he was again made Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and given the added title of Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì.
Wǎn served as the Chief Censor for a second time.
He impeached and investigated without avoidance,
and the powerful elite feared him.
At that time, the Shìlín Guǎn (Scholars’ Forest Hall) was opened west of the city to gather scholars.

Wǎn, along with the Yòuwèi Zhū Chuò and the Tàifǔ Qīng Hè Chēn, took turns lecturing on the imperial annotations to the meaning of the *Lǐjì Zhōngyōng Yì* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Doctrine of the Mean in the Book of Rites).
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
When Hóu Jǐng's forces arrived,
he entered and guarded the Dōngyèmén Gate.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Lìbù Shàngshū.
When the palace city fell,
Wǎn fled,
and traveled externally to Jiānglíng.
Xiāngdōng Wáng, acting as regent,
appointed him Shìzhōng, Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, Xiàngguó Chángshǐ,
with Shìzhōng as before.
He was then dispatched as Chíjié, Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, Xiāngdōng Nèishǐ.
In the second year of Chéngshèng,
he was recalled to serve as Shàngshū Yòupúshè,
and soon after, was additionally appointed Shìzhōng.
The following year,
Jiānglíng fell,
and all court officials were taken captive and brought into the passes.
Wǎn was excused due to illness,
and later died in Jiānglíng,
at the age of sixty-three.
His second son, Jiāo,
whose courtesy name was Shàoyóu,
was quite learned in literature,
and was selected to marry Ānyáng Gōngzhǔ, the eleventh daughter of Tàizōng.
he reached the office of Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
Mìshūchéng,
and was in charge of the records of the Eastern Palace.
Yáo Chá, the Chén Lìbù Shàngshū, said: In the chaos of Tàiqīng,
relatives were estranged and disloyal.
Zuǎn could not reconcile the regional princes
and achieve a harmonious and benevolent administration.
Instead, harboring private grudges,
he created discord in Xiāoxiāng,
which eventually brought calamity upon himself,
not due to loyalty and integrity.
Following this, the fall of Jiānglíng
was indeed rooted in these events.
Considering Zuǎn's character,
he ultimately became a cause of the turmoil in Liáng.
What a pity!
Textual Criticism Notes
Biographies, Volume 29: Xiāo Zǐkè (Disciple Fàn, Zǐxiǎn, Zǐyún)
Xiāo Zǐkè, courtesy name Jǐngchōng,
was a native of Lánlíng,
and the second son of Qí Yùzhāng Wénxiàn Wáng Yí.
During Yǒngmíng,
as a prince, he was enfeoffed as Nánkāng Xiàn Hóu.
At the age of twelve,
he composed a rhyme-prose with his elder cousin, Sītú Jìnglíng Wáng Gāo Sōng,
and Wèijūn Wáng Jiǎn saw it and marveled at him.
Initially, he served as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Huáilíng Tàishǒu.
During Jiànwǔ,
he was promoted to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Wújùn Tàishǒu.
When Dàsīmǎ Wáng Jìngzé raised troops in Huìjī to rebel,
using the name of supporting Zǐkè,
Míngdì summoned Zǐkè's brothers and over seventy of his close relatives into the Western Bureau,
intending to harm them that night.
It happened that Zǐkè had abandoned his commandery and rushed back,
arriving that very day,
so Míngdì stopped.
He appointed Zǐkè as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ.
When Dōnghūn ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Mìshūjiān,
also serving as Yòujūn Jiāngjūn,
and soon after became Shìzhōng.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng,
he was promoted to Fǔguó Zīyì Cānjūn.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
his rank was demoted to Zǐ,
and he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì,
also serving as Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Due to illness, he did not accept the appointment,
and was transferred to Guānglù Dàfū.
Soon after, he became Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ.
Zǐkè, along with his younger brother Zǐfàn and others,
once entered the court to express thanks for a matter.
Gāozǔ received them in audience at the Wéndédiàn,
and leisurely said to them:
"I wish to speak with you brothers.
The treasures of All-under-Heaven
are fundamentally public instruments,
and cannot be obtained through brute force.
If destiny is not due,
even with the power of Xiàng Jí,
one will ultimately fail and perish.
Thus, Bān Biāo’s ‘Discourse on Kingly Mandate’ (Wángmìnglùn) says: ‘What he sought was merely a single gold piece,
yet he finally died, tossing in the ditches and gullies.’
You should not have failed to read this book.
Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng was by nature suspicious and jealous;
among his brothers who possessed even a slight good reputation,
none failed to be poisoned on some pretext.
The only one left was Jǐnghé.
As for the court officials,
those suspected of possessing the Mandate of Heaven and consequently harmed,
suffered continuous wrongful persecution.
However, some were suspected of possessing the Mandate of Heaven but could not be harmed,
and some possessed the Mandate of Heaven but were not suspected.
At that time, though they suspected your grandfather,
they could do nothing against him.
This is a case of suspicion that failed to accomplish harm.
There were also those who were not suspected,
such as Emperor Míngdì of Sòng, who was originally ordinary and overlooked.
How could he have been suspected and thereby spared?
Furthermore, I myself was only two years old at that time.
How could they have known that I was destined for today?
You should know that those who possess the Mandate of Heaven
cannot be harmed by others;
even attempts to harm them will fail.
When I first pacified Jiànkāng city,
officials inside and outside the court all advised me, saying: ‘The era has changed,
the people's minds need unity,
and measures should be taken.’
If I had acted upon this advice at that time,
who would dare say it was improper?
I merely observe that since the time of Jiāngzuǒ,
dynastic transitions have inevitably involved mutual execution,
which damages the spirit of harmony.
That is why the reigns of those states have generally not been prolonged or successful.
This is what is meant by ‘The mirror of Yīn
is not far off; it is in the time of the Xiàhòu.’
This is the first reason.
Second,
although the change from Qí to Liáng is called a dynastic transition,
the situation is different from past times.
Although the period of mourning rites between me and you brothers has been broken for two generations,
our kinship is not distant.
Do not speak only of brothers being kin;
among the brothers in a single family, some interact closely,
and some do not interact.
How much less so among relatives outside the five degrees of mourning?
At the beginning of the Qí regime,
we also shared the sweet and the bitter together,
and the core support was with me.
You brothers are young,
and naturally may not know all the details.
I and you brothers
share the sentiment of being one family.
How could I fail entirely to consider this
and treat you as strangers?
This is the second reason.
That I have achieved this today
was not what I originally intended or sought.
Furthermore, Jiànwǔ massacred and exterminated your family,
subjecting you brothers to misery.
When I raised the righteous army,
it was not only to avenge my own family’s shame,
but also to avenge you brothers.
If you had been able, during the time of Jiànwǔ and Yǒngyuán,
to quell the chaos and restore order,
even if I had risen up in Fán and Dèng,
how could I have failed to lay down my spear and support you?
Even if I had wished not to stop,
my army would have lacked a righteous cause.
Now that I have avenged you,
and the era has changed,
I hope you brothers will dedicate yourselves and repay me.
Furthermore, I seized the opportunity of chaos
and took the realm from the house of Emperor Míngdì;
I did not take the realm from your house.
In the past, Liú Zǐyú claimed to be the son of Emperor Chéng.
Emperor Guāngwǔ said, ‘Even if Emperor Chéng were reborn,
he could not recover the realm,
much less Zǐyú.’
Early in the Liáng dynasty,
when people urged me to execute and exterminate your kin,
I replied just as I spoke about the affairs of Emperor Xiàowǔ’s time: If they truly possess the Mandate of Heaven,
they cannot be killed by me;
if they lack destiny,
why should I hastily carry out such an act?
It would only show a lack of breadth of mind.
Cáo Zhì, being the grandson of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi
and the son of Chénsī,
served Emperor Wǔ of Jìn and became a loyal minister to the Jìn house.
This is an example for you.
You are of the imperial clan;
your bond of sentiment and righteousness differs from others.
I sincerely expect this of you;
you must not again harbor feelings of alienation.
Wait a little while,
and you will naturally know my true thoughts."
Furthermore, during the time of Prince Wénxiàn,
there was a eunuch named Zhào Shūzǔ, who served as the attendant in the inner apartment.
Early in the Tiānjiān era,
he entered the capital to serve as the chief of the Palace Apartment,
residing in the Shòuguāng Palace section.
Gāozǔ called Shūzǔ and said:
"I knew you previously when you were at the Northern Residence (Běi Dì).
Since you are an old acquaintance,
I often give you tasks.
Have you recently seen the young gentlemen of the Northern Residence?"
Shūzǔ respectfully replied:
"Recently, I have mostly been on duty,
and rarely go outside.
Even if I were to temporarily go out,
I would not be able to visit them."
Gāozǔ said:
"If you see the young gentlemen of the Northern Residence,
convey this sentiment of mine: Although I have established a new dynasty today,
my feelings are those of one family;
however, the foundation is not yet fully established.
The reason I have not yet employed the young gentlemen
is not only because it is inappropriate for me right now,
but also because I wish to ensure the young gentlemen are secure.
They should just shut their gates and rest easy;
later, they will naturally see my heart."
Shūzǔ immediately went out and fully relayed the emperor’s words.
Zǐkè was soon sent out to serve as the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Yǒngjiā.
He later returned and was appointed Minister of the Imperial Household (Guānglù Qīng),
and Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān).
He was then sent out to serve as General of Martial Display (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Línglíng (Línglíng Tàishǒu).
In the seventeenth year,
he entered the court to serve as Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì) and General Who Assists the State (Fǔguó Jiāngjūn).
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he was transferred to Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng).
In the third year,
he was transferred to President of the Board of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū).
In the fourth year,
he was transferred to the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù).
In the sixth year,
he was transferred to Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhānshì).
In the second year of Dàtōng,
he was sent out to serve as General Who Pacifies Distant Regions (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Wújùn (Wújùn Tàishǒu).
In the third year,
he died in his official residence in the commandery,
aged fifty-two.
An imperial edict granted him the posthumous titles of Attendant at the Palace (Shìzhōng) and Prefect of the Palace Writers (Zhōngshū Lìng).
His posthumous name was Gōng.
Zǐkè and his sixteen brothers
all served the Liáng dynasty.
Those who were skilled in literature
were five people: Zǐkè, Zǐzhì, Zǐxiǎn, Zǐyún, and Zǐhuī.
Zǐkè once said to his intimate friends:
"As for matters of literature and history,
my younger brothers are all accomplished,
so there is no need for me to strive further.
I only need to retire after my official duties
and be without fault; that is enough."
Zǐkè also studied extensively when young
and was quite skilled in writing,
but he subsequently discarded his writings,
hence no collection of his works has been transmitted.
Zǐcuō
was also famous.
During the Tàiqīng era,
his official position reached Director in the Board of Civil Office (Lìbù Láng).
While fleeing the chaos in Dōngyáng,
he was later killed by bandits.
Zi Fàn’s courtesy name was Jǐngzè,
and he was the sixth younger brother of Zǐkè.
In the tenth year of Yǒngmíng of Qí,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Qíyáng County
and appointed as Táizǐ Xǐmǎ (Attendant at the Crown Prince’s Gate).
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
his noble rank was reduced to Zǐ (Viscount).
He was appointed as Hòujūn Jìshì Cānjūn (Staff Officer and Recorder of the Rear Army),
and then reinstated as Táizǐ Xǐmǎ.
Soon after, he was transferred to Sītú Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education).
He resigned from office due to the mourning period for his birth mother (dīng suǒ shēng mǔ yōu qù zhí).
Zi Fàn was known for his filial nature.
His observance of the mourning rites was known for its intensity (yǐ huǐ wén).
When the mourning period concluded,
he was again appointed Sītú Zhǔbù.
He was successively promoted to Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng (Assistant to the Administrator of Dānyáng),
and then Táizǐ Zhōng Shèrén (Gentleman of the Palace, serving the Crown Prince).
He went out of the capital to serve as the Grand Administrator of Jiàn’ān.
Upon returning, he was appointed Hùcáo Shǔ (Clerk of the Registry of Households)
and Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Gentleman of the Court) under the Grand Marshal, the Prince of Nánpíng.
The Prince loved literary scholars,
and Zi Fàn was especially favored with his grace and attention.
The Prince once said:
“This man is a remarkable talent among the imperial clan.”
He was tasked with composing the Thousand-Character Classic (Qiānzì Wén).
Its lyrics were extremely beautiful.
The Prince ordered his recorder Cài Wěi to annotate and explain it.
From then on, any literary composition within the Prince’s establishment
was drafted by him.
When the Prince died,
Zi Fàn was transferred to Xuānhuì Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Staff Officer for General Xuānhuì),
and then served as Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk) to Hùjūn (General Protector) Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé.
When Zhèngdé became Dānyáng Yǐn (Administrator of Dānyáng),
Zi Fàn was again appointed Xìnwēi Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk for General Xìnwēi) under Zhèngdé,
also holding the position of Yǐn Chéng (Assistant to the Administrator).
He served in official posts for more than ten years,
but never served outside the establishments of princely fiefs (fān fǔ).
He often felt regretful about this.
Since all his younger brothers had achieved prominent positions,
he felt unequal to them.
At this point, he wrote a memorial (jiān) to the court regarding his appointment, saying:
“I have twice accepted the role of Chief Aide to a premier fief.
On this occasion, I have been disgraced twice.
Like a timid bird (cífú) in Hénán,
I rise again from this position.
Due to the different times of my youth and old age,
and the varying days of prosperity and decline,
although I am graced by favor,
I feel ashamed of my advancing years and gray hair.”
In his youth, Zi Fàn’s literary talent and fame were roughly comparable to his younger brothers Zǐxiǎn and Zǐyún,
but his demeanor and deportment were inferior.
Therefore, his official career had its superior and inferior points.
Whenever he read the History of Hàn (Hàn Shū),
regarding the Dù Huǎn brothers,
“five of them reached high office,
but only the middle brother, Qīn, did not reach the highest office but was the most famous.”
He often chanted and recited this,
using it to compare himself.
Soon after, he was appointed Sīmǎ (Commander) for General Xuānhuì, the Prince of Wǔlíng.
He did not take up this post.
He was then appointed Zhōngsàn Dàfū (Grandee for Scattered Appointments),
and transferred to Guānglù (Minister of the Imperial Insignia) and Tíngwèi Qīng (Minister of Justice).
He was sent out to serve as Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Bravery) and Grand Administrator of Shǐxīng.
Upon returning, he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū (Grandee of the Palace),
and transferred to Mìshū Jiān (Director of the Imperial Library).
When Tàizōng (Emperor Xiào Yuán) ascended the throne,
he was summoned to serve as Guānglù Dàfū,
and given the Jia Jīnzhāng Zǐshòu (Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon),
but he did not accept the appointment because of the imminent threat from the enemy.
In that year, when Empress Jiǎn was buried,
he and Zhāng Zǎn were commissioned to compose the ceremonial text (āi cè wén).
When Tàizōng read it,
he said:
“Although the current funeral rites are incomplete,
this text is no less than those of the past.”
Soon after, he fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-four.
After the rebels were pacified,
Shìzǔ posthumously appointed him Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū (Grandee of the Palace with the Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon).
His posthumous title was Wén.
His collected literary works amounted to thirty volumes.
His two sons, Pāng and Què,
both showed literary talent in their youth.
When Tàizōng was Crown Prince,
he and the Prince of Shàolíng once discussed the literary scholars of the Xiāo clan;
Pāng and Què were included among them.
Pāng reached the office of Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng (Gentleman of the Palace, Department of the Secretariat),
and Jìshì (Recorder) for the Prince of Xuānchéng in the Central Army.
He died before Zi Fàn.
Què,
during the Tàiqīng era, successively held the posts of Councillor (Yǒu) to the Prince of Xuānchéng,
and Yòu Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Right) to the Sītú.
After the rebels were pacified,
he went to Jiānglíng
and subsequently perished in Guānxī (the region west of the passes).
Zǐxiǎn’s courtesy name was Jǐngyáng,
and he was the eighth younger brother of Zǐkè.
He was intelligent and bright in his youth,
and King Wénxiàn considered him exceptional,
loving him more than his own sons.
At the age of seven,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Níngdū County.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
following the precedent for sons of princes, he was appointed Jǐshì Zhōng (Palace Attendant).
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
his noble rank was reduced to Zǐ (Viscount).
He was successively promoted to Ānxī Wàibīng (External Military Administrator for General Ānxī),
Rénwēi Jìshì Cānjūn (Staff Officer and Recorder for General Rénwēi),
Sītú Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education),
and Tàiwèi Lùshì (Record Keeper of the Grand Commandant).
Zǐxiǎn had a magnificent appearance;
he was eight *chǐ* tall.
He loved learning
and was skilled in composition.
He once wrote the *Hóng Xù Fù* (Rhapsody on the Wild Goose Prelude).
Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs) Shěn Yuè saw it and praised it, saying:
“This can be called achieving the elevated refinement of Míngdào,
indeed belonging to the stream of Yōutōng.”
He also compiled various accounts of the Latter Hàn Dynasty (Hòu Hàn)
and collated similarities and differences,
creating a complete history (for himself).
He also memorialized to compile the History of Qí (Qí Shǐ).
When the book was completed,
he presented it in a memorial,
and an imperial edict instructed it to be placed in the imperial archives (mì gé).
He was successively promoted to Táizǐ Zhōng Shèrén (Gentleman of the Palace, serving the Crown Prince),
Administrator of Jiànkāng,
Councillor (Yǒu) to the Prince of Shàolíng,
Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng (Assistant to the Administrator of Dānyáng),
Zhōngshū Láng (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),
and temporarily held the post of Zōngzhèng Qīng (Minister of the Imperial Clan Court).
He went out to serve as Grand Administrator of Línchuān.
Upon returning, he was appointed Huángmén Láng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate).
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he was transferred to Zhǎngjiān Shìzhōng (Grand Attendant and Consultant).
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ) greatly admired Zǐxiǎn’s talent,
and also praised his demeanor and eloquence.
Whenever he attended the emperor at imperial banquets,
the emperor would especially look at him and consult him.
The Emperor once casually said to Zǐxiǎn:
“I am composing the *Tōng Shǐ* (Comprehensive History).
If this book is completed,
all other histories can be discarded.”
Zǐxiǎn replied:
“Zhòngní (Confucius) praised the Way of the *Yì*,
eliminated the Eight Records (*Bā Suǒ*),
narrated the regional geographies (*Zhífāng*),
and discarded the Nine Hills (*Jiǔ Qiū*).
That the Holy Sage’s creation agrees with mine
is reaffirmed on this day.”
People at the time considered this a famous reply.
In the third year,
he concurrently held the post of Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University) while retaining his original office.
Gāozǔ’s commentaries on the classics (jīng yì)
had not yet been listed in the academic system.
While Zǐxiǎn was in office,
he memorialized to establish one assistant instructor (zhù jiào)
and ten students (shēng).
He also memorialized to compile the Collected Works of Gāozǔ
and the Record of the Northern Expedition of Pǔtōng (*Pǔtōng Běifá Jì*).
In that year, he was transferred to Guózǐ Jìjiǔ (Libationer of the National University),
and also given the title of Shìzhōng (Attendant and Consultant).
At the school, he successively lectured on Gāozǔ’s commentaries on the Five Classics.
In the fifth year,
he was selected as Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of the Department of Civil Service),
retaining his Shìzhōng title as before.
Zǐxiǎn was reserved and simple by nature,
and rather proud of his talent and spirit.
When he took charge of appointments,
upon meeting scholars and guests of the nine categories (jiǔ liú bīn kè),
he did not speak with them.
He merely lifted his fan and waved it once,
which the officials secretly resented.
However, Tàizōng (Emperor Xiào Yuán) had always greatly respected his character.
When Tàizōng was the Crown Prince,
he often invited Zǐxiǎn for intimate banquets.
Zǐxiǎn once rose to change his clothes,
and Tàizōng said to the seated guests:
“I have heard that extraordinary people occasionally appear.
Today I first knew that it is Minister Xiāo.”
He was highly regarded in this manner.
In the third year of Dàtóng,
he was sent out as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Benevolence) and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
Not long after arriving in the commandery,
he died
at the age of forty-nine.
An imperial edict stated:
“Zǐxiǎn, General Rénwēi and Grand Administrator of Wúxīng,
possessed a lofty and exceptional spirit and grace,
a fine vessel of the imperial clan.
He had not long been administering the region (fēn zhú),
when he abruptly met his demise.
I am filled with grief.
He is posthumously granted Shìzhōng and Zhōngshū Lìng (Director of the Central Secretariat).
Let the mourning begin immediately.”
When requesting a posthumous title for his burial,
a handwritten imperial order (shǒu zhào) stated:
“Relying on his talent and treating others with arrogance (shì cái ào wù),
he should be posthumously titled Jiāo (Arrogant).”
Xiāo Zǐxiǎn 蕭子顯 once wrote an autobiography.
Its summary says:
"I, as the Imperial Tutor of Shàolíng Wáng 邵陵王,
was honored to return to the capital.
Recalling those before me from afar,
there were Táng 唐 and Sòng 宋 of Chǔ 楚,
and Yán 嚴 and Zōu 鄒 of Liáng 梁.
Reflecting on my life,
I was quite fond of literary embellishment.
Although I achieved no fame,
my heart's desire was fulfilled.
Whenever I ascended a height and gazed to the horizon,
or watched things float away by the water,
or felt the wind stir on a spring morning,
or saw the moon bright on an autumn night,
or the early geese first appeared,
or flowers bloomed and leaves fell—
whenever there was an occasion, I responded,
and could never stop myself.
In previous generations, Jiǎ, Fù, Cuī, Mǎ, Hándān, Miào, Lù 賈、傅、崔、馬、邯鄲、繆、路 and their like,
all became prominent through their writing.
Therefore, I frequently presented eulogies,
comparing myself to the ancients.
In the sixteenth year of Tiānjiān 天監,
I first attended the Ninth Day imperial banquet.
Amongst the dense crowd,
I alone received an imperial edict that said: 'The clouds and scenery today are exceedingly beautiful;
how can you not compose a poem?'
After the poem was completed,
another imperial edict descended, saying: 'He can be called a talented scholar.'
I retired and said to others: 'Such a glance of favor
came unexpectedly.
How then can I compare myself to Jiǎ Yì 賈誼?
It is not easy to bear.'
Whenever I composed something,
I particularly lacked laborious thought;
I waited for it to come naturally,
not forcing it with effort.
The poems and rhymed prose I wrote in my youth,
especially the preface to Hóngxù 鴻序—
its style encompassed many forms,
and its literary quality was comprehensive in many ways.
It was quite widely circulated by those who appreciated literature,
thus my reputation spread easily."
Among Xiāo Zǐxiǎn's 蕭子顯 works were the Hòuhàn Shū 後漢書 in one hundred volumes,
the Qí Shū 齊書 in sixty volumes,
the Pǔtōng Běifá Jì 普通北伐記 in five volumes,
the Guìjiǎn Chuán 貴儉傳 in thirty volumes,
and a collection of his writings in twenty volumes.
His two sons, Xù 序 and Kǎi 愷,
both became famous in their youth.
Xù 序,
during the Tàiqīng 太清 period, successively held offices such as Táizǐ Jiālìng 太子家令
and Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
and was also in charge of official documents.
During the rebellion,
he died within the city.
Kǎi 愷,
initially a student of the Guózǐ 國子,
ranked highly in the policy examination.
The province also recommended him as Xiùcái 秀才.
He began his career as Mìshū Láng 祕書郎,
and was promoted to Táizǐ Zhōngshèrén 太子中舍人,
Wángfǔ Zhǔbù 王府主簿,
and Táizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬.
He resigned from office due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was reinstated as Táizǐ Xǐmǎ 太子洗馬,
then promoted to Zhōngshèrén 中舍人,
and was also in charge of official documents.
He was successively promoted to Xuānchéng Wáng Wénxué 宣城王文學,
Zhōngshū Láng 中書郎,
and Táizǐ Jiālìng 太子家令,
again in charge of official documents.
Kǎi's 愷 talent, learning, and reputation
were at the time compared to his father's.
Tàizōng 太宗, while in the Eastern Palace,
early on invited and befriended him.
At that time, Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子 Xiè Gǔ 謝嘏 was dispatched to govern Jiàn'ān 建安.
A farewell banquet was held in Xuānyóu Táng 宣猷堂,
and talented scholars of the time were invited to compose poems,
all using fifteen difficult rhymes.
Kǎi's 愷 poem was finished first,
and its words were also beautiful.
Tàizōng 太宗 sent a message to Xiāngdōng Wáng 湘東王, saying:
"Wáng Yún 王筠 is originally an old master,
but among the younger generation, Xiāo Kǎi 蕭愷 is notable;
he is indeed a talented scholar."
Before this, Gù Yěwáng 顧野王, a Tàixué Bóshì 太學博士, had been ordered to compile the Yùpiān 玉篇.
Tàizōng 太宗 felt that its detailedness and brevity were not entirely appropriate,
and since Kǎi 愷 was learned
and particularly skilled in philology,
he was instructed to revise it with other scholars.
He was promoted to Zhōngshùzǐ 中庶子,
but before he could be formally installed,
he was transferred to Lìbù Láng 吏部郎.
In the second year of Tàiqīng 太清,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng 御史中丞.
Soon after,
Hóu Jǐng 侯景 instigated a rebellion.
Kǎi 愷 was promoted to Shìzhōng 侍中 within the city,
but died in office shortly thereafter,
at the age of forty-four.
His collected works were all lost.
Zǐyún 子雲, courtesy name Jǐngqiáo 景喬,
was the ninth younger brother of Zǐkè 子恪.
At the age of twelve,
in the fourth year of Qiánwǔ 建武 of Qí 齊,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xīnpǔ Xiàn 新浦縣.
He drafted his own petition for the appointment,
which already possessed literary elegance.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān 天監,
his peerage was reduced to a Viscount.
When he grew older, he was diligent in his studies.
Since there was no complete book on the Jìn 晉 dynasty,
he dedicated himself to compiling one in his youth.
By the age of twenty-six,
the book was completed.
He presented it to the throne,
and an imperial edict ordered it to be deposited in the Imperial Library.
Zǐyún 子雲 was by nature calm and quiet,
and did not enjoy seeking official advancement.
At the age of thirty,
he finally began his career as Mìshū Láng 祕書郎.
He was promoted to Táizǐ Shèrén 太子舍人.
He compiled and presented the Dōnggōng Xīnjì 東宮新記,
and was awarded silk by imperial decree.
He was successively promoted to Běizhōngláng Wàibīng Cānjūn 北中郎外兵參軍,
Jìn'ān Wáng Wénxué 晉安王文學,
Sītú Zhǔbù 司徒主簿,
and Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng 丹陽尹丞.
At that time, Xiāngdōng Wáng 湘東王 was the capital's governor,
and deeply appreciated and favored him,
treating him as a friend of humble origins.
He was promoted to Běizhōngláng Lúlíng Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn 北中郎廬陵王諮議參軍,
concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng 尚書左丞.
In the first year of Dàtōng 大通,
he was appointed Huángmén Láng 黃門郎,
then shortly promoted to Qīngchē Jiāngjūn 輕車將軍,
concurrently Sītú Zuǒchángshǐ 司徒左長史.
In the second year,
he entered the court as Lìbù 吏部.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Chángjiān Shìzhōng 長兼侍中.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng 中大通,
he was transferred to Tàifǔ Qīng 太府卿.
In the third year,
he was dispatched as Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn, Línchuān Nèishǐ 貞威將軍、臨川內史.
In the commandery, he was praised for his harmonious governance,
and the people and officials were pleased with him.
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Chángshì 散騎常侍,
then shortly thereafter reinstated as Shìzhōng 侍中.
In the second year of Dàtóng 大同,
he was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì 員外散騎常侍 and Guózǐ Jìjiǔ 國子祭酒,
concurrently holding the position of Nánxú Zhōu Dàzhōngzhèng 南徐州大中正.
Soon after,
he was again made Shìzhōng 侍中.
His positions as Jìjiǔ 祭酒 and Zhōngzhèng 中正 remained as before.
beginning of the Liáng dynasty,
sacrificial animals (shēng quán) were not yet abolished in the suburban and ancestral temples (jiāo miào).
The music lyrics were all composed by Shěn Yuē,
and continued to be used until this point.
Zǐyún first proposed that they ought to be changed.
His memorial stated:
“I humbly reflect that Your Sacred Majesty follows the proper course,
venerating the suburban and ancestral temples (jiāo miào).
Having gained the hearts of the western neighbors,
and understanding the paths of Zhōu and Kǒng,
you have consequently abolished the use of sacrificial animals (láo zǔ).
Your virtue reaches the spirits and deities.
Using only millet (shǔ jì) and water plants (pín zǎo),
you exhaust sincerity in solemn worship.
This system, governing the state,
is indeed as brilliant as the sun and the moon,
and provides instruction for a hundred future rulers;
this is where its importance lies.
Recently, when I held the concurrent post of Purification Official (zhāi guān),
I saw that the songs performed by the musicians
still used the melodies from before the abolition of animal sacrifice.
The bonfire ceremony (liáo) at the Round Altar (Huán Qiū),
still speaks of ‘solemnly preparing the sacrificial animals (shēng quán)’;
The Hán Yǎ (諴雅) at the Northern Suburb (Běi Jiāo),
also performs ‘sacrificial animals and jade are fully prepared (shēng yù kǒng bèi)’;
The ascending song (dēng gē) at the Clear Temple (Qīng Miào),
claims ‘our sacrificial animals are clean (wǒ shēng yǐ jié)’;
During the food offerings (shí jǔ) at the Three Courts (Sān Cháo),
they still sing of ‘red tails and azure scales (zhū wěi bì lín)’.
When the sound spreads through the drums and bells,
it does not accord with the glorious new system.
My duty is to oversee Confucian instruction (rú xùn),
and I find this doubtful.
I do not know whether the music lyrics should be revised and settled or not?”
The imperial decree replied:
“This is merely the officials in charge clinging to obsolete practices (shǒu zhū).
They ought to be urgently changed.”
Consequently, Zǐyún was ordered to compose and finalize them.
The imperial decree stated:
“The lyrics for the suburban and ancestral temples (jiāo miào),
must use dignified language from the classical canons (diǎn gào),
and must not include common or superficial language from philosophical and historical writings (zǐ shǐ wén zhāng).
Moreover, what Shěn Yuē composed
also contains many errors and inaccuracies.”
Zǐyún replied to the decree, saying:
“The offerings and morning sacrifices (yīn jiàn cháo xiǎng),
use the designation 'Yǎ' (雅) for their music.
Logically, we should strictly select from the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng),
which form the perfected teachings of the sages.
However, since the Hàn dynasty, these compositions
have not relied entirely on the Classics;
and what [Shěn] Yuē composed
is even more superficial and mixed.
In the ten pieces I previously revised from [Shěn] Yuē,
I only knew that since the sacrificial animals (shēng quán) had been abolished,
the lyrics ought to be changed.
But I still followed the previous precedent,
not avoiding vulgarity or incompatibility with the style.
Having received Your Majesty’s instruction,
I have finally been enlightened (fā méng).
Although I was originally mediocre and dull,
the path has suddenly become clearly bright.
I shall respectfully follow the completed instructions,
and revise all of [Shěn] Yuē’s compositions.
I shall only take the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng) as the foundation.
Secondly, works such as the Ěr Yǎ (爾雅), the Zhōu Yì (周易), the Shàng Shū (尚書), and the Dà Dài Lǐ (大戴禮),
which belong to the category of canons and edicts (jīng gào),
I humbly believe should also be selectively employed.
I also reviewed the various books concerning Táng and Yú,
and the Hymns of Yīn (Yīn Sòng) and the Odes of Zhōu (Zhōu Yǎ).
While they all focus on praise,
they also separately narrate contemporary events.
The great Liáng dynasty has reformed its practices,
laid down arms and cultivated culture (yǎn wǔ xiū wén),
and established rites and composed music (zhì lǐ zuò yuè).
Its significance surpasses the Three Orthogonals (Sān Zhèng).
Yet, the lyrics composed by [Shěn] Yuē
only generally praised the beauty of the sacred virtue,
and utterly failed to detail the actual creative achievements of the imperial court (huáng cháo zhì zuò).
This violates
the previous structural precedents of the Yǎ and Sòng.
I submit that Your Majesty’s established treatise on music (yuè lùn), concerning pitch pipes and threads (zhōng lǜ wěi xù),
possesses profound and subtle literary thought,
a work appearing only once in an age.
It is as brilliant as the sun and the moon,
an immutable canon,
and the instruction of rites and music (lǐ yuè)
by which perfect governance is achieved.
I have carefully selected and composed one or two phrases,
elucidating the meaning based on each event,
to demonstrate the excellence of the creative works.
Having deliberated deeply for several days,
I have only now managed to complete it.
I respectfully submit it herewith.”
The imperial decree ordered that they all be put into effect.
Zǐyún excelled at cursive and running script (cǎo yān shū),
serving as a model for the age.
He himself said he was skilled at imitating Zhōng Yuáncháng and Wáng Yìshǎo, but slightly altering the script style.
He stated in a reply to an imperial decree:
“In the past, I could not judge discerningly,
but followed what the world valued,
modeling myself after Zǐjìng,
for many years.
When I was twenty-six,
while writing the Jìn Shǐ,
when I reached the biographies of the Two Wángs,
I intended to write an essay on the method of cursive and running script (cǎo yān fǎ),
but the words could not fully express my ideas,
and thus I could not complete it.
I merely touched upon the technique of the 'flying white' (fēi bái) style.
For about the last ten years,
I first saw Your Majesty’s decree, a volume discussing calligraphy (lùn shū),
which debated the power of the brush stroke
and thoroughly analyzed the structure of the characters;
and further stated that Yìshǎo did not reach the level of Yuáncháng,
just as Zǐjìng did not reach the level of Yìshǎo.
From then on, I diligently reflected,
and only then understood the style of running script (yān shì).
I began to change away from Zǐjìng,
and fully modeled myself after Yuáncháng.
Since that time,
I have felt my skill advance.”
His calligraphy was greatly valued by Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng),
who once commented on Zǐyún’s writing, saying:
“The strength of the brush is powerful and spirited,
the heart and hand respond to each other.
His skill surpasses Dù Dù,
and his beauty exceeds Cuī Shí.
He should compete side-by-side with Yuáncháng.”
This shows how much he was appreciated.
In the seventh year [of Pǔ Tōng],
he was sent out as the General of Benevolent Might (Rén Wēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtóng,
he returned and was appointed Minister of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng).
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was again appointed Attendant-in-Chief (Shìzhōng) and Libationer of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ),
concurrently holding the post of Grand Central Regulator of Nán Xú Zhōu (Nán Xú Zhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng).
In the second year,
Hóu Jǐng raided and pressed close,
and Zǐyún fled among the common people.
In the third month of the third year,
the palace city fell.
He fled east to Jìnlíng,
and died of hunger in a monk’s cell at Xiǎnlíng Sì,
aged sixty-three.
The Jìn Shū he authored consisted of one hundred and ten volumes,
and the Dōng Gōng Xīn Jì twenty volumes.
His second son, Tè, courtesy name Shìdá,
was famous early on,
and also skilled at cursive and running script.
Gāozǔ once said to Zǐyún:
“The calligraphy of Zǐjìng
does not reach the level of Yìshǎo.
Recently, seeing Tè’s work,
it has indeed pressed close to yours.”
He successively held office as Auxiliary Writer (Zhùzuò Zuǒláng),
Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Registrar to the Administrator of Xuānhuì (Xuānhuì Zhǔbù),
and Records Official of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Jìshì).
He was sent out as Prefect of Hǎiyán (Hǎiyán Lìng),
but was dismissed due to an incident.
He died
before Zǐyún,
Zǐhuī, courtesy name Jǐngguāng,
was Zǐyún’s younger brother.
In his youth, he immersed himself in books and history,
and also possessed literary talent.
He began his official career as Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng),
and was transferred to Records Official for the Commandant-in-Chief of Nán [Yì] (Nán Zhōngláng Jìshì).
He was sent out as Prefect of Lín'ān (Lín'ān Lìng).
His nature was calm and quiet,
with few vices.
He once attended the Zhòngyún Diàn (重雲殿) to listen to the Emperor lecture on the Sān Huì Jīng.
Upon retiring, he composed a rhyme-prose (fù) commentary on the lecture and presented it,
and was highly praised and appreciated.
He was transferred to Consultant to the Prince of Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng Wáng) and General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī),
concurrently holding the post of Prefect of Xīnfán (Xīnfán Lìng).
Following his principal’s administration, he was successively promoted to Aide with the Status of Exemplar (Yítóng Cóngshì) and Chief Clerk to the General of the Elite Cavalry (Piàojì Chángshǐ),
and then died.
Yáo Chá, Secretary to the Ministry of Personnel of Chén, said: Formerly, Wèi relied on military might to revolutionize the Hán destiny,
Jìn, due to its chief ministers, then shifted the Wèi calendar (dynasty),
which was different from the abdication and succession of antiquity,
where transmission relied on virtue.
Therefore, they suppressed the imperial relatives of the former dynasty,
thereby severing the people's hopes (of restoration).
However, Liú Yè and Cáo Zhì
were still prominent in court;
but upon the Sòng Dynasty, they were treated as disgraced families.
When the Qí Dynasty came,
the Sòng relatives,
were all exterminated.
Their fate (dynasty) did not last long;
this was also a reason for it.
When the Liáng Dynasty revolutionized the state,
it did not adopt previous precedents.
Thus, Zǐkè's brothers and his extended clan members
were all appointed to office according to their talents,
reaching high status and filling the court,
and did not lose their former positions.
How could this only be compared to Wèi being suppressed and Jìn being prominent?
A gentleman knows from this the vast magnitude of Gāozǔ’s spirit,
surpassing previous generations.
Memoir Thirty: Kǒng Xiūyuán, Jiāng Gé
Kǒng Xiūyuán, courtesy name Qìngxù,
was a man from Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Chōngzhī, the Grand Administrator of Dānyáng during the Jìn Dynasty.
His great-grandfather, Yáozhī,
was the Director of the Waterways Department of the Ministry of Personnel during Sòng.
His father, Pèi,
was the Secretary of the Prince of Lúlíng during Qí,
and died early.
Xiūyuán was orphaned at age eleven.
While in mourning, he observed the rites completely.
Every time he saw books written in his father's own hand,
he would weep sorrowfully,
unable to control himself.
Those who saw him could not help but shed tears for him.
Later, he went to Wúxīng and studied the Classics under Shěn Línschì,
broadly grasping the main doctrines.
In the fourth year of Jiànwǔ,
the province nominated him as an Outstanding Talent (Xiùcái).
The Grand Commandant, Xú Xiàosì, reviewed his policy proposals,
greatly admiring them,
and said to those seated with him:
"How could Dǒng Zhòngshū and Huà Língsī surpass this?
He can be called the standard for the younger generation.
Observing this response of his,
he is worthy of being called a talent capable of assisting a king."
Wáng Róng of Lángyé was consistently friendly with him.
He then recommended him to the Minister of Works, the Prince of Jìnglíng,
who made him a Scholar of the Western Residence.
When the Liáng establishment was created,
he and Liú Zhīlín of Nányáng were appointed Erudites of the Imperial University,
which was considered an excellent choice at the time.
When Xiūyuán first arrived at the capital,
he stayed at the residence of his clansman, Kǒng Dēng, the Minister of the Lesser Treasury.
Once, he entered the temple for sacrificial duties.
Fàn Yún, the Palace Attendant, encountered him once,
and highly praised him,
saying:
"I did not expect to suddenly behold your clear countenance.
My baseness and pettiness are instantly dispelled.
Observing the sky through parted fog—
I prove it today."
Later, Fàn Yún ordered his carriage to the gate of the Lesser Treasury Minister.
Kǒng Dēng immediately smoothed his mat and straightened his belt,
thinking the visit was meant for himself.
But then Fàn Yún called solely upon Xiūyuán,
speaking grandly all day long,
and rode home with him in the same carriage.
Dēng felt deeply ashamed.
Shěn Yuē, the Director of the Department of State Affairs, was eminent and esteemed at court.
Carriages filled his gates.
When Xiūyuán occasionally arrived late,
Shěn Yuē would certainly receive him with an open mind,
placing him on his right side (the honored seat),
and discussing literature and meaning.
His respect by cultured people was thus.
Soon after, he was appointed Provisional Staff Officer in the administration of the Prince of Línchuān.
Gāozǔ once asked the Secretary to the Ministry of Personnel, Xú Miǎn:
"The imperial enterprise is now beginning.
I need one person with scholarship and skill who understands court ceremony
to serve as Director of the Ceremonial Bureau of the Ministry of Personnel.
Consider for me,
who is suitable for this selection?"
Miǎn replied:
"Kǒng Xiūyuán's knowledge is clear and comprehensive.
He is deeply familiar with old precedents.
The Diaries of Activity and Repose from Jìn and Sòng, he can recite roughly by heart."
Gāozǔ had long heard of him,
and that very day appointed him concurrently Director of the Ceremonial Bureau of the Ministry of Personnel.
At that time, many things were being altered and established.
Whenever he was summoned and questioned about previous affairs,
Xiūyuán would immediately use what he had recited and recorded to make decisions on the spot,
without ever being hesitant or unclear.
Rèn Fǎng, Director of the Ministry of Personnel, often referred to him as
"Kǒng the Lone Reciter."
He was promoted to Jail Inspector of Jiànkāng.
When he handled lawsuits and settled court cases,
there were seldom any wrongly accused people.
Later, when someone selected was appointed to judicial office,
Gāozǔ still cited Xiūyuán to encourage him.
He was appointed Palace Writer,
then Secretary and Staff Officer to the administration of the Prince of Línchuān, the Minister of Works.
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Left in the Ministry of Personnel.
He impeached officials and maintained discipline in the ceremonial courts,
greatly satisfying the expectations of the court.
At that time, Zhōu Shě, the Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, was compiling the *Yìyì* (Doubtful Meanings of Rites),
gathering materials from Hán and Wèi up through Qí and Liáng.
All of them were researched and collected.
All the memorials and discussions submitted by Xiūyuán
were included in the compilation.
He was appointed Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gates and Serving Attendant,
and then promoted to Chief of the Censors concurrently.
He maintained a stern demeanor and administered the law justly,
avoiding no one.
All officials feared him.
He was appointed Minister of the Lesser Treasury,
and concurrently managed the affairs of the Governor of Dānyáng.
He left the capital to serve as Chief Clerk of the administration of the Prince of Jìn'ān (General Xuānhuì), Grand Administrator of Nánjùn, and Provisional Governor of Jīngzhōu.
Gāozǔ said to him:
"Jīngzhōu controls the strategic point of the upper stream,
its importance surpassing that of other regional commands.
I now entrust a ten-year-old boy to you,
