diligently assist and guide him.
Do not fear the example of Zhōu Chāng's firm defense."
He replied:
"I, your servant, due to my mediocrity and vulgarity,
have undeservedly received your grace and favor.
I shall now measure out my absolute sincerity,
and offer a fraction of it."
The Emperor praised his reply,
and then instructed the Prince of Jìn'ān, saying:
"Kǒng Xiūyuán is a model of moral behavior.
You are still young;
you should take him as your teacher in all matters."
Soon after, the Prince of Shǐxīng, Dàn, replaced the command in Jīngzhōu.
He was again appointed Chief Clerk of Dàn’s administration,
retaining the positions of Grand Administrator of Nánjùn and Provisional Governor as before.
He held office in the province for several terms,
achieving considerable administrative success.
He made decisions with an impartial mind,
and private requests were ineffective.
Gāozǔ greatly commended him,
appointing him Gentleman-Consultant,
and concurrently Director of the Plumed Forest Guard.
He was transferred to Director of the Imperial Library,
promoted to General Illustrating Awe,
and again became Chief Clerk of the administration of the Prince of Jìn'ān, and Grand Administrator of Southern Lánlíng.
He was separately ordered to manage the affairs of Nán Xúzhōu exclusively.
Xiūyuán successively assisted illustrious princes,
gaining great popular acclaim.
The Prince relied heavily upon him.
For strategic military and civil affairs,
every action was taken after consulting him.
The Prince usually established a separate couch in his central chamber,
saying,
"This is Chief Clerk Kǒng’s seat."
No one else was allowed to use it.
His respect was thus.
He was summoned to serve as Minister of the Grand Treasury.
Soon after, he was granted the position of Secretary of the Ministry of Revenue.
After a short while,
he assumed the post of Household Manager to the Crown Prince.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng,
Hóng, the Prince of Línchuān (Governor of Yángzhōu), died.
Gāozǔ discussed with his officials for a long time who should replace the prince in governing the province.
At that time, noble relatives, princes, and dukes
all hoped for the transfer and appointment.
Gāozǔ said:
"I have already found the right person.
Kǒng Xiūyuán’s talent and knowledge are sharp and insightful,
he truly deserves this selection."
He was thus granted the title General Xuānhuì (Illustrating Favor) and made Supervisor of Yángzhōu.
Xiūyuán had first served as Provisional Staff Officer to the Prince of Línchuān;
upon the death of the Prince, he was put in charge of the provincial administration.
Public opinion considered this an honor.
As the capital of the divine prefecture (Jīngzhōu),
the administrative paperwork was abundant and complex.
Xiūyuán handled and resolved matters quickly like flowing water,
and there were no private solicitations (of favor).
In the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
he was granted the additional title Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Gold and Purple,
while remaining Supervisor of Yángzhōu.
He repeatedly submitted memorials declining the honor,
but the Emperor's favorable edicts refused his request.
While in the province, he settled legal disputes by day,
and reviewed ancient texts by night.
Whenever the imperial carriage went on tour,
military and state affairs were always entrusted to him.
died,
an imperial edict was issued summoning Kǒng Xiūyuán to enter the Yànjū Diàn at night,
where he joined the various high officials in deliberating and settling a strategy,
to establish the Prince of Jìn'ān, Xiāo Gāng, as the Crown Prince.
In the fourth year,
he contracted an illness.
Gāozǔ sent palace envoys to inquire about his health,
and supplied medicine,
ten or more times daily.
In the fifth month of that year,
he died,
aged sixty-four.
His dying instructions commanded a simple burial,
requiring only vegetables and simple fare to be offered at seasonal sacrifices and the beginning of the month.
Gāozǔ shed tears for him,
looked back and said to Xiè Jǔ:
"Kǒng Xiūyuán served his office with purity and loyalty,
and held his post with integrity and rectitude.
We had just begun planning to jointly restore the principles of good governance,
and thereby magnify the kingly transformation.
That he suddenly met his demise,
We are truly pained by this."
Jǔ replied:
"This man was pure, firm, strong, and upright—
rarely seen today.
Your humble subject secretly laments this loss for Your Majesty."
An imperial decree stated:
"To attend carefully to the end and commemorate the distant departed,
is the universal rule throughout the ages;
to praise virtue and reward merit,
is the admirable precedent set by the former kings.
Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn, Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū, and Supervisor of Yángzhōu, Kǒng Xiūyuán,
possessed a demeanor and conduct that was upright and proper,
and his refined capacity was profound and elevated.
Rising to prominence and establishing rites,
his reputation was valued highly by the gentry.
When managing affairs in the capital region,
his transforming influence spread and was sung about.
We were just about to raise him up for his benevolence and longevity,
allowing him to harmonize the fixed human relations.
That he suddenly departed forever,
doubles Our sorrow and grief.
He is posthumously granted Sànqí Chángshì and Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū,
bestowed with one set of Grade A timber,
fifty rolls of cloth,
fifty thousand coins,
and two hundred catties of wax.
The day for mourning shall be appointed.
Whatever is required for the funeral arrangements,
shall be provided as needed.
His posthumous title shall be Zhēn Zǐ."
The Crown Prince's personal order stated:
"Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū Kǒng Xiūyuán,
established himself as moderate and upright,
and conducted himself purely and reverently.
In past years, whether traveling west to Zhǔgōng,
or anchoring east at Fén Rǎng,
assisting in the administration of the feudal territories,
he truly exerted his utmost sincerity.
The meticulousness of Ānguó,
and the integrity and purity of Gōngyí,
could not surpass him.
His sudden demise,
fills Us with sorrow and pity.
Now we must raise the mourning rituals,
ensuring the external formalities are fully observed."
Xiūyuán was orphaned young.
He established a determined character,
his demeanor was strong and correct,
he was thoroughly practiced in the structure of governance,
maintained frugality in his personal life,
and mastered literature and the arts.
When holding office and managing affairs,
he did not fear the powerful and abusive.
He constantly took the welfare of the empire as his personal responsibility,
and Gāozǔ deeply trusted and relied on him.
Though he successively held prominent posts,
he committed not the slightest transgression.
His nature was cautious and reserved,
and he had few personal indulgences.
Though he came and went from the imperial inner chambers,
he never spoke of matters within the forbidden palace,
and the world esteemed him highly for this.
He collected books totaling over seven thousand scrolls,
personally collating and editing them.
His memorials, proposals, and impeachment documents,
were compiled into fifteen volumes.
His eldest son, Kǒng Yúntóng,
generally possessed the style of his father,
but fervently believed in Buddhist principles,
observing the sutras and precepts fully.
His office reached Yuèyáng Wáng Fǔ Zīyì and Dōngyángzhōu Biéjià.
His younger son, Kǒng Zōngguǐ,
was bright, keen, and possessed a sense of measure.
He successively served as Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
Sītú Zuǒ Xī Yuàn,
and Zhōngshū Láng.
Jiāng Gé, courtesy name Xiūyìng,
was a native of Kǎochéng in Jìyáng.
His grandfather, Jiāng Qízhī,
was Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng during the Sòng dynasty.
His father, Jiāng Róuzhī,
was Shàngshū Cāngbù Láng during the Qí dynasty.
He was known for his filial conduct,
and died from grief and exhaustion during mourning for his mother.
Gé was intelligent and keen in childhood,
possessing literary talent early on.
By the age of six, he understood how to compose literature.
Róuzhī highly valued and appreciated him,
saying:
"This child will surely bring prosperity to my family."
At the age of nine, he suffered the loss of his father.
He and his younger brother, Jiāng Guān, who was born of the same mother,
were orphaned and poor in their youth.
Having no teachers or friends nearby,
the brothers instructed and encouraged each other,
studying diligently without tiring.
At sixteen, he lost his mother,
and became known for his filial piety.
When the mourning period ended,
he and Guān both went to the Imperial University,
and were appointed as Guózǐ students.
They were recommended as high achievers.
During the Qí dynasty, Zhōngshū Láng Wáng Róng and Lìbù Xiè Tiǎo greatly respected and esteemed him.
Tiǎo once stayed overnight on palace guard duty,
and upon returning, stopped by to visit Gé.
At the time, there was heavy snow.
He saw Gé using tattered bedding and a single mat,
yet engrossed in study without fatigue.
Tiǎo sighed in admiration for a long time,
then removed the jacket he was wearing,
and personally cut half a felt blanket to give to Gé for bedding before leaving.
Sītú, the Prince of Jìnglíng, heard his name,
and invited him to be a scholar at the Western Residence.
At twenty, he was recommended as a talented scholar of Nánxúzhōu.
At that time, Hú Xiézhī of Yùzhāng was acting governor of the province.
Wáng Róng wrote a letter to Xiézhī,
instructing him to recommend Gé.
Xiézhī was then recommending Wáng Fàn of Lángyé.
He consequently replaced Fàn with Gé.
He shed his common clothes and received the imperial summons.
Pūyè Jiāng Shí deeply encouraged and received him.
When Shí became the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
he petitioned to appoint Gé as the Aide in the Prince’s establishment.
At that time, Shí held power that overshadowed the court.
Believing Gé’s talent was sufficient for governing the state,
he ordered him to participate in managing critical state affairs.
Imperial edicts, pronouncements, and official documents,
were all entrusted to him for preparation.
Gé concealed all traces of this involvement,
so outsiders were unaware.
When Shí was executed,
all his retainers suffered punishment,
but Gé alone escaped due to his foresight and cleverness.
He was appointed as Clerk to the Ministry of Ceremonies, and subsequently, Secretary of the Ministry of Carts.
In the first year of Zhōngxīng (501 CE),
Gāozǔ entered Shítou.
At that time, Yuán Áng, the Administrator of Wúxìng, held the commandery and resisted the righteous army.
So, Gāozǔ ordered Jiāng Gé to draft a decree for Áng.
He completed it while seated,
and its language and meaning were elegant and refined.
Gāozǔ greatly admired and praised it,
and consequently ordered him to manage the secretarial affairs together with Xú Miǎn.
When the Prince of Jiàn'ān was appointed Inspector of Yōngzhōu,
he submitted a memorial requesting Jiāng Gé to be his secretary.
Thus, Jiāng Gé was appointed Aide to the General of the North and Chief Clerk,
concurrently holding the position of Magistrate of Zhōnglú.
He and his younger brother, Jiāng Guān, had lived together since childhood,
unable to bear separation.
Jiāng Gé earnestly pleaded for Guān to accompany him.
So, Guān was appointed Provisional Aide to the General of the North,
and concurrently Chief Clerk.
At that time, Shěn Yuē of Wúxìng and Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān both highly appreciated each other.
Fǎng wrote to Jiāng Gé, saying:
"This selection of outstanding talents for the Yōngzhōu court,
for the positions of literary staff,
encompasses both you and your younger brother.
It can be said to be like driving two dragons on a long road,
or galloping a fine steed for a thousand *lǐ*."
While en route in Jiāngxià,
Guān fell ill and died.
Jiāng Gé was in Yōng at the time,
treated with great courtesy by the Prince of the Prefecture,
as if he were a commoner.
When the Prince was recalled to serve as Prefect of Dānyáng,
he appointed Jiāng Gé as Chief Clerk,
concurrently heading the Five Bureaus,
and then promoted him to Palace Attendant,
and Magistrate of Jiànkāng.
He was frequently transferred to be Magistrate of Mòlíng and Jiànkāng.
His governance was clear and severe,
and powerful families feared him.
He was appointed as a Gentleman-in-Waiting of the Central Secretariat,
Assistant Director of the Ministry of Personnel,
and Minister of Agriculture.
He was then reassigned out as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Jìn'ān, with the title of Commander of the Cloud Brigade, Administrator of Xúnyáng, and acting Administrator of Jiāngzhōu Prefecture.
He was transferred to be Chief Clerk to the Prince of Lúlíng, with the title of General of Awesome Benevolence.
His positions as Administrator and acting official remained as before.
His strict integrity made him feared by all cities.
At that time, the young Prince, while acting as governor, often inclined his favors towards his personal retainers.
Jiāng Gé, upholding his uprightness,
refused to sit with these retainers.
Soon after, he was promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánpíng, and Imperial Censor,
impeaching powerful and influential figures,
without any hesitation.
He was appointed Minister of the Imperial Treasury,
then reassigned out as General of Awesome Power, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánkāng, with the title of General of the Northern Central Guard, and Administrator of Guǎnglǐng.
He was then reassigned as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Yùzhāng, with the title of General of the Garrison of the North.
His positions as General and Administrator remained as before.
At that time, Yuán Fǎsēng, the Wei Inspector of Xúzhōu, surrendered and defected.
Jiāng Gé was commanded to accompany the Prince of the Prefecture to garrison Péngchéng.
When the city was lost,
Jiāng Gé, being habitually uncomfortable on horseback,
returned by boat.
Passing through Xiàpī,
he was captured by the Wei people.
Yuán Yánmíng, the Wei Inspector of Xúzhōu, having heard of Jiāng Gé's talent and reputation,
received him with great generosity.
Jiāng Gé claimed to suffer from a foot ailment and did not prostrate himself.
Yánmíng intended to harm him,
but seeing Jiāng Gé's stern and upright demeanor,
he instead respected him greatly.
At that time, Zǔ Jī was also captured.
Yánmíng ordered Jī to compose inscriptions for an *yīqì* (a self-emptying vessel) and a clepsydra.
Jiāng Gé cursed Jī, saying:
"You have received great favor from the state,
yet you have not repaid it.
Now you are writing inscriptions for barbarians,
betraying the imperial court."
Hearing this, Yánmíng
then ordered Jiāng Gé to compose an inscription for the Zhàngbā Temple stele and a text for sacrificing to Péng Zǔ.
Jiāng Gé declined, saying that he had been imprisoned for so long
that he had lost all capacity for thought.
Yánmíng pressed him even more harshly,
threatening to whip him.
Jiāng Gé, with a stern expression, said:
"I, Jiāng Gé, am sixty years old.
Unable to die for my lord,
I would consider it fortunate to die today.
I vow never to write for another."
Yánmíng, knowing he could not be coerced,
stopped.
He was given three *shēng* of hulled grain daily,
barely enough to sustain his life.
When the Wei Emperor requested Yuán Luè, the Prince of Zhōngshān, to return to the North,
Jiāng Gé and Zǔ Jī were released and allowed to return to court.
An imperial edict stated:
"Jiāng Gé, formerly General of Awesome Power, Chief Clerk of the Garrison of the North, and Administrator of Guǎnglǐng,
is intelligent and resourceful,
with a reputation both in and out of office.
In court, he is righteous;
in danger, he is unyielding.
As a chief assistant to the government,
he truly meets with unanimous approval.
He is appointed Chief Clerk to the Prince of Línchuān, the Grand Commandant."
At that time, Gāozǔ was deeply devoted to Buddhism,
and many court officials requested to receive the precepts.
Jiāng Gé deeply believed in cause and effect,
but Gāozǔ did not know this,
thinking that Jiāng Gé did not follow Buddhism.
So, he bestowed upon Jiāng Gé a poem of five hundred characters titled "Awakening to Understanding,"
saying:
"One should diligently strive forward,
and strengthen oneself in virtuous cultivation;
How can one be so obstinate,
like those certain to die in prison?
This I tell Jiāng Gé,
and also all noble gentlemen."
He also sent a personal decree saying:
"The retribution of the world
cannot be disbelieved.
How can you be as stubborn as you were when facing Yuán Yánmíng?"
Jiāng Gé then memorialized to request receiving the Bodhisattva precepts.
He was again appointed Minister of the Imperial Treasury, Chief Clerk, and Commandant.
At that time, the Prince of Wǔlíng was in the Eastern Province,
and was rather arrogant and unrestrained.
The Emperor summoned Jiāng Gé and personally decreed:
"The Prince of Wǔlíng is young,
and Zāng Dùn is weak by nature,
unable to correct him.
I wish to appoint you to replace him as acting governor.
No one but you will do,
and you must not refuse."

So, he was appointed General Who Crushes the Attack, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Wǔlíng, with the title of General of the Eastern Central Guard, Vice-Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery, and acting governor of the prefecture.
Jiāng Gé's protégés and former subordinates,
many of whose families were in the Eastern Province,
hearing that Jiāng Gé was about to arrive,
all brought gifts and waited along the road to greet him.
Jiāng Gé said:
"I generally do not accept gifts.
It is not right for me to accept baskets from former acquaintances alone."
Upon arriving at his post,
he relied only on his official salary,
and his meals never had more than one dish.
The commandery was vast and prosperous,
with hundreds of lawsuits daily.
Jiāng Gé judged and analyzed them,
never having any doubts or delays.
Merits were certainly rewarded,
and transgressions were certainly punished.
The people were at peace, and officials feared him,
causing all cities to tremble.
Wáng Qiān of Lángyá, as Magistrate of Shānyīn,
was notoriously corrupt.
Hearing of Jiāng Gé, he voluntarily resigned.
The Prince of the Prefecture feared him,
and thus held him in elegant respect.
Whenever he attended banquets,
their discussions always revolved around poetry and classics.
The Prince consequently became engrossed in learning and fond of literature.
Diǎnqiān Shěn Chìwén presented the poems composed by the Prince to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ said to the Grand Astrologer Xú Miǎn:
"Jiāng Gé is indeed capable of fulfilling his duties."
He was then appointed Minister of the Ministry of Justice.
When he was about to return,
the people all felt reluctant to part with him,
but he accepted none of their farewell gifts.
The farewell boats were arranged as before,
but Jiāng Gé did not accept any of them.
He only took the single boat provided by the court.
The hull of the boat was uneven,
making it impossible to sleep comfortably.
Someone said to Jiāng Gé:
"Since the boat is unbalanced,
crossing the river will be very dangerous.
You should move heavy objects
to weigh down the light side of the hull."
As Jiāng Gé had no belongings,
he collected over ten pieces of stone from the bank of Xīlíng to balance it.
Such was his incorruptibility and poverty.
Soon after, he became Supervisor of Wújùn.
At that time, the region suffered from famine and desolation,
and bandits roamed openly.
When Jiāng Gé arrived at the commandery,
he only had twenty officially provided guards for himself.
The common people feared that he would not be able to quell the bandits;
they even feared the roaming military officials even more.
The common people were even more afraid of the patrolling military officials.
Jiāng Gé then extensively extended grace and comfort,
and clearly enforced regulations.
The bandits ceased their activities,
and the people and officials were at peace.
When the King of Wǔlíng
went out to govern Jiāngzhōu,
he said:
"I have Jiāng Gé,
whose literary talent is brilliant and refined;
how could I forget him even for a day? He must share my bounty."
He then submitted a memorial requesting Gé accompany him.
He was also appointed as General Mingwēi, Chief Clerk of the Southern Central Guard (Nánzhōngláng Zhǎngshǐ), and Administrator of Xúnyáng.
Later, he was summoned back to serve as Minister of the Treasury (Dùzhī Shàngshū).
He enjoyed praising and promoting commoners,
and extending fame for the younger generation.
Due to this, the scholars and gentry
flocked to him enthusiastically.
At that time, Minister of Personnel (Shàngshū Lìng) Hé Jìngrōng was in charge of selection,
and many of his appointments were ill-chosen.
Gé was inherently strong and upright.
Whenever he attended court banquets,
he offered praise or censure.
Because of this, he was resented by those in power,
so he claimed illness and returned home.

He was appointed as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū), concurrently serving as Commandant of the Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi), and Grand Umpire (Dàzhōngzhèng) of the two provinces Nán Yǎn and Běi Yǎn.
He lived a relaxed and carefree life,
amusing himself with literature and wine.
In the second month of the first year of Dàtóng (535 CE),
he died,
and was posthumously titled Qiángzǐ.
His collected works, in twenty volumes,
circulated in the world.
Gé served successively as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) for eight regional administrations,
Acting Official (Xíngshì) for four princes,
and served as an official with a salary of two thousand *dàn* three times.
He had no concubines or attendants on the side;
his family walls were bare (i.e., utterly poor).
The world esteemed him highly for this.
His eldest son, Xíngmǐn,
was fond of learning and possessed talent and distinction.
His highest office was Gentleman-in-Attendance (Tōngzhí Láng),
but he died early,
leaving five volumes of collected works.
His second son, Cóngjiǎn,
showed literary sensibility early on.
At the age of seventeen,
he wrote the poem "Cǎi Hé Cí" (Picking Lotus Song) to criticize Jìngrōng,
which was admired by people at the time.
He successively served as Administrator-in-Attendance of the Minister of Works (Sītú Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
When Hóu Jǐng caused turmoil,
he was killed by Rèn Yuē.
His son, Jiān, knocked his head until blood flowed,
begging to die in place of his father,
using his own body to shield the blade,
whereupon both were killed.
Everyone under Heaven was heartbroken over this.
The Historian comments: Gāozǔ devoted attention to governance,
and Kǒng Xiūyuán became known for his administrative insight.
Since he encountered the right time,
this was fortunate indeed.
Jiāng Gé was intelligent, sharp, and upright—
was he not also a figure of great renown for his generation?
Biographies, Number 31: Xiè Jǔ and Hé Jìngrōng
Xiè Jǔ, courtesy name Yányáng,
was the younger brother of the Minister of the Central Secretariat, Lǎn.
As a youth, he was fond of learning
and was capable of pure conversation (*qīng yán*).
He was as famous as Lǎn.
When Jǔ was fourteen,
he once presented Shěn Yuē with a five-character verse poem,
which Yuē praised highly.
People of the time created a saying about them:
"The Wáng family has Yǎng and Jù;
the Xiè family has Lǎn and Jǔ."
Yǎng and Jù
were the childhood names of Wáng Yún and Wáng Tài.
He began his official career as a Secretary of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng),
and was promoted to Palace Attendant of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Administrator of the Rapid Cavalry (Qīngchē Gōngcáo Shǐ),
Vice Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng),
Administrator-in-Attendance of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shùzǐ),
Prefect of the Palace (Jiālìng),
and was put in charge of the archives of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
He was deeply appreciated and received by Crown Prince Zhāomíng.
When Rèn Fǎng, Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān), went out to govern Xīn'ān Commandery,
he wrote a farewell poem to Jǔ, which said:
"How can I forget this man, saddened by old age,
who so deeply entrusted himself to this old man?"
This was the depth of his regard.
Once, while attending a banquet in Huálín Park,
Gāozǔ asked Lǎn about Jǔ.
Lǎn replied:
"His knowledge and art far surpass mine,
but only in drinking does he not measure up to me."
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
He was transferred to Palace Administrator of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
still managing the archives.
In the eleventh year of Tiānjiān (512 CE),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the fourteenth year (515 CE),
he was sent out as General Níngyuǎn and Administrator of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Nèishǐ).
His governance was harmonious and well-ordered,
and he greatly won the hearts of the people.
In the eighteenth year (519 CE),
he returned to serve as Palace Attendant,
concurrently Commandant of the Infantry.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
he went out as General Zhēngyì and Chief Clerk of the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi), the Prince of Línchuān.
In the fourth year (523 CE),
he returned to serve as Minister of the Left Quarter (Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū).
That same year, he was transferred to manage the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù),
but was soon dismissed due to an official matter.
In the fifth year (524 CE),
he was reinstated as Palace Administrator of the Heir Apparent,
concurrently General of the Right Army (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn).
In the sixth year (525 CE),
he served again as Minister of the Left Quarter,
concurrently Commandant of the Infantry.
Shortly after, he was transferred to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
and soon appointed Palace Attendant.
He went out to serve as General Rénwēi and Administrator of Jìn líng (Jìn líng Tàishǒu).
While in the commandery, he was clean and quiet in his administration.
The common people were transformed by his virtue,
and the region was肃然 (respectfully ordered).
When he resigned and returned from the commandery,
the officials and common people went to the palace gates requesting a stele be erected.
The imperial edict granted permission.
In the second year of Dàtōng (528 CE),
he returned to serve as Palace Attendant and Minister of the Five Garrisons (Wǔbīng Shàngshū).
Before he took office,
he was transferred to manage the Ministry of Personnel,
retaining his Palace Attendant position.
Jǔ's grandfather, Zhuāng,
twice managed the selection process during the Sòng dynasty.
Up to Jǔ, he served in this capacity three times,
a feat unprecedented in previous generations.
Jǔ was widely learned and well-versed from a young age,
especially adept at esoteric principles (*xuán lǐ*) and Buddhist doctrines.
While serving in Jìnlíng Commandery,
he often held alternating lecture sessions on sutras and treatises with virtuous monks.
The reclusive scholar Hé Yìn traveled from Hǔqiū Mountain to attend.
Such was the prominence of these gatherings.
Previously,
Lú Guǎng, a man from the north who crossed the river, possessed Confucian scholarship.
He served as National University Doctor (Guózǐ Bóshì)
and gave lectures at the academy,
attended by Xu Mǐn, Minister of the Right (Pūshè), and others.
Jǔ went and sat in,
frequently challenging Guǎng.
His arguments were comprehensive and brilliant.
Guǎng deeply admired and submitted to him,
and consequently presented him with the deer-tail whisk he held,
comparing him to the distinguished scholars of old.
In the fourth year (538 CE),
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
In the fifth year (539 CE),
he was promoted to Minister of the Right (Shàngshū Yòupūshè),
retaining his Palace Attendant position.
In the third year of Dàtóng (537 CE),
citing illness, he requested resignation.
He was transferred to Right Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Yòuguānglù Dàfū),
and granted twenty close attendants.
That same year,
he went out to serve as General Yúnhuī and Administrator of Wú Commandery (Wú Jùn Tàishǒu).
Previously,
Hé Jìngrōng had achieved excellent administrative results while governing the commandery,
and was known to the world as "Hé of Wú Commandery" (Hé Wújùn).
When Jǔ took office,
his reputation and achievements were generally comparable to his.
In the sixth year (540 CE),
he returned to serve as Palace Attendant and Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān).
Before he took office,
he was transferred to Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zhānshì) and General of the Flanking Left (Yìzuǒ Jiāngjūn),
retaining his Palace Attendant position.
Jǔ's father, Wěi,
had retired from this same office during the Qí dynasty.
Jǔ repeatedly submitted memorials begging for a different appointment,
but the imperial edict refused.
Only after a long time did he accept the position.
In the ninth year (543 CE),
he was promoted to Minister of the Right (Shàngshū Pūshè),
retaining his Palace Attendant and General positions.
Although Jǔ held a position in the highest executive office,
he was never willing to involve himself in current political affairs.
He frequently claimed illness and requested resignation.
The imperial edict would often grant him leave,
along with handwritten prescriptions
and the provision of premium medicine.
Such was the favor he received.
That same year,
in his current capacity, he participated in managing the selection process.
In the second year of Tàiqīng (548 CE),
he was promoted to Minister of the Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng),
retaining his Palace Attendant and General positions.
That year,
Hóu Jǐng attacked the capital,
and Jǔ died within the siege.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him Palace Attendant, General of the Central Guard (Zhōngwèi Jiāngjūn), and Minister of the Office of the Grand Commandant (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī),
retaining his Palace Attendant and Minister of the Secretariat titles.
His collected works were all lost during the turmoil.
were both famous from a young age.
Gǔ,
during the Tàiqīng period,
successively served as the Heir Apparent's Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),
and went out to serve as the Prefect (Tàishǒu) of Jiàn'ān.
Hé Jìngróng, courtesy name Guólǐ,
was a native of Lújiāng.
His grandfather, Yōuzhī,
was the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng) during the Sòng dynasty;
his father, Chāngyù,
was the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) during the Qí dynasty;
both were famous in previous generations.
Jìngróng, being the son of a renowned family,
at the age of twenty (ruòguān), was selected to marry the Qí Emperor Wǔ's daughter, Princess Chángchéng,
and was appointed Commandant of the Imperial Equipage (Fùmǎ Dūwèi).
Early in the Tiānjiān era,
he served as a Gentleman of the Secretariat (Mìshū Láng).
He successively held the posts of Heir Apparent's Attendant (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Gentleman of the Central Palace (Diànzhōng Láng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
Heir Apparent's Groom (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
Attendant (Shèrén) in the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū),
and Aide to the Secretariat (Mìshū Chéng),
before being promoted to Governor's Aide (Zhìzhōng) of Yángzhōu.
He left the capital to serve as the Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Jiàn'ān.
He governed with purity and fairness and achieved excellent results,
praised by the populace and officials.
Upon returning, he was appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huángmén Láng),
and was repeatedly promoted to Heir Apparent's Zhōngshùzǐ,
Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
and Chief Clerk of the Left (Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ) to the Minister over the Masses (Sītú).
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
he was again appointed Palace Attendant,
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of the Feathered Forest (Yǔlín Jiān).
Soon after, he also concurrently served as the Great Arbiter (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of his native province.
After a while,
he provisionally held the post of Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
His selection and ranking of officials were clear and rigorous,
and he was acclaimed as competent in his duties.
In the fourth year,
he left the capital to serve as General Who Beckons Afar (Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Prefect of Wújùn.
In governing, he diligently showed compassion for the suffering of the people,
settling legal disputes with uncanny wisdom.
He administered the area for four years,
and his governance was ranked the foremost in the realm.
Officials and common people went to the palace gate (què) requesting permission to erect a stele
in his honor, and an imperial decree granted it.
In the second year of Dàtōng,
he was recalled to serve as Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng).
Before taking up the post,
he was again appointed Minister of Personnel,
concurrently holding the title of General of the Right Army (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn).
Soon after, he was additionally granted the title of Palace Attendant.
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
his post was changed to Heir Apparent's Zhōngshùzǐ.
Jìngróng was eight *chǐ* tall,
with fair skin and handsome beard and eyebrows.
He was naturally proud and solemn,
and paid particular attention to the freshness and beauty of his robes and cap.
Whenever he stood in formation at the imperial court,
his demeanor surpassed others.
In the third year,
he was promoted to Vice Director of the Right (Yòu Púshè) of the Department of State Affairs,
participating in the management of official selections,
with his Palace Attendant position remaining as before.
At that time, Vice Director Xú Miǎn, who participated in managing state secrets,
petitioned to resign due to illness.
Consequently, he nominated Jìngróng to replace himself.
Therefore, Jìngróng received this appointment.
In the fifth year,
he was promoted to Vice Director of the Left (Zuǒ Púshè),
was additionally granted the title General Who Proclaims Grace (Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn),
and was allowed to establish staff officers (zuǒ shǐ).
His positions as Palace Attendant and participating manager remained as before.
In the first month of the third year of Dàtóng,
the Vermilion Bird Gate (Zhūquè Mén) caught fire.
Emperor Gāozǔ said to his officials,
"The construction of this gate was low and narrow.
I was just about to rebuild it,
when it suffered Heaven's fire."
Everyone looked at each other, and no one offered a reply.
Jìngróng alone said,
"This is what is meant by Your Majesty 'acting before Heaven, yet Heaven does not disobey.' "
At the time, this was considered a famous reply.
Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Central Authority (Zhōngquán Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Dānyáng (Dānyáng Yǐn).
His positions as Palace Attendant, participating manager, and staff officers remained as before.
In the fifth year,
he entered the court to become Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng).
His positions as Palace Attendant, General, participating manager, and staff officers remained as before.
Jìngróng had long resided in the central government bureaus (táigé).
He was intimately familiar with old precedents,
and moreover, he was intelligent and understood governance.
He was diligent regarding clerical work (bùlǐng);
he handled matters from early morning
until dusk without rest.
Since the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
Prime Ministers (zǎixiàng) had all enjoyed literary pursuits and self-indulgence.
Jìngróng alone diligently handled miscellaneous affairs,
which caused him to be ridiculed and scorned by contemporaries.
At that time, Xiāo Chēn's son, Xūn,
who possessed rather frivolous talent,
composed poems involving the separation and combination of hexagram names to mock him.
Jìngróng treated the situation as if nothing had changed,
and did not concern himself with it.
In the eleventh year,
he was impeached because his concubine's brother, Fèi Huìmíng, who was Aide of the Grain Granary (Dǎocāng Chéng),
stole government rice at night.
He was seized by the enforcement authorities
and sent to the Commandant of the Guards' (Lǐngjūn) office.
At that time, Prince Hédōng, Yù, was the General Commandant of the Guards (Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn).
Jìngróng wrote a letter to seek Fèi Huìmíng's release.
Yù immediately sealed the letter and presented it to the throne.
Emperor Gāozǔ was furious,
and handed the matter over to the Southern Bureau (Nánsī) for investigation and impeachment.
The Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), Zhāng Wǎn, impeached Jìngróng for using his position for personal gain and deceiving the Emperor,
declaring that his crime warranted public execution (qì shì).
An imperial decree specially exempted him from the punishment but stripped him of office.
Originally,
during the Tiānjiān era,
there was a Buddhist monk, Shì Bǎozhì,
who once met Jìngróng
and told him:
"You will surely become noble later,
but in the end, it will be destruction (or defeat) by Hé."
When Jìngróng became Prime Minister,
he believed that someone named Hé would cause his downfall.
Therefore, he suppressed his immediate clan members,
and none of them entered officialdom.
By this time (the impeachment), he was indeed ruined by the Prince of Hédōng.
, Gāozǔ visited the Tóngtài Temple
to lecture on the *Jīnzì Sānhuì Jīng* (Gold-Character Three Wisdom Sūtra)
. Hé Jìngróng requested permission to attend the lecture

. There was also a decree allowing him to attend the court audience on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month
. Soon thereafter, he was appointed Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū
. Before he was formally invested

, hoping that he would be reemployed
. Xiè Yù of Kuàijī sent a letter advising him, saying

, have heard from the roadside
that Your Lordship is now able to attend court daily
, entering and exiting the forbidden palace gates
. Even a drunken guard would likely not dare rebuke you

, extremely fortunate
, extremely fortunate
! I dare to offer congratulations first

; when the letter from Yān first arrived

. Furthermore, a fish with parched gills
does not long for the water of a cup or ladle

, why would they concern themselves with the food inside a cage

; this could be called magnificent

, receiving blame and incurring faults
. Yet you still wish to peer into the court again
, harboring exorbitant expectations
. I secretly do not approve of this for those close to you

. If you act in this way

. I am ashamed that the gentlemen of the realm have not advised Your Excellency of this
. Therefore, I lay bare my heart and liver

?" In the first year of Tàiqīng
, he was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhānshì (Supervisor of the Crown Prince's Household)
, with the title Shìzhōng remaining as before

. Jìngróng moved his family from his residence into the Palace precinct
. Earlier
, Hóu Jǐng had been defeated and retreated at Wōyáng
. Since the true facts could not be ascertained
, rumors claimed that his general Bào Xiǎn had rebelled
, and that Jǐng himself, along with his followers, had perished
. The court was concerned about this
. Jìngróng subsequently met with the Crown Prince
. Tàizōng said to him
: "We have just received new intelligence from north of the Huái River

, Tàizōng frequently lectured personally on the *Lǎo* and *Zhuāng* (Laozi and Zhuangzi) books at Xuánpǔ
. The scholar Wú Zī was then staying temporarily in the Zhānshì Fǔ (Supervisor’s Residence)
, and entered to listen every day
. Jìngróng said to Zī
: "In the past, during the chaos of the Jìn Dynasty
, it was partly due to honoring and elevating esoteric philosophies

, confirming his prediction

, with his original official titles remaining unchanged

, had generations who practiced Buddhism

. Consequently, the frivolous people of the time referred to it

, was Mìshū Chéng (Vice Director of the Imperial Library)

. Yáo Chá, Lìbù Shàngshū (Minister of Personnel) of the Chén Dynasty, said: During the Zhèngshǐ reign of Wèi and the Middle Court of the Jìn Dynasty

. Officials ranked Shàngshū (Minister) and Chéngláng (Vice Director) and above

, no longer concerned themselves

. Only Biàn Kǔn, regarding the affairs of the Secretariat

. Ruǎn Fú said to him

. Isn't this too strenuous

, never once reviewed a single document

. To gaze blankly and sign documents without reading them
is called 'clear and noble'

. The way of petty men grew strong

. Alas

! Biographies, Chapter 32: Zhū Cǎo, Hè Chēn
Zhū Cǎo, courtesy name Yànhé
, was a native of Qiántáng, Wú Jùn
. His father, Zhū Xùn
, was famous for his righteous fervor
, and served officially as Cānjūn (Military Advisor) to the Prince of Jiāngxià during the Qí Dynasty, and as Wúpíng Lìng (Magistrate of Wúpíng).
Zhū Yì was several years old.
His maternal grandfather, Gù Huān, stroked him and said to Yì's grandfather, Zhāo zhī:
“This child is an extraordinary talent,
and he will surely establish your family name.”
When he was ten-something years old,
he liked gathering with groups to gamble (pú bó),
and was quite a trouble to his local village.
After he grew up,
he then disciplined himself and followed teachers,
studying the Five Classics extensively.
He was especially proficient in the *Lǐ* (Rites) and the *Yì* (Changes),
read widely in literature and history,
and was skilled in various miscellaneous arts.
Chess, gambling, calligraphy, and calculation
were all his strengths.
At the age of twenty,
he went to the capital.
The Director of the Secretariat, Shěn Yuē, interviewed him personally,
and jokingly said to Yì:
“You are young,
why are you so immoderate (or unscrupulous)?”
Yì hesitated and did not grasp the meaning.
Shěn Yuē then said:
“In the world, there are only the literary writings and books of Yì (Wényì Yì shū),
and you have taken them all at once.
This can be called being immoderate.”
That year,
he submitted a memorial suggesting that Jiànkāng should establish a prison administration (yù sī),
to be equivalent to the Court of the Judicial Review (Tíng Wèi).
An imperial order directed the Secretariat (Shàng Shū) to discuss it in detail,
and it was adopted.
According to the old system,
one could only obtain official appointment (shì hè) at twenty-five.
At that time, Yì was only twenty-one,
but a special imperial edict promoted him to be Aide to the Councilor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Yì Cáo Cóngshì Shǐ).
Soon after, there was an imperial decree seeking men of exceptional ability.
The Erudite of the Five Classics, Míng Shānbīn, recommended Yì in a memorial, saying:
“I humbly observe that Zhū Yì of Qiántáng,
though young in age,
possesses the virtue of a mature elder.
When alone, he harbors no thoughts of dissipation;
when in obscurity, he carries the countenance of one addressing guests.
His capacity and bearing are grand and profound,
and his spiritual demeanor is sharp as a peak.
He is like a golden mountain ten thousand *zhàng* high,
one strives to climb but cannot reach;
like a jade sea a thousand *xún* deep,
one glimpses but cannot measure.
Furthermore, he is like a scepter newly carved from jade,
or brocade ribbon newly woven.
When struck, he gives forth a ringing sound;
when chosen, he promptly displays his talents.
Judging by his trustworthiness and conduct,
he is not merely rare among ten households;
if he were tasked to carry heavy burdens on a distant journey,
he would certainly be useful for a thousand *lǐ*.”
Gāozǔ summoned him for an audience,
and had him explain the meanings of the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety) and the *Zhōu Yì* (Classic of Changes).
He was greatly pleased with him,
and said to those around him:
“Zhū Yì is truly extraordinary.”
Later, upon seeing Míng Shānbīn,
he said:
“The person you nominated is precisely the right man.”
Subsequently, Yì was summoned to serve as an attendant in the Western Secretariat (Xī Shěng),
and soon concurrently held the post of Erudite of the Imperial Academy (Tài Xué Bóshì).
That year,
Gāozǔ personally lectured on the *Xiàojīng*,
and had Yì hold the book and read aloud.
He was promoted to Director of the Bureau of Rites (Yí Cáo Láng) in the Secretariat (Shàng Shū),
and also served concurrently as Attendant Official (Tōng Shì Shèrén) in the Central Secretariat (Zhōng Shū).
He was successively promoted to Minister of the Court of Dependencies (Hóng Lú Qīng),
and Commander of the Right Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Yòu Wèi Shuài),
and shortly thereafter was granted the special title of Supernumerary Attendant (Yuán Wài Cháng Shì).
In the fifth year of Pǔtōng,
a large-scale northern expedition was launched.
Yuán Fǎsēng, the Inspector of Xúzhōu for the Wèi, sent an envoy requesting to surrender his territory and defect.
An edict commanded the relevant officials to discuss whether the claim was genuine or false.
Yì said:
“Since the royal army began campaigning in the north,
victories and captures have followed one after another.
The territory of Xúzhōu has increasingly been diminished and weakened.
All are willing to submit to Fǎsēng.
Fǎsēng fears disaster is imminent,
thus his surrender must be genuine.”
Gāozǔ then sent Yì to respond to Fǎsēng,
and also ordered the army under Yì to receive and assist him,
submitting to Yì's command.
When he arrived,
Fǎsēng complied with the imperial command
exactly as Yì had predicted.
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sǎn Qí Cháng Shì).
Since Zhōu Shě died,
Yì took over the handling of confidential strategies and plans.
Changes in regional commands,
court ceremonies, national statutes,
and imperial proclamations and edicts
were all jointly managed by him.
Whenever memorials and reports arrived from all four directions,
or administrative records of the bureaucracy,
requiring consultation, deliberation, and decision,
they piled up before him.
Yì composed the wording and set it to paper,
reviewed the matters, and issued his decisions.
His handling was comprehensive, swift, and abundant,
without pausing his brush even for a moment.
In the space of a moment,
all the affairs were concluded.
In the fourth year of Dàtóng,
he was promoted to General of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn).
In the sixth year,
Yì memorialized to lecture on Gāozǔ’s interpretation of the *Lǎozǐ* (Laozi) in the Yíxián Táng (Hall of Fitting Virtue).
An imperial edict granted permission.
When the lecture began,
more than a thousand people—court officials, Daoist adherents, and commoners—came to listen,
making it a grand occasion for the time.
At that time, the Shìlín Guǎn (Hall of Scholar Woods) was also opened west of the city to welcome scholars.
Yì and the Vice Director of the Secretariat, Hè Chēn, lectured alternately daily on Gāozǔ’s interpretation of the *Zhōngyōng* (Doctrine of the Mean) section of the *Lǐjì* (Book of Rites).
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) also summoned Yì to lecture on the *Yì* (Changes) at Xuánpǔ.
In the eighth year,
he was appointed to the additional post of Palace Attendant (Shì Zhōng).
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was promoted to General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn),
and concurrently commanded the Infantry (Bù Bīng).
In the second year,
he was promoted to Central Leader of the Army (Zhōng Lǐngjūn),
retaining his post as Attendant Official (Shèrén) as before.
Gāozǔ dreamed that the Central Plain was pacified.
The whole court offered congratulations.
In the morning, he told this to Yì.
Yì replied:
“This is a sign that all within the four seas will become unified.”
When Hóu Jǐng offered to surrender,
an edict commanded the various officials to deliberate.
The Assistant Director of the Secretariat, Xiè Jǔ, and others thought it inadvisable.
Gāozǔ wished to accept him,
but had not yet decided.
He once rose early and went to the Wǔdé Gé (Wude Pavilion),
and said to himself,
“Our state is enjoying such great peace.
If we immediately accept this territory now,
how can this be appropriate?
If perchance it leads to chaos,
there will be no time for regret.”
Yì perceived Gāozǔ’s subtle intention
and immediately replied:
“The Sage Ruler governs the realm;
this corresponds above to the Azure Heaven.
As for the remaining people of the northern lands,
who among them does not yearn and look up to Your Majesty?
Because they lacked opportunity,
their wishes have not yet been fulfilled.
Now Hóu Jǐng has seized more than half of the Wèi state,
offering his sincerity and presenting terms of submission,
returning from afar to the Holy Court.
Is this not Heaven inspiring his heart,
or men aiding his scheme?
Examining his motives and scrutinizing the matter,
it is truly admirable.
If we do not accept him now,
I fear we will cut off the hopes of future defectors.
This truth is easily seen;
I beg Your Majesty to harbor no doubts.”
Gāozǔ profoundly accepted Yì's words,
and was also influenced by his previous dream.
Consequently, he accepted the surrender.
When Zhēnyáng was defeated and killed,
an envoy returned from Wèi,
reporting that Gāo Chéng, the Wèi Prime Minister, wished to re-establish peace and friendship.
An edict commanded the relevant officials to finalize a proposal.
Yì again judged peace to be the appropriate course,
and Gāozǔ indeed followed his advice.
In the sixth month of that year,
he sent Xiè Tǐng, Magistrate of Jiànkāng, and Xú Líng, Director of the Palace Secretariat (Tōng Zhí Láng), as envoys to the north to establish good relations.
At this time,
Hóu Jǐng was garrisoned at Shòuchūn.
He repeatedly memorialized to break off the peace,
and requested that the envoys be recalled.
He also sent a letter to Yì,
the tone and meaning of which were very urgent.
Yì merely reported the contents of the imperial decree in reply.
In the eighth month,
Hóu Jǐng consequently raised troops and rebelled,
using the punitive expedition against Yì as his justification.
He recruited three thousand soldiers,
and when Hóu Jǐng arrived,
he used these troops to guard the Gate of the Grand Marshal (Dà Sī Mǎ Mén).
Initially,
Jǐng plotted rebellion.
The Prefect of Hézhōu, King Póyáng Fàn, and the Prefect of Sīzhōu, Yáng Yārén, both repeatedly submitted memorials reporting this.
Cái, however, believing Jǐng to be isolated and relying on them for survival,
thought he surely wouldn't do such a thing.
So he told the envoy,
"King Póyáng truly will not allow the state to have even one guest!"
He then suppressed the reports and did not submit them.
Therefore, the imperial court made no preparations.
When the invaders arrived,
all the civil and military officials in the city blamed him.
The Crown Prince also composed "An Ode to the Besieged City,"
the last stanza of which reads:
"Those with high caps and thick shoes,
who feast sumptuously and ride in comfort,
ascend to the crimson ground of the purple heavens,
and push open the golden doors of the jade palace.
They present strategies and offer advice,
proclaim the fortunes and might of governance and punishment.
Because of them, the four borders are filled with ramparts,
and all nations are still unsettled.
We ask, which are the jackals and wolves?
We inquire, who are these vipers and lizards?"
This was meant to refer to Cái.
Cái, feeling ashamed and indignant,
fell ill and died,
at the age of sixty-seven.
An imperial edict stated:
"The late Grand Warden of the Palace Guard, Cái,
possessed a broad and penetrating intellect,
and ample talent and strength.
He advised from within the帷幄 (wéiwò, staff tent)
for many years.
He was still assisting in the affairs of the court
and diligently fulfilling his appointed duties.
His sudden demise before his time
fills us with both sorrow and compassion.
He is hereby posthumously granted the titles of Attendant Censor and Right Executive Assistant of the Department of State Affairs,
and given one set of imperial ceremonial implements.
All necessities for his funeral
shall be provided as required."
It was not customary for the title of Shàngshū (尚書) to be given posthumously.
When Cái died,
Gāozǔ regretted it deeply,
and was about to discuss the matter of posthumous grants.
Among his attendants, some who were close to Cái
then memorialized, saying:
"Although Cái held many nominal positions,
what he truly wished for in life
was to hold the position of an enforcer of the law."
Gāozǔ, honoring his long-held aspiration,
made this special posthumous grant.
Cái held positions of power for over thirty years.
He was skilled at discerning the subtle intentions of the ruler,
and adept at flattery to cater to the emperor's will,
thus he was especially favored and trusted.
His official career ranged from Gentleman-in-Waiting to Attendant Censor,
four offices all adorned with mink tails.
From Commander of the Right Guard to Grand Warden of the Palace Guard,
four positions all allowed him to drive with official escorts.
This was unprecedented in recent times.
Cái and his sons owned a series of residences from Cháogōu to Qīngxī,
complete with terraces, ponds, and amusements.
Whenever he had leisure, he would visit them with guests.
Gifts from all directions,
wealth and goods, piled up.
He was naturally parsimonious,
never dispensing charity.
His valuable delicacies would rot,
and every month he would discard over ten cartloads,
without even sharing them with his sons in their separate quarters.
The "Lectures on the Rites and Changes," "Ceremonial Regulations," and "Collected Works" he compiled, totaling over a hundred chapters,
were mostly lost during the chaos.
His eldest son, Sù,
served as Doctor of the National Academy;
his second son, Rùn,
was a Sītú Yuán (司徒掾, Assistant in the Ministry of Works).
Both met their end in the rebellion.
Hè Chēn, courtesy name Guóbǎo,
was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
His paternal uncle, Yáng,
was a Commandant of Infantry,
and considered a great Confucian scholar of his generation.
When Chēn was young,
Yáng taught him the classics,
and he grasped their meaning upon first hearing.
Yáng was astonished,
often saying:
"This child will achieve nobility through his understanding of the classics."
After Yáng's death,
Chēn's family was poor.
He often traveled to Zhūjì
to sell grain to support himself.
In his free time, he would study,
especially excelling in the Sānlǐ (三禮, Three Rites).
Initially,
Yáng gathered students in his hometown to teach.
Now, they also relied on Chēn.
During the Pǔtōng (普通) era,
the Prefect, King Línchuān, appointed him as Libationer and Aide-de-camp.
When Chēn first arrived in the capital,
Gāozǔ, hearing of his scholarship,
summoned him to the Wéndédéng (文德殿, Hall of Literary Virtue).
He was pleased after conversing with him,
and said to the Right Executive Assistant Xú Miǎn:
"Chēn truly possesses a generational legacy."
He was then appointed Gentleman-in-Waiting to the Royal Domain,
and soon concurrently served as Doctor of the Imperial University.
He gradually rose to the positions of Military Advisor to the Central Guard and Executive Secretary of the Department of State Affairs,
participating in ceremonial matters.
He was successively promoted to Grand Master of Remonstrance,
while retaining his position as Executive Secretary.
He also served as Registrar to King Póyáng of the Western Expedition,
and concurrently as Assistant Executive of the Left in the Department of State Affairs,
becoming full-time after a year.
An edict commanded Chēn to compile a new method for posthumous titles,
which is still in use today.
At that time, the Crown Prince debated
that at the end of the Dàgōng (大功, Major Mourning) period, one could crown a son or marry off a daughter.
Chēn refuted this, saying: "The imperial directive states that
at the end of Dàgōng, one may crown a son and marry off a daughter,
but not crown oneself or marry oneself.
Judging by the ancient texts,
I am still somewhat perplexed.
The rites of marriage and capping
were originally performed by the father.
A person without a father
may cap themselves.
Therefore, when Dàgōng and Xiǎogōng (小功, Minor Mourning) are mentioned,
they are always presented as 'capping a son and marrying off a daughter' in the text,
not implying that one
may only do so for a son
but not for oneself.
At the end of the Xiǎogōng period,
one may indeed marry oneself,
yet it also states
'capping a son and marrying a wife,'
the meaning of which becomes even clearer.
Therefore, by first listing
the two mourning periods,
and consistently specifying 'capping a son and marrying off a daughter'
at the end of the sentence,
the meaning of marrying oneself becomes apparent.
Since it is clear that one can marry oneself at the end of Xiǎogōng,
it follows that one can cap oneself at the end of Dàgōng.
This
is a condensed statement that reveals the underlying principle.
If it is argued that because one observes Dàgōng for a father,
and a son observes Xiǎogōng,
and Xiǎogōng is a lighter mourning,
one may therefore cap a son and marry a daughter for him,
while Dàgōng is a heavier mourning,
thus
one may not marry or cap oneself—
then at the end of Xiǎogōng,
unless it explicitly states that the mourning for father and son is different,
it should not again mention
'capping a son and marrying a daughter.'
If it is argued that the text for Xiǎogōng
states that one may marry oneself,
but the text for Dàgōng does not state that one may cap oneself,
hence it is understood that one in Dàgōng
may not perform auspicious rites for oneself,
but only cap a son or marry off a daughter for him—
I believe that
not performing auspicious rites while in mourning
is fundamentally because auspicious and inauspicious events cannot intermingle.
Although a son at the end of Xiǎogōng
may perform capping and marriage,
he still requires his father to cap
and marry him.
If a father at the end of Dàgōng may cap his son and marry off his daughter,
this implies no obstruction in the rites for auspicious and inauspicious events;
if there is no obstruction,
how could he not cap
or marry himself?
If capping and marrying oneself would be obstructed,
how then could capping a son and marrying off a daughter be permissible?
Now, to permit capping a son but forbid capping oneself,
this is what perplexes
Chēn.
Furthermore, the imperial directive reasons:

then one in Dàgōng with reduced mourning cannot cap a son or marry off a daughter either.'
Upon careful consideration of this directive,
if it means that one in
Dàgōng with reduced mourning cannot cap a son or marry off a daughter,
then one in Xiǎogōng with reduced mourning also cannot cap oneself or marry oneself.
This would mean that all those in Dàgōng or Xiǎogōng with reduced mourning cannot perform capping
or marriage.
The ancient texts should then say 'if in reduced mourning, then not permissible,'
how could it only refer to a junior prematurely deceased child?
Now, it does not speak of reduced mourning generally,
but specifically cites a junior prematurely deceased child,
which indeed has its own meaning.
For
After being married off,
or having remarried,
the person who was married off
has a Dàgōng (大功) relationship with their natal sisters.
If it is a Dàfū (大夫) serving as a Shì (士) father,

For capping and marriage,
the principle is no different.
The reason for this is that
when married out, there is one who receives me,

It is intended to make light of
this and favor that;
though this mourning服 (fú) is reduced,

In the past, those who were Qīqīn (期親),

As for
Qī (期) reduced to Dàgōng (大功),

a reduction and lessening with order.
As for mourning for marriage and capping,

Only for the mourning of Xiàshāng (下殤)

stated that they do not marry.
This is because of their young age;
the grief of untimely death is deep.
Since there is no receiving the thick (mourning) from another surname,

Therefore, it is specifically stated that they do not marry,

Therefore, in all cases of reduced mourning,

stated that they do not marry.
If the principle is like this,

Moreover, the record says,

To speak of Xiàshāng (下殤)

to speak of Xiǎogōng (小功) means it cannot include Dàgōng (大功).
If in fact, all reduced mourning for Dàgōng (大功) and Xiǎogōng (小gōng) cannot be capped or married,

This might not be the meaning of the text.
This is also what Chēn (琛) doubted.
So, Chēn’s (琛) proposal was followed.
He was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍).
Previously, the Nán Zuò (南坐) in the Shàngshū (尚書) did not wear marten fur (diāo 貂);

Shortly after,

Chēn’s (琛) family wealth was abundant;

Throughout his various positions,
Chēn (琛)

Whenever he met Gāozǔ (高祖),
their conversations often lasted for a long time.
Therefore, in the palace (shěng zhōng 省中), a saying emerged:
"Hè Yǎ (賀雅) goes up to the hall and doesn't come down."
Chēn’s (琛) demeanor was elegant and refined,

He was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì (散騎常侍),

At this time,
those whom Gāozǔ (高祖) had appointed to office

Chēn (琛) then submitted a memorial detailing various matters, stating:
"I have received the grace of being promoted,
yet I have not been able to perform a single duty;
holding the responsibility of offering advice,
I have also not been able to recommend a single word.
I humbly hear
that 'a benevolent father does not love a useless
son,

This is why I sigh

I now presume to speak on current affairs,
listing them below.
This is not
to offer counsel,
nor to present advice.
I keep my thoughts sealed within my chest,
not speaking to my wife or children.
My words are without embellishment;
if edited, they are burned.
If they are fortunate enough to be heard,
I ask that they be carefully considered.
If they do not align [with your wishes],

The first matter states: Now, the northern borders are subservient,
weapons are laid down and peace prevails.
This is precisely the time for production, accumulation, education, and training.
However, the population of the empire is declining,
which is indeed
the urgent task of today.
Although all areas are suffering from devastation and displacement,
it is even worse outside the passes.
Commanderies (jùn 郡) cannot endure the overall control of the provinces (zhōu 州),
and districts (xiàn 縣) cannot endure the levies and reductions of the commanderies.
They harass each other,
unable
to manage their administration,
focusing only on responding to requisitions and collections.
The common people cannot bear their lot and
move away,
some relying on influential families,
others gathering in fortified settlements.
They flee out of necessity,
not by choice.
The state's taxes and levies outside the passes are rather light;
yet, annual rents and taxes
often lead to arrears and accumulation.
Meanwhile, the people lose
their peaceful homes.
Is this not the fault of the governors and magistrates?
The eastern border's population is sparse,
all due to the frequent imperial envoys.
A dog does not bark at night,

Now,
in large states and large districts,
those bearing imperial decrees by boat

even remote villages
and distant towns
are all reached.
Every time an envoy arrives,
they cause
disturbance;
moreover, this accumulated harassment

Incompetent district magistrates

while cunning and vicious senior officials

corrupt and cruel.
Even if there are honest and fair ones,
the commandery still restricts them.
Therefore, district magistrates holding their seals
rarely have their performance evaluated;
ordinary people abandon their occupations,
and many become vagrants.
Although imperial edicts for the restoration
of occupations are issued annually,
and graces of tax remission are frequently bestowed,
they ultimately cannot return to their homes.
The second matter states: The compassionate heart of the sagely ruler,

let alone the countless
common people.
Yet, the provinces and commanderies have no will to care for the people.
Thus, the whole world looks up eagerly,

If there is pain that needs relief and medicine,

Today, the reason why all local officials (zǎishǒu 宰守) throughout the empire are inclined towards
greed and cruelty,

The abuses of extravagance and excess

Moreover,
if one eats food covering a square area before them,

Today's banquets and celebrations

The produce of the
Lù Tái

only greedy corruption,

The third matter states: Your Imperial Majesty takes upon the burden of the common people as your responsibility,

Now the
Wèi Shì (魏氏) are in a peaceful alliance,

If you refer to
the court with this point,

If you think that the merit-making (gōngdé) activities

expense.

Also,
Not the slightest speck concerns the state.
If wealth is acquired and used lawfully,

regret that what they have taken is little;

The brave and the cowardly are different;

The brave can be tasked with advancement and acquisition;

If, for example, Shūqí [Shūqí] were tasked with defending Xīhé [Xīhé],

If Wú Qǐ [Wú Qǐ]

If Wú Qǐ [Wú Qǐ] were not heavily employed,

You said,

“Those who achieve supreme governance must prioritize simplicity and purity.”
These words are excellent.
The Master said,
“When
his person is correct,
things proceed without command;

I have refrained from sexual relations for over thirty years,

I have calculated that
I have
not slept in the same room as a woman

This is also known
by everyone.
Since birth, I have not consumed alcohol.
Since birth, I have not been fond of music.

I
emerge at the third watch (around midnight) to handle affairs.
