I am at a loss for how to reply.
You also said,
“All the various bureaus submit memorials,
deceitfully competing to seek advancement.”
Who exactly is this again?
Which one again is the deceitful affair?
If outsiders are now prevented from presenting
affairs,
is this permissible according to righteousness?
No one is neglecting their duty,
but should their duties be abolished?
If duties are abolished, the people will fall into disorder.
If the people are in disorder, can the state be secure?
This is what is meant by
giving up eating due to choking.
If we cut off the submission of memorials,
who will bear the responsibility?
A person who is fully trusted and delegated to,
how can such a one be found?
Therefore, the ancients said:
“Listening exclusively breeds wickedness,
and relying solely on one person causes chaos.”
This is like Èr Shì [Èr Shì] entrusting Zhào Gāo [Zhào Gāo],
or Empress Yuán Hòu [Yuán Hòu] handing power to Wáng Mǎng [Wáng Mǎng].
When the deer was called a horse,
there eventually came the calamity of Yán Yuè [Yán Yuè] at Wàng Yí [Wàng Yí].
Wáng Mǎng [Wáng Mǎng] also eventually usurped the tripod of the Hàn [Hàn] dynasty.
You said,
“blowing apart the fur to find flaws.”
Who, again, are the people whose flaws are being sought?
“Splitting the skin and dividing the fibers,”
who, again, are these people?
As for the matters of
“severity and harshness”
and “punishing and banishing,”
who, again, are all these people?
You also mentioned
“offices, bureaus, residences, and markets.”
Which ones ought to be abolished?
Which ones ought to be reduced?
Regarding “state formalities and military preparations,”
which
ones ought to be reduced?
Which ones are not yet needed?
Regarding “garrisons and relay stations in the four directions,”
which ones are useless?
Which ones obstruct the people?
Where is construction being undertaken that oppresses the people?
Where
are funds being spent on things that are not urgent?
What amounts to
“punishment and summoning”?
What amounts to
“taxation and levies”?
The court has never had these matters.
What are the methods for achieving peace and rest?
You should specify each of these matters
and report them comprehensively.
You said,
“If the people are not greatly relieved in time,
and we only plan when the matter arises,
we know it will be too late.”
According to your words,
what currently constitutes a great imposition of labor upon the
people?
Where is this happening?
You said,
“The state is exhausted and the people are weary.”
If your words are truly sincere,
you must ultimately specify the matters;
you cannot merely speak vaguely.
Indeed, one who can speak of something
must also be able to implement it.
The arts of enriching the state and strengthening the military,
the appropriate means of assisting the people and reducing labor,
and the methods for issuing orders to near and far,
all ought to be listed comprehensively.
If they are not listed comprehensively,
then this is
Deceiving the Imperial Court
and merely displaying empty eloquence.
Whenever a person undertakes something,
they must first examine themselves internally.
Only those who are flawless
can justly punish others.
You must not extensively criticize those inside and outside [the court]
without speaking fully about the actual events.
I await hearing your serious memorial again;
I will review it,
entrust it to the Shàngshū,
and circulate it throughout the realm.
Hopefully, the chaos of the straying sheep will be permanently eliminated,
and the harmful steeds will long
cease;
the beauty of reform
will be seen again today.”
Hè Chēn received the imperial edict
and only apologized for his faults,
daring not to make further criticisms.
After a long time,
he was promoted to Tàifǔ Qīng.
In the second year of Tàiqīng (548 CE),
he was promoted to Yúnqí Jiāngjūn and Zhōngjūn Zhǎngshǐ to the King of Xuānchéng.
Hóu Jǐng raised troops and attacked the capital (Jīngshī).
The King moved into the inner Tái (Palace City),
leaving Hè Chēn and the Sīmǎ Yáng Jiǎo to defend the Eastern Residence (Dōngfǔ).
The bandits soon attacked and captured the city,
allowing their soldiers to rampage and kill.
Hè Chēn was speared but not immediately killed.
The bandits found him
and carried him to the foot of the palace gate (Quēxià).
He asked to see the Púshè Wáng Kè and the Lǐngjūn Zhū Yì,
urging them to open the city gate and let the bandits in.
Wáng Kè and the others rebuked him.
He stopped, weeping,
and the bandits carried him away again to Zhuāngyán Sì (Temple) for treatment.
The following year,
the Tái City could not be defended,
and Hè Chēn fled back to his hometown.
In the winter of that year,
the bandits advanced to invade Kuàijī.
They captured Hè Chēn again and sent him out of the capital (Dū),
making him Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū.
Later, he suffered from illness and died
at the age of sixty-nine.
The writings compiled by Hè Chēn, including the *Sānlǐ Jiǎngshū*, the *Wǔjīng Zhìyì*, and various ritual procedures,
totaled over a hundred chapters.
His son, Xǔ,
in the early Tàiqīng period (547–548 CE),
went from being a Yuàn to the Yítóng, Marquis of Xīchāng,
to serving outside as the Grand Administrator of Bāshān.
While in the commandery, he encountered rebellious soldiers and died.
Chén Lìbù Shàngshū Yáo Chá said: Xiàhóu Shèng once said:
“A scholar worries about not understanding the Classics and their principles;
if the Classics and their principles are clear,
attaining high office (Qīngzǐ) is as easy as picking up a mustard seed from the ground.”
Zhū Yì and Hè Chēn both rose from humble origins,
met the opportune time with their classical learning,
and achieved nobility and prominence,
fulfilling this saying.
However, Zhū Yì then sought favor and trust,
held responsibilities, and possessed power,
yet he was unable to assist the ruler according to the Dào (the proper way);
he merely sought tolerance and flattery.
When the invasion was brought upon and the state was ruined,
it was truly due to Zhū Yì.
Since the disaster and hardship were made manifest,
his crime was not clarified,
and even after his death,
his honors and posthumous gifts were still exceptional.
Since punishment was not applied,
rewards were also excessive.
If instruction and deterrence are neglected,
how can one govern the state?
Therefore, the gentleman knows that concerning the chaos of Tàiqīng,
how could it have avoided this outcome?
Chapter 33 of the Biographies: Yuán Fǎsēng, Yuán Shù, Yuán Yuàndá, Wáng Shénniàn (Yáng Huá), Yáng Kǎn (son Kūn), Yáng Yārén
Yuán Fǎsēng
was a collateral relative of the Wèi clan.
His founding ancestor was Emperor Dàowǔ.
His father, Zhōngkuí,
was the Prince of Jiāngyáng.
Yuán Fǎsēng served Wèi,
holding office successively as Guānglù Dàfū.
Later, he was made Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of all military affairs in Xúzhōu, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xúzhōu,
stationed at Péngchéng.
In the fifth year of Pǔtōng (524 CE),
the Wèi dynasty experienced great chaos.
Yuán Fǎsēng consequently held his garrison and proclaimed himself emperor,
eliminating those who disagreed with him,
establishing his sons as kings,
and deploying his generals and commanders,
intending to plan for restoration.
Soon after, the Wèi chaos gradually stabilized,
and they were about to attack Yuán Fǎsēng.
Yuán Fǎsēng became fearful,
and thus dispatched envoys to submit,
requesting to become a vassal state.
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) granted this,
appointing him Shìzhōng and Sīkōng,
and enfeoffing him as Duke of Shǐ'ān Commandery,
with an income of five thousand households.
When the Wèi army was already pressing near,
Yuán Fǎsēng requested permission to return to the court.
Gāozǔ sent the Zhōngshū Shèrén Zhū Yì to welcome him.
Upon his arrival,
he was treated with great favor and distinction.
At that time, the court was engaged in inviting and gathering supporters,
and soothing and pleasing those who had submitted.
Yuán Fǎsēng was bestowed with a grand residence, female musicians, and gold and silk,
in amounts too numerous to count over time.
Because Yuán Fǎsēng, during his days in Wèi,
had long held responsibilities on the borders,
and often engaged in plunder,
killing a great number of people,
he requested troops for self-defense.
An imperial decree granted him a hundred men with armor and weapons,
who accompanied him when entering and exiting the forbidden palace (Jìntà).
In the second year of Dàtōng (528 CE),
he was given the additional title of Guānjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtōng (529 CE),
he was transferred to Chējì Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year (532 CE),
he was advanced to Tàiwèi
and concurrently held Jīnzǐ Guānglù.
In that same year,
he was established as the Lord of Eastern Wèi,
but he did not take the position.
He was subsequently appointed Shǐchíjié, Sànqí Chángshì, Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn, with the protocol of Kāifǔ Tóng Sānsī, and Governor of Yǐngzhōu.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he was summoned as Shìzhōng and Tàiwèi
and concurrently held the position of Jūnshī Jiāngjūn.
He died,
at the age of eighty-three.
His two sons, Jǐnglóng and Jǐngzhòng,
followed Yuán Fǎsēng to court during the Pǔtōng period.
Jǐnglóng was enfeoffed as the Duke of Dùnyáng County,
with an income of one thousand households.

He went out to serve as Chíjié, Dūdū of military affairs in thirteen provinces including Guǎngzhōu, Yuèzhōu, Jiāozhōu, and Guìzhōu, Píngnán Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng (531 CE),
he was summoned as Shìzhōng and Ānyòu Jiāngjūn.
In the fourth year (532 CE),
he became Zhēngběi Jiāngjūn and Governor of Xúzhōu,
and was enfeoffed as the Prince of Péngchéng,
but he did not take the position.
Soon after, he was appointed Shìzhōng and Dùzhī Shàngshū.
In the early Tàiqīng period (547–548 CE),
he again became Shǐchíjié, Dūdū of military affairs in thirteen provinces including Guǎngzhōu, Yuèzhōu, Jiāozhōu, and Guìzhōu, Zhēngnán Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
He traveled as far as Léishǒu,
where he suffered from illness and died
at the age of fifty-eight.
Jǐngzhòng was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhījiāng County,
with an income of one thousand households.
He was appointed Shìzhōng and Yòuwèi Jiāngjūn.
In the third year of Dàtōng (529 CE),
his income was increased,
making the total two thousand households,
and he was also granted a troupe of female musicians.
He went out to serve as Chíjié, Dūdū of military affairs in thirteen provinces including Guǎngzhōu and Yuèzhōu, Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn, Píngyuè Zhōnglángjiāng, and Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
During the Dàtóng period (535–546 CE),
he was summoned as Shìzhōng and Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn.
His older brother, Jǐnglóng, later served as Governor of Guǎngzhōu.
When Hóu Jǐng started his rebellion,
he used the fact that Jǐngzhòng was a member of the Yuán clan
and sent a messenger to entice him,
promising to support him as the sovereign.
Jǐngzhòng then raised troops,
intending to descend and join Hóu Jǐng.
At that time, Chén Bàxiān, the Military Supervisor of Xījiāng, and Wáng Huáimíng, the Governor of Chéngzhōu, etc., raised troops and attacked him.
Chén Bàxiān addressed his assembled men, saying:
“The Imperial Court considers that Yuán Jǐngzhòng has allied himself with the bandit,
plotting to endanger the state and its altars.
We are now sending Bó, the Duke of Qūjiāng, to be the Governor,
to pacify and garrison this province.”
When the assembled men heard this,
they all abandoned their armor and dispersed.
Jǐngzhòng then hanged himself and died.
Yuán Shù, courtesy name Jūnlì,
was also a near relative of the Wèi.
His grandfather was Xiànwén Dì.
His father was Xī,
Prince of Xiányáng.
Shù served the Wèi as Minister of the Court of the Imperial Clan (Zōngzhèng Qīng).
When the chaos of Ěrzhū Róng occurred,
he returned to the state (Liáng) in the eighth year of Tiānjiān (509 CE).
He was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yè,
with an estate of two thousand households,
and appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì).
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng (525 CE),
he was responsible for receiving Yuán Fǎsēng upon his return to court.

He was promoted to Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Yǐng, Sī, and Huò Three Prefectures (Dū Dū Yǐng Sī Huò Sān Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General of the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Yǐng Prefecture (Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His estate was increased to three thousand households in total, including the previous grant.
He campaigned against the southern Man bandits
and pacified them.
He was given the additional titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and General Who Pacifies the West (Ānxī Jiāngjūn),
and his fief was further increased by five hundred households.
In the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng (530 CE),
he was summoned to serve as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General Who Guards the Right (Zhèn Yòu Jiāngjūn).
In the fourth year (532 CE),
he became Bearer of Credentials, General Who Guards the North (Zhèn Běi Jiāngjūn), and Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs for the Northern Expedition (Dū Dū Běi Tǎo Zhū Jūnshì),
and was granted an accompanying band of wind and percussion instruments (gǔchuī yī bù).
He launched an attack against the Wèi,
assaulting Wèi’s Qiáochéng.
He captured it.
However, when the Wèi general Dúgū Rúyuàn arrived to reinforce the area,
he subsequently besieged Shù.
The city fell and Shù was captured.
He died of frustration in the Wèi territory,
at the age of forty-eight.
His son, Zhēn,
during the Dàtóng period,
requested permission to accompany the Wèi envoy Cuī Chángqiān to Yè to bury his father.
Upon returning, he was appointed Palace Gentleman of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
In the early Tàiqīng period,
after Hóu Jǐng surrendered,
he requested the relatives of the Yuán clan,
wishing to elevate one of them as sovereign.
An imperial edict enfeoffed Zhēn as the Prince of Xiányáng.
He was sent back north with the ceremonial honors due to a Son of Heaven.
He returned upon the defeat of Jǐng.
Yuán Yuàndá
was also a collateral descendant of the Wèi.
His grandfather was Míngyuán Dì.
His father was the Prince of Lèpíng.
Yuàndá served the Wèi as Director of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Lìng) and Governor of Yǐng Prefecture (Yǐngzhōu Cìshǐ).
During the Pǔtōng period,
when the great army launched a northern campaign
and attacked Yìyáng,
Yuàndá offered his prefecture in submission.
An imperial edict enfeoffed him as the Duke of Lèpíng,
with an estate of one thousand households,
and bestowed upon him a magnificent residence and female musicians.

He was subsequently dispatched to serve as Bearer of Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Xiāng Prefecture (Dū Dū Xiāngzhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Xiāng Prefecture (Xiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng (530 CE),
he was summoned to serve as Palace Attendant, Grand Master of the Center (Tài Zhōng Dàfū), and General Who Assists the Left (Yì Zuǒ Jiāngjūn).
In the third year of Dàtóng (537 CE),
he died,
at the age of fifty-seven.
Wáng Shénniàn
was a native of Qí, Tàiyuán.
In his youth, he enjoyed Confucian studies,
and was especially clear on the inner canons (Buddhist texts).
He started his official career in Wèi as a Prefectural Chief Clerk (Zhōu Zhǔbù).
He gradually rose to be the Administrator of Yǐngchuān (Yǐngchuān Tàishǒu).
He subsequently held his commandery and submitted.
When the Wèi army arrived,
he crossed the Yangzi River with his family.
He was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Nánchéng County,
with an estate of five hundred households.
After a while,
he was appointed Chief Administrator of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Nèishǐ).
He later served successively as Chief Administrator of Wǔyáng and Xuānchéng,
achieving distinction in administration in all of them.
Upon his return, he was appointed Minister of the Imperial Stud (Tài Pú Qīng).

He was sent out to serve as Bearer of Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Qīng and Jì Two Prefectures (Dū Dū Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì), General Who Inspires Awe (Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Qīng and Jì Two Prefectures (Qīng Jì Èr Zhōu Cìshǐ).
Shénniàn was fundamentally upright and firm,
and wherever he served, he strictly prohibited licentious shrines.
At that time, in the northeast of Qīng and Jì Prefectures, there was Shílù Shān bordering the sea.
There was previously a temple to a god there,
where wicked shamans deceived and confused the common people.
People from near and far came to pray,
causing extremely great wastage.
When Shénniàn arrived,
he immediately ordered the temple to be demolished,
and the local customs were consequently reformed.
During the Pǔtōng period,
when a great northern expedition was launched,
he was summoned to serve as General of the Right Guard (Yòu Wèi Jiāngjūn).
In the sixth year (525 CE),
he was promoted to Bearer of Credentials, Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, and General of Fangs and Claws (Zhǎoyá Jiāngjūn),
retaining his position as General of the Right Guard.
He fell ill and died,
at the age of seventy-five.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him his original office and the Governorship of Héng Prefecture (Héngzhōu Cìshǐ),
and concurrently provided a full band of wind and percussion instruments.
His posthumous name was Zhuàng.
Shénniàn was skilled at horsemanship and archery in his youth
and did not decline even in old age.
He once held two swords and shields in his hands before Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng),
crossing them left and right,
and galloping his horse back and forth,
surpassing all others in the group.
At that time, there was also Yáng Huá,
who was skilled at performing the ‘Terrifying Military Ride.’
Together, they were the most marvelous and swift performers of the time,
and Gāozǔ deeply admired and praised them.
His son, Zūnyè,
served up to the position of Minister of the Imperial Stud.
When he died,
he was posthumously granted General Who Inspires Awe (Xìn Wēi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Qīng and Jì Two Prefectures,
with a full band of wind and percussion instruments.
His second son, Sēngbiàn,
has a separate biography.
Yáng Huá
was a native of Qiúchí, Wǔdū.
His father, Dàyǎn,
was a famous Wèi general.
Huá was courageous and strong in his youth,
and his appearance was grand and imposing.
Empress Dowager Hú of Wèi coerced him into an illicit affair.
Huá feared that disaster would strike him,
so he led his private retainers and troops to defect.
Empress Dowager Hú yearned for him incessantly
and composed the lyrics for the “Yáng Báihuá Song,”
which she ordered the palace women to sing day and night while linking arms and stamping their feet.
The lyrics were extremely sad and mournful.
Huá subsequently served in numerous military expeditions
and achieved combat merit.
He successively held the offices of Minister of the Imperial Stud,
Director of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèi Shuài),
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Yìyáng County.
During the Tàiqīng period,
when Hóu Jǐng was causing chaos,
Huá wished to establish his resolve and integrity,
but his wife and children were captured by the rebels.
Consequently, he surrendered to Jǐng,
and died among the rebels.
Yáng Kǎn, courtesy name Zǔxīn,
was a native of Liángfǔ, Tàishān.
He was a descendant of Xù, the Han Administrator of Nányáng.
His grandfather, Guī,
when Emperor Wǔ of Sòng governed Xú Prefecture,
was appointed Libationer and Aide (Jìjiǔ Cóngshì) and Grand Central Rectifier (Dà Zhōngzhèng).
When Xuē Āndū surrendered Péngchéng to the north,
Guī was consequently trapped in Wèi territory.
Wèi bestowed upon him the titles of General of the Guards (Wèi Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Yíng Prefecture (Yíngzhōu Cìshǐ).
His father, Zhǐ,
was a Wèi Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng)
and Grand Master of Brilliant Goodness with Gold and Purple (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū).
Kǎn was exceptional and magnificent in his youth,
standing seven feet and eight inches tall.
He had an refined fondness for literature and history
and was extensively versed in books and records.
He particularly enjoyed the *Zǔo’s Commentary on the Spring and Autumn Annals* (*Zuǒshì Chūnqiū*) and the military strategies of Sūn Wú.
At the age of twenty (Ruò Guàn), he achieved merit while accompanying his father in Liáng Prefecture.
During the Zhèngguāng period of Wèi,
he gradually became a divisional general (biéjiāng).
At that time, there was a Qiāng leader in Qín Prefecture named Mòzhē Niànsheng
who occupied the prefecture and rebelled,
proclaiming himself emperor.
He then sent his younger brother Tiānshēng to lead troops to attack and seize Qí Prefecture,
and subsequently raided Yōng Prefecture.
Kǎn served as a subordinate general (piānjiāng),
attached to Xiāo Bǎoyǐn, and went to suppress the rebellion.
He secretly went on patrol
and waited for an opportunity to shoot Tiānshēng.
Tiānshēng immediately fell upon the sound of the bowstring,
and his troops subsequently dispersed.
For his merit, Kǎn was promoted to Bearer of Credentials, Grand General Who Attacks the East (Zhēng Dōng Dà Jiāngjūn), Commissioner Overseeing the Eastern Route (Dōng Dào Xíngtái),
appointed concurrently as Administrator of Tàishān (Tàishān Tàishǒu),
and advanced in peerage to the Marquis of Jùpíng.
Initially,
his father always harbored the ambition of returning south,
and often said to his sons:
“How can a man remain long detained in a foreign land?
You should return to serve the Southern Court (Dōngcháo).”
Kǎn reached this point, he intended to mobilize the Hé and Jǐ Rivers regions to fulfill his late father's ambition.
Yáng Dūn, the Inspector (Cìshǐ) of Yǎnzhōu,
who was Kǎn's cousin,
secretly learned of this [plan],
and occupied the province to resist Kǎn.
Kǎn then led 30,000 elite troops to attack him,
but did not overcome him,
so he subsequently built more than ten forts to defend [his position].
The Imperial Court's rewards and appointments [given to Kǎn]
were the same as those given to Yuán Fǎsēng.
They dispatched Yáng Yārén and Wáng Biàn to lead troops to meet and support him,
and Lǐ Yuánlǚ to transport and supply grain and arms.
The Emperor of Wèi (Wèi Dì), hearing of this,
sent an envoy to appoint Kǎn as General-in-Chief of Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Minister of Education (Sītú), and Duke of Tàishān Commandery (Tàishān Jùngōng),
and to permanently serve as Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ).
Kǎn executed their envoy in a public display.
The Wèi people were greatly alarmed,
and ordered the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Púyè), Yú Huī, to lead several hundred thousand troops,
while Gāo Huān, Ěrzhū Yángdū, and others arrived in succession.
They besieged Kǎn in more than ten layers,
inflicting heavy casualties.
The arrows within the stockade were exhausted,
and the Southern army did not advance.
Thereupon, he broke through the siege at night and exited,
fighting and marching,
and only after one day and one night did he exit the Wèi territory.
When they reached Zhākǒu,
there were still over ten thousand men
and two thousand horses.
As they were about to enter the South,
all the soldiers spent the entire night singing mournful songs.
Kǎn then apologized, saying:
“You gentlemen miss your homeland,
and naturally cannot follow me.
Please choose freely whether to leave or stay;
we part company here.”
Thereupon, they each bowed their farewells and departed.
In the third year of Dàtōng [529 CE], Kǎn arrived at the capital.

By imperial decree, he was appointed Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì), Area Commander-in-Chief of Campaigning Forces in Xiáqiū (Dūcū Xiáqiū Zhēngtǎo Zhū Jūnshì), General Pacifying the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Xúzhōu (Xúzhōu Cìshǐ).
Furthermore, his elder brother Mò and his three younger brothers, Chén, Jǐ, and Yuán,
were all appointed Inspectors (Cìshǐ).
Soon after, Kǎn was appointed Area Commander-in-Chief for Northern Campaigns (Dūcū Běitǎo Zhū Jūnshì),
and went out to garrison Rìchéng.
As Chén Qìngzhī happened to suffer a defeat,
the advance was halted.
In that same year,
an imperial decree appointed him Bearer of Credentials (Chíjíe), General of Cloud-like Banners (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Qīng and Jì Provinces (Qīng Jì Èrzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the fourth year of Zhōng Dàtōng [532 CE],

an imperial decree appointed him Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), Area Commander-in-Chief of Forces in Xiáqiū (Dūcū Xiáqiū Zhū Jūnshì), General Pacifying the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ),
to follow Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) Yuán Fǎsēng on the northern campaign.
Fǎsēng had previously reported, saying:
“I have an old acquaintance with Kǎn,
and I wish to be allowed to travel together with him.”
Gāozǔ then summoned Kǎn and asked about his strategy,
and Kǎn thoroughly presented his plans for advance and conquest.
Gāozǔ then said:
“I know that you wish to travel with the Grand Commandant.”
Kǎn replied:
“Since I pulled myself away [from the North] and returned to the court,
I have always thought of serving unto death.
However, I have truly never wished to travel with Fǎsēng.
Although the Northerners call me a Wú [Southerner],
the Southerners already call me a Lǔ [Barbarian].
If I travel with Fǎsēng now,
it will merely be a matter of ‘birds of a feather flocking together,’
which would not only contradict my original intention,
but would also cause the Xiōngnú [Northern barbarians] to despise the Hàn.”
Gāozǔ said:
“The court urgently requires you to go this time.”
He was then appointed by imperial decree as Grand Army Commandant (Dà Jūnsīmǎ).
Gāozǔ said to Kǎn:
“The position of Army Commandant (Jūnsīmǎ) has been abolished for a long time;
this office is established now specifically for you.”
When the army reached Guānzhú,
Yuán Shù again suffered a defeat at Qiáochéng.
The campaign was abandoned,
and he returned to become Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
In the fifth year,
he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Gāochāng County (Gāochāng Xiànhóu),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
In the sixth year,
he went out to serve as General of Cloud-like Banners (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Tàishǒu).
The Mǐnyuè custom was to favor rebellion,
and previous Grand Administrators had been unable to suppress it.
When Kǎn arrived, he attacked them,
executing their leaders, such as Chén Chēng and Wú Mǎn.
Consequently, the commandery was thoroughly pacified,
and no one dared to violate the peace.
After a while,
he was recalled to serve as Commander of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zuǒ Wèishuài).
In the third year of Dàtóng [537 CE],
the imperial carriage visited the Lèyóu Park (Lèyóu Yuàn),
and Kǎn was present at the feast.
At that time, the Ministry of the Lesser Treasury (Shàofǔ) reported the completion of a newly manufactured double-edged lance (shuò),
twenty-four *chǐ* long [approx. 18 feet],
and 1.3 *chǐ* in circumference [approx. 10 inches].
Gāozǔ then bestowed a horse upon Kǎn,
ordering him to test the weapon.
Kǎn took the lance and mounted the horse,
striking and stabbing left and right,
demonstrating the utmost of his skill.
Gāozǔ praised him for it.
He also composed a thirty-couplet poem about the martial banquet and showed it to Kǎn.
Kǎn responded to the imperial poem instantly at the banquet.
Gāozǔ read it and said:
“I have heard that the benevolent possess courage;
now I see that the courageous possess benevolence.
This can be called the lasting tradition of Zōu and Lǔ,
and proof that heroes and sages do not cease to appear.”
In the sixth year,
he was promoted to Chief Clerk of the Left under the Minister of Education (Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ).
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Bureau of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū).
At that time, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Lìng), Hé Jìngróng, was powerful;
although Kǎn served alongside him in the department,
he never visited him socially.
When the eunuch Zhāng Sēngyìn went to wait upon Kǎn,
Kǎn said:
“My seat is not for eunuchs.”
He ultimately refused to receive him.
The public opinion at the time praised his integrity and rectitude.
In the ninth year,
he was sent out to serve as Bearer of Credentials (Shǐ Chíjíe), General of Martial Vigor (Zhuàngwǔ Jiāngjūn), and Inspector of Héngzhōu (Héngzhōu Cìshǐ).
In the first year of Tàiqīng [547 CE],
he was recalled to serve as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
As there was a major northern campaign,
Kǎn was subsequently appointed Bearer of Credentials (Chíjíe) and General Establishing Martial Prowess (Guānjūn),
and oversaw the construction of the Hánshān Weir (Hánshān Yàn).
The weir was completed within twenty days.
Kǎn advised the commander-in-chief, the Marquis of Zhēnyáng (Zhēnyáng Hóu), to use the high water to attack Péngchéng,
but the advice was not accepted.
Soon after, major Wèi reinforcements arrived.
Kǎn repeatedly advised taking advantage of their long journey to strike them,
and the following morning, he again urged engaging in battle,
but neither suggestion was followed.
Kǎn then led his troops out to garrison the top of the weir.
When the main forces were defeated,
Kǎn formed ranks and retreated slowly.
In the second year,
he again became Minister of the Bureau of Population (Dūguān Shàngshū).
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled
and captured Lìyáng,
Gāozǔ asked Kǎn for a strategy to defeat Jǐng.
Kǎn replied:
“Jǐng's rebellious nature has been evident for a long time;
he might rush forward recklessly.
We should urgently occupy Cǎishí,
and order the Prince of Shàolíng (Shàolíng Wáng) to attack and seize Shòuchūn.
If Jǐng cannot advance,
and loses his base of operations if he retreats,
his ragtag troops
will naturally collapse.”
The debaters insisted that Jǐng would not dare to immediately approach the capital,
and so Kǎn’s plan was shelved.
Instead, Kǎn was ordered to lead over a thousand cavalry to garrison Wàng Guómén.
When Jǐng reached Xīnlín,
Kǎn was recalled to assist the Prince of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Wáng) as Area Commander-in-Chief of all forces within the city (Dūcū Chéngnèi Zhū Jūnshì).
Since Jǐng had arrived suddenly,
the common people rushed into the city,
causing chaos in both public and private affairs,
and all order was lost.
Kǎn then categorized and distributed the defensive duties,
using members of the imperial clan to coordinate them all.
The soldiers competed to enter the armories
and seized weapons and armor for themselves.
The officials in charge could not prohibit them.
Kǎn ordered several people executed,
and only then was the disorder stopped.
When the rebels pressed close to the city,
everyone was fearful and anxious.
Kǎn falsely claimed to have received an arrow-letter,
stating
“The Prince of Shàolíng (Shàolíng Wáng) and the Marquis of Xīchāng (Xīchāng Hóu) have already reached nearby roads.”
The multitude then felt slightly reassured.
The rebels attacked the Dōngyè Gate (Dōngyè Mén),
and the fires they set were very intense.
Kǎn personally resisted and counteracted them,
dousing the flames with water.
The fire was extinguished.
He drew his bow and shot and killed several men,
and the rebels then retreated.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and General of the Army Staff (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn).
There was an imperial decree sending five thousand *liǎng* of gold,
ten thousand *liǎng* of silver,
and ten thousand bolts of silk,
to be bestowed upon the fighting men.
Kǎn declined the gift.
However, he privately awarded and rewarded
his own subordinates, numbering over a thousand men.
The bandits used pointed-roof wooden asses (siege engines) to attack the city.
Arrows and stones could not stop them.
Kǎn made "pheasant-tail torches" (zhìwěijù),
attached iron arrowheads to them,
poured oil onto them,
threw them onto the asses, and burned them.
Soon they were all consumed.
The bandits then raised earthen hills on both the east and west sides,
intending to overlook the city.
The people in the city were terrified.
Kǎn ordered underground tunnels to be dug,
secretly drawing away the soil,
so the hills could not stand erect.
The bandits next built siege towers for scaling the walls (dēngchénglóuchē),
more than ten zhàng high,
intending to shoot down into the city.
Kǎn said:
"The towers are high but structurally weak.
When they move forward, they are bound to collapse.
We can lie down and watch them;
there is no need to prepare defenses."
When the towers were moved, they indeed collapsed,
and everyone submitted (to his judgment).
Since the bandits had frequently attacked without success,
they built a long siege embankment (chángwéi).
Zhū Yì and Zhāng Wǎn discussed launching an attack against it.
Gāozǔ asked Kǎn about this.
Kǎn said:
"It cannot be done.
The bandits have attacked the city for many days,
and since they could not take it,
they built the long embankment,
merely wishing to lure those in the city who might surrender.
If we attack now,
if the force sent out is too small,
it will not be enough to defeat the bandits;
if it is large,
then if we suffer a sudden defeat,
they will trample each other in a rush.
The gate is narrow and the bridge is small,
which will certainly lead to a great disaster and defeat.
This would be showing weakness,
not demonstrating royal might."
(Gāozǔ) did not follow (this advice),
and subsequently sent more than a thousand men out to fight.
Before they could engage,
they fled merely at the sight of the enemy.
Indeed, they rushed into the water while fighting for the bridge,
and more than half of them died.
Previously,
Kǎn's eldest son, Zhuó, was captured by Jǐng (Hóu Jǐng),
and brought and held below the city walls to be shown to Kǎn.
Kǎn said to him (Jǐng’s messenger):
"I have risked my entire family to repay the sovereign's kindness,
and still regret that it is not enough.
How could I consider the fate of this single son?
I hope you will quickly kill him."
A few days later, (Zhuó) was brought again.
Kǎn said to Zhuó:
"I long presumed you were dead.
Are you still alive?
I have dedicated myself to the state,
swearing to die on the battlefield.
I will never allow my actions to be swayed by you."
Thereupon, he drew his bow and shot at him.
The bandits, moved by his loyalty and righteousness,
did not harm him either.
Jǐng sent the Yítóng, Fù Shìzhé, to call Kǎn out and speak, saying:
"The Prince (Hóu Wáng) has traveled far to inquire about the Son of Heaven.
Why do you remain closed off and resistant,
failing to admit him promptly?
You, Shàngshū, are a high official of the state;
you should open the matter to the imperial court."
Kǎn replied:
"After General Hóu fled (from the North),
he dedicated himself to our state.
He was entrusted with the crucial post of Fāngchéng,
where enormous responsibility was placed upon him.
What troubles or distress did he face
that suddenly caused him to raise troops?
Now he drives a rabble of soldiers,
reaching the walls of the Royal City,
allowing bandit horses to drink from the Huái (River),
and arrows to fall upon the Imperial Palace.
Is there any subject of the Emperor who would go this far?
I am deeply indebted to the state's great kindness,
and it is my duty to receive and execute the court's strategies
solely for sweeping away this great rebellion.
I cannot carelessly accept flimsy arguments,
and open the gates to welcome a thief.
Please express my regrets to the Prince,
and advise him to determine his own fate quickly."
Fù Shìzhé further said:
"The Prince served his lord with utmost loyalty,
but his efforts were not recognized by the court.
He merely wishes to report directly to the Supreme One (the Emperor) in person,
so as to eliminate the treacherous sycophants.
Since he is currently engaged in military matters,
he has come to court wearing armor.
How can this be called rebellion?"
Kǎn said:
"His Sacred Majesty has reigned over the Four Seas for nearly fifty years.
He is brilliant, wise, and discerning,
illuminating everything, however hidden.
What treacherous sycophant could possibly be present in the court?
If one seeks to disguise one's wrongdoing,
one will naturally resort to deceitful words.
Moreover, the Prince personally raises sharp blades
and directs them toward the imperial palace.
Is this how one serves his lord with utmost loyalty,
exactly like this?"
Fù Shìzhé had no response.
He then said:
"During my time in the North,
I have long admired your manner and virtue.
I have always regretted that throughout my life,
I have not been able to meet you face-to-face.
I wish to take off my military uniform
and have a proper audience with you."
Kǎn removed his helmet for him.
Fù Shìzhé gazed at him for a long time before leaving.
His reverence and admiration by the people of the North was thus demonstrated.
Later, due to heavy rain,
the earthen hills inside the city collapsed.
The bandits took advantage of this and were about to enter.
Fierce fighting could not hold them back.
Kǎn then ordered many fires to be thrown,
creating a "fire wall" to cut off their path.
He then slowly built a wall near the [yǐng],
and the bandits could not advance.
In the twelfth month,
he contracted a sickness and died within the Imperial Palace (Tái),
aged fifty-four.
An imperial decree granted him the funeral furnishings of the Eastern Park (Dōngyuán Mìqì),
five hundred bolts each of cloth and silk,
and three million cash.
He was posthumously appointed Shìzhōng and Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
and granted a set of military music (gǔchuī).
Kǎn was heroic and brave from a young age;
his physical strength surpassed that of ordinary men.
The bow he used required more than ten shí of drawing weight.
He once stepped up a wall at the Yáo Miào Temple in Yǎnzhōu,
climbing straight up five xún (measures of height),
and moving sideways for seven steps (jì).
At Sì Qiáo Bridge there were several stone statues,
eight chǐ tall,
and ten arm-spans in circumference.
Kǎn grabbed them and struck them against each other,
shattering them all completely.
Kǎn's nature [Xìng] was extravagant,
and he was skilled in music [yīnlǜ].
He personally composed the two melodies Cǎilián and Zhuògē,
which had a great, fresh appeal.
His concubines and maids stood arrayed,
indulging in the utmost luxury and decadence.
He had a zither player named Lù Tàixǐ,
who wore antler horn finger picks seven inches long.
Another woman, Zhāng Jìngwǎn,
had a waist circumference of one chi and six cun.
People at the time all praised her ability to dance "in the palm."
Furthermore, there was Sūn Jīngyù,
who could bend her back until it touched the ground,
and retrieve a jade hairpin from the mat with her mouth.
The imperial court bestowed upon him the singer Wáng É'ér,
and the Eastern Palace also gifted the singer Qū Ǒuzhī;
both were skilled in all manner of marvelous melodies,
unmatched in their generation.
When he first proceeded to Héngzhōu,
he constructed a three-room, beam-connected floating studio [shuǐzhāi] built upon two boats [chā],
adorned with pearls and jade,
and decorated with embroidered silks.
He elaborately set up curtains and screens,
displayed female musicians,
cast off the moorings with the tide,
and set out wine overlooking the waves.
Along the banks and beside the water,
observers choked the path.
During the Dàtóng era,
the Wèi envoy Yáng Fěi,
who had previously studied with Kǎn in the North,
received an imperial decree ordering Kǎn to invite Fěi to a banquet.
There were more than three hundred guests,
and the vessels were all made of gold, jade, and assorted treasures.
Three orchestras of female musicians performed.
By evening,
more than a hundred serving maids
all held golden floral candles.
Kǎn could not drink alcohol,
yet he enjoyed entertaining guests and socializing.
He spent the entire day offering and returning toasts,
sharing their drunkenness and sobriety.
His nature was generous and tolerant,
and he possessed great capacity [qìjú].
Once, while returning south and reaching Liánkǒu,
he hosted a banquet.
A guest named Zhāng Rúcái
got drunk on a boat, causing a fire,
which spread and burned more than seventy vessels.
The amount of gold and silk consumed by the fire was countless.
When Kǎn heard of this,
he paid no attention whatsoever,
and ordered the wine service not to cease.
Rúcái was ashamed and terrified,
and hid himself away.
Kǎn reassured and comforted him, arranging for his return,
and treated him as before.
His third son was Kūn.
Kūn's courtesy name [zì] was Zǐpéng.
He followed Kǎn inside the capital [Táinèi].
When the city fell,
he fled to Yángpíng.
Hóu Jǐng summoned him back
and treated him extremely well.
When Jǐng was defeated,
Kūn secretly planned [to act against him],
and followed him as he fled eastward.
Jǐng was defeated in battle at Sōngjiāng,
leaving only three small boats.
He sailed out to sea, intending to go toward Méngshān.
It happened that Jǐng was tired and sleeping during the day.
Kūn said to the sea pilot:
"Where is there a Méngshān here?
You must only listen to my orders."
They then headed straight for Jīngkǒu.
When they reached Húdòuzhōu,
Jǐng woke up,
and was greatly alarmed.
He asked someone on the shore,
who said
that "Guō Yuánjiàn is still in Guǎnglíng."
Jǐng was overjoyed,
and planned to seek refuge with him.
Kūn drew his sword and shouted at the sea pilot,
forcing him to head toward Jīngkǒu.
Jǐng attempted to jump into the water.
Kūn drew his knife and struck him.
Jǐng then ran into the boat,
and tried to cut a hole in the vessel with a small knife.
Kūn stabbed and killed him with a spear [shuò].
Emperor Shìzǔ appointed Kūn as Chíjié, Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, Commander-in-Chief [Dūdū] of military affairs in Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu, Míngwēi Jiāngjūn, and Governor [Cìshǐ] of Qīngzhōu.
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chāngguó County,
with an estate of two thousand households.
He was granted five million cash,
five thousand shí of rice,
and one thousand bolts each of linen and silk.
He also held the post of Administrator [Tàishǒu] of Dōngyáng.
When campaigning against Lù Nà,
he was promoted to Sànqí Chángshì.
After pacifying Xiázhōng,
he was appointed Governor of Xījìnzhōu.
After defeating Guō Yuánjiàn at Dōngguān,
he was promoted to Envoy with Credentials [Shǐ Chíjié], Xìnwǔ Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Dōngjìnzhōu.
In the third year of Chéngshèng (554 CE),
when Western Wèi besieged Jiānglíng,
Kūn rushed to reinforce it but did not arrive in time.
He followed Wáng Sēngyīn to campaign against Xiāo Bó in Lǐngbiǎo.
Hearing that Grand Commandant [Tàiwèi] Sēngbiàn was defeated,
he returned,
but was routed by Hóu Tián.
He was killed at Yùzhāng,
at the age of twenty-eight.
Yáng Yārén, courtesy name Xiàomù,
was a native of Jùpíng in Tàishān.
In his youth, he was swift, brave, and courageous,
and served the commandery as Chief Clerk [Zhǔbù].
During the Pǔtōng era,
he led his brothers in returning to the state from Wèi,
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Guǎngjìn County.
During campaigns in the area between Qīngzhōu and Qízhōu,
he accumulated merit,
and was gradually promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì and Administrator of Lìyáng.
In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (532 CE),
he was appointed Chíjié, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in Qiáozhōu, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Qiáozhōu.
In the seventh year of Dàtóng (541 CE),
he was appointed Commandant of the Left Guard of the Crown Prince [Tàizǐ Zuǒwèilǜ].
He was then sent out as Chíjié, Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the four provinces of Nán Sìzhōu, Běi Sìzhōu, Yùzhōu, and Chǔzhōu, Qīngchē Jiāngjūn, and Governor of Běisìzhōu.
When Hóu Jǐng surrendered,
an imperial edict commanded Yārén to oversee Huán Hézhī, the Governor of Tǔzhōu,
Zhàn Hǎizhēn, the Governor of Rénzhōu, and thirty thousand elite troops,
to hasten to Xuánhù to receive Jǐng.
He was subsequently made Commander-in-Chief of military affairs in the seven provinces of Yùzhōu, Sìzhōu, Huáizhōu, Jìzhōu, Yīnzhōu, Yìngzhōu, and Xīyùzhōu, and Governor of Sìzhōu and Yùzhōu,
garrisoned at Xuánhù.
As Hóu Jǐng was defeated at Wōyáng,
and the Wèi forces gradually approached,
Yārén feared that food supplies would run short.
He therefore returned to Běisì,
and submitted a memorial offering an apology.
Gāozǔ was greatly angered
and reprimanded him.
Yārén was afraid,
and subsequently stationed his troops on the Huái River.
When Hóu Jǐng revolted,
Yārén led his subordinates to enter and provide aid.
In the second year of Tàiqīng (548 CE),
since Jǐng had already broken the alliance,
Yārén, along with Zhào Bóchāo and the Prince of Nánkāng, Huìlǐ, jointly attacked the rebels at Dōngfǔchéng.
Instead, they were defeated by the rebels.
When Táichéng fell,
Yārén met Jǐng,
and was detained by Jǐng,
who made him Minister of the Five Departments [Wǔbīng Shàngshū].
Yārén constantly contemplated rising up.
He said to his confidants:
"I am but a common person,
yet I received favor from the imperial court.
Ultimately, I could not repay this service
in return for such profound grace.
The state is in peril,
and I could not die for it.
I have clung to life and managed to avoid death,
until this day.
If I should end my life like this,
my resentment would never cease."
Following this, he wept,
and those who saw it were saddened.
In the third year [of Tàiqīng, 549 CE],
he fled to Jiāngxī.
Several hundred of his former subordinates welcomed him.
As he prepared to head to Jiānglíng,
upon reaching Dōngguǎn,
he was killed by the sons of Xún Bódào, the former Governor of Běixúzhōu.
The Official Historian [Shǐ Chén] comments: Gāozǔ overthrew the regime and received the Mandate,
initiating a brilliant and precious fortune.
Wherever his majesty and virtue spread,
there were none who did not embrace him and come forward.
All sacrificed their lives and devoted themselves to hardship,
following one another in succession.
When those like Yuán Fǎsēng entered the state,
grace and favor were bestowed upon them all.
Their positions were important and their responsibilities vast,
dining with bells ringing and tripods set forth—
how fine this was!
However, Yáng Kǎn and Yārén faced the disaster of Tàiqīng,
and both exhausted their loyalty in serving the state.
Kǎn did not yield when facing danger,
and Yārén upheld righteousness until his death.
They may be called men whose wills were like pine and bamboo,
and whose hearts were hard as iron and stone.
The martyrs of old—
surely this refers to them!
Collective Biographies Thirty-Four: Sīmǎ Jiǒng, Dào Gài, Liú Xiǎn, Liú Zhīlín (Younger Brother Zhīhēng), Xǔ Mào.
Sīmǎ Jiǒng, courtesy name Yuánsù,
was a native of Wēn, Hénèi.
His great-grandfather, Chúnzhī,
was the Grand Minister of Agriculture (*Dà Sī nóng*) and Prince Jìng of Gāomì during the Jìn dynasty.
His grandfather, Ràngzhī,
was a Supernumerary Attendant (*Yuánwài Chángshì*).
His father, Xiè,
was skilled in the Three Rites (*Sān Lǐ*).
He served in Qí, reaching the position of Academician of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐ Bóshì*).
Jiǒng inherited the family scholarship in his youth,
applied himself diligently and with specialized focus,
never letting a scroll leave his hand.
The books concerning ritual texts
he had generally read throughout.
Liú Huán of Pèiguó was considered the patriarch of the Confucians;
he praised Jiǒng's learning
and appreciated him greatly.
In his youth, he was close friends with Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān;
Fǎng also highly esteemed him.
He first served as a student of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐ Shēng*),
and began his career as a Gentleman of the Imperial Edict (*Fèng Cháoqǐng*).
He gradually moved up to Acting Staff Officer (*Xíng Cānjūn*) in a princely establishment.
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
an imperial decree ordered knowledgeable scholars to manage the Five Rites (*Wǔ Lǐ*).
The relevant authorities recommended Jiǒng to handle the Auspicious Rites (*Jiā Lǐ*).
He was appointed Libation Assistant (*Cíbù Lángzhōng*) in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū*).
At this time, ritual and music were being newly established.
Many of Jiǒng's proposals were implemented.
He was appointed Commandant of Infantry (*Bùbīng Xiàowèi*),
concurrently serving as Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén*).
Jiǒng's learning was particularly proficient in ceremonial matters (divination and calculation).
Regarding the auspicious and inauspicious rites of the state,
famous contemporary scholars like Míng Shānbīn and Hè Yáng, when doubtful and unable to determine a conclusion,
all sought his final decision.
He was successively promoted to Regular Gentleman (*Zhèngyuán Láng*) and Advisory Staff Officer (*Zīyì Cānjūn*) to the General Who Guards the South (*Zhènnán*),
retaining his concurrent post as Attendant Gentleman (*Shèrén*).
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Right of the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Yòuchéng*).
He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk (*Zhǎngshǐ*) to the General of Grand Awe (*Rénwēi*) and Administrator of Chángshā (*Chángshā Nèishǐ*).
Returning, he was appointed General of the Cloud Cavalry (*Yúnqí Jiāngjūn*),
concurrently serving as Vice President of the Censorate (*Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng*).
Shortly thereafter, he was formally appointed to the latter post.
In the sixteenth year (of Tiānjiān),

he was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Nánkāng (*Nánkāng Wáng*), General Who Proclaims Awe (*Xuānyì*), concurrently managing military affairs of the princely establishment, the commandery, and the Shítou Garrison (*Shítou Shù*).
Although Jiǒng held an external position,
he received an imperial order allowing him to register his name and receive inquiries at the Wéndé Hall and Wǔdé Hall
without restriction on the day.
In the seventeenth year,
he was promoted to Chief Clerk to the Prince of Jìn'ān (*Jìn'ān Wáng*), General Who Manifests Awe (*Míngwēi*).
He died shortly thereafter.
The Prince ordered the Recorder (*Jìshì*), Yǔ Jiānwú, to compile his writings into ten scrolls.
He also compiled one hundred and twelve scrolls of notes on the rites and protocols of the Auspicious Rites (*Jiā Lǐ Yízhù*).
Dào Gài, courtesy name Mòuguàn,
was a native of Wǔyuán, Péngchéng.
His great-grandfather, Yànzhī,
was General of the Cavalry (*Piàojì Jiāngjūn*) during the Sòng dynasty.
His grandfather, Zhòngdù,
was Aide-de-Camp (*Cóngshì Zhōngláng*) to the Prince of Jiāngxià, General of the Cavalry.
His father, Tǎn,
was Secretariat Director (*Zhōngshū Láng*) during the Qí dynasty.
Gài was orphaned and poor in his youth.
He and his younger brother, Qià, were both intelligent, astute, talented, and scholarly.
They were recognized early by Rèn Fǎng,
and consequently their reputation grew.
He began his career as Left Attendant (*Zuǒ Chángshì*) in a princely state,
and transferred to Acting Staff Officer (*Xíng Cānjūn*) in the Judicial Section of the Rear Army (*Hòujūn Fǎcáo*).
He successively held the post of Gentleman of the Palace (*Diànzhōng Láng*).
He was sent out to be Administrator of Jiàn'ān (*Jiàn'ān Nèishǐ*).
He was promoted to Secretariat Director (*Zhōngshū Láng*),
concurrently serving in the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*),
and then Chief of the Household to the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ*).
When Yì, the Prince of Xiāngdōng (*Xiāngdōng Wáng*), became Grand Administrator of Kuàijī (*Kuàijī Tàishǒu*),
he made Gài Chief Clerk (*Zhǎngshǐ*) to the General of Light Chariots (*Qīngchē*), concurrently managing the affairs of the princely establishment and the commandery.
Emperor Gāozǔ instructed the Prince, saying:
"Dào Gài is not merely carrying out tasks for you;
he is sufficient to be your teacher.
Whenever there is a decision regarding action or inaction,
you must always consult him."
He suffered the grief of his mother's death.
He observed the mourning rites completely.
The court commended him.
Even after the mourning period concluded,
he continued to eat vegetarian food and wear coarse cloth for several years.
He was appointed Attendant-in-Ordinary (*Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì*),
Vice President of the Censorate (*Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng*),
Minister of the Grand Treasury (*Tàifǔ Qīng*),
Minister of the Census (*Dūguān Shàngshū*),
Chief Clerk of Yǐngzhōu and Grand Administrator of Jiāngxià (*Jiāngxià Tàishǒu*),
and was given the title General Who Summons the Distant (*Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn*).
He returned to the capital to serve as Minister of the Left Populace (*Zuǒmín Shàngshū*).
Gài was eight *chǐ* tall.
He possessed a beautiful demeanor
and was skilled in refined deportment.
In the offices he governed, he maintained purity and integrity.
His nature was also simple and frugal.
He did not indulge in music or women.
His chambers were empty and plain;
he kept no concubines or maidservants nearby.
Regarding his external attire and carriages,
he did not pursue splendor or luxury.
His caps and shoes were changed only once every ten years.
His court robes were sometimes worn and patched.
He announced his approach and cleared the road
merely to observe the formalities of court regulations.
A while later,
due to an incident, he was demoted to Grand Master of the Palace with Gold and Purple (*Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū*).
Soon after, he was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (*Sànqí Chángshì*), Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*), and Libationer of the Directorate of Education (*Guózǐ Jìjiǔ*).
Gài was always cautious and sincere,
and was especially favored and received by Emperor Gāozǔ.
Whenever they met,
their conversation would last from dusk until dawn.
In the rock garden and pond at Gài's residence, there was a strange rock.
Emperor Gāozǔ jokingly bet him for it,
along with a copy of the *Lǐjì* (Record of Rites).
Gài lost both items.
Before presenting them,
Emperor Gāozǔ said to Zhū Yì:
"Do you think Dào Gài's forfeits can be sent yet?"
Gài, gathering his court tablet, replied:
"Since I am a subject serving the ruler,
how dare I commit a breach of etiquette?"
Emperor Gāozǔ laughed heartily.
His intimacy and affection for him were like this.
Later, he lost his sight due to illness.
An imperial decree granted him the titles of Grand Master of the Palace with Gold and Purple and Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary,
allowing him to retire to his residence to recover.
Gài's family was harmonious and peaceful,
and the brothers were especially affectionate toward each other.
Originally, he and his younger brother Qià always shared a study room.
After Qià's death,
he converted that study into a Buddhist temple.
Consequently, he stopped eating meat and fish,
eating only vegetarian food for the rest of his life.
He built a small room separately
where he performed rites and chanted scriptures with monks morning and evening.
Emperor Gāozǔ sent him purified vegetarian food three times a month,
showing extremely generous favor.
There was a Yánxián Temple (*Yánxián Sì*) on Jiǎngshān,
which had been founded by Gài's family across generations.
Therefore, the official salary he received during his life
was all used to supply it;
he took virtually nothing for himself.
He was also by nature not fond of socializing.
He was only close friends with Zhū Yì, Liú Zhīlìn, and Zhāng Wǎn, who shared his aspirations.
When he was confined by sickness to his home garden,
his gate was quiet enough to trap sparrows (i.e., few visitors came).
However, these three gentlemen (*Sān Jūn*) always announced their approach and made a detour during festivals and holidays
to visit and inquire after him.
They would set out wine, reminisce about their lives,
enjoy themselves thoroughly, and then depart.
Just before he died,
he entrusted Zhāng (Wǎn) and Liú (Zhīlìn) to instruct his descendants regarding simple funeral rites.
He died at the age of seventy-two.
An imperial decree posthumously restored him to his former office.
A collection of his writings in twenty scrolls circulated in the world.
Contemporaries compared the brothers Gài and Qià to the Two Lù (Lù Jī and Lù Yún).
Therefore, Emperor Shìzǔ presented a poem saying:
"The age of Wèi prized the Double Dīng (Dīng Yí and Dīng Yì),
The Jìn court hailed the Two Lù,
But how can they compare to the Two Dào of today,
Who resemble the bamboo braving the cold?"
His son, Jìng,
courtesy name Yuánzhào,
was Acting Staff Officer of the Legal Section (*Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn*) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West (*Ānxī*).
He was an Attendant Gentleman to the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Shèrén*),
and died young.
Jìng's son, Jìn,
was clever and insightful from an early age.
He began his career as Assistant Editor (*Zhùzuò Zuǒláng*).
He successively held the posts of Attendant Gentleman to the Heir Apparent,
Clerk (*Zhǔbù*) to the Prince of Xuānchéng (*Xuānchéng Wáng*),
Equerry to the Heir Apparent (*Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ*),
and Gentleman of the Palace in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng*).
He once accompanied Emperor Gāozǔ on a visit to Jīngkǒu.
Upon ascending the Běigù Tower, the Emperor ordered poems to be composed.
Jìn immediately completed his poem upon receiving the command.
The Emperor read it and showed it to Gài, saying:
"Jìn is definitely a talented young man.
I suspect that perhaps your writings heretofore were actually done by Jìn."
He then bestowed upon Gài a set of linked verses (*Liánzhū*), saying:
"Grind the ink to give wings to your composition;
The brush tip flies to write the correspondence.
As a flying moth rushes toward the fire,
how can it begrudge the burning of its body?
If old age has already arrived,
you may entrust the task to the young Jìn."
His recognition and appreciation for him were thus.
He was appointed Assistant to the Governor of Dānyáng (*Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng*).
During the chaos of the Tàiqīng era,
he went to Jiānglíng and died there.
Liú Xiǎn, courtesy name Sìfāng,
was a native of Xiāng, Pèiguó.
His father, Zōng,
was Administrator of Jìn'ān (*Jìn'ān Nèishǐ*).
Xiǎn was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth,
and was known as a child prodigy by his contemporaries.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was recommended as a Xiùcái.
He was appointed as the Aide to the Commander of the Central Army, Prince Línchuān, upon shedding his civilian clothes.
Shortly after, he was appointed as the Fa Cáo.
Xiǎn loved learning
and was broadly knowledgeable and well-versed.
Rèn Fǎng once obtained a damaged scroll with missing sections,
on which the characters were fragmented.
He showed it to various people,
but none could identify it.
Xiǎn said it was a lost chapter deleted from the ancient Shàngshū.
Fǎng checked the Zhōu Shū,
and it was indeed as he had said.
Fǎng greatly admired and marvelled at him.
When he was in mourning for his mother,
after the period of mourning ended,
Shàngshū Lìng Shěn Yuē ordered his carriage to visit him.
At the meeting, he quizzed Xiǎn on ten topics from the Classics and Histories,
and Xiǎn answered nine of them.
Yuē said:
"This old man is dim-witted and forgetful,
and cannot be questioned;
nevertheless,
I will try a few things,
but not all ten."
Xiǎn asked him five questions,
and Yuē answered two.
Lù Chuí heard of this and sighed, saying:
"Master Liú can be called an extraordinary person.
Even if Píngyuán of our family visited Zhāng Zhuàngwǔ,
or Wáng Càn met Bójiē,
they would certainly not have such an exchange."
Such was the praise and admiration he received from eminent figures.
When Yuē became the Taìzǐ Shǎofù,
he appointed him as Wǔguān Yuàn,
and shortly after, he concurrently served as Tíngwèi Zhèng.
Wǔbīng Shàngshū Fù Zhāo, who was in charge of literary works,
was compiling the national history
and appointed Xiǎn as his assistant.
In the ninth year,
the Wǔ Dū Xuǎn system of the Shàngshū was reformed for the first time.
Xiǎn concurrently served as Lìbù Láng in his original post.
He was also appointed as the Waìbīng Cānjūn for Sīkōng, Prince Línchuān,
and later promoted to Shàngshū Yícáo Láng.
He once composed a poem for the imperial court.
Shěn Yuē saw it and praised its beauty.
At that time, Yuē's suburban residence had just been completed,
so he commissioned a calligrapher to inscribe it on the wall.
He was dispatched as Jìshì Cānjūn for Prince Línchuān.
After the pacification of Jiànkāng,
he re-entered service as Shàngshū Yícáo Shìláng,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was dispatched as the Magistrate of Mòlíng,
and then appointed Jìshì for Piàojì, Prince Póyáng,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was successively promoted to Bùbīng Xiàowèi and Zhōngshū Shìláng,
with his Shèrén position remaining unchanged.
Xiǎn, along with Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng, Liú Zhīlín of Nányáng, and Gù Xié of Wújùn,
held positions together within the forbidden palace.
They taught and befriended each other,
and contemporary people all admired them.
Xiǎn was broadly learned and had a strong memory,
surpassing Péi and Gù.
At that time, Wei people presented ancient artifacts
with embossed characters,
which no one could identify.
Xiǎn examined the text and read it
without any difficulty or hesitation.
He verified the year and month,
and not a single character was wrong.
Gāozǔ greatly commended him.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒchéng
and appointed Guózǐ Bóshì.
He was dispatched as Zhǎngshǐ for Xuānyuǎn, Prince Yuèyáng,
managing the affairs of the prefecture and state.
Before he took up the post,
he was promoted to Zhǎngshǐ of Yúnhuī, Prince Shàolíng, and Prefect of Xúnyáng.
In the ninth year of Dàtóng,
the Prince moved his garrison to Yǐngzhōu,
and he was appointed Píngxī Zīyì Cānjūn,
and granted the title Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn.
He died that year
at the age of sixty-three.
His friend Liú Zhīlín petitioned the Crown Prince, saying:
"Zhīlín has heard
that if Yí and Shú, and Liǔ Huì,
had not encountered one word from Zhòngní,
then the starving man of Xīshān,
and the dismissed scholar of Dōngguó,
how could their names have spread to later generations?
Indeed!
One born with a seven-foot stature
eventually becomes earth for a single coffin.
The matter of immortality
is entrusted to epitaphs.
One who possesses pearls and embraces jade,
yet whose name is not proclaimed until death,
is truly worthy of a long sigh,
and who surpasses this?
I secretly grieve for my friend Liú Xiǎn of Pèiguó,
who treasured literary arts,
diligently researched profound subjects,
was exceptionally intelligent,
and stood out from the crowd.
Having died in Yǐngdū,
his soul returns to the capital.
The day for selecting his tomb site is set,
and a tombstone must be carved.
Zhīlín has already briefly compiled his deeds and actions,
and now humbly presents them.
I earnestly wish for Your Benevolent Grace
to bestow your sagely prose,
to bring glory to his dry bones,
and comfort his departed soul.
Presumptuously bringing this to your esteemed ears,
I tremble beyond measure."
The Crown Prince then granted a memorial inscription which read:
"Fánruò drew forth its essence,
Kōngsāng gave forth its sound.
Their distinct qualities were prized,
their music and renown spread.
Who could compare to him?
A handsome and eminent scholar.
His rites were established in youth,
his achievements shone in maturity.
He fully absorbed the classics and histories,
diligently studied profound principles.
He never forgot what he saw once,
remembering it after a single glance.
Like consulting Jiǎ Kuí,
or asking Bóshǐ.
His talent emerged like an awl through a sack,
his learning complete, he entered officialdom.
Having assisted in judging cases,
he then grasped the fragrant orchid.
He struggled in the Phoenix Pond,
he gave way to others at the Imperial Academy.
He participated in inner court affairs,
and assisted regional lords externally.
The slanting light has already departed,
it sinks into the western flow;
all rivers reach the sea,
then return to follow the eastern current.
The bustling soul returns,
the drifting boat is empty.
White horses face the suburbs,
red streamers turn away from Gǒng.
Dust of the wilds rises and falls,
mountain clouds are light and heavy.
Lǚ covers the book mound,
Yáng returns to the dark tomb.
Heed their example,
the road ends at the earthen mound.
Tender vines are just spreading,
clustered branches daily entwine.
Willows sprout in spring,
birds shiver and gather their down.
The vast sky is always dark,
a cold spring uniquely bubbles forth.
He is buried beside his old tomb,
his fragrance endures and follows. "
Xiǎn had three sons: Yǒu,
Chí,
Zhēn.
Zhēn became famous early.
Liú Zhīlín, courtesy name Sīzhēn,
was a native of Nièyáng, Nányáng.
His father, Qiú,
was the Guózǐ Bóshì of Qí,
posthumously honored as Wénfàn Xiānshēng.
at eight years old was able to compose essays.
At fifteen, he was selected as Mào cái and presented a policy essay.
Shěn Yuē and Rèn Fǎng saw him and considered him extraordinary.
He started his career as Níngshuò Zhǔbù.
Wáng Zhān, the Lìbù Shàngshū, once visited Rèn Fǎng.
He happened upon Zhīlìn sitting there.
Fǎng said to Zhān:
"This is Liú Zhīlìn of Nányáng,
whose scholarship is excellent but has not yet taken office.
He is one whom the Shuǐjìng should select and promote."
Zhān immediately appointed him Tàixué Bóshì.
At that time, Zhāng Jì had just been appointed Shàngshū Púyè.
He entrusted Fǎng to write a memorial declining the post.
Fǎng ordered Zhīlìn to write it on his behalf.
He took up the brush and finished it immediately.
Fǎng said:
"The fine spirit of Jīngnán
truly possesses extraordinary talent.
His future career will certainly surpass mine."
Yuè Ǎi, the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
who was Zhīlìn's maternal uncle,
submitted impeaching memorials to the Xiàntái,
which were all drafted by Zhīlìn.
He was promoted to Píngnán Xíng Cānjūn,
Shàngshū Qǐbù Láng,
Yánlíng Lìng,
and Jīngzhōu Zhìzhōng.
When Tàizōng governed Jīngzhōu,
Zhīlìn was subsequently promoted to Xuānhuì Jìshì.
Zhīlìn was devoted to study, clear, and judicious.
He extensively read various texts.
At the time, Liú Xiǎn and Wéi Léng both had strong memories.
Whenever Zhīlìn discussed matters with them,
they were all unable to surpass him.
He returned and was appointed Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Shìláng,
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was promoted to Zhèngyuán Láng,
Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
and Jīngzhōu Dàzhōngzhèng.
He was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng,
Hónglú Qīng,
and again concurrently served as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was sent out to serve as Zhēngxī Póyáng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ and Nánjùn Tàishǒu.
Gāozǔ said to him:
"Your mother is advanced in years and virtue.
Therefore, I ordered you to return to your hometown dressed in silk brocade,
to fulfill the duties of honoring and supporting her."
Later, he was transferred to serve as Xīzhōngláng Xiāngdōng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ,
retaining the position of Tàishǒu.
Earlier,
when Zhīlìn was in the Jīng Commandery office,
he once temporarily resided in the Nánjùn administrative office.
He suddenly dreamt that the former Tàishǒu, Yuán Tuàn, said to him:
"You will later become the Tàishǒu with the broken arm,
and reside right here."
Zhīlìn later indeed injured his arm,
and consequently governed this commandery.
He mourned his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he was summoned to be Mìshū Jiān,
also supervising Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
He was sent out to manage affairs in Yǐngzhōu.
Zhīlìn was internally unwilling to go out,
and firmly declined.
Gāozǔ issued an imperial rescript written in his own hand, saying:
"I have heard that when one has a wife and children,
filial piety towards parents declines;
when one has high rank and salary,
loyalty towards the sovereign declines.
Since you are satisfied internally,
it is natural that you forget the principle of serving the public good."
Consequently, he was impeached and dismissed by the relevant officials.
After a long time,
he served as Tàifǔ Qīng,
Dūguān Shàngshū,
and Tàicháng Qīng.
Zhīlìn loved antiquity and cherished the unusual.
In Jīngzhōu, he collected dozens or hundreds of types of ancient vessels.
There was one vessel resembling a basin,
capable of holding one *hú*.
It had gold-inlaid characters on it.
No one at the time could recognize them.
He also presented four types of ancient vessels to the Dōnggōng.
The first type was
two carved bronze *chīyí* *kē*.
Both handles were silver-inlaid.
The inscription said:
"Made in the second year of Jiànpíng."
The second type was
two ancient *zūn* carved with gold and silver inlay.
It had a seal script inscription saying:
"Made in the year Qín Róngchéng Hóu traveled to Chǔ."
The third type was
one foreign bathing ewer.
The inscription said:
"In the second year of Yuánfēng,
presented by the kingdom of Qiūcí."
The fourth type was
one anciently manufactured bathing basin.
The inscription said:
"Made in the second year of Chūpíng."
At that time, the Heir King of Póyáng, Fàn, obtained the original version of the *Hàn Shū* that Bān Gù had presented.
He presented it to the Dōnggōng.
The Huáng Tàizǐ ordered Zhīlìn, along with Zhāng Zuǎn, Dào Gài, Lù Xiāng, and others, to compare and collate the differences.
Zhīlìn itemized ten differences in detail.
The summary stated:
"Examining the ancient *Hàn Shū* text, it states, 'On the *jǐyǒu* day, the twenty-first day of the fifth month of the sixteenth year of Yǒngpíng,
Láng Bān Gù presented it,'
but the modern text lacks the date characters for the memorial's submission.
Furthermore, examining the ancient text, the biographies are entitled 'Zhōngpiān,'
while the modern text calls them *zhuàn* (biographies).
Furthermore, the modern *zhuàn* records the deeds and conduct of Bān Biāo,
but the ancient text says, 'Zhì begot Biāo,
who has his own biography.'
Furthermore, the modern text's Basic Annals, Tables, Treatises, and Categorized Biographies are not arranged consecutively,
but the ancient text arranges them consecutively,
totaling thirty-eight scrolls.
Furthermore, in the modern text, the Imperial Affines section is after the Western Regions section.
In the ancient text, the Imperial Affines section follows immediately after the Imperial Annals.
Furthermore, in the modern text, the Gāo Five Sons, Wén Three Kings, Jǐng Thirteen Kings, Wǔ Five Sons, and Xuān-Yuán Six Kings are mixed in the order of the various biographies,
whereas in the ancient text, all the Princes follow the Imperial Affines section,
placed before the Biographies of Chén and Xiàng.
Furthermore, the modern text's account of Hán, Péng, Yīng, Lú, and Wú states, 'Xìn was merely a starving servant;
Bù was truly a branded convict;
Yuè was also a petty thief;
Ruì dwelt in the rivers and lakes.
They rose like clouds and vaulted like dragons,
transforming into Marquises and Kings.'
The ancient text's account states, 'Huáiyīn was resolute and determined;
bearing a sword, he traveled around.
The heroic sons of the state
were truly Péng and Yīng.
Transforming into Marquises and Kings,
they rose like clouds and vaulted like dragons.'
Furthermore, the ancient text has the thirty-seventh scroll,
which explains pronunciation and clarifies meaning,
to aid in correct interpretation,
but the modern text lacks this scroll."
Zhīlìn enjoyed composing essays.
He extensively studied the ancient style.
He often discussed books with Péi Zǐyě of Hédōng and Liú Xiǎn of Pèiguó,
thereby becoming friends.
At this time, the *Zhōu Yì*, *Shàng Shū*, *Lǐ Jì*, and *Máo Shī* all had the exegetical commentaries written by Gāozǔ.
Only the *Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn* was still incomplete.
Zhīlìn therefore wrote "Ten Sections on the General Meaning of the *Chūnqiū*,"
"Ten Sections on the *Zuǒ Shì*,"
and "Ten Sections on the Similarities and Differences among the Three Commentaries,"
totaling thirty items, and presented them.
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
He replied by imperial edict, saying:
"I have examined the *Chūnqiū* exegesis you compiled.
The discussion in this document
has subtle wording and profound intent.
In the teachings of the chronological history,
the language is clear but the underlying meaning is complex.
Qiū Míng transmitted the style of Zhūsì;
Gōngyáng received the scholarship of Xīhé.
Duó Jiāo's explanations are irrelevant;
Xiáqiū's theories have no merit.
Hú Mǔ followed in the footsteps,
and Zhòng Shū called it flourishing.
Gǔ Liáng followed the old ways,
and Qiān Qiū was the most sincere.
Zhāng Cāng transmitted the *Zuǒ Shì*,
and Jiǎ Yì adopted Xún Qīng's teachings.
The origins branched out,
and the objectives led to different results.
The detailed and the brief are confusedly mixed;
this has been the case for a long time.
Previously, in my youth,
I once studied and pondered these texts.
Since having set them aside,
nearly five *jǐ* have passed.
Moreover, the winter days are short,
and state affairs rarely give leisure.
I rise after midnight,
having no time to thoroughly investigate.
I must wait until the summer season,
and try to retrieve and study them.
If reviving the old allows me to seek out the answers,
I will respond separately to your questions."
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
when Hóu Jǐng caused a rebellion,
Zhīlìn fled the danger and returned to his hometown.
Before reaching it,
he died at Xiàkǒu,
at the age of seventy-two.
His collected writings, compiled before and after, totaled fifty scrolls,
and circulated in the world.

十四入太學，
受毛詩，

晚而覆講，
座下聽者常數十百人，
因撰風雅比興義十五卷，
盛行於世．
尤曉故事，
稱為儀注之學．
起家後軍豫章王行參軍，
轉法曹，

遷驃騎大將軍儀同中記室．
文惠太子聞而召之，
侍講于崇明殿，

永元中，
轉散騎侍郎，

與司馬 Jiǒng 同志友善，
僕射 Jiāng Shí 甚推重之，
號為
「經史笥」 ．
天監初，
吏部尚書 Fàn Yún 舉 Mào 參詳五禮，
除征西鄱陽王諮議，
兼著作郎，

時有請封會稽禪國山者，

Mào 以為不可，
因建議曰： 臣案舜幸岱宗，
是為巡狩，

考績柴燎，

刻石紀號」 ．
此緯書之曲說，
非正經之通義也．
依白虎通云，
「封者，
言附廣也；
禪者，
言
成功相傳也」 ．
若以禪授為義，
則禹不應傳啟至桀十七世也，
湯又不應傳外丙至紂三十
七世也．
又禮記云：
「三皇禪奕奕，
謂盛德也．
五帝禪亭亭，

三王禪
梁甫，

若謂
「禪奕奕為盛德者，
古義以 Fúxī、 Shénnóng、 Huángdì，
是
為三皇．
Fúxī 封泰山，
禪云云，
Huángdì 封泰山，
禪亭亭，
皆不禪奕奕，
而云盛德，
則無所寄
矣．
若謂五帝禪亭亭，

Zhuānxū 封泰山，
禪云云，
Dìkù 封泰山，
禪云云，
Yáo

Shùn 封泰山，
禪云云，
亦不禪亭亭，
若合 Huángdì 以為五帝者，
Shǎohào 即 Huángdì
子，
又非獨立之義矣．
若謂三王禪梁甫，
連延不絕，
父沒子繼者，
Yǔ 封泰山，
禪云云，
周成王封泰山，
禪社首，
舊書如此，
異乎禮說，
皆道聽所得，
失其本文．
假使三王皆封
泰山禪梁甫者，
是為封泰山則有傳世之義，
禪梁甫則有揖讓之懷，
或欲禪位，
或欲傳
子，
義既矛盾，
理必不然．
又七十二君，
Yíwú 所記，
此中世數，
裁可得二十餘主： Fúxī、 Shénnóng、 Nǚwā、 Dàtíng、 Bǎi
Huáng、 Zhōngyāng、 Lìlù、 Lílián、 Hèxū、 Zūnlú、 Hùndùn、 Hàoyīng、 Yǒucháo、 Zhūxiāng、 Gétiān、 Yīnkāng、 Wúhuái、 Huángdì、 Shǎo
Hào、 Zhuānxū、 Gāoxīn、 Yáo、 Shùn、 Yǔ、 Tāng、 Wén、 Wǔ，
中間乃有 Gònggōng，
霸有九州，
非帝之數，
云何得有七
十二君封禪之事？
且 Suìrén 以前至周之世，
未有君臣，
人心淳朴，
不應金泥玉檢，
升
中刻石．
Suìrén、 Fúxī、 Shénnóng 三皇結繩而治，
書契未作，
未應有鐫文告成．
且 Wúhuái 氏，
伏
Xī 後第十六主，
云何得在 Fúxī 前封泰山禪云云？
Yíwú 又曰
「惟受命之君然後得封禪． 」
周成王非受命君，
云何而得封泰山禪社首？
Shénnóng 與 Yándì 是一主，
而云 Shénnóng 封泰山禪云云，
Yándì 封泰山禪云云，
分為二人，
妄亦甚
矣．
若是聖主，
不須封禪；
若是凡主，
不應封禪．
當是齊桓欲行此事，
Guǎn Zhòng 知其不可，
故舉怪物以屈之也．
秦始皇登泰山，
中坂，
風雨暴至，
休松樹下，
封為五大夫，
而事不遂．
漢武帝宗信方
scholars.
He broadly summoned Confucian scholars.
Wearing pībiàn (leather caps) and inserting their ritual jade tablets into their belts (jìnshēn),
they sacrificed an ox and performed the rites.
[Huo] Shàn alone went up with him.
Afterwards, Zihóu died suddenly,
and his foot was injured by this incident.
Later, upon the reign of Wèi Míngdì,
he ordered Gāotáng Lóng to compile the ritual procedures.
Hearing of Lóng's death,
[Míngdì] sighed and said:
"Heaven does not wish for my undertaking to be completed;
Gāo Shēng has abandoned me and is gone."
During the Tàishǐ era of Jìn Wǔdì, he wished
to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices.
However, by the Tàikāng era, the debate was still unsettled,
and ultimately, he did not carry them out.
Sūn Hào sent the concurrent Sīkōng Dǒng Cháo and the concurrent Tàicháng Zhōu Chǔ to Yángxiàn to perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices on Guó
Shān.
What merit or virtue
do these gentlemen of the present court possess?
They do not reflect upon the ancient ways yet desire to perform Fēng and Shàn;
this is all because the sovereign delights in fame above,
and the ministers flatter the intent below.
Furthermore, the Fēng and Shàn ceremonies
do not originate from the orthodox canons.
Only the Zuǒ Zhuàn mentions
that "Yǔ assembled the feudal lords at Tú Shān,
and ten thousand states held jade and silk,"
but it does not call this Fēng
Shàn.
Zhèng Xuán had the style of Cān and Chái (ancient diviners),
unable to trace the orthodox canons,
and specialized in believing the books of the Wěi Hòu (apocryphal texts and prognostications).
This is erroneous.
The Lǐ Yún states:
"Serve Heaven according to the methods of Heaven;
serve Earth according to the methods of Earth;
ascend famous mountains to perform the Zhōng sacrifice to Heaven;
use auspicious soil to offer the Xiǎng sacrifice to the Emperor in the suburb."
The burning of brushwood on Dàizōng (Mount Tài)
is what is meant by 'according to the mountain.'
Therefore, the Qū Lǐ says:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,"
which is correct.
Moreover, there is one sacrifice for praying for grain (Qígǔ),
and one for thanking for grain (Bàogǔ).
The Rites do not explicitly show praying to or thanking the Earth,
but extending the text implies it.
The Yuè Jì says:
"The Great Music
is in harmony with Heaven and Earth;
the Great Rites are in measure with Heaven and Earth.
Due to harmony, the myriad things are not lost;
due to measure, Heaven is sacrificed to and Earth is worshipped."
The 'myriad things are not lost' means
that Heaven gives them birth
and Earth provides them sustenance.
Therefore, we know that the Earth also has Qí and Bào sacrifices.
This means Heaven is sacrificed to three times a year in the suburbs,
and Earth is worshipped three times.
The Zhōu Guān mentions Yuánqiū and Fāngzé.
Combined, these are three ceremonies:
the suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth.
Thus, the Xiǎo Zōngbó says:
"Laying out the altars for the Five Emperors in the four suburbs."
This is the suburban sacrifice for 'receiving the vital breaths' mentioned in the Yuè Lìng.
The Shùn Diǎn says:
"In the second month of the year, he made an eastern tour
and hunt,
reaching Dàizōng."
South in the summer,
west in the autumn,
north in the winter,
completing a cycle every five years.
If this were the Fēng and Shàn ceremony,
why would it be so frequent?
These are the Nine Suburban Sacrifices (Jiǔ Jiāo),
all being orthodox
principles.
As for the Great Lǚ sacrifice in the southern suburb,
it is not a regular sacrifice.
The Dà Zōngbó says:
"When the state has a major incident, then perform the Lǚ sacrifice to the Supreme Deity."
The Yuè Lìng says:
"In mid-spring, when the xuánniǎo
arrives,
sacrifice is offered to Gāoméi."
This is also not a regular sacrifice.
Therefore, the Shī Jīng says:
"They performed the Yīn and the Sì sacrifices
to avoid being without a son."
There is also the Yú prayer (for rain),
which is also not a regular sacrifice.
The Lǐ says:
"Yú
is a sacrifice against flood or drought."
Thus, the combined suburban sacrifices to Heaven and Earth are three;
the special suburban sacrifices to Heaven are nine;
and the extraordinary sacrifices are three more.
Examining the Classics states:
"The Zōng sacrifice to Wén
Wáng is performed in the Míngtáng,
to be associated with the Supreme Deity."
Although the Yú sacrifice and the Míngtáng sacrifice are sacrifices to Heaven,
they are not in the suburbs.
This makes the Heaven sacrifices sixteen,
and the Earth sacrifices three.
Only the Great Dì sacrifice is not included in this number.
The Dà Zhuàn says:
"The King performs the Dì sacrifice to the ancestor from whom he originated,
and associates that ancestor with the sacrifice."
It differs from the regular sacrifices,
which is why it is called
greater than the seasonal sacrifices.
Considering the Xì Cí says:
"The composition of the Yì is
expansive, great, and fully prepared.
It contains the way of Heaven,
the way of Earth,
and the way of Man,
combining the three
cosmic powers and doubling them,
hence six.
These six are none other
than the ways of the three cosmic powers."
The Qián Tuàn says:
"Great indeed is the originating power of Qián!
All things rely on it for their beginning,
and it governs Heaven.
Clouds
move and rain is dispensed;
the categories of things flow into form;
the great light concludes and begins;
the six positions are completed in their seasons."
This implies that a sacrifice should be performed every six years,
and the originating power of Kūn is also like this.
The way of sincerity and reverence
is fulfilled
and complete in this.
As for Fēng and Shàn,
