it is not something I dare to hear about."
Gāozǔ graciously accepted this,
and consequently elaborated and praised the deliberation,
responding with an imperial decree.
Requests [for Fēng and Shàn] were consequently halted thereafter.
Ten years later,
he was transferred to become the Household Administrator of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Jiālìng).
According to the old rites of Sòng and Qí,
the suburban sacrifices to Heaven (Jiāo Tiān) and the sacrifices to the Thearchs (Sì Dì) all used the ceremonial robe (Gǔn Miǎn).
In the seventh year of Tiānjiān,
Mào first requested the creation of the Great Fur Robe (Dà Qiú).
Up to this point,
when ceremonies were held at the Hall of Light (Míngtáng),
the ritual specifications still said
"wear the ceremonial robe (Gǔn Miǎn)."
Mào refuted this, saying:
"The Rites state, 'Wear the Great Fur Robe and the cap (Dà Qiú ér Miǎn),
sacrifices to the August Heaven Supreme Thearch (Hàotiān Shàngdì) should also follow this.'
This is precisely because the Gods of Heaven (Tiān Shén) are honored and distant,
requiring sincerity and simplicity.
Now, in general sacrifices to the Five Thearchs (Wǔ Dì),
the principle does not allow for embellishment."
The change to wearing the Great Fur Robe (Dà Qiú)
started from this point.
Furthermore, an imperial edict was issued asking:
"Generally, when seeking Yīn and Yáng,
one should follow its corresponding category.
Now, during the rain sacrifice (Yú Jì), we burn firewood (fán chái).
Using fire to pray for water,
I am skeptical of this intention."
Mào replied:
"Regarding burning firewood during the rain sacrifice (Yú Jì fán chái),
there is no mention of it in the Classics.
This is precisely because earlier Confucian scholars (xiān rú) did not consider it properly.
Examining the poem 'Yún Hàn' (Cloudy Han) from the era of King Zhōu Xuān, it says: 'Above and below we offer and bury,
there is no spirit not honored.'
Máo's Commentary (Máo Zhù) states: 'Above means sacrificing to Heaven,
below means sacrificing to Earth.
Offer the silks,
bury the objects.'
From this, it can be said that
when sacrificing to Heaven and Earth for drought,
there are mentions of offering and burying,
but no mention of burning firewood.
If one argues that sacrifices to the Five Thearchs (Wǔ Dì) must involve burning firewood,
then the current rites at the Hall of Light (Míngtáng)
also do not include this practice.
Moreover, the Rites also say, 'Bury a minor sacrifice (shǎo láo) to sacrifice to the Seasons (Jì Shí).'
The functions of the Seasons are those of the Five Thearchs (Wǔ Dì).
This is further proof that firewood is not used.
In the past, the Altar for Rain (Yú Tán) was located in the south, the position of ultimate Yáng,
which contradicted seeking the spirits (of water/Yīn).
Although it has already been moved to the east,
the rite of burning the offering (shí chái) has yet to be reformed.
I request that the use of firewood be stopped,
and the sacrificial animals and related objects
should all be buried in a pit (kǎn yì),
in accordance with the meaning of 'Yún Hàn' from the time of King Zhōu Xuān."
The emperor ordered that all of this be followed.
Regarding all rituals and rites,
he made many corrections and revisions.
Because of a foot ailment, he was sent out to serve as the Administrator of Shǐpíng (Shǐpíng Tàishǒu).
His administration gained a reputation for competence.
He was promoted to Palace Attendant Consultant (Sànqí Chángshì),
and transferred to be the Administrator of Tiānmén (Tiānmén Tàishǒu).
In the third year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) summoned various scholars (zhū rú) to participate in compiling the notes for the Chángchūn Yì Jì.
In the fourth year,
he was appointed Palace Manager (Zhōng Shùzǐ).
In that year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-nine.
He authored four scrolls of biographical records (Xíng Jì)
and a collected work (jí) of fifteen scrolls.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, said: Sīmǎ Jiǒng had broad and comprehensive Confucian scholarship;
Dào Gài was excellent and quick in literary meaning;
Xiǎn, Mào, and Zhī Lín intensely studied and thoroughly mastered the subject.
They were all employed in busy and convenient positions in the Classics,
responding to questions around the emperor.
This was indeed the duty of Yán and Zhū.
However, Gài and Zhī Lín eventually achieved prominence and honor,
frequently receiving high ranks.
But without meeting the right timing,
how could they have attained this official career?

Biographies, Chapter Thirty-Five: Wáng Guī (Liú Jué, Zōng Lǐn), Wáng Chéng, Chǔ Xiáng, Xiāo Jiè (Cóng Fù Xiōng Qià), Chǔ Qiú, Liú Rǔ (younger brothers Lǎn, Zūn), Liú Qián (younger brothers Xiàoshèng, Xiàowēi, Xiàoxiān), Yīn Yún, Xiāo Jǐ.
Wáng Guī, courtesy name Wēimíng,
was a native of Línyí, Lángxié.
His grandfather, Jiǎn,
was the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) of Qí and the Duke Wénxiàn of Nánchāng.
His father, Qiān,
was the Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Jīnzǐ Guānglù Dàfū) and the Marquis Ān of Nánchāng.
When Guī was eight years old,
he was mourning his deceased birth mother.
His mourning showed profound natural filial piety.
Grand Commandant Xú Xiàosì would shed tears whenever he saw him,
calling him "Filial Child" (Xiàotóng).
His uncle, Jiǎn, also valued him highly,
often saying:
"This child is the thousand-li colt of our family."
At the age of twelve,
he could generally comprehend
the main principles of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng).
When he grew up,
he was fond of learning and possessed eloquence.
The prefecture nominated him as an Outstanding Talent (Xiùcái),
and the commandery welcomed him as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
He started his official career as a Collator (Mìshū Láng),
and was successively promoted to Palace Gentleman of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Chief Clerk to the Prince Ānyòu of Nánkāng (Ānyòu Nánkāng Wáng Zhǔbù),
and subsequently Equerry of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ).
In the twelfth year of Tiānjiān,
the Hall of Supreme Ultimate (Tàijí Diàn) was rebuilt.
When the work was finished,
Guī presented a Rhapsody on the New Palace (Xīn Diàn Fù).
The writing was highly skilled.
He was appointed Vice Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Chéng).
He subsequently served as Central Palace Gentleman of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōng Shèrén),
Registrar of the Left Western Office under the Minister of the Multitude (Sītú Zuǒ Xī Shǔ),
and Attendant Officer (Cóngshì Zhōngláng).
When Prince Jìn'ān, Jiāng, was sent out to govern Nánxú Zhōu,
he highly selected his subordinates
and appointed Guī as Consultant to the General of the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī Zīyì Cānjūn).
After a long time,
he was sent out to serve as the Administrator of Xīn'ān (Xīn'ān Tàishǒu).
He resigned due to mourning his father.
When the mourning period ended,
he inherited the peerage as Marquis of Nánchāng County (Nánchāng Xiàn Hóu).
He was appointed Palace Attendant and Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng).
An edict ordered him, along with Yīn Jūn of Chén Commandery, Wáng Xī of Lángxié, and Zhāng Miǎn of Fànyáng, to serve the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng).
They were all treated with courtesy by Crown Prince Zhāomíng.
When the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng) served as the Capital Administrator (Jīng Yǐn),
he hosted a banquet gathering with court officials,
and assigned Guī to devise the drinking rules.
Guī calmly replied:
"Since the establishment of the Jiāng Zuǒ (East of the Yangtze),
there has been no such precedent."
Xiāo Chēn, Grand Master of Eminent Merit (Tèjìn), and Fù Zhāo, Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Jīnzǐ), were present,
and both declared his statement insightful.
At the beginning of Pǔtōng,
Chén Qìngzhī led the northern expedition.
He captured and restored Luòyáng.
All the officials offered congratulations.
Guī retired and said:
"The Daoists say,
it is not the achieving of success that is difficult,
but maintaining the success that is difficult.
The Jié bandits have been roaming like ghosts
for a long time now.
Huán Wēn gained it only to lose it again,
and Sòng Wǔ ultimately failed to achieve success there.
Our army is isolated and unsupported,
penetrating deep into enemy territory.
Our influence cannot reach,
and the supply line is hard to sustain.
I fear that this campaign
will become a source of disaster."
Soon after, the imperial army was destroyed.
His grasp of the opportunities and dynamics of affairs was often like this.
In the sixth year,
Gāozǔ held a farewell banquet for the Prefect (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu, Yuán Jǐnglóng, at the Wéndé Diàn.
He commanded the assembled officials to compose poems,
all utilizing fifty rhymes.
Guī took up his brush and immediately presented his composition;
his writing was moreover excellent.
Gāozǔ commended him,
and on that very day appointed him as a Grandee Remonstrant (Shìzhōng).
In Dàtōng third year,
he was promoted to Minister of the Five Military Bureaus (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and shortly thereafter took charge as Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
In Zhōngdàtōng second year,
he was sent out as General Zhēnwēi, Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Wáng), Commander of Cavalry (Piàojì).
That year,
the Prince was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ),
and he subsequently served as Administrator of Wújùn (Wújùn Tàishǒu).
The chief clerk, Ruì Zhēnzōng, had his home in Wú.
Former governors and administrators had all devoted themselves to him.
At this time, when Zhēnzōng returned on leave,
Guī treated him very coldly.
When Zhēnzōng returned to the capital,
he secretly reported that Guī
"did not manage the affairs of the commandery."
Shortly thereafter, he was summoned to serve as Minister of the Left People's Bureau (Zuǒmín Shàngshū).
More than a thousand officials and common people of the commandery went to the palace gates requesting that he be allowed to stay.
They submitted memorials three times,
but the Emperor did not permit it.
Soon after, while retaining his original office, he was concurrently made General of the Right Army (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn).
Before he had taken up the post,
he was again made Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and Palace Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
concurrently leading the Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
Guī declined, citing illness, and did not accept the appointment.
He built a residence at Sòngxī Sì (Monastery) on Zhōng Shān and lived there.
In Dàtóng second year,
he died,
aged forty-five.
An imperial edict granted him posthumously the titles of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì) and Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Guānglù Dàfū),
with a funeral stipend of 200,000 cash
and one hundred bolts of cloth.
His posthumous title (Shì) was Zhāng.
The Crown Prince went out to mourn,
and issued an order to Yì, the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng), saying:
"Wēimíng last night suddenly passed away;
this is profoundly painful and sorrowful.
His demeanor and charisma were powerful and correct,
his spirit was distinguished and radiant like a high peak,
his traces were unique for a thousand *lǐ*,
like a hundred-foot tree without branches [i.e., straight and lofty].
His literary argumentation was broad and masterful,
his talent and learning were superior and abundant.
His spirit of unrestraint was profound,
and his *háo liáng* spirit was especially strong.
He was truly a brilliant man.
In an instant he passed like a fleeting shadow,
permanently returning to the long night.
The gleam of the golden knife is hidden;
the long Huái River has dried up.
Last winter,
we already grieved for Master Liú;
now, in the first month of the cold season,
we again mourn Student Wáng.
The grief of losing both
is truly no empty statement."
Guī compiled the variations among various schools concerning the Later Hàn dynasty,
writing annotations for the *Xù Hàn Shū* (Continuation of the Book of Hàn) in 200 scrolls,
and a collection of his writings in 20 scrolls.
His son was Bāo,
courtesy name Zǐyuān.
At seven years old, he could compose literature.
His maternal grandfather, Minister of Works (Sīkōng) Yuán Áng, loved him
and said to his guests:
"This child will certainly embody the essence of my household."
Upon reaching manhood (Ruòguàn),
he was nominated as *Xiùcái* (Flourishing Talent).
He was appointed to Secretarial Editor (Mìshū Láng),
then Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén).
Due to mourning for his father, he left office.
When the mourning period ended,
he inherited the peerage of Marquis of Nánchāng (Nánchāng Hóu).
He was appointed Erudite of the Prince of Wǔchāng (Wǔchāng Wáng Wénxué),
Mounted Escort to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
concurrently managing the records of the Eastern Palace.
He was promoted to Aide to the Minister of Education (Sītú Shǔ),
then Vice Director of the Secretariat (Mìshū Chéng),
and later sent out as Administrator of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Nèishǐ).
During the Tàiqīng period,
Hóu Jǐng captured the capital city.
Dàxīn, the Duke of Dāngyáng (Dāngyáng Gōng) and Prefect of Jiāngzhōu, surrendered the entire province to the rebels.
The rebels then turned to attack Nánzhōng.
Bāo nevertheless held the commandery and resisted the siege.
In Dàbǎo second year,
Shìzǔ commanded that Bāo be summoned to Jiānglíng.
Upon arrival,
he was appointed General Zhōngwǔ and Administrator of Nánpíng (Nánpíng Nèishǐ).
Shortly thereafter, he was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) and Grandee Remonstrant (Shìzhōng).
In Chéngshèng second year,
he was promoted to Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Púyè),
continuing to participate in personnel selection matters,
and was additionally granted the title of Grandee Remonstrant (Shìzhōng).
That year,
he was promoted to Left Vice Director (Zuǒ Púyè),
retaining his administrative duties as before.
In the third year,
Jiānglíng fell,
and he entered Zhōu territory.
Bāo wrote the *Yòu Xùn* (Instructions for the Young)
to admonish his sons.
One chapter states: Táo Shìhéng said:
"In the past, Dà Yǔ did not begrudge a large piece of jade but valued every inch of time."
Why do scholars not recite books?
Why do warriors not practice archery on horseback?
If,
during the deep winter's long nights,
or the bright summer's extended days,
you make your dwelling solemn,
raise your walls high,
permit no confusion or mixing at your gate,
and restrict loud cries while sitting,
by using this method to seek learning,
then you will be
a follower of Zhòngní (Confucius);
by using this method to write literature,
then you will have ascended the hall like Jiǎ Shēng.
In antiquity, basins and platters had inscriptions,
and tables and staffs carried warnings.
Advancing or retreating was guided by them,
and glancing up or down observed them.
The poem of Wén Wáng says:
"There is none who does not have a beginning,
few are able to have a proper end."
Establishing oneself and practicing the Way requires
consistency from beginning to end.
"In moments of haste or distress, one must adhere to this"—
are these the
words of a noble man?
The Rú (Confucian) School maintains distinctions of rank between the honored and the humble,
and degrees of solemnity for auspicious and inauspicious events.
The ruler faces south and the minister faces north;
this is the principle of Heaven and Earth.
Tripods and sacrificial blocks are odd-numbered, while bamboo baskets and wooden dishes are even-numbered;
this is the principle of Yīn and Yáng.
The Dào School seeks to abandon the limbs and body,
reject sharp senses and intelligence,
cast off righteousness and sever benevolence,
and separate the physical form from knowledge.
The principle of the Shì (Buddhist) School is
to perceive suffering, cut off accumulation,
realize
extinction, follow the Way,
clarify causes, distinguish effects,
and transform ordinary people into sages.
Although these teachings have differences in rank,
their meaning ultimately leads to guidance and attraction.
I began with juvenile learning
and reached the age of knowing fate (zhī mìng).
I have
revered the teachings of Zhōu and Kǒng (Confucius),
and also followed the discussions of Lǎo (Lǎozǐ) and Shì (Buddhism).
Since the time of the lower Jiāng region (Jiāng Zuǒ),
this heritage has not declined.
If you can cultivate this,
it is my greatest wish."
Previously,
Liú Jué of Pèiguó and Zōng Lǐn of Nányáng both assisted in the restoration of the dynasty with Bāo,
participating together in the military counsel.
Liú Jué, courtesy name Zhòngbǎo,
was the seventh-generation descendant of Zhēnzhǎng, the Governor of Dānyáng during the Jìn Dynasty.
In his youth, he was upright and possessed great capacity.
Starting as a student of rites at the Imperial University (Guózǐ), he achieved high distinction in the archery examination.
He served as Magistrate of Nínghǎi (Nínghǎi Lìng).
Gradually, he was promoted to Recorder and Staff Officer (Jìshì Cānjūn) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng),
and then transferred to Central Recorder (Zhōng Jìshì).
During the Tàiqīng period,
when Hóu Jǐng caused turmoil,
Shìzǔ assumed authority upriver.
Most of the correspondence and proclamations were entrusted to Jué.
Jué exerted all his strength and loyalty,
and was highly recognized and rewarded.
He successively held the posts of Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng),
and Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
In Chéngshèng second year,
he was promoted to Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) and Libationer of the Imperial University (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ),
retaining his other posts as before.
Zōng Lǐn, courtesy name Yuánlǐn.
His eighth-generation ancestor, Chéng,
was the Administrator of Yídū Commandery during the Jìn Dynasty.
Following the eastward migration during the Yǒngjiā period,
his sons and grandsons subsequently resided in Jiānglíng.
Lǐn was intelligent and fond of learning in his youth;
he was tireless day and night.
The locals called him
"The Juvenile Scholar" (Tóngzǐ Xuéshì).
During the Pǔtōng period,
he served as Concurrent Recorder (Jìshì) in the Princely Establishment of the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
then transferred to Judicial Affairs (Xíngyù),
retaining management of secretarial documents (shūjì).
He successively held the posts of Magistrate (Lìng) of Línrǔ, Jiànchéng, and Guǎngjìn, among others.
Later, he served Shìzǔ as Assistant Administrator (Biéjià) of Jīngzhōu.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Cavalier Attendant (Shàngshū Láng),
enfeoffed as the Marquis of Xìn'ān County (Xìn'ān Xiàn Hóu),
with a stipend of one thousand households.
He was successively promoted to Aide in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Lángzhōng),
Minister of the Five Military Bureaus (Wǔbīng Shàngshū),
and Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
In the third year of Chéngshèng (554 CE),
Jiānglíng fell,
and he, along with Jiǎo, were taken into the territory of Zhōu.
Wáng Chéng, courtesy name Ānqī,
was the son of Púshè Jiǎn.
At the age of seven, he mastered the Zhōu Yì (Book of Changes),
and was selected to enroll as a student in the National University (Guózǐ Shēng).
At the age of fifteen,
he achieved high honors in the examination (shè cè),
and was appointed Attendant in the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng).
He successively held the posts of Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Literary Reader to the Prince of Nánkāng (Nánkāng Wáng Wénxué),
Companion to the Prince of Shàolíng (Shàolíng Wáng Yǒu),
and Middle Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén).
He resigned his post due to mourning for his father.
When the mourning period ended,
he resumed the post of Middle Palace Attendant (Zhōngshèrén),
and was successively promoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Palace Gate (Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng),
concurrently serving as Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì).
At that time, wealthy nobles and gentry
all valued literary pursuits (wénxué),
and few dedicated themselves to classical scholarship (jīngshù).
Only Chéng uniquely favored it.
Whenever he spoke or offered commentary,
he followed the manner of a scholar (rúzhě).
While in the university, he instructed the students
and expounded upon the meanings of the Lǐ (Rites) and the Yì (Changes).
In the fifth year of Zhōngdàtōng (533 CE),
he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) with Extended Duties (Zhǎng Jiān),
and shortly thereafter transferred to Libationer of the National University (Guózǐ Jìjiǔ).
Chéng’s grandfather, Jiǎn, and his father, Jiǎn, had previously held this office.
Three generations serving as National Instructor (Guóshī)
was unprecedented in previous eras,
and the people of the time considered it a great honor.
After a long time,
he was dispatched externally as General Róngzhāo (Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
His governance was lenient and benevolent,
and the officials and common people were pleased with him.
He had not served for a full year
when he died in the commandery,
at the age of forty-one.
His posthumous title was Zhāngzǐ.
Chéng’s nature was modest, noble, and principled.
At that time, Zhū Yì, of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi), held power at court.
Whenever he took a day off,
carriages and horses invariably crowded his gate.
There was a man from Wèijùn named Shēn Yīng who was fond of provocative speeches and lofty arguments,
which often offended those in power.
He often pointed at Yì’s gate and said:
"Those converging here
are all driven by profit.
The only ones capable of not coming
are the Elder and Younger Wáng of Dōngyáng."
The Younger Dōngyáng
was Chéng’s younger brother, Zhì.
At that time, only Chéng, his younger brother, and Chǔ Xiáng did not visit Yì’s gate.
They were praised for this at the time.
Chǔ Xiáng, courtesy name Shìjǔ,
was a native of Yángzhái, Hénán.
His great-grandfather, Yuān,
was the Grand Tutor (Tàizǎi) and Duke Wénjiǎn of Qí,
who assisted in establishing the Qí Dynasty.
His grandfather, Zhēn,
was the Grand Minister of Sacrifices (Tàicháng) Mùzǐ.
His father, Xiàng,
courtesy name Jǐngzhèng.
When he was only a few years old,
his parents died successively.
Xiàng grieved and wasted away like a grown man,
which his relatives and connections all considered remarkable.
When he grew up,
he was refined, elegant, and possessed great capacity.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Xiàng was selected to enroll as a student in the National University (Guózǐ Shēng).
He began his career as Attendant in the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng),
and was promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
and Cavalier Attendant of the Palace (Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng).
He was dispatched externally as Governor of Ānchéng (Ānchéng Nèishǐ).
Upon his return, he was appointed Groom to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
Middle Palace Attendant (Zhōngshèrén),
and was successively promoted to Central Aide to the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi Cóngshì Zhōngláng),
Gentleman-in-Attendance at the Palace Gate (Huángmén Shìláng),
and Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Wáng) under the General Guarding the Right (Zhèn Yòu).
After a short while,
he was recalled to court as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) with Extended Duties (Zhǎng Jiān).
Xiàng’s bearing and manner were dignified and handsome;
his eyebrows and eyes were perfectly defined.
Whenever he took his place in the court procession,
he was the focus of the crowd's gaze.
In the fourth year of Dàtōng (530 CE),

he was dispatched externally as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Lúlíng (Lúlíng Wáng) under the General of the Center of the North (Běi Zhōngláng) and General Quelling Distant Lands (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn).
Three years later,
he died in office.
His maternal cousin, Xiè Jǔ, composed his grave inscription,
which summarized his qualities as:
"His comprehensive governance fostered brilliance;
Zǐsōng (Yuán Xiàn) would be ashamed of his capacity;
wine returns beneath the moon,
the wind clears above the qín."
Critics believed this analogy perfectly captured the man.
Xiáng first became a student of the National University (Guózǐ Shēng),
and attained high honors.
He experienced mourning for his father.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Attendant in the Imperial Library (Mìshū Láng),
and was successively promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
and Registrar (Zhǔbù) to the Prince of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Wáng).
In the fifth year of Zhōngdàtōng (533 CE),
Gāozǔ hosted a banquet for his officials at the Lèuyóu Park.
He issued a special decree commanding Xiáng and Wáng Xùn to compose a twenty-rhyme poem,
with a time limit of three *kè* (quarter-hours).
Xiáng composed and presented his poem immediately upon standing,
which Gāozǔ found remarkable.
On that day, he was transferred to Literary Reader to the Prince of Xuānchéng (Xuānchéng Wáng Wénxué),
and shortly thereafter promoted to Companion (Yǒu).
At that time, the posts of Companion and Literary Reader to the Prince of Xuānchéng carried two grades higher than those for other princes,
so Xiáng received an accelerated promotion to these offices.
Critics of the time praised this decision.
He was dispatched externally as Administrator of Yìxīng (Yìxīng Tàishǒu).
In governance, Xiáng maintained integrity,
reduced excessive severity,
and eliminated extravagant expenditure.
The hundred clans found peace under him.
At the western pavilion of the commandery, there was an ancient tree
that had been withered and dead for many years.
When Xiáng arrived in the commandery,
it suddenly sprouted new branches and leaves.
The people all believed this was due to the positive influence of his virtuous governance.
When his term expired,
the officials and common people went to the palace gates to petition for his retention,
and the imperial decree granted their request.
Soon after, he was summoned to serve as Aide in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù Láng).
When he left the commandery,
the people, regardless of age, followed him to the border,
weeping and bowing their farewells.
Xiáng handled minor appointments (xiǎo xuǎn) impartially and clearly,
and did not change his mind due to personal pleas or connections.
He was known for being fair and equitable (píngyǔn).
Shortly after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng).
After a time, he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
concurrently heading the Supervisor of the Yǔlín (Yǔlín Jiān),
serving in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
He was dispatched externally as Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu).
He had not served a full year in the commandery
when he was dismissed due to official business.
Shortly thereafter, he resumed the post of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sànqí Chángshì),
serving in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng).
In the second year of Tàiqīng (548 CE),
he was promoted to Interim Minister of Personnel (Shǒu Lìbù Shàngshū).
In the winter of that year,
Hóu Jǐng besieged the palace city.
While inside the siege, Xiáng entered mourning for his mother,
and died from extreme grief (huǐ),
at the age of forty-four.
An imperial edict granted him his former office posthumously.
Xiáng had filial piety in his youth.
When he was serving as Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
his mother became gravely ill,
so he invited Buddhist monks (shāmén) to pray for blessings.
In the middle of the night, a strange light was suddenly seen outside the door,
and a snapping sound (tán zhǐ) was heard in the air.
By dawn, the illness was cured.
Everyone believed this was achieved through Xiáng’s sincere devotion.
Xiāo Jiè, courtesy name Màojìng,
was a native of Lánlíng.
His grandfather, Sīhuà,
was Administrator with the Status of the Three Ducal Ministers (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) and Attendant Cavalier (Shàngshū Púshè) during the Sòng Dynasty.
His father, Huìqiàn,
was Minister of the Left Bureau of Commoners (Zuǒmín Shàngshū) during the Qí Dynasty.
Jiè (Xiāo Jiè) was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
possessed ability and insight,
widely studied the Classics and Histories,
and was also skilled at composing literature.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán (era) of Qí,
he received his first official post as Zuòzhù Zuǒláng.
In the sixth year of Tiānjiān (era),
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shèrén.
In the eighth year,
he was promoted to Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng.
In the twelfth year,
he transferred to Zhǔkè Láng.
He was sent out to serve as the Magistrate of Wú (Wú Lìng),
where he established a great reputation and outstanding achievements.
Xiāngdōng Wáng heard of Jiè's fame,
wished to associate with him,
and submitted a memorial requesting his service.
In the third year of Pǔtōng (era),
Jiè was thus appointed Zīyì Cānjūn to Xiāngdōng Wáng.
In the second year of Dàtōng (era),
he was appointed Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.
In the second year of Dàtóng (era),
when Wǔlíng Wáng served as the Cìshǐ of Yángzhōu,
Jiè was appointed Fǔ Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Prefecture).
He was clean and honest in office,
and was praised by the imperial court.
Gāozǔ said to Hé Jìngróng:
"Xiāo Jiè is very poor;
he should be placed in charge of a commandery."
Jìngróng had not yet replied,
when Gāozǔ said:
"Shǐxīng Jùn has lacked a capable administrator for some time,
and the people in the southern mountains (Lǐngshàng) are quite unsettled.
Jiè can be appointed there."
Consequently, he was sent out to serve as the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Shǐxīng.
When Jiè arrived at his post,
he proclaimed his authority and benevolence,
and the entire region became orderly and secure.
In the seventh year,
he was summoned back to serve as Shàofǔ Qīng,
and shortly thereafter was further appointed Sànqí Chángshì.
When the post of Shìzhōng (Attendant in Ordinary) became vacant,
the selection officials nominated Wáng Jūn and three others,
but none pleased the Emperor.
Gāozǔ said:
"This position has been vacant in Our court for a long time;
it is appropriate to use Xiāo Jiè for it."
Jiè was widely learned and had a strong memory;
responding to the emperor's inquiries,
he offered corrections and guidance on many issues.
Gāozǔ valued him greatly.
He was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū.
Whenever there was a major military or state affair,
Gāozǔ would always first inquire and consult with Jiè.
Gāozǔ said to Zhū Yì:
"He is a talent fit for the position of Duānyòu (Chief Minister)."
In the second year of Zhōngdàtóng (era),
he resigned due to illness,
but Gāozǔ refused with a gracious edict.
However, he ultimately refused to resume his duties,
so Gāozǔ sent the Palace Usher Púyè, Wèi Xiáng, to formally appoint him Guānglù Dàfū.
During the Tàiqīng (era),
Hóu Jǐng was defeated at Wōyáng and fled,
entering Shòuyáng.
Gāozǔ ordered the defense chief, Wéi Àn, to admit him.
Jiè heard this and submitted a memorial of remonstrance, saying: "I, your subject, afflicted with illness at home,
humbly hear that Hóu Jǐng, defeated at Wōyáng,
surrendered his life with only a single horse.
Your Majesty does not regret the former disasters,
and again commands that he be received.
I have heard that the nature of a treacherous
person does not change,
and the wickedness in the world is all the same.
Previously, Lǚ Bù killed Dīng Yuán to serve Dǒng Zhuó,
but ultimately executed Dǒng and became a rebel himself;
Liú Láo betrayed Wáng Gōng and
submitted to Jìn,
but then turned against Jìn to cause rebellion.
Why is this?
The wolf cub has a wild heart,
and fundamentally lacks a tamed nature;
the analogy of raising a tiger
inevitably leads to the disaster of being devoured when it is hungry.
Hóu
Jǐng is of the savage-hearted breed,
belonging to the category of the wild barbarians (míngdí).
With his vicious and cunning talent,
he received the immense favor of Gāo Huān,
his position barely inferior to the highest officials,
and holding the office of a regional governor (Fāng Bó).
Yet, before Gāo
Huān's tomb dirt was even dry,
he immediately turned around and counter-attacked.
When his rebellious strength failed him,
he then fled to Guānxī to escape death;
when Yǔwén would not tolerate him,
he therefore threw himself upon us.
The reason Your Majesty
previously did not reject this small trickle (of surrender),
was simply wishing to use a surrendered Hu (barbarian) from a vassal state to attack the Xiōngnú,
hoping only for the achievement of a single battle.
Now that he has lost his army and territory,
he is simply
a common fellow on the border.
Your Majesty cherishes this common fellow and abandons the goodwill of an allied state (Yǔ Guó);
I secretly disapprove of this.
If the state still awaits the morning when he changes his tune,
hoping for his efficacy at the end of the year,
I secretly believe Hóu Jǐng is certainly not a loyal servant till year's end;
abandoning his homeland as if casting off sandals,
and turning his back on
his ruler and kin as if discarding weeds.
How could he possibly be someone who admires Your sacred virtue from afar,
and serves as a pure subject loyal to Jiānghuái (the South)?
His deeds are clear,
there is no room for doubt.
If one corner (of the issue) is already like this,
how can one
fully enumerate all the corresponding examples?
I, your subject, am infirm with age and afflicted by illness,
and should not rashly interfere in court affairs;
but Chǔ Náng, facing death,
maintained the loyalty of defending Yǐng,
and Wèi Yú, on the verge of demise,
also possessed the integrity of remonstrating after death.
I am undeserving to be counted among the elders of the imperial clan (Zōngshì Yílǎo),
but how dare I forget the heart of Liú Xiàng (i.e., loyal remonstrance).
I humbly beg Your Heavenly Compassion,
to briefly consider these dangerous and anxious words."
Gāozǔ read the memorial, sighed,
but ultimately could not act upon it.
Jiè's nature was noble and straightforward;
he had few companions.
He only enjoyed literary gatherings and drinking parties with his paternal cousin Chēn, his cousin Shìsù and Qià, and his younger cousin Shú,
people at the time compared this to the Wūyī gatherings of the Xiè clan.
Earlier,
Gāozǔ summoned more than twenty talented young men,
hosted a banquet, and composed poetry.
Zāng Dùn was unable to complete his poem and
was penalized with one *dǒu* (measure) of wine.
Dùn drank it all,
his complexion unchanged,
speaking and laughing naturally.
Jiè immediately completed his work once he put brush to paper,
and his writing required no correction.
Gāozǔ praised both men, saying:
"Zāng Dùn's drinking,
and Xiāo Jiè's writing,
are the splendors of this occasion."
He died at home
at the age of seventy-three.
His third son, Yǔn,
was initially appointed Jiān Sànqí Chángshì and sent on a diplomatic mission to Wèi.
Upon return, he served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
later reaching the rank of Guānglù Dàfū.
Qià, courtesy name Hóngchēng,
was Jiè's cousin (son of his paternal uncle).
His father, Huìjī,
was the Lìbù Shàngshū of Qí,
and held a great reputation in previous generations.
at the age of seven,
he could nearly recite the *Chǔ Cí* (楚辭, Songs of Chu).
When he grew up,
he loved studying and was extensively knowledgeable,
and was also skilled at composing literature.
During the Yǒngmíng (永明) era of Qí (齊),
he became a Guózǐ Shēng (國子生, Student of the National University),
was recommended as a Míng Jīng (明經, Scholar of Classics),
starting his career as a Zhùzuò Zuǒ Láng (著作佐郎, Assistant Secretary in the Bureau of Archives),
and was promoted to Xī Zhōngláng Wài Bīng Cānjūn (西中郎外兵參軍, Adjutant to the General of the West).
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
he served as Qián Jūn Pōyáng Wáng Zhǔbù (前軍鄱陽王主簿, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Pōyáng, General of the Vanguard) and Shàngshū 囗 Bù Láng (尚書囗部郎),
then was promoted to Tàizǐ Zhōng Shèrén (太子中舍人, Palace Administrative Aide to the Crown Prince).
He left to serve as Nán Xú Zhōu Zhì Zhōng (南徐州治中, Chief Clerk of Nán Xú Prefecture).
Since this was a critical prefecture near the capital region,
involving thousands of officials/clerks,
those who had previously held this post had all amassed great wealth.
When Qìa held the post,
he kept himself pure and strictly followed his duties,
not accepting a single gift or offering,
and his wife and children could not avoid hunger and cold.
Returning, he was appointed Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng (司空從事中郎, Secretariat Supervising Officer under the Minister of Works),
and then became Jiàn'ān Nèishǐ (建安內史, Governor of Jiàn'ān Commandery),
but was dismissed due to an incident.
After a long time,
he was appointed Hù Jūn Cháng Shǐ (護軍長史, Chief Clerk to the General Protecting the Army),
Běi Zhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn (北中郎諮議參軍, Adjutant Counselor to the General of the North),
promoted to Tàifǔ Qīng (太府卿, Minister of the Imperial Treasury),
and Sītú Línchuān Wáng Sīmǎ (司徒臨川王司馬, Marshal to the Prince of Línchuān, Minister of Education).
At the beginning of the Pǔtōng (普通) era,
he was commissioned as Yuánwài Sǎnqí Chángshì (員外散騎常侍, Supernumerary Palace Retainer),
concurrently serving as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞, Vice President of the Imperial Censorate),
but was dismissed due to public business.
After a while,
he became Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì (通直散騎常侍, Palace Retainer with Direct Access).
Qìa possessed literary talent in his youth.
Gāozǔ (高祖) ordered him to compose the stūpa inscriptions for Tóng Tài Sì (同泰寺) and Dà Àijìng Sì (大愛敬寺),
and his writing was very beautiful.
In the second year,
he was promoted to Sǎnqí Chángshì (散騎常侍, Palace Retainer).
He left to serve as Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn (招遠將軍, General Who Beckons the Distant) and Línhǎi Tàishǒu (臨海太守, Governor of Línhǎi Commandery).
His governance was pure and peaceful,
he did not advocate for strict harshness,
and the local populace benefited from it.
Returning, he was commissioned as Sītú Zuǒ Chángshǐ (司徒左長史, Chief Clerk on the Left to the Minister of Education).
He was also commanded to compose the stele inscription for the Dāngtú Yàn (當塗堰, Dāngtú Dam),
the language of which was also rich and elegant.
In the sixth year,
he died while in office,
at the age of fifty-five.
An imperial edict was issued for officials to mourn him,
bestowing 20,000 cash,
and fifty rolls of cloth.
His collected works, in twenty *juǎn* (卷, scrolls),
circulated in the world.
Chǔ Qiú (褚球), courtesy name Zhòngbǎo (仲寶),
was a native of Yángzhái (陽翟) in Hénán (河南).
His great-grandfather, Shúdù (叔度),
was General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ Jiāngjūn) and Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州) during Sòng (宋);
his grandfather, Ài (曖),
was Tàizǎi Wài Bīng Cānjūn (太宰外兵參軍, Adjutant of External Affairs under the Grand Tutor);
his father, Huì (繢),
was Tàizǐ Shèrén (太子舍人, Palace Administrative Aide to the Crown Prince);
all of whom married Sòng princesses.
Qiú was orphaned and poor in his youth,
but he was deeply committed to study
and possessed talent and insight.
Jǐngsù (景素), Prince of Jiànpíng (建平) during Sòng,
was executed in the Yuánhuī (元徽) era,
leaving only one daughter alive.
His former subordinates, Hé Chāngyù (何昌𧜛) and Wáng Sīyuǎn (王思遠), hearing of Qiú’s integrity,
married this daughter to him,
and thereby promoted his reputation.
Serving in Qí (齊), he began his career as a probationary staff officer (Xíng Cānjūn) under the General Who Conquers the Barbarians (Zhēnglǔ),
shortly thereafter taking charge of the Legal Section (Fǎ Cáo),
and was promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) for the Princess of Qǔjiāng (曲江) under the General of the Right (Yòujūn).
He left to serve as the Magistrate of Lìyáng (溧陽),
where he was pure and honest,
living only on his official salary.
He was appointed Píng Xī Zhǔbù (平西主簿, Chief Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the West).
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he was promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (太子洗馬, Gatekeeper to the Crown Prince),
Sǎnqí Shìláng (散騎侍郎, Gentleman Attendant),
and concurrently Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (中書通事舍人, Secretariat Administrative Aide).
He left to serve as the Magistrate of Jiànkāng (建康),
but resigned due to mourning for his mother.
He was recalled to his original post,
which he firmly refused to accept.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Běi Zhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn (北中郎諮議參軍, Adjutant Counselor to the General of the North),
soon after promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (中書郎, Director in the Central Secretariat),
and again concurrently held the post of Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was appointed Yúnqí Jiāngjūn (雲騎將軍, General of the Cloud Cavalry),
repeatedly holding concurrent posts as Tíngwèi (廷尉, Chief Justice),
Guānglù Qīng (光祿卿, Minister of the Imperial Household),
while his Shèrén post remained unchanged.
He was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞, Vice President of the Imperial Censorate).
Qiú was naturally upright and strong-willed,
and would not yield to anyone.
While in the Xìan Sī (憲司, Censorate), he performed his duties admirably.
In the fourth year of Pǔtōng,
he left to serve as Běi Zhōngláng Cháng Shǐ (Chief Clerk to the General of the North) and Nán Lánlíng Tàishǒu (南蘭陵太守, Governor of Nán Lánlíng).
Returning to the capital, he became Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì,
concurrently Supervisor of the Yǔlín (羽林, Feathered Forest Guard).
In the seventh year,
he was promoted to Tàifǔ Qīng (Minister of the Imperial Treasury).
Shortly thereafter,
he was promoted to Dūguān Shàngshū (都官尚書, Minister of Justice).
During the Zhōng Dàtóng (中大同) era,
he left to serve as Rénwēi Línchuān Wáng Cháng Shǐ (仁威臨川王長史, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Línchuān, General of Benevolent Awe) and Jiāngxià Tàishǒu (江夏太守, Governor of Jiāngxià),
but due to illness, he did not take up the post.
He was reassigned the title Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫, Grand Master of the Imperial Household).
Before being commissioned,
he again became Tàifǔ Qīng,
and concurrently Colonel of the Bùbīng (步兵, Infantry).
He was soon promoted to Tōngzhí Sǎnqí Chángshì,
Mìshū Jiān (祕書監, Director of the Imperial Library),
and concurrently Supervisor of Literary Composition (Zhùzuò).
He was promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Cháng Shǐ (Chief Clerk on the Left to the Minister of Education),
his posts as Chángshì and Zhùzuò remaining unchanged.
Since Sūn Lǐ (孫禮) of Wèi (魏) and Xún Zǔ (荀組) of Jìn (晉),
that a Chief Clerk (Tái Zuǒ) wore sable adornments,
began only with Qiú.

Soon after, he left to serve as Zhēn Wēi Jiāngjūn Qīng Chē Hédōng Wáng Cháng Shǐ (貞威將軍輕車河東王長史, Chief Clerk to the Prince of Hédōng, General of Solemn Awe, General of Light Chariots) and Nán Lánlíng Tàishǒu (Governor of Nán Lánlíng).
Returning to the capital, he became Sǎnqí Chángshì,
concurrently commanding the Infantry.
Soon thereafter, he submitted a memorial requesting retirement,
but the imperial edict did not allow it.
He was shortly re-commissioned as Guānglù Dàfū,
and given the additional title of Jǐshì Zhōng (給事中, Attendant Official).
He died in office,
at the age of seventy.
Líu Rú (劉孺), courtesy name Xiàozhì (孝稚),
was a native of Ānshàng Lǐ (安上里) in Péngchéng (彭城).
His grandfather, Miǎn (勔),
was Sītú (司空, Minister of Works) and Zhōngzhāo Gōng (忠昭公, Duke Zhōngzhāo) during Sòng.
His father, Quān (悛),
was Tàicháng (太常, Minister of Ceremonies) and Jìng Zǐ (敬子, Viscount Jìng) during Qí.
Rú was quick-witted and intelligent in his youth,
and could compose literature at age seven.
At the age of fourteen,
he was in mourning for his father.
He damaged his health and became bone-thin,
which his clan members and peers all found remarkable.
When the mourning period ended,
his uncle, Tiàn (瑱), was serving in Yìxīng Jùn (義興郡),
and took Rú along when he went to his post.
He often kept Rú by his side,
saying to his guests:
"This child is the bright pearl of our family."
When he grew up,
he had handsome looks and bearing,
his nature was amiable and gentle,
such that even his family members never saw him express joy or displeasure.
His home prefecture invited him to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
He began his career as a probationary staff officer (Xíng Cānjūn) in the Legal Section (Fǎ Cáo) under the General of the Center (Zhōng Jūn).
At that time, Shěn Yuē (沈約), the General Guarding the Army (Zhèn Jūn), heard of his fame,
and invited him to be his Chief Clerk.
He often went on outings and feasts with Yuē, composing poetry,
and was greatly admired and praised by Yuē.
He was successively promoted to Tàizǐ Shèrén (Palace Administrative Aide to the Crown Prince),
Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk) to the Prince of Línchuān, General of the Center (Zhōng Jūn Línchuān Wáng),
Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (Gatekeeper to the Crown Prince),
and Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng (尚書殿中郎, Director in the Ministry of State Affairs).
He left to serve as the Magistrate of Tàimò (太末).
While in the county, he achieved pure administrative merit.
Returning, he was appointed Jìn'ān Wáng Yǒu (晉安王友, Companion to the Prince of Jìn'ān),
and then transferred to Tàizǐ Zhōng Shèrén (Palace Administrative Aide to the Crown Prince).
Rú loved literature in his youth,
and his nature was quick and swift.
He once composed a *fù* (賦, Rhapsody) on the plum while attending the Emperor,
completing it immediately upon receiving the command,
without needing to revise the writing.
Gāozǔ greatly praised and admired him.
Later, while attending a banquet at Shòuguāng Diàn (壽光殿, Shòuguāng Palace),
the Emperor commanded the officials to compose poems.
At that time, Rú and Zhāng Shuài (張率) were both drunk,
and had not yet finished.
Gāozǔ took Rú’s writing tablet and inscribed a joke upon it, saying:
"Zhāng Shuài is the beauty of the Southeast,
Líu Rú is the talent of Luòyáng (雒陽),
You should finish as soon as you grasp the brush—
Why have you tarried so long?"
His being favored and cherished was like this.
to become Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
concurrently serving as Palace Attendant and Drafter of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén).
Soon after, he was promoted to Household Director of the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Jiālìng);
other duties remained as before.
He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Wáng), who held the title Pacifying General (Xuānhuì),
concurrently managing the affairs of the Assistant Administrator of Dānyáng Commandery (Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng).
He was promoted to Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ),
and Director of the Personnel Bureau of the Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū Lìbù Láng).
He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng), who held the title General of Swift Chariots (Qīngchē),
concurrently managing the affairs of the Assistant Administrator of Kuàijī Commandery (Kuàijī Jùn Chéng).
He was dismissed due to official business.
After a while,
he was appointed to Secretariat Recorder of the Princely Establishment (Wáng Fǔ Jìshì),
Gentleman-Consultant (Sǎnqí Shìláng),
concurrently serving as Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Qīng).
Successively, he was promoted to Minister of the Privy Treasury (Shàofǔ Qīng),
Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education (Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ),
and Vice Censor-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
He was widely regarded as competent in his duties.
In the second year of Dàtōng (Dàtōng Èr Nián, 528 CE),
he was promoted to Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sǎnqí Chángshì).
In the third year (529 CE),
he was promoted to Minister of the Census (Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū),
concurrently holding the position of Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi).
In the fourth year of Zhōng Dàtōng (Zhōng Dàtōng Sì Nián, 532 CE),
he was sent out to be Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Línchuān (Línchuān Wáng), who held the title General of Benevolent Awe (Rénwēi), and Administrator of Jiāngxià (Jiāngxià Tàishǒu),
receiving the added title of General of Chaste Awe (Zhēn Wēi Jiāngjūn).
In the fifth year (533 CE),
he was appointed General of Tranquilizing Distances (Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn) and Chief Clerk of the Minister of Education (Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ).
Before he took the post,
this was changed to Minister of Judicial Administration (Dūguān Shàngshū),
concurrently holding the position of General of the Right Army (Yòujūn Jiāngjūn).
In the fifth year of Dàtóng (Dàtóng Wǔ Nián, 539 CE),
he served pro tem as Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū).
That same year,
he was sent out to be General of Illustrious Awe (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Administrator of Jìnlíng (Jìnlíng Tàishǒu).
While serving in the commandery, he governed peacefully,
and was praised by the officials and the people.
In the seventh year (541 CE),
he returned [to the capital] to become Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng),
concurrently holding the position of General of the Right Army (Yòujūn).
That same year,
he was again made Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū),
but resigned his post due to mourning his mother.
While observing mourning, before the expiration of the term,
he died from extreme grief (huǐ),
aged fifty-nine.
His posthumous title was Filial Son (Xiàozǐ).
Shěn Rú while young was equally famous as his cousins, Shěn Bāo and Shěn Xiàochuò.
Shěn Bāo died young,
and Shěn Xiàochuò was repeatedly dismissed from office,
so their ranks were never high;
only Shěn Rú achieved prominence and wealth.
He possessed a collection of literary works in twenty scrolls.
His son, Shěn Chú,
was an Editor (Zhùzuò Láng),
but died young.
Shěn Rú had two younger brothers: Shěn Lǎn,
and Shěn Zūn.
Shěn Lǎn's courtesy name was Xiàozhì.
At sixteen, he mastered the *Lǎozi* (Lǎo) and the *Changes* (Yì).
He successively served as Attendant Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng).
Due to mourning his birth mother,
he built a hut by her tomb.
For two full years,
his mouth did not taste salt or curds (dairy),
and in winter, he only wore a single layer of cloth.
His family, fearing he could not endure the mourning,
secretly placed charcoal beneath him in the middle of the night.
Shěn Lǎn, benefiting from the warmth, managed to sleep.
When he woke and realized what had happened,
he cried out, wailed, and vomited blood.
Emperor Gāozǔ, hearing of his extreme filial nature,
frequently visited and saw him.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Assistant Director of the Left in the Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng).
His nature was intelligent and quick-witted.
There were seven hundred clerks (lìshǐ) in the Ministry of Personnel (Shàngshū);
he could remember all of their names upon meeting them once.
While in office,
he was honest and upright, showing no partiality.
His elder sister's husband, Vice Censor-in-Chief Chǔ Yīn,
and his cousin, Director of the Personnel Bureau Shěn Xiàochuò,
had both accepted bribes while in office.
Shěn Lǎn impeached them,
and they were both dismissed from their positions.
Shěn Xiàochuò resented this
and once said to others:
"Dogs bite passersby,
but Shěn Lǎn bites his own family."
He was sent out to be Administrator of Shǐxīng (Shǐxīng Nèishǐ).
In governing the commandery, he was particularly zealous for clean integrity.
He returned and was again made Assistant Director of the Left (Zuǒ Chéng),
dying in office.
Shěn Zūn's courtesy name was Xiàolíng.
In youth, he was refined and elegant,
possessing scholarly conduct,
and excelled at literary composition.
He began his career as an Editor (Zhùzuò Láng),
then Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén).

Successively, he was promoted to Secretariat Recorder (Jìshì) in the Princely Establishments of Jìn'ān Wáng, who held the titles Pacifying General (Xuānhuì) and General of the Cloud Cavalry (Yúnhuī) [in two separate stints].
He was greatly respected as a guest.
He was transferred to Administrator of Nán Xú Zhōu (Nán Xú Zhōu Zhìzhōng).
When the Prince later became the Governor of Yōng Zhōu,
Shěn Zūn was again recruited to be Consultant to the General who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Zīyì Cānjūn), concurrently serving as Magistrate of Qí County (Qí Xiàn Lìng).
In the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng (Zhōng Dàtōng Èr Nián, 530 CE),
the Prince was established as the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ).
Shěn Zūn was then appointed Palace Assistant to the Crown Prince (Zhōngshùzǐ).
Shěn Zūn, from the time he followed the Prince in his feudal state (fān) until he was in the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
due to their long-standing favor,
received exceptional affection and treatment;
none of his peers could compare.
In the first year of Dàtóng (Dàtóng Yuán Nián, 535 CE),
he died in office.
The Crown Prince deeply lamented and regretted his death,
and issued an order to Shěn Xiàoyí, Shěn Zūn's cousin and Magistrate of Yángxiàn, which said: "The worthy Palace Assistant (Zhōngshùzǐ)
has suddenly passed away.
Can this grief be adequately expressed!
His filial piety and fraternal affection were pure and deep,
his moral standing firm and steadfast.
Internally, he contained the luster of jade;
externally, he displayed limpid
clarity.
His excellent reputation and fine fame
spread among officials and friends;
his words and actions corresponded,
consistent from beginning to end.
He was comprehensively rich in literature and history;
polished jade (wǎnyǎn) formed his intellect.
His compositions and verses were expansive and abundant,
crafting brilliance
out of black and yellow [colors].
He used famed humility to characterize his nature,
and positioned himself as difficult to promote.
He never sought audience with the Ministers (Gōngqīng)
or formed connections for glory or profit.
Therefore, those recently promoted did not recommend him,
nor did Dù
Wǔ know of him.
Since the office of Ruǎn Fàng [at Hánán],
and the post in Yěwáng [the Crown Prince's domain],
he has been sheltered beneath our gates [in the establishment]
for over five years.
His colleagues have been promoted,
and many latecomers have advanced,
yet he remained tranquil
and reserved,
not caring about the difference [in rank].
Such a steadfast resolution
is truly hard to find.
[This attitude] surpasses [the story of] Wú Qǐ viewing the precious jewel in Xīhé,
and Yáng Xióng walking alone along the Eastern River (Dōng Jiāng).
What is recorded in the books
certainly does not exceed this.
When I was formerly in Hànnán,
he was continuously the Secretariat Recorder (shūjì).
When I condescended to govern Zhūfāng,
he sat easily at the head [of the staff].
On fine days and lovely scenes,
during clear breezes and moonlit nights,
when the osprey boat was just setting off,
and the red
egret slowly cried out,
there was never a day when he did not follow me,
nor a moment when we did not meet.
When the wine was done and our ears grew warm,
we spoke of our ambitions and composed poems,
assessing loyal and worthy men,
and discussing and praising literature
and history.
Of the three beneficial friends,
he was truly one of them.
When he spread governance in the lower county [Qí Xiàn],
even before establishing excellent governance [for long],
he was able to make the people harbor thoughts of regret upon his departure,
and tame pheasants abounded in the fields.
This is also a single feather
of the magnificent phoenix,
sufficient to verify his five virtues.
Recently, while in the Eastern Palace (Chūnfāng),
we were once again able to meet and talk.
Although the Director of Dependencies (Bówàng) had no duty to introduce guests,
and the Director of Imperial Instruction (Sīchéng) had many strict regulations,
we
relied on our old friendship to occasionally meet;
but this man suddenly died,
which is truly regrettable and painful.
The saying, 'Heaven only blesses the good,'
must be empty talk.
How could Heaven's recompense
be like this?"
Thinking of your sincerity in grief and lamentation,
how can
it ever cease? It is gone, what can be done?
Throwing down the brush, I feel sorrowful and mournful.
Yesterday, I intended to write an epitaph and inscription
and compile a collection for him.
My own inadequacy and lack of virtue
meant that during his lifetime I could not promote or praise him,
allowing
him to fully employ his talents.
Now writing an inscription and compiling a collection
—how does it benefit what is past?
Therefore, the feeling of deep regret and sorrow
cannot be stopped.
Liú Qián
, courtesy name Xiàoyí,
was the younger brother of Mìshūjiān Xiàochuò.
He was orphaned in childhood
and encouraged his brothers in diligent study.
They were all skilled in literary composition.
Xiàochuò often said:
"Sān Bǐ Liù Shī (Three Writers, Six Poets)."
The "Three" referred to Xiàoyí,
and the "Six" referred to Xiàowēi.
In the fifth year of Tiānjiān (506 CE),
he was nominated as a Xiùcái.
He began his official career as Zhènyòu Shǐxīng Wáng Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn (Adjutant Serving as Judge under the Prince of Shǐxīng, General Who Guards the Right),
following the princely administration to Yìzhōu,
concurrently serving as Jìshì (Secretary).
When the Prince returned and became Zhōngfǔjūn (General Who Soothes the Military),
he was transferred to Zhǔbù (Master of Records),
and then promoted to Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng (Palace Affairs Director in the Department of State Affairs).
He was commanded to compose the stele inscription for the Golden Buddha statue at Píngděng Sì in Yōngzhōu.
The writing was extremely grand and beautiful.
When Jìn'ān Wáng Gāng went out to govern Xiāngyáng,
he was invited to serve as Ānběi Gōngcáo Shǐ (Director of Merits under the General Who Pacifies the North).
He left the post due to mourning for his mother.
When the Prince was established as Crown Prince,
Xiàoyí's period of mourning ended,
and he was appointed Xǐmǎ (Horse Washer, an official title in the Eastern Palace).
He was promoted to Zhōngshèrén (Attendant).
He went out to serve as Róngzhāo Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Military Awe) and Yángxiàn Lìng (Magistrate of Yángxiàn).
He achieved much-praised merit,
and was subsequently promoted to Jiànkāng Lìng (Magistrate of Jiànkāng).
In the third year of Dàtóng (537 CE),
he was promoted to Zhōngshū Láng (Director in the Central Secretariat).
Due to an official matter, he was demoted to Ānxī Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Adjutant under the General Who Pacifies the West),
concurrently serving as Sànqí Chángshì (Attendant-in-Ordinary).
Upon returning from his mission to Wèi,
he was reinstated as Zhōngshū Láng.
After a short time,
he provisionally served concurrently as Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works, Right Division),
and also concurrently as Níngyuǎn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the General Who Pacifies Afar), administering the affairs of both Péngchéng and Lángyá Commanderies.
He was repeatedly promoted, reaching Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs),
concurrently serving as Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Vice President of the Censorate).
While in office, he impeached and corrected misconduct without fear or favor,
and was praised at the time.
In the tenth year,
he went out to serve as Fúbō Jiāngjūn (General Who Subdues the Waves) and Línhǎi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Línhǎi).
At that time, the administrative network was lax and broad,
and the common people often did not abide by the prohibitions.
Xiàoyí, upon arriving in office,
promulgated the regulations and statutes.
He exerted himself to pacify and comfort the people,
and the entire territory was united,
resulting in a great reform of customs.
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtóng (546 CE),
he entered the capital to serve provisionally as Dūguān Shàngshū (Minister of Revenue).
In the first year of Tàiqīng (547 CE),
he went out to serve as Míngwēi Jiāngjūn (General Who Manifests Awe) and Yùzhāng Nèishǐ (Administrator of Yùzhāng).
In the second year,
when Hóu Jǐng attacked the capital,
Xiàoyí sent his son Lì to lead three thousand troops from the commandery
to join the former Héngzhōu Cìshǐ Wéi Càn in providing aid.
In the third year (549 CE),
the Palace City fell.
Xiàoyí was pressured by the former Lìyáng Tàishǒu Zhuāng Tiě
and lost the commandery.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he died of illness,
aged sixty-seven.
Xiàoyí
and especially devoted in his inner conduct (domestic virtues).
His second eldest brother, Xiàonéng, had died young.
Xiàoyí served his widowed sister-in-law with great respect.
Regarding all household matters, large or small,
he would first consult her before making a decision.
He and his wife served her morning and evening,
never failing in propriety.
The world praised him for this.
He had a collected work in twenty volumes
circulating in the world.
His fifth younger brother, Xiàoshèng,

successively held the posts of Shàolíng Wáng Fǎcáo (Judge under the Prince of Shàolíng), Xiāngdōng Wáng Ānxī Zhǔbù Jìshì (Master of Records and Secretary under the Prince of Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West),
and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
He went out to serve as Xìnyì Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xìnyì),
but was dismissed due to an official matter.
After a long time,
he was reinstated as Shàngshū Yòuchéng (Vice Director of the Right in the Department of State Affairs),
concurrently serving as Sànqí Chángshì.
Upon returning from an embassy to Wèi,
he became Ānxī Wǔlíng Wáng Jǐ Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to Prince Jǐ of Wǔlíng, General Who Pacifies the West) and Shǔjùn Tàishǒu (Administrator of Shǔjùn).
During the Tàiqīng period,
Hóu Jǐng captured the capital.
Jǐ usurped the title of emperor in Shǔ
and appointed Xiàoshèng as Shàngshū Púshè (Vice President of the Department of State Affairs).
During the Chéngshèng period,
he followed Jǐ out of Xiákǒu (the Gorge entrance).
The army was defeated,
and he was captured and imprisoned.
Emperor Shìzǔ soon pardoned him
and reinstated him as Sītú Yòu Zhǎngshǐ.
His sixth younger brother, Xiàowēi,
first served as Ānběi Jìn'ān Wáng Fǎcáo (Judge under the Prince of Jìn'ān, General Who Pacifies the North).
He was transferred to Zhǔbù,
but left the post due to mourning for his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ,
and repeatedly promoted to Zhōngshèrén,
Shùzǐ (Attendant),
and Shuàigēng Lìng (Director of the Office of Astronomy).
In all these roles, he was concurrently in charge of records.
In the ninth year of Dàtóng (543 CE),
when a white sparrow gathered at the Eastern Palace,
Xiàowēi presented an encomium.
Its diction was very fine.
During the Tàiqīng period,
he was promoted to Zhōngshùzǐ (Attendant),
concurrently serving as Tōngshì Shèrén (Secretarial Attendant).
When Hóu Jǐng caused rebellion and disorder,
Xiàowēi managed to escape the besieged city.
He followed the Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Liǔ Zhònglǐ westward,
but when they reached Ānlù,
he contracted an illness and died.
His seventh younger brother, Xiàoxiān,
served as Wǔlíng Wáng Fǎcáo and Zhǔbù.
When the Prince moved to Yìzhōu,
he followed the administration and was transferred to Ānxī Jìshì (Secretary to the General Who Pacifies the West).
During the Chéngshèng period,
he and his elder brother Xiàoshèng both followed Jǐ's army out of Xiákǒu.
After the army was defeated,
he reached Jiānglíng.
Emperor Shìzǔ appointed him Huángmén Shìláng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate),
and he was promoted to Shìzhōng (Palace Attendant).
The brothers were all skilled in five-character poetry
and were highly regarded by the world.
Their collected works were caught in the chaos,
and are now not fully extant.
Yīn Yún, courtesy name Guànshū,
was a native of Chángpíng, Chénjùn.
He was unconventional in character
and did not restrict himself by minor observances.
However, he did not associate recklessly,
and his gate was without inappropriate guests.
He applied himself diligently to studies,
and was broadly knowledgeable in many texts.
While he was young, Hé Xiàn of Lújiāng met him
and greatly admired and praised him.
During the Yǒngmíng period,
he served as Yídū Wáng Xíng Cānjūn (Adjutant Acting for the Prince of Yídū).
Early in the Tiānjiān period,
he served as Xīzhōng Láng Zhǔbù (Master of Records for the General of the Center-West) and Hòujūn Línchuān Wáng Jìshì (Secretary for the Prince of Línchuān, General of the Rear Army).
In the seventh year (508 CE),
he was promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (Palace Attendant and Gentleman),
concurrently serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén (Secretarial Attendant in the Central Secretariat).
In the tenth year,
he was appointed Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng,
concurrently serving as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng,
and also concurrently as Zhōngshū Shèrén.
He was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the Directorate of Education),
Shìdú (Attendant Lecturer) to Crown Prince Zhāomíng,
Xīzhōng Láng Yùzhāng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the Prince of Yùzhāng, General of the Center-West),
and concurrently Supervisor of the Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng (Assistant Administrator of Dānyáng).
He was successively promoted to Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (Attendant-in-Ordinary),
Mìshūjiān (Director of the Imperial Library),
and Sītú Zuǒ Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk of the Minister of Works, Left Division).
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng (525 CE),
he served in the Dōnggōng Xuéshì Shěng (Scholars' Department of the Eastern Palace).
In the third year of Dàtōng (529 CE),
he died,
aged fifty-nine.
Xiāo Jǐ
zi Déxuán, was the son of Qí Qǔjiāng Gōng Yáoxīn.
At the age of ten,
he was able to compose literature.
He was orphaned early,
and had nine younger brothers,
all of whom were young children.
Jǐ's profound affection and harmony
were known throughout the court and the countryside.
He was of a gentle and mild nature,
without contention with others,
and was pure, poor, and self-reliant.
He loved learning
and was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts.
Yáng Gōngzé, the Inspector of Xiāngzhōu,
was a former subordinate of Qǔjiāng.
Whenever he saw Jǐ,
he would say to others:
"This son of Kāng Gōng
can be said to be Huán Língbǎo reborn."
〔一二〕When Gōngzé died,
Jǐ wrote an elegy for him.
He was then fifteen years old.
Shěn Yuē saw it and was amazed,
saying to his uncle Cài Zǔn:
"Yesterday I saw the elegy for Yáng Píngnán by your excellent nephew.
It is no less than the works of Xīyì,
and it verifies the blessings of Kāng Gōng's accumulated virtues."
He began his career as a Zuǒ Láng in the Bureau of Authorship,
then became Lúlíng Wáng Wénxué,
Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and was in charge of records.
He was promoted to Shùzǐ,
Zhōngshū Shìláng,
and Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng.
In his later years,
he devoted himself exclusively to Buddhism.
He served as the Administrator of Xīn'ān,
a commandery abundant in mountains and waters,
which was particularly to his liking.
He traveled according to his nature,
and thus wrote an account of it.
He died in office.
His son Wéi,
zi Yuánzhuān,
〔一三〕also had literary talent.
He rose to the positions of Tàizǐ Shèrén
and Yǒngkāng Lìng.
The court historian remarked: "The likes of Wáng Guī
all achieved fame and reputation.
Having met with favorable times,
their talents and abilities were each displayed,
which is excellent.
Xiāo Qià's compositions at Dāngtú
showed him to be a magnificent wordsmith.
Liú Xiàoyí and his brothers
all became prominent through their writings.
Gentlemen know that the Liáng dynasty had indeed produced talented individuals."
Textual Notes
Biographies 36: Zāng Dùn (younger brother Jué), Fù Qí
Zāng Dùn,
zi Xuānqīng, was a native of Jǔ, Dōngguǎn.
His great-grandfather Táo was
Sòng Zuǒ Guānglù Dàfū.
His grandfather Tánzhī was
Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū.
His father Wèizhēn
was widely read in literature and history,
and possessed talent and ability. In his youth, he was recognized by his maternal cousin Zhōu Yǒng of Rúnán.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
he began his career as a Lǐngjūn Zhǔbù.
The person he served was
Qí Wǔdì.
Upon entering Qí,
he successively held the positions of Tàiwèi Jìjiǔ,
Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng,
Jìshì for the two princely establishments of Jiàn'ān and Lúlíng,
Qiánjūn Gōngcáo Shǐ,
Tōngzhí Láng,
Zhōngzhèng of Nánxúzhōu,
and Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng.
When Gāozǔ pacified Jīngyì
and established his hegemon's residence,
Dùn was appointed Piàojì Xíngyù Cānjūn.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed Hòujūn Zīyì Zhōngláng and Nánxúzhōu Biéjià.
He entered the court as Huángmén Láng
and was promoted to Yòujūn Ānchéng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ and Shǎofù Qīng.
He was then sent out as Administrator of Xīn'ān,
where he earned a reputation for competence.
Returning to court, he served as Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
Sīnóng Qīng,
and Tàiwèi Zhǎngshǐ.
He observed mourning for his birth mother,
living in a hut by her tomb for three years.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Tíngwèi Qīng.
He was sent out again as Ānchéng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ and Jiāngxià Tàishǒu,
and died in office.
Dùn, as a child, studied the Five Classics under the recluse Zhūgě Qú of Lángxié,
mastering their chapters and sentences.
Qú always had dozens or hundreds of students,
but Dùn, among them,
never formed close associations or rivalries.
Qú found him extraordinary
and exclaimed:
"This student is a great talent,
fit to be a king's advisor!"
He first served as Fǔjūn Xíng Cānjūn,
then was promoted to Shàngshū Zhōngbīng Láng.
Dùn had a handsome demeanor
and good deportment.
Whenever he presented reports,
Gāozǔ was very pleased.
He was appointed concurrently Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén,
then Ányòu Lùshì Cānjūn,
while retaining his position as Shèrén.
Dùn was filial.
While on night duty with his father at the Tíngwèi,
his mother, Lady Liú, at home,
suddenly died during the night.
His left middle finger suddenly ached,
preventing him from sleeping.
At dawn,
a messenger from home indeed reported the terrible news;
such was his spiritual connection.
Before his mourning period for his mother was over,
his father also died.
Dùn observed mourning for five years,
not leaving his hut.
His body became emaciated and withered,
so much so that his family no longer recognized him.
A local, Wáng Duān, reported his situation,
and Gāozǔ praised him,
ordering repeated exhortations to make him desist.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng,
then transferred to Zhōngshū Láng,
again concurrently Zhōngshū Shèrén,
promoted to Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng,
and served as Dōngzhōngláng Wǔlíng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ,
managing affairs for the princely establishment, prefecture, and state,
and concurrently as Huìjī Jùn Chéng.
Upon his return, he was appointed Shǎofù Qīng,
concurrently Bùbīng Xiàowèi,
and then promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng.
Dùn was upright and resolute by nature,
and served very competently in the Censorate.
In the second month of the fifth year of Zhōngdàtōng,
Gāozǔ visited Tóngtài Temple to lecture,
and held a grand assembly for the four monastic orders.
Tens of thousands of people were present.
A trained elephant, presented by Nányuè,
suddenly went wild among the crowd.
The imperial carriage, feather guards, and all those assembled were terrified and scattered.
Only Dùn and Sǎnqí Láng Péi Zhīlǐ remained composed and fearless.
Gāozǔ greatly praised them.
Soon, an edict was issued,
adding the title of Sǎnqí Chángshì.
Before he was invested,
another edict stated:
"To command the entire six armies,
one must not appoint those without talent.
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng and newly appointed Sǎnqí Chángshì Dùn
possesses loyal and careful intentions,
and is discerning and cautious in his actions.
He is fair and impartial in office
and diligent and dedicated in his duties.
He will surely be able to manage these military affairs.
He may concurrently lead the armies (Lǐngjūn),
and retain his former position as Chángshì."
In the second year of Dàtóng,
he was promoted to Zhōng Lǐngjūn.
The Lǐngjūn oversaw the critical military affairs of the empire,
and the supervisory duties were many.
Dùn was quick-witted and capable,
with strong character,
skilled at handling complex matters,
and his official duties were well managed.
In the Tiānjiān era,
Xiāo Jǐng, Marquis of Wúpíng, held this position,
and gained a good reputation.
Now, Dùn succeeded him.
In the fifth year,
he was sent out to serve as Rénwēi Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Wú County.
He had not held the office for a full term
when he submitted his resignation due to illness.
He was appointed Guānglù Dàfū
and given the Golden Seal and Purple Cord.
In the seventh year,
when his illness improved,
he was reinstated as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the ninth year,
he died,
at the age of sixty-six.
An imperial edict mourning his death was issued that very day.
He was posthumously granted Shìzhōng,
with the position of Lǐngjūn retained as before.
He was provided with funeral items from the Dōngyuán Mìqì,
one set of court robes,
one suit of clothes,
and money and cloth varying according to rank.
His posthumous name was Zhōng.
His son, Zāng Chángbó,
courtesy name Mènghóng,
was Internal Historian of Guìyáng.
His second son, Zhòngbó,
was Magistrate of Qū'ā.
Zāng Dùn's younger brother was Zāng Jué.
Zāng Jué, courtesy name Xiànqīng,
was also praised for his competence and integrity.
He first served as a mobilizing Staff Officer for the Xīzhōng Láng,
and then as Shàngshū Zhǔkè Láng.
He entered the court to concurrently hold the position of Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was successively promoted to Zhèngyuán Láng,
Hónglú Qīng,
while retaining the position of Shèrén as before.
He was promoted to Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
but before taking up the post,
he was sent out as Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān.
The commandery was located amidst mountains and seas,
where bandits and fugitives often gathered.
Although the previous officials with a salary of Two Thousand Dàn had raised troops to suppress and arrest them,
the banditry did not cease.
Upon Zāng Jué's arrival,
he proclaimed virtuous governance and moral transformation.
All the vicious elements
came out carrying their children on their backs,
the residents returned to their occupations,
and trade and travel flowed smoothly.
However, his administration was strict, harsh, and lacked compassion.
He would apply caning and penalties to officials and common people even for minor offenses.
The common people called him
"Zāng Hǔ" (Tiger Zāng).
Upon returning, he was appointed Cányì Cānjūn to the Píqí, Prince of Lúlíng,
and again concurrently served as Shèrén.
He was promoted to Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì,
concurrently serving as Sīnóng Qīng,
retaining the position of Shèrén as before.
In the eighth year of Dàtóng,
he died in office,
at the age of forty-eight.
Throughout Zāng Jué's time in office,
matters within his jurisdiction, major issues, and cases that the Lántái and Tíngwèi could not decide,
were ordered to be all referred to Zāng Jué.
Zāng Jué's discernment and judgment were precise and detailed,
and he always found the proper resolution.
After Zāng Jué died,
there was someone who beat the drum of appeal and lodged a complaint,
requesting that the matter be referred to a "pure and upright Shèrén."
Gāozǔ said:
"Since Zāng Jué is gone,
there is no one to whom this matter can be referred."
This shows the extent to which he was recognized.
His son, Fù Cāo,
was Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng.
Fù Qí, courtesy name Jǐngpíng,
was a native of Língzhōu in Běidì.
His great-grandfather, Fù Rén,
was the Tàicháng of the Sòng dynasty.
His grandfather, Fù Yǎn,
served as Magistrate of Shānyīn during the Qí period,
and possessed administrative talent.
He was promoted directly from county magistrate to Inspector of Yì Prefecture.
His father, Fù Huì,
during the Tiānjiān era,
held the offices of Magistrate of Shānyīn and Jiànkāng in succession.
He also had a reputation for ability,
and his highest office reached Píqí Cányì.
Fù Qí first became a student of the Mingjīng section at the Guózǐ.
He began his official career as Zuǒ Chángshì to the Prince of Nánkāng.
He was promoted to Xíng Cānjūn,
concurrently serving as Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng.
He resigned due to mourning his mother,
and observed the rites of mourning fully.
After the mourning period ended,
he was disabled by illness for a long time.
At that time, the Northern Altar (Běijiāo) was being reconstructed.
Fù Qí was initially appointed to supervise the construction work.
When the project was completed,
he was appointed Magistrate of Shǐxīn.
Among the county residents, there was a man who died after being beaten by an antagonist during a fight.
The deceased's family reported the case to the commandery.
The commandery arrested the culprit
and subjected him to intensive interrogation and torture.
He ultimately refused to admit guilt.
The commandery then transferred the jail and the case to the county.
Fù Qí immediately ordered his restraints removed
and questioned him with gentle words.
He immediately confessed.
By law, he was subject to the death penalty.
As the winter solstice festival was approaching,
Fù Qí released him to return home,
instructing him to return to prison one day after the festival.
The court functionaries strenuously objected, saying:
"Such things existed in ancient times,
but they cannot be practiced now."
Fù Qí said:
"If he should betray trust,
the county magistrate shall take the blame;
you officials need not worry."
The man ultimately returned exactly as scheduled.
The Grand Administrator was deeply amazed and praised him,
and immediately reported the situation.
When Fù Qí later left the county,
all the people, regardless of age,
came out beyond the border to bow and send him off.
The sound of their weeping and wailing
was heard for dozens of Lǐ.
Upon reaching the capital,
he was appointed Tíngwèi Zhèng,
and concurrently served as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén.
He was promoted to Jìshì Cānjūn to the Níngyuǎn, Prince of Yuèyáng,
retaining the position of Shèrén as before.
He was sent out as Magistrate of Jiànkāng,
but was dismissed for a matter related to public affairs.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Shèrén.
He was successively promoted to Ānxī Zhōng Jìshì,
and Zhènnán Cányì Cānjūn,
retaining the concurrent position of Shèrén as before.
Fù Qí
was broadly knowledgeable and skilled in diplomatic debate.
During the Dàtóng period,
peace was established with Wèi.
Their envoys came twice a year,
and Fù Qí was constantly tasked with meeting them.
In the first year of Tàiqīng
he was successively promoted to Grand Coachman (Tàipú),
Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng),
while retaining his position as Palace Attendant (Shèrén).
He served in the palace for over ten years,
handling crucial and confidential affairs,
second only to Zhū Yì.
In the winter of this year,
Xiāo Yuānmíng, the Marquis of Zhēnyáng and Governor of Yùzhōu, led his troops to attack Péngchéng.
His army was defeated and he was captured by Wèi.
In the second year
Xiāo Yuānmíng sent an envoy back,
stating that the Wèi people wished to reopen friendly relations.
An imperial edict ordered the relevant officials and close ministers to determine a course of action.
Zhū Yì, the General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi), said:
“Gāo Chéng’s intention
is likely to continue the friendly ties,
not breaking the former peace.
The frontier can thereby achieve quietude from bandits and rest for the people,
which is beneficial to the state.”
The deliberators generally agreed with this.
Fù Qí alone said:
“Since Gāo Chéng has just attained his ambition,
and his power is not weak,
why would he need peace?
This must be a ruse;
thus he arranged for the Marquis of Zhēnyáng to send an envoy,
causing Hóu Jǐng to suspect that Zhēnyáng would be exchanged for him.
If Hóu Jǐng feels uneasy,
he will surely plan disaster and rebellion.
If we now permit Chéng to establish friendly relations,
we will fall exactly into his trap.
Moreover, Péngchéng
lost an army last year, and the army suffered another defeat recently at Wōyáng.
If we immediately seek peace now,
it will further display the weakness of the state.
If you follow my humble opinion,
this peace agreement should not be granted.”
Zhū Yì and others adamantly insisted,
and Gāozǔ consequently followed Yì’s suggestion.
When the peace envoys were dispatched,
Hóu Jǐng indeed held this suspicion,
and repeatedly submitted memorials requesting the envoys be recalled.
The emperor merely gave evasive replies.
By the eighth month,
he raised an army and rebelled.
In the tenth month,
he invaded the capital,
and requested that Zhū Yì be executed.
In the third year
Fù Qí was promoted to General of the Central Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn),
with his position as Palace Attendant remaining unchanged.
In the second month,
Hóu Jǐng submitted a memorial before the palace gate,
begging to be granted the four prefectures east of the Yangtze
to settle his subordinates,
promising to lift the siege and return to his post.
An imperial edict granted this.
An oath was then sworn west of the city,
