and Hóu Jǐng requested that the Prince of Xuānchéng be sent out to accompany him.
Fù Qí strongly insisted that the Prince of Xuānchéng was too important as the emperor’s legitimate successor
to be allowed to go,
and instead the Duke of Shíchéng, Dà Kuǎn, was sent to accompany him.
After the alliance with Hóu Jǐng was concluded,
the civil and military officials in the city were ecstatic,
hoping the siege would be lifted.
Fù Qí alone said to the assembly:
“The rebel raised his army in revolt,
and seeks peace before achieving his goal.
With the sentiments of a barbarian and the heart of a beast,
he absolutely cannot be trusted.
This peace will ultimately be a deception by the rebel.”
Everyone resented and blamed him for this.
When Hóu Jǐng broke the alliance,
none failed to sigh in admiration.
Soon after, there was an imperial decree
that, in recognition of Fù Qí’s diligent service,
he be enfeoffed as Marquis of Nánfēng County,
with an estate of five hundred households,
but he adamantly declined to accept.
When the palace city fell,
Fù Qí, suffering from illness, left the siege area
and died in his residence.
Yáo Chá, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, said: Whenever affairs are undertaken, success is determined by planning;
thus, in ten thousand endeavors, no strategy will be overlooked.
This statement is truly reliable.
Fù Qí recognized the falsity of the Qí state’s peace offer
and can be said to have been skilled in strategic planning.
If Fù Qí’s proposal had been adopted at that time,
the disaster and turmoil of the Tàiqīng era
would certainly not have occurred.
Shēn Zǐ said:
“One word relied upon,
and the world submits.”
Is this not what is meant?
Biographies, Chapter 37: Wéi Càn, Jiāng Zǐyī (disciple Four, son Five), Zhāng Shěng, Shěn Jùn, Liǔ Jìnglǐ
Wéi Càn, courtesy name Chángqiàn,
was the grandson of the Chariot and Cavalry General (Chēqí Jiāngjūn) Ruì,
and the son of Fàng, the Governor of Northern Xūzhōu.
He inherited his father’s temperament,
loved scholarship, and championed integrity.
He was eight feet tall
and had a very imposing appearance.
Initially, he served as Adjutant in the staff of the Prince of Jìn’ān (Jìn’ān Wáng) under the Cloud Banner (Yúnhuī),
and was shortly appointed Judge (Fǎcáo),
then promoted to Adjutant of External Military Affairs (Wàibīng Cānjūn),
concurrently serving as Adjutant of Central Military Affairs (Zhōngbīng).
At that time, Yǔ Zhòngróng of Yǐngchuān and Zhāng Shuài of Wú Jùn,
both renowned figures of the older generation,
were colleagues with Wéi Càn in the same administration,
and maintained friendly relations despite the age gap.
When the Prince was transferred and appointed to Yōngzhōu,
Wéi Càn followed and was transferred to Record Keeper (Jìshì),
concurrently serving as Adjutant of Central Military Affairs as before.
When the Prince was established as Crown Prince,
Wéi Càn was promoted to Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
and entered the Eastern Palace to serve as Leader of the Imperial Guards (Lǐngzhí).
He resigned his post to observe mourning for his father.
Soon after, he was recalled to service as General Who Elicits Remoteness (Zhāoyuǎn Jiāngjūn),
and once again served as Leader of the Imperial Guards.
After the mourning period ended,
he succeeded to the title Marquis of Yǒngchāng County,
and was appointed Consultant (Zīyì) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng under the General Who Guards the West (Ānxī).
He was successively promoted to Grand Coachman of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Pú),
and General of the Left Guard (Zuǒwèi Shuài),
retaining his concurrent position as Leader of the Imperial Guards.
Due to old favors, Wéi Càn
was entrusted with close responsibilities.
Although his posts changed frequently,
he always remained in the palace guard.
He gained considerable prestige and reputation,
but was arrogant
and not well regarded by his peers at the time.
Zhū Yì, the General of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi), once sharply said to Wéi Càn at a drinking party:
“How dare you already present a face fit for a General of the Central Army (Lǐngjūn) to people!”
In the eleventh year of Zhōngdàtóng
Before he could be installed,
he was sent out as Bearer of Credentials (Chíjié), Area Commander (Dū) of all military affairs of Héngzhōu, General Who Pacifies the Distant (Ānyuǎn Jiāngjūn), and Governor of Héngzhōu.
The Crown Prince went out to see him off at Xīntíng,
and held Wéi Càn’s hand, saying:
“This will not be a long separation between us.”
In the first year of Tàiqīng
not long after Wéi Càn arrived at the prefecture,
he memorialized requesting to resign his post.
In the second year,
he was summoned to serve as Sànqí Chángshì.
Wěi Càn returned to Lúlíng.
Hearing that Hóu Jǐng was rebelling,
he immediately inspected his troops,
gathering five thousand elite soldiers
and one hundred horses,
and traveled quickly to assist.
Upon reaching Yùzhāng,
he received an order reporting
"the rebels have already crossed Héngjiāng."
Càn immediately consulted with the Grand Administrator (Nèishǐ) Liú Xiàoyí to plan countermeasures.
Xiàoyí said:
"If the situation is truly this critical,
there must be a separate imperial decree.
How can we lightly trust a lone messenger
and rashly cause alarm?
Perhaps it is not true."
At that time, Xiàoyí was hosting a banquet.
Càn was furious,
smashing his cup on the ground and saying:
"The rebels have already crossed the Yangtze River (Jiāng),
immediately threatening the palaces,
and cutting off both water and land routes.
How can there be time for reports?
Even if there is no imperial decree,
how can we remain complacent?
How could Wěi Càn possibly drink wine today!"
He immediately rode out on horseback
and organized his troops for departure.
Just then, the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Duke of Dāngyáng Dàxīn, sent an envoy requesting Càn's presence.
Càn quickly rode to see Dàxīn and said:
"Among the upstream border garrisons,
Jiāngzhōu is the closest to the capital.
Considering your Highness’s inclination and plan,
you should indeed be at the forefront.
However, the middle reach of the river holds great responsibility
and requires coordination and contact;
the garrison cannot be left vacant.
For now, simply demonstrate strength,
move the garrison to Pénchéng,
and send a subordinate general to follow me;
that should suffice for the task."
Dàxīn agreed with this
and sent the Middle Commander (Zhōng Bīng) Liǔ Xīn leading two thousand soldiers to accompany Càn.
Càn left all his family dependents in Jiāngzhōu
and proceeded rapidly by light boat.
Upon reaching Nánzhōu,
Càn's maternal cousin (Wàidì), the Inspector of Sīzhōu, Liǔ Zhònglǐ, also arrived at Héngjiāng, leading over ten thousand infantry and cavalry.
Càn immediately sent provisions and armaments to supply them,
and distributed his private gold and silk to reward the soldiers.
Previously,
the General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn), Prince of Póyáng Fàn, had also sent the Inspector of Xī Yùzhōu, Péi Zhīgāo, along with his eldest son Sī, from Héféi,
leading the troops from west of the river (Jiāngxī) to hurry to the capital (Jīngshī).
They garrisoned at Zhānggōng Zhōu,
awaiting the arrival of the various armies from the upper reaches.
At this time,
Zhīgāo sent boats to ferry Zhònglǐ across,
and they combined their forces, advancing to garrison at Wángyóu Yuàn.
Càn proposed appointing Zhònglǐ as the Grand Commander (Dà Dūdū),
and informing the various downstream armies.
Péi Zhīgāo, relying on his age and rank,
felt ashamed to be subordinate to him,
and thus said:
"His Excellency Liǔ (Liǔ Jiéxià) is an Inspector (Zhōujiàng).
Why must I also be subject to his discipline (whip and board)?"
For several days, no decision was reached.
Càn then spoke forthrightly to the assembly:
"Now we are jointly answering the national emergency,
and our duty lies in eliminating the rebels.
The reason we recommend Inspector Liǔ of Sīzhōu
is precisely because he has long defended the borders,
and is already feared by Hóu Jǐng;
moreover, his soldiers and horses are elite,
none surpass them.
If we discuss rank order,
Liǔ is below Càn;
if we speak of age,
he is also younger than Càn.
It is solely for the sake of the state
that we should no longer argue.
In today's situation,
the priority is harmony among the generals.
If people are not united,
the great task will fail.
Duke Péi is an established veteran of the court,
whose age and virtue are already high.
How can he harbor personal feelings
and obstruct the great plan?
Càn requests permission to resolve this matter for all of you."
He then went by himself in a single boat to Zhīgāo’s camp,
and sternly admonished him:
"If the previous deliberation of the generals
is not agreeable to Yùzhōu,
know that the two palaces are in imminent danger,
and the cunning bandit is overwhelming the heavens.
Ministers and sons must strive together with one heart.
How can we contradict each other?
If Yùzhōu insists on maintaining a difference of opinion,
then the arrowheads will immediately find their mark."
Zhīgāo lowered his head and wept, saying:
"I have received great national favor,
and naturally should lead the soldiers.
I merely regret my advanced age and infirmity,
which prevent me from dedicating my life.
I look eagerly to Governor Liǔ (Liǔ Shǐjūn) to jointly pacify the fierce rebellion,
assuming the consensus had already been reached,
and that my old self was no longer needed.
If there must be suspicion,
I am willing to show you my loyal heart."
Thereupon, the generals settled the discussion,
and only then was Zhònglǐ able to advance his troops.
They next reached Xīntíng.
The rebels formed a battle array at Zhōngxīng Sì.
They held their positions until evening,
and then each side withdrew.
That night,
Zhònglǐ entered Càn’s camp,
organizing the various armies.
They were to fight the next day.
Each general had assigned positions to defend,
and Càn was ordered to station at Qīngtáng.
Qīngtáng was directly on the road to Shítou.
Càn worried that since the stockade walls had not yet been erected,
the rebels would surely fight for it.
He was quite apprehensive,
and said to Zhònglǐ:
"This subordinate official lacks the talent to repel invaders;
I only wish to die for the country.
Your Excellency must carefully consider what is appropriate,
so as not to suffer loss or defeat."
Zhònglǐ replied:
"The stockade at Qīngtáng,
being close to the river bank (Huáizhǔ),
is where we intend to berth all our provisions, supplies, and ships.
This is a crucial matter,
and only you, Elder Brother, can handle it.
If you feel the troops are few,
I will dispatch more forces to assist you."
He then sent the General of the Imperial Retinue (Zhí Gé Jiāngjūn) Liú Shúyìn with troops to assist Càn,
leading his division to advance both by water and land.
At that time, it was dim and foggy.
The soldiers lost their way.
By the time they reached Qīngtáng,
the night was already half over,
and the fortifications were not yet complete by dawn.
Jǐng climbed the gate tower of Chánlíng Sì,
saw that Càn’s camp was not yet established,
and immediately led his elite soldiers to attack.
The Deputy Commander (Jūnfù) Wáng Chángmào advised holding the stockade and awaiting them,
but Càn refused.
He ordered the Army Commander (Jūnzhǔ) Zhèng Yì to strike back,
and commanded Liú Shúyìn to use the naval forces to cut off the rebels’ retreat.
Shúyìn was cowardly and dared not advance,
so Yì was defeated.
The rebels followed their victory into the camp.
Càn's attendants tried to lead him away from the rebels,
but Càn did not move.
He continued to shout at his sons and younger relatives to fight hard.
When almost all his soldiers were dead,
he was consequently killed,
at the age of fifty-four.
Càn’s son Ní and his three younger brothers Zhù, Jǐng, and Gòu, as well as his cousin Áng, all died in battle.
Several hundred of his relatives also died.
The rebels sent Càn’s head to the palace gate
to display it to those inside the city.
Tàizōng heard of it and wept, saying:
"The hope of the state
rested entirely on Lord Wěi.
How unfortunate
that he was the first to die on the battlefield."
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the title General Protector of the Army (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn).
When Shìzǔ pacified Hóu Jǐng,
he was posthumously granted the canonical title Zhōngzhēn (Loyal and Constant).
Posthumous appointments were also granted to Zhù, Jǐng, Gòu, and Ní, all as Palace Clerks (Zhōngshū Láng),
and Áng as Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì).
Càn's eldest son was Zāng,
courtesy name Jūnlǐ.
He successively served as Secretariat Bureau Clerk of the Three Dukes (Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng),
Commandant of the Heir Apparent's Establishment (Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ),
and Commander of the Eastern Palace Guards (Dōnggōng Lǐngzhí).
When Hóu Jǐng arrived,
he led troops to garrison at Xīhuá Mén.
When the city fell,
he fled to Jiāngzhōu,
gathered his old troops,
occupied Yùzhāng,
and was subsequently murdered by his own subordinates.
Jiāng Zǐyī, courtesy name Yuánzhēn,
was a native of Kǎochéng, Jìyáng.
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Tǒng, Sànqí Chángshì of the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Fǎchéng,
served as a court attendant (Fèng Cháoqǐng) during the Tiānjiān era.
Jiāng Zǐyī 少年時便喜好學習，
有志向和操守，
因為家境貧寒，缺乏供養，
於是終身素食。
起初擔任王國侍郎，
奉朝請。
他請求允許到秘閣觀閱書籍，
Gāozǔ 答應了他，
並下敕令讓他在華林省值守。
他的姑夫、右衛將軍 Zhū Yì，
權勢顯赫，在朝中擔任要職，
休沐之日，
賓客雲集，
但 Jiāng Zǐyī 從未登門拜訪，
其高潔如此。
他逐漸升遷為尚書儀曹郎，
出任 Suíchāng 和 Qū'ē 兩縣的縣令，
都留下了良好的政績。
後被授予通直散騎侍郎之職。
又出任戎昭將軍、
南津校尉。
他的弟弟 Jiāng Zǐsì，
曾任金部郎，
Dàtóng 初年，
升遷為右丞。
兄弟二人的性情都剛烈。
Jiāng Zǐsì 自右丞之位上呈奏疏，
極力陳述政事的得失，
Gāozǔ 非常讚賞他，
下詔令尚書省詳細審議並施行。
左民郎 Shěn Jiǒng 和少府丞 Gù Yú 曾上奏事情不獲批准，
Gāozǔ 厲聲呵斥他們，
Jiāng Zǐsì 於是快步上前代替 Shěn Jiǒng 等人應對，
言辭非常激切，
Gāozǔ 怒而下令將他捆綁起來，
Jiāng Zǐsì 踞地不從，
Gāozǔ 的怒氣也因此消解，
於是釋放了他，
但仍免去了他的職務。
等到 Hóu Jǐng 造反，
攻陷 Lìyáng，
從 Héngjiāng 準備渡江時，
Jiāng Zǐyī 率領舟師一千餘人，
在下游準備阻擊他，
他的副將 Dǒng Táoshēng 家在長江以北，
於是與其黨羽四散逃走。
Jiāng Zǐyī 於是退回 Nánzhōu，
重新收攏餘眾，
徒步前往京師。
叛賊也隨後而至，
Jiāng Zǐyī 稟告 Tàizōng 說：
「叛賊的包圍尚未合攏，
仍然可以出擊蕩平，
如果營壘一旦堅固，
就無處施展武力了。」
他請求與他的弟弟 Jiāng Zǐsì、Jiāng Zǐwǔ 率領所屬的一百餘人，
打開 Chéngmíngmén 門去挑戰叛賊。
Tàizōng 答應了。
Jiāng Zǐyī 於是身先士卒，
拔出長戈獨自前進，
眾叛賊從兩側夾攻他，
跟隨的人沒有一個敢於繼上，
Jiāng Zǐsì、Jiāng Zǐwǔ 見事態危急，
互相拉著奔向叛賊，
都遇害了。
詔書說：
「故戎昭將軍、通直散騎侍郎、南津校尉 Jiāng Zǐyī，
前尚書右丞 Jiāng Zǐsì，
東宮直殿主帥 Jiāng Zǐwǔ，
他們的禍事和犧牲已經聽聞，
實在令人憐憫和悲傷，
為國犧牲的待遇應當加等，
這也是舊有的規章。
可追贈 Jiāng Zǐyī 為給事黃門侍郎，
Jiāng Zǐsì 為中書侍郎，
Jiāng Zǐwǔ 為散騎侍郎。」
Hóu Jǐng 平定後，
Shìzǔ 又追贈 Jiāng Zǐyī 為侍中，
諡號 Yìzǐ；
Jiāng Zǐsì 為黃門侍郎，
諡號 Yìzǐ；
Jiāng Zǐwǔ 為中書侍郎，
諡號 Lièzǐ。
Jiāng Zǐyī 續寫了《黃圖》以及 Bān Gù 的
「九品」之說，
並有辭賦文章數十篇，
流傳於世。
Zhāng Shèng 字 Sīshān，
是鎮北將軍 Zhāng Jì 的兒子。
他少年時方正雅致，
有志向和操守，
善於清言。
他的父親在 Qīngzhōu 任職時，
被當地百姓所殺害，
Zhāng Shèng 感於家禍，
終身素食布衣，
手不持刀刃。
被州府舉為秀才。
起初擔任秘書郎，
歷任太子舍人，
洗馬，
司徒左西掾，
中書郎。
出任永陽內史，
回京後被授予中軍宣城王司馬、散騎常侍之職。
又出任鎮南湘東王長史、尋陽太守。
Zhōngdàtóng 元年，
被徵召為太府卿，
不久升遷為吳興太守。
Tàiqīng 二年，
Hóu Jǐng 圍攻京城，
Zhāng Shèng 派遣弟弟 Zhāng Yī 率領郡兵數千人前往救援。
Tàiqīng 三年，
宮城陷落，
御史中丞 Shěn Jùn 避難東歸，
Zhāng Shèng 前往拜訪並對他說：
「叛賊猖獗，
國家危亡受辱，
正是我等臣子效命之時。
如今我想收集兵力，
據守在貴鄉。
如果天道無靈，
忠義之節無法伸展，
即使因此而死，
也實在沒有遺憾。」
Shěn Jùn 說：
「鄙郡雖小，
仗義抗逆，
誰敢不從呢！」
於是堅決勸 Zhāng Shèng 舉義。
於是 Zhāng Shèng 收集士卒，
修繕城壘。
當時 Shàolíng Wáng 東逃至 Qiántáng，
聞訊後，
派遣檄文授予 Zhāng Shèng 征東將軍之職，
加秩中二千石。
Zhāng Shèng 說：
「朝廷危急，
天子蒙難，
今日我怎能有心情，
再接受榮耀的封號呢！」
於是留下了檄文。
叛賊的行臺 Liú Shénmào 攻破 Yìxīng，
派遣使者勸說 Zhāng Shèng 說：
「如果早日投降歸附，
當仍以郡守之職安置你，
並再加爵賞。」
Zhāng Shèng 命人斬殺其使者，
隨後派遣軍主 Wáng Xióng 等人率兵在 Lí Dú 迎擊他們，
擊敗了 Liú Shénmào，
Liú Shénmào 敗退。
Hóu Jǐng 聽聞 Liú Shénmào 戰敗，
於是派遣他的中軍 Hóu Zǐjiàn 率領精兵兩萬人，
協助 Liú Shénmào 攻打 Zhāng Shèng，
Zhāng Shèng 派遣軍主 Fàn Zhìlǎng 出郡西迎戰，
被 Liú Shénmào 所敗，
退回郡中。
叛賊騎兵乘勝焚燒柵欄，
柵內眾軍士氣渙散。
Zhāng Shèng 於是脫下戎服，
坐在聽事廳中，
叛賊持刀逼近他，
他始終不屈服，
於是將 Zhāng Shèng 逮捕並送給 Hóu Jǐng，
Hóu Jǐng 在都市中將他處刑，
他的子弟一同遇害者有十餘人，
當時他六十二歲。
叛賊平定後，
Shìzǔ 追贈他為侍中、中衛將軍、開府儀同三司。
諡號為 Zhōngzhēnzǐ。
Shěn Jùn 字 Shūyuán，
是吳興武康人。
他的祖父 Shěn Xiàn，
是齊國的散騎常侍，
在《齊史》中有傳。
Shěn Jùn was widely learned when young,
possessing talent and capability.
He successively served as Magistrate of Shānyīn, Wú, and Jiànkāng,
all while maintaining a reputation for competence.
He entered government service as Zhōngshū Láng (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat),
and then Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng (Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs).
When Hóu Jǐng approached the capital city,
he was promoted to Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Imperial Censor-in-Chief).
At this time, external reinforcements had all arrived,
and Hóu Jǐng submitted a memorial requesting peace,
which the imperial edict granted.
After the alliance was made,
Jǐng, knowing that there was sickness and plague within the city,
again harbored treacherous designs,
and hesitated to leave.
After several days,
the Crown Prince ordered Shěn Jùn to visit Jǐng’s location.
Jǐng said:
"It is already becoming warm;
it is no longer the time to move.
With an army of 100,000 men,
how can we possibly depart?
I wish to remain and render service to the imperial court.
You must inform the court of this for me."
Shěn Jùn replied:
"General, this assertion of yours
means that your intent is to capture the city.
The military supplies and provisions within the city
can still last for one hundred days.
The General’s own stored provisions are exhausted,
while the state's reinforcement armies are gathering outside.
Upon what will your army of 100,000 men
depend?
Yet you utter these words,
seeking to coerce the imperial court, is that it?"
Jǐng placed his blade across his knee
and glared at him, shouting a rebuke.
Shěn Jùn, maintaining a stern demeanor, rebuked Jǐng, saying:
"Your Excellency is personally a subject of the Emperor,
yet you raised troops against the palace gate.
The Sacred Ruler extended his grace, pardoning your transgression,
and an alliance has already been concluded.
The blood of the covenant has not yet dried,
yet you are turning your back on it.
Shěn Jùn is sixty years old
and moreover an envoy of the Son of Heaven.
Life and death are determined by fate;
how could I fear the blade of a rebellious minister!"
He walked out without looking back.
Jǐng said:
"That is a true Sīzhí (Director of Justice)."
However, he secretly resented him.
When Zhāng Shèng was defeated,
he requested Shěn Jùn be handed over to him in order to kill him.
Liǔ Jìnglǐ
was the grandson of the Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establisher of a Prefecture with Authority Equal to the Three Dukes), Qìngyuǎn.
His father, Jīn,
was the Crown Prince's Zhānshì (Chief Administrator).
Jìnglǐ and his elder brother, Zhònglǐ,
were both famous from a young age for their courage and valor.
He started his career as Zuòzuò Zuǒ Láng (Assistant Gentleman of the Secretariat),
and was gradually promoted to Prefect of Fúfēng.
When Hóu Jǐng crossed the Yangtze River,
Jìnglǐ led three thousand cavalry and infantry to answer the call for reinforcement.
Upon arriving at the capital,
he occupied the Qīngxī Dài embankment,
and frequently fought against Jǐng.
He was the first to ascend and penetrate the enemy lines,
establishing a considerable reputation for military might.
When the Terrace City (Táichéng) fell,
Jìnglǐ and Zhònglǐ were both received by Jǐng.
Jǐng sent Zhònglǐ to plan operations upstream,
keeping Jìnglǐ as a hostage,
and made him Hùjūn (Protector of the Army).
When Jǐng gave a farewell banquet for Zhònglǐ at Hòuzhǔ,
Jìnglǐ secretly said to Zhònglǐ:
"Jǐng is attending the meeting now.
I, Jìnglǐ, will hold him,
and you, elder brother, draw your waist-saber
and immediately hack him to death.
Even if I die, I will have no regrets."
Zhònglǐ admired his bold words
and agreed.
When they had been drinking several rounds,
Jìnglǐ signaled to Zhònglǐ.
Zhònglǐ saw that the guards were strict,
and dared not move.
Thus, the plan did not succeed.
Later, when Jǐng launched an expedition against Jìnxī,
Jìnglǐ and the Prince of Nánkāng, Xiāo Huìlǐ, conspired to attack his city.
They fixed a date and were about to depart,
but the Marquis of Jiàn'ān, Xiāo Bēn, found out and informed against them,
and consequently, they were executed.
The Court Historian remarks: If righteousness is valued above life,
as declared in the ancient canon,
this is indeed what the former sages treasured.
Therefore, Mèngzǐ (Mencius) stated that life is what I desire,
and righteousness is also what I desire.
If these two cannot both be attained,
one should choose righteousness over life.
Men like Zhāng Shèng and his companions
sacrificed their bodies and died for their loyalty,
going to their deaths as if returning home.
Their heroic spirit and resolute energy
have covered the past and the present,
letting gentlemen know that the Liáng dynasty indeed had loyal subjects.
Biography Collection Thirty-Eight: The Eleven Princes of Tàizōng, and The Two Sons of Shìzǔ
Tàizōng's Empress Wáng bore the Afflicted Crown Prince Dàqì,
and the Prince of Nánjùn, Dàlián;
Concubine Chén Shūróng bore the Prince of Xúnyáng, Dàxīn;
Lady Zuǒ bore the Prince of Nánhǎi, Dàlín,
and the Prince of Ānlù, Dàchūn;
Lady Xiè bore the Duke of Liúyáng, Dàyǎ;
Lady Zhāng bore the Prince of Xīnxīng, Dàzhuāng;
Concubine Bāo Zhāohuá bore the Prince of Xīyáng, Dàjūn;
Lady Fàn bore the Prince of Wǔníng, Dàwēi;
Concubine Chǔ Xiūhuá bore the Prince of Jiànpíng, Dàqiú;
Lady Chén bore the Prince of Yì'ān, Dàxīn (same name, different character);
Lady Zhū bore the Prince of Suíjiàn, Dàzhì.
The rest of his sons
are not recorded in this book.
The Prince of Xúnyáng, Dàxīn, had the courtesy name Rénshù.
He was intelligent and perceptive in his youth,
and skilled at composition.
In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (532 CE),
as an Imperial Grandson, he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Dāngyáng,
with an estate of 1,500 households.
In the first year of Dàtóng (535 CE),

he was appointed as Envoy with Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of the Military Affairs of Yǐng, Nán, Běi, Sī, Dìng, and Xīn Six Prefectures, General of Light Chariots, and Governor of Yǐng Prefecture.
He was thirteen years old at the time,
and Tàizōng, considering his youth,
feared he might not grasp the feelings of the people,
and admonished him, saying:
"Regardless of whether matters are big or small,
fully entrust them to the acting officials.
You do not need to concern yourself with even the slightest detail."
Although Dàxīn did not personally manage the affairs of the prefecture,
his every pronouncement was in accord with reason,
which astonished and convinced everyone.
In the seventh year (541 CE),
he was summoned to serve as Shìzhōng (Attendant-in-Ordinary) and concurrently Military Commander of Shítóu Garrison.
In the first year of Tàiqīng (547 CE),
he was sent out as General of the Cloud Banners and Governor of Jiāng Prefecture.
In the second year (548 CE),
Hóu Jǐng invaded the capital district.
Dàxīn recruited and assembled soldiers,
and people from near and far returned to him.
His forces reached several tens of thousands,
and he led them along with the armies from the upper reaches of the river to reinforce the imperial palace.
In the third year (549 CE),
when the city fell,
the Marquis of Shàngjiǎ, Xiāo Sháo, fled south
and proclaimed a secret imperial edict,
adding the title Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Regular Attendant),
and advancing his designation to General Who Pacifies the South.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xúnyáng,
with an estate of 2,000 households.
Initially,
Zhuāng Tiě, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Lìyáng, surrendered the city to Hóu Jǐng.
Afterward, he brought his mother and came to defect.
Dàxīn, considering Tiě to be an old general,
treated him with great courtesy.
Military affairs
were completely entrusted to him,
and he was subsequently made Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Yùzhāng.
Hóu Jǐng repeatedly sent troops westward to raid and pillage.
Dàxīn always ordered Tiě to defeat them,
and the bandits were unable to advance.
At that time, Fàn, the Prince of Póyáng, led his forces, abandoned Héféi,
and camped at Zhàkǒu,
waiting for all the reinforcing troops to gather,
intending to advance together.
Dàxīn heard of this
and sent an order for Fàn to move west,
stationing him at Pénchéng.
The grain and provisions supplied were very generous,
and he sought to collaborate with him to eliminate the disaster.
Soon after, Zhuāng Tiě occupied Yùzhāng and rebelled.
Dàxīn ordered Wéi Yuē (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn) and other generals to attack him.
Tiě was defeated
and again begged for surrender.
Sì, the Heir Apparent of Póyáng, had previously associated with Tiě.
Therefore, he praised him, saying his talent and strategy were extraordinary,
and moreover, he was an old general.
If they wished
to undertake a great enterprise, they should utilize his strength.
If he surrendered to Jiāngzhōu,
his life would certainly not be spared.
Sì requested to intercede for him.
Fàn agreed.
Consequently, he sent the general Hóu Tián to lead five thousand elite soldiers to rescue Tiě,
and they attacked and destroyed the camps of Wéi Yuē and the others by night.
Dàxīn was greatly alarmed upon hearing this.
Thus, a rift arose between the two principalities,
and popular support became divided.
Rèn Yuē, a general of Jǐng, plundered territory until he reached Pénchéng.
Dàxīn sent Wéi Zhì (Sīmǎ) to resist the battle,
but he was defeated.
At that time, he still had over a thousand brave men under his command.
They all advised him, saying:
"Since there are no provisions,
it is difficult to hold the position securely.
If you proceed quickly by light cavalry to Jiànzhōu
to plan for a future endeavor,
that would be the best strategy."
Dàxīn was undecided.
His mother, Chén Shūróng, said:
"Currently, the Son of Heaven (Shèng Yù) is advanced in years,
and the Crown Prince (Chǔ Gōng) is well.
You have long failed to attend to their presence.
Are you not thinking of going to pay respects at the court?
Moreover, I am old,
and you wish to travel far across dangerous roads,
with insufficient provisions?
How can you be called a filial son?
I absolutely will not go."
Thereupon, she beat her chest and wept bitterly.
Dàxīn then stopped the plan.
Subsequently, he made peace with Rèn Yuē.
In the autumn of the second year (of Dàbǎo),
he was killed,
at the age of twenty-nine.
Dàlín, Prince of Nánhǎi, courtesy name Rénxuān.
In the second year of Dàtóng,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Níngguó County,
with an estate of 1,500 households.
He was intelligent and perceptive in his youth.
At the age of eleven,
he suffered the loss of his mother, Zuǒ Fūren.
His weeping and emaciation
made him known for his filial piety.
Later, he entered the National University (Guóxué),
passed the Mingjīng examination with the highest grade (Jiǎkē),
and was appointed Gentleman of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng).
In the eleventh year (of Dàtóng),
he became Acting Attendant at Court (Zhǎng Jiān Shìzhōng).
He was appointed General of the Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn) and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies of Lángyé and Péngchéng.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
he was appointed Bearer of Credential (Shǐ Chíjié), General Xuānhuì,
and stationed at Xīntíng.
Soon after, he was recalled,
stationed at Duānmén,
and appointed Area Commander-in-Chief (Dūdū) of the various military affairs south of the city.
At the time, those who debated suggested seizing outside goods and wealth,
intending to use them for rewards and gifts.
Dàlín alone said:
"Goods should be used to reward scholars,
but cattle can be used to feast the army."
He ordered cattle to be brought,
obtaining over a thousand head,
and those inside the city relied on this to feed the soldiers.
In the first year of Dàbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nánhǎi Commandery,
with an estate of 2,000 households.
He was appointed Bearer of Credential, Area Commander-in-Chief of the military affairs of Yángzhōu and Nánxúzhōu, General Ānnán, and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yángzhōu.
He was also appointed General Āndōng and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Wú Commandery.
At that time, Zhāng Biāo raised an army for righteousness in Kuàijī.
The Wú natives Lù Lìnggōng and Yǔ Mèngqīng of Yǐngchuān, among others, urged Dàlín to flee and join Biāo.
Dàlín said:
"If Biāo succeeds,
he will not need my strength;
if he is defeated,
it will be attributed to my persuasion.
I cannot go there."
In the autumn of the second year (of Dàbǎo),
he was killed in the commandery,
at the age of twenty-five.
Dàlián, Prince of Nán Commandery, courtesy name Rénjìng.
In his youth, he was outstanding and unrestrained,
and skilled at composition.
His manner was refined and elegant,
he possessed delicate ingenuity,
had a subtle understanding of music,
and was also proficient in painting.
In the second year of Dàtóng,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Línchéng County,
with an estate of 1,500 households.
In the seventh year,
he entered the National University together with the Prince of Nánhǎi,
passed the examination with the highest grade (Jiǎkē),
and was appointed Gentleman of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
In the tenth year,
Gāozǔ visited Zhūfāng.
Dàlián and his elder brother Dàlín accompanied him.
Gāozǔ asked:
"Have you practiced horsemanship?"
They replied:
"We your subjects had not yet received an imperial decree,
and did not dare to practice casually."
An edict commanded that horses be given to them to try.
The Dàlián brothers rode the saddle back and forth,
each mastering the movements of galloping,
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased
and immediately bestowed upon them the horses they rode.
When they submitted a memorial of thanks,
the wording was also exceedingly beautiful.
On another day, Gāozǔ said to Tàizōng:
"Yesterday, I saw Dàlín and Dàlián.
Their bearing is charming,
and sufficient to comfort my old age."
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng),
transferred to Attendant at Court (Shìzhōng),
and shortly thereafter concurrently supervised the military affairs of Shítóu Garrison.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,
he was appointed Bearer of Credential, General of the Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn), and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dōngyángzhōu.
When Hóu Jǐng invaded the capital,
Dàlián led a force of forty thousand to respond.
When Táichéng (the Palace City) fell,
the reinforcing armies dispersed,
and he returned to Yángzhōu.
In the third year,
Tián Lǐngqún, a mountain bandit from Kuàijī, gathered tens of thousands of followers and came to attack.
Dàlián ordered Zhāng Biāo (Zhōngbīng Cānjūn) to attack and execute him.
In the first year of Dàbǎo,
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Nán Commandery,
with an estate of 2,000 households.
Jǐng subsequently sent his generals Zhào Bó'chāo and Liú Shénmào to attack him.
Dàlián prepared his defenses and awaited them.
Coincidentally, his general Liú Yì handed the city over to the bandits.
Dàlián abandoned the city and fled.
Upon reaching Xìn'ān,
he was captured by the bandits.
Hóu Jǐng made him General of the Light Chariots (Qīngchē Jiāngjūn) and Acting Governor of Yángzhōu,
and later promoted him to General Píngnán and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Jiāngzhōu.
Dàlián, having been forced into the hands of the invaders,
sought to escape.
He thus made an agreement with the bandits, saying:
"Military and civil affairs,
I will not involve myself in them.
To determine whether I am alive or dead,
you only need to listen for the sound of the bell."
He wished to restrict those who saw him,
and thereby manage his escape.
The bandits also believed him,
but the plan was not yet executed.
In the autumn of the second year (of Dàbǎo),
he was killed,
at the age of twenty-five.
Ānlù Wáng Dàchūn, courtesy name Rénjīng.
When young, he widely studied books and records.
His nature was innately filial and cautious,
his physique and appearance were magnificent and imposing,
and his waist circumference measured ten *wéi* (circles).
In the sixth year of Dàtóng (540 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Xīfēng County,
with an assigned population of 1,500 households.
He was appointed Minister Attendant of the Central Secretariat (*Zhōngshū Shìláng*).
Later, he became General Who Pacifies the Distant (*Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn*),
and was put in charge of the military affairs of the Shítóu Garrison.
When Hóu Jǐng invaded,
Dàchūn fled to Jīngkǒu,
followed Shàolíng Wáng (Xiāo Lún) to aid the capital,
and fought at Zhōngshān,
where he was captured by the rebels.
After the capital city fell,
in the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Ānlù Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.
He was sent out as Barrier-holding Envoy, General of the Cloud Banners (*Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn*), and Governor of Dōngyáng Prefecture (*Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ*).
In the autumn of the second year (551 CE),
he was killed,
at the age of twenty-two.
Liúyáng Gōng Dàyǎ, courtesy name Rénfēng.
In the ninth year of Dàtóng (543 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Liúyáng County,
with an assigned population of 1,500 households.
He was intelligent and alert when young,
and had a handsome appearance and demeanor,
and was especially beloved by Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ).
In the third year of Tàiqīng (549 CE),
when the capital city fell,
and the rebels had already mounted the walls,
Dàyǎ still ordered his attendants to fight back.
As the number of approaching rebels gradually increased,
he then lowered himself down by rope.
Due to his deep indignation, he contracted an illness,
and passed away,
at the age of seventeen.
Xīnxīng Wáng Dàzhuāng, courtesy name Rénlǐ.
In the ninth year of Dàtóng (543 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Gāotáng County,
with an assigned population of 1,500 households.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīnxīng Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.

He was sent out as Barrier-holding Envoy, Area Commander of All Military Affairs in Nánxú Prefecture (*Dūdū Nánxúzhōu Zhū Jūnshì*), General Who Manifests Awe (*Xuānyì Jiāngjūn*), and Governor of Nánxú Prefecture (*Nánxúzhōu Cìshǐ*).
In the autumn of the second year (551 CE),
he was killed,
at the age of eighteen.
Xīyáng Wáng Dàjūn, courtesy name Rénfǔ.
His nature was generous and steady;
he did not idly jest or play around.
When he was seven years old,
Gāozǔ once asked him what book he was reading,
and he replied,
"I am studying the *Shī* (Classic of Poetry)."
Gāozǔ then ordered him to recite from memory.
His tone and rhythm were clear and elegant,
so Gāozǔ then bestowed upon him a scroll of calligraphic work by Wáng Xīzhī.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Xīyáng Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.
He was sent out as General Who Spreads Benevolence (*Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn*) and Governor of Dānyáng (*Dānyáng Yǐn*).
In the second year (551 CE),
he oversaw Yáng Prefecture (*Yángzhōu*),
but retained his General title.
In the autumn, he was killed,
at the age of thirteen.
Wǔníng Wáng Dàwēi, courtesy name Rénróng.
He had a handsome demeanor and appearance,
and his eyebrows and eyes were like a painting.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Wǔníng Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.
In the second year (551 CE),
he was sent out as General Who Commands Trust (*Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn*) and Governor of Dānyáng (*Dānyáng Yǐn*).
In the autumn of that year,
he was killed,
at the age of thirteen.
Jiànpíng Wáng Dàqiú, courtesy name Rén tǐng.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Jiànpíng Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.
His nature was intelligent and mature early.
Initially,
when Hóu Jǐng besieged the capital city,
Gāozǔ, who habitually turned his heart towards Buddhism,
made vows every time,
saying,
"If there are sentient beings who ought to receive all kinds of suffering,
I shall extend my body to substitute and endure it."
At that time, Dàqiú was only seven years old.
Hearing this, he was surprised and told his mother:
"Since the Official Family (the Emperor) is like this,
how dare I, your son, decline."
Thereupon, he paid homage to the Buddha six times a day,
also saying,
"If there are any sentient beings who ought to receive bitter recompense,
Dàqiú shall receive it in their stead."
His precocious wisdom was like this.
In the second year (551 CE),
he was sent out as General of Light Chariots (*Qīngchē Jiāngjūn*), concurrently managing the military affairs of the Shítóu Garrison.
In the autumn of that year,
he was killed,
at the age of eleven.
Yì’ān Wáng Dàxīn, courtesy name Rénlǎng.
When he was four years old,
his mother, Lady Chén, died.
He thereupon grieved and became emaciated,
as if he were an adult.
When Gāozǔ died,
Dàxīn went to offer consolation to Tàizōng (Emperor Jiǎnwén).
He choked with sobs, unable to control himself.
Those around him who saw this
all wiped away their tears.
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Yì’ān Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.
In the second year (551 CE),
he was sent out as General Who Pacifies the Distant (*Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn*), and Administrator of the two commanderies of Lángyá and Péngchéng.
Before he could take up his post,
he was killed,
at the age of eleven.
Suījiàn Wáng Dàzhì, courtesy name Rén yīng.
When young, he was robust and had courageous spirit.
When the capital city fell,
he sighed, saying:
"A great man will surely be able to exterminate the bandit hordes."
His wet nurse was shocked,
and covered his mouth, saying:
"Do not speak carelessly;
calamity will approach."
Dàzhì smiled, saying:
"Calamity arriving is not due to these words."
In the first year of Dàbǎo (550 CE),
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of Suījiàn Commandery,
with an assigned population of 2,000 households.
In the second year (551 CE),
he served as General Who Pacifies the Distant (*Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn*),
and was killed,
at the age of ten.
The sons of Shìzǔ (Emperor Yuán): the Loyal and Stout Heir Apparent Fāngděng was born by Consort Xú;
the Pure and Benevolent Heir Apparent Fāngzhū was born by Lady Wáng;
as for the Lamenting and Cherished Crown Prince Fāngjǔ,
this book does not record who gave birth to him,
but there is a separate biography;
Emperor Jìng was born by Virtuous Consort Xià.
As for the rest of his sons,
this book does not contain biographies for them.
The Loyal and Stout Heir Apparent Fāngděng, courtesy name Shíxiàng,
was the eldest son of Shìzǔ.
His mother was Consort Xú.
When young, he was intelligent and quick-witted,
possessed outstanding talent,
was skilled in horsemanship and archery,
and was particularly adept at ingenious crafts.
By nature, he loved forests and springs,
and particularly enjoyed a life of freedom and ease.
He once authored a treatise, saying:
"Man's life in this world
is merely like a white colt passing a crack.
One pot of wine
is sufficient to nourish one's nature;
one basket of food
is sufficient to delight one's form.
Born among the mugwort and rushes,
buried in the ditches and ravines upon death—
what difference is there
between a clay coffin and a stone sarcophagus?
I once dreamt I was a fish,
and then transformed into a bird.
When I was in that dream,
what joy was there like it?
When I awoke,
what anxiety was similar to this?
This is truly because my situation is far inferior to that of fish and birds.
Therefore, fish and birds fly and swim,
acting according to their will and nature,
while my advances and retreats
are determined by those in control.
I fear touching something if I raise my hand,
and fear falling if I shake my foot.
If only I could ultimately join fish and birds in their roaming,
then leaving the human world would be like slipping off a worn sandal."
Initially,
Consort Xú lost favor due to jealousy,
and Fāngděng felt uneasy about it.
When Shìzǔ heard about this,
he also disliked Fāngděng.
Fāngděng became even more fearful,
which is why he composed the treatise to express his aspirations.
It happened that Gāozǔ wished to see the eldest sons of the various kings.
Shìzǔ sent Fāngděng and others to attend.
Fāngděng joyfully boarded the boat,
hoping to avoid sorrow and humiliation.
When they reached the Yáoshuǐ River,
they encountered Hóu Jǐng's rebellion.
Shìzǔ summoned them back.
Fāngděng reported,
"In ancient times, Shēn Shēng did not begrudge his death;
how could Fāngděng cling to his life?"
Shìzǔ read the letter with a sigh,
knowing there was no intention of returning.
So he allotted ten thousand infantry and cavalry,
and sent them to aid the capital.
Whenever the rebels attacked,
Fāngděng would invariably expose himself to arrows and stones.
When the palace city fell,
Fāngděng returned to Jīngzhōu,
gathered soldiers and horses,
and greatly earned the people's support.
Shìzǔ then began to praise his ability.
Fāngděng also advised building and repairing city walls and stockades,
to guard against unforeseen events.
Once completed,
watchtowers were visible to one another,
extending over seventy *lǐ* in circumference.
Shìzǔ viewed them with great pleasure,
and entered to tell Xú Fēi:
"If I had another son like this,
what more would I have to worry about?"
Xú Fēi did not reply,
but withdrew weeping.
Shìzǔ was enraged by this,
and therefore exposed her disgraceful conduct,
posting it on the grand pavilion.
When Fāngděng entered and saw it,
he felt even more imperiled.
At that time, the King of Hédōng was the *cìshǐ* of Xiāngzhōu,
and would not obey the orders of the *dūfǔ*.
Fāngděng then requested to go and conquer him.
Shìzǔ granted it,
appointing him *dūdū*,
and ordered him to lead twenty thousand elite troops on a southern expedition.
Before Fāngděng departed,
he said to his close associates:
"In this expedition of mine,
I am certainly destined to die;
if I die in a worthy cause,
why should I cling to life?"
When they reached Máxī,
the King of Hédōng led his army to meet them in battle.
Fāngděng attacked him,
his army was defeated,
and he drowned.
He was twenty-two years old at the time.
When Shìzǔ heard of it,
he did not grieve.
Later, reflecting on his talent,
he posthumously granted him the titles of *shìzhōng*, *zhōngjūn jiāngjūn*, and *Yángzhōu cìshǐ*.
His posthumous name was Zhōngzhuàng Shìzǐ.
And a ritual to summon his soul was performed to mourn him.
Fāngděng had annotated Fàn Yè's *Hòuhànshū*,
but did not complete it.
His compiled *Sānshíguó Chūnqiū* and *Jìngzhùzǐ*
circulated in the world.
Zhēnhuì Shìzǐ Fāngzhū, courtesy name Zhìxiāng,
was Shìzǔ's second son.
His mother was Lady Wáng.
As a child, he was intelligent, alert, and widely learned,
understanding Lǎo and Yì,
and skilled in abstruse discussions.
His demeanor was clear and outstanding,
and his arguments were sharp and incisive.
He was especially beloved by Shìzǔ,
and his mother, Lady Wáng, was also favored.
When Fāngděng was defeated and died,
Shìzǔ said to him:
"Unless something is removed,
how can something else rise?"
He then appointed him *zhōngfǔjūn* to serve as his deputy,
and also sent him out as *Yǐngzhōu cìshǐ*,
to garrison Jiāngxià,
with Bào Quán as the acting official,
to defend against the lower reaches.
At that time, Shìzǔ had sent Xú Wénshèng to supervise the various armies,
who was in a stalemate with Hóu Jǐng's general Rèn Yuē.
Fāngzhū, relying on Wénshèng being nearby,
did not attend to military affairs,
but spent his days with Bào Quán in drinking and gambling.
Hóu Jǐng, knowing this,
then dispatched his general Sòng Zǐxiān to lead several hundred light cavalry,
to attack him by a secret path.
It happened to be dark and stormy.
When Zǐxiān arrived,
the common people ran to report,
but Fāngzhū and Bào Quán still did not believe it,
saying:
"Xú Wénshèng's large army is downstream,
how could the barbarians come?"
He only then ordered the gates closed,
but the rebel cavalry had already entered.
The city thus fell,
and Zǐxiān captured Fāngzhū and returned.
When Wáng Sēngbiàn's army reached Càizhōu,
Jǐng then killed him.
Shìzǔ posthumously granted him the titles of *shìzhōng* and *dàjiāngjūn*.
His posthumous name was Zhēnhuì Shìzǐ.
The imperial historian comments: Among the sons of Tàizōng and Shìzǔ,
although they expanded their territories,
their era belonged to a time of chaos and upheaval.
Being captured by bandits,
many died unnatural deaths.
Alas!
It is lamentable.
Collated Notes
Biographies, Volume 39: Wáng Sēngbiàn
Wáng Sēngbiàn, courtesy name Jūncái,
was the son of Right Guard General Shénniàn.
He came to surrender with his father during the Tiānjiān era.
He began his career as Left Attendant of the King of Xiāngdōng's state.
When the king served as Administrator of Dānyáng,
he was transferred to be a Staff Officer in the administration.
When the king went out to govern Kuàijī,
he also served as Middle Military Staff Officer.
When the king served in Jīngzhōu,
he was still appointed Middle Military,
within the specified term.
At that time, Wǔníng Commandery rebelled.
The king ordered Sēngbiàn to suppress and pacify it.
He was promoted to Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Wǔníng.
Soon after, he was promoted to Zhènyuǎn Jiāngjūn and Grand Administrator of Guǎngpíng.
When his term expired,
he returned to serve as Registrar in the king's administration,
and Staff Officer as before.
When the king was summoned to be Protector-General,
Sēngbiàn also served as Chief Clerk of the administration.
When the king served in Jiāngzhōu,
he was still appointed Yúnqí Jiāngjūn Sīmǎ,
and garrisoned Péngchéng.
Soon after, he supervised Ānlù Commandery,
but returned not long after.
Soon he became Grand Administrator of Xīncài,
still holding the title of Sīmǎ,
and retaining his generalship as before.
When the king was appointed to Jīngzhōu,
he became Consulting Staff Officer in the Zhēnyì Jiāngjūn's administration,
granted a stipend for a thousand people,
and replaced Liǔ Zhònglǐ as Grand Administrator of Jìnglín,
his title changed to Xióngxìn Jiāngjūn.
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
the king ordered Sēngbiàn to temporarily hold the *jié*,
and fully supervise a naval force of ten thousand,
also carrying provisions to go to aid.
He had just reached the capital,
when the palace city was overrun,
and the Son of Heaven was in distress.
Sēngbiàn, together with Liǔ Zhònglǐ and his brothers, and Zhào Bóhào and others,
first submitted to Jǐng,
and then entered the court.
Jǐng confiscated all their military supplies,
but treated them with great kindness and appeasement.
Not long after,
he sent Sēngbiàn back to Jìnglín.
Thereupon, traveling twice the usual speed,
he went west to join Shìzǔ.
Shìzǔ, acting on imperial authority,
appointed Sēngbiàn as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn.
When Jīng and Xiāng were suspected of wavering,
and the army commander suffered a defeat,
Shìzǔ again ordered Sēngbiàn and Bào Quán to lead troops to suppress them.
He allocated soldiers and provisions
and set a date for them to depart.
At that time, Sēngbiàn's subordinates from Jìnglíng had not all arrived yet,
and he wished to wait for them to gather
before setting out.
He said to Bào Quán,
"You and I have both been commanded to campaign in the south,
but if the army's morale is like this,
what do you plan to do?"
Quán replied,
"Since we have received the imperial strategy
and are leading valiant and strong men,
this task is like melting snow with hot water;
why worry so much?"
Sēngbiàn said,
"That is not so.
What you say
is merely the usual talk of a literati.
Hédōng has few military talents,
but their weapons are strong,
preserving their strength to await the enemy.
Unless we have ten thousand elite soldiers,
it will not be enough to control them.
My Jìnglíng armored soldiers
have experienced many battles;
I have already sent for them,
and they should arrive soon.
Although there is a deadline,
it can still be reiterated.
I wish to go with you to speak of this to the emperor,
hoping for your assistance."
Quán replied,
"The success or failure of this undertaking
depends on this expedition.
As for the propriety of delay or speed,
we must ultimately obey the emperor."
Shìzǔ was by nature severe and suspicious.
When he vaguely heard their words,
he thought they were procrastinating and unwilling to go,
and gradually became angry.
When Sēngbiàn was about to enter,
he said to Quán,
"I will speak first,
you can act as my subordinate."
Quán again assented.
When they met Shìzǔ,
Shìzǔ greeted them and asked,
"Are you ready?
What day will you depart?"
Sēngbiàn answered fully as he had just said.
Shìzǔ was furious,
clutched his sword, and sternly said,
"Are you afraid to go?!"
Then he rose and went inside.
Quán was terrified and turned pale,
not daring to speak at all.
A moment later,
he sent dozens of attendants to arrest Sēngbiàn.
When Sēngbiàn arrived,
Shìzǔ said,
"You defy orders and refuse to go,
this is to conspire with the rebels.
Now there is only death."
Sēngbiàn replied,
"As Sēngbiàn has long enjoyed official emoluments,
my worry and responsibility are truly heavy.
To face execution today,
how could I harbor resentment?
I only regret not seeing my elderly mother."
Shìzǔ then struck him,
hitting his left thigh,
and blood flowed to the ground.
Sēngbiàn fainted,
and only revived after a long time.
He was immediately sent to the Grand Judge,
and his sons and nephews were also arrested
and all imprisoned.
At that time, the army of Yuèyáng Wáng attacked Jiānglíng.
The people were agitated,
and the defense preparations were uncertain.
Shìzǔ sent his attendants to the prison
to ask Sēngbiàn for advice.
Sēngbiàn fully articulated his strategy,
and was immediately pardoned and made Governor of the Inner City.
Soon after, Yuèyáng retreated in defeat.
Bào Quán was unable to overcome Chángshā,
so Shìzǔ ordered Sēngbiàn to replace him.
He enumerated Bào Quán's ten crimes,
and sent the palace attendant Luó Chónghuān to lead three hundred imperial guards
to depart with Sēngbiàn.
Upon arrival,
they sent a message to Quán saying,
"Palace attendant Luó has been ordered
to bring Wáng Jìnglíng."
Quán was greatly astonished,
and looked to his左右 (attendants) saying,
"If I can have Wáng Jìnglíng assist me in planning,
the rebels will not be difficult to pacify."
Soon after, Chónghuān entered first with the imperial decree,
and Sēngbiàn followed with the imperial guards.
Quán was just dusting his mat,
sitting and waiting for them.
When Sēngbiàn entered,
he sat with his back to Quán
and said,
"Lord Bào,
you are guilty.
The imperial decree orders me to arrest you;
do not treat this as a personal matter."
Then he told Chónghuān to read out the decree.
Quán immediately descended to the ground
and was arrested by the side of the couch.
Sēngbiàn then organized the generals and commanders,
and concentrated their efforts on the siege,
and thus pacified the land of Xiāng.
Hóu Jǐng sailed down the Xiāng River (Jiāngxī) and invaded.
His army reached Xiàshǒu.
Sēng Biàn was made Grand Commander (Dà Dūdu),
leading the Administrators (Cìshǐ) of Bāzhōu, Chúnyú Liàng; the Administrator of Dìngzhōu, Dù Kān; the Administrator of Yízhōu, Wáng Lín; and the Administrator of Chēnzhōu, Péi Zhīhéng, among others,
all heading to Xīyáng.
When the army reached Bālíng,
they heard that Yǐngzhōu had already fallen.
Sēng Biàn consequently occupied Bālíng city.
Shìzǔ then commanded Xú Sìhuī, the Administrator of Luōzhōu, and Dù Zè, the Administrator of Wǔzhōu, to meet with Sēng Biàn at Bālíng.
After Jǐng had captured Yǐngchéng,
his troops increased greatly,
and his followers were extremely fierce.
He was preparing to advance and invade Jīngzhōu.
He therefore sent the pseudo-Yítóng, Dīng Hé, commanding five thousand troops to guard Jiāngxià,
and his great general Sòng Zixiān, leading ten thousand vanguard troops, advanced upon Bālíng.
Jǐng himself followed with all his ferocious bandits, advancing by land and water.
Consequently, the garrisons and patrols along the river
surrendered at the mere sight of them.
The bandits’ scouting parties reached Yǐnjī.
Sēng Biàn moved all the rice and grain from the river islands
and sank all public and private ships in the water.
When the bandits’ vanguard reached the river mouth,
Sēng Biàn ordered his various armies
to man the ramparts and hold fast,
lowering their flags and muffling their drums,
acting as if no one were there.
The next day,
the bandits crossed the river.
Light cavalry reached the base of the city wall
and asked:
“Who is inside the city?”
The reply was:
“It is Commandant Wáng (Wáng Lǐngjūn).”
The bandit said:
“Tell Commandant Wáng (Wáng Lǐngjūn),
the situation being as it is,
why does he not surrender early?”
Sēng Biàn sent a person to reply:
“If the main army just heads towards Jīngzhōu,
this city will certainly not be an obstacle.
Sēng Biàn and his entire household are in the grip of others;
how can he simply surrender?”
After the bandit cavalry departed,
they soon returned
and said:
“Our King has arrived.
Why does Commandant Wáng (Wáng Lǐngjūn) not come out to meet the King?”
Sēng Biàn did not reply.
After a while,
they seized Wáng Xún and others and brought them to the base of the wall.
Xún wrote a letter attempting to persuade those inside the city.
Jǐng led his ships and assembled them all at Běisì.
He also divided them to enter the inner harbors,
landed on the banks to repair roads,
widely erected shelters,
and displayed his troops on the ridge east of the city.
They cut down weeds and bamboo thickets,
opened eight paths toward the city,
and sent five thousand “rabbit heads” (elite troops) for a close-quarters, fierce assault.
Those inside the city simultaneously beat drums and shouted,
arrows and stones rained down.
Since many bandits were killed,
the bandits consequently withdrew.
Shìzǔ further ordered General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn), Hú Sēngyòu, to lead troops down to reinforce Sēng Biàn.
That same day,
the bandits attacked Bālíng again,
engaging in ten separate actions by water and land,
beating drums and sounding horns,
launching close-quarters assaults and hacking their way up.
From atop the city wall, they dropped timber, hurled fire, and threw large stones.
The casualties were extremely numerous.
The bandits retreated in the afternoon,
and then constructed a long stockade surrounding the city.
They massively arrayed their warships and vessels,
using turret ships to attack the southwest corner of the water defense section of the city.
They also sent men across to the island bank,
dragging bundles of sticks and pushing "shrimp carts" (siege equipment) to fill the area,
and drawing up protective wagons close to the city wall.
This continued for two days before stopping.
The bandits also erected wooden trebuchets (jiégāo) on their ships,
gathered reeds, and set fire to them
in order to burn the water stockade.
However, the wind was unfavorable,
so they burned themselves and retreated.
After being repeatedly defeated and frustrated in battle,
and with the bandit commander Rèn Yuē having been captured by Lù Fǎhé,
Jǐng subsequently burned his camp and fled during the night,
returning his army to Xiàshǒu.
Shìzǔ assessed the merits and distributed rewards,
appointing Sēng Biàn as General Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Jiāngjūn), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī, and Administrator of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ).
He was enfeoffed as the Duke of Chángníng County (Chángníng Xiàn Gōng).
Thereupon, Shìzǔ commanded Sēng Biàn to immediately lead all the Bālíng forces,
moving downstream to attack Jǐng.
The army reached Yǐngchéng
and advanced on Lǔshān on foot.
Zhī Huàrén, the commander of Lǔshān city,
was one of Jǐng’s cavalry generals.
He led his followers in fierce fighting,
but the combined forces utterly routed them.
Huàrén subsequently surrendered.
Sēng Biàn then directed the various armies to cross the river and attack Yǐng,
immediately entering the outer city (Luóchéng).
Sòng Zixiān gathered his forces like ants in Jīnchéng (the inner city) and resisted the defense,
but the attack had not yet succeeded.
Zixiān ordered his follower Shí Línghù to lead three thousand troops,
to open the gate and sortie to battle.
Sēng Biàn again utterly routed them,
capturing Línghù alive
and beheading a thousand men.
Zixiān’s forces retreated to hold Cāngmén,
where they were protected by the river’s natural defenses.
The combined armies attacked,
but after repeated battles failed to overcome them.
Since Jǐng heard that Lǔshān had already fallen,
and that the Yǐng garrison had again lost the outer city (Luóchéng),
he led his remaining troops, traveling double speed, back to Jiànyè.
Zixiān and the others were exhausted and pressed,
having nowhere to go.
They begged to surrender Yǐngchéng,
and return personally to Jǐng.
Sēng Biàn pretended to grant their request,
ordering that one hundred ships be provided,
to make them complacent.
Zixiān believed it to be true,
and floated his vessels, preparing to depart.
Sēng Biàn commanded Dù Kān to lead one thousand elite warriors,
scaling the battlements,
simultaneously beating drums and shouting,
descending upon Cāngmén in a surprise attack.
The naval commander Sòng Yáo led turret ships,
secretly surrounding the river on all sides like gathering clouds.
Zixiān fought and traveled simultaneously,
reaching Báiyáng Pǔ.
There, he was utterly defeated,
and Zixiān was captured alive and sent to Jiānglíng.
He then led the various armies to advance to Jiǔshuǐ.
The pseudo-Yítóng bandits Fàn Xīróng and Lú Huīlüè still held Pénchéng.
When Sēng Biàn’s army arrived,
Xīróng and the others consequently forced the Administrator of Jiāngzhōu (Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ), the Duke of Línchéng (Línchéng Gōng), to abandon the city and flee.
Shìzǔ conferred upon Sēng Biàn the titles of Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Lìng), and General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East (Zhēngdōng Dà Jiāngjūn).
He was granted an entourage with drums and horns.
Sēng Biàn was further ordered to temporarily halt at Jiāngzhōu,
and wait until all the armies were assembled,
and then advance again at the appropriate time.
After a while,
Shìzǔ commanded all the Jiāngzhōu armies to launch a joint major offensive.
Sēng Biàn then submitted a memorial concerning the Emperor’s unfortunate news
and reported it to Jiānglíng.
He subsequently led more than a hundred high-ranking generals,
who jointly signed a petition urging Shìzǔ to take the throne immediately.
As he was preparing to advance his army,
he presented another memorial.
Although these petitions were not yet followed,
they all received gracious replies.
The details are found in the Basic Annals (Běnjì).
Sēngbiàn then set out from Jiāngzhōu
and pointed directly toward Jiànyè.
He first ordered Hóu Zhèn (刺史, Cìshǐ, i.e., Governor) of Southern Yǎnzhōu to lead elite soldiers in light boats
to attack the garrisons at Nánlíng and Quètóu, and other places.
As soon as they arrived, they overcame them.
Prior to this,
Chén Bàxiān led a host of 50,000
and departed from Nánjiāng;
his vanguard, 5,000 strong,
traveled until they reached Pénkǒu.
Bàxiān was bold and unconventional, possessing many strategies;
his fame overshadowed Sēngbiàn’s,
and Sēngbiàn feared him.
Having arrived at Pénkǒu,
he met with Sēngbiàn at Báimáozhōu.
They ascended the altar and swore an oath.
Bàxiān composed the text for it, which read:
“The rebellious minister Hóu Jǐng,
a cruel Jié and a petty Hu (barbarian),
defied Heaven without restraint,
constructed treacherous wickedness,
violated his grace and duty to us,
plundered our state,
poisoned our people,
and destroyed our altars of state.
Our High Ancestor, Emperor Wǔ, was spiritually sagacious and brilliant,
illuminating the world,
working tirelessly for the myriad common people,
fostering and nurturing the ten thousand masses
as if they were his parents,
for fifty years.
He pitied Jǐng when he returned in distress,
saved Jǐng from imminent execution,
placed Jǐng in crucial positions,
and elevated Jǐng with extraordinary honors.
How little did our High Ancestor do for Jǐng?
How little grievance did our common people have against Jǐng?
Yet Jǐng used long halberds and strong crossbows
to oppress the court,
chewed with his saw-like teeth in the surrounding plains,
cruelly devoured all sentient beings,
gouged out livers and chopped off feet,
finding boundless satisfaction,
and exposed bones and burned corpses,
without deeming it too brutal.
High Ancestor restricted his diet and lived in a humble palace;
at ninety years of age,
he suppressed his will and contained his dignity,
only to end his life infuriated by the hands of the bandit.
The late Emperor (Dàxíng Huángdì) was mild, solemn, respectful, and silent,
greatly upholding the grand name—
how did he wrong Jǐng,
that Jǐng again inflicted cruel poison?
All the imperial descendants, from infants in swaddling clothes
up to those who had completed the mourning rituals (sīgōng),
faced extreme knives and chopping blocks,
being both slaughtered and minced.
How can any man within the borders of the world,
who calls himself a subject of the King,
eats the grain of men,
and drinks the water of men,
endure hearing this agony
without grieving in his heart?
How much more so for this servant Sēngbiàn
and this servant Bàxiān, etc.,
who bear the charge from Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì, the Prince who is called the pillar of the state—a charge undertaken with weeping blood and contained sorrow—
and who have received grace reaching from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet?
We have generationally benefited from the virtue of the former dynasty,
and personally hold the responsibility of generals and commanders.
If we cannot pour out our loyalty and exert ourselves wholeheartedly
to jointly punish this treacherous rebel,
cleanse the shame from Heaven and Earth,
and avenge the grievance of our sovereign and father,
then we are unfit to be born with spiritual essence and consciousness,
wearing Heaven above and treading Earth below.
Today, the Prime Minister (Xiàngguó), due to his ultimate filial piety, has received a subtle response from Heaven,
and his spiritual might has been unleashed.
He has already defeated the bandit hordes
and captured their marshals,
leaving only Jǐng himself,
who still remains in the capital.
This servant Sēngbiàn and this servant Bàxiān shall coordinate the generals and commanders,
share one heart and common purpose,
and surely execute the wicked villain,
honor and support the Prime Minister,
allow him to inherit the grand enterprise,
and preside over the suburban sacrifices.
If, in the campaign ahead, there is any achievement
or any reward obtained,
and this servant Sēngbiàn, etc., does not push himself forward and yield to others,
but instead leads the troops personally,
then the spirits of Heaven, Earth, the Ancestral Temple, and the Hundred Deities
shall jointly punish and condemn us.
This servant Sēngbiàn and this servant Bàxiān shall work together with one heart
and not deceive or mistreat each other.
If there is any transgression,
may the bright spirits destroy us.”
They then ascended the altar, smeared blood on their mouths,
and jointly read the covenant text.
Tears ran down their lapels,
and their demeanor was impassioned.
When the Royal Army arrived near Nánzhōu,
the bandit commander Hóu Zǐjiàn and others led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry to challenge them from the shore.
They also used a thousand small, fast boats (zhōu[⻖㫒]) carrying soldiers,
each having eighty oars on both sides;
the oarsmen were all Yuè people,
moving back and forth to launch sudden attacks,
their speed surpassing wind and lightning.
Sēngbiàn then signaled the small boats
to all retreat,
and made the large battleships moor tightly along both banks.
The bandits, believing the navy intended to withdraw,
scrambled to advance against them.
The assembled forces then rowed the large battleships,
cutting off their return route.
Sounding the drums and shouting loudly,
they joined battle in the middle of the river.
The bandits all jumped into the water.
Sēngbiàn immediately supervised the various armies as they followed the current downstream,
advancing to the outer fort (Dòuchéng) of Shítóu.
They established connecting camps to press the bandits.
The bandits then built five forts horizontally along the ridge to resist and defend.
Hóu Jǐng personally led his forces out
and fought a major battle with the Royal Army north of Shítóu City.
Bàxiān said to Sēngbiàn:
“This ugly captive is a roaming ghost;
his measure of iniquity is now full.
He has evaded punishment and is seeking death,
wishing for a final showdown.
Our forces are numerous while the bandits are few;
we should divide their strength.”
He immediately dispatched two thousand powerful crossbows to attack the bandits' two western forts,
and then commanded them to form battle lines to confront the bandits.
Sēngbiàn was in the rear, waving his signal and ordering the army forward,
and they again achieved a great victory.
Lú Huīlüè, hearing that Jǐng had been defeated,
surrendered Shítóu City.
Sēngbiàn led his army in and occupied it.
When Jǐng retreated,
he fled north to Zhūfāng.
At this time, Jǐng’s scattered soldiers fled and reported to Sēngbiàn.
Sēngbiàn ordered his generals to enter and occupy Táichéng.
That night,
the soldiers gathering lumber accidentally started a fire,
which burned the Tàijí Hall and the East and West Halls, among others.
At that time, the soldiers looted the capital,
stripping and exposing the scholars and common people.
Those citizens who were seized and bound
could not even keep their undergarments.
They rounded up residents en masse and forced them to pay ransoms.
From Shítóu to the East City,
the sounds of wailing along the Huái River
shook the capital.
Consequently, the common people were disillusioned.
Sēngbiàn ordered Hóu Zhèn and Péi Zhīhéng to lead five thousand elite armored troops
east to pursue and attack Jǐng.
Sēngbiàn captured the bandit faction members Wáng Wěi and over twenty others
and sent them to Jiānglíng.
The pretender Administrator (Wěi Xíngtái) Zhào Bó Chāo surrendered to Hóu Zhèn from Wúsōngjiāng.
Zhèn immediately sent him to Sēngbiàn.
Sēngbiàn said to Bó Chāo:
“Lord Zhào,
you were laden with great grace from the state,
yet you joined the rebellion.
Regarding today’s situation,
what do you intend to do?”
He then ordered him sent to Jiānglíng.
After Bó Chāo departed,
Sēngbiàn looked back at his seated guests and said:
“In the past, the court only knew of Zhào Bó Chāo;
how could they have known Wáng Sēngbiàn?
Now that the state has been overthrown,
it has been restored by me.
The rise and fall of men
is truly unpredictable.”
The guests all stepped forward and praised his achievements and virtues.
Sēngbiàn, suddenly serious,
then falsely replied:
“This is solely due to the divine virtue of the Sage Sovereign
and the obedience of the commanders.
Although this old man abusively occupies the position of military leader,
what power does he possess?”
Thereupon, the rebellious bandits were all subdued,
and the capital was captured and secured.
Emperor Shìzǔ ascended the imperial throne
and, based on Sēngbiàn’s achievements,
promoted him to General-in-Chief Guarding the West (Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn) and Minister of Works (Sītú).
He was granted twenty additional armed guards (jiābàn jiàn),
renamed Duke of Yǒngníng Commandery,
with an income of five thousand households.
His positions as Attendant-in-Chief (Shìzhōng), Director of the Chancellery (Shàngshū Lìng), and holder of ceremonial music and standards (gǔchuī) remained as before.
seizing all their military supplies;
Lǐ Hóngyǎ also led his troops from Línglíng, exiting via Kōnglíngtān,
claiming to assist in the suppression of Nà.
The court did not yet understand his true intentions,
and regarded this with deep concern.
They therefore dispatched the Attendant Secretary Luó Chónghuān to summon Sēngbiàn to proceed and join the Piàojì Jiāngjūn, the Marquis of Yífēng, Xún, on the southern campaign.
Sēngbiàn accordingly took command of Dù Zè and the other various armies,
setting forth from Jiànyè.
When the army reached Bālíng,
an imperial edict appointed Sēngbiàn as the Dūdū Dōngshàng Zhūjūnshì,
and Bàxiān as the Dūdū Xīshàng Zhūjūnshì.
Previously, Bàxiān had yielded the position of Area Commander to Sēngbiàn,
but Sēngbiàn did not accept it.
Therefore, Shìzǔ divided the command into Eastern and Western Area Commanders,
and both proceeded on the southern expedition.
At this time, Nà and his followers had moved down and occupied Chēlún,
constructing fortifications on both river banks,
and blocking the flow of the water in front.
Their officers and soldiers were fierce and brave,
all survivors of a hundred battles.
Sēngbiàn was cautious of them,
and dared not advance rashly.
He thus gradually constructed connecting forts to pressure the bandits.
When the bandits saw that the imperial forces dared not engage in open battle,
they all grew slack and careless.
Sēngbiàn took advantage of their lack of preparation,
ordering the armies by land and water to attack them,
personally grasping the banner and drum,
to signal advances and retreats.
Consequently, the various armies rushed out competing with one another,
and fought a great battle at Chēlún.
Fighting fiercely alongside the Piàojì Xún,
they captured two of their fortifications.
The bandits were utterly defeated,
fleeing on foot to take refuge and defend Chángshā,
forcing the residents
to enter the city and resist the siege.
Sēngbiàn pursued them closely,
and commanded the construction of ramparts to besiege the city.
He ordered all the armies to widely establish palisades and stockades for the siege,
and Sēngbiàn went out and sat on a mound to personally supervise the work.
The bandits recognized Sēngbiàn from afar,
and knowing he was unguarded,
the bandit leaders Wú Zàng, Lǐ Xiánmíng, and others led a thousand crack troops,
opened the gate and rushed out suddenly,
advancing directly beneath their shields,
heading straight toward Sēngbiàn.
At that time, Dù Zè and Dù Kān were attending him,
and the armored guards numbered only about a hundred men.
They immediately descended and dispatched men to engage the bandits.
Lǐ Xiánmíng rode an armored horse,
followed by ten horsemen,
shouting loudly and charging forward.
Sēngbiàn remained seated on his camp stool (húchuáng),
and was not disturbed by them.
He then directed the brave troops,
and consequently captured Xiánmíng,
immediately beheading him.
The bandits then retreated back into the city.
Originally,
when Lù Nà resisted with his troops and rebelled internally,
he used Wáng Lín as a pretext,
saying,
"If the court releases Wáng Lín,
Nà and his followers will naturally surrender."
At that time, all the armies were advancing simultaneously,
and this was not granted.
However, since the Wǔlíng Wáng held forces in the upper reaches of the river,
causing alarm and fear both internally and externally,
Shìzǔ then dispatched Lín to negotiate a settlement.
Following this, Xiāngzhōu was pacified.
Sēngbiàn returned to Jiānglíng,
and was consequently commanded by edict to assemble the armies for a western expedition.
He oversaw a naval force of twenty thousand,
and the Imperial Carriage went out to Tiānjū Sì to see him off.
Soon afterward, the Wǔlíng Wáng suffered a defeat,
and Sēngbiàn withdrew his troops from Zhījiāng back to Jiānglíng,
then returned to garrison Jiànyè.
In the same month,
after staying for a short time,
he returned again to Jiānglíng.
The Qí Zhǔ Gāo Yáng dispatched Guō Yuánjiàn to lead twenty thousand troops,
marshalling a great fleet of ships at Héféi,
intending to plan an attack on Jiànyè.
They also sent their great generals Xíng Jǐngyuǎn, Bù Dàhànsà, Dōngfāng Lǎo, and others to lead forces in succession.
At that time, Chén Bàxiān was garrisoning Jiànkāng.
Having heard of this matter,
he urgently reported it to Jiānglíng.
Shìzǔ immediately ordered Sēngbiàn to proceed to Gūshú,
and stay there to guard the area.
Prior to this, he had ordered the Yùzhōu Cìshǐ Hóu Tiàn to lead three thousand crack armored troops to build ramparts at Dōngguān,
in order to repel the northern invaders.
He summoned the Wú Jùn Tàishǒu Zhāng Biāo and the Wúxīng Tàishǒu Péi Zhīhéng to join Tiàn at the pass.
They subsequently fought the Northern army,
and utterly defeated them.
Sēngbiàn then led his assembled troops back to Jiànyè.
In the third month, on the Jiǎchén day, of Chéngshèng Sān Nián (554 CE),
an imperial edict stated:
"To commend the outstanding and promote the worthy
is praised in the classical canons of Qín (ancient records);
for the superior to bring peace to the inferior
is known to be the system of Hàn.
By these means, the stellar influences of the court are aligned from above,
and the grand plan is supported from below.
Shǐchíjié, Shìzhōng, Sītú, Shàngshū Lìng, Dūdū Yáng Nánxú Dōngyáng Sān Zhōu Zhūjūnshì, Zhènwèi Jiāngjūn, Yángzhōu Cìshǐ, and Kāiguó Gōng of Yǒngníng Jùn, Sēngbiàn:
His demeanor is profound and steady,
and his style is comprehensive and farsighted.
His conduct is a model for the scholars,
his words reflect his cultured person.
His scholarship penetrates the Nine Schools,
his military skill encompasses the Seven Strategies.
In recent years during campaigns,
moving from west to east,
the troops were not exhausted,
and the people had no complaints.
As the royal enterprise faced difficulties and challenges,
he truly managed both the simple and the perilous.
It is fitting that he harmonize this Central Court (Zhōng Tái),
and receive the highest generalship;
we rely on him to organize the realm,
and assist our court policies.
He is promoted to Tàiwèi and Chējì Dàjiāngjūn,
all other positions remain as before."
later,
he was grieving the death of his mother, the Grand Mistress (Tàifūrén).
Shìzǔ sent the Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng) and the Court Gentleman Usher (Yèzhě) to supervise the funeral arrangements,
and conferred a posthumous title by decree, calling her Zhēnjìng Tàifūrén.
The Mistress’s surname was Wèi.
Shénniàn, at the beginning of the Tiānjiān era, commanded his followers to occupy Dōngguān,
then retreated to hold the area west of Cháohú near Héféi,
and subsequently married her,
giving birth to Sēngbiàn.
Her nature was extremely peaceful and gentle,
and she was good at comforting and receiving people.
Everyone, both inside and outside
the family gate, cherished her.
Previously,
when Sēngbiàn was imprisoned,
the Mistress wept and walked on foot,
intending to enter and beg for pardon,
but Shìzǔ refused to grant her an audience.
At that time, the Crown Prince (Shìzǐ) Zhēnhuì was favored by Shìzǔ,
and was often involved in commanding major military and state affairs.
The Mistress went to the inner palace gate (Gé),
stating that she had failed in her instructions (Wúxùn).
She was weeping and sobbing bitterly,
and everyone pitied her.
When Sēngbiàn was released,
the Mistress sternly admonished and encouraged him;
both her words and expression were severe.
She said:
“When a person serves their sovereign,
they must only be loyal and ardent.
This not only protects and blesses the current generation,
but also extends fortune to their descendants.”
When Sēngbiàn succeeded in recovering the former capital (Jiùjīng),
and his achievements covered the realm,
the Mistress remained modest and humble,
and did not use her wealth and high status to arrogantly slight others.
The court and the common people all praised her,
calling her an enlightened and wise woman (Míngzhé Fùrén).
When she passed away,
she was greatly lamented and mourned.
Furthermore, because Sēngbiàn’s meritorious deeds were massive and serious,
his mother's funeral rites were enhanced.
When the coffin was about to return to Jiànkāng,
he again sent a Court Gentleman Usher (Yèzhě) to the river islet where the boat was moored to offer condolences and sacrifices.
He commanded Wáng Póu, the Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè), to write the eulogy, which stated:
“Indeed, your lineage based the foundation on Wǔzǐ,
and your clan flourished through Yángyuán.
Your excellence illuminated others like reflecting gold,
and your virtue was as gentle as warm jade.
You earned praise for your feminine conduct (nǚzé),
and also followed the words of a wife.
You examined books and maps as in a mirror,
and discussed rhetoric and writings.
Your teachings passed down ritual implements (zǔdòu),
and your instructions reached Píngyuán.
Like Chǔ Fā leading troops,
and Mèng Kē achieving virtue,
you employed loyalty and respect,
modeling the state based on your own family.
Your demeanor was glorious and trustworthy,
and served as a model for the people.
Thus, we have commanded the troops,
and deployed our armies;
filling this role (gǔnzhí),
suddenly possessing Guī and Méng.
The mother is ennobled by the son;
truly, you were thus elevated.
Auspicious commands sincerely converged,
and marks of favor were magnified.
Dwelling in high station, you could descend;
residing in nobility, you remembered humility (chōng).
Felicity was supported by a good beginning,
and glory embraced a fine conclusion.
Yānzī has seen evening,
the reeds are in early autumn.
A galloping team of horses is hard to recall,
raging waves cannot be held back.
Turning from Lóngmén to look west,
passing Xiàshǒu and floating east.
Crossing the distant peaks of the Sāngōng,
passing the diverging streams of the Sānjiāng.
The ridges are dense and steep,
obscuring the floating clouds.
The mighty Jiāng and Hàn Rivers
rush past like this.
The inscription banner and the former streamer,
the structure destroyed, leaving the stele.
We set up the offerings upon this empty boat,
imagining that the departing soul is aware.
Alas, grievously sad!”
In the tenth month of that year,
Yǔwén Hēitài, the Chancellor (Xiāng) of Western Wèi, sent troops totaling 50,000, including the forces of the Prince (Wáng) of Yuèyáng,
intending to attack Jiānglíng.
Shìzǔ sent the Chief Scribe (Zhǔshū) Lǐ Yīng to summon Sēngbiàn from Jiànyè,
appointing him Grand Governor (Dà Dūdū) and Governor of Jīngzhōu (Jīngzhōu Cìshǐ).
A separate edict instructed Sēngbiàn, saying:
“Hēitài has violated the treaty,
and suddenly raised his ax (commenced warfare).
Most of the state’s fierce generals
are in the lower reaches (downriver).
The troops of Jīng and Shǎn
are entirely lacking in strength and courage.
You must lead your courageous troops (píhǔ),
set out immediately on the road (xīngyán),
travel twice the normal speed (bèidào jiānxíng),
and hasten to relieve this dire distress (dàoxuán).”
Sēngbiàn then commanded Hóu Tián, the Governor of Yùzhōu (Yùzhōu Cìshǐ), and others to serve as the vanguard,
and Dù Sēngmíng, the Governor of Yǎnzhōu (Yǎnzhōu Cìshǐ), and others to serve as the rearguard.
After the arrangements were complete,
he said to Yīng:
“The Tàitroops are fierce and brave;
it is difficult to contend directly with their sharp edge.
If all our forces concentrate,
I will proceed directly to the Hànjiāng River
and cut off their line of retreat.
When supplying provisions over merely a thousand *lǐ*,
people still show signs of hunger;
how much more so for bandits crossing several thousand *lǐ*?
This is the time when Sūn Bìn defeated Páng Juān.”
Soon after, the capital city (Jīngchéng) fell,
and the Emperor passed away (gōngchē yànjià).
When Emperor Jìng (Jìngdì) first ascended the throne of Liáng,
Sēngbiàn was involved in establishing him.

By imperial decree, he was promoted to General of Cavalry (Piàojì Dàjiāngjūn), Director of the Imperial Secretariat (Zhōngshū Jiān), Grand Governor of All Military Affairs Inside and Outside (Dūdū Zhōngwài Zhū Jūnshì), and Recorder of the Department of State Affairs (Lù Shàngshū).
He consulted with Chén Bàxiān regarding punitive expeditions.
At that time, Gāo Yáng, the ruler of Qí, also intended to install Yuānmíng, the Marquis of Zhēnyáng, as the successor to Liáng.
Thereupon, he wrote a letter to Sēng Biàn, saying:
“The State of Liáng has been unfortunate;
misfortunes and difficulties have followed one another.
Hóu Jǐng ravaged Jiànyè,
and Wǔlíng raised arms in Bā and Hàn.
Your resolve reached the dark heavens,
your spirit pierced the bright sun.
You united your strength and minds,
and wiped out the ugly rebels.
Everyone with feeling,
none failed to sigh in admiration;
