how much more so our neighboring state,
which had previously discussed and reported these matters.
But the western bandits took advantage of the gap,
and again attacked and assaulted.
The ruler of Liáng was unable to firmly defend Jiānglíng,
and perished alongside his ancestral altars.
Before Our royal army could reach him,
he had already surrendered and been defeated.
Officials and people, great and small,
were all entirely captured by the bandits.
We looked south with concern,
and anger and lamentation filled Our bosom.
Given your loyalty as a subject,
We believe your heart must be choked up and shattered.
We hear that you provisionally established a son from a branch line,
issuing orders from Jiāngyīn.
He is barely a little over ten years old,
extremely young and weak.
Liáng’s misfortunes are not yet finished,
and bearing this burden will surely be difficult.
If the sacrifices are handled by the ruler of Wèi,
and governance is controlled by the Níng clan.
A weak trunk and strong branches,
is what has been feared throughout history.
We regard all under Heaven as Our home,
and employ the Great Way to save all beings.
Because the State of Liáng has been ruined and destroyed,
We cherish our old friendship.
To preserve those in peril and rescue the fallen,
is Our duty on this very day.
In aiding the endangered and continuing the succession,
We seek not lasting gain, but upholding virtue.
That Marquis of Zhēnyáng,
is the nephew of Emperor Wǔ of Liáng;
a descendant of Chángshā.
Considering his age and stature,
he is capable of stabilizing Jīnlíng.
Therefore, We establish him as the ruler of Liáng,
and install him in that state.
We thus command Gāo Huàn, the Prince of Shàngdǎng, to command all the generals,
and escort him across the Yangtze,
moving like thunder and speeding like wind,
to help sweep away the hateful rebels.
Gāo Yuè, the Prince of Qīnghé,
previously went to rescue Jīngchéng.
His army passed Ānlù,
but since he could not reach in time,
Our vexation and regret are truly deep.
We fear that the western bandits might ride the tide
and again invade Jiāngzuǒ.
Now [Gāo Yuè] is moving to station at Hànkǒu,
to meet with Layman Lù (Lù Fǎhè).
You should agree to Our good plan,
urge on your commanders,
arrange your ships and vessels,
and welcome the current king (Yuānmíng).
Gather and control your fierce and brave forces,
uniting hearts and strength in a single effort.
The western Qiāng are an unorganized rabble;
they are fundamentally not powerful bandits.
It is merely because Xiāngdōng was timid and weak
that this universal ruin resulted.
With Our army now,
where can we go without conquering?
Establish a good strategy,
and fulfill Our expectations.”
Zhēnyáng accepted the dispatch and escort from Qí,
and was about to reach Shòuyáng.
Zhēnyáng frequently sent letters to Sēng Biàn, both before and after,
discussing the intention of returning to the state and continuing the succession,
but Sēng Biàn did not accept it.
When Zhēnyáng and Gāo Huàn arrived at Dōngguān,
Sànqí Chángshì Péi Zhīhèng led troops to resist the battle,
suffered defeat,
and Sēng Biàn consequently plotted to accept Zhēnyáng,
thereupon settling the rites between ruler and minister.
The memorial said:
"Since the Qín troops invaded Shǎn,
your servant immediately prepared to rush to the rescue.
Just as I was boarding the boat,
Jīngchéng had already fallen.
I immediately dispatched Liú Zhōu to enter the state,
fully expressing my sincere loyalty.
Initially, the meritorious nobles surrounding the court
all shared this covenant.
Since Zhōu did not return for a long time,
public sentiment became suspicious and resistant.
Recently, upon receiving the decree brought by the palace envoy,
I again sent messages to various places to seek counsel.
Opinions were disparate,
and nothing was firmly decided.
Only recently did I receive a letter from Hóu Tián,
showing the document from the western bandit Quán Jǐngxuān,
ordering that the original manuscript be presented.
Observing the generals and commanders,
they are indulging in excesses similar to Tàishǐ.
If we were one morning to defy the Great State [Qí],
your servant would not regret being pulverized into dust,
but I mourn that the fortune of Liáng would be eternally severed from restoration.
I humbly wish that Your Majesty would immediately cross the Jiāng River,
relying on the might of Imperial Qí,
and depending on Your Majesty's supreme sagacious strategy,
establish the ruler based on seniority.
The vengeance and retribution can be anticipated,
and the altars of soil and grain will shine again.
Death itself would not be regretted.
I request the appointment of the separate envoy Cáo Chōng to rush this memorial to the Qí capital.
I will continuously send subsequent memorials to inform you.
I humbly and eagerly await the urgency of paying respects to you."
Zhēnyáng replied:
"Jiāng Gǎo arrived,
conveying the full extent of your public loyalty and righteousness.
The state and ruling house have suffered disorder,
accumulating over many years now.
Three sovereigns have been humiliated,
and the four seas are boiling over.
Heaven appoints a Grand Counselor [Sēng Biàn]
to assist and save the original dynasty,
widely relieving this distress and difficulty,
and establishing our ancestral temple.
Even hermits in the wilderness
still anticipate the arrival of the proper ceremony.
How could the Imperial branches of the ruling house
wait in vain?
Hearing that I am returning to the state,
I understand your lofty intentions.
However, recently commissioning envoys a second time,
perhaps their message was not fully conveyed.
Since you consulted with the high officials
and inquired of the border regions,
traveling back and forth,
it naturally took a month or so.
Now that the envoy has arrived,
it truly fulfills my expectations.
This is indeed establishing our Xiāo Zōng again,
and greatly reviving our state of Liáng.
The billions of common people
will all receive this favor,
and the altars of soil and grain and the ancestral temples
will have nothing to be ashamed of.
Recently, when the army was stationed at Dōngguān,
I frequently sent messengers to Péi Zhīhèng,
showing him the appropriateness of the matter.
His response was arrogant and belligerent,
which greatly shocked all who heard and saw it.
The Prince of Shàngdǎng deployed troops to guard us,
desiring to secure the volatile situation.
Yet, that ignorant fellow
suddenly counter-attacked.
Before our vanguard banner was even raised,
they instantly scattered themselves.
The feeling of alarm and grief
only increases my sorrow.
The Prince of Shàngdǎng sighed deeply with self-reproach,
did not take the heads [of the slain],
and furthermore honored the dead with mounds and trees,
decorated the coffins, and provided thick burial rites,
striving to fulfill proper courtesy.
The great virtue of the Qí court
truly moves the spirits and the people.
I am about to rely on the Imperial might
and respectfully depend on the Grand Counselor,
to punish the rebellious bandits in Xiányáng
and execute the renegade sons in Yúnmèng.
With unified hearts and combined strength,
we will successfully stabilize the state.
Regarding the letter from Quán Jǐngxuān that you showed me,
the various generals in the upstream regions
originally possess loyalty and strategy.
Abandoning kin to side with enemies
is likely not what they would do.
Preventing treachery and settling chaos
ultimately rests upon you.
I shall temporarily pause at Dōngguān
and await further communication,
as I do not yet know whether I will be met by water or land, or where.
Now, establishing a state and setting up a ruler
is recorded in historical documents.
Entering into alliances and exchanging hostages
is a tradition dating back since ancient times.
If your loyalty and integrity
move the Blue Heavens above,
and the generals conspire together
and certainly hold no wavering allegiance,
then the Qí army will turn back its banners;
it is righteous that they will not cross the Jiāng River.
If there is any breach of this promise,
I swear by failure and defeat.
I shall conceal the banners and wait anxiously,
expecting the return of the messenger.
Cáo Chōng is presenting the memorial to the Qí capital;
he has already been dispatched.
Below Wèiqiáo,
I only await your word;
North of Sìshuǐ,
there is already weeping and fear."
Sēng Biàn again sent a second memorial, saying:
"Yuánwài Chángshì Jiāng Gǎo has returned.
I respectfully received the imperial decree concerning your movements.
The compassionate and righteous influence of Great Qí
has been extended to neighboring states,
showing pity for disaster and rescuing those in difficulty,
displaying this great principle.
All the relatives of the Imperial house
are honored to receive it,
and the officials of Jiāngdōng
all know to rely upon it.
Now, although we perform the ritual oath, we do not forget sincerity;
sincerity truly comes from the heart.
I respectfully dispatch Xiǎn, my seventh son,
and Liú, who is Xiǎn’s mother, as well as my nephew Shìzhēn,
to serve as hostages there.
Furthermore, I have sent Zuǒmín Shàngshū Zhōu Hóngzhèng to Lìyáng to respectfully welcome you.
Boats float upon the Jiāng River,
awaiting the crossing of the 'single dragon';
the clean palace and red steps
await the entry of the six-horse carriage.
The ten thousand states turn their hearts,
sharing the glory of Jìn Wén's return.
The Three Virtues will be successfully proclaimed,
and the deliberation of Sòng Chāng will flow forth.
Since the state's fortune is flourishing,
the altars of soil and grain will have an offering.
Then all officials will exert their integrity,
repaying the great benefaction from Great Qí,
pooling our strength to exhibit our humble abilities,
and demonstrating loyalty to Your Majesty.
Now I send Lìbù Shàngshū Wáng Tōng to present this memorial and make it known."
Sēng Biàn then requested that Jìng Dì be made the Crown Prince.
Zhēnyáng replied again:
"Shàngshū Wáng Tōng arrived,
again conveying your message.
I know that you intend to send your virtuous nephew Shìzhēn as a sincere hostage,
and I fully understand your concern for the state.
Furthermore, treating the jade tree in your courtyard
and the bright pearl in your palm
without burdening your heart,
your will is set on assisting and saving.
How can this not be working diligently for our altars of soil and grain,
and broadly aiding our state and ruling house?
The feeling of admiration and gratitude
makes me forget sleep and waking.
Jìn'ān Wáng, possessing the solemn status of being heir apparent in Dōngjīng,
is the virtuous successor in Xīdū.
Inheriting and guarding the Imperial House,
how could this not meet the people's expectations?
However, the world is afflicted by chaos and disorder,
and it is appropriate to establish a senior ruler.
Since he is immature and still a child,
it is difficult for him to succeed to the inheritance.
The virtues of Chéng and Zhāo [Emperors]
have been rare since ancient times;
the perils faced by Chōng and Zhì [Emperors]
are found in every age.
I, the lone man, encountered adversity in fortune,
and had no thought of surviving.
Suddenly, I received unprecedented grace,
leading to this extraordinary undertaking.
Reflecting on my own lack of virtue,
my apprehension and fear are already profound.
If a successor is to be established,
the position fundamentally belongs to the Imperial lineage.
Swearing by heart and mouth,
I intend only Jìn'ān.
If these words prove false,
may the spirits strike me down."
Examining what has been shown now,
deeply fulfills my original intention.
My feelings of relief and comfort,
cannot be expressed in words or images.
But the weight of your (Gōng's) worries and toils,
is already due to the grace of Qí;
your feelings of loyalty and righteousness,
extend again to the second state of Liáng.
How could the masses, both Huá and Yí,
not cherish your reputation?
How could the bright spirits of the ancestral temples
not respond to you?
You should immediately turn your standards (your journey),
and proceed towards Lìyáng.
We expect the hostages and dependents,
to be brought there immediately.
That the gathered troops shall not cross (the river),
has already been set down in the covenant document.
This is the gracious policy of the Sage Lord of Great Qí,
and the promise of the Heroic King of Shàngdǎng.
To gain what is desired and then break faith,
will ultimately not be done.
I merely await our meeting,
which will not be long delayed.
Our homeland is not far,
yet wherever I look, I weep and sob."
Sēngbiàn sent the hostages to Yè.
Zhēnyáng requested to cross with three thousand guardsmen.
Sēngbiàn feared they would cause trouble,
and only accepted one thousand dispersed soldiers,
and simultaneously dispatched the imperial dragon boat and ceremonial chariot to welcome him.
On the day Zhēnyáng crossed the river (Jiāng),
Sēngbiàn held the oar midstream,
not daring to approach the bank.
Afterwards, they met together at the Pǔ of Jiāngníng.
After Zhēnyáng had ascended the false throne,
he immediately granted Sēngbiàn the titles Dà Sīmǎ, Superintendent of the Crown Prince Tutor (lǐng Tàizǐ Tàifù), and Governor of Yángzhōu (Yángzhōu Mù),
the rest (of his titles) remained as before.
Chén Bàxiān, who was then Sīkōng and Governor of Nán Xúzhōu,
detested Sēngbiàn's vacillation.
He consulted with his generals,
and consequently raised an army of one hundred thousand men from Jīngkǒu,
arriving by both water and land,
launching a surprise attack on Jiànkāng.
Consequently, when the naval forces arrived,
Sēngbiàn was habitually residing in Shítou Chéng.
On that day, he was currently attending to official business.
Soldiers had already climbed over the northern wall and entered,
and the Southern Gate then urgently reported that troops were arriving.
Sēngbiàn and his son Wěi hastily rushed out of the inner chamber;
only a few dozen trusted retainers remained around them.
When all the enemy forces arrived,
Sēngbiàn had no plan left.
He therefore stood upon the tower of the Southern Gate, begging for his life and bowing in supplication.
Bàxiān immediately ordered them to set the tower ablaze.
Sēngbiàn and Wěi then descended and were captured.
Bàxiān said:
"What crime did I commit,
that you wished to reward the Qí army by having them attack me?"
He further said:
"Why did you totally lack any defensive preparations?"
Sēngbiàn replied:
"Trusting you at the North Gate,
why is this considered lack of preparation?"
That night, they were executed.
His eldest son, Yǐ,
in the beginning of the Chéngshèng era, served successively in office, reaching the rank of Shìzhōng.
Previously,
when Sēngbiàn pacified Jiànyè,
he sent Bàxiān to guard Jīngkǒu.
He (Sēngbiàn) made absolutely no defensive preparations (against Bàxiān).
Yǐ repeatedly spoke about this concern,
but Sēngbiàn did not listen,
and eventually suffered this disaster.
When the Western Wèi raided Jiānglíng,
Shìzǔ sent Yǐ to supervise all military affairs within the city.
When Jīngchéng fell,
Yǐ followed Wáng Lín into Qí,
and became the Administrator of Jìnglíng Commandery.
Qí sent Lín to guard Shòuchūn,
intending to seize the territory south of the Yangtze (Jiāngzuǒ).
After Chén pacified Huáinán,
they captured Lín and executed him.
When Yǐ heard that Lín was dead,
he went out south of the commandery city,
climbed atop a high mound, wailed and wept,
and died after a single fit of anguish.
Yǐ's younger brother, Bān,
possessed high aspirations and integrity in his youth.
He followed Shìzǔ,
and when Jīngchéng fell and was destroyed,
he was captured by Western Wèi.
The Official Historian comments: Since Hóu Jǐng's rebellious invasion,
Shìzǔ held the upper reaches (of the Yangtze),
entrusting Sēngbiàn with the commandership of the entire army of Chǔ.
When he succeeded in quelling the disaster and rebellion,
his achievement was indeed remarkable.
When evaluating merit,
he deserved the reward of the highest ranks.
Jìng Dì, due to the importance of being the successor established by Gāozǔ,
and the prestige of Shìzǔ succeeding to the body politic (as Emperor),
should have, upon the fall and destruction of Zhǔgōng,
rightly deserved the imperial succession.
Sēngbiàn's position was that of a general and prime minister.
His duty was to preserve loyalty like Yī (Yī Yǐn) and Huò (Huò Guāng);
instead, he was coerced by the Qí army,
and established a collateral descendant (Zhēnyáng) on the side.
If he merely desired to practice loyalty and righteousness,
how far away was true loyalty and righteousness?
Since the path of establishing the state was damaged,
his schemes for self-preservation were inadequate.
He brought about his own destruction.
How tragic!
Arrayed Biographies Forty: Hú Sēngyòu, Xú Wénshèng, Dù Zè (Elder brother Àn, Younger brother Yòu'ān, Elder brother's son Kān), Yīn Zichūn
Hú Sēngyòu, courtesy name Yuànguǒ,
was a man from Guānjūn, Nányáng.
In youth, he was brave and resolute,
possessing military talent.
He served Wèi, reaching the rank of Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū.
In the second year of Dàtōng (528 CE), he returned to the kingdom,
and frequently submitted sealed memorials.
Gāozǔ valued him,
appointed him Acting Commander (Jiǎjié), General Who Surpasses Military Might (Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn), and Commander-in-Chief of Wéndé,
and tasked him with defending Xiàngchéng.
When the city fell,
he was again captured by Wèi.
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtōng (529 CE),
when Chén Qìngzhī escorted Yuán Hào, the Prince of Běihǎi of Wèi, into Luòyáng,
Sēngyòu was again able to return to the kingdom.
He was appointed Administrator of the two commanderies of Nán Tiānshuǐ and Tiānmén.
He governed well.
By nature, he enjoyed reading,
but he could not compose or arrange words elegantly.
However, whenever he was at official banquets,
he invariably insisted on composing poetry.
His literary style was rustic and coarse,
and he was frequently ridiculed.
Sēngyòu remained happy and unperturbed,
believing himself to be truly skilled,
and his boasting became even more excessive.
Later, he served Shìzǔ,
as the Recorder and Adjutant (Lùshì Cānjūn) for the General Who Guards the West (Zhènxī).
When Hóu Jǐng rebelled,
the western Jǔ barbarians revolted.
Shìzǔ ordered Sēngyòu to suppress them,
commanding him to execute all their leaders.
Sēngyòu advised against this,
offending the Emperor's intention, and was imprisoned.
In the second year of Dàbǎo (551 CE),
Hóu Jǐng raided Jīngshǎn (Jīngzhōu and Shǎnzhōng),
and besieged Wáng Sēngbiàn at Bālíng.
Shìzǔ then summoned Sēngyòu from prison,
appointed him Acting Commander (Jiǎjié), General of Martial Might (Wǔměng Jiāngjūn),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Xīnshì County,
ordering him to go to the rescue.
As Sēngyòu was about to depart,
he said to his son:
"You should open two gates:
one gate designated Vermilion (Zhū),
and one gate designated White (Bái).
If I achieve success (auspicious), I will enter through the Vermilion Gate;
if I suffer misfortune (inauspicious), I will enter through the White Gate.
I shall not return unless I achieve victory."
Shìzǔ heard this and admired his spirit.
When he reached Yángpǔ,
Jǐng dispatched his general Rèn Yuē leading five thousand elite troops,
to occupy Báijì,
waiting for Sēngyòu from afar.
Sēngyòu proceeded west via a different route.
Yuē thought Sēngyòu had retreated out of fear of him,
and pursued him quickly,
catching up to him at Qiānkǒu in Nán'ān.
He shouted to Sēngyòu, saying:
"Wú boy (Wú'ér)!
Why don't you surrender immediately?
Where are you running off to?"
Sēngyòu did not speak to him,
secretly withdrawing backwards,
until he reached Chìshā Tíng.
There, he met Lù Fǎhé, who had arrived,
and immediately joined forces with him to attack Yuē.
They thoroughly defeated him,
captured Yuē, and sent him to Jiānglíng.
Hóu Jǐng heard of this and subsequently fled.
Shìzǔ appointed Sēngyòu Shìzhōng and Superintendent of the Army General (lǐng Jūnjiāngjūn),
summoning him back to Jīngzhōu.
In the second year of Chéngshèng
he was promoted to Chējì Jiāngjūn (General of Chariots and Cavalry) and Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establishing a Staff Equal to the Three Dukes),
and the rest of his appointments remained as before.
When the Western Wèi invaders arrived,
Sēng Yòu was appointed Dūdū Chéngdōng Zhūjūnshì (Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs East of the City).
The Wèi army launched attacks from four sides,
advancing simultaneously on a hundred paths.
Sēng Yòu personally braved the arrows and stones,
supervising the battle day and night.
He encouraged his officers and soldiers,
and was clear in his rewards and punishments.
The multitude was all moved by him
and unanimously fought to the death.
Wherever they advanced, they destroyed and eliminated the enemy,
and the rebels dared not approach.
Shortly thereafter, he was struck and killed by a stray arrow,
aged sixty-three at the time.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Xuān of Liáng) heard of it
and rushed to him, weeping over his body.
Thereupon, those inside and outside the city were terrified and panicked,
and the city subsequently fell.
Xú Wénshèng, courtesy name Dàomào,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His ancestors served as generals in Wèi.
His father, Qìngzhī,
at the beginning of Tiānjiān,
led over a thousand men and surrendered from the north.
He died on the way before arrival.
Wénshèng then took command of his troops,
gradually establishing merits and achievements.
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) greatly favored and cherished him.
At the end of Dàtóng,
he was appointed Chíjí, Dū Níngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Níngzhōu with credentials).
Prior to this,
the prefecture was located in a remote and secluded area.
The various Mán (barbarians) under its jurisdiction did not understand moral teachings;
they were greedy for wealth and goods,
and robberies and usurpations were frequent.
Former governors had been unable to control them.
Wénshèng treated them sincerely and comforted them,
showing them both prestige and virtue.
The Yí and Liáo (barbarians) were moved by this,
and their customs subsequently changed.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
upon hearing of the national crisis,
he recruited several tens of thousands of men and came to the rescue.
Shìzǔ praised him

and appointed him Chíjí, Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Attendant-in-ordinary), Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard), Dū Liáng Nán Qín Shā Dōng Yì Bā Běi Bā Liùzhōu Zhūjūnshì (Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs of the Six Prefectures: Liáng, Southern Qín, Shā, Eastern Yì, Bā, and Northern Bā), Rénwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Benevolent Might), and Qínzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Qínzhōu),
entrusting him with the strategy for the eastern campaign.
Thereupon, Wénshèng led the various armies eastward
and reached Wǔchāng.
He encountered Rèn Yuē, a general under Hóu Jǐng,
and subsequently held a standoff with him for a long time.

Shìzǔ further ordered Hùjūn Jiāngjūn (Protector General) Yǐn Yuè, Píngdōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the East) Dù Yòu'ān, and Bāzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Bāzhōu) Wáng Xún, among others, to join him,
all of whom were placed under Wénshèng's command.
They attacked Rèn Yuē at Bèijī.
Yuē was severely defeated
and retreated to defend Xīyáng.
Wénshèng advanced to occupy Lúzhōu,
and again held a standoff.
Hóu Jǐng heard of this
and led a large force westward to reinforce Yuē,
arriving at Xīyáng.
Wénshèng dared not engage in battle.
All the generals said:
"Jǐng's naval forces advanced rashly
and are also very hungry and fatigued.
We can seize this opportunity to attack them
and will surely win a great victory."
Wénshèng refused.
Wénshèng's wife, Lady Shí,
was previously in Jiànyè.
Now,
Jǐng transported her back to him.
Wénshèng was deeply grateful to Jǐng
and secretly exchanged communications,
having absolutely no intention of fighting.
The troops were all angry and resentful.
Dù Yòu'ān and Sòng Zuò, among others, then led their respective forces and advanced alone,
fighting with Jǐng.
They soundly defeated him
and returned with captured boats and ships.
It happened that Jǐng secretly dispatched cavalry which used a side path to raid and capture Yǐngzhōu.
Panic and fear spread through the army,
which subsequently suffered a great rout.
Wénshèng fled back to Jīngzhōu.
Shìzǔ nonetheless appointed him Dūdū Chéng Běimiàn (Area Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Front of the City).
He had also accumulated a great deal of stolen goods and filth.
Shìzǔ was greatly angered
and issued an edict reproaching him,
listing his ten crimes,
and stripped him of his official titles and peerage.
Since Wénshèng had lost military authority,
he secretly harbored resentment and grievances.
Shìzǔ heard of this
and subsequently imprisoned him.
At that time, Rèn Yuē had been captured
and was confined with Wénshèng.
Wénshèng said to Yuē:
"Why did you not surrender earlier,
causing me to reach this point?"
Yuē replied,
"I did not see the tracks of your horses outside the gates;
how could I rush to surrender?"
Wénshèng had no answer
and subsequently died in prison.
Dù Zè
was a native of Dùlíng in Jīngzhào.
His ancestors migrated from the north to the south
and settled in Xiāngyáng in Yōngzhōu.
His descendants made it their home.
His grandfather, Língqǐ,
was a Qí Gěishì Zhōng (Attendant-in-ordinary in Qí).
His father, Huáibǎo,
was ambitious and principled in his youth,
always seeking opportunities to distinguish himself.
When Gāozǔ's righteous army moved east,
he followed Nánpíng Wáng Wěi to remain and garrison Xiāngyáng.
During Tiānjiān,
he gradually established achievements and merits,
and his office reached Xiāoměng Jiāngjūn (General of Gallant Ferocity) and Liángzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Liángzhōu).
At the beginning of Dàtóng,
when Wèi's Liángzhōu Cìshǐ Yuán Luō submitted the entire prefecture,
Huáibǎo was further promoted to Dū Huàzhōu (Area Commander-in-Chief of Huàzhōu).
He served during the time when Yáng Shào, the Di King of Wǔxīng under the jurisdiction of Qínzhōu, rebelled.
Huáibǎo attacked and defeated him.
In the fifth year,
he died at his post.
Zè was Huáibǎo's seventh son.
In his youth, he possessed ambition and spirit,
and was renowned in his hometown for his courage and bravery.
He began his career as Lújiāng Piàojì Fǔ Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (Staff Officer of the Central Army in the establishment of the General of Agile Cavalry of Lújiāng).
When Shìzǔ governed Jīngzhōu,
he served on his staff.
Later he became Xīnxīng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Xīnxīng).
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he followed the Prince of Yuèyáng to attack Jīngzhōu.
Since Shìzǔ had a previous acquaintance with him,
he secretly invited him (to defect).
Zè, along with his elder brother Àn, younger brother Yòu'ān, and nephew Kān, returned to Shìzǔ that night.
Shìzǔ appointed him Chíjí, Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn (General of Trustworthy Might), and Wǔzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Wǔzhōu).
Shortly after, he was transferred to Xuānyì Jiāngjūn (General Who Spreads Righteousness),
concurrently serving as Zhènmán Hùjūn (Protector General Who Guards the Mán) and Wǔlíng Nèishǐ (Administrator of Wǔlíng),
titled Marquess of Zhījiāng County,
with an allotment of a thousand households.
He was ordered to follow Wáng Sēngbiàn in the eastern campaign against Hóu Jǐng.
Upon reaching Bālíng,
it happened that Jǐng came to attack.
He failed to overcome the defenses for several tens of days and then fled.
He was granted Shìzhōng (Court Attendant) and Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Left Guard),
and his rank was advanced to Duke,
with an increase of five hundred households to his allotment.
He subsequently followed Sēngbiàn in pursuing Jǐng to Shítóu
and held a standoff with the rebels at Hénglǐng.
When the battle commenced,
Jǐng personally led his elite forces,
attacking the flanks and crashing through.
Zè intercepted him horizontally from behind the ridge,
and Jǐng suffered a great defeat,
fleeing east to Jìnlíng.
Zè entered and occupied the city.
After Jǐng was pacified,

he was granted Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Attendant-in-ordinary), Chíjí, Dū Jiāngzhōu Zhūjūnshì (Area Commander-in-Chief of All Military Affairs of Jiāngzhōu), and Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Jiāngzhōu),
with an increase of a thousand households to his allotment.
This month,
Qí (齊) general Guō Yuánjiàn (郭元建) attacked Qínzhōu (秦州) Inspector Yán Chāoyuǎn (嚴超遠) at Qínjùn (秦郡).
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) ordered Cè (崱) to go to his aid.
Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) also came from Ōuyáng (歐陽) to join them.
They fought a great battle with Yuánjiàn (元建) at Shìlín (士林).
Bàxiān (霸先) ordered his strong crossbowmen to shoot,
and Yuánjiàn's (元建) forces retreated.
Cè (崱) then unleashed his troops to attack,
and thoroughly defeated them.
Over ten thousand heads were severed,
and more than a thousand men were captured alive.
Yuánjiàn (元建) gathered his remaining forces and fled.
At this time, Shìzǔ (世祖) captured Wáng Lín (王琳) in Jiānglíng (江陵).
His chief clerk, Lù Nà (陸納) and others, then rebelled in Chángshā (長沙).
Shìzǔ (世祖) summoned Cè (崱) and Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to suppress them.
In the second year of Chéngshèng (承聖) era,
they engaged Nà (納) and his forces in battle at Chēlún (車輪),
suffering a great defeat.
Two of their strongholds were captured.
Nà (納) and his forces fled to hold Chángshā (長沙),
and Cè (崱) and others besieged them.
Later, Nà (納) and his forces surrendered.
Cè (崱) then joined Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) in a western expedition against Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王) at Xiákǒu (硤口).
Upon arrival, they immediately defeated and pacified him.
Thereupon, he returned to his garrison,
contracted an illness, and died.
An imperial edict stated:
"Cè (崱),
a scion of an old Jīngzhào (京兆) family,
a descendant of Yuánkǎi (元凱),
whose family traditions include scholarship
and generations of loyalty and integrity.
Since his transfer to the river islets,
his governance was known for integrity and competence.
Promoted from humble beginnings,
he was truly known for his clear and quiet administration.
His sudden demise
fills Our heart with sorrow.
He is to be posthumously granted the title of Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chēqí Jiāngjūn, 車騎將軍),
and given an additional musical ensemble.
His posthumous name shall be Wǔ (武)."
Cè (崱) had nine brothers.
His elder brothers Sōng (嵩), Cén (岑), (巘), Jí (岌), Ní (嶷), Yǎn (巘), Àn (岸), and younger brother Yòu'ān (幼安),
were all famous in their time.
Àn's (岸) courtesy name was Gōnghéng (公衡).
From a young age, he possessed military talent
and was fond of strategies of alliance and conflict.
During the Tàiqīng (太清) era,
he and Cè (崱) together pledged allegiance to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed him with the staff of authority (chíjié, 持節), General Who Pacifies the North (Píngběi Jiāngjūn, 平北將軍), and Inspector of Běiliángzhōu (北梁州),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Jiānglíng (江陵) County,
with a thousand households.
Àn (岸) then requested to take Xiāngyáng (襄陽),
and Shìzǔ (世祖) granted his request.
Àn (岸) then marched day and night,
first going to attack its city,
but failed.
When Yuèyáng (岳陽) arrived,
he fled to his elder brother Yǎn (巘) in Nányáng (南陽).
Yǎn (巘) was at that time the Administrator of Nányáng (南陽).
Yuèyáng (岳陽) soon dispatched forces to attack and capture their city.
Àn (岸) and Yǎn (巘) were both killed.
Yòu'ān (幼安) was by nature extremely filial,
generous,
heroic and brave beyond others.
During the Tàiqīng (太清) era,
he and his elder brother Cè (崱) together pledged allegiance to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed him General of Cloud-like Cavalry (Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn, 雲麾將軍) and Inspector of Xījīngzhōu (西荊州),
and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Huáróng (華容) County,
with a thousand households.
He was ordered to join General Who Pacifies the South (Píngnán Jiāngjūn, 平南將軍) Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) in attacking Hédōng Wáng Yù (河東王譽) at Chángshā (長沙),
and pacified him.
He was also ordered to lead ten thousand elite armored troops
to assist Left Guardian General (Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn, 左衞將軍) Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛) in an eastern expedition against Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Upon reaching Bèijī (貝磯),
they encountered Jǐng's (景) general Rèn Yuē (任約) who came to oppose them.
They then fought,
and utterly defeated him,
beheading his Equal in Rank (yítóng, 儀同) Chìluó Zǐtōng (叱羅子通), Inspector of Xiāngzhōu (湘州) Zhào Wēifāng (趙威方), and others,
and sending their heads to Jiānglíng (江陵).
They then advanced their army to Dàjǔkǒu (大舉口),
where they stood in confrontation with Jǐng (景).
He separately attacked Wǔchāng (武昌),
and captured it.
Jǐng (景) crossed the upper stream of Lúzhōu (蘆洲) to press Wénshèng (文盛) and others.
Yòu'ān (幼安) and the various armies attacked him.
Jǐng (景) was greatly defeated,
and all his boats and ships were captured.
It happened that Jǐng (景) secretly sent forces to raid and capture Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
taking Inspector Fāng Zhū (方諸) and others captive back with them.
People were greatly alarmed.
Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛) fled back from Hànkǒu (漢口).
The various armies were greatly defeated,
and Yòu'ān (幼安) then surrendered to Jǐng (景).
Jǐng (景) killed him,
because of his frequent reversals.
Kān (龕) was
the son of Cén (岑), Cè's (崱) second elder brother.
From a young age, he was brave and skilled in warfare.
Also during the Tàiqīng (太清) era, he and his paternal uncles together pledged allegiance to Shìzǔ (世祖).
Shìzǔ (世祖) appointed him with the staff of authority (chíjié, 持節), Loyal and Martial General (Zhōngwǔ Jiāngjūn, 忠武將軍), and Inspector of Yúnzhōu (鄖州),
Marquis of Zhōnglú (中廬) County,
with a thousand households.
He and his uncle Yòu'ān (幼安) together followed Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to attack Hédōng Wáng (河東王),
and pacified him.
He then followed Sēngbiàn (僧辯) downstream,
and, following Xú Wénshèng's (徐文盛) army, arrived at Bālíng (巴陵).
Hearing that Hóu Jǐng (侯景) had raided and captured Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
and was moving west and about to arrive,
he and Sēngbiàn (僧辯) and others held Bālíng (巴陵) to await him.
When Jǐng (景) arrived,
he besieged it for several tens of days,
but failed to take it and fled.

He was promoted to Minister of the Grand Treasury (Tàifǔ Qīng, 太府卿), General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Jiāngjūn, 安北將軍), Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Dìngzhōu (Dū Dìngzhōu Zhūjūnshì, 督定州諸軍事), and Inspector of Dìngzhōu (定州),
and given the additional title of Palace Attendant in Ordinary Service (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì, 通直散騎常侍),
with an increase of five hundred households.
He then followed Sēngbiàn (僧辯) in pursuit of Jǐng (景) to Jiāngxià (江夏),
and besieged its city.
Jǐng's (景) general Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙) abandoned the city and fled.
Kān (龕) pursued him to Yángpǔ (楊浦),
and captured him alive.
In the third year of Dàbǎo (大寶) era,
the allied armies reached Gūshú (姑孰).
Jǐng's (景) general Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒) met them in battle.
Kān (龕) and Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先), Wáng Lín (王琳), and others led the elite troops to attack him,
and greatly defeated Zǐjiàn (子鑒).
They then reached Shítou (石頭).
Jǐng (景) personally led his faction to join battle.
Kān (龕) and the allied armies fought bravely,
and utterly defeated Jǐng (景).
Jǐng (景) then fled eastward.
His merits were considered the greatest,
and he was appointed General Who Pacifies the East (Píngdōng Jiāngjūn, 平東將軍) and Inspector of Dōngyángzhōu (東揚州),
with an additional enfeoffment of a thousand households.
In the second year of Chéngshèng (承聖) era,
he again joined Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) in suppressing Lù Nà (陸納) and others at Chángshā (長沙),
and they surrendered.
He was also summoned to suppress Wǔlíng Wáng (武陵王) at Xīlíng (西陵),
and also pacified him.
Later, Jiānglíng (江陵) fell.
Qí (齊) appointed Zhēnyáng Hóu (貞陽侯) as successor to the Liáng (梁) lineage,
and appointed Kān (龕) as Inspector of Zhènzhōu (震州) and Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興).

He was also appointed General Who Guards the South (Zhènnán Jiāngjūn, 鎮南將軍), Supervisor of All Military Affairs in Nányùzhōu (Dū Nányùzhōu Zhūjūnshì, 都督南豫州諸軍事), Inspector of Nányùzhōu (南豫州), and Marquis of Lìyáng (溧陽) County,
and granted a musical ensemble;
he was also given the additional titles of Palace Attendant (Sànqí Chángshì, 散騎常侍) and Grand General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn, 鎮東大將軍).
It happened that Chén Bàxiān (陳霸先) raided and captured the capital,
arresting Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) and killing him.
Kān (龕) was Sēngbiàn's (僧辯) son-in-law.
As Administrator of Wúxīng (吳興),
because Bàxiān (霸先) was not of noble birth,
and his troops were disorderly,
during the days he served in the military administration,
he never took Bàxiān (霸先) seriously.
And when he became the Administrator of his own commandery,
he always used the law to discipline Bàxiān's (霸先) clan,
showing no leniency.
Bàxiān (霸先) resented him deeply.
When Sēngbiàn (僧辯) was defeated,
Kān (龕) then held Wúxīng (吳興) to resist him.
He sent his military deputy Dù Tài (杜泰) to attack Chén Qiàn (陳蒨) at Chángchéng (長城),
but was in turn defeated by Qiàn (蒨).
Bàxiān (霸先) then sent general Zhōu Wényù (周文育) to attack Kān (龕).
Kān (龕) ordered his cousin Běisǒu (北叟) to go out and resist,
but he was again defeated by Wényù (文育).
He fled to Yìxīng (義興).
Bàxiān (霸先) personally led his forces to besiege him.
It happened that Qí (齊) general Liǔ Dámó (柳達摩) and others raided the capital.
Bàxiān (霸先) was afraid,
and so returned and made peace with the Qí (齊) people.
When Kān (龕) heard that the Qí (齊) army had returned,
he surrendered,
and was then killed.
Yīn Zǐchūn (陰子春), courtesy name Yòuwén (幼文),
was a native of Gūzāng (姑臧) in Wǔwēi (武威).
At the end of the Jìn (晉) Yìxī (義熙) era,
his great-grandfather Xí (襲),
followed Sòng Gāozǔ (宋高祖) in his southward migration,
and settled in Nánpíng (南平).
His father, Zhìbó (智伯),
was a neighbor of Gāozǔ (高祖)
and they were good friends in their youth.
He once entered Gāozǔ's (高祖) bedchamber
and saw a wondrous five-colored light.
He then grasped Gāozǔ's (高祖) hand and said:
"You will surely achieve great nobility later;
you will not be a mere subject.
The world is in turmoil,
and those who will bring peace to the common people,
will it be you?"
Gāozǔ (高祖) said:
"Fortunately, do not speak too much."
Thereupon, their friendship grew closer,
and whenever Gāozǔ (高祖) had needs,
it was as if he was visiting an external treasury.
When Gāozǔ (高祖) ascended the throne,
he held office as Inspector of Liáng (梁) and Qín (秦) Prefectures.
Zǐchūn,
in the early Tiānjiān reign,
started his career as Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn,
and Xīyáng Tàishǒu.
In the Puǒtōng reign,
he was successively promoted to Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and Nánliángzhōu Cìshǐ;
then again promoted to Xìnwēi Jiāngjūn, Dūdū Liáng Qín Huá Sānzhōu Zhūjūnjì, and Liáng Qín Èrzhōu Cìshǐ.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
he suppressed the rebellious Man in Xiá zhōng,
and pacified them.
He was summoned to be Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn,
and later promoted to Shìzhōng.
During Hóu Jǐng's rebellion,
Shìzǔ ordered Zǐchūn to accompany Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn Wáng Sēngbiàn in attacking Shàolíngwáng in Yǐngzhōu,
and pacified him.
He then, with Zuǒwèi Jiāngjūn Xú Wénshèng, marched east to attack Hóu Jǐng.
Upon reaching Bèijī,
they encountered Jǐng.
Zǐchūn fought bravely,
surpassing all other generals,
and repeatedly defeated Jǐng.
However, as Yǐngzhōu was captured,
the army was subsequently defeated and retreated.
In the second year of Dàbǎo,
he died in Jiānglíng.
His grandson, Hào,
was well-known in his youth.
He began his career as Fèngcháoqǐng,
and successively held the post of Shàngshū Jīnbù Láng.
Later, he entered Zhōu.
He compiled twenty juan of Qiónglín.
The court historian says: Hú Sēngyòu was renowned for his courage and competence;
he captured banners and defeated enemies numerous times.
When he sacrificed his life for his country,
dying for the king's cause,
even the loyal and valiant of ancient times
could not surpass him.
Xú Wénshèng initially established merits,
but failed to maintain his reputation until the end,
which was unrighteous.
Dù Zè understood the principles of change and adaptation,
and knew what was proper to support and what to oppose.
Furthermore, he frequently commanded armies,
repeatedly annihilated rebels and invaders.
His achievements and contributions were outstanding,
and he ultimately became a meritorious official of the restoration.
How righteous!
Collation Notes

Biography Forty-one: Xiàoxíng: Téng Tán’gōng (Xú Pǔjì, Wǎnlíng Nǚzǐ), Shěn Chóngsù, Xún Jiàng, Yǔ Qiánlóu, Jí Fēn, Zhēn Tián, Hán Huáimíng, Liú Tánjìng, Hé Jiǒng, Yǔ Shāmí, Jiāng Fú, Liú Jì, Chǔ Xiū, Xiè Lìn.
The Classic states:
"Filial piety
is the root of virtue."
This is the greatest among the people,
and what a state prioritizes!
Gāozǔ, in establishing his enterprise and founding his dynasty,
rectified himself and transformed customs.
The degenerate customs were reformed,
and the art of governance through filial piety was established.
Each time he issued decrees,
he extended distant commendations.
Yet, with harmony widespread in every household,
few sought peculiar or extraordinary reputations.
Concealed virtue became a trend,
and those who surpassed the multitude humbly took their place.
What was made manifest to sight and hearing
was indeed very little.
Now, these are compiled to record what might otherwise be lost.
Téng Tán’gōng was
a native of Nánchāng, Yùzhāng.
When he was five years old,
his mother, Yáng Shì, suffered from a fever
and longed for cold melon.
Such melons were not locally produced,
and Tán’gōng searched everywhere but could not find one.
He was filled with sorrow and grief.
Soon, he met a monk who asked him the reason.
Tán’gōng told him everything.
The monk said:
"I have two melons;
I will give you one."
Tán’gōng bowed in thanks,
then took the melon home
and offered it to his mother.
The whole household was astonished.
They searched for the monk,
but his whereabouts were unknown.
When his parents died,
Tán’gōng abstained from food and drink for ten days,
and was so overwhelmed with grief that he vomited blood,
fainting and then recovering.
In deep winter, he wore no padded clothes,
and ate only vegetables for the rest of his life.
Every anniversary of their death,
he was consumed by longing and grief,
lamenting day and night.
Outside his gate were two evergreen trees.
At times, a divine light would suddenly rise from the trees,
and soon Buddha images and attendant figures would appear,
radiant and conspicuous,
entering through the gate.
Tán’gōng's family, old and young,
all bowed in worship.
After a long while, it disappeared.
People, both lay and monastic, near and far, spread the story.
Tàishǒu Wáng Sēngqián invited Tán’gōng to be Gōngcáo,
but he firmly declined.
Wáng Jiǎn, who was then with Sēngqián in the prefecture,
referred to him as Téng Zēngzǐ.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
Lù Lián, on an imperial mission to inspect customs,
reported his deeds.
Tán’gōng had three sons,
all of whom had good conduct.
At that time, there was Xú Pǔjì,
a native of Línxiāng, Chángshā.
While mourning his parent and before burial,
a fire broke out at his neighbor's house,
and spread to his dwelling.
Pǔjì wailed and threw himself onto the coffin,
shielding it with his body from the fire.
Neighbors rushed to rescue him;
he was already unconscious from the burns,
and it took several days for him to recover.
In Wǎnlíng, Xuānchéng, there was a woman who slept in the same bed as her mother.
Her mother was attacked by a fierce tiger.
The daughter screamed and fought the tiger,
causing all its fur to fall out.
The tiger carried her for ten-some li,
then finally abandoned her.
The daughter carried her mother back;
she still had breath,
but died after some time.
Tàishǒu Xiāo Chēn offered condolences;
he reported her deeds,
and an imperial edict commended her family gate.
Shěn Chóngsù, courtesy name Sīzhěng,
was a man of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His father, Huáimíng,
was the Cìshǐ (Governor) of Yǎnzhōu during the Sòng Dynasty.
Chóngsù suffered the loss of his father at the age of six,
and his weeping and leaping exceeded the prescribed rites.
When he grew up,
he hired himself out as a copyist to support his mother.
At the beginning of the Jiànwǔ era of Qí,
he began his career as a Fèngcháoqǐng.
At the end of the Yǒngyuán era,
he was promoted to Sītú Xíng Cānjūn.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he became Cānjūnshì (Military Advisor) to the Prince of Póyáng, who served as Qiánjūn (General of the Vanguard).
In the third year,
the Tàishǒu (Administrator) Liǔ Yùn appointed him as Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk).
Chóngsù followed Yùn to the commandery,
and returned to fetch his mother.
His mother died.
Chóngsù, having failed to attend her during her illness,
was determined to kill himself.
No water or liquid passed his lips.
He cried loudly day and night,
and for ten days he was nearly lifeless.
His brothers said to him:
"The funeral rites have not yet been performed.
To suddenly destroy yourself
is not the way of complete filiality."
When Chóngsù arrived at the burial site,
he did not avoid rain or snow,
leaning on the grave mound in deep sorrow.
Every night, fierce beasts came and gazed upon him,
making sounds resembling sighs.
As his family was poor and lacked the means for the final burial,
he resorted to begging for an entire year
before he was finally able to perform the interment.
Afterward, he built a hut beside the tomb.
Believing that his initial mourning rites had been incomplete,
he decided to observe mourning for another three years after the burial.
For a long time, he ate only wheat chaff,
abstaining from salt and vinegar.
He sat and slept on a single mat,
which caused him to swell up from weakness and be unable to rise.
The commandery and county reported his extreme filiality.
When Gāozǔ heard of this,
he immediately dispatched a Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretary of the Palace Secretariat) to console and encourage him.
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued, which stated:
"Qiánjūn Shěn Chóngsù,
has shown noble conduct since youth,
observing mourning beyond the rites.
Because his mourning period was not yet completed,
he was unable to perform the grand burial.
Believing that begging took up a whole year,
and that many sorrowful rites were missed,
he intends, on the morning of eternal remembrance,
to begin a second three-year mourning period.
Although his sentiment is pitiable,
the rites have clear regulations.
He should be commanded to remove his mourning clothes immediately
and be promoted to Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ (Mounted Escort to the Crown Prince).
This will honor his family gate
and strengthen moral instruction."
Chóngsù obeyed the edict and removed his mourning clothes,
yet his weeping and crying were like those in mourning.
He firmly declined the official position,
vehemently submitting petitions to resign.
After a year, he was finally permitted to serve as the Magistrate of Yǒngníng.
Believing that his salary had come too late to support his mother,
his sorrow and remorse intensified.
He could not bear the grief,
and died while serving in the county.
He was thirty-nine years old at the time.
Xún Jiàng, courtesy name Wénshī,
was a man of Yǐnyīn.
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Dàbǎo (Grand Guardian) Xù of Jìn.
His grandfather, Qióng,
at the age of fifteen,
avenged his father in Chéngdū Market,
and was known for his filiality.
At the end of the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
he crossed the Huái River to join the cause of Wǔlíng Wang Yì (Prince Yì of Wǔlíng),
and was killed by the pursuing troops of the Chief Culprit.
He was posthumously granted the title Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng.
His father, Fǎchāo,
served as the Magistrate of Ānfù at the end of the Zhōngxīng era of Qí,
and died in office.
When the news of the death arrived,
Jiàng wept so bitterly he collapsed, losing consciousness.
His body became completely cold,
and he did not revive until nightfall.
Afterward, he rushed to the funeral.
Whenever he stayed overnight by river banks or islets,
merchants and travelers could not bear to hear his cries.
Before his mourning period was finished,
his elder brother, Fěi, began his career as the Tàishǒu (Administrator) of Yùlín.
While campaigning against the Lǐ bandits,
he was struck by a stray arrow
and died on the battlefield.
When the coffin returned,
Jiàng met it at Yùzhāng.
Upon seeing the boat, he threw himself into the water.
People nearby rushed to save him,
and he barely survived.
After arriving,
his family was too poor to hold a timely burial.
He observed the mourning for his father concurrently with the mourning for his brother,
remaining within his mourning hut for four years.
Since tying up his hair (for mourning),
he never combed or washed it again,
and all his hair fell out.
He cried constantly;
when his voice failed, he continued with silent weeping.
The corners of his eyes were inflamed and sore.
His body was withered and emaciated,
skin and bone barely held together,
and even his family members hardly recognized him.
The commandery and county reported his condition.
Gāozǔ issued an edict and dispatched a Zhōngshū Shèrén to order him to cease mourning,
promoting him to Zuǒ Chángshì (Left Attendant) of the Kingdom of Yùzhāng.
Although Jiàng resumed ordinary dress,
his wasted appearance worsened.
His maternal grandfather, Sūn Qiān, admonished him, saying:
"The Lord above governs the realm through filiality.
Your actions surpass those of the ancients,
which is why a clear edict was issued,
promoting you to this post.
Not only is the command of the sovereign and father (substitute) difficult to refuse,
but it also serves to spread your fame to later generations.
Those who are glorified are not solely yourself."
Jiàng then accepted the appointment.
Ultimately, he died at home due to his debilitation,
at the age of twenty-one.
Yǔ Qiánlóu, courtesy name Zǐzhēn,
was a man of Xīnyě.
His father, Yì,
was Sītú Zhǔbù (Chief Clerk of the Minister over the Masses).
He was summoned but did not attend,
possessing a lofty reputation.
Qiánlóu was fond of learning in his youth,
often lecturing on and reciting the Classic of Filial Piety (Xiàojīng).
He never showed dismay before others.
The lofty scholars Liú Qiú and Zōng Cè of Nányáng both admired and marveled at him.
He began his career as Zhǔbù of his home prefecture,
and was promoted to Píngxī Xíng Cānjūn.
He was posted out as the Magistrate of Biān,
where his governance achieved outstanding results.
Previously,
the county territory suffered greatly from fierce tigers.
When Qiánlóu arrived,
all the tigers crossed over and moved to the border of Línjǔ.
People at the time believed this was due to the influence of his benevolent transformation.
At the beginning of the Yǒngyuán era of Qí,
he was appointed Magistrate of Chánlíng.
Less than ten days after reaching the county,
Yì became ill at home.
Qiánlóu was suddenly startled in his heart,
and his entire body was covered in sweat.
That very day, he abandoned his post and returned home.
His family was astonished by his sudden arrival.
At that time, Yì had been ill for only two days.
The physician said:
"To know whether the illness is worsening or improving,
one must taste the excrement to determine if it is sweet or bitter."
Yì suffered from dysentery.
Qiánlóu immediately took some and tasted it.
As the taste became sweeter and smoother,
his heart became increasingly worried and distressed.
By evening,
he repeatedly knocked his forehead on the ground toward the Northern Dipper,
begging to trade his life for his father's.
Soon, he heard a voice in the air saying:
"Zhēngjūn's (The Summoned Gentleman's) lifespan is exhausted,
and cannot be extended.
Since your sincere prayer has reached us,
we can only extend it until the end of the month."
On the last day of the month, Yì died.
Qiánlóu observed mourning beyond the prescribed rites,
living in a hut beside the tomb.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne,
he intended to appoint him.
Zhènjūn (General Who Guards the Army) Xiāo Yǐngzhòu personally wrote a letter urging him,
but Qiánlóu firmly refused.
When the mourning period was complete,
he was appointed Xītái Shàngshū Yícáo Láng (Director of the Bureau of Rites in the Western Secretariat).
Liáng tái was established,
Dèng Yuánqǐ was appointed Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yìzhōu,
and he nominated Qián Lóu to be Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) of the Prefecture and Administrator (Tàishǒu) of the two commanderies, Bāxī and Zǐtóng.
When Chéngdū was pacified,
the city contained mountains of treasures and valuables.
Yuánqǐ divided them all among his subordinates,
but Qián Lóu took nothing whatsoever.
Yuánqǐ disliked his standing out from the crowd,
and said sternly:
"Why is the Chief Clerk the only one acting this way!"
Qián Lóu, showing he did not wish to disobey,
requested several chests of books.
Soon after, he was appointed Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Shǔjùn.
He was pure and simple in office,
and the common people benefited from it.
When Yuánqǐ died in Shǔ,
his troops and retainers all dispersed,
but Qián Lóu personally oversaw the embalming and burial rites,
and carried the funeral casket back to his homeland.
Upon returning, he became a Director (Láng) of the Treasury Department (Jīnbù) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū),
and was promoted to Aide (Cānjūn) in the Secretariat (Jìshì) of the Central Army (Zhōngjūn Biǎojì).
When the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng) was established,
he served the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) in reading, holding his original post.
He was greatly recognized and valued.

An imperial edict commanded that he, along with the Crown Prince's Vice Minister (Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ) Yīn Jūn, the Palace Attendant (Zhōngshèrén) Dào Qià, and the Erudite of the National University (Guózǐ Bóshì) Míng Shānbīn, etc.,
should take turns daily instructing the Crown Prince on the meanings of the Five Classics (Wǔjīng Yì).
He was promoted to Palace Attendant (Sànqí Shìláng) and Grand Arbiter (Dà Zhōngzhèng) of Jīngzhōu.
He died
at the age of forty-six.
Jí Fēn, courtesy name Yànxiāo,
was a native of Liánsháo in Fēngyì Commandery,
and his family had resided for generations in Xiāngyáng.
Fēn possessed filial piety from a young age.
When he was eleven years old,
he suffered the mourning of his birth mother.
Water and gruel did not enter his mouth;
he nearly destroyed his health,
and his relatives and friends found him remarkable.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
his father was the Magistrate (Lìng) of Yuánxiāng County in Wúxīng Commandery.
He was falsely accused by corrupt officials
and arrested and taken to the Court of the Judicial Review (Tíngwèi).
Fēn, aged fifteen,
wailed and wept in the main roads,
pleading with the Dukes and Ministers (Gōngqīng).
Passersby who witnessed this
all shed tears for him.
Although his father was fundamentally innocent,
he was ashamed of being interrogated by officials,
so he falsely admitted guilt,
and his crime was punishable by death (Dàpì).
Fēn then beat the Drum of Appeal (Dēngwén Gǔ),
requesting to die in his father's stead.
Gāozǔ found this remarkable,
and commanded Cài Fǎdù, Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (Tíngwèi Qīng), saying:
"Jí Fēn's request to die to redeem his father
is truly admirable in its righteousness.
However, being
a young child, he might not have initiated this intention himself.
You should severely threaten and coax him
to elicit the true facts."
Fǎdù received the imperial order and returned to his office.
He grandly displayed chains and fetters,
lined up the judicial officials,
and asked Fēn severely:
"You requested to die in your father's stead,
and the imperial command has granted this.
You should immediately submit to the law.
However, the tortures of knives and saws are extreme.
Are you truly able to die?
Furthermore, you are a mere boy;
your intent could not reach this level.
You must have been instructed by someone.
What is that person's name?
You must list it clearly in your answer.
If you have any regret or different thought,
we will also permit it."
Fēn replied:
"Although this prisoner is young and weak,
how can he not know that death is terrifying and dreadful?
But considering my younger brothers are immature and small,
and only this prisoner is the eldest,
I cannot bear to see my father receive the death penalty
while I prolong my own breath.
This is why I made the firm decision in my heart
and appealed to His Majesty (Wànshèng).
Now I wish to sacrifice my life in uncertainty
and entrust my bones to the earth.
This is not a trivial matter.
How could I have been instructed by others?
The bright decree permits the substitution,
which is no different from ascending to immortality.
How could I possibly have second thoughts?"
Fǎdù knew that Fēn's sincerity was genuine
and could not be suppressed or bent.
He changed his expression to a gentle one and persuaded him, saying:
"The Sovereign (Zhǔshàng) knows your honored father is innocent
and will soon release him.
Observing your brilliant and outstanding demeanor,
you are truly a fine youth.
If you now retract your statement,
fortunately, father and son can both be saved.
Why must you use this splendid youth
to suffer the cauldron and cleaver (tānghuò)?"
Fēn replied:
"Even creatures like beetles, fish fry, and ants
still cherish their lives.
How much more so for a human being;
who would wish to be smashed to powder?
However, my father is entangled in a severe prosecution,
and the penal code must be strictly applied.
Therefore, I resolved to perish,
hoping to prolong my father’s life.
I now close my eyes and crane my neck
to await the great execution.
My feelings are exhausted and my intention is finalized;
I have no further words to reply."
When Fēn was first imprisoned,
the prison clerk, following the law, applied chains and fetters liberally.
Fǎdù took pity on him,
ordering the removal of two of the shackles
and replacing them with a smaller one.
Fēn refused to listen,
saying:
"I, Fēn, requested to die in my father's stead.
For a condemned prisoner,
the shackles should only be increased,
how can they be reduced?"
He ultimately did not remove the shackles.
Fǎdù reported the full details to the Emperor,
and Gāozǔ then pardoned his father.
Wáng Zhì, Prefect (Yǐn) of Dānyáng, sought the records of his case at the Court of Judicial Review,
and also requested to visit his residence.
He intended, at the beginning of the year,
to nominate him for selection as a truly filial son (Chúnxiào).
Fēn said:
"How strange, Prefect Wáng!
Why do you underestimate Fēn so much?
If the father is disgraced, the son should die;
this principle is self-evident.
If I, Fēn, were shameless enough
to accept this nomination,
that would mean acquiring fame by exploiting my father's situation—
what an extreme disgrace!"
He refused the offer, and the matter ceased.
At the age of seventeen,
he was recruited and appointed Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù) of his home province.
He was sent out to supervise Wànnián County.
He temporarily held the post for a full month,
and moral governance was widely effective.
Returning from Yōngzhōu to Yǐngzhōu,
the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiāngzhōu, Liǔ Chén, again summoned him to serve as Chief Clerk.
Later, his townsman Péi Jiǎn, the Assistant (Chéng) to the Prefect of Dānyáng Zāng Dùn, and the Arbiter (Zhōngzhèng) of Yángzhōu Zhāng Zè jointly recommended Fēn,
holding that his filial conduct was utterly sincere
and that he was clear and knowledgeable in the *Yìjīng* and *Lǎozǐ*.
An imperial edict ordered the Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) to honor and commend him.
Previously,
when Fēn's father was implicated in the crime,
Fēn developed an anxiety illness (jì jí).
Later, it flared up, and he died.
Zhēn Tián, courtesy name Yànyuē,
was a native of Wújí in Zhōngshān,
and his family had resided for generations in Jiānglíng.
His grandfather, Qīnzhī,
was the Magistrate (Lìng) of Chángníng;
his father, Biāozhī,
was a Provincial Attendant (Zhōucóngshì).
Tián lost his father when he was several years old;
his grief was moving, just like an adult's.
His family, pitying his youth,
fed him rice mixed with meat broth,
but Tián refused to eat it.
At the age of eight,
he asked his mother,
regretting that he had been born too late to know his father,
and then wept bitterly for several days.
Suddenly, he seemed to have a vision,
and when he described the appearance
it matched his father.
People at the time regarded this as filial inspiration.
Though the family was poor,
he always managed to provide delicacies for his mother.
During the period of mourning,
he built a hut beside the grave.
There was a bird of mixed black and yellow colors
that gathered in the tree by the hut;
it chirped when Tián cried,
and stopped when his crying ceased.
There was also a white sparrow that nested and roosted in his hut.
The regional commander, Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn (始興王憺), memorialized his conduct.
An imperial edict declared:
“We empty Our heart and admire the virtuous;
Our thoughts are filled with them, waking and sleeping.
We instruct those regional officials
to exert themselves in searching and promoting them.
Since Tián's filial conduct is truly exceptional,
and his reputation is manifest throughout the land,
he greatly aids in upholding customs and reforming practices,
providing much benefit.
The reports from governors and magistrates,
in spirit, are the same as Our own personal observation.
His residence and neighborhood should be commended and honored,
and he should be granted a noble rank.”
Tián's highest official post was Ānnán Xíng Cānjūn (安南行參軍).
Hán Huáimíng (韓懷明),
a man from Shàngdǎng (上黨),
was living as a sojourner in Jīngzhōu (荊州).
When he was ten years old,
his mother suffered from *shīzhù* (屍疰) (a type of illness),
and each time it flared up, she was critically ill.
Huáimíng prayed, knocking his head on the ground beneath the stars at night.
The cold was exceedingly bitter at the time.
Suddenly, he smelled a fragrance,
and someone spoke from the air, saying:
“The boy's mother will be completely well soon;
do not wear yourself out.”
Before dawn,
his mother had fully recovered.
The local people were astonished by this.
He lost his father at fifteen,
and his grief nearly destroyed his nature.
He carried earth to build the grave mound,
refusing all gifts and assistance.
After the mourning period ended,
he and his fellow villager Guō É (郭黁) together studied under Liú Qiú (劉虬) of Nányáng (南陽).
One day, Qiú stopped lecturing
and stayed alone weeping.
Huáimíng secretly asked the reason.
Qiú's family members replied:
“It is the anniversary of his maternal grandfather's death.”
At that time, Qiú's mother had also already died.
When Huáimíng heard this,
he stopped his studies that very day,
returned home, and devoted himself to caring for his mother.
Qiú sighed, saying:
“Student Hán will not have the regret of Yúqiū (虞丘).”
His family was poor,
so he constantly worked hard to provide sweet and crispy foods,
delighting and playing by his mother's knee,
never leaving her side day or night.
His mother died of old age
at ninety-one.
Huáimíng did not let water or food pass his lips for ten days,
and his wailing never ceased.
A pair of white doves nested above his hut;
they raised their young and were so tame
they seemed like domestic fowl.
They left only after he removed his mourning clothes.
After concluding the mourning,
he ate only vegetables for the rest of his life,
and his clothing and bedding remained unchanged.
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
the Prefect, Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn (始興王憺), memorialized this matter.
The commandery repeatedly summoned him, but he never accepted office,
and he died at home.
Liú Tánjìng (劉曇淨), courtesy name Yuánguāng (元光),
was a man from Lǚ (呂) in Péngchéng (彭城).
His grandfather, Yuánzhēn (元真),
was the Grand Administrator of Huáinán (淮南).
He committed a crime while holding that commandery post.
His father, Huìjìng (慧鏡),
visited court officials seeking clemency one by one,
with extreme sincerity and earnestness,
and thereby became known for his filial piety.
Tánjìng was earnest in his conduct and possessed his father’s style.
He was appointed Zuǒ Chángshì (左常侍) of the Ānchéng (安成) Principality.
His father died while serving in a commandery.
Tánjìng rushed to the funeral,
and went without food or drink for several days;
he fainted and then revived.
Each time he cried, he vomited blood.
After the mourning period was over,
his emaciation and distress developed into illness.
It happened that there was an imperial edict
for scholars and gentry to each recommend candidates in the four categories.
Tánjìng's uncle, Huìfěi (慧斐), recommended him to fulfill the Filial Conduct category.
Gāozǔ (高祖) then appointed him Magistrate of Hǎiníng (海寧).
As Tánjìng's elder brother had not yet been appointed to a county post,
he yielded the position to his brother,
and was instead appointed Ānxī Xíng Cānjūn (安西行參軍).
After his father’s death,
his service to his mother was especially pure and utmost;
he personally prepared the gruel and broth,
not entrusting it to others.
When his mother was ill,
he did not loosen his belt (or take off his clothes).
When his mother died,
he abstained from water and food for nearly ten days.
His mother’s coffin was temporarily interred at Yàowáng Sì (藥王寺).
As the weather was cold,
Tánjìng wore only a single layer of coarse cloth
and built a hut at the burial site.
His wailing continued day and night without cease,
moving travelers along the road.
He died before completing one full year of mourning.
Hé Jiǒng (何炯), courtesy name Shìguāng (士光),
was a man from Qián (灊) in Lújiāng (廬江).
His father, Zǔn (撙),
was a Tàizhōng Dàfū (太中大夫).
At age fifteen, Jiǒng
received instruction from his elder cousin Yìn (胤);
within one year, he was conversant with the commentaries of the Five Classics.
Jiǒng was fair
and had a handsome appearance.
His elder cousins Qiú (求) and Diǎn (點) frequently praised him, saying:
“Shūbǎo (叔寶) is spiritually clear,
Hóngzhì (弘治) has clear skin.
Now looking at this child,
it is as if Wèi (衞) and Dù (杜) are again before our eyes.”
Jiǒng always admired tranquility and withdrawal,
and was not happy to pursue official advancement.
His uncle, Chāngyù (昌𧜛), said to him:
“Qiú and Diǎn have already retreated to lofty seclusion;
you should not do so again.
Moreover, for a gentleman, whether to serve or retire
is also just one path among others.”
At nineteen,
he was appointed Clerk of Yángzhōu (揚州 Zhǔbù).
He was nominated as a Xiùcái (秀才),
and successively promoted to Xíng Cānjūn (行參軍) in a Princely Establishment,
and then Lang (郎) of the Military and Armory Departments (Bīng, Kù Bù Èr Cáo 尚書兵、庫部二曹郎) of the Secretariat.
He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Yǒngkāng (永康 Lìng),
where he was noted for his harmonious governance.
Returning, he became the Secretary within the Jurisdiction of Rénwēi Nánkāng Wáng (仁威南康王 Xiànnèi Jìshì),
and was promoted to Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (治書侍御史).
When his father was ill for several days,
he did not loosen his belt (or take off his clothes),
nor did he comb his hair or bathe.
Within two days,
his appearance had drastically changed.
When his father died,
his loud lamentation never ceased.
He used a straw mat for a pillow and slept on the bare ground.
His waist became hollow and his feet swelled.
Ultimately, he died from this devastation of grief.
Yǔ Shāmí,
was a man of Yǐngchuān.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Yǔ Bīng, the Sīkōng of Jìn.
His father, Yǔ Pèiyù,
served as Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ and Chángshā Nèishǐ.
During the Shēngmíng era of Sòng, he was executed due to the affair of Shěn Yōuzhī.
Shāmí was just born at that time.
When he reached five years old,
his birth mother made him colored clothes,
but he consistently refused to wear them.
When his mother asked him the reason,
he wept and replied:
"Our family suffered such calamity and cruelty—
what is the use of these things!"
After he grew up,
he wore coarse cloth and ate only vegetables for the rest of his life.
He first served as Zuǒ Chángshì for the Kingdom of Línchuān Wáng,
and was promoted to Zhōngjūn Tiáncáo Xíng Cānjūn.
When his legitimate mother, Lady Liú, fell ill and was confined to bed,
Shāmí attended her side morning and evening,
without loosening his clothing.
Whenever acupuncture or moxibustion was required,
he would always test it on himself first.
When his mother died,
he did not take water or liquid for several days.
He did not remove his mourning garments (cuī dié) for the entire mourning period,
nor did he leave the confines of the mourning hut.
He wailed and lamented day and night,
which his neighbors could not bear to hear.
The tomb was located in Xīnlín,
and over a hundred lone pines
grew naturally beside the grave.
His cousin, Yǔ Yǒng, the Dūguān Shàngshū, submitted a memorial detailing his condition,
suggesting he should be nominated for the Pure Filial Piety category.
Gāozǔ summoned him, praised him,
and appointed him as Shè Lìng.
After returning, he was made Qīngchē Shàolíng Wáng Cānjūnshì.
He followed the administration to Kuàijī
and again suffered the loss of his birth mother.
During the return journey to the capital for the mourning,
while crossing the Zhèjiāng River,
they encountered a storm midstream,
and the boat was about to capsize.
Shāmí embraced the coffin and cried out.
Soon after, the wind subsided.
This was due to the power of his filial devotion (xiào gǎn).
When the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Xìnwēi Xíngyù Cānjūn, concurrently Dānyáng Jùn [rank unknown], and was consecutively promoted to Níngyuǎn Lùshì Cānjūn,
and then transferred to Sīmǎ.
He was sent out to serve as Chángchéng Lìng,
where he died.
Jiāng Fú, courtesy name Hánjié,
was a man of Jìyáng Kǎochéng.
His father, Jiāng Qiàn,
was Guānglù Dàfū.
Fú was filial by nature from a young age.
At thirteen,
when his father suffered from an eye ailment,
Fú nursed him for nearly a month,
without loosening his clothing.
One night, he dreamed of a monk who said:
"The person suffering from the eye ailment
will definitely recover if he drinks Huìyǎn water."
When he woke up and told the dream,
no one could understand it.
Fú's third uncle, Jiāng Lù, was close friends with the monk Zhìzhě Fǎshī of Cǎotáng Sì,
so they went to visit him.
Zhìzhě said:
"The Wúliàngshòu Jīng says: 'The Eye of Wisdom (Huìyǎn) sees the truth
and can cross to the other shore.'"
Qiàn subsequently, through Zhìzhě, petitioned to dedicate his dwelling in Niútún Lǐ within the bounds of Tóngxià Xiàn as a temple,
and requested a noble name for it.
The imperial reply stated:
"Loyal officials and filial sons
often receive divine responses (gǎn yìng).
In the Jìn dynasty, Yán Hán
was sent medicine by the unseen world.
Recently, I saw Zhìzhě,
who informed me that your second son received a dream message
about drinking Huìyǎn water.
Huìyǎn is the name of one of the Five Eyes.
If you wish to establish a temple,
it can be named Huìyǎn."
When construction commenced,
an old well was uncovered.
The well water was clear and cold,
different from common springs.
They used the water, as instructed in the dream, to wash the father's eyes and boil medicine,
and he gradually felt relief.
Consequently, he recovered.
People at the time called this "Filial Response" (Xiào Gǎn).
When Nánkāng Wáng served as Nán Xú Zhōu Governor,
he summoned Fú to be Yíng Zhǔbù.
Fú was quiet by nature,
loved the profound discourses of Lǎo and Zhuāng,
and was especially adept at Buddhist doctrines.
He took no pleasure in advancing his career.
When his father died,
Fú built a hut by the grave (lú yú mù),
and wailed continuously all day long.
He died a little over a month later.
Liú Jì, courtesy name Shìxuǎn,
was a man of Píngyuán.
His grandfather, Liú Chéngmín,
was the Jì Zhōu Cìshǐ of Sòng.
His father, Liú Wénwèi,
was Zhèngyuán Láng of Qí.
When Jì was nine years old,
he could recite the Zuǒshì Zhuàn,
and his clan and relatives were all impressed.
At fourteen, he mourned his father,
possessing utmost sincerity (zhì xìng).
Every time he cried, he would vomit blood.
His family was poor.
He and his younger brothers, Liú Yǎo and Liú Xiāo, encouraged each other earnestly in their studies.
When he grew up,
he was extensively learned and widely versed.
In the Tiānjiān era,
he began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng,
and was gradually promoted to Xuānhuì Jìn'ān Wáng Fǔ Cānjūn,
concurrently serving as Xiànnèi Jìshì.
He was sent out to be Xīchāng Xiāng.
Upon returning, he served as Shàngshū Zhǔkè Shìláng.
Before a year had passed,
he was appointed Hǎiyán Lìng.
Jì governed two counties successively,
and was known for his benevolent administration (hé lǐ).
Upon returning, he became Jiànkāng Zhèng.
This was not to his liking.
A short time later,
he was dismissed due to illness.
Soon after, he was appointed Jiànkāng Lìng,
but did not accept the post.
When his mother, Lady Míng, fell ill,
Jì, already fifty years old,
did not loosen his clothing for seventy days.
He recited the Guānshìyīn Jīng,
reaching tens of thousands of repetitions.
One night, he received a dream message,
seeing a monk who said:
"Your mother's lifespan is complete,
but because your sincerity and devotion are so earnest,
I shall extend it for her."
She died more than sixty days later.
Jì built a hut by the grave
and mourned and lamented beyond the prescribed rites.
A pair of white cranes often tamely hovered and circled beside the hut.
The recluse Ruǎn Xiàoxù sent him a letter to try to persuade and restrain him.
Jì's longing and grief did not cease,
and he died before the mourning period ended,
at the age of fifty-two.
He authored eight volumes of Shìsú Yǔ and
ten volumes of collected writings (wén jí).
His younger brother Yǎo is in the Biography of Literary Scholars (Wénxué Zhuàn),
and Xiāo is in the Biography of Recluses (Chǔshì Zhuàn).
Chǔ Xiū,
was a man of Qiántáng, Wú Jùn.
His father, Chǔ Zhòngdū,
was skilled in the Zhōu Yì
and was considered the best of his time.
In the Tiānjiān era,
he served consecutively as Wǔjīng Bóshì.
Xiū studied his father's profession from a young age,
was also conversant in the Xiàojīng and Lúnyǔ,
was skilled in letter writing (chǐ dú),
and had some understanding of literary composition (wén zhāng).
He first served as Shìláng for the Kingdom of Xiāngdōng Wáng,
and was gradually promoted to Qīngchē Xiāngdōng Fǔ Xíng Cānjūn,
concurrently serving as Guózǐ Zhùjiào.
When Wǔlíng Wáng served as Yáng Zhōu Governor,
he invited Xiū to be Xuānhuì Cānjūn and Xiànnèi Jìshì.
Xiū was utterly filial by nature.
During his father's mourning, he became emaciated beyond the prescribed rites,
which led to suffering from a cold ailment (lěng qì).
When he later mourned his mother,
he did not take water or liquid for twenty-three days,
fainting and then reviving.
Every time he wailed, he vomited blood,
and consequently died from the devastation (huǐ).
Xiè Lìn, courtesy name Xīrú,
was a man of Yángxià, Chén Jùn.
He was the eighth-generation descendant of Xiè Ān, the Tài Fù of Jìn.
His father, Xiè Jīng,
was Běi Zhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn.
Lìn was five years old.
Whenever his parents had not yet eaten,
the wet nurse wished to make Lìn eat first.
Lìn said:
"I truly do not feel hungry."
When urged to eat, he ultimately would not comply.
His maternal uncle, Ruǎn Xiàoxù, heard of this and sighed, saying:
"If this child stays at home, he is the equal of Zēngzǐ;
if he serves a ruler, he is the match of Lìn Shēng."
Therefore, he named him Lìn.
Gradually, he was taught the Classics and Histories.
After merely glancing at them, he could recite them fluently.
Xiàoxù often said,
"He is the Yángyuán of our family."
When he suffered the loss of his father (was in mourning),
he wailed bitterly day and night.
He wasted away until only his bones remained standing (he was severely emaciated).
His mother, Lady Ruǎn Shì, constantly watched over him herself, trying to comfort and restrain him.
After the period of mourning was completed,
the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), Xiāo Zǐxiǎn, memorialized regarding his supreme conduct,
promoting him to be Acting Staff Officer of the Judicial Section (Făcáo Xíng Cānjūn) in a Princely Establishment,
and he was subsequently promoted several times, reaching Staff Writer for Foreign Military Affairs (Wàibīng Jìshì Cānjūn).
At that time, sweet dew (Gānlù) fell upon the Shìlín Guǎn.
Lìn presented an encomium (sòng).
Gāozǔ praised him,
and consequently issued an edict commanding him to compose the Monument Inscription of Virtuous Rule for the Inspector of Běi Yănzhōu, Xiāo Kăi.
He was also commanded to compose the Encomium on the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhōngyōng Sòng) dedicated to the Prince of Xuānchéng.
In the first year of Tàiqīng (547 CE),
he was transferred to Cavalier Attendant (Sănqí Shìláng),
concurrently holding the post of Cavalier Regular Attendant (Sănqí Chángshì),
and was dispatched as an envoy to Wèi.
Coincidentally, Hóu Jǐng offered up his territory and defected,
and troops clashed on the border.
Lìn's mother feared he would not be able to return,
and died from emotional distress.
When Lìn returned and entered the territory,
that evening he had an ominous dream.
At dawn, he resigned his post and rushed home.
Upon arriving,
he wailed bitterly and vomited blood.
His breath stopped for a long time (he fainted),
and no water or gruel passed his lips.
Relatives and friends feared for his life,
and facing him, grieved sorrowfully.
They strongly urged him to drink some gruel.
Lìn initially forced himself to accept it,
but ultimately could not ingest it.
After more than a month,
he died one night while leaning over the coffin.
He was thirty-eight years old at the time.
Lìn composed several dozen pieces of poetry, rhapsodies (fù), steles, and encomia.
The Imperial Historian said: Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) stated,
"Grief does not destroy one's nature,"
teaching the people not to injure the living by mourning the dead.
Therefore, regulations for mourning rites were established,
providing structure and refinement for them.
Gāo Chái and Zhòng Yóu embraced the teachings of the sages.
Zēng Shēn and Mǐn Sǔn reverently practiced filial piety.
Some allowed no water or gruel to pass their lips
and wept tears of blood throughout the year.
How could they not know that their wounds were great and their pain deep,
and that the yearning expressed in the *Lù Ě* poem was urgent?
This is what is meant by: when the former kings instituted the rites,
the worthy submitted to them.
As for [Qíng] Qiū and Wú,
they ultimately perished through self-destruction.
People like Liú Tánjìng, Hé Jiǒng, Jiāng Fú, and Xiè Lìn,
also share the intent of those two men.

Memoir Forty-Two: Confucian Scholars (Rúlín): Fú Màróng, Hé Tóngzhī, Fàn Zhěn, Yán Zhízhī, Hè Yáng (Zǐgé), Sīmă Jūn, Biàn Huá, Cuī Líng'ēn, Kǒng Qiān, Lú Guǎng, Shěn Jùn (Tàishǐ Shūmíng), Kǒng Zǐqū, Huáng Kǎn.
The Hàn dynasty, having inherited the legacy of Qín's book burning,
greatly promoted Confucian instruction.
The students in the Imperial University
numbered tens of thousands.
The schools (hóngshè) in the commanderies and states
were entirely filled.
Those studying in the mountains and marshes
sometimes had marketplaces established near them.
Such was its flourishing state.
During the disorder at the end of the Hàn,
this path subsequently declined.
After the Zhèngshǐ reign era of Wèi,
the study of profundity and emptiness (Xuánxū) was still favored,
and Confucian scholars became few.
At that time, men like Xún Yǐ and Zhì Yú,
although they revised and established new rites
and reformed official positions,
were unable to change customs or alter trends.
From this time onward, the Central Plains were ruined,
and the elite (yīguān) were exterminated.
The region East of the River (Jiāng Zuǒ) was established in haste,
with not a moment to spare.
Down through the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
the National Academy (Guóxué) was occasionally established,
but encouragement and instruction were not widespread.
Its establishment lasted less than ten years;
it was merely for the sake of appearances.
Its disuse lasted for many generations;
its abandonment was swift.
No schools were established in the villages.
High officials (Gōngqīng) rarely mastered classical learning.
The great Confucians at court
studied alone and were unwilling to nurture the masses.
Later generations were isolated and uncultivated;
they possessed the classics but had nowhere to study and practice them.
The Three Virtues (Sāndé) and the Six Arts (Liùyì)
had long been abandoned.
