When Gāozǔ possessed the realm,
he deeply lamented this situation.
He issued edicts seeking learned scholars,
to regulate the Five Rites (Wǔlǐ),
establish the Six Tones (Liùlǜ),
revise the calendar (Dòulì),
and standardize weights and measures.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (505 CE),
an edict stated:
"During the two Hàn dynasties, those promoted as worthy
were all masters of classical learning.
They embraced the elegant Way,
thus establishing their name and completing their conduct.
Since the Wèi and Jìn eras, frivolity and extravagance have reigned;
Confucian education has faded away.
Moral integrity (Fēngjié) has not been established;
this is the cause.
We adjourn court late in the day
reflecting on hearing of outstanding individuals.
To recruit scholars and obtain the right men
is truly to reward them.
We shall establish one Erudite of the Five Classics (Wǔjīng Bóshì) for each Classic,
widely open the school houses,
and invite new talents to enter."
Thereupon, Míng Shānbīn of Píngyuán, Shěn Jùn of Wúxīng, Yán Zhízhī of Jiànpíng, and Hè Yáng of Kuàijī were appointed Erudites (Bóshì),
each presiding over one academy.
Each academy had several hundred students,
and they were provided with grain and rations.
Those who excelled in the examination (shècè tōngmíng)
were immediately appointed as officials.
Within ten-odd years,
those carrying classics and bearing satchels gathered like clouds in the capital.
Students were also selected and sent to Yúnmén Shān in Kuàijī
to receive instruction from Hé Yìn of Lújiāng.
Erudites (Bóshì) and Libationers (Jìjiǔ) were sent out separately
to the prefectures and commanderies to establish schools.
In the seventh year (508 CE),
another edict stated:
"To establish a state and rule the people,
establishing education is the foremost task.
To refine one's person and sharpen one's conduct
depends upon classical learning.
We founded the enlightened mandate
and gloriously reside within the realm.
Although We cultivate refined learning
and concurrently promote literature and the arts,
the number of useful men is not yet broad,
and the fundamental aims are still wanting.
This is not simply to mold the noble youths
and bring them into compliance with standards,
but We desire to formally emphasize modesty and respect for age,
setting an example from the family to the state.
Now that Our influence and instruction have spread,
the barbarians (Róng) and the Chinese (Xià) share the same customs,
it is proper to greatly open the schools,
extensively inviting the sons of officials (zhòuzǐ).
We must strive for the Ten Relationships (Shílún)
and promote the Three Virtues (Sāndé),
so that Our governance extends widely
and profound words are manifested."
Thereupon, the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ), Imperial Princes (Huángzǐ), imperial relatives (Zōngshì), and marquises (Wánghóu) began their studies there.
Gāozǔ personally lowered his imperial carriage
to offer sacrifices to the Former Teachers and Former Sages.
This was followed by feasts and discussions,
and they were rewarded with bundles of silk.
How numerous and orderly they were!
How expansive and grand!
The practice of the Great Way (Dàdào) was thus renewed.
Fú Màróng, Hé Tóngzhī, and Fàn Zhěn
already had renown in the world.
Among the Confucian scholars of the time,
Yán Zhízhī and Hè Yáng, among others, were the first to receive this selection.
They are now all appended to the Memoir of Confucian Scholars (Rúlín Zhuàn).
Fú Màróng, courtesy name Gōngyí,
was a native of Ānqiū in Píngchāng.
His great-grandfather, Tāo,
was an Assistant in the Imperial Library (Zhùzuò Láng) during the Jìn dynasty.
His father, Yìnzhī,
was Chief Clerk to the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Zhǔbù) during the Sòng dynasty.
Mànróng was orphaned early,
and resided as a sojourner with his mother and elder brother in Nánhǎi.
In youth he was devoted to study,
skilled in the Lǎo (Lǎozǐ) and the Yì (Yìjīng),
and was unconventional and fond of making grand statements.
He often said:
“Hé Yàn doubted nine matters in the Yìjīng;
in my view,
Yàn fundamentally did not study,
thus I know that Píngshú (Hé Yàn's courtesy name) had shortcomings.”
He gathered disciples and taught as his profession.
He served as Acting Cānjūn (Staff Officer) to the General of Agile Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn).
Emperor Míngdì of Sòng was fond of the Zhōu Yì,
and assembled court officials to lecture in the Qīngshǔ Diàn.
He commanded Mànróng to hold the classic (and lecture).
Mànróng naturally possessed fine demeanor and presence;
the Emperor compared him to Jī Shùyè (Jī Kāng),
and ordered the man of Wú, Lù Tànwēi, to paint an image of Shùyè and bestow it upon him.
He was promoted to Sītú Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Minister of Works).
When Yuán Càn was Dānyáng Yǐn (Administrator of Dānyáng),
he requested Mànróng to serve as Jiāngníng Lìng (Magistrate of Jiāngníng).
Upon returning to the capital, he was appointed Shàngshū Wàibīng Láng (Secretary of the Bureau of External Military Affairs).
At the end of the Shēngmíng era,
he served as Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General Who Assists the State) and Nánhǎi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Nánhǎi).
In the beginning of the Qí Dynasty,
he became Tōngzhí Sànqí Shìláng (Gentleman-in-Attendance and Consultant, Through Communicating).
In the beginning of the Yǒngmíng era,
he was appointed Tàizǐ Shuàigēng Lìng (Prefect of the Palace Gate Guard for the Crown Prince),
attending the Crown Prince during lectures.
Wèi Jiāngjūn (General of the Guards) Wáng Jiǎn formed a deep friendship with him,
ordering him to collaborate with Sīmǎ Xiàn of Hèněi and Lù Chéng of Wújùn to compile the *Sāngfú Yì* (Meaning of Mourning Clothes).
After it was completed,
[Wáng Jiǎn] also wished to define the rites and music (lǐyuè) with him.
Coincidentally, Wáng Jiǎn passed away.
He was promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng (Gentleman of the Central Secretariat) and Dàsīmǎ Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Staff Officer to the Grand Marshal),
then sent out to serve as Wǔchāng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Wǔchāng).
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he returned to the capital and was appointed Zhōngsàn Dàfū (Grandee of the Palace).
At that time, Emperor Míngdì did not highly value Confucian scholarship.
Mànróng's residence was east of the Wǎguān Sì (Wǎguān Monastery).
He set up a high seat in the reception hall.
Whenever he had guests, he would ascend the high seat to lecture and explain.
His students usually numbered several dozens or a hundred people.
When the Liáng State was established,
because Mànróng was an old scholar,
he was summoned and appointed Sīmǎ (Marshal),
then sent out to serve as Línhǎi Tàishǒu (Administrator of Línhǎi).
In the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
he died in office,
at the age of eighty-two.
He composed collected commentaries (*Jíjiě*) on the *Zhōu Yì*, the *Máo Shī*, and the *Sāngfú*,
and definitions (*Yì*) for the Lǎo (Lǎozǐ), Zhuāng (Zhuāngzǐ), and *Lúnyǔ* (Analects).
His son, Jǐ,
is recorded in the *Biographies of Worthy Officials*. Hé Tóngzhī,
courtesy name Shìwēi,
was a man of Qián in Lújiāng,
and the sixth-generation descendant of Yùzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Yùzhōu) Hé Yùn.
His grandfather, Hé Shàozhī,
was Yuánwài Sànqí Chángshì (Supernumerary Palace Attendant) during the Sòng Dynasty.
His father, Hé Xīn,
held the rank of Fèng Cháoqǐng (Gentleman Serving at Court) during the Qí Dynasty.
Tóngzhī loved the Three Rites (*Sānlǐ*) in his youth.
He studied independently, guided by his own mind,
working hard and focusing intently.
His hands never stopped handling the scrolls.
He read three hundred chapters of ritual discussions (*Lǐ Lùn*),
and generally knew them by heart.
At that time, Tàiwèi (Grand Commandant) Wáng Jiǎn was the acknowledged master of Confucianism.
He greatly admired and respected Tóngzhī.
Tóngzhī began his official career as Yángzhōu Cóngshì (Attendant Official of Yángzhōu).
He subsequently became a scholar (*Xuéguan*) at the Zǒngmíng Guǎn,
and was frequently promoted to Sītú Chējì Cānjūn Shì (Staff Officer to the Minister of Works and General of Chariots and Cavalry),
and then Shàngshū Cíbù Láng (Secretary of the Bureau of Sacrifices).
During the Jiànwǔ era of the Qí Dynasty,
he served as Zhènběi Jìshì Cānjūn (Secretarial Staff Officer to the General Who Guards the North),
attended the Crown Prince during lectures,
and concurrently held the position of Dānyáng Yì Zhōngzhèng (Impartial Judge of the Dānyáng District).
At that time, Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry) Liú Huán and the recluse scholar Wú Bāo had both already died.
Among the great scholars in the capital district,
only Tóngzhī remained.
Tóngzhī clearly mastered ritual methods and precedents.
All ritual precedents regarding auspicious and inauspicious matters of the state
were decided by him.
His reputation was highly regarded by the world.
He successively held the posts of Bùbīng Xiàowèi (Colonel of Infantry) and Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the National University).
Soon after, he was promoted to Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Staff Officer to the General of Agile Cavalry),
and then transferred to Sīmǎ (Marshal).
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
when the capital was in military disorder,
Tóngzhī regularly assembled students to lecture and discuss,
tirelessly and diligently.
In the beginning of Zhōngxīng,
he was appointed Xiāojì Jiāngjūn (General of Vigorous Cavalry).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he highly respected Confucian scholarship,
and appointed Tóngzhī as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs).
At this time, all state institutions were being established from scratch.
Tóngzhī determined policies based on ritual law,
providing many benefits.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (503 CE),
he died in office,
aged fifty-five.
Gāozǔ deeply mourned and regretted his death,
and intended to posthumously bestow an official rank upon him.
According to precedent, no Zuǒchéng received posthumous ranks,
but an imperial decree specially granted him the rank of Huángmén Shìláng (Gentleman of the Yellow Gate).
Confucian scholars considered this an honor.
He authored about one hundred chapters of essays, rites, and definitions.
His sons were Hé Cháoyǐn and Hé Cháohuì. Fàn Zhěn,
courtesy name Zǐzhēn,
was a man of Wǔyīn in Nánxiāng.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Jìn Ānběi Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the North) Wāng.
His grandfather, Fàn Qúzhī,
was Zhōngshū Láng (Secretary of the Central Secretariat).
His father, Fàn Méng,
died young.
Zhěn was orphaned and poor in his youth,
serving his mother with filial piety and reverence.
When he had not yet reached adulthood,
he heard that Liú Huán of Pèiguó had gathered a crowd for lectures,
and he went there to follow him.
He excelled beyond the ordinary and studied diligently.
Huán greatly admired him
and personally performed the capping ceremony for him.
He spent many years under Huán's tutelage.
When leaving to return home,
wearing straw sandals and cloth clothing,
he walked barefoot on the road.
Huán's house was frequented by many wealthy visitors traveling in carriages and on horseback.
When Zhěn was among them,
he felt no shame or embarrassment.
When he grew up,
he mastered classical doctrines extensively,
specializing particularly in the Three Rites (*Sānlǐ*).
His nature was straightforward,
and he liked provocative statements and lofty arguments,
which were not appreciated by his fellow scholars and friends.
He was only close with his maternal younger cousin, Xiāo Chēn.
Chēn was famous for his eloquence,
but always respected Zhěn's simplicity and depth.
He began his official career in Qí as Níngmán Zhǔbù (Clerk to the General Who Pacifies the Barbarians),
and was repeatedly promoted to Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng (Secretary of the Palace Bureau of the Department of State Affairs).
In the middle of the Yǒngmíng era,
the Qí established peaceful relations with the Wèi state (Northern Wèi),
exchanging envoys annually.
They specially selected talented and scholarly gentlemen
to serve as diplomatic envoys (*Xíngrén*).
Zhěn, along with his cousin Fàn Yún, Xiāo Chēn, Yán Yòumíng of Lángyé, and Péi Zhāomíng of Hédōng, successively led missions,
and all became famous in the neighboring state.
At that time, Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng greatly gathered guests and retainers,
and Zhěn was also included.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he was promoted to Lǐngjūn Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk to the General of the Guard).
He was sent out to serve as Yídū Tàishǒu (Administrator of Yídū),
but resigned due to mourning for his mother.
He returned to reside in Nánzhōu.
When the righteous army (of Xiāo Yǎn) arrived,
Zhěn came to welcome them, dressed in black mourning clothes.
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔdì of Liáng) had a long-standing friendship with Zhěn from the Xī Dǐ (Western Residence);
he was very pleased to see him.
When the city of Jiànkāng was pacified,
Zhěn was appointed Jìn'ān Tàishǒu (Administrator of Jìn'ān).
While in the commandery, he was clean and frugal,
relying only on his official salary.
He administered affairs for four years,
and was then summoned to serve as Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs).
When Zhěn left and returned (to the capital),
although he sent nothing to his relatives,
he only sent gifts to the former Shàngshū Lìng (Director of the Department of State Affairs), Wáng Liàng.
When Zhěn served the Qí Dynasty,
he and Liàng were colleagues serving as Secretaries in the same office,
and they were old friends.
By this time, Liàng had been dismissed and abandoned at home.
Since Zhěn had welcomed the royal army (Liáng),
his ambition lay in holding power.
However, his expectations were not fully met,
and he was often discontented.
Therefore, he privately associated closely with Wáng Liàng,
allegedly to defy the current trend.
Later, he was eventually implicated due to Liàng and banished to Guǎngzhōu.
The details are found in Wáng Liàng’s biography.
Initially,
when Zhěn was in the era of Qí Shì (the Southern Qí Dynasty),
he once served Jìnglínɡ Wánɡ Zǐliáng (Prince Xiāo Zǐliáng of Jìnglínɡ).
Zǐliáng devoutly believed in Buddhism,
but Zhěn vehemently proclaimed that there was no Buddha.
Zǐliáng asked:
“If you do not believe in cause and effect (karma),
how can there be wealth and nobility in the world,
and how can there be lowliness and poverty?”
Zhěn replied:
“The birth of a person is comparable to a single tree of blossoms;
they bloom from the same branch,
and all open from the same stem.
Carried by the wind, they fall.
Naturally, some brush past curtains and fall onto mats and couches,
while others pass fences and walls and fall beside cesspits and filth.
Those who fall onto the mats and couches,
Your Highness is such a one;
those who fall into the filth,
this humble official is such a one.
Although nobility and lowliness are certainly different paths,
where, ultimately, is the cause and effect?”
Zǐliáng could not refute him
and found him deeply strange.
Zhěn withdrew to discuss the principle
and authored the *Shénmièlùn* (*Treatise on the Extinction of the Soul*), stating: Someone asked me:
“The extinction of the spirit (shén) —
how do you know that it is extinguished?”
I reply:
“The spirit is the body,
and the body is the spirit.
Therefore, if the body exists, the spirit exists;
if the body perishes, the spirit is extinguished.”
The questioner asks:
“The body (xíng) is designated as unconscious,
the spirit (shén) is named as conscious.
Consciousness and unconsciousness
are immediately different in reality.
The spirit and the body,
logically, cannot be one.
That body and spirit are immediately identical
is something I have not heard.”
I reply:
“The body is the substance of the spirit,
the spirit is the function of the body.
Thus, the body refers to the substance,
and the spirit speaks of its function.
The body
and the spirit
cannot be different from one another.”
The questioner asks:
“If the spirit is not substance,
and the body is not function,
and they are prohibited from being different,
where does this principle reside?”
I reply:
“The names are different, but the entity is one.”
The questioner asks:
“If the names are already different,
how can the entity be one?”
I reply:
“The relation of the spirit to the substance
is like the sharpness to the knife;
the relation of the body to the function
is like the knife
to the sharpness.
The name ‘sharpness’ is not the knife,
and the name ‘knife’ is not the sharpness.
However, without the sharpness, there is no knife;
without the knife, there is no sharpness.
I have not heard of the knife disappearing while the sharpness remains,
so how could the body perish while the spirit survives.”
The questioner asks:
“The case of the knife and the sharpness
may be as you say,
but the principle concerning the body and the spirit
is not like that.
Why do I say this?
The substance of wood is unconscious,
but the substance of a person
is conscious.
Since a person has a substance like that of wood,
yet possesses a consciousness different from wood,
is it not the case that wood has only one aspect,
while a person has two?”
I reply:
“How strange is this statement!
If a person had a substance like wood, which served as the body,
and also had a consciousness different from wood, which served as the spirit,
then your argument would be valid.
But now, the substance
of a person,
that substance is conscious;
the substance of wood,
that substance is unconscious.
The substance of a person is not the substance of wood,
and the substance of wood is not the substance of a person.
How could there be a substance like wood
and furthermore a consciousness different from wood?”
The questioner asks:
“The reason the substance of a person differs from the substance of wood
is merely because the person is conscious.
If a person were unconscious,
how would they differ from wood?”
I reply:
“A person does not have an unconscious
substance,
just as wood does not have a conscious form.”
The questioner asks:
“The physical remains of the deceased—
are they not the unconscious substance?”
I reply:
“That is no longer the substance of a person.”
The questioner asks:
“If that is the case,
then a person truly has a substance like wood,
and possesses a consciousness different from wood.”
I reply:
“The deceased possess a substance like wood,
but
do not possess a consciousness different from wood;
the living possess a consciousness different from wood,
but do not possess a substance like wood.”
The questioner asks:
“The bones of the deceased—
are they not the physical body of the living?”
I reply:
“The form of the living is not the form of the dead,
and the form of the dead is not the form of the living.
The distinction has already been transformed,
how can the physical body of the living
become the bones of the dead?”
The questioner asks:
“If the physical body of the living is not the bones of the dead,
if it is not the bones of the dead,
then it ought not to come from the physical body of the living.
If it does not come from
the physical body of the living,
then where did these bones come from to arrive here?”
I reply:
“It is the physical body of the living
that transforms into the bones of the dead.”
The questioner asks:
“Although the physical body of the living transforms into the bones of the dead,
is it not because of life that there is death?
We thus know that the dead substance is still the living substance.”
I reply:
“It is like a flourishing tree transforming into a withered tree.
The substance of the withered tree,
how can it be the entity of the flourishing tree!”
The questioner asks:
“The flourishing entity transforms into the withered entity,
but the withered entity is immediately the flourishing entity.
The silk entity transforms into the thread entity,
but the thread entity is immediately the silk entity.
What distinction is there?”
I reply:
“If the withered is immediately the flourishing,
and the flourishing is immediately the withered,
then it ought to drop its leaves when flourishing,
and bear fruit when withered.
Furthermore, a flourishing tree ought not to transform into a withered tree,
because if flourishing
is immediately withered,
there would be nothing left to transform.
If flourishing and withering were one,
why wouldn't it wither first and then flourish?
Why must it flourish first and then wither?
What is the reason?
The meaning of silk and thread
is also
refuted by this argument.”
The questioner asks:
“When the form of the living perishes,
it ought to be instantly and completely extinguished.
Why then does it still take the form of death,
continuing its course without ending?”
I reply:
“The entity
of life and extinction
must necessarily proceed in sequence.
Indeed, that which is born suddenly must die suddenly;
that which is born gradually must die gradually.
That which is born suddenly
is like a flash or a squall;
Those that come into being gradually
are animals and plants.
To have suddenness and to have gradualness
is the principle of things.”
Question:
“If the form is the spirit,
are the hands and the like also the spirit?”
Answer:
“They are all parts of the spirit.”
Question:
“If they are all parts of the spirit,
and the spirit is capable of thought (lǜ),
should the hands and the like also be capable of thought?”
Answer:
“The hands and the like should be able to possess the
knowledge of pain and itch,
but not the thought (lǜ) of right and wrong.”
Question:
“Are knowing (zhī) and thought (lǜ)
one or different?”
Answer:
“Knowing (zhī) is thought (lǜ).
When shallow, it is knowing;
when deep, it is thought.”
Question:
“If so,
there should be two types of thought (lǜ).
If thought is twofold,
is the spirit twofold?”
Answer:
“The human body is only one;
how can the spirit be twofold?”
Question:
“If it cannot be twofold,
how can there be the knowing of pain and itch,
and furthermore, the thought of right and wrong?”
Answer:
“Just as hands and feet are different,
yet together constitute one person,
although right and wrong, pain and itch are also different,
they all together constitute one spirit.”
Question:
“The thought of right and wrong
does not pertain to the hands and feet;
to what place does it pertain?”
Answer:
“The thought of right and wrong
is presided over by the heart-organ (xīnqì).”
Question:
“Is the heart-organ (xīnqì) the heart among the Five Zàng
or not?”
Answer:
“It is.”
Question:
“What special difference do the Five Zàng possess
that the heart alone has the thought of right and wrong?”
Answer:
“What difference do the Seven Apertures possess,
yet their specific functions
are not equal?”
Question:
“Thought (lǜsī) has no fixed location;
how do you know that it is presided over by the heart-organ (xīnqì)?”
Answer:
“The Five Zàng each have their specific duties,
but none are capable of thought (lǜ).
For this reason,
we know the heart is the origin of thought.”
Question:
“Why is it not attached to the eye or other parts?”
Answer:
“If thought (lǜ) could be attached to the eye part,
why is the eye not attached to the ear part?”
Question:
“The essence of thought (lǜtǐ) has no root,
thus it can be attached to the eye part;
the eye has its own root,
and does not need to be attached to other parts.”
Answer:
“Why
does the eye have a root while thought (lǜ) has no root?
If it truly had no root in my form,
and could be universally attached to a different place,
then the emotions of Zhāng Jiǎ
could be attached to the body of Wáng Yǐ,
and the nature of Lǐ Bǐng
entrusted to the frame of Zhào Dīng.
Is that so?
It is not.”
Question:
“The form of the Sage (shèngrén) is just like the form of an ordinary person,
yet there is a difference between the ordinary and the sacred.
From this, we know that form and spirit are separate.”
Answer:
“It is not so.
That which is refined gold
can illuminate;
that which is base cannot illuminate.
If there is refined gold that can illuminate,
how can there be base matter that does not illuminate?
How could the spirit of the Sage (shèngrén) be attached to the
vessel of an ordinary person,
or the spirit of an ordinary person entrusted to the body of the Sage (shèngrén)?
Therefore, the eight colors (bācǎi) and double pupils (chóngtóng),
the appearances of Xūn and Huá;
the dragon face and horse mouth,
the countenances of Xuān and Hào—
these are external differences in form.
The heart of Bǐ Gān,
with its seven apertures and corner arrangement;
the gall bladder of Bó Yuē,
which was as big as a fist—
these are the distinctions in the heart-organ (xīnqì).
From this
we know that the Sage’s (shèngrén) fixed nature
always transcends the common sphere.
Not only does his Way transform all living things,
but his form also surpasses the myriad things.
To equate the bodies of the ordinary and the sacred
is something I dare not accept.”
Question:
“You say that the form of the Sage (shèngrén) must be different from that of the ordinary person.
May I ask: Yáng Huò resembled Zhòng Ní,
and Xiàng Jí resembled Dà Shùn.
Shùn and Xiàng, Kǒng and Yáng,
had different wisdom but similar forms.
What is the reason for this?”
Answer:
“Stones resemble jade but are not jade;
chickens resemble phoenixes but are not phoenixes.
Things indeed possess such resemblances,
and so people should naturally be like this.
The appearances of Xiàng and Yáng are similar only superficially, not truly similar.
If the heart-organs (xīnqì) are not equal,
mere appearance is of no benefit.”
Question:
“The difference between the ordinary and the sacred,
where their forms and organs are not identical,
is acceptable.
However, the Sages (shèngrén) attain the ultimate principle,
and rationally there should be no duality.
Yet Qiū and Dàn had differing appearances,
and Tāng and Wén
had varied looks.
That the spirit does not match the appearance
is thus made even clearer.”
Answer:
“Sages (shèngrén) are identical in their heart-organ (xīnqì),
but their forms do not necessarily have to be identical,
just as horses may have different coats but run equally fast,
and pieces of jade
may differ in color but share equal beauty.
Therefore, the Jìn Jí and the Jīng Hé
are valued equally high as linked cities;
Huáliú and Lùlí
both can travel a thousand miles.”
Question:
“I have now heard
that form and spirit are not separate,
and that when the form perishes, the spirit is extinguished—
this principle is certainly appropriate.
May I ask concerning the Classic that says: ‘Establish for them ancestral temples,
and offer sacrifices to them as guǐ (ghosts or spirits)?’
What does this mean?”
Answer:
“This is the teaching of the Sage (shèngrén),
intended to soothe the hearts of filial children
and encourage the intentions of the wicked and depraved.
To give spiritual clarity to it
is what is meant.”
Question:
“Bó Yǒu wore armor,
and Péng Shēng appeared as a pig.
The historical writings clearly record these events.
Can it be merely a pedagogical device?”
Answer:
“Monsters and anomalies are vast and confusing;
they
may or may not exist.
Those who die violently are many,
but they do not all become ghosts (guǐ).
Péng Shēng and Bó Yǒu,
why were they alone able to do that?
If they suddenly became a man or a pig,
they were not necessarily the sons of the rulers of Qí and Zhèng.”
Question:
“The Yì (Classic of Changes) says: ‘Therefore, knowing the circumstances of guǐshén (ghosts and spirits)
is analogous to Heaven and Earth, and does not conflict with them.’
It also says: ‘Loading guǐ onto one cart.’
What do these meanings refer to?"
Why?"
He replied:
"There are birds,
there are beasts;
this is the distinction between flying and walking.
There are humans,
there are ghosts;
this is the distinction between darkness and light.
Whether a human, upon destruction, becomes a ghost,
or a ghost, upon destruction, becomes a human,
is not known."
The question was asked:
"Knowing that the spirit is extinguished,
what advantage is there in that?"
He replied:
"Fótú (Buddhism) harms governance,
Sāngmén (monks) corrupt customs.
Startling like the wind and rising like the fog,
they rush and proliferate without
ceasing.
I mourn their failings,
and seek to rescue those drowning in them.
Now, those who exhaust their wealth to flock to the monks,
and ruin their families to chase after the Buddha,
but do not pity their relatives,
nor show compassion for the poor and destitute—why is this?
It is truly because the desire to benefit themselves is deep,
and the intention to aid others is shallow.
Thus, when they give a meager measure (guīcuō) to a poor friend,
feelings of stinginess show in their expression;
when they donate a thousand *zhōng* (measures) to a rich monk,
feelings of
joy overflow in their face and hair.
Is this not because monks promise manifold future blessings,
while friends offer no recompense for a leftover sheaf of grain?
They hasten to give, neglecting the relief of immediate suffering,
focusing solely on accumulating virtue for themselves.
Furthermore, they are confused by vague and obscure words,
frightened by the suffering of Àbí (Avīci) hell,
tempted by extravagant and baseless rhetoric,
and elated by the joys of Dōushuài (Tuṣita) heaven.
Therefore, they abandon the Confucian robes (fēngyè),
don the horizontal monastic robes (héngyī);
they discard sacrificial vessels (zǔdòu),
and set forth their water bottles and begging bowls (píngbō).
Every family abandons their loved ones,
every person cuts off their lineage.
This results in soldiers being defeated in the ranks,
officials being absent from the government offices,
grain being exhausted
by the idle wanderers,
and wealth being depleted on clay and wood (idols).
Hence, villainy does not cease,
and songs of praise remain stifled.
Because of these things,
their influence never stops,
and their harms are endless.
If
creation is derived from nature,
and the multitude of things are unified by a singular process of transformation,
suddenly existing by themselves,
and vanishing instantaneously into nothingness;
coming, they are not welcomed;
departing, they are not pursued.
Following the principles of Heaven,
each would rest content in their nature.
The common people would be content in their fields,
the superior men would maintain their tranquility and simplicity.
They would farm and eat;
food would not be exhausted.
They would rear silkworms and clothe themselves;
clothing would not be depleted.
The lower classes would have surplus to provide for the upper classes,
and the upper classes would govern by non-action (wúwéi) and wait upon the lower classes.
Life could be preserved,
the state could be strengthened,
rulers could achieve hegemony—
by employing this Way."
When this discourse was released,
the court and the common people were in uproar.
Zǐliáng assembled monks to challenge him, but they could not overcome him.
Zhěn remained in the south for many years,
then he was recalled to the capital (jīng).
Upon arrival,
he was appointed Zhōngshū Láng (Secretary of the Central Secretariat) and Guózǐ Bóshì (Erudite of the Directorate of Education),
and died while holding office.
His collected writings totaled ten scrolls.
His son, Zǐxū,
courtesy name Chángcái.
He transmitted his father’s learning,
and started his career as Tàixué Bóshì (Erudite of the Imperial University).
Xū had rhetorical talent.
During the Dàtóng era,
he often concurrently served as Zhǔkè Láng (Director of Foreign Guests),
receiving and dealing with the northern envoys.
He was promoted to Píngxī Xiāngdōng Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Aide to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West),
and attended to the Prince of Xuānchéng for his studies.
He was sent out to serve as Pōyáng Nèishǐ (Administrator of Pōyáng Commandery),
and died in that commandery.
Yán Zhízhī,
courtesy name Xiàoyuán, was a native of Zǐguī, Jiànpíng Commandery.
His grandfather, Qīn,
served the Sòng dynasty as Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì (Regular Attendant, Palace Counselor of General Affairs).
When young, Zhízhī was skilled in Zhuāngzǐ and Lǎozǐ,
capable of esoteric discussion (Xuányán),
and proficient in *Sāngfú*, *Xiàojīng*, and *Lúnyǔ*.
When he grew up,
he comprehensively studied Zhèng's commentaries on the rites, the *Zhōuyì*, the *Máoshī*, and the *Zuǒshì Chūnqiū*.
His nature was pure, filial, cautious, and generous,
and he did not use his talents to elevate himself above others.
When young, he suffered the grief of his father's death;
consequently, he remained vegetarian for twenty-three years.
Later, he contracted a cold-sickness (fēnglěng jí),
and only then did he stop.
During the Yǒngmíng era of the Qí dynasty,
he began his career as Lúlíng Wángguó Shìláng (Gentleman of the Principality of Lúlíng).
He was promoted to Guǎnghàn Wángguó Yòuchángshì (Right Attendant of the Principality of Guǎnghàn).
When the Prince was executed,
no one in the principality dared to look (at the body).
Zhízhī alone rushed to weep,
personally managed the funerary preparations and embalming,
and went barefoot to escort the coffin to the gravesite.
He constructed the tomb for him.
Only after the burial was complete did he return.
People at the time admired his righteousness.
During the Jiànwǔ era,
he was promoted to Yuánwàiláng (Supernumerary Gentleman) and Sànqí Chángshì (Regular Attendant).
Soon after, he served as Kānglè Hóu Xiàng (Chancellor to the Marquis of Kānglè).
While in the county, he was honest and upright,
and the people and officials praised him.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (503 CE),
he was appointed Hòujūn Qíbīng Cānjūnshì (Aide to the Cavalry Division of the Rear Army).
Gāozǔ issued an edict seeking broadly learned scholars to manage the Five Rites (Wǔlǐ).
The relevant officials proposed Zhízhī to manage the Rituals of Mourning (Xiōnglǐ).
In the fourth year (505 CE),
Wǔjīng Bóshì (Erudites of the Five Classics) were established for the first time.
Each opened a schoolhouse for teaching,
and Zhízhī was concurrently appointed Wǔjīng Bóshì.
Zhízhī's schoolhouse was located in Cháogōu,
and the students usually numbered over a hundred.
When Zhízhī lectured,
students from all five schools certainly came,
and listeners numbered over a thousand.
In the sixth year (507 CE),
he was promoted to Zhōngfǔjūn Jìshì Cānjūn (Record Keeper and Aide to the General of the Central Army),
still concurrently holding the position of Bóshì.
In the seventh year (508 CE),
he died at his schoolhouse,
aged fifty-two.
Since he fell ill,
Zhízhī refused to accept his official salary (lǐngfèng).
His wife and children were consequently destitute.
When he died,
there was no place to hold the funeral rites.
His students purchased a house for him,
and only then could the funeral be properly conducted.
Zhízhī was naturally benevolent and compassionate,
and loved to perform unseen virtuous deeds.
Even when alone in a dark room,
he never slackened in this practice.
Once, when young, he was traveling in the mountains,
and saw a sick person.
Zhízhī asked his name,
but the person could not answer.
He loaded him onto his cart and returned together,
arranging for medical care.
Six days later, the man died.
Zhízhī provided a coffin, dressed the body, and buried him,
never knowing where the man was from.
Once, traveling alongside Shèntáng,
he saw a sick person lying by the side of the embankment.
Zhízhī descended from his carriage and asked the reason.
The man said his surname was Huáng,
his family originally from Jīngzhōu,
and he worked as a laborer for hire.
Since his illness had become critical,
the boat master, about to depart,
had abandoned him on the bank.
Zhízhī’s heart was moved with pity.
He loaded him up and returned to treat him.
After a year, the man surnamed Huáng recovered.
He requested to serve as a slave for the rest of his life to repay the great kindness.
Zhízhī refused,
provided him with funds and provisions,
and sent him away.
Many of his righteous deeds were like this.
He compiled the *Xiōnglǐ Yízhù* (Notes on the Rites of Mourning) in four hundred seventy-nine scrolls.
Hè Yáng,
courtesy name Délǐan, was a native of Shānyīn, Kuàijī Commandery.
His grandfather, Dàolì,
was skilled in the Three Rites (Sānlǐ).
He served the Sòng dynasty as Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng (Secretary of the Three Dukes in the Department of State Affairs) and Jiànkāng Lìng (Magistrate of Jiànkāng).
Yáng 少 (shào) transmitted the family business.
During the Qí (Qí) period, Liú Huán (Liú Huán) of Pèi Guó (Pèi Guó) served as the Prefectural Aide (Fǔ Chéng) of Kuàijī (Kuàijī).
Upon seeing Yáng, he deeply appreciated and distinguished him.
He once visited Zhāng Róng (Zhāng Róng) of Wú Jùn (Wú Jùn) together with Yáng,
and pointing at Yáng, he said to Róng:
“This young man possesses spiritual intelligence and sharp wit;
he will become the patriarch of Confucian scholars in the future.”
When Huán returned,
he recommended him to be a student in the Guó Zǐ (Guó Zǐ) academy.
He passed the examination for the study of the classics (Míng Jīng),
served as the Libationer (Jì Jiǔ) of Yáng Zhōu (Yáng Zhōu),
and soon concurrently served as the Assistant Instructor (Zhù Jiào) of the Guó Zǐ.
He successively held the posts of Attendant (Fèng Cháo Qǐng),
Academician (Bó Shì) of the Imperial University (Tài Xué),
and Assistant (Chéng) of the Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tài Cháng).
He resigned his post due to mourning his mother.
At the beginning of Tiān Jiān (Tiān Jiān),
he was reinstated as Assistant of the Grand Master of Ceremonies.
The responsible department nominated him to manage guest rites.
He was summoned for an audience and spoke on the meaning of rites and righteousness.
Gāo Zǔ (Gāo Zǔ) was impressed by him,
and issued an edict for him to attend court on the new moon and full moon,
and participate in the lectures at Huá Lín (Huá Lín).
In the fourth year,
when the Five Academies (Wǔ Guǎn) were first established,
Yáng was concurrently appointed Academician of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng Bó Shì).
He received a separate edict to settle the rites for the Crown Prince (Huáng Tài Zǐ)
and compile the meanings of the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng Yì).
Yáng observed all former practices regarding rites.
At that time, Gāo Zǔ was initiating the establishment of rites and music,
and many of the suggestions Yáng proposed
were implemented.
In the seventh year,
he was appointed Commandant of the Infantry (Bù Bīng Xiào Wèi),
and Overseer (Lǐng) of the Academicians of the Five Classics.
In the ninth year,
he contracted an illness.
Medical staff were dispatched to inquire about his health.
He died in the academy
at the age of fifty-nine.
His writings included commentaries (Jiǎng Shū) on the Lǐ (Lǐ), Yì (Yì), Lǎo (Lǎo), and Zhuāng (Zhuāng);
several hundred essays on comprehensive discussions (Bó Yì) for the court;
and one hundred forty-five volumes of regulations on guest rites (Bīn Lǐ Yí Zhù).
Yáng was particularly proficient in the Lǐ (Lǐ).
The students in the academy often numbered in the hundreds,
and dozens of his disciples passed the Míng Jīng (Míng Jīng) examination and responded to the imperial policy questions (Duì Cè).
He had two sons.
Gě (Gě) had the courtesy name Wénmíng (Wénmíng).
When young, he was versed in the Three Rites (Sān Lǐ).
Upon growing up,
he comprehensively studied the Xiào Jīng (Xiào Jīng), Lún Yǔ (Lún Yǔ), Máo Shī (Máo Shī), and Zuǒ Zhuàn (Zuǒ Zhuàn).
He began his career as a Gentleman-in-Attendance (Shì Láng) in the Princely State of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Wáng Guó), concurrently serving as Academician of the Imperial University.
He attended upon the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng) for reading.
He was commanded to lecture on the Rites for the three princes—of Shàolíng (Shàolíng), Xiāngdōng, and Wǔlíng (Wǔlíng)—at the Yǒng Fú (Yǒng Fú) residence.
He was gradually promoted to Provisional Staff Officer (Xíng Cān Jūn) in the establishment of the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
and then transferred to the Directorate of Rites (Yí Cáo Láng) of the Department of State Affairs (Shàng Shū).
Soon after, he was appointed Magistrate (Lìng) of Mòlíng (Mòlíng),
and then promoted to Academician (Bó Shì) of the Guó Zǐ (Guó Zǐ).
He lectured and taught at the academy,
and his students often numbered several hundred.
He was dispatched outside the capital as the Advisory Counselor (Zī Yì Cān Jūn) to the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng), who was the General of the Western Region (Xī Zhōng Láng),
and concurrently held the post of Magistrate of Jiānglíng (Jiānglíng Lìng).
When the Prince first established a school in his residency,
Gě was appointed to oversee the Libationer of the Confucian Forest (Rú Lín Jì Jiǔ).
He lectured on the Three Rites,
and many gentry (yī guān) from Jīng (Jīng) and Chǔ (Chǔ) attended.
He twice served as Supervisor (Jiān) of Nánpíng Commandery (Nánpíng Jùn) before and after,
and was cherished by the people and officials.

Soon after, he was given the title General of Upright Awe (Zhēn Wēi Jiāng Jūn), concurrently serving as Chief Clerk (Cháng Shǐ) to the General Who Pacifies the West (Píng Xī), and Administrator (Tài Shǒu) of Nán Commandery (Nán Jùn).
Gě was fundamentally filial.
He often regretted that his pursuit of office (tān lù) prevented him from working the fields (dài gēng),
and that he failed to adequately support his parents.
During his time in Jīng Zhōu (Jīng Zhōu), he served in various commanderies and districts.
The salary and emoluments he received
were not kept for his wife and children.
He solely intended to return to his hometown and build a temple
to express his gratitude and remembrance.
In the sixth year of Dà Tóng (Dà Tóng),
he died while in office
at the age of sixty-two.
His younger brother, Jì (Jì),
was also versed in the Three Rites.
He successively served as the Director (Láng) of the Department of Sacrifices (Cí Bù Láng) of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently serving as the Palace Secretarial Aide (Tōng Shì Shè Rén) of the Central Secretariat (Zhōng Shū),
and was successively promoted to Commandant of the Infantry,
Gentleman of the Yellow Gate (Huáng Mén Láng) of the Central Secretariat,
and concurrently Compiler (Zhù Zuò).
Sīmǎ Yún (Sīmǎ Yún), whose courtesy name was Zhēnsù (Zhēnsù),
was a native of Wēn (Wēn) in Hénèi (Hénèi).
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Cháo Liè Wáng (Cháo Liè Wáng) Chéng (Chéng), General of the Cavalry (Piào Jì Jiāng Jūn) of the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty.
His grandfather, Liàng (Liàng),
was the Provisional Director (Cóng Shì Zhōng Láng) for the Minister of Works (Sī Kōng) of the Sòng (Sòng) dynasty.
His father, Duān (Duān),
was an Attendant (Fèng Cháo Qǐng) during the Qí (Qí) dynasty.
Yún was orphaned and poor but loved learning.
He studied under Liú Huán (Liú Huán) of Pèi Guó (Pèi Guó),
and with strong effort and focused concentration,
he was deeply appreciated and distinguished by Huán.
When he grew up,
he was widely versed in the classics and techniques,
and was particularly proficient in the Three Rites.
During the Jiàn Wǔ (Jiàn Wǔ) period of the Qí dynasty,
he began his career as an Attendant (Fèng Cháo Qǐng),
and was promoted to Provisional Staff Officer in a Princely Establishment (Wáng Fǔ Xíng Cān Jūn).
At the beginning of Tiān Jiān (Tiān Jiān),
he served as Director of Administration (Zhì Zhōng) for his home province,
and was appointed Magistrate of Jìyáng (Jìyáng Lìng),
where he achieved clean governance.
He was summoned into the capital and appointed Director of the Department of Sacrifices (Cí Bù Láng) of the Department of State Affairs.
In the seventh year,
Ānchéng Tàifēi Chén shì passed away.
Ānchéng Wáng Xiù, the *cìshǐ* of Jiāngzhōu, and Shǐxīng Wáng Dàn, the *cìshǐ* of Jīngzhōu,
both submitted memorials requesting to be relieved of their duties due to their compassionate mother.
The imperial edict did not permit it.
They returned to their original posts.
However, as the Tàifēi passed away in the capital,
there was no one to preside over the funeral rites.
The *shèrén* Zhōu Shè debated, saying:
"Hè Yànxiān said, 'A son of a compassionate mother does not observe mourning for the compassionate mother's relatives.
A wife does not follow her husband to mourn for her compassionate mother-in-law.
This is because the *xiǎogōng* mourning attire has no precedent to follow.'
Yǔ Wèizhī said, 'Not only does a son not follow his mother to mourn her relatives,
a grandson also does not follow his father to mourn his compassionate mother.'
it is clear that there is no mourning attire for a compassionate grandmother.
Reflecting on the sorrow within the family,
it cannot be treated as ordinary.
According to the auspicious rites of a father,
all sons receive condolences.
Now, for the sons of the two princes,
on the day of assuming mourning attire,
they should wear plain clothes for one day
From this,
An imperial decree said:
"Since the two princes are far away,
their sons should preside over the sacrificial rites."
"The *Lǐ* says, 'A white hat and black sash are the crown of the sons and grandsons.'
Thus, the attire of the heir apparent should be different from the usual.
He may wear fine cloth clothing,
with a silk collar and sash,
and not listen to music for three years.
Furthermore, the *Lǐ* and *Chūnqiū* state
that a *shùmǔ* is not offered sacrifices for generations,
which probably refers to those without royal decree.
Since Wú Tàifēi was appointed by imperial decree,
and the rites of Ānchéng were used,
then she should be enshrined in the ancestral temple.
The destruction of the shrine should only occur when the kinship of five generations ends.
Although Chén Tàifēi's mandate was equally significant,
since the compassionate grandsons do not observe mourning,
there is no reason for her to be worshipped in the ancestral temple for generations.
The son performs the sacrifice, and the grandson stops it.
This conforms to the classical texts."
Gāozǔ thereupon ordered the ritual officials to deliberate on the mourning attire for the emperor's compassionate mother.
Yún debated:
"According to the five grades of mourning attire system of the Sòng dynasty,
an imperial prince observes mourning for his nursemaid.
According to the rites, a *shùmǔ* who has been compassionate to oneself
should observe the *xiǎogōng* mourning system.
According to the *Zēngzǐ Wèn*,
Zǐyóu said, 'To mourn a compassionate mother as one's own mother,
is this according to the rites?'
In ancient times, a nobleman had a tutor outside
and a compassionate mother inside.
They were appointed by the sovereign to educate the son.
What mourning attire is there?'
Zhèng Xuán's commentary says, 'This refers to the son of a sovereign.'
If the son of a sovereign does not observe mourning,
then it is understandable that the son of a king does not observe mourning.
Also, the *Sāngfú Jīng* says, 'The son of a *jūnzǐ* for a *shùmǔ* who has been compassionate to oneself.'
The commentary says, 'A son of a *jūnzǐ*
is the son of a noble person.'
Zhèng Xuán cited the *Nèizé*,
stating that the three mothers only applied to high officials and grandees.
From this,
the mourning attire for a compassionate mother
does not extend upwards to the five ranks of heirs
nor downwards to the sons of the three types of officials.
If those who observe mourning are limited to high officials and grandees,
then considering that the sons of feudal lords do not even have this mourning,
how much more so should it be applied to imperial princes?
I suggest that according to the rites, this should be abolished
to correct the confusion of previous generations."
Gāozǔ thought otherwise.
He said:
"The *Lǐ* mentions 'compassionate mother'
in three categories: Firstly, a concubine's son who has no mother
is raised by a concubine who has no son.
They are designated mother and son,
and observe three years of mourning.
This is what the *Sāngfú Qīcuī* chapter refers to as 'a compassionate mother as one's own mother.'
is raised by a concubine.
She provides compassionate and utmost care.
Although the love is equal,
for the son of a principal wife,
the concubine has no claim to be a mother.
However, due to deep affection and significant service,
*xiǎogōng* mourning is observed.
The *Sāngfú Xiǎogōng* chapter does not directly state 'compassionate mother'
but says 'a *shùmǔ* who has been compassionate to oneself,'
clearly distinguishing it from the three-year compassionate mother.
The third is when the son is not motherless,
but a person of lower status is chosen to look after him,
equivalent to a teacher or guardian,
yet not without compassion.
Hence, she is also called a 'compassionate mother.'
Since a teacher or guardian has no mourning attire,
then this compassionate mother also has no mourning attire.
one is chosen to be the son's teacher;
the next is the compassionate mother;
the next is the nursemaid.'
This is a clear statement.
This statement about choosing 'various mothers'
means choosing persons to be these three mothers,
not choosing the mothers of one's brothers.
How do we know this?
If she were a brother's mother who already had a son,
then she would be a senior concubine.
The rites for a senior concubine
indeed have special additions.
How could a junior concubine who has given birth
then be relegated to a nursemaid?
This is not permissible.
Also, for a person with many brothers,
this might be acceptable in terms of righteousness.
But if it is a newborn son,
would all three mothers immediately be lacking?
From this,
it can be inferred that the 'various mothers' mentioned in the *Nèizé*
refer to the three mothers,
clearly not the mothers of one's brothers.
What Zǐyóu asked about
was precisely the compassionate mother who served as a teacher or guardian,
not the three-year or *xiǎogōng* compassionate mother.
Is this not proof that the compassionate mother who serves as a teacher or guardian has no mourning attire?
Zhèng Xuán did not distinguish the three types of compassionate mothers,
mixing them in his explanations,
citing the lack of mourning for one
to annotate 'compassionate to oneself.'
The errors of later generations
indeed stem from this.
The *Jīng* says 'son of a *jūnzǐ*.'
Although this originated from grandees,
it implies that if grandees are already like this,
then above this,
it should be even more so.
Thus, the commentary says, 'A son of a *jūnzǐ*
is the son of a noble person.'
The general term 'noble'
encompasses everything.
The *Jīng* and its commentary are interdependent
and illuminate each other.
Thus, the meaning of 'compassionate care'
extends to grandees and above.
The Sòng dynasty's regulation on this matter
was not contrary to the meaning of the rites.
Its abrupt abolition
is truly questionable."
Thereupon, Yún and others requested to revise and finalize according to the imperial decree: If the son of a principal wife
has his mother pass away and is raised by his father's concubine,
he shall observe five months of mourning.
This shall apply equally to both noble and humble,
and be made a permanent regulation.
Yún was successively promoted to *Wángfǔ Zīyì* and *Quánzhī Zuǒchéng Shì*,
and soon after was appointed *Shàngshū Zuǒchéng*.
He was sent out as *Shǐxīng Nèishǐ*
and died in office.
His son, Shòu,
inherited his father's profession
and was learned in the *Three Rites*.
During the Dàtóng era,
he held successive official positions as *Shàngshū Cíbù Láng*,
and was sent out as *Qǔ'ē Lìng*.
Biàn Huá, courtesy name Zhāojiū,
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Jìn Piàoqí Jiāngjūn, Zhōngzhēn Gōng Hú.
His father, Lúnzhī, was a *Gěishìzhōng*.
Huá was orphaned and poor in his youth but loved learning.
At the age of fourteen,
he was summoned and appointed a *Guózǐshēng*,
mastering the *Zhōu Yì*.
When he grew up,
he studied all five classics extensively,
and was a good friend and fellow student of Píngyuán Míng Shānbīn and Kuàijī Hè Yáng.
. He was successively promoted to Fèng Cháoqǐng
, and Acting Military Advisor to the General Who Attacks the West
. Early in the Tiānjiān reign
, he was promoted to Military Advisor to the Prince of Línchuān
, concurrently serving as Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ (National University)
. He was transferred to Clerk and Military Advisor for the Prince of Ānchéng
, concurrently serving as Academician of the Five Classics (Wǔjīng Bóshì)
, gathering disciples and teaching
. Huá was widely read and possessed skillful eloquence
. In explaining the Classics and analyzing principles
, he was the foremost scholar of his time
. Since the establishment of the Jiāngzuǒ (Eastern Jìn period)
, the study of musicology (Zhōnglǜ) had been lost
. It was only with Huá that it was understood again
. He was promoted to Director of the Rites Bureau (Yí Cáo Láng) of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū)
. He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Wú
, where he died
. Cuī Líng'ēn
, was a man from Dōngwǔchéng, Qīnghé
. In his youth, he devoted himself earnestly to study
. Following teachers, he thoroughly mastered the Five Classics
, specializing particularly in the Three Rites (Sānlǐ) and the Three Commentaries (Sānzhuàn)
. He previously served in the North as Academician of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Bóshì)
. In the thirteenth year of Tiānjiān, he returned to the state
. Emperor Gāozǔ, valuing his Confucian scholarship
, elevated him to serve as Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Attendance (Yuánwài Sǎnqí Shìláng)
. He was successively promoted to Commandant of the Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi)
, concurrently serving as Academician of the Guózǐ
. Líng'ēn gathered disciples and lectured
; those who attended were usually several hundred people
. His nature was simple and rustic, lacking grace
; but when he elucidated the Classics and analyzed principles
, it was extremely refined and subtle
. The elder Confucians in the capital universally praised and respected him
. Assistant Instructor Kǒng Qiān particularly admired his scholarship
. Líng'ēn initially studied the interpretation of the *Zuǒzhuàn* by Fú
, which was not followed in Jiāngdōng
. When he later changed to explain Dù's interpretation
, in every phrase and sentence, he regularly brought up Fú's arguments to challenge Dù's
. Consequently, he compiled the *Zuǒ Shì Tiáoyì* (Categorized Meanings of Master Zuǒ) to clarify these points
. At that time, there was another Assistant Instructor, Yú Sēngdàn, who was also expert in Dù's scholarship
. He therefore composed the *Shēn Dù Nán Fú* (Upholding Dù and Challenging Fú)
, in response to Líng'ēn
. Both works circulated concurrently in the world
. Sēngdàn
, was a man from Yúyáo, Kuàijī
. He taught the *Zuǒ Shì*
, and those who listened also numbered several hundred
. In his comprehensive understanding of principles and rules
, none could surpass him at that time
. Previously, when Confucians discussed Heaven
, they mutually maintained the two theories of Hún (Celestial Sphere) and Gài (Celestial Canopy)
. Those discussing Gài could not reconcile it with Hún
, and those discussing Hún could not reconcile it with Gài
. Líng'ēn established a theory
, uniting Hún and Gài as one
. He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Chángshā (Chángshā Nèishǐ)
. Upon his return, he was appointed Academician of the Guózǐ
; his lecture audience became especially large
. He was sent out to serve as General Who Manifests Awe (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Inspector of Guìzhōu
, and died in office
. Líng'ēn compiled and annotated the *Máo Shī* (Mao Edition of the Book of Odes) in twenty-two chapters
, compiled and annotated the *Zhōu Lǐ* (Rites of Zhōu) in forty chapters
, composed the *Sānlǐ Yìzōng* (Essentials of the Meaning of the Three Rites) in forty-seven chapters
, the *Zuǒ Shì Jīng Zhuàn Yì* (Meanings of the Zuǒ Shì Classic and Commentary) in twenty-two chapters
, the *Zuǒ Shì Tiáolì* (Categorized Rules of Master Zuǒ) in ten chapters
, and the *Gōngyáng Gǔliáng Wénjù Yì* (Meaning of the Phrases and Sentences of the Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng Commentaries) in ten chapters
. Kǒng Qiān
, was a man from Shānyīn, Kuàijī
. In his youth, he served as a disciple to Hé Yìn
. He mastered the Five Classics
, particularly excelling in the Three Rites, the *Xiàojīng* (Classic of Filial Piety), and the *Lúnyǔ* (Analects)
. He lectured on these tens of times
, and his students also numbered several hundred
. He successively held the post of Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ
, and served as Academician of the Five Classics three times
. He was promoted to Director of the Sacrificial Bureau (Cíbù Láng) of the Department of State Affairs
. He was sent out to serve as the magistrate of the two counties, Hǎiyán and Shānyīn
. Qiān was a Confucian scholar
, and was not skilled in governance
. He achieved nothing notable in the counties
. During the chaos of Tàiqīng
, he died at home
His son, Chǔxuán
, was quite knowledgeable in literature
. His official position reached Academician of the Imperial University (Tàixué Bóshì)
. Qiān’s elder brother's son, Yuánsù
, was also skilled in the Three Rites
, and possessed great renown
, but died young
. Lú Guǎng
, was a man from Zhuō, Fànyáng
. He claimed to be a descendant of Chén, the Attendant Gentleman in the Retinue of the Minister of Works (Sīkōng Cóngshì Zhōngláng) during the Jìn dynasty
. Chén perished during the chaos of Rǎn Mǐn
. Among the old clans of the Central Plain of Jìn
, Chén had descendants
. Guǎng, in his youth, was expert in the Classics
, and possessed Confucian scholarship
. He returned to the state during the Tiānjiān reign
. Initially, he was appointed Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Attendance
. He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Shǐ'ān
, but was dismissed due to an incident
. After a time
, he was appointed General Who Crushes the Attack (Zhéchōng Jiāngjūn)
, provided with a thousand troops for the northern campaign
. Upon return, he was appointed Commandant of the Infantry
, concurrently serving as Academician of the Guózǐ
, lecturing extensively on the Five Classics
. At that time, among the Confucian scholars who came from the North were Cuī Líng'ēn, Sūn Xiáng, and Jiǎng Xiǎn
. All gathered disciples and lectured
, but their accents and rhetoric were rustic and clumsy
. Only Guǎng’s discussions and arguments were pure and elegant
, not resembling a person from the North
. The Director of the Department of State Affairs (Púyè), Xú Miǎn
, who was also knowledgeable in classical studies
, deeply appreciated and favored him
. Soon thereafter, he was promoted to Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sǎnqí Chángshì)
, retaining his post as Academician
. He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk to the Heir-Apparent of the Prince of Guìyáng, General Who is Trusted and Martial (Xìnwǔ Guìyáng Sì Wáng Zhǎngshǐ), and Administrator of Xúnyáng
. He subsequently served as Chief Clerk to the Prince of Wǔlíng
, retaining his post as Administrator
, and died in office
. Shěn Jùn, courtesy name Shìsōng
, was a man from Wǔkāng, Wúxīng
. His family had been farmers for generations
. Jùn, however, was fond of learning
. Along with his maternal uncle, Tàishǐ Shúmíng, he studied under his kinsman, Shěn Língshì
. He remained under his tutelage for many years
, reviewing his lessons day and night
. If he sometimes dozed off
, he would immediately strike himself with a rod
. Such was his dedication
. After Língshì died
, he then went to the capital
, traveling extensively among lecture halls
. Consequently, he gained a comprehensive mastery of the Five Classics
, specializing particularly in the Three Rites
. Initially, he served as Commandant of the Royal Kingdom (Wángguó Zhōngwèi)
. He was gradually promoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance
, and concurrently served as Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ
. At that time, Lù Chuí, Director of the Personnel Bureau (Lìbù Láng), wrote a letter to Xú Miǎn, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Púyè), recommending Jùn, saying
: "Yǔ Jìdá, Academician of the Five Classics, needs to be replaced
. I calculate that the government certainly wishes to carefully select the right person
. Among all the books of the sages that can be lectured upon
, the theories must be founded upon the *Zhōu Guān* (Rites of Zhōu)
. Thus, the book *Zhōu Guān*
, is truly the source and foundation of all the Classics
. This scholarship has not been transmitted
, for many years and generations
. Northerners Sūn Xiáng and Jiǎng Xiǎn have also studied it
, but their pronunciation differs between Chǔ and Xià (South and North)
, so students do not attend their lectures
. Only Assistant Instructor Shěn Jùn
, is particularly skilled in this book
. Recently, when he opened his lecture hall
, scholars such as Liú Yán, Shěn Hóng, and Shěn Xióng
, all came down from their seats carrying their texts
, receiving instruction facing north
. Not one failed to sigh in admiration and submit
, and people had no dissenting comments
. I, your younger brother, suggest that this man should be employed immediately
, instructing him to specialize entirely in this one field of study
, going through it and starting anew
. This will cause the orthodox canon of the Sages
, which has been abandoned, to flourish again
, and this expertise, lost for generations
, to be transmitted to future students.' "
Miǎn followed this advice
, and memorialized Jùn to concurrently serve as Academician of the Five Classics
. He lectured at the academy
, with audiences often reaching several hundred people
. He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Huáróng
. Upon returning, he was appointed Supernumerary Gentleman-in-Attendance
, and concurrently served again as Academician of the Five Classics
. At that time, Hè Chēn, Secretariat Drafter (Zhōngshū Shèrén), was compiling the *Liáng Guān* (Official Regulations of Liáng) by imperial decree
. He then proposed that Jùn and Kǒng Zǐqū be assigned as Scholars (Xuéshì) of the Western Secretariat
, to assist in the compilation and recording
. When the book was completed
, he was appointed to concurrently serve as Palace Secretary to the Secretariat (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén)
. He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Wǔkāng
, and died in office
. His son, Wén'ē
, inherited his father's profession
, specializing particularly in the *Zuǒ Shì Zhuàn*
. During the Tàiqīng reign
, he was promoted from Assistant Instructor of the Guózǐ to Academician of the Five Classics
. Other inheritors of Jùn's profession
, included Zhāng Jí from Wú Jùn and Kǒng Zǐyún from Kuàijī
. Their official positions both reached Academician of the Five Classics and Director of the Sacrificial Bureau of the Department of State Affairs
was a man of Wū Chéng, Wú Xīng,
and a descendant of Tài Shǐ Cí of Wú.
In youth, he was skilled in Zhuāng and Lǎo,
and simultaneously studied the *Xiàojīng* and the *Lǐjì*.
His understanding of the Three Arcana (*Sān Xuán*) was particularly profound,
and was considered the best of his generation.
Whenever he lectured,
there were usually more than five hundred listeners.
He successively served as National University Assistant Instructor (Guózǐ Zhùjiào).
Shàolíng Wáng Lún was fond of his scholarship,
and when he was sent out to govern Jiāngzhōu,
he took Shū Míng to the garrison.
When the Prince moved to Yǐngzhōu,
Shū Míng again followed the residence.
Wherever he went, he lectured and taught,
and scholars outside the Jiāng region all transmitted his teachings.
In the thirteenth year of Dàtóng (547 CE),
he died,
aged seventy-three.
Kǒng Zǐ Qū,
was a man of Shānyīn, Kuàijī.
He was orphaned and poor in youth but loved learning.
While farming, cultivating, chopping wood, and gathering,
he always carried books with him.
Whenever he had spare time, he recited and read.
He diligently exerted himself,
and consequently mastered the classics and arts,
especially excelling in the Ancient Text *Shàngshū*.
He first served as Attendant (Shìláng) to the Heir Prince of Chángshā,
concurrent with National University Assistant Instructor (Guózǐ Zhùjiào).
He lectured on the *Shàngshū* forty times,
and the listeners often numbered several hundred.
When Palace Secretary (Zhōngshū Shèrén) Hé Chēn received an imperial decree to compile the Officials of Liáng,
he petitioned for Zǐ Qū to become a Scholar of the Western Department,
assisting in the compilation and recording.
After the work was finished,
he was concurrently appointed Attendant for Overseeing Literature (Sīwén Shìláng),
but he did not take up the post.
After a long time, he concurrently held the posts of Minister of Guests (Zhǔkè Láng) and Palace Secretary (Shèrén),
while retaining his position as Scholar.
He was successively promoted to Attendant in the State of the Prince of Xiāngdōng,
Palace Regular Attendant (Chángshì),
Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng),
and then Aide to the Duke of Lújiāng (Yúnhuī Lújiāng Gōng Jìshì Cānjūn).
He was then transferred to concurrently serve as Palace Secretary of the Central Secretariat for Internal Communication (Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén).
Soon after, he was promoted to Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
retaining his Palace Secretary post.
When Gāozǔ compiled the Commentaries and Sub-Commentaries on the Five Classics (*Wǔjīng Jiǎngshū*) and the *Kǒngzǐ Zhèngyán*,
he specifically ordered Zǐ Qū to consult various books
to serve as scholastic evidence.
When the task was finished,
an imperial decree ordered Zǐ Qū, Zhū Yì (Right Guard), and Hé Chēn (Left Assistant) to preside over the Classics (teaching) on alternating days at the Scholars’ Pavilion (Shìlín Guǎn).
He was successively promoted to Gentleman-Consultant (Tōngzhí Zhèngyuán Láng),
retaining his Palace Secretary post.
In the first year of Zhōngdàtóng (546 CE),
he died in office,
aged fifty-one.
Zǐ Qū authored a total of twenty scrolls of *Shàngshū* Meanings (*Shàngshū Yì*),
thirty scrolls of Collected Annotations on the *Shàngshū* (*Jízhù Shàngshū*),
a continuation of Zhū Yì’s Collected Annotations on the *Zhōuyì* in one hundred scrolls,
and a continuation of Hé Chéngtiān’s Collection of Rites Treatises (*Jílǐ Lùn*) in one hundred fifty scrolls.
Huáng Kǎn,
was a man of Wújùn,
and a ninth-generation descendant of Huáng Xiàng, the Prefect of Qīngzhōu.
Kǎn loved learning in his youth,
and studied under Hé Yáng.
He devoted himself wholly to the specialization,
thoroughly mastering his studies,
and was particularly knowledgeable about the Three Rites (*Sānlǐ*), the *Xiàojīng*, and the *Lúnyǔ*.
He began his career concurrently serving as National University Assistant Instructor (Guózǐ Zhùjiào).
He lectured and spoke at the school,
with several hundred listeners.
He compiled fifty scrolls of the Commentary and Sub-Commentary on the *Lǐjì* (*Lǐjì Jiǎngshū*).
When the work was completed and submitted,
an edict ordered it to be deposited in the Imperial Library (Mì Gé).
Soon after,
he was summoned to Shòuguāng Hall to lecture on the meanings of the *Lǐjì*.
Gāozǔ praised him,
appointed him Supernumerary Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng),
while retaining his Assistant Instructor post.
He was utterly filial by nature.
He regularly recited the *Xiàojīng* twenty times per day,
comparing it to the *Guānshìyīn Jīng* (Avalokiteśvara Sutra).
When his mother died,
he resigned his post and returned to his hometown.
The Prince of Shàolíng, Píngxī, admired his scholarship
and welcomed him with generous gifts.
After Kǎn arrived,
he contracted a heart illness.
In the eleventh year of Dàtóng (545 CE),
he died at Xiàshǒu,
aged fifty-eight.
The ten scrolls of the Meanings of the *Lúnyǔ* (*Lúnyǔ Yì*) that he compiled,
along with the Meanings of the *Lǐjì*, were highly regarded by the world,
and scholars transmitted them.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, said: In the past, Shūsūn Tōng discussed the classics on horseback,
and Huán Róng studied diligently amidst chaos.
When peace was achieved,
they attained glory and favor,
as did those like Cuī, Fú, Hé, and Yán, who followed suit.
Màn Róng and Tóng Zhī lectured on the Way during the late Qí dynasty
and did not change with the times.
Hé Yáng, Yán Zhízhī, and their contemporaries,
when they met with Liáng's promotion of Confucianism and reverence for the Way,
all reached high offices.
Through the power of examining antiquity,
these gentlemen all achieved their utmost.
Fàn Zhěn wore the black headband, sought fame through luck,
and did not achieve his ambition.
This was fitting.
Biography Forty-Three: Literature I: Dào Hàng, Qiū Chí, Liú Bāo, Yuán Jùn, Yǔ Yúlíng (younger brother Jiān Wú), Liú Zhāo, Hé Xùn, Zhōng Róng, Zhōu Xīngsì, Wú Jūn.
In the past, the histories of Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù
both included a biography for Sīmǎ Xiāngrú.
Although Xiāngrú did not participate in major affairs of the Hàn court,
this inclusion was based on the particular brilliance of his writing.
Bān Gù also wrote biographies for Jiǎ, Zōu, Méi, and Lù,
including them based on their literary ability.
Fàn Yè’s *Book of the Later Hàn* contains the Biographies of Literary Garden (*Wényuàn Zhuàn*),
and the detail concerning the persons recorded therein
is already extensive.
However, coordinating the state with the warp of ritual and music,
and communicating past and present while describing virtue and vice,
is impossible without literature.
Thus, those who rule the world
all sincerely appreciate its meaning.
The learning of the officials
universally values and honors its Way.
From antiquity until now,
this has never changed.
Gāozǔ was intelligent and literary in thought,
gloriously dwelling over the realm.
He widely sought out the refined scholars,
issuing edicts to collect exceptional individuals.
The flourishing of literary works
splendidly accumulated.
Whenever he went on an excursion,
he would immediately order his officials to compose poems.
Those whose compositions were excellent
were rewarded with gold and silk.
Those who approached the palace court to present *fù* or *sòng* (rhapsodies or eulogies)
were sometimes granted an audience.
Among those in office
were Shěn Yuē, Jiāng Yān, and Rèn Fǎng,
whose literary talent
was exquisitely unmatched at that time.
As for those like Dào Hàng of Péngchéng, Qiū Chí of Wúxīng, Wáng Sēngrú of Dōnghǎi, and Zhāng Shuài of Wújùn,
some entered to serve duty in Wéndé Hall,
or attended banquets in Shòuguāng Hall;
they were all later selections.
Yuē, Yān, Fǎng, Sēngrú, and Shuài are discussed separately based on their achievements.
Now we append the biographies of Dào Hàng and others who were scholars and literati,
including those active until the Tàiqīng period,
in the Biographies of Literature.
Dào Hàng,
courtesy name Mào Xiè, was a man of Wǔyuán, Péngchéng.
His great-grandfather, Yànzhī,
was a General of Sòng.
His father, Huī,
was Minister of the Five Armaments (Wǔbīng Shàngshū) of Qí.
Hàng was intelligent and keen as a child.
When he was five years old,
Huī copied ancient poems onto a screen.
Hàng asked to be taught to read them once,
and was immediately able to recite them
without missing anything.
When he grew up, he was diligent in study.
He was skilled in composing prose
and proficient in seal and cursive scripts.
His demeanor was admirable,
and his appearance was pleasing.
During the Jiànwǔ reign of Qí,
he began his career as the Administrator of the Legal Section of the Rear Army.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was promoted to Principal Clerk of the General Who Conquers the Barbarians.
When Gāozǔ first came to power,
he sought out and promoted virtuous and outstanding talents,
and deeply admired his abilities.
When the Eastern Palace was established,
he was made a Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting.
At that time, the Academy of Scholars was set up in the Wéndé Diàn,
and highly talented and learned scholars were summoned to serve there as academicians,
tasked with collating and editing historical records.
An imperial edict granted Hàng full access.
At that time, Gāozǔ hosted a banquet at Huáguāng Diàn,
and ordered his officials to compose poems.
Hàng alone was instructed to compose a two-hundred-character poem,
to be completed within three kè.
Hàng composed and presented it immediately,
and its writing was exceptionally beautiful.
Soon after, as Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting, he was put in charge of the Eastern Palace's secretariat and the excellent policy documents of the Cabinet of Scattered Cavalry.
In the third year,
an imperial edict stated that officials of the Department of State Affairs who were upright and capable, or exceptionally talented, should be made Gentlemen.
Hàng was appointed Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng Cáo.
Hàng's paternal cousins, Gài and Qià,
both possessed talent and fame,
and at that time, they successively served as Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng.
The contemporary world regarded this as an honor.
In the fourth year,
he was promoted to Grand Tutor's Attendant-in-Ordinary.
Hàng was not boastful,
did not discuss the faults of others,
and was good friends with Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān and Fàn Yún of Nánxiāng.
In that year,
he was promoted to Assistant of Dānyáng Yǐn,
but due to illness, he could not perform his duties,
and was transferred to Consultative Aide to the General of the Northern Central Army.
In the fifth year,
he died in office,
at the age of thirty.
Gāozǔ deeply grieved and lamented his passing,
and issued an edict granting him twenty thousand coins
and thirty bolts of cloth.
He authored over a hundred poems and rhapsodies.
Qiū Chí, courtesy name Xīfàn,
was a native of Wúxīng Wūchéng.
His father, Língjū,
was talented and famous,
and served in Qí, reaching the office of Grand Master of the Central Court.
Chí was able to compose essays at the age of eight,
and Língjū often said that his spirit and bones resembled his own.
Xiè Chāozōng, Yellow Gate Gentleman, and Hé Diǎn, recluse, both saw him and were impressed.
When he grew up,
the prefecture appointed him as Administrator,
he was recommended as a Cultivated Talent,
and was appointed Erudite of the Imperial Academy.
He was promoted to Acting Administrator of the Grand Marshal,
but left office due to his father's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he was appointed Administrator of the Western Central Army.
He was successively promoted to Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng,
but left office due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period,
he again served as Gentlemen of the Diànzhōng,
and was promoted to Registrar Administrator of the Chariots and Cavalry.
When Gāozǔ pacified Jīngyì,
and the Duke's Residence was established,
he was brought in as Principal Clerk of the Hussar General.
He received great courtesy and respect.
The exhortations to advance King Liáng and the special rituals
were all written by Chí.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was appointed Palace Attendant.
Soon after, he was promoted to Palace Attendant, concurrently serving as Magistrate of Wúxīng District and Academician of the Wéndé Diàn.
At that time, Gāozǔ wrote a series of "linked pearls,"
and ordered dozens of officials to follow suit.
Chí's writing was the most beautiful.
In the third year of Tiānjiān,
he was sent out as the Administrator of Yǒngjiā,
but did not perform his duties well in the commandery
and was impeached by the relevant authorities.
Gāozǔ, loving his talent,
shelved the impeachment.
In the fourth year,
when Liánchuān Wáng Hóng, General of the Central Army, led a northern expedition,
Chí served as Consultative Aide,
and was in charge of the secretariat.
At that time, Chén Bózhī was in the north,
and came to resist with the Wèi army.
Chí persuaded him with a letter,
and Bózhī subsequently surrendered.
Upon his return, he was appointed Palace Attendant,
and was promoted to Senior Administrator to the Grand Minister of Education.
In the seventh year,
he died in office,
at the age of forty-five.
His collected poems and rhapsodies were circulated in the world.
Liú Bāo, courtesy name Xiàocháng,
was a native of Péngchéng.
His grandfather, Miǎn,
was the Minister of Works of Sòng.
His father, Xuān,
was the Prince's Attendant-in-Ordinary of Qí.
Bāo's father died when Bāo was four,
and when he was six or seven,
he often wept upon seeing his paternal uncles.
At that time, his paternal uncles Quān and Huì, among others, were all prominent and noble.
Bāo's mother thought he was afraid
and was angry with him.
Bāo replied:
"I was orphaned early and too young to understand.
I heard that my paternal uncles resembled my father greatly,
so my heart felt like weeping;
there was no other intention."
With that, he choked up and sighed,
and his mother also wept bitterly.
Initially,
Bāo's parents and two elder brothers had successively died,
and were all temporarily interred.
When Bāo was sixteen,
he began to move the burial site,
managing the reburial himself.
He did not rely on his paternal uncles,
and it was all completed within a short time.
Huì often sighed in admiration of him.
In his youth, he loved learning
and was capable of composing essays.
He began his career as Acting Administrator of the Legal Section of the Minister of Education,
but did not take the post.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
because he was the younger brother of the King of Línchuān's consort,
he was directly promoted from Principal Clerk of the General Who Conquers the Barbarians to Merit Officer of the King's Central Army.
He was successively promoted to Gentleman of the Treasury Bureau of the Department of State Affairs,
Assistant of Dānyáng Yǐn,
Assistant of the Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince,
Gentleman of the Diànzhōng of the Department of State Affairs,
and Chief Administrator of Nánxú Prefecture.
He was dismissed due to official matters.
After a long time,
he became Prince's Gentleman-in-Waiting,
in charge of the secretariat,
and lectured at Shòuguāng Diàn.
Since Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he promoted literary scholars who were junior to him.

Bāo, his paternal cousin Xiàochuò, his paternal younger brother Rú, Dào Gài of the same commandery, Gài's younger brother Qià, his paternal younger brother Hàng, Lù Chuí of Wújùn, and Zhāng Shuài were all recognized for their literary talent,
and frequently attended banquets.
Although their official advancements occurred at different times,
their rewards and gifts were not dissimilar.
In the tenth year of Tiānjiān,
he died,
at the age of thirty.
On his deathbed,
he called upon his friend Liú Zhīlìn of Nányáng to entrust him with his funeral arrangements,
emphasizing simplicity and frugality.
Bāo had a reputation for ability in office.
His character was gentle yet upright.
When interacting with people,
he would directly point out their faults,
but afterwards would praise their virtues.
He concealed nothing in his feelings,
and thus scholars and friends alike admired and lamented him.
Yuán Jùn, courtesy name Xiàogāo,
was a native of Chénjùn Yángxià,
and an eighth-generation descendant of Huàn, Superintendent of the Palace in Wèi.
Jùn was orphaned early,
and was earnestly devoted to learning.
His family was poor and had no books,
so he always borrowed them from others.
He would always transcribe them,
setting himself a daily quota of fifty sheets.
If the number of sheets was not reached,
he would not rest.
He was slow of speech,
but skilled in writing.
When the righteous army conquered Jīngyì,
Póyáng Wáng Huī garrisoned in Pògāng to the east.
Jùn followed the Prince, overseeing the secretariat.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
when the State of Póyáng was established,
Jùn was appointed Gentleman,
and followed the Prince to garrison in Jīngkǒu.
When the Prince moved to Yǐngzhōu,
Jùn concurrently served as Administrator of the Capital Affairs.
Gāozǔ was fond of rhapsodies and poems,
and at that time, those who presented literary works at the Southern Gate were numerous.
Their ornate and beautiful pieces were noteworthy,
and some were praised and promoted.
In the sixth year,
Jùn imitated Yáng Xióng's "Official Admonitions" and presented them.
Gāozǔ praised him,
and bestowed silk upon him.
He was appointed Supernumerary Palace Attendant,
and served directly in the Wéndé Academy of Scholars,
transcribing twenty volumes each of the Shǐjì and Hànshū.
He also received an imperial order to compose new stele inscriptions with Lù Chuí,
the details of which are too numerous to include.
Yǔ Yúlíng
, was the younger brother of Sànqí Chángshì Qiánlóu
