. At seven, he could speak on abstruse philosophy
. When he grew up,
he was astute, learned, and talented in thought
. When Qí Suíwáng Zǐlóng
was governor of Jīngzhōu
, he summoned Yúlíng to be his registrar
and made him, along with Xiè Tiǎo
and Zōng Guài
, copy and compile various books
. When Zǐlóng
was replaced and returned
, Yúlíng
was again appointed as the escorting former registrar
. Zǐlóng
was soon harmed by Míngdì
. His subordinates, fearing and avoiding,
none dared to approach
. Only Yúlíng
and Guài
remained
to manage the funeral affairs
. When Shǐ'ānwáng Yáoguāng
was Fǔjūn
, he appointed Yúlíng
as Xíngcānjūn
, also serving as Jìshì
. At the end of Yǒngyuán
, he was appointed Dōngyáng Suì'ān Lìng
, and was praised by the people and officials
. In the early Tiānjiān era
, he became Jiànkāng Yùpíng
, then was promoted to Shàngshū Gōnglùn Láng
, and waited upon the emperor in Wéndédiàn
. He was sent out as Xiāngzhōu Biéjià
, then promoted to Piàojì Lùshì Cānjūn
, also serving as Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén
. Soon after, he took charge of Nánjùn Yì Zhōngzhèng
, and was appointed Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ
, with his position as Shèrén remaining unchanged
. In former times,
officials of the Eastern Palace
were generally considered clear choices
. The Xǐmǎ
managed literary affairs
and was especially esteemed
. In recent times, for appointments,
only those from eminent families with talent and prestige were chosen
. At that time, Yúlíng
and Zhōu Shè
were both promoted to these posts
. Gāozǔ
said:
"An office is made clean by the person in it
, how can it be limited to eminent families?"
Contemporary opinion considered this excellent
. Soon after, he was promoted to Sànqí Shìláng
and then appointed as Jīngzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng
. He was successively promoted to Zhōngshū Huángmén Shìláng
, with his positions as Shèrén
and Zhōngzhèng
remaining unchanged
. He was sent out as Xuānyì Jìn'ānwáng Zhǎngshǐ
and Guǎnglíng Tàishǒu
, acting in both the prefecture and commandery affairs
, but was dismissed due to official matters
. He was reinstated as Tōngzhíláng
, then appointed Hónglú Qīng
, again holding the post of Jīngzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng
. He died in office
at the age of forty-eight
. His collected works comprised ten volumes
. His younger brother was Jiānwú
. Soon after, he took charge of Jīngzhōu Dà Zhōngzhèng
with his original official title
. He was successively promoted to Zhōnglùshì Zīyì Cānjūn
, Tàizǐ Shuàigēnglìng
, and Zhōngshùzǐ
. Initially,
Tàizōng
, while still a vassal,
had a refined taste for literary scholars
. At that time, Jiānwú
, along with Xú Chī
from Dōnghǎi
, Lù Gǎo
from Wújùn
, Liú Zūn
and Liú Xiàoyí
from Péngchéng
, and Xiàoyí's
brother Xiàowēi
, all received his appreciation and welcome
. When he became the Crown Prince
, he also established the Wéndé Shěng
and appointed scholars
. Jiānwú's
son Xìn
, Chī's
son Líng
, Zhāng Chánggōng
from Wújùn
, Fù Hóng
from Běidì
, Bào Zhì
from Dōnghǎi
, and others were chosen
. In the Yǒngmíng era of Qí
, the literary figures Wáng Róng
, Xiè Tiǎo
, and Shěn Yuē
began to use the four tones in their writings
, considering it a new development
. By this time, the adherence to tones and rhymes
became even more strict
, and the pursuit of ornate and decadent styles
surpassed previous times
. At that time, the Crown Prince
, in a letter to Xiāngdōngwáng
, discussed this, saying: We have nothing to enjoy or wander,
only devoting ourselves to reading
. Our nature is fond of literature
, and from time to time we make short verses
. Although it is but common sound
, we cannot put down our brushes
. We are ashamed of our skills
with the talented people of ancient times
, from the distant Yáng
, Mǎ
, Cáo
, Wáng
, to the recent Pān
, Lù
, Yán
, Xiè
, when examining their choice of words and intention
, they are entirely dissimilar
. If current literature is deemed correct
, then ancient literature is incorrect
; if the former
sages are praiseworthy
, then the current style should be abandoned
. To approve of both
is something I dare not allow
. Moreover, there are those who imitate the writings of Xiè Kānglè
and Péi Hónglú
, which is also quite
. Péi Shì
was a talent for good historiography
but utterly
lacked beauty in poetry
. Thus, to learn from Xiè
is not to reach his essence
but merely to obtain his prolixity
; to emulate Péi
is to ignore his strengths
and only acquire his weaknesses
. Xiè's
skill is indeed impossible to emulate
, and Péi's
plainness is also not worth admiring
. Therefore, those who are opinionated
and those who pursue fame but forget substance
are like
dividing meat among benevolent
beasts
, or showing off their dice game in Hándān
, entering a fish market and forgetting the stench
, and imitating faults to invite disaster
. The elegance of Xiè Shēng
is not something the three thousand
can match
; to imitate Péi Shì
, one fears
that the two Tángs
will not be transmitted
. Hence, a jade zither
and golden flute
are instead ridiculed by untrained eyes
; while common tunes
are more appealing to the ears of Yǐngzhōng
. Spring's lofty melodies
are not harmonized
, and subtle sounds
are lost and not sought after
. Ultimately, they do not meticulously examine every detail
, nor assess the balance of substance and embellishment
; having a different clever mind
, they ultimately shame the skilled hand
. Therefore, a scholar holding jade
and treasures
looks at Zhèngbāng
and knows to retreat
; a person with high hats and green shoes
gazes at Mǐnxiāng
and sighs
Jiǎn zhī fù (簡之賦) and
Zhōu Shēngyì (周升逸)'s arguments
are also excellent works,
hard to encounter again.
Literature has not fallen,
there must be extraordinary talents,
and one who leads them,
if not my brother,
then who?
Every time I wish to discuss it,
there is no one to talk with,
I miss my Zǐjiàn (子建),
to deliberate and discuss together.
Discriminating between the clear and turbid,
making them like the Jīng (涇) and Wèi (渭) rivers;
discussing them like the monthly appraisals,
similar to
those of Rǔnán (汝南).
Once the red and black are decided,
and the yellow is distinguished,
it will make those who harbor rats feel ashamed,
and the unqualified feel disgraced.
It will be like Yuán Shào (袁紹),
fearing to meet Zǐjiāng (子將);
like those
who stole cattle,
remotely ashamed of Wáng Liè (王烈).
Longing for you but unable to see you,
how can my distress be?
During the Tàiqīng (太清) era,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) invaded and captured the capital.
When Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
he appointed Jiānwú (肩吾) as Dùzhī Shàngshū (度支尚書).
At that time, the various regional governors in the upstream areas
all held their prefectures to resist Hóu Jǐng (侯景).
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) issued a forged imperial edict, sending Jiānwú (肩吾) to Jiāngzhōu (江州),
to persuade Dāngyáng Gōng Dàxīn (當陽公大心).
Dàxīn (大心) soon surrendered the entire prefecture to the rebels.
Jiānwú (肩吾) then fled into the territory of Jiànchāng (建昌).
After a long time,
he finally managed to reach Jiānglíng (江陵),
and died shortly thereafter.
His collected works circulated in the world.
Liú Zhāo (劉昭), courtesy name Xuānqīng (宣卿),
was a native of Gāotáng (高唐), Píngyuán (平原).
He was the ninth-generation descendant of Jìn (晉) Tàiwèi (太尉) Shí (寔).
His grandfather, Bólóng (伯龍),
was known for his filial piety during his father's mourning period.
Sòng Wǔdì (宋武帝) decreed that the Heir Apparent and all the princes should go to offer condolences.
His highest office was Shǎofù Qīng (少府卿).
His father, Biāo (彪),
was Qí (齊) Zhēnglǔ Jìn'ān Wáng (征虜晉安王)'s jìshì (記室).
Zhāo (昭) was bright and alert in his youth,
and at seven, he understood the principles of Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊).
When he grew up,
he diligently studied and was skilled at writing.
His maternal cousin, Jiāng Yān (江淹), had praised him early on.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
he began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請),
and was successively promoted to Zhēngběi Xíng Cānjūn (征北行參軍)
and Shàngshū Cāngbù Láng (尚書倉部郎),
soon thereafter appointed Wúxī Lìng (無錫令).
He successively served as Xuānhuì Yùzhāng Wáng (宣惠豫章王) and Zhōngjūn Línchuān Wáng (中軍臨川王)'s jìshì (記室).
Initially,
Zhāo (昭)'s paternal uncle, Róng (肜), compiled various Jin Histories, annotating Gān Bǎo (干寶)'s Jìn Jì (晉紀) into forty volumes.
Later, Zhāo (昭) himself compiled "Hòuhàn Tóngyì" (後漢同異) to annotate Fàn Yè (范曄)'s work,
which was widely praised for its extensive thoroughness.
He was promoted to Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎),
and then went out to serve as Shàn Lìng (剡令),
where he died in office.
His collected annotations to "Hòuhàn" (後漢) were one hundred eighty volumes,
"Yòutóng Zhuàn" (幼童傳) ten volumes,
and his collected writings ten volumes.
His son, Tāo (縚),
courtesy name Yánmíng (言明),
was also fond of learning
and thoroughly understood the Sānlǐ (三禮).
During the Dàtóng (大同) era,
he served as Shàngshū Cíbù Láng (尚書祠部郎),
but soon resigned his post
and did not serve again.
Tāo (縚)'s younger brother, Huǎn (緩),
courtesy name Hándù (含度),
was famous in his youth.
He successively held office as Ānxī Xiāngdōng Wáng (安西湘東王)'s jìshì (記室).
At that time, the western court extensively gathered literary talents,
and Huǎn (緩) was at the forefront.
He was appointed Tōngzhí Láng (通直郎),
and soon promoted to Zhènnán Xiāngdōng Wáng (鎮南湘東王)'s Zhōnglùshì (中錄事),
then followed the prince to Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
where he died.
Hé Xùn (何遜), courtesy name Zhòngyán (仲言),
was a native of Tán (郯), Dōnghǎi (東海).
His great-grandfather, Chéngtiān (承天),
was Sòng (宋) Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (御史中丞).
His grandfather, Yì (翼),
was Yuánwàiláng (員外郎).
His father, Xún (詢),
was Qí (齊) Tàiwèi Zhōngbīng Cānjūn (太尉中兵參軍).
Xùn (遜) could compose poetry at eight,
and at twenty, he was recommended as Xiùcái (秀才) by the prefecture.
Fàn Yún (范雲) of Nánxiāng (南鄉) saw his policy proposals
and praised them greatly,
thus forming a friendship that transcended age.
From then on, every piece of writing or poem he produced,
Fàn Yún (范雲) would invariably admire,
saying to his intimates:
"Recently, when observing men of letters,
their substance often exceeds that of scholars,
but their ornateness harms custom;
those who can encompass both clarity and turbidity,
and balance ancient and modern,
are seen in Hé Shēng (何生)."
Shěn Yuē (沈約) also loved his writings,
and once said to Xùn (遜):
"Every time I read your poems,
I read them three times a day,
and still cannot stop."
Such was the praise he received from famous scholars.
During the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
he began his career as Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請),
and was promoted to Zhōngwèi Jiàn'ān Wáng (中衞建安王)'s Shuǐcáo Xíng Cānjūn (水曹行參軍),
concurrently serving as jìshì (記室).
The prince loved men of letters
and spent his days with them in feasts and entertainments.
When the prince was transferred to Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
Xùn (遜) still managed the secretariat.
He returned to serve as Ānxī Ānchéng Wáng (安西安成王)'s Cānjūnshì (參軍事),
concurrently Shàngshū Shuǐbù Láng (尚書水部郎),
and resigned due to his mother's mourning.
After the mourning period ended,
he was appointed Rénwēi Lúlíng Wáng (仁威廬陵王)'s jìshì (記室),
and again followed the prince to Jiāngzhōu (江zhōu),
where he died shortly thereafter.
Wáng Sēngrú (王僧孺) of Dōnghǎi (東海) compiled his works into eight volumes.
Initially,
Xùn (遜)'s writings and Liú Xiàochuò (劉孝綽)'s were both highly esteemed by the world,
and the world referred to them as
"Hé Liú" (何劉).
Shìzǔ (世祖) wrote an essay discussing them, saying:
"Among those who wrote many poems and were capable, there was Shěn Yuē (沈約);
among those who wrote few but were capable, there were Xiè Tiǎo (謝朓) and Hé Xùn (何遜)."
At that time, there was Yú Qiān (虞騫) from Kuàijī (會稽),
skilled at composing five-character-line poetry,
whose fame was equal to Xùn (遜)'s.
His highest office was Wángguó Shìláng (王國侍郎).
Later, there were also Kǒng Wēngguī (孔翁歸) from Kuàijī (會稽) and Jiāng Bì (江避) from Jìyáng (濟陽),
both serving as Nánpíng Wáng (南平王)'s Dàsīmǎ Fǔ (大司馬府)'s jìshì (記室).
Wēngguī (翁歸) was also skilled at composing poetry.
Bì (避) was learned and insightful,
and furthermore annotated the "Lúnyǔ" (論語) and "Xiàojīng" (孝經).
Both men had collected works.
Zhōng Róng (鍾嶸), courtesy name Zhòngwěi (仲偉),
was a native of Chángshè (長社), Yǐngchuān (潁川).
He was the seventh-generation descendant of Jìn (晉) Shìzhōng Yǎ (侍中雅).
His father, Dāo (蹈),
was Qí (齊) Zhōngjūn Cānjūn (中軍參軍).
Róng (嶸), along with his elder brother Gùn (岏) and younger brother Yǔ (嶼), were all fond of learning,
possessing keen intellect.
Róng (嶸),
during the Yǒngmíng (永明) era of the Qí (齊) dynasty, became a student at the Guózǐ (國子, National University),
understanding the Zhōu Yì (周易).
Wèi Jūn (衞軍, Protector-General) Wáng Jiǎn (王儉) served as Libationer (Jìjiǔ),
and greatly appreciated and welcomed him.
He was nominated as an Outstanding Talent (Xiùcái) from his home commandery.
He began his career as an Attendant Gentleman of a Princely State (Wángguó Shìláng),
and was promoted to Acting Staff Officer to the General Who Comforts the Army (Fǔjūn Xíng Cānjūn).
He was sent out to serve as the Prefect of Ānguó (安國).
At the end of the Yǒngyuán (永元) era,
he was appointed Acting Staff Officer to the Minister of Education (Sītú Xíng Cānjūn).
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān (天監) era,
although the institutions had been reformed,
there was insufficient time to fully implement them.
Róng (嶸) therefore spoke, saying:
“During the turmoil that began in the Yǒngyuán (永元) era,
men secured high rank merely by manipulating their status;
merit was not achieved through military service,
but office was obtained through bribery.
Waving a piece of gold could acquire one of the Nine Ranks (Jiǔliè, high officials);
sending a short letter could recruit one of the Six Regiments (Liù Xiào).
Cavalry commanders (Jì Dūwèi) clog the markets,
and colonels (Lángjiàng) fill the streets.
Although their robes bear ribbons and tassels [symbols of high office],
they still perform the duties of slaves and menials;
although their posts are merely titular (Huángsǎn, sinecures),
they still personally undertake the tasks of common clerks and laborers.
The mixing and confusion of name and reality (title and function)
has never been worse than this.
Your humble servant suggests that military officials who are gentlemen from established clans (sùzú shìrén),
and who already possess positions in the pure register (qīngguàn, high officialdom),
but have acquired additional titles based on military connection,
should all have these titles immediately removed,
to punish those who seek fortune through opportunism.
If they are commoners (hánrén) who have acquired official standing (lìxìng),
let their rank be judged based on their family status (ménpǐn),
and they should not be allowed, merely through military association,
to improperly obtain entry into the pure ranks (qīngjí).
As for the mingled expatriates (qiáo zá) and the Chǔ (楚) savages (cāng),
they should be controlled and pacified.
It is absolutely necessary to strictly cut off their official stipends (lù) and service obligations (lì),
to prevent them from obstructing proper governance,
and grant them nothing more than empty titles.
I respectfully offer this utmost loyalty,
disregarding what public opinion may say."
An imperial decree (chì) ordered the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) to implement this.
He was promoted to Acting Staff Officer to the Prince of Línchuān (Línchuān Wáng) under the Central Army (Zhōngjūn).
When the Prince of Héngyáng (衡陽王), Yuánjiǎn (元簡), went out to govern Kuàijī (會稽),
he appointed Róng (嶸) as the Registrar (Jìshì) of the General Who Pacifies the North (Níngshuò),
exclusively managing literary documents.
At that time, the retired scholar Hé Yìn (何胤) had built a dwelling on Mount Ruòxié (若邪山).
A great flood erupted from the mountain,
washing away trees and rocks,
but this dwelling alone remained intact.
Yuánjiǎn (元簡) commanded Róng (嶸) to compose an Ode on the Auspicious Dwelling (Ruì Shì Sòng) to commemorate it,
the wording of which was highly elegant and beautiful.
He was selected to be the Registrar (Jìshì) for the Prince of Jìn'ān (晉安王), under the General of the Household, West (Xī Zhōngláng).
Róng (嶸) once critically evaluated the five-character poems of antiquity and the present,
discussing their merits and flaws,
naming the work *Shī Píng* (詩評, Critique of Poetry).
Its preface says: When *qì* (vital energy) moves things,
and things affect people,
it thus stirs the nature and feelings,
expressing itself in dance and song.
It seeks to illuminate the Three Powers (Sāncái: Heaven, Earth, Man),
and bring splendor to the myriad existence.
Spirits and deities rely upon it
to receive sacrifices;
subtle mysteries use it to be made known.
Nothing is closer to
moving Heaven and Earth and inspiring ghosts and gods
than poetry.
In antiquity, the words of the Southern Wind (Nán Fēng zhī Cí),
and the Eulogy of the Auspicious Clouds (Qīng Yún zhī Sòng),
their meaning was profound
indeed.
The Xià (夏) dynasty song says,
"How depressed is my heart";
the Chǔ (楚) regional ballad says,
"My name is given as Zhèngzé (正則)."
Although the poetic form was not yet complete,
they are generally considered the earliest beginnings of the five-character
verse.
It was only later, during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, with Lǐ Líng (李陵),
that the form of five-character verse first became clearly defined.
The provenance of the Old Poems (gǔ shī) is remote and vague,
and the generation of their authors is hard to ascertain.
Judging by their literary style,
they are certainly compositions of the Flourishing Hàn (Yán Hàn),
and were not initiated during the declining
Zhōu (周) dynasty.
Since the time of Wáng (王), Yáng (揚), Méi (枚), Mǎ (馬), and their like,
the literary *fù* (rhapsodies) flourished in competition,
but metric chanting (yínyǒng) was rarely heard.
From Commandant Lǐ (Lǐ Dūwèi) up to Consort Bān (Bān Jiéyú),
over the course of nearly a century,
there was only one woman [Bān Jiéyú],
a female writer,
and that was all.
The tradition of the poets
had largely been lost.
Throughout the two hundred years of the Eastern Capital (Dōngjīng, Eastern Hàn),
only Bān Gù (班固) wrote poems on history,
but his style was plain and simple,
lacking literary refinement.
Descending to the Jiàn'ān (建安) era,
Cáo Gōng (曹公) and his sons
were deeply fond of this literary style;
the brothers of Píngyuán (平原),
were flourishing literary pillars;
Liú Zhēn (劉楨) and Wáng Càn (王粲)
served as their wings.
Following them were those who clung to the Dragon and relied upon the Phoenix (i.e., attached themselves to the Cáo family),
joining their entourage,
numbering perhaps a hundred.
This brilliant flourishing
reached its peak at that time.
After that, the tradition gradually declined and faded away,
until
the Jìn (晉) dynasty.
During the Tàikāng (太康) era,
the Three Zhāngs (Sān Zhāng) and the Two Lùs (Èr Lù),
the Two Pāns (Liǎng Pān) and the One Zuǒ (Yī Zuǒ),
revived the tradition and followed in the steps of the earlier kings.
The literary elegance (fēngliú) did not perish;
it was also a revival of literature
itself.
During the Yǒngjiā (永嘉) period,
the veneration of Huáng and Lǎo (Daoism),
and the favoring of empty discourse (xūtán), became prevalent.
The poems of that time
had intellectual content (lǐ) that surpassed their wording (cí),
and were bland and lacking in flavor.
Moving to the area South of the Yangtze (Jiāng Biǎo),
the faint echoes of this trend were still being passed on.
Sūn Chuò (孫綽), Xǔ Xún (許詢), and the lords Huán (桓) and Yǔ (庾),
all wrote plain and classical works resembling treatises on Daoist principles (Dàodé Lùn),
the Jiàn'ān (建安) style was utterly gone.
Earlier, Guō Jǐngchún (郭景純), employing his eminent talent,
innovated
and changed the style;
Liú Yuèshí (劉越石), relying on his pure and steadfast *qì*,
helped establish its beauty.
However, the proponents of the former style were numerous and the innovators few,
so they were unable to move the public.
It was not until the Yìxī (義熙) era,
when Xiè Yìshòu (謝益壽) magnificently
continued their work;
and at the beginning of the Yuánjiā (元嘉) era,
there was Xiè Língyùn (謝靈運),
whose talent was lofty and language rich,
his luxurious splendor difficult to match.
He certainly encompassed and surpassed Liú (劉) and Guō (郭),
and overshadowed Pān (潘) and Zuǒ (左).
Thus, we know that the Prince of Chén (Chén) [Cáo Zhí] was the outstanding figure of Jiàn'ān,
[cont. from 157]
assisted by Gōnggàn (公幹) and Zhòngxuān (仲宣);
Lù Jī (陸機) was the hero of Tàikāng (太康),
assisted by Ānrén (安仁) and Jǐngyáng (景陽);
and Lord Xiè (Xiè Kè) was the grand master of Yuánjiā (元嘉),
assisted by Yán Yánnián (顏延年). These are all the supreme figures of five-character verse,
literary giants born for their times.
Now, four-character verse (sì yán) is concise in wording but broad in meaning.
Drawing inspiration from the *Fēng* (Airs) and *Sāo* (Elegies),
it is easy to produce many such pieces.
Yet, it often suffers from excessive words and limited meaning,
thus it is rarely practiced by the world.
Five-character verse holds the essence
of literary expression,
and is the most flavorful among all compositions.
This is why it is said to meet the taste of the general populace.
Is this not because it describes events and releases forms,
exhausting emotions and depicting objects,
being the most detailed
and immediate way of doing so?
Therefore, poetry contains the Six Principles (Liù Yì).
The first is *xīng* (Stimulus),
the second is *fù* (Description),
and the third is *bǐ* (Comparison).
When the text is complete but the meaning lingers, this is
*xīng* (Stimulus);
using objects to symbolize intent, this is
*bǐ* (Comparison);
directly recording events,
presenting metaphors to depict objects, this is
*fù* (Description).
Expanding upon these three principles,
selecting and employing them,
giving them the backbone of *fēnglì* (strength of manner),
and moistening them with rich literary coloring (dāncǎi),
so that those who savor
them find boundless depth,
and those who hear them are moved in their hearts—
this is the ultimate achievement of poetry.
If one relies solely on *bǐ* (Comparison) and *xīng* (Stimulus),
the trouble lies in the meaning being too deep,
and if the meaning is too deep, the language stumbles.
If one merely uses *fù* (Description)...
Using the *fù* (賦) style,
the trouble is that the meaning becomes shallow;
when the meaning is shallow, the composition becomes diffuse.
Playfulness leads to wandering and shifting,
the writing lacks resting places,
resulting in the flaw of wild and sprawling content.
As for spring breezes and spring
birds,
autumn moons and autumn cicadas,
summer clouds and heavy rain,
winter months and extreme cold—
these are the four seasons that inspire people in poetry.
During joyous gatherings, poetry is entrusted to foster intimacy;
when separated from the multitude, poetry is entrusted
to express grief.
Furthermore, when a minister of Chǔ leaves the borders,
or a concubine of Hàn departs the palace;
perhaps bones lie across the northern wilds,
perhaps the soul pursues the flying tumbleweed;
perhaps one bears a spear guarding the outer frontier,
or the aura of killing dominates the border;
the guest at the frontier has thin clothes,
the lonely lady in the frost-touched chamber exhausts her tears.
Moreover, some officials remove their pendants and leave court,
departing once and forgetting to return;
some women raise their eyebrows and enter favor,
a second glance destroying the state.
All these manifold
circumstances,
stir the mind and spirit—
if not by setting forth poetry, how can their meaning be displayed?
If not by long songs, how can their feelings be released?
Therefore it is said:
“Poetry can lead to unity (social cohesion),
it can express complaint (grief).”
To make
the poor and humble easily content,
and secluded dwelling free from melancholy,
nothing is superior to poetry.
Therefore, among writers and authors,
none fails to love it.
In the customs of scholars today,
this trend is rampant.
Just
able to wear clothes,
and only beginning elementary studies,
they enthusiastically rush into it.
Consequently, common sounds and mixed forms (styles) appear,
each becoming a school's methodology.
As for rich and spoiled youths,
ashamed that their writing
falls short,
they spend the whole morning refining phrases,
and half the night moaning.
When viewed alone, they call it startling and brilliant;
but when viewed by the multitude, it ultimately sinks into flatness and dullness.
Next there are those who are frivolous and unrestrained,
who laugh at Cáo and Líu as
ancient and clumsy.
They claim that Bào Zhāo is superior to the sovereigns of the Golden Age (Xī Huáng),
and that Xiè Tiǎo stands alone through antiquity and modernity.
Yet those who imitate Bào Zhāo ultimately cannot match
"The marketplace is crowded at noon,"
and those who study Xiè Tiǎo can barely achieve
"The yellow bird crosses the green branch."
They merely abandon themselves before the judgment of discerning listeners,
and have no involvement in the literary currents.
I, Zhōng Róng, observe that among the high officials and gentry,
after every extensive discussion,
they invariably take poetry as their topic of conversation.
Following their preferences and desires,
their critiques differ;
Zī and Mǐn
flow together (the pure and impure mix),
vermilion and purple compete with each other,
clamor and contention arise,
and there is no standard to rely upon.
Recently, Líu Shìzhāng of Péngchéng, a man of brilliant appreciation,
was distressed by this confusion,
and intended to compile a *shī pǐn* (poetry critique)
for the current age.
He verbally set forth his standards,
but his writing was not completed.
I, Zhōng Róng, was inspired and composed this work.
Formerly, the Nine Grades assessed men,
and the Seven Summaries (Qī Lüè) judged scholars.
When comparing these assessments with reality,
many certainly did not
match.
But as for poetry as an art,
comparison easily allows it to be known.
By judging according to category,
it is almost the same as games of chance.
The current Emperor (Huángdì) possesses the highest innate talent,
embodies deep and melancholy
profound thoughts.
His writings rival the sun and moon in splendor,
and his learning investigates Heaven and humanity.
Formerly, when he was a noble lord,
he was already hailed as the foremost.
Moreover, now that the eight directions are unified,
and the trend sweeps like wind and rises like clouds,
those who cherish jade stand shoulder
to shoulder,
and those who grasp pearls follow closely.
They naturally glance at Hàn and Wèi without looking back,
and swallow Jìn and Sòng in their breasts.
Assuredly, this is not a matter of farmers’ songs or carriage-side discussions,
daring to create classifications.
This current record by
Zhōng Róng
is merely intended to circulate among the common people,
and be shared during conversation and laughter.
Soon after,
he died in office.
Zhōng Wán, courtesy name Zhăng Yuè,
his official position reached Administrator of the Commandant’s Staff (Fŭ Cānjūn) and Pacifier of Jiànkāng Píng.
He authored the *Liáng Lì Zhuàn* (Biographies of Good Officials) in ten volumes.
Zhōng Yŭ, courtesy name Jì Wàng,
was the Administrator of Yŏngjiā Commandery (Yŏngjiā Jùn Chéng).
In the fifteenth year of Tiānjiān,
an imperial decree commanded scholars to compile the *Biàn Lüè*,
and Zhōng Yŭ also participated in it.
Both brothers had collected literary works.
Zhōu Xīngsì, courtesy name Sī Zuăn,
was a man from Xiàng, Chénjùn,
and a descendant of Kān, Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince (Tàizĭ Tàifù) of Hàn.
His great-grandfather was Níng,
Administrator of the Commander-in-Chief of the West’s Staff (Zhēngxī Fŭ Cānjūn) and Governor of Yídū (Yídū Tàishŏu) during the Jìn dynasty.
Xīngsì's family generationally resided in Gūshú.
When he was thirteen,
he traveled to the capital to study.
After accumulating more than ten years,
he became broadly conversant with historical records and commentaries,
and was skilled at literary composition.
He once walked from Gūshú,
and sought lodging at an inn.
At night, someone said to him:
"Your talent and learning surpass this generation.
At first, you shall be recognized by high-ranking officials,
and finally, you will be known by an enlightened ruler."
When the words ended,
it was impossible to ascertain where he went.
During the Lóngchāng era of Qí,
the Attendant Censor Xiè Fěi served as the Administrator of Wúxīng.
He only discussed literature and history with Xīngsì.
When he was dismissed from the commandery and returned,
he consequently praised and recommended him greatly.
His home province nominated him as a Xiùcái,
and he was appointed Aide to Guìyáng Commandery.
The Administrator Wáng Róng had always admired and favored him,
treating him with exceptional deference.
When Gāozǔ launched the revolution,
Xīngsì presented the *Xiū Píng Fù*,
the writing of which was exquisite,
and Gāozǔ commended him for it.
He was appointed Attendant in the Kingdom of Ānchéng,
and was attached to the Huálín Palace Office.
That year,
Hénán presented horses.
An edict commanded Xīngsì, along with the Expectant Appointees Dào Hàng and Zhāng Shuài, to compose a rhapsody.
Gāozǔ judged Xīngsì's work to be the most refined.
He was promoted to Gentleman-in-Attendance without Portfolio,
and advanced to serve in the Wéndé and Shòuguāng Palace Offices.
At this time,
Gāozǔ converted his former residence at Sānqiáo into Guāngzhái Sì,
and commanded Xīngsì and Lù Chuí to each draft an inscription for the temple stele.
When both were completed and submitted,
Gāozǔ adopted the one drafted by Xīngsì.

Thereafter, the inscription for the Bronze Pillar, the tablet for the Shàntáng, the proclamation for the Northern Expedition, and the composition of a Thousand Character Essay following the rhymes used in Wáng Xīzhī's calligraphy,
were all assigned to Xīngsì to compose.
Each time they were presented,
Gāozǔ invariably praised their quality,
and granted him additional gifts of gold and silk.
In the ninth year,
he was appointed Aide to Xīn'ān Commandery.
When his tenure was completed,
he resumed serving as Gentleman-in-Attendance without Portfolio,
assisting in compiling the National History.
In the twelfth year,
he was promoted to Jǐshìzhōng,
continuing the historical compilation as before.
Xīngsì had previously suffered from *fēngjū* on both hands.
That year, he also contracted a serious illness,
and his left eye went blind.
Gāozǔ stroked his hand,
and lamented, saying:
"Such a man, yet afflicted with such an illness!"
He personally drafted a medical formula for treating the abscesses and bestowed it upon him.
Such was the extent of his appreciation.
Rèn Fǎng also admired his talent,
often saying:
"If Zhōu Xīngsì were not ill,
within ten days he would surely reach the position of Vice President of the Imperial Secretariat."
In the fourteenth year,
he was appointed Aide to Línchuān Commandery.
In the seventeenth year,
he resumed serving as Jǐshìzhōng,
attached to the Western Palace Office.
The Commander of the Left Guard, Zhōu Shě, received an imperial command to annotate the *Lìdài Fù* composed by Gāozǔ.
He memorialized recommending Xīngsì to assist.
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
he died.
His compositions included over a hundred scrolls, such as the *Huángdì Shílù*, *Huáng Dé Jì*, *Qǐjū Zhù*, and *Zhí Yí*,
and a collected literary works in ten scrolls.
Wú Jūn, courtesy name Shūxiáng,
was a native of Gùzhāng, Wúxīng.
His family background was poor and humble.
Wú Jūn, however, was fond of learning and possessed outstanding talent.
Shěn Yuē once saw Jūn's writing,
and praised and appreciated it greatly.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
Liǔ Yùn served as the Administrator of Wúxīng,
summoning and appointing him as Chief Clerk,
and inviting him daily to compose poetry with him.
Jūn's literary style was clear, outstanding, and possessed an ancient flavor.
Enthusiasts sometimes imitated it,
calling it the
"Wú Jūn Tǐ."
When the Prince of Jiàn'ān, Wěi, served in Yángzhōu,
he drew him in to concurrently hold the post of Recorder,
managing documents and correspondence.
When the Prince moved to Jiāngzhōu,
he was appointed Attendant in the Kingdom,
concurrently handling the Prefecture City Bureau.
Upon returning, he was appointed Fèng Cháoqǐng.
Before this,
Jūn had memorialized requesting to compile the *Qí Chūnqiū*.
When the book was finished and presented,
Gāozǔ deemed the book untruthful,
and ordered the Palace Aide Liú Zhīlín to cross-examine him on several points.
Ultimately, he was rambling and could not answer,
and an edict ordered it delivered to the Palace Office to be burned.
He was dismissed from office as a consequence.
Soon after, there was an edict summoning him for an audience,
ordering him to compile a Comprehensive History,
starting from the Three Sovereigns,
up to the Qí dynasty.
Jūn completed the draft work on the Basic Annals and Hereditary Houses,
but only the biographies were unfinished.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
he died,
at the age of fifty-two.
Jūn annotated Fàn Yè's *Hòu Hàn Shū* in ninety scrolls,
authored the *Qí Chūnqiū* in thirty scrolls,
the *Miào Jì* in ten scrolls,
the *Shí'èr Zhōu Jì* in sixteen scrolls,
the *Qiántáng Xiānxián Zhuàn* in five scrolls,
the *Xù Wén Shì* in five scrolls,
and a collected literary works in twenty scrolls.
Before this,
there were Gāo Shuǎng of Guǎnglíng, Jiāng Hóng of Jìyáng, and Yú Qiān of Kuàijī.
All were skilled at literary composition.
Shuǎng,
during the Yǒngmíng era of Qí, presented a poem to the Grand General Wáng Jiǎn,
and was appreciated by Jiǎn.
When he assumed the post of Governor of Dānyáng,
he nominated Shuǎng as a Filial and Incorrupt candidate from the commandery.
In the early Tiānjiān era,
he successively held office as Consultant to the Prince of Línchuān, Commander of the Central Army.
He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Jìnlíng.
He was imprisoned in the jail for an offense.
He wrote the *Huò Yú Fù* to describe his own situation.
His writing was very skillful.
Later, he was pardoned and released.
He died shortly thereafter.
Hóng served as Magistrate of Jiànyáng,
He died because of an offense.
Qiān's office reached the rank of Attendant in the Kingdom.
All of them possessed collections of literary works.
Biography Forty-four: Literature (Part Two): Liú Jùn, Liú Zhǎo, Xiè Jǐqīng, Liú Xié, Wáng Jí, Hé Sīchéng, Liú Yǎo, Xiè Zhēng, Zāng Yán, Fú Tǐng, Yǔ Zhòngróng, Lù Yúngōng, Rèn Xiàogōng, Yán Xié.
Liú Jùn, courtesy name Xiàobiāo,
was a native of Píngyuán, Píngyuán.
His father, Tǐng,
was Inner Prefect of Shǐxīng during the Sòng dynasty.
Jùn was born for a full month,
when his mother carried him back to their home village.
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ era of the Sòng [Dynasty],
Qīngzhōu fell to the Wèi,
and Jùn, being eight years old,
was abducted by someone and taken to Zhōngshān.
Liú Shí, a wealthy man in Zhōngshān, pitied Jùn,
and redeemed him with bundles of silk,
teaching him calligraphy and scholarship.
When the Wèi people heard that he had relatives in Jiāngnán,
they relocated him again to Sānggān.
Jùn loved learning,
but his family was poor.
He lodged under someone's corridor,
self-instructing himself in reading.
He constantly lit hemp torches,
studying from evening until dawn.
If he occasionally fell drowsy,
he would singe his hair;
once awake, he would read again,
staying sleepless all night long.
His energy and spirit were like this.
During the Yǒngmíng era of the Qí [Dynasty],
he managed to return from Sānggān.
He felt that his knowledge was not broad enough,
and sought out unusual books.
If he heard that the capital (Jīngshī) had them,
he would surely go and beg to borrow them.
Cuī Wèizǔ of Qīnghé called him
"The Book Lecher" (Shūyín).
At that time, Prince Zi Láng of Jìnglíng broadly invited scholars.
Jùn, through an intermediary, requested a state post under Zi Láng.
Xú Xiàosì, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), suppressed the request and did not permit it,
instead appointing him as an Attendant Gentleman (Shìláng) for the Prince of Nánhǎi,
which he did not accept.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Míng,
Xiāo Yáoxīn was the Governor of Yùzhōu,
and Jùn served as the Chief of Criminal Justice (Xíngyù) in his administration,
where he was treated with great respect.
Yáoxīn died shortly thereafter,
and for a long time, Jùn was not promoted.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he was summoned into the Western Department (Xīshěng),
where he supervised the collation of confidential texts (Mìshū) with the scholar Hè Zōng.
Jùn’s elder brother, Xiàoqìng,
was serving as the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Qīngzhōu at the time.
Jùn requested leave to visit him,
but was implicated for privately transporting restricted goods.
He was impeached by the relevant authorities,
and dismissed from office.
Xiù, the Prince of Ānchéng, admired Jùn’s scholarship.
When Xiù was transferred to Jīngzhōu,
he brought Jùn in as an Administrator (Cānjūn) in charge of household affairs (Hùcáo).
He provided Jùn with books
and had him compile and copy categories of affairs,
which he named *Lèiyuàn*.
Before the work was completed,
Jùn had to leave again due to illness.
He subsequently traveled to Zǐyán Shān in Dōngyáng,
built a dwelling, and resided there.
He composed the *Shānqī Zhì* (Account of Dwelling in the Mountains),
the writing of which was exceedingly beautiful.
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ) invited literary scholars,
and those with high talent
were often brought forward
and promoted without adherence to rank.
Jùn acted according to his nature
and could not drift along with the crowd.
Gāozǔ rather disliked this about him,
and therefore did not appoint him to a position.
Jùn then composed the *Biàn Mìng Lùn* (Treatise on Distinguishing Destiny) to express his feelings, saying: The Sovereign once spoke with various famous worthies about Guǎn Lù,
lamenting that he possessed extraordinary talent but failed to achieve high office.
There was someone present beneath the red steps
who overheard this discussion
and returned to tell me about it.
I hold that whether a scholar suffers hardship or achieves success
is entirely a matter of Destiny (mìng).
Therefore, I respectfully relate the Heavenly Edict
and offer the following summary:
Your servant observes that Guǎn Lù's native genius was brilliant and grand,
his virtue shining brightly like jade tokens,
truly a hero and outstanding talent within the four seas;
how could he be merely one of the class of diviners and ritual supplicators?
Yet his office stopped at Assistant Prefect of the Palace Lesser Treasury (Shàofǔ Chéng),
and his life ended at forty-eight.
How meager was the Heavenly recompense
and reward?
Therefore, that high talent does not lead to noble office,
and that greedy, gluttonous men hold great positions,
has been lamented since antiquity.
Why
should Gōngmíng be the only one [to suffer this]?
Thus, regarding the Way of Nature and Destiny (xìng mìng),
and the number governing hardship and success (qióng tōng),
sudden deaths and frustrations occur chaotically,
and no one knows how to distinguish them.
Zhòngrèn obscured the source,
and Zi Cháng illuminated the
confusion.
As for those wearing pheasant caps and living in hovels with broken jars for windows,
they must assume that Heaven has predetermined their dates;
while those holding high prestige and residing in noble gates,
say that it is solely summoned by human effort.
Loud, clamorous, and contradictory noises are made,
and various opposing theories arise together.
Xiāo Yuǎn discussed the origin but did not fully elaborate on the ramifications,
while Zi Xuán spoke of the ramifications but did not detail the origin.
Allow me to attempt to explain it, saying: When the Dao generates the ten thousand things,
it is called the
Way (Dào);
when things are generated without a master,
it is called Spontaneity (Zìrán).
Spontaneity means that
things appear to be so,
but one does not know why they are so;
all equally obtain it,
but one does not know how they obtain it.
It urges and
moves, molds and creates, but claims no merit;
all categories of beings are mixed and formed, but not by its strength.
In giving life, it harbors no heart to nourish or foster;
in causing death, how could it harbor the intent to kill or slaughter?
Throwing things into deep springs
is not due to its anger,
nor is raising them to the Milky Way due to its pleasure.
Vast and great,
the myriad treasures transform through it;
firm and pure,
once transformed, it does not change.
What transforms but does not change
is called Destiny (Mìng).
Destiny,
is the command that comes from Heaven.
It is fixed in hidden omens,
and remains unchanged in the end.
Ghosts and spirits cannot participate,
nor can saints and sages scheme against it.
The strength of those who touch mountains cannot resist it,
and the sincerity of those who would overturn the sun cannot affect it.
If it is short, it cannot be delayed even for a moment,
if it is long, it cannot be hastened by the water clock.
Even supreme
Virtue cannot exceed it,
and the highest intelligence cannot escape it.
This is why, in the era of Fàngxūn,
the vast waters overflowed the hills;
and in the time of Tiānyǐ,
metals melted and stones flowed.
Wén Gōng had his
tail cut off,
and Xuān Ní was deprived of his food supply.
Yán Huí’s cluster of orchids withered;
Rǎn Gēng sang of the plantain.
Yí and Shū perished because of the slander of a malicious woman;
Zi Yú was frustrated by Zāng Cāng’s
accusations.
If saints and worthies were still like this,
how much more so the mediocre ones!
Then there is Wǔ Yuán, whose corpse floated on the river currents;
and Sānlǘ (Qū Yuán), whose body sank at the bank of the Xiāng River;
Grand Master Jiǎ
had his ambitions thwarted in Chángshā;
Commandant Féng grew white-haired in the Palace Secretariat (Lángshǔ);
Jūnshān, like a wild swan, sank down,
breaking his graceful wings beneath the high clouds;
Jìngtōng, rising like a phoenix,
shattered his swift pinions in the wind cave:
How could this be because their talent was insufficient or their conduct lacking?
In recent times there was Liú Huán of Pèiguó,
and Huán's younger brother, Jǐn,
both distinguished scholars of their time.
Huán was the Kǒngzǐ of Guānxī;
he mastered the Six Classics,
followed goodness and
guided others,
deeply committing himself to Confucian practice (Rúxíng).
Jǐn, meanwhile, had aspirations fiercer than autumn frost,
and a heart as pure as Kūnlún jade;
standing tall and lofty,
untouched by worldly dust.
Both cultivated virtue within humble gates,
and both spread
their reputations across Heaven and Earth.
Yet their offices were less significant than Attendant Gentleman (Shìláng),
their rank did not ascend to that of a Halberd-Bearer (Zhí Jǐ).
They successively fell and died,
and their ancestral sacrifices ceased to be honored.
Using these two worthies
to speak of ancient times,
we see that: In the past, those with jade-like character and golden demeanor,
brilliant and successful heroes,
were all banished and rejected in their prime years,
hiding their extraordinary talents without being used,
waiting for the vegetation to wither along with them,
and mingling with elk and deer...
died together,
whose fat smeared the plains,
whose bones filled the valleys and ravines,
who perished and are unheard of—
how can they possibly be fully recounted!
In these matters, the High Official (Zǎihéng) compared to the lowly servant (Zàolì),
Róng and Péng
compared to the child who died young (shāngzǐ),
Yī Dùn compared to Qián Lóu,
Yáng Wén compared to Dūn Qià—
all equally obtained their fate through nature,
and did not rely upon talent or intelligence.
Therefore it is said:
“Life and death are
governed by fate;
wealth and honor are determined by Heaven.”
This is what is meant.
However, the substance of fate flows circularly,
and its changes are not singular:
sometimes one wails first and laughs later,
sometimes the beginning is auspicious but the end is calamitous,
sometimes it comes un
summoned by itself,
sometimes it is achieved through the aid of others.
It is tangled and intertwined,
rotating and relying upon hidden factors;
it cannot be proved by a single principle,
nor can it be verified by a single path.
Furthermore, its way is profound and
subtle,
solitary, silent, and sudden;
it has no form by which it can be seen,
and no sound by which it can be heard.
It must control things to manifest its spirit,
and it must rely on people to take form,
like the crown and
pendants of the Son of Heaven,
who delegates the hundreds of officials to manage their duties.
But those who are deluded, seeing the majestic rise of Tāng and Wǔ,
say that suppressing chaos lay in divine achievement;
hearing of the exceptional births of Kǒng and Mò,
say that their genius and wisdom monopolized
extraordinary fame;
observing the sudden transformation of Péng and Hán,
say that fierceness and bravery led to human nobility;
seeing the vermillion sashes of Zhāng and Huán,
say that mastering the classics earned them the blue and purple robes (high office).
How could they know that the powerful force
moves them forward?
Therefore, those who speak (of success) but deny fate
have six delusions (or blind spots).
I request permission to present the outlines (of these delusions): Indeed, beautiful countenances and delicate skin,
or wide mouths and wrinkled noses—
these are differences in physical form.
Flowering in the morning and dying in the evening,
or tortoises and cranes living a thousand years—
these are variations in age.
Hearing words like an echo (quick to understand),
or being too dull to distinguish beans from wheat—
these are distinctions in spirit (or intelligence).
If we certainly know these three things are fixed by Creation,
yet regarding the realms of honor and disgrace,
we uniquely claim they come from man—
this is knowing two fives but not yet recognizing
ten.
This is the first delusion.
A dragon horn on the head and sun-shaped marks on the forehead
are the appearance of emperors;
eyes like the River (wide) and lines like a tortoise shell
are the features of dukes and marquises.
Observing the mirror, one knows one is about to be punished;
pressing the belt buckle reveals one's destined
position.
Stars, rainbows, pivotal points, and lightning
illuminate the signs of Sagely Virtue;
crying at night and gathering clouds
are the dense omens of a rising ruler.
All these signs begin in the preceding period
and are diffused in later generations.
If
one says that driving fierce beasts (Píhǔ),
brandishing a three-foot sword,
entering the imperial palace (Zǐwēi),
and ascending to the path of the Emperor
is the whole story, then one has not grasped the logic of the profound and mysterious,
and has not measured the computations of the spiritual realm.
This is the second delusion.
The villages of Kōngsāng
and their vicinities
turned into great rivers;
the capital of Lìyáng
transformed into fish and turtles.
The Chǔ armies slaughtered the Hàn soldiers,
and the Suī Hé clogged its own flow;
the Qín people buried the Zhào troops alive,
and the boiling noise was like
thunder.
Fire rages on Kūnyuè,
and pebbles are burned along with jade and precious stones;
severe frost falls at night,
and mugwort and orchids perish together.
Even with the outstanding talents of Yóu and Xià,
or the near sainthood of Yī
and Yán,
how could they possibly resist this?
This is the third delusion.
Some say:
The Pearl of Bright Moonlight
cannot be without flaws;
the jade pendant (huáng) of the Xià Hòu
cannot be without defects.
Therefore, Tíng Bó died under the jurisdiction of a county magistrate,
and Cháng Qīng ended his life as an administrator of a park.
It was not that their talent was unexceptional,
nor that their lord was unenlightened,
yet the great brilliance of the Jiélù jade was shattered,
and the night color of the Xuánlí
was spoiled.
Was their measure shorter than the standard ruler?
Consider those like this:
Zhǔfù Yǎn and Gōngsūn Hóng failed the policy examination and were not promoted;
they traveled around lobbying but were not admitted into service.
They tended pigs on Zī
Yuán,
and were rejected by the provincial authorities.
If, hypothetically, they had died suddenly like a fleeting shadow,
perishing quickly in the frost and dew,
their shame and disgrace
would they have been comparable to the ranks of Cuī and Mǎ?
But when they reached the point of opening the Eastern Chamber (holding high office),
having arranged
the five tripods (symbols of high rank),
their fame shone like lightning and spread like wind,
their reputation rushing beyond the seas.
Was it that they were foolish before and wise afterward,
or wrong initially and correct in the end?
Rather, is it that honor and decline have a fixed measure,
and Heaven's mandate has a predetermined
limit?
Yet (they mistakenly believe) ugliness and beauty are self-generated.
This is the fourth delusion.
When the tiger roars, the wind rushes;
when the dragon rises, the clouds gather.
Thus, when Chónghuá stood, Yuán and Kǎi ascended;
when Xīn Shòu was born,
Fēilián advanced.
Yet, in the world, good people are few
and wicked people are numerous;
dark rulers are many,
and enlightened monarchs are few.
But fragrant orchids and foul-smelling dogbane are not kept in the same vessel;
the owl and the phoenix do not fly wing-to-wing.
This
causes Húndùn and Táowù
to follow in the footsteps of heroes atop the Yúntái;
while Zhòngróng and Tíngjiān
plow beneath the rocks.
To stubbornly insist that decline and prosperity reside in oneself,
with no connection to Heaven,
is the fifth delusion.
Those Róng Dí barbarians,
having human faces but animal hearts,
relish peace as if it were poisoned wine.
They take slaughter and execution as their morality,
and incestuous retribution as their benevolence and righteousness.
Although Dàfēng
stood on Qīngqiū,
and Zuòchǐ raged in Huá Yě,
compared to their savage brutality,
they are not worth mentioning.
Since the Metal Element (Jīn Xíng) failed to contend (lost power),
Heaven and Earth were convulsed and overturned,
and those who wore their belts on the left (barbarians) rushed forward with boiling lips,
seizing the
opportunity and erupting like lightning.
They subsequently overthrew Luò,
and toppled the five capitals.
They occupied the ancestral lands of the former kings
and usurped titles in the central prefecture (China).
They contested with the Three Sovereigns for their populace,
and challenged the Five Emperors
for their territories.
Their tribes flourished intensely,
filling Shénzhōu (China).
Alas!
Blessing the good and bringing calamity upon the wicked
is merely empty talk.
Is this not because misfortune (Pǐ) and prosperity (Tài) alternate,
waxing and waning
in succession,
and yet people wrongly obscure this truth?
This is the sixth delusion.
Thus, what is meant by Fate includes:
life and death,
nobility and baseness,
poverty and wealth,
order and chaos,
calamity and blessing.
These ten things are what Heaven bestows.
Stupidity and wisdom...
Goodness and wickedness—
these four are the actions undertaken by humans.
Indeed, the spirit is not that of Shùn or Yǔ,
nor is the mind different from Zhū or Jūn;
talent hangs suspended around the middle path,
resting entirely upon what is habitually practiced.
Therefore, plain silk
has no fixed color,
and black and yellow arise in succession;
as for putrid fish and fragrant orchids,
entering into their presence causes one to change naturally.
Thus, Jì Lù studied under Zhòng Ní,
thereby sharpening the integrity of wind and frost;
while Chǔ Mù consulted Pān Chóng,
leading to the disaster of perversity and rebellion.
Yet the wickedness of Shāng Chén,
whose flourishing deeds brought glory to his descendants;
and the goodness of Zhòng Yóu,
which could not prevent his death by tying up his cap-strings;
this shows that right and wrong stem from
man,
while fortune and misfortune reside in Destiny.
Or perhaps it is that ghosts and spirits harm the excessive,
while August Heaven assists Virtue.
Thus, Sòng Gōng spoke a single word,
and the judicial stars moved thrice;
Yīn Dì mutilated himself,
and clouds came
from a thousand *lǐ* away.
If goodness and wickedness have no tangible proof,
then this meaning is not fully embraced.
Moreover, Yú Gōng heightened his gatehouse in anticipation of his descendants being ennobled,
and Yán Mǔ swept the tomb in anticipation of a funeral.
This is why the noble person continually
strives relentlessly.
If benevolence were to have no reward,
why would one cultivate goodness and establish a reputation?
These are the words of the vulgar crowd.
Now, the words of the Sages
are apparent yet obscure,
subtle yet graceful,
deep and remote and difficult to hear,
vast as the Milky Way and limitless.
Sometimes they establish teachings to encourage the mediocre and lazy,
and sometimes they speak of Destiny to exhaust the limits of innate nature and spirit.
"Accumulated goodness leaves behind surplus blessings,"
is establishing a
teaching;
"The Phoenix bird does not arrive,"
is speaking of Destiny.
Now, to take a fragment of their speech and argue about its essential meaning,
how is this different from creatures that die at sunset discussing the changes that occur throughout the year?
Furthermore, Jīng Zhāo had virtuous fame,
yet the red clouds would not disperse;
Zhōu Xuān prayed for rain,
and the *guī* tablets and *bì* discs were exhausted.
Yú Sǒu planted virtue,
but did not reach the height of Xūn or Huá;
Yán Nián was cruel and barbaric,
but not as excessively ruthless as Dōng Líng.
Their performance of good was uniform,
their wickedness was comparable,
yet misfortune and fortune followed different courses,
and their failure and success displayed differing outcomes.
Can the All-Vast Supreme Lord (Shàngdì)
possibly be like this?
The *Shī* (Classic of Poetry) says:
"The wind and rain were dark as night,
but the rooster crowed without ceasing."
Therefore, when a good person performs good,
how could they ever stop?
Now, eating fine rice and millet,
presenting fodder-fed livestock,
wearing fox and badger fur,
donning thin silk,
observing profound and subtle wonders,
listening to the *qín* and *sè* of Yúnhé—
these are the things that living people
crave;
they are not done in order to gain something.
Cultivating the Dao and Virtue,
practicing Benevolence and Righteousness,
emphasizing Filial Piety and Fraternity,
establishing Loyalty and Integrity,
gradually absorbing the rich moisture of Ritual and Music,
treading the magnificent rules of the Former Kings—
these are the things that the noble person craves;
they are not done in order to gain something.
In that case, the noble person dwells in rectitude, embodies the Dao,
takes joy in Heaven, and knows Destiny.
He understands that certain things cannot be helped,
and recognizes that they
are not dependent on intellect or strength.
When things pass away, he does not summon them back;
when they arrive, he does not repel them;
he is not joyful upon birth,
nor grieved upon death.
A jeweled terrace and a summer house
cannot delight his spirit;
an earthen dwelling
woven with reeds
is not enough to trouble his mind.
He is neither inflated nor bent by wealth and rank,
nor does he anxiously seek what he desires.
How could there be writings like those of Shǐ Gōng or Dǒng Xiàng concerning being unrecognized?
When this discourse was finished,
Liú Zhǎo of Zhōngshān sent a letter challenging it.
In all, there were two further exchanges,
and Jùn provided comprehensive analysis and refutation in his replies.
Coincidentally, Zhǎo died,
and thus did not see Jùn's final reply.
Jùn then wrote a preface to the correspondence, saying:
"Since Lord Liú had presented this challenge,
I happened to be mourning a relative,
and ultimately I failed to deliver the reply.
Soon after, this gentleman departed forever,
transforming into a different entity.
His preparatory remarks and remaining arguments
were preserved but not transmitted.
Someone obtained them from his family and showed them to me,
and I lamented that his voice and countenance were not yet erased,
but the person himself was already gone;
the bamboo slips were still fresh,
but the grass on his grave would soon stand tall.
My tears flowed silently, not knowing where they stemmed from.
Although a steed passing a crack cannot be retained,
and a foot-long ripple vanishes like lightning,
the autumn chrysanthemums and spring orchids
never cease their blooming brilliance.
Therefore, I preserve the gist of his argument
and respond further to its core meaning.
If the words of Mò Dí were without error,
and the discourse in the Xuān Shì Hall had confirmation,
then the trees of Dōngpíng
would incline westward upon gazing towards Xiányáng;
and the spring on Gài Shān
would flow in rhythm upon hearing strings and song.
But alas, the sword hangs over an empty mound;
what can be done about this regret!"
Most of the essays regarding this discourse are not recorded here.
Jùn also once wrote an autobiography,
the summary of which says:
"I compare myself to Féng Jìngtōng,
and there are three ways in which we are similar,
and four ways in which we are different.
Why is this?
Jìngtōng possessed heroic talent surpassing his age,
and his will was as hard as metal and stone;
although I do not measure up to him,
my integrity is bright and passionate—
this is the first similarity.
Jìngtōng encountered the enlightened ruler of the restoration,
but was ultimately never tested or employed;
I met an illustrious sovereign born for this age,
but was also banished in my prime—
this is the second similarity.
Jìngtōng had a jealous wife,
which led him to personally undertake chores like drawing water and grinding grain;
I have a fierce wife,
who likewise caused my family life to be difficult and rough—
this is the third similarity.
Jìngtōng lived during the Gēngshǐ era,
personally grasping the military tally,
leaping onto horseback and eating meat;
while I, from youth until maturity,
have been anxious and joyless—
this is the first difference.
Jìngtōng had a son, Zhòngwén,
who achieved office and established a name;
while my misfortune is the same as Bódào's,
and I shall forever be without an heir—
this is the second difference.
Jìngtōng possessed vigorous physical strength,
growing ever stronger in old age;
while I suffer from the illness of a dog or horse,
and may suddenly die at any time—
this is the third difference.
Although Jìngtōng perished like burnt *zhī* and *huì* orchids,
finally filling a ditch or ravine,
he was admired by famous worthies,
and his grace, strong character, and fragrance
became increasingly glorious over time;
whereas my reputation is silent and desolate,
the world does not know me,
and once my *hún* and *pò* depart,
I shall be just like the autumn grass—
this is the fourth difference.
Thus, I forced myself to write this (self-description),
and leave it for those who delight in such matters."
Jùn resided in Dōngyáng,
and many scholars from Wú and Kuài followed his teachings.
In the second year of Pǔtōng (521 CE),
he died,
at the age of sixty.
His disciples granted him the posthumous title, Xuánjìng Xiānshēng.
Liú Zhǎo, courtesy name Míngxìn,
was a native of Wèichāng, Zhōngshān.
His ancestor six generations removed, Yú,
was a Cavalry General-in-Chief during the Jìn dynasty.
was skilled at composing essays when young.
Once grown, he studied widely.
Serving in the Qí [Dynasty], he began his career as a Fèng Cháoqǐng,
then Gùanjūn Xíng Cānjūn.
In the beginning of Tiānjiān [era],
he was appointed Hòujūn Línchuān Wáng Jìshì Cānjūn,
[then] Mòlíng Lìng,
and then died.
Xiè Jǐqīng,
was a man from Yángxià, Chénjùn.
His great-grandfather was Língyùn,
Línchuān Nèishǐ of the Sòng [Dynasty];
his father, Chāozōng,
was Huángmén Láng of the Qí [Dynasty]: both had great reputations in previous generations.
Jǐqīng, when young, was intelligent and articulate;
the people of the time called him a child prodigy (Shéntóng).
Later, Chāozōng was exiled to Yuèzhōu due to an incident,
the route passed Xīntíngzhǔ.
Jǐqīng could not bear to say goodbye,
and consequently threw himself into the river current.
His attendants quickly rushed to save him,
and he was saved from drowning.
When he observed mourning for his father,
his grief and physical deterioration exceeded the proper rites.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was summoned and appointed Guózǐshēng.
Wénhuì Tàizǐ of the Qí [Dynasty] personally oversaw the policy examination,
and said to the Jìjiǔ Wáng Jiǎn:
"Jǐqīng is fundamentally adept at profound principles (Xuánlǐ).
Now you may question him regarding the meaning of the Classics (Jīngyì)."
Jiǎn received the instruction and posed the questions.
Jǐqīng debated and responded according to the matter at hand;
his words were never hesitant.
Wénhuì greatly praised him.
Jiǎn said to others:
"Xiè Chāozōng has, in effect, not died!"
Having grown up, he loved learning;
he was widely read and possessed literary talent (wéncǎi).
He began his career as Yùzhāng Wáng Guó Chángshì,
and was repeatedly promoted to Chējì Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn,
Xiàngguó Jìjiǔ,
then went out to serve as Níngguó Lìng,
and later entered the court to serve as Shàngshū Diànzhōng Láng and Tàiwèi Jìn'ān Wáng Zhǔbù.
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān [era],
he was appointed Zhēnglǔ Póyáng Wáng Jìshì,
Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng,
and soon became Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ.
For former court gentlemen (láng) who transferred to this position,
people of the time referred to it as "fleeing south" (Nánbēn).
Jǐqīng was somewhat disheartened,
frequently reported illness,
and generally stopped managing the affairs of the Censorate (Tái).
He was transferred to Sànqí Shìláng,
and subsequently promoted to Zhōngshū Láng,
Guózǐ Bóshì,
and Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
Jǐqīng was thoroughly familiar with precedents and ancient practices.
Whenever Púyè Xú Miǎn had doubts or obstacles,
he frequently consulted him.
However, his nature was unrestrained and unconventional;
if he felt like doing something, he would do it immediately,
unbound by court regulations.
He once attended a banquet at the Lèyóuyuàn,
but returned before becoming drunk.
He then went to a wine shop beside the road,
stopped his carriage, lifted the curtain,
and drank opposite the three runners (zōu) in front of his carriage.
At that time, the spectators formed a wall,
but Jǐqīng acted as if nothing was amiss.
Later, while serving in the provincial office,
he wore short underpants (dúbí kūn) at night,
climbed the gallery walkway with his students, drank until drunk, and shouted loudly.
He was censured and impeached by the relevant authorities,
and was consequently dismissed from office.
Soon after, he was reinstated as Guózǐ Bóshì,
and shortly thereafter appointed Hédōng Tàishǒu.
Before his term was complete,
he requested retirement due to illness.
Soon, he was appointed Tàizǐ Shuàigēng Lìng,
and promoted to Zhènwèi Nánpíng Wáng Zhǎngshǐ.
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng,
an imperial decree ordered Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn, Xīchāng Hóu Xiāo Yuānzǎo, to lead the various armies in a northern campaign.
Jǐqīng requested permission to join the campaign,
and was promoted to Jūnshī Zhǎngshǐ,
with the added title of Wēiróng Jiāngjūn.
The army reached Guōyáng but was defeated and retreated.
Jǐqīng was dismissed from office because of this incident.
His residence was in Báiyáng Shíjǐng.
Those in the court who were friendly with him brought wine to visit him,
and his guests filled the seats.
At that time, Zuǒchéng Yǔ Zhòngróng was also dismissed and returned home.
The two men found their temperaments compatible,
and both indulged their feelings and behaved wildly.
Sometimes they rode an open carriage touring the countryside;
when drunk, they would hold a bell (duó) and sing funeral songs (wǎn'gē),
ignoring public criticism.
When Xiāngdōng Wáng was stationed in Jīngzhèn,
he sent a letter encouraging him.
Jǐqīng replied:
"Since your servant reluctantly parted from Nánpǔ,
and retreated to the eastern suburbs,
gazing toward the sun and facing the wind,
I stand awaiting your words.
I reflect upon your kind favor,
attending banquets alongside you,
rowing the cassia oars on the clear pond,
sitting amidst fallen blossoms on the high crag.
The fragrance of orchids permeated the air,
feathered goblets gathered rapidly.
Listening intently to your discourse,
I bathed in the profound current.
Your eloquent argument, like waves and billows,
cannot be adequately compared to a hanging river;
your words, like spring algae,
beautiful writings cannot match.
Everyone looked at each other with moved expressions,
convinced in heart beyond verbal praise.
We did not feel that the spring day was long,
but rather felt that the long night was too short.
Such wonderful gatherings are hard to maintain,
gathering clouds easily drift away.
Although memory speaks of yesterday,
suddenly it is pale autumn.
Your gracious light has not forgotten me,
and humorous words have been sent from afar.
Dismissed and returned home due to an incident,
how could I speak of rest and seclusion?
Since I no longer hold high office,
it is appropriate that I dwell in a single hut.
The hardship of farming life,
truly aligns with your pure instruction.
Originally lacking the ornamentation of a golden bridle,
I do not need jade disks for wealth.
Merely old age causes my body to fail,
and sickness makes my mind obstructed.
Confined and stuck to my mat,
more than seventy days have passed.
Dreams and illusions last only a moment,
yet sorrow lingers in my thoughts.
Realizing finally that this is useless,
I resolved to dispel it myself.
Searching for reason and cleansing my mind,
I take destiny's decree as restorative balm;
humbly checking my appearance in the mirror,
I now substitute physical frailty (zhīlí) for the day-lily (xuānshù) [to forget sorrow].
Thus I can admire your magnificent virtue,
and speak eternally of former sages—
Guǐgǔ living in deep seclusion,
Jiēyú holding himself high,
[Zhuang Zhou] concealing his name in a butcher shop,
[Yán Hú] leaving his trace among the barriers and markets.
These men are distant in time,
but their lingering essence can be imagined.
If the departed possessed knowledge,
how could they not feel wrapped in sorrow in the dark earth,
regrettably separated from the fragrant dust [of the living]?
If the deceased could be resurrected,
they would surely be clothed in light and brilliance,
joyfully participating in gatherings,
allowing this simple old gardener [Jǐqīng]
to be seated in the last place of the humble company.
The days since I left are already distant,
and the chance to attend you again has not yet materialized.
The linked swords and flying ducks [referencing gifts]
are inappropriate metaphors [for my situation].
Cherishing your glorious virtue privately,
I secretly shed tears."
Although Jǐqīng did not maintain strict self-discipline,
he was truly affectionate towards his family.
His elder brother, Cáiqīng, died early.
His son, Zǎo, was orphaned young.
Jǐqīng raised him with the utmost care.
When Zǎo came of age,
he successively held prestigious posts such as Gōngfǔ Jìjiǔ and Zhǔbù.
All this was due to Jǐqīng's encouragement and guidance.
The world praised him for this.
Jǐqīng did not attain a major appointment [after his dismissal],
and died of illness.
His collected writings circulated in the world.
Liú Xié, courtesy name Yànhé,
was a man from Jǔ, Dōngguǎn.
His grandfather was Língzhēn,
the younger brother of Sīkōng Xiù of the Sòng [Dynasty].
His father was Shàng,
Yuèqí Xiàowèi.
Xié was orphaned early.
He was earnestly dedicated to study.
His family was poor, and he did not marry.
He relied on the Śramaṇa Sēng Yòu,
living with him
for over ten years.
Consequently, he became widely versed in the Classics (jīng) and commentaries (lùn).
Thereupon, he distinguished and categorized the sections,
cataloging and organizing them.
The Buddhist canon (jīngzàng) at Dìnglín Sì today
was compiled by Xié.
, he started his official career as a Court Attendant (Fèng Cháo Qǐng)
. Hóng

, the Prince of Línchuān and General of the Central Army (Zhōng Jūn), appointed him to serve concurrently as Secretary (Jìshì). He was promoted to be the Cánjūn (Adjutant) of the Cāngcáo (Granary Section) under the General of Chariots and Cavalry (Chē Qí)
. He left the capital to become the Magistrate (Lìng) of Tàimò
, where his administration achieved clean and distinguished results
. He was appointed Secretary (Jìshì) to the Prince of Nánkāng and General of Rénwēi
, concurrently holding the position of Shèrén (Attendant) for Communications (Tōngshì Shèrén) in the Eastern Palace (Dōng Gōng)
. At that time

, offerings and sacrifices in the Seven Ancestral Temples (Qī Miào) already utilized vegetables and fruits, but the sacrifices in the Two Suburbs (Èr Jiāo) and the Altars of Agriculture (Nóng Shè) still used whole animals (xīshēng)
. Therefore, Liú Xié
memorialized, saying that the Two Suburbs should be reformed to match the Seven Temples. An imperial decree
ordered the Department of State Affairs (Shàng Shū) to discuss it, and the decision was made to follow what Liú Xié
had proposed. He was promoted to Commandant of Infantry (Bù Bīng Xiàowèi)
, while retaining his concurrent post as Shèrén (Attendant)
. Crown Prince Zhāomíng
loved literature and received him with deep affection
. Originally
, Liú Xié
compiled the *Wénxīn Diāolóng* (The Literary Mind and the Carving of Dragons) in fifty chapters, discussing literary styles past and present
, citing examples and arranging them in sequence
. Its preface says: Now, Wénxīn (The Literary Mind)
speaks of the intentions (yòngxīn) used when creating literature
. In the past, there was Juānzǐ's *Qín Xīn* (Heart of the Lute)
and Wángsūn's *Qiǎo Xīn* (Cunning Heart)
. The character "Xīn" (Heart/Mind) is indeed beautiful
, thus it is used here
. Literary writings
times have attained their form through ornate carving (diāorù)
since ancient
. How could this be derived from Zōu Shì's
collective discourses, *Diāolóng* (Carving Dragons)? Now, the universe is vast and boundless
, and outstanding talents (lí xiàn) are numerous and diverse
. Distinguishing the excellent and standing out from the common sort
relies solely on intelligence and skill
. Years and months swiftly fly by
, and the vital spirit (xìng líng) does not remain
. Spreading fame and achieving reality
relies solely on literary creation (zhì zuò)
. Humans resemble the form of Heaven and Earth
, endowed with the nature of the Five Talents (wǔ cái)
. They compare their ears and eyes to
the sun and moon
, and their voice and spirit to the wind and thunder
. Their superiority over the myriad things
is already profoundly spiritual
. Their form is as fragile as grass and trees
, yet their fame surpasses the hardness of metal and stone
. Therefore, when the noble person (Jūnzǐ)
, he cultivates virtue and establishes words
dwells in the world
. Is it because he loves argument
? No, it is a necessity
. My age
was past the standing age (yú lì, i.e., thirty), when I once dreamt at night of holding ritual vessels lacquered in red
, following Zhòngní
southward. When I awoke in the morning
, I was pleased and delighted
. How great
is the difficulty of seeing the Sage
! Was this merely a residual dream granted to an insignificant person
? Since the beginning of mankind
, there has been none like the Master
. To expound and praise the will of the sages
, nothing is better than annotating
the Classics
. However, scholars like Mǎ Róng and Zhèng Xuán
have already thoroughly elaborated upon them
. Even if one had a profound new interpretation
, it would not be sufficient to establish a new school of thought
. Only the application of literature
is truly the branches and leaves of the Classics
. The Five Rites (wǔ lǐ) rely
on it for completion
; the Six Canons (liù diǎn) depend on it for practical use
. Through it, sovereign and minister shine brightly
, and military and state affairs become illustrious
. Examining their origin
, nothing is outside the Classics
. But since the time of the sages
is long
past, literary styles have broken down and scattered
. Writers love the strange
, prizing language that is shallow and deceitful
. They embellish their plumage and value ornamentation
, making elaborate embroidered purses and scarves
. Their departure from the fundamentals is increasing
, leading eventually to error and excess
. For
, the *Book of Zhōu*
, when discussing rhetoric, values simplicity and essence (tǐ yào)
; and our Master Nífǔ
, when presenting his teachings, abominated unorthodox doctrines (yì duān)
. The differences in rhetoric and teachings
should conform to the essential principles
. Consequently, taking up the brush and mixing the ink
, I then
began
discussing literature. Upon detailed observation, those in recent times who have discussed literature are many
. Such examples include Wèi Wén's
*Shù Diǎn* (Disquisition on Canons), Chén Sī's
prefaces and writings, Yīng Yáng's
*Wén Lùn* (Literary Discussion), Lù Jī's
*Wén Fù* (Rhyme-Prose on Literature), Zhòng Qià's
*Liú Bié* (Classification of Genres)
, and Hóng Fàn's
*Hàn Lín* (Forest of Literature). Each illuminates only a corner or crack
, rarely observing the main thoroughfare
. Some critique the talents of their contemporaries
, some evaluate the writings of previous scholars
, some broadly cite the ideas of the refined
, and some briefly summarize the themes of chapters and sections
and the vulgar
. Wèi Wén's *Diǎn* is dense but incomplete
; Chén Sī's writings are argumentative but irrelevant
; Yīng Yáng's *Lùn* is flowery but sketchy
; Lù Jī's *Fù* is clever but fragmented
; the *Liú Bié* is precise but lacks comprehensive effort
and disordered
; and the *Hàn Lín* is shallow and deficient in essentials
. Furthermore, followers like Jūnshān and Gōnggàn
, and groups like Jífǔ and Shìlóng
, generally discussed the meaning of literature
, sometimes appearing
. None of them were able to shake the leaves and find the roots
occasionally
, or observe the ripples and trace the source
. They neither described the admonitions of the former sages
nor benefited the concerns of later generations
. Now, the making of the *Wénxīn*
is rooted in the Dào
, takes the Sages as its masters
, embodies the Classics (Jīng)
, draws upon the Apocrypha (Wěi)
, and transforms the *Sāo*
. The cardinal principles of literature
are thus said to have been fully explored
. As for discussing writing (wén) and brushwork (bǐ)
, I draw boundaries and make classifications
, tracing the origin to manifest the end
, explaining names to clarify the meaning
, selecting writings to define the chapters
, and expounding principles to establish the comprehensive system
. In the upper
, the overall framework is made clear
chapters and above
. Reaching the points of dissecting emotions and analyzing external forms
, encompassing all sections and internal connections
, displaying the spiritual nature
, depicting style and structure (fēng shì)
, including comprehensive connections
, reviewing phonetics and characters
, examining elevation and decline
, praising and criticizing talents and strategies
through temporal sequence
, sighing regretfully over those who understand the music
, and steadfastly defining standards for instruments
—longingly, I write this preface
to control the various chapters
. In the lower chapters and below
, the detailed sections (máo mù) are made manifest
. Establishing principles and defining names
manifest the numbers of the Great Yì (Dà Yì)
. The chapters dedicated to literary function
number only forty-nine
. Now, evaluating a single piece of writing is easy
, but integrating all literary discourses is difficult
. Although I have lightly skimmed the surface
and deeply plumbed the marrow
, there may be nuanced meanings and hidden sources
that seem near
, and instances which the text does not record
yet are distant
are too numerous to count
. When it comes to assessing and criticizing established literature
, if there are points that align with old discussions
, it is not mere copying (léi tóng)
, but rather that the circumstances inherently prevent deviation
. If there are points that differ from previous theories
, it is not difference for the sake of difference
, but rather that the principles inherently prevent uniformity
. Alignment and divergence
do not depend on valuing past or present
; tearing the flesh and separating the fibers
, the only duty
. Holding the reins in the field of refined literature
is seeking the balance (zhé zhōng)
and encircling the treasury of elegant ornamentations
, it may be considered nearly complete
. However, words cannot fully express the meaning
—a difficulty noted by the Sages
—and knowledge lies in the vessel
Guǎn,
how could he establish standards?
The vastness of former ages
has already cleansed what I have heard;
the obscurity of future generations,
perhaps it will obscure their view.
After completion,
it was not yet praised by the trends of the time.
Xié himself valued his writing
and wished to have Shěn Yuē pass judgment upon it.
Yuē was powerful and renowned at the time,
and [Xié] had no means to reach him personally,
so he carried his book,
waited for Yuē to come out,
and presented it to him in front of his carriage,
looking like a merchant selling goods.
Yuē immediately ordered it to be taken and read,
valued it highly,
and said it deeply grasped the principles of literature.
He frequently displayed it on his desk.
However, Xié excelled in Buddhist philosophy in his writing,
and for the temples, pagodas, and steles of famous monks in the capital,
people certainly requested Xié to compose the texts.
There was an imperial edict for him to collaborate with the Śramaṇa Huì Zhèn at Dìnglín Sì to compile scriptural commentaries.
When the work was finished,
he then requested permission to become a monk.
He first burned his sideburns as a vow,
and the edict granted his request.
Thereupon he changed his clothes at the temple,
and changed his name to Huì Dì.
He died before the year was out.
His collected writings circulated in the world.
Wáng Jí, courtesy name Wénhǎi,
was a man from Línyí, Lángyé.
His grandfather, Yuǎn,
was the Sòng Guānglù Xūn (Court Minister of Ceremonial).
His father, Sēngyòu,
was a Qí Xiāojì Jiāngjūn (General of Swift Cavalry).
Jí could compose essays at age seven.
When he grew up, he loved studying,
was widely read, and possessed great talent.
Rèn Fǎng of Lè'ān saw him and praised him.
Once, at a gathering hosted by Shěn Yuē, he composed the poem "Yǒng Zhú" (Ode to the Candle),
which was highly appreciated by Yuē.
Towards the end of the Qí dynasty,
he served as Guānjūn Xíng Cānjūn (Staff Officer),
and was successively promoted to Wàibīng (Chief of Foreign Affairs) and Jìshì (Secretary).
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he was appointed Ānchéng Wáng Zhǔbù (Secretary to the Prince of Ānchéng),
Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng (Secretary in the Ministry of Personnel),
and Tíngwèi Zhèng (Court Judge).
He served successively as Magistrate of Yúyáo and Qiántáng,
but in both cases, he was dismissed.
After a long time,
he was appointed Qīngchē Xiāngdōng Wáng Zīyì Cānjūn (Adviser to the Prince of Xiāngdōng),
following the Prince’s administration to Kuàijī.
Within the commandery were Yúnmén Shān and Tiānzhù Shān.
Jí often toured them,
sometimes not returning for months on end.
He composed poetry upon reaching Ruòxié Xī.
A fragment of it says:
"The cicadas chirp, but the forest is quieter still;
The birds call, but the mountain is more secluded."
At the time, this was considered uniquely transcendent writing.
He returned and served as Dà Sīmǎ Cóngshì Zhōngláng (Staff Officer of the Grand Marshal),
and was promoted to Zhōngsǎn Dàfū (Grand Master of Court Attendance).
Feeling particularly frustrated,
he traveled the market streets on foot,
not being selective about his companions.
When the Prince of Xiāngdōng became Governor of Jīngzhōu,
he drew [Jí] in as Ānxī Fǔ Zīyì Cānjūn (Adviser to the Pacifying West Command),
concurrently holding the post of Zuòtáng Lìng (Magistrate of Zuòtáng).
