He did not attend to county affairs;
he drank wine daily.
If someone came with a lawsuit,
he would whip them and send them away.
A short time later,
he died.
His collected writings circulated in the world.
His son, Bì,
also possessed literary talent,
but died before Jí.
Hé Sīchéng, courtesy name Yuánjìng,
was a man from Tán, Dōnghǎi.
His father, Jìngshū,
was the Qí Zhēngdōng Lùshì Cānjūn (Secretary to the General Who Conquers the East) and Magistrate of Yúháng.
Sīchéng was diligent in his studies when young
and skilled in literary composition.
He began his career as Nánkāng Wáng Shìláng (Gentleman of the Household for the Prince of Nánkāng),
and was successively promoted to Ānchéng Wáng Zuǒchángshì (Left Attendant to the Prince of Ānchéng),
concurrently holding the post of Tàixué Bóshì (Erudite of the Imperial Academy),
Píngnán Ānchéng Wáng Xíng Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Prince of Ānchéng, General Who Pacifies the South),
concurrently serving as Jìshì (Secretary).
He followed the administration to Jiāngzhōu,
and composed the poem "Yóu Lúshān" (Traveling Mount Lú).
When Shěn Yuē saw it,
he praised it highly,
thinking that he himself could not match it.
Yuē had recently constructed a study hall at his suburban residence,
and consequently ordered a skilled calligrapher to inscribe this poem on the wall.
Fù Zhāo often requested Sīchéng to compose Shìdiàn Shī (Poems for the Sacrificial Ceremony to Confucius),
and the language was elegant and refined.
He was appointed Tíngwèi Zhèng (Court Judge).
In the fifteenth year of Tiānjiān (516 CE),
an imperial edict ordered Xú Miǎn, the Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince, to recommend scholars to enter the Huálín garden to compile the *Biǎnlüè*.
Miǎn recommended Sīchéng and four others to fill the selection.
He was promoted to Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ (Imperial Clerk of the Ministry of Justice).
Since the Sòng and Qí dynasties,
this post had become somewhat light,
but at the beginning of the Tiānjiān era, the selection process was once again made rigorous.
In front of his carriage, following the precedent of the Shàngshū Èr Chéng (Two Vice Ministers of the Department of State Affairs), he was assigned three attendants,
who carried the official seal in a green satchel,
this being the old custom because the censorial officials’ seal and ribbon were carried in front of them.
After a while,
he was promoted to Mòlíng Lìng (Magistrate of Mòlíng),
and also entered the palace to concurrently serve as Dōnggōng Tōngshì Shèrén (Aide-de-Camp of the Eastern Palace).
He was appointed Ānxī Xiāngdōng Wáng Lùshì Cānjūn (Secretary to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, General Who Pacifies the West),
and his concurrent post as Shèrén remained unchanged.
At that time, Xú Miǎn and Zhōu Shě were prominent in the court due to their abilities and talent,
and they both admired Sīchéng's learning,
often inviting him over on alternating days.
When Crown Prince Zhāomíng died,
he was sent out to serve as Yī Xiàn Lìng (Magistrate of Yī County).
He was promoted to Xuānhuì Wǔlíng Wáng Zhōng Lùshì Cānjūn (Chief Secretary to the Prince of Wǔlíng, General of Proclaimed Grace).
He died in office,
at the age of fifty-four.
His collected writings numbered fifteen scrolls.
Initially,
Sīchéng, his relative Xùn, and his son Lǎng all excelled in literary fame.
People at the time had a saying:
"The Three Hés of Dōnghǎi,
Zǐ Lǎng is the greatest."
When Sīchéng heard this,
he said:
"This saying is mistaken.
If it must be so (that I am not the best),
then the merit must surely belong to Xùn."
Sīchéng's intention was that the merit ought to belong to himself.
His son Lǎng, courtesy name Shìmíng,
had talent and quick wit early on,
and excelled at philosophical discussion (qīngyán).
Zhōu Shě would discuss things with him frequently
and admired his profound reasoning.
He once composed the *Bài Zhǒng Fù* (Rhapsody on the Ruined Tomb),
imitating Zhuāng Zhōu’s "Horse Whip" style;
the writing was extremely skillful.
People of the time had a saying:
"Among men, the bright and cheerful Hé Zǐ Lǎng."
He successively served as Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (Gentleman Attendant at the Gate)
before being sent out as Guóshān Lìng (Magistrate of Guóshān).
He died,
at the age of twenty-four.
His collected writings circulated in the world.
Liú Yǎo, courtesy name Shìshēn,
was a man from Píngyuán, Píngyuán.
His grandfather, Chéngmín,
was the Sòng Jìzhōu Cìshǐ (Regional Inspector of Jìzhōu).
His father, Wénwèi,
was the Qí Dōngyáng Tàishǒu (Administrator of Dōngyáng).
He had an excellent record of clean governance,
and is recorded in the *Qí Shū Liángzhèng Zhuàn* (Biography of Worthy Administrators in the History of Qí).
When Yǎo was a few years old,
the retired scholar Míng Sēngshào saw him,
and patting him, said:
"This child is truly a colt of a thousand *lǐ*."
At thirteen,
he entered mourning for his father.
Every time he wept,
passersby were moved by his sorrow.
At the beginning of the Tiānjiān era,
he served as Tàixué Bóshì (Erudite of the Imperial Academy) and Xuānhuì Yùzhāng Wáng Xíng Cānjūn (Staff Officer to the Prince of Yùzhāng, General of Proclaimed Grace).
Liú Yǎo, while young, loved learning,
and extensively mastered all books.
Whenever Shěn Yuē, Rèn Fǎng, and those below them
had forgotten something,
they all consulted him.
Once, while sitting with Shěn Yuē, they discussed the sacrificial zūn vessels used in ancestral temples.
Shěn Yuē said:
“Zhèng Xuán, in answering Zhāng Yì,
said they were painted with phoenix tails hanging loosely.
Now that we no longer have these vessels,
they do not conform to ancient practice.”
Liú Yǎo replied:
“This statement may not necessarily be verifiable.
In ancient times, the zūn vessels
were all carved from wood into the shape of birds or beasts,
hollowed out at the head and back
to pour wine in and out.
Recently, during the Wèi dynasty, vessels belonging to Qí Grand Master Zǐwěi used for sending off his daughter were unearthed in Lǔ Jùn.
Among them was a sacrificial zūn made in the shape of a sacrificial ox.
Furthermore, during the Jìn Yǒngjiā era, the bandit Cáo Yí unearthed the tomb of Qí Jǐnggōng in Qīng Zhōu
and also obtained two such zūn vessels,
the forms of which were likewise ox images.
Both finds are ancient preserved artifacts,
proving that the claim is not baseless.”
Shěn Yuē greatly concurred.
Shěn Yuē also said:
“Hé Chéngtiān’s compilation is astonishingly comprehensive.
His book records the affairs of Zhāng Zhòngshī and the Long-necked King.
What is the source for this?”
Liú Yǎo replied:
“Zhòngshī, who was one foot and two inches tall,
is mentioned only in the Lùn Héng.
The Long-necked one is King Píqiān Wáng,
about whom Zhū Jiàn'ān's record of the region south of Fúnán states that he has been immortal from ancient times until now.”
Shěn Yuē immediately retrieved the two books to check,
and everything was exactly as Liú Yǎo had stated.
Shěn Yuē had recently constructed an upper chamber and study at his suburban home.
Liú Yǎo composed two laudatory verses for it,
and presented them, along with other essays he had written, to Shěn Yuē.
Shěn Yuē immediately ordered a skilled scribe to inscribe the verses on the wall.
He then replied to Liú Yǎo in a letter, saying:
“The things I have loved and been fond of throughout my life
are not found among common people,
and the joy of the forests and ravines
is often seized by responsibilities.
The day is late and the path is ending;
this aspiration is passing away.
Yet I still retain a little leisure and remoteness,
seeking feelings that are pure and spacious.
Building this dwelling in the eastern suburbs
is not merely for rest;
it is indeed to somewhat fulfill my long-held wishes
and occasionally gain a period of repose.
The places where Zhòngcháng lived and wandered,
and the beauties described by Xiūliǎn—
my longing and admiration for them are profound but futile;
how can I possibly resemble them?
Because of your great affection for me,
you favored me with two laudatory verses.
The language and polish are beautiful and rich,
and all relevant facts and meanings are fully brought forth.
Between the phrases and rhythms,
light and shadow illuminate each other,
making me immediately feel that this place
is naturally ten times more wonderful.
Thus, I know that the benefit of beautiful composition
is immense.
I shall immediately place them on the wall of the chamber
and read them with admiration, whether sitting or reclining.
The various pieces in the separate scroll
are all masterly creations.
Moreover, the ‘Mountain Temple’ piece is truly inspiring,
and the accompanying pieces by the various worthies are lofty and unusual,
causing smiles and curing illness;
they encompass this meaning.
I hope that when we meet soon,
we can discuss and analyze them together again.”
This shows how much he was praised by Shěn Yuē.
Once, while sitting with Rèn Fǎng,
someone presented Fǎng with ēn wine, but wrote the character `榐`.
Rèn Fǎng asked Liú Yǎo:
“Is this character correct?”
Liú Yǎo replied:
“Gě Hóng’s Zì Yuàn writes it with the wood radical next to `鏩`.”
Rèn Fǎng also said:
“The wine that causes drunkenness for a thousand days
must be an empty claim.”
Liú Yǎo said:
“In Chéngxiāng, Guìyáng, there is ‘thousand-mile wine.’
One drinks it and only becomes drunk upon reaching home;
this is also an example of the same phenomenon.”
Rèn Fǎng was greatly astonished and said:
“I must have forgotten it myself;
I truly do not recall this.”
Liú Yǎo said:
“It comes from the Record of Establishing Commanderies compiled by Yáng Yuánfèng.
Yuánfèng was a person of the Wèi dynasty.
This book also contains his fu,
which mentions ‘Triple Heavy, Five Grades,’
and ‘Shāng Xī Kuǎn Lǐ.’”
They immediately checked Yáng’s record at the time,
and the details were all correct.
Wáng Sēngrú was commanded to compile a genealogy
and asked Liú Yǎo about the origins of bloodlines.
Liú Yǎo said:
“Huán Tán’s Xīn Lùn states: ‘The Grand Historian’s genealogical tables of the Three Dynasties,
with lines running horizontally and diagonally upward,
were all modeled after the Zhōu genealogy.’
Judging by this,
they must have originated in the Zhōu dynasty.”
Wáng Sēngrú exclaimed:
“It can be said that I have learned something I had not heard before.”
Zhōu Shě also asked Liú Yǎo:
“Secretariat officials wear purple satchels,
which are traditionally called a ‘qiè náng’ (carry bag).
What is its ultimate source?”
Liú Yǎo replied:
“The Biography of Zhāng Ānshì states: ‘He held a satchel and wore a brush,
serving Emperor Xiàowǔ for several decades.’
Wěi Zhāo and Zhāng Yàn’s commentaries both state: ‘Tuo
means a bag.
Close officials wear brushes
to await consultation.’”
Fàn Xiù, when compiling his dictionary with pronunciation and explanations,
also consulted Liú Yǎo.
His extensive knowledge and powerful memory
were all of this type.
Later, he assisted Zhōu Shě in compiling the national history.
He was sent out to serve as the Magistrate of Línjīn,
where he achieved good merit.
When his term expired,
more than three hundred people from the county went to the imperial court requesting he remain in office,
which the imperial edict permitted.
Liú Yǎo requested relief due to illness,
and upon returning, he was appointed Staff Officer to the establishment of the Prince of Jìn'ān, Yúnhuī General.
Grand Tutor Xú Miǎn recommended Liú Yǎo and Gù Xié, along with five others, to enter the Huálín gardens to compile the Piānlüè encyclopedia.
When the work was finished,
he held his original post concurrently with Court Judge.
He retired again due to a foot ailment.
He subsequently wrote the Lín Tíng Fù (Rhapsody on the Garden Grove).
Wáng Sēngrú saw it and exclaimed:
“Since the time of the Jiāojū Fù,
there has been no such composition.”
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
he was again appointed Director of Jiànkāng,
and promoted to Director of the Carriage Bureau in the Secretariat.
A few months later,
he was transferred to serve as Director of Ceremonies.
The Grand Minister (Púshè), Xú Miǎn, exclusively entrusted Liú Yǎo with the Secretariat documents and deliberations.
He was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Yúyáo.
While in the county, he was honest and pure;
if people offered gifts,
he refused to accept any.
The Prince of Xiāngdōng issued an instruction praising him.
Upon returning, he was appointed Secretary and Staff Officer to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, Xuānhuì General.
He resigned his post due to mourning his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he again served as Secretary to the Prince’s establishment,
concurrently with Attendant Censor of the Eastern Palace.
In the first year of Dàtōng (527 CE),
he was promoted to Commandant of Infantry,
and his position as Attendant Censor remained the same.
Crown Prince Zhāomíng said to Liú Yǎo:
“Wine is not what you prefer,
yet you hold the office related to wine.
This is only because you are truly worthy of the ancients.”
Soon after, an imperial edict ordered him to replace Péi Zǐyě in managing the affairs of the Director of Imperial Archives.
When Crown Prince Zhāomíng died
and the new palace establishment was founded,
it was customary for none of the former staff to be retained,
but an edict specially retained Liú Yǎo.
He then wrote commentary on the Rhapsody on the Prince’s Death,
which was praised as extensive and thorough.
The Grand Minister (Púshè), Hé Jìngróng, memorialized that Liú Yǎo should be transferred to Advisor in the Prince’s establishment.
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
“Liú Yǎo must first pass through the Central Secretariat.”
He was then appointed Gentleman of the Central Secretariat.
Soon after, he became Advisor and Staff Officer to the Prince of Xiāngdōng, Píngxī General,
concurrently retaining the posts of Attendant Censor and Director of Imperial Archives as before.
He was promoted to Vice Director of the Left in the Secretariat.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he died in office,
aged fifty at the time.
having no particular indulgences.
By nature, he did not boast,
nor did he discuss the faults or merits of others.
When he encountered the Shì Shì (Buddhist) scriptures and teachings,
he always practiced kindness and forbearance.
In Tiānjiān seventeen (518 CE),
when he was observing mourning for his mother,
he permanently ceased eating meat and fish,
maintaining a vegetarian diet and keeping fasts.
When facing death,
he left instructions to be interred in monastic robes,
carried on an open cart,
and returned to be buried in the old grave site.
Wherever a plot could be found
sufficient only to hold the coffin, that would suffice;
no spirit tablet altars or sacrificial feasts were to be set up.
His son complied with these instructions.
From his youth to adulthood, Yǎo
produced many writings.
He compiled the Yàoyǎ, five scrolls (juàn);
the Chǔcí Cǎomù Shū, one scroll;
the Gāoshì Zhuàn, two scrolls;
the Dōnggōng Xīn Jiù Jì, thirty scrolls;
and the Gǔ Jīn Sì Bù Shū Mù, five scrolls.
All were circulated in the world.
Xiè Zhēng, courtesy name Xuándù,
was a man from Yángxià, Chén Jùn.
His great-grandfather, Jǐngrén,
served as the Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Púshè) under the Sòng dynasty.
His grandfather, Zhì,
was Aide to the Minister of Works (Sītú Zhǔbù) under the Sòng.
His father, Jǐng,
was famous in his youth along with his cousin Tiǎo (Xiè Tiǎo).
When Zǐliáng, the Prince of Jìnglíng of Qí, established the Western Residence (Xī Dǐ),
inviting literary scholars,
Jǐng also participated.
During the Lóngchāng period,
he served as Adjutant-Advisor to the Cavalry General (Piàojì Zīyì Cānjūn) for Emperor Míng,
concurrently leading the Secretariat (Jìshì).
He was promoted to Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
and then to Administrator of Jìn'ān (Jìn'ān Nèishǐ).
When Gāozǔ pacified Jīngyì,
Jǐng served as an Advisor to the Hegemon's Prefecture (Bàfǔ Zīyì),
and later as Palace Attendant (Huángmén Láng) in the Liáng Court (Liáng Tái).
In the early Tiānjiān period,
he successively rose to be Minister of Agriculture (Sīnóng Qīng),
Director of the Imperial Library (Mìshū Jiān),
Minister of Population Affairs (Zuǒ Mín Shàngshū),
and General Who Manifests Awe (Míngwēi Jiāngjūn) and Grand Administrator of Dōngyáng (Dōngyáng Tàishǒu).
Gāozǔ intended to appoint him Palace Attendant (Shìzhōng),
but he firmly declined, citing old age,
and requested the purple robes (jīn zǐ).
Before the arrangement was made,
he fell ill and died.
Zhēng was intelligent and astute in his youth;
Jǐng found him exceptional.
He often said to his relatives:
"This child is an extraordinary vessel.
My only worry is his lifespan.
If Heaven grants him his years,
I shall have no regrets."
When he grew up,
he possessed a fine demeanor
and was fond of learning and skilled at composition.
He first served as Judicial Officer (Fǎcáo) under the Prince of Ānchéng (Ān Xī),
then transferred to Gentleman of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Láng) in charge of the Finance Bureau (Jīnbù) and the Three Dukes/Two Offices Bureaus (Sāngōng Èr Cáo).
He then became Secretariat Recorder (Jìshì) for the Prince of Yùzhāng,
concurrently serving as Attendant at the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shèrén).
He was promoted to Adjutant-Advisor to the General Who Pacifies the North (Píng Běi Zīyì Cānjūn),
concurrently Minister Herald (Hónglú Qīng),
with his post as Shèrén remaining the same.
Zhēng was friends with Pèi Zǐyě of Hédōng and Liú Xiǎn of Pèi Guó, who served alongside him.
Zǐyě once composed a *fù* on standing watch during a cold night to present to Zhēng,
and Zhēng responded by composing the *fù* on being moved by a friend (Gǎn Yǒu Fù) in return.
At that time, Yuán Lüè, the Prince of Zhōngshān of Wèi, was returning north.
Gāozǔ held a farewell banquet for him at Wǔdé Diàn,
demanding that poems of thirty rhymes be composed,
with a deadline of three *kè*.
Zhēng completed his in two *kè*.
His composition was extremely fine,
and Gāozǔ reviewed it twice.
He also wrote an essay on releasing captured animals (Fàngshēng Wén) for Yuānyóu, the Marquis of Línrǔ,
which was also admired by the world.
In Zhōng Dàtōng first year (529 CE),
he resigned due to the mourning period for his father.
Subsequently, he again fell into mourning for his mother.
An imperial edict recalled him to serve as General of Upholding Awe (Zhēnwēi Jiāngjūn),
temporarily resuming his former duties.
After the mourning period concluded,
he was appointed Vice Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng).
In the third year (531 CE),
when Crown Prince Zhāomíng died,
Gāozǔ established Gāng, the Prince of Jìn'ān, as the new Crown Prince.
Before issuing the imperial edict,
he summoned only three men for consultation: Hé Jìngróng (Left Assistant of the Department of State Affairs), Kǒng Xiūyuán (General of Proclaiming Grace), and Zhēng.
Although Zhēng’s age and rank were still relatively low at the time,
the trust placed in him was already significant.
In the fourth year,
he was successively promoted to Gentleman of the Palace Secretariat (Zhōngshū Láng),
with the posts of Minister Herald (Hónglú Qīng) and Shèrén remaining unchanged.
In the sixth year,
he was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Yùzhāng, General of the Northern Garrison (Běi Zhōng Láng), and Grand Administrator of Southern Lánlíng (Nán Lánlíng Tàishǒu).
In Dàtóng second year (536 CE),
he died in office,
at the age of thirty-seven.
His friend Wáng Jí of Lángxié collected his writings into twenty scrolls (juàn).
Zāng Yán, courtesy name Yànwēi,
was a man from Jǔ, Dōngguǎn.
His great-grandfather, Tāo,
was Left Grand Master of Splendid Happiness (Zuǒ Guānglù) under the Sòng.
His grandfather, Níng,
was Vice Director of the Right in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Yòu Chéng) under the Qí.
His father, Léng,
was Adjutant (Cānjūn) in the Rear Army (Hòu Jūn).
Yán was known for his filial nature as a youth;
when observing mourning for his father, his devotion brought him illness and renown.
He was an orphan and poor, but diligently studied;
wherever he went, a book never left his hand.
He first served as Gentleman (Shìláng) under the Prince of Ānchéng,
and was later transferred to Palace Attendant (Chángshì).
His cousin, Wèi Zhēn, was appointed Administrator of Jiāngxià Commandery,
and took Yán along to the post.
En route, Yán composed the *Fù* on Camping and Traveling (Túnyóu Fù).
Rèn Fǎng saw it and praised it.
He also composed the Seven Calculations (Qī Suàn),
the language of which was also rich and beautiful.
His nature was reserved and upright.
He never once called upon anyone in society.
Though Assistant of the Department of State Affairs (Púshè) Xú Miǎn wished to meet him,
Yán ultimately refused to go to him.
He was promoted to Acting Adjutant (Xíng Cānjūn) under the General Who Guards the Army (Guānjūn), serving the Prince of Xiāngdōng as a reading attendant (shì dú).
He successively rose to Adjutant (Cānjūn) in the General of Proclaiming Grace's (Xuānhuì) Light Chariot Prefecture (Qīngchē Fǔ),
concurrently serving as Secretariat Recorder (Jìshì).
Yán was widely read and had memorized much of what he studied;
he was especially proficient in the Hàn Shū,
reciting and chanting almost all of it from memory.
The Prince once personally took the catalogue of the Four Sections of Literature (Sì Bù Shū Mù) to test him.
Yán was able to identify one item from each scroll, from *Jiǎ* (A) to *Dīng* (D),
along with the author’s name,
making no omissions or errors.
His extensive learning was thus demonstrated.
When the Prince moved to Jīngzhōu,
Yán followed the headquarters and was transferred to Adjutant in charge of Records (Lùshì Cānjūn) under the General Who Pacifies the West (Ān Xī), General of the Western Garrison (Xī Zhōng Láng).
He successively oversaw Yìyáng and Wǔníng commanderies.
These consecutive posts were all among the southern (mán) and western (zuǒ) tribes.
Previous administrators (jùnshǒu) usually selected military men
to suppress them with troops.
Yán, however, entered the territories alone in a single carriage with only a few disciples.
The various Mán tribes were pleased and submitted,
and banditry thereupon ceased.
When the Prince entered the capital to oversee the military affairs of Shítou Garrison,
Yán was appointed Adjutant in charge of Records (Lùshì) under the General Who Pacifies the Right (Ān Yòu).
When the Prince moved to Jiāngzhōu,
Yán became Adjutant-Advisor to the General Who Guards the South (Zhèn Nán Zīyì Cānjūn),
and died in office.
His collected writings amounted to ten scrolls.
Fú Tǐng, courtesy name Shìbiāo.
His father, Jǐ,
was Administrator of Yùzhāng (Yùzhāng Nèishǐ),
and is recorded in the Biographies of Good Officials (Liáng Lì Zhuàn).
Tǐng was quick-witted in his youth;
at the age of seven, he had mastered the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) and the Lúnyǔ (Analects).
When he grew up,
he possessed talent and intelligence,
was fond of composition,
wrote five-character-line poetry,
and was skilled at imitating the style of Xiè Kānglè.
His father's friend, Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān, deeply admired and praised him,
often saying:
"Under the sun, this boy is without equal."
At the end of the Qí dynasty,
he was nominated by the prefecture as a Promising Talent (Xiùcái).
His examination response was rated first among his contemporaries.
When Gāozǔ’s righteous army arrived,
Tǐng went to welcome and visit him at Xīnlín.
Gāozǔ was very pleased to see him
and called him
"Yán Zǐ" (Yán Huí),
appointing him Acting Adjutant (Xíng Cānjūn) to the General Who Conquers the East (Zhēng Dōng).
He was eighteen years old at the time.
In the early Tiānjiān period,
he was appointed Adjutant in the Central Army (Zhōng Jūn Cānjūn Shì).
His residence was located at Cháogōu.
He lectured on the Lúnyǔ at his home,
and the listeners filled the court.
He was promoted to Magistrate of Jiànkāng (Jiànkāng Zhèng),
but was soon impeached and dismissed.
After a long interval,
he entered the court as Gentleman (Láng) in charge of Ceremonies (Yí Cáo) in the Department of State Affairs.
He was transferred to Secretariat Recorder (Jìshì Cānjūn) under the General of the Western Garrison (Xī Zhōng Láng),
and successively served as Magistrate (Lìng) of Jìnlíng and Wǔkāng.
After resigning from the counties and returning home,
he built a residence in the eastern suburbs
and never again sought office.
possessed a rare great reputation,
and was also skilled at handling the current age.
Those in positions of power within the court
mostly associated with him,
thus he could not long devote himself to reclusion and tranquility.
At that time, Púshè Xú Miǎn took sick leave and returned to his residence. [Tǐng]
sent him a letter to observe his intention, saying: In the past, Shì Dé harbored concern,
and longed for arousal for several days;
Fǔ Sì missed his friends,
and his emotions were burdened for ten days.
Therefore, we know that what the deep heart is tied to,
noble or base, is all the same.
Moreover, your favor
is profound like a familial elder,
your righteousness values a true friend,
your Dào shields the common people,
and your virtue broadly covers all.
Yet, the court and the countryside are vastly separated,
mountains and rivers are distant and different.
Although [your] cough and spittle occasionally reach [me],
your countenance
is not seen.
The sorrow of Dōngshān,
how can one speak of immediate return?
The west wind is affecting,
who can be without thought (of you)?
Furthermore, dwelling in quiet isolation,
I look at my shadow and find no response.
The autumn wind rises
in all four directions,
gardens and groves change color,
the cool wilderness is silent,
and cold insects chirp and cry.
The feelings I hold cannot be simply set aside;
my emotions and thoughts cannot be without refuge.
At times, I resort to chanting poetry;
whenever I move (to write), I fill
pages.
Yáng Shēng was deep and melancholic,
yet his works merely covered an earthen jar (fù’àng);
Huì Zǐ possessed five carts of books,
but the contradictions and refutations were all the greater.
One day I casually offered a small piece of writing,
not expecting such extravagant praise.
I subsequently received your profound kindness,
multiple tablets and letters,
the paper dense and the characters polished.
When reciting them, I could not stop,
but I merely regret that your agreement and endorsement were excessive,
potentially harming precision and accuracy.
In the past, Zǐjiàn did not wish to rashly praise Chén Lín,
fearing
he would be mocked by later generations.
If the remaining commentary is now overly extravagant,
will it not encumber your pure discourse (qīngtán)?
Tǐng has hidden his tracks among the tall grass and weeds;
contact with the outside world is cut off.
Yet, relying on songs and chants,
I have obtained [news] from the carriage drivers and herdsmen.
I respectfully learned that you have been using acupuncture (biānshí),
and are still corresponding freely,
gladdening the heart and pleasing
the ear.
Gradually, you have cast aside [old habits].
Dwelling quietly in honored surroundings,
you are devoted to cleansing yourself.
Fine silks and bamboo music (sìzhú)—
both categories have been instantly dismissed.
Square mats and round tables—
three cups alone remain.
Therefore,
your Dào transforms the region,
and your spirit soars beyond the boundaries.
You practice the strings and recitation,
illuminating the contemplation of reduction (guān sǔn).
I reflect upon Liú Hóu abstaining from grain,
and contemplate Hán Qīng relinquishing honor.
I regard with affection the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū),
and commit my feelings to the Southern Peak (Nányuè).
I delve into and admire the gifts you bring,
aligning myself with the position of a junior follower (xiàfēng).
Although I say this is most fortunate,
I still do not fully comprehend.
Although the imperial Dào is stable and peaceful,
allowing officials to resign and depart swiftly,
men of worth (Yóu
Gēng) find their proper place,
and those in power (Yín Liàng) have a destination.
For those wandering and indifferent,
Zhǎn Shì still rolls up his sleeves (to act);
upon the vast white waters,
Níng Sǒu intends to lift his robes (to cross).
Thus we know that the superior man rescues
others,
and righteousness is not pursued merely for self-interest.
If one desires to wander with Chìsōng Zǐ,
who can truly achieve this?
I wish to urge you toward benevolence and longevity,
thereby securing this abundant blessing.
Although [the Dào] does not speak,
the four seasons continue
their course.
Only then will the black-haired people (qiánshǒu) have shelter,
and the gentry (jiànshēn) not be deprived.
The white colt will not be left in the empty valley,
and even the butcher of sheep (túyáng) will anticipate his reward.
Is this not excellent?
Is this not excellent?
In the past, Dù Zhēn secluded himself in a deep chamber,
and Láng Zōng cut off his traces in the hidden wilds.
This is difficult,
and truly not what I hope for.
Jǐng Dān was lofty and pure;
Xiāngrú was arrogant toward the world.
Yet they still frequently visited powerful
houses,
and behaved with ease and dignity in their hometowns.
I constantly consider this approach to be the greatest,
and I secretly admire it every time.
I am currently considering holding a broom and extending my thoughts,
through Chén Shìzhě [my attendant].
I request that you come during the slack farming season,
without waiting for
an invitation.
Tǐng truly enjoys composing literature,
but does not fit in with the current age,
nor can he shorten his pace or constrain his steps
to accommodate popular trends.
My writings are like chāngzū (fermented vegetables),
mistaken for a favored delicacy by those who are biased.
Therefore, I am not
ashamed of my stubborn ignorance,
nor do I fear the Lóngmén.
In the past, Jìngtōng’s appreciation of Jǐngqīng,
and Mènggōng’s recognition of Zhòngwèi,
merely came from men of wide knowledge,
yet they were considered great achievements.
How much more so when it comes from the revered leader of the age,
making it even more extraordinary!
Recently, because rush mats were unavailable,
and there was a lack of writing paper,
I casually imitate Dōngfāng,
presenting this letter to the Prime Minister (chéngxiàng).
I need to find someone skilled in calligraphy;
I further request that you refine and correct it.
If perchance I meet
Zǐhóu,
I will again prepare a revised tablet.
Miǎn replied, saying: Having read your letter again,
the multiple tablets and missives,
encompassing both action and retreat (chū chù),
mixing words and silence.
The subjects and meanings are thorough and complete,
the intentions profound and far-reaching.
Opening the case and unfolding the paper,
my indignation and admiration
are doubly increased.
You, sir (qīng), sprang forth as a talent from an heroic state (Xióngzhōu),
and entered the court at a young age (ruòguān).
You have thoroughly studied the Hundred Schools
and cultivated the Six Teachings.
Observing your eyes reveals your sharp intellect;
looking at your demeanor shows your brilliance and clarity.
You are like
the famed steed of the State of Lǔ,
surpassing the white crane in the clouds.
When you took up residence in a famous district
and were tested as an official in fertile land,
you were expected to possess the string music and chanting of Wǔchéng,
and the songs and poetry of Tóngxiāng.
How could you be mentioned in the same breath as mere
mediocrities like Zhuó Lǔ?
It is exactly the time when your excellent abilities should be recognized,
and you should receive additional favor and appointment,
adorning yourself with the hairpin and sash,
and being placed among the high ranks.
Yet you wish to emulate far-off models of retirement and emergence (juǎn shū),
using the pretext of wisdom or foolishness.
Since you already know that benefit is a burden,
and understand that when full, words multiply,
your lofty withdrawal from the dust of the world
is truly admirable.
Moreover, with Jīnshāng (autumn) controlling the season,
and white autumn (sùqiū)
taking command of the sequence,
the groves and fields are desolate,
and there is no one to share happiness with.
Lying down upon books and documents,
you wander through Confucian and Daoist (rú xuán) teachings.
Both self and external things are forgotten;
who can be hindered by favor or disgrace?
This truly evokes joy and envy,
and I use
there are differences and similarities.
Now, listening from afar and searching nearby,
arousing my thoughts whether awake or asleep,
like a white colt in an empty valley,
a recluse crane-necked [in anticipation],
considering poverty and lowliness a disgrace,
finding it hard to associate with birds and beasts.
Therefore, I should abandon these
kudzu vines and mosses,
and go forth to follow the yuān-lù (official ranks).
If I do not rely on seclusion or prominence,
would this not be splendid!
My wisdom is insufficient to aid the age;
my talent is ashamed to save the world.
Following the principles received from the court,
I dare not indulge in idleness.
My strength is weak and the path is long;
my sense of shame is constant.
If the world follows the Way (Dào),
what need is there for the people of Yáo
to act?
I am permitted to use my fatigue and illness as an excuse,
and contemplate following a life of leisure and ease.
If, however, carts and writings are unified [i.e., the realm is ordered],
and border guards report no alarms,
music is composed and rites are established,
monuments are inscribed and mountains are sealed,
then I
return to live in my humble cottage
—that would truly be great fortune.
But I have long suffered from asthma (fēng kài),
and now encounter this emptiness and dizziness.
My emaciation resembles Shì'ān;
my frailty is the same as Chángrǔ.
The bureaucratic documents are neglected and abandoned;
the affairs of the court (Tái Gé) have not yet been
managed.
(The illness) pleasures the ear but rots the intestines,
and I cease my duties due to the circumstances.
This is not because I wish to pursue Sōngzǐ [Chì Sōngzǐ]
or remotely admire Liú Hóu [Zhāng Liàng].
If Heaven grants me longevity,
I will naturally attend solemnly to my duties.
To compare myself to those who are not my equals,
I truly feel the words are wasted.
Reviewing the cycles (of my life/thoughts),
I feel lost and dejected.
The pure dust is singularly distant;
white clouds drift aimlessly;
such is the lingering feeling, endless.
You have kindly sent down a letter (shū zhá),
showing me your literary work (wén hàn).
I read it repeatedly until I could recite it,
lingering over the ornamented paper.
Formerly, Zhòngxuān (Wáng Cān) was talented and quick-witted,
and gained fame through Zhōngláng (Cài Yōng);
Zhèngpíng (Xú Gàn) was sharp and
perceptive,
relying on Běihǎi (Kǒng Róng) to establish his reputation.
Looking at the past and judging the present,
I have qualities for which I feel ashamed.
If these writings should form a compilation (juǎn zhì),
I will strive to praise them highly.
Do not let your unique brilliance merely follow your palm,
and idly cause
writers to clench their fists in frustration.
I desire to see you (shì lǘ);
you ought to prepare by sweeping your gate.
I also have thoughts of coming (lái sī),
and going straight to where your couch is suspended (xuán tà).
As for the light moss and fishnet (gifts),
they should be presented separately.
The sighing for the palace
gates (Chéng Què),
when will I cease to harbor this feeling?
I await the Day Lily (Xuān Sū, relief from sorrow).
The letter cannot fully express my thoughts.
Tǐng subsequently entered officialdom,
and soon became Zhìshū of the Nántái.
He accepted bribes related to his duties,
and was due to be investigated and impeached.
Tǐng feared punishment,
and consequently changed his attire to become a Dàorén (Daoist).
After a long time hiding,
he later encountered an amnesty,
and came out at Tiānxīn Sì (Temple).
Coincidentally, the Prince of Shàolíng (Shàolíng Wáng) was appointed Governor of Jiāngzhōu.
He took Tǐng along to the garrison.
The Prince loved literature and scholarly matters,
and Tǐng was greatly favored and treated well.
Tǐng consequently returned to secular life.
He again followed the Prince when he moved his garrison to Yǐngzhōu,
and was summoned to the capital to serve as Jīng Yǐn (Metropolitan Prefect).
Tǐng remained in Xiàshǒu.
After a long time, he returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
During the Tàiqīng reign period,
he traveled as a guest to Wúxīng and Wújùn.
He died during Hóu Jǐng’s rebellion.
He authored *Ěr Shuō* in ten volumes,
and a collected works (Wén Jí) in twenty volumes.
His son, Zhīmìng,
had previously followed Tǐng in serving the Prince of Shàolíng,
acting as Secretary (Zhǎng Shūjì).
During the rebellion,
the Prince was defeated and fled from Yǐngzhōu.
Zhīmìng then surrendered to Hóu Jǐng.
He constantly felt resentment toward the court, due to his father’s incomplete official career.
He deeply resented the court,
and consequently served Jǐng with his whole heart.
When Jǐng attacked Yǐngzhōu
and besieged Bā Líng,
the military proclamations and manifestos
were all written by him.
When Jǐng usurped the throne,
he became a Zhōngshū Shèrén (Secretary of the Palace),
relying exclusively on power and favor,
his influence swaying both the court and the region.
When Jǐng was defeated, he was captured
and sent to Jiānglíng.
He died miserably in prison.
Tǐng's younger brother, Chuí,
also possessed talent and reputation.
He was first introduced by the Prince of Shàolíng,
serving successively as Jìshì,
Zhōng Jìshì,
and Cānjūn (Staff Officer).
Yǔ Zhòngróng, courtesy name Zhòngróng,
was a native of Yǐngchuān Líng.
He was the sixth-generation descendant of Bīng, the Sīkōng (Minister of Works) of the Jìn Dynasty.
His grandfather, Huīzhī,
was the Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng (Vice Censor-in-Chief) of the Sòng Dynasty.
His father, Yī,
was the Jìshì for the Prince of Shàolíng of the Qí Dynasty.
Zhòngróng was orphaned young,
and was raised by his uncle Yǒng.
When he grew up,
he cut off social contact,
dedicating himself entirely to intense study,
holding books in his hands day and night without stopping.
He first served as Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn under the Commandery of Ānxī.
Yǒng was already esteemed and prominent at the time.
Xú Miǎn, the Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū), intended to appoint Yàn Yīng, Yǒng’s son, as a palace official (gōng liáo).
Yǒng wept and said:
"My elder brother’s son was orphaned young,
and his talent is passable.
I wish to use the position that Yàn Yīng has the honor of holding, and pass it to him."
Miǎn agreed,
and consequently transferred Zhòngróng to be Tàizǐ Shèrén (Secretarial Aide to the Crown Prince).
He was promoted to Zhǔbù for the Prince of Ānchéng.
At that time, Liú Xiàobiāo of Píngyuán was also a staff officer for the administration,
and both were received with courtesy by the Prince due to their extensive learning.
He was promoted to Gōngcáo Shǐ of Jìn'ān.
He successively served as Magistrate (Lìng) of Yǒngkāng, Qiántáng, and Wǔkāng.
In governing the counties, he achieved no notable distinction,
and was frequently impeached.
After a long period,
he was appointed Zhōng Jìshì for the Prince of Ānchéng.
When he was about to leave to accompany the administration,
the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ), recalling their former kindness,
specially hosted a farewell banquet,
and bestowed a poem, saying:
"Sūn Shēng ascends the Zhìyáng road,
Wúzǐ heads to Cháogē County.
Neither compares to the promotion in Fánlín,
setting out wine overlooking the magnificent palace."
His peers considered this an honor.
He was promoted to Zīyì Cānjūn (Consultant and Staff Officer) for the Prince of Wǔlíng under the Commandery of Ānxī.
He was appointed Shàngshū Zuǒchéng (Assistant Prefect of the Department of State Affairs).
He was dismissed for failing to investigate and impeach honestly.
Zhòngróng was widely learned,
and had a great reputation in his youth.
He was prone to acting on his temperament and indulging in drink,
and was fond of audacious statements and elevated discussions.
Scholars and friends therefore thought little of him.
Only with Wáng Jí and Xiè Jǐqīng did he share mutual affection and congeniality.
These two were also unruly at the time,
so they followed each other,
becoming wildly unrestrained and drinking heavily,
no longer maintaining restraint or conduct.
After a long time,
he again became Zīyì Cānjūn,
and was sent out to serve as Magistrate of Yī Xiàn.
When the Tàiqīng rebellion occurred,
he was traveling as a guest in Kuàijī.
He encountered illness and died,
at the age of seventy-four.
Zhòngróng compiled miscellaneous philosophical works (Zhūzǐ Shū) in thirty volumes,
and geographical works by various schools (Zhòng Jiā Dìlǐ Shū) in twenty volumes,
*Biographies of Exemplary Women* (Liè Nǚ Zhuàn) in three volumes,
and a collected works (Wén Jí) in twenty volumes: all circulated in the world.
Lù Yúngōng, courtesy name Zǐlóng,
was a native of Wújùn.
His grandfather, Xián,
was the Zhōu Biéjià.
His father, Wán,
was the Níngyuǎn Zhǎngshǐ.
*Yún Gōng* at five years old recited the *Lúnyǔ* and the *Máoshī*.
At nine years old, he read the *Hànshū*,
and was generally able to memorize it.
His paternal great-uncle *Chuí* and *Liú Xiǎn* of *Pèiguó* questioned him on ten matters.
*Yún Gōng* replied without error.
*Xiǎn* sighed in admiration and surprise at him.
When he grew up,
he loved learning and possessed literary talent and quick thought.
The prefecture recommended him as *Xiùcái*.
He was successively promoted to Acting Adjutant (*Xíng Cānjūn*) to the Prince of *Wǔlíng*, *Xuānhuì*, and the Prince of *Xiāngdōng*, *Píngxī*.
*Yún Gōng* had previously composed the stele inscription for the Temple of *Tàibó*.
*Zhāng Zǎn*, the Administrator of *Wúxīng*, passed through the area upon being relieved of his post,
read his text, and exclaimed:
“He is the *Cài Bójī* of today!”
When *Zǎn* arrived at the capital, he took charge of appointments.
He spoke of [Yún Gōng] to *Gāozǔ*.
[Gāozǔ] summoned him to concurrently serve as *Shàngshū Yícáo Láng*.
Shortly thereafter, he obtained the substantive post.
He entered the court to serve in the *Shòuguāng Shěng*,
and using his primary office, he oversaw the affairs of the *Zhùzuò Láng*.
Soon after, he was appointed *Zhùzuò Láng*.
He was successively promoted to *Zhōngshū Huángmén Láng*,
and also continued to manage the editing affairs.
*Yún Gōng* was good at Go.
He often served at the Imperial Presence late at night.
His ceremonial cap accidentally touched the flame of a candle.
*Gāozǔ* smiled and said to him:
“The candle is burning your sable [decoration].”
*Gāozǔ* intended to appoint *Yún Gōng* as *Shìzhōng*,
and therefore used these words to tease him.
At that time, a new "bream fish boat" had been constructed in the *Tiānyuān Chí*.
Its shape was broad and short.
On days when *Gāozǔ* was at leisure,
he often floated on this boat.
Among the court officials, he only brought along *Tàicháng* *Liú Zhilìn*, *Guózǐ Jìjiǔ* *Dào Gài*, and *Yòuwèi* *Zhū Yī*.
Although *Yún Gōng*'s age and rank were still low at the time,
he was also included.
Such was the grace and favor he received.
In the first year of *Tàiqīng* (547 CE),
he died,
at the age of thirty-seven.
*Gāozǔ* mourned and lamented his loss.
He issued an edict written by his own hand, saying:
“The Palace Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and Manager of Secretarial Affairs, *Lù Yún Gōng*,
was highly refined in demeanor and intelligent,
a distinguished talent among the younger generation.
His sudden passing and departure
truly causes deep sorrow.
A mourning ceremony shall be scheduled for a fixed day.
He is to be granted 50,000 cash for funeral expenses,
and forty bolts of cloth.”
*Zhāng Zǎn* was serving as the Administrator of *Xiāngzhōu* at the time.
He wrote a letter to *Yún Gōng*'s uncle *Xiāng* and his elder brother *Yànzǐ*, saying:
“The capital’s messenger arrived,
and I learned that the Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, your virtuous nephew and virtuous younger brother, has perished.
It is not only your esteemed family that has lost a treasure,
but truly all men of understanding share this grief.
My heart aches with pain and regret,
and I cannot stop.
Your virtuous nephew and virtuous younger brother displayed divine spirit and temperament early in life,
distinguished and excellent even in youth.
Whatever passed before his eyes,
scarcely required a second inquiry.
Carrying oranges and embracing plums,
this character originated from his natural disposition;
sitting arrogantly upon stacked firewood,
did not rely on external praise.
When he gathered knowledge through study,
he could immediately establish [the core point];
when questioned to differentiate things,
he mastered the concepts in his mind and understood them independently.
Just as he passed the age of youth,
his rhetorical and artistic skills were fully fluent and harmonious.
Among the many scholars rising and falling [in rank],
he was a brilliant leader in the stream of poetry.
Upon meeting, though there was a difference in age and rank, we walked shoulder-to-shoulder,
abandoning formal bowing ceremonies.
Our feelings and minds were mutually compatible,
forgetting the difference in years and conventional obligations.
We spent mornings strolling and evenings feasting,
continuing like this for a year.
We enjoyed antiquity and reviewed texts,
from dawn until dusk.
Acquaintances known throughout my life
have gradually scattered and disappeared.
How many of them remain in this old man's memory?
The number is scarce.
But regarding this person,
how could one ever miss him?
Joyful hearts and pleasurable affairs
were entrusted to him.
When I was transferred to a post in *Xiāo* and *Xiāng*,
I moored my boat at the bend of the *Luò* River.
Just as we were about to separate,
our intimacy and sincerity became even more apparent.
That evening, stopping near the Imperial Suburb,
we quickly stayed for a night or two.
We lingered, holding hands,
reluctant to part upon taking divergent roads.
In the several years of official travel,
I have been invaded and afflicted by travel sickness.
My awareness and thoughts have become blurred and indistinct,
and I have long been cut off from the world.
Leaning on a table, I dictate orally,
as I intrinsically lack the skill [to write smoothly].
My brush moves like flying,
and I feel much more ashamed.
My old friends from travels in *Jīng* and *Luò*
have all become like clouds and rain.
Only with this person,
did letters and news follow intermittently.
Beyond external appearance and traces,
distance did not separate our affection.
Within the depths of our hearts,
how could the wind and frost change our commitment?
Having served as a guest official for half a cycle,
my intention is focused on returning home.
I look forward daily to returning east,
to renew our former intimacy.
How can it be that this parting
has permanently separated us into different worlds!
At the beginning of our separation,
who can guarantee their own survival?
I only feared that I, in my decline,
would not fulfill our future engagement.
I did not expect that you, in the flower of your age,
would cover your body while still in spring.
The regret of burying jade,
is profound as I reflect on the matter.
I think of the emotion involved in introducing him [to the court],
and how deeply sincere my feelings were.
The relationship between you brothers [and nephew] was profound,
and he was also a deep treasure to your family.
Having suffered this sudden calamity,
what words can possibly express it?
As I write, my sadness increases,
and my words have become disorganized.”
*Yún Gōng*'s cousin, *Cáizǐ*,
also had a reputation for talent.
He successively held the posts of *Zhōngshū Láng* and Advisor to the Prince of *Xuānchéng*,
Internal Attendant to the Crown Prince (*Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ*),
and Minister of the Court of Judicial Review (*Tíngwèi Qīng*).
He died before *Yún Gōng*.
The collected works of *Cáizǐ* and *Yún Gōng*
are both circulated in the world.
*Rèn Xiàogōng*, whose courtesy name was *Xiàogōng*,
was a native of *Línhuái* in *Línhuái*.
His great-grandfather, *Nóngfū*,
was the Inspector of *Nányùzhōu* during the Sòng [Dynasty].
*Xiàogōng* was orphaned young.
He was renowned for his filial piety in serving his mother.
He studied diligently with all his energy.
His family was poor and lacked books,
so he constantly struggled to borrow them from others.
Every time he read a book once,
he was able to recite it with almost nothing omitted.
His maternal grandfather, *Qiū Tuō*,
was an old acquaintance of *Gāozǔ*.
*Gāozǔ*, hearing that he possessed talent and learning,
summoned him to the Western Palace Section to compile history.
He was initially *Fèng Cháoqǐng*.
He was promoted to serve in the *Shòuguāng Shěng*,
and became *Sīwén Shìláng*.
Soon after, he concurrently served as *Zhōngshū Tōngshì Shèrén*.
He was ordered to compose the inscription for the stūpa base of *Jiànlíng Sì* Temple.
He also memorialized to compile the preface to the collected works of *Gāozǔ*.
Both works were rich and splendid.
From then on, he was solely in charge of official documents and writing for the Imperial family.
*Xiàogōng*'s writing was rapid and quick.
Upon receiving an edict, he immediately completed it,
as if he hadn't given it much thought.
Every time he presented a memorial,
*Gāozǔ* invariably praised it.
He was repeatedly rewarded with gold and silk.
In his youth, *Xiàogōng* studied Buddhist scriptures and treatises under the Dharma Master *Yún* at *Xiāosì* Temple.
He understood Buddhist principles.
By this time, he ate only vegetables and upheld the precepts,
believing and accepting them very sincerely.
However, his nature was somewhat self-aggrandizing.
He valued himself above others due to his talent and ability.
Among his contemporaries, he often showed disregard for many,
and the world therefore thought little of this aspect of him.
In the second year of *Tàiqīng* (548 CE),
when *Hóu Jǐng* invaded and pressed upon the capital,
*Xiàogōng* memorialized to recruit troops,
and followed *Xiāo Zhèngdé*,
to garrison the southern bank.
When the rebels arrived,
*Zhèngdé* led his troops to join the rebels.
*Xiàogōng* returned and rushed to the Palace,
but the Palace gates were already shut.
He then fled into the Eastern Administration.
Soon after, [the Eastern Administration] was attacked by the rebels.
When the city fell, he was killed.
His collected works are circulated in the world.
was a native of Línyí, Lángxié.
His ancestor of the seventh generation, Hán,
was during the Jìn Dynasty a Shìzhōng, Guózǐ Jìjiǔ, and the Jìng Hóu of Xīpíng.
His father, Jiànyuǎn,
was broadly learned and possessed moral integrity.
Originally,
when Emperor Hé of Qí was garrisoned in Jīngzhōu,
he appointed Jiànyuǎn as Lùshì Cānjūn.
When Emperor Hé ascended the throne at Jiānglíng,
he made him Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ,
and soon after, concurrently Zhōngchéng.
When Gāozǔ received the abdication (of the Qí dynasty),
Jiànyuǎn refused to eat,
and died of indignation a few days later.
When Gāozǔ heard this, he said:
"I ascended according to Heaven's mandate and the will of the people.
How does this concern the scholars and officials of the realm?
Yet Yán Jiànyuǎn went so far as to do this!"
Xié was orphaned in childhood
and raised by his maternal uncle’s family.
In his youth, he was praised for his talent and character.
He extensively studied all the classics
and excelled in cursive and clerical scripts.
He first received office as Chángshì of the Kingdom of Xiāngdōng Wáng,
and also concurrently served as Jìshì of the administration.
When Shìzǔ left to garrison Jīngzhōu,
Xié was transferred and promoted to Chief Jìshì.
At that time, Gù Xié of Wú Jùn was also in the princely residence,
sharing the same name as Yán Xié.
Their talents and learning were nearly equal,
and the staff within the administration referred to them as
"The Two Xié."
When his maternal uncle, Xiè Jiǎn of Chén Jùn, died,
Xié, owing to the kindness of having been raised by him,
observed the mourning rites usually reserved for paternal uncles,
which was highly regarded by commentators.
Furthermore, moved by the loyal integrity of his family,
he did not seek prominence and advancement.
He consistently declined official summonses and nominations,
contenting himself with serving only in the princely administration.
In the fifth year of Dàtóng (539 CE),
he died,
at the age of forty-two.
Shìzǔ greatly lamented his loss
and composed a "Poem of Nostalgia" to mourn him.
One stanza reads:
"Hóngdū possessed great grace,
Indeed, he contained both flower and fruit.
The wild goose’s progress had yet to ascend,
Superior talent lingered in a minor post."
The five chapters of the *Jìn Xiān Zhuàn* (Records of the Immortals of Jìn)
and the two volumes of the *Rìyuè Zāiyì Tú* (Charts of Celestial and Calamitous Portents) compiled by Xié,
were destroyed in a fire.
He had two sons: Zhīyí,
and Zhītuī.
Both gained fame early.
Zhītuī,
served during the Chéngshèng period, reaching the posts of Zhèngyuán Láng and Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Yáo Chá, Lìbù Shàngshū of the Chén Dynasty, said: Emperor Wén of Wèi asserted that among literary men of antiquity,
few were able to completely preserve their reputation and integrity.
Why is this?
Literature, when subtly expressing one's nature and spirit,
and uniquely extracting one's emotions,
easily leads to slighting one's peers
and inevitably generates arrogance and ostentation.
In major cases, it results in disrespecting nobles and rulers;
in minor cases, it leads to scorn for one's colleagues.
Envy is quickly aroused and slander follows,
and the trouble originates from this.
As for the banishment of Qū and Jiǎ,
and the dismissal of Huán and Féng,
this was not unique to any single generation;
it was surely the calamity brought on by relying on one's own talent.
When scholars encounter an age of enlightenment and refinement,
and display gorgeous literary phrases,
they face no fear of suppression
and do not suffer the troubles of former times.
This is wonderful.
As for the critique by Mister Liú,
it is merely about fate.
As for fate,
the Sages rarely speak of it.
To insist upon it and make it definite
is not the true meaning of the Classics.
Biographies Section 45: Recluses. Hé Diǎn (Younger brother Yìn) Ruan Xiàoxù, Táo Hóngjǐng, Zhūgě Qú, Shěn Yǐ, Liú Huìfěi, Fàn Yuányǎn, Liú Xū, Liú Xiāo, Yǔ Shēn, Zhāng Xiàoxiù, Yǔ Chéngxiān.
The *Yì* (Classic of Changes) states:
"The noble man, retiring from the world, feels no regret,
and standing alone, he feels no fear."
Confucius referred to Cháng Jù and Jié Nì as recluses.
The recluses of antiquity
either felt ashamed merely to hear of dynastic abdication,
or highly declined invitations from emperors and kings,
regarding the rule of the ten thousand chariots (the Empire) as defilement and disgrace,
and went to death without regret.
These men valued the Way over life,
and rarely appeared in the world;
they are the highest class of recluses.
Others accepted office as gatekeepers
or served beneath the pillar (as archivists),
remaining calm and thereby fulfilling their ambitions,
dwelling in defilement without shame on their faces.
This is what is called "the great recluse hiding in the marketplace or court,"
which is the next rank down.
Others exposed their bodies and feigned madness,
acted as if blind or mute, isolating themselves from the world,
abandoned rites and music in order to revert to the Way,
and restrained filiality and compassion without concern.
These preserved their lives and avoided harm,
having attained the Way of great propriety;
this is yet the next rank down.
Nevertheless, all equally preserved the essence of speaking or remaining silent,
possessing the virtue of the quiet, upright person.
How can they be mentioned in the same breath
as those who bury themselves in a chaotic age, striving for gain and courting influence?
They certainly cannot be discussed together!
Mèngzǐ said:
"For people today, regarding rank and emolument,
obtaining them is like living,
and losing them is like dying."
The *Huáinánzǐ* states:
"People all look into still water for a mirror,
not into flowing, murky water."
Those who can raise the pure and stir up the turbid,
and suppress greed and halt contention—
surely these are the recluses!
Since ancient times, emperors and kings
have invariably revered their Way.
Even Táng Yáo could not compel Cháo and Xǔ,
and King Wǔ of Zhōu could not make Yí and Qí surrender.
Emperor Gāo of Hàn, despite his indulgence and arrogance, bowed deferentially to Huáng and Qǐ.
Emperor Guāngwǔ, while adhering to the law, yielded to the wishes of Yán and Zhōu.
From this time forward,
the world has had such people.
During the flourishing period of the Liáng Dynasty,
this virtuous practice was continued and inherited.
These are men whose virtue can be revered
and whose learning and skills can serve as models.
Therefore, they are included in the section on Recluses.
Hé Diǎn, courtesy name Zǐ,
was a native of Qián, Lújiāng.
His grandfather, Shàngzhī,
was Sīkōng of the Sòng Dynasty.
His father, Shuò,
was the Administrator of Yídū.
Shuò had long suffered from a nervous disorder (or paralysis);
he killed his wife without cause
and was executed by law.
When Diǎn was eleven years old,
he nearly died of grief.
When he grew up,
affected by the family tragedy,
he wished to reject marriage and official career.
Shàngzhī forcibly arranged a marriage for him to a woman from the Wáng clan of Lángxié.
After the ritual was completed
and he was about to proceed with the welcoming of the bride,
Diǎn wept profusely,
asking to uphold his original resolve,
and consequently the marriage was called off.
His appearance was dignified and refined;
he was thoroughly versed in all the classics
and skilled in discussion.
His family was originally a major clan,
and many of his relatives and in-laws were high officials.
Although Diǎn did not enter the city government,
he wandered freely among men.
He wore neither hairpins nor belts (i.e., informal attire),
sometimes driving a simple wooden cart,
wearing straw sandals,
allowing his heart to go where it pleased,
returning home only after becoming drunk.
Many scholars and officials admired and followed him.
People at the time called him
"The Open Recluse" (Tōngyǐn).
His elder brother, Qiú,
also lived as a recluse on Hǔqiū Shān in Wú Jùn.
When Qiú died,
Diǎn ate only vegetables and abstained from alcohol
for the entire three years,
and his waist size was reduced by half.
Towards the end of the Sòng Tàishǐ era,
Hè Diǎn was summoned to serve as tàizǐ xǐmǎ;
In the beginning of the Qí Dynasty,
he was repeatedly summoned to serve as zhōngshū láng and tàizǐ zhōngshùzǐ: but he accepted none of them.
He was the closest of friends with Xiè Fěi of Chénjùn, Zhāng Róng of Wúguó, and Kǒng Zhìguī of Kuàijī.
His paternal younger cousin, Hè Dùn,
lived in a garden with a thatched gate,
and Kǒng Zhìguī built a dwelling for him there.
Inside the garden was the tomb of Biàn Zhōngzhēn,
and Hè Diǎn planted flowers beside the tomb.
Every time he drank, he would surely pour out a libation for him.
Previously,
when Chǔ Yuān and Wáng Jiǎn served as chief ministers,
Hè Diǎn said to people:
“I wrote the appraisal for the *Qí Shū Zàn*,
saying, ‘Chǔ Yuān is indeed from a noble clan,
and Wáng Jiǎn is also a glory of the state;
if they do not rely on their maternal relatives,
how can they care for the nation?’ ”
Wáng Jiǎn heard of this,
and wished to visit Hè Diǎn,
but knowing he could not be seen,
he refrained.
Yùzhāng Wáng Yí ordered his carriage to visit Hè Diǎn,
but Hè Diǎn escaped through the back gate.
The Minister of Education, Jìnglíng Wáng Zǐliáng, wished to meet him,
and Hè Diǎn was at Fǎlún Sì at the time.
Zǐliáng then went and invited him.
Hè Diǎn wore a simple head cloth and ascended the mat (seat).
Zǐliáng was endlessly delighted,
and presented Hè Diǎn with the wine cup of Jī Shúyè
and the wine warming vessel of Xú Jǐngshān.
When Hè Diǎn was young, he once suffered from thirst and dysentery,
which accumulated over years without healing.
Later, while holding lectures at Shífó Sì in Wúzhōng,
he slept during the day in the lecture hall,
and dreamed of a Taoist figure whose appearance was extraordinary,
who gave him a handful of pills.
He consumed them in the dream,
and was cured from that point onward.
People at the time believed this was due to the influence of his pure virtue.
His nature was unrestrained and open,
and he loved to give things away.
Gifts were brought to him from near and far,
none of which he refused,
but he immediately redistributed them.
Once, while traveling through Zhūquè Mén Jiē,
someone stole Hè Diǎn’s robe from behind his carriage.
He saw it but did not speak.
A bystander seized the thief and handed him over.
Hè Diǎn then gave the robe to the thief as a gift.
The thief dared not accept it.
Hè Diǎn ordered someone to report the matter to the authorities.
The thief, fearing this,
then accepted it,
and Hè Diǎn urged him to leave quickly.
Hè Diǎn possessed refined judgment of human character,
and selected and promoted many people.
He recognized Qiū Chí of Wúxīng when he was a mere youth,
and praised Jiāng Yān of Jìyáng despite his humble background.
Everything happened exactly as he predicted.
When Hè Diǎn was old,
he also married the daughter of Kǒng Sì of Lǔguó;
Kǒng Sì was also a recluse.
Although Hè Diǎn married,
he did not meet with his wife.
He built a separate house for her to live in,
and no one could understand his intention.
When Zhāng Róng of Wúguó was young, he lost his official post,
and wrote poetry containing lofty and noble sentiments.
Hè Diǎn replied with a poem, saying:
“In former days when I heard of the Eastern Capital,
it was not before receiving the official letter.”
Although this was a joke,
Zhāng Róng was bothered by it for a long time.
When Hè Diǎn married later,
Zhāng Róng finally wrote a poem presenting it to Hè Diǎn, saying:
“Alas, Layman Hé,
at dusk encounters debauchery.”
Hè Diǎn was also bothered by this,
but had no way to explain it away.
Gāozǔ had a previous friendship with Hè Diǎn.
When he ascended the throne,
he issued a handwritten decree, saying:
“In the past, due to abundant leisure,
I was able to visit your secluded path.
Sitting among the tall bamboo,
overlooking the clear pond,
forgetting the present and discussing the past—
what great joy that was!
I have been briefly separated from your garden dwelling
for fourteen years.
The difficulties and obstacles of human affairs
are indescribable.
Since receiving the mandate of Heaven,
I have constantly thought of seeing you.
Though objects and forms are close at hand,
my toil is heavy in the mountain retreat (palace).
Yán Guāng thrust aside the nine layers of palace guards,
stepped through the nine grades (of rank),
spoke of Heaven and man,
and as an old friend,
refused to be subservient.
How did this harm his loftiness?
Wénxiān visited Zǐhuán wearing a leather cap,
and Bókuàng met Wénshū wearing fine gauze.
If one searches through past records,
there is no lack of prior examples.
I now bestow upon you a deer-skin cap and other items.
In a few days,
I hope you can come in.”
Hè Diǎn wore the cap and common clothing and was led into Huálín Yuán.
Gāozǔ was extremely pleased,
composed poems and set out wine,
treating him with the same favor and courtesy as before.
He then issued a further decree, saying:
“The former Gentleman-Recruited Hè Diǎn
holds his way in high esteem,
his ambition rests comfortably in a small space,
he sheds concern for his physical body,
and his spirit dwells in obscurity.
When I consider governing, even when the sun is setting,
I still think of former sages;
how much more so since I personally have him in my time,
and yet he does not join in governance.
The duties of my voice and lips are crucial,
and I must await the wise men of the state.
I sincerely hope that you will kindly comply
and deign to offer advice and suggestions.
He may be recruited as Shìzhōng.”
He declined, citing illness, and did not go.
A further decree was then issued, saying:
“Gentleman-Recruited Hè Diǎn
maintains his integrity beyond worldly affairs,
giving free rein to his spirit outside the dust,
and his manner of easy detachment
comes naturally from afar.
In the past, based on long-held aspirations,
he gave numerous eloquent opinions,
and in looking upon Zǐlíng,
my feelings combine contemplation of the past.
In the past, Zhòng Yú rose above the common world
yet received a stipend from the Hàn court;
Āndào maintained his aloof ambition
yet did not refuse the stipend of the Jìn Dynasty.
These were the great patterns of former generations,
shared by past worthy men.
It should be discussed how to increase his stipend and provisions,
all of which should be delivered to his dwelling.
Whatever daily expenses he requires,
the Imperial Kitchen will provide separately.
Since he is a man of high esteem, let him
by precedent be treated as an official of the court.”
, he died
, at the age of sixty-eight
. An imperial edict stated
: “Hé Diǎn
, the recently appointed Shìzhōng, lived reclusively in the mountains and streams
, and did not change his convictions even in old age
. His sudden demise
causes us double grief and sorrow
. He shall be granted one set of wood materials of the first grade
, twenty thousand in funeral money (fù qián)
, and fifty rolls of cloth
. All matters required for the funeral
shall be managed by the Palace Supervisor (Nèijiān)
.” The Emperor further instructed Diǎn’s
younger brother, Yìn
, withdrew from official life in his youth (ruò guàn)
, maintaining a single principle until his hair turned white
. His heart wandered beyond worldly matters
, and he was not mired in recent trends
; he cast off the restraints of the physical body (xíng hái)
and entrusted himself to profound philosophy (yuǎn lǐ)
. His temperament and disposition achieved excellence
, and when moved by inspiration, his spirit soared higher
; in literary gatherings and in the virtue of wine
, his contemplation spanned distant realms
. When We received the mandate (lù) and the charts (tú)
, We considered expanding our renown and moral influence (shēng jiào)
. The court is filled with noble men (jūn zǐ)
, and it is essential that the honored ones establish refined customs
; in the countryside there are outside officials (wài chén)
, and it is fitting to promote those who are difficult to summon
. We were relying on his pure prestige (qīng huī)
to properly elevate Our great endeavor
. In the past, when he was still a commoner (bù yī)
, Our affectionate regard was established early
; We provided him with the rank of Zhòng Yú
and treated him with the courtesy accorded to Zǐ Líng
. During breaks from governance and reading
, We would summon him, wearing a horned cap (jué jīn)
, and speak profoundly of the Fén and Shè
regions, entrusting Our thoughts to him
. Now that he has suddenly departed for eternity (wàn gǔ)
, Our heart is truly struck with grief
. You, Sir (Qīng), possess pure and deep fraternal devotion
; now that your relative has passed away
, the wish to grow old together (xié lǎo)
has been unexpectedly snatched away
. The lingering, eternal sorrow
is unbearable
. Alas, eternally departed! How can this be borne
!” Diǎn
had no son. Members of his clan designated Chí Rèn
, the son of his paternal cousin Gěng
Yìn

and Zhōu Yóng
as a Mìshū Láng

, and they would return according to schedule
. He entered court service as a Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng

and also provided explanations for the *Lǐjì*

received an imperial command to compile the New Rites (Xīn Lǐ)
. The task was then assigned to Tèjìn Zhāng Xù
to continue and finish it
also died

were appointed to assist Yìn

, he was promoted to Shìzhōng

was related to the Empress’s clan (hòu zú)

was high-ranking and prominent
. Early in Jiànwǔ

. By this time

had resigned from Wúxīng Jùn

and left immediately without waiting for a reply
. Emperor Míng

on Ruòyé Shān

two elder brothers, Qiú
had died first
