as Dàshān (Great Mountain)
was called Xiǎoshān (Small Mountain)
During the Yǒngyuán period
, he was summoned for the posts of Tàicháng
and Tàizǐ Zhānshì
, but he accepted neither
. When Gāozǔ
established his Princely Headquarters (Bà Fǔ)
to serve as Jūnmóu Jìjiǔ
: “I imagine your purity and comfort
, indulging your feelings in the forests and valleys
, which brings great joy
. Since you have internally ceased the battle of the heart
and externally ended the toil of material service
, you nourish harmony through the Way
, and your conduct is flawless
. Ruòyé
commands the beauty of the eastern region
, praised by former generations
, making it a land of pleasure (lè tǔ)
. I was transferred to minor official posts
, moving from the East to the West
. When Our words of understanding regarding philosophy failed to meet
, it resulted in separation and rupture
. I incline my head and look east
; there is no day when I do not think of you
. In our past joyful encounters
, dragging our robes in scholarly circles
, I truly wished to mentally wander (wò yóu) through a thousand years
and hunt and fish among the hundred schools
. Once I began serving as an official
, this aspiration was thwarted
. Because the way of the world has fallen into crisis
and still suffers from calamity and tribulation
, I have thrown up my sleeves many thousands of times
, determined to suppress disaster and misfortune
. I thought I could look through scrolls and discuss philosophy
, placing my feelings in antiquity
—how could I not harbor this thought
? But events have forced my wishes to diminish
. Your pure heart has a modest reliance
, and your dwelling place is far from the mundane
; dwelling amidst the human world
, you are practically a recluse
. You both readily picked up the green cord (symbolizing official rank)
and then cast aside the crimson robes (zhū fú)
. However, principle lies in knowing when to serve and when to withdraw
, and righteousness values adapting to the times
. Your recognition of the beginnings of disaster in the past
truly made you a forerunner
; your aloofness and personal virtue
were admired and sighed over by the perceptive
. Now that We govern the state (bāng)
, poverty and low status are things all should be ashamed of
, and loving benevolence depends on oneself
. Fortunately, there should be no stagnation
. I will write separately
; this letter does not say everything
. I now send a messenger to await and receive news from you
, raising his head and returning with your brushstrokes (letter)
, which will comfort my anxious waiting
.” Yìn
did not come
Gāo Zǔ ascended the throne,
and issued an edict appointing [Yìn] as Tè Jìn and Yòu Guānglù Dàfū.
The handwritten imperial mandate said:
"I have humbly inherited the mandate of the era,
accepting this joyous elevation,
yet I look upon myself as obscured and unlearned,
ignorant concerning the principles of governance.
Although I toil until the sun sets,
hoping to achieve great peace,
the enduring standards of the former kings
are still hidden in strategies and texts,
and the methods for flourishing or declining
depend on the right person.
Moreover, the ways of the world are shallow and declining,
with conflicts and deceptions constantly arising.
To reform customs and change trends
is truly not easy.
If one does not rely on refined scholarship to expand the court,
and use loftiness to guide people,
then where the muddied current flows,
no one knows its limit.
Governing others versus governing oneself,
maintaining personal virtue versus benefiting the world:
in choosing what to gain and what to lose,
which is the more useful path?
Although I am not learned,
I quite enjoy broad ancient knowledge;
I still long for lofty ideals,
and I often feel admiration.
Now that affairs of state are chaotic,
and worry and responsibility must be borne,
I cannot but ask you to temporarily relinquish your retreat in the mountains
to jointly establish the nation's excellence.
I truly hope you deeply understand my past intentions
and do not begrudge getting your feet wet.
I now dispatch Wáng Guǒ, the Commander of the Army (Lǐngjūn Sīmǎ), to proclaim this edict and convey my intent.
I anticipate meeting you soon."
When Wáng Guǒ arrived,
Yìn, wearing simple clothes and a deer-skin turban,
holding a classical scroll,
descended from his couch and knelt to receive the imperial edict,
then sat down on his mat and prostrated himself while reading it.
Yìn subsequently addressed Wáng Guǒ, saying:
"When I was previously at the Qí Cháo, I intended to present two or three matters.
Firstly, I wished to correct the suburban altars (jiāoqīu).
Secondly, I wished to recast the Nine Tripods (jiǔ dǐng).
Thirdly, I wished to erect twin gate towers (quē).
Tradition holds that when the Jìn Shì wished to erect gate towers,
Chéngxiàng Wáng pointed to Niútóu Shān and said, 'This is the Gate Tower of Heaven (tiān quē),'
but this failed to clarify the true meaning of erecting gate towers.
The gate tower (quē)
is called Xiàng Wèi.
One hangs emblems of law upon it,
and takes them down after a full day.
Xiàng (Emblem)
means Law (fǎ);
Wèi (Tower)
means the appearance of being tall and great along the roadside.
The tripods (dǐng) are spiritual vessels,
prioritized by those who possess a state.
Therefore, when Wángsūn Mǎn spoke critically about them,
the Viscount of Chǔ (Chǔ Zǐ) immediately stopped boasting.
The Round Mound (yuánqiū) and the suburban sacrifice (guójiāo)
were traditionally distinct rites.
The Southern Suburban Sacrifice (Nánjiāo) worships the Five Emperors, Línɡ Wēiyǎnɡ, and similar spirits,
while the Round Mound worships the Heavenly Grand Emperor (Tiānhuáng Dàdì) and the Great North Star.
Former generations combining them into the jiāoqīu
was a great error made by earlier Confucians.
Now that the Liáng Dé has announced its beginning,
it should not continue this former mistake.
You should go to the palace and present these matters."
Wáng Guǒ replied:
"I am humble and inferior;
how dare I lightly discuss the national rites?
This should properly await Shūsūn Shēng."
Yìn said:
"Why don't you send the messenger who brought the edict back to court to report,
and stay here to travel with me?"
Wáng Guǒ was astonished and said:
"Such a precedent has never been heard of, neither anciently nor presently."
Yìn said:
"The two chapters of the Tán Gōng
both discuss the beginning of things.
If it begins with you,
why must there be a precedent?"
Wáng Guǒ said:
"If you are now determined to remain aloof from the world,
is there still any possibility that you might dedicate yourself to service?"
Yìn said:
"You merely judge me by the duties imposed.
I am already fifty-seven years old.
Four *dǒu* of rice per month is more than I can eat.
How can I possibly harbor any desire for officialdom?
Previously I received recognition from the enlightened ruler,
and now I am again honored by this grand summons.
I very much wish to go to the palace to express my gratitude;
but recently my waist and legs have become severely debilitated,
so this wish cannot be fulfilled."
Wáng Guǒ returned
and reported Yìn's sentiments to the throne.
An imperial mandate was issued granting him the stipend of a Shàngshū in plain clothes (Báiyī Shàngshū Lù),
but Yìn firmly declined.
A further edict ordered that he be given 50,000 cash monthly from the Shān Yīn treasury,
but Yìn again refused to accept it.
Thereupon an edict was sent to Yìn, saying:
"Recently, scholarship has fallen into decay,
and the ways of Confucianism are nearly exhausted.
Among the gentry and officials in the villages,
few good deeds are heard of.
I always consider how to promote and encourage them,
yet the trend has not shifted.
Sitting by the screen, I frequently sigh in regret.
I originally intended to ask you to temporarily emerge
to guide the younger generation.
Since you are now suffering from infirmity,
this desire remains unfulfilled,
and the weariness of waiting
fills my dreams.
I have prepared a boat with an empty seat,
and must wait until the coming autumn.
I hope that you will graciously fulfill your long-held aspirations.
Among your disciples, how many
are proficient in the Classics and of sound conduct?
I wish to observe these towering talents
and place them in official positions.
You should immediately report their names fully,
to fulfill my diligent expectations."
[The edict] also said:
"In recent years, scholars have become extremely few,
truly because there are no longer gatherings of disciples;
thus, knowledge of the Classics has been abandoned.
Whenever I think of this,
I am filled with emotion.
You are the head of the Confucian school,
and possess intrinsic virtue.
You should instruct those among the younger generation who are motivated
to come to you to receive instruction.
I imagine you will profoundly consider guiding and teaching them,
so that this culture may once again flourish."
Consequently, Hé Zǐlǎng, Kǒng Shòu, and six other individuals were sent to Dōng Shān to receive instruction.
The Administrator (Tàishǒu), Héngyáng Wáng Yuán Jiǎn, showed him profound respect,
often ordering his carriage mid-month to ceremonially stop before Yìn's gate,
discussing matters all day long.
Yìn considered the location of Ruò Xié to be restricted and narrow,
not accommodating his disciples,
so he moved to Qín Wàng Shān.
The mountain had a flying spring;
he built his academy westward,
using the trees for reinforcement,
and relying on the cliff face for walls.
He set apart a small, private chamber,
where he slept and resided.
He personally locked and unlocked the door;
servants and attendants were not permitted to enter.
He cultivated two *qǐng* of land on the mountain side,
and during breaks from lecturing, he would go there with his disciples.
When Yìn first moved
and was about to build his dwelling,
he suddenly saw two men wearing black caps,
whose appearance was very imposing.
They asked Yìn:
"Do you intend to live here?"
Then they pointed to a location and said:
"This spot is extremely auspicious."
Suddenly they were no longer visible,
and Yìn settled there according to their words.
Soon after, the mountain experienced a great flood;
trees and rocks were all uprooted,
but only the room where Yìn resided remained standing firmly and alone.
Yuán Jiǎn therefore ordered Zhōng Róng, the Secretary and Aide (Jìshì Cānjūn), to compose the Ruì Shì Sòng (Ode to the Auspicious Dwelling),
and had it carved on stone to commemorate the event.
When Yuán Jiǎn left the commandery,
he entered the mountain to bid Yìn farewell.
Yìn accompanied him to Dū Cì Dài,
three *lǐ* away from the commandery.
Thereupon he said:
"Since I abandoned worldly affairs,
the path of socializing has been broken.
If it were not for a noble person descending into the mountain wilds,
how could I possibly look upon the city again?
This journey to the dike
ends now, never to be repeated."
They clasped hands and shed tears.
Hé clan crossed the river,
and starting with Chōng, who was Sīkōng of the Jìn dynasty, they were all buried at Xīshān in Wú.
Yìn's family members generally did not live to old age,
only his grandfather, Shàngzhī, reached seventy-two.
When Yìn reached the age his grandfather had lived to,
he then relocated back to Wú,
composing a poem titled "Farewell to the Mountain,"
the words being extremely melancholy.
Arriving in Wú,
he resided at the Western Temple on Hǔqiū, lecturing on sūtras and treatises;
his students followed him again.
Governors and magistrates in the eastern region who traveled through
all came to visit him.
Yìn regularly prohibited killing.
A hunter was once chasing a deer;
the deer ran straight toward Yìn,
lay prostrate, and did not move.
Moreover, there was a strange, crane-like bird,
red in color,
which gathered in the lecture hall,
becoming tame and familiar like a domestic fowl.
Previously,
Fǎshī Zàng of Kāishàn Sì had met Yìn at Qínwàng.
Later, Fǎshī Zàng returned to the capital
and died at Zhōngshān.
On the day he died,
Yìn was at Bānruò Sì
and saw a monk who presented Yìn with an incense burner, a cosmetic box, and a case containing writings,
saying,
"Present this to Jūshì Hé."
Having spoken, the monk vanished.
Yìn opened the case;
it was the Dàzhuāngyán Lùn,
which did not yet exist in the world.
Furthermore, he erected a luminous pearl pillar within the temple,
which then emitted light for seven days and seven nights.
The Grand Administrator, Hé Yuǎn, reported this phenomenon in a memorial.
Prince Zhāomíng Tàizǐ admired his virtue,
and sent the attendant Hé Sīchéng to deliver a handwritten decree to praise him.
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he died,
aged eighty-six.
Before this, Yìn had been ill.
His wife, née Jiāng, dreamed a divine being told her:
"Your husband's lifespan is finished;
since he possesses profound virtue,
he ought to gain an extension of life.
You must take his place."
His wife woke up and recounted the dream,
and shortly thereafter fell ill and died.
Yìn's illness subsequently recovered.
When the time of his death came, Yìn dreamed of a divine woman,
along with about eighty people,
all dressed in caps,
who lined up and came forward.
They all bowed beneath his bed.
He woke up and saw them again,
and immediately ordered the preparation of funerary equipment.
Soon after, his illness flared up,
and he did not attempt to cure it.
Yìn annotated the Bǎifǎ Lùn and the Shí'èrmén Lùn, each in one scroll;
annotated the Zhōu Yì in ten scrolls;
the Máoshī Zǒngjí in six scrolls;
the Máoshī Yǐnyì in ten scrolls;
the Lǐjì Yǐnyì in twenty scrolls;
and the Lǐ Dáwèn in fifty-five scrolls.
His son, Zhuàn,
also did not seek office.
The Prince of Lúlíng appointed him as Chief Clerk,
but he did not take the position.
Ruǎn Xiàoxù, courtesy name Shìzōng,
was a native of Wèishì, Chénliú.
His father, Yànzhī,
was the Attendant Officer to the Grand Commandant of the Sòng dynasty.
When Xiàoxù was seven,
he was adopted by his paternal uncle, Yìnzhī.
Yìnzhī’s mother, née Zhōu, died,
leaving property worth over a million (coins),
which ought to have gone to Xiàoxù.
Xiàoxù accepted nothing,
giving it all to Yìnzhī’s elder sister, the mother of Wáng Yàn of Lángyé.
Those who heard of this all sighed in admiration.
As a child he was profoundly filial,
and his nature was reserved and quiet.
Although he played games with other children,
he found pleasure in digging ponds and building mounds.
At thirteen,
he had thoroughly mastered the Five Classics.
At fifteen,
he underwent the capping ceremony and went to see his father.
Yànzhī cautioned him, saying:
"The three capping rites confer ever-greater respect;
this is the commencement of human relations.
You should strive to encourage yourself
in order to protect your person."
He replied:
"I wish to follow the path of Sōng Zǐ across the vast oceans
and pursue Xǔyóu into the secluded valley,
hoping to preserve this fleeting life
and avoid worldly burdens."
From then on, he secluded himself in one room;
he never left his door except for the customary morning and evening greetings.
His family members rarely saw his face,
so his relatives and friends
called him "Jūshì."
His cousin Wáng Yàn was prominent and powerful,
and often came to his door.
Xiàoxù anticipated that Wáng Yàn would inevitably meet ruin,
so he consistently hid and refused to see him.
Once, he ate some fermented paste that tasted excellent.
When he asked about it,
he was told it had come from the Wáng family.
He immediately spat out what was in his mouth and covered the remaining relish with what he had chewed.
When Yàn was executed,
his relatives were all fearful for themselves.
Xiàoxù said:
"We are related but not faction members;
how can punishment affect us?"
In the end, he escaped implication.
When the Righteous Army besieged the capital,
his family was poor and had nothing to cook with.
His servants secretly stole firewood from a neighbor to keep the fire alight.
When Xiàoxù learned of this,
he refused to eat,
and instead ordered them to dismantle parts of the house for fuel.
The room where he lived contained only a wicker bed,
surrounded by bamboo and trees.
Early in the Tiānjiān era,
the Palace Censor-in-Chief Rèn Fǎng, while seeking his elder brother Lǚzhī,
intended to visit him but did not dare.
He looked from afar and sighed:
"Though his dwelling is near,
the man himself is distant."
Such was the admiration he received from famous contemporaries.
In the twelfth year,
he was summoned along with Fàn Yuányǎn of Wújùn,
but neither reported for duty.
Yuán Jùn of Chénjùn said to him:
"In earlier times,
Heaven and Earth were in chaos,
and worthy men concealed themselves.
Now the path of the world is clear,
yet you still hide away.
Is this permissible?"
He replied:
"Although the virtue of Zhōu flourished in the past,
Yí and Qí were not content to eat ferns and bracken.
When the Hàn dynasty was prosperous,
Huáng and Qǐ felt no regret dwelling in the mountains and forests.
The practice of benevolence rests with oneself.
What concern is it of the human world?
Furthermore, I am hardly comparable to those former worthies!"
Later, while he was listening to lectures at Zhōngshān,
his mother, née Wáng, suddenly became ill.
His brothers wished to summon him.
His mother said:
"Xiàoxù's profound nature communicates with the unseen realm;
he is certain to arrive on his own."
Sure enough, he became alarmed in his heart and returned.
The neighbors sighed in admiration.
To compound the medicine, fresh ginseng was required.
It was traditionally said to grow on Zhōngshān.
Xiàoxù personally traversed secluded and perilous areas,
but did not find it for several days.
Suddenly, he saw a deer walking ahead.
Xiàoxù felt inspired and followed it.
When they reached a certain place, the deer vanished.
He looked closely,
and indeed obtained the herb.
His mother was able to take the medicine
and consequently recovered.
People at the time all attributed this result to his power of filial devotion.
At that time, there was a skillful diviner, Zhāng Yǒudào (張有道), who said to Xiàoxù (孝緒):
"I see your reclusive traces, but your heart is difficult to discern.
Unless we examine it with tortoise shells and milfoil,
there's no way to verify it."
When he arranged the hexagrams,
after manipulating five changing lines,
he said:
"This will be Xián (咸), 'Influence/Wooing.'
It is the method of responsive interaction,
not a sign of auspicious retreat."
Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"How do you know that the later line won't become 'the ninth in the uppermost place'?"
Indeed, it formed the Dùn (遯) hexagram, 'Retreat.'
Yǒudào (有道) sighed and said:
"This is what is meant by 'A fat retreat, nothing that would not be advantageous.'
The image truly corresponds to virtue,
with both heart and traces aligned."
Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"Although I obtained the Dùn (遯) hexagram,
and the 'ninth in the uppermost place' line is not activated,
the path to ascension [to immortality]
means I should now highly decline and take leave, like Xǔ Shēng (許生)."
Thereupon, he composed the Gāoyǐn Chuán (高隱傳, 'Biographies of Lofty Recluses'),
starting from Yán (炎) and Huáng (黃),
and ending at the close of Tiānjiān (天監),
divided into three categories after careful deliberation,
totaling several *juàn* (卷).
He also wrote an essay which stated:
"The essence of the ultimate Way
lies in non-action (*wúwéi*);
the traces of the Sage
lie in alleviating evils.
Evils are alleviated through traces,
but the use of traces deviates from the essence;
since the essence is non-action,
action is not the ultimate of the Way.
However, if traces are not manifested,
then the world cannot be pacified;
if the essence is not thoroughly investigated,
then the Way is truly lost.
Qiū (丘) and Dàn (旦) sought to preserve their traces,
and thus should have temporarily obscured their essence;
Lǎo (老) and Zhuāng (莊) only clarified their essence,
and likewise should have deeply suppressed their traces.
Since traces can be suppressed,
this is why those few masters had something in excess;
since the essence was obscured,
Níqiū (尼丘) was therefore insufficient.
Those who do not grasp the One
lack that clear wisdom;
those who embody the Two
alone possess discerning insight.
[一０] However, the Sage, having reached the extreme of enlightenment,
instead initiated his traces;
the Worthy, not yet having attained the supreme position,
further spoke of his essence.
This is truly because traces are needed to save the world,
and none but a Sage can do it;
the essence truly clarifies principle,
and can be illuminated by the Worthy.
If one can embody this essence and traces,
and comprehend that suppression and elevation,
then the intentions of Kǒng (孔) and Zhuāng (莊)
would be more than half understood."
Nánpíng Yuánxiāng Wáng (南平元襄王) heard of his reputation,
and sent him a letter inviting him,
but he did not go.
Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"It's not that my ambition scorns wealth and status,
but rather my nature fears the imperial court.
If I could be harnessed,
how would I be different from a swift steed?"
Originally,
at the end of Jiànwǔ (建武),
the east gate of Qīngxī Gōng (青溪宮) collapsed inexplicably,
[一一] and a great wind uprooted the willow trees outside the east gate of the Eastern Palace.
Someone asked Xiàoxù (孝緒) about this,
and Xiàoxù (孝緒) said:
"Qīngxī (青溪) is the old imperial residence.
Qí (齊) corresponds to the element Wood;
the east is the position of Wood.
Now that the east gate has collapsed by itself,
Wood must be declining."
The consort of Póyáng Zhōngliè Wáng (鄱陽忠烈王)
was Xiàoxù's (孝緒) elder sister.
The king once ordered his carriage,
intending to visit him,
but Xiàoxù (孝緒) dug through the wall and fled,
ultimately refusing to see him.
His nephews would send gifts annually,
but he accepted none of them.
When people questioned him about it,
he replied:
"It was not my original wish,
therefore I do not accept it."
The stone statue he worshipped
had been damaged before,
and he wished to repair it.
One night, it was suddenly restored,
and everyone found it extraordinary.
In Dàtóng (大同) second year,
he died,
at the age of fifty-eight.
His disciples composed an elegy for his virtues and conduct,
posthumously naming him Wénzhēn Chǔshì (文貞處士).
His works, such as the Qī Lù (七錄) and others, comprising 250 *juàn* (卷),
circulated in the world.
Táo Hóngjǐng (陶弘景), courtesy name Tōngmíng (通明),
was a native of Mòlíng (秣陵) in Dānyáng (丹陽).
Initially,
his mother dreamt of a green dragon emerging from her bosom,
and also saw two celestial beings holding incense burners arriving at her place.
Afterwards, she became pregnant,
and subsequently gave birth to Hóngjǐng (弘景).
As a child, he had extraordinary conduct.
At the age of ten,
he obtained Gě Hóng's (葛洪) Shénxiān Chuán (神仙傳, 'Biographies of Immortals'),
which he studied day and night,
and thus developed the aspiration for nourishing life.
He said to people:
"Looking up at the azure clouds
and seeing the white sun,
I don't feel it's far."
When he grew up,
he was seven *chǐ* (尺) and four *cùn* (寸) tall,
with a brilliant and elegant divine demeanor,
bright eyes and sparse eyebrows,
a slender physique and long ears.
He read over ten thousand *juàn* (卷) of books.
He was skilled in playing the *qín* (琴)
and adept at cursive and clerical scripts.
Before he reached twenty,
Qí Gāodì (齊高帝) became chancellor,
and appointed him as tutor to the various princes,
bestowing upon him the title Fèng Cháoqǐng (奉朝請).
Although he was in a noble household,
he kept to himself and did not engage with external matters,
solely dedicating himself to reading.
Many matters of court protocol and historical precedents
were decided by him.
In Yǒngmíng (永明) tenth year,
he submitted a memorial resigning from his emolument,
and the emperor granted it,
bestowing upon him a bundle of silk.
When he departed,
dukes and ministers bid him farewell at the Zhēnglǔ Tíng (征虜亭),
with splendid tents and provisions,
and carriages and horses filling the roads.
Everyone said that since Sòng (宋) and Qí (齊),
there had been no such event.
Both court and commoners honored him.
Thereupon, he settled in Qūqǔ Shān (句曲山) in Jùróng (句容).
He said:
"Below this mountain is the Eighth Cave Palace,
named Jīntán Huáyáng Zhī Tiān (金壇華陽之天), 'Heaven of Jintan Huayang,'
with a circumference of 150 *lǐ* (里).
In ancient times during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, the three Máojūn (茅君) of Xiányáng (咸陽) attained the Dao,
and came to preside over this mountain,
hence it is called Máoshān (茅山)."
He then established a hermitage on the mountain
and styled himself Huáyáng Yǐnjū (華陽隱居, 'Recluse of Huayang').
He first received talismans, diagrams, scriptures, and methods from Sūn Yóuyuè (孫遊岳) of Dōngyáng (東陽).
He traveled throughout famous mountains,
searching for elixirs of immortality.
Whenever he passed through a ravine or valley,
he would surely sit or lie there,
reciting poetry and lingering,
unable to stop.
At that time, Shěn Yuē (沈約) was the Administrator of Dōngyáng Jùn (東陽郡),
and, respecting his lofty aspirations and integrity,
repeatedly sent letters inviting him,
but he did not come.
Hóngjǐng (弘景) was a man who was
adaptable and cautious,
his presence and reclusion perfectly aligned;
his mind was like a clear mirror,
grasping things as soon as they appeared,
his words never superfluous or contradictory,
and he always became aware of things.
In the Jiànwǔ (建武) era,
Qí Yídū Wáng Kēng (齊宜都王鏗) was killed by Míngdì (明帝).
That night,
Hóngjǐng (弘景) dreamt that Kēng (鏗) bid him farewell.
He then inquired about matters in the netherworld,
and Kēng (鏗) spoke extensively of various secrets and marvels.
Thus, he composed the Mèng Jì (夢記, 'Record of Dreams').
In the early Yuánwáng (永元) era,
he built a three-story tower.
Hóngjǐng (弘景) resided on the top floor,
his disciples in the middle,
and guests on the bottom floor,
thus completely isolating himself from others.
Only one family servant was allowed to attend him.
He particularly loved the sound of the wind in the pines,
and whenever he heard its rustling,
he would be filled with joy.
Sometimes he would wander alone among springs and rocks,
and those who saw him thought he was an immortal.
His nature delighted in writing,
he esteemed the unusual and strange,
he cherished every moment,
and as he grew old, he became even more diligent.
He was particularly adept at Yin-Yang and the Five Phases,
wind-direction analysis and star-counting,
mountains, rivers, and geography,
local produce,
medical arts, and materia medica.
He compiled "Dìdài Niánlì" (Chronicle of Imperial Reigns).
He also once constructed an armillary sphere,
saying,
"This is needed for cultivating the Dao,
not just for court historians."
When the righteous army pacified Jiànkāng,
and he heard discussions of abdicating the throne,
Hóngjǐng cited prognostic charts and oracles,
where in several places, the character
"Liáng"
was formed.
He ordered his disciples to present these.
Gāozǔ had already associated with him early on,
and after ascending the throne,
his favor and courtesy towards Hóngjǐng became even more profound.
Letters and inquiries never ceased,
and officials' carriages were constantly seen arriving.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (507 CE),
he moved to the eastern stream of Jījīn.
He was skilled in the methods of *bìgǔ* (abstention from grains) and *dǎoyǐn* (breathing exercises),
and though over eighty years old, he had the appearance of a strong man.
He deeply admired Zhāng Liáng's character,
saying,
"No ancient worthy can compare."
He once dreamed that the Buddha bestowed upon him a Bodhi prediction,
naming him Shènglì Púsà.
Thereupon, he went to the Ashoka Pagoda in Mào County and made a vow,
receiving the Five Great Precepts.
Later, Tàizōng visited Nánxú Prefecture,
admired his pure conduct,
summoned him to the inner hall,
talked with him for several days, and then he departed.
Tàizōng greatly respected and admired him.
In the early Dàtōng period (527 CE),
he was ordered to present two swords to Gāozǔ.
One was named Shànshèng,
and the other Wēishèng,
〔一二〕both were fine treasures.
In the second year of Dàtóng (536 CE),
he died,
aged eighty-five.
〔一三〕His complexion remained unchanged,
and his limbs were pliable as before.
An imperial edict posthumously appointed him Zhōngsàn Dàfū,
and granted him the posthumous title Zhēnbái Xiānshēng.
Furthermore, a *shèrén* was sent to supervise his funeral.
Hóngjǐng had left instructions for a simple burial,
and his disciples followed them.
Zhūgě Qú, courtesy name Yòuwén,
was a native of Yángdū, Lángyé,
whose family had resided in Jīngkǒu for generations.
Qú served the recluse Guān Kāngzhī in his youth,
and extensively studied the classics and histories.
He then took the recluse Zāng Róngxù as his teacher.
Róngxù, who authored the "Jìnshū",
credited Qú with contributing to its revelations and clarifications,
comparing him to Hú Suì.
In the early Jiànwǔ reign of Qí (494 CE),
Jiāng Sì, acting official of Nánxú Prefecture, recommended Qú to Míngdì, saying:
"Qú is content in poverty and adheres to the Dao,
delights in rites and cultivates poetry.
He has never presented his calling card to local officials
or waited in attendance at government offices.
Given his detached and reclusive nature,
he can promote purity and refine customs.
I request that he be appointed to the position of Yìcáo Cóngshì."
The emperor granted this,
but Qú declined and did not accept.
Xiè Tiǎo of Chén Commandery, then administrator of Dōnghǎi Prefecture, issued an instruction:
"In the past, Zhǎngsūn Dōngzǔ
demonstrated the integrity of Lóngqiū;
〔一四〕Wénjǔ Běizī
was highly praised for his moral conduct.
This served to inspire the greedy and strengthen the weak,
and to uphold exemplary models.
The hermit Zhūgě Qú
is imbued with such lofty character,
following in the footsteps of previous worthies.
Does he conceal a pearl beneath coarse cloth,
or hide jade awaiting its price?
Or is he a solitary, pure recluse
who serves no princes or kings?
I hear that in serving his parents, he endures the hardship of eating beans,
and in providing for them, he has little provision of wild vegetables.
How can I alone enjoy immense wealth
and forget this small share of grain?
He may be sent one hundred *hú* of grain."
During the Tiānjiān era,
Prefect Xiāo Chēn, Inspector Ānchéng Wáng Xiù, and Pōyáng Wáng Huī all treated him with exceptional courtesy.
When Qú mourned his mother, he became emaciated.
Huī repeatedly visited to inquire about him.
After the mourning period ended,
he was recommended as a *xiùcái*,
but did not accept.
Qú was diligent in teaching and guiding,
and students came to him daily.
His residence was small and humble,
unable to accommodate them,
so Prefect Zhāng Yǒu built him a lecture hall.
Qú conducted himself with purity and uprightness,
and his wife and children never saw a change in his expression, whether of joy or anger.
Morning and evening, he was assiduous,
lecturing and reciting without cessation,
and people increasingly revered him for this.
In the seventh year of Tiānjiān (508 CE),
Gāozǔ issued an edict inquiring about him to Prefect Wáng Fèn.
Fèn immediately responded with the full truth.
Before he could be summoned for employment,
he died at home that year.
Qú's twenty volumes of writings
were collected and recorded by his disciple Liú Jiǎo.
〔一五〕
Shěn Yǐ, courtesy name Chǔmò,
was a native of Wǔkāng, Wúxīng.
His father, Tǎnzhī,
was the Director of the Department of State Affairs during the Qí dynasty.
Yǐ was pure and quiet in his youth, with outstanding conduct,
and he admired the character of Huáng Shúdù and Xú Rúzi.
He did not study books for the sake of mere textual analysis,
nor did his writings favor superficial embellishment.
He often stayed alone in a room,
and people rarely saw his face.
Yǐ's paternal uncle, Bó,
was prominent and influential in the Qí era.
Whenever Bó returned to Wúxīng,
guests crowded his gate,
but Yǐ never went to his door.
When Bó visited him,
Yǐ would not step beyond his threshold for greeting or farewell.
Bó sighed, saying:
"Now I know that being noble is not better than being humble."
Soon after, he was summoned to be the Left Chamberlain of Nánjùn Wáng,
but he did not accept.
Yǐ's personal conduct was very refined;
he was filial to his mother and friendly to his brothers,
and was praised and admired by his community.
In the third year of Yǒngmíng (485 CE),
he was summoned to be *Zhùzuò Láng*;
in the second year of Jiànwǔ (495 CE),
he was summoned to be *Tàizǐ Shèrén*;
he did not accept either.
In the second year of Yǒngyuán (500 CE),
he was again summoned to be *Tōngzhí Láng*,
which he also did not accept.
Yǐ had never managed his family estate,
and during the chaos and warfare at the end of Qí,
he and his family ate only once a day.
If anyone offered him fine grain or meat,
he would close his door and refuse.
He only supported himself by gathering firewood and foraging,
and remained perfectly content, never changing his joyful disposition.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (507 CE),
a large-scale northern expedition was launched,
and adult males were conscripted.
Liǔ Yùn, the Prefect of Wúxīng, drafted Yǐ for service.
Lù Rèn, the *Biéjià* of Yáng Prefecture, sent a letter rebuking him.
Yùn was greatly ashamed,
treated Yǐ with generous courtesy, and sent him home.
He died at home that year.
He authored dozens of articles.
Liú Huìfěi, courtesy name Wénxuān,
〔一六〕was a native of Péngchéng.
In his youth, he was widely learned
and skilled in writing.
He began his career as the Judicial Staff Officer for Ānchéng Wáng.
He once returned to the capital,
passing through Xúnyáng on his way.
He visited Kuāngshān,
and called upon the recluse Zhāng Xiàoxiù.
〔一七〕They found great joy in each other's company,
and he resolved to stay there for the rest of his life.
Consequently, he did not re-enter officialdom
and resided at Dōnglín Temple.
He also constructed a garden north of the mountain,
named Lígoù Yuán,
and people at the time called him Lígoù Xiānshēng.
Hùifěi was especially knowledgeable about Buddhist scriptures,
skilled in seal script and clerical script.
While in the mountains, he handwrote over two thousand scrolls of Buddhist scriptures,
and routinely recited over a hundred scrolls.
He practiced the Way day and night,
diligently and tirelessly.
People far and near admired him.
When Tàizōng visited Jiāngzhōu,
he bestowed upon him a small table and a staff.
Commentators said,
“Since Master Yuǎn Fǎshī passed away,
nearly two hundred years had passed,
before we finally had the eminence of Zhāng and Liú.”
Shìzǔ and the Prince of Wǔlíng, among others, sent letters and inquiries without fail.
In the second year of Dàtóng,
he died,
at the age of fifty-nine.
Fàn Yuányǎn, courtesy name Bóguī,
was a native of Qiántáng in Wú Commandery.
His grandfather, Yuèzhī,
was summoned to serve as a Doctor of the Imperial Academy,
but he did not go.
His father, Língyú,
while residing in mourning for his father,
died from wasting away due to grief.
Yuányǎn was a child at the time,
yet his sorrowful yearning and observance of rites were complete,
which his relatives and neighbors found remarkable.
When he grew up, he loved learning,
and broadly mastered the classics and histories,
also excelling in Buddhist doctrines.
However, his nature was humble and respectful,
and he did not use his talents to boast to others.
His family was poor;
he relied solely on garden vegetables for his livelihood.
Once, while he was walking out,
he saw someone stealing his vegetables.
Yuányǎn quickly turned and ran away.
His mother asked him the reason,
and he fully answered with the truth.
His mother asked who the thief was,
and he replied:
“The reason I retreated just now
was fearing he would feel shame and embarrassment.
If I reveal his name now,
I wish you would not disclose it.”
Therefore, the mother and son kept it secret.
Sometimes there was someone crossing the ditch to steal his bamboo shoots.
Yuányǎn thereupon cut wood and made a bridge for them to cross.
From then on, the thieves were greatly ashamed,
and there was no more petty theft in the entire village.
When residing at home, he usually did not leave the city,
and when sitting alone, he was as if facing a severe guest.
Those who saw him all changed their expressions and corrected their demeanor.
Liú Huán of Pèiguó valued him greatly as exceptional,
and once submitted a memorial praising him.
In the second year of Jiànwǔ of Qí,
he was first summoned to be the Adjutant to the General Who Pacifies the North (Ānběi Cānjūnshì),
but he did not go.
In the ninth year of Tiānjiān,
County Magistrate Guǎn Huìbiàn reported on his righteous conduct,
and the Governor of Yángzhōu, Prince Hóng of Línchuān, invited him to serve,
but he did not go.
The following year,
the Prince submitted a memorial recommending him,
but he was ultimately not summoned.
That year he died at home,
at the age of seventy.
Liú Xū, courtesy name Yàndù,
was a native of Píngyuán.
His father, Língzhēn,
was the Prefect of Wǔchāng during the Qí dynasty.
Xū was praised for his pure filial piety as a child.
At the age of a few years,
his parents died successively.
Xū, while in mourning,
wept with childlike devotion,
nearly dying from grief.
All who came to offer condolences grieved for him.
Later he was raised by his paternal uncle.
He served his aunt and his sisters,
with profound filial piety and brotherly affection,
and was praised by his clan.
He lamented his early orphanhood,
and if anyone accidentally mentioned the names he held taboo,
he never failed to feel overwhelmed and shed tears.
His elder brother, Jié, arranged a marriage for him,
setting a date for the wedding.
Xū heard of it and fled into hiding.
He returned only when the matter had been dropped.
The Governor of his home province, Zhāng Jì, invited him to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
but he did not accept.
The relevant official issued a formal summons,
whereupon Xū hung the summons tablet on a tree and fled.
Xū was skilled in Profound Talk (Xuányán),
and especially excelled in Buddhist scriptures.
He once listened to lectures at the various monasteries on Mount Zhōng with his cousin, Liú Xiāo,
and subsequently together they chose a site and built a dwelling in the eastern ravine of Sòngxī Sì,
having the ambition to end their days there.
In the seventeenth year of Tiānjiān,
he died at Xiāo’s dwelling,
at the age of thirty-one.
As he was dying,
he held Xiāo’s hand and said:
“When my breath ceases, immediately shroud the body.
Once shrouded, bury it immediately.
A spirit tablet must not be erected at all,
nor should there be any sacrifices or offerings.
Do not seek an heir.”
Xiāo followed his instructions and carried them out.
His clansmen and closest friends jointly carved stone and erected an inscription,
posthumously styling him the Recluse Xuánzhēn Chǔshì.
Liú Xiāo, courtesy name Shìguāng,
was Xū’s older cousin.
His grandfather, Chéngmín,
was the Governor of Jìzhōu during the Sòng dynasty;
his father, Wénwèi,
was a Regular Official (Zhèngyuán Láng) during the Qí dynasty. His family served as Two-Thousand-Picul officials for generations,
and all had reputations for integrity.
Xiāo showed understanding and wisdom from childhood.
He lost his father at the age of four.
When staying with other children,
he alone would not play or frolic.
At six years old, he recited the *Lúnyǔ* and the *Máo Shī*,
and anything his mind did not understand,
he was able to question and debate.
At eleven,
he read the *Xiāoyáo Piān* (Wandering at Ease chapter) of the *Zhuāngzǐ*,
and said:
“This is understandable.”
A visitor then questioned him,
and he answered each question
with logic and reason.
His family always found this extraordinary.
When he grew up,
he was widely learned and possessed literary talent.
He did not marry and did not enter officialdom.
Together with his younger cousin Xū, he lived in seclusion, pursuing his ideals.
He wandered freely through forests and marshes,
finding enjoyment only in scenery and books.
He always wished to escape the human world,
but because his mother was old, he could not bear to leave her.
He often followed his brothers Jì and Yǎo while they served as officials.
When he was young, he loved giving charity,
making it his duty to relieve the distress of others.
If people sometimes presented him with gifts,
he also did not refuse them.
After a long time, he sighed and said:
“One who receives gifts from others must repay them,
otherwise one will feel ashamed before others.
I certainly have nothing with which to repay people;
how can I constantly feel ashamed?”
In the seventeenth year of Tiānjiān,
shortly thereafter, he wrote the *Treatise on the End of Change* (*Gézhōng Lùn*).
Its words were: “The matters of life and death,
the sages rarely spoke of them.
Kǒngzǐ said:
‘The refined essence and energy form matter,
the wandering soul causes transformation.
To know the characteristics of ghosts and spirits
is similar to
Heaven and Earth but does not contradict them.’
His words are terse,
their meaning is subtle,
the phenomenon is hidden,
and the intention is profound.
It cannot be used for arbitrary judgments,
and it is difficult to obtain an accurate investigation thereof.
I shall briefly indulge in wild talk,
and beg to try to speak of it.
Form and consciousness combine to become life;
soul and body separate and are called death.
When combined, there is activity;
when separated, there is rest and silence.
When there is activity,
everyone recognizes its spirit;
but when it is silent,
no being can fathom where it goes.
When everyone knows it, the meaning is manifest without speaking;
when none can fathom it, the more one argues, the more subtle the principle becomes.
This is why Xūn and Huá failed
to speak of it,
and Jī and Kǒng suppressed the topic and did not elaborate.
Former distinguished worthies
mutually gave rise to different views.
Jì Zhá said:
‘The bones and flesh return to the earth;
the animating spirit goes everywhere.’
Zhuāng
Zhōu said:
‘Life is forced labor;
death is rest.’
Examining these two views,
they seem contradictory.
Why is this?
If the spirit goes everywhere,
then the spirit exists;
if death is rest..."
cease,
the spirit is non-existent.
Yuán Xiàn said:
"The Xiàhòu clan used *míngqì* (spirit articles),
showing the people that there is no consciousness (after death).
The Yīnrén (people of Yīn/Shāng) used sacrificial vessels,
showing the people that there is consciousness.
The Zhōu
people used both,
showing the people doubt."
Examining records
and verifying past statements,
the distinction between existence and non-existence
cannot be fully stated.
If we investigate internal teachings,
judging by
the Buddhist section (Shì bù),
then the words of the various masters can be traced,
and the rites of the Three Dynasties (Sāndài) are not surpassed.
Why is this?
The spirit is the foundation of life;
the physical form is the vessel of life.
Death is when the spirit leaves this vessel
and immediately ceases to be that vessel.
Although the dead cannot return,
the essence and spirit undergo transformation sequentially,
and are never extinguished.
When the spirit leaves this (body),
its knowing function (consciousness) is suddenly vast and clear.
Therefore, the Xiàhòu *míngqì*
show that it does not return.
At that very moment (of transformation),
the *hún líng* (soul/spirit) knows non-extinction.
Therefore, the Yīnrén sacrificial vessels
show that it still exists.
Non-returning aligns with Zhuāng
Zhōu (Zhuāngzǐ),
and still existing aligns with Jì Zhá.
Each obtains one corner,
without harming their overall meaning.
Assuming the reality
of the matter, then (the state) is also nothingness.
Therefore, the Zhōu people had the rite
of using both,
and Nífù (Confucius) gave voice to the concept of the wandering soul.
Is this not the case?
If we discard the arguments of extremity and bias,
and seek the central tenet,
then the criticisms of being unbenevolent or unwise
can
cease.
Now, the physical form
is the substance of non-consciousness;
the spirit
is the nature of consciousness.
Consciousness does not exist independently;
it relies on non-consciousness to establish itself.
Thus, the form
is to the spirit
merely a temporary lodging house.
When death occurs,
the spirit leaves this (place) and goes elsewhere.
Since the spirit has left this (place),
why should the lodging house remain?
Rapid decay is the correct principle.
Since the spirit has gone elsewhere,
what is the purpose of sacrifice?
Sacrifice is a deviation from principle.
Yet the teachings of Jī (the Zhōu royal house) and Kǒng (Confucius) are not like this—
is there a reason for it?
Generally, the rise of rites (*lǐ*) and music (*yuè*)
arose from superficiality and meanness;
the display of sacrificial vessels (*zǔ dòu*) and the arrangement of graves (*zhuì zhào*)
arose from popular custom defects.
Instituting the spirit mat,
displaying the coffin and outer shell (*guó*),
setting out offerings (*kuì diàn*),
and building mounds (*qiū lǒng*)—
these are merely intended to allow filial sons to have a place
for remembrance,
for what benefit are they to the spirit that has already departed?
Therefore, in high antiquity, bodies were covered with brushwood
and discarded in the open fields.
Can we say that Zūnlú, Hèxū, Huángxióng, or Yán
Dì (the Yan Emperor) acted contrary to principle?
Thus, Zǐ Yǔ was sunk in a river;
Hàn Bó used a square pit;
Wén Chǔ was buried in yellow earth;
Shì'ān used hemp ropes (to wrap the body).
These four men
attained principle,
and forgot the teachings (of convention).
If I were to associate with these four men,
then my lifelong ambition would be achieved.
However, long-held habits become routine,
making sudden reform difficult.
If I were to indulge my ambition immediately,
I might not be followed.
Now I wish to cut short the tedious extravagance
and strive to preserve simplicity and ease.
While not going so far as to expose
the corpse (bare burial),
I will deviate from common customs,
so as not to wound the feelings of the living,
yet still conform to the Way of the Perfected Person (Zhìrén).
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Gather the form of the head and feet
and bury it without an outer shell (*guó*)."
This is also
the rite for the poor.
Why should I feel ashamed of it?
Furthermore, Zhāng Huàn used only a headscarf;
Wáng Sù only washed the hands and feet;
Fàn Rǎn was buried immediately upon encoffinment;
Xī Zhēn established no mat
or small table.
Wén Dù used an old boat as an outer shell (*guó*);
Zǐ Lián used an ox cart to carry the coffin;
Shú Qǐ warned against building mounds or graves (*fén lǒng*);
Kāng Chéng (Zhèng Xuán) instructed against consulting omens for auspicious times.
These several gentlemen
still followed
these practices;
how much more should I,
when faced with prosperity and peace (Huá Tàì)!
Now I wish to emulate their excellent conduct
and take it as a rule.
Perhaps this conforms to the Way of the Mean (Zhōngyōng zhī Dào),
and I may avoid the criticism of wasteful spending.
After the breath ceases, there is no need for recalling the *pò* (bodily soul).
Wash the body and encoffin it.
Use one thousand cash to buy a simple coffin, plain old skirts and shirts, clothing, a head covering, a pillow, and shoes.
Apart from these necessary articles for the send-off,
the usual contents
of the coffin,
and the various chamber sacrifices
are absolutely not to be implemented.
The world generally believes the words of Lǐ (Dàosǐ) and Péng (Zǔ),
which can be called delusion.
I take Kǒng (Confucius) and Shì (Buddha) as my teachers,
and am relatively free from this delusion.
Once encoffined,
transport the body on an uncovered cart,
returning to the old hill (ancestral burial ground).
Whatever place is obtained,
if the earth is sufficient to form a pit,
and the pit is sufficient to hold the coffin,
there is no need for bricks or tiles,
no
effort in building mounds or planting trees.
Do not establish sacrificial offerings,
do not place tables or mats,
do not use Lord Máo’s (Máo Jūn) empty seat,
nor Bó Yí’s basin of water.
As for the winter and summer sacrifices (*zhēng cháng*) and subsequent heirs—
these are severed by my words and intention.
Let the matter cease with my person;
this does not harm societal teaching.
All family members, young and old,
relatives both internal and external,
all my friends
and those at my dwelling place,
I sincerely wish you to fulfill my ambition.
Happily, do not
override it.
The following year he died suddenly,
aged thirty-two.
When Xiāo was young, he once sat alone in an empty room.
An old man came to the door
and said to Xiāo:
"Your mental strength is fierce and brave;
you can grasp the essence of life and death;
but you cannot remain long in one place."
He then snapped his fingers and departed.
When Xiāo grew up,
he devoted his mind to studying Buddhism.
There was a man of the Way, Shì Bǎozhì,
whom people of the time could not fathom.
He met Xiāo at Xīnghuáng Sì
and, startled, arose and said:
"You dwell in seclusion studying the Way;
pure and clean, you shall ascend to Buddhahood."
He repeated this three times.
In the spring before Xiāo died,
someone planted a persimmon tree in his courtyard.
Xiāo said to his nephew, Yǎn:
"I will not see this fruit.
You must not speak of it."
He died by autumn,
and people considered him someone who knew his destiny.
His relatives and friends composed a eulogy of his conduct
and posthumously titled him Zhēnjié Chǔshì (Reclusive Scholar of Integrity and Virtue).
Yǔ Shēn, courtesy name Yànbǎo,
was a man of Xīnyě.
In youth, he was sharp, alert, and devoted to study.
He synthesized and mastered the classics, histories, and the hundred schools of thought.
The *wěi* (apocryphal texts), observational divination (*hòu*), calligraphy, and archery,
calculation, and mechanical ingenuity,
were all skills in which he excelled in his time.
However, his nature was tranquil and simple,
and he especially loved forests and springs.
Of his ten *mǔ* estate,
hills and pools occupied half.
He ate vegetables and wore worn clothes,
and did not manage his estate professionally.
Once, when returning by boat from his country cottage,
he was carrying one hundred and fifty *dàn* of rice.
Someone else had loaded thirty *dàn* along with him.
When they arrived at his residence,
the person who had borrowed space said:
“Yours is thirty *hú*,
mine is one hundred and fifty *dàn*.”
Shēn remained silent,
allowing him to take as much as he wished.
A neighbor was falsely accused of theft;
he was investigated and prosecuted,
and falsely confessed.
Shēn pitied him,
and used his books as collateral for twenty thousand cash.
He ordered a student to pretend to be the relative of the accused,
and paid the fine on his behalf.
The neighbor was released,
and thanked Shēn.
Shēn said:
“I pity the innocent of the world;
why would I expect gratitude?”
His actions of this type were numerous.
Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) had been friendly with Shēn when young,
and always held him in high regard.
When he raised his army,
he appointed Shēn as Secretary and Staff Officer (Jìshì Cānjūn) in the Píngxī Prefecture.
Shēn refused the offer.
In his life, he rarely sought close companionship.
Liǔ Yùn of Hédōng wished to associate with him,
but Shēn rejected and would not accept him.
Later, when the Prince of Xiāngdōng (Xiāngdōng Wáng) governed Jīngzhōu,
he commissioned Shēn as Secretary and Staff Officer (Jìshì Cānjūn) in the Zhènxī Prefecture;
he did not accept.
During the Pǔtōng era (520–527),
an imperial edict stated:
“To illuminate and elevate those hidden talent
is the priority of government.
To recognize the worthy and seek out gentlemen
is an urgent matter that occupies our waking thoughts.
Yǔ Shēn of Xīnyě, content with his lot, lives in reclusion,
devoting himself to withdrawal;
in the classics, histories, literature, and arts,
he is broadly versed and practiced.
Yǔ Chéngxiān of Yǐngchuān has mastered the teachings of Huáng and Lǎo (Daoism),
and broadly studied Buddhism.
Both do not compete and do not strive,
content in their simple existence.
They can serve to curb restlessness and strengthen customs.
Shēn is appointed Palace Attendant (Huángmén Shìláng);
Chéngxiān is appointed Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
The provinces and counties are ordered to strongly urge them repeatedly;
we hope they can bend their will,
and we expect them to be the seasonings (of the state).”
Shēn claimed illness and did not attend.
From his later years onward,
he especially adhered to Buddhism.
He established an altar (*dàocháng*) inside his residence,
where he circled and performed rites of repentance (*lǐchàn*),
without ceasing, six times a day.
He recited the *Fǎhuá Jīng* (Lotus Sutra),
once every day.
Later, in the middle of the night, he suddenly saw a Daoist figure,
who identified himself as Yuàn Gōng.
His demeanor was extremely unusual.
He called Shēn “Master Shàngxíng,”
gave him incense, and departed.
In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (532),
while taking a midday nap,
he suddenly woke up startled and said:
“Yuàn Gōng has returned!
I must not remain long.”
His complexion did not change;
as soon as he finished speaking, he died,
at the age of seventy-eight.
Everyone in the household heard a voice chanting in the air:
“Master Shàngxíng has been reborn in the Pure Land of Mí (Mǐ Jìng Yù).”
Gāozǔ heard this and issued an edict saying:
“To recognize goodness and praise conduct
was upheld by former kings.
Yǔ Shēn of Xīnyě,
a pearl of Jīngshān,
the finest wood of Jiānglíng,
has peacefully followed the Southern Way.
He certainly possessed famous virtue,
stood firm in his bitter integrity,
and maintained a solitary, pure, and simple bearing.
His sudden passing fills me with sorrow.
It causes sadness in my heart.
He should be posthumously titled ‘Recluse Zhēnjié’ (Zhēnjié Chǔshì),
to display his lofty character.”
The writings compiled by Shēn: *Dì Lì* (Imperial Chronology) in twenty scrolls,
*Yì Lín* (Forest of Changes) in twenty scrolls,
a supplement to Wǔ Duānxiū's *Jiānglíng Jì* in one scroll,
*Jìn Cháo Zá Shì* (Miscellaneous Affairs of the Jìn Dynasty) in five scrolls,
and *Zǒng Chāoshāo* (General Compilation) in eighty scrolls,
circulated throughout the world.
His son, Mànqiàn, courtesy name Shìhuá,
also earned an excellent reputation early on.
When Shìzǔ was in Jīngzhōu,
he recruited him as Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù),
and promoted him to Central Recorder (Zhōng Lùshì).
Whenever he departed,
Shìzǔ always watched him go,
and said to Liú Zhīlín:
“Jīngnán truly has many virtuous gentlemen.
Although one might praise Guī Tiánfèng,
or consider Huán Jiē pure,
in valuing virtue and marking the extraordinary,
none surpass this son.”
Later, he was transferred to Staff Officer for Consultation (Zīyì Cānjūn).
His written works, *Sāngfú Yí* (Rites for Mourning Attire), *Wénzì Tǐlì* (Styles and Regulations for Writing), *Zhuāng Lǎo Yì Shū* (Commentary on the Meaning of Zhuāngzi and Lǎozǐ),
annotations on the *Suàn Jīng* (Manual of Computation) and the astronomical calculations of the Seven Luminaries (*Qīyào Lì Shù*),
and his composed essays, totaled ninety-five scrolls.
His son, Jìcái,
possessed learning and good conduct.
During the Chéngshèng era (552–555),
he served as high as Secretariat Attendant (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
When Jiānglíng fell,
he followed the standard practice and entered the Pass.
Zhāng Xiàoxiù, courtesy name Wényì,
was a man of Wǎn in Nányáng.
In youth, he served the province as Administrator and Executive Clerk (Zhìzhōng Cóngshì Shǐ).
He suffered the mourning of his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
he became Deputy of the Prince of Jiàn'ān (Jiàn'ān Wáng Biéjià).
After a short time,
he resigned his post and returned to the mountains,
residing at Dōnglín Sì (East Grove Monastery).
He owned dozens of *qǐng* of land,
and several hundred subordinates (*bùqǔ*).
He directed them to farm diligently,
and fully provided for the mountain community (monks).
People near and far came to respect and admire him,
flocking to him like people rushing to market.
Xiàoxiù’s nature was open and direct;
he disliked ostentation.
He constantly wore a hood made of bark cloth (*gǔpí jīn*),
stepped in straw sandals,
and held a fly-whisk made of coir palm skin (*bìnglǘ pí*) in his hand.
He took Cold Food Powder (Hánshísǎn);
even in mid-winter, he was able to sleep on a stone.
He widely engaged with all types of books,
and specialized intensely in Buddhist scriptures.
He was skilled in discourse,
and proficient in official script calligraphy (*lìshū*).
In all skills and arts,
none were unfamiliar to him.
In the third year of Pǔtōng (522),
he died,
at the age of forty-two.
Everyone in the room smelled an extraordinary fragrance.
Tàizōng (Emperor Jiǎn Wén of Liáng) heard of it and mourned him deeply.
In a letter to Liú Huìfěi,
he described his purity and integrity.
Yǔ Chéngxiān, courtesy name Zǐtōng,
was a man of Líng in Yǐngchuān.
In youth, he was reserved, quiet, and possessed strong moral integrity.
Right and wrong never touched his speech;
joy or anger did not show on his face.
No one could observe his feelings.
At a young age, he studied under Liú Qiú of Nányáng.
He possessed a strong memory and sharp comprehension,
excelling beyond his peers.
The Dark Classics (*Xuán Jīng*) and Buddhist scriptures,
none were unmastered by him.
The Nine Streams (*Jiǔliú*) and Seven Summaries (*Qīlüè*),
he fully refined and mastered.
The commandery recruited him as Chief Administrator (Gōngcáo), but he refused.
He then traveled with the Daoist priest Wáng Sēngzhèn to Mount Héng.
Later, due to his younger brother’s illness, he returned to his hometown,
and subsequently lived on Mount Tǔtái.
When the Loyal and Illustrious Prince of Póyáng (Póyáng Zhōngliè Wáng) was in the province,
he admired Chéngxiān’s character and style,
and invited him to associate with him.
He also asked him to lecture on *Lǎozǐ*.
Famous monks from far and near
all came to assemble.
Arguments and challenges arose sharply,
and divergent views competed to be heard.
Chéngxiān calmly responded to them,
and all heard things they had never heard before.
The Loyal and Illustrious Prince especially valued and respected him,
and summoned him as Provincial Chief Clerk (Zhōu Zhǔbù).
The Prince of Xiāngdōng heard of this,
and also commissioned him as Staff Officer for Judicial Affairs (Fǎcáo Cānjūn).
He refused both appointments.
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng,
Liú Huìfěi of Lúshān arrived at Jīngzhōu.
Chéngxiān had a previous acquaintance with him,
and went to visit him.
The students of Jīngshǎn
therefore requested Chéngxiān to lecture on the Lǎozǐ.
Xiāngdōng Wáng (Prince of Xiāngdōng) personally ordered his carriage and came to listen.
They discussed matters the entire day,
and the prince greatly appreciated and welcomed him.
He stayed for more than a month,
and then returned to the mountains.
The Prince personally held a farewell ceremony,
and also presented him with poems.
The hermit praised this gesture.
In that year, he died,
at the age of sixty.
Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel (Lìbù Shàngshū) of Chén, said: Those in the world who slander hermits (chǔshì)
often say they merely steal empty fame
and have no practical use;
there are indeed some who fail to live up to their reputation.
As for the scholarship of Zhūgě Qú,
and the family pedigree (bùfá) of Ruǎn Xiàoxù,
how could it have been difficult for them to gain advancement?
That they ultimately remained in seclusion
was surely just their nature.
Arrayed Biographies (Lièzhuàn) Forty-Six: Knowing When to Stop (Zhǐzú): Gù Xiànzhī, Táo Jìzhí, Xiāo Shìsù
The Yì (Classic of Changes) says:
"The meaning of 'excess' (kàng) is
knowing how to advance but not knowing how to retreat,
knowing how to survive but not knowing how to perish.
Only the sage
knows advancement, retreat, survival, and perishing without losing the correct path!"
The commentary (zhuàn) says:
"Knowing contentment prevents disgrace (rǔ),
knowing when to stop prevents danger (dài)."
If one does not understand advancement and retreat,
nor grasp knowing when to stop and be content (zhǐzú),
the calamities of danger and disgrace
will arrive within a fixed time (qī yuè).
When the ancients advanced,
it was to bring peace to the age and aid in affairs,
and to promote the Way and refine customs.
However, their advancement
brought easy glory and favor,
hence it was seized upon by fools;
their retreat,
meanwhile, involved rigorous virtue and arduous integrity,
hence it was feared and avoided by mediocrities.
Although disaster, defeat, peril, and ruin
are displayed before our eyes and ears,
those who lightly rise up and majestically withdraw (qīng jǔ gāo dǎo)
are few in previous histories.
During the Hàn era, Zhāng Liáng completed his task and withdrew,
feigning illness and refusing grain (quèlì).
Compared to Yuè Yì and Fàn Lí, who reached a state of distress (diānbèi),
this was superior.
Later, Xuē Guǎngdé and the two Shū officials (èr Shū),
handled their departure and appointments with propriety,
and are worthy of praise.
In Yú Huàn’s Wèi Lüè Zhīzú Zhuàn (Record of Contentment),
Fāng Tián and Xú Yú, compared to Guǎn and Hú,
show that their paths were fundamentally different.
Xiè Língyùn’s Jìn Shū Zhǐzú Zhuàn (Record of Knowing When to Stop)
first discusses the scholars of the Jìn era who avoided chaos—
these were perhaps not the right kind of people;
only Ruǎn Sīkuàng abandoned glory and preferred seclusion,
thereby keeping far from danger and disgrace.
The Sòng Shū Zhǐzú Zhuàn includes Yáng Xīn and Wáng Wēi,
all being of the same lineage (liúyà).
During the Qí era, Liú Huán of Pèiguó,
courtesy name Zǐguī,
refused stipends and cherished the Way.
He lived in quiet retirement, cultivating his ambition.
He was not anxious about poverty and lowliness,
nor avariciously obsessed with wealth and status.
He was one of the highest examples of Confucian conduct.
When Liáng possessed the realm,
the way of the petty man receded,
and worthy scholars and high officials were mutually invited to hold positions.
However, those who measured their strength and guarded their aspirations
were unheard of in that generation.
Sometimes there were those who retired from office (zhìshì) and announced their old age,
or those who possessed little ambition and few desires.
The national historians recorded them,
and also called this the Record of Knowing When to Stop.
Gù Xiànzhī, courtesy name Shìsī,
was a native of Wú County in Wújùn.
His grandfather, Gù Jǐzhī,
was General Who Guards the Army (Zhènjūn Jiāngjūn) and Governor (Cìshǐ) of Xiāngzhōu during the Sòng Dynasty.
Before Xiànzhī reached adulthood (ruò guàn),
the province appointed him Aide to the Deliberative Bureau (Yìcáo Cóngshì).
He was recommended as Cultivated Talent (Xiùcái),
and gradually promoted to Palace Attendant to the Crown Prince (Tàizǐ Shèrén),
Director of the Bureau of Statistics (Shàngshū Bǐbù Láng),
and Registrar to the General Who Soothes the Army (Fǔjūn Zhǔbù).
During the Yuánhuī period,
he served as Prefect (Lìng) of Jiànkāng.
At that time, there was a man who stole an ox.
The owner recognized it,
but the thief also claimed it was his own ox.
The testimony and evidence from both families were equal,
and previous prefects had been unable to decide the case.
When Xiànzhī arrived,
he reviewed the circumstances
and said to the two families:
"No need for further talk.
I have found the solution."
He then ordered the ox to be untied,
allowing it to go wherever it wished.
The ox walked directly back to the original owner's house,
and only then did the thief admit his guilt.
His discoveries of treachery and revelations of the hidden
were often of this kind.
People at the time called him "Enlightened Spirit" (Shénmíng).
Regarding entreaties from powerful individuals
or the cruel greed of high officials,
he adhered strictly to the law (jù fǎ zhí shéng)
and showed no partiality or leniency.
His character was also pure and frugal.
He governed vigorously and forcefully,
achieving great public harmony.
Therefore, whenever drinkers in the capital (Jīngshī) obtained a mellow and superior wine,
they would invariably call it
"Gù Jiànkāng,"
meaning the wine was pure and fine.
He was promoted to Manager of Merits (Gōngcáo) to the General of Cavalry and Chariots (Chējì Jiāngjūn), and Friend (Yǒu) to the Prince of Jìnxī.
When Qí Gāodì took power,
he appointed him Staff Officer of Recording (Lùshì Cānjūn) to the General of Swift Cavalry (Piàojì Jiāngjūn),
and promoted him to Aide (Yuàn) of the Western Secretariat to the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
When the Qí Court was established,
he became Gentleman of the Central Secretariat (Zhōngshū Shìláng).
After Qí Gāodì ascended the throne,
he was appointed Administrator (Nèishǐ) of Héngyáng.
Before this,
the commandery had suffered years of plague and epidemics.
More than half the population had died.
Coffins were extremely expensive,
so all the dead were wrapped in reed mats
and abandoned by the roadside.
Upon Xiànzhī’s arrival (stepping down from the carriage),
he sent separate notices to the subordinate counties,
seeking out the relatives and family members,
and ordered them all to provide proper burial (bìn zàng).
For those whose families had died out completely,
Xiànzhī expended the public stipend
and instructed the magistrates (gāngjì) to manage the arrangements.
Furthermore, according to local custom,
when mountain dwellers fell ill,
they invariably claimed that their ancestors were causing misfortune.
They would all open the tombs, split the coffins,
and wash the dry bones with water,
calling this “removing the malevolence” (chú suì).
Xiànzhī enlightened them through explanation,
arguing the distinction between the living and the dead,
that the affairs of one do not depend on the other.
Consequently, the custom changed.
At that time, Wáng Huàn, the Governor (Cìshǐ), had just arrived.
Only Héngyáng alone had no lawsuits.
He sighed and said:
"The transformative influence of Gù Héngyáng is complete!
If all nine commanderies were like this,
what work would I have left to do!"
He returned and served as Chief Aide (Cóngshì Zhōngláng) to the Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi).
He was sent out to serve as Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the General of the Central East (Dōng Zhōngláng), concurrently managing the affairs of Kuàijī Commandery.
Lǚ Wéndù, a native of Shānyīn, was favored by Qí Wǔdì.
He established an estate in Yúyáo
and acted quite arbitrarily and recklessly.
When Xiànzhī arrived at the commandery,
he immediately submitted a memorial requesting its removal.
Later, Wéndù returned to bury his mother.
Officials of the commandery and county rushed to offer condolences,
but Xiànzhī refused to communicate with him.
Wéndù deeply resented this,
but ultimately could not harm him.
He was promoted to Chief Clerk (Zhǎngshǐ) to the Prince of Bālíng, under the General of the Central South (Nán Zhōngláng),
given the additional title of General Who Establishes Might (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn), and concurrently managed the affairs of Wùzhōu.
At that time, the Minister of Education (Sītú), the Prince of Jìnglíng, established military colonies (tún) in the borders of Xuānchéng, Línchéng, and Dìnglíng counties.
He sealed off hundreds of miles of mountains and marshes,
prohibiting the populace from gathering firewood and foraging.
Xiànzhī firmly stated in a memorial that this was unacceptable,
and his words were very sharp and direct.
The Prince replied to him, saying:
"If not for you, I would not have heard this virtuous advice."
He immediately ordered that the prohibition be lifted.
He was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
concurrently Shàngshū Lìbù Lángzhōng.
During the Sòng era,
his grandfather, Jìzhī, had once served in the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
He planted a beautiful tree in the courtyard,
and said to others:
“I am planting this for Xiànzhī.”
By this time,
Xiànzhī indeed held this office.
He was sent out as Zhēnglǔ Chángshǐ, acting in Nányǎnzhōu affairs,
but suffered the mourning period for his mother.
When the mourning period ended,
during the Jiànwǔ reign,
he was again appointed Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng,
leading the Bùbīng Xiàowèi.
Before taking up the post,
he was moved again to Tàizǐ Zhōngshùzǐ,
leading the Wúyì Zhōngzhèng.
He was sent out as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and Línchuān Nèishǐ,
but before reporting,
the assignment was changed to Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Jìnlíng Tàishǒu.
After a short time, he became ill,
submitting a request to resign and return to his hometown.
At the beginning of the Yǒngyuán reign,
he was summoned to serve as Tíngwèi,
but did not accept the appointment.
He was then appointed Yùzhāng Tàishǒu.
There was a chaste woman named Wàn Xī,
who was widowed young and had no son.
She served her parents-in-law with exceptional filial piety.
Her own parents wished to take her back and marry her off,
but she swore to die rather than agree.
Xiànzhī bestowed upon her bolts of silk,
commending her integrity and righteousness.
In the second year of Zhōngxīng (502 CE),
the righteous army pacified Jiànkāng,
and Gāozǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Liáng) became the Governor (Mù) of Yángzhōu.
He summoned Xiànzhī to be Biejù Cóngshìshǐ.
By the time he arrived,
Gāozǔ had already accepted the abdication.
Xiànzhī's wind-disease gradually worsened,
and he firmly requested to return to Wú.
In the second year of Tiānjiān,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū at his home.
Although Xiànzhī had governed various commanderies repeatedly,
his assets amounted to nothing (less than one *dàn* or *shí* measure),
and when he returned,
his dwelling was empty,
and he could not escape hunger and cold.
In the eighth year (of Tiānjiān),
he died at home,
aged seventy-four.
Before his death, he drafted an ordinance,
instructing his sons, saying: “That man emerges from birth and enters death
is a principle akin to day and night.
Since we do not know whence we come in life,
how can we know whither we go in death?
What Yánlíng (Jìzā) said—
'The vital essence returns upward
to Heaven,
the bones and flesh return downward to the Earth,
and the soul and breath go everywhere'—
truly has basis.
Although this might be vague and difficult to verify,
it is assuredly not baseless delusion.
The span of a hundred years
is a period
swift as a fleeting glimpse (through a crack).
I now preemptively establish my final arrangements.
After I close my eyes,
remember to comply fully and carry them out,
and do not deviate from my will.
Zhuāngzhōu and Tán Tái were those who understood life;
Wángsūn and Shì'ān were those who corrected conventional practices.
Wángsūn, Shì'ān,
矫俗者也．
I have not attained their understanding,
nor have I achieved their corrective power.
I have always considered the regulations established by Zhōngdū (Lǐ Yīn),
to be truly rational and agreeable to sentiment.
允理愜情．
The clothing should fully cover the body,
demonstrating adherence to ritual propriety;
the coffin should fully cover the clothing,
sufficient to conceal the odor.
As for objects placed inside the coffin,
none whatsoever are required.
Carry the body in a plain hearse (Chūnchē),
covered with coarse cloth,
so that people will not despise (the extravagance).
Hàn Míngdì, with the dignity of the Son of Heaven,
still offered sacrifices of water in a basin and dried meat and grain;
Fàn Shǐyún (Fàn Bì), the noble martyr,
though esteemed highly,
was also presented offerings of cold water and dry rice.
How much less should I, a humble and ordinary person,
fail to uphold moderation and sincerity?
Rituals should be simple rather than sorrowful—
this reflects the natural affection for kin;
Rituals
should be thrifty rather than extravagant—
this can still be managed according to my wishes.
There is no need to permanently display a memorial table (Língyán).
Only incense and lamps should be set up,
so that those who come to express grief have something to rely upon.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, the anniversary of the death (Jì), and during the annual sacrifice (Xiáng),
you
may temporarily place a small bed
and briefly arrange tables and mats.
Offer only vegetarian dishes,
and do not use livestock (Shēng Láo).
For the Winter (Zhēng) and Autumn (Cháng) sacrifices,
the practice should not be abandoned regardless of wealth or status.
Preparing all the proper items is difficult,
and often leads to negligence
and carelessness.
Sacrificing to the ancestors has its own established old rituals,
which must not be neglected.
For offerings from me downward,
the sacrifices shall only use vegetarian food and seasonal fruit,
and must not follow the practice of former generations.
This is meant to show
the descendants
that they should not forget their parents throughout the four seasons.
Kǒngzǐ said:
'Even if the offerings consist only of vegetable soup and melons,
one must maintain reverence as if fasting.'
The fundamental value lies in sincerity and respect;
why seek complete preparation of all objects?"
He authored several dozen essays of poetry (Shī), prose-poetry (Fù), inscriptions (Míng), eulogies (Zàn), and the *Héngyáng Jùn Jì*.
Táo Jìzhí,
was a man from Mòlíng in Dānyáng.
His grandfather, Mǐnzǔ,
was the Sòng Governor (Cìshǐ) of Guǎngzhōu.
His father, Jǐngrén,
was Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
Jìzhí was intelligent early on,
and Mǐnzǔ loved and admired him greatly.
Mǐnzǔ once placed four boxes of silver lined up before them,
instructing his various grandsons to each take some.
Jìzhí was only four years old at the time,
but he alone did not take any.
When people asked the reason,
Jìzhí replied:
“If there is a gift,
it should first be given to my father and uncles;
it should not yet be distributed to the grandsons.
That is why I did not take any.”
Mǐnzǔ was even more impressed by his brilliance.
At the age of five, he lost his mother,
grieving like an adult.
Previously,
before his mother fell ill,
she had ordered clothes to be dyed outside.
After she died,
the family finally retrieved them.
Jìzhí embraced them and cried sorrowfully,
and all who heard were moved to sadness.
When he grew up, he loved learning
and was indifferent to fame and profit.
He started his career as Guìyáng Wángguó Shìláng,
and Běi Zhōngláng Zhènxī Xíng Cānjūn,
but he did not take up either post.
People at the time called him
“Pìnjūn.”
When the mourning period for his father ended,
Shàngshū Lìng Liú Bǐng, who led the Dānyáng Yǐn,
invited him to serve as Hòujūn Zhǔbù,
and concurrently Jùn Gōngcáo.
He was sent out as Wàngcài Lìng,
but resigned shortly thereafter due to illness.
At that time, Liú Bǐng and Yuán Càn, believing that the power of Qí Gāodì (Xiāo Dàoichéng) was increasing daily,
planned to oppose him.
Bǐng had always highly esteemed Jìzhí,
and wished to decide the strategy with him.
Jìzhí believed that since Yuán and Liú were scholars (Rúzhě),
they were certain to fail and perish.
He firmly declined and did not go.
Soon after, Bǐng and the others were executed.
At the beginning of Qí (Southern Qí),
he served as Shàngshū Bǐbù Láng.
At that time, Chǔ Yuān was Shàngshū Lìng.
Since he had always been good friends with Jìzhí,
he repeatedly appointed him Sīkōng and Sītú Zhǔbù,
entrusting him with the affairs of the headquarters.
When Yuān died,
Shàngshū Lìng Wáng Jiǎn, believing Yuān possessed utmost virtue,
wished to posthumously title him Wénxiào Gōng.
Jìzhí requested, saying:
“Wénxiào is the posthumous title of Sīmǎ Dàozǐ.
I fear that the title itself may not embody complete perfection.
Wénjiǎn would be better.”
Jiǎn agreed to this.
Jìzhí further requested Jiǎn to erect a stele for Yuān,
managing and supervising the project from start to finish.
He demonstrated great administrative integrity,
and people at the time praised him for it.
He was transferred to be the Jìshì Cānjūn for the Tàiwèi.
He was sent out to be the Sīmǎ of the Guànjūn and the Grand Administrator of Dōngguǎn.
While in the commandery, he was known for his "purity and harmony" (Qīnghé).
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng,
and concurrently served as the Sīmǎ of the Zuǒwèi.
He was then transferred to be the Zīyì Cānjūn of the Zhèn Xī.
When Qí Wǔdì died,
Míngdì assumed the role of Prime Minister.
He eliminated those who differed from him,
and Jìzhí was unable to pander to him.
Míngdì became somewhat wary of him,
and so sent him out to be the Chángshǐ of the Fǔguó and the Grand Administrator of Běihǎi.
Being a senior assistant in a frontier post
was rarely undertaken by those of noble birth.
Someone advised Jìzhí to call upon the Emperor to express his gratitude.
When Míngdì saw him,
he immediately retained him,
appointing him as Pìaoqí Zīyì Cānjūn,
and concurrently Shàngshū Zuǒchéng.
He was then transferred to be the Grand Administrator of Jiàn'ān.
His administration emphasized purity and tranquility,
which benefited the common people.
Upon his return, he served as Zhōngshū Shìláng,
then was promoted to Yóujī Jiāngjūn, concurrently Tíngwèi.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
he was promoted to Gěishì Huángmén Shìláng.
He often stated that "once one's official career reaches the rank of two thousand *dàn*,
one's initial wish is fulfilled,
there is no need to busy oneself with human affairs."
Thereupon, he resigned due to illness and returned to his hometown.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he was appointed Tàizhōng Dàfū at home.
Gāozǔ said,
"The Liáng dynasty has come to rule the world,
yet I do not see this man."
In the tenth year,
he died at home,
at the age of seventy-five.
Jìzhí had always been exceptionally pure and ascetic.
He had lived in seclusion for over ten years.
When he died,
his family had nothing but bare walls.
His descendants had nothing with which to shroud and inter him.
Those who heard of it were all saddened by his aspirations.
Xiāo Shìsù
was a native of Lánlíng.
His grandfather, Sīhuà,
was a Sòng Zhēng Xī Yítóng Sānsī.
His father, Huìmíng,
was the Grand Administrator of Wúxīng.
Both had great reputations.
Shìsù became an orphan and poor at an early age,
and was taken in and cared for by his uncle, Huìxiū.
He began his career as a Fǎcáo Xíng Cānjūn for the Qí Sītú,
then was promoted to Zhùzuò Zuǒláng,
Tàizǐ Shèrén,
and Shàngshū Sāngōng Láng.
At the end of Yǒngyuán,
he served as Tàizǐ Xǐmǎ.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
Gāozǔ brought him in as the Zhōngwèi Pìaoqí Jìshì Cānjūn.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
he served as the Yǒu for Línchuán Wáng,
then again as Tàizǐ Zhōngshèrén,
and Dānyáng Yǐn Chéng.
When he was first appointed,
Gāozǔ bestowed eighty thousand coins upon him.
Shìsù dispersed it all among his relatives and friends in a single day.
He was then promoted to Sītú Zuǒ Xīshǔ,
and Zhìzhōng of Nán Xúzhōu.
He had a quiet and retiring nature,
few desires,
loved learning,
and was skilled in "pure conversation" (qīngyán).
Fame and gain were not spoken of by him,
and joy and anger did not show on his countenance.
Whether in society or in office,
he always acted according to his feelings and was straightforward,
never boasting or being arrogant.
He was naturally simple and unadorned,
and gentlemen all respected him for this.
When he was in Jīngkǒu,
he already had the intention of settling there for good,
and so built a house on Mount Shè.
He was then summoned to be Zhōngshū Shìláng,
but he declined the appointment.
He then returned to his mountain dwelling,
living in solitude and avoiding official duties.
No one but his relatives was allowed to reach his fence gate.
His wife,
the daughter of Tàiwèi Wáng Jiǎn,
had lived separately from him for a long time,
and so he had no children.
In the eighth year,
he died.
His relatives and old friends traced his actions and conduct,
and posthumously named him Zhēnwén Xiānshēng.
The historian says: Gù Xiànzhī and Táo Jìzhí
were those who prolonged their lives in retirement;
as for Xiāo Shìsù, his desire for officialdom was even less.
Compared to those who clung to their stipends and indulged in favor,
lingering in the human world,
there was a distinct difference.
