Biographies, Chapter 47: Good Officials: Yǔ Bì, Shěn Yǔ, Fàn Shùzēng, Qiū Zhòngfú, Sūn Qiān, Fú Jǐ, Hé Yuǎn.
Emperor Xuān of Han once believed that
"for government to be peaceful and lawsuits settled,
it depends on good officials of the two thousand *dàn* rank!"
Former historians also said:
"The Grand Administrator of today
is the feudal lord of ancient times."
Therefore, the office of chief official
is known as "cherishing the people."
Thus, guiding virtue, regulating rites,
and transforming customs and traditions
must all come through them.
At the end of Qí, there was chaos and disorder.
Government was controlled by petty individuals.
Taxes and levies arose like clouds,
and corvée labor was limitless.
Most administrators and magistrates relied on powerful families,
each fostering greed and tyranny,
exploiting and extorting,
and distressing the common people.
The world was shaken,
and people had nowhere to turn.
Gāozǔ, while still in the fields,
understood the suffering of the people.
When the Liáng dynasty was established,
he issued a broad and lenient decree,
and the various miscellaneous levies from the chaotic times
were all abolished.
Thereupon, within the four seas,
people were finally able to rest their shoulders.
Upon ascending the throne,
he personally attended to all affairs,
listening to governance until sunset,
seeking out the ailments of the people.
He then dispatched light carriages to inspect local customs,
and set up "lungs-and-stones" (fèishí) to allow the poor to reach him,
endeavoring to show compassion and relief,
and alleviate their urgent distress.
In the first year,
he first abolished the household tax (rénzī)
and imposed a tax on adult males (jìdīng wéi bù).
He himself wore washed clothes,
and the imperial treasury had no ornate decorations.
The palace quarters used no more than silk and colorful fabrics,
no pearls, gems, brocades, or embroidery.
The imperial kitchens removed grand feasts,
serving vegetables daily,
and drinking no more than three cups of wine: thus he led the nation in frugality.
Whenever selecting chief officials,
he sought to choose the incorruptible and impartial.
All were summoned before the emperor,
who personally exhorted them on the principles of governance.
He first promoted Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng Dào Gài to be the Nèishǐ of Jiàn'ān,
and Zuǒmín Shìláng Líu Zōng to be the Grand Administrator of Jìn'ān.
Gài and others, in their official capacities,
were all noted for their integrity.
He also issued an order: if a small county had capable officials,
they would be promoted to large counties;
if a large county had capable officials,
they would be promoted to the two thousand *dàn* rank.
Thereupon, Qiū Zhòngfú, the magistrate of Shānyīn, who had outstanding administrative achievements,
was appointed Nèishǐ of Chángshā.
Hé Yuǎn, the magistrate of Wǔkāng, who was pure and impartial,
was appointed Grand Administrator of Xuānchéng.
Those who were appointed as officials with credentials
often followed suit.
As for Yǔ Bì of Xīnyě and other officials,
they enriched their administration with classical learning,
some spreading benevolence where they served,
others being remembered after they left.
They were truly good officials of later times.
Thus, this chapter on good officials is compiled.
Yǔ Bì, courtesy name Xiūyě,
was a native of Xīnyě.
His father, Shēnzī,
was the Sòng Yōngzhōu Cīshǐ.
When Bì was ten years old,
he suffered the sorrow of his father's death,
and during the mourning period, he became emaciated from grief,
which was praised by his provincial compatriots.
At twenty,
he was appointed Zhǔbù by the province,
passed the Xiùcái examination,
and successively rose to Ānxī Zhǔbù,
Shàngshū Diànzhōngláng,
and Pìaoqí Gōngcáo Shǐ.
He was widely read in various books and
had eloquent speech.
During Qí Yǒngmíng,
when peace was established with Wèi,
Bì was appointed acting Sànqí Chángshì to be an envoy.
Upon his return, he was appointed Sànqí Shìláng,
and oversaw record-keeping in the Eastern Palace.
After *Yùlín Wáng* was deposed,
(he) managed the imperial edicts and pronouncements of the Central Secretariat,
and was sent out to serve as the Assistant Administrator (*Biéjià*) of *Jīng Zhōu*.
Subsequently, (he) was transferred to be the Counselor to the Mid-ranking General of the West (*Xī Zhōngláng Zīyì Cānjūn*),
and later served again as the Assistant Administrator (*Biéjià*) of the commandery (*Zhōu*).
Previous officials (*Gāngjì*)
had all attained wealth and abundance.
When *Bì* served in that capacity again,
he maintained personal integrity and set an example for his subordinates,
completely shutting down requests and influence peddling.
Using cloth blankets and living on simple vegetable food,
his wife and children could not avoid hunger and cold.
*Míng Dì* heard of this and praised him,
issuing a handwritten edict commending his excellence.
His commandery and hometown honored him for it.
(He) was transferred to be the Counselor to the Minister of Works (*Sītú Zīyì Cānjūn*) and the Palace Attendant, Serving in the Central Court (*Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì*).
When *Gāozǔ* pacified *Jīngyì* (the capital area)
and established his paramount administration,
(he) brought him in to serve as the Meritorious Officer (*Gōngcáo Cānjūn*) to the General of Agile Cavalry (*Piàojì*).
(He) was transferred to be the Assistant Director of the Left in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Zuǒ Chéng*).

(He) was sent out to be the Chief Clerk to the General Who Assists the State (*Fǔguó Zhǎngshǐ*), the Assistant Administrator of *Kuàijī Jùn*, concurrently managing the affairs of the commandery government.
At that time, following a period of decline and decay,
the common people faced famine,
and grain prices were high everywhere;
rice reached several thousand (cash per unit).
Many people were scattered and displaced.
*Bì* comforted and managed them, achieving great administrative success.
He only retained his official salary,
his dedication to integrity becoming increasingly strict.
There were times when he did not light a fire for cooking for a whole day.
The Grand Administrator (*Tàishǒu*), *Yǒngyáng Wáng*, heard of this and sent him provisions,
but *Bì* declined to accept them.
In the first year of *Tiānjiān* (502 CE),
he died.
His corpse remained unburied, as there were no means for his shroud,
and the coffin could not be returned (to his home).
*Gāozǔ* heard of this
and issued an edict granting one hundred rolls of silk
and fifty *hú* of rice.
Previously,
*Bì* was a prominent figure among the noble families of Western *Chǔ*,
and had held illustrious official positions early on.
His fellow townsman, *Yuè Ǎi*, was capable and useful,
but had always been at odds with *Bì*,
mutually competing and overriding each other.
*Ǎi* served *Yùzhāng Wáng Yí* of *Qí*.
When *Yí* died,
*Ǎi* was frustrated in his career.
He requested leave from his post as Colonel of Infantry (*Bùbīng Xiàowèi*) to join the garrison and return to *Jīng Zhōu*.
At that time, *Bì* was the Assistant Administrator (*Biéjià*) of the commandery,
and he paid even less attention to *Ǎi*.
When *Gāozǔ* ascended the throne,
*Ǎi*, based on his meritorious service in the Western court, was made Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat (*Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng*).
*Bì* only then obtained the acting position in *Kuàijī*,
which deeply shamed him.
Coincidentally, he received a minor reprimand concerning his official duties.
*Gāozǔ*, considering *Ǎi* was his fellow townsman,
sent (Ǎi) to convey the imperial decree and instruct him.
*Bì* became extremely indignant,
and consequently, fell ill and died.
*Shěn Yǔ*, courtesy name *Bóyú*,
was a native of *Wǔkāng* in *Wúxīng*.
His uncle, *Chǎng*,
served *Jìanpíng Wáng Jǐngsù* of *Sòng*.
*Jǐngsù* plotted rebellion,
and *Chǎng* departed before the plot was exposed.
When (the plot) failed,
(Chǎng) was implicated and imprisoned.
*Yǔ* went to the court (*Tái*) to plead his case,
and managed to obtain his uncle’s pardon,
thereby becoming known.
He began his career as an Administrator (*Cóngshì*) for the commandery and was appointed to Serve in the Central Court (*Fèng Cháoqǐng*).
He once visited *Yīn Nǐ*, the Assistant Director of the Right in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Yòuchéng*) of *Qí*.
*Nǐ* spoke with him regarding government affairs,
and valued his talent greatly.
He said to him:
"Judging by your ability and competence,
you ought to hold this position of mine."
*Jìnglǐng Wáng Zǐliáng*, the Minister of Works (*Sītú*), heard of *Yǔ*'s reputation
and brought him in as an Administrator (*Cānjūn*) for his headquarters,
concurrently serving as the Administrator for Postal Service (*Bùchuán Cóngshì*) for *Yáng Zhōu*.
At that time, *Shěn Huīfú*, the Magistrate of *Jiànkāng*, relied on his influence to slight *Yǔ*.
*Yǔ* strictly disciplined him according to the law,
and the populace feared his strength.
*Zǐliáng* trusted and appreciated him greatly;
even family matters were entrusted entirely to *Yǔ*.
When *Zǐliáng* died,
*Yǔ* subsequently served *Shǐ'ān Wáng Yáoguāng*, the Inspector (*Cìshǐ*).
He was once sent on a mission to register the adult males (*Míndīng*).
He was fast and incurred no resentment.
*Yáoguāng* said to the officer sent with him:
"Why do you not learn from what *Shěn Yǔ* does?"
(Yáoguāng) then ordered him to take sole charge of the commandery's prison affairs.
The embankment (*Dài*) at *Fāng Shān* in *Húshú* County was high and steep.
In the winter months,
travelers, both private and official, found it difficult.
*Míng Dì* sent *Yǔ* to supervise the repairs.
*Yǔ* then opened four drainage outlets (*Hóng*)
and halted travelers to participate in the construction.
It was completed in three days.
A clerical assistant (*Shūzuǒ*) from *Yáng Zhōu* traveled privately
and falsely claimed to be a commandery envoy
refusing to participate in the labor.
*Yǔ* whipped him thirty times.
The clerical assistant returned and complained to *Yáoguāng*.
*Yáoguāng* said:
"*Shěn Yǔ* certainly would not whip you unjustly."
Upon investigation,
it was indeed confirmed that (the assistant) had been deceitful.
*Míng Dì* subsequently sent *Yǔ* to construct the *Chì Shān Táng*.
The expenditure was tens of thousands less than the amount estimated by the skilled construction workers (*Cáiguān*).
The Emperor favored him even more.
In the first year of *Yǒngtài* (498 CE),
he was made the Magistrate of *Jiàndé* County.
He instructed the people that every adult male (*Dīng*) should plant fifteen mulberry trees, four persimmon trees, as well as pears and chestnuts.
Adult females (*Nǚ Dīng*) should plant half that amount.
Everyone was delighted,
and soon the area became a forest.
He left office and returned to the capital (*Jīngshī*),
concurrently serving as acting Director of the Bureau of Selection (*Xuǎncáo Láng*).
He followed *Chén Bózhī*'s army to *Jiāng Zhōu*.
When the righteous army besieged *Yǐng Chéng*,
*Yǔ* persuaded *Bózhī* to welcome *Gāozǔ*.
*Bózhī* wept and said:
"My son is in the capital (*Dū*).
He cannot leave the city,
and I cannot help but care for him."
*Yǔ* replied:
"That is not correct.
People's morale is uneasy,
and all are considering changing their plans.
If you do not plan early,
the followers will disperse and be difficult to reassemble."
*Bózhī* subsequently led his forces to surrender,
and *Yǔ* followed in *Gāozǔ*'s army.
Initially,
when *Yǔ* was in the household of *Jìnglǐng Wáng*,
he was always close to *Fàn Yún*.
At the end of *Qí* (Southern Qí Dynasty),
he once lodged at *Yún*'s place.
He dreamed he was sitting atop a roof beam and pillar,
looking up and seeing characters in the sky that read:
"The residence of the *Fàn* clan."
By this time (of the surrender),
*Yǔ* related this story to *Gāozǔ*.
*Gāozǔ* said:
"If *Yún* does not die (in the conflict),
this dream will be verified."
When *Gāozǔ* ascended the throne,
*Yún* strongly recommended *Yǔ*.
(Yǔ) was promoted from Magistrate of *Jìyáng* to concurrent Assistant Director of the Right in the Department of State Affairs (*Shàngshū Yòuchéng*).
At that time, the realm was newly settled.
*Chén Bózhī* memorialized, recommending *Yǔ* to oversee and accelerate logistics and transportation.
The army and the state were saved (by his efforts).
*Gāozǔ* considered him capable.
(He) was transferred to Director of the Bureau of Equipage (*Shàngshū Jiàbù Láng*),
retaining his concurrent post as Assistant Director of the Right (*Yòuchéng*) as before.
*Yǔ* recommended his clansmen, *Shěn Sēnglóng* and *Sēngzhào*, for having administrative competence.
*Gāozǔ* accepted both recommendations.
(He) left office due to mourning for his mother,
but was subsequently reinstated as General Who Manifests Martial Might (*Zhènwǔ Jiāngjūn*) and Magistrate of *Yúyáo* County.
The prominent clan of *Yú Shì* in the county numbered over a thousand households.
Their requests and visits were like a marketplace.
None of the previous magistrates (*Lìng Zhǎng*) were able to halt them.
From the moment *Yǔ* arrived,
no private solicitation was entertained.
Those who did arrive
were all made to stand below the steps,
and he disciplined them strictly according to the law.
To the south of the county, there was another powerful clan of several hundred households.
Their sons and younger brothers acted aggressively and without restraint,
mutually shielding one another
and greatly enriching themselves.
The common people suffered greatly because of them.
*Yǔ* summoned the older men among them and made them overseers of *Shítóu* Granary.
The younger men he drafted as county servants (*Xiàn Tóng*).
All of them wept loudly on the roads.
From then on, the powerful retreated and hid their tracks.
When *Yǔ* first arrived,
the wealthy local officials all wore bright clothes and fine garments
to distinguish themselves.
*Yǔ* angrily said:
"You are merely low-ranking county clerks!
Why do you try to resemble noble persons?"
He forced all of them to wear straw sandals (*Máng Juè*) and coarse cloth,
standing attendant all day.
If their feet stumbled or they made a mistake,
he would immediately apply the rod or whip.
When *Yǔ* was of low status,
he had once come here himself to sell pottery,
and was insulted by the wealthy.
He therefore used this opportunity to take revenge.
Because of this, the gentry and commoners were alarmed and resentful.
However, *Yǔ* maintained his integrity and guarded his purity,
thus he was able to carry out his intentions.
Later, when the Royal Army launched the Northern Campaign,
Yǔ was summoned to serve as the General Who Establishes Awe (Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn),
supervising the transport of grain supplies,
soon concurrently holding the post of Commissioner of Metropolitan Waterways (Dūshuǐ Shǐzhě).
After a short while,
he was promoted to Minister of the Lesser Treasury (Shǎofǔ Qīng).
He went out to serve as Chief Clerk of the General Who Pacifies the South (Ānnán Zhǎngshǐ) and Governor of Xúnyáng (Xúnyáng Tàishǒu).
When the Inspector of Jiāngzhōu, Cáo Jǐngzōng, was critically ill,
Yǔ administered the affairs of the prefecture and province.
When Jǐngzōng died,
he subsequently became Chief Clerk to Xiāo Yǐngdá (General Who Commands Trust/Xìnwēi),
his position as Governor remaining the same.
Yǔ’s nature was uncompromising and stubborn;
he frequently offended Yǐngdá,
and Yǐngdá resented him.
In the eighth year of Tiānjiān (509 CE),
he entered to offer counsel on affairs,
and his words were exceptionally fervent and stirring.
Yǐngdá changed countenance and said:
“Did the court appoint you to merely act upon your own judgment?”
When Yǔ left,
he said to others:
“Only after I die will I cease;
I absolutely cannot bow my head and comply.”
On that very day,
he was murdered by bandits on the road.
He was fifty-nine years old at the time.
Many believed that Yǐngdá had caused his death.
His son, Xù, repeatedly pressed the lawsuit,
but Yǐngdá also died shortly thereafter,
and the case could not be fully investigated.
Xù therefore wore coarse cloth and ate simple vegetables for the rest of his life.
Fàn Shùzēng, courtesy name Zǐxuán,
was a man from Qiántáng in Wújùn.
As a youth, he loved learning.
He studied the Five Classics (Wǔ Jīng) under Lǚ Dàohuì of Yúháng,
and generally mastered the textual commentary.
Dàohuì’s students often numbered in the hundreds,
but he singled out Shùzēng, saying:
“This child will certainly become the teacher of a king.”
When Crown Prince Wénhuì of Qí and Wénxuān Wáng of Jìnglíng were young,
Gāodì introduced Shùzēng to serve as their teacher and friend.
He began his career as an Attendant Official (Shìláng) in the Kingdom of Jìnxī under Sòng.
At the beginning of Qí,
he reached the position of Chancellor of the Household (Lángzhōng Lìng) in the Kingdom of Nánjùn,
and was promoted to Director of Guests (Zhǔkè Láng) in the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū) and Colonel of the Infantry of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Bùbīng Xiàowèi),
concurrently holding the office of Magistrate of Kāiyáng (Kāiyáng Lìng).
Shùzēng was an outspoken and blunt man;
while in the palace, he frequently offered remonstrance and contention.
Although the Crown Prince could not fully adopt all his advice,
he did not punish him for it.
The Prince of Jìnglíng deeply
esteemed and valued him, calling him
“Zhōu Shě.”
At that time, Shěn Yuē, the Commander of the Left Guard of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Zuǒwèishuài), also compared Shùzēng to Jí Àn.
Because his parents were old,
he requested to return home to care for them.
He was then appointed Grand Master of the Palace (Zhōngsàn Dàfū).
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he was appointed General of Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn),
and went out to serve as Governor of Yǒngjiā (Yǒngjiā Tàishǒu).
His governance was honest and peaceful;
he did not favor harsh severity,
and the local customs benefited from it.
In Héngyáng County, which was under his jurisdiction,
the mountains and valleys were steep and treacherous,
serving as a refuge for criminals and fugitives.
Former officials had tried to suppress them but failed to stop the activity.
Shùzēng, upon arriving in office,
offered them grace and sincerity.
All the members of these criminal groups,
carrying their infants in slings, came out
and two hundred families were registered as official households.
From then on, commerce flowed freely,
and the residents settled peacefully in their professions.
While in the prefecture, he dedicated himself to integrity and honesty;
he accepted no gifts.
Míngdì heard of this and greatly praised him,
issuing an edict to commend him.
He was summoned back to serve as General of Cavalry (Yóujī Jiāngjūn).
The prefecture sent him over 200,000 in ‘old friends’ money (gifts),
but Shùzēng refused all of it.
When he first went to the prefecture,
he did not take his family.
When he returned,
none of his officials carried luggage.
The common people, young and old,
all came out to bow and bid farewell,
their wailing cries heard for dozens of *lǐ*.
During the reign of Dōnghūn [Hòu],
he was appointed Grand Master of the Palace (Zhōngsàn Dàfū),
and returned to his hometown.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he went out in a light boat to the capital court
and subsequently resigned, returning east.
Gāozǔ issued an edict which stated:
“Grand Master of the Palace Fàn Shùzēng,
formerly in the era of Qí,
served his lord with loyalty and integrity.
When he previously governed Yǒngjiā,
he governed his conduct with honesty and frugality.
It is appropriate to increase his honors and rank
in order to encourage pure conduct.
He may be appointed Grand Master of the Center (Tàizhōng Dàfū),
and granted twenty bolts of silk.”
Throughout his life, all the stipends and salaries Shùzēng received
he distributed to others.
When he grew old,
he was left utterly destitute, with nothing to rely upon.
He died in the eighth year of Tiānjiān (509 CE),
at the age of seventy-nine.
He annotated the *Wényán* of the *Yì* [Jīng],
and authored dozens of miscellaneous poems and *fù*.
Qiū Zhòngfú, courtesy name Gōngxìn,
was a man from Wúchéng in Wúxīng.
As a youth, he loved learning.
His paternal great-uncle Língjū possessed a keen eye for judging character,
and always referred to him as a ‘Thousand-*lǐ* Colt.’
At the beginning of Yǒngmíng era of Qí,
he was selected to be a student of the Directorate of Education (Guózǐ Shēng).
He achieved the highest ranking,
but before receiving an appointment,
he returned to his hometown.
His family was poor;
having no means to support himself,
he joined a group of bandits
and provided planning for them,
robbing and plundering the Three Wú regions.
Zhòngfú was intelligent and possessed strategy;
the bandits feared and obeyed him.
All his schemes succeeded,
and thus he was never exposed.
Governor Xú Sì summoned him and appointed him to Chief Clerk (Zhǔbù).
He successively held the posts of Attendant Official (Cóngshì) in Yángzhōu,
Erudite of the Imperial Academy (Tàixué Bóshì),
and Magistrate of Yúhú (Yúhú Lìng).
He gained a reputation for competence.
Governor Lǚ Wénxiǎn was a favored minister at the time,
and he habitually insulted and demeaned the subordinate counties.
Only Zhòngfú refused to yield to him.
He left office due to the mourning period for his father.
When Míngdì ascended the throne,
he was appointed General of Ardent Might (Lièwǔ Jiāngjūn) and Magistrate of Qū'ē (Qū'ē Lìng).
This occurred when Wáng Jìngzé, the Governor of Kuàijī, raised troops and rebelled.
Taking advantage of the court’s lack of preparation,
the news of the rebellion had just arrived,
but the vanguard had already reached Qū'ē.
Zhòngfú said to his officials and the people:
“Although the rebels, carried by victory, are fierce,
they are a temporary rabble and easily dispersed.
If we now collect the ships and vessels,
and breach the Chánggāng Weir,
draining the canal water to block their path,
and manage to hold out for a few days,
the metropolitan army will surely arrive,
and the great affair will be achieved.”
When Jìngzé’s army arrived,
they found the canal drained
and indeed halted their troops, unable to advance.
They subsequently suffered defeat and dispersed.
Because Zhòngfú had merit in resisting and defending,
he was promoted to Magistrate of Shānyīn (Shānyīn Lìng).
He held this post with great renown.
The common people composed a folk song about him which said:
“The two Fùs, Shěn, and Líu,
are not as good as one Qiū.”
The Fù Yǎn father and son, Shěn Xiàn, and Líu Xuánmíng,
had successively governed Shānyīn
and all had administrative achievements.
(The folk song) meant that Zhòngfú surpassed them all.
Towards the end of Qí, governance became chaotic,
and there was significant corruption and bribery.
He was impeached by the judicial authorities,
who intended to arrest him.
Zhòngfú secretly fled,
heading straight back to the capital and presenting himself at the palace gate.
Meeting with a general amnesty,
he escaped prosecution.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was again appointed Magistrate of Shānyīn.
Zhòngfú excelled at resolving difficult issues
and was skilled at adapting to circumstances and change.
His officials and the people respected and submitted to him,
calling him ‘Divine Wisdom.’
His governance was ranked first in the empire.
He held the office for less than a year,
when he was summoned to become Shàngshū Yòuchéng,
then promoted to Zuǒchéng,
and subsequently elevated to Wèiwèi Qīng.
The imperial favor and trust granted him were very great.
When the twin watchtowers (Què) were first constructed,
Zhòngfú was put in charge as Dàjiàng.
When the work was finished,
he was sent out to serve as Ānxī Zhǎngshǐ and Tàishǒu of Nánjùn.
He was transferred to Yúnhuī Zhǎngshǐ and Tàishǒu of Jiāngxià,
managing the affairs of the Yǐngzhōu provincial government.
He suffered mourning for his mother,
but was recalled to provisional duty.
He was removed from the roster due to an incident,
but was later recalled again to serve as Sīkōng Cānjūn.
Soon after, he was transferred to Nèishǐ of Yùzhāng.
While in the commandery, he further exerted himself in maintaining integrity.
After a short while, he passed away,
at the age of forty-eight.
An imperial edict stated:
“Qīu Zhòngfú, the Nèishǐ of Yùzhāng,
was repeatedly tested in great commanderies,
and charged with demonstrating subsequent achievements.
Not only did he avoid regrets and mistakes,
but his administrative achievements were truly outstanding.
His unfortunate death
is truly saddening.
He shall be posthumously granted the title Jǐshì Huángmén Shìláng.”
When Zhòngfú’s coffin was about to return (to his homeland),
the old and young of Yùzhāng cried and clung to the funeral procession,
preventing the wheels of the cart from moving forward.
When Zhòngfú was Zuǒchéng,
he compiled the *Huángdiǎn* in twenty scrolls,
and the *Nángōng Gùshì* in one hundred scrolls.
He also compiled the *Shàngshū Jùshì Zá Yí*,
which circulated in the world.
Sūn Qiān, courtesy name Chángxùn,
was a native of Jǔ in Dōngguǎn.
In his youth, he was appreciated by his relative, Zhào Bófú.
When Qiān was seventeen,
Bófú served as the Cìshǐ of Yùzhōu,
and appointed him as Zuǒjūn Xíng Cānjūn.
He was known for his capable administration.
He left office due to mourning for his father,
and stayed as a sojourner in Lìyáng.
He personally farmed to support his younger brothers and sisters,
and the local community praised his generosity and harmony.
Yìgōng, the Prince of Jiāngxià of the Sòng dynasty, heard of this,
and appointed him Xíng Cānjūn.
He subsequently served in the administrations of the Dà Sīmǎ and Tàizǎi.
He was sent out to become the Magistrate of Jùróng.
He was upright, prudent, and possessed a strong memory;
the county people called him “Divine Intelligence.”
At the beginning of the Tàishǐ reign,
he served Xiūrén, the Prince of Jiàn'ān.
Xiūrén made him Sītú Cānjūn,
and spoke highly of him to Emperor Míng.
He was promoted to Míngwēi Jiāngjūn and the Tàishǒu of the two commanderies of Bādōng and Jiànpíng.
The commandery was situated amidst the Three Gorges (Sānxiá),
which he governed by might and prestige.
When Qiān was about to report to duty,
he was instructed to recruit a thousand men to accompany him.
Qiān said:
“The reason the barbarian tribes (Mányí) are not submissive
is probably due to a failure of proper treatment.
Why should we trouble the military
and incur state expenditure?”
He firmly declined the offer.
Upon reaching the commandery,
he spread the influence of kindness and benevolence.
The Mán and Láoliáo tribes cherished him,
competing to send him gold and treasures.
Qiān consoled and reasoned with them and sent them away,
accepting absolutely nothing.
When captives were seized in raids,
he released all of them back to their homes.
Any salary or emoluments that came from the officials or common people
were entirely forgiven and exempted.
The entire commandery was peaceful,
and his prestige and trustworthiness became widely known.
After serving for three years,
he was summoned back to serve as Fǔjūn Zhōngbīng Cānjūn.
At the beginning of the Yuánhuī reign,
he was transferred to Cìshǐ of Liángzhōu.
He declined and did not proceed to the post,
and was instead transferred to Yuèqí Xiàowèi and Zhǔbù in the administration of the Zhēngběi Sīmǎ.
When the Prince of Jiànpíng was about to raise troops,
he worried about Qiān’s strong integrity,
so he used a pretext to dispatch Qiān as an envoy to the capital,
and only then launched his rebellion.
When the Prince of Jiànpíng was executed,
Qiān was transferred to Zuǒjūn Jiāngjūn.
In the early years of Qí,
he served as Níngshuò Jiāngjūn and the Magistrate of Qiántáng.
He managed complicated affairs with simplicity,
and there were no prisoners confined in the jails.
When he left office,
the common people, knowing that Qiān had not accepted gifts while in office,
loaded up silk fabrics and pursued him to present them.
Qiān refused the gifts.
Whenever he left an official post,
he had no private residence;
he often borrowed an empty official carriage to live in.
At the beginning of the Yǒngmíng reign,
he became Guānjūn Zhǎngshǐ and Tàishǒu of Jiāngxià.
He was impeached for leaving the commandery immediately upon being replaced
and was imprisoned in the Shàngfāng (Imperial Workshop/Jail).
After a short while,
he was released and made Zhōngsàn Dàfū.
When Emperor Míng was about to depose and establish a new ruler,
he wanted to draw Qiān into his trusted inner circle.
He made Qiān acting Wèiwèi,
and provided him with one hundred armed guards.
Qiān did not wish to involve himself in crucial political changes,
and promptly disbanded the armed men.
Although the Emperor did not punish him,
he no longer trusted him.
He was sent out as Sīmǎ to the Nán Zhōngláng.
In the first year of Yǒngyuán of Dōnghūn,
he was transferred to [X X] Dàfū.
In the sixth year of Tiānjiān,
he was sent out as Fǔguó Jiāngjūn and Tàishǒu of Línglíng.
Though already old and frail,
he still vigorously managed the government,
and the officials and common people felt secure under him.
Before this,
the commandery suffered greatly from tiger attacks.
Upon Qiān's arrival, the tigers vanished entirely.
The night he left office,
a tiger immediately harmed the residents.
Whenever Qiān governed a commandery or county,
he always diligently encouraged and instructed farming and sericulture,
striving to maximize the benefits of the land.
The revenue was always higher than in neighboring regions.
In the ninth year,
due to his advanced age,
he was summoned to become Guānglù Dàfū.
After he arrived,
Gāozǔ commended his purity and integrity,
and treated him with great respect and distinction.
Whenever he had an audience,
he still requested a challenging post to prove his worth.
Gāozǔ smiled and said:
“I employ your wisdom,
not your strength.”
In the fourteenth year,
an edict stated:
“Sūn Qiān, the Guānglù Dàfū,
is known for his purity and prudence,
and does not slacken even in old age.
Being of such high age and seniority,
he deserves special treatment.
He shall be granted twenty trusted attendants,
and also provided with assistance (for walking).”
From youth to old age, Qiān
served successively in two counties and five commanderies,
and was everywhere known for his incorruptibility.
His personal life was frugal and simple.
His bed was placed behind a screen made of rush mats (Qúchú Píngfēng).
In winter, he used a cloth quilt and a rush mat.
In summer, he had no mosquito net,
yet when he slept at night, he never suffered from mosquitoes or gnats;
many people found this strange.
Although he was over ninety years old,
he was robust, like a man of fifty.
Whenever there was an imperial audience,
he would always arrive at the palace gates before everyone else.
He devoted himself to benevolence and righteousness,
and his personal conduct far surpassed that of others.
His cousin, Língqìng, who was often ill, stayed at Qiān’s residence.
Once, Qiān returned from an outing and asked about his condition.
Língqìng said:
“I just drank something—the temperature wasn't right—
and now I am still thirsty.”
Qiān withdrew and sent his wife (to attend to him).
There was a man from Péngchéng named Liú Róng,
who was a beggar, gravely ill, and had no home.
His friends carried him to Qiān's dwelling.
Qiān opened up the main hall to accommodate him.
When Róng died,
Qiān provided him with proper funeral rites and burial.
Everyone admired his righteous conduct.
In the fifteenth year,
he died while in office,
aged ninety-two.
An edict granted thirty thousand cash as funeral aid
and fifty bolts of cloth.
Gāozǔ held a period of mourning for him,
and deeply lamented his loss.
Qiān’s cousin, Lián,
was obsequious, calculating, and skilled in officialdom.
During the Qí period, he had already served in major counties,
and as Shàngshū Yòuchéng.
At the beginning of Tiānjiān,
Shěn Yuē and Fàn Yún held power in the court.
Lián dedicated himself to serving them,
and also particularly attached himself to Zhōngshū Shèrén Huáng Mùzhī and others.
Whenever high officials dined,
Lián would invariably submit delicious food daily,
personally frying and seasoning everything by hand,
refusing to shy away from strenuous labor.
Consequently, he managed to become a Lièqīng (High Minister),
Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng,
and the Tàishǒu of Jìnlíng and Wúxīng.
At that time, Guǎnglíng’s Gāo Shuǎng had a talent for treachery and duplicity,
and served as a retainer under Lián.
Lián entrusted him with documents and records.
Gāo Shuǎng once made a request that was not satisfied,
so he created a wooden clog riddle to convey his meaning to Lián, saying:
“It pokes the nose but knows no sneeze,
it is trampled on the face but knows no anger,
it gnaws the teeth to measure steps,
holding onto this, one can surpass others.”
This mocked him for disregarding shame and humiliation,
using them to attain status and position.
Fú Jī, whose courtesy name was Xuányào,
was the son of Mánróng.
In his youth, he inherited his father’s learning,
and could discuss profound principles.
He was renowned alongside Rèn Fǎng of Yuè'ān and Liú Màn of Péngchéng.
He began his career during the Qí dynasty as Fèng Cháoqǐng,
and concurrently served as Tàixué Bóshì.
Soon after, he was appointed Dōngyáng Jùnchéng,
and after his term was complete, he became the Magistrate (Lìng) of Yín.
As Mánróng had already retired at that time,
Fú Jī was frequently placed in external positions,
allowing him to support his parent.
At the end of the Qí dynasty,
he was first appointed Shàngshū Dūguān Láng,
and then Wèijūn Jìshì Cānjūn.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he was promoted to Guózǐ Bóshì.
He resigned due to mourning for his father.
After the period of mourning was complete,
he served as Chēqí Zīyì Cānjūn,
and was successively promoted to Sīkōng Zhǎngshǐ,
Zhōngshū Shìláng,
Qiánjūn Jiāngjūn,
and concurrently Wǔjīng Bóshì.
He was placed in overall charge of the Five Rites affairs, alongside Lìbù Shàngshū Xú Miǎn and Zhōngshū Shìláng Zhōu Shě.
He was dispatched out to serve as Yǒngyáng Nèishǐ.
While governing the commandery, he was clean and pure,
and his administration was peaceful and quiet.
One hundred and fifty-four people, including the commandery resident Hé Zhēnxiù, went to the prefecture (Zhōu) to report on his excellent conduct.

Gāozǔ praised him for it,

Although the commandery produced a lot of hemp and ramie,

His commitment was of this degree.
The subordinate counties Shǐxīn, Suì’ān, and Hǎiníng,

He was summoned to serve as Guózǐ Bóshì,
and concurrently led the Chángshuǐ Xiàowèi.
At that time, Hé Yuǎn, the Nèishǐ of Shǐxīng, had repeatedly demonstrated pure conduct.
Gāozǔ issued an edict promoting him to Huángmén Shìláng,

Fú Jī considered that his reputation and standing had always been ahead of Hé Yuǎn,
and that they both maintained reputations for probity and honesty as officials.
Yet, Hé Yuǎn was repeatedly promoted,
while Fú Jī merely advanced in grade.
His expectations were not met,

He petitioned for his own removal from office.

Yú Hú, the Zhìshū Shìyùshǐ, submitted a memorial, stating: "Your servant has heard that when loyalty and trust are lost,
the way of integrity is diminished;

blackmails the sovereign,

Reasoning from this,

This is naturally the foundation of governance;

He always

sighing

'Guózǐ Bóshì and acting Chángshuǐ
Xiàowèi Fú Jī,
has been clean and fair in governing.

How can a court official, having received an edict like
this,
not lose his wits and break his courage,
blame himself before the relevant authorities,
pluck out his hair and draw out his intestines (in self-mortification),
and offer even a slight apology or justification?
Instead, he simply complied and accepted it,

Given Fú Jī’s insight
and understanding,
he must surely have grasped the import of this instruction,

Consequently, the scholar class has been demoralized,

Examining his actions and seeking his intentions,
there is not a single thing

I humbly submit that Fú Jī, stumbling and downcast,
for over thirty years,
saw the imperial fortune suddenly rise,

washing (the state clean) like the Jiāng and Hàn rivers.
Within the space
of one cycle (twelve years),

Disloyalty and disrespect,
have already

If the law states
this,
Fú Jī is the principal offender."
Your servant respectfully reviews the case: Fú Jī, the Nèishǐ of Yùzhāng,
concealed his flaws while displaying upright conduct,
and relied on perversity to define his motivation.
Both his silence and speech were contradictory,
exhausting both faithfulness and reverence.
He was fortunate to live in a prosperous era,
and was promoted without regard to standard sequence.
The ravines and gorges might be filled,
but his desires were never satisfied.
Blackmailing the sovereign by running East,
how can this be called the return of one who knows contentment?
Abandoning his ambition and taking off his cap,
this differs from the result achieved by those driven by passion.
To crave such richness,
who would not call it hardship?
Wearing the turtle seal and ribbon,
how is it different from being bound in ropes?
It is proper to clarify the code of conduct and discipline,
and sternly rectify the official documents.
Your servants have deliberated together,
and request that based on the evidence,
Fú Jī be dismissed from his current office,
and that all his positions and appointments,
be entirely stripped away.
An imperial edict commanded that no punishment be enacted,
and Fú Jī was consequently able to proceed to his commandery.

Yáo Chá, Minister of Personnel of the Chén Dynasty, said: In previous histories, there were "model officials" (xún lì).
Why was that?
It was because the age necessitated it.
Under Hàn Wǔdì, duties were numerous and villainy arose.
Gentle governance was ineffective;
thus, severe cruelties, executions, and massacres were used to overcome them,
which also led to much resentment and injustice.
When Liáng arose,
it broke the angular into the rounded,
and carved things back into simplicity,
instructing the people in filial piety and fraternal duty,
and encouraging them in agriculture and sericulture.
Consequently, the wicked and cunning transformed into people like Yóu Yú,
and the frivolous changed into the loyal and sincere.
When pure customs had spread,
the people naturally knew what was forbidden.
The people of Yáo and Shùn
could truly be given fiefs house by house,
it is true!
As for harsh officials (kù lì),

Biographies, Chapter 48: Various Barbarians - South of the Sea, Eastern Barbarians, Northwestern Rong Tribes.
The various states South of the Sea
are generally located on islands in the vast ocean, south and southwest of Jiāozhōu.
The nearest are three to five thousand *lǐ* apart,
the furthest are twenty to thirty thousand *lǐ* apart,
and to their west, they border the various states of the Western Regions (Xīyù).
During the Yuándǐng era of the Hàn Dynasty,
General Fúbō (Subduer of Waves), Lù Bódé, was dispatched to open up the Bǎiyuè territory,
and Rìnán Commandery was established.
The various states beyond that border
all offered tribute since the time of Emperor Wǔ.
During the reign of Emperor Huán of the Latter Hàn,
Dà Qín and Tiānzhú both sent envoys along this route to present tribute.
And during the time of Sūn Quán of the Wú state,
he dispatched Zhū Yìng, Aide in Propagating Culture, and Kāng Tài, Gentleman of the Palace, to establish communications there.
The countries they passed through or heard reports of
numbered over a hundred,
and consequently, records and accounts were established.
During the Jìn dynasty, those communicating with the Central Lands were few,
thus they were not recorded by the historians.
When it came to Sòng and Qí,
more than ten states arrived,
and biographies were first written for them.
Since the Liáng established its reign,
those states who honored the Liáng calendar,
performed tribute duties,
and crossed the seas arriving annually,
exceeded the previous dynasties.
Now, selecting the rough details of their customs
and arranging them, this is called the Biographies of the States South of the Sea.
The Kingdom of Línyì
was originally Xiànglín County of Rìnán Commandery in the Hàn Dynasty,
which was the ancient boundary of Yuècháng.
General Fúbō Mǎ Yuán opened up the southern boundary of Hàn,
and established this county.
The territory is approximately six hundred *lǐ* in extent (length and width).
The city is one hundred twenty *lǐ* from the sea,
over four hundred *lǐ* from the border of Rìnán,
and borders Jiǔdé Commandery to the north.
In its southern region,
by water and land routes, over two hundred *lǐ* away,
there is a state of barbarians from the west who also claim kingship.
This is where Mǎ Yuán erected two bronze pillars marking the Hàn boundary.
In that country, there is Golden Mountain (Jīn Shān).
The stones are all reddish,
and gold originates within them.
At night, the gold flies out,
resembling fireflies.
It also produces hawksbill turtle shell, cowry teeth, *jíbèi* cotton, and *chén mù xiāng* (aloeswood).
*Jíbèi*
is the name of a tree.
When its flowers mature, they resemble goose down.
The fibers are drawn out and spun to make cloth;
it is pure white and indistinguishable from ramie cloth,
and it can also be dyed in five colors
and woven into patterned cloth.
*Chén mù* (sinking wood)
is cut down by the locals,
piled up over years,
where it rots away, and only the heartwood remains.
When placed in water, it sinks,
and is thus called *chén xiāng* (sinking incense/aloeswood).
That which neither sinks nor floats
is called *gōng xiāng*.
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there was great chaos.
The Registrar, Qū Dá,
killed the county magistrate and established himself as king.
This was passed down for several generations.
When a later king had no heir,
he established his nephew, Fàn Xióng.
After Xióng died,
his son Yì succeeded him.
In the third year of Xiánkāng of Emperor Chéng of Jìn (337 CE),
Yì died.
His slave, Wén, usurped the throne and established himself.
Wén was originally a slave of Fàn Zhì, a chieftain of the Yí people in Xījuǎn county of Rìnán.
He often herded cattle in a mountain gully
when he found two snakeheads (Channa argus).
They transformed into iron,
so he used them to forge a knife.
When it was finished,
Wén faced a stone and swore, saying:
"If I can chop this stone and break it,
then I shall become king of this country."
He then raised the knife and chopped the stone.
It was as if he were cutting straw,
and Wén's heart was uniquely surprised by this.
Fàn Zhì often sent him to trade in Línyì.
He then taught the king of Línyì how to build palaces and military vehicles and weapons.
The king favored and trusted him.
Later, he slandered the king's sons,
who each fled to other countries.
When the king died without an heir,
Wén pretended to welcome a prince from a neighboring country,
put poison in his drink and killed him,
then coerced the people of the country and established himself.
He raised an army and attacked the small neighboring countries,
swallowing them all up,
and had a force of forty to fifty thousand men.
At that time, Jiāng Zhuāng, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, sent his trusted associates Hán Jí and Xiè Zhì,
one after another, to oversee Rìnán Commandery.
Both were corrupt and cruel,
and all the countries suffered from them.
In the third year of Yǒnghé of Emperor Mù (347 CE),
the court sent Xiàhóu Lǎn to be the Grand Administrator.
His oppression and exploitation were even more severe.
Línyì had previously lacked fertile land
and coveted the rich land of Rìnán,
always wishing to seize it.
By this time,
taking advantage of the people's resentment,
it raised an army and attacked Rìnán,
killing Lǎn
and offering his corpse as a sacrifice to heaven.
They remained in Rìnán for three years
before returning to Línyì.
The Inspector of Jiāozhōu, Zhū Fān, later sent the Supervisor Liú Xióng to garrison Rìnán.
Wén again
slaughtered and annihilated him. He advanced and plundered Jiǔdé Commandery,
harming officials and common people.
He sent an envoy to inform Fān,
wishing to make Mount Héng, the northern border of Rìnán, the boundary.
Fān did not agree
and again sent Supervisors Táo Huǎn and Lǐ Qú to attack him.
Wén returned to Línyì,
but soon after again garrisoned Rìnán.
Five years later,
Wén died,
and his son Fó succeeded him,
still garrisoning Rìnán.
Huán Wēn, the General who Conquers the West, sent the Supervisor Téng Jùn and the Grand Administrator of Jiǔzhēn, Guàn Suì, to lead troops from Jiāo and Guǎng provinces to attack him.
Fó fortified the city and held it firmly.
Suì ordered Jùn to deploy a large force in front,
while Suì himself led seven hundred elite soldiers
and entered by climbing over the ramparts from the rear.
Fó's troops were shocked, panicked, and fled.
Suì pursued them to Línyì,
where Fó then requested surrender.
At the beginning of Shēngpíng of Emperor Āi (357 CE),
he again became a menace, and Inspector Wēn Fàngzhī attacked and defeated him.
In the third year of Lóng'ān of Emperor Ān (399 CE),
Fó's grandson, Xūdá, again attacked Rìnán,
capturing the Grand Administrator, Jìng Yuán.
He then advanced and plundered Jiǔdé,
capturing the Grand Administrator, Cáo Bǐng.
Dù Yuàn, the Grand Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, sent the Protector Dèng Yì and others to defeat him.
Yuàn was then appointed Inspector.
In the third year of Yìxī (407 CE),
Xūdá again attacked Rìnán,
killing the Chief Clerk.
Yuàn sent the Maritime Patrol Supervisor Ruǎn Fěi to attack and defeat him,
slaying and capturing a great many.
In the ninth year (413 CE),
Xūdá again attacked Jiǔzhēn.
Dù Huìqī, acting as Commandery Administrator, fought him,
beheading his son, King Jiāolóng Zhēn Zhī, and his general, Fàn Jiàn, and others,
and capturing Xūdá's son Néng alive,
along with over a hundred other captives.
After Yuàn's death,
Línyì plundered Rìnán and Jiǔdé commanderies every year,
killing and pillaging many people.
〔一０〕Jiāozhōu thus became weak and depleted.
After Xūdá died,
his son Dízhēn succeeded him.
His younger brother Díkǎi's mother fled.
Dízhēn regretted being unable to accommodate his mother's brother (step-brother),
so he abandoned the country and went to Tiānzhú (India),
ceding the throne to his nephew.
The Chancellor, Zàng Lín, strongly advised against it, but he did not listen.
After his nephew was established, he killed Zàng Lín.
Zàng Lín's son then attacked and killed him,
and established Wén Dí, the half-brother of Díkǎi (same mother, different father).
Wén Dí was later killed by Dānggēnchún, a prince of Fúnán.
The high minister Fàn Zhūnóng suppressed the rebellion
and established himself as king.
After Zhūnóng died,
his son Yángmài succeeded him.
In the second year of Yǒngchū of Sòng (421 CE),
he sent envoys to offer tribute,
and Yángmài was appointed King of Línyì.
After Yángmài died,
his son Duō succeeded him.
He admired his father
and again called himself Yángmài.
〔一一〕
The customs of their country: their dwellings are elevated structures
called "yúlán."
Doors and windows all face north.
They write on tree leaves as paper.
Men and women all wrap a horizontal strip of jíbèi cloth around their waists downwards,
which is called "gānmàn,"
also known as "dōumàn."
They pierce their ears and wear small rings.
The noble wear leather sandals,
while the common walk barefoot.
This is true for Línyì, Fúnán, and all countries to their south.
Their king wears ceremonial robes,
adorned with yīngluò (necklaces),
like the ornaments of a Buddha statue.
When he goes out, he rides an elephant,
blows conch shells, beats drums,
is shaded by a jíbèi umbrella,
and uses jíbèi as banners and flags.
The country has no established penal code.
Those who commit crimes are trampled to death by elephants.
Their major clans are called Brāhman.
Marriages must take place in the eighth month.
Women propose to men first,
indicating that men are of lower status than women.
They marry within the same clan.
They have a Brāhman lead the groom to see the bride,
who takes his hand and entrusts herself to him,
and they say a chant:
"Jílì, Jílì" (auspicious, auspicious),
which is considered the completion of the ceremony.
The deceased are cremated in the wilderness,
which is called "huǒzàng" (cremation).
Widows live alone,
with disheveled hair until old age.
The king practices Nígān Dào (Jainism),
casting gold and silver human statues,
ten arm-spans in circumference.
At the beginning of Yuánjiā (424 CE),
Yángmài invaded and plundered Rìnán and Jiǔdé commanderies.
Dù Hóngwén, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, erected his banner intending to attack him,
but stopped upon hearing that a replacement was coming.
Eight years later,
he again attacked Jiǔdé Commandery,
entering the estuary of Sìhuì.
Ruǎn Mízhī, the Inspector of Jiāozhōu, sent the company commander Xiāng Dàoshēng to lead troops to attack him.
They attacked Qūlì city but could not capture it,
so they withdrew.
Thereafter, they frequently sent envoys to offer tribute,
but their plundering did not cease.
In the twenty-third year (446 CE),
Jiāozhōu Inspector Tán Hézhī and General Zhènwǔ Zōng Quán attacked him.
Hézhī sent his Sīmǎ (Chief Clerk), Xiāo Jǐngxiàn, as the vanguard.
Yángmài, hearing of this, was afraid
and wanted to offer ten thousand catties of gold and one hundred thousand catties of silver,
and return the people he had plundered from Rìnán.
However, his high minister Sēng Dá advised him against it,
so he sent the great commander Fàn Fúlóng to garrison his northern border, Qūlì city.
Jǐngxiàn attacked the city
and captured it,
beheading Fúlóng
and capturing countless gold, silver, and miscellaneous items.
Taking advantage of the victory, he advanced directly
and immediately captured Línyì.
Yángmài and his son barely escaped with their lives.
He seized their rare treasures,
all of which were unnamed valuables.
He also melted down their gold statues,
obtaining several hundred thousand catties of gold.
Hézhī later died of illness,
seeing a "Hú god" haunting him.
During the Xiàowǔ, Xiàojiàn, and Dàmíng reigns,
〔一二〕 Fàn Shénchéng (范神成), King of Línyì (林邑), repeatedly sent his Registrar (長史) to present memorials and tribute.
In the first year of the Tàiyù reign of Emperor Míng (明帝),
he again sent envoys to present local products.
During the Yǒngmíng reign of Qí (齊),
Fàn Wénzàn (范文贊) repeatedly sent envoys to present tribute.
In the ninth year of Tiānjiān,
Wénzàn’s (文贊) son, Tiānkǎi (天凱), presented a white monkey.
An imperial edict stated:
“Fàn Tiānkǎi (范天凱), King of Línyì (林邑), residing across the sea,
has sincerely offered his loyalty and reached out to us,
travelling afar to present tribute.
This is truly commendable.
He should be granted a noble title
and bestowed with glory and favour.
He is appointed as Envoy with Credentials (持節), Overseer of all Military Affairs along the Coast (督緣海諸軍事), General Who Awe the South (威南將軍), and King of Línyì (林邑).”
In the tenth year,
and the thirteenth year,
Tiānkǎi (天凱) repeatedly sent envoys to present local products.
Shortly after, he died of illness.
His son, Bìcuìbámó (弼毳跋摩), ascended the throne
and presented memorials with tribute.
In the seventh year of Pǔtōng,
King Gāoshìshèngkǎi (高式勝鎧) sent envoys to present local products.
An imperial edict appointed him as Envoy with Credentials (持節), Overseer of all Military Affairs along the Coast (督緣海諸軍事), General Who Pacify the South (綏南將軍), and King of Línyì (林邑).
In the first year of Dàtōng,
he again sent envoys to present tribute.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng,
the acting King of Línyì (林邑), Gāoshìlǜluóbámó (高式律羅跋摩), sent envoys to present tribute.
An imperial edict appointed him as Envoy with Credentials (持節), Overseer of all Military Affairs along the Coast (督緣海諸軍事), General Who Pacify the South (綏南將軍), and King of Línyì (林邑).
In the sixth year,
he again sent envoys to present local products.
The kingdom of Fúnán (扶南)
is south of Rìnán Jùn (日南郡),
within a great bay west of the sea.
It is about seven thousand *lǐ* (里) from Rìnán (日南)
and over three thousand *lǐ* (里) southwest of Línyì (林邑).
Its capital is five hundred *lǐ* (里) from the sea.
There is a great river, ten *lǐ* (里) wide,
flowing northwest,
then east into the sea.
The kingdom has a circumference of over three thousand *lǐ* (里).
The land is low-lying, flat, and broad.
Its climate and customs are largely similar to Línyì (林邑).
It produces gold, silver, copper, tin, agarwood, ivory, peacocks, and five-coloured parrots.
About three thousand *lǐ* (里) to its south lies the kingdom of Dùnxùn (頓遜),
situated on a sea peninsula.
Its territory spans a thousand *lǐ* (里),
and its capital is ten *lǐ* (里) from the sea.
It has five kings,
all subordinate to Fúnán (扶南).
Dùnxùn’s (頓遜) eastern border connects to Jiāozhōu (交州),
while its western border adjoins the kingdoms outside the territories of Tiānzhú (天竺) and Ānxī (安息),
allowing for trade and exchange.
This is because
Dùnxùn (頓遜) extends into the sea for over a thousand *lǐ* (里),
and the expansive sea has no accessible shores,
so ships have never been able to pass directly through.
At its market,
traders from east and west gather,
with over ten thousand people daily.
Precious goods and treasures
are all available there.
There is also a “wine tree,”
resembling a pomegranate.
Its flower juice is collected and stored in jars,
turning into wine after several days.
Beyond Dùnxùn (頓遜),
on a large island in the great sea,
is the kingdom of Píqiān (毗騫),
eight thousand *lǐ* (里) from Fúnán (扶南).
It is said that its king is twelve *chǐ* (丈二) tall,
with a neck three *chǐ* (三尺) long.
〔一三〕He has been immortal since ancient times,
and his age is unknown.
The king is divine and sacred.
He knows the good and evil deeds of his people and all future events.
The king knows everything,
so no one dares to deceive him.
In the south, he is called the "Long-necked King."
According to their customs,
they have houses and clothes,
and eat polished rice.
Their language
differs slightly from Fúnán (扶南).
There is a mountain that produces gold.
Gold appears naturally on the rocks,
without any limits.
According to their law, criminals are punished
by having their flesh eaten in front of the king.
The country does not receive merchants.
If anyone comes, they are also killed and eaten.
Therefore, merchants dare not approach.
The king always resides in a multi-storied building,
does not eat meat,
and does not worship spirits or gods.
His descendants live and die like ordinary people;
only the king is immortal.
The King of Fúnán (扶南) often sent envoys to exchange letters.
He always presented the King of Fúnán (扶南) with fifty pure gold eating utensils.
Some were shaped like round plates,
others like pottery bowls,
called *duōluó* (多羅),
holding five *shēng* (升),
and still others like smaller bowls,
holding one *shēng* (升).
The king could also write in Tiānzhú (天竺) script.
His writings, about three thousand words,
explained his past lives,
resembling Buddhist scriptures,
and discussed good deeds.
It is also said that Fúnán’s (扶南) eastern border is the great expansive sea.
In the sea, there is a large island.
On the island are various Bó (薄) kingdoms.
East of these kingdoms are the Wǔzhōu (五洲) islands.
Travelling further east across the expansive sea for over a thousand *lǐ* (里),
one reaches the Great Natural Island.
On it, there are trees that grow in fire.
People near the island peel their bark,
spin it into cloth,
making small towels a few *chǐ* (尺) long.
They are indistinguishable from burnt hemp, but slightly greenish-black in colour.
If they become slightly dirty,
they are thrown into fire,
and emerge clean again.
Sometimes they are used as lamp wicks,
and never seem to burn out.
The customs of Fúnán (扶南) originally involved nudity,
tattooed bodies, and unbound hair,
without prescribed clothing.
They had a woman as their ruler,
named Liǔyè (柳葉).
She was young and strong,
resembling a man.
To its south was a border kingdom.
〔一四〕A person named Húntián (混填), who worshipped spirits and gods,
dreamt that a deity bestowed a bow upon him.
He boarded a merchant ship and went out to sea.
Húntián (混填) rose early and went to the temple.
He found a bow under the sacred tree,
and immediately, following his dream, boarded a ship and sailed into the sea,
eventually entering the outer territories of Fúnán (扶南).
When Liǔyè (柳葉) and her people saw the ship arrive,
they wanted to seize it.
Húntián (混填) immediately drew his bow and shot at their ships,
piercing through one side.
The arrow hit a retainer.
Liǔyè (柳葉) was greatly frightened,
and led her people to surrender to Húntián (混填).
Húntián (混填) then taught Liǔyè (柳葉) to wear cloth through her head,
so her body would no longer be exposed.
He then governed her kingdom,
took Liǔyè (柳葉) as his wife,
and their children were made kings over seven cities.
Later, King Hùnpánkùang (混盤況) used deception and force to sow discord among the various cities,
making them suspicious of each other.
He then raised an army, attacked, and unified them.
He then sent his descendants to divide and govern the cities,
who were called "Minor Kings."
Pán Kuàng (盤況) died at over ninety years old.
His middle son, Pán Pán (盤盤), was enthroned,
and the affairs of the state were entrusted to his great general, Fàn Màn (范蔓).
Pán Pán (盤盤) died three years after his enthronement.
The people of the state collectively elevated Màn (蔓) to be king.
Màn (蔓) was brave and strong, possessing strategies and tactics.
He again used military might to attack neighboring states,
all of which submitted to him.
He styled himself the Great King of Fúnán (扶南).
He then built large ships,
traversed the expansive sea,
and attacked over ten states including Qū Dōukūn (屈都昆), Jiǔ Zhì (九稚), and Diǎn Sūn (典孫),
opening up territory five to six thousand *lǐ* (里).
Next, when he was about to attack the state of Jīnlín (金隣),
Màn (蔓) fell ill.
He sent his crown prince, Jīn Shēng (金生), to act on his behalf.
Màn's (蔓) sister's son, Zhān (旃),
who was at that time a general of two thousand men,
usurped the throne from Màn (蔓) and established himself.
He sent someone to deceive Jīn Shēng (金生) and kill him.
When Màn (蔓) died,
he had an infant son named Cháng (長),
who was living among the common people.
When he reached twenty years of age,
he gathered strong men from the state and ambushed and killed Zhān (旃).
Zhān's (旃) great general, Fàn Xún (范尋), then killed Cháng (長) and established himself.
He further improved the internal administration of the state,
built towers and pavilions for enjoyment,
and received guests three or four times in the morning and afternoon.
The common people presented gifts of charred sugarcane, turtles, and birds.
The state law had no prisons.
Those who committed crimes
first fasted for three days.
Then, an axe was heated to extreme redness,
and the accused was made to hold it and walk seven steps.
Alternatively, a gold ring and a chicken egg were thrown into boiling water,
and the accused was made to retrieve them.
If they were innocent,
their hands would be scorched and烂 (làn) (ruined),
but if they were guilty, their hands would not be harmed.
Also, crocodiles were kept in the city moat,
and fierce beasts were caged outside the city gates.
Those who were guilty
were fed to these fierce beasts and crocodiles.
If the animals did not eat them, they were considered innocent,
and were released after three days.
Large crocodiles were over two *zhàng* (丈) long,
shaped like *tuó* (鼉) (alligators).
They had four feet,
a snout six or seven *chǐ* (尺) long,
and teeth on both sides,
sharp as knives and swords.
They usually ate fish,
but also devoured deer and people if encountered.
They were found south of Cāngwú (蒼梧) and in foreign countries.
During the Wú (吳) dynasty,
Zhōngláng (中郎) Kāng Tài (康泰) and Xuānhuà Cóngshì (宣化從事) Zhū Yīng (朱應) were sent as envoys to Xún's (尋) state.
The people of the state were still naked,
except for women who wore 'pierced-head' garments.
Tài (泰) and Yīng (應) said to them:
"The state is truly excellent,
but the people's exposure is strange."
Xún (尋) then ordered the men of his state to wear *héngfú* (橫幅).
*Héngfú* (橫幅)
is now called *gānmàn* (干漫).
Wealthy families made them from brocade,
while the poor used cloth.
During the Tàikāng (太康) era of Emperor Wǔ of Jìn (晉武帝),
Xún (尋) first sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the first year of the Shēngpíng (升平) era of Emperor Mù (穆帝),
King Zhú Zhāntán (竺旃檀) presented a memorial offering tamed elephants.
An imperial edict stated:
"This item incurs no small labor and expense,
detain it and do not send it."
Later, King Jiāochénrú (憍陳如),
originally a Brāhmaṇa from Tiānzhú (天竺),
had a divine voice tell him
"You should be king of Fúnán (扶南)."
Jiāochénrú (憍陳如) was delighted in his heart.
He traveled south to Pán Pán (盤盤).
When the people of Fúnán (扶南) heard of this,
the whole state rejoiced and supported him,
welcoming and enthroning him.
He again reformed the system
and adopted the laws of Tiānzhú (天竺).
When Jiāochénrú (憍陳如) died,
the subsequent king, Chí Lí Bámó (持梨跋摩),
presented a memorial offering local products during the reign of Emperor Wén of Sòng (宋文帝).
During the Yǒngmíng (永明) era of Qí (齊),
King Shéyé Bámó (闍邪跋摩) sent envoys to offer tribute.
In the second year of Tiānjiān (天監),
Bámó (跋摩) again sent envoys to deliver a coral Buddha statue
and offer local products.
An imperial edict stated:
"Fúnán (扶南) King Jiāochénrú Shéyé Bámó (憍陳如闍邪跋摩),
residing across the sea,
has for generations presided over the southern lands.
His sincerity is widely evident,
offering precious tribute through multiple translations.
He should be rewarded and accepted,
and granted an honorable title.
He is appointed General Guarding the South and King of Fúnán (安南將軍、扶南王)."
Today, the people of his state are all ugly and dark,
with curly hair.
They do not dig wells where they live;
dozens of households share one pond for drawing water.
Their custom is to worship heavenly deities.
Heavenly deities are represented by copper statues,
those with two faces have four arms,
those with four faces have eight arms.
Each hand holds something,
perhaps a child,
or a bird or beast,
or the sun and moon.
Their king rides an elephant when going out or entering,
and his consorts and attendants do likewise.
When the king sits, he half-squats with one knee raised,
letting his left knee hang to the ground.
White felt is spread before him,
and a gold basin and incense burner are placed upon it.
According to their state customs,
during mourning, beards and hair are shaved off.
There are four types of burial for the dead: water burial means casting them into the river,
fire burial means burning them to ashes,
earth burial means interring them,
and bird burial means abandoning them in the wilderness.
Their nature is greedy and stingy,
without propriety or righteousness.
Men and women are free to follow their desires in relationships.
In the tenth year,
and thirteenth year,
Bámó (跋摩) repeatedly sent envoys to offer tribute.
In that year he died,
and his illegitimate son, Liú Bámó (留跋摩), killed his legitimate younger brother and established himself.
In the sixteenth year,
he sent the envoy Zhú Dāng Bǎolǎo (竺當抱老) to present a memorial and offer tribute.
In the eighteenth year,
he again sent envoys to deliver an auspicious sandalwood image from Tiānzhú (天竺) and bodhi tree leaves,
along with fire-pearls, turmeric, and storax incense.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (普通),
the second year of Zhōng Dàtōng (中大通),
and the first year of Dàtóng (大同),
envoys were repeatedly sent to offer local products.
In the fifth year,
envoys were again sent to offer live rhinoceroses.
It was also said that their state possessed a Buddha's hair,
twelve *chǐ* (尺) long.
An imperial edict ordered the *shāmén* (沙門) Shì Yúnbǎo (釋雲寶) to accompany the envoys to retrieve it.
Previously,
in the eighth month of the third year,
Gāozǔ (高祖) rebuilt the stupa of King Āyù (阿育王),
from beneath the old stupa were taken *shèlì* (舍利) and Buddha's nails and hair.
The hair was blue-black in color.
When the monks extended it with their hands,
it would lengthen or shorten according to their hands.
When released, it would coil back into the shape of a snail shell.
According to the Saṃgha Sūtra, it is stated:
"The Buddha's hair is blue and fine,
like the fibers of a lotus root stem."
The Buddha Samādhi Sūtra states:
"When I was in the palace, I washed my head,
and measured my hair with a ruler;
it was twelve *chǐ* (尺) long.
When released, it spiraled to the right,
forming a snail pattern."
This is consistent with what Gāozǔ (高祖) obtained.
King Āyù (阿育王) was the Iron Wheel King,
who ruled Jambudvīpa (閻浮提),
the entire world.
After the Buddha's parinirvāṇa,
in one day and one night,
he commanded ghosts and spirits to build eighty-four thousand stupas.
This was one of them.
During the Wú (吳) dynasty, a nun resided there,
maintaining a small monastery.
Sūn Lín (孫綝) later destroyed it,
and the stupa also perished.
After Wú (吳) was pacified,
various Daoists rebuilt it at the old site.
When Emperor Zhōng of Jìn (晉中宗) first crossed the Yangtze River,
it was further repaired and adorned.
During the Xián'ān (咸安) era of Emperor Jiǎnwén (簡文),
the *shāmén* (沙門) Master Ān Fǎshī Chéng (安法師程) was commissioned to build a small stupa,
but he died before it was completed.
His disciple Sēng Xiǎn (僧顯) continued and completed its construction.
In the ninth year of Tàiyuán (太元) of Emperor Xiàowǔ (孝武), a golden finial and dew-receiving basin were added.
After this, in Líshí Xiàn, Xīhé, there was a Hu man named Liú Sàhé who suddenly died from illness,
but his heart area was still warm,
and his family did not dare to bury him immediately.
After ten days, he revived.
He said:
"Two officials arrested me,
and we traveled northwest.
I do not know how far it was,
until we reached the eighteen hells,
where, according to the severity of their karmic retribution,
people suffered various painful tortures.
I saw Guānshìyīn (Avalokiteśvara), who said: 'Your lifespan fate is not yet exhausted.
If you can live,
you should become a Shāmén (monk).
Luòxià, Qíchéng, Dānyáng, and Kuàijī all have stūpas of King Āyù Wáng (Ashoka).
You should go and pay homage to them.
When your life ends,
you will not fall into hell.'
After speaking,
it was as if I fell from a high cliff,
and I suddenly woke up."
Because of this, he left home (became a monk),
named Huìdá.
He traveled around paying homage to the stūpas.
Next, he arrived at Dānyáng,
but did not know where the stūpa was located.
He then climbed Yuèchéng to look around,
and saw unusual colors (or radiance) over Chánggānlǐ.
He approached the spot to pay homage,
and it was indeed the site of the Āyù Wáng stūpa,
which frequently emitted bright light.
From this, he confirmed that there must be *śarīra* (relics).
He gathered a crowd and began digging.
Digging down one *zhàng* (about 10 feet),
they found three stone steles,
all six *chǐ* long.
Inside one stele was an iron casket.
Inside that casket was a silver casket.
Inside that casket was a gold casket,
which contained three *śarīra* and one piece each of nail and hair.
The hair was several *chǐ* long.
They immediately moved the *śarīra* nearby to the north,
opposite the west side of the stūpa built by [Emperor] Jiǎnwén,
and constructed a one-story stūpa.
Sixteen years later,
he again commissioned the Shāmén Sēng Shàngjiā to build it up to three stories;
this is the one [Emperor] Gāozǔ later opened.
When they first dug four *chǐ* into the soil,
they discovered a dragon cave and various scattered treasures left by people in the past, such as gold and silver rings, bracelets, hairpins, and tweezers.
When they reached a depth of about nine *chǐ*,
they finally reached the stone foundation.
Beneath the foundation was a stone casket.
Inside the casket was an iron jar,
which held a silver basin.
Inside the basin was a gold filigree jar,
containing three *śarīra*.
They were the size of millet grains,
perfectly round, radiant, and pure.
Inside the casket there was also a lapis lazuli bowl,
which contained four *śarīra*, hair, and nails.
There were four pieces of nail,
all the color of agarwood.
On the twenty-seventh day of that month,
Emperor Gāozǔ again visited the temple to pay homage,
and held a Wúchā Dàhuì (Great Dharma Assembly),
granting a general amnesty throughout the realm.
On that day,
a gold bowl was filled with water and the *śarīra* were floated in it.
The smallest one sank and did not emerge from the bowl.
Emperor Gāozǔ bowed dozens of times,
and the *śarīra* then emitted light from within the bowl.
After circling for a long time,
it stopped exactly in the center of the bowl.
Emperor Gāozǔ asked the Great Head Monk, Huìniàn:
“Did you see an inconceivable event today?”
Huìniàn replied:
“The Dharma Body is eternally present,
profoundly still and unmoving.”
Emperor Gāozǔ said:
“This disciple wishes to invite one *śarīra* back to the Capital (Tái) for veneration.”
On the fifth day of the ninth month (Jiǔyuè Wǔrì),
he again held a Wúchā Dàhuì at the temple,
sending the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ), various princes, marquises, and court nobles to escort the relic.
On this day,
the weather was bright and pleasant.
The capital was emptied of its inhabitants,
with hundreds of thousands of spectators.
The gold and silver offering implements and other items provided
were all left at the temple for veneration,
and he also donated ten million cash as the temple’s foundational endowment.
Later, on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the fourth year,
Emperor Gāozǔ again visited the temple for a Wúchā Dàhuì,
and erected two stūpa pillars (*chà*).
For each, he used a gold vase,
followed by a jade vase,
to repeatedly contain the *śarīra*, nails, and hair,
which were then placed inside seven-jeweled stūpas.
He then used stone caskets to hold the jeweled stūpas,
and placed them separately beneath the two stūpa pillars.
Also added were piles of treasures—gold, silver, rings, bracelets, and other jewels—donated by princes, marquises, imperial consorts, princesses, common people, and wealthy families.
On the second day of the eleventh month of the eleventh year,
the temple monks again invited Emperor Gāozǔ to the temple to speak on the topic of the Bōrě Jīng (Prajñā Sūtra).
That evening, both stūpas emitted bright light.
He commanded the General Who Guards the East (Zhèndōng Jiāngjūn), Shàolíng Wáng Lún, to compose the inscription for the Great Merit Stele of the temple.
Before this,
in the second year,
he rebuilt the stūpa in Màoxiàn, Kuàijī.
They opened the old stūpa and retrieved the *śarīra*.
He sent Shì Jìngtuō and three other monks from Guāngzhái Sì, along with Palace Attendant Sūn Zhào, to temporarily escort them back to the Capital (Tái).
After Emperor Gāozǔ had paid his respects,
they were immediately sent back to the county and placed under the new stūpa.
This county stūpa was also one of the ones discovered by Liú Sàhé.
During the Xiánhé period of the Jìn dynasty,
Gāo Kuī, the Governor (Yǐn) of Dānyáng, traveled to Zhānghóu Qiáo.
He saw a five-colored light several *chǐ* long emanating from the stream.
Unsure what the marvel was,
he ordered men to dig and look at the place where the light was coming from.
They found a golden image,
but it lacked a halo base.
Kuī then descended from his carriage,
and loaded the image to return.
When they reached the beginning of Chánggān Lane,
the ox refused to move forward.
Kuī then instructed the driver to let the ox go wherever it wished.
The ox pulled the carriage directly to the temple.
Kuī subsequently left the image with the temple monks.
Every time midnight arrived,
the image routinely emitted bright light,
and the sound of metal and stone could be heard in the air.
After one year,
a fisherman named Zhāng Xìshì,
suddenly saw a bronze floral pedestal (base) floating on the water near the river mouth.
Xìshì retrieved it and sent it to the county office.
The county office sent it to the Capital (Tái),
and when it was affixed to the base of the image,
it fit perfectly.
Later, in the first year of the Xián'ān period of [Emperor] Jiǎnwén,
Dǒng Zōngzhī, a man from Hépǔ, Jiāozhōu, was diving for pearls.
At the bottom, he found a halo (radiance) of the Buddha.
Jiāozhōu escorted it to the Capital (Tái),
and when it was affixed to the image,
it matched perfectly again.
From the time the image was obtained during the Xiánhé period,
until the beginning of the Xián'ān period,
more than thirty years passed,
before the halo and base were finally complete.
Initially,
after Gāo Kuī obtained the image,
five Hu monks from the Western Regions came to visit Kuī.
They said:
“Long ago, we obtained an image made by King Āyù Wáng in India (Tiānzhú).
We brought it to Yèxià,
but due to the Hu invasion and chaos,
we buried the image by the river.
Now, searching for it, we have lost track of its location.”
The five men had all dreamed on the same night that the image spoke, saying:
“I have already emerged in Jiāngdōng,
and have been obtained by Gāo Kuī.”
Kuī then escorted these five monks to the temple.
Upon seeing the image, they sighed and wept,
and the image immediately emitted light,
illuminating the halls and rooms.
Furthermore, Huìsuì of Wǎguān Sì wished to make a replica of the image.
The temple abbot, Sēng Shàng, feared that the gold color would be damaged.
He said to Suì:
“If you can make the image emit light
and turn its body westward,
only then can I permit it.”
Huìsuì then earnestly paid homage and made a request.
That night, the image immediately rotated on its seat, emitted light,
and turned its body westward.
The next morning, permission was granted to make the replica.
The base of the image originally had foreign script,
which no one could recognize.
Later, the Tripiṭaka Master (Sānzàng) Qiúbámó recognized it,
saying it was made by King Āyù Wáng for his fourth daughter.
During the Dàtóng period,
the *śarīra* from the old stūpa were retrieved.
An imperial decree commanded the purchase of the residential lands of several hundred families next to the temple,
in order to expand the temple area.
They constructed various halls and chambers, as well as a surrounding corridor for the auspicious image,
making its construction magnificent and exquisite.
The drawings of the *jīngbiàn* (sūtra transformations)
were all executed by the Wu man Zhāng Yáo.
Yáo’s skill in painting (red and blue pigments),
was unmatched during that era.
during Yuánjiā of Sòng Wéndì,
and the Xiàojiàn and Dàmíng periods of [Sòng] Xiàowǔdì,
they all sent envoys to present tribute.
In the first year of Dàtōng (527 CE),
its king sent an envoy to respectfully present a memorial, which stated:
"To the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) of Zhèndàn (China), within Yánfútí, Yángzhōu: Adorned with ten thousand virtues,
respected by all,
just as the sky is pure and cloudless,
bright splendor filling the eye,
the Tiānzǐ's body and mind are pure
and likewise thus.
The monastics and laity are numerous and flourishing,
all benefiting from the brilliant transformation of the Sage King,
saving and delivering all beings,
forever acting as the boat of salvation.
Your subject hears this and rejoices in the good fortune.
We sincerely and reverently salute the feet of the Eternally Victorious Son of Heaven (Chángshèng Tiānzǐ),
bowing our heads in inquiry and greeting.
We now present a meager offering;
we pray that you graciously accept it."
In the fifth month of the first year of Zhōngdàtōng (529 CE),
envoys were repeatedly sent to offer ivory statues and stūpas,
along with several dozen varieties of incense, such as Chén (agarwood) and Tán (sandalwood).
In the eighth month of the sixth year (534 CE),
envoys were again sent, bringing genuine relics (shèlì) from Bódí Guó and painted stūpas,
along with Bodhi tree leaves and Zhāntáng incense.
The state of Dāndān,
in the second year of Zhōngdàtōng (530 CE),
its king sent an envoy to respectfully present a memorial, which stated:
"We humbly understand that the Sage Sovereign possesses ultimate virtue and benevolent rule;
he faithfully honors the Three Jewels (Sānbǎo),
the Buddhist Dharma is flourishing and manifest,
the multitude of monks is diligently assembled,
Dharma activities grow stronger daily,
and the authority is imposing and strict.
Those relied upon in the court and holding state power
are compassionate toward the common people.
The Eight Directions and the Six Harmonies (the entire world),
none fail to submit.
Your civilizing influence reaches the proximity of the various heavens;
it cannot be described in words.
We cannot contain our rejoicing in this good fortune,
as if momentarily paying respects before your honorable feet.
We respectfully present two ivory statues and two stūpas,
along with Huǒqí pearls, gǔbèi cloth, and various fragrant medicines."
In the first year of Dàtóng (535 CE),
envoys were again sent to present items such as gold, silver, lapis lazuli (liúlí), various jewels, fragrant medicines, and other goods.
The state of Gānlì
is located on an island in the Southern Sea.
Its customs are generally similar to those of Línyì and Fúnán.
It produces bānbù cloth, gǔbèi cloth, and betel nut (bīnláng).
Its bīnláng is especially fine,
ranking highest among all nations.
During the reign of Sòng Xiàowǔdì,
the king, Shì Póluólián, sent his Chief Clerk, Zhú Liú, to present gold, silver, and jeweled vessels.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (502 CE),
its king, Qútán Xiūbáluó, on the eighth day of the fourth month, dreamed that he saw a monk,
who said to him:
"There is now a Sage Sovereign in the Central State (Zhōngguó).
Ten years from now,
the Buddhist Dharma will greatly flourish.
If you send an envoy to present tribute and show reverence,
then your territory will be abundant and joyful,
and trade will increase a hundredfold.
If you do not believe me,
then your territory will not be able to secure itself."
Xiūbáluó initially did not believe him.
After a while, he dreamed of the same monk again, who said:
"If you do not believe me,
I shall take you to observe it."
Thereupon, in the dream, he arrived in the Central State (Zhōngguó)
and paid homage to the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ).
When he awoke,
he felt it was extraordinary.
Luó was originally skilled in painting.
He therefore depicted the appearance and features of Gāozǔ as seen in his dream,
adorned it with mineral pigments (dānqīng),
and then sent an envoy, along with a painter, to present a memorial and offer items such as a jade plate.
When the envoy arrived,
they copied the image of Gāozǔ and returned with it to their state.
It matched the original painting exactly.
They consequently placed it in a jeweled casket,
and daily offered rites of reverence.
Later, Báluó died,
and his son Píxié Bámó was established [as king].
In the seventeenth year (518 CE),
he sent his Chief Clerk, Píyuán Bámó, to respectfully present a memorial, which stated:
"To His Majesty, the Eternally Victorious Son of Heaven (Chángshèng Tiānzǐ):
All Buddhas, World-Honored Ones (Shìzūn),
enjoy eternal happiness and tranquility,
possessing the Six Supernatural Powers and Three Clear Insights (sāndá),
and are honored by the world;
this is called the Tathāgata (Rúlái),
worthy of offerings, the Perfectly Enlightened One (Zhèngjué).
[The Tiānzǐ] leaves behind the form of the shèlì (relics),
builds various stūpas and images,
adorning the realm
like Mount Xūmí.
Towns, dwellings, and settlements
are arrayed and filled in sequence;
city walls and public buildings
resemble the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (Dāolì Tiāngōng).
Possessing the four types of troops,
capable of subduing enemies.
The state is tranquil and happy,
free from all suffering and calamity,
the people are harmonious and virtuous,
receiving the transformation of the True Dharma (Zhèngfǎ),
and rejoicing flows everywhere unobstructed.
It is like being on the Snow Mountain (Xuěshān),
where the melted snow water flows forth,
pure and possessing the Eight Virtues (bāwèi),
filling the hundred rivers,
winding and turning,
eventually flowing into the great ocean,
so that all sentient beings
uniformly receive and benefit from it.
Among all nations,
it is uniquely superior and foremost—
