this is called Zhèndàn (China).
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) of Great Liáng, residing in Yángdū (Yangzhou/Capital),
covers the four seas with benevolent protection,
his virtue accords with the heart of Heaven.
Although a human, he is [like] Heaven,
having descended to be born to protect the world,
a precious treasury of merit and virtue,
possessing great compassion for saving the world,
born for us in honor,
and possessing complete majesty and decorum.
Therefore, we sincerely and reverently salute the feet of the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ),
bowing our heads in inquiry and greeting.
We respectfully present a golden lotus (fúróng), various fragrant medicines, and other items;
we pray that you graciously accept them."
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
envoys were again sent to present local products.
, is in the Nánhǎi
. Its territory spans thirty days travel east to west
, and twenty days travel north to south
. It is twenty-four thousand *lǐ* distant from Guǎngzhōu
. The climate and products
, are generally the same as Fúnán
, but it has an abundance of *gōngchén* (gaharu/aloeswood), *pólǜ* (frankincense) and other fragrances
. The custom is that both men and women are bare-chested and wear their hair loose
; they use *gǔbèi* (cotton cloth) for lower garments
. The king and noble ministers, however, add cloths of cloudy silk to cover their shoulders
, using gold cords as belts
, and gold rings pierced through their ears
. The women wear cloths
, and drape themselves with *yīngluò* (beaded necklaces/chains)
. The country builds its walls by piling up bricks
, with double gates and towers
. When the king goes out, he rides an elephant
; there are banners, feathered decorations, flags, and drums
, covered by a white canopy
, and the military guard is numerous
. The people of the country say
, that since the founding of the state, more than four hundred years have passed
. The subsequent heirs grew weak
. There was a worthy man in the royal clan
, and the people of the state were loyal to him
. When the king heard of this
, he placed him in prison
. His fetters spontaneously broke
. The king considered this miraculous
, and therefore dared not harm him
. Instead, he expelled him beyond the border
. He subsequently fled to Tiānzhú
. Tiānzhú married him to the eldest daughter
. Soon after, the King of Lángyá died
, and the great ministers welcomed him back to be king
. After more than twenty years, he died
. His son, Pójiādáduō, succeeded him
. In the fourteenth year of Tiānjiān
, he sent the envoy Āsāduō to present a memorial, which stated
: "Great Auspicious Son of Heaven, Your Majesty: Separated from lust, anger, and delusion
, you pity all sentient beings
, and your compassionate heart is immeasurable
. Your form is majestic and beautiful
, your body bright and glorious
, like the moon in the water
, illuminating the ten directions
. The white *ūrṇā* between your brows
, is white like snow
, its color shines brightly
, also like moonlight
. Worshipped by all *devas* and good spirits
, you maintain the treasure of the correct Dharma
. Pure conduct increases among the populace
, adorning the capital city
. The city walls and palaces are high and steep
, like Mount Gān
. Towers and pavilions are arranged in rows
, and the roads are level and straight
. The population flourishes
, joyful, secure, and stable
. They wear various clothes
, just like heavenly garments
. Among all nations
, yours is the most honored and victorious
. The Heavenly King pities the multitude of beings
, the people are peaceful and happy
, compassion is deep and broad
, disciplinary conduct is pure
, ruling through the transformation of the correct Dharma
, and offering respect to the Three Treasures
. Your illustrious reputation spreads
, covering the world
. The common people are happy to see you
, just as the moon is newly born
. You are likened to the Brahmā King
, the master of the world
, people and gods alike
, none fail to take refuge
. I reverently salute the Great Auspicious Son of Heaven, Your Majesty
, as if you were present before me
. I humbly inherit the legacy of my ancestors
, and rejoice boundlessly
. I now send this envoy to inquire after Your Great Well-being
. I wished to travel myself
, but feared the winds and waves of the great sea would prevent arrival
. I now humbly present a modest offering
, and pray that Your Great Household will graciously accept it
." The state of Póli
, is situated on an island in the sea southeast of Guǎngzhōu
. It is two months' travel distant from Guǎngzhōu
. Its national border spans fifty days' travel east to west
, and twenty days' travel north to south
. It contains one hundred and thirty-six settlements
. The climate is hot
, like the height of summer in the Middle Kingdom
. Grain ripens twice a year
, and grass and trees are perpetually luxuriant
. The sea produces patterned shells and purple cowries
. There is a stone called Hānbèiluó
, which is soft when first mined
, but after being carved into objects and dried
, it becomes extremely hard and strong
. The people of this country wear *gǔbèi* (cotton cloth) like turbans
, and also use it for lower garments
. The king uses patterned silk cloth
, and drapes *yīngluò* around his body
. On his head he wears a gold crown, more than a foot high
, shaped like a ceremonial cap (*biàn*)
, adorned with seven treasures
. He wears a sword decorated with gold
, and sits cross-legged on a high golden seat
, resting his feet on a silver footrest
. The attendant women are all decorated with golden flowers and various treasures
. Some hold white feathered whisks or peacock fans
. When the king goes out
, an elephant draws his palanquin
. The palanquin is made of various fragrant woods
, topped with a feathered canopy and pearl screens
. His entourage blows conches and strikes drums
. The king's surname is Jiāochénrú
. Since ancient times, they have not communicated with Zhōngguó
. When asked about his ancestors or the number of years [of the dynasty], he could not recall
, but he claimed that the consort of King Báijìng was a woman of his country
. In the sixteenth year of Tiānjiān
, he sent an envoy to present a memorial, which stated
: "We humbly understand that the Sagely King deeply trusts and honors the Three Treasures
, raises up *tǎsì* (stupas and monasteries)
, polishing and adorning them majestically
, throughout the entire land
. The main avenues are level and smooth
, clean and without filth
. Terraces and palaces stand in rows
, their appearance is like a heavenly palace
, grand, beautiful, and subtle
, unsurpassed in the world
. When the Sagely Lord travels outside
, the four military divisions are fully assembled
, feathered insignia and attendants lead the way
, filling the space on all sides
. The scholars and women of the capital
, wear beautiful robes and shining ornaments
. The marketplaces are abundant
, piled high with treasures
. The royal laws are pure and well-ordered
, with no mutual encroachment or seizure
. All students arrive
, the Three Vehicles converge competitively
, spreading and explaining the correct Dharma
, like clouds spreading and rain moistening
. [Your virtue] circulates across the Four Seas
, meeting with ten thousand states
. The long river is vast and boundless
, clear, cold, deep, and wide
. All beings draw sustenance
, and nothing can diminish its purity
. Yin and Yang are harmonious and unobstructed
, and disasters and epidemics do not arise
. The Sagely King of Dàliáng's Yángdū is unequalled
. Ruling over the Supreme State
, you possess great compassion
, raising the ten thousand people as your children
. You maintain equality and forbearance
, making no distinction between enemy and kin
. Moreover, you relieve the destitute
, and hoard nothing
. Nothing is left unilluminated
, like the brightness of the sun
; none fail to receive joy
, like the pure moon
. The chief ministers and assistants are worthy and good
, the multitude of officials are loyal and trustworthy
. They serve their superior with utmost loyalty
, their minds harbouring no divergent thoughts
. I humbly believe that the Emperor is my true Buddha
. Your servant is the Ruler of the state of Póli
. I now respectfully bow my head and pay homage at the feet of the Sagely King
. I only wish that the Great King may know this heart of mine
. This devotion has existed for a long time
, it is not merely recent
. Mountains and seas created barriers and distance
, making it impossible to communicate directly
. Therefore, I now send an envoy to present gold mats and other items
, to express this sincere devotion
." In the third year of Pǔtōng

, its king, Píngā, again sent the envoy Zhūbèizhì to present dozens of items, including white parrots, indigo beetles, helmets (*dōumóu*), lapis lazuli vessels, *gǔbèi* cloth, conch shell cups, various spices, and medicines
is several thousand *lǐ* southeast of Dà Yuèzhī.
Its territory is thirty thousand *lǐ* square.
It is also named Shēndú.
During the Hàn era, Zhāng Qiān was sent as an envoy to Dà Xià,
where he saw *qióng* bamboo staffs and Shǔ cloth.
The people of that country said
they bought them in Shēndú.
Shēndú is Tiānzhú (India).
It is likely that the transmitted pronunciations and characters used in translation differed,
but they are actually the same place.
Westward from Yuèzhī and Gāofù,
south to the Western Sea (Xī Hǎi),
and east to Pányuè,
there are several dozen states lined up.
Each state has established a king.
Although their names differ,
they are all Shēndú.
During the Hàn period, it was loosely subordinate to Yuèzhī.
Its customs and settled inhabitants are the same as Yuèzhī,
but the land is low, humid, hot, and damp.
The people are weak and afraid of war,
weaker than Yuèzhī.
The country borders a great river,
named Xīntáo.
Its source is in Kūnlún,
where it divides into five rivers,
collectively named the Shuǐ.
Its water is sweet and excellent.
Below it is genuine salt,
perfectly white in color, like crystal (*shuǐjīng*).

The local produce includes rhinoceroses, elephants, martens, weasels, tortoiseshell, *huǒqí* (fire-gathered gems/opal), gold, silver, iron, woven fabrics with gold threads, gold-skin felt carpets (*jīnpíjì*), finely spun white pile fabric (*xìmó báidié*), good furs, and thick rugs (*tàdēng*).
*Huǒqí* is shaped like mica (*yúnmǔ*),
the color of purple gold (*zǐjīn*),
and possesses luster.
When separated, it is thin like a cicada's wing,
but when piled up, it is thick and heavy like gauze and thin silk (*shāgǔ*).
To its west, it trades in the sea with Dà Qín and Ānxī.
There are many rare treasures from Dà Qín,
including coral (*shānhú*), amber (*hǔpò*), gold and emerald jewels (*jīnbì zhūjī*), fine jade (*lánggān*), turmeric (*yùjīn*), and storax (*sūhé*).
*Sūhé* is made by combining the juices of various fragrant substances and boiling them down;
it is not a single natural material.
It is also said that the Dà Qín people collect the *sūhé*,
first press out the liquid to make aromatic oil (*xiānggāo*),
and then sell the residue to merchants of various countries.
Therefore, it is passed along through intermediaries before reaching the Central States (*Zhōngguó*),
and is not very fragrant.
*Yùjīn* uniquely comes from Jìbīn Guó.
Its flower is distinctly yellow and fine,
similar to the hibiscus (*fúróng huā*) covering the lotus (*lián*).
The people of the country first take it up to the Buddhist temples (*Fósì*).
After many days of fragrant drying,
they discard it.
Merchants then collect it from the temples,
and trade it to other countries.
In the ninth year of Yánxī era of Hàn Huán Dì (166 CE),
Āndūn, King of Dà Qín, sent an envoy who came to present tribute from outside the borders of Rìnán.
This was the only contact during the Hàn dynasty.
The people of that country travel as merchants,
often reaching Fúnán, Rìnán, and Jiāozhǐ.
But among the people of the countries on the southern border, few ever reach Dà Qín.
In the fifth year of Huángwǔ era of Sūn Quán (226 CE),
a merchant from Dà Qín named Qín Lùn arrived at Jiāozhǐ.
Wú Miǎo, the Administrator of Jiāozhǐ, sent him to see Sūn Quán.
Quán asked about the local geography and customs,
and Lùn answered comprehensively.
At that time, Zhūgě Kè was campaigning against Dānyáng
and captured dark, short people from *Yǒu* and *Shè*.
Lùn saw them and said:
"In Dà Qín, such people are rarely seen."
Sūn Quán gave Lùn ten men and ten women,
and appointed Liú Xián of Kuàijī to accompany Lùn.
Liú Xián died on the way,
so Lùn subsequently returned directly to his home country.
During the time of Hàn Hé Dì,
Tiānzhú repeatedly sent envoys to offer tribute.
Later, the Western Regions (*Xīyù*) revolted,
and contact was broken off.
It was not until the second year of Yánxī of Huán Dì (159 CE),
and again in the fourth year (161 CE),
that envoys frequently came to offer tribute from outside the borders of Rìnán.
During the Wèi and Jìn eras,
contact was completely severed and never resumed.
Only during the Wú period did Fàn Zhān, King of Fúnán, send his relative Sū Wù as an envoy to that country.
Departing from Fúnán and heading for the estuary of Gōulì,
they followed the great curve of the sea, heading directly northwest, passing several countries along the bay.
After more than a year, they reached the river mouth of Tiānzhú.
Traveling upstream for seven thousand *lǐ*, they finally arrived there.
The King of Tiānzhú was astonished and said:
"Even from the farthest reaches of the coast,
there are still people like this!"
He immediately called for him (Sū Wù) to observe the interior of the country.
Then he appointed two men, Chén and Sòng, and others, to repay Zhān with four Yuèzhī horses.
He sent Sū Wù and the others back,
and they arrived (back in Fúnán) after a cumulative four years.
At that time, Wú had sent the Gentleman-of-the-Household Kāng Tài as an envoy to Fúnán.
He met Chén and Sòng,
and asked them fully about the geography and customs of Tiānzhú.
They said:
"It is the country where the Buddhist Way (*Fódào*) originated.
The people are honest and generous,
and the land is rich and fertile.
Their king is titled Mòulùn.
In the capital city
the spring water is divided into streams,
which flow around canals,
eventually emptying into the great river.
All its palaces are decorated with carved and engraved patterns.
In the winding streets and markets,
houses and towers are magnificent.
Bells, drums, and music,
clothing, perfume, and flowers,
transport by water and land flows freely.
A hundred types of merchants gather,
bringing rare objects and exquisite treasures,
allowing one to indulge whatever the heart desires.
Sixteen major states, such as Jiāwéi, Shèwèi, and Yèbō, surround it.
They are two or three thousand *lǐ* distant from Tiānzhú.
They all jointly revere and serve it,
considering it to be in the center of heaven and earth."
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān era (502 CE),
its King Qūduō sent Chief Clerk Zhú Luódá to present a memorial, which stated:
"I humbly hear that your country rests by rivers and borders the sea.
The mountains and rivers provide complete defense,
and all wonders are present.
The decoration of the land
is like a transformed city (*huàchéng*).
Palaces are splendidly adorned,
streets and alleys are flat.
The populace is abundant,
joyful, prosperous, and peaceful.
When the Great King travels abroad,
the Four Corps accompany him.
You are sacred, enlightened, benevolent, and loving,
and do not harm living beings.
Ministers and people within the country
follow the Righteous Dharma (*zhèngfǎ*).
The Great King is benevolent and sagely,
transforming them with the Way (*dào*).
You show compassion to all creatures,
and none are abandoned.
You constantly cultivate pure precepts,
guiding those who fail to uphold them.
The supreme Dharma vessel (*fǎchuán*)
rescues those who are sinking.
Officials and common people
receive happiness and are without fear.
All heavenly deities protect and uphold you,
ten thousand spirits attend you.
Heavenly Māra (*Tiānmó*) submits,
and none fail to pay homage and look up to you.
The King's person is majestic and solemn,
like the sun at its first rising.
Your benevolent grace universally moistens (the people),
just like great clouds.
Among the lands of Zhèndàn (China),
you are the most supremely excellent.
The land where your subject resides
is protected by Shǒuluó Tiān (Maheśvara/Śiva),
keeping the country peaceful and happy.
Kings have succeeded kings
without ever being broken off.
Within the country are images made of the Seven Treasures (*qībǎo*),
decorated with all kinds of wonders.
Your subject personally practices self-discipline,
following the Dharma of the Transforming King.
Your subject's name is Qūduō.
We are a royal lineage spanning generations.
We sincerely wish that the Great King’s sacred body be at peace.
Now, we bring the ministers and common people of this country,
and the mountains, rivers, and treasures,
all to be subservient [to you].
Throwing our five limbs to the ground (prostrating),
we dedicate our sincerity to the Great King.
The envoy, Zhú Dádūo, has always been loyal and trustworthy;
it is for this reason that he is now dispatched.
Should the Great King require any rare or exotic items,
we shall all respectfully send them.
This territory
is entirely the Great King's domain.
The King's laws and the way of goodness
shall all be followed and implemented.
We pray that envoys of trust between our two countries will travel ceaselessly.
When this envoy returns,
we wish to be granted an envoy [from your side],
to fully proclaim your sagely decrees
and prepare instructions for what is proper.
With utmost sincerity,
we hope for a return response that is not empty.
If what we have stated is deemed acceptable,
we request that you adopt and receive it.
We now respectfully present a glass spittoon (*liúlí tuòhú*), various spices, *gǔbèi* cloth, and other items."
Shīzīguó
is a neighboring country to Tiānzhú (India).
The climate there is temperate
with no distinction between winter and summer.
The five grains grow according to what people sow,
without requiring specific seasons.
The country originally had no human inhabitants;
it was merely occupied by ghosts, spirits, and dragons.
Merchants and traders from various countries came to trade with them.
The ghosts and spirits were not visible in form,
but they brought out rare treasures
and displayed the price they were worth.
The merchants took them according to the price.
People from various countries heard of the pleasantness of this land,
and consequently flocked there.
Some decided to stay,
and thus it became a great nation.
In the early years of the Yìxī reign period of Jìn,
it first sent an envoy to present a jade statue.
It took ten years to arrive.
The statue was four *chǐ* and two *cùn* high;
the jade color was pure and lustrous,
and the craftsmanship was exceedingly unique,
scarcely appearing to be man-made.
This statue remained in the Wǎguān Temple throughout the Jìn and Sòng dynasties.
The temple already contained five Buddhist statues personally crafted by the recluse Dài Āndào,
and Gù Chángkāng's painting of Wéimó (Vimalakīrti).
The people of the time referred to these as the "Three Masterpieces."
Later, during Qí Dōnghūn's time,
the jade statue was finally destroyed.
First the arms were severed,
then the body was taken
to make hairpins and bracelets for his favored concubine, Pān Guìfēi.
In the sixth year of Yuánjiā of Sòng,
and again in the twelfth year,
its king, Chàlìmóhē, sent envoys bearing tribute.
In the first year of Dàtōng,
the later king, Jiāyèjiāluōhēlíxié, sent an envoy who presented a memorial, saying:
“Respectfully addressing the wise lord of Great Liáng: Though mountains and seas separate us distinctly,
communication and messages flow continuously.
I humbly understand that the Emperor’s virtue and morality are high and far-reaching;
your coverage and support are like Heaven and Earth,
your illuminating wisdom is equal to the sun and moon.
Beyond the four seas,
there is none who does not follow you.
All kings of neighboring states
all present tribute,
to demonstrate the sincerity of their admiration for righteousness.
Some sail the seas for three years,
or travel by land for a thousand days,
fearing your might and cherishing your virtue,
no distance prevents them from arriving.
Since the time of my previous kings,
we have fundamentally relied only on cultivating virtue,
governing without severity.
We serve the True Dharma and guide the world,
rejoicing when people do good,
celebrating as if it were our own body.
We wish to jointly propagate the Three Treasures with Great Liáng,
to deliver those who are difficult to transform.
Upon the return of this message,
I humbly await your imperial decree.
Now I present a small offering;
I hope you will deign to accept it.”
Among the countries of the Eastern Barbarians (Dōngyí),
Cháoxiān (Joseon) is the largest.
It received the civilizing influence of Jīzǐ,
and its implements still retain aspects of ritual and music, it is said.
During the period of Wèi,
the regions east of Cháoxiān, such as Mǎhán and Chénhán,
had continuous communication with China.
Since Jìn crossed the Yangtze River (Jiāng),
those who traveled east across the sea
included Gāogōulí and Bǎijì (Baekje).
During the Sòng and Qí periods, they regularly sent tribute and offerings,
and when Liáng arose,
there was an increase in this practice.
Fúsāngguó
had not been heard of in former times.
During the Pǔtōng reign period,
a Daoist monk claimed to have arrived from there;
his account of its origins was exceedingly detailed,
so it is recorded here as well.
Gāogōulí
trace their ancestry to Dōngmíng.
Dōngmíng was originally the son of the king of Gāolí of the Northern Barbarians (Běiyí).
When King Lí traveled out,
his chambermaid became pregnant afterwards.
When King Lí returned,
he intended to kill her.
The chambermaid said:
“Previously, I saw a vapor in the sky like a large chicken egg
descend upon me,
and consequently, I became pregnant.”
The king imprisoned her,
and later she gave birth to a boy.
The king placed him in a pigsty,
but the pigs breathed upon him with their mouths,
and he did not die.
The king considered him divine,
and allowed him to be taken and raised.
When he grew up, he was skilled in archery.
The king was wary of his fierce ability
and again wanted to kill him.
Dōngmíng then fled.
He went south to the Yānzhì River,
struck the water with his bow,
and fish and turtles all floated up to form a bridge.
Dōngmíng crossed on it.
He arrived in Fúyú and became its king.
His subsequent offshoots formed the Gōulí lineage.
That country
was the Xuántú Commandery of Hàn.
It is located east of Liáodōng,
a thousand *lǐ* from Liáodōng.
During the Hàn and Wèi eras,
it bordered Cháoxiān and Wèi to the south,
Wòjǔ to the east,
and Fúyú to the north.
In the fourth year of Yuánfēng of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
Cháoxiān was conquered,
and Xuántú Commandery was established.
Gāogōulí was made a county subordinate to it.
In its center is Liáoshān,
where the Liáoshuǐ originates.
Their king capitalizes below Wándū,
which has many great mountains and deep valleys.
There are no plains or marshes.
The common people live by depending on this terrain,
and drink water from the mountain streams.
Although they are permanent residents,
they lack good fields.
Therefore, it is their custom to be thrifty with food.
They like to build elaborate palaces and houses.
To the left of where they dwell, they erect a large building
to sacrifice to ghosts and spirits.
They also offer sacrifices to Língxīng (the star spirit) and the gods of soil and grain (Shèjì).
Their nature is fierce and impetuous;
they enjoy raiding and plundering.
Regarding their officials,
they have Xiāngjiā, Duìlú, Pèizhě, Gǔzōujiā, Zhǔbù, Yōutái, Shǐzhě, and Zàoyīxiānrén.
The superior and inferior ranks each have their distinctions.
Their speech and various matters
are largely the same as Fúyú;
their temperament and clothing, however, differ.
Originally there were five clans (zú):
Xiāonú Bù,
Juénú Bù,
Shùnnú Bù,
Huānnú Bù,
and Guìlóu Bù.
Originally, the Xiāonú Bù provided the king,
but being weak,
the Guìlóu Bù replaced them.
During the Hàn period, they were bestowed with clothing, turbans (cè), court robes, and drums and horns (gǔchuī).
They habitually received these from Xuántú Jùn.
Later, they became slightly arrogant
and no longer went to the commandery.
They merely built a small city on their eastern border to receive them,
and even now, this city is still named Cègōulóu.
The term “Gōulóu”
is the Jùlí name
for “city.”
Regarding the appointment of officials,
if they appoint a Duìlú, they do not appoint a Pèizhě;
if they appoint a Pèizhě, they do not appoint a Duìlú.
It is their custom to enjoy singing.
Men and women in the settlements throughout the country
gather in groups every night to sing and play.
Their people are clean, pure, and self-satisfied.
They are skilled at storage and brewing.
When kneeling and bowing, they extend one leg.
Their walking pace is always fast (a trot/run).
In the tenth month, they hold a great assembly to sacrifice to Heaven.
Its name is
Dōngmíng.
For their public assemblies, their clothing
is adorned with brocade, embroidery, gold, and silver.
What the Dàjiā and Zhǔbù wear on their heads resembles a turban (cè) but lacks a rear covering;
the Xiǎojiā wear a Zhéfēng,
which is shaped like a cap (biàn).
There are no prisons in their country.
When someone commits a crime,
they assemble the various *jiā* officials to deliberate and execute the person,
confiscating their wives and children.
It is their custom to enjoy licentiousness;
men and women often run away together and entice each other.
Once married,
they immediately begin gradually preparing burial clothes.
For death and burial,
they use an outer coffin (guǒ) but no inner coffin (guān).
They favor lavish burials;
all gold, silver, wealth, and money are expended on the funeral rites.
Piled stones form the burial mound (fēng),
and pines and cypresses are planted in rows.
If the elder brother dies, the younger brother marries the sister-in-law.
All their horses are small,
and suited for climbing mountains.
The people of the state esteem spirit and strength.
They are skilled with bows, arrows, swords, and spears.
They have armor and helmets (kǎijiǎ),
and are accustomed to warfare and fighting.
Wòjǔ and Dōnghuì are both subject to them.
Early in Wáng Mǎng’s reign,
he mobilized Gāolí (Gōugōulí) troops to attack the Hú (barbarians).
They did not wish to go,
but were forced to be dispatched.
They all fled outside the frontier and became bandits and marauders.
The commanderies and prefectures laid the blame upon the Marquis of Jùlí, Zōu.
Yán Yóu lured him in and executed him.
Wáng Mǎng was greatly pleased,
and renamed Gāogōulí to Xiàgōulí.
At this time, they were merely a Marquisate.
In the eighth year of Guāngwǔ,
the King of Gāogōulí sent envoys to pay tribute.
He was then first referred to as king.
Between the reigns of Shāng and Ān,
their king, named Gōng,
repeatedly raided Liáodōng.
Cài Fēng, the Administrator of Xuántú, campaigned against him but could not suppress him.
When Gōng died,
his son Bó Gù was established.
Between the reigns of Shùn and Hé,
they repeatedly invaded Liáodōng again, raiding and plundering.
In the second year of Jiànníng (of Emperor Líng),
Gěng Lín, the Administrator of Xuántú, campaigned against them,
killing and capturing several hundred people.
Bó Gù consequently submitted and became subservient to Liáodōng.
When Gōngsūn Dù dominated the lands east of the sea,
Bó Gù established friendly relations with him.
When Bó Gù died,
his son Yīyímō was established.
Yīyímō had already repeatedly raided Liáodōng since the time of Bó Gù,
and also accepted more than five hundred households of refugee Hú.
During the Jiàn'ān period,
Gōngsūn Kāng led an army to attack them,
defeated their state,
burned their towns and settlements,
and the surrendered Hú also rebelled against Yīyímō.
Yīyímō subsequently built a new state.
After this, Yīyímō again attacked Xuántú.
Xuántú and Liáodōng combined their forces and attacked,
severely defeating him.
When Yīyímō died,
his son Wèigōng was established.
Wèigōng possessed courage and strength.
He was skilled with saddled horses,
and good at archery and hunting.
In the second year of Jǐngchū (of Wèi),
when the Grand Tutor Sīmǎ Xuānwáng was dispatched leading troops to campaign against Gōngsūn Yuān,
Wèigōng sent a Zhǔbù and a Dàjiā commanding one thousand soldiers to assist the army.
In the third year of Zhèngshǐ,
Wèigōng raided Xī'ānpíng.
In the fifth year,
Wúqiū Jiǎn, the Inspector of Yōuzhōu, led ten thousand men out of Xuántú to campaign against Wèigōng.
Wèigōng commanded twenty thousand infantry and cavalry to meet the army.
A great battle was fought at Fèiliú.
Wèigōng was defeated and fled.
Jiǎn's army pursued him to Xiàn,
hoisted the carts, tied up the horses,
climbed Wándūshān,
slaughtered the populace of his capital,
and decapitated and captured more than ten thousand people.
Wèigōng fled far away with only his wife and children.
In the sixth year,
Jiǎn attacked him again.
Wèigōng took only light forces and several *jiā* officials and fled to Wòjǔ.
Jiǎn sent General Wáng Qí to pursue him,
penetrating more than a thousand *lǐ* into Wòjǔ,
reaching the southern border of Sùshèn.
He carved a stone inscription to commemorate his achievement.
He also went to Wándūshān,
inscribed Bùnàichéng, and then returned.
After this,
they reestablished relations with Zhōngxià (the Central Plain/China).
During the Yǒngjiā chaos of Jìn,
the Xiānbēi, Mùróng Huì, occupied Chānglí, Dàjí Chéng (Great Spiny City).
Yuán Dì appointed him Píngzhōu Cìshǐ (Governor of Píngzhōu).
The King of Gōulí, Yǐ Fúlì, frequently raided Liáodōng.
Huì could not restrain him.
Fúlì died.
His son, Zhāo, succeeded him.
In the first year of Jiànyuán (era) of Kāng Dì,
Mùróng Huì’s son, Huǎng, led troops to attack him.
Zhāo engaged in battle,
was utterly defeated,
and fled alone on horseback.
Huǎng pursued the victory to Wándū,
burned its palaces and houses,
and returned with more than fifty thousand captured men.
In the tenth year of Tàiyuán (era) of Xiàowǔ,
Gōulí attacked the commanderies of Liáodōng and Xuántú.
Hòu Yān’s Mùróng Chuí sent his younger brother, Nóng, to attack Gōulí,
and recovered the two commanderies.
Chuí died.
His son, Bǎo, was established.
He appointed Gōulí King Ān as Píngzhōu Mù (Shepherd of Píngzhōu),
and enfeoffed him as King of the two states, Liáodōng and Dàifāng.
Ān first established the officials of Zhǎngshǐ (Chief Clerk), Sīmǎ (Commander), and Cānjūn (Adjutant).
Later, he partially possessed the Liáodōng Commandery.
Down to his grandson, Gāo Liǎn,
during the Yìxī era of Jìn Ān Dì,
he first submitted memorials and engaged in tributary duties.
Successive states of Sòng and Qí all granted him noble ranks and positions.
He died at over a hundred years old.
His son, Yún.
During the Lóngchāng era of Qí,

he was appointed Sāi Chíjìe (Bearer of Credential), Sànqí Chángshì (Cavalry Attendant-in-Ordinary), Dūdū Yíng Píng Èr Zhōu (Area Commander-in-Chief of Yíng and Píng two provinces), Zhēng Dōng Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Conquers the East), and Lèlàng Gōng (Duke of Lèlàng).
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he promoted Yún to Chējì Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief of Chariots and Cavalry).
In the seventh year of Tiānjiān,
an imperial edict stated:
“Gāolí King, Lèlàng Jùn Gōng Yún,
has shown sincerity and loyalty.
His tributary envoys arrive continuously.
It is proper to elevate his rank and title,
and thus extend the court's standards.
He may be appointed Fǔ Dōng Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Soothes the East), Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī (Establisher of a Staff with the Ceremonial Privileges of the Three Dukes).
His titles of Chíjìe, Chángshì, Dūdū, and King remain as before.”
In the eleventh year,
and the fifteenth year,
he repeatedly sent envoys to pay tribute.
In the seventeenth year,
Yún died.
His son, Ān, was established.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
an edict instructed Ān to inherit the enfeoffment and rank,
becoming Chíjìe, Dū Yíng Píng Èr Zhōu Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Yíng and Píng two provinces), and Níng Dōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Pacifies the East).
In the seventh year,
Ān died.
His son, Yán, was established.
He sent envoys to pay tribute.
An edict allowed Yán to inherit the rank.
In the fourth year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
the sixth year,
the first year of Dàtóng,
and the seventh year,
he repeatedly presented memorials offering local products.
In the second year of Tàiqīng,
Yán died.
An edict allowed his son to inherit Yán’s rank and position.
Bǎijì (Baekje):
Its ancestors were the three Hán states of the Eastern Yí (Eastern Barbarians).
The first is called Mǎ Hán,
the second is called Chén Hán,
and the third is called Biàn Hán.
Biàn Hán and Chén Hán each comprised twelve states.
Mǎ Hán comprised fifty-four states.
The large states had over ten thousand households.
The small states had several thousand households.
Totaling more than a hundred thousand households.
Bǎijì was one of these.
Later, it gradually grew strong and large,
annexing the various small states.
Its state was originally located east of Liáodōng, along with Gōulí.
During the Jìn era, since Gōulí partially possessed Liáodōng,
Bǎijì also occupied the territories of the two commanderies, Liáoxī and Jìnpíng.
They established the Bǎijì Commandery themselves.
During Jìn Tàiyuán,
King Xū.
During Yìxī,
King Yú Yìng.
During Sòng Yuánjiā,
King Yú Pí.
They all sent envoys to present captured people.
Yú Pí died.
His son, Qìng, was established.
Qìng died.
His son, Móu Dū, was established.
Móu Dū died.
His son, Móu Tài, was established.
During Qí Yǒngmíng,
Tài was appointed Dūdū Bǎijì Zhū Jūnshì (Supervisor of Military Affairs of Bǎijì), Zhèn Dōng Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Guards the East), and King of Bǎijì.
In the first year of Tiānjiān,
Tài’s title was promoted to Zhēng Dōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Conquers the East).
Soon after, he was defeated by Gāogōulí.
For several years he was weak and diminished.
He moved his residence to the land of Nán Hán.
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
King Yú Lóng first again sent envoys to present memorials,
stating:
“We have repeatedly defeated Gōulí,
and now we have finally established good relations with them.”
And Bǎijì became a strong state again.
In that same year,
Gāozǔ issued an edict saying:
“The Acting Dūdū Bǎijì Zhū Jūnshì, Zhèn Dōng Dàjiàngjūn, King Yú Lóng of Bǎijì,
guards his domain across the sea,
performs his tributary duties from afar.
His sincerity and loyalty have arrived,
and We commend this.
It is proper to follow the old precedent
and grant him this glorious appointment.
He shall be appointed Sāi Chíjìe, Dūdū Bǎijì Zhū Jūnshì, Níng Dōng Dàjiàngjūn (General-in-Chief Who Pacifies the East), and King of Bǎijì.”
In the fifth year,
Lóng died.
An edict again appointed his son, Míng, as Chíjìe, Dū Bǎijì Zhū Jūnshì, Suí Dōng Jiāngjūn (General Who Soothes the East), and King of Bǎijì.
The city where he governed was called Gùmá.
The towns were called Yánlǔ,
which is equivalent to the commanderies and counties of Zhōngguó (China).
His state had twenty-two Yánlǔ,
which were all occupied by his sons, younger brothers, and members of the imperial clan.
Their people are tall.
Their clothes are clean and neat.
Their state is close to Wō (Wa/Japan),
and many people are tattooed.
Now, their language and attire are roughly the same as Gāolí (Goguryeo),
but they differ in that they do not hold their arms out when walking,
nor do they stretch their feet out when bowing.
They call a hat *guān*,
a short jacket *fù shān* (double robe),
and trousers *kūn* (underpants/drawers).
Their language incorporates that of Zhū Xià (the Central States),
and it is said to be a remnant custom of Qín and Hán.
In the sixth year of Zhōng Dàtōng,
and the seventh year of Dàtóng,
he repeatedly sent envoys to present local products.
He also requested the meaning of scriptures like the Nièpán Jīng (Nirvana Sutra) and a scholar (Bóshì) specializing in the Máoshī (Classic of Poetry),
along with artisans and painters.
An imperial order was issued to provide all of these.
In the third year of Tàiqīng,
unaware that the capital was besieged by bandits and rebels,
he still sent envoys to pay tribute.
When they arrived,
seeing the palace walls desolate and ruined,
they all wailed loudly and wept.
Hóu Jǐng was enraged
and seized them.
When Jǐng was defeated,
they were finally able to return to their state.
Xīnluó (Silla):
Their ancestors were originally of the Chén Hán lineage.
Chén Hán is also called Qín Hán.
They are ten thousand *lǐ* away.
Tradition says that during the Qín era, refugees fleeing forced labor came and settled in Mǎ Hán.
Mǎ Hán also ceded its eastern border territory for them to live in.
Because they were Qín people,
it was therefore named Qín Hán.
Their language and names for things resemble those of Zhōngguó people.
They call a state *bāng*.
They call a bow *hú*.
They call a bandit *kòu*.
They call serving wine *xíng shāng*.
They all call each other *tú* (comrade),
which is not the same as Mǎ Hán.
Furthermore, the King of Chén Hán was often chosen from among the Mǎ Hán people.
This was hereditary succession.
Chén Hán could not establish its own king independently.
This shows that they were people who had moved and settled there.
They were controlled by Mǎ Hán.
Chén Hán originally had six states,
which gradually divided into twelve.
Xīnluó was one of these.
Their state is located more than five thousand *lǐ* southeast of Bǎijì.
Their land is bordered by the great sea to the east.
To the north and south, it borders Gōulí and Bǎijì.
During the Wèi period, it was called Xīnlú.
During the Sòng period, it was called Xīnluó,
or sometimes Sīluó.
Their state was small,
and unable to send envoys independently.
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
the king, whose surname was Mù and given name Qín,
first sent envoys, following Bǎijì, to present local products as tribute.
Their customs call the wall (or capital city) *Jiànmóluó*,
their inner settlements are called *Zhuópíng*,
the outer ones are called *Yìlè*.
These are equivalent to *Jùn* and *Xiàn* (Commanderies and Counties) in the Central States.
The state has six *Zhuópíng*
and fifty-two *Yìlè*.
The land is fertile and beautiful,
suitable for growing the five grains.
They have much mulberry and hemp,
and they make fine silk and cloth.
They domesticate oxen and ride horses.
Men and women are separate.
Their official titles
include *Zibēnhànzhī*, *Qíhànzhī*, *Yèhànzhī*, *Yīguòzhī*, and *Qíbèihànzhī*.
Their caps are called *Yízǐlǐ*,
their short jackets are called *Wèijiě*,
their trousers are called *Kēbàn*,
and their boots are called *Xǐ*.
Their bowing and walking are similar to those of *Gāolíb* (Goguryeo).
They have no written script;
they cut notches in wood for records.
Their language only becomes intelligible through *Bǎijì* (Baekje).
As for *Wō* (Wa),
they themselves claim to be descendants of *Tàibó*.
The custom is for all to tattoo their bodies.
They are more than twelve thousand *lǐ* away from *Dàifāng* Commandery,
generally lying east of *Kuàijī*,
separated by a vast distance.
Traveling from *Dàifāng* to *Wō*,
following the ocean route,
passing through the *Hánguó* (Korean states),
sometimes eastward, sometimes southward,
after more than seven thousand *lǐ* one first crosses a sea.
The sea is over a thousand *lǐ* wide;
it is named *Hànhǎi*.
This leads to the state of *Yīzhīguó*.
Again crossing a sea of over a thousand *lǐ*,
is the state named *Wèilúguó*.
Then, traveling southeastward overland for five hundred *lǐ*,
leads to the state of *Yīdūguó*.
Again traveling southeastward for one hundred *lǐ*,
leads to the state of *Núguó*.
Again traveling eastward for one hundred *lǐ*,
leads to the state of *Bùmíguó*.
Then, traveling southward by water for twenty days,
leads to the state of *Tóumǎguó*.
Then, traveling southward by water for ten days,
and overland for one month,
leads to the state of *Yěmǎtáiguó*,
which is where the King of *Wō* resides.
Its officials include *Yīzhīmǎ*,
next is *Mímǎhuòzhī*,
next is *Núwǎngdī*.
The people cultivate millet, rice, ramie, and hemp,
raise silkworms and mulberries, and weave cloth.
They have ginger, cinnamon, oranges, pepper, and perilla.
They produce black pheasants, pearls, and green jade.
There is a beast like an ox,
named the mountain rat (*shānshǔ*).
There is also a great snake that swallows this beast.
The snake's skin is so hard it cannot be cut;
there are holes on its surface,
which open and close suddenly.
Sometimes there is a light,
if one shoots and hits it,
the snake dies.
The products of the land are generally the same as those of *Dān'ěr* and *Zhūyá*.
The climate is warm,
and the customs are not licentious.
Both men and women wear their hair tied in a knot without covering.
The rich and noble use brocade, embroidery, and variegated silks for caps,
resembling the *Húgōngtóu* (Barbarian Elder's Cap) of the Central States.
For eating and drinking they use *biāndòu* (bamboo and wooden ritual vessels).
When they die,
they have a coffin but no outer casing;
they heap up earth to make a burial mound.
All people are fond of wine.
Customarily, they do not know the correct new year,
and many live to an old age,
often reaching eighty or ninety,
sometimes even a hundred years old.
By custom, there are more women than men;
the noble may have four or five wives,
the commoners still have two or three wives.
Women are not lascivious or jealous.
There is no theft,
and few disputes or lawsuits.
If someone violates the law,
for minor offenses, their wife and children are confiscated;
for serious offenses, their clan is exterminated.
During the *Guānghé* era of Emperor Língdì of the Hàn,
the state of *Wōguó* fell into chaos;
they attacked and fought each other for years,
until they jointly enthroned a woman named *Bēimíhū* as king.
Bēimíhū had no husband;
she served the Way of Ghosts (*guǐdào*)
and was able to deceive the masses.
Therefore, the people of the state installed her.
She had a younger brother who assisted her in ruling the state.
Since becoming king,
few people saw her;
she had a thousand female servants attending her,
and only one man was allowed to enter and exit to convey her messages and commands.
The palace where she resided
was constantly guarded by soldiers.
In the third year of *Jǐngchū* of the Wèi (239 CE),
after *Gōngsūn Yuān* was executed,
Bēimíhū first sent envoys to pay tribute,
and Wèi designated her as the King of Wō Friendly to Wèi (*Qīnwèiwáng*),
granting her a golden seal and a purple ribbon.
During the *Zhèngshǐ* era,
Bēimíhū died.
A male king was subsequently enthroned,
but the state did not submit,
and they reverted to attacking and killing one another.
They then again enthroned *Táiyǔ*, a relative of Bēimíhū, as king.
Afterward, a male king was again enthroned,
and they all received titles and mandates from the Central States.
During the time of Emperor Āndì of the Jìn,
there was *Wō* King *Zàn*.
When Zàn died,
his younger brother *Mí* was enthroned.
When Mí died,
his son *Jì* was enthroned.
When Jì died,
his son *Xīng* was enthroned.
When Xīng died,
his younger brother *Wǔ* was enthroned.
During the *Jiànyuán* era of the Qí,

Wǔ was granted the staff of authority and appointed Military Governor of the Six States of *Wō*, *Xīnluó*, *Rènnà*, *Jiāluó*, *Qínhán*, and *Mùhán*, and General Who Guards the East (*Zhèndōng Dàjiāngjūn*).
When Emperor Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Wǔ's title was promoted to General Who Conquers the East (*Zhēngdōng Dàjiāngjūn*).
To the south of this is the state of *Zhūrúguó* (Dwarf State),
where the people are three or four *chǐ* tall.
Further south are the states of *Hēichǐguó* (Black Teeth State) and *Luǒguó* (Naked State),
more than four thousand *lǐ* away from *Wō*,
reachable by boat in about one year.
Furthermore, ten thousand *lǐ* to the southwest are the Sea People (*hǎirén*);
their bodies are black and their eyes are white,
they are naked and ugly.
Their flesh is delicious,
and travelers sometimes shoot and eat them.
The state of *Wénshēnguó* (Tattooed Body State)
is seven thousand *lǐ* or more northeast of *Wōguó*.
People’s bodies are tattooed like beasts,
and they have three marks on their foreheads;
those with straight marks are noble,
those with small marks are common.
The local customs are joyful,
goods are abundant and cheap,
and travelers do not need to carry provisions.
They have houses,
but no walled cities.
The palace where their king resides
is decorated with gold, silver, and precious ornamentation.
Surrounding the building is a moat,
ten *zhàng* wide,
filled with mercury.
When it rains, the water floats atop the mercury.
For markets, they use precious jewels.
Those who commit minor offenses are whipped and caned;
those who commit capital offenses are left for fierce beasts to devour.
If the accused is wrongfully charged, the fierce beasts avoid them and do not eat them;
after a night has passed, they are pardoned.
The state of *Dàhànguó* (Great Han State),
is five thousand *lǐ* or more east of *Wénshēnguó*.
They have no weapons,
and do not wage war.
The customs are all the same as *Wénshēnguó*, but the language is different.
: In the first year of Yǒngyuán of Qí
, a śrāmaṇa (Buddhist monk) named Huìshēn
from that country came to Jīngzhōu
"Fúsāng is over 20,000 *lǐ* east of the great Hàn country (Dàhàn Guó)
. The land is located east of the Central States (Zhōngguó)
. Its soil has many Fúsāng trees
, and thus it is named after them
. Fúsāng leaves resemble those of the *tóng* tree
, but when they first sprout, they are like bamboo shoots
. The people of the country eat them
. The fruit is red and resembles a pear
. They weave the bark into cloth for clothing
, and also use it for floss
. They build plank houses
. They have no inner or outer city walls (chéngguō)
. They have writing
, using Fúsāng bark as paper
. They have no weapons or armor (bīngjiǎ)
, and do not engage in war
. The law of the country
provides for southern and northern prisons
. Those who commit light offenses enter the southern prison
; those with heavy offenses enter the northern prison
. If there is a general amnesty, the southern prison is pardoned
, but the northern prison is not
. For those in the northern prison
, males and females are paired together
. A son born becomes a slave at eight years old
; a daughter born becomes a serving maid (bì) at nine years old
. The person who committed the crime
does not leave until death
. If a nobleman (guìrén) commits a crime
, the state holds a great assembly
, seating the criminal in a pit
, and they feast and drink facing him
, separating from him as if parting forever in death
. They draw a ring of ash around the pit
. If there is one ring, the punishment is limited to the offender himself (píngtuì)
; two rings extends it to the descendants
; three rings extends it to seven generations
. They name the king Yǐqí
. The first rank of nobleman is called Dàduìlú
; the second rank is Xiǎoduìlú
; and the third rank is Nàduōshā
. When the king travels, he has drums and horns to lead his procession
. The color of his clothing changes according to the year
: *Jiǎyǐ* years are blue-green (qīng)
; *Bǐngdīng* years are red (chì)
; *Wùjǐ* years are yellow (huáng)
; *Gēngxīn* years are white (bái)
; *Rén'guǐ* years are black (hēi)
. They have oxen with extremely long horns
. They use the horns to carry things
, holding up to twenty *hú*
. For vehicles, they have horse carts, ox carts, and deer carts
. The people of the country raise deer
, just as the Central States (Zhōngguó) rear cattle
. They make cheese/yogurt (là) from milk
. They have *sānglí* (mulberry pears)
that do not spoil for a year
. They have many grapes (Pútáo)
. Their land has no iron, but possesses copper
. They do not value gold or silver
. Markets are free of taxes or assessments (zūgū)
. Regarding their marriages
: The fiancé builds a house outside the gate of the bride's family
. Morning and evening he sprinkles water and sweeps
. If after a year the woman is not pleased
, he is driven away
. Only if they are mutually pleased do they marry
. The wedding ceremonies are generally the same as in the Central States (Zhōngguó)
. For the funeral of parents (qīn)
, they do not eat for seven days
; for the funeral of grandparents (zǔfùmǔ)
, they do not eat for five days
. For brothers, paternal uncles, paternal aunts, elder sisters, or younger sisters
, they do not eat for three days
. They establish a spirit tablet (líng) or a divine image (shénxiàng)
, and offer homage morning and evening
. They do not wear mourning clothes (cuīdié)
. When a successor king (sìwáng) is enthroned
, he does not attend to state affairs for three years
. Their customs originally lacked the Dharma (Fófǎ)
. In the second year of Dàmíng of Sòng
, five *Bhikṣus* (bǐqiū) from the country of Jìbīn Guó
traveled to their country
, and instructed the people to become monastics (chūjiā)
. Consequently, the customs were changed
Huìshēn further said:
"Over a thousand *lǐ* east of Fúsāng is the Women's Country (Nǚ Guó)
, their complexion is very pure white
. Their bodies are covered in hair
, and their hair is long, draping to the ground
. When the second or third month arrives
, they vie to enter the water and become pregnant
. They give birth to children in the sixth or seventh month
. The women have no breasts on their chests
. Hair grows on the back of their necks
, the roots of which are white
. The hair contains a milky juice
, which they use to nurse their children
. At one hundred days they are able to walk
, and after three or four years they become adults
. They are alarmed and avoid meeting people
, especially fearing husbands/men (zhàngfū)
. They eat salty grass (xiáncǎo) like birds and beasts
. The leaves of the salty grass resemble those of *xiéhāo*
, but their fragrance is sweet and their flavor is salty
." In the sixth year of Tiānjiān
, a person from Jìn'ān
crossed the sea
. He landed
, and found people residing there
. The women were like those in the Central States (Zhōngguó)
, but their language could not be understood
. The men had human bodies but dog heads
, and their voices sounded like barking
. Their food included soybeans (xiǎodòu)
. Their clothes were like plain cloth
. They built structures of packed earth
; their shape was round
, and their doors were said to be like small holes (dòu)
. Regarding the various Róng tribes of the Northwest
: During the Hàn dynasty, Zhāng Qiān first opened the route to the Western Regions (Xīyù)
, and Gān Yīng subsequently reached the Western Sea (Xīhǎi)
. Some sent imperial hostages (shìzǐ)
, and some presented tribute
. Although the armies were strained and military efforts extreme at that time
, victories were barely achieved
. Compared to previous generations
, the strategic reach was far less
. During the Wèi period, the three sides stood like a tripod
, engaging in daily warfare (gāngē)
. After the Jìn clan pacified Wú
, they achieved little peace
. They merely established the officials of *Wùjǐ*
, and the various states did not submit or follow them
. Following this, the Central Plain (Zhōngyuán) suffered devastation and chaos
, the Hú people rose one after another
, and the Western Regions (Xīyù) were separated from Jiāngdōng
, preventing interaction even through multiple interpreters (chóngyì)
. Lǚ Guāng's invasion of Qiūcí
was merely a barbarian attacking barbarians
, and was not carried out under the directive of the Central States (Zhōngguó)
. Since then, the various countries have divided and merged
; their victories, defeats, strength, and weakness
are difficult to record in detail
. Although bright pearls and kingfisher feathers (cuìyǔ)
filled the inner palace (hòugōng)
, fine horses like *Púshāo* and *Lóngwén*
rarely entered the outer government offices (wàishǔ)
. When the Liáng dynasty received the mandate
, those who acknowledged the legitimate calendar (zhèngshuò) and paid homage at the court
included the countries of Qiúchí, Dàngchāng, Gāochāng, Dèngzhì, Hénán, Qiūcí, Yútián, and Huá
. Now, we compile their customs
to form the account of the Northwestern Róng
The King of Hénán,
his ancestors originated from the Xiānbēi Mùróng clan.
Originally,
Mùróng Yìluògān had two sons.
The eldest illegitimate son was named Tǔyùhún,
and the legitimate son was named Huī.
When Luògān died,
Huī inherited the position.
Tǔyùhún avoided him and moved west.
Huī pursued him to keep him,
but the cattle and horses all ran west,
refusing to return.
Consequently, they journeyed westward up Lǒng,
crossed Fúhǎn,
went out southwest of Liángzhōu,
and settled at Chìshuǐ.
Their land was south of Zhāngyè,
west of Lǒngxī,
and south of the Hé (Yellow River),
hence it was taken as their designation.
Its territory extended east to Diéchuān,
〔三一〕 bordered Yútián to the west,
touched Gāochāng to the north,
and connected to Qínlǐng in the northeast,
spanning over a thousand *lǐ* (Chinese miles).
It was anciently the land of Liúshā.
There was a scarcity of grass and trees,
and little water.
There was ice and snow in all four seasons,
with particularly heavy rain and hail only in the sixth and seventh months.
When it was clear, wind blew sand and gravel,
often obscuring the light.
The land produced wheat but no other grains.
There was Qīnghǎi, several hundred *lǐ* square.
If mares were pastured near it,
they would invariably conceive foals.
The locals called these "dragon offspring,"
hence their country had many good horses.
They had houses,
interspersed with *bǎizǐzhàng* (tents made of felt),
which were *qiónglú* (yurts).
They wore robes with small sleeves,
trousers with narrow openings,
and tall, long-skirted hats.
Women wore their hair braided.
Later, Tǔyùhún’s grandson, Yèyán,
was quite literate.
He claimed that his great-grandfather Yìluògān was first enfeoffed as Duke of Chānglí,
and "I am indeed the son of the Duke’s grandson."
According to ritual, the father’s personal name was used as the state’s clan name,
so they took the surname Tǔyùhún,
which also became the state’s name.
By the time of his last grandson, Āchái,
they first received official titles from the Central Plain.
His nephew Mùyán,
at the end of Sòng Yuánjiā era, again styled himself King of Hénán.
Mùyán died,
and his cousin Shíyín succeeded him.
He then used written documents,
built cities,
and constructed palaces.
His lesser kings also built residences.
There was Buddhism in the country.
Shíyín died,
and his son Dùyìhóu succeeded him.
Yìhóu died,
and his son Xiūliú succeeded in his place.
During Qí Yǒngmíng era,

Dài (Xiūliú) was appointed as Envoy with Imperial Credentials, Area Commander of Xīqín, Hé, and Shā three prefectures, General Who Guards the West, Protector-Colonel of the Qiāng, and Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two prefectures.
When Liáng arose,
Dài was promoted to General Who Conquers the West.
Dài died,
and his son Fúliánchóu inherited the title.
〔三二〕 In the thirteenth year of Tiānjiān,
he sent envoys to present two gold-mounted agate goblets.
He also memorialized to establish a nine-story Buddhist temple in Yìzhōu,
which was granted by imperial edict.
In the fifteenth year,
he again sent envoys to present a red dancing dragon colt and local products.
His envoys sometimes arrived two or three times a year,
or once every two years.
Their land bordered Yìzhōu,
and trade was constant.
The people, attracted by its profits,
often went there,
teaching them writing,
and acting as interpreters for them.
They gradually became more cunning and intelligent.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
they again presented local products.
Chóu died,
and his son Hēluózhēn succeeded him.
In the third year of Dàtōng,
he was appointed by imperial edict as General Who Pacifies the West, Protector-Colonel of the Qiāng, and Inspector of Xīqín and Hé two prefectures.
Zhēn died,
and his son Fófǔ inherited the title.
His crown prince also sent envoys to present a white dragon colt to the Crown Prince.
In the country of Gāochāng,
the Kǎn clan was in power.
Later, it was attacked and conquered by Jǔqú Màopú’s brother Wúhuì, the King of Héxī.
Their king, Kǎn Shuǎng, fled to Ruìruì.
Wúhuì occupied it and claimed kingship,
but his rule perished after one generation.
The people of the country then established the Qū clan as king,
named Jiā.

Yuán Wèi granted him the titles of General of Chariots and Cavalry, Minister of Works, Area Commander of all military affairs in Qínzhōu, Inspector of Qínzhōu, and Founding Duke of Jīnchéng Commandery.
He died after twenty-four years in office,
and was posthumously titled King Zhāowǔ.
His son Zǐjiān,

held the titles of Envoy with Imperial Credentials, General-in-Chief of Agile Cavalry, Regular Mounted Attendant, Area Commander of all military affairs in Guāzhōu, Inspector of Guāzhōu, Founding Duke of Héxī Commandery,
〔三三〕 and Gāochāng King with Concurrent Authority of the Three Excellencies, and succeeded to the throne.
His country was formerly the land of Chēshī.
It bordered Hénán to the south,
connected to Dūnhuáng to the east,
adjoined Gūicí to the west,
and bordered Chìlè to the north.
It established forty-six garrisons,
including Jiāohé, Tiándì, Gāoníng, Línchuān, Héngjié, Liǔpó, Wūlín, Xīnxīng, Yóuníng, Shǐchāng, Dǔjìn, Báilì, etc.
〔三四〕 These were all their garrison names.
The officials included Four-Garrison Generals and various other generals,
Chief Clerk,
Aide-de-camp,
Palace Attendant Cadet,
Middle Army Cadet,
Conveyance Secretary,
Conveyance Clerk,
Counselor,
Commandant,
and Chief Scribe.
The language of the people of the country was largely similar to that of the Central Plain.
They had the Five Classics, historical records of successive dynasties, and collected works of various philosophers.
Their facial features resembled those of Gāolí.
They braided their hair and let it hang down their backs,
wearing long-bodied, small-sleeved robes and wide-crotched trousers.
Women braided their hair but did not let it hang down,
wearing brocade sashes, necklaces, rings, and bracelets.
Marriage involved six rites.
Their land was high and dry.
They built city walls of earth,
constructed houses with wood,
and covered them with earth.
The climate, hot and cold, was similar to Yìzhōu.
They cultivated all nine grains,
and people mostly ate fish, mutton, and beef.
They produced good horses, grape wine, and rock salt.
There were many trees and plants.
The fruit of a certain plant was like cotton pods,
with threads inside like fine hemp,
called *báidiézǐ*.
The people of the country often collected it to weave into cloth.
The cloth was very soft and white,
and used in trade.
There were "court crows"
that gathered every morning in front of the king’s palace,
forming ranks.
They were not afraid of people and dispersed only after sunrise.
During the Dàtóng era,
Zǐjiān sent envoys to present a singing salt pillow, grapes, good horses, felt carpets, and other items.
The country of Huá
was a branch of Chēshī.
In the first year of Hàn Yǒngjiàn,
the Eight Huá people assisted Bān Yǒng in attacking the northern barbarians and rendered meritorious service.
Yǒng memorialized for the Eight Huá to be appointed Marquis of the Rear Department Who Befriends Hàn.
From Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
communication with the Central Plain ceased.
Not until the fifteenth year of Tiānjiān,
did their king Yàndàiyīlì first send envoys to present local products.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
they again sent envoys to present a yellow lion, white sable furs, Persian brocade, and other items.
In the seventh year,
they again presented a memorial and tribute.
When the Yuán Wèi resided at Sānggān,
Huá was still a small country
subordinate to Ruìruì.
Later, it gradually became powerful,
conquering the neighboring states of Bōsī, Pánpán, Jìbīn, Yānqí, Qiūcí, Shūlè, Gūmò, Yútián, Jùpán, and others,
expanding its territory by over a thousand *lǐ*.
The land is warm,
with many mountains, rivers, and trees,
and produces the five grains.
The people of the country use lamb meat as their staple food.
Its beasts include lions and two-legged camels;
the wild donkeys have horns.
The people are all skilled archers,
wearing small-sleeved, long robes,
and using gold and jade for belts.
Women wear furs,
carving wood into horns on their heads,
six *chǐ* long,
which they adorn with gold and silver.
There are few women,
so brothers share a wife.
They have no walled cities;
they use houses for dwellings,
opening doors facing east.
Their king sits on a gold couch,
moving according to the annual Jupiter cycle (*Tàisuì*),
and receives guests while sitting next to his wife.
They have no written script;
they use carved wood as tallies.
When communicating with neighboring countries,
they employ Hú (barbarians) from those neighboring states to write in Hú script,
using sheepskin as paper.
They have no official ranks.
They serve the God of Heaven and the God of Fire.
Every day they go outside their doors to worship the gods before eating.
Their kneeling involves a single bow and then they stop.
For burial, they use wood as the outer coffin.
When parents die,
the son cuts off one ear,
and immediately after the burial is completed, it is considered auspicious.
Their language requires a translator from Hénán before it can be understood.
Zhōugǔkē Guó
is a small country bordering Huá.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
it sent envoys accompanying Huá to present local products.
Hēbátán Guó
is also a small country bordering Huá.
All countries neighboring Huá
have clothing and appearance similar to Huá.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
it sent envoys accompanying the Huá envoys to present local products.
Húmìdān Guó
is also a small country bordering Huá.
In the first year of Pǔtōng,
it sent envoys accompanying the Huá envoys to present local products.
Báití Guó.
The king’s surname is Zhī and his personal name is Shǐjīyì.
Their ancestors were likely a separate branch of the Hú of the Xiōngnú.
When Hàn Guànyīng fought the Xiōngnú,
he beheaded one Báití horseman.
It is now located east of Huá Guó.
It is six days' journey from Huá,
bordering Bōsī in the west.
The land produces millet, wheat, melons, and fruits.
The food is generally similar to Huá.
In the third year of Pǔtōng (522 CE),
it sent envoys to present local products.
Qiūcí
is an ancient country of the Xīyù (Western Regions).
During the time of Hòu Hàn Guāngwǔ (25–57 CE),
its king, named Hóng,
was killed by Xián, the King of Shāchē,
and his clan was wiped out.
Xián installed his son Zéluó as the King of Qiūcí,
but the people of the country subsequently killed Zéluó.
The Xiōngnú established Shēndú, a nobleman of Qiūcí, as king,
and thereafter it belonged to the Xiōngnú.
However, Qiūcí was always a large country during the Hàn Era.
Its capital was called Yánchéng.
When Wèi Wéndì first ascended the throne,
it sent envoys to offer tribute.
During the Jìn Tàikāng era (280–289 CE),
it sent a prince to serve at the court.
In the seventh year of Tàiyuán (382 CE),
Fú Jiān, the Lord of Qín (Former Qín), dispatched General Lǚ Guāng to attack the Xīyù.
When he reached Qiūcí,
Bó Chún, the King of Qiūcí, fled with his treasures,
and Lǚ Guāng entered his city.
The city had three walls;
the outer wall was comparable in size to the city of Cháng'ān.
The houses and rooms were magnificent,
decorated with *lánggān*, gold, and jade.
Lǚ Guāng established Zhèn, the younger brother of Bó Chún, as king before returning.
From this time onward, communication with the Central Plain ceased.
In the second year of Pǔtōng (521 CE),
King Níruìmózhūnàshèng sent envoys bearing a memorial and tribute.
Yútián Guó
is part of the Xīyù.
Late in the Hòu Hàn Jiànwǔ era (c. 56 CE),
King Yú was defeated by Xián, the King of Shāchē,
and relocated to become the King of Líguī.
Xián installed Yú’s younger brother Jūndé as the King of Yútián.
He was tyrannical,
and the common people suffered because of him.
During the Yǒngpíng era (58–75 CE),
Dūmò, one of his kinsmen, killed Jūndé.
The Elder Xiūmòbà then killed Dūmò
and established himself as king.
After Bà died,
his older brother's son, Guǎng, was enthroned.
Later, he attacked, captured, and brought back Xián, the King of Shāchē,
and killed him.
Consequently, Yútián became a powerful nation,
and all the small countries in the northwest submitted to it.
Its land has much flooding and sandy soil/gravel,
but the climate is warm,
suitable for rice, wheat, and grapes.
There is water that yields jade,
named the Jade River (Yùhé).
The people of the country are skilled at casting bronze vessels.
Its seat of government is called Xīshān Chéng.
It has houses, rooms, markets, and wells.
Its fruits, gourds, vegetables, and greens are the same as those in the Central Plain.
They especially revere the Buddhist Dharma.
The chamber where the king resides
is decorated with vermilion paintings.
The king wears a golden headband
which resembles the hat of the Húgōng (Barbarian Duke) today.
He receives guests while sitting next to his wife.
The women in the country all braid their hair
and wear furs and trousers.
The people are respectful;
when meeting each other, they kneel,
and their kneeling involves placing one knee to the ground.
For writing, they use wood as pens and tablets,
and jade as seals.
When the people receive a message (letter),
they wear it on their heads before opening the tablet.
During the time of Wèi Wéndì (220–226 CE),
King Shānxí presented famous horses.
In the ninth year of Tiānjiān (510 CE),
it sent envoys to present local products.
In the thirteenth year (514 CE),
it further presented Bōluópó Bùzhàng (a type of textile/tapestry).
In the eighteenth year (519 CE),
it further presented a glazed jar.
In the seventh year of Dàtóng (541 CE),
it further presented a foreign carved jade Buddha statue.
Kěpán Guó
is a small country west of Yútián.
It borders Huá Guó to the west,
adjoins Jìbīn Guó to the south,
and connects with Shālè Guó to the north.
Its seat of government is located in a mountain valley.
The city circumference is over ten *lǐ*.
The country contains twelve cities.
The customs are similar to Yútián.
They wear cotton cloth,
donning long, small-sleeved robes
and narrow-cuffed trousers.
The land is suitable for wheat,
which they rely on for food.
They have many oxen, horses, camels, sheep, etc.
It produces fine gold and jade.
The king’s surname is Gěshā Shì.
In the first year of Zhōng Dàtóng (546 CE),
it sent envoys to present local products.
Mò Guó
is the Qiěmò Guó of the Hàn Era.
It has over ten thousand households capable of warfare.
It borders Dīnglíng to the north,
Báití to the east,
and Bōsī to the west.
The natives cut their hair short,
wear caps,
and small-sleeved garments.
When making shirts, they leave the neck open but sew the front closed.
They have many oxen, sheep, mules, and donkeys.
Its king is Ānmòshēnpán.
In the fifth year of Pǔtōng (524 CE),
he sent envoys to offer tribute.
The country of Bōsí,
its ancestors included King Bōsìní.
His descendants adopted the given name of the royal father as their clan name,
which then became the name of the country.
The country has a city,
which is thirty-two *lǐ* in circumference.
The city wall is four *zhàng* high,
and all have towers and observatories.
Inside the city are several hundred thousand rooms of houses,
and outside the city are two or three hundred Buddhist temples.
Fifteen *lǐ* west of the city is an earth hill;
the hill is not excessively high,
but its momentum connects over a great distance.
In it are vultures that devour sheep,
which the local people consider a great menace.
In the country is the *yōubōtán* flower (Udumbara flower),
fresh and beautifully endearing.
It produces *lóngjū* horses.
In the Xiánchí (Pool of Harmony) grow coral trees,
one or two *chǐ* long.
There are also amber, agate, pearls, and *méijī*, etc.,
but they are not considered precious domestically.
Gold and silver are used for market purchases.
The marriage custom: after the betrothal gifts are complete,
the son-in-law takes several dozen people to welcome the bride.
The son-in-law wears a brocade robe with gold thread
and brocade trousers with lion designs,
and wears a heavenly crown.
The bride also does the same.
The bride’s brothers then come to take her hand and hand her over.
The ceremony of husband and wife
is thus forever completed.
The country borders the Guó country to the east,
and the Pólúomén country to the west and south,
and the Fànlì country to the north.
In the second year of Zhōngdàtōng (530 CE),
they dispatched an envoy to present a Buddha tooth.
The country of Dàngchāng
is in the southeast of Hénán,
the northwest of Yìzhōu,
and the west of Lǒngxī.
It is a branch of the Qiāng people.
In the era of Emperor Xiàowǔ of Sòng,
its king, Liáng Guànchōng, first presented local products.
In the fourth year of Tiānjiān (507 CE),
King Liáng Míbó came and presented licorice and *dāngguī* (angelica root).

An imperial edict appointed him as Envoy with Credentials (*Shǐ Chíjíe*), Area Commander-in-Chief of the armies of Hé and Liáng two prefectures, General Pacifying the West (*Ānxī Jiāngjūn*), Commandant of the Eastern Qiāng (*Dōng Qiāng Xiàowèi*), Governor of the Hé and Liáng two prefectures (*Cìshǐ*), Duke of Lǒngxī (*Lǒngxī Gōng*), and King of Dàngchāng (*Dàngchāng Wáng*),
and bestowed upon him the Golden Seal (*Jīn Zhāng*).
When Míbó died,
his son Mítài succeeded him.
In the seventh year of Dàtóng (541 CE),
he was again granted his father's rank and position.
Their clothing and customs are generally the same as those in Hénán.
The country of Dèngzhì
is located within the borders of Xīliángzhōu.
It is a separate branch of the Qiāng people.
Generations were known as Bearer of Credentials (*Chíjíe*), General Pacifying the North (*Píngběi Jiāngjūn*), and Governor of Xīliángzhōu (*Cìshǐ*).
During the time of Emperor Wén of Sòng,
King Xiàng Qūdān sent an envoy to present horses.
In the first year of Tiānjiān (504 CE),
an edict appointed Xiàng Shūpéng, King of Dèngzhì, as Area Commander-in-Chief of the armies of Xīliángzhōu,
and gave him the title General Pacifying the North (*Ānběi Jiāngjūn*).
In the fifth year (508 CE),
Shūpéng sent an envoy to present four hundred *jīn* of *huángqí* (astragalus root)
and four horses.
Their custom is to call a cap *tūhé*.
Their clothing is the same as that of Dàngchāng.
The country of Wǔxīng
was originally Qiúchí.
Yáng Nándāng proclaimed himself King of Qín.
Emperor Wén of Sòng sent Péi Fāngmíng to subdue him,
and Nándāng fled to Wèi.
His elder brother's son Wéndé again gathered a crowd at Jiālú.
Sòng then conferred upon him rank and position.
Wèi again attacked him,
and Wéndé fled to Hànzhōng.
His cousin Sēngsì again established himself
and garrisoned Jiālú again.
When he died,
Wéndé's younger brother Wéndù succeeded.
He appointed his younger brother Wénhóng as Administrator of Báishuǐ (*Báishuǐ Tàishǒu*),
garrisoning Wǔxīng.
In the Sòng era, Wénhóng was made King of Wǔdū (*Wǔdū Wáng*).
The country of Wǔxīng
dates from this point.
Nándāng's relative, the younger brother Guǎngxiāng, again attacked and killed Wéndù,
and established himself as King of Yīnpíng (*Yīnpíng Wáng*) and Garrison Commander of Jiālú (*Jiālú Zhènzhǔ*).
When he died,
his son Jiǒng succeeded.
When Jiǒng died,
his son Chóngzǔ succeeded.
When Chóngzǔ died,
his son Mèngsūn succeeded.
In the Yǒngmíng era of Qí,
Yáng Língzhēn, the Duke of Qiúchí and Governor of Nánliángzhōu under the Wèi dynasty, occupied Nígōngshān and offered allegiance.
In the Qí era, Língzhēn was appointed Governor of Běiliángzhōu (*Cìshǐ*) and Duke of Qiúchí (*Qiúchí Gōng*).
When Wénhóng died,
his relative Jíshǐ was made Governor of Běiqínzhōu (*Cìshǐ*) and King of Wǔdū (*Wǔdū Wáng*).
In the beginning of the Tiānjiān era (504 CE),

Jíshǐ was appointed Envoy with Credentials, Area Commander-in-Chief of the armies of Qín and Yōng two prefectures, General Assisting the State (*Fǔguó Jiāngjūn*), Commandant Pacifying the Qiāng (*Píng Qiāng Xiàowèi*), Governor of Běiqínzhōu (*Cìshǐ*), and King of Wǔdū (*Wǔdū Wáng*).
Língzhēn was appointed General of the Champion Army (*Guānjūn Jiāngjūn*).
Mèngsūn was appointed Acting Bearer of Credentials (*Jiǎjié*), Inspector of Shāzhōu (*Shāzhōu Cìshǐ*), and King of Yīnpíng (*Yīnpíng Wáng*).
When Jíshǐ died,
his son Shàoxiān inherited the rank and position.
In the second year (505 CE),

Língzhēn was appointed Bearer of Credentials (*Chíjíe*), Area Commander-in-Chief of the armies of Lǒngyòu, General of the Left (*Zuǒ Jiāngjūn*), Governor of Běiliángzhōu (*Cìshǐ*), and King of Qiúchí (*Qiúchí Wáng*).
In the tenth year (513 CE),
Mèngsūn died.
An imperial edict posthumously granted him the titles General Pacifying Shā (*Ānshā Jiāngjūn*) and Governor of Běiyōngzhōu (*Cìshǐ*).
His son Dìng inherited the enfeoffment and rank.
When Shàoxiān died,
his son Zhìhuì succeeded.
In the first year of Dàtóng (535 CE),
Hànzhōng was recaptured.
Zhìhuì sent an envoy to submit a memorial
requesting to lead four thousand households to return to the State.
An imperial edict permitted it,
and immediately established this area as Dōngyìzhōu.
The country borders Qínlǐng to the east,
and connects with Dàngchāng to the west.
It is eight hundred *lǐ* from Dàngchāng,
four hundred *lǐ* south of Hànzhōng,
three hundred *lǐ* north of Qízhōu,
and nine hundred *lǐ* east of Cháng’ān.
It originally had one hundred thousand households,
but this has been gradually reduced generation after generation.
The prominent clans there are the Fú clan and the Jiāng clan.
Their language is the same as that of the Central Plains.
They wear black caps (*tūqímào*),
long robes with small sleeves,
trousers with small openings,
and leather boots.
The land is planted with nine kinds of grain.
Marriages follow the six rites.
They know how to write letters.
They cultivate mulberry and hemp.
They produce pongee silk (*chóu*), thin silk (*juàn*), fine cloth, lacquer, wax, pepper, etc.
The mountains yield copper and iron.
The country of Ruìruì
is presumably a separate branch of the Xiōngnú.
In the Wèi and Jìn eras,
the Xiōngnú were divided into several hundred thousand tribes,
each with its own name.
Ruìruì was one of these tribes.
Since the Yuán Wèi moved south,
they consequently seized control of the former territory.
They have no walled cities.
They practice animal husbandry, following water and grass,
and use felt tents (*qiónglú*) as their dwellings.
They braid their hair,
wear brocade,
robes with small sleeves,
trousers with small openings,
and high-topped boots (*yōngxuē*).
Their land suffers from bitter cold;
in the seventh month, broken ice extends across the river.
In the Shēngmíng era of Sòng (477-479 CE),
Wáng Hóngguǐ was sent as an envoy there,
to invite them to jointly attack Wèi.
In the first year of Jiànnyuán of Qí (479 CE),
Hóngguǐ first arrived in their country.
The king led thirty thousand cavalry
and emerged more than three thousand *lǐ* southeast of Yānránshān.
The Wèi people closed the passes and dared not fight.
Afterward, they gradually diminished and weakened.
In the Yǒngmíng era (483-493 CE),
they were defeated by the Dīnglíng
and became a smaller state, moving their settlements south.
In the Tiānjiān era (504-519 CE),
they first defeated the Dīnglíng
and recovered their former territory.
They began to build a walled city,
named Mùmòchéng.
In the fourteenth year (515 CE),
they sent an envoy to present a coat of black sable fur.
In the first year of Pǔtōng (520 CE),
they again sent an envoy to present local products.
Thereafter, they visited every few years.
In the seventh year of Dàtóng (541 CE),
they again presented one horse
and one *jīn* of gold.
That country is capable of using ritual arts to sacrifice to heaven and cause wind and snow.
They face the bright sun ahead,
and immediately afterward, mud and slush overflow.
Therefore, when they are defeated in battle, no one can pursue them.
If this is done in the Central Summer (China proper),
it becomes cloudy but does not rain.
When asked for the reason,
they replied that it was because of the *jùn*.
The Court Historian (*Shǐchén*) says: The various kingdoms of the islands south of the sea, the Eastern *Yí*, and the Northwest *Róng*,
whose territories reach the distant fringes and borderlands,
each possess their own boundaries and domains.
If their mountains are strange or their seas unusual,
and they harbor unusual creatures or peculiar species,
it was unheard of in former antiquity,
and not recorded in previous documents.
Therefore, we know that beyond the Nine Provinces (*Jiǔzhōu*),
and outside the Eight Desolations (*Bāhuāng*),
to differentiate their regions, products, and soils,
it is impossible to exhaust their limits.
Since *Gāozǔ* embraced them with virtue,
their court tributes arrive annually.
How excellent this is!

Biographies Forty-nine: Prince of *Yùzhāng*, Zōng (Yùzhāng Wáng Zōng); Prince of *Wǔlíng*, Jì (Wǔlíng Wáng Jì); Prince of *Línhè*, Zhèngdé (Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé); Prince of *Hédōng*, Yù (Hédōng Wáng Yù).
Xiāo Zōng (Zōng), Prince of *Yùzhāng* (Yùzhāng Wáng), courtesy name Shìqiān,
was the second son of *Gāozǔ*.
In the third year of *Tiānjiān* [504 CE],
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of *Yùzhāng* Commandery (Yùzhāng Jùnwáng),
with a stipend of two thousand households.
In the fifth year [506 CE],

he was sent out to serve as Bearer of the Staff (*Shǐchíjié*), Area Commander (*Dūdū*) of Military Affairs of *Nán Xúzhōu*, General of Majestic Benevolence (*Rénwēi Jiāngjūn*), and Governor (*Cìshǐ*) of *Nán Xúzhōu*.
Soon after, he was promoted to General of the Northern Palace Guard (*Běi Zhōngláng Jiāng*).
In the tenth year [511 CE],
he was transferred to Area Commander of Military Affairs of *Yǐng*, *Sī*, and *Huò* three prefectures, General of the Cloud Banner (*Yúnhuī Jiāngjūn*), and Governor of *Yǐngzhōu*.
In the thirteenth year [514 CE],
he was transferred to General Who Pacifies the Right (*Ānyòu Jiāngjūn*), overseeing the military affairs of the *Shítou* garrison.
In the fifteenth year [516 CE],
he was transferred to General of the Western Palace Guard (*Xī Zhōngláng Jiāng*),
concurrently General Protector of the Army (*Hùjūn Jiāngjūn*).
He was again transferred to General Who Pacifies the Front (*Ānqián Jiāngjūn*), and Administrator (*Yǐn*) of *Dānyáng*.
In the sixteenth year [517 CE],
he again became General of the Northern Palace Guard and Governor of *Nán Xúzhōu*.
In the second year of *Pǔtōng* [521 CE],
he entered the court to become Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*) and General Who Guards the Right (*Zhènyòu Jiāngjūn*).
He was given subordinate officials.
Originally,
his mother, Lady of Attendance (*Shūyuán*) Wú, having come from the palace of the Frivolous Duke of Qí (Qí Dōnghūn Gōng), gained the favor of *Gāozǔ*.
She gave birth to Zōng after seven months.
Many in the palace were suspicious of this.
When Lady Wú’s favor declined and she became resentful,
she presented arguments suggesting the questionable paternity.
Thus, Zōng harbored this doubt.
Once grown,
he possessed talent and scholarship,
and was skilled at writing compositions.
*Gāozǔ* treated his sons according to ritual,
and their court audiences were not very frequent.
Zōng resented not being recognized.
Every time he was sent out to a feudatory command,
Lady Wú followed him to the garrison.
When he reached the age of fifteen or sixteen,
he still stripped naked and frolicked in front of her,
making no distinction between day and night.
Everyone, inside and outside [the household], held foul discussions.
While Zōng was in *Xúzhōu*,
his administration and punishments were cruel and violent.
Moreover, he possessed great strength,
controlling galloping horses with his bare hands.
He often went out secretly at night,
without any fixed schedule or measure.
