Whenever an imperial decree or message from *Gāozǔ* arrived,
he would invariably show his anger and resentment on his face,
and none of his subordinates dared to speak about it.
In a separate room, he secretly offered sacrifices to the seven ancestral temples of the Qí (Southern Qí) clan.
He also wore civilian clothes and went to *Qǔ'ē* to pay respects at the tomb of Emperor Míng of Qí (Qí Míngdì).
However, he still had no way to be completely sure of himself.
He heard a popular belief that if the blood of a living person is dripped onto the bones of a dead person,
and it permeates [the bone],
then they are father and son.
Zōng then secretly opened the tomb of the Frivolous Duke of Qí,
took out the bones,
and dripped the blood from his arm onto them to test it.
He also killed a random man,
took his bones and tested them,
and both tests showed positive results.
From this point on, he constantly harbored treacherous intentions.
In the fourth year [523 CE],

he was sent out to serve as Bearer of the Staff, Area Commander of Military Affairs of *Nán Yǎn*, *Yǎn*, *Xú*, *Qīng*, and *Jì* five prefectures, General Who Pacifies the North (*Píngběi Jiāngjūn*), and Governor of *Nán Yǎnzhōu*.
He was granted a set of drums and pipes (*gǔchuī*).
Hearing that Xiāo Bǎoyín, Prince of Jiàn'ān of Qí, was in Wèi (Northern Wèi),
he sent men into the North to establish contact with him,
addressing him as uncle.
He promised to surrender his commandery and submit to him.
At this time, a major Northern Expedition was launched.
In the sixth year [525 CE],
Yuán Fǎsēng, a Wèi general, surrendered *Péngchéng*.
*Gāozǔ* then ordered Zōng to serve as Area Commander of the massed forces,
to garrison *Péngchéng*,
and face off against the Wèi general, Yuán Yánmíng, Prince of Ānfēng.
As *Gāozǔ* considered that the military engagement had lasted long,
fearing that discord might arise,
he ordered Zōng to withdraw his troops.
Zōng feared that if he returned south, he would lose the opportunity to meet Bǎoyín again.
So, accompanied by several riders, he fled to Yánmíng during the night.
Wèi appointed him Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*), Grand Commandant (*Tàiwèi*), Duke of Gāopíng, and Prince of Dānyáng,
with a stipend of seven thousand households,
three million cash,
three thousand bolts of hemp and silk,
one thousand bolts of patterned silk,
fifty horses,
five hundred sheep,
and one hundred male and female slaves.
Zōng then changed his name to Zuǎn,
with the courtesy name Déwén.
He observed the most severe mourning (*Zhǎncuī*) for the Frivolous Duke of Qí.
Consequently, the relevant authorities petitioned to strip him of his titles and territory,
remove him from the imperial genealogy,
and change his surname to Bèi (Perverse/Traitorous).
Soon after, an imperial edict restored his status,
and his son, Zhí, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Yǒngxīn,
with a stipend of one thousand households.
In the second year of *Dàtōng* [528 CE],
when Xiāo Bǎoyín rebelled in Wèi, holding *Cháng'ān*,
Zōng fled north from *Luòyáng*,
intending to join him.
He was captured by a ferry official,
and the Wèi people killed him.
He was forty-nine years old at the time.
Previously,
when Zōng was dissatisfied with his lot,
he once composed the poems "Listening to the Chimes" (Tīng Zhōng Míng) and "Lamenting Falling Leaves" (Bēi Luò Yè),
to express his feelings.
The main ideas are: Listening to the Chimes:
You should know I am in the Emperor’s City.
The uneven sounds are hard to count;
in disorder, a hundred sorrows arise.
The departing sound hangs distant and deep;
the returning echo lingers and is urgent.
Who
pities the time-teller
laboring painfully on the Jiànzhāng Terrace?
Listening to the Chimes:
Listen, listen, it comes not from one place.
Holding jade and clutching jewels, I cast them away in vain;
climbing pines and plucking cassia, who will approve of me?
Former friends and old loves are scattered east and west,
just
like falling leaves that will never be gathered again.
Where does the drifting lone goose find rest?
The lingering parting crane cries at midnight.
Listening to the Chimes:
Listening to this, how endless it is!
More than twenty years
I have been stuck within the capital’s domain.
Gazing into the bright mirror,
my countenance wearies;
my cloud-like sorrow and sea-like longing are merely
hidden and repressed.
His "Lamenting Falling Leaves" says: Lamenting falling leaves,
they flutter down in layer upon layer.
Falling and then flying,
they scatter and depart, never to return.
Lamenting falling leaves,
the falling leaves lament.
Human life is like this,
once scattered, it cannot be recovered.
Lamenting falling leaves,
when will the falling leaves return?
Though formerly sharing a common root,
they are no longer connected even slightly.
Those who saw these pieces at the time were all saddened.
Xiāo Jì (Jì), Prince of *Wǔlíng* (Wǔlíng Wáng), courtesy name Shìxún,
was the eighth son of *Gāozǔ*.
In his youth, he studied diligently,
possessing literary talent.
In his writing, he disliked frivolous style,
and possessed great integrity.
In the thirteenth year of *Tiānjiān* [514 CE],
he was enfeoffed as the Prince of *Wǔlíng* Commandery (Wǔlíng Jùnwáng),
with a stipend of two thousand households.

He successively held positions as General Who Pacifies the Distant (*Níngyuǎn Jiāngjūn*), Grand Administrator (*Tàishǒu*) of the two commanderies of *Lángyá* and *Péngchéng*, General of Light Chariots (*Qīngchē Jiāngjūn*), and Administrator of *Dānyáng* (*Dānyáng Yǐn*).
He was sent out to be Grand Administrator of *Kuàijī*,
and soon, that commandery was reorganized into *Dōng Yángzhōu*.
He remained as Governor (*Cìshǐ*),
and was granted Bearer of the Staff (*Shǐchíjié*) and General of the Eastern Palace Guard (*Dōng Zhōngláng Jiāng*).
He was recalled to court to be Palace Attendant (*Shìzhōng*),
and oversaw the military affairs of the *Shítou* garrison.
He was sent out to be General Who Proclaims Grace (*Xuānhuì Jiāngjūn*) and Governor of *Jiāngzhōu*.
He was recalled to court to be Bearer of the Staff, General Who Proclaims Grace, Area Commander of Military Affairs of *Yáng* and *Nán Xú* two prefectures, and Governor of *Yángzhōu*.

Soon after, this was changed, and he was appointed Bearer of the Staff (*Chíjié*), Area Commander of Military Affairs of *Yì*, *Liáng*, and thirteen other prefectures, General Who Pacifies the West (*Ānxī Jiāngjūn*), and Governor of *Yìzhōu*.
He was granted an additional set of drums and pipes.
In the eleventh year of *Dàtóng* [545 CE],

he was appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (*Sǎnqí Chángshì*), Grand General Who Conquers the West (*Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn*), and honored with the establishment of a fully staffed office, equal to the Three Councilors (*Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī*).
Initially,
during the Tiānjiān (天監) reign,
the Tàiyáng Gate (太陽門) was shaken,
and the characters formed said:
“Shào Zōng liáng wèi wéi Wǔ Wáng (紹宗梁位唯武王)” (The Wǔ Wáng alone shall continue the lineage and inherit the Liáng throne).
Interpreters believed that the Wǔ Wáng (武王)
was the King of Wǔlíng (武陵 Wáng),
and consequently, the court and commoners focused their attention on him.
When the Tàiqīng (太清) reign arrived,
Hóu Jǐng (侯景) rebelled,
but Jǐ (紀) did not go to provide aid.
After Gāozǔ (高祖) died,
Jǐ (紀) then usurped the title in Shǔ (蜀).
He changed the reign name to Tiānzhèng (天正).
He established his son Yuánzhào (圓照) as Crown Prince,
Yuánzhèng (圓正) as the King of Xīyáng (西陽),
Yuánmǎn (圓滿) as the King of Jìnglíng (竟陵),
Yuánpǔ (圓普) as the King of Nánqiáo (南譙),
and Yuánsù (圓肅) as the King of Yídū (宜都).

He appointed Huī (撝), the Administrator (Tàishǒu, 太守) of the two commanderies of Bāxī (巴西) and Zǐtóng (梓潼) and Marquis of Yǒngfēng (永豐 Hóu), as General-in-Chief Who Conquers the West (Zhēngxī Dà Jiāngjūn, 征西大將軍) and Inspector of Yìzhōu (益州 Cìshǐ, 刺史),
and enfeoffed him as the King of Qínjùn (秦郡).
The Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ, 司馬) Wáng Sēnglüè (王僧略) and the Directing Military Advisor (Zhíbīng Cānjūn, 直兵參軍) Xú Pēng (徐怦) both firmly remonstrated,
but Jǐ (紀) thought they were disloyal to him,
and killed them all.
The Marquis of Yǒngfēng, Huī (撝), sighed, saying:
“The King cannot be saved!
Good men are the foundation of the state,
yet now he executes them in opposition.
What else can be expected but ruin! ”
He also said to his close associates:
“In the past, Huán Xuán’s (桓玄) reign name was Dàhēng (大亨).
Those who understood the matter called it ‘èr yuè liǎo (二月了)’ (finished in the second month),
and indeed, Xuán’s defeat actually occurred in mid-spring.
This year’s name is Tiānzhèng (天正),
which, structurally, is ‘yī zhǐ (一止)’ (one stop/cease).
How can he last long? ”
In the fourth month of summer in the fifth year of Tàiqīng (太清),
Jǐ (紀) led his army eastward down to Bājùn (巴郡),
using the excuse of suppressing Hóu Jǐng (侯景),
but planning instead to seize Jīngshǎn (荊陝).
Hearing that Western Wèi (Xī Wèi, 西魏) was invading Shǔ (蜀),
he sent his general, the Inspector of Nánliángzhōu (南梁州 Cìshǐ), Qiáo Yān (譙淹), to turn back his troops and rush to aid.
In the fifth month,
the Western Wèi general Yùchí Jiǒng (尉遲迥) led his forces and pressured Fúshuǐ (涪水).
Yáng Qiányùn (楊乾運), the Inspector of Tóngzhōu (潼州 Cìshǐ), surrendered the city to him.
Jiǒng (迥) divided his troops to garrison and defend it,
and immediately hastened toward Chéngdū (成都).
On the day Dīngchǒu (丁丑),
Jǐ (紀) reached Xīlíng (西陵).
His ships covered the river,
and his banners and armor shaded the sun (or shone brightly).
His military appearance was exceedingly grand.
Shìzǔ (世祖) ordered the Garrison General (Hùjūn Jiāngjūn, 護軍將軍) Lù Fǎhé (陸法和) to build two fortifications on opposite banks at Xiákǒu (硤口),
to guard the river and block Jǐ (紀).
At this time, Lù Nà (陸納) had not yet been pacified,
and the Shǔ (蜀) army was again pressing forward.
Public sentiment was anxious and disturbed,
and Shìzǔ (世祖) was worried about this.
Fǎhé (法和) reported emergencies,
which continued daily for ten days.
Shìzǔ (世祖) then released Rèn Yuē (任約) from prison
and appointed him Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ) to the King of Jìn’ān (晉安 Wáng).
He withdrew the forbidden troops (imperial guard) to assign to him;
and also sent the General Who Proclaims Valor (Xuānměng Jiāngjūn, 宣猛將軍) Liú Fēn (劉棻) to hasten west with Yuē (約).
In the sixth month,
Jǐ (紀) built connected fortresses
and attacked and cut the iron river obstructions.
Shìzǔ (世祖) again released Xiè Dárén (謝答仁) from prison and appointed him Commandant of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi, 步兵校尉).
He assigned him a regiment of troops
to proceed upriver to Fǎhé (法和).
Shìzǔ (世祖) wrote a letter to Jǐ (紀), saying:
“The Emperor respectfully inquires of the King of Wǔlíng (武陵 Wáng), who holds the False Yellow Axe (Jiǎ Huáng Yuè, 假黃鉞) and Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi, 太尉): Since the Jiǔ Lí (九黎) invaded and assaulted,
and the Sān Miáo (三苗) plundered and disturbed,
heaven has long suffered misfortune and chaos.
The barbarian invaders (Xūnchǒu, 獯醜) have taken advantage and oppressed us.
They have massacred the people and destroyed the monumental gates (Xiàng Wèi, 象魏),
leaving the royal palace fields barren.
I rest upon a spear and gaze eastward,
and float westward weeping tears of blood.
I have lost my beloved sons in two regions,
and lack the eight hundred vassal states.
My body is covered with chain mail,
and my hand has been pierced by stray arrows.
Then, the tragedy of the ‘wind and tree’ (death of a parent),
caused ten thousand regrets to entangle me;
the sorrow of ‘frost and dew’ (grief over ancestors),
caused a hundred worries to gather consequently.
I strike my heart and drink gall;
my will is not set on self-preservation.
It is only because the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Zōngshè, 宗社) hangs by a thread
and the whales and sharks (rebels) have not yet been cut down,
that I taste gall and await the dawn,
diligently enacting Heaven’s punishment,
alone utilizing the four eyes (of state vigilance),
and wielding the eight powers (of imperial authority) from my seat.
Although I have established altars to await generals
and drawn back curtains to receive scholars,
when repelling the forces at Chìbì (赤壁),
I had no strategy from Lǔ Sù (魯肅);
when burning the grain at Wūcháo (烏巢),
I did not consult Xún Yōu (荀攸).
My talent and wisdom are nearly exhausted,
and my gold and treasure are almost depleted.
I have received no inch of help from the side,
and have experienced every peril and obstruction.
Thus I succeeded in beheading the Cháng Dí (長狄) at Jūmén (駒門),
and defeating Chī Yóu (蚩尤) at Fēngmù (楓木).
Since my grievances and shame have been purged,
and there is no dust (trouble) in the realm,
I manage the four directions
relying entirely on one force (my own).
Now I shall share this peace and order
with the regional officials.
The height of summer is blazing and intense.
How fares my younger brother?
All the civil and military officials
must be weary and exhausted.
I now dispatch the Cavalier Attendant in Ordinary (Sǎnjì Chángshì, 散騎常侍) and Inspector of Guāngzhōu (光州 Cìshǐ), Zhèng Ānzhōng (鄭安忠),
to convey my previous intentions.”
He further ordered him to explain his intentions to Jǐ (紀),
promising that Jǐ (紀) could return to Shǔ (蜀)
and retain sole authority over Mínfāng (岷方).
Jǐ (紀) did not follow the command,
and replied with a letter maintaining the etiquette appropriate for family members.
On the day Gēngshēn (庚申),
Jǐ’s (紀) general Hóu Ruì (侯叡) led his troops along the mountains intending to plan an advance.
Rèn Yuē (任約) and Xiè Dárén (謝答仁) engaged in battle with them
and defeated them.
Soon thereafter, Lù Nà (陸納) was pacified,
and all the various armies rushed west.
Shìzǔ (世祖) again wrote a letter to Jǐ (紀), saying:
“My dearest Dàzhì (大智)!
In the last month of the season, the heat is vexing,
melting metal and cracking stone.
Gathered mosquitoes sound like thunder,
and foxes are sealed away for a thousand *lǐ*.
With such a jade body (you),
you suffer hardship in the marching ranks.
When I look to the west,
how distressed I am for you.
Since the Xūnchǒu (獯醜) relied on their strength and oppressed us,
and the Jié Hú (羯胡) rebelled and shifted allegiance,
I am one day older than you (the senior brother),
and happen to have the merit of pacifying the rebellion.
I receive this joyful elevation,
and the mandate belongs to me.
If you would only send an envoy,
it is what I truly await.
If you say otherwise,
I shall throw down my brush here.
Fraternal love between brothers
means sharing the same form and spirit.
If the elder brother is fat and the younger brother is thin,
there is no chance of replacing the other;
the days of yielding dates and sharing pears
and sharing joy are long gone.
The Shànglín (上林) park stands quietly,
hearing the mournful cries of the four birds;
in Xuānshì (宣室) Hall, the maps are laid out,
and I sigh that the initiator of all things (our father) is long departed.
My heart truly loves you,
but the letter cannot express all that I wish to say.”
Dàzhì (大智)
was Jǐ’s (紀) courtesy name (bié zì).
Jǐ (紀) sent Lè Fèngyè (樂奉業), whom he had appointed Minister of Finance (Dùzhī Shàngshū, 度支尚書), to Jiānglíng (江陵),
to discuss reconciliation and submission,
agreeing to return to Shǔ (蜀) according to the previous directive.
Shìzǔ (世祖) knew that Jǐ (紀) was certain to be defeated,
and therefore refused and did not permit it.
On the day Bǐngxū (丙戌),
Fú Shēng (苻昇) and Xú Zichū (徐子初), commoners of Bādōng (巴東), executed Gōngsūn Huǎng (公孫晃), the commander of Jǐ’s (紀) Xiákǒu (硤口) fortress,
and surrendered to the assembled forces.
Wáng Lín (王琳), Sòng Cuò (宋簉), Rèn Yuē (任約), Xiè Dárén (謝答仁), and others then advanced and attacked Hóu Ruì (侯叡),
capturing his three fortifications.
Consequently, more than ten fortresses on both banks all subsequently surrendered.
General Fán Měng (樊猛) captured Jǐ (紀) and his third son, Yuánmǎn (圓滿),
and killed them both at Xiákǒu (硤口).
He was forty-six years old at the time.
The relevant officials submitted a memorial requesting the cancellation of his registration in the imperial genealogy.
Shìzǔ (世祖) granted this,
and bestowed upon him the surname Tāotiè (饕餮) family.
Initially,
when Jǐ was about to usurp the imperial title,
there was more than one strange anomaly.
The most extraordinary of these
was a pillar in the Bǎi Hall of the inner chamber which, around its joints, grew flowers.
Their stems numbered forty-six;
they were fluttering and lovely,
resembling lotus flowers.
An observer said:
"Wáng Dūn relied on flowers,
this is not a good omen."
Jǐ's reign title was Tiānzhèng,
which secretly corresponded with Xiāo Dòng.
Everyone said that the character Tiān (天) was
"two people" (二人),
and
the character Zhèng (正) was
"one stopping" (一止).
Dòng and Jǐ both usurped the throne
and perished after one year.
Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé (臨賀王正德), whose courtesy name was Gōnghé (公和),
was the third son of Línchuān Jìnghuì Wáng (臨川靖惠王).
When young, he was rough and dangerous,
not restrained by rituals and conventions.
Initially,
since Gāozǔ (高祖) had no sons,
he adopted Zhèngdé as his son.
When Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
Zhèngdé immediately aspired to the position of Heir Apparent.
Later, when Zhāomíng Tàizǐ (昭明太子) was established,
Zhèngdé was enfeoffed as Xīfēng Hóu (西豐侯),
with an estate of five hundred households.
From then on, he harbored resentment and expectations,
and entertained unlawful designs.
He cast sidelong glances at the palace screen
and coveted exploiting calamities and anomalies.
In the sixth year of Pǔtōng (普通),
he was appointed Light Chariot General (qīngchē jiāngjūn, 輕車將軍) based on his role as Palace Gentleman Attendant (huángmén shìláng, 黃門侍郎),
and was allowed to appoint subordinate officials.
Shortly after,
he fled and defected to Wèi (魏).
The relevant authorities memorialized to strip him of his titles and fiefdom.
In the seventh year,
he fled back from Wèi.
Gāozǔ did not hold this against him.
He was restored to his titles and fiefdom,
and was subsequently made General Who Subdues the Barbarians (zhēnglǔ jiāngjūn, 征虜將軍).
In the fourth year of Zhōngdàtōng (中大通),
he served as General Who Inspires Military Prowess (xìnwǔ jiāngjūn, 信武將軍) and Administrator of Wújùn (吳郡 Tàishǒu).
He was summoned to serve as Attendant at the Palace (shìzhōng, 侍中) and General Who Consoles the Army (fǔjūn jiāngjūn, 撫軍將軍),
and was allowed to appoint subordinate officials.
He was enfeoffed as Prince of Línhè Commandery (Línhè Jùnwáng, 臨賀郡王),
with an estate of two thousand households,
and was additionally given the title General of the Left Guard (zuǒwèi jiāngjūn, 左衞將軍).
However, his brutal nature intensified daily,
and he gathered vagrants and runaways.
Hóu Jǐng (侯景), knowing he harbored wicked intentions,
secretly ordered someone to induce and persuade him,
and firmly bound him to an agreement.
Hóu Jǐng sent a letter to Zhèngdé, saying:
"Currently, the Son of Heaven is advanced in age,
corrupt officials are destabilizing the state,
laws and statutes are confused,
and government orders are inverted.
In Jǐng's view,
failure is inevitable and only a matter of days.
Moreover, Your Royal Highness originally belonged
to the line of the Heir Apparent but were subsequently deposed and humiliated.
All righteous gentlemen in the realm
secretly feel pain over this.
In the context of Jǐng's foolish loyalty,
how can he not feel indignant?
Now the four seas are trembling with anxiety,
and their hearts turn towards Your Royal Highness.
How can Your Royal Highness attend to such private feelings
and abandon these countless people?
Although Jǐng is not valorous,
he truly intends to exert himself.
We wish the Prince would graciously comply with the common people
and appreciate this sincere request."
Zhèngdé read the letter and was greatly delighted, saying:
"Hóu Jǐng's intention secretly aligns with mine;
this is heaven's aid."
Thereupon, he agreed to it.
When Jǐng reached the river,
Zhèngdé secretly transported empty boats,
falsely claiming to be fetching reeds,
and thus ferried Jǐng across.
The court was unaware of his plot
and still ordered Zhèngdé to guard Zhūquè Bridge (Zhūquè Háng, 朱雀航).
When Jǐng arrived,
Zhèngdé led his army and advanced together with Jǐng.
Jǐng enthroned Zhèngdé as the Son of Heaven,
changed the year name to Zhèngpíng Yuánnián (正平元年),
and served as Chancellor (chéngxiàng, 丞相).
When the Terrace City (Táichéng, 臺城) fell,
they restored the title Tàiqīng (太清),
and demoted Zhèngdé to Grand Marshal (dàsīmǎ, 大司馬).
Zhèngdé expressed resentment.
When Jǐng heard this,
fearing he might cause a mutiny,
he issued a false imperial edict and executed him.
Hédōng Wáng Yù (河東王譽), whose courtesy name was Chóngsūn (重孫),
was the second son of Zhāomíng Tàizǐ.
In the second year of Pǔtōng,
he was enfeoffed as the Duke of Zhījiāng County (Zhījiāng Xiàn Gōng, 枝江縣公).
In the third year of Zhōngdàtōng,
he was re-enfeoffed as Prince of Hédōng Commandery (Hédōng Jùnwáng, 河東郡王),
with an estate of two thousand households.
He was appointed General Who Pacifies the Distant (níngyuǎn jiāngjūn, 寧遠將軍) and Military Supervisor of Shítóu Garrison (Shítóu Shùnjūnshì, 石頭戍軍事).
He was sent out to serve as Administrator of Lángyé (琅邪) and Péngchéng (彭城) commanderies.
Upon returning, he was appointed Attendant at the Palace and Light Chariot General,
and was allowed to appoint subordinate officials.
He was sent out to serve as Southern Central Protector (nán zhōngláng jiàng, 南中郎將) and Governor of Xiāngzhōu (湘州 Cìshǐ).
Not long after,
Hóu Jǐng invaded the capital.
Yù led his troops to reinforce the defense.
When he reached Qīngcǎo Lake (Qīngcǎo Hú, 青草湖),
the Terrace City fell.
An imperial edict ordered the troops to return to base,
and Yù returned to his garrison in Xiāngzhōu.
At that time, Shìzǔ (世祖) was garrisoned at Wǔchéng (武城).
Zhāng Zàn (張纘), newly appointed Governor of Yōngzhōu (雍州 Cìshǐ), secretly informed Shìzǔ, saying:
"The Prince of Hédōng is raising troops,
and the Prince of Yuèyáng (Yuèyáng) is hoarding provisions.
They are conspiring together for mischief
and plan to attack Jiānglíng (江陵)."
Shìzǔ was greatly alarmed.
He returned by land
and sent Consultant Zhōu Hóngzhí (周弘直) to Yù's location
to supervise his grain and troops.
Yù said:
"We each have our own military headquarters;
why suddenly involve others?"
The envoy was sent back and forth three times,
but Yù did not comply.
Shìzǔ was furious
and sent his heir, Fāngděng (方等), to attack him,
but Fāngděng was instead defeated and killed by Yù.
Shìzǔ then ordered Bāo Quán (鮑泉), Governor of Xìnzhōu (信州 Cìshǐ), to suppress Yù,
and concurrently sent a letter detailing the consequences (of fortune and calamity),
promising to forgive him if he changed his ways.
Yù did not reply.
He repaired and deepened the city moat
to implement a strategy of resistance and defense;
he said to Bāo Quán:
"A defeated general
is hardly in a position to speak of bravery.
If you wish to advance, then advance;
there is no need for many words."
Quán garrisoned his army at Shíguǒ Temple (Shíguǒ Sì, 石槨寺).
Yù led his troops to counterattack,
but was unsuccessful and returned.
Quán advanced his army to Júzhōu (橘洲).
Yù again attacked him with his full force,
but could not prevail.
As it was already dusk,
and the soldiers were exhausted,
Quán seized the opportunity to launch an attack,
and routed them completely,
beheading three thousand men,
and drowning more than ten thousand others.
Yù subsequently burned the outer city and settlements of Chángshā,
and drove the residents into the inner city.
Bāo Quán positioned his army to besiege it.
Yù was brave and fierce from youth,
and possessed courage;
he was able to comfort and care for his soldiers,
and greatly won the hearts of the masses.
Even though he had been besieged for a long time,
and communications were completely severed,
the defense remained solid.
Later, Shìzǔ again sent Commander-in-Chief Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to replace Bāo Quán in attacking Yù.
Sēngbiàn built earthen mounds overlooking the city,
and attacked fiercely day and night.
Arrows and stones rained down like water,
and more than half of the officers and soldiers in the city were killed or wounded.
Yù, distressed and in urgent straits,
secretly fitted out seagoing vessels,
planning to break through the siege and escape.
Coincidentally, his subordinate general Mùróng Huá (慕容華) led Sēngbiàn into the city.
Yù looked around and saw that all his attendants had scattered,
and he was subsequently captured.
He said to the guards:
"Do not kill me.
If I could just see the Seventh Official (Shìzǔ) once
to expose these slanderous scoundrels,
I would die without regret."
The official in charge said:
"The received order does not permit it."
Thereupon, they executed him,
and sent his head to the garrison in Jīngzhōu.
Shìzǔ returned his head for burial.
Initially,
when Yù was about to be defeated,
he secretly pulled out a mirror to look at his face,
but did not see his head.
He also saw a tall person covering a roof,
using both hands resting on the ground to peer down into his study (zhāi).
He further saw a white dog as large as a donkey,
emerging from the city,
and its location became unknown.
Yù greatly disliked this,
and shortly thereafter, the city fell.
The court historian says: Xiāo Zōng and Xiāo Zhèngdé were both rebellious and frenzied,
bringing about their own destruction and extermination;
it was fitting.
During the invasion of Tàiqīng,
Xiāo Jǐ, relying on the resources of Yōng and Shǔ,
consequently did not exert himself to assist the Emperor (qín wáng) and rush to the aid,
nor fulfill the duty (jié) of a subject and son.
When the bandit Jǐng was executed and suppressed,
he only then began to raise troops.
The army moved out without proper justification (wú míng),
thus creating his own source of misfortune and disaster.
Alas!
That he suffered the punishment (fá) of Guǎn and Cài,
was surely brought upon himself.
Biography Fifty: Hóu Jǐng
Hóu Jǐng, courtesy name Wànjǐng,
was a native of Shuòfāng,
or perhaps a native of Yànmén.
When young, he was unrestrained,
and feared by his villagers.
When he grew up,
he was fierce, brave, and physically strong,
skilled in riding and archery.
He was selected to serve as a garrison soldier (shù bīng) in the Northern Commandery (Běi Zhèn),
and gradually established meritorious achievements.
In the first year of Wèi Xiàochāng,
a garrison soldier of Huáishuò Commandery, Xiānyú Xiūlǐ,
raised a rebellion in Dìngzhōu,
attacking and capturing commanderies and counties.
There was also Tǔjīn Luòzhōu, a garrison soldier of Róuxuán Commandery,
who led his followers,
and again invaded Yōu and Jì,
joining with Xiūlǐ.
Their combined forces numbered over one hundred thousand.
Later, Xiūlǐ was killed,
and his subordinates scattered.
Gě Róng, the commander of Huáishuò Commandery, then gathered them up.
He attacked and killed Tǔjīn Luòzhōu,
taking all his troops,
and they referred to him
as "Bandit Gě" (Gě Zéi).
In the fourth year (of Wèi Xiàochāng),
Emperor Míng of Wèi died.
His Empress, of the Hú clan, governed the court (lín cháo).
The General Tiānzhù, Ěrzhū Róng, entered from Jìnyáng and assassinated the Hú clan Empress,
and also executed her relatives.
Jǐng initially brought his private troops to meet Róng.
Róng greatly admired Jǐng,
and immediately entrusted him with military affairs.
At that time, Bandit Gě was pressing south.
Róng personally led an expedition,
ordering Jǐng to be the vanguard.
Upon reaching Hénèi, he attacked and utterly defeated them.
He captured Gě Róng alive.
Based on his merit, Jǐng was promoted to be the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Dìngzhōu and Director of the Grand Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái),
and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Púyáng Commandery (Púyáng Jùn Gōng).
From this time on, Jǐng's prestige and fame were established.
After a while,
Emperor Shénwǔ of Qí (Gāo Huān) became the Chancellor (Xiàng) of Wèi,
and again entered Luò to execute the Ěrzhū clan.
Jǐng again surrendered with his troops to him,
and was subsequently employed by Shénwǔ.
Jǐng’s nature was cruel and tyrannical.
He governed the army with strict order.
However, the treasures and wealth obtained from destruction and plunder
were all distributed and bestowed upon his officers and soldiers.
Therefore, all were willing to be used by him,
and wherever he went, he was often victorious.
He assumed overall command of military power,
second only to Shénwǔ.
Wèi appointed him Minister of Instruction (Sītú) and Director of the Grand Secretariat for the Southern Route (Nándào Xíngtái).
He commanded a force of one hundred thousand,
exercising total control over Hénán.
When Shénwǔ became gravely ill,
he said to his son, Chéng:
“Hóu Jǐng is cunning and full of schemes,
unpredictable and difficult to understand.
After I die,
he certainly will not serve you.”
He then wrote a letter summoning Jǐng.
Jǐng knew of this,
and feared disaster would reach him.
In the first year of Tàiqīng,

he consequently dispatched his Secretary to the Grand Secretariat (Xíngtái Lángzhōng), Dīng Hé, to come and present a memorial requesting surrender, which read: Your servant has heard that when limbs and torso are united,
then the four seas (the world) are peaceful;
when those above and below are suspicious and disloyal,
then the borders and territory are split apart.
Thus, when Zhōu and Shào were united in virtue,
the tributes of Yuècháng
arrived;
when Fēi and Wù were disaffected,
it was why the feudal lords rebelled.
This is the cause of success and failure,
and is the same throughout antiquity and the present day.
In the past, your servant stood shoulder to shoulder with the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) of Wèi, King Gāo (Gāo Huān), exerting effort together,
to jointly pacify sources of trouble,
support the imperiled and uphold the ruler,
and assist the state (shè jì).
Since the revival (zhōng xīng),
there was no campaign I did not
join.
From Tiānpíng until now,
I have always been the first to go out when there was an issue.
When attacking cities, they always fell;
in open battle, the enemy was certainly destroyed.
My physical strength was consumed upon the saddle and armor;
my loyalty and devotion were exhausted in my small heart.
Riding upon
this opportunity,
my rank reached that of the high ministers (dǐng fǔ).
It is right that I should vow to die, exhausting my duty,
to repay the imperial grace bestowed upon me,
to drop my head and spill my guts,
and suddenly never harbor duplicity.
Why must I, through writing (hàn mò),
suddenly discuss
this matter?
What your servant regrets is that dying without righteousness is
not done by true heroes.
Your servant does not cherish his life,
but only fears that his death would be without benefit.
Now, the Chancellor (Chéngxiàng) has suffered illness,
and governance proceeds from his son, Chéng.
Chéng is naturally treacherous and suspicious,
touching upon all matters with doubt and jealousy.
Flatterers and sycophants advance one after another,
jointly plotting destruction.
Although the distribution
of territories is not yet complete,
he repeatedly sent letters issuing summons,
disregarding the safety of the state (shè jì),
only fearing that his private family power could not be established.
With sweet words and generous gifts,
he schemes to eliminate the loyal and the upright.
If his father
should pass away,
what grace will be granted?
Fearing slander and dreading execution,
I refuse and will not return.
Thus, I display my troops in Rǔ and Yǐng,
and hold banners in Zhōu and Hán.
Consequently, together with Gāo Chéng, Governor (Cìshǐ) of Yùzhōu;
Bào Xiǎn, Governor of Guǎngzhōu; Sīmǎ Shìyún, Governor of Yǐngzhōu; Láng Chūn, Governor of Jīngzhōu;
Lǐ Mì, Governor of Xiāngzhōu; Xíng Zǐ
cái, Governor of Yǎnzhōu; Shí Chángxuān, Governor of Nányǎnzhōu; Xǔ Jìliáng, Governor of Qízhōu; Qiū Yuánzhēng, Governor of Dōngyùzhōu; Kězhūhún Yuàn, Governor of Luòzhōu;
Yuè Xún, Governor of Yángzhōu; Méi Jìchāng, Governor of Běijīngzhōu; Yuán Shénhé, Governor of Běiyángzhōu, and others—
all are regional supervisors (mù bó) of Hénán,
commanders (shuài zhǎng) of large regions,
each
secretly forming private plans,
determining to meet under the banner (yǐng huì).
We are feeding the horses and concealing the spears,
waiting for the moment to strike.
East of Hángǔ,
west of Xiáqiū,
all wish to return their allegiance to the Sage Court,
to rest their shoulders
under virtuous rule,
exerting their strength with one heart,
and die without changing their resolve.
Only the few regions of Qīng and Xú
merely need a broken letter (a brief note),
and they will hurry here via a post-relay station (yì),
without needing military strategy.
Furthermore, the rift between your servant and the Gāo clan is already formed.
When disaster loomed and I was graciously summoned,
I previously did not comply.
Even if he recovers (píng fù),
there will ultimately be no way for reconciliation.
South of the Yellow River (Huáng Hé),
the area
under your servant’s jurisdiction,
is as easy to turn over as one’s palm.
Attaching themselves to your benevolent influence (fù huà) is not difficult.
All the officials look up reverently,
listening for your servant to initiate the call.
If Qí and Sòng are pacified,
we will slowly attend to Yān and Zhào.
I humbly consider
that Your Majesty’s net of heaven is widely opened,
and is about to unify script and gauges (shū guǐ).
Hearing this small petition (cùn kuǎn),
you should surely grant it magnanimously (pèirán).
When Dīng Hé arrived,
Gāozǔ summoned his officials for a court conference.
Xiè Jǔ, the Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè), and the opinions of the various ministers (Bǎibì)
all stated that receiving Hóu Jǐng was improper,
but Gāozǔ did not follow this opinion and accepted Jǐng.
his son Chéng succeeded him,
who was Wénxiāng Dì.
Gāozǔ then issued an edict to enfeoff Jǐng [Hóu Jǐng] as Hénán Wáng (Prince of Henan),
Great General, Commissioner with Staff, General Supervisor of all military affairs north and south of the Hé Nán, and Grand Secretariat (Dà Xíngtái),
authorized to act immediately upon receipt of orders,
following the precedent of Dèng Yǔ,
and granting him one complete set of drums and pipes (Gǔchuī).
Qí Wénxiāng sent Great General Mùróng Shàozōng to besiege Jǐng at Chángshè.
Jǐng requested aid from the Western Wèi.
The Western Wèi sent their Prince of Wǔchéng, Yuán Qìng, and others to lead troops to relieve him.
Shàozōng then retreated.
Jǐng again requested troops from Yáng Yārén, the Inspector of Sīzhōu.
Yārén sent Chief Clerk Dèng Hóng to lead troops to the Rǔ Shuǐ (Ru River).
Yuán Qìng's army also fled during the night.
Thereupon, [Jǐng] occupied Xuánhù and Xiàngchéng,
requesting that inspectors be dispatched to secure them.
An edict appointed Yáng Yārén as Inspector of the two prefectures, Yùzhōu and Sīzhōu,
relocating his garrison to Xuánhù;
and Yáng Sījiàn, the Administrator of Xīyáng, as Inspector of Yīnzhōu,
garrisoned at Xiàngchéng.
Since Wèi had recently lost its commander-in-chief,
and Jǐng had also taken Hénán and submitted to them,

and his words disrespectful.
Póyáng Wáng Fàn, stationed at Héféi,
and Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Yáng Yārén both repeatedly memorialized that Jǐng harbored rebellious intentions.
Lǐngjūn Zhū Yì said:
“Hóu Jǐng has only a few hundred rebellious renegades.
What can they do?”
He suppressed these reports and did not submit them,
and instead increased rewards,
thus making Jǐng's treacherous plot even more resolute.
He also learned that Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé resented the imperial court
and secretly ordered a liaison,
to which Zhèngdé agreed to initiate from within.
In the eighth month,
Jǐng finally raised troops in rebellion,
attacking Mǎtóu and Mùzhà,
capturing Tàishǒu Liú Shénmào and Shùzhǔ Cáo Qiú, and others.
Thereupon, an edict appointed the governor of all provinces, Póyáng Wáng Fàn, as Nándào Dūdū,
〔一七〕Běixúzhōu Cìshǐ Fēngshān Hóu Zhèngbiǎo as Běidào Dūdū,
Sīzhōu Cìshǐ Liǔ Zhònglǐ as Xīdào Dūdū,
and Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì Péi Zhīgāo as Dōngdào Dūdū,
to jointly attack Jǐng.
They crossed from Lìyáng.
Also, Kōufǔ Yí Tóng Sān Sī, Dānyáng Yǐn, Shàolíng Wáng Lún was ordered to hold the jié,
and oversee all the armies.
raising the standard to attack
the north, the bears and tigers
rose together,
conquering and recovering the Central Plain.
Jīng, Xiāng, Guǎng, and Yǐng already belong to Guān Yòu,
while Xiàngchéng and Xuánhù also serve the Southern
Court.
It is fortunate that you took them yourself;
why need the trouble of imperial favor?
However, strategies are not singular,
and principles have ten thousand paths.
For your majesty’s plan,
nothing is better than ceding territory for a dual peace,
creating a tripartite pillar
stalemate.
Yān, Wèi, Jìn, and Zhào are sufficient for supporting your stipends,
while Qí, Cáo, Sòng, and Lǔ shall all return to Dàliáng.
This allows your servant to devote his strength to the Southern Court,
strengthen good relations in the north,
and allow bolts of
silk to circulate freely,
while military chariots remain still.
Your servant establishes contemporary merit,
and your majesty completes the ancestral undertakings,
each preserving our borders,
personally enjoying the harvests,
with the hundred surnames peaceful and settled,
and the four
peoples dwelling securely.
How is this compared to driving farmers from the fields,
confronting powerful enemies on three fronts,
avoiding conflict at the beginning and end,
yet taking the arrow and spearhead in the heart and belly?
Even if Tàigōng
served as the general,
he could not achieve survival.
If this task is assigned to a highly enlightened person,
how can success be achieved?
Furthermore, I recall your letter stating
that my wife and children are all detained by the Minister of Justice (Sīkòu).
Using this as leverage,
you perhaps hope I will return.
This must be due to narrow-minded suspicion,
failing to recognize the greater meaning.
Why is this?
In the past, Wáng Líng attached himself to Hàn,
yet did not return even though his mother was there.
Tàishàng was held captive by Chǔ,
yet still asked for the broth naturally.
How much more so my mere wife and children,
that I should worry about them?
If you think killing them
is beneficial,
I cannot stop you even if I wished to.
If killing them causes no harm,
and you merely execute them,
the burden of the family rests with your majesty,
how does it concern your servant?
As for what Zūndào reported,
it was quite accurate;
but being in bondage,
he probably did not convey everything thoroughly.
Therefore, I reiterate my statement
to discuss the details further.
I hope for a sound plan,
and that you will
favor me with a timely reply.
However, in the past, my relationship with the Covenant Lord
was like the qín and sè zithers;
slanderous people intervened,
turning us into enemies.
Holding the bowstring and grasping the arrow,
I involuntarily feel sorrow.
Tearing the silk to write this
letter,
I know not what more I can express.
In the twelfth month,
Jǐng led his army to besiege Qiáochéng but could not take it.
He retreated and attacked Chéngfù,
taking it.
He further sent his mobile secretariat’s Vice Director Wáng Wěi and Left Administrator Wáng Zé to the palace gate to present a proposal,
requesting that one of the Yuán youths be installed as the Lord of Wèi,
supported by the northern expedition.
This was granted.
An edict was issued dispatching Prince’s Retainer Yuán Zhēn as the Prince of Xiányáng.
Upon crossing the Jiāng (Yangzi River),
he would be allowed to assume the nominal position,
and imperial carriages and attendants were supplied to him.
Qí Wénxiāng again sent Mùróng Shàozōng to pursue Jǐng.
Jǐng retreated into Wōyáng,
still having several thousand horses,
tens of thousands of armored soldiers,
and over ten thousand chariots.
They faced off north of the Wō River.
Jǐng’s army ran out of food.
The soldiers were all Northerners
and were unwilling to cross south.
Their generals, including Bào Xiǎn, led their respective divisions to surrender to Shàozōng.
Jǐng’s army scattered.
He then, with a few close attendants on horseback, crossed the Huái River from Xiáshí.
Gradually gathering scattered troops,
he gained eight hundred cavalry and infantry,
and fled to Shòuchūn.
The regional supervisor, Wéi Àn, admitted him.
Jǐng memorialized requesting a demotion,
but a gracious edict refused it,
and he was still appointed Governor of Yùzhōu,
his original office remaining the same.
Since Jǐng occupied Shòuchūn,
he harbored rebellion.
He conscripted all residents of the affiliated cities
as soldiers,
temporarily suspending the assessment of market value and land taxes.
He allocated the daughters of the common people entirely to his generals and soldiers.
He also memorialized requesting ten thousand bolts of brocade
for the soldiers’ robes.
Zhū Yì, the Commander of the Guards (Lǐngjūn), argued
that the brocade in the imperial treasury was only sufficient for distribution as rewards near and far,
and should not be used for military uniforms in the border city.
He requested sending blue cloth instead.
Jǐng received the cloth
and used it all for robes and shirts,
thus favoring the color blue.
Furthermore, believing the weaponry provided by the court
was mostly not excellent,
he memorialized requesting blacksmiths from Dōngyě
to restart manufacturing.
An order was issued to supply them all.
After Jǐng's defeat at Wōyáng,
he made many demands,
but the Imperial Court was magnanimous
and never refused him.
Previously,
Zhēnyáng Hóu Yuānmíng, the Governor of Yùzhōu, commanded the various armies to besiege Péngchéng.
His army was defeated and he was captured by Wèi.
At this time,
he sent an envoy back conveying Wèi’s request to renew their previous good relations.
In the second month of the second year,
Gāozǔ again made peace with Wèi.
Jǐng was alarmed upon hearing this,
and hurriedly memorialized, strongly remonstrating,
but Gāozǔ did not heed him.
Thereafter, his memorials became arrogant
and his language disrespectful.
Póyáng Wáng Fàn, who was garrisoned in Héféi,
and Yáng Yārén, the Governor of Sīzhōu, both repeatedly memorialized stating that Jǐng harbored rebellious intentions.
Lǐngjūn Zhū Yì said:
"Hóu Jǐng is just a few hundred rebellious bandits;
what trouble can he cause?"
They suppressed these reports and did not submit them,
while continually increasing rewards and gifts,
which is why his treacherous plot further succeeded.
Knowing that Línhè Wáng Zhèngdé resented the Imperial Court,
he secretly sent agents to negotiate an alliance.
Zhèngdé promised to provide internal support.
In the eighth month,
Jǐng consequently raised troops and rebelled,
attacking Mǎtóu and Mùzhà,
seizing the Administrator Liú Shénmào and Garrison Commander Cáo Qiú, and others.
Thereupon, an edict appointed Póyáng Wáng Fàn, the Governor of Hézhōu, as Commander-in-Chief of the Southern Route (Nándào Dūdū),
Fēngshān Hóu Zhèng Biǎo, the Governor of Běixūzhōu, as Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Route (Běidào Dūdū),
Liǔ Zhònglǐ, the Governor of Sīzhōu, as Commander-in-Chief of the Western Route (Xīdào Dūdū),
and Péi Zhīgāo, the Regular Attendant and Palace Aide to the Emperor (Tōngzhí Sànqí Chángshì), as Commander-in-Chief of the Eastern Route (Dōngdào Dūdū).
They were to jointly suppress Jǐng,
crossing the river from Lìyáng.
Furthermore, Shào Líng Wáng Lún, who held the titles of Minister-Director (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī) and Administrator of Dānyáng, was ordered to hold the ceremonial staff (chíjié)
and supervise all armies.
In the tenth month,
Hóu Jǐng left his central army general Wáng Xiǎnguì to guard Shòuchūn Chéng (City),
led his army out, falsely heading toward Héféi,
then attacked Qiáozhōu,
where the Assistant Defender Dǒng Shàoxiān opened the city gates and surrendered to him.
He captured the Regional Inspector (Cìshǐ), the Marquis of Fēngchéng, Tài.
Gāozǔ heard of this,
and dispatched the Crown Prince’s Palace Attendant (Tàizǐ Jiālìng), Wáng Zhì, leading three thousand troops, to patrol the Jiāng (Yangzi River) and establish defenses.
Jǐng advanced to attack Lìyáng,
the Grand Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Lìyáng, Zhuāng Tiě, sent his younger brother Jūn, leading several hundred men, to raid Jǐng’s camp by night.
They failed to succeed,
and Jūn was killed in battle.
Tiě subsequently surrendered to him.
Xiāo Zhèngdé had previously dispatched dozens of large ships,
falsely claiming they carried reeds (dí),
but actually equipping (troops) to ferry Jǐng across.
When Jǐng reached Jīngkǒu,
and was about to cross,
he worried that Wáng Zhì would obstruct him.
Soon after, Zhì retreated without apparent reason.
Jǐng heard of this but did not yet believe it,
so he secretly sent scouts to observe.
He told the envoy:
“If Zhì has truly retreated,
you must break a branch from a tree east of the Jiāngdōng to serve as confirmation.”
The scouts returned as instructed,
and Jǐng was greatly pleased, saying:
“My task is accomplished.”
He then crossed the river from Cǎishí,
with several hundred horses,
and a thousand soldiers.
The capital was unaware of it.
Jǐng immediately divided his forces and attacked Gūshú,
capturing the Grand Administrator of Huáinán, the Marquis of Wénchéng, Níng,
and subsequently reached Cíhú.
Thereupon, an imperial edict appointed the Regional Inspector of Yángzhōu, Prince Dàqì of Xuānchéng, as the Commander-in-Chief of all military affairs within the city (Dūdu Chéngnèi Zhū Jūnshì),
and the Minister of Revenue (Dūguān Shàngshū), Yáng Kǎn, as General of the Military Counselors (Jūnshī Jiāngjūn) to assist him.
The Marquis of Nánpǔ, Tuī, guarded Dōngfǔ Chéng (East Prefecture City),
the Duke of Xīfēng, Dàchūn, guarded Shítóu Chéng (Stone City),
and the Chief Clerk to the General of Swift Cavalry (Qīngchē Zhǎngshǐ), Xiè Xǐ, guarded Báixià.
After this, Jǐng arrived at the Zhūquè Háng (Vermilion Bird Bridge).
Xiāo Zhèngdé had previously been stationed in Dānyáng Commandery,
and at this point,
he led his division to join Jǐng.
The Prefect of Jiànkāng, Yǔ Xìn, led more than a thousand troops and encamped north of the bridge.
Seeing Jǐng arrive at the bridge,
he ordered the bridge dismantled.
They had only removed one boat (section of the bridge),
when he abandoned his army and fled to Nántáng.
The remaining troops then closed the bridge again and ferried Jǐng across.
The Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) gave the horse he was riding to Wáng Zhì,
assigned him three thousand elite soldiers,
and sent him to reinforce Yǔ Xìn.
When Zhì reached the Headquarters of the General of the Guard (Lǐngjūn Fǔ),
he encountered the rebels.
Before forming a battle array, he immediately fled.
Jǐng, taking advantage of the victory, reached the palace gates.
The Duke of Xīfēng, Dàchūn, abandoned Shítóu Chéng and fled.
Jǐng sent his General of Equivalent Rank (Yítóng), Yú Zǐyuè, to occupy it.
Xiè Xǐ also abandoned Báixià Chéng and fled.
Jǐng then attacked the city by a hundred routes,
carrying torches and burning the Dà Sīmǎ (Grand Marshal) Gate and the various Eastern and Western Huá Gates.
The people inside the city were caught off guard,
and had not yet made preparations.
They then drilled holes in the gate towers,
pouring water down to extinguish the fires,
which were finally put out after a long time.
The rebels also hacked at the Dōngyèmén (East Side Gate), about to open it.
Yáng Kǎn drilled through the door panel,
and stabbed several people to death,
whereupon the rebels retreated.
They also climbed the walls of the Eastern Palace (Dōnggōng),
shooting arrows into the city.
That night,
Tàizōng recruited men to go out and burn the Eastern Palace.
The terraces and halls of the Eastern Palace were thus completely destroyed.
Jǐng also burned the Mǎ (Horse) barracks west of the city, the Shìlín Guǎn, and the Tàifǔ Sì (Grand Treasury Office).
The next day,
Jǐng built several hundred wooden donkeys (siege vehicles) to attack the city.
Flying stones were thrown down from the city walls,
shattering everything they hit.
Jǐng attacked fiercely but failed to overcome the defenses,
suffering many casualties.
He therefore ceased the assault,
and constructed a long siege embankment to cut off internal and external communication.

He sent a petition requesting the execution of Zhū Cāo, the General of the Central Guard (Zhōng Lǐngjūn); Lù Yàn, the Commander of the Crown Prince’s Right Guard (Tàizǐ Yòu Wèishuài); Xú Lín, who concurrently held the position of Less Palace Minister (Jiān Shǎofǔ Qīng); and Zhōu Shízhēn, the Director of the Arsenal (Zhìjú Jiān), among others.
Inside the city, reward decrees were also shot out:
“Anyone who can cut off Jǐng’s head,
will be granted Jǐng’s rank,
along with one hundred million coins,
ten thousand bolts each of coarse cloth and silk,
and two troupes of female musicians.”
In the eleventh month,
Jǐng installed Xiāo Zhèngdé as emperor,
who immediately ascended the false throne in Yíxián Táng (Hall),
and changed the reign name to Zhèngpíng.
Originally,
a nursery rhyme contained
the words “Zhèngpíng,”
so he established this designation to match it.
Jǐng appointed himself Chancellor (Xiàngguó) and General Supporting Heaven (Tiānzhù Jiāngjūn).
Zhèngdé married his daughter to him.
Jǐng again attacked Dōngfǔ Chéng (East Prefecture City).
He deployed a hundred-foot high tower chariot,
which hooked and pulled down all the battlements,
and the city subsequently fell.
Jǐng ordered his General of Equivalent Rank (Yítóng), Lú Huīlüè, leading several thousand men,
carrying long swords, to stand flanking the city gate,
and drove out all the civil and military officials inside the city naked.
The rebels crossed weapons and slaughtered them,
with over two thousand killed.
The Marquis of Nánpǔ, Tuī, was killed on that day.
Jǐng ordered Zhèngdé’s son, Xiànlǐ, and the General of Equivalent Rank, Lú Huīlüè, to guard Dōngfǔ Chéng.
Jǐng then built a dirt mountain both east and west of the city to overlook the interior.
Those inside the city also constructed two mountains in response,
with princes and dukes and all those below them carrying earth on their backs.
Initially,
when Jǐng arrived,
he immediately hoped to conquer the capital,
and his orders were very clear,
not offending the common people.
However, since he failed to take the city,
morale faltered,
and fearing that all the reinforcement armies would assemble,
and his own forces would surely scatter,
he unleashed his troops to kill and plunder.
Corpses piled up, blocking the roads.
Wealthy households and influential families
were recklessly stripped bare.
Their daughters, wives, and concubines
were all taken into the military camps.
When the dirt mountains were being built,
without regard for noble or humble status,
construction continued day and night without rest.
They were arbitrarily beaten and whipped.
Those who were exhausted or weak were consequently killed to fill the mountains,
and the sound of wailing and crying
echoed between heaven and earth.
The common people dared not hide,
and all came out to join him.
Within ten days,
his forces reached tens of thousands.
Jǐng’s General of Equivalent Rank (Yítóng), Fàn Táobàng, secretly sent an envoy offering submission and begging to surrender.
The matter was exposed, and he was subsequently killed.
At this time,
Prince Lún of Shàolíng, leading the Duke of Xīfēng, Dàchūn, and the Duke of Xīngàn, Dàchéng,

the Marquis of Yǒng'ān, Què; the General Who Surpasses Martiality (Chāowǔ Jiāngjūn), the Marquis of Nán'ān Township, Jùn; the former Regional Inspector of Qiáozhōu, Zhào Bóchāo; the Regional Inspector of Wǔzhōu, Xiāo Nòngzhāng; and the Colonel of Infantry (Bùbīng Xiàowèi), Yǐn Sīhé, and others,
totaling thirty thousand cavalry and infantry,
departed from Jīngkǒu,
and immediately occupied Zhōngshān.
Jǐng’s faction was greatly alarmed.
They prepared ships and boats, all wishing to flee and disperse.
Jǐng divided his forces and sent more than ten thousand men to resist Lún.
Lún attacked and heavily defeated them,
beheading over a thousand men.
The next morning,
Jǐng again arrayed his troops north of Fùzhōushān.
Lún also formed ranks to await him.
Jǐng did not advance,
resulting in a standoff.
When evening arrived,
Jǐng led his army back.
The Marquis of Nán'ān, Jùn, led several dozen cavalrymen to provoke him.
Jǐng turned his army around and engaged in battle,
and Jùn retreated.
At that time, Zhào Bóchāo was arrayed north of Xuánwǔ Hú (Lake),
saw that Jùn was in peril,
but did not rush to his aid.
Instead, he led his army forward and fled.
The allied armies fell into chaos because of this disturbance,
and were completely routed.
Lún fled to Jīngkǒu.
The rebels captured all the baggage train, weapons, and armor,
beheading several hundred men,
and taking more than a thousand prisoners alive.
They captured the Duke of Xīfēng, Dàchūn; Lún’s Chief Clerk (Sīmǎ), Zhuāngqiū Huìdá;
the General of the Imperial Guard (Zhíhé Jiāngjūn), Hú Zǐyuē; and the Prefect of Guǎnglíng, Huò Jùn, among others.
They were brought to the city walls to be paraded,
and forced to claim
that “Prince Shàolíng has already been captured.”
Only Jùn stated,
“The Prince suffered a small setback,
but he has already returned to Jīngkǒu with his entire army.
Those inside the city must only hold firm,
and reinforcements will arrive soon.”
The rebels struck him with swords,
but Jùn’s speech and expression remained unchanged.
Jǐng respected his righteousness and released him.
On that day,
Sù, Heir Apparent of Póyáng, and Péi Zhīgāo reached Hòuzhǔ,
and established a camp at Càizhōu.
Jǐng divided his forces to garrison the southern bank.
In the twelfth month,

Hóu Jǐng manufactured various siege implements, including mobile towers (fēilóu), ramming carts (tóngchē), wall-scaling carts (dēngchéngchē), battlement-hooking carts (gōudiéchē), approach bridge carts (jiēdàochē), and fire carts (huǒchē),
all several zhàng high,
with some carts having up to twenty wheels.
They were displayed before the imperial gate,
and were to be used simultaneously in a hundred avenues of attack upon the city.
He used the fire carts to burn down the large tower at the southeastern corner of the city.
The rebels then used the momentum of the fire to assault the city.
Those on the city walls released fire,
completely burning their siege equipment.
The rebels then retreated.
They also built earth mounds (tǔshān) to press close to the city.
Those inside the city dug tunnels (dìdào) to draw in the earth mounds,
and the rebels could not sustain them.
They burned their siege implements,
and returned into their barricades (zhà).
The General of Military Talent (Cáiguān Jiāngjūn), Sòng Ní, surrendered to the rebels.
He subsequently devised a plan for them:
diverting water from Xuánwǔ Hú to flood Táichéng.
The water outside the city rose several chi,
and the imperial thoroughfare before the gate became a raging torrent.
They also burned the residences, camps, and temples on the southern bank,
nothing was left intact.

Liǔ Zhònglǐ, the Governor (Cìshǐ) of Sīzhōu; Wéi Càn, the Governor of Héngzhōu; Chén Wénchè, the Administrator (Tàishǒu) of Nánlíng; Lǐ Xiàoqīn, the General Who Proclaims Ferocity (Xuānměng Jiāngjūn), and others,
all came to provide assistance.
The Heir Apparent (Shìzǐ) of Póyáng, Sī, and Péi Zhīgāo also crossed the Jiāng (Yangtze River).
Zhònglǐ established a camp south of Zhūquè Háng,
Péi Zhīgāo camped at Nányuàn,
Wéi Càn camped at Qīngtáng,
Chén Wénchè and Lǐ Xiàoqīn were stationed in Dānyáng Jùn, and the Póyáng Heir Apparent, Sī, camped south of Xiǎo Háng.
They all built barricades along the Huái (River).
When dawn arrived,
Jǐng only then became aware.
He ascended the gate tower of Chánlíng Sì (Monastery) to observe them.
Seeing that Wéi Càn’s camp perimeter had not yet been completed,
he first crossed with his troops and attacked him.
Càn resisted the battle but was defeated.
Jǐng beheaded Càn and displayed the head beneath the city walls.
Liǔ Zhònglǐ heard of Càn’s defeat,
and without waiting to don his armor,
he hurried to the location with several dozen cavalry.
He encountered the rebels and engaged in battle,
slaying several hundred heads,
and more than a thousand men drowned after jumping into the water.
Zhònglǐ penetrated deeply,
but his horse became mired in the mud,
and he also suffered serious wounds.
After this, the rebels dared not cross the bank.
Shàolíng Wáng Lún, along with Línchéng Gōng Dàlián and others, assembled on the southern bank coming via the eastern route.

Xiāngdōng Wáng Yì, the Governor of Jīngzhōu, dispatched his Heir Apparent Fāngděng, along with the acting Grand Administrator (Sīmǎ) Wú Yè, and the Administrator of Tiānmén, Fán Wénjiǎo, to head down to the capital (Jīngshī).
They camped in front of Xiāngzǐ’àn.
Lǐ Qiānshì, the Governor of Gāozhōu, and Yáng Yārén, the former Governor of Sīzhōu, also led troops that arrived subsequently.
Soon after, the Póyáng Heir Apparent Sī, Yǒng'ān Hóu Què, Yáng Yārén, Lǐ Qiānshì, and Fán Wénjiǎo led their forces across the Huái (River).
They attacked the rebels’ barricade in front of Dōngfǔ Chéng,
and broke it.
They then established a camp east of the Qīngxī River.
Jǐng dispatched his General of Equal Dignity (Yítóng), Sòng Zǐxiān, to station himself at the residence of Nánpíng Wáng,
setting up barricades along the west bank of the water to hold the line against them.
Jǐng’s provisions were gradually exhausted.
By this point, rice bushels numbered several hundred thousand,
and fifteen or sixteen tenths of the population were eating each other.
Initially,
when the relief troops arrived at the north bank,
the common people, supporting the old and leading the young, waited for the royal army.
As soon as they managed to cross the Huái,
they immediately competed in plundering.
Those among the rebel faction who wished to withdraw themselves (from the rebellion),
hearing of this, all ceased (their attempts).
When the rebels first arrived,
those inside the city could only barely hold fast.
For the matter of quelling and settling the disturbance,
they placed their hopes on the relief army.
Subsequently, forces from the four directions gathered like clouds,
their number reported to be a million men.
They maintained continuous camps against the enemy,
for more than a month now.
Disease and plague afflicted the city,
and more than half the people died.
Jǐng had been requesting peace since the beginning of the year,
but the imperial court had not yet granted it.
Now, as the situation became desperate, they finally consented.
(Jǐng) requested to cede the four prefectures west of the Jiāng (Yangtze),
and also asked that Xuānchéng Wáng Dàqì be sent out,
only then would he lift the siege and cross the Jiāng.
He also promised to send his General of Equal Dignity, Yú Zǐyuè, and Assistant Director (Zuǒchéng), Wáng Wěi, into the city as hostages.
Fù Qí, the Commandant of the Central Army (Zhōnglǐngjūn), argued
that because Xuānchéng Wáng was a highly important direct heir,
it was impermissible to consent to this.
Instead, he requested that Shíchéng Gōng Dàkuǎn be sent out.
The imperial edict consented to this.
Consequently, an altar was established outside Xīhuá Mén (West Glorious Gate).

They dispatched Wáng Kè, the Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs (Shàngshū Púyè); Shào, the Marquis of Shàngjiǎ Township (Shàngjiǎ Xiāng Hóu) and acting Court Attendant (Shìzhōng); and Xiāo Cuō, the acting Gentleman-in-Waiting (Sǎnjì Chángshì), along with Yú Zǐyuè, Wáng Wěi, and others,
to ascend the altar and swear the covenant together.
Liǔ Jīn, the General of the Left Guard (Zuǒ Wèi Jiāngjūn), exited below Xīhuá Mén.
Jǐng exited his barricade gate,
facing Jīn from afar.
They slaughtered a sacrifice and smeared themselves with blood (in ritual oath).
Nánkāng Sì Wáng Huìlǐ, the Governor of Nányānzhōu; Xiāngtán Hóu Tuì, the former Governor of Qīngzhōu and Jìzhōu; and Xīchāng Hóu’s Heir Apparent Yù led thirty thousand troops,
arriving at Mǎqióng Zhōu.
Jǐng was concerned that the Northern Army might advance from Báixià,
cutting off his route on the Jiāng.
He requested that all of them be ordered to assemble on the southern bank.
The imperial decree then ordered the Northern Army to advance to Jiāngtán Yuàn.
Jǐng memorialized, stating:
"Yǒng'ān Hóu and Zhào Wēifāng repeatedly insulted your servant across the barricades,
saying, 'The Son of Heaven may have sworn an oath with you,
but I will eventually drive you out.'
I request they be summoned into the city;
then I will immediately set off" ．
The imperial decree summoned both of them.
Jǐng further memorialized, saying:
"A message from the western bank arrived, stating that
Gāo Chéng has already gained Shòuchūn and Zhōnglí.
Having no place to securely settle,
I temporarily request the use of Guǎnglǐng and Qiáozhōu.
Once I conquer and obtain Shòuchūn and Zhōnglí,
I will immediately return them to the court."
Previously,
Liú Miǎo of Péngchéng persuaded Jǐng, saying:
"The Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn) has halted troops for a long time,
attacking the city without taking it.
Now, relief forces are gathering like clouds;
it will not be easy to defeat them.
I hear that military provisions cannot last a month,
the supply routes are cut off,
and there is nothing to plunder in the fields.
Whether we succeed or fail hangs in the balance,
the time for decision is now.
It would be better to beg for peace,
preserve your army, and return.
This is the best strategy."
Jǐng agreed with his words,
and therefore requested peace.
Later, he learned that the relief army’s commands were inconsistent,
and they would ultimately fail to achieve their goal of supporting the sovereign.
Moreover, he heard that the deaths from disease inside the city were increasing,
and there would certainly be those who responded (to his actions).
Jǐng’s strategist, Wáng Wěi, again advised him, saying:
"Your Excellency, as a subject, you raised troops in rebellion,
surrounding and guarding the imperial palace,
already exceeding ten tendays (one hundred days).
You have harassed and humiliated the imperial consorts and mistresses,
and defiled the ancestral temples.
Holding this position today,
where can you find a place to settle?
I wish Your Excellency would observe the changing circumstances."
Jǐng agreed with this,
and then raised a memorial, stating: Your servant has heard
that "writing does not fully convey speech,
and speech does not fully convey meaning."
However, meaning is not expressed without speech,
and speech is not fully conveyed without writing.
This is why your servant, filled with accumulated indignation,
cannot remain silent.
I humbly consider that Your Majesty possesses sagely wisdom,
and is endowed with multiple talents and arts.
In the past, due to the decline of the age,
you soared like a dragon over the Hàn and Miǎn (Rivers),
pacifying the wicked and eliminating chaos,
successfully avenging family grievances.
After that, you followed in the footsteps of previous kings,
gloriously dwelling south of the Jiāng,
modeling yourself on Wén and Wǔ,
and tracing back to Yáo and Shùn.
Furthermore, as the state of Wèi declined,
there was no powerful enemy externally,
and thus
you were able to take Huálíng in the west,
and enclose the Huái and Sì rivers in the north.
You established good relations with the Gāo family;
light carriages (messengers) followed one after another,
and the border regions were free from worry
for more than ten years.
You personally governed all affairs of state,
painstakingly laboring
in the path of governance.
You edited and corrected the remaining writings of Zhōu and Kǒng (Confucius),
and expounded upon the profound mysteries of True Suchness (zhēnrú).
Your years enjoyed are long,
and your direct lineage is like a stable rock.
In the arts and achievements of a sovereign,
none can compare.
This is why your servant, though leaping about in a remote corner,
sighed while looking toward the Southern Wind (the South).
How could I have expected that the reputation differed from the reality,
and what was heard was not the same as what was seen?
Since your servant dedicated his person and recorded his name,
The deeds, both former and latter,
and the memorials previously presented,
have already been fully detailed.
Unable to restrain my indignation,
I again present this appeal to Your Majesty: Your Majesty maintained peace with the Gāo [Shì] (Gāo clan),
for more than twelve years (yì jǐ),
boats and carriages traveled back and forth,
visible along the roads,
surely intending to share misfortune and pity suffering,
sharing prosperity and equating sorrows;
how could you
accept the allegiance of this humble official,
covet the lands of Rǔ and Yǐng belonging to your official,
and immediately sever good relations north of the Hé (Yellow River),
issue a proclamation cursing Gāo Chéng,
entrap his envoy who had not yet returned
in the tiger's mouth (danger),
raising troops and beating the
drums,
invading and pressuring Péng and Sòng?
Now, when enemy states fight each other,
they cease upon hearing of a death;
even the friendship of common men
involves entrusting orphans and committing one's life;
how could there be a ruler of ten thousand chariots
who forgets righteousness
when seeing benefit, acting like this!
This is the first failure.
I and Gāo Chéng
already held deep enmity,
morally we could not belong to the same state,
and returning to the Dào (the righteous path) was necessary.
Your Majesty appointed me Supreme General,
entrusting me with independent command,
granting me musical instruments and female entertainers,
chariots, robes, bows, and arrows.
I accepted the command without demur,
truly intending to repay your kindness.
I was planning to hang my banner high upon Sōng and Huà (Mts.),
display my flag throughout Jì and Zhào,
swiftly sweep away the disorder,
and truly restore order throughout the land
(yǔ nèi);
(so that) Your Majesty, clad in court robes, could cross the Jiāng (Yangtze River),
announce your achievements at Dōng Yuè (Mt. Tài),
making Dàliáng equally glorious with Xuān and Huáng (the Yellow Emperor),
and I would compare my merit to Yī (Yī Yǐn) and Lǚ (Lǚ Shàng),
passing down abundance to future generations,
and having my name recorded on bamboo
and silk (bamboo and silk records).
This was truly the ambition of my life.
However, Your Majesty wished to divide the achievement,
and was unable to fully entrust me,
sending me to attack north of the Hé,
while intending to personally lead the campaign in Xú Fāng (the Xú region).
You dispatched the incompetent
Zhēnyáng,
and appointed the arrogant and greedy Hú and Zhào.
As soon as they saw the banners and drums (of the enemy),
they scattered like birds and dissolved like fish.
Mùróng Shàozōng, seizing the victory, swept through the area,
and none of the garrisons at Wōyáng failed to abandon
their armor.
The disaster struck faster than covering the ears against sudden thunder,
and scattered forces could not secure the overall integrity.
This caused your official to be distressed and lose my base,
and my wife and children were slaughtered.
This is truly where Your Majesty has deeply failed your official.
This
is the second failure.
When Wéi Àn guarded Shòuyáng,
his troops amounted to less than a cohort (yī lǚ).
Mùróng’s fierce vanguard
wished to water their horses in the Cháng Jiāng (Yangtze River).
If I had not retreated to secure Huáinán,
the outcome would have been unpredictable;
once they subsequently fled,
the border gained peace.
You ordered me to serve as Governor of this prefecture (zhōu),
to act as a defensive barrier.
I was just about to gather the remaining survivors,
comfort and pacify them,
encourage the troops and feed the horses,
and certainly fight a subsequent battle,
to bury the bodies at Hánshān,
and wipe away the disgrace of Wōyáng.
Your Majesty, having lost spirit and courage,
had no determination left to defend,
and immediately believed Zhēnyáng's deceitful memorial,
requesting
renewed peace talks.
Your official repeatedly argued firmly,
but you doubted and refused to listen.
Being fickle and contradictory like this,
even a child would be ashamed of it;
how much more so for a ruler,
who is duplicitous in his virtue (èr sān qí dé).
This is the
third failure.
Now, for those who shrink back, hesitate, and delay,
there are established military laws.
Zǐyù suffered a minor defeat,
yet was executed by Chǔ;
Wáng Huī failed to follow the rules,
and was executed by Hàn.
Zhēnyáng commanded tens of
thousands of elite armored troops,
with equipment piled up like mountains.
Mùróng had light troops,
fewer than a hundred chariots,
yet (Zhēnyáng) could not resist,
and personally suffered imprisonment.
As the Emperor's nephew (yóu zǐ),
to be bound and presented before the enemy’s court,
it was truly fitting that his name be removed from the imperial registry,
and his blood used to anoint the war drums.
Your Majesty, however, never pursued accountability,
pitied his pathetic survival,
and wished to use this humble official
to arrange a trade (for him).
Should the
methods of a ruler
be like this?
This is the fourth failure.
Xuánhù is a great dependency,
historically known as Rǔ and Yǐng.
Your official brought the prefecture to submit internally,
but Yáng Yārén resolutely refused to enter (it);
after he did enter,
he abandoned it without reason,
yet Your Majesty
never suspected or blamed him,
instead allowing him to return and reside in the Northern Directorate (Běi Sī).
Since Yārén abandoning it
was not deemed a crime,
my acquiring it should not be deemed a merit.
This is the fifth failure.
My retreat and defeat at Wōyáng
was not a fault of the battle (itself),
but truly resulted from Your Majesty and your officials collectively misjudging the situation.
When I returned to Shòuchūn,
I showed no sign of regret,
respectfully serving the Imperial
Court,
concealing wickedness and extolling goodness.
Yārén, knowing he abandoned the prefecture,
gnashed his teeth in sighing resentment,
feeling inward shame and fear,
and thus memorialized that your official intended to rebel.
If one intends to rebel, there must be tangible evidence.
What
proof or verification was there?
Yet you instantly accepted the false accusation,
and Your Majesty never investigated or debated the matter,
but silently believed and accepted it.
How can someone who falsely accuses another of the greatest crime
still serve the ruler shoulder to shoulder
with him?
This is the sixth failure.
Zhào Bóchāo rose from incompetence,
and was appointed regional governor (fāng bó).
He only preyed upon the common people,
stockpiling soldiers and horses,
not desiring to establish merit for the state,
but merely seeking wealth
and nobility for himself.
He distributed bribes to influential favorites,
seeking to buy reputation.
Zhū Cǎo and his ilk
accumulated gold and valuables from him,
subsequently causing everyone to praise Hú and Zhào,
comparing them to the historical Guān (Yǔ) and Zhāng (Fēi),
deceiving the Imperial
ear (tiān tīng),
and treating it as truth.
In the campaign at Hánshān,
he brought female entertainers with him.
Immediately upon hearing the enemy drums,
he fled along with his concubines,
not waiting for Zhēnyáng,
which is why not a single wheel returned.
Discussing
this crime of his,
he ought to have been exterminated along with his nine generations of kin;
yet, because he paid bribes to the palace inner circle (zhōng rén),
he was reinstated to his prefecture official post.
If Bóchāo committed no crime,
then what account should be taken of my merit?
If rewards and punishments have no rule,
how can one govern the
state?
This is the seventh failure.
I have always governed my subordinates strictly,
without encroaching on property.
Customs duties and market taxes
were all completely suspended or forgiven.
The people of Shòuyáng
cherish the relief and restoration.
Péi Zhītì and others assisted...
The garrison was there,
and fearing that your servant would restrict them,
they fled back without cause;
they also informed your servant that they intended to rebel.
Your Majesty did not rebuke them for disobeying orders and abandoning their posts,
but instead accepted their slanderous insinuations.
To treat your servant thus,
where can I find peace?
This is the eighth fault.
Although your servant's talent falls short of the ancients,
I have indeed experienced many things.
In governing the people and leading the multitude,
from youth to old age,
since I was young, I have been active,
often without a single unexecuted plan.
But when I committed myself to the
Dao,
I exhausted my loyal counsel,
yet every time I presented a memorial,
it was suppressed.
Zhū Cǎo arbitrarily controlled the military,
Zhōu Shízhēn was in overall charge of arms,
Lù Yàn and Xú Lín superintended
grain and silk.
All of them explicitly sought bribes;
without payment, nothing would proceed.
[二四] The truth of matters beyond the border
was decided in the secretariat of the Shèrényuàn;
the appointment of generals and the dispatching of armies
required memorials to the designated
authorities.
Your servant had no bribes to offer,
and thus was suppressed and obstructed.
This is the ninth fault.
The Prince of Póyáng garrisoned Héféi,
bordering your servant.
I respected him as a member of the imperial lineage,
always treating him with deference;
yet the heir-prince was cowardly and weak,
merely feigning preparedness and defense.
When your servant had an
envoy,
he would certainly attack and shoot at them,
sometimes publicly declaring your servant to be a rebel,
or accusing your servant of minor faults.
To attract and secure loyalty requires propriety;
how can a loyal and valiant person endure this?
This is the
tenth fault.
The remaining matters
cannot be fully enumerated.
Caught between advancement and retreat, I was in a dire straits,
and frequently submitted memorials.
My words were direct and my language strong,
which displeased the Dragon's Scales,
and thus a stern imperial edict was issued,
and I was immediately
to be attacked.
Shùnhuá was truly filial,
yet he still fled from his vicious father's rod;
Zhào Dùn was loyal and virtuous,
yet he did not punish the regicide.
What kinship or crime do I have,
that I should sit and await
annihilation?
Hán Xìn was heroic and exceptional,
he defeated Xiàng Yǔ and established the Hàn dynasty,
but in the end was cooked by a woman,
only then regretting Kuǎ Tōng's words.
Each time your servant reads historical accounts,
my heart often laughs at this.
How can I follow their overturned carriage,
and gratify Your Majesty's sycophantic officials?
Therefore, I have raised the army of Jìnyáng,
to cross the Chángjiāng amidst chaos,
wishing to ascend the scarlet steps,
tread upon the
patterned stone,
verbally present what is right and wrong,
point out what is good and bad,
execute the wicked officials by Your Majesty's side,
and cleanse the corrupt governance of the imperial court.
Then I shall return to guard my fief,
to preserve my loyalty and integrity;
this is your servant's utmost wish.
On the first day of the third month,
the people within the city, deeming Jǐng to have broken his oath,
raised beacons and beat drums, shouting.
Thereupon, Yáng Yārén, Liǔ Jìnglǐ, and the heir of Póyáng, Sì, advanced to the north of Dōngfǔ City.
Before their palisades were even erected,
they were attacked by Sòng Zǐxiān, one of Jǐng's generals,
and utterly defeated.
Several thousand drowned in the Huái River.
The rebels sent their severed heads to the palace gates.
Jǐng again sent Yú Zǐyuè,
requesting peace once more.
Emperor Wǔ sent the Imperial Censor-in-Chief Shěn Jùn to Jǐng's location.
Jǐng had no intention of leaving,
and Jùn firmly admonished him.
Jǐng was enraged,
and immediately released the water from in front of the stone gate,
attacking the city by a hundred routes,
day and night without ceasing.
The city then fell.
Thereupon, all imperial regalia, clothing, and playthings, as well as the concubines of the rear palace, were plundered.
Princes, marquises, and court officials were rounded up and sent to Yǒngfú Province,
and the guards of the two palaces were removed.
Wáng Wěi was made to guard Wǔdé Hall,
Yú Zǐyuè was stationed at Tàijí East Hall.
A forged imperial edict proclaimed a general amnesty throughout the realm,
and Jǐng declared himself Grand Commander, Controller of All Domestic and Foreign Military Affairs, and Recorder of the Imperial Secretariat,
retaining his titles of Attendant Censor, Bearer of the Imperial Insignia, Grand Chancellor, and Prince.
Initially,
the piled corpses in the city could not be buried in time,
and there were those already dead but unburied,
or about to die but not yet expired.
Jǐng gathered them all and burned them,
the stench was perceptible for over ten *lǐ*.
The Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Bāo Zhèng, was critically ill;
the rebels dragged him out and burned him.
He writhed in the flames
for a long time before expiring.
Thereupon, all supporting armies dispersed.
Jǐng issued a forged edict saying:
"Recently,
traitorous officials usurped authority,
almost endangering the state.
Thanks to the Chancellor's brilliant rise,
assisting my person,
the regional commanders, governors, and prefects may each return to their original posts."
Xiāo Zhèngdé was demoted to Attendant Censor and Grand Marshal,
and all officials were restored to their ranks.
Jǐng sent Dǒng Shàoxiān to lead troops to attack Guǎnglíng.
The Inspector of Nányǎn Province, the heir of Nánkāng, Huìlǐ, surrendered the city to him.
Jǐng appointed Shàoxiān as Inspector of Nányǎn Province.
Initially,
the Inspector of Běiyǎn Province, the Marquis of Dìngxiāng, Zhī, and the Marquis of Xiāngtán, Tuì,
along with the former Inspector of Tóng Province, Guō Fèng, had jointly raised an army
to provide aid.
By this point,
Fèng plotted to join Jǐng with Huái'yīn.
Zhī and the others were unable to restrain him,
and all fled to Wèi.
Jǐng appointed Xiāo Nòngzhāng as Inspector of Běiyǎn Province.
The provincial people raised troops to resist him.
Jǐng sent the Palace Guard Commander Qiū Zǐyīng and the Palace Guard General Yáng Hǎi to lead troops to reinforce.
Hǎi killed Zǐyīng
and led his army to surrender to Wèi.
Wèi then occupied Huái'yīn.
Jǐng again sent the Commissioner Yú Zǐyuè and Zhāng Dàhēi to lead troops into Wú.
The Administrator of Wújùn, Yuán Jūnzhèng, welcomed their surrender.
After Zǐyuè and the others arrived,
they plundered Wú,
greatly extorting provisions,
forcing and abducting women and children,
and cruelly oppressing the populace.
There was no one in Wú who did not resent and hate them.
Thereupon, they each erected city walls and palisades to defend themselves.
In this month,
Jǐng moved his garrison to Xīzhōu,
and sent Commissioner Rèn Yuē as the Southern Circuit Administrator,
garrisoning Gūshú.
In the fifth month,
Gāozǔ passed away in the Wéndé Palace.
Previously,
after Táichéng had fallen,
Jǐng first sent Wáng Wěi and Chén Qìng to pay respects to Gāozǔ.
Gāozǔ said:
“Where is Jǐng now?
You may summon him.”
At that time, Gāozǔ was seated in the Wéndé Palace.
Jǐng then entered the court,
with five hundred armored soldiers as his personal guard,
and ascended the hall wearing a sword.
After bowing,
Gāozǔ asked:
“You have been in military service for a long time;
surely you are not too weary?”
Jǐng remained silent.
He then asked again:
“From which province are you,
that you dare to come here?”
Jǐng again could not answer,
and his attendants answered for him.
Upon leaving,
he said to Xiānggōng Wáng Sēngguì:
“I have often stood in the saddle facing the enemy,
with arrows and blades crossing,
yet my spirits were calm and unhurried,
without any fear.
Today, upon seeing Xiāo Gōng,
I was intimidated;
is this not the inviolable might of Heaven?
I must not see him again.”
Although Gāozǔ’s external power had been diminished,
his spirit remained indignant.
At times, when matters were reported to him,
he would frequently reject them.
Jǐng deeply respected and feared him,
and also did not dare to press him.
Jǐng sent soldiers to stand guard inside the palace chambers.
Gāozǔ asked Zhìjújiān Zhōu Shízhēn:
“Who are these people?”
He replied:
“The Chancellor.”
Gāozǔ then wrongly said:
