“What Chancellor?”
He replied:
“It is Chancellor Hóu.”
Gāozǔ angrily said:
“His name is Jǐng,
what do you mean Chancellor!”
Thereafter,
for every request made,
many were not to his liking.
Even his imperial meals were curtailed,
and he consequently grieved and fell ill, and passed away.
Jǐng then secretly withheld the news of his death,
and provisionally interred him in the Zhāoyáng Palace.
Outside, none of the civil or military officials knew of it.
After more than twenty days,
the imperial coffin was moved to the Tàijí Front Hall,
and the Crown Prince was welcomed to ascend the imperial throne.
Thereupon, he issued a false edict pardoning people from the north who had been enslaved,
hoping to gain their service.
He also sent Yítóng Lái Liàng to lead troops to attack Xuānchéng.
Xuānchéng Nèishǐ Yáng Huá lured Liàng and beheaded him.
Jǐng again sent his general Lǐ Xiánmíng to punish Huá,
but Huá surrendered the commandery.
Jǐng sent Yítóng Sòng Zǐxiān and others to lead their forces eastward to Qiántáng.
Xīnchéng Shùzhǔ Dài Sēngyì held the county and resisted them.
[二五]
This month,
Jǐng sent Zhōngjūn Hóu Zǐjiàn into Wú’s army,
to arrest Yú Zǐyuè and Zhāng Dàhēi and return them to the capital for execution.
At that time, Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ Línchénggōng Dàlián held the province,
and Wúxīng Tàishǒu Zhāng Shèng held the commandery.
From Nánlíng upwards,
everyone was holding their ground.
The area where Jǐng’s commands were effective
was only west of Wújùn
and north of Nánlíng.
In the sixth month,
Jǐng appointed Yítóng Guō Yuánjiàn as Shàngshū Púyè, Běidào Xíngtái, and Commander of all Jiangbei military affairs,
stationed in Xīnqín.
Local people Lù Jí, Dài Wénjǔ, and others raised an army of over ten thousand men,
killed Jǐng’s Tàishǒu Sū Dányú,
and proclaimed former Huáinán Tàishǒu Wénchénghóu Níng as their leader
to resist Jǐng.
Sòng Zǐxiān heard of this and attacked them.
Jí and the others abandoned the city and fled.
Jǐng then divided the two counties of Hǎiyán and Xūpǔ in Wújùn to form Wǔyuán Commandery.
At this point,
Jǐng killed Xiāo Zhèngdé in the Yǒngfú Province.
He enfeoffed Yuán Luó as Xīqín Wáng,
and Yuán Jǐnglóng as Chénliú Wáng.
[二六] More than ten of the Yuán clan’s sons and younger brothers were enfeoffed as kings.
He appointed Liǔ Jìnglǐ as Shǐchíjié, Dàdūdū,
subordinate to the Grand Chancellor,
to participate in military affairs.
Jǐng sent his Zhōngjūn Hóu Zǐjiàn, Jiānxíngtái Liú Shénmào, and others to lead an army on an eastern campaign,
which conquered Wúxīng.
They captured Tàishǒu Zhāng Shèng and his son and sent them to the capital,
where Jǐng had them both killed.
Jǐng appointed Sòng Zǐxiān as Sītú,
Rèn Yuē as Lǐngjūn Jiāngjūn,
Ěrzhū Jìbó, Chìluó Zǐtōng, Péng Jùn, Dǒng Shàoxiān, Zhāng Huàrén, Yú Qìng, Lǔ Bóhé, Hēxī Jīn, Shǐ Ānhé, Shí Línghù, Liú Guīyì,
all as Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī.
This month,
Póyáng Sìwáng Fàn led troops to Zàkǒu.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Xúnyángwáng Dàxīn intercepted him and moved westward.
Jǐng moved his camp to Gūshú.
Fàn’s generals Péi Zhītì and Xiàhóu Wēishēng surrendered to Jǐng with their forces.
In the eleventh month,
Sòng Zǐxiān attacked Qiántáng.
Dài Sēngyì surrendered.
Jǐng established Qiántáng as Línjiāng Commandery,
and Fùyáng as Fùchūn Commandery.
He appointed Wáng Wěi and Yuán Luó both as Yítóng Sānsī.
In the twelfth month,
Sòng Zǐxiān, Zhào Bóchāo, and Liú Shénmào advanced to attack Kuàijī.
Dōngyángzhōu Cìshǐ Línchénggōng Dàlián abandoned the city and fled.
Liú Shénmào was sent to pursue and capture him.
Jǐng appointed Péi Zhītì as Shǐchíjié, Píngxī Jiāngjūn, Hézhōu Cìshǐ,
and Xiàhóu Wēishēng as Shǐchíjié, Píngběi Jiāngjūn, Nányùzhōu Cìshǐ.
This month,
an envoy from Báijì arrived.
Seeing the city and its surroundings in ruins,
he wailed outside the Duānmén gate.
Passersby who saw this could not help but shed tears.
Jǐng was greatly enraged when he heard this,
and sent him to be confined in Xiǎozhuāngyán Temple,
not allowing him to enter or exit.
In the first month of Dàbǎo First Year,
Jǐng issued a false edict to promote himself, granting forty palace guards,
and providing feathered banners and drums for his front and rear entourages,
and establishing Left and Right Chángshǐ and four Cóngshì Zhōngláng.
Former Jiāngdū Lìng Zǔ Hào raised an army in Guǎnglíng,
beheaded Jǐng’s Cìshǐ Dǒng Shàoxiān,
and proclaimed former Tàizǐ Shèrén Xiāo Miǎn as Cìshǐ.
He also allied with the Wèi people for support,
and issued proclamations far and wide,
intending to campaign against Jǐng.
Jǐng was greatly alarmed when he heard this,
and immediately led Hóu Zǐjiàn and others out of Jīngkǒu,
gathering forces by land and water.
Hào fortified the city and defended it.
Jǐng attacked the city
and captured it.
Jǐng had Hào torn apart by chariots as a public display,
and all, young and old, in the city were beheaded.
He appointed Hóu Zǐjiàn as Supervisor of Nányǎnzhōu affairs.
This month,
Jǐng summoned Sòng Zǐxiān back to Jīngkǒu.
In the fourth month,
Jǐng appointed Yuán Sīqián as Dōngdào Xíngtái,
stationed in Qiántáng.
He appointed Hóu Zǐjiàn as Nányǎnzhōu Cìshǐ.
Wénchénghóu Níng raised an army in Wúxī Xiāng,
and within ten days,
his forces reached ten thousand.
He led them westward.
Jǐng’s Xiānggōng Mèng Zhèn and Hóu Zǐróng attacked and defeated them,
beheaded Níng,
and sent his head to Jǐng.
In the seventh month,
Jǐng established Zòujùn as Xīyǎnzhōu,
and Yángpíngjùn as Běiyǎnzhōu.
Rèn Yuē and Lú Huīlüè attacked Jìnxī Commandery
and killed Póyáng Shìzǐ Sì.
Jǐng appointed Wáng Wěi as Zhōngshū Jiān.
Rèn Yuē advanced and raided Jiāngzhōu.
Jiāngzhōu Cìshǐ Xúnyángwáng Dàxīn surrendered to him.
Shìzǔ, upon hearing that Jiāngzhōu had fallen,
sent Wèijūn Jiāngjūn Xú Wénshèng to lead his forces down to Wǔchāng
to resist Yuē.
Jǐng again issued a false edict to promote himself to Xiàngguó,
enfeoffed the twenty commanderies including Tàishān as Hànwáng,
and granted him the privilege of not needing to rush when entering court,
of being addressed without his personal name during salutations,
and of wearing a sword and shoes when ascending the hall,
following the precedent of Xiāo Hé.
Jǐng appointed Liǔ Jìnglǐ as Hùjūn Jiāngjūn,
Jiāng Xúnyì as Xiàngguó Zuǒchángshǐ,
Xú Hóng as Zuǒsīmǎ,
Lù Yuē as Yòuchángshǐ,
and Shěn Zhòng as Yòusīmǎ.
This month,
Jǐng led his fleet up to Wǎnkǒu.
In the tenth month,
robbers killed Wǔlín Hóu Zī at Guǎngmòmén.
Zī often entered and exited Tàizōng’s bedchamber,
which Jǐng’s faction resented,
and so they harmed him.
Jǐng again issued a false imperial edict, saying:
"The visible celestial phenomena hang in the sky,
the four seasons take their standard from the Chén and the Dǒu;
all creatures grow upon the earth,
and the ten thousand things look up for illumination to the Great Luminaries.
Therefore, when governing effortlessly before the screen,
the eight corners of the world converge;
when bearing the charts and establishing the proper position,
the nine domains submit together.
Thus, the rulers who took names from the clouds or titles from the waters,
and the descendants of the Dragon Officials and Human Sovereigns,
none failed to receive signs from the Hé and the Luò Rivers,
and perform the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices on Dàizōng.
The four barbarian tribes hastened,
and the myriad states came to court.
Listening widely to the reigns of Yú and Xià,
their Way was ever renewed.
Extending to Shāng and Zhōu,
this was never changed.
But when Yōu and Lì lacked strength,
military horses bred in the suburbs;
when Huì and Huái lost control,
barbarian dust encroached upon the imperial path.
Consequently, wolves and jackals freely spread their poison,
invading the dwelling places of Yī and Yuè;
the Xiǎnyǔn became terribly rampant,
nesting in Xián and Luò.
Since the Jìn tripod moved east,
many years and ages have passed.
The Plains of Zhōu have not been recovered,
and the time has been truly long.
Although Sòngzǔ attempted strategic planning,
he stopped his long-term plan halfway;
Qí proposed treaties of peace and alliance,
but only fruitlessly exhausted the envoys.
Our Great Liáng received the mandate and became Emperor,
emerging from Zhèn and ascending to the Imperial seat.
All regions submitted to benevolence,
and the wide territories imbibed the transformation.
We opened up borders and expanded territory,
crossing the Hànhǎi while raising the whips;
those who came to court and offered audience,
equaled the scale of Túshān, wheel tracks matching.
The dark tortoise emerged from the Luò River,
the white pheasant returned to Fēng.
The northern frontier shared the same script,
and the barbarian heavens followed the same tracks.
We did not expect Gāo Chéng, being arrogant and unruly,
to slaughter the state of Wèi,
inciting both Huá and Yí,
and failing to fulfill his duty to the ruler.
Consequently, he cast wolfish glances and invaded from the north,
turning his horse's head southward.
It happened that Heaven detested the darkness and deceit,
and the number of wicked followers was exhausted.
The dragon and leopard responded to the era,
and the wind and clouds met at the appointed time.
The Chancellor, the Prince of Hàn,
possesses superior virtue and heroic bearing,
truly granted by Heaven;
his magnificent strategies and brave plans
originate from his own mind.
The pearl fish showed an omen,
and Chén and Mǎo aligned in brilliance;
he analyzed the Six Tāo,
managing the four realms meticulously.
His patterns rose like a leopard changing its coat,
the phoenix gathered and the coiled dragon soared;
flapping his wings, he came in dignity,
descending bearing the charts.
When he first took charge of governance,
he truly initiated the campaign first,
serving this great plan,
and was able to eliminate the Xūn wicked.
It was only because the Emperor ascended (to Dǐnghú),
and the six dragons rested their carriage;
that the weapons temporarily ceased,
and the Nine Punishments were not yet fully executed.
But their wickedness ripened and reached its fullness,
and the chief perpetrator (Gāo Chéng) died.
His younger brother Yáng continued the rebellion,
prolonging the steps toward chaos.
Though the sound of Yáng is different,
he shares the same destructive manner;
he stealthily usurped a false title,
his heart hoping to wield the executioner's axe.
The ruler and officials by the Fēng River,
presented maps and begged for aid;
the common people of Guānhé,
weeping blood, requested troops.
All wished to serve the nation's spirit,
and longed to see the Imperial transformation.
We, though deficient and dull,
succeeding to the military task,
hope to save the populace of Yáo,
and aspire to pacify the tracks of Yǔ.
Moreover, carriages and robes are used to reward merit,
and titles become prominent because of deeds.
When the Zhōu army conquered Yīn,
the title Yīngyáng originated with Shàngfǔ;
when Hàn campaigned against the Róng and Dí,
Míng Yǒu truly began the position of Dùliáo.
How much more so now, with divine planning and sagacious calculations,
so profound they are hard to fathom,
with great achievements and glorious merits,
deeds surpassing description and comparison,
how can we use those standard titles
to preserve and secure this state?
The Chancellor may be granted the titles Yǔzhòu Dà Jiāngjūn and Dūdu Liùhé Zhū Jūnshì.
All other appointments remain as before."
When he presented the text of the edict to Tàizōng (Xiāo Yì),
Tàizōng exclaimed in astonishment:
"Does the General truly hold the title of the Universe (Yǔzhòu)?"
Qí sent its general Xīn Shù to besiege Yángpíng.
Jǐng's Circuit Commissioner, Guō Yuánjiàn, led troops to reinforce it,
and Shù retreated.
Xú Wénshèng entered Bèijī.
Rèn Yuē led the naval forces to meet him in battle,
but Wénshèng utterly defeated him.
He then advanced his army to Dàjǔkǒu.
At this time, Jǐng was garrisoned at Wǎnkǒu.
The capital was weak and defenseless.
Nánkāng Wáng Huìlǐ and the Administrator of Běi Yǎnzhōu, Chéng Qīn, planned to attack Jǐng.
Jiàn'ān Hóu Bēn learned of their plot
and informed Jǐng.
Jǐng sent men to arrest Huìlǐ, along with his younger brother Qíyáng Hóu Tōnglǐ, Liǔ Jìnglǐ, and Chéng Qīn,
and executed them all.
In the twelfth month,
Jǐng issued a false edict enfeoffing Bēn as Jìnglíng Wáng,
rewarding him for exposing the Nánkāng plot.
In this month,
Zhāng Biāo raised a revolt in Kuàijī.
He attacked and captured Shàngyú.
Jǐng’s Grand Administrator, Cài Tái Yuè, attacked him,
but could not suppress him.
By this point,
Biāo had also captured Zhūjì, Yǒngxīng, and other counties.
Jǐng sent the Yítóu Tián Qiān, Zhào Bóchāo, and Xiè Dārén eastward to campaign against Biāo.
In the first month of the second year,
Biāo sent a detached general to raid Qiántáng and Fùchūn.
Tián Qiān advanced his troops and engaged them in battle,
and defeated them.
Jǐng appointed Wáng Kè as Tàishī,
Sòng Zixiān as Tàibǎo,
Yuán Luó as Tàifù,
Guō Yuánjiàn as Tàiwèi,
Zhāng Huàrén as Sītú,
Rèn Yuē as Sīkōng,
Yú Qìng as Tàizǐ Tàishī,
Shí Línghù as Tàizǐ Tàibǎo,
Hēxī Jīn as Tàizǐ Tàifù,
Wáng Wěi as Shàngshū Zuǒ Púyè,
and Suǒ Chāoshì as Shàngshū Yòu Púyè.
Xiāo Yōng, the Governor of Běi Yǎnzhōu, plotted to surrender to Wèi.
The matter was exposed,
and Jǐng executed him.
In this month,
Shìzǔ sent the Governor of Bāzhōu, Wáng Xún, and others to lead forces down to Wǔchāng to assist Xú Wénshèng.
Rèn Yuē requested reinforcements from Xītái,
and sent an urgent appeal to Jǐng.
In the third month,
Jǐng personally led a force of twenty thousand men
westward to reinforce Yuē.
In the fourth month,
Jǐng arrived at Xīyáng.
Xú Wénshèng led his naval forces to engage him,
and Jǐng utterly defeated him.
Jǐng discovered through reconnaissance that Yǐngzhōu was undefended,
and short of troops.
He then sent Sòng Zixiān to lead three hundred light cavalry in a surprise attack, capturing it.
He captured the Governor Fāng Zhū and the Acting Administrator Bào Quán,
and seized all the family members of the Wǔchāng army.
Xú Wénshèng and his colleagues heard this,
suffered a major defeat,
and fled back to Jiānglíng.
Jǐng pressed his advantage and continued westward.
Initially,
Shìzǔ (世祖) sent the Commandant Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) to lead his troops eastward to relieve Xú Wénshèng (徐文盛).
The army reached Bālíng (巴陵).
Coincidentally, Jǐng (景) arrived,
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) therefore strengthened his defenses and resisted him.
Jǐng (景) set up a long siege line,
built earth mounds,
and attacked day and night,
but could not overcome them.
Sickness and plague spread within the army,
and more than half the men died or were wounded.
Shìzǔ (世祖) sent the General Who Pacifies the North, Hú Sēngyòu (胡僧祐), leading two thousand soldiers, to rescue Bālíng (巴陵).
When Jǐng (景) heard this,
he sent Rèn Yuē (任約) with several thousand elite soldiers to intercept and attack Hú Sēngyòu (胡僧祐).
Hú Sēngyòu (胡僧祐) and the lay Buddhist Lù Fǎhé (陸法和) retreated to and held Chìtíng (赤亭) to await the attack.
Rèn Yuē (任約) arrived and engaged them in battle.
He was soundly defeated,
and Yuē (約) was captured alive.
When Jǐng (景) heard of this,
he fled that night.
He appointed Dīng Hé (丁和) as the Governor of Yǐngzhōu (郢州),
and left Sòng Zǐxiān (宋子仙), Shí Línghù (時靈護), and others to assist Hé (和) in defense.
He assigned Zhāng Huàrén (張化仁) and Yán Hóngqìng (閻洪慶) to guard Lǔshān (魯山) City.
Jǐng (景) then returned to the capital (Jīngshī).
Wáng Sēngbiàn (王僧辯) then led his troops eastward,
reached Hànkǒu (漢口),
and attacked Lǔshān (魯山) and Yǐng (郢) cities,
both of which fell.
From this point on, wherever the various armies went, they achieved victory.
Jǐng (景) then deposed Tàizōng (太宗),
and imprisoned him in Yǒngfú Shěng (永福省).
When the draft of the imperial edict was ready,
he forced Tàizōng (太宗) to copy it.
When he reached
“The former Emperor was mindful of the importance of the sacred vessel (the throne),
and considered the security of the altars of soil and grain (the state),”
he sighed, wept, and choked with sobs,
unable to stop himself.
On that day,
Jǐng (景) welcomed Dǒng (棟), the Prince of Yùzhāng (豫章), to the imperial throne.
He ascended the front hall of the Tàijí (太極) Palace.
A general amnesty was proclaimed throughout the empire,
and the reign era was changed to Tiānzhèng (天正) First Year.
A whirling wind arose from Yǒngfú Shěng (永福省),
blowing all its ritual objects and cultural relics upside down or broken.
Those who saw it were all terrified.
Originally,
after Jǐng (景) had stabilized the capital district (Jīngyì),
he immediately harbored ambitions of usurpation,
but believing that the four directions still needed pacification,
he did not immediately enthrone himself.
However, since he had suffered military defeat at Bālíng (巴陵),
lost armies at Jiāng (江) and Yǐng (郢),
had fierce generals annihilated externally,
and felt his heroic spirit inwardly discouraged,
he wished to falsely assume the grand title,
and thus fulfill his wicked intention.
His strategist Wáng Wěi (王偉) said,
“Since ancient times, when the imperial cauldron (the throne) is moved,
deposition and enthronement are necessary.”
Therefore, Jǐng (景) followed his advice.
When his Grand Commandant Guō Yuánjiàn (郭元建) heard this,
he rushed back from Qínjùn (秦郡),
and remonstrated with Jǐng (景), saying:
“The reason the armies from the four directions have not arrived is
precisely because the two palaces (Tàizōng and Dǒng) are safe.
If you proceed with regicide and rebellion,
incurring the hatred of the whole empire,
once the opportunity is lost,
even regret will be too late.”
Wáng Wěi (王偉) stubbornly insisted, and Jǐng (景) did not follow the advice.
Jǐng (景) then falsely issued an edict in Dǒng’s (棟) name,
posthumously honoring Zhāomíng (昭明) Crown Prince as Emperor Zhàomíng (詔明 Huángdì),
the Prince Ān (安) of Yùzhāng (豫章) as Emperor Ān (安 Huángdì),
the Consort Jìng (敬) of Jīnhuá (金華) as Empress Jìng (敬 Huánghòu),
Lady Wáng (王), the Grand Consort of the State of Yùzhāng (豫章), as the Empress Dowager,
and Consort Zhāng (張) as the Empress.
He appointed Liú Shénmào (劉神茂) as Minister of Works (Sīkōng),
Xú Hóng (徐洪) as General Who Pacifies the South,

and Qín Huǎngzhī (秦晃之), Wáng Yè (王曄), Lǐ Xiánmíng (李賢明), Xú Yǒng (徐永), Xú Zhēnguó (徐珍國), Sòng Chángbǎo (宋長寶), and Yǐn Sīhé (尹思合) were all made Administrators, Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers (Yítóng Sānsī).
Jǐng (景) gave the Consort of the deceased Crown Prince to Guō Yuánjiàn (郭元建).
Yuánjiàn (元建) said:
“How can a Crown Prince’s consort be degraded to become another man’s concubine?”
In the end, he refused to meet her.
On the night of Rén’yín (壬寅) in the tenth month,
Jǐng (景) sent his Palace Commandant Pēng Jùn (彭儁) and Wáng Xiūzuǎn (王脩纂) to present wine to Tàizōng (太宗), saying:
“The Chancellor believes Your Majesty has endured sorrow long enough,
so he has ordered your servants to present a cup of wine.”
Tàizōng (太宗) knew they were about to murder him.
He thereupon drank the wine deeply,
and when drunk, he returned to his bedchamber.
Wáng Xiūzuǎn (王脩纂) used a towel filled with earth placed upon his abdomen,
and thus he collapsed (died).
His corpse was clad in court robes,
and he was secretly buried in a thin coffin near the wine storehouse north of the city.
Previously,
Tàizōng (太宗) had been imprisoned for a long time,
and no court official could gain access to him.
He feared disaster was imminent,
and was constantly ill at ease.
Only the Palace Attendant Yīn Bùhài (殷不害) was later gradually allowed entrance.
Tàizōng (太宗) pointed to the palace where he resided and said to him:
“Páng Juān (龐涓) should die beneath this place.”
He also said:
“Last night I dreamed I swallowed earth.
You try to interpret this for me.”
Yīn Bùhài (殷不害) replied:
“In the past, Chóng Ěr (重耳) was given a lump of earth (as a sign of allegiance),
and eventually returned to the State of Jìn (晉國).
The dream Your Majesty had
might correspond to this.”
Tàizōng (太宗) said:
“If there is truly a sign from the spirits,
I hope this prediction is not false.”
When he was murdered at this time,
it was indeed done with earth.
In this month,

Jǐng’s (景) Minister of Works and Eastern Circuit Mobile Secretariat Liú Shénmào (劉神茂), Administrators Yǐn Sīhé (尹思合), Liú Guīyì (劉歸義), Wáng Yè (王曄), and the General of Cloud Banners, Yuán Yūn (元頵), Prince of Sānggān (桑乾), along with others, occupied Dōngyáng (東陽) and submitted [to Shìzǔ].
They subsequently sent Yuán Yūn (元頵) and the detached generals Lǐ Zhàn (李占) and Zhào Huìlǎng (趙惠朗) down to occupy the mouth of the Jiàndé (建德) River.
Yǐn Sīhé (尹思合) captured Jǐng’s (景) Grand Administrator of Xīn’ān (新安), Yuán Yì (元義),
and seized his troops.
Zhāng Biāo (張彪) attacked Yǒngjiā (永嘉).
Qín Yuǎn (秦遠), the Grand Administrator of Yǒngjiā (永嘉), surrendered to Biāo (彪).
In the eleventh month,
Jǐng (景) appointed Zhào Bóchāo (趙伯超) as the Eastern Circuit Mobile Secretariat,
to garrison Qiántáng (錢塘).
He sent Administrator Tián Qiān (田遷), Xiè Dárén (謝答仁), and others to lead troops eastward to attack Liú Shénmào (神茂).
Jǐng (景) falsely issued an edict in Xiāo Dǒng’s (蕭棟) name,
bestowing upon himself the rites of the Nine Marks of Favor (Jiǔ Xī),
and establishing officials from the Chancellor downward.
When the prepared ritual items were displayed in the courtyard,
a wild bird suddenly flew over Jǐng (景).
It had red feet and a scarlet beak,
and its form resembled a mountain magpie.
All the rebel followers were terrified,
and though they rushed to shoot at it, they could not hit it.
Jǐng (景) appointed Liú Quàn (劉勸), Qī Bà (戚霸), and Zhū Ānwáng (朱安王) as Administrators, Equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers, with Establishment of a Household (Kāifǔ Yítóng Sānsī).
He appointed Suǒ Jiǔshēng (索九昇) as General Protector of the Army.
Hóu Zǐjiàn (侯子鑒), the Governor of Southern Yǎnzhōu (南兗州), presented a white river deer.
A white rat was caught in Jiànkāng (建康) and presented [as an omen].
Xiāo Dǒng (蕭棟) attributed this (the omen) to Jǐng (景).
Jǐng (景) appointed Guō Yuánjiàn (郭元建) as the Governor of Southern Yǎnzhōu (南兗州),
retaining his titles of Grand Commandant (Tàiwèi) and Northern Mobile Secretariat (Běi Xíngtái) as before.
Jǐng (景) again falsely issued an edict in Xiāo Dǒng’s (蕭棟) name,
posthumously honoring his grandfather as Grand General (Dà Jiāngjūn),
and his father as Chancellor (Chéngxiàng).
He crowned himself,
with twelve strings of beads (liú),
erected imperial banners and flags,
had clearance rituals performed when he went out or returned,
rode the golden-hubbed carriage (Jīngēn Chē),
used six horses,
prepared the five seasonal auxiliary carriages,
established the ceremonial staffs (Máotóu Yúnhǎn),
used the Bāyì (八佾) dance in his music,
and utilized the Gōngxuán (宮懸) arrangement of bells and stands,
all exactly following the former imperial protocols.
Jǐng again forged Xiāo Dòng's edict,
abdicating the throne to himself.
Thereupon, at the Southern Altar,
brushwood was burned in sacrifice to Heaven,
he ascended the altar to receive the ritual objects of abdication,
all according to the previous rites.
Ceremonial music was carried on carts,
camels bore the sacrificial victims,
snares and traps were placed on the palanquin,
and he sat with his feet dangling.
The crystal ornament (biāo) on the sword Jǐng wore suddenly fell off,
and he picked it up himself.
As he was about to ascend the altar,
a rabbit ran out in front of him,
and soon disappeared.
Furthermore, a white rainbow pierced the sun.
Jǐng returned and ascended the Tài Jí Qián Diàn (Front Hall of the Grand Ultimate),
declared a general amnesty,
and changed the reign era to Tài Shǐ Yuán Nián (First Year of Tàishǐ).
He enfeoffed Xiāo Dòng as Huái Yīn Wáng (Prince of Huaiyin),
and imprisoned him in the surveillance office (jiān shěng).
The pseudo-officials proposed changing
"jǐng bì" (warning of clearance)
to
"yǒng bì" (perpetual clearance),
to avoid Jǐng's given name.
He changed the Liáng statutes to the Hàn statutes,
changed the Zuǒ Mín Shàng Shū (Minister of the Left Populace) to Diàn Zhōng Shàng Shū (Minister of the Palace Interior),
the Wǔ Bīng Shàng Shū (Minister of Five Armies) to Qī Bīng Shàng Shū (Minister of Seven Armies),
and the Zhí Diàn Zhǔ Shuài (Commander of Palace Interior Guards) to Zhí Qǐn (Chief of the Sleeping Chamber Guards).
Jǐng appointed up to ten or more officials to the posts of the Sān Gōng (Three Dukes),
and there were especially many Yí Tóng (Equaling the Three Dukes in Status) positions;
some rode a single horse alone,
holding the reins themselves.
His Zuǒ Pú Shè (Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs), Wáng Wěi, requested the establishment of the Seven Shrines (Qī Miào).
Jǐng said:
"What are the Seven Shrines?"
Wěi replied:
"The Son of Heaven sacrifices to his ancestral fathers for seven generations,
hence the establishment of the Seven Shrines."
He also requested the taboo names (huì) of the seven ancestors,
and ordered the Tài Cháng (Grand Minister of Ceremonies) to prepare the sacrificial rites.
Jǐng said:
"I do not recall my former generations,
only my father (Ā Yé) named Biāo."
Hearing this, everyone secretly laughed.
A member of Jǐng's faction knew that Jǐng's grandfather was named Zhōu,
but for the rest, Wáng Wěi fabricated their names and positions,
making Hóu Bà, the Sì Tú (Minister of the Masses) of the Hàn Dynasty, the founding ancestor (shǐ zǔ),
and Hóu Jǐn, a recluse scholar (zhēng shì) of the Jìn Dynasty, the seventh generation ancestor (qī shì zǔ).
Thereupon, he posthumously honored his grandfather Zhōu as Dà Chéng Xiàng (Grand Chancellor),
and his father Biāo as Yuán Huáng Dì (Founding Emperor).
In the twelfth month,
Xiè Dá Rén, Lǐ Qìng, and others arrived at Jiàn Dé,
attacked the stockades of Yuán Yūn and Lǐ Zhàn,
thoroughly defeated them,
and captured Yūn and Zhàn, sending them to Jǐng.
Jǐng cut off their hands and feet and displayed them publicly until
they died after a full day.
On the first day of the first month of the second year of Jǐng's reign,
he held court facing the imperial balcony.
Since Jǐng had suffered defeat at Bā Qiū,
and his forces were almost exhausted,
fearing that the Qí people might take advantage of the opportunity and form pincers with the Western armies,
he dispatched Guō Yuán Jiàn to lead infantry towards Xiǎo Xiǎn,
and Hóu Zǐ Jiàn to lead a naval force toward Rú Xū,
displaying their military strength at Féi Shuǐ,
to demonstrate their martial prowess.
Zǐ Jiàn reached Hé Féi,
attacked the outer wall (Luó Chéng),
and overcame it.
Guō Yuán Jiàn and Hóu Zǐ Jiàn soon heard that the Imperial Army (Wáng Shī) was approaching,
so they burned the residences of the common people in Hé Féi,
withdrew their forces,
Zǐ Jiàn secured Gū Shú,
and Yuán Jiàn returned to Guǎng Líng.
At that time, Xiè Dá Rén attacked Liú Shén Mào;
Shén Mào's subordinate generals, Wáng Yè and Lì Tōng, both held their outer camps and surrendered to Dá Rén.
Liú Guī Yì, Yǐn Sī Hé, and others were frightened,
and each abandoned their cities and fled.
Shén Mào, isolated and in peril,
subsequently surrendered to Dá Rén.
Wáng Sēng Biàn's army reached Wú Hú,
and the commandant of Wú Hú fled during the night.
Jǐng dispatched Shǐ Ān Hé, Sòng Cháng Guì, and others leading two thousand soldiers,
to assist Zǐ Jiàn in defending Gū Shú.
He recalled Tián Qiān and others back to the capital (Jīng Shī).
In this month,
Guō Cháng, a member of Jǐng's faction, presented a foal that had grown horns.
In the third month,
Jǐng went to Gū Shú,
inspected the ramparts and stockades,
and further cautioned Zǐ Jiàn, saying:
"The Westerners are good at naval warfare,
you must not compete directly with them;
Rèn Yuē's defeat last year
was precisely due to this.
If we can engage in a battle combining cavalry and infantry,
we will surely be able to defeat them.
You should just strengthen the walls and observe their moves."
Zǐ Jiàn then abandoned his boats and landed,
closing his camp and refusing to fight.
Sēng Biàn and the others consequently halted their army for more than ten days.
Jǐng’s faction was greatly pleased,
and informed Jǐng, saying:
"The Western Army fears our strength
and will surely try to escape.
If we do not strike,
we will lose the chance."
Jǐng again ordered Zǐ Jiàn to prepare for a naval engagement.
Zǐ Jiàn then led over ten thousand infantry and cavalry across the islet (zhōu),
and simultaneously advanced with the naval forces.
Sēng Biàn counter-attacked,
thoroughly defeating them,
and Zǐ Jiàn barely escaped with his life.
Jǐng heard of Zǐ Jiàn's defeat,
was greatly terrified, shedding tears,
covered his face and lay down with his blanket.
After a long time, he finally rose,
and sighed, saying:
"I have mistakenly ruined you, my Lord (Nǎi Gōng)!"
Sēng Biàn advanced his army to Zhāng Gōng Zhōu.
Jǐng assigned Lú Huī Lüè to guard Shí Tóu,
and Hé Xī Jīn to guard Hàn Guó Chéng.
He forced all the common people and the families of the soldiers to move inside Tài Chéng (the Palace City).
Sēng Biàn burned Jǐng's water stockades,
entered the Huái River,
and reached the islet near Chán Líng Sì.
Jǐng was greatly alarmed,
and therefore established stockades along the Huái River,
stretching from Shí Tóu to Zhū Què Háng (Vermilion Bird Bridge).
Sēng Biàn and the various generals then built interconnected camps and stockades on the high ground west of Shí Tóu Chéng,
reaching as far as Luò Xīng Dūn.
Jǐng was terrified,
and personally led Hóu Zǐ Jiàn, Yú Qìng, Shǐ Ān Hé, Wáng Sēng Guì, and others
to establish stockades northeast of Shí Tóu for defense.
He ordered Wáng Wěi, Suǒ Chāo Shì, and Lǚ Jì Lüè to guard Tài Chéng,
and Sòng Cháng Guì to guard Yán Zuò Sì.
He sent men to excavate the tomb of Wáng Sēng Biàn's father,
break open the coffin, and burn the corpse.
Wáng Sēng Biàn and the others advanced their camps north of Shí Tóu Chéng.
Jǐng arrayed his troops and challenged them to battle.
Sēng Biàn led the assembled forces in a fierce attack,
and thoroughly defeated Jǐng.
Hóu Zǐ Jiàn, Shǐ Ān Hé, and Wáng Sēng Guì each abandoned their stockades and fled.
Lú Huī Lüè and Hé Xī Jīn both surrendered with their cities.
After Jǐng was defeated and retreated,
he did not enter the palace;
he gathered his scattered troops
and stationed them below the palace gate (Què),
intending to flee and hide.
Wáng Wěi seized his reins and remonstrated, saying:
"Since ancient times, has there ever been a Son of Heaven who flees?
The palace guards now
are still enough for one more battle.
How can you just flee,
abandoning this place? Where do you intend to go?"
Jǐng replied:
"When I was in the North, I fought Hè Bá Shèng,
defeated Gé Róng,
and gained fame in Hé and Shuò,
being a man of the same kind as Gāo Wáng (Prince Gāo).
Now I came south, crossed the Great River,
took Tài Chéng as easily as turning my hand,
fought Shào Líng Wáng (Prince of Shaoling) at Běi Shān (North Mountain),
and defeated Liǔ Zhòng Lǐ on the South Bank—
all things you personally witnessed.
The matter of today
is probably Heaven destroying me.
You protect the city well.
I will make a final stand."
He looked up at the stone watchtower (shí què),
paced back and forth, and sighed for a long time.
He then placed his two sons in leather bags and hung them on his saddle,
and fled east with more than a hundred cavalry, including his Yí Tóng (Equaling the Three Dukes in Status) Tián Qiān and Fàn Xī Róng.
Wáng Wěi abandoned Tài Chéng and fled in hiding.
Hóu Zǐ Jiàn and others fled to Guǎng Líng.
Wáng Sēngbiàn dispatched Hóu Tián leading the army to pursue Hóu Jǐng.
Hóu Jǐng reached Jìnling,
he kidnapped the Grand Administrator Xú Yǒng and fled east to Wújun,
advanced and next stayed at Jiāxīng,
Zhào Bóchāo occupied Qiántáng to resist him.
Hóu Jǐng retreated back to Wújun,
reaching Sōngjiāng,
but Hóu Tián's army arrived suddenly,
Hóu Jǐng’s followers had not yet formed ranks,
and all raised banners requesting surrender.
Hóu Jǐng could not control them,
so he and several dozen trusted associates fled in a single small boat,
pushing his two sons into the water,
entering the sea from Hùdú.
Reaching Húdòuzhōu,
Yáng Kūn, formerly a Palace Attendant of the Crown Prince, killed him,
and sent the corpse to Wáng Sēngbiàn.
The head was sent to Xītái.
The corpse was exposed in the marketplace of Jiànkāng,
the common people scrambled to butcher, mince, and devour it,
They burned the bones and scattered the ashes.
Those who had suffered his calamities,
then mixed the ashes with wine and drank it.
When Hóu Jǐng’s head reached Jiānglíng,
Shìzǔ ordered it impaled in the marketplace,
after which it was lacquered,
and delivered to the Military Arsenal.
Hóu Jǐng’s height was less than seven *chǐ*,
but his eyebrows and eyes were refined and handsome.
His nature was suspicious and cruel,
and he loved slaughter.
When punishing people, sometimes he would first chop off their hands and feet,
cut their tongue and perform rhinotomy,
so that they died only after a full day.
He once established a large pounding mortar at Shítóu,
and anyone who broke the law,
were all pounded to death.
His brutality was thus extreme.
Since usurping the throne,
he often wore a white gauze cap,
but still draped himself in a dark blue robe,
or used an ivory comb inserted in his topknot.
He often laid out rugs and bamboo traps,
wore boots, and sat with his feet hanging down.
Sometimes he would ride a horse alone for amusement inside the palace,
or use a crossbow to shoot crows and birds in Huálínyuán.
His strategist Wáng Wěi did not permit him to go out lightly,
whereupon he became depressed and resentful,
and further lost his ambition.
The palace hall where he resided constantly had owls screeching,
Hóu Jǐng hated this,
and always sent men to search the mountains and fields to hunt and capture them.
During the Pǔtōng period,
a nursery rhyme went:
“Cyan clothes and a white horse come from Shòuyáng.”
Later, Hóu Jǐng indeed rode a white horse,
and his soldiers all wore cyan clothes.
The horse he rode,
whenever they were about to win a battle,
it would stomp its feet and neigh loudly,
its spirit would be vigorous and outstanding;
when they fled in defeat,
it would certainly lower its head and refuse to advance.
Initially,
during the Zhōngdàtóng period,
Gāozǔ once dreamt at night that the regional governors and administrators of the Central Plains all brought their territory to surrender,
the entire court acclaimed this as a blessing,
and when he awoke, he was extremely pleased.
The next morning, he saw Zhū Yì, the Secretariat Drafter,
and told him the dream.
Zhū Yì said:
“Is this not a sign that the realm is about to unify,
and Heaven’s Way has shown the omen beforehand?”
Gāozǔ said:
“I rarely dream,
to be inspired thus last night,
is truly enough to comfort my heart.”
When the Tàiqīng 2nd year came,
Hóu Jǐng indeed defected and submitted,
Gāozǔ was overjoyed and pleased,
believing it was connected to divine power,
and thus debated accepting him,
but his intention was still undecided.
He once went out to attend to affairs at night,
and reached Wǔdégé,
saying to himself:
“My state is like a golden bowl,
without a single flaw or crack.
If I now accept territory,
how can this be appropriate?
If perchance it leads to chaos,
it will be too late for regret.”
Zhū Yì immediately responded:
“Your sagely brightness rules the realm,
responding to the azure Heaven above.
The remnant populace of the northern lands,
who does not admire and look up to you?
It is only because they lacked opportunity
that their hearts were previously unrealized.
Now Hóu Jǐng occupies more than ten *zhōu* in Hénán,
dividing half of the Wèi territory,
offering sincerity and submitting allegiance,
coming from afar to submit to the sacred court.
How can this not be Heaven enticing his heart,
and men assisting his plan?
Examining his intentions and judging the matter,
it is quite commendable.
If we now refuse and do not accept him,
I fear we will cut off the hopes of future defectors.
This is truly easy to see,
I beg Your Majesty to have no doubt.”
Gāozǔ deeply accepted Zhū Yì's words,
and also believed his previous dream,
and thus finalized the decision to accept Hóu Jǐng.
When Zhēnyáng was defeated and overthrown,
and the border garrisons were terrified and disturbed,
Gāozǔ was already anxious about this,
saying:
“What I have done now,
is it not exactly what happened to the Jìn family?”
Before this,
Táo Hóngjǐng of Dānyáng, who lived secluded on Huáyángshān,
was widely learned and knowledgeable.
He once wrote a poem that said:
“Yífǔ was allowed to be dissolute,
Píngshū sat discussing emptiness,
unexpectedly the Zhāoyángdiàn
turned into the Chán Yú Palace.”
At the end of Dàtóng,
scholars competed to discuss profound doctrines,
and did not practice military affairs.
At this point,
Hóu Jǐng indeed occupied the Zhāoyángdiàn.
During the Tiānjiān period,
the monk Shì Bǎozhì said:
“The tailless puppy goes mad by itself,
before it dies it will bite and injure men,
in a moment it will perish by itself,
starting from Rǔyīn, dying in Sānxiāng.”
He also said:
“The mountain family's little boy will indeed bare his arm,
and glare like a tiger before the Tàijídiàn.”
The tailless puppy,
and the mountain family's little boy,
both resemble a monkey.
Hóu Jǐng subsequently overthrew and trapped the capital,
and inflicted poison and harm upon the imperial clan.
During the Dàtóng period,
Zhū Dān, the Grand Medical Director, once served inside the Forbidden Palace.
Not long after,
he dreamt at night that a dog and a sheep were both on the imperial throne.
He awoke and was disturbed by it,
and told someone:
“Dogs and sheep,
are not good things.
Now they occupy the imperial throne,
will there be a rebellion?”
Soon after, the Son of Heaven suffered humiliation,
and Hóu Jǐng ascended the main palace hall.
When Hóu Jǐng was about to be defeated,
there was a Buddhist ascetic named Sēng Tōngdàorén,
whose mind and temperament were like madness,
drinking wine and eating meat,
no different from ordinary people.
He had traveled in the world for several decades,
and his name and hometown
were unknown to anyone.
His early words were hidden and mysterious,
and were only verified after a long time.
People all called him Shéli.
Hóu Jǐng deeply trusted and respected him.
Hóu Jǐng once shot arrows with his followers in the rear hall.
At that time Sēng Tōng was seated there.
He snatched Hóu Jǐng’s bow and shot at Jǐngyángshān,
shouting loudly:
“I have already got the slave!”
Later, Hóu Jǐng again held a feast gathering his associates,
and also summoned Sēng Tōng.
Sēng Tōng took meat, dipped it in salt, and offered it to Hóu Jǐng.
He asked:
“Is it good?”
Hóu Jǐng replied:
“My only regret is that it is too salty.”
Sēng Tōng said:
“If it is not salty, it will rot and stink.”
Indeed, his corpse was later sealed with salt.
Wáng Wěi,
was a man from Chénliú.
In his youth he possessed talent and learning.
Hóu Jǐng’s memorials, petitions, letters, and declarations,
were all composed by him.
Once Hóu Jǐng attained his goal,
the plans for usurpation and seizure
were all Wěi's stratagems.
When he was imprisoned and sent to Jiānglíng,
he was boiled in the marketplace.
Among the common people, those who had suffered his tyranny,
all cut and roasted his flesh to eat.
The historian says:
The Way is not always smooth,
and Fortune knows no constant tranquility.
Thus, adversity and prosperity are fated,
and flourishing and decline succeed each other.
The time of difficulty, the *yángjiǔ* cycle,
is perhaps upon us now.
As for the insignificant fellow, Hóu Jǐng,
who rebelled against and betrayed his own state—
whose sagacity could not safeguard him
and whose courage was not outstanding—
yet [it was] Wáng Wěi who acted as his chief strategist,
bringing about this treason and malice.
Leading his vile horde,
he crossed the river and proceeded straight ahead.
With long halberds and powerful crossbows,
he destroyed the palaces and towers.
Disaster enveloped the Imperial Center,
and suffering spread everywhere among the populace.
He unleashed his arrogant and tyrannical intent,
achieving the disaster of usurpation and robbery.
Alas!
When a state is about to perish,
evil portents must descend.
Although we call this human affairs,
it is suppressed by the timing of Heaven.
Formerly, Yí Yì brought chaos to Xià,
the Quǎn Róng plagued Zhōu.
In the Hàn dynasty, Mǎng and Zhuó spread disaster,
and in the Jìn dynasty, Dūn and Xuán caused calamity.
When compared to this Jié bandit,
his brutality is even greater than theirs.
What sorrow!
